TL;DR: Firewatch is a beautiful, short narrative game with a believable central relationship and a mystery that becomes genuinely gripping for a while. The buildup worked better than the payoff for me, but it’s an easy recommendation if you enjoy walking simulators and story-focused games. 7/10.

The first thing that stands out is how beautiful it is. The forests, mountains, sunsets and colors give the whole game a distinct identity. Just walking around is pleasant.

And walking is most of what you do. Firewatch is very much a walking simulator: explore the park, climb or rappel when needed, inspect things, and talk to Delilah over the radio. Navigation is probably the closest thing it has to a gameplay system, where you use a map and compass to work out where you are instead of simply following a marker. It’s simple, but it works.

The story starts surprisingly heavy. That opening hits hard, although the game never reaches that emotional weight again. Henry’s relationship with Delilah works much better throughout. After months of talking over the radio, their connection feels believable, and by the end I did care about them.

The central mystery was the strongest part for me. Around the middle of the game I wanted answers immediately. Unfortunately, the explanation didn’t fully live up to that buildup. The conclusion itself wasn’t necessarily bad, but parts of the whole situation felt a little too hard to believe.

The dialogue choices also seem to just deciding how Henry responds than actually changing anything meaningful. And, because the game only lasts around four hours, its lack of actual gameplay never became boring or repetitive. It tells its story, does what it wants to do, and gets out.

A very emotional short story. My first round took roughly 3 hours, its both relaxing and a bit on your toes. I did have some bugs where the action (from pressing a button to climb up) didn't happen and the player only moved a bit, but honestly its just a small thing and it worked in the end. 

Do be warned that if you're currently dealing with some emotional matters, I would recommend waiting a bit before playing the game as it can be quite emotional.

Firewatch is a beautifully written game with a remarkable sense of place. Its warm lighting, rich colour palette and finely detailed environments bring the Wyoming wilderness to life, and the unhurried pace invites you to linger in it rather than rush through. The voice acting is the standout. Henry and Delilah's radio exchanges feel natural and believable, and the dialogue choices let you shape a relationship that feels like your own. The gameplay is deliberately modest, built around exploration, navigation and interaction. That restraint is its strength, because nothing competes with the characters or the mystery that slowly unfolds around them. The blend of exploration, conversation and slow-burning storytelling held my attention from start to finish. For anyone seeking a short, emotional and memorable experience, I wholeheartedly recommend it.

I finally got around to playing Firewatch after being intrigued by its premise way back when it first came out. I am generally a fan of this type of game (Gone Home, What Remains of Edith Finch, and so on), and I am more than happy to play a lowkey, slow boil, walking simulator if the plot and characters are strong. I am sorry to report that this game does not have a particularly compelling plot or strong characters. I do not wish to spoil anyone who has not yet played, but this biggest issue that this game has is its lack of identity. It waffles between a slice-of-life story and a mystery thriller, and in the end it does neither of these things well. The characters do not behave rationally starting early on in the game (not reporting a serious problem to authorities involving missing people because questions would be "annoying"). From here, the characters become less and less believable, and then by the halfway point of the game, we lose out on the genuine character moments that occur between the two of them in lieu of them becoming more and more paranoid about a situation that ends up being entirely resolved (with a neat and tidy bow) in the last 30 minutes of the game. If you can get this game on deep discount, it's worth seeing for yourself if the story clicks for you, but otherwise, do not pay full price for this game.

Mysteries in narratives have always been complicated for me. Almost every mystery novel, video game, whatever... I love it on what I call the "unknown side," when there are still many possibilities for what the answer to everything actually is. The mystery, the not knowing, creates the best atmosphere and is when the story feels the most gripping.
But when the reveal arrives, it can be so disappointing that it ♥♥♥♥♥ on the entire story.
I usually have this problem with stories that seem supernatural, where there is an entire exploration and debate over whether something supernatural is actually going on. And then, in the end... it turns out the supernatural really does exist! That's the recipe for a story I'll 100% hate and call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, albeit purely because of personal preference. If you don't establish that your story is fantastical, or that fantastical elements are genuinely possible within its world, don't make that the big reveal!
All of this is to say that Firewatch indeed has a mystery narrative, and many times I feared it would disappoint me, especially with the larger conspiracy surrounding the story.
But the reveal, which I won't spoil, is so human. So anticlimactic. So soul-shatteringly real. It breaks you. And I absolutely applaud the narrative for that.
Firewatch understands something about mystery that I think a lot of stories get wrong: Sometimes the answer doesn't need to be bigger than the mystery. Sometimes reality is more devastating precisely because it isn't supernatural, conspiratorial, or fantastical. The mystery works because of all the possibilities you imagine while you're still on the "unknown side." And when the truth finally arrives, it feels painfully human.
It is true that this is a walking sim. Don't expect much "game" beyond an interactive, roughly three-hour story where you walk around, explore, and occasionally get lost for a while. But I bought this game because I knew I needed exactly that: solitude, walking around in nature, and a quiet place to exist for a few hours.
The game provides that beautifully, with gorgeous scenery and an environment that makes the story hit even harder. Especially at the point in life I'm currently in, and with the feelings I've been grappling with during this time, that aspect of the game hit me much harder than I expected.
So I think I'll review Firewatch less as a game and more as a piece of writing. And as a piece of writing, I applaud it. Standing ovation.
This is exactly how I think a mystery should be handled in a dramatic, realistic story. The dialogue feels real. The environment feels real. The mystery respects the fact that sometimes the most devastating answer is simply a human one.

review:
To start with the positives this game is really pleasant to look at. The visuals are beautiful and calming and the environment does a great job of making you feel isolated in nature. Sadly that is probably the only positive thing I can say about the game.




SPOLERS BELOW 





Knowing Henrys backstory, I found it pretty frustrating that so much of the dialogue was focused on him impulsively flirting with Delilah. This is a man who was unable to take care of his sick wife to the point where her family had to take her away and that already makes it difficult to sympathize with him. I could have understood this more if his time working as a fire lookout was actually about reflecting on his drinking, his decisions and the fact that he left his sick wife alone at home so he could go to a bar.

The way Henry treated his wife almost like she was dead weight even though he never openly admitted it was honestly pretty heavy. What bothered me even more was how the game handles his relationship with Delilah. At the end some of the dialogue choices make it feel like Henrys main purpose for isolating himself was to leave his past behind, almost as if his wife would simply disappear if he kept flirting with another woman. Throwing away years of commitment for someone you have never even met in person is not a great look for someone who was supposedly in a "happy" marriage.

Delilah also bothered me for similar reasons. She was hesitant to report the death of a kid in the cave because she was afraid she would be blamed for it. Even if she never intended for anything bad to happen she eventually realized that her actions played a part in what happened and still chose to avoid the consequences. I understand that the characters are supposed to be flawed but I didn't find their decisions interesting in any way. They are supposed to be grown adults in their 40s but their actions said otherwise. 

As for the story itself I honestly found it pretty underwhelming. I bought this game because I saw all the positive reviews and because I love nature, especially the idea of complete isolation. I expected the game to give me more of that experience but my expectations were probably way too high.

After finishing it, the main thing I took away from the story is that it is about escaping and running away from your problems. It's not really about finding solutions or facing them. It feels like Henry uses the isolation to escape from his responsibilities and find some peace at a time when his family and wife needed him the most.

For these reasons I'm giving the game 2 out of 5 stars.

Firewatch:

I started playing Firewatch during that magical period of my life between “It’s complicated” and “It’s over.” You know the one. That beautiful emotional wasteland where you're technically single, technically not single, and somehow still losing arguments with someone who isn't even there. So naturally, I decided to escape into the wilderness.

You play Henry, a likeable but somewhat stoic man who runs away from his problems and takes a job as a fire lookout, spending his days doing manual labour, wandering through the woods and staring dramatically into the middle distance. And before you judge the man too harshly: his wife died, you heartless bastards. Have some empathy.

Then, somewhere between the trees and the static, comes a voice over the radio. A beautiful voice. The kind you could listen to for hours. Suddenly, being alone in the woods doesn't seem like such a bad idea anymore.

Days 1–2: “I've come here to disappear.”
Days 3–77: “So anyway, there's this woman I've been talking to…”

You spend the game exploring the wilderness, solving a mystery, uncovering increasingly strange things and developing a relationship with someone you've never physically met. Basically, Tinder for emotionally damaged people with walkie-talkies.

Then the final stretch arrives. The mystery unfolds, the wilderness starts feeling very different, and an emergency evacuation is called. Suddenly, it's time to leave.

I went in expecting a walking simulator with pretty scenery and some decent dialogue. Instead, I got emotionally mugged by a woman with a radio, and underneath all the mystery and humour, Firewatch understands something rather uncomfortable: sometimes you don't go somewhere to find yourself. Sometimes you go somewhere because you don't know what else to do.

I recommended if you're going through some ♥♥♥♥. You might come out with a little perspective, and possibly an unhealthy attachment to a woman you've only ever spoken to through a radio.

Firewatch is less of a game and more of an interactive story.  Outside of "using a map to navigate" there basically isn't any gameplay, besides walking around.  Choices appear to have very little meaning and exploration slows the story down while adding more or less nothing to your experience (with possibly a single exception).  So, that is to say, exploration is not really rewarded, despite the world feeling inviting.  It's an interesting choice to make a big inviting world, but basically waste your time for exploring it.

On top of that, it's actually pretty buggy.  Navigation with mouse and keyboard is strange (with my speed sometimes being slowed for no reason) and interactable (like padlocks) will sometimes move you away from them when you try to click on them, instead of actually interacting with them.  I'm genuinely shocked they haven't patched this game's bugs by now, given its success.

All that having been said, if your expectations are in the right place, the story (once it gets going) is really quite good and the main cast deliver their dialogue (of which there is a TON) extremely well.  The ultimate resolution of the story is generally strong and satisfying, at least in regards to the mysteries presented, and the characters conclusions are... well... what you make of them.

If you are merely interested in an interactive story, Firewatch delivers in spades.  If you want a game to play, you will probably be disappointed.  It took me a while to reset my expectations, but once I did, I enjoyed the ride.

Initially it's all quite calm, you're wandering around in the forest, carrying out your duties, having conversations with Delilah and gradually finding out more about one another. Afterwards, things begin to become strange and you end up having to work out what's really going on there. I quite enjoyed the way the mystery developed gradually since it made you start making connections and begin to think that there must be something much larger going on.

I believe it is in the conclusion that the game actually makes its main point. Since you spend such a large part of the game becoming absorbed in the mystery, it's easy to forget why Henry was even out here in the first place. There isn't instead some grand conspiracy or a perfectly clear explanation for you to discover. The focus is rather on Henry using this place as a means of escaping from his actual life and having to come to terms with the fact that he can't remain there indefinitely. I found that message to be very good and it made the ending have a different impact on me.

The music is also very good and matches the game well. I probably prefer the landscapes too. The entire forest has a pretty pleasant atmosphere, and it never grew boring just to walk about and enjoy the views.

The game is short and doesn't offer a lot of gameplay, but I don't think that's necessary. What matters most is the story, the conversations, the atmosphere and the characters. By the time I'd finished it, I had the feeling that I had actually experienced something rather than have simply gone through another game.

[h1]Firewatch[/h1]
[b]First-person narrative adventure | ~5 hours[/b]

[h2]What it's about[/h2]
It's the summer of 1989. You play as Henry, a man who takes a job as a fire lookout in the Shoshone National Forest in Wyoming, largely to put some distance between himself and a life that has become hard to face. Your world is a watchtower, a map, a compass, and miles of pine and canyon in every direction.

Your only human contact is Delilah, your supervisor in another tower across the valley, reachable by handheld radio. The whole game is built on that connection: you report in, she teases you, you decide what to tell her and what to keep to yourself. Then small strange things start happening in the forest, and the two of you begin piecing together what's going on while the fire season closes in.

Mechanically it's simple. You walk, climb, rappel, navigate by reading an actual paper map rather than following a marker, and you talk.

[h2]What it does well[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Writing and performance.[/b] The dialogue between Henry and Delilah is the best thing here — funny, awkward, warm and evasive in the way real conversations are. Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones deliver it with a naturalism that makes the radio feel like a lifeline rather than a menu.
[*][b]A place you actually inhabit.[/b] Olly Moss's art direction gives the forest a bold, poster-like palette — burnt orange dusk, deep blue night, haze-yellow afternoon — that makes every vista feel composed on purpose. Paired with map-and-compass navigation instead of waypoints, you genuinely learn the terrain, and by the end you know your way home.
[*][b]Tension without threat.[/b] Nothing in these woods can kill you, yet the middle stretch is quietly nerve-wracking. The unease comes from isolation, imagination and Chris Remo's restrained score rather than jump scares.
[*][b]Pacing that respects your time.[/b] A single summer told in a handful of hours, with no filler. It also makes a nearly ideal first game: forgiving controls, nothing to master, and short enough to finish in a couple of sittings without losing the thread.
[/list]

[h2]Worth knowing[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]The ending is quieter than the build-up.[/b] Firewatch cares more about what the mystery does to Henry than about the mystery itself. If you spend the middle hours building elaborate theories, you may come away feeling the payoff is quieter than the setup promised — though on its own terms, that quietness is the point.
[*][b]Your choices shade rather than steer.[/b] Dialogue options change the texture of Henry and Delilah's relationship, not the events. Replays mean new lines, not a new story.
[*][b]It's short, and light on "game".[/b] Anyone looking for systems to master or challenge to overcome won't find much. What you're buying is a story and a place.
[/list]

[h2]Summary[/h2]
Firewatch is a small, near-perfect piece of storytelling. It takes a premise with almost nothing in it — one man, one tower, one voice on a radio — and makes it completely absorbing through writing, performance and a forest you come to know by heart. Its restraint is deliberate: the light mechanics, the modest length and the understated ending are all in service of a story about loneliness, escape, and the strange intimacy of talking to someone you've never seen.

[b]A short game that leaves a long shadow. Worth playing, and worth sitting with once the credits roll.[/b]

Firewatch is an absolute masterpiece of narrative-driven gaming, expertly capturing how a serene, peaceful escape can suddenly curdle into a horrid sense of paranoia and dread, reinforced by standout scores across the board: a 9/10 for Story thanks to its heartbreakingly human narrative about running from grief, a 9/10 for Atmosphere through its masterclass in sound design and visual tension that makes you feel constantly watched and walking on edge, an 8/10 for Audio/Voice Acting for the incredible chemistry between Henry and Delilah over the radio, and a 6/10 for Freedom since the exploration is largely linear and guided rather than a sprawling open-world sandbox. You step into the boots of Henry, taking a lookout job in the vast wilderness with your only lifeline being a radio and Delilah across the valley, balancing the heartwarming intimacy of building an authentic connection with a creeping dread where the quiet beauty of nature twists into a suffocating nightmare, proving that the most terrifying things aren't just the secrets we run from, but the unseen presence waiting in the woods with us.

Visually, the game is an incredibly beautiful experience. The intense, pastel cel-shaded look—without black outlines—is super cool. The highly atmospheric soundscape and the sometimes Zen-like background music complement the relaxing vibe.

The exploration-based, story-driven, walking-sim-style gameplay is also very laid-back. The only real gameplay element, aside from the on-screen prompts to press buttons when interacting with objects, is navigating the world using a map and compass, which greatly enhances immersion (if you want, you can even disable the HUD and the “I’m here” marker on the map).

Be warned that the story starts off very sad, but in the middle section—in keeping with the game’s likely message of escapism—it becomes quite laid-back. To build suspense, the second half is sprinkled with a bit of mystery, thriller, and drama. I found 90% of the story to be very good and exciting; only the resolution could have been a bit more creative in my opinion. However, it serves as a good reminder that escapism isn’t real and that we players, too, must eventually return to the real, less fantastical world. Thankfully, not everything is spoon-fed to you, leaving plenty room for interpretation and reflection :).

It’s worth specifically highlighting that the voice acting (in English) is absolutely brilliant—top Hollywood standard! I’d say it’s the best I’ve heard so far.

Bottom line: Even though the story doesn’t quite hit the mark (for me), I’d highly recommend this fantastic “game” (aka. story-driven walking sim) to anyone who can appreciate a melancholic, laid-back mystery story and values art over “photorealism”. I think this is a game that will stay with you long after the credits roll.

It took me a few sittings to finish Firewatch simply because I could never find the right time to sit down and complete it. Then, on an off day, I finally decided to finish it, and boy, did it make me question a lot of things. The ending is nothing like the usual fairytale payoff most games condition us to expect; there’s no grand revelation, no perfect romance, and no satisfying “everything worked out” conclusion. Instead, when the credits roll, you’re left sitting there wondering what the game was actually trying to tell you.

It slowly starts to click that Firewatch is really a game about escapism. [spoiler] Henry escapes his life and his wife’s illness by disappearing into the wilderness. Delilah escapes her own responsibilities and guilt, while Ned retreats into the forest after Brian’s death rather than confronting his grief. [/spoiler] Even we, the players, are doing the same thing, escaping our daily routines and problems for a few hours, immersing ourselves in someone else’s life. Maybe that’s why the ending feels so strangely empty and real. Firewatch doesn’t give you the escape you were hoping for; it reminds you that eventually, you have to go back.

First of all, the navigation is pretty confusing, and the distances you have to walk are way too long. If I’m going to spend that much time walking around, I feel like there should at least be more interesting scenery, things to discover, or different interactions along the way.

Secondly, the story is very short, and there’s basically no side content at all. I think the beginning, middle, and ending are fairly well balanced, but during the middle part, I never really found myself full of questions or particularly invested in the mystery.

I also don’t understand why the game seems to focus so much on its technical and visual side while giving less attention to the story. If you’re making a game that only lasts around 4.5 hours, I think the story should be much more impactful and memorable.

Despite all of that, it’s an okay way to spend 4.5 hours. But I definitely don’t think this game is worth its price.

I was recommended this game by a couple friends, and seeing as it was quite short I gave it a go. And I can confidently say it was an incredible recommendation, and despite it only taking me roughly 4 hours to beat, it is easily more memorable and impactful than a lot of 20-30 hour titles I've played, despite it ultimately being a walking simulator.

The first point I'd like to mention is the graphics. The stylized look of the game paired with the gorgeous lighting make the game really stand out from the crowd. I could honestly spend hours walking through these environments and always find it relaxing.

And whilst a lot of the game can be relaxing, the game can easily take a tonal turn. Hell, the game starts off with a massive tonal shift before you've even gotten to the main course. The game is an exceptional example of tone through ambience and setting, and a first playthrough is sure to be a thrilling ride. Though I will say, the ending felt mildly underwhelming for everything that happened - though that very well could be the intention.

The performances from the voice actors for Henry and Delilah also deliver stellar performances which really put you in the right mood for the events of the game, and even to this day lines from key points still stick with me.

The soundtrack although simplistic on analysis is still brilliant at getting you in the right headspace. I often find myself playing some of the tracks whenever I see a sunset out on a walk.

It's a short but brilliant experience that I definitely recommend.

Firewatch is a seminal narrative adventure set in the 1989 Wyoming wilderness, following a fire lookout named Henry and his radio-bound supervisor, Delilah. The Narrative & Writing (9/10) is exceptional, driven by realistic dialogue and an authentic, evolving relationship between the two leads. The Visuals & Atmosphere (9/10) feature a striking, stylized art direction by Olly Moss with incredible lighting and environmental mood. The Gameplay (5/10) is intentionally minimal, consisting mostly of walking, using a map and compass, and selecting dialogue choices under time pressure. The Story Arc & Ending (6/10) remains polarizing, as the mystery's resolution intentionally subverts expectations in a way that disappointed some players.

➕ Industry-leading voice acting and natural dialogue flow between Henry and Delilah
➕ Beautiful, iconic art style with brilliant environmental lighting and atmospheric design
➕ A deeply personal, grounded story that tackles grief, isolation, and escapism
➖ Gameplay is essentially a "walking simulator" with minimal interactive depth
➖ The final act and resolution subvert the thriller build-up in a way that can feel anticlimactic

Although this game has been regarded as a "walking simulator", it's not that bad considering you can jog and the map is not that long (10 minutes jogging to get from West to East). Most of the gameplay is free-roam, meaning you can progress the story when you feel like it, as long as you have the equipment to do so (rope for climbing, axe for spiky bushes).
Without going too deep into the story, you take on the role of Henry, a married man that decided to take a job listing to (NOT) go sit in a tower all day and look out for smoke, and the only one to keep him company through a walkie-talkie is Delilah, his boss, to whom he has to report anything he finds. Things start easy, put out fires, watch out for smoke, ward off drunk teens, but then you start suspecting that this forest has more secrets than people oughta know about...
That's it, no more spoilers, go play it yourself. I'm sure you'll enjoy it!

Now, for the achievements:
5 are story-related.
2 are obtainable as soon as Day 2:
 - Use up all the film in the disposable camera you find with the rope backpack;
 - Find the Turtle in the SouthWest lush forest and adopt it.
3 are obtainable as soon as Day 77:
 - Go to the burned down cabin that you found when hiking for the wires in Day 2 and open the stove;

I've only played maybe one first person game on a flat screen in the past ten years, so it could just be that, but the controls in this felt very.. off. I used a dual shock style controller. For some reason you can't re-bind the buttons. And the default config never clicked for me throughout my playthrough. It didn't help that there seemed to be way more buttons than even necessary for a game that consists of walking and talking. All in all, Firewatch just feels janky.

It doesn't help that the world is absolutely full of invisible walls. These walls funnel you through the extremely linear path that you're supposed to take. I understand why they did that, but you get hung on on all kinds of invisible objects at every turn. I've gotten stuck on rocks, trees and at a few points started floating backwards.

And this leads to why I'm not recommending this. There really is no actual game here. You have zero choices to make in regards to anything. Sure there are some dialog picks but they have no real effect on anything. Maybe they mention the type of dog you owned or something but it's all meaningless. You have no problems to solve, no real directions to choose, nothing meaningful to collect (maybe there's an achievement for picking up books?).. this really could have been an animated short. You could watch someone else play through this on youtube and get the exact same experience. Actually that would be better since you wouldn't be the one getting frustrated. All you do is walk the path, which triggers story elements, which are almost entirely sound bytes. Occasionally you have to press A to do an animation to get over a log or something. That's it, that's the "game".

Some games give you a world to conquer. Others give you a world to disappear into. Firewatch gives you somewhere to hide. Only to slowly show you that running away doesn't mean leaving anything behind. At first, Firewatch seems almost too simple. You spend your days alone in the Wyoming wilderness, climbing mountains, clearing trails, reporting smoke, and talking to someone you've never met through a crackling radio. There are no armies to defeat, no cities to save, no grand adventure waiting around every corner.

And yet, somehow, that quiet becomes the adventure... Henry isn't a chosen hero. He's just a man trying to escape a life that has become too heavy to carry. The forest gives him distance from everything he's running from, but it also forces him to sit with the thoughts he's been avoiding. Every empty path and every silent evening in the watchtower feels like a reflection of his own loneliness. The heart of Firewatch isn't the mystery surrounding the forest. It's the relationship built over the radio. Delilah feels like one of the most genuine companions in gaming despite never appearing beside you. Through small conversations, jokes, awkward moments, and things left unsaid, you slowly form a connection with someone who is just as lonely as you are.

What makes Firewatch special is how it plays with your expectations. It makes you search for hidden meanings, bigger explanations, and something waiting beneath the surface. But instead of giving you a simple answer, it leaves you with something much more human! And that is the realization that not every problem has a dramatic solution. Sometimes life is messy because people are messy.

The beauty of Firewatch comes from its atmosphere. The warm colors of the forest, the quiet moments watching the sunset, and the feeling of being completely alone in nature create a world that feels both peaceful and strangely unsettling. It's a place where you can feel safe and lost at the same time. Firewatch isn't about discovering what's hiding in the woods. It's about discovering what you're hiding from yourself. It's about regret, loneliness, connection, and the difficult truth that escaping your problems is much easier than facing them. Some stories give you closure. Firewatch gives you something different.. 

A moment of reflection...

And even after the final radio call ends, there's a good chance you'll still be thinking about the conversations that never happened and the things that were left unsaid. 9/10

[h2]Nota Geral | Overall Rating[/h2]

[b]Firewatch é a prova de que uma narrativa bem escrita, apoiada por uma dublagem excepcional, consegue carregar uma experiência inteira sem precisar de combate, puzzles complexos ou qualquer artifício de jogabilidade tradicional. A Campo Santo criou algo raro: um jogo sobre duas pessoas conversando por rádio em meio a uma floresta isolada de Wyoming, e mesmo assim consegue construir tensão, mistério e um vínculo emocional genuíno entre Henry e Delilah que fica na cabeça muito depois dos créditos subirem. É uma das melhores experiências narrativas que já joguei.[/b]

[i]Firewatch is proof that a well-written narrative, backed by exceptional voice acting, can carry an entire experience without needing combat, complex puzzles, or any traditional gameplay tricks. Campo Santo created something rare: a game about two people talking over radio in the middle of an isolated Wyoming forest, and it still manages to build tension, mystery, and a genuine emotional bond between Henry and Delilah that stays with you long after the credits roll. It's one of the best narrative experiences I've ever played.[/i]

[h2]Jogabilidade | Gameplay[/h2]
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

[b]A jogabilidade é minimalista de propósito, focada em exploração e no simples ato de caminhar pela floresta usando mapa e bússola pra se orientar. O que faz isso funcionar tão bem é como o rádio se torna a verdadeira mecânica central: cada decisão de diálogo com Delilah muda sutilmente a dinâmica entre os dois personagens, e a simplicidade da jogabilidade nunca atrapalha, ela só existe pra servir a história, que é onde o jogo realmente brilha.[/b]

[i]The gameplay is deliberately minimalist, focused on exploration and the simple act of walking through the forest using a map and compass to find your way. What makes this work so well is how the radio becomes the true central mechanic: every dialogue decision with Delilah subtly shifts the dynamic between the two characters, and the gameplay's simplicity never gets in the way, it exists solely to serve the story, which is where the game truly shines.[/i]

[h2]Duração | Duration[/h2]
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

[b]A duração é perfeita pra esse tipo de experiência. São poucas horas, mas cada uma delas é usada com propósito, sem nenhum momento de enchimento. É o tipo de jogo que você termina numa sessão só, sente o peso emocional do final, e não sente falta de mais conteúdo, porque a história contada é exatamente do tamanho que precisava ser.[/b]

[i]The length is perfect for this kind of experience. It's only a few hours, but every one of them is used with purpose, with no filler moments. It's the kind of game you finish in a single sitting, feel the emotional weight of the ending, and don't miss more content, because the story told is exactly the size it needed to be.[/i]

[h2]Enredo | Story[/h2]
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

[b]O enredo é o grande triunfo do jogo. A relação entre Henry e Delilah, construída inteiramente através de diálogos por rádio, é escrita com uma naturalidade e química que poucos jogos conseguem replicar, e o mistério em torno do que está acontecendo na floresta mantém a tensão crescente do início ao fim. É uma história sobre fuga, solidão e as consequências de decisões passadas, contada de um jeito íntimo e pessoal que faz cada revelação parecer genuína, não forçada.[/b]

[i]The plot is the game's great triumph. The relationship between Henry and Delilah, built entirely through radio dialogue, is written with a naturalness and chemistry that few games manage to replicate, and the mystery surrounding what's happening in the forest keeps the tension building from start to finish. It's a story about escape, loneliness, and the consequences of past decisions, told in an intimate, personal way that makes every reveal feel genuine, not forced.[/i]

[h2]Visual[/h2]
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

[b]Visualmente, Firewatch é deslumbrante. A direção de arte estilizada, com uma paleta de cores quentes que captura perfeitamente o pôr do sol sobre as montanhas de Wyoming, cria uma das florestas mais bonitas já retratadas em um jogo. Cada área tem uma identidade visual própria, e a fotografia natural do cenário reforça a sensação de isolamento e beleza selvagem que a história pede.[/b]

[i]Visually, Firewatch is stunning. The stylized art direction, with a warm color palette that perfectly captures the sunset over the Wyoming mountains, creates one of the most beautiful forests ever depicted in a game. Every area has its own visual identity, and the natural scenery's photography reinforces the sense of isolation and wild beauty the story calls for.[/i]

[h2]Áudio | Audio[/h2]
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

[b]A dublagem é o que realmente eleva o jogo a outro patamar. Cissy Jones e Rich Sommer entregam performances excepcionais como Delilah e Henry, transmitindo cada nuance emocional através apenas da voz, já que os dois praticamente nunca se encontram fisicamente na tela. A trilha sonora sutil complementa perfeitamente os momentos de introspecção e tensão, e os sons ambientais da floresta reforçam a sensação de solidão que permeia toda a experiência.[/b]

[i]The voice acting is what really elevates the game to another level. Cissy Jones and Rich Sommer deliver exceptional performances as Delilah and Henry, conveying every emotional nuance through voice alone, since the two practically never meet physically on screen. The subtle soundtrack perfectly complements the moments of introspection and tension, and the forest's ambient sounds reinforce the sense of loneliness that permeates the entire experience.[/i]

It had a lot of good moments especially in the first half, and set up a strong immersive mood and interesting narrative mechanics that I was excited about. But then it developed a red herring story that uses up the rest of the runtime of the game. It was so close to being good, but they focused on side characters that don't matter and don't connect to the main characters. The voice acting is wonderful, and along with the visuals, carries the game. The dialog writing is odd, the way they speak is 2010s not 1970s, but I accepted it. The narrative is awful: the big reveal is disappointing, then the main relationship ends abruptly. It feels like a movie that ran out of budget and couldn't film a real ending. Looking back on the plot now that I know the mystery's big reveal, a lot of events in the game don't make plausible sense. Like other weak mystery stories, the buildup is great but then the reveal ruins it and make you feel you wasted your time.

Dementia is a key part of the narrative, and the writers have put zero work into learning about it. They have a heartless view of the difficulty and complexity of being a caretaker for someone with that illness. The writers are trying to tell a story about the futility of running from your problems, but ironically they don't engage with what it would actually be like to be in the main character's situation. In the end, they moralize about him needing to go home and face it. But he already has faced it, and there isn't necessarily anything further to do besides process his grief. They similarly use the "crazy PTSD veteran" trope in a shallow and unconvincing way. It's just bad writing.

I had been making dialog choices assuming my choices would matter somehow, but your picks only affect the immediate responses you get. There were a handful of things that seemed like clues to reward players who thoroughly explored the world, but they were just flavor and didn't expand the story, it feels like a waste of time to have called in every item.

Also as a walking simulator, the walking is glitchy. You often get stuck on things, and at one point whenever I tried to interact with objects like the yellow cache boxes or the gate, it made me sprint backwards(?) instead of interacting. The only reason this wasn't a game breaking bug was that I found that mashing R2 would interact and break the backwards sprint. Also if you have vsync disabled, walking breaks entirely!

I almost never write Steam reviews. In fact, this is my first one.

But if you're even thinking about buying this game, just do it. Sale or no sale. If you're looking for a great single-player experience, spend your money on this before you spend it on anything else.

The best way I can describe Firewatch is: it's like a thriller movie... except you're the one living through it.

If you're going into this expecting something like 911 Operator or a fire lookout simulator where you just answer radios all day, you're in the wrong place. And if you're looking for a horror game, this isn't that either.

What this game is, is a surprisingly simple single-player adventure with a story that completely pulls you in if you let it. You never really know what's coming next.

At first, you're trying to understand your character's thoughts and make the choices you think he would make. Then you find yourself wondering if he should leave his old life behind and move on. Five minutes later, none of that even matters anymore.

One moment it's funny. The next it's heartbreaking. Then suddenly it's incredibly tense. Halfway through, you're no longer sure what's actually happening... or even what kind of game you're playing anymore.

I don't want to spoil anything, because discovering it for yourself is exactly what makes this game special.

I'd play it again in a heartbeat.

Not a very good game in my opinion for the asking price. I am very glad that I had bought this for like 3 euros when it was on sale.

Firewatch is a shockingly buggy and unpolished game. They have these wooden logs in the level that you can walk up to, press the spacebar and your character will play an animation of him climbing over it. It's cute but you can break it extremely easily. In most cases, there is nothing stopping you from walking up to the log from the side, getting on top of it, looking down and triggering the prompt to climb it while you are standing on top of it which will result in your character grabbing onto thin air and climbing over nothing, resulting in your flying in the air over the log in this very strange state where gravity only pushes you down when moving, meaning you can stay flying there as long as you want. You can also trigger this bug when  you attempt to climb a log that is half sunk into the ground and you start climbing it from the elevated point. Maybe the programmers had assumed that the logs would always be placed on a perfectly flat ground and that the level designer(s) would place them in tight passages that wouldn't allow you to walk up onto them from the side. The reason why I'm making such a big deal out of this is because this is a 20 euro game and any playtester would have been able to catch this immediately.

That's not all the bugs though, for example, when you interact with the door in your tower, the game will play an animation of the character opening the door and walking through it. The issue is that if you are looking slightly upwards or slightly downwards, your camera will snap up for couple of frames and then snap back into the correct place. It's absolutely nauseating! Or another example: Since there is no jump button, there is a mechanic where you look at the place where you want to jump to, press a button and the character will play a jump animation and automatically move to the desired location. The issue is that the camera just snaps into the position and can snap upwards or downwards for a couple frames like with the door animatons. Maybe the game knows how unpleasant and motion sickness inducing this is so sometimes you get spared and get no jumping animation and your character just unceremoniously flies to the jumping destination with his idle animation still playing. Thanks game!

Or yet another example: Walking and moving around is extremely janky and unpolished which is kind of an issue for a walking simulator. They have this mechanic where you cannot walk off of edges and your character will get automatically stopped. Why? Well it's so that they can have pre-set places where you get a janky and jerky animation of the character walking off of a ledge and dropping down. I'm assuming they implemented it like this as they didn't want to spend an eternity placing and aligning millions of invisible walls around edges, so they added an automatic system for it instead. The issue is that the "prevent the player walking over an edge and dropping down" system is poorly implemented and you often end up getting stuck on top of rocks or small little bushses and have to spend like a minute, fiddling around the controls to get off. I don't think I have ever played a game where you can nearly get stuck by just walking on top of a small protruding rock in the ground. 

And The first person animation are way too snappy and walking into a wall at an angle (or attempting to walk over an edge at an angle) will result in the walk animation completely spazzing out and blinking between the idle animation and move animation. Again, this is a 20 euro game and a playtester would have caught this instantly.

I found the gameplay loop itself to be deeply unsatisfactory and disjointed. Navigating the world is very disorientating, everything looks the same so you have to constantly use the janky map which is bafflingly mapped to the "m" key which forced me to always take my hand off of the mouse and go hunting for it on my keyboard which is not what I would call seamless. The story itself is also pretty uninteresting [spoiler]and the big reveal in the  the cave is not very shocking or sad in any way[/spoiler]. Maybe it's because the first time I attempted to [spoiler]walk over the dead kid to progress, my player character instead snapped into the idle animation, started flying away from the kid and then teleported infront of it, the camera snapped down and the game crashed, forcing me to replay that entire section again.[/spoiler]

While the atmosphere and the art direction are pretty nice, the story commits the greatest possible sin in fiction: being pointless. It might as well not have happened at all. It’s like the writer set out to set up plot lines and resolve them in the most mundane, least interesting way possible. There’s dialogue and action decisions at various points, too, but none of them materially affect the outcome, beyond a character saying a different line.

[spoiler]
* The girls who get reported missing? They just went for a joyride and ended up in jail.
* The love interest? She just flirts for no reason and is not at all interested in the protagonist.
* The shady research facility out in the woods? It’s just a perfectly ordinary scientific installation tracking the movement and behaviors of fauna. (This is actually not even a mystery really; it’s quite obvious to any player right from the start.)
* The main characters being spied on? It’s just a crazy veteran messing with them for no reason.
* The protagonist’s personal problems surrounding his sick wife? Nothing gets resolved by the end one way or another. The trip to the wilderness was a waste of time that just put a pause on things and he returns home neither better nor worse than he left.
[/spoiler]

If the message is that running away from your problems doesn’t achieve anything, I guess it’s applicable, but it falls flat because it just feels like the narrative is incompetently constructed instead.

I really enjoyed playing this short, atmospheric game.

The story is bittersweet, the world is beautiful, and the game does a great job of building tension and suspense at key moments. The characters are complex and endearing, and the voice acting is absolutely phenomenal.

The main gameplay loop is essentially a walking simulator. You complete one objective at a time by hiking from point A to point B, then back again, repeating the process throughout the game.

My only real complaint is the navigation. The map isn't huge, but it's almost entirely made up of dense forest, and the game doesn't hold your hand at all. There's no minimap, so you're forced to rely on a physical map and compass that your character has to pull out every single time you want to check your location. While this certainly adds to the realism and immersion, players with a poor sense of direction (like me) will probably spend a lot of time lost and wandering around. I could have finished the game in about four hours if I hadn't spent so much time trying to find my way and backtracking.

Overall, it was a very enjoyable experience. I recommend it to anyone looking for a relaxing, atmospheric game with beautiful scenery, plenty of hiking, a touch of mystery, and excellent dialogue between its characters.

They were right when they say that affordable indie experiences change you. I got this game for the whopping sum of 3.90 bucks and every minute of those 3 hours 20 where met. I knew the game from somewhere — at this point I don't even bother trying to remember how I heard about stuff. The game just doesn't let me down. It was a short while and that's why I wanted to play it since I just 100% completed Gran Turismo 4 a week ago. It just gives me so much immersion for what it is that it just deserves a spot up there, the only other game that had me on a paper map with a compass was Far cry 2 which is an outliar in terms of ubisoft. The graphics were also gorgeous and really did get the most of what a Wyoming sunset looks like. As for the music it's a really strong point here, everytime a song cam on breaking the quietness of the wild it just sent chills down my spine and that's because one it's amazingly fitting for this american pastoral scene but secondly also because as far as the detective work and the plot go, this just had me on my damn toes — the prime example would be the first time you get to see that shadow meddling around at your tower. And here the real shiner let's be real is the story, talking about which I found the gameplay really fitting unlike some people who were really annoyed at the thought of a "walking simulator" as they call it" and yeah that's what you get for your picturesque setpiece, but if I really wanted to play something high octane I would rather be on Metal gear rising or something man. So yeah, the laid back slower paced roaming around really helped me take in those aforementioned visuals and sound (nice tortoise by the way). It starts with a kind of RPG choice based intro to set you up in the world putting in the process the weight of a dementia affected wife and not so young dog that I did get to pick. Although you never get to see said wife (you do see a picture in the tower) more on that in a bit, you get to see the Henry's mental state and gymnastics all throughout. The game shines in a really unique manner that I have never and hope to never see again (please be a once in a lifetime experience), it is the fact that even though you interact with people on the job — mainly Delilah — you never and I mean ever get to see a single face during the whole thing. And as far as the narrative goes, I really really admire the implications and weight that this can hold. It brings mystery and doubt all the way and helps to wrap it up great with a clear and concise ending. Now the fact that I never got to see a single soul with whom I interacted led me to some hasty conclusions while playing that make me theorize about events in the game and particular relationships. My thought process sparked mainly from that scene where Henry gets a call from Delilah in the middle of the night that turns into a discussion with your wife only to be reminded around the next day that you called her only to start mumbling about you wife. That could very well be fatigue and exhaustion from such predicaments but the game lets you more than once wonder in your dialogue options if you were — I don't know — perhaps imagining things and hallucinating things. And I know that the wife Alzheimer's is real because she has a picture but I still wonder if maybe just maybe Henry had a mental illness of his own, I mean they never tell you what really happened that night and it just makes me wonder if he couldn't have experienced a bit of schizophrenia at some point. While the body is real and his dad sure is too considering how long he's been there, as I said some of this stuff doesn't get cleared and it's better that way. Anyways, I don't know if the community made hundreds of videos dissecting that since I didn't really interact with the community, only saw some people talking about the walking. Futhermore, great stuff and I am left satisfied with that money spent.

cons and pros section:

PROS:
-delilah is a fun VA and even though the protagonists VA doesnt keep up most of the time it was fun enough dialogue.
-atmosphere is pretty dang good. the few random fun happenings are entertaining and the area has a general mystique that makes you want to walk further for a while.
-the in-game map and compass are VERY good. not just in appearance and aesthetic, but also in functionality. down to how it marks important things you come across with a nice key to follow and everything. you would benefit greatly from turning off your location showing on the map and also turning off the interface (until you start handling items, you might want to see the options those have per item in the bottom right of the screen so turn interface on for that).
-the integration of the limited film camera throughout the game was well done and complimentary to a game like this.
-spamming the option to smash the locked gate in the cave made me laugh a lot.
-the "moral" of the story, aka the overall outcome of the main characters life problems, were nice story elements especially in the setting

CONS:
-(the biggest con imo)a game about traversing geometry where you regularly get stuck on things, including a bug that turning v-sych off makes your movement completely break lmao. even with v-sych on sometimes you can get stuck so badly you need to reload an earlier save. explore, but at your own risk. docks satisfaction points continuously.
-the free-roaming elements to the game dont feel like they should really be explored since you are more or less streamlined by a progression system in order to be able to traverse the map. they even go as far as having you end up traversing the whole maps walkable area throughout the story if you just choose one way to go each time. making it so that you might as well just never explore extra out side of where youre already going for the main objective.
-the classic "if you interact with the wrong thing too early you will get cutscened to the next part of the game without being able to see everything else" happens.
-although the dialogue can be entertaining the modern speech used does tend to leave you with a suspension of disbelief if you are wanting immersion in the story and setting, which is the 1980's.
-the paranoia that forms [spoiler] when you finally enter the fenced in area [/spoiler] feels very forced in a way where it really forces a certain method of thought that seems very conspiratorial and therefore very unbelievable. removing its impact from the story at hand.

A engaging and compelling narrative driven game, let down by poor pacing and threadbare exploration.

The core of Firewatch is an engaging character study excellently performed by Rich Sommer (Henry)
and Cissy Jones (Delilah). Their performance is the driving force of the narrative and really helps sell the developing relationship of the two leads. The two only communicate via radio and thus it is up to the player to control how much Henry reports to the disembodied Delilah. It's a testament to the strength of the performance that I looked forward to every snippet of conversation and every piece of witty banter.

Unfortunately their performance is let down by gameplay that, in many ways, is substandard. Firewatch belongs to genre that is (often dismissively) referred to as 'walking simulators'. While I personally have no problem with a game taking a more narrative focus, moving away from more challenge and skill based engagement, the strength of such games is often determined by the interweaving of environment and narrative. In this regard I found Firewatch lacklustre. The national park that Henry finds himself is surprisingly lifeless, often serving as little more than padding between narrative encounters. While there are some lite navigational challenges, Firewatch rarely rewards exploration. Straying from the beaten path often only serves to pad playtime.

Despite this, Firewatch remains a pretty comfortable recommend. The strength of the core performances are so strong, and the game short enough, that the lack of engaging gameplay or exploration should not be enough to deter anyone looking for a narratively rich experience.

This game isn't really about the gameplay. It's about the story it tells along the way. Therefore one needn't expect much from the game part of the game, and that's fine, but we're still stuck with the game portion, focused on writing as the devs may have been. The game starts by filling you in on your life prior to its events, with you choosing some of what those events are, which does affect dialogue later. Minimally. This is sporadically interrupted by segments of gameplay that teach you some controls, but they're almost completely pointless, only introducing you to walking, and clicking on things to interact iirc. After gameplay truly begins, you are introduced to a new mechanic occasionally, though they all are the same. Click interactable, receive passage. You would expect that to imply progression gating like HMs in pokemon, but no. There's no returning to an area you couldn't access before. Every received method is for only that part of the game, and the ones that come after. There is an item you receive which you are advised to use in a way that implies it will be an investigative aid, but no. It doesn't come up again at any point. The only puzzle in this game is navigating the perpetual fog. Basically, I was given a lot of potential toys, only to be disappointed by all of them.

As for my complaints of polish, much of the game is really hard to see. For a game partially about walking through beautiful nature, much of it can't be seen because swathes of the game are relatively monotone, and occasionally foggy. There are also no settings for antialiasing/mipmapping or FOV. Animated actions for your character commonly bug out if you aren't in just the right place, causing you to move at high speeds with flyhacks on in a direction of the interaction prompt's choice. Lastly, I could see into/under a lot of the rocks throughout the landscape, and I wasn't even going off the beaten path. No QC. Kept my computer a bit warmer than it felt like it should've as well.

You step into the role of Henry, a fire lookout who spends the summer in a remote watchtower deep in the woods, with his only connection to the outside world being Delilah, whom he talks to over the radio. Story-wise, it's not quite as profound as What Remains of Edith Finch, but honestly, it doesn't need to be — Firewatch is playing a different game altogether, and it does what it does really well. The tension builds up nicely over time, you're constantly wondering what's actually going on, and the resolution feels satisfying.

TLDR:the main reason you would play this game is for the story.
Overall it's a slow burn, the game is heavily dialogue & story heavy but I think that serves to the game's strength, but there's still a fair bit of gameplay in light puzzle, parkour, and rock climbing sections.  In addition there's tonnes of little easter eggs (even stuff from other games, movies, & media) there's hidden passages/dialogue options that you don't necessarily have to explore/activate to progress the story but provide alot of incite into the characters' backstories.

If you're still not convinced about the story, i'll give you some non descript examples of what makes it so good: not only do the characters directly tell you stuff, but you can parse information about what kind of person from the way they speak, like small slip-of-the-tongue moments, where characters actually hesitate & choose to withhold information from you tell you alot about the characters and keep your mind occupied trying to connect the dots which makes the characters intriguing and mysterious & keep you begging to learn more, with environmental story telling there's tonnes of objects/trinkets you can pick up & examine which gives alot of clues into what kind of hobbies & personalities certain characters have, (even if you haven't met them directly). sometimes the characters will chat about something earlier in the game, make some promise, etc, and initially you won't think too much of it, but later on, just exploring your watchtower's room, you'll come across an object that confirms the characters went through with their promise, and you can't help but chuckle. And this is done without the game even leading you on to discover it, it's up to you as the player to discover these moments that sometimes even lead to more OPTIONAL dialogue which will make you wonder how many other easter eggs the devs put effort into for stuff 60% of players wont even run into, it's incredibly rewarding to take your time and choose your own path through the forest as that extra time exploring always pays off.

For those interested in a spoil free summary of my essay, firstly it's a bit more subjective, beyond the literal setting of the game, with all the spoilers & plot twists, that I won't get into. For some short context this review was a originally differently worded, I did an indepth analysis of the characters, but I went back and realised I wanted people to actually play the game themselves, and then draw their own opinions about each character rather than take what I say as face value, so everything below is a bit vague and might sounds insane, but the beauty of Firewatch, is that the symbolism isn't shoved in your face, everything i'm about to say is so subtly hinted by the devs, you could finish this game, and never realise any of it, but if you take your time to enjoy the journey, rather than rushing to the end, you'll see.

To me, the game isn't just about being in a forest, it's an analogy that forces the player to question the morality of this concept called "Escapism": running away from your problems if you will. The beauty of it is that the game doesn't present escapism as a black & white topic, Ingame you'll run into and interact with other characters and it becomes obvious they all have unique issues/flaws/traits/guilts, but it's not really your place to judge because the developer's put you in a tough spot on purpose, mostly because of your character own fatal flaw for 'running away' and getting a job out in the Shoshone national park is a certain someone, (who this flaw is gets explained extremely early so it's not much of a spoiler but you'll learn more as you play and get opportunities to fill in the gaps) The developers highlight Isolation in several ways including diegetic sounds, wind, and the symbolic imagery of a forest as not only as place of reflection & recovery, but isolation isn't just used in the literal sense, it's used symbolically, think about it, when you have an argument, a bad take, or controversional opinion, it's often said "You're on your own". Hence why I believe that the forest is the perfect analogy and environment to explain how escapism is neither good or bad. and initially you feel guilty about your character's past (rightfully so), but as the game goes on, you run into other characters with their own problems/commitments they're running from, and you can't help but feel for sorry for some of them, as well as judge other characters (however the devs make you contemplate if it's really your place to judge) One thing I only realised on my second playthrough was the Forest-fire which not only serves as an overarching passive 'antagonist', but the symbolism of the Forest Fire slowly creeping into your character's henry & his coworker's mind slowly realising they cant ignore their responsibilities as a Fire-lookout by just gossiping and having fun all summer, serves as a sort of "symbolic karma" prediction of what ignoring their relationship issues will result in. The ending of the game:
[spoiler] was to many players quite underwhelming with tonnes of the characters' redemption arcs remaining unfulfilled/incomplete, but it honestly serves to the developers' argument as  despite all the fun you had with delilah, +uncovering the truth behind what happened to Brian, whether you think they were in the wrong for running away, in any other situation would be clear cut: wrong, but since you persevered with them and carried the guilt with them, it's not clear, the ending reminds you regardless of what you think of Henry, delilah, and ned, their issues are waiting for them back in the city, & ironically your own issues & commitments in real life are waiting for you when you finish the game, the developers force you accept that the people you hate in real life might have some truth to why they act the way they do.[/spoiler]. 

And again, everything i've just said is like the "B plot" in the symbolism & messaging, there's a whole other can of worms with the literal events of the story in the "A Plot" which I'll let you experience yourself.

Although i'd still have to say that game was amazing, it's a slow burn of mystery & detective-work like conspiracy, it's about the journey not the destination, silly goofy dialogue with milennial humour'ed characters and it shows. 10/10.

I went into Firewatch expecting a relaxing walking simulator, and while it definitely delivered on the peaceful atmosphere, it surprised me with how invested I became in the story.

The environments are beautiful, the dialogue feels natural, and the slower pace gives you time to really take everything in. Just when I thought I had the game figured out, it threw in a few twists that had me saying "oh crap" more than once.

It's not an action game, and it doesn't try to be. It's about exploration, mystery, and the relationship between the characters, and it does those things incredibly well.

My only complaint is that I wish it had been longer. By the time I reached the end, I wasn't ready for it to be over. I would have happily spent several more hours exploring the world and following the story.

If you enjoy story-driven games with gorgeous scenery, fantastic voice acting, and a mystery that keeps you hooked, I highly recommend Firewatch.

What really elevated it to an art piece for me was the use of the camera. You only have a limited number of photos, so you end up being careful with each shot, choosing to capture only the most meaningful moments or beautiful scenery. All I can say is: take your time with this game. It isn’t meant to be rushed—just slow down and enjoy it.

[b]Rating: 7/10 – Good[/b]

[b]Firewatch[/b] is one of those games that, at least in my opinion, kind of understays its welcome. It is a very [b]Good[/b] experience. The art style and world are absolutely visually stunning, simply gorgeous to look at and very fun to explore. On top of that you have great character writing and a very interesting story that, despite not being a massive fan of how they decided to end things, I found very enjoyable.

The characters are great and I love their relationship, on top of that you’ve got a great mystery but in the end it just kind of feels like someone adapted a full-length novel trilogy into a single movie and had to rush through some stuff. Personally I think the game could’ve benefited from not rushing through practically 90% of the days and allowing you to experience more of the relationship building that is very core to the game’s experience. Additionally, I think the core mystery at the heart of [b]Firewatch[/b]’s is very interesting but, in the end, it just didn’t feel quite fleshed out enough to me with a lot of reveals being stuffed into the finale rather than being strewn across the game. (Although maybe I just missed some stuff, the world is surprisingly large).

Overall, despite some complaints, [b]Firewatch[/b] is a very [b]Good[/b] short game that is totally worth playing. Although I do think that the high price can be a bit of a turn-off since the game is very short, but its quality is undeniably very high. I’d definitely recommend checking it out if you haven’t yet.

It starts off pretty strongly for a dialog + exploration heavy based game, but the ending was overall a little unsatisfying to me. While I wasn't hoping for a romance between Henry and Delilah, it felt a little disappointing that there isn't much of a conclusion, which left me mildly unsatisfied. Does he go to his wife, or does he abandon her? What ends up happening to Ned? And Delilah? It's all open to interpretation, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it is the downfall to this game for me. 

Regardless of the choices you make, Henry still inevitably flirts with Delilah and vice versa, even going so far as to stop wearing his wedding ring, and I wasn't too interested in that part of their dynamics. Yeah, he's lonely and needing some human connection while out there for months, just as Delilah, but it didn't sit quite right with me. And it leaves me to wonder if she does that with other new members each summer? If not, what makes Henry so special? 

Throughout the storyline you quickly realize that Henry isn't capable of properly taking care of his sick wife and drinks a lot, and inevitably came out to this place as a poor attempt to run away from his responsibilities and guilt -- pretty similarly to Delilah, who spends her summers here after failing to be there for her (ex) boyfriend after he lost a family member. Both of them drink as an attempt to escape, but ultimately it doesn't do either of them any good. That is a recurring point throughout the entire game. The rare moments we get of Henry sharing his feelings of guilt and when he talks about Julia was well done in my opinion.

The dialogue between the two was very well done, I especially enjoyed some of Delilah's witty remarks, but on occasion it felt as if she didn't really care? There were a handful of moments where she wouldn't comment on anything reported by Henry which felt a little strange and ultimately pointless to have him point out to her over the walkie.

Though it isn't a major issue, there were a few technical aspects that I did not enjoy while gaming, more specifically whenever climbing/jumping and using the axe. The jerky camera movements were quite nauseating, and while there's only a minimal amount of that you end up doing throughout the entire game, the very last portion of the game has a lot of it and it was pretty annoying to me. 

Takes about 3.5-4 hours to finish everything, and it's worth trying out once; though it's not a game I'd find myself playing again. Regardless, I'd give it a solid 6/10.

Firewatch is an adventure game about a fire lookout named Henry who’s out there in his area alone, and his only way of communication is with his supervisor, Delilah, on a walkie-talkie, where they build their relationship as the days progress. As the days progress, however, some form of mystery builds up when Henry thinks he’s being watched by someone other than Delilah. After going through horror games, I wanted to play something different where I could make my own decisions through character studies, and this was one that I’ve been wanting to play. I remember watching YouTubers play this very interesting game, especially since it was made by the same people who did the first season of The Walking Dead, which I also remember loving. So with this one, I had a solid time with Firewatch, even if it’s a bit of an unsatisfying experience that hurt the game for me. I really like how it started, from making decisions from the get-go when it comes to creating your character from your backstory, while having the soothing music to back it up. The graphics are very interesting because it's like a smoother Hello Neighbor with the glossy animated look of the forest and the character design that you can kind of tell looks low-budget, but they worked around it to make it stunning. The music is so calming, so meditative, and so relaxing that it builds so much onto exploring the forest that it feels like a journey.

The character interactions and the dialogue tree are honestly the best part of the game because of how intricate the conversations are, with choices that are interesting to choose; you don’t know what to pick first. The voice acting brings these dialogues to life so naturally that it feels like I'm listening to an actual conversation, and you’re just sucked in. I love Delilah being smart with Henry, and she is just having fun with him to make the experience fun for him since he’s going through a lot of things regarding his wife and why he came over here. The gameplay mechanics are a lot of fun that, as I said, you’re just exploring the forest, collecting things and trash, climbing up and down with ropes, and figuring out the mystery as well. I was loving the build-up of the mystery that I was trying to figure out just as much as Henry was, and it was getting me super engaged. But what it all led up to, however, was when the game hurt itself. It was such a letdown of a resolution that it felt like it didn’t want to have any form of satisfaction, even if it’s trying to be satisfyingly unsatisfying. People praised it for being realistic in the process of where it all lead up to, and I can understand that, but there needs to be a payoff, and this game didn’t give me that. I also find some of the technical aspects a problem when climbing on tree stumps that are unnecessarily difficult to climb up where sometimes I don’t even know what I’m doing wrong. Firewatch still managed to be a fun game even if the ending was just so disappointing.

Welp, that kinda sucked. I've been wanting to play this game for a while. How could I not? The trailer, the landscapes, the premise, the positive reviews.. it all got me interested. A mystery in the woods? hell yeah! but unfortunately, the game just didn't land for me.

Since this is a walking simulator, the gameplay is very simple: follow directions, go from point A to point B and talk to the person on the radio while you do it. Because of this, I expected the story to blow me away or, at the very least, hook me in. Instead, 3h in, I was bored out of my mind, still wondering what the game was about.

Then some things started happening and I thought "finally, the slowest burn in the world is gonna pay off", [i]but it never really did[/i]. There was so much potential for so many different interesting, dark stories. It was so easy to make up conspiracy theories while investigating, but there was no big mind-blowing plot in the end.

The protagonist is likeable and the dialogue is fine, but nothing I'll remember. He has a sad backstory isn't relevant to the game (besides it being mentioned every now and then and the reason he's there), but you start the game by going over it and making choices about it that don't really seem to matter or change much. There's barely any music, so I can't say that's a selling point either. Some people got attached to Delilah, I never fully trusted her.

There are a lot of books, items and food laying around but you can't really do anything with them. Like, at some point you're supposed to pick up some supplies and only take the ones that were dropped for you and not for other people but why would you take the rest? You don't eat, drink, sleep, read or anything. There's no point or "hard choice to make for your own survival".

I don't know, it was just not for me.

I've seen so many reviews and recommendations about this game, which thrilled me a lot. As a guy who loves fast paced games and shooting, I always have space for a lovely, slow and peaceful story based game. 

Now, games like these, like Firewatch, are the ones that some people call "walk simulators", and it's understandable if you're not the type of person who doesn't care about listening to people, which is another aspect about Firewatch. 
No there isn't much to say about the gameplay, although I do agree with some saying that it's not that engaging, unique or revolutionary.

But let's just make this review done. 
Firewatch it's a story about people, they make decisions, mistakes and think. These are not characters built for the plot, they are built to experience stuff after experiencing a lot in their lives, just like you.
The gameplay is focused on your decision to what to say in a conversation, which was amazing, I was very engaged in Henry's conversations. You climb, find stuff and use some equipment for your tasks.


One tip I should give you is, don't feel like you have much right to judge or review the human characters in this game because they feel very real and if you think they're unrealistic or generic, is because you didn't meet every person in this world and you know how to talk to ONLY a certain type of people. 

No, I can't relate to these characters (cuz I'm a 23 old guy who's still "trying" in life), but I can feel their connections and emotions, their way to show struggles, doubts, happiness. There are bits where I felt myself nervous or just anxious for the characters, and it's not only because the game makes me care for them after some time, but because they show emotions that I felt myself too, and for others too.

Overall, the game is already 10 years old, and it aged pretty well in terms of visual looking and standards (no AI back then, just pure natural art).

The ending, NO SPOILER, at first kinda disappointed me, but then I realised that life sometimes is just like that. The ending of a chapter of your life might be more different than you expect. Life is still going, we are going to experience more, and there is no guarantee that we are going to end a story the way we wished. Things happen just like that, we can't go back and we can't always fix everything in our lives. We only get to choose what to do and how to handle things, how we grow through them and not how it's going to end.

Firewatch taught me some things to remember: we're all experiencing different lives, we all love in different ways. It taught me to remember, without being stuck in the past.
