[h1]HENRY THE HUNK [/h1]

Firewatch is easily one of the best walking simulators ever made. Compared to many games in the genre, the exploration here feels much more interactive. Instead of simply following markers, you actually have to navigate using a physical map and compass, which keeps you engaged and makes the journey feel immersive rather than repetitive. That said, there were still a few moments where the long walks between destinations started to feel a little slow.

Thankfully, the incredible voice acting completely carries the experience whenever that happens. The performances are genuinely outstanding. I honestly can’t think of many games with voice acting this natural and believable. The dialogue is exceptionally well written too — funny, emotional, awkward, tense, and heartfelt exactly when it needs to be. Henry and Delilah are both fantastic characters, and watching their relationship grow throughout the game feels authentic and surprisingly layered compared to what most games usually attempt. I really enjoyed every conversation between them.

The ending, however, might divide people. Personally, I expected something different. The story keeps building tension and mystery as you progress, making you eager to uncover the truth. When the conclusion finally arrives, I’ll admit I felt a little disappointed at first. It’s not a bad ending by any means — actually, it’s quite thoughtful and realistic — but it may not match the expectations some players build up along the way. Whether it works for you will mostly come down to personal preference.

Even so, the game absolutely nails almost everything else. The art direction is stunning, the soundtrack is beautiful, the atmosphere is unforgettable, and the storytelling is deeply moving. At several points, I genuinely wished the game would go even further and introduce more gameplay mechanics, simply because the world and characters are so compelling that you never want the experience to end.

One of the biggest downsides is definitely the length. The main story only takes around 4–5 hours to complete, and there isn’t much replay value afterward. That’s fairly common for narrative-driven walking simulators these days, but in a game this good, you naturally want more time with the characters and world. I felt the same way with The Suicide of Rachel Foster — short experiences, but memorable ones. The hours you spend in Firewatch are incredibly high quality, though I still wish there had been more side activities, achievements, or optional discoveries to encourage replaying it. There are a few small easter eggs scattered around the map, but not enough to make a second playthrough feel very different.

The world itself also feels slightly less open than it first appears. Early on, the map gives off this huge sandbox-like impression, but over time you realize it’s more like a series of connected paths and carefully designed “tunnels.” Beautiful tunnels, admittedly, but still more limited than expected. I also would’ve loved to see the environment feel a little more alive overall, with more wildlife interactions or dynamic details scattered throughout the forest.

Still, none of these complaints stopped me from loving the experience. Firewatch is a pure walking simulator, and it fully embraces that identity. The game occasionally teases the idea of becoming something bigger or more gameplay-heavy, but it never really goes in that direction. And honestly, that’s okay. The emotional journey, atmosphere, and character writing are strong enough to carry the entire experience on their own.

Pros

* Stunning art style and scenery
* Incredible voice acting
* Excellent storytelling and dialogue
* Beautiful soundtrack and atmosphere
* Short, but emotionally powerful experience

Cons

* Very short (around 4–5 hours)
* Limited replay value
* Some players may want deeper gameplay systems
* The world could feel more alive and interactive

I finished Firewatch in a single day, and honestly... I was disappointed that it ended so soon. That's probably the biggest compliment I can give it. I became so invested in the story that I didn't want it to end, and I'll definitely be replaying it again in the future.

The first thing that stood out to me was how beautiful the game is. The art style is stunning, and every part of the Wyoming wilderness feels peaceful and immersive. Whether you're watching the sunrise from the lookout tower, hiking through the forest, or simply stopping to admire the scenery, the world is a joy to explore.

The narrative is excellent. The conversations between Henry and Delilah feel natural, believable, and surprisingly personal. I genuinely looked forward to every radio call, and the mystery kept me curious from beginning to end. The voice acting is fantastic, and the soundtrack complements the atmosphere perfectly. It's one of those rare games where the world feels alive, even though you're often alone.

There were a couple of small glitches during my playthrough, but nothing that affected my enjoyment. At one point I spotted a mysterious floating tree sticking out of the ground... I decided to accept that as perfectly normal and carried on with my adventure!

The achievements are straightforward and enjoyable to earn, especially if you're aiming for 100%. One small heads-up: one of my achievements didn't appear on Steam straight away. If that happens, don't panic. Closing the game and starting a Free Roam save fixed it for me, and there are some excellent Steam guides that explain how to trigger it if you're still having trouble.

Firewatch isn't a game filled with action or combat, and that's exactly why I enjoyed it. It's a relaxing, emotional, and memorable experience that lets the story, characters, and atmosphere take centre stage.

If you're looking for a beautiful narrative-driven game with fantastic voice acting, gorgeous scenery, and a mystery that keeps you engaged from start to finish, I'd highly recommend Firewatch.

My only complaint? I wish it had lasted longer.

This game is sort of what I expected, but at the same time isn't even close. At first it may seem like a relaxing walking simulator. Which most certainly is. But it's quite more than that. When I started it I thought it was a choose-your-own-adventure type thing, in a way it is. Through the game you're offered dialogue choices when talking to your new friend from the next nearest watchtower. Every time your start the game you can build a vastly different relationship and experience the same story differently. The story is great considering it's just you - the player communicating with the only human around there.

Except for great storytelling, the voice acting is done incredibly well which helps the immersion and accents the intimacy between the characters. Speaking of immersion, the nature scenery is coloured beautifully. Everywhere you look you feel like watching a painting at the gallery.

While this game might be a walk in the park for the most part, it can get creepy and unsettling at times. I wouldn't call it a straight up horror game, but it sure feels like that sometimes. It speaks for itself how great of an atmosphere this game can create.

I realize that there are people unsatisfied with the ending, but to be honest, I like the way it ends. I believe that the ending was purposely made the way it is. I surely recommend playing this at least once in a lifetime. It's short and might be a glorified walking sim, but it's truly a unique gaming experience. Although the game is not everybody's cup of tea.

First of all, it's worth mentioning that this game is primarily a "walking simulator." If you are expecting a non-cliché story built around a massive mystery or action-packed conspiracy, this ain't the game you're looking for.

I finished the game in a mere five hours, and throughout the entire journey, I felt like I was watching a great movie rather than playing a video game. The graphics are absolutely gorgeous; the soft lines and diffuse lighting heavily reminded me of "The Witness".

The music and overall ambience were also incredible, kicking in at the exact moment they were needed most -whether you are taking in a beautiful landscape, arguing with a coworker, or stumbling onto something that feels slightly off.

I loved how the game introduces us to the characters. It lets you define the protagonist's personality early on, allowing you to develop his habits and traits as the story progresses. The dialogue feels incredibly intimate and meaningful, like listening to two real human beings talking about their lives, fears, and decisions. I felt privileged just to be a part of it.

It's clear the developers designed every single detail with intention. For instance, early on you are given a disposable camera with 18 shots. Throughout the game, you'll naturally take pictures of various things, strange occurrences, landscapes, or potential evidence.

[b][Warning: Spoilers Ahead][/b]

[spoiler] At the very end of the game, seeing those 18 pictures roll during the credits delivers a profound realization. You find out there was no grand conspiracy; it was just a grounded tragedy of a father losing his son. The mystery wasn't actually that deep. Looking back at your photos, you realize that the tone of your journey, whether it felt dark and paranoid or beautiful and serene, was entirely defined by what you chose to focus on and capture. It leaves you with a wonderful sense of how uniquely the experience was tailored to you. [/spoiler]

Playing firewatch today -- as i write, on the 17th of may, 2026 -- is strange. I can't recall a time i didn't faintly know about it; it was one of the first games i -wanted- to play as a tween. I never did, until now. In many ways, the thing itself will inevitably be less than i would've expected. It's essentially a linear path tip to tail; it has choices, but not very many, and few matter in a game-y way. Post-firewatch, it's hard to take firewatch itself as a piece of adventure art without it feeling less. Yet less is not, in any way, lesser. For a game set in a vast expanse of wilderness, and one mired in an inescapeable froth of ideas, of culture, of the legacy of the new deal, of the 1980s, of "the adventure game", of conspiracies and mysteries, it felt personal and close. For a game in love with the freedom of exploration and hiking, and for one in many ways about this notion of freedom, it's a purposeful and segmented thing. Reading and hearing about firewatch and mostly knowing how it ended already could not have in any way prepared me for the experience of it. For the experience of being alone in an expanse, yet being in a world always close to my chest. For bonding with someone -- and as someone -- and letting that link be what mattered far, far beyond what the Shoshone can cut one off from. I felt, for a time, as someone else; someone not myself, but whom i knew, and who i really cared for. I felt his flaws and, stuck with them, how much of a person there can be around them. I could feel in a sinking pit in my chest that i knew Dee, and that i knew her well enough to recognize her avoidance of connection; i knew her well enough, too, to know how much she could connect with people. 
Firewatch, though a game about a freeing space free from people, is a game about constraints; constraints of character, but also of life; constraints upon what we can and cannot do, but also of how much our choices can truly impact us. Constraints of who we are and who we can be with. And it's a game about flourishing with those constraints, about how little they can mean in the face of the paths we can take. It's a game with one ending, but also a game with as many endings as it has players; a game defined by what we make of our choices much more than the particular choices we make. A game where remarking upon things is the main mechanic, but a game where the things that drive you, the unremarked upon, are the story. A beautiful game.
I feel i knew Henry, and i knew Dee. I wish them well. In my mind, my Henry knew how to get well. And i dearly hope he was able to move on. As i played Firewatch i could not shake the impression that i knew this place, this game, this art, once, too; that, though i was experiencing it for the first time, i was coming against the smallness and tenderness of something i once before failed to fully grasp, so mired in its beauty that i was. I don't think i will ever be able to capture that feeling again -- but in its rarity is also its value. Even if the best games are those that stick with you and to which you return, in one way or another, eventually, some of the very best are also ephemeral, experiences you can only have once and feelings you will forget and there is no use trying to cling to. I felt a lot playing Firewatch. I really, really wish it well, even if we won't see each other again. A part of me can pretend we will, even if i know better. If i pretend, maybe missing it can be warm, too.

You get pulled into the sublime; the awe-inspiring, magnificent, and spellbinding qualities of nature. The story itself is pretty short and easy to go through in about 1-2 hours. It is safe to say that after those first 2 hours, I was left staring at my screen as the credits rolled. I can't recommend this enough. I first picked it up when I was about 12 or so, and I came back to it a few months ago while I was going through some mental issues that I won't get into here. But it really helped me get through them, by reminding me of a better time in my life. It is such a beautiful yet depressing game with an amazing story.

I've played through Firewatch several times at this point, and it just keeps holding up. The art style is still gorgeous, and not just because half the gaming world used screenshots from it as wallpapers for years. The whole experience of being alone in a Wyoming fire lookout, talking to Delilah over the radio, slowly unraveling something strange in the woods, is one of those rare games that nails its atmosphere completely. I'm also still absolutely convinced that one of the people you talk to in the game is secretly the real villain behind everything, but I won't say more than that until you've played it yourself. Short, beautiful, and unforgettable.

Firewatch has a gorgeous art style and a fantastic soundtrack. That's probably the best thing about it. You play as a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness, and the only human connection you have is a walkie-talkie with your supervisor, Delilah.
The dialogues are fine. Nothing terrible, but nothing exceptional either. What saves the experience is the voice acting, which is superb. Henry and Delilah feel like real people with their own problems, and their performances carry the whole game. The story is okay, but again, nothing spectacular. This is not a game you will remember when someone asks for "games with an above-average story."
What I don't like about Firewatch is that several passages feel too much like a walking simulator. You just hold W while listening to conversations. The game is also very short, you can easily finish it under 5 hours.
TLDR; I would recommend the game only on a sale for people who enjoy atmospheric walking games and don't expect a mind-blowing narrative.

Firewatch lives or dies entirely on whether its atmosphere and characters are enough to carry you through, and for a lot of people they are. The setting does genuine work. The Wyoming wilderness feels expansive and isolated in a way that grounds the relationship between Henry and Delilah, and that relationship is the actual game regardless of what else is happening around it. The voice acting sells it and the writing has a naturalism to it that most games in this space don't manage.

The problem is that the mystery the game builds around itself never pays off in a way that matches the investment it asks for. It spends most of its runtime suggesting something larger is happening and then resolves into something deliberately mundane, which is a valid artistic choice but one that leaves a lot of players feeling like they were promised something that never arrived. That's not a misreading of the game, it's a reasonable response to how it positions itself.

The walking simulator label is fair here more than it is for most games it gets applied to. There is very little friction between you and the ending. You walk, you talk on the radio, occasionally you make a dialogue choice that shapes tone more than outcome, and then it's over. If that loop isn't working for you emotionally the game has almost nothing else to offer, and that's a real limitation regardless of how well executed the individual pieces are.

I promise not to spoil anything plot wise. I would describe the game as an action walking simulator. The story has you taking a job as a fire lookout in Shoshone National Forest, Wyoming. You rely on a paper map and compass to navigate the forest. You explore the foreet, interact with objects by picking them up, and communicating with your boss, Delilah, via walkie talkie as you spend almost an entire summer in your tower and protecting the forest. When prompted to speak with Delilah, you are usually given three dialogue options to pick from that remind me very much of the speech options from any game made by Telltale Games. There's a timer to make a selection and the selections generally follow certain personality types that vary but thats not always the case. Which IMO, helps the narrative and gives you a clearer understanding of the protagonist's personality. There is some very light platforming as well while exploring.

Visually, the game is stunning and has that somewhat cell shaded look that reminded me of Borderlands, but was not distracting with how super cartoony/anime it could have been. The forest has diverse and unique sections, you can really tell that one section was made and just copied and pasted throughout the map. There's different colored rocks, boulders, cliffs, trees, bodies of water, you name it.

Where Firewatch shines is the dialogue itself. The voice actors do an incredible job of creating strong and unique personalities, the witty sarcasm and banter is enjoyable and at times hysterical. I've never felt so connected to a character that I couldn't see or play as like I did with Delilah. The game deals with some difficult adult themes and topics in a way that creates sorrow and empathy towards the characters but doesn't drown out their positive interactions with each other. I cannot get over the flow of the conversations between the two when they talk. It feels so genuine and realistic. I could easily picture this conversation happening IRL. It's not perfect, it doesnt feel forced, and the tones change. It's hard for me to imagine that the conversations were read from a script because of how natural to human speech it feels.

Firewatch also excels at creating and building tension and suspense in its plot. I found myself genuinely questioning what was real and what wasn't. I convinced myself I figured out the plot and potential twists about 4 or 5 times only to discover I was more wrong with each and every guess. I want to make it clear that despite this tension and suspense, this game is not a horror game or thriller by any stretch of the imagination.

If you're an achievement/trophy hunter, this game is incredibly easy and you can get all 10 achievements/trophies in about 5-10 hours depending on how well you can navigate the map.

Sadly, Firewatch is an incredibly short game. I managed to beat it and get every achievement in under 6 hours of playtime. There isn't much to do in the game other than progress the story. No side quests, collectibles, or any incentive to explore the map other than to take in the beauty's of the graphics and the world that was created. I'm still not going to spoil the plot, but I did read on the game's Wikipedia page that one of the biggest criticisms of the game was its ending. It's hard for me to not agree with that and I would describe it as a combination of disappointing and underwhelming. Also like any game made by Telltale Games, there is little replay ability here. Your choices in dialogue and in the game have zero repercussions nor change the narrative. At best, it changes the responses and conversations you have with Delilah. But there is a really cool mode in the special features section where you can replay the game with developer commentary on.

TLDR: Firewatch is an indie darling and worthy of your time. It's incredible narrative, voice acting, and graphics should not be missed. These will more than make up for the fact the game is incredibly short and has a lackluster ending.

I went into Firewatch expecting a chill hiking simulator and came out emotionally attached to a disembodied voice on a walkie-talkie. Not sure how that happened, but here we are.

You play as a guy who runs away from his problems… only to realise the forest has excellent acoustics for overthinking. The gameplay is basically: walk, look at pretty trees, climb things that definitely violate workplace safety laws, and make dialogue choices that will haunt you later at 2am.

And the disposable camera you get to snap pics with and then actually see them after you’ve finished, was easily my favourite touch.

Is it action-packed? No.
Will you fight enemies? Also no.
Will you become emotionally compromised over a radio conversation? Unfortunately yes.

Firewatch is a short, unique, but rich experience.

Everything in this game ties together to create a very distinct set of feelings. One moment you are able to dissociate with everything going around you, the next you are brought back to the reality of the situation. For a short period of time, it's able to put you in the shoes of someone going through a rough patch of their life and portray the mixed and conflicting feelings going on in their head. Earlier on, it feels like it tries to romanticize the idea of running away from situations and responsibilities, but it ends up teaching that whatever is coming to you, you are going to have to face it earlier or later. 

The game is beautiful and is accompanied by great dialog and voice acting. This plus an intriguing and mysterious plot create an engaging and full experience. Gameplay-wise, it felt too simple at times, but that's to be expected since it's advertised as a walking simulator. There's no active input to be made. You are given tasks to be completed, which are made up of going to a certain spot, interacting with something, and then coming back to your tower. With the passing of time and the consequent experience gained by the MC every day because of the totally different situation that he was put in from his normal life, at times it felt like this experience should be showcased as well in the gameplay. You will progressively unravel the story and build up relationships with moments of great tension. 

Without delving into spoilers, the story is overall good. It has its highs and lows, but I have to say that the ending, or more specifically the lack of choice in the turning out of things, felt really underwhelming. Maybe that was done by choice, but even then it felt too poor of a choice after so much dialog and building up. With some tweaks, this really could have been a perfect game.

I can’t really recommend Dear Esther anymore. Not because it isn’t important, but because it feels like a prototype of something greater. It walked so games like Firewatch could run.

And Firewatch really does run.

From the moment I started, I had that rare feeling. That this is going to be something special. And it fully delivers on that promise.

I won’t spoil the story, games like this live and die on discovery. You play as a man taking on a job in the wilderness. How he got there, why he’s there, and what unfolds… that’s the experience. There are plenty of deep-dive analyses out there if you want to dissect it, but this is one you should feel first, not study.

Gameplay-wise, yes, it’s a walking simulator. You’ll spend most of your time moving through the environment. But calling it just that undersells it. There’s enough interaction, enough intentional design, that it feels grounded as a game, not just a passive experience. The conversations, the small choices, the pacing, they all matter.

Where it truly shines is atmosphere.

The visuals are stunning in a very deliberate way. The art style isn’t chasing realism. It’s building mood. The warm color palette, the lighting, the way the forest feels both inviting and isolating… it pulls you in. You don’t just move through the world. You linger in it.

And the sound design elevates everything. The sparse musical cues hit exactly when they should. The dialogue feels natural, unforced, and carries the emotional weight of the entire experience. It’s one of those games where silence is just as important as sound.

What really stuck with me, though, is how human it feels. There’s no grand spectacle, no over-the-top twists for the sake of it. Just people, distance, and the things left unsaid. It trusts you to sit with that, and that’s where it hits hardest.

It’s not for everyone. If you’re looking for challenge, systems, or constant engagement, this isn’t that kind of game. But if you’re willing to slow down, pay attention, and let it unfold at its own pace, it’s absolutely worth your time.

I give this a tentative thumbs up.

If you like grounded story based games which use the experience of playing a game to add immersion to the story, then this game is good for you.

If you like the idea of exploring a forest, living in a fire watch tower, and being isolated 99% of the time, then this game is for you.

If you like mysteries, conspiracies, and flawed characters who are never all good or all evil, then this game is for you.

This game DOES NOT have any interest in appealing to you with some kind of mind blowing level design, sound track, or tight gameplay controls. There's no unique mechanics. There's very little actual gameplay beyond moving from point A to point B and interacting with the world to do your job or explore it. It's not for you, if that is what you want.

It isn't here to judge you if that's what you want, or pat you on your back if you like what it's here to present. It's just a story that exists to be told, about a world where there are no supernatural entities, space aliens, or blazing wars. And in that context it explores very well the concept of using a video game to facilitate a short story, and to help really draw the player into the first person experience of the main character. A man who isn't Master Chief. He's not the faceless self insert for everyone to potentially be. He is his own person with his own life that he has lived, and you get to ride along for some of the ups and the downs involved in that life. 

My only complaint really is that, although this is a complete story, it also feels like a single chapter in a bigger one and I am uncomfortable with not getting full closure on some things. But I guess that's just how life is. 

So, yeah, this game gets a thumbs down when it comes to being what I expect most video games to actually be. It's more of a story you live than a game you play. But it perfectly achieves exactly what it wants to do, and for people who want what this game offers, and it wears what it offers on its sleeve I assure you, then this is the game for you. Definite thumbs up in that category.

Firewatch is one of those games that slowly sneaks up on you. At first, it feels like a peaceful escape — just you, a map (that I was terrible at reading so please prepare yourself my fellow bad navigators), and miles of beautiful wilderness. But somewhere between getting lost for the third time and stopping to admire yet another tree, it becomes something more. 🙂

The scenery is honestly stunning. There were so many moments where I just paused and thought, “Okay wow… this is actually gorgeous.” Especially the lake. It’s the kind of game that makes you slow down, even when you’re slightly frustrated.

What really pulled me in, though, was the story. It feels very human — quiet, a little messy, and surprisingly deep and emotional. The conversations, the atmosphere, the sense of connection… it all builds up in such a natural way that you don’t even realize how invested you’ve become until you really care.

I’ll keep this spoiler-free, but I’ll admit a part of me wanted something a bit more for the ending. A happier kind of closure I guess. But at the same time, I get it because tt feels real, and maybe that’s the point — not everything wraps up neatly, even when you wish it would.

Overall, Firewatch is perfect for a chill, reflective gaming session — it’s about the journey, the atmosphere, and the feelings it leaves you with afterward. Even if you get lost a few times along the way as sometimes when you lose your way, you find yourself. 🙂

Firewatch isn't a game you play for complex combat or fast-paced action; you play it for the incredibly raw, human experience. The art direction is breathtaking—almost every sunset over the Wyoming wilderness feels like a painting. But the real masterpiece here is the relationship between Henry and Delilah. The voice acting and radio banter are so organic that you feel the humor, the growing isolation, and the creeping paranoia right alongside them.

It’s a brilliant, tightly paced mystery about trying to escape your real-world problems, only to realize you can't hide in the woods forever. A beautiful, immersive, and unforgettable story that completely hooks you from start to finish. Highly recommended.

The Breakdown
Pros:

Atmospheric Excellence: The stylized 1989 Wyoming setting is one of the most beautiful environments in gaming history.

Top-Tier Writing: The dialogue feels like a real conversation between two flawed adults, not a scripted video game.

Emotional Depth: It handles heavy themes like isolation, guilt, and loss with incredible maturity.

Pacing: It doesn’t overstay its welcome, keeping the tension high throughout the mystery.

Cons:

Minimal Gameplay: If you want puzzles or combat, this "walking simulator" style might not be for you.

One-and-Done: Once the mystery is solved, there isn’t much reason to replay it immediately.

Short Runtime: It’s a 4-hour experience—easy to accidentally finish in a single sitting if you get hooked.

[h1] My review on firewatch [/h1] 
truly an incredible game, this is the peak of story games.
this game is so great because it has the attribute most story games miss, and in my opinion one of if not the most important aspects of a story game, which is personal connection with the main character. 
[b] ill try not to spoil the game here [/b] when you start the game, you get to "shape" the story of how the main character ended up in this situation, and then it throws you in the game. i quite like that, it made me feel like im about to experience a new life. the main character clearly feels ashamed of his actions, and we get to experience the same feelings as him all throughout the game, towards the end of the game, we face challenges, and make a whole "conspiracy theory" i guess you could say that and collect notes, find clues, everything feels like a big investigation, but towards the end of the game, we realize this wasnt about us at all, the problem was simple, and instead of feeling relieved, we (and the main character) feel some sort of emptiness. the end of the game was a bummer to a lot of people as well, we did so much and the end was just bland. i really liked this ending, since it isnt just a "happy ending everythings good now" type of ending, its just making us feel betrayed, and the main character just goes back to deal with the problems he ignored and ran away from all this time. truly amazing how the player and the main character felt throughout this journey, they both felt the same emotions.
another thing about the game is that even though were in a big forest that looks like its fully free to explore, almost every path is blocked off, which i dont think was the devs being lazy, i think its also representing the illusion of freedom we have in the game, we ran from our problems to start something new, but everythings so linear, and when you get so close to achieving the things you wanted, something goes wrong, and you start all over again. the ending presents this quite well.

Firewatch is interesting for two reasons -- its a cornerstone of the 'walking simulator' genre, where gameplay is trivialised to tell a story. This would be the end of it, if Firewatch didn't have a compelling story. But it does, and its worth of the playthrough for that reason alone.

The second reason it is interesting is because of why it attracts negative reviews. Without spoilers, many of the reviewers are unhappy with the narrative direction the story takes and the feeling you get at its conclusion. That conclusion is why I recommend the game, and saying anything more about it would give too much away in what is a short title. However, some will find it disatisfying, and that requires the player to ask why they feel that way. And that question, if the story does what it needs to do, is why it is compelling.

A short "Walking simulator" that is immersive and inspiring not in spite of its minimalism, but because of it. In the 4 hours it took me to complete the game, the game ran me through a plethora of emotions, from complete relaxation, to extreme paranoia, to relief, to sorrow. And I mean EXTREME paranoia. For a game that [spoiler]never actually SHOWS you anything scary or jumpscarey[/spoiler], it still had me looking behind my back SEVERAL times.

The game is best enjoyed when you immerse yourself into its world and really enjoy the sights of the national park. The visuals, sound design, music, and voice acting are all intricately planned to make you really feel like you're in a forest, or to make you sh*t your pants when they wanted to. Delilah, in particular, makes for a perfect companion to your journey. Her sarcasm but earnestness leaves one wishing that the days with your fellow lookout would never end.

And what is there to say about the writing that hasn't been said. The story has one key message: [spoiler]you can escape for a bit, but you have to face reality again[/spoiler]. All the characters tackle this message in one way or another, and at some point we must too. In particular the ending really hit it out of the park: [spoiler]There is no govt conspiracy, no serial killer, no secret dementia/secret twin plot, and no grand adventure. At the end of the day, there's just what you have waiting for you at home[/spoiler].

Where the game falls flat for me, funnily enough, is the climax scene of the whole story! I wish everything after that point had just a little more to give! A little bit more from Henry, Delilah, and[spoiler]the Goodwins[/spoiler]! Just a little bit more to see what their brain thinks of the whole truth of the matter. I will also say (and this is not a criticism) that there is a lot of subtle detail one has to do to figure out the entire picture of the mystery: details which may be easy to miss for some, which may detract from the experience. Oh and the animations bug out sometimes.

Overall I recommend it for anyone who doesnt mind wandering around through a mountain park and extinguishing whatever little fires they can find, and who really enjoy a mystery all about messing with your head and blurring the lines between delusion and reality. Or, if you just really REALLY love nature.

During the first Act you really get the feeling that your “buddy” Dehila is actually just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with you and perhaps she has lost her mind and is stalking you (there are references throughout the game that firewatchers go mad out in the wilderness).  Then during the second act you find a secure secret camp with government-grade surveillance equipment and detailed notes about you and Dehila, it’s real, it has all been real – it seems that you truly have been the target of a government psyop.  There are multiple beds and evidence of a wide scale structured operation. 
Then, the incredibly truncated nonsense third act happens.  Apparently just some random guy named Ned was, somehow, actually behind it the whole time – for really no reason … and the fact that you found an entire government site just days earlier doesn’t matter (or maybe Ned was somehow using the site, despite it being secured when you found it … idk it’s stupid). [h2]Pros[/h2]
[list]
    [*][b]Emotionally touching story[/b]: the game tries to put the player inside Henry’s POV, a protagonist troubled by the weight of his dramatic situation with his wife while interacting with another troubled soul, his boss Delilah… the bond that develops between them opens up numerous possibilities (I’ll come back to this later…)
    [*][b]The dialogue is the game’s strongest element[/b]: it never feels artificial and is executed excellently
    [*][b]Picturesque Wyoming setting[/b], very pleasant visually
    [*][b]Very well-crafted animations[/b]
    [*][b]Enjoyable soundtrack[/b] that follows the emotional progression of the narrative without ever overdoing it
    [*][b]Excellent UI management[/b], things only appear when they’re needed
    [*][b]Relaxing and well-crafted sound effects[/b]
    [*][b]Extremely easy to platinum[/b] (I’ll come back to this as well…)
[/list]
[h2]Neutral[/h2]
[list]
    [*][b]Very short length[/b], completable in a single afternoon (3 hours like)
    [*][b]The cartoon art style[/b]… some people may like it, others may not; I personally feel it clashes slightly with the game’s emotional immersion
    [*][b]The quality of the assets[/b] (textures, polygons) [b]is okay[/b], for a game of this scope it works fine, nothing extraordinary tho
    [*][b]The gameplay focuses on navigating the forest environment[/b] while maintaining the emotional relationship between the two characters (I’ll come back to this ahaha)
[/list]
[h2]Cons[/h2]
[list]
    [*][b]Controls feel a bit stiff[/b], the controller’s stick dead zones are too large and movement in general doesn’t feel very fluid
    [*][b]A chapter (or day) selection would've been very welcome[/b], since some achievements are missable (which makes the platinum tedious)
    [*][b]Navigating certain menus is clunky[/b] when using a controller
[/list]
[h2]A separate discussion about the ending, gameplay and the overall success of the concept[/h2]
IMHO, [b]Firewatch unfortunately suffers from a somewhat confused concept[/b]: the multiple dialogue responses with Delilah suggest alternative narrative paths, even though there is only one ending. This ending is generally considered disappointing, not living up to its potential… but I actually think it makes sense. [spoiler]Disappointment is the central element of the ending, the same emotion Henry feels toward the potential new partner, a bitterness that invites him to face the problems he’s been trying to escape from (after all Julia is still his wife and abandoning her during her illness would hardly be a good ending)[/spoiler].

This narrative formula therefore works conceptually, but the disappointment experienced by the player is a double-edged sword. That kind of emotion isn’t particularly welcome in a product that relies so heavily on emotional engagement.

[b]One way to address this would've been to add alternative endings[/b]: dialogue choices would gain real meaning and players’ emotional expectations would be satisfied while still preserving the concept of the disappointment (even reinforcing it further!). But that’s a more complex discussion.
[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
Wasted potential, but [b]it’s far from a bad game[/b], quite the opposite. It remains a small video game gem worth discovering. Recommended without too much enthusiasm and without major reservations.

I went into Firewatch expecting a chill walking simulator, but honestly it ended up being way more memorable than I thought.

The whole game takes place in the Wyoming wilderness where you play as Henry, a fire lookout spending the summer alone in a tower. The environment is beautiful in a very calm, almost lonely way. The art style isn’t realistic, but it’s gorgeous. Every sunset, foggy morning, and forest trail just feels peaceful but also slightly mysterious.

What really carries the game though is the dialogue between Henry and Delilah. The conversations feel natural, like two real people just talking over a radio while trying to deal with their own lives. Sometimes it's funny, sometimes awkward, sometimes surprisingly emotional. You start the game thinking it's just about watching for fires, but slowly it builds this feeling that something strange might be happening in the forest.

The exploration part, honestly, had me lost so many times. I kept trying to figure out my way, restarting the same day just to get back to the lookout tower and begin again. That frustration of getting turned around... it was a struggle, but oddly it made the journey feel real.

One thing people should know is that this game is very story focused. If you’re expecting action or complex gameplay, this isn’t that. It’s more about the experience, the characters, and the feeling of being alone in the wilderness.

If you like narrative games and strong writing, Firewatch is definitely worth playing at least once.

Firewatch is a game you could talk about for hours because of its color palette, atmosphere, and beautiful soundtracks. But what about its dialogues? About two years ago, I randomly started playing Firewatch on my friend’s PlayStation on a summer night out of boredom and played for around two hours. Unfortunately, I never had the chance to continue. A few weeks ago, I bought it and started again.

The game pulls you in from the very beginning with Henry’s background and loneliness. The sincere and very realistic-feeling dialogues with Delilah are written so well that I kept wondering where the conversation would go next and I even got lost a few times while heading to objectives. Two real people finding themselves here while trying to escape something in their own ways feels very relatable. Many of their conversations are meaningful and the game even rewards you with small, sweet easter eggs at the end.

Most games use cutscenes to show you the story. Firewatch doesn’t. Instead, you experience the story naturally through conversations with Delilah while actually playing. It doesn’t try to shock you with a crazy twist ending. Firewatch offers something different: simplicity. And I think that’s the hardest and most valuable thing to achieve.

That element gave the story a depth I wasn’t prepared for, and it made the whole journey feel much more human and personal.

The atmosphere is incredible. The Wyoming wilderness feels alive, peaceful, and isolating all at once. Walking through nature, alone with your thoughts (and a voice on the radio), creates a unique kind of immersion that few games manage to achieve. It gently reminded me that sometimes nature can help us escape, even if only temporarily, from the bigger issues we’re dealing with.

There’s something powerful about the solitude in this game. Being alone out there, away from everything, feels like a chance to clear your mind and process life in a different way. Firewatch is emotional, beautifully written, and quietly impactful. I absolutely loved it.

I have a complicated relationship with this game, having pirated it way back when it came out and really disliking it back then. I was also young back then and went into it with a sour disposition for the same reason I didn't pay for it - half-writing it off under the oft-thrown-about label of "Walking Simulator". Recently, I played a couple other National Park horror/mystery games (namely [i]Radiolight[/i] and [i]Fears to Fathom: Ironbark Lookout[/i]), which took a lot of DNA from Firewatch to mixed effect and made me somewhat nostalgic for a game I didn't like very much. I thought that now, as a more mature and experienced person, I would give it another try in the hopes that I would get more out of it. It's happened before, it could happen again. Besides, it was like five bucks in the winter sale.

But nah. [i]Firewatch[/i], I still hate you so much. 

I don't hate this game because it's bad, mind you. I actually find the majority of this game to be pretty good. There's not much in terms of proper gameplay outside of walking around and reporting stuff over the radio, but the conversations that result (more on that later) are often charming enough to make it somewhat engaging to look for things around the park to talk about. The art style is also gorgeous to this day, and there's some truly beautiful sights to see around the park, especially at sunset, and the soundtrack - while not something I would casually listen to - is a great backdrop for wandering this chunk of wilderness. It's relaxing to just walk around and explore, seeing the sights, idly chatting over the radio, and there's even a camera to snap a couple pictures of vistas you particularly enjoyed. Good stuff. 

So, this is all pretty positive so far, I'll admit - but this is one of the fundamental problems with [i]Firewatch[/i]. 

All of this is in service of a story that left me scratching my head and wondering what the point was. Ostensibly, this is supposed to be a mystery game, and that aspect is actually not bad, if a little haphazard with its introduction to the story, kind of just popping into the narrative at a certain point. The resolution isn't entirely logical, and there's many logical leaps in the actions of the antagonist, but a lot of this can be attributed to that antagonist's characterization, so I don't entirely mind.  I didn't like this resolution much when it came out, but now I think its fine. Had everything else wrapped up in a satisfactory fashion, I'd probably be flipping this to a recommend and not writing this right now, but here we are. 

You play as Henry, a man whose wife contracted early-onset dementia, leaving him alone, sad, and looking to get away from it all, hence why he takes up the position of a fire lookout. She doesn't remember who he is, her family snatched her away and hates his guts, and so here we are. Your only company is your supervisor Delilah, who you speak to over the radio and report things to. Their relationship is meant to be the real crux of the game, and their voice acting and dialogue tends to be great and one of the best aspects of the game. They're characters with defined personalities, but this relationship that the game hinges on is awkward paced and with a resolution that makes the mystery plotline seem like a work of absolute art in comparison. The progression of their attachment to each other is very strange and the game skips over vast swathes of time that really could have been used to further develop their relationship in a way that would resolve almost all of these issues. 

The resolution of their relationship at the end of the game is just deeply unsatisfying. This is intentional to a degree, but in combination with the resolution of the mystery, it really just leaves you sitting there wondering what the point of playing any of this was. Maybe that feeling is the point, but it doesn't mean I like it. Maybe the game is a character study of these two people, but the more I ruminate on it, the more I feel like neither of these characters actually has much depth to them outside of Henry and his wife's whole deal - which is something I also don't like because the game throws a lot of really bizarre messaging out there and seems to really want him to not move on and live his life outside the shadow she cast. Odd. 

The game seems to want you to get really invested in this relationship, but I just wasn't having it. I liked the dialogue, I liked the banter, but I didn't find much of their closeness believable at all and Delilah in particular is charming but a real piece of work when you get down to it and really think about her after the fact. Again, probably the point. Your mileage may vary. 

The other problem actually is with the gameplay, and that's that while walking around is fun, there's not much firewatching you get to do. You check out smoke plumes a couple times, and other times you go around hunting for tools, but there's entire implied mechanics like the Osbourne Fire Finder that actually aren't mechanics and never utilized. I actually really wanted to just have Henry do his damn job, but the game never allows for that to happen outside of a few spots. It's also pretty buggy, which is something I didn't remember. I had to restart the game twice (thank god it's short) because Henry got his ass clipped on top of the climbing tope tie-off rocks and stumps and I couldn't get down no matter how much I spastically jiggled him around.

Anyway, yeah. [i]Firewatch[/i]. I give it a "Don't Recommend" almost entirely because Steam doesn't allow for any nuance with this kind of thing, but it might still be worth picking up on a deep sale just to wander the national park and take photos. Just don't expect to get anything rewarding out of it.

As she guides you through your objectives, reacts to your observations, and engages in personal conversations, a believable relationship begins to form. The dialogue feels natural and well-written, and while player agency is somewhat limited, the game provides a convincing illusion of choice. Keep in mind the relatively short runtime – it took me around four hours to complete – so you may want to consider picking it up on sale.

[i]Firewatch tells the story about Henry, who's searching for some life changes after his wife developed dementia. To clear his head, he starts a job as a fire lookout at the distant Shoshone National Forest. His only contact in the wilderness is his supervisor Delilah, who also uses the isolation of the forest to find an escape from her own burdens.[/i]

The gameplay is based on [u]completing small tasks and exploring[/u] the national park around the firewatch tower while following a bittersweet plot that unfolds through radio dialogues between Henry and Delilah.

The natural atmosphere and vibrant surroundings are lovely designed and add a sharp contrast to the [u]tense storyline[/u] that builds a more and more unsettling feeling. Firewatch is definitely not a cozy hiking or exploration game, it's more about emotional bonding and character development. The [u]beautiful visuals[/u] and the mystery of the plot keeps you hooked, but in the end it’s the connection between Henry and Delilah that stays with you the most. I'm in love with games that explore psychological connections and Firewatch makes it deeply fascinating to see how isolation turns a connection into a form of escapism far away from reality.

[b]Overall, Firewatch is a masterpiece in [u]atmospheric storytelling[/u] and definitely [u]worth the price of 20€[/u]. It’s a must-play for anyone who loves deep, psychological, story-driven games.[/b]

Firewatch – Intimate Storytelling in the Wilderness

Developed by Campo Santo and published by Panic, Firewatch is a narrative-driven adventure set in the Wyoming wilderness. Players control Henry, a man seeking escape from personal turmoil by working as a summer fire lookout. His only connection to the outside world is Delilah, his supervisor, communicating via radio.

The game’s greatest strength lies in its writing. Dialogue feels natural, nuanced, and emotionally grounded. Player choices subtly shape tone and relationships rather than major plot outcomes, reinforcing the game’s focus on character over spectacle. The art direction, inspired by vintage national park posters, delivers striking landscapes filled with warm hues and atmospheric depth.

Mechanically, Firewatch is minimal. Exploration, light environmental interaction, and conversation form the core gameplay loop. Some may find the linear structure and understated ending unsatisfying, but the restraint aligns with its themes of isolation and imperfect closure.

Though short, the experience is cohesive and memorable. It prioritizes emotional authenticity over traditional gameplay systems, resulting in a reflective, mature narrative journey.

However, the silence of the forest eventually makes the voices you ran away from clearer. Firewatch gently but firmly reminds us that no matter how far you go, you cannot escape yourself. The solitude spent in that tower turns into a bittersweet yet healing experience, teaching you that you must eventually face your feelings.

There's a lot to say about this game. As for celebration of this game's 10 year anniversary coming up, I figure it would be a good idea to write a review. This review will likely contain spoilers, for anyone who cares, so I can summarize everything by saying this game is worth the price if you enjoy story games that reward exploration with more story and lore. (If you're anything like me)

I've played this game on a few different specs. I don't have the specifics down to motherboard, RAM, and Processors, but I can tell you this game ran perfectly on my 1080, 2080 Super, 3080, and 5080. There are some bugs I encountered, but overall didn't mean much.

Visually, this game is still holds up. A rather unique art style for the time the game was released in. The color palette works extremely well, especially during sunrise/sunset. In my opinion, one of the best segments in the game for visual effects is when you walk through the Aspen Grove on the way to the campsite. The sun rays going through the trees, the fog just being finely tuned to not be overbearing and not so you can see so far into the distance to ruin a shot because of the world border. It keeps you well immersed. The Aspen Grove is such a flex in visual splendor that works so well. Definitely could've gotten away with more areas and scenes like that, but I'm not complaining. (SPOILERS FROM THIS POINT ONWARD, SKIP IF SOMEHOW HAVEN'T PLAYED OR SEEN THIS GAME BEFORE AND YOU CARE ABOUT THEM)

For the story, it does a great job at telling you what you need to know, as long as you pay attention and are open to explore. The game does have a certain amount of replayability via different dialogue, maybe trying to do something differently, maybe even paying closer attention to detail on your second or third playthrough to make your own theories for some of the things this game doesn't tell you. (Which is a part of the fun, deal with it) The main character is running from his problems, which is something I'm sure a lot of us want to do, and here we get to see it play out. Honestly, this game halfway made me want to do this same position of a fire lookout at one point, but I don't think I'm quite cut out for that line of work lol. What starts out as a game that makes you think you'll be preventing fires, takes a completely different turn. And honestly, I think that's for the better, as you can only have so much of a game just 'putting out and preventing fires' before it gets too boring/asinine. The game's description summarizes the story pretty well by saying your only emotional hotline is via a handheld radio. The game does allow you to explore by Day 3, though half the map will already be mostly explored by then. Though, I believe it's main purpose is to explore the burned down cabin you walk by in Day 2, as a racoon spawns there on Day 3 inside the furnace, which leads to a pretty niche but very interesting piece of lore to the game. Otherwise, it's just a burned down cabin that isn't explained further. Some parts about the cabin are left to interpretation, which is half the fun. It leaves a portion to fan theories, which is good for the game in the long run. The kind of companionship you grow with Delilah makes you think there's hope, even if everything played out poorly with Julia. More on that later. Then, the story shifts to keep you on your toes, leaving you paranoid every step of the way. Worried you'll be knocked out from behind again, maybe a jumpscare or two. Then you find out the 'research site' was just an elaborate hoax. I will admit it seems slightly outlandish for everything to be run by Ned, but at the same time, it has a bit of creative freedom for it being a story game, so I'm more than willing to let it slide since it works so well in the end. The game does a good job at foreshadowing the climax. The Goodwins disappear suddenly, old pack left by Brian, missing person posters, and how often focus is shifted to the Goodwins. It's a part of this subtle buildup that makes the climax more impactful than you'd expect. Once you find Brian, everything clicks and you think about everything that has happened leading up to that point. Then you get the confession from Ned, and the truth is unknown. We do not know the beginning or middle, only what the end result is. Was it an accident? Was it intentional? Ned kept blackmail of Henry and Delilah just in case, so we'll never know.

There's a fair amount of comedic relief in the game, which will get you a chuckle out of you on the first time playthrough. Next, I'll be talking about the extra features of the game, AKA the audio commentary. I personally love when game have this, and I hate that games don't follow this route anymore. I believe it sets apart the passion projects from just another attempt at revenue, and it proves to improve quality by giving players insight to details they may not have known before. The beginning tapes introduce you to the beginnings of the game design, intro, and programs built into the game. I'm not developer-coded enough to understand all of what was being talked about, but I was nerd enough to listen the whole time. Finding out Forest Byrnes could be surfed originally and was removed was highly disappointing, I will say. It definitely could've been a free roam feature. #JUSTICE4SURFING!! The next few tapes talk about various details of the game, and the ones I noted down was that the developers were afraid of frying graphics cards at the time of the game's release. I cannot state enough how much modern games do NOT care for optimization. Even my 1080 ran this game at high settings, from what I can remember. Now, in the age where 30series+ are almost required to play minimum settings on modern games, this is a very, very nice change of pace and I appreciate the developers for thinking about this. It DOES beg the question though.. if this game would ever receive a remaster, how far could it go? Only in my dreams, unfortunately. There was also talks of trying to find the Teen's campsite and how early players didn't look up, playing into the Gamer Debuff of losing the ability to look vertically into the sky. I'm glad to know this has always been a thing. There were also several mentions of a Firewatch sequel, quite a tease, but honestly, as much as I hate to admit it, I think this game is fine the way it is. A sequel would threaten to shake everything apart that was built up. Unless the sequel has nothing to do with Henry or Delilah, then that'd be fine. In which case, I'm all for another Firewatch. I reached the Admin Sundial (that's what I called it), and messed with the various buttons for different ambiences. There was a setting that basically set it to like midnight and it felt like I was playing a Slender game. It was oddly fitting. On Day 33, there's a tape in which Skype is mentioned, and GOD does it make me feel old. I never even knew Day 34 existed and only found out via the audio commentary. Ben said in the audio on Day 34, that morally, no one took all the supplies for themselves. I sure didn't. I skipped the credits like a chud and found out that Jared Emerson-Johnson was a part of the development of the game, and it all makes sense. (Shoutout to Delilah's VA as well)

The ending. I still can't decide if I hate it or love it. I think that's a part of the magic. No one in this story really got a happy ending. Dave and Ron, Delilah and Henry, Ned and Brian. At best, it was bittersweet. This ending works well, because if we saw and met Delilah, I don't believe we'd be satisfied. I personally felt like it was a message to do what you have to do. Nothing good lasts forever, but you should be grateful for what is, not what can be. My original review was much, much longer, but Steam has limited my characters, so that's as long as the review is going to be. Might make a google doc, idk.

Firewatch’s mechanics are deceptively simple but deeply effective. At its core, it’s a walking simulator, but movement, exploration, and communication are mechanically intertwined to deliver a unique experience. Traversing the Wyoming wilderness relies on intuitive controls and a responsive map/compass system, making navigation satisfying and tension‑building without ever feeling tedious.

The radio dialogue system is the heart of the game’s mechanics. Choosing how and when to respond to Delilah isn’t just narrative — it’s an interactive loop where timing and tone influence relationship dynamics. Conversations happen in real time, which makes your choices feel active rather than passive, reinforcing engagement through mechanical feedback rather than stats or points.

Exploration mechanics are subtle but meaningful. Climbing, investigating points of interest, and using tools like binoculars or notes all feed into a gameplay loop that rewards observation and curiosity. Puzzles aren’t traditional; they’re environmental challenges that rely on careful attention to surroundings and context, tying directly into the tension and pacing systems.

Even simple systems like note‑taking, climbing ladders, or opening doors contribute to player agency, giving the sensation that every action matters in your investigation. The combination of movement, environmental interaction, and dialogue choices forms a loop where mechanics and story reinforce each other seamlessly.

10/10 — simple, intuitive mechanics that turn exploration and conversation into engaging gameplay loops.

I did finish the game, so that's something. But I kept expecting an actual "game" at some point. Instead, the whole thing is just a guided tour of a burning national park. And it's not burning for the first couple of months, LOL. If you enjoy following instructions and listening to a story told in tiny bits and pieces while your character is out chasing down misbehaved teenagers and tromping around abandoned campsites (not by choice, but because you must follow all instructions as they are given in order to "advance" to the next scene), then this is for you.  I was hoping for something a bit more interesting.

I think this would have been better as a movie, or as an even more on-the-rails story game. The dialog options and actions you can take would reasonably suggest a wider divergence of branching storylines than the game delivers on.

It's possible to sequence break the dialogue by just moving through the environment at a brisk pace, even when it makes sense for the main character to be in a hurry. Instead of having dialog trigger automatically at specific locations, perhaps it would have been better to add that dialogue to a queue, waiting until the current conversation is finished. To be fair I got this idea from Hades, which came out 4 years after this game, but to be unfair this problem should have come up in playtesting and they still decided to ship it.

It's also possible to break narrative logic. By just hurrying when it makes sense to hurry, it's possible to have something on screen while the dialog says it looks different [1].

In terms of narrative, I get wanting to write the story they did, but the dialog choices undercut their ability to do that. It gives player agency to let the protagonist behave and think in certain ways, skips a few days, and then you find out that the protagonist started behaving a different way the moment they were offscreen because of the assumptions the dialog makes [2].

The graphics were gorgeous for their time, but 10 years later the focus on realism has left them looking okay. I vividly remember watching Markiplier do a Firewatch playthrough around 9 years ago. At the time I was obviously younger and far too immature to understand the message behind the game or the themes surrounding it, so I chalked it up to being "just another walking sim." Fast forward to now after taking the nostalgia bait and jumping into the game personally, my opinion has drastically changed. 

We play as Henry, a man who is shrouded by guilt and feels he has no other choice but to escape from his spiraling life for a change of scenery, so he applies for a fire watching job in the papers, thus where the game begins. The main selling point for me is how great this game is at depicting isolation. If you have ever had a setback, or maybe you just want a different perspective on things, that alone should be enough for you to want to give this game a shot. Everything feels so real, almost like you are in the tower alongside Henry, with nothing to do but pace through your thoughts. That's not to say there aren't distractions though. Whether it be Delilah telling you to go to another outpost for information or maybe you found a boombox blasting "Push Play by Cheap Talk. Everything still leads back to the main reason you came to the forest in the first place. I could be generic and say the message behind this game is about "Not running from your problems!" but that would be selling it short. At its core, the game is about acceptance and how not doing so can completely alter who you once were. Every character is also an example of this, which solidifies those feelings. My words could mean nothing, and maybe I am just dragging a simple plot, but that's what I took away from this game, and why it cut so deep for me. Anyways, the atmosphere, voice acting, and music are all amazing, even the humor plays a massive role in making it feel the way that it does. Cozy. 

All of those great things being said, this game is a bit pricey at $20. You get around 4-5 hours of content, and that's reaching. Also its nearly a decade old, the price point is just a little outdated. I would wait for a sale and pick it up for a quarter of that price. Firewatch is truly a 1/1 experience though, and I would recommend it to anyone. Even if it means a little splurging. 10/10

Firewatch is one of my favourite games. Every now and again I dip back in and spend some time in Shoshone National Forest, and I want to take a quick minute to say why I think you should to. 

Whilst this game has occasionally been branded as a 'walking simulator', there's clearly so much more to it then that. You play as Henry, a newly recruited firewatcher sometime in the mid 1980's. You've gone out into the woods to get away from life, for reasons that are worth finding out for yourself. His senior, Delilah, is another firewatcher who you communicate with via radio. 

Firewatch gives you space to simply dialogue with her, exploring both Henry and Delilah's lives with both endearing banter and heartfelt conversations on some very familiar, earnest topics. You can respond in many ways, and in each of my playthroughs I've really enjoyed the different conversations you can have. Ultimately, this is a story-driven narrative, so the dialogue is really what shines for me. 

But there's a mystery within the beautiful woodland you find yourself in, and as the summer progresses, it's up to Henry and Delilah to unravel it. Obviously I won't spoil anything in this review, but it creates just enough space for you to want to chase down answers in the short runtime. 

What Firewatch does best is create an atmosphere that's relaxing at times, wholesome in others, and certainly stressful for a minute or two. The playable area is stunning, and between muddying Henry's hiking boots and listening to the subtle, peaceful score that accompanies you, it's easy to see why it's so popular.

If you're still reading this, I won't steal anymore of your time. But you can complete this game with all achievements in under five hours very easily, and you'll have a blast doing so. 

Have fun!

A lovingly made, compact, story-driven solo game where you spend the majority of your time hiking trails in a national park.  The game effectively creates a sense of space and being off the grid working as a firewatcher in a national park in 1989.  The narrative building system reminded me of other story-based games I enjoyed like What Remains of Edith Finch.  Parts of the narrative are controversial, but I won't get into that here as it should be experienced first.  Some of the story I had issues with made more sense to me on further reflection.  I had some issues with the movement system - a few times I got stuck on invisible objects and I had to do a level restart once.  Fortunately the game does not bother with an inventory or progression system, and instead wisely keeps the focus on the story and the scenery, which at times feels like walking into an Ansel Adams photograph.  I would recommend this game for a relaxing outdoor playing experience with minimal distractions.

Your choices don't matter in the game and you are shoehorned into the same story even when it doesn't make sense. I think I would have enjoyed the game more if it either didn't present options that it will ignore anyways or if the game expanded to work with (rather than against) your choices. 

The game looks beautiful, the voice acting is excellent, and I don't mind the linear story progression as this is a walking sim at it's core. That all said, I didn't feel any emotional impact from this game because it gives you dialog options that [i]seem[/i] to give you choice, but then the game still forces situations to happen that don't make sense. For example, [spoiler] if you refuse to set the surveillance camp on fire, then Ned just sets it on fire anyways...which doesn't make sense because Ned would either die from the wildfire or be found out when help arrives to deal with the wildfire.[/spoiler] Also, [spoiler]I didn't flirt with Delilah, so it's not a big deal that she left me behind at the end,[/spoiler] so I didn't feel any emotional impact from the story. Since this game is a walking sim, if the story dialog choices don't matter, then I don't see the point in playing this game vs watching a video. 

Lastly, I experienced bugs that required me to restart the day to progress. I always stayed to the linear story, so I imagine there are a more bugs for players that explore around the map or delay doing the immediate goal.

I paid full price for the game which I do not recommend. At $5 or below, I would recommend the game if you're okay that Firewatch will tell you a specific story, rather than tailor the story to the dialog options you chose.

[h1] CONS: [/h1]
[list]
    [*] The story’s ending is very disappointing undermining the strong buildup.

    [*] The game does a poor job explaining basic controls—I had to dig through the settings just to figure out how to run.
    [*] On the first day, the main character is clearly wearing a ranger uniform, yet NPCs still call him a weirdo, which makes no logical sense.

    [*] Some objectives are poorly highlighted and hard to spot, leading to unnecessary frustration.

The story starts off promising, with strong voice acting, good humor, and impressive visuals that made me genuinely interested in what would happen next. Unfortunately, the ending completely drops the ball and leaves the entire experience feeling unsatisfying.

Firewatch is a first-person narrative adventure video game developed by Campo Santo. Set in the forests of Wyoming in the late 1980s, the game places the player in the role of Henry, a man who takes a job as a fire lookout to escape personal problems, including a relationship marked by illness and emotional distance.

The experience focuses almost entirely on "storytelling" and "exploration". The game’s central relationship is between Henry and Delilah, his supervisor, with whom he communicates exclusively via radio. Through well-written dialogue and response choices, the player shapes Henry’s personality and the dynamic between the two characters, resulting in a believable and emotionally nuanced connection.

Visually, Firewatch stands out for its stylized art direction, featuring colorful landscapes inspired by minimalist illustrations that convey both beauty and isolation. The soundtrack and sound design further enhance the introspective atmosphere, creating a constant sense of loneliness, mystery and contemplation.

In terms of gameplay, it is deliberately simple: walking, exploring, interacting with objects, and making narrative decisions. This may feel limited to players seeking complex mechanics or action, but it aligns with the game’s approach, which prioritizes emotional immersion over traditional challenge.

The most debated aspect of Firewatch is often its ending, which avoids conventional resolutions in favor of a more realistic and human conclusion. This choice may feel unsatisfying to some players, but it reinforces the game’s central themes: escapism, expectations and the difficulty of confronting reality.

Overall, Firewatch is a standout work within the narrative genre. It is neither a long game nor one focused on replayability, but it delivers an intimate, reflective and memorable experience, especially recommended for players who value "well-told stories and realistic character development".

Firewatch represents a compelling example of video games as an introspective medium. It does not rely on action or complex mechanics, but on atmosphere, dialogue, and psychological depth. The true narrative unfolds not on the screen, but within the player’s own mind.

Assuming the role of Henry, a man escaping personal tragedy through isolation, the player witnesses a classic avoidance coping strategy. The silence of the wilderness offers no relief; instead, it amplifies unresolved emotional conflict. Henry’s relationship with Delilah, conducted exclusively via radio, becomes a subtle study of projection, as the player constructs an image of her based on assumptions and expectations.

The game handles uncertainty with remarkable restraint. Gradually emerging suspicion feels organic rather than forced, accurately mirroring cognitive processes that arise when information is incomplete. The ending deliberately avoids conventional closure, reinforcing the authenticity of the experience.

Firewatch ultimately confirms that video games can function as a legitimate platform for existential reflection and psychological exploration.

Firewatch 8/10, Walking Simulator That Walked Into My Feelings

Hours played: One very emotional hike
Genre: Sad Man Goes Outside

Firewatch is a game where you:

- Walk around a beautiful forest
-  Talk on a radio
 - Avoid your real-life problems

You play as Henry, a guy who makes some bad life decisions and then takes a job as a fire lookout to not think about them

Gameplay includes:
* walking
* climbing things
* picking up random objects
* staring at scenery while contemplating your entire existence

If you’re expecting combat, crafting, or skill trees this is not that game. This is a **vibes-first, thoughts later** experience.

Delilah (The Voice That Carries the Game)

Most of the game is just you talking to Delilah over a walkie-talkie.

Somehow this results in:

* better chemistry than most RPG romances
* jokes that feel natural
* emotional moments that sneak up on you

You will care about this voice.
You will also project a lot onto this voice.
The game is aware of this and lets it happen.

* Art style: stunning
* Colors: chef’s kiss
* Music: calm, lonely, slightly unsettling

The forest feels peaceful until it suddenly feels *too* quiet, and you start thinking:

> “Am I alone… or *alone* alone?”

This is a story about:

 escapism
 guilt
 loneliness
 and how running away does not magically fix things

It lets you build theories, get paranoid, and feel clever then gently reminds you that real life is often messier and less dramatic than that.

Some people hate this.
Some people think about it for years.

Pros

- Great voice acting
- Gorgeous art direction
- Short, focused, memorable

Cons

- If you want action, you will be disappointed
- Ending will divide people
- You may finish the game and just sit there

But read that book 'The Singular Mind' if you're in a similar spot. It'll certainly help.

I was incredibly impressed with Firewatch. What I really love is the old adventure games, although they are not always as good in reality as they are in memory. What's really impressive is when a real adventure game (not action adventure, which is completely different) build a new mechanic into the game. The flawed Moebius: Empire Rises had that. To some extent the sword fights in The Secret of Monkey Island had that. In terms of gameplay, Firewatch has that. Henry, the player character, must get to know the area that he's watching for fires, but he comes across reasons to get out of the watchtower and look around.

There are three parallel stories in Firewatch. First, the story of Henry's marriage. I was very moved by it. I started really caring about Henry, and, to some extent, about his wife, Julia. There's the story of the relationship between Henry and his supervisor, Delilah. Their dialogue makes the bulk of the game. And then there is story of Henry's investigation of Two Forks, the area he's watching.

Many game stories have a problem with story scope. It's often all about saving the world or one country (usually the US). There is none of that in Firewatch. True, Henry is supposed to help protect the area against fires, but he's hardly a hero. He got the job mostly because it requires no qualifications. It never happens that he sees a fire, even a tiny one, without Delilah seeing too. No, the stakes in Firewatch are the stakes of the story: what can Herny do, if anything, about his complicated marriage? What is the nature of the relationship between Henry and Delilah? And what exactly is happening at Two Forks?

The fact that the stakes are so slow means that it is extremely easy to identify with them. When Henry senses danger, it's not from a horde of zombies. Rather, it's beacuse some thing around him don't add up. That's extremely easy to identify with.

Also, the voice acting is amazing. The only completely unrealistic thing about this game is how beautiful the voices of those characters are. We've come a long way. If you want to see how bad it used to be, go look at the voice version of King's Quest 5 on YouTube. People got actually paid for that. Sure, for the voices, they just picked people around the office, but I'm sure they got paid for that work. The standards definitely have changed. For adventure games, I think that Oxenfree set the new bar, and it's a high one.

Anyway, I was wrapped, intermitently, with suspense, fear, and a sense of deep compassion. Also these two characters can sometimes be funny, but not in a way that diminishes the seriousness of their situation.

This is what I would call a game for adults. Not as in "explicit" but in the way that Bergman, Fellini or Ozu make films for adults. I love it when things are just pure fun. But this was a daring attempt and going the other way, and I think it succeeded fully.
