[h3]Quick Summary:[/h3]
Unable to cope with watching the person he loved slowly slip away due to illness, and being forced into a life he never wanted, a man tries to escape by taking a job in a forest far away from the city. In the place he goes to, we experience an interesting and mysterious story, accompanied by stunning landscapes and a voice on the radio — someone who, just like him, is also running away from their own life. There isn’t much to say about the gameplay; it is entirely a walking simulator. Other than occasionally getting stuck while walking — which forced me to save and reload — there isn’t anything else going on mechanically. The story is interesting, the narration is well done, and the scenery is absolutely amazing. It’s a game that can be 100% completed in about 4 hours, and after finishing it, players who want can freely roam around this beautiful world.
[h3]Score for those who don’t want to read till the end: [b]8/10[/b][/h3]

[h3]1- Introduction and Expectations[/h3]
I started this game while playing Clair Obscur, mostly to change things up a bit and because I had just bought it. I had heard a lot of praise about its storytelling and had been curious about it for some time. Before buying it, I already knew that it was a walking simulator and that I shouldn’t expect much in terms of gameplay, so everything I experienced while playing was exactly in line with my expectations, which left me satisfied.

[h3]2- Gameplay | No score for gameplay, but -1 point due to issues[/h3]
There isn’t much to say about the gameplay. As I mentioned in the first part of the review, this is a walking simulator, so I’ll keep this section short and won’t include it in the scoring. However, even though the gameplay mainly consists of walking, I deducted 1 point from the overall score due to the problems I experienced while walking.

Especially in the later parts of the game, after certain animations like jumping or dropping down from a height, the character can get stuck and stop moving even on flat ground. This can be very frustrating, because it doesn’t get fixed unless you save and reload. Since the game only took me around 4 hours to finish, it didn’t cause major issues, but even for such a short experience, it was enough to get on my nerves.

[h3]3- Story and Atmosphere | Story: 9/10, Atmosphere: 10/10[/h3]
The game is entirely built around storytelling and atmosphere. The story is generally well written, somewhat emotional, but overall mysterious and interesting. To avoid spoilers, I won’t go into too much detail about the story, but in general, we experience the events of a man who starts working at a fire lookout tower to escape from what he went through after a tragic event involving the person he loved. We experience this through conversations over the radio with another person and through the events we witness along the way. I deducted 1 point because I wasn’t fully satisfied with the ending of the story and because I expected it to be a bit longer.

There is a lot to say about the atmosphere: the trees, the colors, the sounds of nature, and the sense of peace you feel while wandering around are all excellent. This is a kind of peace that you can’t really find in real life, but you can find it here. I didn’t take any photos myself, but there are plenty of opportunities for in-game photography, and some scenes could easily be used as wallpapers. Because of this, I’d say the atmosphere is the strongest aspect of the game.

[h3]4- Pros and Cons[/h3]
[b]Pros:[/b]
+ Engaging story
+ Amazing atmosphere
+ Free roam mode for a chill experience
[b]Cons:[/b]
- Getting stuck during gameplay
- The ending of the story was not satisfying

[h3]5- Replayability and Recommendation[/h3]
I don’t think the story has much replay value. It’s memorable, short, and not something you’re likely to forget easily. However, it can still be enjoyable to jump into the free roam mode from time to time just to relax and explore. I would recommend playing this game even just for its atmosphere, but the story is definitely worth experiencing as well. It’s a short game and very cheap on sale, so I think everyone should try it at least once.

[h3]6- Score[/h3]
Even though I didn’t include gameplay in the scoring, I deducted 1 point due to the issues I experienced. I also deducted 1 point because I wasn’t satisfied with the ending of the story. The atmosphere, however, gets a full score. My score: [b]8/10[/b]

It sucks that I didn't enjoy this one because this really is my type of game. My disappointment doesn't even stem from the somewhat high expectations that were set any time I heard about this game. The moment the game begins, the music and narrative sweep you away... it's the moment you begin in the Firewatch tower that everything begins to go up in flames. 

Without spoiling anything, I have to start by saying that I was really up and down on whether or not I wanted to continue. Mostly because being slightly bored with the walking. The dialogue between the main characters kept me engaged and it was that first whiff of mystery that caused me to think that maybe I was wrong and that I should continue on. 

It wasn't until the mystery started to unravel where I realized I just did not care for the execution of the story. And it didn't help that the game is extremely boring when it comes to actual gameplay. I love myself talking/walking sims, but there's gotta be a high level of engagement for it to work and it just doesn't here. By the time the major revelation is unraveled, I just didn't care. 

The characters deserved so much more because I did find them interesting and nuanced. It was just everything else that bogged them down. One of the worst parts of the game that distracted me from the character dialogue was absolutely the technical performance. For the first time I had to go out of the game settings to lower my frame limit because I kept running into invisible walls and my walking pace would significantly slow down. It was atrocious and annoying and took me out of the moments until I figured out how to resolve the issue. 

These writers are talented, it's just that their talent was wasted on a mystery that felt off, choices that really don't matter or play into the story all that much, and an all-round story that was just too boring and needed something more. I like that others love this game so much, it was just a big miss for me.

I obviously LOVED the location as well of course, I can’t express how much I love American pine forests/Pacific Northwest-adjacent environments. Firewatch is a decent game with some great writing, I had fun for the 4 hours it took me to complete the game, but the plot started to get stale towards the end and I wasn't a huge fan of my ending.  The game is incredibly short too, probably over half of my playtime was just cutscenes/pause menu.  However, the characters are entertaining throughout the game and the plot builds on itself well, bringing together a very interesting and mysterious story.  The 2 characters and their interactions are really the focus of the game, and the writer did a great job bringing them to life.  Both of them feel like real people with real personalities.  Besides the flushed-out dialogue, characters, cutscenes, unfortunately the game is really just a strand-type game and you're simply walking from point A to point B to get the next exposition dump.  Also, sometimes which direction to go and what to do next can be unclear if the cutscene is skipped, or partially skipped.  The outcome I got wasn't what I intended either, but I guess I have to play the game again and correct my dialogue options if I want to get the ending I was looking for.  Still worth $5 anyday for a quick afternoon playthrough.

The writing and voice acting are excellent, and they make the interactions feel natural and human. You’re constantly aware of your choices and how they shape the tone of the relationship, which keeps you emotionally invested.

Firewatch is short and sweet, but it delivers a strong emotional impact. It beautifully portrays human emotions, loneliness, and connection through simple but powerful storytelling.

If you enjoy story-driven games focused on dialogue, atmosphere, and emotional interaction, Firewatch is definitely worth playing.

Firewatch is a masterclass in atmosphere and emotional tension that proves you do not need combat to create a gripping experience. It turns the simple act of walking through the Wyoming wilderness into a deeply personal narrative about isolation, regret, and the human need for connection.

​You play as Henry, a man who retreats to a lookout tower to escape his life, only to find himself entangled in a mystery that feels increasingly voyeuristic and paranoid. The core of the game is the radio dialogue between Henry and his supervisor, Delilah. The writing is so natural and the voice acting so superb that you forget you are talking to a person you have never actually seen.

​The art style is breathtaking, with sunsets that make you want to stop playing just to stare at the horizon. It is a short, focused experience that understands exactly when to build tension and when to let the silence of the forest speak for itself. It is not just a "walking simulator"; it is a beautiful, heart-wrenching study of two people hiding from the world.

Firewatch is quiet in a way that’s loud as hell.

I finished this game and just sat there. No music. No menus. Just staring. That’s how you know it worked.

This isn’t about combat, skill trees, or winning. It’s about loneliness, escape, and the lies we tell ourselves when real life gets too heavy. You play as a man running away from his problems, and the game never lets you forget that — no matter how far into the woods you go.

The dialogue is unreal.
Natural. Awkward. Funny. Painfully human. The conversations with Delilah feel more real than most “choices matter” games ever manage. Every pause, every joke, every uncomfortable silence says something.

The world is beautiful but empty — and that’s the point.
Wide forests, crackling radios, distant smoke. You’re alone, but not really. And that tension between comfort and isolation slowly messes with your head in the best way.

And the ending…
No spoilers. Just this: Firewatch doesn’t give you what you want. It gives you what you need. It respects you enough to let things be unresolved, messy, and real.

This game understands that sometimes there’s no big answer.
No villain. No fix. Just people, pain, and moving forward anyway.

Firewatch isn’t long, but it stays with you.
I’ll be thinking about this one for a long time.

Firewatch really impressed me with its art style. It’s not going for hardcore realism, but that’s exactly why it works so well. The visuals are clean, atmospheric, and genuinely beautiful without trying too hard.
The story is very engaging, especially the prologue, which immediately pulls you in emotionally. It sets the tone perfectly and makes you care about what’s going on from the start. The characters are another strong point. Their chemistry feels natural, and I really liked how the game explains things through dialogue instead of throwing obvious tutorials at you. It feels organic and immersive.
What holds the game back from a higher score are the bugs. There are several moments where you randomly glitch around, and some animations look straight-up broken, like the game briefly forgot how it’s supposed to work. It doesn’t completely ruin the experience, but it does break immersion more than it should.
Overall, Firewatch is a strong narrative-driven experience with great atmosphere and characters. Technically a bit rough in places, but still absolutely worth playing if you value story and mood over perfect polish.

Now.. everything else.

Firstly, it's a bad [i]game[/i], not a [i]bad[/i] game. The storytelling are its strengths, but I would argue its similar to old Telltale games like The Walking Dead where it has an interesting plotline but nothing to do outside of that plotline except walk around, dialogue, and explore and wait for the next story trigger.

Up next.

The first plot you're following is a romance plot in the first sections of the game after the exposition about your character (which personally, I would've been more engaged in following compared to the actual game). Then, you're 'romancing' or bantering with your (technically) boss despite the lack of professionalism in the radio dialogue here.[spoiler]She's drunk one of the first time she speaks with you, and is a rather interesting start.[/spoiler] There are also a bunch of plotlines you follow that are kind of unrelated to the story, which starts to drag but is tolerable.

So you reach about the halfway point. BOOM! [spoiler]You find out there's a stalker![/spoiler]Panic rises with the tonal shift of the game and starts dragging the focus away from the romance into 'two people surviving.. together' that average plot with two people. And by the way, right now, you're the only one who can do anything about it (recklessly, mind you) exploring everything.

When you investigate and, for some reason, do not die to the antagonist of this story, an interesting plot device (that while had been worked on, elaborated, and discussed in the early sections of the story leading up to it, is still frankly such a great timed interruption to the investigation) ends the story.

Congratulations. You walk away with an ambiguous ending. It's hollow too.

It was a nice game. People complain about the plot but really, sometimes the greatest mystery isn't about the unrealistic things that's going on around you, or that could be going on around you. Sometimes the greatest mystery is people. Why they do the things they do. Why can't everything just be normal and peaceful. 

Delilah is a gal that lives in the moment (or so I believe). Henry is a guy who's trying to figure out what the hell he's to do now. Ned is a mental case that got his familial life taken away from him by his own mistake. And I think that's the mystery of the game: who these people are, why they're here in the middle of nowhere instead of being wherever living their life and what are they gonna do next in their boring, mundane lives. In other words, people.

People are a real mystery. And life too, consequently. It's not as exciting as conspiracies maybe but nonetheless interesting. Every minute of your life could be your last. Someone may break into your house to kill you, or just run up to you on the street and plunge a knife in your throat (and who's to say that in a few years a certain chain of events won't transpire that'd turn you into such a person?). Or your brain could suddenly pop a vein and you'll die from bloodloss in the middle of the night. Your friends and family, if you have them, would react differently too. Some would accept your sudden death, some may find it weird and decide to investigate, some would have no strong feelings, etc. And that, I think, is our grand mystery.

Why these things happen. Why you were destined to die, and whether your death was destined in the first place whether it's via the actions of a person or your own body deciding it's just time for you to go. And why people act the way they act and do the things they do. The thing is, your death may not be even random. Many cases of abuse happen between family members, who's to say a relative of yours wouldn't decide to murder you one day? Or someone you've never seen before but who's been seeing you almost every day. It's not like these things can't happen to you.

When you really think about it, people are a bigger mystery than any conspiracy you can possibly come up with. Sometimes you can't help but wonder why they do the things they do, what events in their life shaped them to be the person they are now with their current set of ideals if present. Firewatch is a game about people. Not exaggerated or broken characters just ordinary individuals dealing with the weight of their own lives. At its heart, the game is about escape the ways people run from responsibility, grief, or emotional strain, and how those attempts to disconnect can reveal more about them than the problems they’re avoiding. You play as someone who retreats into the quiet isolation of the Wyoming wilderness, and the game leans into that feeling of getting away from everything. The routine tasks, the long walks, the small disturbances in the forest they’re intentionally mundane, grounding you in a space that feels both peaceful and lonely. The real emotional pull comes from the relationship that develops over the radio. The conversations are thoughtful, vulnerable, often surprisingly honest, and they gradually reveal how both characters are using this distance to confront or avoid their own issues. The dialogue is the soul of the game, turning simple exchanges into meaningful moments.

One of Firewatch’s strengths is how it blends this personal connection with a sense of unease that slowly builds in the background. The game never relies on big twists or dramatic reveals instead, it focuses on the tension that comes from uncertainty, isolation, and not fully understanding what’s happening around you. It uses atmosphere, sound, and the environment to keep you on edge without ever breaking the grounded, human tone of the story. By the time the journey reaches its end, Firewatch doesn’t try to provide a clean moral or a neatly wrapped conclusion. Instead, it reflects the messy way life often unfolds where closure isn’t guaranteed, and where people sometimes leave things unresolved because they don’t know how to face them. Ultimately, Firewatch is less about mystery and more about the emotional landscapes people carry with them. It’s a quiet, immersive experience that sticks with you not because of what happens, but because of why people do the things they do.

[h2]Short Summary[/h2]
[b]Firewatch[/b] is a masterclass in atmospheric storytelling. It delivers a stunning, emotional journey through the Wyoming wilderness, defined by incredible voice acting and a lingering sense of isolation.

[h2]The Breakdown[/h2]

[table]
[tr]
[td][h3]What We Loved[/h3][/td]
[td]The conversational choice system creates an intense, believable bond between characters. The stylized art direction and excellent voice acting carry the entire experience.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][h3]Minor Annoyances[/h3][/td]
[td]The gameplay is mechanically shallow and often labeled a "walking simulator." The ending subverts mystery tropes in a way that feels anticlimactic to some.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][h3]What It's About[/h3][/td]
[td]It explores escapism and the inability to run from life's problems. It is a story about isolation, paranoia in the deep woods, and the fragility of human connection over distance.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][h3]How It Plays[/h3][/td]
[td]Exploration acts as a vehicle for dialogue delivery. You navigate using a map and compass, serving as a pacing mechanism to separate story beats rather than a complex challenge.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][h3]Core Tone[/h3][/td]
[td]The game shifts between introspective melancholy and tense paranoia. Yet, it remains consistently warm, banter-filled, and human throughout the journey.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][h3]Genre Context[/h3][/td]
[td]Comparable to [b]Gone Home[/b] or [b]What Remains of Edith Finch[/b], focusing on narrative immersion over skill-based mechanics.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][h3]Technical Snapshot[/h3][/td]
[td]Visually stunning with a distinct art style. However, the Unity engine struggles occasionally with minor performance hitches on specific hardware.[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

[h2]The Bottom Line[/h2]

[h3]Who Is This For?[/h3]
Players seeking a mature, short narrative experience who value atmosphere, dialogue, and emotional resonance above all else.

[h3]Who Is This Not For?[/h3]
Those demanding complex gameplay loops or high-octane action, or anyone easily frustrated by endings that prioritize realism over Hollywood closure.

[quote]If you are willing to trade mechanical depth for a beautiful, haunting story about human flaws, this trip to the woods is essential.[/quote]

[h2]Main Review[/h2]

You play as Henry. You are a man fleeing a personal tragedy involving your wife's early-onset dementia. You take a job as a fire lookout in the Shoshone National Forest during the summer of 1989. You are a lonely observer in a tower, but the game hints you might be a participant in a conspiracy. The premise is grounded in the idea that you can run to the middle of nowhere, but you cannot outrun who you are. The narrative hook is immediate. It pulls you into a web of escapism and the hard reality of the choices you left behind.

The gameplay is minimal by design. You traverse a semi-open wilderness using a map and compass. You engage in a conversational choice system via walkie-talkie with your supervisor, Delilah. This is the core loop. The navigation is light puzzle-solving. It never challenges your reflexes. Instead, the walking serves as a pacing mechanism. It gives the dialogue room to breathe. The interactions feel natural. You are not solving the world's problems. You are just a guy on a radio. Some will call this shallow. Others will see it as the perfect vehicle for the story.

The world of [b]Firewatch[/b] is a character itself. The art direction by Olly Moss is vibrant and stylized. It masks the technical simplicity of the assets. The sound design immerses you completely in the Wyoming wild. The narrative pacing begins as a slow-burn slice-of-life. It accelerates into a tense thriller. It maintains a consistent, leisurely stroll through the environment. The tone balances warmth and banter with deep introspection and paranoia. You feel the isolation. You feel the connection to the voice on the other end of the radio.

[b]Firewatch[/b] is a short, impactful 4-5 hour experience. It is a linear journey with little replay value beyond seeing different dialogue options. It is a memorable mood piece. The primary criticism often lands on the ending. It subverts mystery tropes. It refuses to give you a grand conspiracy. It gives you reality instead. This feels like a fizzle to some. It feels poignant to others. Technically, the voice acting is flawless. The engine can suffer from minor stuttering. Despite these flaws, the value lies in the emotional weight. It is a flawed gem, but a gem nonetheless.

Short story-oriented walking simulator. My wife completed it years ago but I just decided to try it. The review contains some spoilers! You have been warned.

What I liked:

* Amazing intro. Very atmospheric, made me sad in a good way, got some tears.
* Good sountrack. I listened to the album before the game and it was another incentive to play it.
* Lovely visual style. I'm a big fan of The Long Dark and this is another watercolor Unity game with distinct style.
* Has a bit of gameplay for a standard walking simulator. And walking is quite good. I especially liked the ability to run endlessly. Helps a lot when you know the map already.
* Not a bad overall story and radio interactions. It's a one shot experience but a pleasant one.
* The ability to save where you want and turn autosaves off (f**k the games like "What remains of Edith Finch" where you don't even understand if the game was saved at all).
* The ability to turn off location on the map. I like some compass and map orienting in my games.
* Handwritten info added to the map dynamically. I adore this since classic Silent Hills!
* Great idea with [spoiler]the photos you have taken appearing in the credits. Actually helps to finish watching them. And the final photos by the camera owner add greatly to the story.[/spoiler]
* Love how the world [spoiler]becomes harsher till the end[/spoiler], adds to the atmosphere.

What I disliked:

* Bugs. Had some tiny stuttering on a new PC with 4080 SUPER. Had frequent animation bugs. Like when you try to climb the rocks and Henry just walks backwards into the air instead! Saving and loading helps but still, such things happened not once but several times. The [spoiler]turtle was flying in the air when I found it.[/spoiler]
* Bad collision physics. I was stuck on some rocks and trees several times. But most of the time wagging the controller sticks for half a minute helped me escape this predicament.
* The world is too small and empty. It would be cool if the game was longer and had some more exploring and actual gameplay. I don't even understand why did they implement a free roam mode instead of making the area larger and more interesting.
* The lack of [spoiler]actual choices. Nothing you tell or don't tell Delilah matters at all in the end.[/spoiler]
* Optional achievements are meh and sometimes even stupid. For example, I [spoiler]discovered an old house on my own on the day I checked the wires. But the racoon event can trigger only much later. Why did you do this? Why do I need to go to that place again? The cassette with the song - why can't I listen to it if I found it??[/spoiler]
* Bad sound design. The music is cool but the forest and ambient sounds are poor and strange. Something that sounds like wooden drumming? Why, what does it mean? Constant repetitive rustling in the grass.
* You can take and look at many items but they are mostly useless. And you can't even put most of them away accurately, just drop randomly.
* The world drawing details are significantly poorer at the edges of the map. You really see that there's almost nothing there.
* Hilariously bad axe usage animation! No one chops trees the way Henry does in real life!

Overall, the game has its flaws but I still recommend it. Good tiny attempt to tell a story within a picteresque nature setting. Enjoyable little jorney for a couple of evenings. And the intro really impressed me, a solid one.

Quick Description:
-It's always difficult to review a game almost 10 years after it released.  I bought Firewatch a few years ago for less than $2 and have been meaning to play it.  I really loved the strong voice acting, the unique visual style, and early on was really excited to explore the world around me.  I read a review where the reviewer mentioned that they really enjoyed the first half and absolutely hated the second half.  This is exactly how I felt.  I was shocked at how little enjoyment I received in the closing couple of hours.  I started out rooting for the two main leads, and over time, found them far less likeable, far less logically consistent, and far less relatable.  I assume that the point of this game is to shed light on the isolation, loneliness, and exhaustion that every day life and grief can have on us as human beings.  But I just didn't find any of this to be very satisfying.

Consensus:
-Bottom Shelf Game (Tier 5 and makes up 10% of my reviews).  It's okay that this game feels a big janky and buggy, b/c it's almost 10 years old.  I knew that there would be plenty of slow exploration and linear progression.  I don't have a problem with any of that.  I just started to feel less connected to the dialogue and characters with every second that passed.  I'm aware that this may be exactly the point of this game and it was done intentionally by the devs.  There are tons of games that handle grief, depression, paranoia, and loneliness in a far more interesting and rewarding way imo.  For all of these reasons, I won't be recommending Firewatch.

It's left me speechless. I don't even know where to begin in describing this game.
Despite only being around 3-6 hours of a story, you'll find fully fledged 30 hour stories can feel shorter. Playing as Henry, you take a summer job as a fire lookout, in the hopes of getting away from his personal life. Your only live interaction with another human is Delilah, another lookout in a region not far from you. 

This is a game about human connection, processing our past, solitude, and countless other things that are intentionally left open to interpretation.

This isn't an action-packed game, you can't die, you can't attack, it is an even more muted version of Death Stranding - a walking simulator. Do not be swayed by this diagnosis though, for the player who values a deep narrative, this is the right game. It can be finished in one sitting, what's the harm?

You may walk around, climbing rocks and repelling down slopes, but the content goes beyond that. There isn't another game that can have my heart pounding all whilst doing nothing in-game. 

There's so much to talk about. It never really feels like the game has one central theme. If anything, I'd say the one central theme is simply Henry, as a person, and subsequently people as a whole, who often go through a similar situation. For one, the entire premise is a dive into the process of guilt, lengths of love, and the processing of emotions. Henry comes to Firewatch as a means of getting away from his life, his mistakes, and the struggles he had with Julia, and all throughout the came she plays a central role to Henry. By the end, we see that time alone does not heal, you must first take the [i]time[/i] to process our emotions, and how it affects us. Henry isn't healed by the end of the game, Julia is still with him, appearing in his dreams. 

Side-note, the atmosphere is incredible, there's truly something about it that just nails the forest and nature. Dialogue is also probably the best I've seen, it feels so natural, makes us believe these are not characters. I mean, just through the tone, you, like any normal irl interaction, can pick up certain cues and intentions. Stutters and silence are surgically  placed in dialogue to introduce conspiracy, leading to my next point.

Within the theme of Henry, comes with it this deep sense of paranoia that is very overtly shown through the plot of an external party listening in on Henry and Delilah, and it's so incredibly pulled off. Everything about this game is ambiguous. Could Delilah just be Julia in a different state? Was Delilah real? Was she on our side? Was she conspiring with Ned? Why didn't she just meet us whilst dropping off the walkie talkie? Most of these, of course, aren't greatly viable, however the game introduces the instability of the storyline for us to have those thoughts in the first place. In a way, it represents us in our states of guilt and grief, we are constantly switching between how we perceive events, and we often struggle to find a conclusion that we're happy with.

The game has flaws, for sure. The ending is certainly a point of content. Whilst I couldn't help but desire some sort of relationship to come out of Delilah and Henry, I can understand the ending to an extent. Henry came to get away, only to find that running from a wave is just setting yourself up for failure. I think, this entire period for home was a period of self-realisation. I feel it's safe to say there was [i]some[/i] love between Henry and Delilah, although it feels like at times Delilah wasn't reciprocating it. Point, some love isn't mean to last, we experience it, we appreciate it, we learn from it, and we move from it. I think this was what D+H were. Lessons. Whilst I wish there was a little more development for Delilah, Henry grew to learn that you must face the oncoming wave, and let it wash over you. Fighting, running from it, will only cause you to drown.

I'm sort of happy that the storyline ended up being a crazed father trying to cover up his sons death. There are plot holes sure (how does he know these details about Julia?), but I couldn't have really imagined it being some big government conspiracy or aliens. This feels more grounded, it connects better, not everything in life has a climax, sometimes things simply pass. 

I could go on and on and on, but this is one of those games you really wanna replay just to better understand everything, and replay I will.

I particularly am a very emotional person. Get immersed easily, get empathetic and understand characters. I can say without a doubt, this is one of the games with best narrative I ever played. The way it's made, for you to choose different options, from serious to sentimental, makes you slowly build an actual relationship with Delilah yourself, not just Henry. Instead, you get so immersed into the world you feel like Henry at moments. It's truly a really well-written game.

As for criticism I would change how some skill-gates are presented. I was stuck for like 15 minutes when I encountered the "Nuts" part, definitely took me a while to figure it out. Nonetheless, I'd say its a really thought design. The places you are forced to go don't really seem forced, instead it's completely natural.

I finished it, put the controller down, and just sat there. The woods were still in my head. The sunset colors, the lonely tower, the radio crackling with Delilah’s voice. The scenery and world building amazed me. It felt real in a quiet way. The kind of place I could almost smell and hear. Pines, wind, distant thunder, my own footsteps.

But then the story ended and I caught myself thinking, “Wait, is that it?”
No big twist that fixes everything. No grand answer. Just people, trying to run from their own mess, and failing in slow motion.

It took me a couple of hours to process that.
Is the story just that. Or is life just like that.
You try to escape, you disappear for a while, you take a job in the middle of nowhere, but your problems still wait for you like patient ghosts.

Playing Firewatch felt like pressing pause on my life. For a moment, I got to be nobody. No expectations. No labels. No one who knows my past. Just a person in the woods, walking, talking, looking at trees and skies that do not care who I am. Instead of acting how people expect me to act, I could act how I feel. I could make choices without the usual guilt of not trying hard enough to be “better”.

The game reminded me that running away does not solve anything. The pain, the regrets, the unresolved things, they stay. They wait. But distance can shrink them. Out there, my own problems felt less overwhelming, less loud. They were still real, but not as big as the sky above the forest.

So maybe Firewatch is not about a mystery in the woods. Maybe it is about that short, fragile time when you step out of your life and see it from far away. It does not fix you. It does not save you. It just gives you a summer where you can breathe, ask hard questions, and admit that you are tired.

And somehow, for me, that felt enough.

If you want action, puzzles, or big twists, this won’t scratch that itch. But if you’re into quiet, reflective narrative games with gorgeous visuals and great performances, Firewatch is absolutely worth a play.

Firewatch is just one of those games. It's quite short but it has some weight to it. The storytelling is excellent at leading you down one path while setting up another. There is some setup, but for the most part, significant events blindside you, leaving a lasting impact. Unfortunately I watched a YouTuber play through the whole thing when it came out so I knew about the big stuff going in. But now as an adult, I picked up on so many other details that I missed before. 

Firewatch is a game about many things. It's a game about forgetting, a game about running away from your hardships. It's a game about coping in some of the best and worst possible ways. And above all, it's a game about self reflection. Firewatch is a story game more than anything else. Don't go in expecting riveting gameplay because most of this is a walking sim. Pay attention to the nature, to what is being said on the radio, to what Henry is thinking throughout the game. If you can get past excessive swearing, then you should pay attention to Delilah as well. It was nice to have a male character dealing with emotional stuff. Not for that alone, but for the ability to make him be open about it. Henry doesn't have to be closed off, you can let him open up about his issues and he'll do it. Rare healthy protagonist moment.

A lot of the story of Firewatch is told to you directly, but a good chunk is through environmental details. Being out in the open nature starts off as pretty nice. It's relaxing and beautiful being out there. Later on though, you begin to feel vulnerable. It's too open, too normal. I love how that simple change in vibe was executed in the story and how much weight it put on the closing act. For a game that only lasted just shy of 5 hours for me, that was some grade A execution. 

I really don't have much else to say without delving into spoiler territory and my comments on the audio design are just "good." For it being a 2016 game, there are a surprising amount of bugs still in the game. Many of which were pretty blatant and didn't take much looking to find. There are animation issues, lighting problems, and I could sometimes see object ID text through solid objects. Those aren't game ruining but the animation stuff could mess with your immersion which I didn't care for. 

All in all, I really enjoyed Firewatch. If you haven't played it and are interested, then definitely give it a shot. Firewatch is an experience you'll play once, but you'll likely not forget it.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Firewatch as a game is supposed to give one a one-of-a-kind walking-simulator-experience through the wilderness in Wyoming. From the very first seconds you are presented with the backstory of the main character, Henry and his reasons for choosing a quiet and isolated summer. The game transports you into the topic of mental and physical health, with a moral dilemma that is building up as you keep playing the game. The game wants you to feel sorry for Henry from the very first lines, but at the same times gives you the false impression that you have a choice in his backstory. No matter what you pick, the outcome will be the same: you end up in the wilderness and Julia is still sick, you still end up meeting Delilah and in time, your character still ends up developing feelings for the woman behind the radio, besides you actively choosing to stay “loyal” to your wife. Personally, this was the part that annoyed me the most about the game. I did not like the characters from the very first beginning, and I could not really figure why. To me they felt very forced, like the people who wrote the script tried way too hard to make them relatable, that it got to the point of a very kitsch movie script in my head. The lines the characters were using, only managed to make me feel some sort of second-hand embarrassment, to the point I could not enjoy the walking simulator itself but be happy that I could not hear Delilah’s voice anymore. Delilah did not interest me in the slightest, even though I understand her role was to test Henry and his mental health, as well as his loyalty to his wife. She failed to impress me, which only upset me more in the end, when after actively choosing to stay loyal, Henry still followed the developer’s script to fit the ending they chose. If one connects this aspect to the ending of the game, the whole game feels rushed. I managed to sit down on a Saturday evening and play it through, which is not a problem, because one can understand that Firewatch is an indie game, developed to deliver a story and an “unique” experience. At some point, the game tried to develop some kind of supernatural element, which one can agree that it makes you develop interest: what if the advertising for the job was just for an experiment? I think the game would have been more enjoyable in my eyes, if it had this unique plot twist in the middle. Instead, towards the end, they change the entire narrative and blame everything that happened and the only “horror” elements to one singular character that you don’t meet but get to know through Delilah and other elements in the game. The addition of Ned to reach the conclusion out of the “horror” arc, made the whole game feel like the developers ran out of ideas, or had to meet a deadline of some sort and just decided to flat out cut the narrative and go for a very cliché ending.

Firewatch is a game about working as a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness. It was on deep discount some time ago and it looked promising, so I decided to pick it up.
The year is 1989. You are Henry, an ordinary guy whose wife got very sick recently, so he decides to accept a job in the middle of nowhere to get away from the everyday pressure of life. You arrive in the Shoshone National Forest in the beginning of summer, eager to get started on your new job. Aside from the forest critters, your only company will be your boss Delilah, with whom you'll be talking using a walkie-talkie. A watch tower in the valley will be your home for the remainder of the summer season, while Delilah is holed up in the command center at the top of the hill. Everything seems rather idyllic at first, but you'll soon realize that you got more than you bargained for when you signed up for this job.
Firewatch is basically a walking simulator with elements of psychological thriller. The gameplay follows a pretty unique concept consisting of walking, hiking and communicating with your boss. You’ll be responsible for monitoring an open-world perimeter while taking direction from Delilah and reporting your findings to her. Communication between you and Delilah is very realistic and highly interactive, often presenting choices that can influence the direction of the story. 
Firewatch surrounds you with a quiet sense of solitude and isolation, lulling you into relaxation before shifting into moments of unexpected suspense. The graphics are simple and yet beautiful at the same time, presenting the wild nature in an artistic manner. Sadly, the game world is limited in size and seems rather empty. More on that note, the whole game is pretty short and the story feels a little unfinished. Still, in this case, quality definitely outweighs quantity.

Firewatch is short, but memorable. In fact, I’ve never encountered a game quite like it before. If you enjoy games that focus on exploration or conversation, this one is absolutely worth a go.

Firewatch is a slow burn that rewards patience with authenticity. What begins as a quiet summer job in the Wyoming wilderness becomes one of the most natural, human conversations I’ve ever had in a game. The writing and voice acting are exceptional, the environment feels alive in subtle ways, and even getting lost feels meaningful. Despite a deliberately slow start, its emotional buildup crescendos into a thoughtful story about guilt, connection, and the kind of loneliness you can only hear over a radio. At just four to five hours long, it’s short, satisfying, and stays with you long after the credits roll.

Honestly, the game is really beautiful. The atmosphere is amazing and it truly makes you feel the isolation and that there’s no one around you. That’s what made me get attached to it, whether wanting to uncover the mysterious things happening or just talking and connecting with Delilah. What I loved the most is how immersive it was; it really pulled me into its world and felt like a nice, light experience overall.

I wander, I enjoy a beautiful landscape, I make someone interesting discoveries, I choose dialogue options that just get ignored later on, and I deal with someone on the other end of a radio who I get very annoyed at by the end, but at least she keeps the game going.

It's described as a game about adults having adult conversations about adult things.  As far as I can tell, that means saying the word "♥♥♥♥" a lot.  And I guess talking about relationships.

The graphics were enjoyable and the voice acting and directing only slightly diminished the immersion.  But the choices I made didn't seem to be reflected with what later happened.  Once, I had the option to suspect somebody of something, but when I felt that the evidence pointed somewhere else, I chose dialogue options to insist they didn't do it.  Later, with no new developments, my character said how that person was probably guilty.  What was the point of my dialogue choice, then?

One of the most frustrating moments was after my character was beaten unconscious by an assailant and my character said to the supervisor on the other end of the radio, "I've just been assaulted!" and her response was "we can't report that, no one would believe us."  Lol what?

In the end, this game suffers some of "Gone Home" syndrome: where the final outcomes are so dull it pains me to reflect back on them.  Thankfully, it is not as bad as Gone Home.

The constant guessing on what's going on, the fear of what could be out there and the tension that keeps heightening as you uncover the plot (Special mention to the good soundtrack). I really wish the payoff was worth the hype. Found myself pretty happy with the experience, but very disappointed with how it all turned out in the end. Don't let all this deter you from trying this game out. There's a lot more to it than that. 

Overall, Firewatch is a great experience and a shining example of "the journey is the reward". I really wished it took what it built to great heights.

[h1][b][i]"Firewatch"[/i][/b][/h1]
[h2][u]Overview[/u][/h2]
Life itself is complex and difficult. There are both pleasant moments and sad ones. Sometimes, when life becomes unbearably difficult, you can afford to disconnect for a certain period to reboot your burned-out brain. The game tells us about such a moment in the life of the main character Henry.
At the beginning of the game, we get introduced to our supervisor, the area and the workplace where our hero will be for a certain time. During the game, we will encounter not only the expected events for the firewatch, but also a certain mystery. The solution to which will lie entirely on our shoulders.
Despite the straight narrative, the game has a wonderful visual style (screenshots of which can be taken as desktop wallpapers), a wonderful dialogue system with Delilah (by choosing certain phrases we can both build relationships or destroy them), an interesting and mysterious plot (the outcome of which is very interesting to spectate). The only thing that may disappoint you, like me, is the ending of the game. Yes, it is so realistic, like life. But still, I was hoping for a better ending for Henry until the very end...
[h2][u]Pros:[/u][/h2]
[list]
[*]A wonderful visual style of the game and shader graphics.
[*]The sound and music in the game are well chosen and very well show both the emotions of the situations, and the state of nature and the environment.
[*]Lively dialogues, both from the main character and our supervisor Delilah, which you can listen to and listen to, watching their development.
[*]An interesting and mysterious plot that draws you in the more you play it.
[*]The choice of phrases during the dialogue affects the building of relationships.
[*]The absence of markers in the HUD. Delilah told you the location you need to go to? You open the map, find the location and set off. Although, to be honest, in most cases you can intuitively get to the appropriate location.
[*]An additional mode in which you can listen to audio cassettes from the developers and get to know the game's story better. In addition, while playing in this mode, the map will be updated with certain concept models and concept art. So it is worth to try to play it for another try.
[/list]
[h2][u]Cons:[/u][/h2]
[list]
[*]Corridor gameplay. You as the main character will not have anything special to do on the map due to the need to have a certain tool, or a blocked location. In other cases, the particular location may not having anything until a certain moment in the plot.
[/list]

This game has no idea what it wants to do.

At first, it feels like an introspective, grounded experience about looking for solitude in the woods, with a lot of immersion-oriented mechanics that seem to support this. You navigate around using a paper map and compass, gather items to gradually increase your exploration opportunities, and spend time on side activities while learning about the characters and their personal life dramas. There’s also quite a bit of variation in dialogue options and objectives’ solutions, which hint at a branching narrative or at least a Telltale-style "_ will remember that" adventure.

Then it suddenly does a complete 180 both story- and gameplay-wise, time-skipping through the remaining buildup to become a fast-paced and tense conspiracy thriller, of all things. The slower exploration aspect is brushed aside in favor of a tight narrative game where you quickly move from one story marker to another, while the established backstories or player’s choices become irrelevant in the face of a mystery that gets thicker and bolder by the minute.

Then another 180 throws it away too for the sake of an abrupt "realistic" conclusion – except, funnily enough, it feels just as contrived and random as the preceding conspiracy. You can spend a whole evening enumerating all the forced coincidences, inconsistent behaviors and barely explainable loose ends of this story, which is a feat for something that only lasts 5-6 hours.

Needless to say, the final product looks like a jack of all trades who excels at nothing. It’s as if the developers got too attached to every cool little thingie they implemented and never properly considered the overall experience, so 50% of the result ended up sabotaging the other 50% of the result.

And if you decide to read between the lines, like many of the game’s vocal proponents seem to do, then the picture becomes even worse due to how condescending and disproportionately critical to the characters (and, by extension through a meta layer, to the players) this story is.

The MC is faced with a crappy, heavy, unwinnable family situation, cooks in it for a while the best he can, then dares to wish for a few months of solitude, and that’s supposed to represent "running away from your problems"? The characters have scary, abnormal things happen to them, like being spied on or getting assaulted in broad daylight, yet somehow it’s purely their fault for giving in to paranoia and coming up with crazy theories? The two leads are clearly on the same wavelength and enjoy each other’s company, but that’s dismissed as another symptom of escapism because, uh… middle-aged people aren’t supposed to make new connections unless they fully unload their emotional baggage first? It all just lacks basic human empathy. Or basic narrative planning. Or both, really.

Then again, it might be just the latter. The audio commentary mode has a lot of developer conversations about various technical challenges, like making a dynamic skybox from scratch with gradients or manually unloading certain parts of the map to improve performance, and while I have no doubt it took skill and effort to properly tackle those details, I also feel like it distracted them from focusing on the broader aspects of game design. Creating a consistent, organic experience takes either a very clear vision from the start or a very firm resolve to cut out and redo things, and it seems that this small dev team had neither.

At first, I honestly thought Firewatch was going to be another calm, walking-simulator type of game. But as soon as I started playing, I got completely hooked. It’s calm, relaxing, and atmospheric... yet at the same time, it carries this quiet, lonely, uneasy feeling that makes it unique. I was so glad I decided to play it.

The story is easily the main strength of the game, right alongside the atmosphere, art style, and the amazing character interactions. It genuinely felt like watching a movie ... it starts slow, funny, and lighthearted. The banter between Henry and Delilah had me smiling, and I actually enjoyed doing all the little tasks she gave me. But as the story begins to unfold, you start to feel that something isn’t right. You don’t know what it is, but that mystery pulls you in deeper and deeper. I loved every bit of it. And the voice acting ... man, both of them absolutely nailed it. Every line sounded natural, emotional, and real.

The atmosphere and music are another highlight. You might be walking somewhere for a task, or just exploring, and the world is quiet ... all you hear are the sounds of wind, insects, and birds. Then suddenly, the music fades in... and uff, it’s magical. I also loved interacting with random things during exploration. Like when I found that cute little turtle, or that weird abandoned cabin on a hill , small moments like those made the world feel alive and mysterious at the same time.

And that ending... well, let’s just say it was bittersweet but realistic. I personally loved it. I won’t say too much about it, but it made me emotional. It felt like a reflection of real life.. how we used to spend time with friends, laughing, playing, making memories... and then life gets busy, people drift apart. Sometimes someone enters your life, you share something special, and then they’re gone. That’s what Firewatch made me feel... nostalgic, a little heavy, but grateful

If you're thinking about getting Firewatch, you probably should. It's quick, simple, and cheap on sale.

But I think the game is very interesting story wise. It has a way of making you care about its two main characters, and others by extension even in a short time. But first and foremost, this game is an allegory for things we're all familiar with. Guilty of, even. It's about escapism and running away, which is very interesting coming from a game. We play games to escape from reality, to focus on something else, to experience a good story, or to be calm. and this one presents itself as a relaxed experience, "to be calm". Overall, it is, but much like real life, you find yourself worrying about all of these grand things you don't have control of and overthinking. But much like a lot of the events in this game, it's never really that bad in reality. That's why a criticism of Firewatch is that it's underwhelming, because we're so used to these insane adventures that don't want you to think, and even if it's story focused, most don't make you feel the need to look inward.  It doesn't have to be crazy, scary, complicated, mentally draining, or heartbreaking. Or on the opposite end, happy-go-lucky, overly comedic, insanely cheerful, or heartwarming. Sometimes it's just normal. Just... human. Play it, and you'll see what I mean.

1. Impressions from playing through the game
I didn't expect to be able to get through the game so quickly. Perhaps the developers expected players to spend more time exploring the world, but I always had a specific task that I wanted to complete as quickly as possible.

2. Visuals and sound
The graphics are impressive: beautiful landscapes, unique design, and very atmospheric music. All of this creates a strong sense of immersion. There were also some annoying lags during gameplay: when attempting to perform an action, the character would “move back” and I had to try again and again. Once, the radio disappeared from my hand.

3. Story and characters
The story hooked me right from the start, especially the introductory part. However, there weren't enough moments in the game that allowed me to connect with the main character on a deeper level. He seemed realistic, with human weaknesses and quirks, but his dilemmas didn't elicit any sympathy from me. At the same time, this can be considered a plus: the hero really feels like a living person. However, I would not be interested in spending time with him. 

For some, the game can be a very powerful experience thanks to its atmosphere and moral conclusions, but for me personally, it turned out to be superficial. Thanks to the developers for the game — it was still an interesting experience!

No matter where you run from your problems, they will chase you. There's no conspiracy, no monsters, no crazy plot twists and or some dramatic answer, its only simple reality. The point is, we'll eventually snap back to reality. It might sound bittersweet, but it's worth it, because problems must be solved, no matter what.

[h1] ПЛАМЕННЫЙ ВАЙОМИНГСКИЙ ИНЦИДЕНТ [/h1]

Firewatch напоминает Death Stranding в миниатюре, где основное занятие – исследование живописных локаций и выполнение рутинных задач. И хотя хайп вокруг Firewatch вполне понятен, лично для меня она оказалась проектом, скорее, средним по качеству.

Firewatch по сути, "симулятор ходьбы" с неплохой графикой, в котором вы исследуете лесные тропы, чтобы разобраться с различными происшествиями. Однако, несмотря на приятный визуальный стиль, игра не поражает ни выдающимся сюжетом, ни "захватывающей" атмосферой. Если бомбить прям принципиально, то игра нередко бесит микрофризами, пропадающими обьектами, а также моментами, когда главного героя отбрасывает с сторону, при взаимодействии с каким нибудь вентилем или замочной скважиной.

Прохождение Firewatch занимает немного времени, и одним из ее ключевых, в плохом смысле слова элементов является иллюзия выбора. В начале игры вам предоставляется возможность сформировать историю знакомства главного героя, Генри, с его девушкой. В дальнейшем ваши решения немного влияют на реплики в диалогах по рации с вашим наставником, Делайлой. Тем не менее, эти изменения не добавляют истории глубины или нелинейности. И как бы вы не хотели - собираете вы улики, мусор или открываете все или не все ящики с припасами, конец будет один, как и развитие истории после пролога, с МИЗЕРНЫМИ изменениями.

Стоит ли играть в Firewatch? Если вы ищете расслабляющую и атмосферную игру, в которой можно просто бродить по красивым локациям и наслаждаться неспешным повествованием, то Firewatch может вам понравиться. Firewatch – это игра для тех, кто умеет расслабляться и получать удовольствие от простых вещей. Конечно, разработчики могли бы постараться над историей лучше, но, имеем что имеем.

[h1] THE FIERY WYOMING INCIDENT [/h1]

Firewatch resembles Death Stranding in miniature, where the main activity is exploring scenic locations and performing routine tasks. And although the hype around Firewatch is quite understandable, for me personally it turned out to be a project of rather average quality.

Firewatch is essentially a "walking simulator" with good graphics, in which you explore forest trails to deal with various incidents. However, despite the pleasant visual style, the game does not impress with either an outstanding plot or an "exciting" atmosphere. If you make a joke out of principle, then the game often infuriates with microfreezes, missing objects, as well as moments when the main character is thrown aside when interacting with some valve or keyhole.

Firewatch takes a little time to complete, and one of its key elements, in the bad sense of the word, is the illusion of choice. At the beginning of the game, you are given the opportunity to form the story of the acquaintance of the main character, Henry, with his girlfriend. In the future, your decisions will have a bit of an impact on your conversations over the radio with your mentor, Delilah. However, these changes do not add depth or non-linearity to the story. And no matter how much you want to, whether you collect evidence, trash, or open all or not all of the supply crates, the end will be the same, as will the development of the story after the prologue, with SCANTY changes.

Is it worth playing Firewatch? If you are looking for a relaxing and atmospheric game where you can just wander through beautiful locations and enjoy a leisurely narrative, then Firewatch may appeal to you. Firewatch is a game for those who know how to relax and enjoy simple things. Of course, the developers could have tried to work on the story better, but we have what we have.

A short, spooky experience of being a Firewatcher in an isolated national park. A lot of the "spook" factor comes from how isolated the game feels, and at wondering what could be lurking somewhere in the woods, but it was overall just a really interesting game. You work alongside one of your neighboring towers, manned by your boss, by talking over the radio and keeping an eye out for fires or other dangers of the area. But things keep seeming to happen, and the quiet summer you'd hoped for may be out of your reach. 

Contemplative is a word that comes to mind. There is a lot of time spent hiking around the woods, and it gives a relatively realistic sense of pathfinding and navigation. You do have a map, but it can become bothersome to stop and pull it out each time, so you start to rely on signs and pathways, checking in every now and then to see how you're progressing. I enjoyed that aspect.

I also really enjoyed the story aspect, where there was a lot of suspense and enough spook to keep me engaged. The ending really nailed home the contemplative, and I would say...value neutral? Messaging of the game. Whatever you have decided through the course of the narrative is what you have decided; the ways that you have interpreted the events are the way they are, and I felt like each option was equally available and acceptable. 

I just really enjoyed the game, I think it was a solid experience, particularly since it often goes on sale so cheaply. Worth a couple hours of your time!

Walking through the woods has never felt so unsettling…

Firewatch is a first-person narrative game that throws you into the boots of Henry, a man looking to escape his messy life by becoming a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness. It’s quiet, reflective… until it isn’t. What starts as a relaxing hike through nature quickly shifts into something tense, emotional, and a bit haunting.

What really stood out to me was how the game kept me constantly on edge. There’s this brilliant sense of something’s not quite right, even when you’re just strolling through pine trees. That looming feeling of danger - despite the lack of actual threat - was done incredibly well. There were moments where I genuinely felt anxious and disorientated, especially when I lost my bearings in the woods. Not knowing where I was or what might be coming gave the whole experience a sharp edge.

The story itself is interesting, but I will say the ending felt a bit rushed. After everything the game built up, it kind of just… wrapped up with a “get to the chopper” moment. I wanted more emotional closure or at least a bit more meat on the ending’s bones. That said, I’m curious how different choices affect the story. I’ve only done one playthrough (around 7 hours), but it does make me wonder if things could’ve played out a little differently.

Delilah and Henry—the only two voices you really hear - were handled well. Their banter and relationship felt natural, layered, and often funny or deeply sad. It’s one of the game’s strongest points, for sure.

Visually, the forest is beautiful. Some great photo-worthy spots and a really lovely colour palette - especially the sunsets. But there were a few parts of the game that felt a bit unpolished. Not buggy or broken, just slightly underdeveloped, like the devs had big ideas but didn’t get the chance to fully flesh them out.

Would I recommend it? Definitely. Firewatch might not have the deepest plot or the longest playtime, but it leaves an impression. If you like moody, story-driven games that make you feel something, it’s well worth the walk.

The Uneasy Quiet of the Wyoming Wilderness!

Firewatch is a masterclass in atmosphere. From the moment you take on the role of Henry, stationed in an isolated watchtower, the game pulls you into a world that feels breathtakingly beautiful yet unnervingly fragile. The quarrying silence of the wilderness is deceptive—peaceful on the surface, but carrying an undercurrent of dread that slowly creeps in until you’re second-guessing every rustle of leaves and flicker of shadow.

The story unfolds with an unsettling elegance. At first, it’s about routine patrols, playful banter with Delilah on the radio, and the sense of escaping into nature. But then things twist. Strange noises, shadowy figures in the distance, and hints of something sinister lurking behind the trees start to erode the safety of your solitude. It’s not a jump-scare type of horror—it’s the slow burn kind, where your own imagination fills the silence with unease. By the time the quarry sequence and its creeping tension hit, you’re gripping the controller, heart racing, convinced something—or someone—is about to break the fragile quiet.

What makes Firewatch incredible is how it blends intimacy and intensity. The bond between Henry and Delilah grounds the story emotionally, while the mystery keeps you perched at the edge of your seat. It’s rare for a game to make you feel both connected and deeply unsettled at once, but Firewatch nails it. By the end, you walk away not only impressed by its storytelling but haunted by its atmosphere.

Firewatch is one of those story-driven games that sticks with you long after the credits roll. You play as Henry, a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness, communicating almost entirely with your supervisor, Delilah, over the radio. What starts as a quiet summer job quickly turns into a mystery that had me hooked until the very end. The atmosphere is top-notch: stunning visuals that make every sunset screenshot-worthy, paired with a soundtrack that knows exactly when to kick in. Gameplay is pretty minimal (lots of walking, some light exploration and decision-making), but that’s not a flaw here. It keeps you focused on the story, the environment, and the choices you make in conversations. If you’re looking for an action-packed adventure, this isn’t it. Firewatch, developed by Campo Santo, is a breathtaking journey that weaves together stunning visuals, heartfelt storytelling, and an immersive atmosphere to create an unforgettable gaming experience. Set in the sun-drenched, vibrant wilderness of Wyoming’s Shoshone National Forest in 1989, this first-person adventure game casts you as Henry, a fire lookout seeking solace from a complicated past. What unfolds is a poignant exploration of human connection, isolation, and self-discovery, wrapped in a mystery that keeps you hooked until the final moments.

From the moment you step into Henry’s boots, Firewatch captivates with its art direction. The game’s painterly aesthetic, with its bold color palette of warm oranges, lush greens, and twilight purples, transforms the forest into a living, breathing character. Each vista, from towering pines to shimmering lakes, feels handcrafted with care, inviting you to pause and soak in the beauty. The dynamic day-night cycle and subtle environmental details—like the rustle of leaves or the flicker of a distant campfire—create a world that feels alive and responsive.

The heart of Firewatch lies in its narrative, driven by the relationship between Henry and Delilah, his supervisor, who communicates solely through a walkie-talkie. Their witty, authentic banter, brought to life by stellar voice performances from Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones, feels like eavesdropping on real conversations. The dialogue choices allow you to shape Henry’s personality and his bond with Delilah, making their evolving relationship feel deeply personal. The story deftly balances humor, vulnerability, and tension, tackling themes of grief, trust, and escapism without ever feeling heavy-handed.

Gameplay in Firewatch is elegantly simple, focusing on exploration and environmental storytelling. You navigate the forest, uncover clues, and piece together a mystery that grows increasingly eerie as strange occurrences unfold. The pacing is deliberate, allowing you to immerse yourself in the solitude of the wilderness while unraveling the plot at your own rhythm. The walkie-talkie serves as both a narrative tool and a gameplay mechanic, letting you check in with Delilah to share discoveries or seek guidance, which keeps the experience intimate and engaging.

The sound design is equally remarkable, with a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack by Chris Remo that perfectly complements the game’s emotional beats. The soft strums of acoustic guitar and ambient forest sounds enhance the sense of solitude and wonder, while subtle audio cues heighten the tension during the game’s more suspenseful moments.

If there’s a critique, it’s that Firewatch is relatively short, clocking in at about four to six hours, and some players might crave a more complex resolution to its mystery. However, the game’s focus on emotional depth over sprawling mechanics feels intentional, prioritizing quality over quantity. The ending, while bittersweet, stays true to the story’s themes, leaving you with a lingering sense of reflection.

Firewatch is a masterclass in storytelling and atmosphere, a game that lingers long after the credits roll. It’s a love letter to the wilderness, to human connection, and to the messy, beautiful complexities of life. For anyone seeking a game that’s as thought-provoking as it is visually stunning, Firewatch is a must-play—a glowing ember in the vast forest of gaming.

Firewatch is a story-driven, walking sim that has you playing the role of a seasonal fire lookout working in the Shoshone National Forest. The game can be completed within three to five hours depending on how much time you spend randomly exploring the world. 

The game has a minimalist design to keep the player's focus on the story and visual environment which are the game's two main strengths. There is not much variation in music and sound effects, just enough to create an ambience that fluctuates between the calm of the empty wilderness and the suspense of the unknown. The art design is also minimalist, reminiscent of 1980's Saturday morning cartoons. Having a more realistic setting would have helped with the immersion but nonetheless had its own charm. And then there are the clunky game mechanics which involves walking around the forest while navigating over various fallen logs and steep slopes. 

There are no puzzles, fights, strategy, or action of any kind. The game is all about the story. Thus, if you need something more than just a compelling narrative to stay engaged with a video game, Firewatch might not be for you. However, for those that are looking for a good piece of fiction to interact with, then yes, I definitely recommend this game. The dynamics between the characters, their backstories, the environment, and the predicament they find themselves in creates a unique and engrossing story that will keep you engaged until the end. 

The prologue could be accused of being emotionally manipulative but I have to admit it worked to good effect, drawing me into the story quickly and established the setting. A common complaint with the game is the ending, which I can understand (without going into spoilers), however, I personally liked the ending for the reason that it felt.... "real". The way the characters interact and the choices you help them make, creates a believable world, an underestimated quality in keeping one engaged with a story that feels genuine. Firewatch is a great alternative to spending an afternoon with a good book.

This game is far from perfect, but is still an amazing piece.

First the good things. The environment, art style and voice acting are the major highlights for me. The park is beautiful, couple this with the amount of dialogue options available in game it makes exploring or back tracking actually enjoyable and it never really felt like a chore. Seeing Henry and Delilah's relationship grow and evolve overtime was what made me stick through til the end.

Next is the mediocre. The Ending, as everyone has pointed out, is rather ehhhh. It leaves a lot of loose ends that are never really answered, but not in a cool theorising mysterious way but in more of a 'did the devs run out of time?' kind of way. It makes the last portion feel rather lackluster. Although discovering the [][][][] in the cave was actually a really sad yet awesome part. Especially the stuff that follows with [][][].

Finally the bad. The games physics and it's use of invisible walls makes things feel so constricted at times. I wanna feel like I'm in a forest, not locked in a mime's sex dungeon. It also breaks immersion too. I mean I've seen Henry traverse rough terrain and cliff faces but he can't jump over a foot tall boulder cause 'oh uh yeah, invisible wall...' Really? Also I brought this game on sale not even realising its original price was $30. I recommend waiting for a sale, as a $30 game should NOT have the following issues...

Achievements bugs. One achievement requires encountering an animal. If you encounter the animal but have alt-tab'd at any point during your playthrough then tough luck cause now the achievement won't trigger. Now you gotta reset the day and make the arduous journey back just to encounter the same animal.
And the other achievement requires finding a hidden item. Well guess what? I couldn't even get it during normal gameplay as the item kept clipping out of the map whenever I entered the area. I had to play free roam just to get it. I'd say a solid extra 30 minutes of my playtime was purely trying to get these last two achievements. How infuriating.

Despite the flaws mentioned I still think it's a good game that everyone should try at least once. Don't bother with the achievements unless you're a completionist and definitely wait for it to go on sale.

[h1]❓ What is this[/h1]
Firewatch (2016) is a first-person narrative adventure developed by Campo Santo and published by Panic. It’s a story-driven experience set in the Wyoming wilderness, blending exploration, mystery, and emotional dialogue.

[h1]❔ How I played[/h1]
Completed the story in around 5 hours. Focused on dialogue choices and explored side paths to uncover environmental details and notes. Played on an RTX 4060 with Ryzen 5 5500, where performance was generally smooth but I noticed occasional input lag during movement and camera control.

[hr][/hr]
[h1]🕹️ Gameplay[/h1]
Gameplay revolves around walking, climbing, and interacting with objects, but its real strength lies in the radio dialogue system. Every choice shapes Henry’s relationship with Delilah, making conversations feel alive and natural. The intrigue builds through mysterious occurrences in the forest, giving a sense of paranoia and suspense. Still, the limited mechanics can feel shallow, and technical hiccups like input lag occasionally break immersion.

✅ Pros:
+ Strong, branching dialogue choices that feel human and authentic
+ Immersive exploration with a strong sense of place
+ Gradual mystery that creates tension and unease
+ Smooth controls and clean interface

❌ Cons:
- Minimal interactivity outside of dialogue and exploration
- The buildup of suspense is stronger than its resolution
- Minor issues even on modern hardware

[hr][/hr]
[h1]📖 Story[/h1]
The story explores loneliness, escapism, human vulnerability, and trust. Henry is running from personal struggles, while Delilah uses humor and distance to hide her own. Their relationship, formed entirely through radio conversations, is believable and emotionally layered.

The central intrigue-a sense that something sinister is happening in the forest-keeps tension high but ultimately ends on a grounded, almost anticlimactic note. Personally, the main story felt intriguing but not fully polished, as if the ending was finished in a rush. The emotional weight remains strong, but the lack of refinement leaves a bittersweet impression.

[h1]🎨 Visuals & Sound[/h1]
The painterly art style creates a stunning vision of American national parks-golden sunsets, thick forests, and vast horizons. It captures the feeling of solitude in nature while keeping a warm, stylized look.

The soundtrack by Chris Remo is subtle and atmospheric, leaning on acoustic tones and ambient soundscapes. It’s not bombastic, but it perfectly complements the mood of both calm exploration and quiet unease.

[h1]⚙️ Performance & Replayability[/h1]
Runs well overall on modern systems, but occasional input lag can be noticeable. Replay value comes mainly from experimenting with dialogue paths, though the core story beats remain the same.

[hr][/hr]
[h1]💡 Verdict[/h1]
For me, Firewatch stands out as one of those rare indie games that really nails the feeling of isolation, connection, and mystery. The story pulled me in, even if the ending felt a bit rough and unfinished. Still, the time I spent with Henry and Delilah had weight, and exploring those quiet forests with the soundtrack in the background left a lasting impression.

This is not just a walking sim where your main task is to grab something on the one side of the map and then return to your base. This game is something bigger. Even though it's not a horror game, Firewatch can give you goosebumps and a feeling that someone is right behind your back.
