Not every time you need to save the kingdom, rescue the princess or slay the dragon. Not every time you must overthrow the galactic empire or defeat primordial evil. Not every story is an epic tale about heroic battles and cosmic struggles. Sometimes all you need is just a simple walk through a wild forest and talk to a fellow human.  

If I could describe Firewatch in one word, it would be — mundane. This is a game about regular activities that you, me and everyone could perform every day. About stories of normal people living their normal lives and having oh not-so-epic problems, failures and successes. You will not experience grand talks and deep thoughts and yet this game is far away from being simple. Imagine dealing with subtlety and minimalism when playing but at the same time focusing more on this vague feel of being…. watched?

Our protagonist is Henry — a middle-aged man with a difficult, yet not tragic past. His wife got early dementia, and was forced to be with her family because the dude cannot handle taking care of her by himself. Then he later stumbled on a job advertisement about a Ranger gig in Shoshone National Park. He took the job and met — only through radio tho — a woman named Delilah, a fellow Ranger and his supervisor, with whom later he created a friendly bond. And then things get a little darker, but it mostly smokes and mirrors, because the story itself is focusing more about human relations than surviving in the wild and other mysterious shenanigans. The game teases us with something extraordinary, but due to not being long (5hrs max with doing all achievements) it quickly discards that kind of narrative, funneling to “big” reveals and explanations. To be honest I expected something more after two first in-game days, but then the plot started literally galloping forwards.

From the gameplay perspective this game is nothing more than a walking simulator. Don’t be fooled by the game world being an open wildlife area, it is mostly composed from little places connected by corridors surrounded by invisible walls, like to hills too steep to climb, bushes or cliffs accompanied by Henry’s inability to jump on his own. There are some tasks you need to do every day but mostly they are connected to the story and you don’t need to rush to complete them. So for the majority of time you will be walking from place to place, picking items needed to progress (ropes, axe) checking supply caches and listening to dialogues between characters. They are dynamic by the way — you need to initiate conversation and then respond within a limited time window, so pay attention to it.

The game shines when focusing on Henry’s and Delilah dynamic. Both of them are middle-aged, both had hard times in the past, both are more grounded and realistic in approach to reality and lack this youthful naivety. They know they are in Shoshane for a moment, so aside from a little flirting and teasing each other from time to time they do not try to establish some deeper connection. And yet they do not shy from opening more about their past experiences, struggles and life in general. Overall, I think the main theme of Firewatch is about the human inability of creating deeper human connection. We sail through the surface but are too afraid to dive deeper because we don’t want to get hurt when exposing our true self to another person.

Now. It's over. Go home or something.

Atmosphere Without Substance

Firewatch immediately hooked me with its premise. The idea of retreating into the Wyoming wilderness, stepping into the boots of a lonely fire lookout, and slowly unraveling a mystery through conversations with Delilah sounded like the perfect recipe for a narrative-driven adventure. And visually, the game nails it — the art direction is stunning, the landscapes are gorgeous, and the soundtrack captures the mood beautifully. Sadly, beyond that initial immersion, the experience left me feeling disappointed.

The biggest issue is how little there is to actually do. Gameplay boils down to walking long distances, picking up a few objects, and choosing dialogue options. While I don’t expect a walking sim to be action-heavy, the interactivity here feels extremely limited. There are moments where tension should build — strange noises in the woods, hints of surveillance, the sense of being watched — but instead of evolving into clever mechanics or meaningful choices, everything funnels back into the same linear path.

The story itself, while intriguing at first, ultimately falls flat. The setup teases mystery and danger, but the resolution is underwhelming and leaves a lot of threads dangling. Rather than a satisfying payoff, it feels like the narrative fizzles out. The relationship with Delilah, meant to be the emotional core of the game, is strong in parts but inconsistent — sometimes the writing feels natural and warm, and other times it slips into awkward or rushed exchanges that break the immersion.

On top of that, pacing is a problem. Large stretches of the game involve walking through the same environments with little variation, which becomes tedious. By the time I reached the ending, I wasn’t feeling reflective or emotional — just let down by how abruptly it all wrapped up.

I respect Firewatch for its artistry and atmosphere, and I understand why some people connect with it. But for me, the shallow gameplay, uneven writing, and unsatisfying conclusion made it feel more like a missed opportunity than the powerful narrative experience it promised to be.

Firewatch is a short but deeply atmospheric narrative adventure that left me both satisfied and curious for more. Set in the Wyoming wilderness, you play as Henry, a fire lookout spending the summer in isolation, at least until your radio crackles to life with the voice of Delilah, your supervisor, and a slow-burn mystery begins.

The writing is sharp and natural, and the dialogue between Henry and Delilah is the emotional core of the experience. While the mystery is engaging, it ultimately resolves more quietly than I expected, which left me with mixed feelings.  It was realistic, yes, but maybe a touch anticlimactic.  I also felt as though the game were a bit too short.  Another two or three hours of story content would've clinched this for me.  As for the story itself, it was beautiful.  (8/10)

The controls are flawless. Everything from walking the trails to climbing rocks feels smooth and intuitive, and the minimalist HUD keeps you immersed without distraction.  I played the game exclusively on my Deck, and I ran into no issues whatsoever.  (10/10)

The visual beauty is where Firewatch truly shines. The art style is stunning in warm, painterly landscapes that shift beautifully with the time of day and weather. Every view feels like a postcard you want to frame. (10/10)

The audio design is solid, with subtle environmental sounds that make you feel like you’re really out in the woods. However, aside from a few well-timed music cues, the soundscape sometimes felt a little sparse, which occasionally undercut the tension or atmosphere. (6/10)

Firewatch is a visual and emotional journey worth taking. It’s a game you don’t play for action, but for the experience of inhabiting a place, listening to a story unfold, and feeling just a little less alone until the credits roll.  (8/10)

So, what can I say about this game? First of all, I really enjoyed the story — it kept me in suspense the whole time. The gameplay is simple, nothing too complex, but still fun and engaging. The characters are fairly well-developed, and I appreciated them. Overall, I definitely recommend it!

Lovely little walking simulator. Firewatch had been on my "planning to play" list for almost a decade, and now that I've finally played through it, I can say that I should have picked it up sooner.

The gameplay is somewhat static and doesn’t really offer anything exciting. Instead, the game is driven by its story and "hollow" atmosphere. I expected there would be some puzzles to enhance the gameplay, as is common in these types of games, but I didn’t come across any.

What first got me interested in the game was it's low poly art style back in 2016. It really does fit the game well and likely helped keep it under budget. Speaking of the budget, they clearly didn’t want to hassle themselves with character models and animations. most characters are only heard over the radio (or distance), and the few you do see are shown from a distance or obscured. It’s a clever way to maintain immersion without stretching resources too thin.

All in all, Firewatch is a memorable experience, even if the gameplay itself is minimal. What it lacks in interactivity, it makes up for with atmosphere, strong voice acting (dialog sometimes TOO childish), and a story that keeps you engaged until the end. It’s not a game for everyone, but if you’re into narrative driven games with a unique visual style, it’s definitely worth your time, just don’t expect much beyond walking and talking.

Overall, very good game, would recommend but only on sale, I don't think it is worth $20

The mood, the mystery, and the tension, are very well-crafted. Having that invisible voice, a character who you can only communicate with via radio, does a great job at creating the feeling of joint isolation. 
While it is a fairly linear game, you are still free to explore a fair amount of the map, and I enjoyed doing that.

The negatives:
Caution if you suffer from motion sickness in games. Some of the movements, especially when you're climbing up or down a ledge, were a little nauseating.
There are several options you can choose with the dialogue, but they don't seem to actually affect the game at all other than things like choosing the name of an animal. It's the sort of game that would be ripe for multiple endings based on your choices, but ended up being far more linear which feels like a wasted opportunity.
After thinking about it, the story itself was just a disappointment to me. I struggle to make a lot of it make sense, especially when the build up was so good. (Last night I literally dreamt up a better ending, with a twist, than the one in game!)

Overall, if you're wanting a short game, get it in a sale. It is decent. But I wouldn't recommend full price myself.

Firewatch is a narrative-driven adventure game that stands out for its emotional storytelling, rich atmosphere, and stunning art direction. Developed by Campo Santo and released on Steam in 2016, it offers a deeply personal, contemplative experience set against the backdrop of the Wyoming wilderness. At first glance, it presents itself as a mystery-thriller, but beneath that lies a much more intimate exploration of loneliness, guilt, and the fragile ways people try to connect.

You play as Henry, a man who has taken a summer job as a fire lookout in the Shoshone National Forest. The game opens with a quiet but powerful sequence that outlines Henry’s motivations: his wife is suffering from early-onset dementia, and he has chosen to retreat from his life rather than face it directly. This prologue, delivered through interactive text choices, immediately sets a somber, human tone that lingers throughout the game. As Henry, your only real companion is Delilah, another lookout stationed miles away. Their relationship unfolds through voice communication via walkie-talkie, forming the emotional core of the experience.

The dialogue between Henry and Delilah is where Firewatch truly shines. It's written with nuance and subtlety, capturing the awkwardness and vulnerability of two strangers forming a bond under unusual circumstances. Their conversations shift from witty banter to deeply personal confessions, and the choices you make influence the tone of their relationship, though not necessarily the outcome. The game doesn’t rely on branching paths or multiple endings—its power comes from how real the characters feel, not from how much control you have over them.

Visually, Firewatch is striking. The use of bold, stylized colors and dramatic lighting turns the wilderness into a painterly world that feels both isolated and alive. Time of day and weather effects are used to great atmospheric effect, reinforcing the mood of each narrative beat. Whether you’re hiking through golden forests at sunset or trudging through foggy, overcast mornings, the game’s environment constantly evokes a sense of place and emotional tone. It’s not a vast open world, but every inch of the map feels purposeful and artfully crafted.

Gameplay in Firewatch is minimal by design. There are no puzzles in the traditional sense, no combat, and no inventory systems. You walk, explore, and talk. You’ll navigate the terrain using a map and compass, examine objects, and respond to Delilah’s comments. The game keeps interactions grounded in realism—pulling out your map, opening supply boxes, and climbing rocky paths are all handled with a physicality that maintains immersion. While some players may find the lack of traditional gameplay mechanics limiting, those who come for the story and atmosphere will likely find it refreshing.

As the story progresses, a sense of unease creeps in. Strange occurrences and mysterious clues begin to surface, leading Henry and Delilah into a subplot that hints at conspiracy or even paranoia. While this mystery keeps the tension high, it ultimately serves more as a vehicle for character development than a twist-filled thriller. The resolution of the plot is understated and realistic, avoiding melodrama in favor of emotional authenticity. Some players may find this unsatisfying if they expect a more conventional payoff, but others will appreciate the grounded conclusion that ties back into the game’s themes of isolation and emotional escape.

The sound design and voice acting further elevate the experience. The ambient audio—chirping birds, rustling leaves, distant thunder—makes the forest feel alive. Cissy Jones and Rich Sommer, who voice Delilah and Henry respectively, give layered performances that bring the characters to life with wit, pain, and charm. Their chemistry carries the game, making even the most mundane interactions feel significant.

Firewatch is not a game for everyone. Those looking for action, challenge, or replayability may not find it here. But for players who value narrative, atmosphere, and emotional depth, it offers a memorable, affecting journey. It's a story about people trying to navigate their lives and find meaning in the aftermath of personal loss. It’s about the comfort of a voice in the dark, and the limits of escapism. With its beautiful setting, powerful writing, and heartfelt performances, Firewatch is one of the most compelling narrative experiences in modern gaming.

[b]TLDR[/b] Beautiful and atmospheric walking simulator, stellar writing and voice acting, somewhat undercut by underwhelming plot and ending. [18/20⭐, 6h🏅, 1/5💡]

[b]Context[/b] A quintessential walking simulator, where you play as an isolated firewatcher placed deep in a national park. When I first played Firewatch many years ago, I was mind-blown by the experience; I have to admit that upon revisiting, it didn’t hit quite as hard the same impact, but it remains an essential entry for those interest in narrative-driven adventure games.

[b]Writing[/b] You play as Harry, who has taken a firewatching job in a remote USA national park to escape personal problems back home. The only contact you have is through a radio with Delilah, an experienced firewatcher stationed in a neighboring tower. As the game progresses, mysterious occurrence affect Harry’s solitude and he starts learns more about his tower’s past occupants.

The writing is as good as it gets, exploring themes of trauma, isolation and human connection without feeling pretentious. Each dialog choice you make affects your relationship with Delilah and future interactions in nuanced ways, but I found it a bit disappointing that the plot itself is fully linear. In fact, the plot is perhaps the game’s weakest point, with a heavy-handed and non-climatic ending, with many narrative threads turning out to be red herrings or receiving underwhelming closure. 

[b]Aesthetics[/b] The visuals are stylized and relatively simple, but they perfectly capture the sweeping landscapes and quiet isolation—and, eventually, the sense of impending danger—that defines the experience. The human habitats are impressively detailed, hinting at a larger world beyond Harry’s experience. The ambient soundtrack is minimal and unobtrusive, surfacing just at the right moments. The voice acting is top-notch, one of the best I’ve experienced in a game, Delilah in particular standing out.

[b]Gameplay[/b] The game plays essentially as a walking simulator, you are given a map and a compass and are tasked with exploring the national park; parts of the part are blocked until you find proper equipment. The world is “open”, in the sense that you can freely explore every open area in any order. However, the apparent expansion of the wilderness is mostly an illusion, as you are mostly confined to walking predefined paths, and most of the areas are only unblocked as you progress the game. The disposable camera is also a neat feature that adds to the immersion.

There is nothing that can be considered challenging in the gameplay, and you can’t die or reach any deadends. The game auto-saves but you can also manually save at any point (although only 4 slots, not even enough to revisit all chapters).

[b]Value[/b] It took me less than 5h to beat the 5 days/chapters of the game, and then an additional half an hour to get all achievements due to a buggy collectible that didn’t spawn. After finishing the game you can also explore the world freely. You can also play the game with director’s commentary, which I found quite interesting (didn’t fully explore it as it would require another complete playthrough). You cannot revisit previous chapters other than using the 4 save slots. Choices you make affect your relationship with Delilah, which result in a different experience due to how central that is to the game and the character’s evolution, but the plot is linear and there is a single ending ([spoiler]the “bonus” ending is not an ending[/spoiler]).

Feel like there is a bit of a poor sell with the sense of isolation endemic to most walking sims (and no, that is not a derisive term, it's a genre and they can be good or bad like any other genre) but that's hardly an issue in-game given how it unfolds. On that, I do feel it kind of pushes its themes a little hard, but I think only so much it harms the sense of choice more than the entire experience. It is nevertheless a really good example of the genre itself, striking an excellent balance between visual style and quality and refraining enough from its underlying cartooniness without also trying too hard to be taken seriously. This is of course predominantly represented by a truly command vocal performance on part of the leads, which I think is easily the best part of the game and is good enough to save a few stilted lines of dialog and weaker plot threads. Other than the very end it is also well-paced and doesn't overstay its welcome. It is a little buggy, and while I don't usually care that much if it's something immersion breaking it's annoying, and that's definitely worth counting against a game this old, but it's far from so bad I'm going to make the whole review negative over it. It's a really short adventure that has a lifespan of maybe about 3-5 hours if you are not skipping through the narrative (you shouldn't, as it's the only selling point of it) so Firewatch doesn't overstay it's welcome, even though you'll probably wish that it did. 

In sum, without spoilers you are a guy who were given choices on how he deals with the situations in his life, but inevitably resulting in you needing some time away from everything and everyone, therefor you begin your new journey as a Firewatch, embracing the wilderness and an isolated life and only having your boss at the radio as someone you can communicate with, there on it'll be about your adventures as a firewatch

Firewatch is a beautiful game. The visuals are stunning, the voice acting is some of the best in the industry, and the characters themselves are written to be really likeable and relatable. The atmosphere is amazing and the tension in the general hiking sections is so thick you could cut it with a knife. 

Firewatch is also one of the most boring gaming experiences I've had in a long time. I finished the game; partly due to it's short length. I even went back and got the two or three achievements I had missed the first time. But god, does this game meander about way too much for such a short runtime.

First major problem: the story. Like I said, the characters are likeable and interesting, and voiced acted really really well. But the game's short runtime actively works in it's detriment. People have gone over Firewatch's ending over and over again, over what it means for the context of the story and how it related to it's themes. I believe the ending is a whole heaping pile of bollocks and that the writers ran out of time and had to quickly come up with something. The game is focused around a "mystery", but the game has a total of like, 4 relevant characters throughout the whole thing, so it's incredibly obvious what's going on the second you give it a second or two of genuine thought. Which you'll have a lot of time to do, considering long stretches of the game are completely absent of character dialogue (which is in my opinion, the best part of the game, and for reasons's I'll speak on later, no character dialogue means one of the most boring parts of the game). Being a "mystery" story, you'd expect a lot of twists and turns throughout. Instead you get 4.5 hours of semi-interesting filler dialogue between the two main characters and all the rest of the plot building is done in about 10 minutes at the start and 10 minutes at the end. The game is filled with different threads and "red herrings" that either get addressed like an hour later, fizzle out quietly, or simply get forgotten about. Seriously, why was Delilah being so secretive about that one call near the beginning of the game? As far as I know, the game literally never addresses this moment after the fact.

So if the story is lacking substance, the gameplay has to supplement it to create an enjoyable experience. Unfortunately, Firewatch is a walking simulator. The gameplay is holding W and Shift, occasionally pressing space to do scripted parkour sections, and picking dialogue options from a list. That's it. for around 4-5 hours, that's all you're doing. Beyond this monotony, I have a major gripe with the gameplay (or lack thereof). It's the missed opportunity that is the "exploration". if someone tells you this game is an "exploration" game, they're lying. The map isn't small, but it certainly isn't large enough to warrant going off the beaten path. And it's not like there's anything to *do* off the beaten path, either. They gave you this visually stunning area to explore and put nothing in it to actually do. You visit the majority of the map as part of the story anyways, so exploring has little to no use. Ludonarrative dissonance really hampers any sense of exploration that could have been had, either. For the uninitiated, ludonarrative dissonance is when a game's story and gameplay conflict with each other. In Firewatch, it's because the story is so tense. One thing Firewatch does very well is atmosphere. The subtle music, the sounds of the forest, and the narrative implications of the whole thing [spoiler] (the fact that you realise someone's definitely been watching you for most of the game) [/spoiler] are done very very well, and just add to the beautiful graphics. However, in such a tense scenario, where you're always feeling like you NEED to get to the next thing NOW, because it's almost always urgent, [spoiler] The girls and their fire, going to Wapiti Station, whenever you return to your lookout tower at night, etc. [/spoiler], exploration feels significantly less important. Henry in-game wouldn't be giving a crap about exploring right now, so why should I? There's a mystery to get to the bottom of! The game's inclusion of a self-guiding navigation system where you have to use familiar landmarks and knowledge of the area to get around from time to time is such a cool concept I'm disappointed they didn't expand on. Firewatch's map tells you everything you'd need to know, including where you are and where you need to go. Throughout the game Henry'll even fill in them map with routes to follow, so why not just let the player do this themselves? Let the player make their own paths, navigate on their own. It'd even encourage exploration, since you'd have to use environmental clues to help you where you're going. Maybe this idea would've gone against the spirit of the game (it probably does, to be honest), but it would have given me SOMETHING to do for 5 hours instead of just pressing forward and listening to dialogue. 

Do I recommend Firewatch? I'm on the fence. Behind all the critique's I've listed, lies a very visually beautiful game with some of the best atmosphere, character writing, and voice acting of a game in recent memory. I feel like the best takeaway is this: If Firewatch was a movie or short film, it'd be outstanding. But as a form of interactive media through a video game, it falters in all unique aspects that make the medium interesting. People take the piss out of "movie games", but at least those are interactive in the sense that you can pick alternate paths to experience different stories. Firewatch is linear, so it doesn't even get *that* luxury. 

It's short, so I'd only buy it if it was heavily discounted (I'm talking below like $8).

"Firewatch" is a cornerstone of a genre of games that I think deserves wider appreciation than it gets from the mainstream. That genre is the "Walking Simulator", and while those who DO appreciate them, know how immensely effective they can be, but the audience at large often write them off as "boring". You follow a character through what is typically a linear story, and while there are often gameplay elements thrown in (like exploration) for good measure, usually the main draw is the story or the experience of the game. "Firewatch" manages to be simple and complex at the same time, telling a very personal tale, that hits all the right beats, while also managing to be a unique and very fulfilling mystery. I would just say that if you've never tried a game like this, but you like movies, games, great stories, and can tolerate not carrying a gun in EVERY game, then this is a great Walking Simulator to try first. Then if you like it, move on to "What Remains of Edith Finch", "Soma", "The Unfinished Swan" or one of the many other great experiences offered in this underappreciated genre. "Firewatch" is a beautiful game, and highly recommended.

Got this game because I heard so many good things about it. It seems like a game that you can play from your couch, nice and easy, no twitch reflexes needed, with a good and gripping story. And for the most part it is, except for the last thing. The story seems good at first, and I think most people who reviewed this game positively must not have finished playing it or something, because while it may seem interesting and intriguing at first, it absolutely falls flat and ends with a fart noise like a whoopee cushion. It starts very emotionally charged, and intriguing, with a sob story about you and your wife which [spoiler] develops Alzheimer's disease [/spoiler] very early in life, and you have a lot of binary choices to make, which in the end make no difference whatsoever. Then you go work for a national park as a fire watch, in a very remote location, and your only contact is your boss, a woman as lonely as you are, with a bit of an alcohol problem. She starts being a bit clingy to you and soft pushes a bit of a relationship, but at the same time there are some signs that she might not be who she says she is, and I started to be more and more intrigued by the story. They also enrich the context with a missing kid from a few years ago, a possible child murderer in the area, and a pair of missing teens that they make look like they might have been kidnapped by that murderer, or that he might even be yourself. They make it seem like your wife's condition is something out of the ordinary and fishy, and it might also affect you and you don't even know it. Interesting stuff, right? I wanted to play more. But unfortunately there is where  the fun ends, and if you play the last hour of the game you will feel a deep disappointment, and the nagging thought that developers had enough of it and wanted to end it as soon as possible. Anything explained about your wife's condition? No, just story context to explain your character's state of mind and nothing more. Anything explained about the shadiness of Delilah? Nope, never mentioned again. What was all that thing with the [spoiler] scientists and the research bases[/spoiler]? Nothing, they were just there. Do you end up with Delilah and she moves in with you to be a happy dysfunctional couple? [spoiler] Nope! She just decides to leave you there in the middle of a wildfire and go back to her old boyfriend. Amazing! [/spoiler]. And the explanation for the missing and dead children? Weak and implausible. So yeah, my recommendation would be, get this game for free or deep deep discount, play the first 3h and uninstall. Make your own ending and be happy with it.

Loneliness, Pine Trees, and the Woman in My Ear

Firewatch is the kind of game that sneaks up on you. One minute you’re hiking through the Wyoming wilderness in your ranger-issued shorts, trying to figure out how a couple of drunk teens managed to set half the forest on fire with fireworks, and the next you're emotionally spiraling because a woman with a devastatingly sexy voice on the radio asked how you're really doing.

This isn’t a shooty-bang-bang game. There are no dragons. No inventory management. No high-octane car chases. Just you, the wilderness, a walkie-talkie, and a job watching for fire. Sounds boring, right? It’s not. It’s haunting. It’s funny. It’s beautiful. And somehow, it becomes one of the most intimate games I’ve ever played.

You play as Henry, a man who took a job in the middle of nowhere to escape his own wreckage of a life. The setup is simple: you sit in a tower, spot fires, report back. But what makes this game burn is Delilah—your supervisor, your only friend, and the woman whose voice slowly becomes your entire emotional support system.

And that voice? Delilah’s voice is dangerous.

Sultry, sarcastic, warm, and wounded—every time she speaks, it’s like whiskey being poured over an old wound. I found myself hiking through brush, not to complete an objective, but just to get to the next conversation. She’s flirty. She’s funny. She’s human. And somehow, you fall in love—not with her face, not with her body (you never even see her), but with the idea of her. With the sound of her. With the company of her.

Firewatch is brilliant in that way. It lets you fall for someone using nothing but a voice and a radio signal. And when the world starts unraveling around you—mystery, paranoia, fire closing in—Delilah is your anchor… even when you’re not sure if you can trust her.

Gameplay-wise, it’s a walking sim, yes. You walk. You talk. You occasionally climb rocks and swat away branches like a sweaty philosopher. But the real journey is internal. It’s about grief, connection, and what it means to be seen by someone, even if they’re hundreds of miles away.

The art style? Gorgeous. Like an oil painting of the American West lit on fire at golden hour. The soundtrack? Sparse and perfect. The story? Quietly devastating. No big plot twists. No happy endings. Just real, raw emotion wrapped in pine needles and smoke.

Final verdict? Firewatch is a short game with long echoes. It’s about healing, about escape, about two broken people clinging to each other through static. I didn’t want to leave that tower. I didn’t want to lose that voice in my ear. And when the game ended, I sat in silence and wondered how a voice I never saw could feel more real than half the characters in my life.

So here’s to Delilah. Wherever you are, radio girl… I still think about you.

[h1]A beautiful story about escaping from reality[/h1]
[h2]8.6/10. Get it on sale, right now.[/h2]
[hr][/hr]
[h3][b]TL; DR[/b][/h3]
This is a story about escaping from problems. Your character escapes from a horrible tragedy unfolding in his life by picking up this job, where he works with similar coworkers to uncover a mystery surrounding grief, denial and regret. The dialogue stood out to me the most; it was smooth, organic, and well-thought even with overlapping events from the player randomly exploring. I felt like I was talking to a real person behind the radio. I agree with some critics that the game could be longer, BUT I disagree on the plot and pacing (see below) – it is perfect. Can’t comment much on graphics since I’m on a lower end device, but that doesn't matter to me since story is the main appeal. If you love a good narrative, the Stanley Parable, and tend to explore every nook and cranny of a game, this is a must-try. If you tend to skip cutscenes, love action, and over-the-top stories about saving the world, this probably isn’t for you.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]
[/h2]


[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Some people see this as an over-glazed “walking simulator”. I can see where they are coming from, especially since hike lengths are long and the scenery can get a little repetitive. (But then again, it’s a forest. What do you expect? Space Cows?) The main entertainment is the dialogue itself. Talking to the other firewatcher about your past lives, stumbling across interesting finds, replying wittily to her questions and having a conversation until you inevitably annoy her and she turns off her radio. [i]Oops, sorry.[/i] To call for some constructive criticism, I wished that you could interact with your surroundings more beyond taking photos; pick up interesting finds, more wildlife interactions, etc. Overall, the game still does a good job to keep you engaged as you slowly hike towards your destination.


Game is polished and bugs are non-existent, with me only encountering a slight camera glitch while climbing a rope on one occasion that I was quickly able to fix. The game runs below minimum specs – not remarkably well, but it runs. I experienced frequent crashes due to my laptop overheating (11th Gen i7 integrated graphics, 16GB shared RAM), which made me lose most of my playtime. Bummer. A quick tune down of the resolution and using a laptop cooler solved that. The music is nothing to write home about, but still does a great job setting the mood, especially during tense moments. 




[h2]Plot & Pacing[/h2]
Below are some personal opinions on the common critiques. No spoilers, but reading may impact your enjoyment if you decide to play. I suggest you only read this if you’re really undecided. 


[b][i][u]The game skips too far ahead in time[/u][/i][/b]

I think the overall timeline of events for the main story is quite fair. You can’t expect one to live in an isolated tower in the middle of the forest and have some life-changing event happen every single day. However, I do agree that we don’t get to see enough of the lives of the characters. I really wished that we could live through days where the character does menial tasks and just go about their day. Maybe the developers cut it out as that would make the game feel too dragged-out and “boring”. I hoped that we could get the option to skip unimportant days, but still be given the option to play them if we want. 



[b][i][u]The plot’s resolution is too anticlimactic. They could have done a lot more with it[/u][/i][/b]

Yeah, having the character go through a wild story could generate a more mainstream appeal. I get that it’s a videogame and many people think the ending is half-baked. However, I think that the ending is quite reasonable given the firewatcher’s circumstances. Not every ending has to be over-the-top and ends with him saving the world. I think the ending they went with aligns with the message of the game the best. I would certainly love to see an alternate ending to firewatch; maybe your decision influences multiple endings? I’m satisfied with how the game concludes and don’t find it lacklustre in any way



[b][i][u]The plot feels rushed after the resolution[/u][/i][/b]

People get that perception as the game very quickly ends after you find out the truth. However, if you take the time to collect the notes, notice the items scattered in storage caches, and pay attention to the dialogue, you can see that the story is well thought-out. I think this is the kind of game which feels rushed, if you rush. Choosing to run whenever possible instead of strolling slowly and appreciating the full dialogue would definitely impact your experience. 


 (Spoiler Warning) I think superal1983 in [url=https://gamefaqs.gamespot.com/boards/168646-firewatch/73300254] this old thread [/url] illustrates these viewpoints well. 




[h1]Should you get it?[/h1]
Players with lower end devices may have to tune down the resolution, but the trade off is more than worth it. This is a slow game that requires you to slow down, appreciate the worldbuilding/plot and the bigger implications of what the game is trying to tell you. There’s a free roam mode and a developer’s commentary mode which is always cool but I doubt there’s much replayability for the main story beyond the second or third replay. I’ll come back and change this if I’m ever proven wrong. For full price, this game leaves some aspects to be desired at 15 dollars. That’s a lot of money to spend for 3-5 hours of short (but quality) gameplay for the main story. However, getting this on sale at 80% off for less than 3 bucks is an absolute steal. If it’s not discounted, this game is at least worth a wishlist until a sale comes around.

A game this short bugging out more often than others ten times its length is absurd. There is a ridiculously high chance that interacting with an object will have you slide along the floor uncontrollably while your character attempts, fruitlessly, to complete a long winded animation. Play on any device that can hit over 120 FPS and the game will simply stop letting you walk backwards by creating an ever growing invisible wall across the land. Baffling, really.

This game gets a lot of praise for the interactions between the two protagonists, Delilah and Henry. Delilah is written with all the grace and nuance of an insufferable lead in a low tier romantic comedy that swears anyone she speaks to will fall in love with her. You can, hilariously, stone wall her the entire game. It will affect nothing, however, as any pretense of branching paths or dialogue is shattered at every step. Nary a choice you make will matter and the game will proceed as ordained by the devs. Why there are even dialogue options is confounding. Though I guess scrolling through choices offers a slight break from stumbling around the linear and boring environments.

Henry is an unlikable oaf whose every line of dialogue made me wish the tumble he takes at the beginning was fatal. There is no dialogue choice that makes him any less annoying or whiny. While you have the illusion of choice when determining how Henry interacts with Delilah, you are absolutely stuck playing a chud.

The insufferability of the two leads, with whom you will spend the entirety of the game with, of course, could be worthwhile, if the story was at all satisfying. What little mystery and intrigue there is to be found leads nowhere with a twist that announces it self from a mile away, There's something to be said here about escapism, responsibility, the harsh realities of life, sure, but it is conveyed through the most mediocre vehicle possible.

TL;DR - Firewatch is a great game with a gut punching but grounded story and a world oozing with atmosphere. If you like summer forest vibes and a good story then this game is for you and I wholeheartedly recommend it.

Now for the longer answers. 

The story itself I found very enthralling, especially the chemistry and banter between the two main protagonists. The air of mystery as you progress I think added a nice touch of suspense.  I can maybe imagine people being dissatisfied with there not being a bigger payoff but personally I think that's what makes the story so great for me, it is grounded and at the end of the day that feels like what this game was going for from the start. 

In regards to graphics, it is pretty visible that it is an older game made by an indie studio, but I don't think they aged horrendously. The painterly vibe fits the setting and the world itself feels fleshed out through atmosphere to the point where the graphics themselves kinda take a background to the visual storytelling. 

My only complaint with this game, and it is a pretty big one, is the way I had to fight the jank to try and finish it. Now I should say, I played this on Linux, via Proton emulation and not the native port, so it is possible that the fault is entirely on my end and the native port works fine. Still I think it's important to note for anyone else possibly looking to play this game on Linux, I encountered a plethora of bugs that forced me to save and restart my game multiple times and pulled me out of the flow of the story. Most notable was getting constantly stuck in terrain and being able to barely walk, interacting with things like ropes, logs, bush obstacles causing my character to instead uncontrollably walk off in a random direction and among other things (moderate spoiler alert) [spoiler]the cave gate opening visually but not really allowing me to walk through[/spoiler]. I haven't tested if the game does this only on Proton, or the native port as well, so take from this what you will.

[h2] THE GOOD [/h2]
[list]
    [*] The music is just great, one of the best game soundtracks in my personal opinion.

    [*] It's visually appealing, the art style and approach they took with it is nice.

    [*] The dialogue with Delilah is nice, Delilah is a charismatic woman, she becomes a friend to accompany you during the times of very lonely walks through Firewatch's forest.

    [*] Getting 100% Achievements completed is always satisfying, and this game doesn't require you to go through 5 different playthroughs to Perfect the game, it doesn't even require you to look up a guide, which is always nice.
[/list]

[h2] THE BAD [/h2]
[list]
    [*] Not enough gameplay mechanics, it's a walking simulator, and the main thing that keeps you going as you walk is the Radio and Delilah, without that you're just left bored at times, and although the game is relatively short, you still feel VERY slow with everything you do, every jog, every animation to jump down, rappel, it is all slow even after doing the same mechanic 50 times, the duration of the animations continue to feel sluggish and slow.

    [*] Not enough unique looking areas, most areas look the same, I get that it's a forest, but at the same time it's a video-game, and they could've done more with it

    [*] The game's ending doesn't justify the journey, again, Firewatch at it's core just feels like "They could've done more" for more about that, spoilers ahead: [spoiler] Firewatch puts a lot of emphasis on the relationship of Delilah and the MC Hank, Hank has a wife who suffers from Dementia, and Hank sees a LOT of behavioral psychology, human mind and relationship dynamics books laying around in supply caches or just around the forest, all of these things I mentioned, played a very little role in what felt like the rushed ending of Firewatch, just off all of the things I mentioned, you could probably imagine a lot of cool, thoughtful or even mind-blowing endings for the game, I had a lot of theories running in my mind while getting close to finishing the game, but at the end, none of that was explored, and we hit the credits screen without even fully concluding Hank's story with his wife Julia, or his relationship with Delilah, we never even got to see Delilah as a matter of fact.[/spoiler]
[/list]

[h1]Firewatch – 100% Completion Review[/h1]
[i]All achievements earned, every conversation path explored, every hidden location and secret discovered[/i]

[b]Firewatch is not about what happens. It is about how it makes you feel.[/b]
As a completionist experience, it is short, focused, and beautifully crafted. But what lingers most is the emotional undercurrent, not the checklist.

You play as Henry, a man escaping personal grief by working a summer job in the Wyoming wilderness. What follows is a walking sim with real weight, driven almost entirely by dialogue and the growing relationship between Henry and his supervisor, Delilah. You never see her. You only hear her. And somehow, that makes the connection more powerful.

[b]The writing is exceptional.[/b]
Conversations feel natural, sometimes awkward, sometimes cutting, sometimes playful. Dialogue options shape the tone of the relationship more than the plot, but small choices do carry emotional consequences. A full completion run means reloading key moments to see alternate dialogue, and it is worth doing.

[b]Visually, the game is striking.[/b]
Stylized landscapes shift with time of day and weather. Every trail, every lookout point, every cave feels hand-placed to guide your eye without ever breaking immersion. Exploration is gentle but purposeful.

The ending is divisive. Some will want more closure. Others will recognize that the ambiguity is part of the point.

[hr]

[b]Firewatch is a quiet, human story told through movement, silence, and voice.[/b]
Completing it does not reveal new mechanics. It reveals new shades of meaning. And that, in a game like this, is everything.

Playing Firewatch is like going to an art show and watching a cotton candy be spun to life only for it to instantly dissolve in the rain once the guy hands it to you. But the weird thing is… the disappointment in seeing the cotton candy dissolve is intentionally part of the experience. 

That is to say, Firewatch is a tight 3-hour story with strong characterization, beautiful environments, and a relaxing vibe that teeters on the brink of tension… but ultimately amounts to nothing. I understand what they are going for, but I’m not sure it works in the context of a game.

In Firewatch, you are a man named Henry whose wife has dementia and has moved to the other side of the planet to be away from you. You’ve taken up a Fire Lookout position and do some chores around the Oregon wilderness while talking to your boss over the radio. 

You play vignettes consisting of a handful of days during your time on the job. Along the way, a mystery unfolds, causing you to hike from one side of the territory to the other multiple times. Firewatch wants to lean into the feeling of navigating and feeling lost, but you’ll quickly master the map and get a sense for where things are. I never used the compass once in the entire game. 

Ultimately, the mystery feels… unresolved. Not in the sense that it is bad, but in the sense that there are some hanging lose threads and no answers for them. It’s plain and unfortunately unsatisfying… but that’s the point. 

The journey is arguably more important than the destination. Firewatch does an excellent job of creating tension, paranoia, and mystique. The characterization is excellent. The vibes are strong. If you’re looking for a movie-length game that captures the feeling of the outdoors in a low-stakes, low-stress environment, then Firewatch may be for you.

My girlfriend and I played "Firewatch" as a couples' activity - except with less hiking and more dialogue. The game is designed for adults, not because of its mature content (although there is some of that), but because it understands relationships better than most games.

Firewatch isn't just a game—it's an emotional work of art that demonstrates how much depth, feeling, and atmosphere an interactive experience can have. From the very first minute, the atmospheric world of the Wyoming forest captivates you—with its vibrant sunsets, rustling treetops, and the impressive expanse of nature. It's as if you're actually standing there.

The strength of Firewatch lies not in its action or complex gameplay, but in its calm, profound narrative. You play Henry, a man grappling with his past while working as a fire watcher in the wilderness. The only human voice you hear is that of your superior, Delilah—and this is where the game unfolds its true magic.

The dialogues between Henry and Delilah are incredibly realistic, funny, sometimes sad, and always touching. It doesn't feel like a game, but rather like a real conversation you're having—full of emotion and humanity.  The decisions you make may seem small at first glance, but they shape your personal path through the story and make the experience unique.

What also makes Firewatch so perfect is the fantastic sound design. Every footstep on dry leaves, every distant rumble of thunder, every musical note is perfectly placed. The soundtrack is minimalist, but that's precisely what makes it so effective—it hits you in the heart at exactly the right moment.

The graphics are also beautiful. They're stylized, almost like a painting, and create an atmosphere you won't forget. You'd want to walk through these woods forever, watch the sunset, and listen to the wind.

Firewatch is a quiet but powerful game. It's a meditation on loneliness, memory, closeness, and loss—and that's precisely what makes it so perfect. Anyone who thinks video games are just shooting games or puzzles will be proven wrong here.

Conclusion:
Firewatch isn't a typical game—it's an experience you feel. A perfect blend of story, atmosphere, dialogue, and art.  If you haven't played it yet, you're missing out on one of the most beautiful, human games of all time.

Have you ever heard of Checkov's Shotgun? The developers of this game clearly had not.

It's a strong literary premise that, if you introduce a story element, you have 2 more acts to use it. If you begin your story with a shotgun hanging on mantle above the fireplace, by the end of the story, that shotgun needs to come into play in some way. This cuts out unnecessary fluff and filler, and focuses the audience's attention on things that matter. This premise has been around for ages, and is generally used to great effect, keeping audiences engaged and entertained. A recipe for success if you will in any artistic medium. This game fails this premise on every level.

Now, you can, of course (especially in a mystery) use red herrings to throw the audience's expectations for the real reveal. However, many story elements here have no follow up at all, and there is no real reveal at the end, meaning there are no real red herrings, just a weak and meandering plot.

Like others have said, kind of cool, but nowhere near worth $20. Maybe $10 at best. It's 4 hours long and there's no replayability at all. The story just kind of, ends, rather anticlimactically. It starts heading towards some deep dark mystery, but concludes shorty after with what was, imo, an unsatisfying ending. Really wish I could get a refund, but alas, 4.1 hours is outside the window. Had i known it was this short going in, I would have waited for a sale.

It really felt like they were headed down a much longer road full of twists and turns, but they ran out of funding and had to do *something* to complete the story for release. The ending really comes out of left field, and not in a good way... everything you've experienced up to it lends itself towards some big mystery, but they just pull the rug out from under you and that's it, roll credits. No epilogue, no sense you did anything that mattered, just a B-story "mystery" that doesn't amount to a whole lot. I understand that a main theme of this game is boredom and disappointment with life, but I don't play games to be bored and disappointed. This is a game that would have been better as a short film or a novella at half the price.

I really didn't have any expectations going into this game except that I expected it to be pretty, and it was definitely that. The plot had a lot more suspense and drama than I expected, and there were points where I was on the edge of my seat with nerves. 

But, the plot was a bit of a disaster. Henry [spoiler]leaving his wife with early onset dementia behind to go take a job for 10 weeks away from it all[/spoiler] establishes him as a unlikable person, and so I expected the plot to be about character growth and development. But it... wasn't. They set up this whole thing, where all Henry has for company is Delilah on the other other end of the walkie-talkie, and his thoughts and memories. But then it ends up being... nothing, really, because we're embroiled in a paranoia-driven thriller mystery. Which was like, fine, except the reveal of the whodunnit comes completely out of left field in a meaningless way. 

Then the ending is just unsatisfying in many ways. I'm not sure if you're meant to [spoiler]want to start a relationship with Delilah[/spoiler] because if you don't, the plot fizzles out horribly. And if you are, that's so unbelievably ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up in every way imaginable and surely -- surely that's not how it was supposed to resolve? 

So... the ending fell super flat for me, a lot of plot holes were never resolved, and the entire setup was kind of meaningless. But game purty, and as someone who generally dislikes 1st person games, I wasn't super bothered by it here, which is a point in its favor. And I was easily able to enjoy grinding the whole thing out in one gaming session.

So for $5 or less, sure, it's worth it to have played the game. But know that the ending is pretty awful (like was it even finished, or rushed? It's that bad...) and it's really only worth playing for the visuals alone. For that reason I really don't feel comfortable recommending it.

This has got to be one if not the best indie games to ever exist. 

Firewatch is a phenomenal, story-rich experience filled with secrets scattered across its breathtaking landscapes—and features some of the most likeable characters I’ve ever encountered. 

You play as Henry, a middle-aged man whose wife suffers from Alzheimer's. Though she’s still alive, she’s emotionally and physically distant, having moved to Australia to be cared for by her family. Meanwhile, Henry grieves her lost identity in the isolation of Wyoming, where the game takes place. Seeking escape, he takes a job as a firewatcher—a role as solitary as it sounds. But he soon discovers he’s not alone in using isolation as a coping mechanism. Enter Delilah, a witty and empathetic woman he communicates with via radio. And with that, the premise is set—now let’s dive into the details. 

I’m not exaggerating when I say the game’s art style is jaw-dropping. The lighting—especially the volumetric effects—is both soft and vibrant, contributing to that classic “rounded” Unity engine aesthetic found in many indie titles. Recently, I’ve gravitated toward games with a dreamlike quality, and Firewatch fits that mold perfectly. It blends stylized realism with painterly visuals so effectively that it feels like living inside a commercial—except, in this case, the commercial is the product. I imagine their marketing team had an easy time with this one. Regardless of the weather or time of day, the game’s environment is consistently beautiful. 

Let’s talk about the characters, because I can’t go another paragraph without mentioning them. Man, I’m genuinely excited just thinking about it—Henry and Delilah are phenomenal. Their banter is natural and often hilarious, filled with sarcastic quips, emotional honesty, and moments of vulnerability. When one of them is scared or upset, the other instinctively jumps in to lighten the mood, reflecting a deep emotional connection. Their chemistry is flawless, their values aligned, and their conversations feel raw and authentic—as if they were real friends trying to lift each other out of darkness. 

And the voice acting is some of the best I’ve ever heard. Cissy Jones brings Delilah to life with effortless charm and emotional nuance, while Rich Sommer nails Henry’s dry wit and underlying melancholy. What truly elevates their performances is the use of natural stuttering—those little verbal hiccups like “I—I—I uh…” add a realism that few voice actors pull off convincingly. It’s especially impressive considering Delilah has no on-screen face to convey emotion. Yet, through voice alone, Jones perfectly captures every subtle shift in tone. 

Even the silence in Firewatch is expressive. The distant rustle of trees, the occasional chirp of birds, and the melancholic strum of the soundtrack punctuate the loneliness with just enough presence to keep you from drifting too far. The way this game blends silence with the occasional strum of a guitar or plucking of a single string is both relaxing, intriguing, AND mysterious, depending on the moment. Isn’t it mad how one simple sound can have such a different emotional reaction when used in different contexts? Madness. 

Moreover, the story itself is well-paced and emotionally grounded. A mysterious figure in the shadows, the case of two missing girls, and a spreading wildfire create an undercurrent of tension throughout the narrative. Despite numerous time skips, nothing feels forgotten. Delilah frequently references past events, and even seemingly minor updates maintain a sense of continuity. The way the game balances grounded realism with hints of psychological suspense is masterful. For a time, you genuinely feel like you’re being stalked by something supernatural—but the final, mundane explanation brings it back to reality. You’re just a regular person in a bizarre situation. And that’s what grounds the story so well: it constantly reminds you that you’re vulnerable, ordinary, and human. 

The gameplay, while relatively minimal, holds its own within the context of the experience. Walking, occasional jogging, and frequently consulting a compass or paper map are standard mechanics for a game like this—especially one so firmly rooted in realism and a deliberate disconnect from modern technology. 

This game feels like summer, if that makes sense—and a significant reason for that is its non-reliance on digital tech. As you explore and collect information, you can occasionally radio Delilah to ask questions about specific objects. You’ll also come across physical tools: a disposable camera for capturing scenic moments, and an axe for clearing paths blocked by trees or branches. Everything feels tangible and grounded. 

One of my favorite features is the paper map. Instead of relying on a digital HUD or auto-navigation, you’re required to manually mark and zoom in on the map yourself. It’s physical and intentionally low-tech—just like the compass, which reacts naturally to your environment. It may seem basic, but there’s something incredibly refreshing about seeing real-world tools integrated authentically into gameplay, especially in an era dominated by over-designed UI and high-tech interfaces. 

This commitment to tactile, analog mechanics gives Firewatch a unique charm that most modern titles can’t replicate without venturing far from convention—or revisiting design approaches long left behind. 

A bit of analysis here—Henry’s character really stands out to me, and I want to share my interpretation. From what I’ve gathered, escapism plays a central role in how Henry copes. He frequently mentions that drinking is his last resort, especially if this whole “firewatcher thing” doesn’t help him feel any better. It seems he expects to isolate himself in a harsh, unforgiving environment, and rather than confront the demons that haunt him, he tries to drown them out through solitude—choosing a place with zero distractions and zero immediate gratification. 

But this very decision sets him up for repeated failure, which we see unfold throughout the game. Henry often brings up his wife, even dreaming of her calling him through the walkie-talkie. To me, it’s evident that his attempt to lose himself in work has only intensified his inner turmoil—it hasn't healed him, but instead pulled his demons closer to the surface. 

Delilah isn’t without her own baggage either. She struggles, arguably, just as much. Still grieving a breakup from over a decade ago, Delilah takes a more social—yet equally avoidant—approach. She drinks, deflects, and flirts as a means of escape. It’s immediately clear from how she avoids discussing her own emotions, often turning personal questions around rather than answering them directly. From Henry’s perspective, this becomes even more noticeable as their bond deepens. 

What truly stood out to me was a small but powerful moment near the end of the game. Delilah tells Henry that she plans to take the rescue helicopter out and that it’ll return for him later—even though he’s the last one left. On the surface, it seems like a simple logistical choice. But I instantly recognized it for what it was: avoidance. Why? Because I’ve done it myself. The dynamic between Henry and Delilah over the radio is not unlike an online friendship—close, emotionally rich, but physically distant. Delilah is clearly anxious about meeting someone she’s only known through that virtual space. 

Later, Henry has the option to invite Delilah back to Boulder, and she replies that she might drop by eventually—a vague promise that reeks of hesitation and emotional delay. To me, it’s another sign of her deflection: pushing decisions into the future to avoid confronting them now. Again, I’ve been in that exact position. That was my interpretation, anyway.

-it's fairly short, especially if you don't take time to explore and suss out other points of interest

Overall, this game is a perfect example of needing something in between a  thumbs up or down:  for as long as it lasts it's fun enough to play and you'll genuinely want to find out what happens next, but the unsatisfying ending combined with there being very little reason to revisit the game after you have completed it makes this a hard sell. I am still pretty new to the walking sim genre, but I fear this game will be hard to top. I played it in one sitting, I just needed to know the ending!

The graphics are fairly simple, but the style fits the story so well; it makes you want to sit there and just exist for a while, which is exactly what Henry came there for. The landscapes are gorgeous, and yet once the story progresses, that beauty is mixed with an eerie feeling that is perfect for the plot.

The pacing of this game feels very immersive in the sense that you can't rush it. You're stuck in the wilderness, and no matter what happens, you can't just teleport back to the lookout; you have to travel to and from every place you visit. I loved the little shortcuts you discover as the game goes on, it was just like in real life when you visit and area often and you start figuring out little shortcuts, on top of preventing the game from getting tedious.

The characters were very compelling; Henry's story is of course very sad, but that's what made me appreciate the scenery of the game so much. He's a character who lost everything, and that makes you want to appreciate the littlest things.
I fell in love with Delilah instantly. Her wits, her charm, everything. She is very charismatic, in a way that doesn't feel forced at all. The interactions between Henry and her were so well written, and truly make you feel the weight of being completely alone in the wilderness. Delilah is Henry's only contact, so in a setting like this, it makes sense that they became so close this fast, especially with the weird things that keep happening to them throughout the game. I wish there was just a bit more options as to the way you reply and interact with Delilah, but that's truly just a detail.

The game does a truly fantastic job at making you feel the weight of the loneliness as the story progresses. [spoiler] You start doubting Delilah's intentions and trustworthiness [/spoiler], and the fact she's the only person you can depend on drives you nuts.

My favorite part of the game though, is how the game manages to make you feel the stress, the need to watch over you shoulder, to look into the trees, without having any real jumpscare ([spoiler] aside from the one time you get knocked out [/spoiler]). Knowing that someone out there is watching you, listening to you while you're so vulnerable out in the woods was enough to be highly stress inducing without incorporating horror game tactics, which I'm really thankful for as someone who hates horror games.

The ending truly wrecked me. I was hoping it would be an Appalachian style nutjob stalker case, and yet finding out the truth just made the game that much more profound; the tragedy, the guilt Delilah goes through, it mad eme cry a little.

Overall one of my favorite games so far, and I really wish I could play it again for the first time.

I believe the game is focusing a little bit too much on the story in a way that encroaches on the playing experience. I wish some kind of small routine was perhaps given to the player to (like a real fire watcher) outside of simply following the main plot's events.

[b][More gameplay spoilers ahead][/b]

In my opinion the game could really benefit some kind of simple daily tasks like checking that the main paths are cleared up, no tree fell down in the night, that the crates are still in good shape, nothing that needs to be overly complicated. But just some kind of small routine that makes the player feel a little bit more in the boots of a real fire watch. I really like our home and really would love to have it a bit more interactive. This would provide perhaps a bit longer play time (and more replayability for some) while still allowing for the main plot to continue on side of course. This is especially true for the times where we are just thrown "60 days later" by the magic of a black screen, or when we are getting teleported home by the end of day because we finished the event to do.
Please let walk home, close the door, turn of the ligths and go to sleep so I feel more like in a game than just watching a movie.

For those that want to escape, if only for a little while.

It's a tale as old as time: someone takes to the wilderness in order to leave their problems behind, searching for space, or clarity, or maybe to disappear entirely.  Through dialog options, you can somewhat guide the protagonist's own reasons for this, but nothing is ever handed to you concretely. Several months ago, I played through Firewatch for the first time in a last ditch effort to get my mind off of imminently losing a long term relationship. While I didn’t know that within just a few hours I would be dumped, I did know that something bad was happening and, whatever it was, it was going to hurt me dearly. I scrambled to find some sort of activity I could do that I hadn’t attached thoughts of my then-partner to, settling on this game after being in my backlog for almost a year.

On one hand, I think it was maybe the best thing that I could have experienced in those crucial, agonizing hours. On the other, the emotions I felt made me feel somehow significantly worse. I didn't know why, but that new sinking feeling in my chest helped me process what was happening so much more than I had originally thought.

Every few months, when grief visits me in unexpected ways, I pick up the game again and replay the whole story, usually in one sitting. This time around, however, I decided to take copious breaks (mostly because I was extremely sick at the time,) but also so I could thoroughly enjoy the dev commentary. In doing so, I had a lot more chances to really understand what made me click with the game in the first place and why it matters so much to me.

This game isn’t a grand adventure with complicated gameplay or difficult achievements. It’s simply a story about broken people trying to escape their problems and making terrible mistakes along the way. Throughout the game, as the stakes and smoke rises, all you can do is pray that everything, in some way, will end up okay. And as you hold onto that fleeting hope, it only becomes more and more apparent just how impossible that's actually going to be. While this game has an incredible amount of choices that can change much of the plot, there is no series of dialog and no actions in what you do that can change how the story ends. Yes, there is a small alternative ending where Henry can choose not to take the helicopter lift out, but the larger story and everything before that very last second is unchangeable, despite your countless choices. Henry will always just barely miss seeing Delilah. Julia will always be deteriorating an ocean apart. Dave will always have his feelings unrequited by Ron. Brian will always be dead at the bottom of a hole. And the forest will always burn.

This is not a satisfying game and, to its credit, it’s not remotely trying to be. It is as raw as it is brutal. It leaves a terrible taste in your mouth that can’t be washed out. You finish this game feeling awful, knowing that this beautiful world and those deep relationships have literally burnt to the ground. And in the most backwards and strange way, that’s exactly the kind of game I need when the going gets tough. Sometimes, what you need is a swift kick in the gut to understand that even when the world collapses in on itself, it’s better to have had the ability to make choices than to not have had them at all.

These characters, and by extension you, walk away from this game not with a feeling of accomplishment, but simply with a new perspective and a sliver of possible foresight. There are only a few other games I know that can effectively do something as difficult yet important as this, namely Night in the Woods, but this one stands far and above. While you may have faith that Henry will make that journey to reunite with Julia or continue his relationship with Delilah wherever that may be, that’s something we never get the chance to see or even be confirmed to us. Henry enters the Shoshone a battered and broken man, and yet he leaves it more world-weary and more shattered than he was when he arrived. In a way, you do the same. Wishing you had just a little bit more time or had the chance to have had that last conversation. And yet, you never get to, making you savour that little amount of time that you did get to have.

This has become one of my favorite games ever, and even though my connection to the game is rooted in grief, that very reason is what has allowed me to find so much solace when all else fails. As time goes on and I better understand this game, I also better understand myself and find new perspectives in mourning. I can wholeheartedly say that this game has indescribably helped me come to terms with not getting the closure that I desperately needed. Sometimes, you don’t get that chance and it’s tragic and heartbreaking and cruel all the same. But being able to live through pain like that and seeing tomorrow having got to experience something as beautiful as this is sometimes all you could ask for. That makes it worth it in the end, the ability to say “No matter how brief, at least I was here. At least I made a difference to someone.”

A beautiful, atmospheric slow burn
Firewatch is a truly atmospheric and beautifully crafted game. It’s a welcome change of pace from the usual fast and action-packed titles out there.
You follow a well-written, linear story, but the game gives you plenty of room to explore and discover small extras scattered throughout the world. You’re slowly drawn into Henry’s life and surroundings, and it’s easy to lose yourself in the calm, quiet wilderness.
At the beginning, you shape some "flavor" elements of Henry’s past — small choices that define his life before he escapes into this remote job. These personal touches go a long way in building a connection between the player and the character.
The game is slow, but deliberately so. It tells a story at its own pace, and while the path is linear, there’s enough freedom to wander off and uncover bits of a world that feels lived-in and real.
Conclusion: Firewatch isn’t about action or challenge — it’s about atmosphere, emotion, and storytelling. And in that, it absolutely delivers.

Firewatch is a beautifully crafted narrative adventure set in the Wyoming wilderness. With stunning visuals, rich atmosphere, and deeply personal storytelling, it pulls you into the quiet yet emotionally charged life of Henry, a fire lookout. The voice acting—especially the dynamic between Henry and Delilah—is top-notch, making the experience feel intimate and real. It’s a short game, but one that lingers long after it ends.

I'd be remiss if I didn't say that this game didn't really hit as much as I'd like it to. With that being said, I don't regret playing this game. It's not mechanically or graphically complex, but there is an emotional through-line that I did grasp to have more layers than previously thought.

 My first play-through found me frustrated and honestly a bit bored considering that on my end, I kept getting lost with where to go, and at the end just found myself wanting the game to just end. However, on my achievement hunter run, where I was more familiar with where I was going, I was more able to fully grasp the story as I didn't find myself distracted by taking a wrong turn.  As to which I say, I found myself sympathizing for my character, and Delilah, your only other form of interaction.

The wilderness in which you find yourself is visually nice initially, tho personally, its awe wore off as I didn't seem to quite stick with me. I will say however that at night, paired with the stars becomes stunning to look at. 

Overall, it was alright for me. It's more grander themes of escapism and to grieve that which is not dead but no longer with you was realized to me by sources outside of the game itself. I appreciate the game for the concept itself of constricted emotional connection. Even if it didn’t strike a deep chord while playing, I respect the quiet space it carved out; for reflection, for loneliness, and for the kind of conversations that linger long after the fire’s gone out.

Firewatch is a short adventure walking-sim game with a significant focus on open world exploration and mystery. The gorgeous natural environments and strong sense of atmosphere provided by the dynamic day & night cycle make the walking sim part quite enjoyable, however the way the mystery ends up being resolved leaves a bit to be desired.

The story mainly revolves around two main characters, both middle aged and not too happy about how their lives have gone so far. What fills out the open world exploration are frequent conversations between the two. The writing and voice acting do a good job of making the relationship interesting to follow. Their experiences of grief and desire to find themselves wanting to work in isolated spaces like the fire lookout tower inform what themes the game is going to tackle.

The mystery element plays well with how the characters are basically isolated from the rest of the world and how their traumas affect their ways of thinking. Unfortunately, I find that the final portion of the game sneaks up a little bit too fast on you. I feel like there could be an hour or two more to give the story beats some more space. While I sort of understand why the mystery was resolved the way it was, I think the execution could be better.

Overall, the atmosphere, exploration and the relationship of the two main characters provide a good walking sim journey that can be finished in one sitting.

Firewatch is a touching narrative-driven game with an appealing art style and superb voice acting.  

You experience the Wyoming wilderness as Henry, a man whose life circumstances drove him to accept a summer job that requires living in total isolation -- except for his manager Delilah on the other end of a walkie-talkie.  The gameplay is minimal, simply walking from point A to B, and serves mostly as a vehicle for the interactions between Henry and Delilah.  These interactions are where one really "plays" Firewatch.  You choose how Henry responds to Delilah and watch their relationship develop.  

Music is sparse and impactful when present.  Most of the time, you're listening to sounds of the wilderness and chirps from your radio.  The voice acting is convincing and really helps sell the experience (it better be on-point since it's front and center in this game).  

My only criticism is that I encountered a few bugs, one of which halted my progress and required me to restart a level.  Another time, my character couldn't walk unless he was holding his map.  In yet another instance, I encountered a visual bug that made everything seem out of focus.  These latter two bugs resolved with saving/loading the game.

Overall, Firewatch is a fun short single player game (my playthrough lasted 7 hours).  If you're looking for something chill after a tough week at work, this might be the game for you.

This game has already become a classic and it would be very problematic to say anything new about it. In general terms, it can be described as a kind of beautiful story. Playing the game, I had the same feeling as reading Turgenev's "Notes of a Hunter" - you need to be able to convey the beauty of nature so vividly. But, this is not just graphomania The main thing here is not the gameplay or the graphics, but the plot, the characters themselves. The environment is just there to reveal the main idea, which could be described as follows: "a bad deed will lead to more bad deeds and so on in a circle that knows no end." 

Although, initially I thought that the game tells how Americans experienced the "patriotic act", which was canceled literally a year before the release of the game: a constant feeling of being watched, hopelessness, leading to despair (it is enough to remember how Delilah literally had a panic attack when she found out that she and Henry were being watched). But, like the melody of the march by composer Prokofiev from the opera "The Love for Three Oranges", the plot at first sets you up for one thing, taking a major key, and then suddenly turns everything upside down and throws you into a minor key.

It was pretty fun, finished the whole thing in an all-nighter. 

The first time you go somewhere can be a bit slow and annoying, but once you figure out the path you can just sprint through it later on. Sometimes the game won't allow you to walk up a gentle slope or jump over the dreaded triangle-shaped rock, since the spacebar only allows you to jump over the square-shaped rocks, and that can be annoying on the first run, but again, you'll learn the routes pretty quickly.

The story is pretty enjoyable, and (avoiding spoilers) it's cool how the environment evolved with each new day. The ending had nice closure, but I didn't like the big twist, and it felt like a lot of stuff left unexplored, especially if you don't want to believe the answer to the story. 

All in all, I'd recommend on sale, maybe even when not on sale (I got it on sale). Very nice!
