[h2]📝 Quick Thoughts[/h2]
Won't include spoilers but reading this review might give away something you might want to know or experience for yourself. This is mostly how I feel about the game, not about what this game is.

[h3]📖 Story (Main plot + Narrative)[/h3]
The main story has a powerful base to it. It makes sense, and it's very well written. You can feel that a lot of thought was put behind each section of the story or each incident that happens in the game. The presentation of the main story is perfect.

[h3]📚 Side Content/Side Stories[/h3]
I didn't see any side content or side story, it's just the main plotline and everyone is a part of it. You can finish the game and walk around in free roam, that's mostly it.

[h3]🎭 Characters (Main + Side)[/h3]
A substantial amount of thought is put behind every character in the game. Just like visual novels where you choose one option out of many, you talk to Delilah the same way, except, she remembers everything, not just for the next response but for the entirety of the game. There are other characters which at first feel like background mobs, but surely you're going to think about them once you're AFK.

[h3]🎶 Sound & Music[/h3]
Music is immersive. When I say immersive, I mean, it changes with what's happening and it fits right. That, and the selection of the music tracks, very nice. Whether it's a beautiful morning, a suspenseful corner, a dark cave, or a shocking reveal. You'll feel it. The noise that MC makes, the sound of items you interact with, even the walkie-talkie static, it fits right, it's not annoying.

[h3]🎤 Voice Acting[/h3]
Voice acting is REALLY well done, you can feel the emotions if you have ears for it. I loved it!

[h3]🎨 Visuals (Graphics + Art Style)[/h3]
Since I played it on a good PC, it looked fantastic. I often stopped playing and just ... looked at my screen. This is the type of art style I won't mind using as a wallpaper. It's not realistic at all, it doesn't try to be, and still, it's gorgeous.

[h3]🎮 Gameplay Experience[/h3]
To me, it's a cozy game. There are no stressful game-sequences or timed challenges. Controls are basic and simple. No complex puzzle solving or spending your night finding clues to open a box. It feels like a restricted open world game which you can play linearly. The game doesn't let you run off of a cliff, which is a good thing.

[h3]🌍 World Building & Level Design[/h3]
The forest is beautiful. The terrain is believable. The map sections and region locking is really well done. The day-night cycle never felt intrusive. When the atmosphere of the game changes, you will clearly feel it. I sure did.

[h3]⚙️ Game Performance (Loading, Bugs, Framerate)[/h3]
There are no intrusive loading screens, once you start the game, you'll play all of it. However, there are some bugs when you switch apps (Alt + Tab), it won't register achievements and sometimes audio goes bye-bye. There's also a minor bug where you walk off when you interact with an item in front of you. Apart from this, I didn't face any crash. I personally didn't notice any frame drops or screen tearing.

[h3]🏆 Extras (Achievements, Grind, Replayability)[/h3]
Most people will consider this game a single playthrough game. There are, however, different choices you can make to experience different interactions and conversations. There is virtually no grinding in this game. You can choose to find trash and pick it up (clean it) but there's no reward for it. Achievements are relatively easy to 100%. You can play the entire game without any outside help, and then 100% it within a couple of hours (or minutes) on your second playthrough.

[h1] Mid Life Crisis Simulator [/h1]
I worked in HSE and one of my jobs was to assess the needs of people who are fire fighters and implement them because they have to do night shifts and what's not. It made me nostalgic playing this game and experiencing their POV. Even though the main character is not a fireman but a lookout for fires, I feel that itself is a real challenging job and somewhat simillar job. 

[b] Story: Okay [/b]
I did not find the story depressing or that much sad because life happens, you move on. You realize when you are 31, nothing surprises you anymore. The story starts off with a man who had a rocky relationship with his wife and took a job to get away a bit. It's an interesting vacation like job but still challenging. You meet your supervisor who is a very nice lady and you communicate with her through a radio. It's a nice LDR remote working relationship. Things happen during your stay, mysterious person following your tracks, strange science teams and some drunks. You also direct the story a bit like a visual novel, so the second time you play it, you are still entertained. The story does emphasize about fire hazards/safety quite a bit which is very good information for normal people. 

[b] Characters: Okay [/b]
I don't think there is much development except the guy going through a phase in his life. I think he is a lumberjack type of guy who does like nature and is good with an axe. The supervisor is mysterious and they have an interesting relationship with twists and turns. There's the guy's wife Julia also, then some side characters. There is not much of a strong BG info about others except the main character. The story is not striking and it's not oscar worthy but it fits I guess. 

[b] Gameplay [/b] 
Had some performance issues which the SSD fixed, can't play with discord voice in the BG then it lags must be my potat laptop but eh. It's a basic walking simulator where you are equipped with the map but I did need some time to get used to the paths and such, it's challenging, the navigation. You also open fire lookout caches, read notes, gather useful items and travel from various parts of the map. I felt the gameplay would have more interesting stuff to do and did expect some survival stuff like the forest, but oh well. I liked that you could play the second time with commentary and that the photos you took can be converted into prints which is a real nice marketing strategy within the game. 

[b] Art and music [/b]
The art is nice and scenic. Real relaxing. The music is okay. Voice acting is good. 
The dialogue between the characters are great, some dark humor and sarcasm.  it made by bf laugh he liked it.

You need to stop alt tabbing out of the game, turn on manual saving instead of auto and then go ahead before getting bugged ones.

Its a good game, to be honest, but Steam should certainly add some nuance to the review system. While I would not like to give it a negative review, I do not necessarily think that this is anything revolutionary either, however. For starters, I want to focus in on the good. This game is a very story driven experience, and the characters are all very well written. Each felt like they were three dimensional, and each had their own issues and faults that they played in to. None of them were perfect people, everyone did bad and good things for reasons that were understandable. Certainly the warning in the description about the matter being intended for adult audiences should be heeded, however. While the subject matter was not dark per se, it did deal with adult issues, with people who do not always take the moral choices - depending on player - making it something of mature piece. The characters were exceptional, and the story was short enough to keep it simple to point of being involved yet not missing out on anything. Another amazing point was the soundtrack, as well as the graphics. Both were really well done, and I want to mention it. The issues start to arise with the gameplay and some inconsistencies in the narrative. Gameplay wise, it is a walking simulator. There is not much to say about it other than that, but it could have been made a lot better with some more parkour or something, as that would have fit the story. To me, however, it was just a touch too boring as is, and could have been equated more to a visual novel with how minimal it all was. Further, there were some bugs. Interacting with something in your hand would send you walking back at times, or interacting with rope and such sometimes would be difficult to do for the small hit boxes/buttons or whatever they are called to get something to be used. The most damning, however, was simply how slow it all felt to me. The sprint mode felt painful at times, as did the repelling and climbing. The chapters cut when I felt it would have been labelled tedious, but it still felt too long to get from one place to another. In terms of the narrative, in a spoiler free context, the starting portion could have easily been put into the game in some cinematic or small bits of gameplay/glimpses into what was happening. It did not need to be text on a screen for five-ten minutes, only to delve into a boring walk just to give exposition. The medium of a video game, I feel at least, lets you really live through the eyes of the character. It would have been a lot more meaningful to show what was happening rather than start the game out with a huge exposition dump that felt cheap in its delivery. [spoiler]Out of the spoiler free context, some plot points simply felt out of place, and disconnected from the main story. It seemed to me that this was the story of a man gradually losing interest in his ill wife, and growing close to another woman who also has feelings for him, but does not act on them out of her morals. This would have been great all by itself, but the developers felt the need to add a mystery and the murder of a little boy by his father in it to create conflict. This wouldn't have been so bad if it didn't branch off into investigating researchers, getting threatening tapes, and just stuff that adds horror but simply did not feel naturally introduced. All these points leading to the mystery being revealed simply felt disjointed and random, especially the "whodunnit" but with the teenaged girls.[/spoiler] Is it a good game? Yes. Its a pretty great story minus some minor flaws, has a great voice cast, has amazing characters, and is almost completely bug free gameplay. However, it is not the best walking-sim out there, and I certainly believe that it is not worth what it is currently being sold at. Three hours of your life for a very compelling play, but its nothing revolutionary. 100%, however, get it on a sale. Its not a waste of time to go in blind, and I thought it very enjoyable, if overpriced on the modern market for these sorts of games.

I wasn't sure whether or nor i'd recommend Firewatch for a moment. I thought back over my choices and thought that I got the version of the ending that I was supposed to - I wasn't about to use my wife's ailment as an excuse for cheating, so when the ending rolled around I thought "Hey, that makes sense, this Delilah seems pretty suspicious anyways so I dodged a bullet on that one"

Then I find out that, in fact, that's the ending *everyone* gets. The game always drops the conspiracy angle, makes a bunch of half-assed overtures to try and explain the dissonance between what was shown versus what we actually got, and that even if you wanted to roleplay someone who, like Delilah, has a barely functional moral compass - you *still* get the same ending. Suffice to say, I felt that was kind of a betrayal of concept. I could look past the graphical bugs I ran into, or the poor pathfinding or getting stuck on rocks and tweaking out, because this is ultimately a story game first, and the gameplay is more of a vestige of what people would expect to have, like an interactive movie. But then I come to find that your choices barely matter, and the ending is always the same anyways.

I don't know what it is about the mid 2010's and the slew of titles that barely had gameplay, professed that your choices mattered, and then failed to deliver on said promise, but I can't say I'm unhappy that that time has passed. If the ending had made better sense, or if the choices had actually mattered, then perhaps I would have given a cautious recommendation, but ultimately that isn't the reality. Firewatch is a game that stokes it's flame to bursting, and then quietly fizzles itself out before it can accomplish anything with it. Maybe get it on sale, or better yet, watch someone else play. The experience of seeing someone else play this game is almost identical to what you would get doing it yourself.

Firewatch isn’t loud about anything. The air is quiet, the colours soft, and the loneliness feels familiar in a way that stirs something old inside you. It doesn’t shove grief in your face or hold your hand through resolution. It just lets you walk, slowly, through the kind of quiet that says more than words ever could, long enough for you to hear the things you’ve been trying not to say.

You play as Henry, who takes a job watching for wildfires in the Wyoming wilderness after his wife’s illness and their unravelling life leave him emotionally stranded. He doesn’t fight. He doesn’t try to fix. He just… leaves. And the story never punishes him for the urge to retreat, for finding comfort in emptiness, for choosing the peace of doing a job no one sees or thanks him for.

But solitude doesn’t mean isolation. Over a radio, you meet Delilah. And slowly, you open up to each other. It’s messy, funny, intimate, and vulnerable. You speak into a radio and hope the voice on the other end stays. You hold your breath, waiting for the next reply, pretending it’s enough.
It isn’t. You know it isn’t. But some of us only speak our truth when we think nothing will come of it, when we’re safe behind the distance.

Firewatch is warm, aching, quiet. It’s a beautifully lonely piece of storytelling.
If you’ve ever needed space before you could speak, if you’ve ever left something unfinished but not forgotten, this one will stay with you.

If this is meant to be a hiding place, it fails, gracefully. Because even in the wilderness, you’re eventually asked to come back. To choose. To do.

And maybe that’s the quiet message we are meant to see in it: Some doors don’t close when you leave. They remain open, just enough, for you to come back and try again.

Sometimes, escaping doesn’t take you away from pain—it just gives it a place to echo louder. Firewatch is about that echo. The one between trees, between breaths, between two strangers on a radio.

You walk through wild beauty, but it's never just a hike. Every trail carries weight: of grief, of guilt, of not knowing what you’re doing—but walking anyway. Because what else is there?

Then there’s Delilah. Her voice isn’t just company. It’s connection. It's warmth in a cold place. It’s something you didn’t know you needed until it makes you laugh. Until it makes you stay.

There’s no saving the world. No epic climax. Just moments. Quiet, human moments. And in those, Firewatch finds something most games never even look for: the ache of being alive.

You’ll finish it with a lump in your throat, a heart slightly bruised, and a memory that lingers like the smell of pine after rain.

You won’t want to say goodbye. Not to her. Not to the woods. Not even to Henry.

Just… stay a little longer.

Firewatch isn’t just a walking simulator — it’s a slow-burn masterpiece that wrapped me in warmth, mystery, and melancholy all at once. From the moment Henry steps into his lonely watchtower, you can feel the isolation of the Wyoming wilderness pressing in. The art style? Gorgeous. Those bold, warm colors and sweeping landscapes make every sunset feel like it was painted just for you.

The real magic is in the dialogue. Your only connection is Delilah’s voice over the radio, and somehow, that bond becomes one of the most real and human relationships I’ve ever experienced in a game. The banter is natural, witty, and full of subtle emotional hooks that slowly reel you in. One moment you’re laughing together about supply drops, the next you’re quietly admitting things you didn’t even realize you were holding onto.

The mystery? Perfectly paced. Weird noises in the woods, locked fences, a shadow of someone watching you from afar — it keeps you uneasy without ever needing a jump scare. Every breadcrumb pulls you deeper into both the investigation and your connection with Delilah.

The sound design seals it. The rustle of leaves, distant thunder, the soft crackle of your radio — it’s immersive to the point where you feel the crisp evening air on your skin.

Final Verdict: 10/10 — Firewatch isn’t just a game, it’s an experience. It’s quiet, human, and achingly beautiful. I came for the mystery, stayed for the connection, and left feeling like I’d just said goodbye to someone I’d known my whole life.

Firewatch começa em 1975, em Boulder, Colorado, contando com textos e sons de bar para apresentar a história de Henry e Julia, um casal que se conhece por acaso e rapidamente se apaixona. Eles adotam um cachorro e fazem planos para o futuro, até que Julia, com apenas 41 anos, desenvolve demência precoce. Incapaz de lidar com a deterioração da esposa e do relacionamento, Henry aceita um trabalho como vigia de incêndios florestais no Parque Nacional de Shoshone, buscando fuga e silêncio.

No posto de vigia, Henry se comunica por rádio com Delilah, outra vigia, cuja voz guia e acompanha sua jornada. A relação entre os dois se desenvolve por meio de diálogos, onde o jogador pode escolher tons mais flertantes, distantes ou amigáveis. Apesar de lembrar um simulador de romance, Firewatch é muito mais — trata-se de solidão, trauma, fuga e tentativa de redenção.

A narrativa ganha tensão quando aparecem mistérios: uma figura sombria, adolescentes desaparecidas, uma cerca misteriosa e equipamentos de vigilância. Tudo leva a Henry a explorar uma caverna, onde descobre o corpo de Brian, um garoto que morreu em um acidente de escalada. Seu pai, Ned, ex-vigia, escondeu o corpo e vive isolado desde então, espionando Henry.

O jogo termina com um incêndio florestal se espalhando e Henry sendo evacuado, sem encontrar Delilah pessoalmente. O desfecho é propositalmente inconclusivo e melancólico — sem encontros românticos, sem reconciliações definitivas, apenas duas pessoas lidando com suas perdas de formas distintas.

A experiência emocional do jogador é intensificada pela atmosfera sonora, pelos visuais deslumbrantes e pela sensação constante de que algo está prestes a dar errado. A comparação com incêndios florestais simboliza a dor e a cura: destrutiva, mas também renovadora.

Por fim, o jogador reflete não apenas sobre os personagens, mas sobre sua própria vida, lembranças e perdas — como o narrador, que comprou Firewatch motivado por um sonho sobre alguém do passado. O jogo se transforma em um espaço para processar emoções, e essa conexão pessoal é o que o torna tão poderoso.

//

Firewatch begins in 1975 in Boulder, Colorado, using on-screen text and bar ambiance to introduce the story of Henry and Julia, a couple who meet by chance and quickly fall in love. They adopt a dog and make future plans, until Julia, at just 41, develops early-onset dementia. Unable to cope with his wife’s decline and their crumbling relationship, Henry takes a seasonal job as a fire lookout in Shoshone National Forest, seeking escape and solitude.

At the lookout tower, Henry communicates via radio with Delilah, another lookout whose voice guides and accompanies him through his journey. Their relationship develops through dialogue options, allowing the player to choose a flirtatious, distant, or friendly tone. While it may resemble a dating sim at times, Firewatch is ultimately about loneliness, trauma, escapism, and the search for redemption.

The story builds tension as mysteries unfold: a shadowy figure, missing teenagers, a mysterious fenced-off area, and surveillance equipment. All clues lead Henry into a cave, where he discovers the body of Brian, a boy who died in a climbing accident. His father, Ned, a former lookout, had been hiding in the forest ever since, spying on Henry and avoiding the world, unable to deal with his grief.

The game ends with a wildfire spreading out of control and Henry being evacuated, never actually meeting Delilah face-to-face. The ending is purposefully unresolved and melancholic—no romantic climax, no neat closure, just two people coping with loss in different ways.

The emotional impact on the player is deepened by the game’s sound design, stunning visuals, and a constant sense that things might take a dark turn. Wildfires serve as a metaphor for grief—destructive, but also regenerative.

In the end, the player is left reflecting not just on the characters but on their own life, memories, and losses—just like the narrator, who bought Firewatch after a dream about someone from the past. The game becomes a space to process emotions, and that personal connection is what makes Firewatch so powerful.

1. Story & Atmosphere – 9/10

Firewatch drops you into the shoes of Henry, a man escaping a crumbling personal life to take a job as a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness in 1989. The story kicks off with a gut-wrenching text-based prologue that traces Henry’s relationship with his wife, Julia, and her descent into early-onset dementia—a sequence that’s as heartbreaking as it is effective. From there, the game shifts to the Shoshone National Forest, where your only companion is Delilah, your supervisor, who chats with you over a walkie-talkie.

The narrative thrives on the evolving bond between Henry and Delilah, built entirely through radio conversations that feel natural, witty, and deeply human. The writing is sharp, blending humor, tension, and vulnerability in a way that makes you care about these two flawed souls. The mystery that unfolds—hinting at conspiracies and unseen threats—keeps you hooked, though the resolution might leave some wanting more. The atmosphere is a standout: the isolation of the forest, paired with eerie silences and subtle sounds, creates a hauntingly immersive vibe.

Pros:

✅ Emotional, character-driven story with brilliant dialogue.

✅ Tense, mysterious atmosphere that plays on isolation.

✅ Stellar voice acting that brings Henry and Delilah to life.

Cons:

❌ Ending feels underwhelming compared to the buildup.

2. Gameplay: Exploration & Interaction – 7/10

Firewatch is a first-person adventure—or “walking simulator,” if you will—that prioritizes exploration and dialogue over traditional gameplay mechanics. You roam the forest with a map and compass, tackling simple tasks like investigating smoke or tracking down clues. The lack of combat or complex puzzles keeps things minimalistic, which suits the game’s introspective tone but might disappoint players craving action.

The dialogue system is the real star, letting you choose how Henry responds to Delilah—whether he’s sarcastic, earnest, or guarded. These choices shape their relationship, though they don’t drastically alter the story’s path. It’s simple but effective, making every chat feel personal. The pacing can drag at times, and the limited interactivity might not satisfy everyone, but it fits the game’s quiet, reflective nature.

Pros:

✅ Intuitive exploration with a satisfying map-and-compass system.

✅ Dialogue choices add depth to character interactions.

✅ Minimalism enhances the story’s mood.

Cons:

❌ Gameplay lacks variety or challenge.

❌ Slow pace can feel repetitive.

3. Open World & Exploration – 8/10

The Shoshone National Forest is small but stunningly crafted. It’s not a sprawling open world like some modern titles, but every inch feels purposeful. From sun-drenched trails to shadowy canyons, the stylized art direction—courtesy of Olly Moss—turns the wilderness into a living painting. The day-night cycle and shifting weather add to the immersion, making each hike visually spectacular.

Exploration is rewarding in a subtle way: you’ll stumble across notes, abandoned camps, and scenic vistas that flesh out the world’s history. There’s no fast travel, which forces you to engage with the environment, though the compact map means you’re never truly lost. It’s a contained experience, but one that invites you to linger and soak in the details.

Pros:

✅ Gorgeous, cohesive world design.

✅ Subtle environmental storytelling.

✅ Compact yet immersive exploration.

Cons:

❌ Limited scope might feel restrictive to some.

4. Technical Performance & Graphics – 9/10

Visually, Firewatch is a treat. Its bold, painterly aesthetic—think warm oranges, cool blues, and soft shadows—sets it apart from photorealistic games. The forest feels alive, with rustling leaves and flickering light filtering through the trees. The soundtrack, composed by Chris Remo, is understated yet evocative, perfectly complementing the mood. Voice acting is top-notch, with Rich Sommer (Henry) and Cissy Jones (Delilah) delivering performances that carry the game.

On the technical side, it’s mostly smooth, though the original PC release had some bugs and performance hiccups. By 2025, most issues have been ironed out across platforms, including the Nintendo Switch port. It’s not a demanding game, so it runs well even on modest hardware.

Pros:

✅ Striking art style and lighting.

✅ Exceptional voice acting and sound design.

✅ Stable performance on modern systems.

Cons:

❌ Early technical issues linger in memory for some players.

Firewatch is an atmospheric masterpiece that creates a dense, immersive mood with minimal means. From the very beginning, the vast and beautiful Wyoming wilderness feels calming—yet there’s an underlying sense of unease. As seemingly harmless events unfold, a slow realization creeps in: something isn’t right. But maybe it’s all in your head? After all, you're completely alone, far away from civilization.

This isolation is captured perfectly. The world feels vast yet small, lonely yet never truly empty. You rarely see other people, but you constantly communicate via radio with Delilah, the only person in the game you can speak to. These conversations—brilliantly written and performed—carry much of the game’s emotional depth.

The sound design also plays a crucial role. The ambient noises of nature—the rustling wind, cracking branches, distant chirping—make you forget you’re in a game. Music is used sparingly, but when it does appear, it hits with maximum impact.

Despite its short playtime, Firewatch tells more than many hundred-hour open-world games. It is subtle and mysterious, rarely offering clear answers—but when it does, you can never be sure they are the truth. It creates a unique atmosphere, balancing tranquility and tension, relaxation and unease, vulnerability and control.

The gameplay itself may not be for everyone—it’s basically a walking simulator, an interactive experience that prioritizes storytelling and emotions over action or puzzles. But for those who embrace it, Firewatch delivers a story that lingers long after the credits roll. As I walked down the final path, I felt like I had lived through an entire adventure—yet it had only been a few hours. Firewatch is a timeless work of art.

Firewatch is one of those games that sticks with you long after the credits roll. It’s a beautifully crafted, story-driven experience that drops you into the Wyoming wilderness as Henry, a man coming to work as a fire lookout, trying to escape his messy life. Your only real connection is with Delilah, your supervisor, who you talk to over a handheld radio—and from there, things slowly unravel into a gripping mystery.

I won’t say too much about the story (since that’s what really makes the game shine), but exploring the gorgeously rendered forest, making choices that shape Henry’s relationship with Delilah, and uncovering secrets along the way was an unforgettable experience. It’s not a super long game—I finished 100% in just under 7 hours, with some idle time—but it’s absolutely worth playing.

That said, it’s not without its flaws. There are a few more bugs than I expected, and I did notice some traversal stutters here and there. Also, the later part of the story felt a little rushed—I would’ve loved to experience more days firsthand instead of skipping ahead so much. But even with those minor issues, Firewatch is an emotional, atmospheric, and visually stunning adventure that I’d highly recommend.

My main complaint about the game is that it feels clunky to play at times. The character gets stuck on stones and branches easily while just walking around. During some moments it feels like his character model is a bit too big, resulting in him getting stuck in places he shouldn't be. For example, the reeling in the watchtower, when walking back and forth it got a bit stuck from time to time, or when in the cave while jumping up and down these larger stones. 

A comment on the ending. It was a bit underwhelming. The choices I made for Henry leaned towards him being a guiltridden, but loyal and faithful husband. With some people, it doesn't matter how much quality time you spend with them, how deeply you get to know them, you're nothing more than an experience and a memory in the past.

It would be amazing if these small issues could be addressed. I’ve read that if you send the developers a screenshot, they can sometimes patch specific spots. But realistically, given how many little areas like this exist, it would probably require a full playthrough to catch them all — and after all, this game has been out since 2016, so that’s understandable.

Overall, I still recommend it! It’s a cool, short game with a lovely story. Just keep in mind that if smooth gameplay is very important to you, it might not be a perfect experience. If you can grab it on sale, it’s well worth it.

For the sake of Delilah's love for puns, I would say that Firewatch felt pedestrian. I really liked the promise of the game and the start of it ~1st hour, and I wanted to like the rest of it... Vibes, coziness, exploration, it all disappear for me the more I played.
I couldn't stop myself from thinking about what if Firewatch was a novel? It definitely felt like it would be a better novel than a game (especially in audiobook format). In the context of Firewatch, game medium offers developers 3 unique opportunities that they haven't used or didn't flesh out. Let's deal with everything in order.

[b]Gameplay:[/b] Very streamlined. It felt like the game take your hand and pull you along all the time. I totally understand that this game is about story and not the gameplay per se, but hear me out. Each diversion to explore a location wouldn't benefit in anything. No Easter eggs, no interesting stuff lying around, waiting to be explored. Nothing. Just one raccoon. Each mechanic (or resources for that mechanic) introduced in the game at the very convenient time to get through the location that time gated by the plot. They could just add more stuff along the way when you're hiking, so it would not feel like get from point A to point B all the time, which started to feel like a chore pretty quickly.

[b]Plot & choices:[/b] I felt robbed. Why make any choices in dialogues for the whole game if at the end the result is the same ? I—and maybe Henry too—felt another heartbreak. Maybe it's just me getting older and becoming a sucker for good endings, but developers teased relationships between Delilah and Henry. For me, it felt very natural that 2 broken souls that took that job would try to heal each other afterward. Is it so hard to introduce a "good" ending if you choose all positive dialogue options? Because dialogues itself were the most positive thing about the game. I really enjoyed them and I wanted more of them. I guess that introduces the idea of utter boringness in the wilderness very well—when the only person you can speak to is on a walkie-talkie with you. You develop a connection to that person.
With that chill introduction, for the 1st hour of the game, I expected a more relaxed game. Maybe it's more on me than on the game, but it made me wonder why each game tries to bring action and thriller motives when it doesn't need to? I would be totally happy to do mundane tasks as a forester/fire watcher, rather than feel ominous thrill for 3 hours. [spoiler]Who thrashed your room at the tower? Are girls got killed? By who? Who the hell smashed my head with a rock or something? Why and how someone listening and recording our talks with Delilah?[/spoiler] The game always put questions into your head, like you're some sort of detective, which isn't the bad thing per se, but it didn't work for me in that story. The majority of the time I just concentrated on the anxious nature of the game rather than enjoying it.

[b]Visuals & Audio:[/b] Could be better. It's not about chunky style. It just wasn't breathtaking enough, which I expected from that type of game. If not the gameplay should entertain you while you're hiking from point A to point B, then the visuals and audio (except the dialogue, which I discussed previously). Locations were fine, but that's it, not great. Music often turned on unexpectedly when you press a hidden trap panel, which sounded really weird, like you got to the boss room, but boss is nowhere near. And the general vibe of rather tense music to increase suspense of the plot didn't work for me as well.

To conclude my point, If Firewatch was a novel:
1. The dialogues would be fleshed out, and there will be more of them by the nature of the medium, and that's great.
2. Thriller idea feels like would suit much better for something like 50,000-60,000 words with good pacing.
3. Descriptions of surroundings could paint so much better picture than what I saw.
4. We wouldn't lose a lot of the gameplay, because it was almost point-and-click game, but in 3D.
5. Useless choices would be cut off, and we didn't lose a lot from it.

At the end of the day, it might be just not the game for me. But I reckon it's not the game for everyone, maybe not even for the most people. Still, I enjoyed some parts of Firewatch, but I can't recommend it for the majority of people.

The biggest complaint from this game's detractors is that they weren't completely satisfied with the ending -- and I don't really agree fully. I think that sometimes people forget that this game is meant to be grounded in reality.

The story, dialogue, voice acting, and landscape design are fantastic. Those are the biggest pros of this game, and you can tell this was a passion project for the devs. All of your dialogue options and ways of answering questions affect even the smallest things, and the devs put a lot of thought and had to record a TON of extra voice lines to accommodate different playstyles and dialogue choices. Super cool.

Slightly buggy physics in the game is probably the only real pain point I have. I got stuck on seemingly invisible terrain a few times.

This game gets a BIG recommend for me. I even played through the second time with dev commentary on and it was fantastic.

Initially I made a review of Firewatch and DID NOT recommend the game, but i have changed my mind.

Firewatch is a first-person narrative-driven adventure set in the Wyoming wilderness in 1989. You play as Henry, a man escaping his troubled past by taking a job as a fire lookout. Your only contact with the outside world is Delilah, your supervisor, whom you communicate with via radio.

As you explore the forest, strange events begin to unfold, leading you on a mystery that is both deeply personal and unsettling. The game focuses on storytelling, atmosphere, and player choices, making it a cinematic and emotional experience rather than an action-packed one.

[h2] ✅The Good [/h2]


[h3] 🖼️ 1. Stunning Visuals & Atmosphere[/h3]
Firewatch has a unique art style to the game, it's almost slightly cartoonish with the look of an oil painting, but together, it looks brilliant. The sunsets are a marvel to look at and the whole forest, although huge, has a peaceful yet eerie vibe

[h3]🎭 2. Fantastic Story & Character Writing[/h3]
The emotional depth of the story is one of Firewatch's biggest strengths.

Henry and Delilah’s conversations feel natural and realistic, thanks to top-tier voice acting and a well-written script.

Themes of loneliness, regret, and human connection are explored in a way that feels mature and thought-provoking.

[h3]🎙️ 3. Some of the Best Voice Acting in Gaming[/h3]
Rich Sommer (as Henry) and Cissy Jones (as Delilah) deliver incredibly nuanced performances, making the relationship between the characters feel genuine and emotionally compelling.

Dialogue choices feel organic, giving you room to shape the tone of your conversations.

[h3]🌲 4. Engaging Exploration & Mystery[/h3]
The game starts as a relaxing wilderness experience but gradually builds tension, making the unfolding mystery feel gripping and suspenseful.

There’s a real sense of isolation and paranoia as events escalate.

[h3]🎵 5. Beautiful Soundtrack & Sound Design[/h3]
The ambient sounds of the forest (birds chirping, wind rustling through trees) make the world feel alive.

The soundtrack is subtle yet impactful, enhancing the emotional moments of the story.

[h2]❌ The Bad[/h2]


[h3]⏳ 1. Short Playtime & Limited Replayability[/h3]
I completed the entire game in 1 evening, it took me just over 3 hours and i wasn't rushing. There also isn't much replayability to Firewatch unless you want to select different dialogue options between Henry and Delilah but for me that isn't worth it and in my opinion, 3 hours is far too short for a game to be completed


[h3]📜 2. The Ending is Divisive[/h3]
This really upset me, frankly, the ending is terrible. 
After the game building suspense and really gripping me throughout the whole story, I was expecting some plot twist or something more interesting than what happened, the game ended and I was certain that there must be something more that I haven't uncovered yet, I was wrong, the game just has a terrible ending

[h3]🚶‍♂️ 3. Limited Gameplay Mechanics[/h3]
Firewatch is essentially a walking simulator, with no real puzzles, combat, or deep mechanics.

I guess this is ok for a game that is ONLY 3 hours long, but take what you will from that.

[h3]🌎 4. Open World Feels Underused[/h3]
While the world is beautiful and immersive, there are few reasons to explore beyond the main story path.

You can roam the environment, but there’s little reward for doing so.

[h2]🎯 Final Verdict[/h2]
🔥 Firewatch is one of the best narrative-driven adventure games out there, offering a deeply personal story, stunning visuals, and top-tier voice acting. However, its short length, limited interactivity, and divisive ending left me feeling a little bit like Firewatch could have had more to give.

🎖️ Score: 7/10 – A must-play for fans of story-driven games, but those looking for deep gameplay mechanics or a grand mystery may be left wanting more.

Criticism surrounding videogames can often revolve around what a game isn't trying to be. Its unsatisfying timeline; its uncomfortable protagonists; its uninteresting gameplay. While it's completely valid to have personal preferences towards what games you find interesting (and frankly those should be embraced), there is a point to be made about separating feelings from critique, a point that can be learned and practiced through analysis.

This leads me to Firewatch, a game I feel is prone to this type of critique. And what I find most interesting about Firewatch, is exactly what many of its players seemed to be opposed to: it decidedly is not a satisfying videogame. The story presented will not wrap up any bows; the character dynamics are going to feel strange to some degree; the gameplay will have you feeling lost and potentially even frustrated. Firewatch is a story about the inevitability of escapism and reality blending together. While you may be able to see yourself in this game's simulated wilderness, and perhaps find it as a means of comfort, you are not granted the ability to escape for long-- not unlike Henry or Delilah. You have to be reminded of the existence of reality.

You may enter this forest if you choose to, but it shall not let you stay.

Without spoiling much there is a somewhat mysterious plot that takes place over the course of the game, so the game is more than just wandering around a forest. While it’s not a very long game, taking me just over 5 hours to 100%, and it does have more bugs than I would expect from such a short and fairly simple game, and it does suffer from traversal stutters; it was an absolutely fantastic experience that I paid 2 or 3 dollars for. I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys slower paced story rich games and can enjoy a game that his little to no gameplay.

Simulation Experience

The weakest parts of Firewatch are the start and the end, and it certainly does have its problems. 

But man, the parts in between are captivating and tension-strung - the mystery, sense of loneliness and the fact you're all alone in the woods by yourself save for a voice at the end of a walkie talkie...it's such a great concept. And sometimes, that concept really shines through.

The soundtrack/sound design helps a lot with settling you into that mindframe, and lost in the Yellowstone forest, trudging and taking it in to appreciate the surroundings, and it giving you a moment to breathe and reflect, is part of the experience imo.
It reminds me of my own hiking trips, how cathartic it can be to just be out wandering and resting your thoughts, away from daily life's stressors.

The art direction is gorgeous; many have mentioned how the landscapes in this game make for some fantastic wallpapers. Vibrant, lush colours painted in different lighting scenarios throughtout points of the story look amazing especially.

The gameplay is nothing to write home about, but Firewatch was never about the gameplay being the forefront runner. And as someone who doesn't mind narrative games, this is ok with me but I can see someone who plays more regular games getting frustrated or bored.

The story is a big part of the game and I'll admit I'm not entirely certain how much my decisions influence the story, but I have to assume it's not much if the main story beats are mostly the same for everyone.
As with my main opinion of the game, it has some very strong moments that I think are worth experiencing Firewatch for. 
But, it's let down by writing that at times feels like it meanders too much like it's building up to something, only to then not have a pay off.
The main mystery is still good and has a conclusion, however it lacks the consequences of it.
 
Before I played this, I've seen a lot of people talk about a cliffhanger.
And I will say I agree only to a certain extent. 
The ending does have closure, only it feels rushed and leaves more questions than there are answers, which left me feeling confused and a smidge irate. 

Even despite that, as I said earlier, I think this is a game worth playing if you have your expectations in check.
I only wish it was a bit more organised and coherent than what we ended up getting.

Firewatch is a walking simulator that evolves into a mystery in its final stages before it all fades away. This game explores themes of isolation and delves into feelings of solitude and sadness. It is a game about grief.

As I mentioned earlier, this game primarily functions as a walking simulator. Thus, the gameplay isn't particularly exciting; however, exploring the forest can be quite soothing. It encourages a sense of calm; there isn't much to do except hike around, fix things, and discover your surroundings, along with experiencing getting stung by a bee, being startled by a raccoon, adopting a turtle, and occasionally getting hit in the head.

The beginning of Firewatch features a poignant story. As you hike up the mountain, you receive flashbacks of the past, learning how Henry met his wife, how they fell in love, how they spent their time together, and how everything changed once Julia developed Alzheimer’s. This makes for an emotionally charged experience. Henry struggles to escape his sadness, trying to forget that his beloved wife is forgetting him, while a father copes with the death of his son, creating a powerful emotional journey. That said, the ending of Firewatch was disappointing, yet it also felt fitting. Although there was no grand conspiracy, twist, or perhaps a happy ending, the conclusion felt like a true ending—an end to evading the real world, an end to trying to forget your grief, and an end to both summer and the job you took. It's hard to express in words, but the ending is crafted in a way that leaves everything open to your interpretation. Did Henry reunite with his wife? Did he leave? Did he and Delilah ever meet? It’s up to you to decide, which, in my view, was a wise choice. This makes the game more memorable than others because the ending prompts you to ask questions and encourages you to fill in the narrative with your own imagination.

It took me a while to finish this game. Originally, I started it a few years ago... left it unfinished in my backlog, then picked it back up and started over from beginning to end in one sitting. In terms of playtime, it will not amount to much. I think of it as an experience that's closer to watching a movie than playing a video game. TLDR: I think it's worth it. I'd happily pay for this game for the same amount I'd be spending at the movie theaters, if not a bit more.

The game is quite pretty. It has a bit of a cartoony (for lack of a better word) style, but manages to still capture the visual majesty of American national parks. The colors are gorgeous and the setting works well to intensify the paradoxical feelings freedom and isolation out in the wilderness. The invisible walls do occasionally break the flow, but I personally did not find it frustrating since this was clearly intended to be a linear experience. 

Getting the gameplay stuff out of the way: this is a walking sim. You will mainly be traveling from Point A to Point B and pressing interaction and dialogue prompts. There is a decent amount of backtracking going on, which may seem tedious at times, but as you get more familiar with using the map and the environment, it becomes more tolerable. For the [i]most[/i] part, it's packaged fairly well. I was stuck at a couple of points, but the solutions were not actually obtuse or anything. I'm just spotty at problem solving sometimes. Overall - it doesn't really offer much in terms of gameplay/mechanics. But obviously, this is not what the game is about. 

The game is centered around conversations and exchanges between two people working as fire lookouts in a national forest. Without spoiling anything, the dialogue is deliberately crafted to reveal aspects of their personalities rather than their backgrounds. The dialogue is also supported by excellent voice acting, among the best I've ever heard in video games, to be honest. The story itself is not exactly remarkable, but this game isn't selling a great story - it's selling great characters. 

...And that is a point which I believe some reviewers are missing when they say the conclusion (again - I'm not spoiling anything, I just want to address a common criticism) fell flat. The writing is fairly grounded from the very beginning, and because of the increasing tensions and twists that occur throughout the chapters, people may have developed expectations about where the plot is headed. I would argue that those expectations are misguided, and that the writers were fully aware about "reining it in" at the end. But of course, this is just my opinion. I find the realism refreshing in a medium dominated by cliches, character tropes, melodrama, and extreme power fantasies. 

Firewatch will probably stay in my head for a while, in the same way that a good book will stay in my head long after I turn the final page. It was not profound in the sense that it was enlightening, but in the sense that it touched on something very viscerally human - when we seek avenues to escape the troubles and tragedies that plague our lives, they may only remind us of what is actually important in the end.

When Firewatch was released in 2016, critics and players alike showered it with praise, calling it an emotional, immersive, and beautifully written experience. But after playing it, I can’t help but ask: Was everyone playing the same game???

A Mystery Without a Meaningful Conclusion

The game starts with an interesting premise: However, the game never delivers a satisfying conclusion. The mystery seemingly resolves itself without any real impact, and major plot threads feel underdeveloped or abandoned. What starts as an eerie and suspenseful journey quickly loses its momentum, leaving me wondering what the point of it all was. 

One of the biggest frustrations this game is how disconnected it makes you feel. You never truly interact with another character face-to-face but instead only through voices on a radio, audio tapes, or distant silhouettes. You cannot even see Delilah. She’s with you the entire game, talking to you, guiding you, sharing jokes, and even opening up emotionally—but when you finally get the chance to meet her at the end, she’s already gone. (╯‵□′)╯︵┻━┻ like WTF...

It almost feels like the developers ran out of budget or time and decided to wrap things up as quickly as possible, leaving players with an underwhelming and rushed resolution.

Not recommended.

Is it a game? By definition, it's not. Firewatch is an interactive experience.
Does it look nice? Yes it does.
Does it have a good story? Meeeeh.. it does have a story. Nothing spectacular. No idea what everybody's raving about.
Does it have gameplay? No. None. Mechanically it's as empty as California's water reserves.

TBH, it would have fared a lot better as a movie. Because with Firewatch what you essentially have is a movie where story is bogged down by long uneventful treks through bushes and brushes with annoyingly long unnecessary interaction animations (climbing, I'm looking at you!). It gets to the level so bad where you actually start avoiding any trail that has non-gradual terrain, because walking long-way around is probably faster than going through 8 canned animations.
And the gameplay. Oh Lord... it's nonexistant. No, turning a flashligt on & off is not a gemeplay feature. No, walking to an interactable and pressing a button to progress the story is NOT a game mechanic. No, watching the grass grow and occasionally selecting a timed dialogue option does not constitute a high skill challenge.

To sum it up, it's pretentious. Should've been a movie, that would've saved you 3 hours of your life.

Firewatch Review: A Hauntingly Beautiful Story of Isolation and Connection
Rating: 8.5/10

Pros:
✔️ Stunning visuals and immersive atmosphere
✔️ Excellent voice acting and character writing
✔️ Engaging mystery with emotional depth
✔️ Well-paced storytelling and environmental storytelling

Cons:
❌ Some loose ends in the story
❌ Limited interactivity beyond walking and dialogue

Review:
Firewatch is a unique narrative-driven adventure that immerses players in the vast wilderness of Wyoming, blending mystery, personal drama, and psychological tension. Developed by Campo Santo, the game puts you in the role of Henry, a man seeking escape from his troubled past by taking a summer job as a fire lookout. Your only human connection is Delilah, your supervisor, who communicates via radio, leading to some of the best voice-acted conversations in gaming.

The game excels in atmosphere, with breathtaking landscapes that shift between tranquil beauty and eerie solitude. The writing is sharp, and the evolving dynamic between Henry and Delilah feels incredibly real, balancing humor, flirtation, and emotional weight. As the mystery unfolds—strange occurrences, missing persons, and the feeling of being watched—the game builds tension without relying on cheap scares.

However, Firewatch does leave some unanswered questions, and while the conclusion is poignant, some players may find it lacking resolution. That said, the journey is what makes Firewatch special, not just the destination.

For those who enjoy story-driven experiences, emotional narratives, and atmospheric exploration, Firewatch is a must-play. It’s not about action or puzzles—it’s about human connection, loss, and the weight of solitude.

I initially didn't dislike this enough to downvote it, but by the time I finished writing this review I had changed my mind. Since this is marketed as a "Story Rich" game, and the story really turned my stomach in places, I can't in good faith recommend it. Which is a shame, because I could wander around in the beautiful natural-park landscape for hours, but I just could not - I repeat COULD NOT - stand Delilah. If the writers were truly shooting for an insufferable, morally irresponsible woman to the nth degree, I suppose they did a good job, because I was so grateful when Henry finally muted her a$$ and I discovered we could ignore her even when he didn't. Take the following shining examples of her character:

[list]
[*] Constantly getting drunk on the job - how are you going to spot forest fires and save lives if you're barely lucid? Also, how much respect can you possibly inspire as a supervisor this way?
[*] "Two girls disappeared under suspicious circumstances while camping and skinny-dipping in a remote park. There's [i]no way[/i] it could be foul play. But if they turn up dead, then... I guess? I don't want to talk to the cops though, so I'm not going to say anything until that happens." - [b][i]Then proceeding to lie to the cops.[/i][/b] Need I say more, or are you also 1000% fed up with this woman?
[*] A kid's intact, loaded backpack turns up in the middle of nowhere, with his name tag still on it. [b]Normal people:[/b] Something bad could have happened, no one would leave essential survival gear behind like this, we should ask after him. [b]Delilah:[/b] Idk, maybe he just didn't need it anymore and went home...?
[*] Failing to report on a lookout bringing his kid (against the rules) to the park. Kid dies in a climbing accident. Delilah proceeds to throw herself a pity party when she finds out, because she's clearly suffered the most in this situation.
[*] Her intentions towards a guy who's mourning his lost relationship with his beloved wife, who has dementia. Surely, the most crass, distasteful move in this situation would be to try and start something with such a guy, implying that he can just ditch his poor sick wife. [b]Delilah:[/b] Challenge Accepted! (The utter AUDACITY!)
[*] And a final round of stand-up citizen vibes: "I know we have to evacuate ASAP because the park's burning down and could take us with it. I'm going to leave right now, Henry, I just don't feel like waiting any longer. (Nothing to do with you rejecting me or anything.) Don't worry, I'm sure the help will come back for you. That's their job."
[/list]

And that's just what I remember, based on accidentally initiated / forced conversations (I began to skip the dialogue/reporting options whenever I could). Henry may be a little dull, and I won't even get started on Ned, but Delilah really killed the story for me. Why the game tries to shoehorn her in as a romantic interest is beyond me. Must every story with a man and woman in it end with them getting together? Should basic decency and grace regarding a preexisting relationship be damned? Whatever happened to that poor, atrophied word known as "friendship"? I guess people always get desperate and messy when they're lonely enough, right?

Finally, although I was happy to see there was a "Free Roam" mode (and wish this game had been just that to begin with), the controls are a little lacking for a landscape that just begs to be explored. Being able to jump only in limited places, and not even starting out with basic tools like, say, rope or axe, kind of broke the immersion of a wilderness-based game. I should not have to make it through 50-75% of the main story before being able to chop down branches. I'll probably come back to this game eventually just to wander around (as best as I can) for the sky and forest views, but if I hadn't already spent over 3 hours on it, I think I'd have tried for a refund.

Given what Firewatch is pitched as I think it fails. For a game in the wilderness, the world feels incredibly static and unalive. The environment feels more like a haunted house with nature wrapping paper. This might serve better if the "who done it" plot had a better mystery with a stronger cast of characters, but the one-dimensional dialogue consistently caused me to care less and less about the narrative. I'll admit, one thing that Firewatch does excellently is storytelling through sound design. The mix of walkie-talkie, music, and natural sounds led to some really tense moments; unfortunate then that all of the build-up is followed by a let-down.

SPOILER thoughts about narrative below, this is a mystery game after all...
[spoiler] I think when it comes to endings, it ought to be less about the surprise factor and more about whether or not what happens feels earned by the character and more importantly the audience. I think we're meant to see Ned Goodwin as the father who watched his son die whom he very much loved, and because of grief never knew how to return to the civilized world. Contrastingly, Henry has been watching his wife die and chooses to run away to the wilderness. The question we have throughout the game is whether or not Henry will ever return home to continue to care for his wife even in the face of death. He does ultimately return home, not by choice, but rather by a sort of deus ex machina i.e. a forest fire ending the game. Rather than experiencing Henry processing his grief, we are spoonfed a shallow love story as our only hope. Often the wilderness and camping are used as a way to escape, but also a processing tool. Ultimately, rather than tackling the difficult topics and exploring the potential complexities of marriage, the narrative attempts to side-step it all, and it truly just does not fulfill. [/spoiler] 

Is it weird then that after all of this, I still think Firewatch attempts something unique here? Even though the whole does not add up to the sum of its parts, this game sets a target for what can be done with new methods of video game storytelling. We do not need hours of cutscenes or massive open worlds, but rather an environment worth exploring and a narrative worth uncovering. Perhaps Campo Santo's next game will rise to the occasion.

Firewatch: The Most Overrated Hike You’ll Ever Take

Alright, let’s talk about Firewatch. People act like this game is some profound emotional experience, but let’s be real—it’s just a glorified nature walk with a radio. You wander around the woods, chat with a woman who’s never actually there, and pretend your dialogue choices matter. Spoiler: they don’t.

The game starts strong, I’ll give it that. The intro hits you with some sad backstory, and you think you’re about to embark on some deep, mysterious journey. But by the end, it’s like, that’s it? The “big twist” is about as shocking as finding out your DoorDash driver ate some of your fries.

Visually? Gorgeous. The art style is fantastic. But at the end of the day, it’s still just walking. You’re essentially playing as a guy on a midlife crisis retreat with zero real agency. 

Look, if you love the whole "walking simulator with feelings" genre, you might dig it. But if you want actual gameplay keep away

Firewatch is a walking simulator story game. The game took me a short 4 hours but they used those hours to the best, the story constantly had me hooked, and the environment of the game fills in those quiet gaps very well. Easily recommend, even more so if on sale.

Firewatch is an unforgettable journey through the serene yet haunting landscape of the Shoshone National Forest. Set in 1989, you step into the boots of Henry, a fire lookout stationed in a remote tower, tasked with the quiet yet profound responsibility of keeping watch over the wilderness. The beauty of the game lies not only in its stunning visuals but in its emotional depth, where the landscape becomes a backdrop for personal reflection and mystery.
The narrative, masterfully told through your interactions with Delilah—your witty, often poignant supervisor—is gripping. With only a walkie-talkie as your connection to the outside world, you’ll find yourself unraveling clues that build a sense of suspense and intrigue. The game seamlessly blends peaceful exploration with subtle psychological tension, making each new discovery both thrilling and introspective.
Firewatch isn't just about solving a mystery; it's about the journey itself—one of solitude, connection, and self-discovery. A truly compelling experience that will stay with you long after the credits roll. Highly recommended for anyone who enjoys emotional storytelling wrapped in a beautiful, immersive world.

Firewatch is a short narrative tale of a man named Henry, who does a stint of time as a fire lookout in a national park to escape from trauma in his personal life. He talks with his supervisor, Delilah, via walkie-talkie throughout the game, who initially gives him simple tasks to attend to as a lookout. After a brief period of time though, strange things start happening around the pair, and they both become wrapped into a mystery that could uncover some hidden secrets of the national park, threatening those who wish to keep those secrets buried for good. Firewatch plays almost entirely as a walking simulator, given a map to loosely traverse the park at your own pace and encountering new hints and secrets regarding the mystery along the way. I felt that the gameplay was simple yet relaxing, and the scenery you walk around is absolutely gorgeous, with some beautiful forests, lakes, and trails to navigate through. The dialogue between the two main characters was charming and felt incredibly organic. The story was mostly intriguing, but if I had to give the game one gripe it's that the ending felt a little flat. There's a pretty big climax build-up for the hour before the end, and then when the resolution occurs it feels kinda...eh? Like I suppose the story is resolved *technically*, but I guess I just expected maybe a little bit more of...something. That being said, I got the game for I think $5 on a sale, and it was absolutely worth $5 for a relaxing and engaging mystery. Even for full price I'd probably still recommend Firewatch, just maybe don't hold your breath for an absolutely amazing ending.

Starting off with the story, it will leave you on the edge of your seat. Questioning what is real, only to be hit with the hard truth of reality by the end in one of the most shocking scene I have seen in a game to date. It uses fantasy, to ground you.

It's biggest appeal going in is the atmosphere and sense of adventure you get once you first hop into the game. It is one of the most gorgeous games I have ever played, and certain landscapes will somehow through simple layouts make your jaw drop. This is by far the biggest strength of the game but it unfortunately held back through one major issue.

I found myself often being pulled out of the atmosphere to face, not nature blocking my path, but poorly designed "invisible" barriers. What may once be enough distance between a bush and a tree to fit through, will another time be too tight. It would be one thing if this was a one off, as natural barriers can often be hard to pull off, but for how reliant on atmosphere this game is, they should have found a fix for this.

Moreover, the game (when you pull out your map) will remind you where you need to go, yet it fails to mention details anywhere that were said in the conversation with Delilah prior, just the vague area. It is one thing to not have told us details on how to get there in the first place, but you will often forget or second guess the specific directions you were told to reach the area, which will leave to extra time wasted, wandering about the completely wrong loop.

To sum up these thoughts, it is a unique adventure, boggled down by simple fixes that could have been addressed easily, but were not. Leaving this game, I will not remember just the highlights it wants me to remember, but also the needless infuriating parts also. However, I still recommend this game, but not at the base 20 euro price tag. You will want to experience this game, but it can wait.

I discovered Firewatch through a random TikTok video, and I'm so glad I gave it a chance. I didn’t expect this game to be as captivating as it turned out to be. From the very beginning, the story pulls you in with its mystery and emotional depth, and the emotions I felt after finishing this game stayed with me long after the credits rolled.
Unlike some players, I didn’t find the ending underwhelming at all. It wraps up in a way that feels honest to the story and its themes, leaving room for reflection. The beauty of Firewatch lies in its ability to let you make choices that shape how the narrative unfolds, allowing each player to imagine their own version of the story. 
Visually, this game is breathtaking. The stunning landscapes of Wyoming’s Shoshone National Forest are beautifully rendered, immersing you in a world of towering pines, glowing sunsets, and rolling hills. The graphics make every moment feel like you’re walking through a painting.
What truly elevates Firewatch is its character development and voice acting. Henry and Delilah feel real, their conversations natural and heartfelt. The dialogue builds a genuine connection, making their story all the more impactful.
The music is another standout. Every track is perfectly timed and beautifully composed, amplifying the emotional beats of the game. It’s one of those soundtracks that sticks with you long after the credits roll.
Overall, Firewatch is a masterpiece of storytelling, atmosphere, and emotion. It’s not just a game—it’s an experience. If you’re on the fence about buying it, I strongly recommend it. You won’t be disappointed.

[h2]A Visually Stunning and Flawlessly Acted Masterpiece[/h2]
[h3]Rating: 10/10[/h3]
Firewatch is an absolute masterpiece and an essential experience. It is a first-person adventure set in the stunning, visually arresting Shoshone National Forest, where you play as Henry, a fire lookout escaping a complicated past. 

The game is driven almost entirely by the brilliant, naturalistic voice acting between Henry and his supervisor, Delilah, conducted solely over a walkie-talkie. It feels so real.

Its storytelling is masterful, blending a compelling central mystery with a profound, emotional examination of human connection, grief, and self-discovery. 

The art direction is breathtaking, making every moment of exploration feel like stepping into a vibrant, living painting.

[h3]Time?[/h3]
The story is between 4 to 5 hours. It took me about 8 hours to 100%

[h3]Final Verdict[/h3]
This is a must-play for anyone who values superb writing, emotional depth, and atmosphere in video games. Buy this if you love narrative adventures, "walking simulators," or beautiful games that tell a mature, character-driven story.

It's about Fear, I feel. Not as in horror, or even terror, but a growing sense of unease, despair, disappointment, anger, sadness, all just gnawing in your head, stuck at the back of your mind like plaque.

And so, you run, and it follows... it manifests itself again in the discomfort of unfamiliar people, irritated by a younger generation that's impossible to relate to, a mysterious stranger keeping tabs on you bringing about paranoia... the escapist fantasy of the outdoors isn't magically a different world than the one you lived before, the isolation of Shoshone National Park just draws the fear out from inside you, finding scraps of it in everything.

There's more I can say, but to sum my thoughts up, (and without spoiling because like all games, it really is best enjoyed blind) I found Firewatch to be a deeply moving exploration of Isolation, Escapism, and Consequence, impossible to evade as they are.

My only complaint is that even though I would say I took my time with the narrative, and explored around and enjoyed the conversations I had, the runtime of the game was still fairly short, finishing in 4 hours. I think being able to finish it in one sitting made it more enjoyable than it would have been if it were overly drawn out, though.

The TLDR; you're going to have a good time if you expect a 70s / 80s style bottle movie. You're going to have a moderately good time if you want to be awed by nature. You're going to have a less good time if you want to brilliantly untangle a mystery.

I finally got around to _Firewatch_. The nature design was great, I kept getting lost more than in real forests and wall hugging like an idiot got you jammed in dead ends obstructed by plant noise. The nature design was also terrible, it felt like a videogame level in the worst possible way, full of unimpressive border blocks and silly gates; you felt physically railroaded to the story. The ludo-narrative dissonance eventually got to me: it should absolutely be possible to fall, drown, faint if the environment itself is to hold any menace. You should certainly be threatened by the fire, and once I realised how empty the pyrotechnics are, the ending deflated a lot.

It gets a bit spoilery below.

Story wise, I think it wants to have its cake and eat it on multiple levels. It wants to be a spooky mystery story that gets tied up in a neat little bow, and it also leans very heavily on how unreliable a narrator you are about what's actually going on - but it doesn't actually commit to it and leaves you to do 100% of the labour to get anything out of that angle. I tried to play the character as a frank, hard stuck alcoholic - there's enough great expressive choice here. Will you notice the ring? Put it back on? What items are you trying to save when you flee? What cap is your go-to? What do you think is worth photographing? But when the game chooses to respond to your choices it feels very clumsy. The snoop reports break the fourth wall when you're supposed to be paranoid or tense, and the romance of convenience / desperation with Delilah is formally appropriate, but also kind of tired. I did enjoy her conveying an actual character, which I had no faith would actually happen.

Also, I hated hated hated how telescoped the days get near the end. The start in random point on map, deliver plot beat, cut to day transition part. I had ideas of my own on how to resolve the mystery, but I wasn't allowed any agency to explore them. I get they wanted to build momentum, and not have an 80 hour game where 76 hours are pointless meandering, but fighting the loading system is not my idea of immersion. And I guess that's my main point of contention with the game; it's good at being a 70s movie character study, but I wanted a more immersive experience.

Firewatch is a rarity in the gaming sphere in that, like its few peers, fully utilise the interactivity of the game format to delve into the human experience and connections, letting the player make organic choices that influence relationships and outcomes. It is a short yet impactful experience that leaves you wanting more from the story, yet it still achieved the objective that it set out to accomplish: to give a glimpse into another person's life that could almost be a reality. Many video games released now rely on superhuman characters and satisfying plot conclusions that make the players feel powerful and contented. But life isn't like that. Things rarely resolve neatly, and often you have to come to terms with that, and keep moving forward, doing what you have with what you can. This is what Firewatch is about. It is about relearning what life is, and what we do from here can make all the difference.

This is a deeply personal game, that I don't think I will replay anytime soon, or maybe ever. Because, I don't want to sully my experience of this playthrough, ever. I know I would be unable to experience these raw emotions for a second time, so I'll always remember and love this game, but it has to collect dust in my steam library. - The game is pretty short, it took me less than 5 hours to complete it. I am sure that there is more to discover but the end came so fast... And a day ends the moment all is done, you have no option to continue until you return back to your stand.
- There are some little but annoying issues like finding the spot where to grab the rope, small rocks you can step on from one side but the character will not step down on the other side even when it is like 5 cm to the ground, radio playing music over the music background of the game or inaccurate areas to interact with items. Also, every time you put down your map it will hide your compass as well and you are unable to walk faster when you have a map in your hands. Faster walking did not work at the very end as well, no idea why. Some bigger items can't be fully inspected because walkie-talkie was covering part of the item. Or it was at least hard and uncomfortable.
- Most of your answers over the radio are time limited, you have to choose in few seconds. In some cases I was unable to even read all options in such short period and it was even more complicated when you were doing something else by that time, like climbing or reading game tips.
- Maybe it was just me, but some game mechanics were not clear at the beginning like that some events can be reported only when you point on it. I have missed all time limited ones at the very beginning of the game because a moment later the event was gone and I was unable to find what was highlighted a second before.  I have always stopped and completed the conversation before I did any further action in later gameplay.
- There is no option to ask for a specific information again or, in most cases, to ask for a general help. You can communicate only in case you are contacted or you have something to report. However, the game is pretty easy and guides you more or less so the hardest is to get oriented at some locations and find your way through bushes. 
- You might be disappointed by the game end, not just because it comes so soon but also because it might not reflect the way you direct your answers and how did you understood the relationship of Henry and D. But this is individual.

An honest review of Firewatch

The feeling when I was first playing this game reminded me of my favorite game, Outer Wilds. The exploration, making theories about the story of it all, and Firewatch does exceptionally well in these aspects. But where Outer Wilds's ending filled me with feelings of happiness and conclusion, Firewatch just left me unsatisfied.

The entire game is building up to this "big bad" throughout the story. There are tiny clues spread across the world map hinting at who is up to this madness that you and your boss have been put through. But in the end, the game concludes with you finding out that it was a random kids dad who you don't even meet. And when you find this, the characters don't really seem concerned and just go on with the plan to evacuate the forest. The game ends with you having one final chat with your boss, and then just leaving on a helicopter.

I would give the GAME (excluding the ending) an 8/10. I really enjoyed my experience playing through Firewatch. I loved the visuals and just how peaceful it was to explore at your own pace. But with the ending being so, disappointing, I would give Firewatch overall an 5/10. All of the work you put into the mystery of this game just feels, robbed. 

Did I enjoy this game? Somewhat. Is it worth 20$? No, not at all. I finished the entire game in just under 3 hours and it doesn't feel worth it for a game of this price. If you want to play this game, I recommend getting it on sale. 

In conclusion, I think that the main game is good, but the ending puts it to shame. I wouldn't recommend this game because of its ending. If you enjoy this game, (or it's your favorite) that's fine, but I personally didn't like it.

I watched a lets play of this game when it came out, but by now I forgot everything. This game fits my fav subcategory of games: "like a good book you read in the afternoon” It is short compact beautiful experience.
The story is captivating and full of mystery and tension, yet the woods are peaceful. The art styles use of colors is just *chefs kiss* and the soundtrack is one of my most favorite ones.
Some people dislike the ending but I liked it, I think it was fitting, quite poetic. The game isn’t a fantasy, it is based in real life. Its about grieve, running away, isolation, relationships and the purpose they have during a certain live period. 

The biggest negative in my opinion is the lack of explorations.  It is a walking sim, you will be asked to go to a point a, then b, then c and so on.
