Don’t Trust the Walkie-Talkie Lady
You’re here to watch for fires, but Delilah on the walkie-talkie keeps dragging you into her drama. Here’s why you shouldn’t listen to her:

1. Bad Advice: “Go check out that spooky noise!” Meanwhile, she’s cozy in her tower. Don’t fall for it.

2. Distracting Drama: She’s vague, dodgy, and keeps secrets. Focus on the job, not her soap opera.

3. Red Flags Everywhere: She’s too chill about illegal stuff and ignores danger signs. Trust your gut, not her.

4. You’re Not Her Pawn: Next time she says, “Go investigate,” remind her you’re not her errand boy.

Enjoy the forest, do your job, and don’t let Delilah’s charm ruin your peaceful retreat!

[i]Firewatch[/i] is a first-person adventure game developed by Campo Santo, set in the Wyoming wilderness in 1989. You take on the role of Henry, a fire lookout, communicating with Delilah, your supervisor, via radio. The game focuses on exploration, narrative, and emotional storytelling.
[hr]
[b][h2]Gameplay[/h2][/b]
    [b]Exploration:[/b] The game emphasizes navigating the Shoshone National Forest with a map and compass, solving occasional puzzles along the way.
    [b]Dialogue Choices:[/b] Your relationship with Delilah evolves based on your dialogue choices, which shape the narrative.
    [b]Mystery Elements:[/b] As the story unfolds, strange events add tension and mystery, driving the plot forward.
[hr]
[b][h2]Visuals and Atmosphere[/h2][/b]
    [b]Art Style:[/b] Featuring a beautiful, painterly art style, the game uses vibrant colors to create a stunning and immersive world.
    [b]Sound Design:[/b] Top-notch voice acting and ambient sounds enhance the atmosphere, pulling you into the experience.
    [b]Environmental Storytelling:[/b] Clues scattered throughout the world deepen the narrative and reward exploration.
[hr]
[b][h2]Story and Themes[/h2][/b]
    [b]Character-Driven:[/b] The narrative delves into themes of isolation, loss, and human connection, creating a deeply personal experience.
    [b]Ambiguity:[/b] The story leaves some elements open to interpretation, encouraging thoughtful reflection.
    [b]Emotional Impact:[/b] The intimate story and character interactions leave a lasting emotional impression.
[hr]
[b][h2]Pros[/h2][/b]
    [b]Well-Written Dialogue:[/b] The natural and engaging conversations between Henry and Delilah make their relationship feel authentic.
    [b]Stunning Atmosphere:[/b] A combination of striking visuals and immersive sound design creates a captivating world.
    [b]Emotional Depth:[/b] The narrative is powerful, resonating on a personal level.
[hr]
[b][h2]Cons[/h2][/b]
    [b]Linear Gameplay:[/b] The game follows a linear path with limited replayability, and choices have a minimal impact on the overall outcome.
    [b]Short Length:[/b] With a playtime of about 3-6 hours, some may find the game too brief.
[hr]
[b][h2]Conclusion[/h2][/b]
[i]Firewatch[/i] is a standout narrative adventure that excels in storytelling and atmosphere. Its emotional depth and immersive world make it a memorable experience, even if its linear nature and short length may not appeal to everyone.

[b]Rating: 8.5/10[/b]

I endeavor to provide constructive and respectful criticism. I will begin with negatives but may the reader keep in mind I am only beginning there and I DO recommend this game.

ISSUES
- While movement in general feels good, some obstacles require an animation to traverse (climbing, jumping across gaps, dropping down from ledges, etc.) and they feel jarring, do not always transition smoothly, and can be somewhat buggy. On the plus side, this does cause me to naturally choose paths which involve fewer of these obstacles when possible which likely reflects an actual hiker's decisions as well.
- The Supply Caches only feel significant from a navigation standpoint (map notes and locating yourself on the map if you have that disabled) and not from what you find within them, seeming to defeat the idea of a supply cache. They highlight the fact that you don’t really need anything in the game. While that fact itself isn’t necessarily a problem, constantly reminding us every time we open a cache that ‘oh, right what was I hoping would be here I have no use for anything’ is immersion breaking
- The narrative conclusion feels underwhelming. Without giving spoilers, I’ll say that this disappointment has nothing to do with the answers to the physical mystery present in the game, but the fact that Henry’s backstory and personal dilemma seems in many ways forgotten about during the bulk of the plot despite how often it is mentioned. This becomes particularly confusing and concerning in regards to his interactions with Delilah.
- While it does have a good story, the game is overly focused on telling it quickly. When playing a game for the first time I try to move at the pace the game seems intended to be played at. With that said, the way the game and the narrative interact give no space for exploration. Instead, you are given a prompt to go to a certain place with some urgency and once each narrative piece for the day concludes the day is ended against your will and it moves on to the next day that something relevant to the plot happens. While you can choose to explore at various points, doing so would require ignoring what is going on at the time in the narrative.

POSITIVES
- The narrative itself is rather gripping and interesting. It sets up a good mystery and gives a conclusion to that mystery which was properly set up.
- The ambience to the game is phenomenal
- The radio mechanic is innovative. It is easy to use and serves the game practically while also somewhat simulating the feeling of actually using a walkie-talkie. 
- The chemistry between Henry and Delilah is perfect. The dialogue rarely feels annoying, instead I found myself honestly enjoying interacting via the dialogue prompts with Delilah. Simply talking was a quality experience.
- The terrain and scenery feels realistic but diverse.

Overall I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good mystery and some wanderlust.

An eight-year-old work, with a very short campaign, but still delivers a lot.

Yes, I spent more time in this game than its campaign actually requires. I have the habit of exploring every detail and breaking down to the fullest the works I engage with, and I feel there’s a lot to say about Firewatch, because it’s much more than it first appears to be.

Two key ideas run through our mind throughout the experience: grief and escapism.

Primarily focused on the narrative, Firewatch has some horror elements, but I want to focus on the drama that drives all the events: the protagonist, Henry. He’s not a very educated, handsome, or delicate man, but he was loved for being authentic and sincere.

''You... you're pretty.''

The weight of his emotional pain and his desire to escape it lead him to isolation. We’re talking about a man destroyed by his wife Julia’s degenerative illness and the guilt of not knowing how to handle the situation. Henry, unable to bear the pain, flees to the solitude of the woods, taking an impulsive job. Yet, even in seclusion, he finds that it’s impossible to escape from himself.

Right from the start, we’re directly and impactfully presented with Henry’s memories: “You meet her at a bar.” Julia is brilliant, humorous, and Henry quickly falls in love. Over time, however, their relationship begins to crumble: “Julia starts forgetting things. Little things, at first.” The decline progresses, eventually destroying everything Henry thought was solid. When asked how to handle it, he hesitates: send her to family in Australia or care for her on his own? Neither option seems enough. So, Julia’s family takes her away from him, while he sinks into drinking, rumination, and self-degeneration.

Weakened and emotionally adrift, Henry becomes vulnerable to the forces acting around him. Delilah, his supervisor and sole human connection, is initially charismatic and helpful but gradually reveals herself to be as ambiguous as the mysteries surrounding the forest.

“Hey, is someone out there?” – A mysterious figure seems to stalk him, amplifying his terror and paranoia. Delilah, in turn, appears concerned, but it’s left implied that she knows something but withholds information, carefully choosing what to share, always guiding Henry in a way that seems convenient to her. The stalker watching him from the shadows intensifies his doubts and vulnerabilities, making him more and more a prisoner of his own mind and the environment surrounding him.

It’s in this stage of mystery and uncertainty that Firewatch’s story unfolds.

Well, all this happens in the first two days of the game. Quite a lot to digest, right? Moving on, I’ll try to be a bit more concise.

The plot develops from here. We have a total of 78 days, not all of which are shown to the player, but even so, we can see that some things happen through the excellent dialogues presented during the days we participate in.

We can notice an increasing closeness between Henry and Delilah as they begin to share more about their lives, interacting more intensely. Their relationship starts to become more like that of partners, which further strengthens their bond but also brings to light the growing divergences throughout the plot. They begin to get to know each other more deeply, revealing traits of their personalities and behaviors, establishing a communication that feels organic and natural, making the dialogues more genuine and loaded with tension. This gradual process of closeness leads to a decisive moment: as their relationship grows, so does their unease. Mysteries accumulate, and the puzzles become denser. The forest, in its solitude, seems to harbor more than just nature. The threats of the stalker’s presence and the questions about what is really happening begin to eat away at Henry, who finds himself increasingly trapped between the desire to find answers and the need to escape it all. The mounting tension leads to moments of uncertainty, constantly manifesting without the game needing to use traditional horror elements or appeals. Here, Firewatch uses a subtle atmosphere where the mystery never stops tormenting the player. In every gesture of Henry, in every word from Delilah, there’s some weight, or a doubt lodged.

As the game moves into its final stages, the closeness between Henry and Delilah evolves. What seemed like a professional and distant relationship begins to transform into something more personal, almost intimate. But this also brings insecurity, with suspicions and some inconsistencies in Delilah’s speech taking over. The stalker, always present in the shadows, seems to feed off the tension between them, adding more layers of confusion and uncertainty. And while all this happens, the forest, with its almost deafening silence, becomes more of a metaphor for Henry’s mind: a maze he doesn’t quite know how to navigate. As the secrets begin to unfold, the story gains new layers. Henry, immersed in his own emotions and solitude, starts uncovering more of what’s behind the events around him. However, things are not easy to decipher. Every clue he finds seems to generate more doubts, as if the truth were a puzzle piece that never quite fits. And in the end, we have the resolution of the mystery and the conclusion of Henry’s journey, which seems to reach its end without him fully understanding what happened. But in Firewatch, the answer isn’t simple, and there is no great revelation of something monumental. It all turns out to be just a local tragedy, people tormented by a past they couldn’t leave behind, just like the stalker, who turned out to be a figure from Delilah’s life, as everything pointed to. The true resolution comes through acceptance. Henry finally confronts his own demons and, in some way, understands that escape is not the answer. He realizes that to find peace, perhaps one must face the pain and grief, not as something to avoid but as something that is part of who he is.

Note: I didn’t do all the possible endings, I don’t know how much things change depending on the decisions you make, but I decided that Henry should return to his wife and face his past, his own reality to be overcome, leaving that forest behind.

Other than that, what else can I add here? I would like to emphasize that the characters are charismatic, have very natural interactions, and this makes you sympathize with them and easily feel their struggles. This helps a lot in guiding the narrative, as good characters contribute to a more engaging plot, not to mention the atmosphere, the sounds of the environment, which have a tangible presence and greatly help in building a reflection of the emotional state of the characters, which is loneliness, isolation. Even the beautiful landscapes, the warm colors of the sunset, and the vibrant tones of some parts of the forest carry a certain melancholy that aligns with the inner suffering of both characters, especially Henry.

And this is my reading of this work. I hope you enjoyed it, until next time.

Firewatch is a game that brings itself to the forefront among the recently abundant 'Walking Simulations'. I say 'walking simulation' because first of all it's not a survival game or a game with a lot of mechanics and a lot of things to do. Those who have played Dear Eshter or Gone Home will understand what I mean, and even though they are similar, Firewatch stands out in many ways.

First of all, Firewatch is a story-driven game. But it doesn't do this with cutscenes or anything like that. You will be in dialog with the person on the other end of your radio throughout the game. With very well written dialogs, the game draws you in comfortably and you find yourself wondering what will happen next as a result of the developing events.

One of the most important things you have to do is to find your direction. With map and compass in hand, you try to find your way to your mission and you get lost a lot. The map is covered with lots of trees and hillsides, so you can get lost a lot, but the environment looks so beautiful that you can find yourself looking around. Since it's mostly an open world game, you have the opportunity to walk around before your mission. However, you cannot reach some areas immediately because you need the necessary tools. Apart from that, there are material boxes left for the fire lookouts, which is the job you do in the environment. In each box you can find some unnecessary items and you can also find new map information for you to explore.

You will be in contact with the person in the other watchtower with the radio that has been with you since you first started working as a fire lookout. You can get information or chat with your radio for many important or unimportant things in the game. Some of your answers are in multiple options and you can say whatever you want. This adds a very different flavor to the story because some of the things you talk about can be brought up again. Apart from that, every once in a while you can talk about your personal life or the mission over the radio to keep the story going. This is the part that sets it apart from other walking simulators because it draws you in as you talk and makes you like the characters.

Apart from walking and exploring, you use some equipment, so it doesn't feel like a game left completely unattended. The reason I say this is because some walking simulations lack a lot of mechanics, so there are a lot of things that are missing. This game, on the other hand, has some platforming elements. Crossing the street, going up and down ropes or clearing your path with an axe.

Graphically, it is very satisfying. There is a lot of detail in the environment. We never see Henry, the main character, but we can see his hands and body all the time. The animations are very fluid, like a Pixar movie. The day-night cycle changes according to the story, but you don't realize that the transitions are pre-written, they are very smooth.

The music comes out very rarely, but again, it's crafted according to the story and when it does, it hits the spot and focuses you on the story.

The gameplay may seem short compared to other games. I finished it in 5 hours, but I can say that it is enough for other games of this genre I have played. You experience the story a lot, but the ending may not satisfy everyone. I think it was written very realistically. If you say that this is a game and it should be written in a crazy way, I can't say otherwise, but this game shows that storytelling can be done in a great way without being too fantastic.

In conclusion, Firewatch is not a game that everyone can play and enjoy. It's not a game with tons of game mechanics, puzzles or shooting. But it is a very pleasant experience. And when I say experience, it's definitely not a “Dear Eshter” style game that tells a story as you walk. It has mystery, humor, and sometimes it gives you goosebumps. I definitely recommend it to those who like this genre.

[h1][b]Firewatch: The Solace of Escapism and Its Impermanence[/b][/h1]

         Firewatch isn’t one of those games that got you hooked with groundbreaking and exciting gameplay mechanics, but instead by its narrative and atmospheric, immersive world—taking place in a dense and scenic forest brought to life and stylized by the stunning art style, with every frame being screenshot-worthy. A recipe for a very inviting journey, one that is both mysterious and comforting. These are the elements that both hooked the players and also served as the core part of the game as well. 

[h2]Act I: The Pursuit of Comfort During Hard Times[/h2]

         You’re put in the shoes of Henry, who went through years of hard times and tragedies. Who’s out seeking solace and comfort by taking a fire lookout job. As we had a brief glimpse through the years of his life, we already formed somewhat of an emotional connection with Henry. Solely through dialogue options and some images, leaving the rest for us to imagine. The gameplay consists of you, a fire lookout, completing tasks and daily routines with mystery elements sliding in through events that occurred during your time in the forest. The game also featured a character Delilah, who lives in another lookout tower, giving you tasks and guiding you through the process. This is very important as the game is incredibly and intentionally barren and lacks human interactions. With Delilah being your only human companion to talk and share your thoughts with, through very human-like dialogues. This effortlessly forms a connection between the player and Delilah, who’d venture alongside the player throughout the whole game via the radio, a communication device that’d shape and play a very significant role in the game’s narrative overall.

[h2]Act II: The Transience Nature of Escapism[/h2]

         Throughout the story, the story plays out almost like a mystery/investigation game, with many mysteries for us to solve. All of this helps spice up the story and distract us and Henry away from the demons and the ghosts of his memory and hardships that he’s running away from. But ultimately, that still isn’t the main focal point of the story. And the people who assumed it to be, are left disappointed after the ending.

         The story wraps up as we finally unearthed the mystery and the whereabouts of Ned Goodwin and his son Brian, while the forest fire marches deeper and deeper into the forest and our vicinity. As we found out the fate of Brian Goodwin and learned about the person who had been stalking us the whole game to be Ned Goodwin, we also learned about how he is very so different than us. After the tragic death of his son, he essentially cut himself off from the outside world and lived on as a hermit in the area, unable to accept the fact, deal with the reality, or even report the incident to the authorities. He served as an extreme example of what the protagonist Henry could be if he chose to run away from his own tragedies completely, just like Ned did in his own. But unlike Ned, Henry still isn’t completely detached from the whole point of this temporary escapism holiday away from his problems. And ultimately, as the story wraps itself up, Henry and Delilah who both came here to run away from their own tragedies, choose to go on their separate ways and back into dealing with their own demons. In the end, depending on your perspective, Henry would realize and eventually go back to face reality, rather than keep running away from it.

[h2]Act III: The Dilemma of Going Back to the Reality[/h2]

         The ending, while seemingly disappointing and unfulfilling, is ultimately the whole point of it, and the story as a whole. Something that some players do forget. Henry chose to take the job as a way to seek solace somewhere away from all the chaos that he couldn’t bear any longer. And those who thought the game would end up with a happy ending, with two of them getting together and flying away in a chopper into the sunset, would end up being disappointed. As no matter how good their chemistry and relationship they had, or could potentially be in the future. There is still the elephant in the room being both of them deciding to go back to fighting their own battles. And especially for Henry who's left with a lesson and a newfound motivation to go back into it. And in the end, no matter how blissful escapism is, deep down we all know that it never lasts. All of this is being the ultimate lesson for Henry, but also for us players who probably got the game to run away and seek solace from the chaos of the real world as well.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]

The story is exceptionally well narrated, while not very complicated or groundbreaking, it certainly don't need to be in order for it to be great. And even if we pushed the story aside, this is still a solid walking simulator with an very well crafted environment and a solid art style. I personally picked it up on sale for just over a dollar, and honestly I think the game would still be worth it in its full price. 

An absolute gem of an indie game, although its not a hidden gem, it is very well deserved of its recognition and the sales and reviews already speaks for itself. A short, bittersweet and memorable ride. And though it is kind of a one-time experience, it certainly isn't a story that is designed to be replayable. And besides, it only took one playthrough to get its message across loud and clear.

It is dishearteningly common nowadays to find people complain about how XYZ story game is woke because the main character is not what they expected them to look like or that what gender they expected them to be. Even tho Firewatch itself is very far away from this topic, I feel like this game surely goes on to show how video games does not need characters with looks or something that fits into the stereotypical idea of a game character to have great attachment.
The main protagonist of Firewatch Henry and the main supporting character Delilah don't even get their physical appearance showed throughout the game, but the level of attachment you end up building with these characters is immense.

We never see Henry's face, even though he is the lens through which we experience the game’s story. He isn’t a muscular action hero or a glamorous icon, he’s an ordinary middle-aged ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up man who is in a messy chapter in his life. What makes Henry extraordinary is his humanity—the humour, vulnerability, and raw emotion.
Similarly we never see Delilah's face, and are left to imagine her appearance based on her words, her humour, and the stuff about her life she chooses to share. Yet, by the end of the game, Delilah feels as vivid and real as any other character.
This is where Firewatch truly shines - it demonstrates that connection doesn’t depend on physicality. Delilah’s charm, vulnerability, and wit unfold naturally when we talk to her. She’s imperfect and deeply human, with her own insecurities and regrets. These things make her relatable.

This also shows one of Firewatch's core themes: the power of connection in isolation. Delilah’s voice always feels comforting in the lone wilderness. Her absence at the game’s end reminds us how deeply we can care for someone based solely on shared moments and conversations we had, and not their physicality.
In a medium often obsessed with photorealistic character models instead of actual character building, Firewatch offers a very different and refreshing perspective. 

Calling any game in general “woke” simply because its characters aren't similar to traditional expectations reveals an unwillingness to engage with the complexity of storytelling. Firewatch shows that characters, like people, are more than their outward appearances. It’s their thoughts and emotions that make them memorable.

Halfway through playing the game I searched for reviews, and found people describing the ending as underwhelming. I didn't quite understand why — not even after unlocking all the achievements — until I finally realized that the game's mainstream appeal lies in Henry and Delilah developing an emotional connection. What disappointed people was precisely the fact that Henry and Delilah never meet. Looking back, I awkwardly remembered that I never shared anything about Julia with Delilah throughout the game, deflected her flirtatious remarks, and played deaf to her teasing. And then it struck me — I related far more to Ned, who knew deep down he had made terrible mistakes yet was too cowardly to face reality; and to Dave, who carried emotions as deep and heavy as the ocean but kept a calm facade just to keep life moving.  
I was drawn to this game because ChatGPT recommended it as "a space for awake eyes and ears beyond the numbness of reality". In the end, it reminded me of how much of a mess my own emotional world still is, how my choice to seal off my emotions from others and painstakingly construct a solitary inner world remains unconventional, even alien. The only solace I found was that, during the fleeting hours I spent wandering the rocky trails and caves, I felt a solid, unspeakable emotional connection with the lonely souls of Shoshone National Forest, and with all the players who had ever been comforted by this game. And that, I realized, was enough. Henry leaving the Wyoming wilderness still has to return to a world revolving around his wife with dementia; Ned, exposed and forced out of his solitary life, likely faces an uphill struggle to find his next psychological sanctuary; and we, shutting off the game and returning to our daily lives, will once again grind away our patience in the 9-5 monotony until we grow weary and wither. The game and life share the same theme: brief escapes are always followed by the inescapable force of long separations. Fate listens to neither your explanations nor your pleas — it just moves forward. Yet, on some random warm spring Saturday nights, we might find ourselves thinking about these kind smiles and gentle people, these books, these songs, these games that remind us we are not alone and we can still find noble souls to talk to: tiny, fragile beams of light that, in the prolonged darkness of life, illuminate our path. I'm grateful for and deeply admire this kind of light.

[h3][b]An Uneasy Stroll Through the Woods[/b][/h3]

Firewatch isn’t a game you play for the gameplay - it’s essentially a walking simulator. You’re dropped into a lonely forest and try to unravel an ongoing mystery. That’s it. It’s more about the experience than the mechanics, and it honestly does a decent job of immersing you in its world.

That said, this game made me feel deeply uncomfortable the entire time. The atmosphere is eerie, and I never felt at peace or relaxed. It always felt like something could go horribly wrong at any moment.

The story, however, left a lot to be desired. Maybe I missed something, but the climax didn’t land for me. At its core, it feels like a story about people who are having a rough time and are looking for some form of escape. I couldn’t really relate to the cast, and while that might be a personal thing, it left me feeling disconnected.

One thing I will say is the chemistry between the main character and Delilah is amazing. The voice acting is phenomenal, and their banter felt really natural and engaging. But even that came with its own uneasiness - it felt wrong to encourage their relationship, especially considering the protagonist’s personal situation.

I don’t think I can wholeheartedly recommend Firewatch, but I also don’t think it’s not worth your time. It’s a short and immersive experience that plays out like an interactive film. If you’re curious, give it a shot - it might resonate more with you than it did with me. If not, watching a video essay might give you the same takeaway, minus the immersion.

Firewatch is a first person narrative driven game. Our protagonist, Henry, has taken a job as a fire lookout in a national park in Wyoming. He's trying to get away from the world after suffering some personal issues. Over the radio, he meets Delilah, who is stationed in another tower. As the season progresses they exchange stories and get to know each other more and more. The strong point of the game is its dialogue and character development. The voice acting is well done, and the sound work really makes you feel like you're somewhere wild and remote. The environments are beautiful and vibrant; there are gorgeous vistas, there are forests, and there are mountain views. The gameplay itself is uninspired, with mundane tasks to accomplish initially, and as the story unfolds the exploration becomes more interesting. Firewatch is a short but immersive experience that does taper off towards the end, yet is worth the playthrough.

This game would have been fully realized if Delilah became villainous, as she had Shodan or GladOS potential.  

As a first-person walking simulator taking place in the 1980s, this is a good-looking game with an artistic flair that matches the 80s era.  Your character’s background of a middle-aged man looking for reprieve from tragic life circumstances in a picturesque wilderness is quietly compelling, until you must deal with the intrusive banter from Delilah.  I almost wish that I did not lower my character by entertaining her, as you have the option to mostly ignore her, but I did talk to her to try and flush out a plot, which turned out to be a far-fetched mystery that would have been more interesting if it fully committed to an unbelievable, fantastical yarn.

This was an okay 4-5 hour experience to completion.  There is no incentive for replay, as it is linear and without combat, and it features a companion who I did not jive with and would have loved for the story to take a dark turn, and my mission becomes one to hunt down and destroy Delilah.  Needless to say, I am perhaps not this game’s intended audience.

[h2]An immersive adventure worth a brief detour[/h2]

[b]Buy it if...[/b] you like short, atmospheric and narratively driven experiences. Firewatch starts with some surprising emotional weight and unfolds a tense mystery right up until the end. The mechanics are simple: patrol your assigned woods, find new forestry tools, and open up new paths. At around 3hrs in length, it's a great palate cleanser in a world of +60hrs RPGs. Definitely worth getting on sale!

[b]Avoid it if...[/b] you’re looking for a deep story, or for complex gameplay. Firewatch hits its emotional beats well, and with (mostly) understated character moments. Those moments are brief, however, and by the end I felt the cast was mostly reacting to the story instead of being at the center of it. That shift works if you enjoy what is revealed in the final chapters, but I felt the ending failed to match the strength of the first few in-game days.

Very few games get me emotional. Firewatch proved to be one of those. Despite being released long ago, this gem of a game continues to resonate through its stunning visuals, superb voice acting, and a story that cuts straight to the heart of human nature.

At its core, the game delivers a powerful message about confronting personal problems. Through its story, it illustrates how futile it is to run from our problems – they follow us like shadows, persistent and unavoidable. The protagonist's journey serves almost as a mirror, reflecting our own tendencies to seek escape rather than face difficult truths. It really resonated with me, because it reminded me how I do those same things.

The games story reminds us that while building fantasy realities might offer temporary comfort, the true growth comes from having the courage to face and reshape our current reality- *your* reality.
The game stands as evidence to how video games can also have a intriguing narrative to become powerful vehicles for emotional and personal growth. It proves that video games can also be a work of art as much as the next thing. 
I can't recommend this game more than I already am. Play it. It is an incredible experience.

This game follows you, Henry. You take a job as a lookout on the fire watch service of the Shoshone National Forest in Wyoming after your wife moves in with her parents when her dementia gets too severe for you to continue caring for her. The beginning of the game focuses very heavily on Henry's decision to run away from his wife, Julia, rather than choosing to visit her at her family's place. 

Shortly after arriving, however, you begin to notice that there is plenty 'off' near your lookout. You find a fenced off area of the park that your boss, Delilah, didn't know about. Things go missing, someone breaks into your watch tower, and find records of your past conversations with Delilah that you both assumed were private. After a while of gathering clues about the area, you discover that a man named Ned was in your tower years ago, and is hiding the details surrounding the death of his kid son, of which he is responsible for. 

The way the games handles this story is elegant, dropping details of it here and there, but never spelling it out for you. You have the opportunity to investigate unique and interesting areas, read notes and talk to Delilah about the people who were hear before you, and discover hints about Ned's actions throughout the entire experience. While the game is linear with the main story and ending being identical across all play-throughs (barring one secret ending that you can activate at the very end of the story by literally doing nothing) the decisions you make along the way inform the lens by which you view the experience, changing the game in novel and interesting ways for each individual who plays it. 

I really like this game, and I will definitely be adding it to my list of must play favorites that I will recommend to everyone. If you are digging through the reviews looking for motivation to get it, allow me to be that motivation. GET THIS GAME. You will love it!

After playing and finishing Firewatch, I’m left with mixed feelings, especially about the ending.

The graphics are undeniably stunning, and the game does a great job of immersing players in the beauty and solitude of nature. At times, the environment felt truly alive, with the dense forests and serene landscapes adding to the overall atmosphere. The story starts with an interactive flashcard sequence that introduces Henry, the main protagonist, and gives a glimpse into his life and struggles with Julia. It’s a simple yet effective way to establish a strong emotional foundation.

The game’s pacing is slow at the beginning but gradually builds up to an intense and mysterious atmosphere. This is, in my opinion, where Firewatch truly excels. The creeping paranoia, the eerie sense of being watched, and the blend of deep forests with calming areas created a unique and captivating experience. The atmosphere is the game’s strongest point. At times, it felt creepy, mysterious, and downright unsettling, which kept me hooked throughout the story.

However, I have some significant criticisms, particularly regarding the movement mechanics. The controls often felt clunky and unpolished, which hurt my immersion. On multiple occasions, I got stuck between trees, rocks, or even patches of grass, forcing me to restart the game. Additionally, the movement speed felt sluggish, and going downhill was painfully slow—so much so that it became frustrating and distracting from the plot.

Then there’s the ending, which left me feeling disappointed. While the buildup to the climax was gripping, the conclusion felt shallow and anticlimactic. The idea of Henry being manipulated by Ned and Delilah had potential, but the resolution didn’t deliver the payoff I was hoping for. I expected a major plot twist or a dramatic unfolding of events, but instead, it fizzled out. I also wish the game had leaned harder into the idea of Delilah and Ned collaborating—it would have added a fascinating layer to the story. While some players might interpret this as a fan theory, I believe it should have been made canon by the developers.

In conclusion, Firewatch shines in its atmosphere and visual presentation, but its technical flaws and unsatisfying ending hold it back from greatness. That said, I recommend buying this game on sale. It’s a colorful, story-rich mystery that can be entertaining at times, despite its shortcomings.

firewatch is on it's surface a game about a mystery, but when you scratch the surface a little it becomes obvious that the game really is about grief and how people handle it. Many find it's ending unsatisfying, however if you understand the true meaning, you will be able to appreciate how real and human the ending is.

SPOILERS:
Review contains only spoiles. 












The theme of escapism runs deep here. Running away from your problems doesn’t solve them—it only delays the inevitable. Henry embodies this perfectly, mirroring Delilah and Ned in their shared refusal to confront reality. Ned, for example, avoided facing the truth about his son’s death, retreating entirely from the world. Similarly, Henry tries to escape his crumbling life by isolating himself in the wilderness. But by the end of the game, it’s clear he remains broken, stuck in the same unresolved state.

Delilah’s words cut through his denial: “You came here to escape your problems, and they’re still there in front of you.” When Henry asks her to come to Boulder with him, she refuses—not because she doesn’t care for him, but because she recognizes his deeper issue. He’s still running, avoiding, and looking for external solutions instead of confronting his own turmoil. That’s why she tells him to go back to Julia, even though Julia likely won’t remember him.

Delilah pushes Henry to face his problems—not for Julia’s sake, but for his own. He needs to confront the mess, even if the solution is imperfect or painful. A terrible solution, after all, is better than none at all.

To me, this makes the ending perfect. It’s why this story stands out as one of the best in video game history. Video games themselves are a form of escapism, giving us a way to momentarily forget life’s difficulties. But Firewatch turns that concept on its head, forcing both Henry and the player to acknowledge that no matter how far you run, your problems will always follow you.

Firewatch is a walking simulator in the best possible way—if walking through gorgeous forests while emotionally unpacking your life choices and occasionally freaking out over cryptic events sounds like your idea of fun, this game is for you.

Graphics and Atmosphere
Imagine Bob Ross painted a national park while whispering, "Let's add a happy little sunset here," and you'll have a good idea of what Firewatch looks like. The visuals are so stunning that I wanted to live in this world—until I remembered I hate bugs and can't read a map. Wyoming never looked so good, and probably never will again.

Sound Design and Music
The sound design is chef’s kiss. From the soothing crunch of your boots on a dirt trail to the occasional rustling of "wait, what was that?" in the bushes, the audio makes you feel like you're actually there. Chris Remo's soundtrack is a mix of tranquil and "I think something’s about to happen," perfectly complementing the vibe of "I'm relaxed but also slightly panicked."

Gameplay
Do you enjoy hiking? How about emotionally charged conversations? Firewatch has you covered. The gameplay is simple but satisfying: walk around, solve minor navigation puzzles, and talk to your only connection to the outside world—a voice on a radio who is equal parts charming and suspiciously good at roasting you.

Using the map and compass feels nostalgic for anyone who’s ever been hopelessly lost in the woods, except this time you can't blame Google Maps. It’s like Boy Scouts, but with existential dread instead of merit badges.

Story and Writing
The story is where Firewatch truly shines. It’s like a campfire tale, except instead of s'mores, you’re served a buffet of emotional depth and compelling dialogue. Your radio buddy is witty, sarcastic, and so well-voiced that you'll find yourself talking back to her out loud. (Just me? Cool.)

Without spoiling anything, the narrative is a mix of mystery, heartache, and "wait, is this about me?" It’s the kind of story that makes you feel like you're making important decisions, even if the most impactful one is deciding whether to report a suspicious tree.

Pros
Visually stunning enough to make you consider moving to the wilderness. (Don't.)
Dialogue that feels so natural, you'll wonder if the writers have been spying on your awkward conversations.
A story that sticks with you, even after you’ve rage-quit over trying to find the next trail.
Cons
It’s short, but hey, so is a rollercoaster, and no one complains about those.
If you’re looking for action-packed gameplay, this isn’t it. Unless you count wrestling with your own emotions as "action-packed."
Final Thoughts
Firewatch is like a fine craft beer: it’s rich, unique, and may leave you a little sad when it’s over. It’s also the only game where I’ve shouted, “Oh no, I think I made a mistake!” about both a dialogue choice and accidentally wandering into the wrong part of the forest.

Play this game if you love beautiful scenery, deep stories, and the kind of introspection that feels like therapy (but cheaper). Just make sure you’re emotionally ready for it. And bring a compass.

Aside from being very boring, the game's biggest crime is that it somehow makes the great outdoors feel claustrophobic. In one scene you are crawling through a narrow cave, in another you are walking around the edge of a lake, and they feel almost exactly the same, navigation-wise.

For a game that's all about character, there is very little to the characters. What fans call "minimalist storytelling" might be more accurately described as "not having much going on in the writing department". 90% of what's interesting about the game's writing takes place during the opening exposition at the start of the game. Dialogue frequently goes nowhere, presumably so that players can project depth onto the characters without the devs having to bother to characterize them themselves.

There is exactly one plot point of any consequence, which would be totally fine in a free, 15-minute game, but made almost all of my three-hour playthrough feel like a slog. I only wish I'd finished it an hour sooner so I could still get a refund.

If you're interested in this game, do yourself a favor and go watch an edited-down highlights reel on YouTube instead. Maybe a decade ago this game was a breath of fresh air, but in 2025 you can find a hundred better indie games for online for about $2 each.

In short I really recommend this game but if you are one of those persons who needs more than an opinion here are some reasons why I find that this game is one of the best I have played in a while:

The story is quite short and it took me around 3 to 4 hours to complete. Despite the story looks fairly simple at the start as you are doing normal things that a fire watcher is expected to do like exploring the forest, locating any persons that could be dangerous to the forest as they are lighting up a fire, there is a 'threat' and a mystery that you as a player is encouraged to uncover and from there you get more information about your fire watcher partner and her experiences as a fire watcher. I found the story interesting as there were quite a lot of twists that I personally wasn't expecting and I found myself sympathising with some of the characters and it had quite a natural flow and it didn't seem like 3 hours of gameplay as I was immersed in the game and the setting and the story of the characters.

The controls are quite simple and they introduce a couple of mechanics as you progress through the story, but they are introduced nicely as it is natural the way that they are implemented. Despite this game was launched in 2016, the visuals and the art hold pretty well up until this day and I really like the settings and the music that went along the tension of the story. It runs really nicely and I didn't experience any lags or bugs which is always a plus. The map is quite big to explore (but heads up, the map is a sandbox) and despite there are limits to the map, it doesn't feel small in the slightest as the story forces you to explore all of it and go from point A to point B.

Overall I will replay the whole game again to collect all the trophies in a couple of weeks and I can't recommend this game enough to someone who wants a cozy adventure, someone who wants to discover a mystery or if you just like the art style and the way that the game looks give it a try!

Firewatch is a primarily narrative driven story game that has you walk around the Wyoming wilderness interacting with varying different points of interest while communicating with another firewatch person via walkie talkie. It’s developed by Campo Santo and published by Panic, alongside of Camp Santo. It released back in Feb 9 of 2016. 

I’m going to be extremely brief with this one. The story and narrative is strong, and this entire experience basically hinges on that because everything else is relatively weak. The pacing is good, and character development can vary slightly dependent on dialogue options that you choose, although overall the outcome will be somewhat the same. The game centers around exploring the wilderness and interacting with different points of interest that often come in the form of stumps or rocks that allow you to traverse different areas that would normally be inaccessible. Controls are fine. There apparently is expanded controller support that was implemented back in December of 2021 on steam, a staggering 5 years after the games release. I never played with a controller, just keyboard and mouse. There is no difficulty to the game nor option for it, just the one fairly linear experience. Visually it’s a well stylized game and it’s aged well at this point. Animations and their details are limited, constrained to what you’ll mostly see by interacting with travel points to get from point a to point b. Music pops up here and there, but doesn’t have much impact. It’s somewhat forgettable. Sound effects for various actions are also limited. The voice acting is strong, which is good given how heavily the game relies on it’s plot and narrative pushing the story forward. Rich Sommer (Henry) and Cissy Jones (Delilah) do a phenomenal job. The dialogue is witty and very human. The direction here was excellent. Environment variety is limited, it’s all forest. Some of it’s burned. Exploration is normally rewarded in the form of additional dialogue or new lore. There’s no endgame content to speak of, and the only reason you would go back and play it again would be to get achievements that you missed, or to experience the games free roam mode within it’s special features on the main menu, unlocked through completing the story at least once. 

Performance wise the game runs well, almost always at a buttery 144fps. I experienced no crashes during my time with it. That being said, the game is riddled with annoying bugs and inconveniences. Henry can become detached from the topology of the floor beneath him when interacting with a traverse point and he will slide in a random direction. This happens frequently. Modeling on rocks are incomplete within a cave. If you interact with a locked cache and then escape out of the interaction during dialogue that is playing on the radio, specifically when you are prompted to provide a response to Delilah, the game will lock you in place. You can look around, but are unable to press escape to bring up the pause menu or press literally any controls to bring up any menu or move away from the cache. This resulted in having to Alt + F4 to restart the game. If Henry is running towards the edge of a large drop off and continues running forward without interacting with it, he can once again become detached from the topology of the floor map and slide down the edge to the floor beneath it. This also happened several times. If Henry pulls up his map during walkie dialogue and is prompted for a response, you will be unable to select a response so long as the map is pulled up, and will have to put it away in order to select an option. Given how quickly some of the response timers expire, it’s entirely possible the player can miss responding, or being able to read the options in time if they bring up their map to check their bearings at the wrong moment. Certain items (such as the turtle) have the chance to not spawn, and these are tied to achievements. The game by default is set to autosave, so unless you know about it, it’s also entirely possible to have a run where an interactable item just doesn’t spawn. 

Achievement hunting in this one is a pain as well. There is no chapter select, so if you miss some achievements during your initial playthrough, you’ll have to play it all the way back through to the point where you can grab whatever you missed. Because of it’s design there’s a lot of sitting around waiting for responses to happen, so it can take a minute to progress through the story if you’re looking for just the one achievement you missed. See also the turtle achievement above. Sometimes it won’t spawn, so you’ll have to reload. Not a huge deal if you have autosaving disabled, but that’s enabled by default. Poor design in my opinion. 

Firewatch’s strongest point is it’s well structured story and superb voice acting direction helping to drive it forward, while it’s weakest points is it being riddled with annoying bugs, poorly designed mechanics and world interaction, achievement items not spawning, and missing quality of life features like chapter select. 

Final verdict is 3/5. I recommend this to players that are largely invested in story telling games with less to none game features and mechanics, but only under the condition that it’s on sale. This is one long interactive movie essentially. I won’t return to this game, but I did enjoy the story the first time around and can appreciate it.

Firewatch is an immersive story experience that keeps you enthralled into finding out whats going on, whilst providing you with a relaxed, yet sometimes tense, narrative.

If you're looking for a game that is short but rich in story then this is the game for you.

Overall I enjoyed the Firewatch experience, and it was the first game I played on Steam Deck, which ended up being a good pairing. 

The gameplay is typical for a walking simulator, you explore the map, make observations and discoveries, and the plot reveals itself to you over time. I mostly enjoyed the moment to moment exploration, small talk on the radio with our new friend Delilah, and learning about the main characters' backstories. 

At the point where the game starts trying to work in an actual plot and mystery, I enjoyed that well enough but the payoff was disappointing enough that I kind of wished they hadn't bothered with it in the first place. So despite ending on a slightly weak note, I found the experience to be worthwhile as a whole. 

Firewatch might be a little overhyped but it's still worth checking out.

Firewatch is a masterpiece. From the moment you step into the boots of Henry, the isolated fire lookout, the game draws you into its world with stunning visuals, an emotionally gripping story, and some of the most memorable voice acting I've ever heard. The beautiful wilderness of Wyoming feels alive, with its sweeping landscapes and dynamic weather effects that set the tone perfectly for the introspective journey ahead.

The relationship between Henry and Delilah, his only contact in the world, is the heart of the game. Their conversations are witty, heartfelt, and real, and I found myself deeply invested in their evolving bond. The writing is top-notch, and the emotional depth it brings to the story is incredible.

The pacing is perfect. There's a sense of mystery that keeps you hooked, as you explore the forest and uncover secrets. The gameplay itself is simple but engaging, focusing more on narrative and character development than traditional action. It's not about fast-paced combat; it's about the journey, the solitude, and the introspection that comes with being alone in such a vast, beautiful place.

If you're looking for a game that combines stunning visuals, a deep and emotional story, and a tranquil yet haunting atmosphere, Firewatch is an absolute must-play. It’s a rare gem that will stay with you long after the credits roll. A solid 10/10.

It's an okayish game. It plays like a visual novel and not so much like a game, which really isn't my cup of tea. I don't think it lives up to the hype it got post-release. I do admit that the game's scenery can be quite pretty, although I wasn't expecting it to be poly graphics.

As other people have already said, it's more of a hiking simulator than a tower watching experience, and it's very story-focused. The dialogue adds a lot of flavor to the game, but everything else you do is pretty much all predetermined.

My biggest specific gripes are:

1. The camera panning. As someone who's prone to experiencing motion sickness, most of the game isn't that bad once you get used to it, but I dislike the way that the camera pans around whenever you interact with environmental obstacles. For example, I really hope that in real life I don't swing my line-of-sight around and stare at my boots every time I hop over a log when hiking, or that I don't tilt my head sideways 90 degrees and swing it around wildly every time I use a hammer. This game does that; it's stupid. It just feels like those forced object interactions to jump and climb don't increase the realism that much and are distracting when in the middle of hiking .

2. Lack of free choice. As far as I can tell, the events in the game are predetermined. You don't choose to take an alternate route, because the game is designed so that there's often only one way you can take. 
It feels like there's no point in wandering off and exploring anywhere besides where the game objective is, because either you won't be able to get there, or you'll be forced to go back there later on anyway for a game objective. It really takes the fun out of exploring.

3. Somewhat cumbersome travel mechanics. When hiking, it's easy to get lost sometimes. Checking the map helps prevent this, but it's a bit annoying to repeatedly pull up and zoom in on the map and compass. You kinda have to put the map down afterwards because you can't run and hold the map at the same time. Running makes you go a bit too fast, but walking feels too slow sometimes, there's not a happy medium. Luckily the world you move around in is actually pretty small, so it's manageable. I wish you could jump or travel over rocks, but unfortunately you can't.

I thoroughly enjoyed Firewatch for its engaging plot and well-crafted story. The pacing was solid, though I do think it could have been a bit slower and the game could have been slightly longer to really savor the experience.

Visually, the game has a warm, somewhat cartoonish style that gives it a unique charm. The protagonist's arms even reminded me of the TF2 Heavy, which added a fun touch. The landscapes are stunning, with adorable raccoons and gorgeous lighting, especially during dusk and dawn.

The gameplay mechanics are good overall, but I would have preferred the ability to place items instead of just tossing them. Thankfully, I didn’t run into any technical issues during my playthrough.

Henry and Delilah are well-developed characters, and their dialogue, especially Delilah’s, was really compelling. [spoiler]I did feel a bit sad that Delilah was only a voice in the end and we never actually saw her in the game.[/spoiler]

The atmosphere of the game is incredibly immersive, and the walkman feature during free roam really enhanced that feeling. I do wish there were more opportunities for casual conversations with Delilah even in  free roam. The soundtrack and sound design were excellent, though I would’ve loved to hear songs from the Lake Cheap Talk from album Let's Get Electric - 1987 by Cheap Talk sadly it wasnt added to the walkman during free roam.

For me, the most memorable moments were the conversations with Delilah and playing as Henry, gradually growing fond of her and navigating the unfolding drama together. [spoiler]The climax, involving a grieving father unable to find closure after losing his son, was both intense and heartbreaking. A particularly sad moment for me was when Delilah didn’t wait for Henry at the end.[/spoiler]

I’d definitely recommend Firewatch to anyone who enjoys a good adventure game or walking simulator. It might not be everyone’s cup of tea, and it can be a bit of a double-edged sword, but the immersive story could easily translate into a great movie or book. All in all, it’s a beautifully crafted game that's definitely worth experiencing.

A very solid adventure game all around with a great sense of immersion.

The writing in the game coupled with the setting is this game's strong suit and, by the end of the game, becomes charming in its own right. The development of the relationship between Delilah and Henry is very grounded and genuinely comes off as plausible things people would actually talk about being isolated in the wilderness in the manner the game portrays--from just talking about everyday things, getting on each other's case in a joking manner and all-around shooting the ♥♥♥♥, to the occasional moment of emotional vulnerability. Each of the two clearly are not perfect people and have their own varying vices which are dealt with in different ways. It's very human and very, very well executed.

Environment wise, yuuuup, that looks like a forest, alright. But for real, the art style is very nice and lends itself to allowing you to stumble upon some truly beautiful scenes of canyons, vistas and forest clearings, they knew they popped off on the environmental design so much they even give you a camera to snap a few photos that are then shown back to you when the credits roll. My only criticism as far as the design goes, is that it sometimes feels very easy to get 'stuck' on a particular piece of geometry (rocks, mostly) and you need to wiggle yourself out of them, but even then, that's just a minor complaint. I don't think I have any real issues other than that.

The only thing I felt overall, outside of minor nitpicks, is that the conclusion and wrapping up of the narrative was a little unsatisfying. Not in an everything falls to bits sort of way, but just in a sense that it feels like it's missing a little something. Regardless though, I would say that if you're looking for a very emotionally human game, then this is one of the few that you cannot go wrong with.

This game is the definition of short and sweet. The story is great and even though it's not fully open world so it isn't "replayable" (unless you want to experience the linear story multiple times), although I believe you can explore at your own pace in one of the special features. But why explore at all? One simple reason: this game is beautiful. The graphics look so good, they're not fully realistic, it's more like a painting that you can't help but stare at in awe and I think that's better than it just looking like real life. It gives it its own little unique feel that no other game I've played has replicated, at least as far as I remember. I felt so immersed in the characters and their relationships and in the end I do think that the moral of the story is, do not be afraid to face what's ahead of you. Sometimes you just need a break, an escape from your problems, an escape from life as a whole, but in the end you have to realise that you have to face your problems and can't escape them forever. I picked this game up for 2 euros and got an experience I won't forget anytime soon, 9/10, I feel like it was a bit too short but if it was any longer it might have been too stretched out, so I think it hits a sweet spot.

TLDR: Great game, pick it up if you can, preferably on sale, either way you'll get a great experience. The graphics are breath-taking and the story is great.

I just finished Firewatch, and wow, what an amazing experience! The game pulls you in with its beautiful visuals and keeps you hooked with its emotional story and characters.

You play as Henry, a guy escaping some tough times with his wife, Julia. The way the game shows their relationship through flashbacks is so touching and real. Then there’s Delilah, your boss on the radio, who’s funny, sarcastic, and sometimes really deep. Talking with her felt so natural, like I was actually building a connection.

Oh, and I can’t forget Mayhem, the dog! Even though he’s only in the prologue, he added such a sweet and emotional touch to Henry’s backstory.

The mystery of the game is gripping, but what I loved most was how it explored loneliness and human connection. Plus, the world is stunning—every sunset and forest view is jaw-dropping, and the music sets the perfect mood.

If you’re into games with great stories, deep characters, and beautiful vibes, I can’t recommend Firewatch enough. It’s one of those games that really sticks with you.

[h1] A beautifully made game, but the advertising misled me [/h1] 

I want to start by acknowledging that Firewatch is a visually stunning game with excellent voice acting and an intriguing premise. From a technical and artistic standpoint, it’s clear that a lot of care went into its creation. However, my personal experience with the game was marred by misleading advertising and significant gaps in the plot.

When I purchased Firewatch, I was under the impression by its description and marketing that it was a relaxing, atmospheric adventure. The game was often described as a “vibe” / atmospheric game, with an emphasis on exploration and introspection. However, I quickly discovered that the tone of the game veers heavily into psychological horror. The sense of tension, dread, and unease pervades much of the experience, which was entirely different from what I was expecting.

As someone who is very sensitive to horror themes, this left me feeling deeply uncomfortable. Had the advertising been more upfront about this tonal aspect, I would have avoided the game altogether. This isn’t an issue of the game being bad but rather that it was mismarketed. The lack of clarity in the description made me feel blindsided.

Other than the advertising, the game leaves many plot points unresolved or open to interpretation. While some might find this ambiguity compelling, I found it frustrating. It felt like the game was setting up a deeper narrative that never fully paid off, leaving me with more questions than answers.

Ultimately, I can see why some people love Firewatch. It is a unique, immersive experience. But for anyone considering it, be aware that it’s not the relaxing, soul-soothing game it may appear to be. If you’re sensitive to psychological tension or prefer clear resolutions in storytelling, this might not be the game for you.

Firewatch is one of those rare games that feels more like an experience than just a game. From the moment I stepped into its world, I was completely captivated by its stunning visuals and engaging story.

The art direction is phenomenal. The game doesn’t aim for photorealism but instead uses a beautifully stylized aesthetic that captures the grandeur of Wyoming's wilderness. Every sunrise, every valley, and every winding trail is like a painting come to life. The vibrant colors and dynamic lighting make even the simplest moments—like walking through a forest—breathtaking. This isn’t just a game; it’s a visual feast that makes exploration feel rewarding in itself.

The story is where Firewatch truly shines. You play as Henry, a man seeking solace as a fire lookout after a personal tragedy. The connection you build with Delilah, your supervisor on the other end of a walkie-talkie, is one of the most authentic and emotionally engaging relationships I’ve ever experienced in gaming. The dialogue is sharp, witty, and, at times, deeply moving.

What starts as a simple job of watching for fires evolves into a layered narrative filled with mystery, personal introspection, and emotional weight. The game masterfully balances moments of quiet reflection with tense, heart-pounding twists. I found myself hanging on to every word of dialogue, every clue, and every small detail that pushed the story forward.

While the gameplay isn’t the main focus, it complements the narrative perfectly. The exploration feels organic, and the radio conversations flow naturally as you walk through the wilderness. It’s a slow burn, but one that rewards patience with an unforgettable story.

Firewatch is an unforgettable journey that combines breathtaking visuals with one of the most engaging stories I’ve ever encountered in gaming.

Firewatch is a wonderful experience.  I'm not quite sure how to classify it, though. It's a bit of a walking simulator, adventure, and suspense game, with some humor thrown in there.  You play as Henry, who is working as a lookout for wilderness fires over a summer season.  His only human contact is via walkie-talkie, to his boss.  Henry is trying to escape his life's difficulties, which I'm sure many of us can empathize with. The graphics are charming for a 9 year old game, the voice acting is excellent, and the near-solitary immersion is very well done.   You go through a lot of emotions playing the game as you work through some background plot stories.

The controls are simple and easy to understand/use, since you don't have to worry about things like entering an inventory to use items, etc. This lets you focus on the environment and the tasks at hand, which are also not overly complex.  This is a good game to play when you just want to appreciate the environment and plot without too much other complexities interfering.  The soundtrack also helps to set the mood and is great to listen to.

If I had any criticism with this game, it has to do with the ending.  No spoilers, but since I was emotionally tied to the game by the time I reached the ending, I personally found it to be a bit anti-climactic.  That said, while I subjectively didn't love the ending, I do understand why the developers chose to end the game the way they did.  Their ending has its own meaning which I can appreciate, despite it seeming superficially anti-climactic.  For information's sake, your choices throughout the game are somewhat limited and ultimately don't change the outcome or path of the plot.  That said, this is not marketed as a "choices matter" game, so that did not bother me, but it seemed to annoy some previous players.

If this game is on sale, it's a no-brainer.  Buy it.

The graphics are amazing, with colorful sunsets, quiet forests, and a feeling of being alone in nature. The music fits perfectly, making the world feel peaceful but also a little mysterious.

The gameplay is simple—you walk around, explore, and use a map and compass. There’s not a lot of action, but it fits the game’s focus on the story. The game is also pretty short, which might disappoint some players.

Overall, Firewatch is a game that tells a great story and makes you think about connection and loneliness. If you like games with strong stories, this one is worth playing.

The gameplay was suitably simple whilst also including enough interactivity so that I didn't at any point feel that the game was tedious really. The use of radio prompts on various items within the environment was fantastic, and the delivery of the commentary felt realistic. There were mysteries that felt exciting throughout.

The reason I just couldn't bring myself to recommend it is simply that the ending is just very anti-climactic, in a way that lessened the rest of the game in my view.

--- SPOILERS AHEAD ---

[spoiler]I am slightly torn on this as in a way, the ending did surprise me. Its shock factor comes from how little shock there is. It's very down-to-earth by the end, and we're shown that the story was never really about some wild conspiracy. It's just a relaxed story about a guy who's struggling with his way forward after a tragedy. His adventure throughout Firewatch serves to teach him, as the protagonist, that he can't just keep trying to escape his struggles, and he needs to finally confront his reality and care for his wife. It's a decent moral for the whole story.

I just wish that I, as the player of this game, could have been given *something* more interesting at the end. The justification for Ned doing all that he did was rather odd, is there really nothing more to it than that he just went mad after losing his son? Why target the lookouts? What was the point in all the psychology reports? Why go to so much effort to scare Henry? Why later point Henry to his hideout? These things are hardly explained in any way that was satisfying to me.

I get also that the whole thing with the teens was just another non-mystery. The protagonists were in their own heads so much that they made more of it than it was. Yet, I still feel like, as a player, I wanted something more from that thread.

I guess the only conclusion I can make is that, although I appreciate the game's demonstration of how in reality, these great mysteries most of the time are almost certainly being hugely inflated by our own imagination; the reason that I play games is because I *enjoy* exercising my imagination. It all feels an interesting piece of art, but a dull video game. I don't play games wanting to be disappointed.[/spoiler]

Firewatch: A Masterpiece of Narrative and Atmosphere

"Firewatch" is a shining example of how video games can transcend mere entertainment to become profound works of art. Developed by Campo Santo, this 2016 first-person adventure game masterfully combines breathtaking visuals, an emotionally gripping story, and unforgettable character dynamics to create an experience that stays with players long after the credits roll.

A Visual and Atmospheric Feast
Set in the Wyoming wilderness during the summer of 1989, "Firewatch" immediately immerses you in its vibrant, painterly landscapes. Each frame feels like a work of art, with lush forests, rolling hills, and dramatic sunsets rendered in a warm, almost dreamlike palette. The game’s environment is not just a backdrop but a living, breathing character of its own, shaping the mood and heightening the sense of isolation and discovery.

Complementing the visuals is the masterful use of sound. From the rustling of trees to the distant calls of wildlife, every audio cue enhances the sense of being truly alone in the wilderness. Chris Remo’s hauntingly beautiful score punctuates the narrative at just the right moments, evoking emotions ranging from quiet introspection to heart-pounding tension.

A Story of Connection and Mystery
At its core, "Firewatch" is about the human need for connection. You play as Henry, a man seeking solace in the wilderness after personal turmoil. His only link to the outside world is his supervisor, Delilah, with whom he communicates via a handheld radio. The voice acting by Rich Sommer (Henry) and Cissy Jones (Delilah) is nothing short of stellar, bringing authenticity and depth to their evolving relationship. Their banter, laced with humor, vulnerability, and tension, is the beating heart of the game.

As you navigate the wilderness, a gripping mystery unfolds, blending personal drama with elements of suspense. The game masterfully balances moments of quiet introspection with bursts of intrigue, keeping you engaged without ever feeling contrived. The narrative choices allow you to shape Henry and Delilah’s relationship, adding a layer of personal investment that makes the story feel uniquely yours.

Gameplay That Serves the Story
While the gameplay mechanics are simple—exploring, interacting with objects, and navigating the environment—they never feel limiting. Instead, they serve the story, allowing you to focus on the emotional and thematic core of the game. The navigation system, which relies on a map and compass, adds to the immersive experience, reinforcing the sense of being alone in the wilderness.

Themes That Resonate
"Firewatch" is a deeply human story, exploring themes of grief, escapism, and the complexities of human connection. It poses questions about responsibility and the ways we cope with personal loss, leaving players to reflect on their own lives long after the game ends.

Conclusion
"Firewatch" is a masterpiece not because of groundbreaking mechanics or action-packed sequences, but because of its ability to tell a deeply resonant story within a beautifully crafted world. It’s a testament to the power of video games as a medium for storytelling, offering an experience that is as thought-provoking as it is visually stunning. For anyone seeking a game that prioritizes narrative and atmosphere over traditional gameplay tropes, "Firewatch" is an absolute must-play.

Without spoiling too much, this game does a lot of super good stuff, and I don't have a lot of criticism, so I'll start off with the only bad stuff I can really say - The game isn't super polished. There were a couple of floating trees, bizarrely low resolution textures, a few typos, and I ended up clipping into something about ten times throughout my playthrough. The default fov is 55, which though easily fixed through a registry edit, it would have been nice to have a slider in the options menu. I mean seriously, who the ♥♥♥♥ plays at 55 fov?

That being said, all the rest is good stuff. The game isn't afraid to take time where it's needed, but keeps the pacing incredibly snappy and quick. The world feels big but not too big, and looks absolutely gorgeous. The sound design is excellent and adds so much to the immersion. The game is long enough for you to get attached to these characters, but short enough to play in a single sitting. All of the little motions your character does are fully animated, and all of the animation in the game looks great.

The writing and voice acting are excellent, which allows the game to have some serious emotional weight. It's no OMORI, but it doesn't slack on making the characters feel real, and charming, and human. It still definitely feels like the scope of an indie game, but it's delivered to the standard of a much higher budget game.

The game design is also very good. Even though you're wandering through the forest and can techincally go wherever you want, it always feels clear where you need to go and how to get there, without yellow-painting anything. As the story progresses, it feels natural to explore new places, and each place leads to the "next" one in a way that doesn't just happen on its own. I feel like without the care put into the design, Firewatch could have easily been a very 6/10 game, if that makes sense. Good, but not that good. But instead, everything fits together perfectly. I'd say it's an 8.5/10 game.

And on top of all of it, it's fun. The gameplay is simple, you spend a lot of time walking, but it feels important while you're doing it. I think a lot of that comes from the pacing, you constantly want to know what's coming next, while also being aware that you can take as long as you want.

Basically, it's really good, and if you think you would like it, you definitely will.

Has some good things about it, but overall was a rather big disappointment. 
Good: If you like this sort of stuff, the dialogues on the radio throughout the game are pretty great and fun. I wouldn't say there was anything particularly meaningful said there, only barely brushing on some thought-provoking stuff, but it was still by far the most interesting part of the game. The atmosphere of the game, some of the visuals and the first-person feel of it all were pretty good too. Was rather funny at times too.

Bad (more of that imo): First, the story is really anticlimactic and doesn't make much sense. There's not really any kind of point it tries to make or anything that is actually accomplished at the end of the day. It's comparable to basically a summer adventure that you've made some good memories on but that's about it. Which in itself is not so bad a thing, but is certainly not what you expect from a story-driven game that is praised for provoking thought. It has some good moments and cool ideas, but it fails to develop them well - turns to the kind of "plot twists" that nobody expects because they'd just be a stupid choice. Not all of it was bad, but overall it felt really lackluster, disppointing, unsatisfying and lacking a bigger direction.
While the gameplay was not terrible, it was very frustrating a lot of the time and had a lot of really weird things about it. The way each day/segment ends is always really abrupt an odd,  It also always works against your interest, cuts off when you have some kind of idea of what to do or wanna go somewhere, but almost never lets you skip the hike through the entire forest so you can got to X. Navigating through the forest is also just a massive pain and at first is pretty fun, but towards the end of the game it's really frustrating and annoying. On one hand, you're supposed to feel like you're just in a wild, open forest with no clear paths set out, but then the way it's all actually designed forces you to follow designated, rigid paths which are easy to miss, confusing and tedious. It would be less of a problem if you didn't have to walk everywhere every time, but you do, so you better learn where eery path goes on the first trry.
Also, a rather minor thing, but still a big disappointment - there's not really any fire. You don't really deal with anything important, dangerous or serious. You walk around, find objects and talk on the radio, that's about it. All the fire's in the background and you almost never interact with it. 
Your choices are also supposed to make a difference, but at no point it really ever felt like they mattered at all. Unless it's between the choice of actually talking on the radio or just missing out on the main part of the game on purpose. 

In general, it's just a really disappointing and anticlimactic game with a lot of really odd choices and tedious game design. It's got some really nice things about it, but it's about as impactful of a story game as a generic crime thriller is lifechanging literature. If you just want to play it for the vibes and maybe some fun time, then it's pretty good, but if you're looking for something more this isn't really it.
