Just finished Firewatch and wow… what a game. It’s super short but somehow it totally pulls you in. Playing as Henry, stuck in a Wyoming forest and talking to Delilah over the radio, felt surprisingly emotional. The dialogue feels real and the way your choices shape the story is subtle but cool.

The atmosphere is everything. The forest looks gorgeous, the lighting and sounds make it feel alive, and some moments legit made me stop and just look around. The sense of isolation mixed with mystery keeps you hooked the whole time.

Gameplay is simple, mostly walking and exploring, but the story makes up for it. Some parts got me really curious, and the ending… wow, it hit harder than I expected.

It’s not perfect — it’s short and some puzzles are super easy — but honestly, it doesn’t matter. The story and vibe are what make it stick.

If you like story-driven games, mysteries, and gorgeous settings, Firewatch is worth it. Definitely left me thinking about it after I finished.

Some directions the game leads you seem like plot devices and it's a little disappointing to have a ton of polish and cohesiveness then those loose ends. But man, it was a very, very up=and-down game that pulled out different emotions from you, and it is so immersive. Its shorter length kept it from being overwhelming for me, despite my wish for an ending to all storylines. Firewatch is simply a unique and magical combination of a video game and an interactive movie.

The ambient sounds and visuals are top-notch, creating an immersive experience that draws you into the heart of the park. The dynamic between Henry and Delilah is engaging and realistic, and it helps drive the emotional depth of the narrative.

It’s not just the gameplay that shines, but the emotional journey you take alongside Henry. It’s a game about loneliness, connection, and discovery, all wrapped in a stunningly atmospheric environment.

If you're looking for a deeply emotional and visually captivating experience, Firewatch is an adventure you should definitely check out. Highly recommended!

Недавно я прошел Firewatch, и мне стоит сказать, что это была невероятно сильная игровая история, оставившая отпечаток. Игра на самом деле заставила меня почувствовать себя немного как в какой-то другой реальности — без всякой магии или сверхъестественного, но при этом с необычным, почти интимным ощущением от происходящего.

Я начал играть, не зная, чего точно ожидать. Firewatch — это не какой-то традиционный экшен, и на первый взгляд может показаться, что это просто прогулка по лесу с элементами симулятора, но как только ты вникаешь в атмосферу, понимаешь, что все не так просто.

Главный герой, Генри, — человек, который решает уйти от проблем и начать новый этап жизни. Его история, как и все, что с ним происходит, подается через диалоги с его напарницей, Делайлой, которая контролирует ситуацию через рацию. Само повествование держит тебя в напряжении, несмотря на отсутствие экшен-сцен или каких-то глобальных угроз. Вместо этого игра сосредоточена на эмоциональной глубине персонажей, их отношениях и их прошлом. Это почти как путешествие не только через лес, но и через самих себя.

Графика тоже стоит отдельного внимания. Природа в Firewatch выглядит потрясающе, и каждый кадр можно воспринимать как картину. Бескрайние леса, горы, озера — все это выглядит ярко, живо и красочно, создавая атмосферу уединения, но в то же время и какой-то опасности, скрытой на горизонте.

Музыка в игре — просто шикарная. Визуально и аудиально игра поддерживает нужное настроение, и даже в моменты тишины ты ощущаешь, что все не так уж спокойно, как может показаться на первый взгляд. Это идеальное сочетание для того, чтобы погрузиться в мир игры.

Не могу не отметить и то, что игра поднимает важные вопросы о жизни, одиночестве, переживаниях и принятии решений. Это не просто прогулка по лесу, это очень личный опыт, который заставляет задуматься о том, как мы взаимодействуем с другими людьми, как они влияют на нас и какие тайны мы скрываем от окружающих.

В конце концов, Firewatch — это игра, в которой важно не то, что ты делаешь, а как ты это переживаешь. Если ты готов к эмоциональной и атмосферной поездке, где каждый диалог и каждое решение имеют значение, эта игра определенно тебе понравится. Лично я остался очень доволен и точно порекомендую ее всем, кто хочет чего-то более глубокого, чем просто экшен или стрелялки.

I liked it, but I cannot wholly recommend. 

Pros: The scenery looks nice, the voice acting is superb, and the story, at least the dialogue, was very engaging. The interaction between H and D, along with the progression of the mystery, were the best parts of my experience. The writing was more vulgar than I expected, but it didn't throw me off too much. 

Cons: The ending felt so disappointing and was the main reason I didn't love Firewatch. [spoiler] The main character loses his connection to someone he grew extremely close to and does not change his feelings on how to approach his wife. There was potential for massive character growth, but the snippet we see into this person's life does not contain it. [/spoiler] Perhaps that was the point, or I missed another message the writers wanted to convey. I also believe the gameplay could have been more involved. The environment doesn't have many interactable elements, and you never see the wildlife you would expect to find while hiking around a national park (aside from the single elk in the opening sequence). The sound design is excellent, but I wanted to see ducks when I looked towards the duck sounds. I can understand not using human models so the character/player feels more isolated, but the world feels emptier than I believe it was meant to be. I don't want to come off as "the gamer that complains about graphics or silly little details", but it would have added to my experience greatly. 

I can only recommend Firewatch if there is a discount. I want to emphasize that there is definitely something here; I appreciated this work as a piece of art and had a laugh or two. Unfortunately, the best word to describe my final thoughts is "dissatisfied".

Firewatch Review – A Beautiful, Frustrating Journey

Firewatch is an emotional and immersive experience, and while I absolutely loved the story and the world it builds, I have to admit—going for 100% completion nearly drove me over the edge. The Ol’ Shoshone achievement in particular was brutal and made me almost want to give up entirely. That said, I did push through and got the full 100%—a personal victory that felt well-earned.

Tip for Completionists:
If you're aiming for 100%, make sure to disable auto-save and manually save before attempting tricky achievements, especially Ol’ Shoshone. It’ll save you a lot of frustration and repetition.

Despite the challenges, the game itself is amazing. The narrative, voice acting, and atmosphere are top-notch. It’s a slow burn, but incredibly rewarding if you’re into character-driven stories with emotional depth. The setting is beautifully crafted, and the sense of isolation is palpable in the best way possible.

This one might be an oldie, but it’s definitely worth your time. I’d absolutely recommend it—just go in prepared if you’re a completionist.

Firewatch is a gorgeous, beautifully voice-acted walking simulator with minimalist cartoonish views and an enthralling narrative that hooks the player in a captivating conspiracy within Firewatch’s secluded Wyoming National Park. Firewatch begins with a gutwrenching intro, not unlike the beginning of Up, that manages to convey the same emotion with only text and hopeless decisions. The intro introduces the arc of Henry, the protagonist, and his wife Julia’s love story till their eventual battle with her dementia. The story takes place over 79 Days with many time skips that allow a humorous and personable relationship to bud between Henry and Delilah. These two Fire watchtower park rangers never actually meet each other in the full game but develop a connection over their radios. I won’t say much about the story as it’s easily the game’s best aspect — it’s best to go in blind. You start off by completing menial tasks until you fall under suspicion in a disappearance case that only grows into a greater conspiracy. Apart from the radio transmissions, the game’s primary mode of advancing the story is through journals and notebook pages scattered across the world. You slowly trek around a surprisingly expansive park with an assortment of interesting landmarks and secrets to discover along your path. Even though at times, the 6-mile walks could be tedious; it’s all the other elements — story, visuals, the beautiful sounds of nature all around you, and finally, the fitting light guitar and piano songs — that play throughout the experience — along with the fairly engaging side activities and investigations that come within the package that make it so great. As Campo Santo’s first and last game, it was a lovely introduction to their almost watercolor art style and engrossing writing, and it’s a damn tragedy that they were absorbed by Valve: I only hope that their writing talent goes towards creating a fun HL3 ;)

I want to firstly say I have mixed feelings on this game, and that I recommend getting it on sale.

Technically speaking, the game is weak. Its kind of just a walking simulator that breaks up walking with animations. And even the few interactables in the world tend to have some issues. Animations ending too early, dropping you at the wrong point, or causing your to just straight up move in an unintended direction with no way to break out. Softlocked me once or twice in my playtime, had to load a previous save and try again. This seems like something that should have popped up in playtesting and been fixed for the amount of times it had occurred to me. Story's ending is kind of weak if you didn't find all the bonus things that aren't required for the story, too many loose threads (which does encourage a second playthrough). Even with all the information, there's no real moral to the story, or even a solid conclusion. You kind of just experience it, which I suppose is fine for most. You arrive, you participate, you leave. The mysteries get solved and you get sad. The side objectives are pretty few and far between, mostly tied down to your exploration. And it feels like some of these systems could have been fleshed out just a little bit more. For instance, collecting all the books doesn't really have any benefit other than being able to fill your bookshelf. But the game never even tells you its possible, and you can't 'save' them the way you can with papers. You have to lug each one by hand back to your watchtower. Last bad thing, the choices in the stories dialogue change so very little. I enjoyed hearing differing voicelines on the second playthrough, but the only 'choices' that really affect the outcome of anything are what you choose in the text section at the beginning. It really feels like this game was created the way it was to avoid having to animate other people besides yourself, but a lot of the core moments in the story are sort of distant from the player as a result. You really have to roleplay the role you've been given, rather than experiencing the player's background. And your choices don't really matter anyways.

There is good in this game though, hence the recommended status. It's pretty, the music is great, and the character dialogue is very well written too. There's not a line or delivery that feels out of place in the whole runtime. If you're here for story, the games got it. Like walking in the woods? This may not be a one-for-one, but it's pretty darn good. It's cool to go exploring, to talk with Delilah (the voice on the radio), to solve the mystery at hand. The game genuinely had me deeply interested throughout, even if the ending was a little weak. For such a short game, you get real connection with these characters the same way you would with any novel. I think the mild obsession with books in the game tells a little about the world-builders in a non-straightforward way, because its evident they know how to write. Anyways, I can't say much more without forwarding a game playthrough. If you don't mind a little jank and enjoy e-novella type games, this is absolutely something you should take a look at. Being an outdoorsman myself I have quite a bit of appreciation for the content, but I think anyone willing to enjoy some scenery will enjoy the game.

The first time you enter the cabin you'll notice a whole bunch of various household items you can interact with. After all, the game is about being a fire lookout, so it makes sense that you spend quite a lot of time in the cabin and do things in it, right? You have supplies, a stove, a coffee pot, a mug, wait a minute, can you cook a coffee and enjoy some cozy juicy roleplay in this atmospheric, story-rich adventure? Nah, sorry, you can only pick things up, look at them and then drop carelessly. That's the whole interactivity of the objects in the environment. The max you get is rotating a book so that you can read the back cover.

They added a d20 dice to the game for story reasons, but can you roll the dice? Sure you can, but it will never stop rolling infuriatingly slowly, even on a level flat surface. Being teased with something cool and then getting trolled is a thing this game does constantly.

That lazy interaction system is not only bad in itself but it also ruins the story at times. You see a framed photograph of [spoiler] your wife, who is now very sick [/spoiler], and of course, you would pick it up to take a better look but guess what, the only thing you can do afterward is toss it down like you would throw a dirty paper plate into a garbage bin. That doesn't make sense at all and is very disappointing.

The dialogues you have over the radio aren't much better in quality, and the options you get are sometimes so bad and uncalled for, I wouldn't want to pick any of those. Would you prefer being unreasonably aggressive or awkwardly over-apologetic? Luckily, you can ignore the dialogue and say nothing. Whatever you choose to do won't affect anything, except for you, the player who personally experienced that interaction. Maybe the dialogues are written like that by design since the characters have their issues but still, it's not fun.

The walking part of this walking simulator has some serious issues as well. Being permanently stuck between floorboards or being unable to step over a branch that a dog could carry and having to walk around it is frustrating. The camera is so unnecessarily shaky, it's like you're playing a bobblehead. You hop over a log or get on top of a rock and the camera does this insane animation as if you were doing some sick parkour moves. After a while, you learn to disengage your attention during these crazy interactions and it's not what you would expect from a game about enjoying hiking.

None of the features in this game are properly tuned or free of bugs, and there aren't even that many of the features. Trying to climb a rope will sometimes put you in an invisible wagon and carry you away in a random direction. The dialogues are timed events, and sometimes the time you get is too short, especially considering that your input could be blocked with something else. The lighting bugs out and changes when you look around. Even the Steam achievement system is scuffed and you will likely miss both missable and unmissable achievements. I finished the entire game but only got 1 out of 10, which is somewhat close to how I rate the overall experience.

There were some interesting moments, but the negatives outweighed them heavily. Firewatch could be a decent movie, but as an interactive experience it's just bad, so if you want to enjoy it, just watch a playthrough on YouTube. It's free of charge, free of frustration, and will save you from the hassle of clicking the mouse and holding W.

Firewatch is one of those games I wish I could play for the first time again.

It isn’t a long game and there isn’t loads of action, but that honestly isn’t the point. Most of the experience is just walking through the forest, talking over the radio and slowly learning more about Henry, Delilah and what’s happening around you.

The atmosphere is easily the best part. The art style is beautiful, the music fits perfectly and even the quiet moments feel important. Walking through the forest alone can feel relaxing one minute, then genuinely unsettling the next.

A few things I really liked:

- The visuals are simple but stunning
- Henry and Delilah actually feel like real people
- The voice acting is genuinely brilliant
- The radio conversations make exploring much more interesting
- The mystery keeps you wanting to find out what happens next
- The soundtrack and atmosphere work perfectly together
- It doesn’t drag itself out longer than it needs to

The conversations between Henry and Delilah are what made the game memorable for me. Their relationship feels natural, awkward and believable instead of sounding like two characters reading scripted dialogue. I actually cared about what they were saying, which is rare for a game this short.

The story also does a good job of making you question everything. At times I had no idea what was actually happening or who could be trusted, and exploring alone made the whole situation feel much creepier.

I know some people don’t like the ending, and I understand why. It isn’t some massive dramatic conclusion that answers everything perfectly. It feels more realistic and bittersweet, which honestly suited the rest of the game for me.

Is it action-packed? No.

Is it particularly long? Not really.

Did it still leave more of an impact on me than games five times its length? Definitely.

Firewatch is beautiful, emotional and slightly unsettling in a way that’s hard to explain without spoiling it. It left me feeling a bit empty when it ended, but in the best possible way.

Firewatch is an intriguing experience, even if the gameplay boils down to little more than navigating to specific locations on a map. The beautiful visuals and engaging dialogue help make the journey feel worthwhile, but it’s hard to ignore the limitations of player agency.

While the game offers a variety of dialogue choices and ways to interact with the world, it’s disappointing to realize that these decisions have no real impact on the story’s progression. This makes the narrative feel more linear than it initially appears, which might leave some players wanting more depth.

The story itself is compelling, pulling you in with its mysterious and intimate tone. However, the ending leaves something to be desired—it feels underwhelming compared to the buildup, lacking the emotional punch that could have made the conclusion truly memorable.

Ultimately, Firewatch feels more like watching an indie film than playing a traditional video game. That’s not necessarily a bad thing, but if you’re looking for meaningful choices or a more dynamic conclusion, you might walk away feeling slightly unsatisfied. Still, the journey itself is worth experiencing for its storytelling and atmosphere.

It took me a little over three hours to complete, and in that time, I found myself fully immersed in the story, which demands to be played in a single sitting. The voice acting in Firewatch is absolutely top-notch, with the performances from the two lead characters—Henry and Delilah—bringing an emotional depth that anchors the entire narrative. Their dialogue feels incredibly natural, allowing the relationship between them to develop in an organic way. It’s this dynamic that makes the story so compelling, as the game explores themes of loneliness, isolation, and the human need for connection.

Complementing the visuals and voice acting is a soothing, atmospheric soundtrack that perfectly matches the mood of the game. The music enhances the experience without overwhelming it, allowing players to lose themselves in the quiet tension of the story.

At its core, Firewatch is a deeply emotional journey that touches on real-world issues like stress, anxiety, and depression. The game captures the psychological weight of dealing with personal loss, mental health struggles, and the yearning for escape in a way that’s both subtle and powerful. The story doesn’t shy away from exploring the complexity of human emotions, and it leaves you reflecting long after the credits roll. 

In conclusion, Firewatch is an experience that resonates deeply. It’s a game that not only tells a compelling story but also explores the inner turmoil and emotional struggles that come with facing one’s fears and confronting personal demons. It’s an experience that will stay with you, prompting you to think about the nature of relationships, isolation, and the importance of human connection, long after you’ve finished playing.

The best thing about Firewatch is how, for lack of a better word, real it feels. The game may be stylized and unrealistic visually, but there's a very tactile, grounded sense to it as you explore. The characters too feel very real. Henry and especially Delilah feel like real, complicated people and I was instantly sold on their interactions. I think a lot of this is due to some very good voice acting.

I know at the time it was controversial, but I'm overall pretty happy with how the game ended. I don't think there was any way for there to be an actual grand conspiracy that wouldn't feel ridiculous in a grounded game like this one. The ultimate anticlimax also serves the game's themes. Delilah and Henry were both so quick to jump to the idea of a grand conspiracy, of the whole world screwing them over because they wanted their problems to be fantastical and not their fault, not the mundane struggles they were trying to escape from. Having it all turn out to be mistakes, paranoia, and pointless human tragedy just reinforces the message that there's no running from the struggles of everyday human life. I think not seeing Delilah is also a good thing. Finally seeing a character you've known only by their voice can be easily screwed up.

I feel like the game could have been longer, and possessed a few more sections that encouraged exploration and isolation. After the beginning, Firewatch becomes very linear and this extends to the game's design. The world is not as open as it looks, and you're confined to very linear paths for a lot of it. It can break immersion, especially when it doesn't look like there should be any good reason you can't access a certain area. This hampers the game quite a bit for me, it makes traversing the same paths back and forth feel like more of a chore than it should in a game this pretty.

I have a handful of other small quibbles. It's a little annoying how Henry refuses to place down any object normally. It almost makes me not want to pick anything up because I know it's going to end up on the floor in a few seconds. It just looks and feels silly. I also wish there was more music. The tracks the game does have are good, but there's just so few of them.

An intriguing and thought-provoking work of art that I can suggest that anyone experience...once at least. "Firewatch" is one of two titles (Along with "Edith Finch") given as examples of great walking simulators and it succeeds well enough that I agree with this consensus. It has the right blend of interactivity, exploration and narrative to carry the short runtime, but I (and most reviewers) agree that the strength of the plot dips near the end. The conclusion not only lacks catharsis but seems nonsensical the more time that is spent thinking about it. Despite this depressing denouement, the core gameplay remains enjoyable throughout and the exploration aspect works. The graphics are more than satisfactory and soundscape is serviceable. On the whole, I would rate "Firewatch" as just about worth a few hours and $2, but the player will probably draw more from the experience of the midgame than the ending.

Firewatch is a unique & interesting game. The game is so unique that it’s unlike anything I’ve played & the game does not fit neatly into any one genre. I would describe Firewatch as an interactive movie, walking simulator, suspense game. One playthrough of Firewatch took me roughly 9 hrs. But I play games slowly, so a typical gamer could finish the game in perhaps 4-5 hours.

 Firewatch is polished & high quality. The game has a good frame rate & quality, smooth gameplay. Moreover, the game offers intuitive & responsive controls. Also, the game is easy yet not boring or shallow. And, the game’s art design is stylized. It’s eye-catching & interesting, looking like a realistic painting.

Firewatch boasts some of the best voice acting I’ve heard in a game. The performances are believable & compelling. The stellar voice acting carries the game; the phenomenal voice acting makes the game stand out, given that a major part of the game are the conversations by radio the MC has with Delilah. Since you never see Delilah, the voice acting does the heavy lifting.

Let’s discuss the game’s ending without spoilers. Many people don’t like the ending. To be fair, the ending is straightforward & anticlimactic. But the ending is also surprising, shocking & profound. To me this shows the genius of the developers. I ended up liking the ending once I understood it (I had to Google it as the ending’s meaning is profound & hard to see). I loved that I came away from the game with such thought-provoking & deep commentary on the human condition.

Firewatch does have some flaws. The biggest flaw is the mediocre & disappointing free-roam mode. After you beat the game, you can free roam the beautiful game world. But you don’t keep the tools you gained from beating the game. Hence, large parts of the game world are unavailable for free roam. This was a huge disappointment for me.

Another flaw, although minor, is that the game does not have auto-walk or auto-run. So you have to manually walk & run. Thankfully, the game map is not huge. Even still, it was annoying & rather tedious to have to constantly hold the movement buttons.

Another minor flaw is that in one aspect, the game suffers from a lack of realism. The game takes place in a forest, yet there are almost no animals. This is unrealistic. Just realize that Firewatch is not an animal-watching game.

Finally, despite the game's name, you never actually do any fire watching. Instead, you do a lot of hiking. Personally, this flaw did not bother me because I wanted a hiking simulator game. But I could easily see this flaw bothering some players, maybe many.

In conclusion, Firewatch is a prime example of video games as art. It’s amazing to see what the video game medium can produce. I highly recommend Firewatch, especially if you’re looking for something unique & want a memorable experience. I know I’ll be thinking about this game for a long time.

Took me around 6.3 hours, according to Steam - but Firewatch is in the books. Firewatch is a walking-sim type of adventure game, as most of the time you'll be walking around to the next location to find an item, use a certain item, and get the next cut-scene and/or choice. You will make choices, which shape the actual story & lines, for the most part - even if it might not actually shape the actual ending itself.

After a relationship that has had its ups & down, you take a job as a fire lookout in a big watchtower in 1989. All kinds of incidents happen in Wyoming here in this location and you're to take care of them how you see fit. Without giving too much away here, the story's really good & what you decide in the opening stuff and say to Delilah on the radio will shape the journey itself.

The game ran also well for the most part at 1080p at mostly 60fps, except for a few frame-drops here and there w/ the game maxed-out. Not a big deal w/ the frame-drops here and there, as this isn't an action game and it doesn't happen a ton.

Regardless, the story will hit you hard once you get to the end & find out what likely really happened, even though there's so much other stuff Lore-wise that feels like other stuff might or might not have happened or been a part of this madness; depends on how you look at & feel about some of this extra Lore, as it could be there as "red herrings" or actually might be important threads. Some of it, feels up to interpretation - but, maybe extra playthroughs & combing through everything could possibly help that out.

Regardless, this walking sim and story was really good and I certainly enjoyed my 6.3 hours with it or so.

Firewatch is a masterpiece, and a game that utilizes all of its mechanics, storybeats and atmosphere beautifully. Every time I got up to go to the bathroom, or go do something else, I felt like I was stepping out of a different world; it's that immersive. I'm an avid hiker, and the way this game encompasses nature, the outdoors, and the way it uses that to cultivate environmental storytelling is so impressive. It also helps that the game's art style is breathtaking. I took so many screenshots during this playthrough, and they aren't even really screenshots I put any genuine effort into, but I still love them all. It's so effective in its visual design, and so aesthetically pleasing.

The story and specifically characters also definitely serve as a highlight of the experience, and probably THE main highlight for most. From the opening section, I pretty much already knew I was going to like this; and it didn't disappoint. I absolutely marveled Henry and Delilah's dynamic together, and thought it served as a genuinely really interesting portrayal of two people connecting in the same environment despite never actually seeing each other at all. The dialogue and natural chemistry these two have with each other is just so well presented, and it's probably my favorite part of the overall game. It also helps that the actual plot, and mystery is engaging to a fault, never fully cluing in the player.

Overall, Firewatch is an interesting game for those who like story/character focused games, but it's not without it's share of flaws. The game largely focuses on your relationship with your boss, Delilah, a fellow ranger posted in a nearby firewatch tower, and the unraveling of a mystery that develops as the story progresses.

[u]Pros[/u]
[list]
    [*]The dialogue - This is where the game shines brightest. The voice acting is great and the banter between your character and Delilah feels real, and human, and the way you choose to respond to her (or not) can have interesting impacts on dialogue later in the story.
    [*]An Interesting and well developed world - The map isn't just a desolate forest, it's filled with natural sights and the evidence of human activity both past and present, giving you the sense that this is a world that has been lived in, and is alive.
    [*]The intricate plot and how it is interwoven with different events and dialogue as the game progresses. However, certain story beats can feel a little hollow at times (arguably there's simply not enough time in the game to build emotional investment into certain things that the game might want you to be invested in).
    [*]The music often does a great job at setting the tone in any given scene.
[/list]

[u]Cons[/u]
[list]
    [*]The price/playtime ratio: This is a very short game, easily completed within a single evening (4-6 hours), so if you're looking for your money to buy you more entertainment than that, consider waiting for a sale.
    [*]Walking around the world and limited exploration - This is what you spend the vast majority of your playtime doing, but I didn't find it particularly interesting; in other words, it's a bit of a walking simulator. For a game about being out in the wilderness I expected the exploration to be a highlight of the game, but often it felt like "fun on rails" typically there's only one way to get from one place to another, and if you stray from the trail for more than a moment you'll discover the invisible walls that prevent any pathfinding you might want to do on your own. The logs,and ledges you have to climb over, and the ropes you have to climb up and down (essentially any time the game prompts you to press the space bar) can feel tedious and don't seem to add much to the game. There are a few minor secrets to be discovered in small areas, but not many. Unfortunately, the game's world is much more linear than it appears.
    [*]Graphics and graphical glitches - Overall the graphics for this game are alright, they didn't really draw me into the game's world as much as I had hoped, but that is perhaps more of a personal preference thing. The bigger issue to me is that there were semi-frequent graphical glitches which detracted from my immersion (in what is supposed to be an atmospheric and immersive game). There was a fair share of floating trees and rocks, a fair amount of clipping with interactive objects (for example, I once had a climbing rope disappear halfway into a cliff side), and some points in the game where the lighting just didn't seem to work quite right.
    [*] This last one is a minor thing, but your character is a middle aged man who is somehow able to frequently drop 12-15 feet straight down off of rock ledges without even a little grunt of pain when his knees should have been practically destroyed. Just another little thing that detracts from the immersion.
[/list]

So, if you like story games, give this game a shot when it's on sale, it's still pretty decent entertainment for an evening.

[b]Honestly, I didn't expect Firewatch to be so well written and voiced. I went into it blind not knowing what to expect, and it’s always a win when you get sucked right in, like one does with a good book.[/b]

You could have a seemingly boring game, but if the story is captivating and engrossing, it'll carry it leaps and bounds - not saying the gameplay here is boring, just be mindful it is an 'active' walking sim similar to 'The Vanishing of Ethan Carter'. Here, you go about each day performing duties as a Firewatch volunteer, all the while conversing with others over a walkie-talkie. It breaks up the feeling of isolation nicely, otherwise solace is there should you choose to ignore calls.

Thematically, it starts off with a love story, a tragedy which makes you take up a job as a ranger in the middle of nowhere. How you deal with things and what you ultimately decide on pans out through self-reflection, dialogue and your actions - it's a 'journey not destination' type of experience and we all need some of those once in a while. I liked the use of a bushfire, and not a traditional storm, to symbolise a growing threat and impending doom in the plot. There is a darker tone to the story, though I'll let you discover that on your own.

Only two gripes, getting stuck on geometry is a thing with occasional invisible walls and janky vaulting mechanics. Some of the responses to choose from yield very aggressive/accusatory discussion threads, a tone I personally wouldn't have assumed judging by the choices.

[b][i]All in all, I thoroughly enjoyed Firewatch. It's a great story driven game - about spending the summer in a desolate nature reserve, running away from tough troubles, only to have to face them eventually anyway.[/i][/b]

[h1]A Remarkable Adventure Game That Accomplishes So Much With So Little[/h1]
Took me many years to finally play this but man am I glad I got around to it. [i]Firewatch[/i] is a game that puts you in the shoes of a man who is trying to rediscover himself after a grave misfortune. The player gets to play out this tragic backstory in a sort of 'choose your own adventure novel' style opening that honestly felt like the video game equivalent of the prologue scene from Pixar's [i]Up[/i]. After sinking its hooks in, the game is ready to set you off on an adventure where you work as a fire watch for a few months while trying to get your life back on track.

The overwhelming majority of the story is delivered from the protagonist and another fire watch who radios you throughout the story. Their relationship blossoms and the mundane begins to seep in initially as you complete rudimentary tasks around the forest with simple objectives and excellent pacing of radio conversations that perfectly fill the space of time you spend traveling around the camp sites. There are no animated faces you will come across, no fail states, less than a handful of voice acted characters, and a simplistic art style. Despite this, however, this game made me laugh, cry, cheer, shriek, and legitimately got under my skin at one point. And it all culminates in an ending that is very quiet yet haunting and hints at a tremendous future for all the characters involved.

It's hard to think of much to criticize about this game, as it sets out to achieve something relatively simple, yet emotional, and it succeeds at that. I suppose one issue is just the lack of any real puzzle solving. All the mysteries and secrets you stumble by on your various treks through the forest conveniently all tie up nicely in the final hour, which does make the world feel as small as it actually is. But that shouldn't detract from what is an excellent one and done adventure that, in spite of the lack of replay value, I'll still probably revisit years later when I similarly feel aimless and want to share the experience with someone special. That is how terrific the writing is. And honestly, how many games can you say that about?

The game’s narrative is immersive and thought-provoking, with each conversation adding layers to the characters and the mystery unfolding around you. The voice acting is superb, and it feels like you’re truly building a relationship with Delilah, even though you're separated by miles of wilderness. Every decision, every response feels meaningful, which makes the story feel personal.

The visuals are stunning, offering beautiful, painterly views of Wyoming’s wilderness. The art style creates a sense of tranquility, which contrasts wonderfully with the subtle tension that builds as the mystery unravels. You’re constantly wondering what's around the corner, not just in terms of the landscape but in the storyline as well.

Overall, Firewatch offers a refreshing, intimate experience that’s more about human connection and self-discovery than action-packed moments. If you’re looking for a game that values story and atmosphere, this one is a must-play.

🌟[h1]  Overrated and Full of Missed Opportunities 🌟[/h1]

This game came so close to being great, but I have to disagree with a lot of the praise it gets.

[b]🔆 Visuals 🔆[/b]
The [u]scenery is ABSOLUTELY beautiful.[/u] I really enjoyed exploring the forest, and it did help distract me from the fact that you’ll be walking A LOT. 

[b]🔆 Characters 🔆[/b]
The [u]voice acting is excellent[/u], and I loved the little backstories we get. The writing is solid, and the occasional banter between characters felt natural. 

[b]🔆 Gameplay 🔆[/b]
Smooth and easy to play—no complaints here.

[b]🔆 Story 🔆[/b]
Here’s where things fall apart for me. The game does a lot of building and teasing—constantly making me wonder if Henry was losing it, if Delilah was hiding something, or if Ned was really as bad as she claimed. The setup was so good, with conspiracy theories running wild in my head as things escalated.

But the story with the child? [u]It was so empty[/u]. When I finally discovered him, I couldn’t even process the emotions I was supposed to feel. The death of a child is, of course, tragic—but the game gives us so little to work with that I [u]wasn’t emotionally invested[/u]. What does this even have to do with the larger story? Why does Delilah hate Ned so much? It felt like a missed opportunity for a deeper connection.

And the situation with the teenage girls? What was that all about? They set off fireworks, I scold them, they call me names, then they go missing—Delilah asks if we should tell the police, I say yes, and she goes behind my back and doesn’t report it? What?! Then after all that build-up, they’re just found drunk and in jail? Who asked for this subplot? It added nothing to the story and felt like a distraction to the fact that there is truly nothing more to this game.

[b]🔆 The Ending 🔆[/b]
WHYYYYY?! I wasn’t expecting or hoping for a romantic relationship with Delilah, but I still don’t understand how she could just leave me in the middle of a fire?! Her excuse: "I couldn't bring myself to see you in person." Okay... but I’m literally in a burning forest right now? Sure, a second helicopter comes to save me, but wow, what a way to close things off. And Ned? I just felt bad for the guy by the end of it all. His story [u]could’ve been explored in a more meaningful way.[/u]

[b]🔆 Final Thoughts 🔆[/b]
All in all, I just don’t get it. As you can see, I have so many questions and can’t grasp how people enjoy this game. But hey, to each their own, I guess.

If this review catches your eye, let this first sentence warn you that this game is not a fire watch simulator.   If that is what you are looking for, this is probably not for you. Some games allow your to design characters and pick multiple dialogue options to lead to different narrative outcomes.  That is not this game.  This game, like a novel, tells a story through its defined main characters.  

The visual style of the game struck a unique balance of style, graphic design choice, and color palette which maintained both a high frame-rate and brilliant visuals. The cell style graphics kept mostly 60fps frame-rates on my Steam Deck with only a few stutters.  The style of animation was not distracting, and overall the verisimilitude and presence felt during game-play lead to a highly engaging experience. I started the game on the last day of a fall camping trip, and finished the evening of my return home. I feel as that choice contributed positively to the feeling of presence I felt in playing.

As hinted at previously, the results of the dialogue choices in Firewatch are mostly fixed, and the characters cannot be customized or built to your preference. You can't deviate from the story being told.  This isn't a failing on the designer's part. To customize these things would have broken the very story being told.  Firewatch feels like a novella, and the many mystery books you can inspect along the way seem to be a nod to more of a literary flair. The story unfolding before you is conveyed through a middle aged man and woman communicating via a handheld radio. Firewatch weaves a bittersweet tale of [spoiler] escapism [/spoiler] and loss intertwined through the main story arch .  If you are dealing with or have dealt with loss, or perhaps a serious illness, you may find yourself connecting with these characters in the woods.  I didn't spoiler tag most of this, as its in the introduction (perhaps even the thing I did spoiler tag), but I'll leave a word out here as it felt to me like the bigger part of the twist depending on how you yourself played through the game and connected to the story. 

The game is short, it's doable in an evening for even a busy adult. I think that was perhaps a good choice.  There are some small achievement hunt activities, and collectible aspects of the game if you are inclined (I wasn't). I played through the main story arc, it held my attention fully, and I put the game down and had a good think.  I'll likely uninstall now that the story has been told. Perhaps I'll revisit in a few years for a re[strikethrough]read/strikethrough]play.  Honestly at the end of my time with Firewatch I think I might have valued a reflective hour sipping a whisky by the fire as a cathartic debrief.  If you decide to play, and the ending doesn't  land with you,  consider spending a few minutes unplugged and just thinking about why.

review:
TL/DR: It's a walking sim with a weird plot and clunky mechanics
Firewatch has great visuals and voice acting, and does a good job of creating suspense and getting you interested in the story. However, I literally could not bring myself to finish the game due to the incredibly frustrating game play. I won't spoil the plot, but in my opinion it wasn't interesting enough to warrant the literal HOURS I had to spend wandering around finding where I was supposed to go. There are also small optimization issues that really irritated me. For example, even though the game gives you no directions and you're supposed to read a map to figure out where to go, you physically cannot sprint with your map and compass out. Speaking of the compass, any time you use your radio (which you use A LOT) it forces you to put away your compass, which you will most likely immediately pull out again. I was really interested in the plot, but that interest was quickly replaced by anger due to the incessant amount of aimless, clunky wandering. If you enjoy slow paced games I'd say you'll love this title, but if you have ADHD like I probably do you might want to skip this one.

Beautiful game, in both scenery and story. Both of our main characters are likable, funny and their chemistry is perfect. I've seen this game get a lot of hate in the past for the ending but I think it fits well. Henry used this job and the forest as a temporary escape from his problems, and it was time for him to go home and face reality.

Good short binge game. Definitely worth picking up anytime on sale. The art style alone is gorgeous and the dialogue between Henry and Delilah. Heart breaking beauty in the narrative paired with visuals around every corner worthy to be your next wallpaper. Hell, it may even inspire you to take a spontaneous trip to go hiking with some friends, and you will love every moment with nature.

Some spoilers ahead:

Fantastic scenery and voice acting; the voice actors really did well. And the way the story unfolds is fantastic, but they quickly fizzle out. The guy you play as, and the woman you talk to over the radio - Delilah - are not much to praise, nor to take any special note of.

What I mean by that, is that I wish there were more archetypes presented in dialogue choices - as there were numerous instances where the presented choices were nothing that I would say - especially whenever Delilah started to lose her ♥♥♥♥ and somewhat began to turn on you; the presented dialogue choices in those instances with her certainly did not help her to calm down and get a grip... nor to have her respect you. 

Delilah herself seems to be extremely manipulative, and when times got tough, she came off as... well... a ♥♥♥♥♥ with no penance. Perhaps that was intentional on the Developers' part, and if so, then that's just a personal gripe of mine instead of constructive criticism.

There are several different tasks that the Player can go on, and they all are REALLY interesting, but most of them just... fizzle away in excitement/curiosity. 

And you'd think that with nearly 3 months of constant communication via radios, and even sexual and flirtatious banter, that the two of you would have met in the flesh, and - if you chose to warm-up to her, that she would have waited for you during the evacuation and would have been much more willing to come with you back to your home. The ending was extremely disappointing because you will always get the same outcome - no matter your relationship that was developed with Delilah.

About the ending with Delilah never waiting for the Player: The Developers should have given different explanations (rescue team insisted, dragged her away because of smoke inhalation maybe…) But the complete shutdown at the end didn’t feel right when compared to the relationship the Player had with her during the game (if the Player chose to warm up to her intimately.) I would have appreciated a more hopeful ending, like exchanging phone numbers if you will, where they talk about meeting up (before or after they “put their affairs in order”, or whatever), having a dinner, decide to talk about what happened, continuing a relationship (be it friendship, romantic, or just professional.)

TL;DR: I finished this game in around 4 hours, all in one go. Voice acting and scenery is solid, but the RPG element is very much lacking in most parts - along with a dissatisfying ending that always ends the same way. And the only human connection you have, is a manipulative ♥♥♥♥♥. This game is NOT worth 20$ considering the playtime and my less-than-stellar experience. Would not recommend.

Set in the Wyoming wilderness, the game’s art direction is stunning, with vibrant, painterly landscapes that shift beautifully as the story unfolds. The real star here, however, is the dialogue between the protagonist, Henry, and his supervisor, Delilah, which feels natural and engaging, giving the story a deeply personal touch.

While Firewatch is light on gameplay, focusing more on exploration and choices, its strength lies in its storytelling and the tension of isolation in the wilderness. The game’s pacing, combined with its evolving mystery, keeps you hooked. However, some may find its abrupt ending unsatisfying. Overall, Firewatch is a unique, introspective experience that prioritizes emotion over action, leaving a lasting impression.

Firewatch isn't a bad game; this is more of a mixed review than a negative one. 

There is genuine effort to be seen at every moment, be it the charming art style, the soundtrack, or the surprisingly impressive voice acting. The work invested into this game is apparent and recognised, but despite that effort and care, and a sound setup for an intriguing story, Firewatch falls short in its execution.

To keep it brief, the game's story sets various pieces in motion, only for most of them to fizzle out into nothing substantial; the primary mystery, once revealed, doesn't live up to the anticipation that is otherwise competently built up during the game's events. The banter between the two primary characters is fun and at most times convincing in its delivery, but for all of their development - and much like the mystery - there isn't a particularly satisfying ending; everything is left very open-ended, which might be intentional.

At its full price, I wouldn't recommend Firewatch, but for a decent discount it will reliably provide a few hours of intriguing story telling.

If you're not immediately punched in the gut by the first ten minutes of gameplay, you're not in the correct headspace for this game. The backstory of Henry, the playable character, must be something you carry with you for the entirety of the experience. This established narrative is the fire that you are about to watch burn for the next three hours. 

Henry is a coward. I mean that he is dominated by his fear. His fear has already ruined his life, soaked him in gasoline and tossed him a match. Fear has denied him healthy social interactions, relationships, and robbed him of parenthood. Fear put a bottle in his hand and made him unable to care for his wife. It's driven him out to the middle of nowhere to hide, at the top of a tower like a cornered cat. 

However, Henry has you, the player, making him do all manner of heroic acts. You make him surprise himself with his own bravery, you are like a spirit of divine intervention driving him onward to solve a great mystery. More incredible still, everything you do will expose even greater cowards in your midst.

Just as the employees are only able to watch the fire burn and not extinguish it, so too goes the story with Henry and all that is consuming him internally. I realized somberly that the moment I relinquished control over Henry he'd go right back to being overwhelmed by his circumstances, scampering away again at the first hint of adversity. The only redeeming acts he was ever responsible for, occurred while I was at the helm. He is a tragic husk doomed to keep burning until his ashes scatter. All I'd shown him in those hours of divine inspiration was a glimpse into his own dark fate to come, and that there was no brighter path to steer him towards. He is alone, but he's not the only one.

For me Firewatch is and always will be an absolute masterpiece that I could fully immerse myself in. With characters that feel real, phenomenal voice acting, a very interesting story with great underlying messages and lessons, and of course the absolutely BEST visuals I have EVER seen in any game no matter the graphics. Walking through this world was an incredible experience and I at multiple points just stopped and looked around at the stunning scenery.

Of course I can not say that this game is perfect, or at least I can't say that it's perfect for everyone, because it isn't. There s a couple of minor things in the game that people say are flaws, but there is one big thing that divides people on whether to love or hate this game, and that is of course the story and escpecially the ending. Now don't get wrong, I loved the story, it was thrilling, thought provoking and beautiful. Even a lot of people who view the story as a giant flaw think so, but the ending is just something that a lot of people can't enjoy and for some people it ruins the entire game.

The ending is to many lackluster and dissapointing, people leave the game felling empty and unfulfilled, which I totally understand. I was not prepared for the ending myself, because it was so different from all other games, but that is also one of the reasons I really like the ending. Even though it ended a bit more abrubtly than I was was expecting, I still found myself sitting down and just thinking about it and all it's different meanings for a while after I finished it. 
Many would say that the ending wasn't well thought out, but I strongly disagree, Firewatch is a game about [b] isolation, running away and escaping[/b], and why doing it isn't all bad. In that way I think the ending absolutely succeded, because that is exactly what the ending was about. [spoiler] In the end Henry was left behind alone by Delilah, [i] exactly like what Henry did with Julia in the prologue [/i], it shows us the other perspective when Delilah runs away from her problem of having to meet Henry after all that has happened. And just like with what Henry did in the prologue, this isn't necessarily a bad thing, because sometimes people just need to escape and no one can tell someone that it's right or wrong, because everyone is diffrent  and no one can fully understand anyone other than themselves. [/spoiler]

This why I belive that Firewatch is an absolute mastepiece and a incredibly worthwhile experience. I have bought this game multiple times on different platforms and absolutely recommend that you buy it, however after all I've said, it's up too you to judge whether you will actually like the game or not.

I purchased this game back in 2016 and it sat in my Steam Library for years without me ever touching it (2024 now). I had a day off work today and was looking for a game to play when I came across this dusty gem in the list. I'm not too big of a fan when it comes to walking simulator type games. There's gotta be a story or some element that keeps you engaged. The Long Dark is one of the best examples of this IMO. Most games similar to these have some type of element of engagement in them, but more often than not, you find things are too drawn out and its more a game about walking than something that makes it feel unique. Firewatch is not this way. The story was paced perfectly and held my interest the entire playthrough. I remember buying this game years back because of the similar art style to Bethesdas' Dishonored games or Hinterlands' The Long Dark. Playing through this game now was time well spent! It's a very laid back experience, more of a psychological thriller relying on situations that build up suspense and a sense of threat just around the corner. The world is beautifully made. The Devs did a great job in making the map feel not crazy busy and easy to navigate. I would have liked the story to be a little longer or maybe the implementing of some sort of challenges to make me want to return to the game once I completed the story. Character development was A1 if you ask me. Really great job of building a characters personalities through small details and motivations revealed. Choosing dialogue was an added plus, too. Though sometimes I did find myself choosing one option and the tone of voice was angrier or more annoyed or cocky, which is not how I wanted the direction of the conversation to go. All around great game just wish I had more of a reason to keep it installed and come back to it. 7.5/10

[h2] Watching for Fires and Life Reflecting in the Brave Wyoming Wilderness [/h2]
To me, September marks the start of the Spooky Season (which runs until October 31st). But before I start playing games that feel appropriate for the time of year, I wanted to play something to end the summer. That would be [i]Firewatch[/i], a gorgeous and memorable game with a great story and superb performances.

In 1989, a man named Henry ran away from his problems and took a job he found in a newspaper as a fire lookout for the summer. Sitting high atop a mountain in the beautiful Wyoming wilds, it’s our job to keep the forest safe from fires. However, we aren’t doing this job alone. Our only source of communication comes from our boss, Delilah, who is situated in another lookout tower far from ours. Throughout the course of the game, we’ll explore the environment unknown to us and take it all in while exploring an engaging mystery set in the heart of the great outdoors. In ways, our choices will impact what happens next. Will we be the same man we were at the start of the summer, or will we be forever changed?

I want to first talk about how beautiful this game looks. The developers have perfectly captured the beauty of the great outdoors and the Wyoming wilderness, so much so that there were times when I was playing when I would just sit back and take in everything. I would listen to the wind blowing, trees and other plants rustling, and see the sun shine through the trees. Adding in the game’s sound design made for a very relaxing experience throughout. Furthermore, what also helped keep me engaged was the game’s narrative, especially the mystery elements. Though, similar to Henry and Delilah, the later portions of the game can make one slightly paranoid with the idea of being watched.

With the game’s story, there’s something pretty realistic about it. Henry tries to get his mind off his problems and get away from them, his hesitance on whether to go see his wife or return to Boulder, Colorado, but deciding in the end to go to her. A lot of his backstory relating to him and his wife Julia feels real. It’s all very emotional and very heart-wrenching that I was able to sympathize. His relationship with his boss, Delilah, also felt pretty realistic, even though we never actually saw her and only talked over the radio. It was very clear from the get-go that she uses humor to shield from her personal life, but as we progress, we get to learn a bit more about her.

Even though this game is from 2016, I still don't want to spoil too much because this was so good that I think everyone needs to check it out at least once.

Firewatch is a short but sweet experience. It's your classic walking simulator story game, but it does it very well. The story is grounded in the characters we meet and learn about as time goes on, and the major beats are well set up and feel impactful. You have choices at almost every turn, changing subtle but meaningful details of the world and the people in it while keeping the overall story the same. Everyone who has played this game has experienced Firewatch, but not everyone has experienced [i] my [/i] Firewatch. Most of the story is delivered through dialogue between yourself and a neighbouring fire lookout which makes getting to know and understand the two characters very easy. Even after only 4 hours, I feel like i know these people and their relationship is believable.

Before playing, I saw some people saying that the navigation is clunky, and I only agree in the sense that real navigation with a map and compass is clunky, especially in a forest. As a Scout, it gave me a bunch of nostalgia of hiking through woods, up mountains and down roads while navigating with nothing but a map, compass and pen. My only complaint is that the game was maybe a bit too short to properly learn how to navigate the park, as I would've loved to be walking around confidently by the end, but whether that's a problem for other people is down to them personally.

Overall, great little experience with a well written story and great voice acting from the cast. Would recommend

I had heard little about Firewatch back in 2016 when it dropped.
That was during the time where Unity Inde titles were really booming.
I heard it was wonderful, a bit of controversy some time after that, and then nothing.

so here i am, 8 years later, and what do i think about it?
TLDR: I enjoyed it. The story could easily lose you if you don't empathize or immerse yourself in the characters or the story, or have a hard time doing so.

The story kept my interest, it was fun to explore the forest around me- then it lost me.

It was tense, it made me nervous, i was anxious to see what happened next- then... it ended.
I'm left feeling like there's something i missed, like a second ending, a continuation of events, or some other part of the puzzle, but the puzzle is done, and the piece that's missing was designed to be missing. I bought it like that.

Now, that's not necessarily a bad thing. It asked me questions and allowed me to answer them as the character in a way that made sense.
It has a lot to say about abandonment, relationships, and mental health.

It was easier for me to empathize with the main character, both me and the person i was streaming to both have family members suffering from dementia, and the game asks questions concerning what distance is a healthy amount of distance-
and i wish this game leaned more into that discussion.
How relationships can be strained, how your actions have a consequence for others should you choose to act, or a lack of action.
But once the mystery started, it became harder to keep track. I was invested because there was some sense of danger, and characters i came to empathize might be hurt or killed, and- being a game designer, the game kept alluding to obstacles that would crumble or falter, and there were times it happened, and times it didn't.

Which, kept the suspense, until the mystery was over, then the game ends.

I know its 8 years ago, and even though I'll still be vague about the ending and what exactly happens, I'll still put it under a spoiler tag.
--
[spoiler]It went out with an "I did it" kind of confession, and then quickly ended with- what you expect, an out of control fire.
Which- i don't really know how to feel, having it end so quickly, and not exactly wrap up the 'right things'.
The message is clearly 'People make simple mistakes that affect them and others around them for the rest of their lives', but it doesn't really expand on that past there being a comment about what you do about it.
Then you start talking about what your next steps are in life, and... that's it! 

I got a quick little text-based beginning about Henry's wife, why don't we get a short epilogue while the credits roll, explaining what he chose to do when he got home?[/spoiler]
--

I remember seeing something about the ending briefly in 2016, maybe that set my expectations, but i don't remember anything but orange colors and Delilahs name being said in a questioning voice. So maybe that set my expectations to be a sad ending. Which, maybe i got, considering.

But either way, I'm left with a thought, and that thought is "It happened too fast."
Even so, i had fun, and I won't pretend like i didn't enjoy my experience.

I could see another version of myself not liking the game.

And if your the type to not immerse yourself in a game in attempt to take its story seriously, maybe its not for you. 
As for me?

[h1]EXCELLENT NARRATIVE EXPERIENCE BUT CLUNKY NAVIGATION[/h1]
Firewatch is a decent explorative walking simulator, with an attractive art style and strong emphasis on voice overs that will convincingly put you in the shoes of a rookie fire lookout. Being a fire lookout, you are to spend your time in the lookout tower and out in the open, while being in constant touch with your supervisor, through a walkie-talkie. The script and the voice overs being superb, make the conversations feel life-like and create an immersive experience. 

My summary on the game:
    
[table]
[tr]
	[td][b]Story & Presentation[/b][/td]
	[td][b]7.5/10[/b][/td]
	[td]The story can be broken up as - the character's past, present and future. The game does a good job in carrying forward the weightage of the character's past into his present life as a rookie fire lookout. As I do not want to spoil away the experience, I am not going to comment on the ending. Through, the conversations you have with your supervisor, the story takes shape. The presentation has depth. Overall, it was a good experience.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
	[td][b]Gameplay[/b][/td]
	[td][b]5.5/10[/b][/td]
	[td]Clunky movements and non-intuitive navigation. Feels like a fat guy walking simulator, which may be acceptable at times, as your character is little on the fat side. But getting stuck on stones? Come on! Also, one other aspect that was disappointing is - you don't get to see any wildlife. The whole forest is practically dead and you feel like you are the only one out there.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
	[td][b]Gameplay Length[/b][/td]
	[td][b]7/10[/b][/td]
	[td]Around 5 to 6 hours to complete the game. Just when you start enjoying the life of a lookout, the game is almost done. The map in the game being decently big, could have made use of few side missions and more exploration.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
	[td][b]Graphics[/b][/td]
	[td][b]7.5/10[/b][/td]
	[td]The art style looks unique and great, though at times looks like an orangey mess. The game looks great on 4k.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
	[td][b]Sound[/b][/td]
	[td][b]9/10[/b][/td]
	[td]Truly amazing voice overs/script, which is the strong point of this game. Conversations feel real. Forest and other ambient sounds are decent as well.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
	[td][b]Controls[/b][/td]
	[td][b]9/10[/b][/td]
	[td]Simple to learn right away in an easy to use layout. Easy to play on both KB+M and controller.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
	[td][b]Difficulty/Challenges[/b][/td]
	[td][b]6/10[/b][/td]
	[td]Being a walking simulator, the game is easy and casual, apart from the clunky movement and navigation. However, the one aspect that can truly frustrate you is - the buggy achievements that don't unlock, requiring you to restart the game. Make sure you create multiple saves.[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

For a casual and excellent narrative experience, Firewatch is a good game, if you are willing to overlook it's clunky navigation mechanics and buggy achievements.

Firewatch is not just a game; it's a journey into the human psyche. If you're looking for an experience that blends stunning visuals, captivating narrative, and raw emotional depth, look no further. This game will haunt you in the best way possible.

Firewatch is an intricate tapestry woven from the threads of solitude, mystery, and the unspoken bonds between two distant souls. Spoiler free review: 

Firewatch is much more story-based than I expected. Based on the description, I figured the game would have me completing daily, management-type tasks with a slowly developing story which I could explore at my own pace. Rather, Firewatch is very much a walking simulator/interactive movie which you can complete in four hours. 

This being said, I do recommend buying the game on sale. 

Visuals: 10/10. The game has a cartoony realism graphical style much like Subnautica. The lighting and environments are great. 

Performance: 7/10. I'm running the game on a 2080ti, 3700x and 16gb of Ram with an M.2 SSD. I do have a 3440x1440p ultrawide monitor, but I was still a bit disappointed by fairly regular stuttering (once every 15 minutes or so). 

Story: 8/10. For me, the story lost it's impact as it proceeded. If you've seen the movie Up, then I'd compare the opening to that film. It is a deeply emotional backstory for our character which was done brilliantly. The relationship you have with the person on the other end of the radio is also satisfying with well-written dialogue. I did however think the game proceeded too quickly with the mystery element, and I wanted more buildup first. The mystery was also not particularly engaging to me and felt cliche. The ending did redeem the story a bit. 

Overall, I recommend buying this game on sale. Keep in mind I live in New Zealand and at full price this game is $28.99 NZD, which is a lot for a 4 hour walking simulator. I believe I bought the game at 50% off and I consider that to be absolutely worth the money.

I’ve replayed this game multiple times, and each time, I discover new layers to the characters and story. The feeling of solitude, combined with the eerie mystery that unfolds, creates an atmosphere that stays with you long after the credits roll. "Firewatch" is more than just a game; it’s a poignant reminder that while we may want to escape our problems, true peace only comes from facing our demons head-on. If you haven’t experienced this masterpiece yet, you’re missing out on a journey that’s as emotionally rich as it is visually stunning.

[h1] A Unique, Emotional Human Experience [/h1]
On its own, [i] Firewatch [/i] seems like just another indie game with decent graphics and a decent story, but after playing it, I'm finding out about just how beautiful this game is at its core. I first noticed this game back when it first released back in 2016, at the height of the PS4/Xbox One era, but nothing ever compelled me to pick it up until I found it on-sale and decided to see what the fuss was about years later. 

What I discovered was a game that grips you to your core in terms of storytelling. You play as Henry, a 39 year old married man who, in order to escape the reality of personal turmoil, becomes a lookout at Shoshone National Forest in 1989. There, he meets his supervisor, Delilah, who lives in a neighboring lookout tower north of where Henry is posted. Delilah becomes the sole voice that Henry communicates with the most throughout the story and through the player's own choices - can forge a new relationship with her. 

All the while, as Henry and Delilah work together and get to know one another more, a mystery brews in the background of the story. Like a forest fire, the embers grow with each passing day until the mystery envelopes every aspect of the story. Paranoia seeps in and you're left wondering what's going on, who's watching you in the forest, and if all of this is just a bad dream come alive. 

At its core, I feel that [i] Firewatch [/i] is a real human story - one that reflects over love, life, family - the problems that we face as human beings, and the resolve needed in order to overcome them. Sometimes we get the outcome we want - but the reality we often face is that we don't. This game is a rollercoaster of a story that envelopes you into feelings of peace, of happiness, and all the while intrigues you with the mystery that besets Henry and Delilah and how you both work to figure it out together. 

It's not a perfect game, but a game absolutely worth experiencing. 

[hr][/hr]
[h2] The Things I Liked [/h2]
[h3] Simple Gameplay Mechanics [/h3]
The mechanics are very simple. You can run, walk, and use an action button to traverse crevices, jump, rappel, and so on. There are no combat mechanics, the game keeps it simple in that regard. You can pick up items, examine them, keep an eye on your dynamic map (that updates as you walk across so that way you know where you are at all times), and explore new areas around the map. The game doesn't make itself so complex in this regard, so the simplicity of the controls is something I really enjoyed. 

[h3] Well-Written Dialogue & Voice Acting [/h3]
Dialogue is one of the more consistent mechanics, where you can communicate often with Delilah on your walkie-talkie. You can report to her observations that unlock new dialog tree options or can choose to stay quiet, which can lead to a more reserved conversation. In my playthrough, I decided to be more flirtatious, romantic with Delilah, and that unlocked wonderful new conversations with her. 

With that in mind, I've got to say that Cissy Jones and Rich Sommer absolutely rocked in their voice roles as Delilah and Henry respectively. There was unmatched chemistry in the way they interacted with one another and it felt like a [b] real [/b] and believable conversation between two people in that situation. For a game where you lack facial animations, the voice work more than compensates for it. Outstanding. 

[h3] Maximized Graphics with Low Resources [/h3]
The graphics are very good for 2016 and for the type of game being played. It sort of reminds me of a much more refined [i] The Long Dark [/i] style of animation. It's cartoonish with a blend of realism but the game seems to use its resources well to depict the landscape as beautiful as it does for such a small storage space. 

[h3] Musical Score [/h3]
The soundtrack was one of the best parts of the game. There was something serene about it - so connected with the story and vibe of the environment. My favorite tracks are "Canyon Sunset" and "Calm After the Storm".  

[hr][/hr]
[h2] The Things I Didn't Like [/h2]
[h3] Controversial Ending [/h3]
Without spoiling too much more than I already have, I'm still pretty conflicted about the ending. It's something of a bittersweet ending. The game will play out as you see fit for the story, so you may arrive to a different conclusion than I did, but I sort of wanted more in the end - actual closure - which eludes the Henry I played. Although, the game sticks true to its theme in the way it portrays itself - we often do not get closure in real life - and the game doesn't shy away from reminding you of that fact. 

...and that's pretty much it. There wasn't really much I didn't like about the game at all. I really enjoyed it. I'm not sure about how high the replay value is, but it's certainly a title worth replaying to show your friends who've never played it before. 

[hr][/hr]
[h2] All in all, I'd give it a 9.5/10 [/h2]
Even a decade later, [i] Firewatch [/i] holds its own against the blazing and unpredictable wildfire of time. It's a story that a lot of adults can relate to as it touches on mature themes like family, death, marriage, and the meaning of life. We can all relate to Henry's plight in some way, as well as relate to Delilah too. The two of them create such an amazing duo that sets the foundation to the rest of the story. While the ending isn't what I expected [i] or preferred [/i], it's still an ending that reminds us of the reality of life and how we should all enjoy the moments we have for we never know what tomorrow might bring and what new wildfire we may have to endure.

It's difficult to levy any criticism against this game without spoilers, so it's best to just say: great journey, poor destination. Most of the game is spent hiking off the beaten path in scenic Wyoming; while certain paths are reused several times, it still feels fresh because of changes to the environment and the story's progression. The story is just another modern slice-of-life that could've been resolved by having a chat with Dad, but the results would've been depressing for the main character either way. There's also some decent tension with Taco Bell Mild-strength horror elements, but it's nothing you'll lose sleep over and is eventually resolved. The main issue with the story is the ending which felt quite rushed, with a certain character seemingly scapegoated for all of the mysterious situations that happen throughout the game. 

Despite how short this walking sim is, I still managed to run into several game-breaking bugs with environment interactions. Running vanilla Windows 10 with no peripherals plugged in except KB&M and headphones (no controllers attached), there were several instances where interacting with an object would cause my character to moonwalk away 10 feet each attempt until I restarted the game. Also, the first time this happened, my character ended up awkwardly noclipping out of the map. Given that this game barely has any actual gameplay in it, and the fact that the game is eight years old, it's really appalling that there's any gamebreaking bugs in it. As an additional nitpick, there's also issues with clipping throughout the environment, like tall grass and plants clipping into supply drop boxes. It's not a huge issue, but, given how much of the game focuses on the environment, the lack of simple polish is surprising.

Movie game value proposition should be considered in a separate category from most other video games because of their lack of replay value and (usually) short length. Consider purchasing this as if you were buying a movie ticket; this is a $20 three hour game written by a Xanax'd out Millennial west coaster (dogs are not children). This is honestly difficult to recommend... Not because it's a bad game, but because of the poor value proposition. I've played several other Walking Simulators that had more impactful and memorable stories but this is elevated by the environments and voice acting instead of the writing. Worth getting on a sale if you're a fan of these types of games, but you're not going to convince your CoD/FIFA addicted dudebro friend that "video games are art too!" with this.
