I recommend this game with a caveat: You need to be the kind of guy that enjoys "walking simulator" type games, otherwise this game won't have much for you. But if you do like those, there's considerably more substance in Firewatch than in most other games of its genre.

You start the game with a couple of text prompts relaying the life of Henry, your character, that explains why he ended up in a watch tower in the middle of a nature reserve in Wyoming, USA. Soon after your arrival, you're tasked by your handler and fellow firewatcher, Delilah, with doing mundane things like cleaning up the forest and asking a couple of teenagers disturbing the peace to calm down, and also gather supplies. You only ever communicate with Delilah over a walkie-talkie that you bring with you everywhere, and you start casual conversations with her, and report back various findings to her. You eventually form a friendship which could grow into something more than a friendship, while you exchange life stories to each other, and you get to learn about some of the other people Delilah got to meet and interact with during her tenure as a watcher.

After a couple of days on the job, things start to get weird, and you begin to discover that things around the place aren't as idyllic as they may seem, and you set out to figure out exactly what's going on.

The gameplay entails you walking around the nearby nature reserve and interacting with supply boxes, items on the floor, and rappelling up and down cliffsides while going from place to place to move the story along. Outside of talking to Delilah, there isn't much else to do than admire the admittedly very pretty scenery.

The game is also not very long. It can be beaten in its entirety in about 3-4 hours, so if you're the kind of person that weighs the "value" of a game purely by playtime, you should wait for a steep discount for this one. Granted, I got this while it was on sale for dirt cheap (I think it was like 3€ or so), so this might have colored my perception of the game a bit, but overall, if you're into walking sims, this one is one of the better ones.

Firewatch is a remarkable entry in the genre of “walking simulators,” blending impeccable writing, stunning art direction, and stellar voice acting. Set against the backdrop of Wyoming’s wilderness, the game invites players to step into the shoes of Henry, a fire lookout tasked with patrolling the Two Forks Woods.

The narrative unfolds over an entire summer, with each “day” serving as a chapter. The vibrant colors – bold reds, yellows, and oranges – paint a beautifully immersive landscape, courtesy of renowned illustrator Olly Moss. The narrow passage through Thunder Canyon, the serene Jonesy Lake, and the mysterious Medicine Wheel all feel like real places, despite the stylized visuals.

The heart of Firewatch lies in the radio conversations between Henry and his supervisor, Delilah. Their relationship feels authentic, even without on-screen faces. Delilah’s emotional armor cracks just enough to reveal her humanity, while Henry grapples with his past life in Boulder, Colorado. The tension, humor, and occasional fear keep players engaged throughout.

However, the ending – without spoilers – left some players wanting more. While the journey is captivating, the resolution may not satisfy everyone. Still, Firewatch remains a must-play for its unique storytelling and emotional depth.

Firewatch is a game that lingers in your thoughts long after you’ve put down the controller. Its flaws are forgivable, given the overall experience. If you appreciate character-driven narratives and atmospheric exploration, this game is well worth your time.

[i]Firewatch[/i] is a short story-driven walking simulator with attractive semi-low-poly graphics with a naturalistic aesthetic. The narrative is told through the lens of a troubled middle-aged man in a mid-life crisis and bounced off a forward and similarly storied female colleague on the radio. Their relationship, as well as the ones in their previous lives, are explored in the backdrop of the Wyoming wilderness, nominally as they watch for forest fires. But mysteries abound in these woods, and you should get to the bottom of it all.

I greatly enjoyed playing [i]Firewatch[/i]. The story was compelling and well-executed. I had my suspicions throughout, but it was laid out cleverly and I was never exactly sure what to think, or how reliable of a narrator I really even was. I found it appropriately exciting and emotional.

The game is visually beautiful. You're led to explore the game world at a pretty comfortable pace, getting just enough novelty without feeling rushed or overwhelmed. While I found the dense forest easy to lose myself in, the map tool and compass you're provided make it trivial to orienteer.

Game mechanics are pretty simple and largely movement-based (jump over this gap, climb down this rope, etc.). The focus is really on the story and the environment, which gave the game a refreshing feeling. Performance was good and I experienced no meaningful bugs.

Strong recommendation!

I have completed Firewatch a couple of days ago and I was honestly not sure whether I'd recommend it or not at first. Curiously enough I bought it on a sale or as part of some bundle a long time ago, can't really remember. It's been gathering dust in my library for a while until I stumbled on someone's video playing Firewatch. I only watched a couple of hours of gameplay but it was enough to persuade me to install and play myself.

The world is heavily stylised and it is gorgeous. The lighting, the attention to detail. The game feels warm and comfortable. Why would I not recommend it then?

- It's an absurdly short game. It only takes 3-4 hours to complete.
- price, and this is the biggest factor here. The amount of content is simply not worth the asking price (without a sale discount).
- story was a huge letdown. It masterfully built up suspense, but crashed so hard at reveal.
- world is dead, i.e. you visit a section of the map and that's it, you basically never go back to it again.
- It's buggy. I've gotten stuck on fallen trees a number of times. There was a particular shrub-covered passage that I had to go through to progress the story that bugged out on me. 
- Controls feel odd. Both the key mappings and how the character handles in the world. It does not feel good or natural to interact with objects.
- technical issues - I could not change game resolution no matter how much I've tried. I know this may be a mac specific issue, but other games do not have same problem, so the game was not very well tested on macs. Not the end of the world on its own, but certainly adds to problem pile.

Dammit, I really wanted to like this. I'd put a neutral recommendation if I could, since the game seemed to have resonated with so many people. 

In the beginning, I was along for the ride. The intro of quick choices setting your character up, as well as setting the context, was a great way to bond as it felt like the player had some impact on the game. And, maybe there was impact. Obviously, the story told would be slightly altered by some of the choices.

But what you end up having is a janky walking simulator; It's simulating an open wilderness, that is incredibly locked down and forces the player to follow the set path. At best you can choose if you want to run around a mountain going left, or right. If you steer of the path, weird collisions happen with fallen trees, rocks and mountains. Not once was I almost stuck between some rock and the Invisible Wall™ after trying to take a shortcut. Or, being sneaky and going through bushes instead of following the open trail.

The characterization and storytelling was good. And the visuals, especially the lighting, were excellent. But, the game had too much of an obvious one-track to draw me in, and too often the movement was so limited, that it pulled out of the immersion.

5/10, don't regret buying it on sale at least :)

First of all, I'd like to say that if I could put a neutral review, I would.

The game is nice, it's somewhat suffering of having been hyped up by some of my relatives in my case, but it still was a very nice game.

My issue with it, like some others have pointed out, is the ending. There is in this game a part of the story that is dedicated to solving a mystery, and the game manages to hype you up about this mystery throughout the story. The problem is that, in the end, the solution to that mystery is kind of a letdown, in my opinion.

In the four hours I've played, I feel like I've still mostly enjoyed myself. There are some bugs that, while they are annoying, can be bypassed if you persevere and keep trying to go past it (some interactables are broken, and your character starts being pushed away from them instead of using them. Keep trying and it'll eventually work). The issue, to me, is that this could've been better without the mystery part. This could have been a great little slice of life game. But the mystery, its ending and the lack of different endings for your character's story are making what would be a great game into an okay game, to me.

Overall, the artistic direction is good, the music is very chill and nice, the voice acting is really good, the dialogue is great, got some laughs out of me. The characters are really well written, and I got attached to them. The gameplay is simple, slightly janky at times, but it works out well. However, the overarching story of the game is lacking imo, I've had the ending figured out by the 2h mark, and the only thing that made me keep going was that I felt it was too simple for it to be all there is. And once that is done, the ending is sorely lacking. Some dialogue in the game makes it feel like you might be developping something between the two main characters, but in the end it falls short, and it doesn't seem to be impacted by your choices.

So yes, I don't think this game deserves a negative review for that, but I am still slightly disappointed.

EDIT: After watching some stuff about the game, theories and all, I can say I've missed some things. That being said, the things that I've missed don't actually make the experience that much better, if better at all in my opinion. The payoff for those elements isn't there either, and they themselves don't bring anything more to the game, I feel.

I got it on sale and would be angry if I had paid full price, especially as the entire game was about a brief 4 hours with a plot that honestly feels like it could fit into a 1 to 2 hour movie better. As it is, it's just "meh".

Some other reviews say they identify with the main character. What? Henry is a jerk that makes really questionable decisions throughout the game. If the relevant party in the game had [b]really[/b] wanted to kill him, he'd be dead several times over because he takes no real action that would prevent them from doing that. In fact, well after he thinks he's in danger, he walks into a really obvious trap [spoiler]when he's locked in the cave[/spoiler] because he "has to know" what's going on. He's like the character in a horror movie that [i]insists[/i] on breaking away from the group first and going into the basement of the haunted house alone to find out what's happening, except that that this game is not that genre so [spoiler]he survives at the end[/spoiler].

There are also plenty of signs right in the intro that he was not good for Julia, even before [spoiler]she began suffering from early onset dementia[/spoiler]. Depending on the options chosen in the intro, he's dismissive when she brings up the topic of kids, completely and wildly unsupportive of her career (no matter which option you pick), possibly alcoholic, and neglectful of either the initial signs of her problems and/or her ongoing care afterwards. There are intro options that make him look [i]better[/i], but none that make him look [i]good[/i]. Julia's parents thought she could have done better than Henry? They were right.

I'm not really sure what the point of the story is. Some people have taken a message that you can't run away from your problems, but... he more or less does successfully? If he suffers anything worse than a guilty conscious for leaving his wife in her family's care for the summer, it's not obvious, and if he does visit her again, it's only because he's got [i]some[/i] moral complexity instead of being a complete sociopath, The problems he has in woods weren't any logical consequence of his decision to leave and take the job; if he had been at one of the other stations instead, he never would have encountered [spoiler]Ned[/spoiler] and it would have been a relatively uneventful summer. So the events of the game just seems to be just one damned thing after another.

The level design has so many spots where invisible walls or trivial obstructions block you. Apparently, we can jump from 10 to 15 feet up off a cliff onto solid rock without doing serious knee damage as a long drop, but sliding down what looks like a 5 ft gently sloping bit of gravel is out of the question without a rope, and going through some slightly denser vegetation can also be no-go depending on what was needed for the map.

It's not all bad. I did like some of the attention to detail about the late 1980s era the game takes place in, like the music from the boombox and red-eye from the flash on the disposable camera showing up at the end. The story could have been good and interesting with a little more work and had its moments when it looked like there was a [spoiler]X-files-esq government conspiracy[/spoiler].

For comparison, I liked _Gone Home_, and _Dear Ester_.

This whole game serves as an allegory for why you shouldn't run away from your problems. The setting and the characters all play their part in driving this narrative, and it does so incredibly.

Life isn't about wallowing in the bleak moments, or trying your best to escape from them, life is about salvaging meaning from those same bleak moments. Life is always going to be full of hardships, and running away from them doesn't solve anything. This game is a beautiful example of that.

There's nothing wrong with enjoying the occasional distractions from our everyday lives, but you also shouldn't lose sight of what's important. You can take a new job far away, drink lots of alcohol or play video games all you want, but all that does is delay the inevitable. When life gets rough, it's up to you to make the correct decisions to better your situation, and losing yourself in temporary bids of escapism will only make the challenges ahead more difficult to face.

Firewatch is what I believe many would call a walking simulator kind of game. Having never played one before, I didn't expect it to have been one of my favourite games that I've played in recent times and a personal must play. Even when there isn't any dialogue I would find myself still content with just walking as I enjoyed the beautiful landscapes around me and the amazingly composed soundtrack. Despite playing on low graphics, I would occasionally just take moments to stare at a view of the mountain range or sunset which seemed to be what the game devs knew players might do because there's a camera mechanic that seemingly has little value other than to take pictures of these types of moments and thankfully are able to be downloaded it seems. Lastly, I wanted to say that the game is very well written as I'd find myself emotionally invested in all the characters despite only having been with them a short while. While I don't often replay games, I definitely find myself wanting to play again with higher graphics and to be able to experience the story another time.

Firewatch, developed by Campo Santo, is a stunning first-person adventure game that combines breathtaking visuals, an engaging narrative, and a thought-provoking ending.

The game balances moments of calm and introspection with suspense and urgency, keeping players engaged throughout. Its open-ended conclusion encourages reflection and leaves room for interpretation, elevating Firewatch from a simple adventure game to a memorable narrative experience.

In conclusion, Firewatch’s beautiful visuals, compelling story, and thoughtful ending create an emotionally resonant and visually stunning game. Whether you're an avid gamer or seeking a unique experience, Firewatch is a journey worth taking.

I enjoy walking simulators, but I feel like this should have been a 90-minute movie, instead of a 4-to-5-hour video game.

Like most walking simulators, the gameplay loop is basically just doing chores, with only the story driving you forward. Unfortunately, I found the story to be really inconsistent, especially since the game lets you choose your own dialogue to shape it. You can be panicky, mean, silent, etc. but the events play out the exact same way. 

Example: the entire game, I kept the main NPC lady at arm’s length, with cold and aloof dialogue choices. Yet, she suddenly starts flirting with me like we’re drowning in sexual tension. It makes no sense, so why even let me choose?

The plot itself revs up in the mid game, but unfortunately finishes with a whimper. The payoff isn’t worth all the work. Without a satisfying ending, I realized I spent the past few hours just…. well, walking. At least the setting is unique; though it’s made up of mediocre graphics. 

It might be worth it if you’re desperate for a narrative, but there are a ton of better walking simulators out there.

The game has several "[i] phases [/i]", each accompanied by an excellent soundtrack and beautifully crafted environments. I recommend playing the game without any delay and experiencing the beautifully written story of Henry.

Story Wise: 10/10 I loved this games story telling its was a very exciting and emotional game there are many exciting  moments when playing the game and doing missions, because you want to develop the story and find out more, and there was always new stuff that made you want to know what would happen even more.

Gameplay Wise: 7.5/10 I liked the games mechanics alot they are very good and flawless, the only thing i didn't like about it was that you didn't really get to do stuff yourself you just had to press a button and the character would do it for you which i wasen't a big fan of, but if you just like chill walking sims this is for you. But it's also very easy to get lost on the trails and go the wrong way if you don't look at the map. 

Visuals/Looks: 10/10 I love the look of the game it's very beautiful, Looks high quality and real but at the same time cartoonish, the colors blend very well, the brightness is on point nothing wrong with the games looks at all.

Music: 10/10 The music really plays a big part in games and i think that they nailed the music in this game, it helps you get into a scenario very well, the music fits the intense moments and the relaxing ones.

Pc Performance: I don't have a high end pc or anything but i could run the game on the highest graphic settings with little to no lag, so if you think that your pc might not be able to run smooth in the game thats no the case.

The ending: ?/10 As everything is coming together with all the little storylines, uncertainty about the main character's the game just ends, and you have no real idea what the characters have ahead of them other than them leaving and going back to their normal life.

Playtime: It's not a long game it takes about 4h to complete or less depending on what you are looking to do, for me it took around 5h+ because i kept going the wrong way. But i completed the game in one sitting because i found it very enjoyable. 

Is it worth buying yes 100% if you don't have the money for it wait for it to go on a sale and buy it.

So I've finally played FIREWATCH - after 5 years of "hallucinating" this to be a horror game. (I've played Blair Witch a ridiculous amount of time) Now that I've finished it, and after reading about everything the game offers (from in-game content to wikis and retrospective posts), here's what I think.

(it's more like a personal note anyway, but thank you if anyone bothers to read this review)

The game has a good plot. And that story is composed of some of the best dialog and voice acting I've heard in a game, something along the lines of DBH or Subnautica. The game also has a detailed-rich art style, which should be pointed out, especially when someone 8 years later says that the game has appealing visual quality. 

So a gripping story, graphics that can withstand the modern level of visual quality, and great dialog/voice acting. What else could I ask of a game for me to mark it as "not recommend"? 

People would say because of the ending. I wouldn't put it as one of my reasons. I adore Campo Santo's choice of ending. After all the hype - from the flirty romantic relationship between Henry and Delilah to the death of Brian Goodwin and Henry's conspiratorial mystery that turns out to be Ned Goodwin, FIREWATCH abruptly ends, without you ever meeting Delilah, each of you going separate ways, and an awkward "goodbye". It ends "in a way that feels mundane but refreshingly human" (Jordan Oloman, Green Man Gaming). It's an ending that keeps you wondering, not a cliffhanger for the next episode, but it shows the blatant truth: There was no conspiracy, there was no flirty spark, and Henry should either move on or go back to care for his wife. I love the simplicity of it - it's another case in life where there's no girl or medal for the hero, and life progresses.

So why 'negative'? One word: Replayability. It's annoying to see how much more Campo Santo could have built upon this powerful short story. The game utilizes dialog options from walkie-talkies, from which could be used to spark multiple paths for exploration, without having to change the final ending. It's already done in the game (if you stay professional while talking to Delilah, she would go very curt and scary unlike the usual plot) - I am shocked that this wasn't explored further. Simple things like asking Delilah to fully report the 'missing' (air quotes because in the end, they weren't), or committing to finding Ned rather than fleeing, or simply taking all the resources from the supply drop.... all that can lead to a mountain to brainstorming, let alone changing the ending. It had so much potential to be more than just a story. 

I get that I am taking a note out of Quantic Dream's baby, but this game, with its powerful art, great voice acting, and plot, could be more, if not similar. And I fully believe the team could've done more, knowing that they lent their talent to Half-Life Alyx 4 years after Firewatch. 

Nevertheless, I ended my first run-through of Firewatch with a smile on my face. The game is fantastic, and it will be something that I'll keep in the back of my mind when I work my way towards my first Indie Game. Looking forward to what the studio is cooking for its 2nd game!

Lots of games strive to be philosophically meaningful and fall flat on their butts by causing their players too much confusion or being too obvious about it. Firewatch manages to not just toe the line between these two, but create a whole game thriving in this space where others have failed. It shows you the beauty of finding a butterfly in a meadow, and the horror of a deep, dark, underground cave system without making the player motion sick from twists in the story.

The graphics are divine. The only problems I experienced were not being able to walk on normal ground, which was fixed by saving and reloading the game whenever I got stuck. Another issue was easily getting lost, but you're walking around in the middle of the woods; that's bound to happen. I always found my way back to the right trail without needing to cry or look up an online guide. There is no complicated button spamming, there is no timed moments, there are no difficult puzzles. This game is incredibly accessible for everyone once you get over the mildly irritating but easy to learn controls. The subtitles said the exact same things the dialogue did, nothing was too difficult to read or access. Again, it's an accessibility dream, which is difficult to find in story-rich games [think of Detroit: Become Human or OMORI]. Best of all, there's no jumpscares, and it gives you plenty of time to walk through the map and look at the pretty scenery.

The voice acting, while cheesy and a little unrealistic at points, remained consistent throughout and felt incredibly real in the tense moments. Even the flawed bits didn't take away from the story; just added a bit of charm.

And maybe the core reason why I like this game is because it is one of the rare pieces of media that can fundamentally change you. The ending left me with questions, but none of them were relevant to the story that I saw played out; only what would happen after. The ending, while being ambiguous, leaves you with a sense of closure whilst leaving you wondering: "What's going to happen to them?". Many stories fail to do this. Firewatch, a game, succeeded with flying colors.

TL;DR: would buy if it were $30, joyous that it's only $20, scheduling another therapy appointment

Besides the set pieces in the map, the characters typically only talk to progress the story. There would be times where I would be listening to the main conversation topic at the time, and the entire thing would be glossed over because I found a small conversation topic like Garbage or something about a trail. Another issue is Achievements. I've recently been achievement hunting in games to completion and this game has a major flaw. There are achievements scattered around the map, like a turtle companion, etc. But, they seem to only be on that specific day, or after a specific day. Terrible design when it comes to wanting to go back to collect them only to realize you have to restart the entire day over (except for the last day, because there isn't anything you can do). In order for someone to get an achievement they missed, if they didn't have a save, is to restart the game entirely. The "free roam option" offers no achievements (from what I've seen when I looked for 2 of them).

A wildfire (or forest fire, bushfire) is an unplanned, uncontrolled and unpredictable fire in an area of combustible vegetation.[1][2] Depending on the type of vegetation present, a wildfire may be more specifically identified as a bushfire (in Australia), desert fire, grass fire, hill fire, peat fire, prairie fire, vegetation fire, or veld fire.[3] Some natural forest ecosystems depend on wildfire.[4] Wildfires are different from controlled or prescribed burning, which are carried out to provide a benefit for people. Modern forest management often engages in prescribed burns to mitigate fire risk and promote natural forest cycles. However, controlled burns can turn into wildfires by mistake.

Wildfires can be classified by cause of ignition, physical properties, combustible material present, and the effect of weather on the fire.[5] Wildfire severity results from a combination of factors such as available fuels, physical setting, and weather.[6][7][8][9] Climatic cycles with wet periods that create substantial fuels, followed by drought and heat, often proceed severe wildfires.[10] These cycles have been intensified by climate change.[11]: 247 

Naturally occurring wildfires can have beneficial effects on those ecosystems that have evolved with fire.[12][13][14] In fact, many plant species depend on the effects of fire for growth and reproduction.[15] Some natural forests are dependent on wildfire.[16] High-severity wildfires may create complex early seral forest habitat (also called snag forest habitat). These types of forest may have higher species richness and biodiversity than an unburned old forest.

Wildfires can severely impact humans and their settlements. Effects include for example the direct health impacts of smoke and fire, as well as destruction of property (especially in wildland–urban interfaces), and economic losses. There is also the potential for contamination of water and soil.

Wildfires are a common type of natural disaster in some regions, including Siberia (Russia), California (United States), British Columbia (Canada), and Australia.[17][18][19][20] Areas with Mediterranean climates or in the taiga biome are particularly susceptible. At a global level, human practices have made the impacts of wildfire worse, with a doubling in land area burned by wildfires compared to natural levels.[11]: 247  Humans have impacted wildfire through climate change (e.g. more intense heat waves and droughts), land-use change, and wildfire suppression.[11]: 247  The carbon released from wildfires can add to carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere and thus contribute to the greenhouse effect. This creates a climate change feedback.[21]: 20

Natural occurrences that can ignite wildfires without the involvement of humans include lightning, volcanic eruptions, sparks from rock falls, and spontaneous combustions.[22][23]

Human activity
Sources of human-caused fire may include arson, accidental ignition, or the uncontrolled use of fire in land-clearing and agriculture such as the slash-and-burn farming in Southeast Asia.[24] In the tropics, farmers often practice the slash-and-burn method of clearing fields during the dry season.

In middle latitudes, the most common human causes of wildfires are equipment generating sparks (chainsaws, grinders, mowers, etc.), overhead power lines, and arson.[25][26][27][28][29]

Arson may account for over 20% of human caused fires.[30] However, in the 2019–20 Australian bushfire season "an independent study found online bots and trolls exaggerating the role of arson in the fires."[31] In the 2023 Canadian wildfires false claims of arson gained traction on social media; however, arson is generally not a main cause of wildfires in Canada.[32][33] In California, generally 6–10% of wildfires annually are arson. The spread of wildfires varies based on the flammable material present, its vertical arrangement and moisture content, and weather conditions.[36] Fuel arrangement and density is governed in part by topography, as land shape determines factors such as available sunlight and water for plant growth. Overall, fire types can be generally characterized by their fuels as follows:

Ground fires are fed by subterranean roots, duff on the forest floor, and other buried organic matter. Ground fires typically burn by smoldering, and can burn slowly for days to months, such as peat fires in Kalimantan and Eastern Sumatra, Indonesia, which resulted from a riceland creation project that unintentionally drained and dried the peat.[37][38][39]
Crawling or surface fires are fueled by low-lying vegetative matter on the forest floor such as leaf and timber litter, debris, grass, and low-lying shrubbery.[40] This kind of fire often burns at a relatively lower temperature than crown fires (less than 400 °C (752 °F)) and may spread at slow rate, though steep slopes and wind can accelerate the rate of spread.[41] This fuel type is especially susceptible to ignition due to spotting (see below).
Ladder fires consume material between low-level vegetation and tree canopies, such as small trees, downed logs, and vines. Kudzu, Old World climbing fern, and other invasive plants that scale trees may also encourage ladder fires.[42]
Crown, canopy, or aerial fires burn suspended material at the canopy level, such as tall trees, vines, and mosses. The ignition of a crown fire, termed crowning, is dependent on the density of the suspended material, canopy height, canopy continuity, sufficient surface and ladder fires, vegetation moisture content, and weather conditions during the blaze.[43] Stand-replacing fires lit by humans can spread into the Amazon rain forest, damaging ecosystems not particularly suited for heat or arid conditions.[44]

NO SPOILERS REVIEW:
Game: I would give this game a solid 4/10. It wasn't very long - I'd expect a $20 game to buy me at least 10 hours of gameplay, but it only took me about 4.5, and I was messing around a lot. The controls are easy to figure out, the map is decently sized, and the running speed is JUST fast enough that I didn't mind the absence of a 'sprint' mechanic. 

Vibes: The game has a lot going on in a good way.  The visual and sound design is beautiful, and the pacing is good. The acting is... decent, I suppose. Going to be honest, I got real tired of listening to Henry's voice after about 2 hours. But I also radio'd every single time I possibly could, so maybe that's on me.

Story: (and without spoilers), I was HOOKED towards the middle but the ending fell very flat (ooh bad pun).
I wish that the underlying narrative behind Henry and his character development aligned more with the external story. I was excited for a climactic emotional resolution, something that would make me cry - but no, it served me nothing more than an eyebrow raise. The real disappointing part is that this beautiful concept and art style warrants an Outer Wilds-esque emotional resolution... like, that is kind of the promise behind this genre of game, that's why I spent $20 on it instead of waiting until it was free on Epic. It's the entire appeal. Without that emotional resolution, I'm just left feeling ripped off. Ultimately, the characters never fully developed, nobody learned anything. The whimsy melted away and I was pulled into a simulation that felt uncomfortably... bureaucratic. 

TLDR: the vibes are there, but the narrative was disappointing.

Title: Firewatch Review: A Masterful Blend of Storytelling and Atmosphere

Introduction:
Firewatch, developed by Campo Santo and released in 2016, is a game that defies easy categorization. It's not a traditional action-packed adventure or a puzzle-solving extravaganza. Instead, Firewatch is an experience—a journey into the heart of human emotion and the mysteries of the natural world. In this review, we'll explore why Firewatch stands out as a great game, examining its narrative depth, character development, visual splendor, and atmospheric sound design.

Narrative Depth:
At the heart of Firewatch lies its compelling narrative, which unfolds like a gripping mystery novel. Players step into the shoes of Henry, a man grappling with personal demons who takes a job as a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness to escape his troubles. As Henry explores his surroundings and communicates with his supervisor, Delilah, via radio, players are drawn into a tale of intrigue, betrayal, and self-discovery. The narrative of Firewatch is expertly crafted, weaving together themes of isolation, grief, and the search for meaning in a vast and indifferent world. Every conversation, every discovery, adds layers of depth to the story, keeping players engaged from start to finish.

Character Development:
One of Firewatch's greatest strengths is its rich and nuanced characters, particularly Henry and Delilah. Despite never meeting face-to-face, the relationship between Henry and Delilah is the emotional core of the game. Through their radio conversations, players witness the evolution of their bond, from initial skepticism to genuine friendship and beyond. Henry's journey is one of personal growth and redemption, as he confronts his past mistakes and learns to embrace the present moment. Delilah, meanwhile, is a complex and enigmatic figure, her wit and charm masking deeper layers of vulnerability and insecurity. The dynamic between Henry and Delilah is beautifully realized, thanks to the game's sharp writing and stellar voice acting, making them feel like real people with real hopes and fears.

Visual Splendor:
Firewatch is a visual feast for the senses, with its stunning art direction and breathtaking environmental design. Set against the backdrop of the Wyoming wilderness, the game's vibrant color palette and stylized graphics create a sense of immersion unlike any other. From the towering trees of the forest to the tranquil waters of the lake, every inch of Firewatch's world is a sight to behold. The game's dynamic lighting and weather effects further enhance the sense of realism, with each sunrise and sunset casting a different hue over the landscape. Whether exploring a lush meadow or navigating through a dense thicket, players will find themselves constantly awestruck by the beauty of Firewatch's visuals.

Atmospheric Sound Design:
Rounding out the sensory experience of Firewatch is its atmospheric sound design, which transports players to the heart of the Wyoming wilderness. From the gentle rustling of leaves in the wind to the distant calls of wildlife, every sound in Firewatch feels authentic and immersive. The game's ambient soundtrack, composed by Chris Remo, perfectly complements the mood and tone of each scene, whether it be one of serenity or suspense. The use of sound is integral to building atmosphere and heightening tension, making Firewatch a truly immersive experience from beginning to end.

Conclusion:
In conclusion, Firewatch is a masterful blend of storytelling, atmosphere, and gameplay that sets a new standard for narrative-driven experiences in gaming. From its compelling narrative and rich character development to its stunning visuals and atmospheric sound design, every aspect of Firewatch is meticulously crafted to draw players into its world and keep them captivated until the very end. Whether you're a seasoned gamer or someone looking for a unique and unforgettable experience, Firewatch is a game that demands to be played and cherished.

A solemn, evocative examination of self-imposed isolation in the face of grief, Firewatch is a game that excellently blends peaceful exploration with complex human drama, served with a side of unhinged paranoia. It's a simple, sometimes intentionally boring experience that involves a lot of wandering and limited equipment interaction, but this means that even the most uninitiated player can approach it and enjoy it, so long as they have a basic ability to read a map and a compass. Even then, Firewatch practically rewards you for getting lost and taking in its landscape at your own pace, containing lots of branching radio dialogue, and several charming secrets that make this one of the best nature getaways in the indie gaming landscape.

So I've finally found the opportunity to play through this indie darling of 2016. And let me start by saying that I thoroughly enjoyed it.
A short but sweet one-and-done type of a game. Its brief playtime (4-5 hours) doesn't take anything away from the impact Firewatch has. I'd actually call it a strength, as anything significantly longer would potentially detract from the final experience by making it feel unnecesarily padded out and risk that the player would start to feel dissatisfied with the lack of deeper game mechanics.
Propelled forward by a strong story with incredible voice acting performances in the spotlight, Firewatch with its beautifully stylized wilderness really immerses you in its world and creates atmosphere that's simultaneously relaxing and cozy, yet unnerving and tense. The groundedness and mundanity not only making it way more relatable than the standard "go save the world" hero's journey you'd find in most games, but also significantly scarier than most survival horror games, despite Firewatch definitely not being what you'd call a horror game.
Go play it, preferrably with as little prior information about it as possible. It's touching and sweet, melancholic, yet funny, scary, yet beautiful, all in the span of 4 hours. It's a game that values your time and I appreciate that.
One small gripe. I'd love it if there was an option in the menu that would disable the player position showing on the map to make the experience even more analog and the navigation bit more challenging.

I want to say that the initial presentation of the game was amazing. Between the talented voice acting, and the game's general art style, it's easy to tell that this game was made with love and passion.

My main issue about the game is its consistency. Its a game that presents itself as a story driven exploration game about love, regret, healing, self-discovery, and mystery - but it concludes in a way that leaves those sensations lingering in the air with no fully drawn knot made to tie everything off.

========================================Spoilers=======================================

I was drawn to the game because it had an enticing narrative about healing and discovery, something that I personally, was looking for. The game does a good job at presenting the MC's emotions of fear, pain, avoidance, anxiety, and regret. His radio partner, Delilah, is also a vibrant and complex character with her own unique quirks and mannerisms.

My main issue is that the game only has one ending, the mystery seems to solve itself, the MC and Delilah don't really change and their relationship never evolves - I'd go as far to say as they become jaded with one another. They decide to conclude the shocking mystery they uncover by straight up lying about it and bitterly agreeing to part ways. And in the final scene, and the last line of dialogue... the game has an open ending where you are left interpret things for yourself even though there's not much to interpret.

Just from the vibrant dialogue, and its choose-your-own-response type of narrative, I could have seen this story ending in multiple different ways. There could have been a good ending, a bad ending, a bittersweet ending, but they settle for just one that is just straight up bitter. Perhaps the devs and writters were on a tight budget, or perhaps they were on a time limit, perhaps the authors actually intended for the story to end this way to trigger some very broad reflection - whatever the case was, it felt like something was missing, that there were still pieces of the puzzle to put together.

Regardless of what the situation may be: healing, self-discovery, and reflection require people to make choices that will make or break who someone is as a person and how they develop. And I would have liked to seen this in Firewatch, and I believe I was tricked into thinking that was the case when I first played this game

All in all, Firewatch IS a nice game, but I believe it had the potential to have a far greater impact on its player-base and to allow us to look even deeper into both ourselves and the MC. But, alas, it didn't quite execute all the way.

I will start by saying, that this is not a game for kids, maybe even not a game for teenagers. That's not to say that is deals with excessive adult content or anything like that, but it is very much mature in nature. Anyone looking for a straight horror game or some one-note action adventure is not going to be satisfied by this game.

The game is a walking simulator to its core, all the while focused on a developing relationship between two middle aged people, stuck out in the middle of nowhere. It's steeped in midlife issues, dealing in themes such as mental illness, paranoia and isolation. It's not one great, black cloud however, and there are a lot of genuinely funny moments throughout. It's a slow burn throughout (no pun intended) and there are a number of twists and turns that slowly unravel over the course of five hours. Without wanting to spoil anything, things often boil down to character's imaginations getting away from them. There is however one sinister plot element hanging over the whole thing which in my opinion makes this worth playing.

Walking sims, when done correctly, can be great. I don’t need nonstop waves of entertainment and action for me to walk away from a game feeling satisfied. But this is a walking sim for the sake of being a walking sim. It very much feels like the graphics were made first and then the developers all looked at each other and said, “Uh. Okay. Now what?”

You go to point A, do something tiny, go to point B. Again, this is fine when done correctly. But with a map so small and constrained, I’ve never gotten lost more in my life. On top of that, every corner starts to blend in and look the same after the first 1-2 hours of gameplay.

The story itself was inching along, too. The gameplay chore made me check out during character development and main storyline because I knew once the talking stopped, I’d be forced to walk across the entire map again for the 30th time.

There wasn’t a minute of fun in the entire game leading up to the point I gave up. So it’s uninstalled and will never be revisited. From the small amount of time I gave the game, that was far more than enough time to realize I’m not interested in walking around in circles for hours for the sake of finishing some random game I’ve had collecting dust in my game library.

One night, amidst the consequence of severe burnout thanks to a stack of university papers and various assignments due, I opened up steam and spied through tired eyes the gem that was Firewatch. It looked like just the break a stressy depressy student needed. The art, the nature, the aesthetic and promises of a tale about escaping messy lives by retreating into the wilderness. I was starstruck. 

Verily, I checked my bank account and noted a distinct lack of funds to safely purchase this game. A moment passed, two moments, three. "♥♥♥♥ it", I say and click the purchase button.

Within 10 minutes I had all but neglected the stack of academic papers that demanded my attention and was hypnotised by the immediate journey I was taken through in Firewatch. It was all that I needed, all that I wanted. The music enthralled me, the gentle aura of a promising getaway had me entranced from the moment I clicked play. Then it came... A chill adventure turned dark, menacing. Conspiracies and mysteries arose and I was left with baited breath as I dared to journey onwards. Night came and the hours passed by as the addiction of this adventure gripped at me. Midnight passed, then 1am, then 2am. But I dare not stop as I simply must see this journey to its conclusion.

A wild ride of 5 hours later. I was a changed man. This game both saved me from extreme burnout and absolutely ruined me from the emotional journey I had undergone. My only critique is that the ending left me somewhat... wanting, a common lament among the players as I understand. But the journey itself was worth every ounce of my affection.

To those who feel like you need a break from stress of the real world. I most wholeheartedly recommend this game. It'll change you forever

A depressed man escaping from taking care of his fiance who has dementia and an alcoholic woman who seems to be enjoying life but its a facade and is also escaping from her problems. Which lead to pretty deep and interesting conversations between the two that really make you think when you apply it to your own life. People claim its a walking simulator, and it sure is, but I never got the feeling of being bored or just wasting my time doing a fetch errand. All the tasks felt purposeful and even when you were just walking, it was combined with dialogue so it felt quick going from point a to point b. I do have to admit, I cannot stand Henry. Don't get me wrong, I pity the man, but my god was he not the sharpest tool in the shed and really hard to get myself immersed as he would act very unrelatable. I mean getting flustered over panties or being slow at understanding what Delilah was getting at with Cottonwood creek felt like I was playing a typical isekai main character. The dialogue was definitely the highlight of the game, very well written script that felt as if it was a real conversation with chemistry and insanely good voice acting. But lets get to the bad part and warning, spoilers ahead. The twist felt anticlimactic. I mean we were building all this anticipation that the government is doing some shady ♥♥♥♥, using us as test subjects and we're on this journey to bust it up and find out the truth behind this sketchy Wyoming wilderness. All that building up and trying to guess the twist just to get revealed it was some random character called Ned behind it all and I gotta say, it felt like a slap to the face. I actually let out a sigh when I heard his voice and realized it was all him. Felt like there was a big potential to make the twist crazy but the developers settled for the realistic/boring choice and I was not satisfied. Also the game was super buggy, which is surprising because its been 8 years since it was released and its still unpolished. Another pet peeve was getting constantly lost and having to bring up the map hundreds of times felt really annoying and broke the immersion. So while I really did enjoy the game (until the end), the ending really left a sour taste in my mouth and I felt unfulfilled. This game is just difficult to recommend to others. Its a shame that this game could've been amazing but I guess we got the bad timeline. Firewatch is a game I expected more out of, but perhaps that is intentional. 

The game begins with a very beautifully written and presents an example of a real life issue that instantly made me reflect on my own life and loved ones. Throughout the game, you're taken on this emotional journey with compelling, genuine characters that were brought to life with the help of incredible voice acting. Exploring the forests of Wyoming was simply beautiful (albeit frustrating at times since I lost my sense of direction frequently) furthering the themes of the game and greatly enhancing immersion. The story builds up nicely, but ultimately, Firewatch emphasizes the journey over the destination, and I believe it's important to approach the game with this perspective to avoid the disappointment that some players experienced.

[h2] Mystery? [/h2]
Firewatch is marketed as a "mystery game," but the actual mysteries within it feel quite insignificant. If your sole focus is on uncovering the truth and reaching the ending, then you might not enjoy yourself. That was how I personally felt when I finished it myself and found myself saying "that's it?" out loud. However, if you immerse yourself in Firewatch and really take the time to savor the beautiful scenery, engage in the conversations, and think about how you feel in the shoes of the protagonist, then I definitely think you'll find an emotional journey that is quite special.

[h2] Verdict [/h2]
While I don't believe Firewatch to be the most revolutionary or unique game in its genre, it offers about 4 hours of intriguing story, wonderful characters, and easy 100% completion. If the game's concept interests you, I would recommend giving it a try.

While even most positive reviews agree that the ending is disappointing, I feel it's disappointing to such an extreme that it flips an otherwise adequate game to a "would not recommend."

This game certainly is a walking sim.  The visuals are appealing, the sound quality is solid.  The first few hours really are a treat exploring the woods and getting to know your auditory companion.

But after a while, the exploration wears out its welcome a bit.  It's amazing how often you can get lost when the exploration is so restrictive, forcing you on to criss-crossing routes by bounding them with impassible rocks or trees.  Stopping every 10 seconds to awkwardly pull up your map gets old after the 200th time.  But you keep going, because the story has you hooked.

And that story is composed of some of the best dialog and voice acting I've heard in a game.  It really hooks you in and gets you excited for your next gaming session (or the next in-game day if you're binging it).

Until the end.  As everything is coming to a crescendo...all the little storylines, bits of intrigue, uncertainty about both the main character's and supporting character's future...the game just...ends.  The supporting character becomes much more anxious, quiet, and even a bit standoffish toward the end, you share an awkward goodbye, and then have no real idea what either of those characters have ahead of them other than "going home."

I know it's an artistic tool to leave things vague and open to the imagination of the player, but it's just so unsatisfying to invest so much time into building this relationship and getting wrapped up in so many of these little storylines only to have maybe one or two half-resolved at best.  You decisions mean nothing other than changing a few lines of dialog...so like other users say, you're just as well off watching a Youtube playthrough and not getting too invested in it.
Worth it if you like story walking sims.

Before buying, it's important to understand what this game is, and what it's not.

I've seen many people calling Firewatch an exploration game, a survival game, a "puzzle/mystery" game (similar to Outer Wilds), etc ...

Firewatch is none of the above. It is a story-driven, linear adventure game. There are no puzzles to solve, there's no survival aspect, and there's no "proper" exploration (since the game is, again, linear). This isn't to say that you can't enjoy the atmosphere of the game and its world, but it is definitely not focused around you exploring the map freely.

If anything, i'd say Firewatch is closer to a mystery novel, or movie. There's not much interaction required from the player. You go from point A to point B, recover new clues, watch the story unfold, and repeat these steps until the end.

That said, the narration of the story is quite good and the pacing makes the whole experience very enjoyable.

I'd give Firewatch a good 8/10 rating. Price is reasonable as well (though the game could be a tad longer imo as there are some unexplained aspects of the story that remain after the ending).

It's hard to explain why I don't recommend this game without spoilers, so I'll try my best not to spoil anything, but it mainly has to do with the storytelling techniques, so this will have LIGHT spoilers.

The story of this game surrounds two people in fire watchtowers talking to one another and developing a friendship over the course of a summer while they observe the forest for fires. 

I think the concept for the story is incredibly interesting, but my problem with the game is I feel like it tried to speedrun the character development process, and I really think this game would've worked much better as a slowburn, or at least a slower burn than it was. 

I felt some attachment to the two fire watchers, but out of the theoretical 120 days the game is supposed to take place, the player experiences little to none of it, and time skips past most of the 120 days, so when the two fire watchers start bonding more, it feels like their bonding comes out of nowhere, which made me feel left out of the story I was supposed to be a part of.

I'm not trying to say that the game should've never timeskipped and given us 2,880 hours of the most boring content imaginable, but I wish we would've gotten more small bonding moments between the characters, and more lore surrounding the other characters mentioned by the firewatchers, whether that be given in the environment of the game, or through the conversations between the firewatchers.

Again, without attempting to spoil anything, a decent amount of the emotional impact is supposed to come from the characters we never meet or speak with that the firewatchers discuss, and I do think the impact is lessened by how little we learn about those characters.

I want to end my review by saying that this is strictly personal preference. There is so much I admire about this game, from the development team's involvement with the Stanley Parable, to the environment present within the game, to the dialogue that we do get from the two firewatchers. But when a game is supposed to be story heavy, I can't recommend it when I get to the end and feel nothing.

This will be the first review I've ever written for a game. Firewatch is more than deserving of that title. 

I rarely, if ever, play story games, and I just so happened to pick up Firewatch due to an interest in wildlife preservation and the types of jobs that go along-side fire-watchers, as well as the many incredible reviews this game has raked in over the years. 

I fell in love with the aesthetic of the game the second I started playing. It is just enough stylised with just enough beautiful nature scenery. This game truly does have some of the most beautiful scenery I have ever seen in a game. I could stare at any frame from any point in the game for hours on end.

 The longer I played, the more intrigued I became. I started making my own hypotheses, and used the, albeit limited, amount of choice in my actions to further investigate what I believed was happening in the story. And yet, despite my constant investigative work, the game would continuously throw me right back out to where I started. 

This game truly has captured how to make a compelling story that keeps you thinking through every second of game play. Even when the game had finished, I still believed there must be more to the story. It was a truly fascinating game, that never once made me feel like I was wrong, but only that I had found new information that meant I had to rethink my hypothesis.

Yes, for sure, there will be people who dislike this kind of, open-ended, campaign that seems like it just doesn't go anywhere. I don't think those people are wrong. This game is not going to entertain everybody. Honestly, I would love more closure on the story. I would. However, that does not mean I did not think this game is one of the best story games out there, as long as you're okay with not getting a concrete answer to many of the questions you will have during this game. 

This game is great for people who are okay with not knowing the answer to everything, who love to make up theories, most of which will probably not be even close to the truth. That is what Firewatch is good for. It lets you make up your own story, even though it already has it's own. 

Just get the game. If you spent all this time reading this entire review, then you should just buy the game. It's worth it, I promise.

Firewatch is a game that is able to create a truly cozy and relaxing atmosphere. From the quiet moments in the forest to exploring the beautiful environment, the game manages to create a captivating and inviting atmosphere. The warm visual design and the detailed, serene natural environment bring you into a peaceful forest world, like being in a cool and protected place away from the hustle and bustle of the outside world.. Also the interaction between the main characters, Henry, and Delilah, his friendly supervisor, also adds a cozy element to the game. Their relaxed and humorous conversations help create a warm and familiar relationship between the characters, making you feel like you're in the midst of a light conversation with a close friend... Firewatch also uses music cleverly to enhance the atmosphere. The soft soundtrack and stunning natural scenery form a perfect combination to stimulate a sense of comfort and tranquility, making you feel relaxed while exploring this vast and beautiful world.

Do I think this game is good? Yes.
Did I enjoy it? Yes.
Do I think other people playing it would enjoy it? Yes.
So why am I not recommending it? Well, it's mostly a walking simulator with a podcast in the background. A really good podcast that is! But it's not enough for me to recommend it to someone. The game feels almost like a demo, like the whole game was building up to something bigger that you never got to. And aside from that, after playing through it a second time... there's no real replay value. It ultimately felt a bit rushed, I wish they could've expanded the story and the map a bit more on it to make you connect with the people that you talk to on your radio or that you read about, but after finishing the game you just feel like you missed something... then go back into the game and find nothing.

Again, the game itself isn't bad and if the price tag was 5-10$ I would recommend it, but not as it is.

[h1][b] TLDR: A short walking-simulator game about unraveling a mystery in the Colorado forest. It has solid foundations, but I can’t help in thinking Firewatch needs to be grander in scope.[/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
✅Nature vibes
✅Mystery undertones
✅Reduces backtracking

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖No FOV slider, you have to go into the registry
➖Occasional sluggish/buggy movement and interactions
➖Lack of any real exploration

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative/Length) – [7/10] [/b] [/h1]
Game World: Firewatch takes place inside a small forested area in Colorado during the late 1980s where it's your job to act as the “Paul Blart, Forest cop” by watching out for fires, hence the name Firewatch. The forest consists of many paths and areas only accessible after you procure tools from advancing through the story. The area is big enough to where it takes maybe 15-20 minutes to hike from one end to the other. 

Narrative: There are two major plot points: The backstory of your character, Henry, and the mystery of your firewatch station. Henry’s problems are the entire reason he’s doing the firewatch job so as you go through the plot of the firewatch job, you learn more about how Henry feels about the situation with his wife. 
The other plot as the mystery of the firewatch station is presented well enough. I like how the mystery is kept under wraps for most of the game as you uncover bits and pieces, the player can start to wonder who the culprit is. Due to how short Firewatch is, you only really have a handful of choices of who is the driving force behind the mystery, so unfortunately, this is pretty easy to guess. 
The ending [spoiler]I felt was a bit of a letdown. You found out that Ned was behind the mystery, but you’ve only had a single one-sided conversation with him and are supposed to take everything as if it was the truth. [/spoiler] 
Overall, I wish Firewatch took more time in setting up the narrative. The game could have easily doubled in length while using this time to flesh out the characters more, or perhaps add more little quirks to the story. Something as innocent as making a sandwich, needing to leave for a minute, then coming back to a bite in the sandwich would provide volumes to the unsettledness of the mystery.  

Length: Short game, I finished it in about 4 hours. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Controls/Mechanics/Difficulty) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
Controls: Subpar. I had so many issues moving this guy. Sometimes he didn’t want to walk on the path. Sometimes he didn’t want to use an action like breaking down overgrowth. Sometimes I would just get literally stuck. In the course of my 4 hour journey, this occurred multiple times and I even had to reload the game twice due to being completely stuck. Really buggy controls. Henry has the climbability of a champion rock climber with the maneuverability of a dude on ‘My 600-Lb Life’.
At the very least, props to the devs for eliminating the need for constant backtracking by having the story warp you back to where you need to go. Even after only 4 hours I was getting slightly annoyed with the movement. 

Mechanics: Walking simulator 90% of the time. The other 10% you use various equipment such as map and compass, signal tracker, axes, ropes. Firewatch doesn’t even have any real exploration. The entire game is walking from one point of importance to the next. Even if you deviate from the path, there’s not much worth seeing aside from the decent at best graphics. 

Difficulty: Easy, it's essentially a visual novel with some interactivity. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/UI/Performance) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
Quality: Firewatch at times looks good, at best, and looks like a 90’s Disney movie, at worst. The forest is somehow both beautiful and low-res. It's odd. Like the game just seems like a low-polygon generation of a detailed forest. 
There is no FOV slider, an egregious error in a first person game. 

UI: Minimalistic. Aside from the compass and map, the only thing ever on your screen is a crosshair. 

Performance: Runs good with no issues on my desktop. Constant 250+ frames
i9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD
[h1] [b] Audio (Sound Effects/Music) – [7/10] [/b] [/h1]
Sound Effects: Good. The sound does a good job at providing a calming nature aspect while also adding some occasional elements of spookiness. The voice acting was good and the conversations seemed natural. 

Music: Minimal. I was surprised the game is selling a soundtrack when I think I heard two, maybe three, songs during the entire 4 hours. 
[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [2/10] [/b] [/h1]
Not great, aside from achievements, there are some small dialog choices to make, but I don’t believe Firewatch has any sort of massive replay factor. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
Firewatch almost feels like a demo. What it presents is a good, solid foundation. I just want more of it. I feel almost unsatisfied in that I was presented with something interesting, but it was over too quickly, it was too small, and I want more of the setting, more of the characters, and more of the mystery. 
Especially when you consider the non-sale price of $20, what you get almost feels like half a book. Still, I adore what is there with my only real gripe being the buggy movement, the game is great and I want to see a sequel. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes [/h1]
But make sure you get it on sale. $5-7 is a fair price for Firewatch

I've played this for the first time over the last couple of days and I think the label of "disappointing" it sometimes gets is a bit strong. I think I'd go for "unfulfilling". The setup of the story opens up lots of intriguing possibilities to weave a story that will haunt your thoughts for some time (like What Remains of Edith Finch does), but a lot of the roads it could go down turn out to be dead-end streets, and the mystery fizzles out in exactly the way they're hoping the forest fire will, without ever really burning bright.
The device of each warden being in their own tower, out of reach, is on the one hand a smart metaphor for their emotional isolation, but on the other a real barrier to caring about them as much as I'd have liked, and the way the characters act (or don't act) is somewhere between criminally lackadaisical and frustratingly solipsistic.
I'd rate the whole game as pretty good, but not a "must play". If you're in the right frame of mind, and it's on sale, then you can get things out of it - but I can't bring myself to give it an unqualified recommendation. Which is a shame, because I think these people have a great game in them.

Firewatch is an immersive first-person adventure game that captivates players with its unique narrative and stunning visuals, and offers a rich, character-driven story set in the Wyoming wilderness.
The story centers around Henry, a fire lookout assigned to monitor the Shoshone National Forest. Players experience the solitude of the wilderness, the mystery surrounding a series of strange events, and the development of a complex relationship with Delilah, another lookout, through radio communication. The narrative is engaging, filled with emotional depth, and presents players with choices that shape their experience.
Visually, Firewatch is a very nice to look at. The game boasts a distinctive art style with a palette that reflects the natural beauty of the setting sun against the vast forests and towering mountains. The day-to-night transitions and dynamic weather add to the game's atmospheric depth, making the player feel truly isolated in the expansive outdoors.
Overall, Firewatch is an exceptional game that offers a unique blend of storytelling, visual artistry, and voice acting. It's a thought-provoking experience that stays with you long after the credits roll. The game is a testament to the power of interactive storytelling and is a must-play for those who appreciate a narrative that explores the human condition and the complexities of interpersonal communication. Firewatch is not just a game; it's an unforgettable journey through the wilds of both nature and the human heart.
Firewatch gets a 7/10.

A game where you role-play as a forest ranger and solve a mystery with your only companion being on the other side of the radio. Story is short but interesting, with some of the best voice acting I've ever come across. Audio design is fantastic, and while the graphics isn't crazy complex the stylized art style does a pretty good job and I'd say it fits the overall aesthetic quite well. Gameplay isn't particularly deep but the manual, hands-off approach to everything was refreshing - you really do feel like an actual ranger when navigating the wilderness with nothing but a map and a compass. The game nails the atmosphere of the wilderness, and the manual navigation enhances the immersion . 

There are some complaints. I wish the map was an actual open area rather than an illusion of an open area with forced borders. Movement was also quite buggy, I'd sometimes get stuck on top of a rock for absolutely no reason. I also faced a random bug when trying to open a locker and then cancelling, which rendered me stuck in place and only able to rotate the camera (and see through myself!). Fortunately the game is structured on day-basis, so a quick "restart the day" fixed it and I wasn't set back too far.

Overall, for a 4 hour game it's pretty good. I tend to not have high hopes for indie games because they're cheaper, but this one still managed to surprise me with the story and voice acting. The radio companion character is well written and an easy favorite, very memorable. I enjoyed it all the way from start to finish.

Firewatch is a narrative-focused walking simulator that’s just a step shy of brilliance. It features picturesque visuals in a style reminiscent of the great Saul Bass’ and high-quality voice acting: just look at the reviews praising Delilah’s “sexy” voice. With strong presentation, the last remaining factor is its story, and this is where the game begins to struggle.  

The remainder of Firewatch is a middling performance that tries to deliver an unfocused narrative that fails to meet its potential. Players are introduced to a premise that covers the theme of grief and loss but also takes a weird turn as light elements of horror and mystery begin to appear. This would be fine but Firewatch’s short length gives little room for these elements to breathe and characters are left undeveloped and on unsatisfying terms. There’s also the addition of frustrating technical issues. Henry often does not traverse terrain when prompted and there’s a bug preventing one of the achievements unless you reload your save.

Firewatch ultimately has a lot going for it, but also noticeable downsides. If you are patient enough to wade through a lukewarm story in exchange for excellent audiovisuals, then this title is for you. For me, this is one of the rare cases where Steam Reviews would benefit from having a “mixed” recommendation option.

If Steam had a review score between recommended and not recommended, I'd use it here, because I don't want to give this game a thumbs down. 
The positives:
- It has gorgeous visuals 
- The characters are well-realized thanks to the excellent vocal performances, even if the dialogue distinctly feels like millennial 30yo's writing 1980s 40yo's 
 -The dialogue system of the walkie-talkies keeps you engaged and gives you some wiggle room to define Henry's character, even if it ultimately doesn't affect the story
The negatives:
- Many slow, canned animations for mounting cliffs and climbables. These were so numerous and so pace-breaking that it seriously hampered my desire to explore. The path from the cave to the outlook is a perfect example: 3-4 cliffs in a row where you get to watch Henry do the same animation, slowly lugging his ass up. This pays off well the first time you do it -- Henry's totally out of breath by the time you reach the top -- but on return trips, I dreaded every second of it. God help you if you try to climb up a rope. I understand we're not playing a super-human, but I would have accepted a little incongruence between the movement mechanics and Henry's abilities for the sake of the player.
- I found the story ultimately unfulfilling. The premise is great, the characters are interesting, but the game fails to capitalize on these. Without giving too much away, much of the story centers around a mystery involving the two main characters, where you're intentionally left in the dark for most of it. In about the last half hour, you discover a vital clue, then the ever-absent antagonist simply tells you what the mystery was. From a whodunnit perspective, it was unsatisfying. Mystery aside, in a way, you could look at the antagonist as an alternate version of our main characters, someone who isolated themselves in nature to avoid their real problems, taken to the extreme. Drawing parallels is about as good as you'll get because otherwise, despite being very character-focused, none of the characters change significantly or have much of anything profound to say for themselves or for the story's greater themes. You could say it's a vignette, but then it's a vignette where not much happens. Whether this was a choice or whether they ran out of time or money is unclear. When people say "the game just sort of ends", this is what they're referring to.

A couple of gaming rec subreddits got the horn for Firewatch recently, and as someone who loves a good narrative experience in gaming, I thought I'd check it out.

Without any spoilers, the writers clearly have experience dealing with loved ones with dementia. I've been through that experience myself over the last couple of years, and Firewatch is spot on in how it portrays the experience. If you're someone who is in that position, take it from my regrets: see them while you can. It will hurt. It will ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hurt. But you'll regret it if you lose the opportunity, especially if you feel you ought to have done better.

As for the main narrative, it's slow at first. The main plot hooks take about half the game to kick in. Once they do, there's a thrilling 90 minutes or so progressing from the introduction of those plot hooks to the denouement. Pay attention to what's going on around you early on, though; it's all relevant.

Gameplay-wise, it could be better. I experienced several bugs, largely relating to clipping into environment and having movement restricted by it; but also one which caused me to need to quit to progress - not great for an immersive story experience. At times, it's not entirely clear where one is relative to paths on the map, and very early you'll likely be frustrated by a lack of clarity regarding what scenery is capable of being traversed (some might say the game needs some yellow paint). With that being said, it's serviceable and carries the story well enough to not force the player out.

I think Firewatch excels in its coverage of some sensitive topics through the medium of a fairly compelling story. With that being said, I don't think it benefits from being a video game. I'm glad to have played it, but I'd rather have watched a film, I think.

This game suffers from a MAJOR technical issue relating to the physics engine, rendering it more or less unplayable on some modern hardware.

The game doesn't support VRR and doesn't include a framerate limiter, meaning your only option (aside from resorting to external hacks) is to enable V-Sync, which is implemented horribly in this game/engine, and adds 100-200ms of input lag, making the game unenjoyable.

The story also feels like something written with the explicit purpose of being sad and getting "the feels" out of people, which IMO is a cheap way to get emotions. I didn't feel interested enough in the story to continue fighting the technical issues this game has.

[b] Pros: [/b]

[b] Atmospheric Setting: [/b] The game’s visuals are stunning, capturing the serene yet haunting landscapes of the forest. The changing weather and day-night cycle add to the immersive experience.
[b] Compelling Story: [/b] Firewatch weaves a tale of loneliness, loss, and human connection. The radio conversations with your supervisor, Delilah, provide emotional depth and drive the narrative forward.
[b] Character Development: [/b] Henry and Delilah are well-written characters, and their interactions feel genuine. Their evolving relationship is the heart of the game.
[b] Mystery and Intrigue: [/b] The forest conceals secrets, and as you explore, you uncover strange occurrences that keep you engaged. The tension builds gradually, leaving you eager to discover the truth.

[b] Cons: [/b]

The gameplay for some might be limited, as it's not about action or complex puzzles. It's a walking simulator with occasional choices.

The game can be completed in a few hours, which may want you yearning for more.

[b] Verdict: [/b]

Firewatch is an emotional journey that resonates long after the credits roll. If you appreciate storytelling, character-driven experiences, and a touch of mystery, this game is well worth playing.
