I had rather mixed feelings on this one, so please note whether I hit thumbs up or down in the end, it's more a case of hovering somewhere in the middle. I will also have a section at the bottom with a few minor spoilers, but I don't know how to do the censor bar so I'll still be as abstract as possible.

So, what we have here is a walking simulator, one of the fabled games that are barely a game. I've no real opinion on this genre as I haven't had all that much exposure to it. I liked both the Stanley Parable and the Beginners Guide, but I also think the Chinese Room's lack of desire and/or ability to actually create gameplay for Amnesia a Machine for pigs hamstrung what could have been a much better game. I think I have dear Esther and Layers of Fear in my Steam Library and will play them at some point.  If you don't know, these are games that are mostly very minimal in terms of gameplay, usually mostly walking around exploring and experiencing a story. Some would call this an intentional artistic expression, some would call it small studios doing the best with what they have. It's a genre term that honestly borders on insult a lot of the time when used to describe a game, and I've definitely used it myself when games feel a bit deficient on the gameplay side. As there's next to no gameplay for me to review, I'll talk about the environment and story.

So, environment. The game looks really nice. It's got quite a cartoony art style, and I find they usually age very well, and this game is no exception. There's some really nice sound design as well, wind and leaves rustling, small animal noises and the like. I choice I really like is that the game doesn't have much in the way of UI overlay. You have a paper map, compass and verbal instructions. Whilst there's markers on the map, they are limited to there, so in order to get around you have to do some good old fashioned orienteering, which does absolute wonders for immersion. Sure the environment doesn't look hyper realistic, and it is still very gamey, lots of narrow paths and canyons funnelling you about, but with the sound and you actually having to put effort into navigating it very much feels quite real. The story only actually sends you to about half of it, so it feels decently large as well and there's some scope for additional exploration. I'd say the Forest does it's environment better, but it's a larger and much longer game than this. What I'm trying to say is that I love how much effort has gone into making the setting feel very real. I'm from Ireland and have never been into a massive North American Forest, but after playing this I really want to.

So, story. This is the part that I have pretty mixed feelings about, but I'll keep any spoilerish stuff vague and in a second paragraph at the end. You play as a guy  called Henry who has come out to work for the forestry service by sitting in a watchtower keeping an eye for forest fires all summer, lest smokey the bear smite mankind for our failure to prevent them. His wife is suffering from early onset dementia, something he's struggling to deal with. He makes a friendship with his supervisor, a woman called Delilah who he chats to frequently over the radio, and something of an emotional affair begins to develop. I really like both the characters in this, they are well written and well voice acted, and I was quite engaged in their conversations. Maybe sounding cliched, but they very much felt like real people, multi layered and flawed. Unfortunately for them, there are some odd goings on. A pair of campers vanish after their campsite is destroyed, someone appears to be stalking and quite hostile to Henry. There's a fire on the horizon and more are starting. Delilah appears friendly but will also go miles out of her way to deliver something for Henry to the south rather than just going to his tower. Whilst I think it could have done with a slower burn, It really builds up a pretty gripping sense of intrigue and paranoia as it goes on. Now unto mild spoilers.
.
.
.
.
.
.
So, sadly to say, as gripping as I found it, the story ends on a pretty sour note. Whilst I like the final conversation between Henry and Delilah, the rest of the plot just comes to an abrupt and rather disappointing conclusion. Without saying too much, it basically turns out that it was all just a big misunderstanding. It's not Life is Strange or Mass Effect 3 ending bad, but it's honestly not great, and I find myself walking away wondering what all of the hype was about.

 I don't regret taking the journey, as the environments are great and it was really engaging while it lasted, but it's sadly one that ends with you unexpectedly slipping and breaking your leg rather than reaching your destination.

Firewatch is another top-shelf masterpiece that I proudly display in my library. Your name is Henry. You're out in the woods away from your (sadly) dementia-ridden wife, forest-ranging the days away with only another ranger, Delilah, to speak to. The woods are more than they seem, but don't worry, there's nothing supernatural here.

I loved Firewatch's art style and music (Chris Remo strikes again!). When North Backcountry played midway, I legitimately had to stop and put my head between my hands to process the crashing wave of nostalgia and emotions surfacing within me, as if summoned by the music itself. i also found myself stopping several times in-game to watch the trees shifting in the wind or the sun filtering between branches. I've never been to the forests of Wyoming, but this game sure felt like a warm slice of it, albeit pixelated, beautified, and less wolf'ed and bear'ed.

I loved how you could just walk in Firewatch without saying much, as if you're actually hiking the trails and taking in nature. The bits of dialogue with Delilah helped curb the loneliness, but for those who don't mind it, you have the option of not responding to Delilah most of the time, leaving you to silently take in the scenery. It's a pretty good walking sim in that regard, complete with forest ambience.

The build-up of suspense when you find out [spoiler]someone has been listening to your conversations with Delilah[/spoiler] as well as [spoiler]being attacked/seeing a mystery man following you around[/spoiler] to the [spoiler]deer research camp[/spoiler] was unsettling, which was probably the point. It all comes crashing down when you find out the truth, however, which is, well... quite sad.

[spoiler]I can't explain how deeply and viscerally sad I felt when I saw Brian's body in the cave. All I could think about was how in pain Ned must've been to lose his son. Sure, Delilah says he might not have been the best father (♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, in her words) but the man had PTSD and probably just wanted to spend some time with his kid too. Ned tried his best and Brian was decently happy, evidenced by the makeshift forts, photos, and plans you'll be privy to near the end. That's why I didn't agree with Delilah when she insulted Ned. In fact I saw it more as her projecting onto him because of her own guilt of inaction, which would've potentially saved Brian otherwise. If I were Ned, I'd want to spend my days hiding away from people after losing my son AND still struggling with PTSD too, knowing I inadvertently contributed to his death even though all I wanted was to teach him cave rappling.[/spoiler] I don't think anyone in the game was truly in the wrong, however. People cope with grief, loss, and pain differently. Whether by avoidance or self-depreciation.

TL;DR, Firewatch to me feels like a long journey of people coping with grief, solitude, and pain. Henry lost his wife, in a way, to dementia. It's clear he still loves her-their photo, the midnight sleepwalking/dreaming/mumbling, the option to still keep their marriage troubles private from Delilah-but because of her condition, Henry has to face the painful truth that his marriage might not be what he hoped it to be, nor the same for the woman he loved. Delilah and Ned had to deal with the pain of [spoiler]losing Brian[/spoiler], one ridden with mental illness and hiding away from society, the other helpless and quitting their job entirely. This is not an easy game to swallow. The wonderful music and art certainly does nothing to reduce the intense emotions that might be conjured up while playing, but I say experience it at least once and come out anew.

A Journey of Discovery: A Firewatch Review

Firewatch isn't just a game; it's an immersive experience that captivates from the first moment. Set against the stunning backdrop of the Wyoming wilderness, it's a narrative-driven adventure that seamlessly blends breathtaking visuals, evocative storytelling, and immersive gameplay.

From the moment you step into the shoes of Henry, a fire lookout with a troubled past, you're drawn into a world that feels familiar and mysterious. Through radio conversations, the bond between Henry and his supervisor, Delilah, forms the heart of the experience. Their exchanges are witty, engaging, and incredibly human, profoundly connecting you to their journey.

What truly sets Firewatch apart is its masterful storytelling. Without relying on grandiose set pieces or over-the-top action sequences, the game manages to evoke a range of emotions, from laughter to sorrow, as you uncover the mysteries lurking beneath the tranquil surface of the forest. Every decision you make feels meaningful, shaping the story's outcome in subtle yet significant ways.

Visually, Firewatch is a work of art. The stylized graphics, dynamic day-night cycle and weather system create a living, breathing world that begs to be explored. Whether trekking through dense forests, scaling steep cliffs, or gazing out over shimmering lakes, every corner of the wilderness feels meticulously crafted and brimming with detail.

The remarkable aspect of Firewatch is its ability to evoke a sense of introspection. As you wander through the wilderness, grappling with Henry's personal demons and the mysteries that surround him, you can't help but reflect on your own life and the choices that have brought you to this point.

Ultimately, Firewatch isn't just a game about solving puzzles or completing objectives; it's a journey of self-discovery and emotional resonance. It's a testament to the power of storytelling in gaming, proving that you don't need flashy graphics or bombastic gameplay to create a truly memorable experience. If you're looking for a game that will linger in your thoughts long after you've finished playing, look no further than Firewatch.

In Firewatch you play as a man named Henry. You know little about him other than the fact that his wife was diagnosed with alzheimers in her 40s, and for whatever reasons at this point unknown to the player, Henry decides to leave her in the care of her family and takes a job in the woods as a fire watchman. It's there that he comes into contact with another watchman, Delilah, and in what seems like a simple job, a number of issues will be brought to light that leave it to you to investigate. I love this game. For what may seem like a simple walking simulator, I still enjoyed my time walking through the lush woods, pulling out my map to make sure that I was going the right way and being sure to hit up every lockbox possible to expand my knowledge of the surrounding area. That being said, where Firewatch truly shines is in it's story, but more specifically, it's conversations between Delilah and Henry. The thing that got me hooked on this game was the relationship between these two, truly brought to life by both of these character's voice actors. Although their playful dialogue is mostly lost in the second half of the game due to the rising tensions in their situation, I would be lying if I didn't run to every location Delilah told me to go, wanting to hear the next line of dialogue between the two. I don't want to say much more about this game because it is basically a playable movie and saying anything about it would be like spoiling it, so if you like story-rich games but also not just standing around listening to a wall of dialogue, I would highly recommend Firewatch. Also, there's this part in the game where you stumble across a disposable camera, which you can use to take photos of any pretty scenery you come across. I completely forgot about this feature, and I was only reminded of it when the credits rolled and a bunch of blank photos were shown on the screen, definitely meant to be filled with pictures I took. Kind of makes me wanna go back and play it again.

"Firewatch" Is a game about isolation and coping with problems, a first-person storytelling game set in a National Forest In Wyoming. With a unique art style and captivating story, the game becomes successful even though it is an indie game. This hidden gem is for the audience who like good narratives, beautiful landscapes, and love to solve the mysteries.

You are playing as Henry, after finding out that his wife "Julia" has dementia, Henry is taking a job as "Firewatch" at Shoshone National Forest. After some long walk up to the mountain, Henry is stationed at "Two Fork Lookout" and gets paired with "Delilah" his supervisor, whom we will communicate with through a walkie-talkie for an entire game. Together, both of them need to watch for any fire or thing that can be a source of fire and stop it before it gets out of hand. After some time, the big mystery reveals itself that every conversation between him and Delilah is getting recorded by someone and that someone takes their audio and edits it like they are the murderer. Both of them need to who are spying on them, why are they spying on them and how to fix this problem.

The game mechanics itself is not anything fancy. The gameplay mechanics are very bland, A lot of walking, hiking, looking where to go, and taking pictures along the way. But, with very unique and beautiful sceneries walking around and taking pictures is very relaxing and enjoyable. Another big thing about this game is indeed the story. The story of this game is engaging, and very "Real". Every character has their own personality and desires and we can see these types of people in real life.

I thought this game was one of a kind. The story is very engaging, It is so engaging that it makes me complete an entire game in 1 sit, sure some people might think that the ending is “Underwhelming” and get a lot of criticism for it. But, for me, the end of this game really taught me a lot of lessons in life whether it is “Don’t run away from your problem.”, or “Maybe the problem isn't as big as we think.“For the game's perspective, this game's scenery is very charming, with its unique art style and beautiful lighting, this 2016 game is still very beautiful even by today's standards. Lastly is the audio, the audio of this game is very relaxing and can make you feel the essence of the National Forest In Wyoming.

Overall, The graphics are outstanding no matter how long time passes and how much the gaming industry develops as a whole. The sound is also very charming and relaxing. And lastly, the storytelling of this game is captivating and full of twists and turns. This game is easily 9 out of 10 for me.

While this was an exceptionally well-done atmospheric game, the game to me isn't quite worth the price or the hype that's surrounding it. It's more akin to a "short story" than a game, just so happening to be first-person. The story is well-acted (from a voice acting perspective), and unveils itself quite well. However, the game's pacing suffers from jolts of excitement without a lot of connection to a larger plot, coupled with a somewhat lackluster ending. There a few mechanics that could have been done a bit better as well, such as detecting your intent to climb or descend a rope (one must be standing in just the right spot for it to engage). All-in-all, a nice little quick game that is begging for this to be an opening chapter to a larger story, or a game that shouldn't be more than $9.99 (given the content).

In terms of atmosphere and art style, it's top-notch. The actual in-game artwork is quite nice, sets the atmosphere well, and blends perfectly with the sounds and soundtrack. It renders well for my PC, and the Steam Deck, so it's not a terribly complex game visually. There could be a few more solid indicators of paths, however, I think part of the "fun" of the game is exploring the area and using your map as you would if you were actually hiking. Having said that, there are a few annoyances to point out.

For starters, this is another Unity-based game which allows for the "examine" mechanic, where you pick up items to then look at them, but not to do anything. This game is full of a ton of items which get you thinking "Wait, should I take this? Is this important somehow?", and they all turn out to be useless (save for a few plot-items).

While being curious what specific items do or how they affect things is a slight peculiarity, having to re-engage the "run" setting every time you equip and then de-equip the map is frustrating. If there's no stamina, and no consequence for running versus walking (as far as I can tell; such as noise in stealth areas, etc), then why offer the option to walk? Traversing the map takes a while, and for those with a poor sense of direction, you'll be looking at the map more often than perhaps you ought to be.

Speaking of which, you can't use the radio and the map at the same time, and your companion will be talking to you on their schedule, which interrupts your ability to respond, as each response is on a timer. I felt a bit panicked every time the countdown to send a response back kicked in, and I couldn't get out of the map screen fast enough (which I doubt was the developer's intention).

Plot-wise, the mystery of the Shoshone is quite compelling. At least at first. It goes from "ooh, what's going on here?" to the characters contemplating a vast conspiracy way too quickly. Knowing that Valve acquired Campo Santo after this game got me thinking about the mysterious world of Black Mesa and Aperture Science, with overtones of conspiracies and black sites with government controls and experiments. This was a bit over-the-top for me, and absolutely none of what I was building this up to be in my head compared to the actual plot. Playing this 2016 title today got me also thinking of Stranger Things, with its 80s vibe, and frequent mentions to off-brand Dungeons and Dragons and weird sci-fi aspects belies its true (dare I say somewhat lackluster) plot.

I'm fine with the game not needing to be an extravagant sci-fi or 80s horror or crazy conspiracy happenings in the forest type plot, but I'd like some more backstory and motivation. When the story peaked, I was left wondering the motivations of the person in question. I get the whole "crazy-from-tragedy" thing, but it felt rushed. One minute I'm standing in a camp, and the next minute the game ends. It felt anticlimactic.

Should the game have vastly different experiences each play-through, where each choice I can make will add swaths of new content into the game so that I can, in fact, hear the backstory of the antagonist, I'd just say to heck with that. I don't want to have to replay a game multiple times (especially when there's so much walking) to unlock every possible line of dialog. Crucial components in storytelling shouldn't be optional, hard to access, or a secret.

I'm torn between recommending and not recommending this game. On the one hand, it was very fun to play and unfold the story, learning about a mystery in a gorgeous setting. Both voice actors, Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones did a fantastic job pulling you into the story much in the same way that John William's music elevated the classic Indiana Jones movies. On the other hand, the game was captivating enough that I'm ultimately disappointed at the ending. I can forgo some of the mechanics issues (especially when it moves your character randomly, as if it can't figure out how to close the gap between your position and the position required to engage with an object like a rope) if the story was ultimately satisfying. For such a great set-up, the game peters out towards the end, making me question whether folks were burn out a bit towards the end. Even in the game, time passes in harsh jumps from weeks to months, as if to say "Yep, nothing much happened here" when it should be using the opportunity to build the world a bit more.

I liken this game to Portal quite a bit. It was a short game that delighted us all. However, it had a great twist, ending, and set of mechanics. Given Firewatch doesn't have mechanics, it really needed to boost up its story, or deliver Chapter 2. Portal wasn't meant to be a full game, it was at most a preview of some new game mechanics done in a fun way. Portal 2 gave us the backstory we craved, and expanded upon a lot of mechanics in a way that felt balanced between story, puzzles, and gameplay. I'd be happy with Firewatch if it were free as part of a bundle, or if Firewatch 2 (much in the same vein of Portal 2) dropped and gave us something bigger. For now, I'd have to urge people to wait for a Steam sale to get their money's worth. A promising start, but a lackluster payoff. I'm excited to see what the Campo Santo folks will produce in the future.

Environmental narrative adventure games, often mockingly and reductively called, "walking simulators," have basic interactivity to let the story take center stage.  The design is very simple, but some games have taken the formula to an advanced level.  Firewatch was one of them.

I've been aware of this game since it released eight years ago and I watched about half of it as played by Miss Fushi.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cz2SnARtuq4&list=PLZw7lO5V0lry-kcc0VQCuH7mB4SblFvwM

There was never any plan for me to buy or play the game, but they were practically giving it away for $2.  I bought it and when I went to play it, I did my usual check of PC Gaming Wiki.  It turns out there was a VR mod I didn't know about: https://raicuparta.itch.io/two-forks-vr

This mod is outstanding and it improved my enjoyment of Firewatch by leaps and bounds.  I wish it wasn't motion controllers only, but I'm used to this by now.  For some reason, it's standard for VR modders to reject the option of playing the game with an HMD for an immersive perspective, but while still using normal controls.

I said Firewatch was an "advanced" "walking sim" because, like “Valley” or “What Remains of Edith Finch,” it creates a light gameplay experience to increase the player's involvement.  Firewatch has vast numbers of dialogue options, rather than a linear narrative.  This makes it a uniquely replayable environmental narrative adventure game.

As far as I know, the plot is the same, so it's really only replayable if you like the style of the dialogue.  I enjoyed the relationship between the two characters, but I hated the way their personalities were written.

This is supposed to be set in the mid-1980s, but both the man and the woman speak like 2010s urban millennials that grew up on 2000s-era "cringe comedy."  They're relentlessly sarcastic, relish being willfully socially awkward, have childish dispositions, and present their thoughts and feelings through thick layers of self-aware irony.

These are the hallmarks of "millennial writing" and use of this style has hopelessly dated Firewatch to the mid-2010s.  As the writers no doubt intended, the style of both the dialogue and voice acting are cringeworthy.  Perhaps not intended, they have put me off from replaying it to see other ways the conversations can play out.

I also thought the misdirections used to achieve plot twists and surprising revelations weren't that clever and felt too contrived or manipulative.

There were aspects I didn't like about Firewatch, but the overall experience was very immersive and enjoyable.  The gradual buildup of smoke over time from the once-distant "Flapjack Fire" (all the possible names were deliberately corny - it's IRONIC bro!) became overwhelming by time the fire was on the doorstep of my watchtower.  Virtual reality intensified the effect of the smoldering forest.

I wrote way more about this game than I'd meant to.  This is the end of the review.

Firewatch: Where the Bears are Less Scary Than Your Midlife Crisis (But Just Barely)

Imagine a choose-your-own-adventure story, except instead of space pirates or winning the lottery, you're...a middle-aged fire lookout. That's Firewatch, folks. Buckle up for a hilarious journey of existential dread, questionable moustache choices, and walkie-talkie banter that's more awkward than a family reunion with your ex.

Meet Henry, a man who's traded in his corporate grind for a mountaintop shack. Picture Dwight Schrute on vacation, minus the beets and plus a whole lot of existential angst. He's joined by Delilah, his ever-patient supervisor whose voice is the only thing keeping him from full-blown hermit mode. Their conversations are a goldmine of comedy, ranging from philosophical musings on loneliness to arguments about the best way to heat a can of beans (spoiler alert: it's not with a magnifying glass, Henry).

The game throws you curveballs like a rogue squirrel with a grudge. Strange messages appear, cryptic figures lurk in the shadows, and the tension builds faster than a campfire fueled by gasoline. Is there a conspiracy? Are bears actually plotting world domination? Or is it just Henry's overactive imagination, fueled by too much instant ramen and questionable decisions?

The beauty of Firewatch is that it never takes itself too seriously. You'll laugh, you'll cringe, you might even shed a tear (or two, or three, depending on your emotional stability). The developers knew exactly how to balance the humor with the suspense, keeping you guessing until the very end (and even then, you might be left with more questions than answers).

Just remember, this ain't your typical action-packed adventure. There's no slaying dragons or wooing princesses here. Instead, you'll be battling existential dread, dodging awkward silences, and mastering the art of making a decent cup of instant coffee. So, if you're looking for a game that's more "Eat, Pray, Love" meets "Lost" than "Call of Duty," then Firewatch is your spirit animal.

Here's the bottom line:

Pros: Hilarious dialogue, beautiful scenery, surprisingly deep story, walkie-talkie banter that will make you snort-laugh.
Cons: No dragons, Henry's mustache is questionable, existential dread may linger after playing.
Final verdict: Firewatch is a must-play for anyone who enjoys a good laugh, a good story, and a healthy dose of self-reflection. Just don't expect to emerge unscathed. You might just find yourself questioning your life choices and craving a can of beans (heated properly, of course).

P.S. If you do play, keep an eye out for the mysterious "Mysterious Figure." Trust me, you won't regret it. (Or maybe you will. But hey, that's all part of the Firewatch experience!)

This is a mystery game with lots of clues and conversations leading your mind all over the place, we had so many questions about each event and were discussing and theorising all the possibilities of each character and what could be going on it was absolutely fantastic. There wasn't a single game moment that was boring (such as grinding or backtracking), each step and conversation was purposeful in continuing the story onward and ALWAYS took a turn to what we expected to happen. As an extra plus note- it was quite funny in places too! Playing this game was like playing through a great story book and although I love online shooters and strategy games, this was a very creative and refreshing change of pace and I already set out to buy more games like this.

Music was great, the tone was great, voice acting was great, pacing was great and although some people completed this in a few hours we took 7 hours to complete and it felt like a very rich amount to play through!

You can tell the team that made this game really cared about making it a success and we look forward to their next one too. One little extra and decent aspect is you get a camera in the game and at the end not only do you get to see all your photos but you can also enter your email address and view them or download them which is something I haven't come across before and makes this game even more fulfilling and involving.

The suspense of the middle part of the game was good but ultimately falls flat at the end of the game. This game has its charms however and is pretty unique. If you feel like playing it I would recommend you to get it for a good discount because I don't see the full price to be justified.

So, during this winter break, I went on a journey through the captivating world of Firewatch—a game that has left a lasting mark on my gaming experience. As someone who cherishes atmospheric adventures and gripping narratives, Firewatch quickly became one game that I enjoyed a lot, captivating me with its stunning visuals, immersive story, and very relaxing gameplay.

From the moment I booted up Firewatch, I was greeted by a mesmerizing landscape of the Wyoming wilderness. The vibrant colors and stylized visuals drew me in, making me feel like I was stepping into a painting come to life. Every step I took felt like a leap into the unknown (but also a kind of familiar environment), with the rustling leaves and distant wildlife adding to the sense of immersion.

As I assumed the role of Henry, a fire lookout tasked with monitoring the forest for signs of danger, I found myself drawn into a mystery that unfolded with each passing day. The game's writing was so absorbing, with dialogue that felt like genuine conversations between real people. And the voice acting is simply superb, breathing life into the characters and making me feel like I was right there with them. Fun fact: The actor playing Henry is Rich Sommer, known from Mad Men. 

What struck me most about Firewatch was its ability to evoke a sense of relaxation. I know it is a cliché, but as a walking simulator game, it wasn't about the destination—it was about the journey itself. Whether I was wandering through the forest or looking out over a beautiful scenery, I always felt a profound sense of peace. In a world filled with noise, Firewatch offered a welcome break—a chance to slow down and appreciate the beauty of nature.

Firewatch is a regular video game, but it's also a journey of discovery and self-reflection. It's about finding a little refuge in the middle of uncertainty, and don't we all need that in these times. It took me only a bit less than four hours to finish it, but it is well worth it, especially now when you can get it on sale for a couple of bucks. 

So, if you're looking for a truly immersive gaming experience, I wholeheartedly recommend checking out Firewatch.

Summary:
Beautiful art style, good story, good atmosphere, well done. A little boring to traverse at times. Probably overpriced - get it if it's on sale.

  I make games myself, and if I could make a game half as good-looking as this, my life would be complete. If you like the visual style of the screenshots on the store page, the majority of the game looks like that.
  Of course, visuals aren't the only aspect of a game, and this one comes with a compelling story to boot. I won't spoil anything, but it's written very well, and, at times, it really invokes the sense of loneliness that's apparent at the start. The ending is something some people may complain about, but I quite like it. I think it's very fitting for this game.
  The gameplay is mostly walking from place to place, and in the beginning of the game it's good because it allows time to take in the environments. Later in the game, it gives time for the story to sink in. For myself, I ruined it because I watched a full playthrough of this game, expecting never to buy it for myself, but I can see how it would aid the gameplay.
  That brings me to my only major complaint, though, and that's the price. I completed this game in three hours flat, and compared to other games, it didn't provide the same value. It doesn't really have replayability, by nature of a heavily story-based game, but Outer Wilds, another game with very little replayability, took me eighty hours to finish completely, and it costs five dollars more. 
  I got this game while it was on sale for two dollars, and it's more than worth it at that price point. In fact, I'd easily pay ten dollars for it. My advice is to wait for a sale, because the price is a little steep. 
  I would recommend playing the game over watching a playthrough - playing it gives more of the full effect of the game.

Verdict: Recommend, but wait for a sale if you can.

When you start the game, you're meant to sympathize a lot with Henry. Not fully empathize, but at the very least, you can understand the decisions he makes in the prologue. When I played the game, I tried to lean into role playing his character as best as I could. I figured Henry is a person who needs some strong introspection, and that some time away from people will probably be painful, but at least helpful.

Enter your boss, Delilah. Do you want to develop a friendship, and possibly romantic relationship with this person, or do you want to keep the relationship strictly professional? Just kidding, you don't get a choice. The game guides you in certain direction worse than if you were in the Truman Show. A big issue for me is that no matter how many times you tell Delilah, that you're not interested in talking about your past, she keeps prying again, and again, and again.

If I wanted to have my boundaries crossed in a conversation, I could talk to my relatives. I don't need to have it happen in a video game.

There's a lot of discussion about the ending. Some debate whether or not you should've been able to see Delilah at least once. I couldn't have cared less about meeting her. I couldn't stand talking to her. This whole game is simply about trying to get the player to commit an emotional affair with someone. It blows.

TL/DR: A Short, Chill Exploration/Hiking Game w/ Mostly-Great Writing. 8/10

Things I liked:

      •  The music is good and atmospheric, with a chill vibe except when it needs to not be.
      •  The dialogue is great, natural and well-written (or improvised?)
      •  The graphics are smooth and, if a little cartoony, well done.
      •  Story was generally good, with a neat twist, though the ending wasn't my fav (see more below)

Things I was just okay with:

      •  Total game length was ~4 hours - could've used a bit more to see/do
      •  Run speed was a little slow
      •  Lots of things to interact with that had no reason for interaction (books, cleaning supplies, etc)
      •  Ending: No spoilers, but I wasn't thrilled with the ending and felt somewhat let down. As a storyteller/novelist, I can understand [i]why[/i] they went the way they did, but I would've done it differently

Things I didn't like:

      •  There was a bit too much going all the way across the map and back, retracing your steps. I know it's a hiking game, but come on. NOTE: This wouldn't have been an issue with a faster 'jogging mode.'
      •  The timer on responses on the radio - this felt like a forced pacing issue where they were trying to make it feel like you needed to hurry.

While the ending was surprising and not as satisfying as I would have liked (wish the dialogue and the character building would have led to different outcomes), the game as a whole is powerful. Between the characters dealing with their own challenges, the scenery, the sound track. Just wow!

In an era focused on live services and games that expect hundreds of hours of playtime, Firewatch is a lovely departure from that norm and a reminder that a game's impact isn't simply a function of its length. The relatively grounded stakes of the story and minimal UI help put the player in Henry's shoes, making the exceptional writing further deepen the player's connection to the protagonist and the story as a whole. The art direction also helps immerse the player, being close enough to realism to feel intimately familiar, yet separated enough from reality to allow the game's beauty to shine through. The gameplay does struggle slightly, as contextual button prompts struggle to consistently appear, and climbing sequences with no challenge other than pressing A are far less fulfilling than the navigational challenges that appear in the rest of the game. Nonetheless, Firewatch remains an excellent game for its whole duration, and I would highly recommend it to anyone looking for a few hours of escape into a wonderful world and heartfelt narrative.

Let me tell you a story to exemplify how great this game is. This is not just a game to me it’s a life long friend. 

One evening sometime around February of 2016 while I was spending time with my parents and grandparents at their log cabin home in California a YouTube notification popped onto my phone screen. My family was making dinner or something and I had nothing but free time and a warm fireplace to snuggle up to. When I opened the video I was greeted by the classic Markiplier “Hello everybody my name is..” 


What I had not known that evening was that I had so luckily happened to have stumbled upon the single greatest single player game of all time. From the timeless graphics to the stunning scenery I was swept from my cozy fireside couch and flung deep into Shoshone National Park. 



This game’s quality is breathtaking and second to none. But most importantly, no other form of media have I found that resembles an iota of the genuine humanity that is portrayed by this game. To this day I want to take a summer and work at a watchtower. To this day I yearn to just tour that great park and witness its beauty firsthand. Few games have ever made me feel such a strong attraction.



Though I had watched the entire series Markiplier had done on the game, I remained attached to this game like a leach. When my room was remodeled two years later in the 8th grade Firewatch posters were the first on the wall. Later, in my freshman year of high school after I had spent an entire summer making money to buy a gaming setup. The first game I bought once steam had installed was none other than Firewatch. 


Maybe it was the thrilling story or the equally beautifully crafted graphics that brought me to the game, but I wonder if there wasn’t another factor. Henry, the middle aged beer bellied protagonist, and I, a skinny insecure teen, had something in common with each other. We were both terribly lovesick and hopelessly depressed. 


For me Firewatch became an unconscious therapy. An escape. A reminder that good people exist even in bad lighting and that opportunities exist everywhere. A reminder that nature heals and so can I.



One scene in particular stands out to me when looking back on my fond memories of this game. One day Delilah asks Henry what he looks like. Each answer responds in banter and fun, but then she asks about my eyes. And suddenly I’m not playing as Henry anymore. 


For years throughout every play-through I’ve done in that game my answer was never just what Henry would have said. It was me and they were always tired. So very tired. 


Since then years have came and went. Life happened and things got better. I soon had forgotten the game, but recently it’s been back on my mind. This time I hope I can finally tell Delilah that my eyes are happy. 


So very happy.

Not bad, not quite good either. Firewatch is a walking simulator with decent graphics and a really fleshed out dialogue. Despite its short length, I had the misfortune of encountering the same bug several times (the character getting pushed away from an item when trying to interact with it), which isn't game-breaking, but still a bit annoying. Other than that, I didn't find any other technical problems.

Most of the critiques of the game concern the ending, which isn't exactly accurate. Trying not to spoil anything, the characters' decisions at the end are coherent with their behaviour throughout the game. The issue of the ending feeling anticlimactic is part of a larger problem that encompasses the entire story and has a lot to do with the protagonist's motivation for becoming a fire warden in the first place.

This motivation is explained at the beginning and essentially is a desire for escapism and refuge from his personal tragedies. From that, one would expect the protagonist to undergo some events during his fire watch that would alter his outlook on the problems he was trying to escape from in the first place. Maybe it doesn't have to be something exactly like that, but the protagonist should have some kind of growth or development. Apart from that, there could also be some insight into the life of a fire watch, how the protagonist tries to fight boredom while spending so much time alone in a watchtower, etc.

Instead, the game goes in a completely different direction and presents a mistery that's unrelated to the protagonist. In itself, this sub-story is decent: the problem is the absence of interaction between the events surrounding the protagonist and his personality. He unravels the mystery, seems to learn nothing from it and [spoiler]returns to the civilised world[/spoiler]. The main cause of the great disappointment at the end is the realisation that the characters haven't had any kind of growth from this experience and that the protagonist is a hollow vessel for presenting some mystery. Many players expected [spoiler]something to happen between Henry and Delilah[/spoiler] because that, at least, would be a conclusion to the story.

A one-dimensional protagonist wouldn't be a problem if the game focused on the mystery and nothing else, but Henry and Delilah (protagonist and co-protagonist respectively) talk constantly about why he decided to take that job and his background in general, so the game clearly wants the player to focus on this aspect as well, which doesn't develop in any significant way and therefore leads to disappointment because of failed expectations.

Taking all of this into consideration, I'd recommend the game if you're interested in a 4-5 hour story with no heavy gameplay and a decent mystery, but without getting too invested in the characters. The dialogue is really well written; it's the overarching story that has problems. Besides, the game has a massive discount more often than not, so it can cost you next to nothing and you can see for yourself what you think of the story.

As a side note, I experienced a number of bugs (animation glitches, textures glitches, getting locked into animations, etc.) which 1. make the game feel unpolished and 2. seem a bit more unacceptable considering how small scale the gameplay actually is; it's weird to me how these things didn't come up all the time in playtesting. An example is that every time I pulled out my second radio, its texture was incredibly fuzzy on half of the face; or sometimes terrain would unrender in front of me before rendering after a moment; or sometimes I'd get locked into grabbing the rope, as my player model would try to shimmy towards it but would instead just keep shimmying; or sticky ledges; and so on and so on. 

Overall, can't really recommend this game, it's easy to build mysteries and sell and aesthetic, both of which this game does well, but delivering on either is hard and that is what should be praised.

The dialogue between Delilah and Henry is incredible, and the voice acting is phenomenal and feels so authentic. I don't know how to feel about this game. It has a very strong beginning, gorgeous graphics and one of the best ambient sound & voice-acting performances I have witnessed. You care about the characters and their relationships; there are funny moments, relatable moments, sad moments, goosebumps, shock, tension, mystery, adventure, curiosity, and thrillers. But I would be lying if I said that the game was great. In many moments, you are just walking from one place to another, to another, to another without anything interesting happening, and that's fine at the beginning, but after about 2 hours, it gets bland and repetitive. It has a good but also anticlimatic ending, which is also fine. I think that the game tries to be too many things at the same time, and that leads to non-proportional pacing.
And this being a walking simulator makes you think that the walking aspect is alright, howerer the oppesite is true; nearly all of the forest looks similar so you are DEPENDENT on the map, but you cant look at the map while walking so you need to peek all 15 seconds on it and to do so you need to stop and stand still. That is acceptable, in spite of that you cant even run while holding the map so each time you stop to look at the map (which is very often) you have to press M each time and then press M again to close it to then press R to run (which is about 20% faster that walking, i wouldnt even call it running, more like a powerwalk). Yet using the map it sometimes leads you to 
dead ends although the map shows that there should be a way.
The negative aspects I mentioned don't matter all that much, and the game would still be great, but there are sadly game-breaking bugs where you get stuck, for example, in a tree and have to restart a whole day you have already spent about 20 minutes in, and that can be annoying, along with the character sometimes not wanting to walk to a side, and you have to move the camara and only walk with W until you get to a part where you can walk normally again with WASD. I looked it up, and it seems as if other people also experienced that, so if you are able to look past some bugs that may or may not force you to redo 20 minutes worth of gameplay, you will be awarded with a heart-touching game.

Overall, I would rate it an 8/10, without the annoying game-breaking bugs 8,5/10.

"Firewatch" is a truly masterful creation that combines exceptional visual style with a thoroughly engaging and intricate plot. The game offers a unique experience where players are immersed in their surroundings and the unfolding characters.

Right from the start, "Firewatch" impresses with its visual appeal. The Wyoming wilderness is meticulously reproduced, and the art design imparts a unique and atmospheric character to the entire game. Sound effects and the musical score enhance the emotional power of the narrative, adding an extra layer to the overall atmosphere.

The storyline of "Firewatch" unveils complex human relationships and dramas that capture attention and pique interest. The unfolding narrative combines mystery with emotional tension, creating an almost hypnotically appealing experience.

While the gameplay may seem relatively straightforward, featuring exploration and interaction, it contributes to the intensity of the bond between players and characters. While some may criticize the game's short duration, it trims unnecessary elements, emphasizing the strength of the content.

In conclusion, "Firewatch" offers an exciting adventure that successfully blends superb design, a well-crafted plot, and a magical experience. It is a game that leaves a profound impression and is a must-play for any fan of adventure puzzles and thrilling experiences.

[h1] Don't Understand the Hype [/h1]

I'll preface this by saying story-driven games are not typically my cup of tea. That being said, the high level of praise for this game on its story, voice acting, and visuals made me curious, so I picked it up on sale.

Boy am I glad I didn't pay full price. The story is a major letdown. Half of it is a character study on you and Delilah; the other half is a mystery-thriller about the strange happenings in the woods.

[h3]Characters / Voice Acting:[/h3]

Let's start with the character study portion. To me, the characters are woefully unlikable and unrealistic. The two of you are constantly exchanging snarky one-liners and sarcastic quips. It's supposed to be funny but I found it obnoxious especially since the game's opening establishes you as a middle-aged adult. It seems the writers' idea of an adult is someone who constantly makes references to drinking, other drugs, and dropping F-bombs. 

I will admit, I'm an adult and as such I curse and drink quite frequently, but the execution here is frankly irritating. From the very beginning your "supervisor" comes off as an unprofessional weirdo. The whole thing feels like it's written by a 16 year old, someone who still thinks drinking and cursing is inherently "cool", and as a result, the characters feel and act like teenagers, complete with sexual references that are utterly cringe-inducing.

About an hour in I realized the game telegraphs which dialogue interactions are central to the plot and which ones aren't. I found myself skipping the non-essential dialogue, only engaging when necessary, so I wouldn't have to listen to my supervisor's inane babbling as much. And it truly is inane - the extra dialogue adds nothing to the plot and nothing positive to the experience as a whole, unless I suppose you are in fact 16.

As I result, I completed the game in just over 3 hours. If it were any longer, I probably wouldn't have finished it. There is a branching dialogue system, but I refuse to replay the game even if it had any impact on the overall story, which, from what I understand from other reviews, it doesn't.

[h3]Plot (the mystery):[/h3]

The plot itself is okay. There were some points where I felt the execution was creative and interesting. The mystery is intriguing even if the characters' reactions to events are not (there are several points where the characters make strange and nonsensical conclusions as the writers attempt to intensify the mysteriousness of what's happening). However the resolution is unbelievable, in the sense that it's difficult to believe because of how illogical it is.

[h3]Mechanics:[/h3]

Mechanics are bare bones as many have said. I knew going into it that this game was not about the mechanics, so I don't hold its lack thereof against it. However, I will say I encountered several small glitches, which given the short playtime means at least one glitch per hour, a number that seems quite high considering how simple your interactions are.

[h3]Visuals / Atmosphere / Exploration:[/h3]

Visuals are fine: they did a good job of changing up your environment and making your Firewatch station feel "lived in". But let's be honest, if I want to go on a pretty walk in the woods, I can do that in real life. The only reason to do so in a video game is to experience something not available in reality, or something you wouldn't WANT to experience in reality, a.k.a the plot, which as I've stated, has its moments but is ultimately anti-climactic.

The only thing left is the undefinable "sense of exploration". The game promises "secrets and discoveries to be made over every hill". I can only assume they're referring to the supply boxes scattered throughout the woods, because they're the only things out there aside from plot elements and a few distinctive landmarks. You barely even run into any animals: I counted two. I opened quite a few supply boxes - and [spoiler] aside from necessary equipment and map notes[/spoiler], there is nothing interesting or of use in any of them. Just pointless notes, fake books, and pine cones.

[h3]Conclusion:[/h3]

For $20, you're better off renting a few good movies for a good story.

Like many others I had this game offered with a huge discount, and since I love wilderness, hiking and a good mistery I gave it a look. I was going to title this "needs work, a lot", but since the game was released eight years ago I don't see many chances to see it -actually- developed. It will probably stay in the discount bin and it's a shame, because it has some points.
- The story: I won't say it's good or bad. It's a story, it pretends to be gritty and realistic so you take it as it is. In some way it -is- refreshing, and the "blind romance" is an interesting device. The problem is - it's simple, and short, leaving you with a "meh" in your mind that comes not from anticlimax or what. And...
- The choices: in the presentation it reads: "your choices influence the outcome". This is a big NO: the story will go on the same way no matter what. Soon you are not even left with a reasonable illusion that the plot is not railroaded, and you're led by the nose all the time, anyway. It would be honest to present it as "visual novel without visual contact AND choices".
- the setting: this for me was, and is, the strong suit. The wilderness is nice. The landscapes are decently rendered, still there are things that put me off: boulders that look like concrete slabs, and you have to LOOK for them, bugs that block you or make you move in strange ways. The map is small, the paths are fixed, you can do a little sightseeing and take photos, tank you very much.

To recap, it's a demo at best, and it's not very kind selling it at full price; it's also a little late I guess to see it -seriously- overhauled and extended to become the game it could be. A pity, indeed.

I had a really great time with Firewatch. For a studio's first game, it feels expertly crafted - the setting, tone, and style all fit together perfectly to tell its story, with riveting twists and turns that kept me guessing from start to finish. I really loved how the story plays with your expectations, setting up narrative threads that could resolve in any number of ways, really pulling you into the sense of paranoia that Henry develops over the course of his summer in the wilderness, with nothing but a distant voice over the radio for company. The walking simulator part of the game controls excellently, which is truly essential for a game like this where there's very little proper gameplay outside of the traversal and dialogue options, and I really appreciated that even the map was a physical object that you had to manipulate to read properly. Even with its rather short four-hour length, I feel like you really get some bang for your buck with Firewatch (though I'd suggest waiting for a sale because it routinely gets deep discounts), and if you have any interest at all in narrative-driven walking sims like this, I'm not sure there's a better one to experience. All the more reason that it's a shame the developers were gobbled up by Valve to do approximately nothing at all...

[h1]Embracing the Wild: A Firewatch Adventure[/h1]

[h2]Story[/h2]
Firewatch, like a well-told campfire story, weaves a narrative tapestry that pulls you into its wilderness embrace. Set against the backdrop of the Wyoming wilderness, you step into the boots of Henry, a fire lookout with a past as rugged as the landscapes he navigates. The beauty of Firewatch lies not just in the scenic vistas but in the subtle complexities of human connections. The dialogue feels authentic, akin to sharing tales under the stars with a trusted companion. As you unravel the mysteries that echo through the trees, the emotional depth resonates, creating an unforgettable journey. "You're not lost. You're here," the game whispers, and you can't help but be captivated by the call of the wild.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Navigating the forested expanse feels like a dance with nature, where every step immerses you deeper into the storyline. The gameplay is a testament to simplicity's power, emphasizing exploration, decision-making, and a pinch of survival. The day-to-day tasks of a fire lookout become an engaging rhythm, punctuated by moments of suspense and discovery. The bond with your witty and unseen supervisor, Delilah, adds a layer of charm to the experience. It's a dance that balances solitude with companionship, mirroring the delicate steps of a forest creature. Firewatch is a game that reminds us that the journey can be as rewarding as the destination.

[h2]Graphics[/h2]
The visuals of Firewatch are a masterpiece painted with strokes of wilderness grandeur. The art style captures the essence of a vibrant national park, inviting players to lose themselves in the scenic splendor. As the sun sets over Shoshone, the warm hues blend seamlessly with the forest greens, creating a visual spectacle that mirrors the beauty of nature. The attention to detail in the environment, from the rustling leaves to the distant mountain peaks, is a testament to the developers' commitment to creating an immersive experience. It's a canvas that invites you to pause and soak in the majesty of the outdoors, much like a breathtaking view from a mountaintop lookout.

[h2]Sound[/h2]
Firewatch's soundtrack is a symphony of the wilderness, with each note harmonizing with the rustling leaves and distant calls of wildlife. The sound design is a journey in itself, enveloping you in the ambience of the forest. Delilah's voice, a constant companion through your walk in the woods, adds a human touch to the solitude. The dialogue is delivered with such finesse that it feels like a conversation with a close friend. The minimalist approach to sound effects accentuates the tranquility of the woods while punctuating moments of tension. It's a sonic experience that enhances the emotional resonance of the narrative, making Firewatch an auditory adventure worth savoring.

[h2]Overall[/h2]
Firewatch is not just a game; it's an ode to nature, storytelling, and the human spirit. Its narrative prowess, coupled with engaging gameplay and breathtaking visuals, creates a harmonious symphony of gaming delight. While some may argue about the abruptness of the ending, the journey itself is so compelling that it overshadows any reservations. Should you embark on this adventure? Without a doubt. Firewatch beckons you to leave the familiar trails and embrace the wild unknown. It's not just a game; it's a journey into the heart of the untamed, where every step is a choice, and every choice resonates like a ripple in a tranquil lake. So, gear up, embrace the mystery, and let the call of the wild guide you through this unforgettable experience.

[h1]Yellow Trees, Red Flags, and One Very Expensive Therapy Session[/h1]

[h2]Welcome to the World’s Least Helpful Summer Job[/h2]
Firewatch casts you as Henry, a man who heads into the Wyoming wilderness in 1989 to work as a fire lookout after life on the outside gets a little too heavy to carry normally. Your only real human connection is Delilah, your supervisor on the other end of a handheld radio, and the game very quickly turns that setup into something more intimate, more suspicious, and much messier than “man looks at trees for a season.” It’s a first-person mystery, sure, but more than that it’s a game about running away from your problems and then discovering your problems have surprisingly good cardio.

[h2]A Postcard from Heaven, Mailed from an Emotional Sinkhole[/h2]
I still think Firewatch looks fantastic. Not "holy crap I can see that hair on his nose" fantastic, but actually artistic, which is rarer than the industry likes to admit. The color palette does a ridiculous amount of work: warm oranges, bruised sunsets, deep forest shadows, all of it making the place feel beautiful and faintly dangerous at the same time. It doesn’t chase realism like a dog chasing a car. It picks a mood, commits to it, and makes the whole game feel like a national park poster designed by someone going through a quiet breakdown. That was the right call.

[h2]Two Voices, One Radio, and a Masterclass in Making Silence Feel Loud[/h2]
The sound is half the game’s magic. Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones do so much with timing, hesitation, flirtation, deflection, and the little conversational stumbles that make people sound like people instead of dialogue trees wearing skin. The score by Chris Remo knows when to step in and when to get the hell out of the way, which is a skill more games should learn instead of arriving with an orchestra every time you open a door. Firewatch understands that loneliness is not always silent. Sometimes it sounds like a crackling radio and someone trying very hard to sound normal.

[h2]Walking, Talking, and Quietly Falling Apart in Good Lighting[/h2]
On a pure mechanical level, Firewatch is not exactly out here bench-pressing game design. You walk, you look, you talk, you pick dialogue options, and you follow the thread. That’s the package. If someone goes in expecting systems, challenge, or the kind of interactivity that lets them knock over a crate and call it immersion, they may bounce off it hard enough to achieve orbit. But I think the restraint mostly works. The limited mechanics keep the attention where it belongs: on mood, pacing, and the push-pull between what Henry says, what he avoids saying, and what the game quietly suggests about him. It is not mechanically rich, but it is mechanically focused, and there’s a difference.

[h2]The Mystery Is Real, It’s Just Not the One Your Brain Ordered[/h2]
This is the part that made Firewatch stick with me. The story sets you up to expect one kind of payoff and then hands you something sadder, smaller, and more human instead. I like that. A lot. The game is about loneliness, avoidance, guilt, fantasy, and the stories people build so they don’t have to stare directly at the hole in the middle of their life. That means the ending was always going to annoy some people, especially if they wanted the whole thing to go full conspiracy thriller and start foaming at the mouth. But for me, the refusal to turn into a dumb twist machine is exactly why it works. Firewatch looks you in the eye and says, “No, sorry, your pain does not get to become cool.” Brutal. Correct. Excellent.

[h2]Beautiful, Sharp, and Slightly Up Its Own Ass[/h2]
What Firewatch does well, it does extremely well. The atmosphere is immaculate, the voice work carries real emotional weight, and the writing is observant in a way that feels rare even now. It can be funny without getting desperate, tender without getting syrupy, and uneasy without resorting to some idiot jumping out of a cupboard. But it also has limits, and they are not tiny. The actual choice-and-consequence side is thinner than the game’s tone initially suggests, the mystery can feel like a deliberate bait-and-switch if you want harder answers, and the whole thing is over quickly enough that if it doesn’t get its hooks into you early, you’ll spend the rest of it admiring the scenery and waiting for a deeper cut. I think it lands. I also think it absolutely knows it’s clever, which is fine right up until it starts admiring itself in the mirror a bit too long.

Firewatch is one of those games that a certain kind of player will adore and another kind will dismiss as “walking around talking about feelings,” which is funny because, yes, that is literally part of the product and it happens to be good. I think it’s a beautiful, well-acted, emotionally intelligent game that understands the difference between mystery and fantasy, and between connection and projection. It’s not perfect, and it’s definitely not trying to entertain people who need every game to hand them a shotgun and a skill tree. But when it works, it really works wonders. It leaves you with that odd, sour little feeling that the summer meant something, even if nobody came out of it cleaner. Frankly, that’s more than most games manage after twenty extra hours and three unnecessary boss fights.

Also your character claims he's unable to continue on some paths because it's blocked by brambles that are 3 feet high, it's just dumb. It's hard for me to immerse into this world when the characters turn away in the opposite direction from an impossible path that is so obviously not a big deal if he just does some minor manoeuvring of his body around the brambles through some bushes and trees. There are huge time jumps going from day 3 to like day 60 something, then 70 something, that caught me off guard. They are trying to show a passage of time but it doesn't offer any sense of stakes. There is some intrigue of stuff going on but there's no urgency to solve it day by day, it's just ok well I still have a job to do so skip ahead 50 days, and then during all that time we can imagine him just sleeping in his tower and walking around the forest every day therefore it's not interesting for the player to experience. Firewatch, developed by Campo Santo (who debuted as their first game), is a captivating narrative-driven game that revolves around the protagonist, Henry, a Firewatch Park Ranger. The game offers a unique blend of exploration, mystery, and emotional storytelling, making it a standout experience in the gaming world and an instant hit for Campo Santo games.

The central focus of Firewatch is the character of Henry, who takes on the role of a Firewatch lookout in the vast and beautifully rendered Wyoming wilderness. Henry is a complex character who seeks solace and an escape from the challenges of his everyday life. As players delve into the game, they are quickly immersed in the stunning terrain of Wyoming, featuring cliffs, waterfalls, caves, and majestic mountains that serve as the backdrop for the unfolding narrative.

The narrative takes an intriguing turn when Henry establishes communication with his supervisor, Delilah, voiced by Cissy Jones. The relationship that develops between Henry and Delilah becomes a cornerstone of the game, and the strength of their bond is shaped by the player's decisions. The beauty of Firewatch lies in its ability to weave an emotionally charged tale that is deeply influenced by the choices players make throughout the game.

Decision-making plays a pivotal role in Firewatch, impacting the dynamic between characters. As players navigate the lush and expansive Wyoming wilderness, they are confronted with choices that affect the narrative direction and the characters' interactions. The consequences of these decisions are not only reflected in the dialogue but also in the overall atmosphere and tension of the game.

The Wyoming terrain, meticulously crafted and rendered, serves as more than just a backdrop; it becomes a character in itself. The Cliffs, waterfalls, caves, and mountains create a sense of isolation and contemplation, emphasizing the solitude that both Henry and the player experience. The attention to detail in the environment enhances the immersive storytelling, making the exploration of the wilderness an integral part of the overall gaming experience.

Firewatch is not just a game; it's an emotional journey that explores themes of loneliness, self-discovery, and the complexities of human relationships. The voice acting adds a layer of authenticity to the characters, making their connection with players even more profound.

In conclusion, Firewatch stands out as a remarkable narrative-driven game that successfully intertwines the beauty of its Wyoming setting with a compelling story centered around the character of Henry. The choices players make resonate throughout the game, shaping the narrative and the relationships that unfold. Firewatch is a masterclass in atmospheric storytelling that will leave players reflecting on their journey long after the credits roll.

Firewatch won me over because it turns a simple first-person mystery into something much more personal through dialogue, atmosphere, and pacing. Firewatch is not built around complex mechanics, and that is part of its strength. What stood out the most to me was the connection between Henry and Delilah, the way the Wyoming wilderness feels both beautiful and isolating, and how the soundtrack and visual style support that mood. It is a short game, and some people may want more from its ending, but its identity is very clear. 

In my experience, it was an easy game to get absorbed in. I really liked exploring the landscape, listening to the conversations, and watching the story build a very specific emotional tone in just a few hours. I also think it is fair to mention that achievement hunters may run into a few annoying issues, and anyone expecting heavy gameplay systems may find it too light. Even so, I recommend it to players who value atmosphere, strong writing, and short narrative experiences. Not so much for someone looking for action or a lot of mechanical depth.

Firewatch is a neat game. That's how I would put it. I've been hearing its name thrown around everywhere throughout the years and it's always been one of those games where it's on my radar but I never really bothered playing or looking into it. I had no idea what this game was about but finally gave in and bought it when I saw it was on sale. Let me just say, first impressions with the graphics were great, the scenery is gorgeous and was great for me because I love taking photos in games. 

From what I could tell while playing, it was a story game, but as I kept playing through it I was trying to figure out *what* kind of story game it was and what it was trying to tell. An hour in or so I begin to think that this is actually some type of horror game, and I was actually expecting for any second for something to jump out at me because the vibe the game was giving truly was that of a horror or suspense game. And as the game goes on, I am really convinced this is a horror game even though nothings happened, the whole setup with the walkie talkies and that random tent out in the forest with a ton of equipment made me feel like there was something bigger at play, and then, nothing ever happened (without trying to spoil much) it all turns out to be one thing and then that's it, there's nothing else to figure out, and it sort of feels... I don't know, underwhelming? I get that not every game needs this super crazy plot twist and story, but I think this is the type of game that could have benefited from it. Hell, at the end you don't even get to meet Delilah, the person you've been talking to the entire game, it just ends and you're left with a feeling of "That's it?" I just wish there was more to it I guess, but maybe that's the point, that not everything needs complicated and sometimes things can be simple and still beautiful, or maybe I'm grasping at the straws here trying to figure out what the purpose was behind this game besides being a playable book. Maybe that's all it was meant to be though.

Regardless, it is a good game and clearly well made, I still enjoyed playing it so I'm going to recommend it, but I ask that you don't go in expecting for a lot of stuff to happen, go in with a mindset that you are going on a hike, take your time and look at the scenery, to appreciate the humor in the conversations, it's a game to play and relax with, like laying in bed while reading a book. 6/10 personally.

One thing that kept bugging me throughout my playthrough was the navigational system. A big part of real backcountry hiking is routefinding, and this game has disappointingly little of that, instead forcing you into designated trails. In the game our character is pretty limble; he can hop on rocks, jump gaps, rappel down cliffs, climb up small cliffs, etc. But he can only do those things *on trail.* if you stray off the path you hit barriers, often in the form of small cliffs, boulders, trees, etc. These barriers often look passable, but for some reason our character just won't traverse them. I kept finding myself running into small boulders and getting annoyed when the character refuses to jump on top of them, even though he climbs cliffs & jumps between boulders just fine *on trail.* This made navigation really annoying at times, because I kept having to make sure I was on trail and not being misled by terrain that looks passable but actually isn't.

Firewatch doesn't take much skill, and it doesn't even take a lot of brains. It takes more graphics card than it takes skill and brains combined and you can run this thing on a potato if you don't use the most expensive lighting setting. It is very much a 3D interactive visual novel rather than a game. There's not much to it... You just put yourself in the shoes of somebody going through a life experience, and wonder what it would be like to be that guy. A lot of reviewers don't like this game because it's boring, and/or the ending is unsatisfying. Both of those things are... kinda true. Granted, it's probably a lot less boring to play this game than it would be to actually work the job that it's depicting -- that of a fire lookout. (Though, that's not saying much, since most fire lookouts seem to give the impression that it is the most profoundly boring job that you can possibly imagine).

However, I still immensely enjoyed the game and couldn't help but play through it a few times just to know what secrets I missed. And... I can't really tell you why I did that... It's just some story. Henry (the player character) is just some middle-aged guy. The setting is just somewhere in the Shoshone. Your job is just looking out for fires. (Though of course, the plot focuses on everything but said fires, even if you are very much aware that that's your job).

I know that after having discussed this game with other players that the theme of the story is about how we run away from our problems sometimes, and how choosing to do that affects us and others, and just -- I don't know, the coping strategies we have when we get stressed about life, and trauma, and any kinda pain... or whatever... But also it just feels so profoundly... ordinary. My first impression was that the theme of the story is that ♥♥♥♥ Happens Sometimes™ and that's it. It felt like I was back in middle school reading The Old Man and the Sea when I finally experienced the ending. It's like the whole thing is just some low-key sad story you'd hear from your dad, or your uncle, or even just a total stranger you'd strike up a conversation with at a random bar. And then maybe they finish the story by giving you some of Uncle Barry's Very Own Life Advice™. Or maybe they wouldn't, and when they're done talking, you'd both just sit there thinking about life.

So, if it feels so ordinary, why play this game instead of reading some dusty old book titled "Memoirs of a Park Ranger/Fire Lookout/etc.?" Well, first of all, probably because (quite like myself) you're ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ illiterate. Also, maybe because this game features Cissy Jones. (Not to understate the talents of Rich Sommer or any of the other voice cast; they are all incredibly talented, and each of their jobs on this game is a masterpiece. But... hnngg.. Cissy Jones... save me...) And also it's just good art. The visuals are extremely well-made and beautiful. The sound design and the music seems to perfectly fit everything. Delilah (played by Cissy Jones) is always trying to sound as sexy as possible, all the time, and is really good at it. All of the artists and writers just put their whole ♥♥♥♥♥ into this ♥♥♥♥♥. Every part of the game is an artistic masterpiece. These are all good reasons to play, but it's also just... believable? And maybe "believable" is just something I was more surprised and interested to see in a video game than I would have been to see in a book? And maybe that's the only thing that stands out? I don't know. But, I enjoyed it.

Since it's a video game instead of a book, you experience the story in an interactive and visual way, and maybe for this particular story, it makes you feel more like it's real. You feel more like you can understand how Henry feels. This game just gives you a lot of emotions, which is something that some people pursue, and I guess that was what I was pursuing. If that sounds like yourself, then, I can recommend this game to you. Go. Take off for the woods. It's a place where there ain't no shoulds... or something.

TL;DR: I'm kidding. I genuinely don't think that I can, in good conscience, recommend this game to you if you can't read all that. I don't have any TL;DR. I know it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ War and Peace up there, but I'm sorry, this is one of those games.

Firewatch is a fun and creative narrative that let's you sink away from reality and get immersed in a world full of story and mysteries. Not one moment of this game was unenjoyable for me and while the game is rather short, there are additional modes (under the special features) that are available to play if you want to continue exploring. 
PROS:
- The artstyle of this game is beautiful. Looks impressive in all stages and locations in the game.
- The gameplay feels connected to the story. While there isn't anything mindblowing about the gameplay (it's mainly a lot of exploration), everything gameplay wise is connected to the story. There are easter eggs hidden althroughout the map and everything you discover has some sort of backstory to it.
- The characters. You'll hear 2 characters voices for the majority of the story, Henry (who you play as) and Delilah, another worker who's been there for years. Neither of the characters feel bland, they both have personality and depth and backstory to them. They both are likable and feel like regular, interesting people.
- The story. The game starts off with giving you Henry's backstory, of meeting his wife Julia who suffers from dementia early on in her life and eventually, when Henry and Julia are both in their 40s, she has to move back to her parents house in Australia because she was too much responsibility for Henry to take care of. It's a dark backstory, and Henry takes the firewatch job to clear his mind. I won't go much further than that (since this is the beginning of the game) but the game feels pretty emotional at times. There's so much you learn about all the characters (even the ones that aren't Henry and Delilah) that you can find yourself feeling bad for them. I enjoyed the story so much that I really hope a sequel to this game is in the works.

CONS;
- The end of the game. This isn't a huge con, I just wish that there could have been something more. The whole game it feels like everything is leading to something big and the ending is somewhat inconclusive. You get told what each character plans to do in the end but I wish there was like a "1 year later" type of thing so we end up finding out what happens next. Again it's not a huge thing I just wish we got to know.
- The length of the game. I feel that the length wasn't stretched out (which is good) but I also feel like there could have been more. Not a whole lot like I mentioned, just something small to let the player know what happens next. This also brings up the topic of price, and I think this game when it's at it's full price is around $30 but I'm not entirely sure.
