Firewatch is an exploration adventure game set in the wilderness of Wyoming.  As the protagonist, Henry, you chose to become a firewatch ranger to get away from your life and be in solitude.  During your adventure you meet, via radio only, Delilah who is another ranger at another watch tower.  During the course of the game you will deal with campers, wildlife, and fires.  The true highlight of this game is the dialogue between the two characters.

The graphics for this game remind of The Witness, but with more animation making it much more alive.  The different times of day are beautiful as the lighting really paints a masterpiece especially as the light goes through leaves and branches of the trees.  The only drawback on the graphics that I had was that the motion of the camera made me nauseous.  I had to mess with the FOV and it was better, but the motion of the camera really follows the players head and motion which can be a bit more than you are used to.  The only other game that made me feel this way was 3D Sonic, other than that I'm not weak when it comes to motion.  I was able to overcome it with settings though and was able to complete the game.

The sounds are great.  Nature sound like what nature should sound like, there's music in areas where mystery or suspense is occurring, but again the true highlight is the dialogue.  The voice acting is spot on and the conversation that you engage in are very real and natural.  The person who wrote the script for this game should be handling movie scripts because this was beyond what most games offer and beyond what most movies offer as well.

Between the graphics, sounds and the dialogue this game truly immerses you in an atmosphere most games just can't create.  The backstory evolves, the characters evolve, and it's just a really good mixture of all of the above for the making of a great game.

The game is short, which is great because it is afterall just an exploration game where you are hiking around the mountains and through the trees.  But the storyline and gameplay last just long enough where it doesn't feel drawn out where it overstays its welcome and you are able to truly enjoy the whole game rather than feel like you are doing meaningless tasks just to add more time to the game.

While I wouldn't buy this for the full price, I think that it is a pleasant experience to have so check it out for sure if it's half price or even less.

A GAME ABOUT ESCAPISM 

  Firewatch, one of the most beautiful games ever made, and one that was in my backlog ever since 2016. Now, 8 years after the release, I was finally able to play it, and that was good, it was good because im sure that the "me" of 2016 would have hated or just disliked this game, but now with a more mature mind, I can see what the Campo Santo team was aiming for, and that message hitted me like a brick.

  About the story, it shows us the brief tale of a man named Henry, that lives a normal life. The beginning of the game gives us some options of how Henry met Julia, his wife. In the end, Julia is diagnosed with dementia, and starts to live with her parents in another country. Henry then finds a job vacancy for forest lookout in Shoshone National Forest, Wyoming. There he meets another employee, a woman called Delilah, that has years of experience in that occupation.

  The gameplay is slow paced, everything is meant to be an experience, you are isolated in that wilderness alongside Delilah, the narrative and the way the characters are written keeps the player engaged and interested in what will happen next. In the first days you do basic forest watch stuff, until by the end of the game, stuff gets out of hand and both you and Henry starts to question whether is all everything real or not... And just like real life, most of the problems are simply we having an overreaction for a problem that is simple to solve.

  The games makes sure to show that Henry is there to escape from his problems and the ending is a remind of that, there is a big red herring being shown in the entire game with an awesome build up, that just show to us how reality is. Firewatch is a game about two individuals with problems and troubled pasts, and what happens to individuals that don't take responsabilities of their choices. In this game you can confiscate illegal objects and clean the forest, but that doesn't change anything, the player does that because that's the main character work. Henry in the end strives that he need to move on which is a huge contrast to Delilah, that thinks that she can always escape when a problem is on her face.

  The end is open to total interpretation, the question whether Delilah or Henry story ends there is pointless. Both of them continue to live their lives as usual. The question though, is asked to the player, do you live your life thinking that you are a victim and flee from everything that once made you happy just to avoid a fate that feels unfair? Are you someone that fully identify yourself with your suffering and nurture until it closes you forever, like a shell? Or are you capable of decide that being here, making the choices we can, and getting to continue taking part and connecting in human life, is reason enough to take responsibility for protecting fragile things and fixing broken ones. We can decide that it’s not about fault, being a hero, winning, or getting rewarded. It’s just about the truth. We’re the ones who are here now when help is needed, and if we don’t help, no one else will. Are you like Henry, or like Delilah?

  Firewatch in itself is about how we deal with what we can’t escape, and what we owe to ourselves to uphold our commitments, a game real as it gets, about humans and humans lifes.

One of the best narrative driven "Walking Simulator" type games. In particular the voice acting and writing are top notch, especially between Henry, the main character, and Delilah, his boss, who you only ever hear on the radio. The game hits you with emotional and very realistic human story-lines from the very beginning. 

The main gameplay is navigating your watch area and completing objectives Delilah gives you (example, go tell off some teenagers setting off fireworks in the park). You use your compass and map so its a bit more interactive. What's really unique is the main mechanic where you use your walkie talkie to point out everything and talk to Delilah. I found myself making sure to comment on most everything I saw to Delilah. I just wanted to know more about her, or hear what genuinely funny joke she would make about something, or just share what I was seeing with her. The magic of the game really is that relationship where you don't really know Delilah but that is the only person you speak to for the whole game. I'm a sucker for those types of stories, where you bond with an unknown person over an unusual situation (and some beautiful scenery). 

The game builds up mystery for you to uncover, and many found the ending disappointing. I found the ending actually great, and its clever how the game builds on the player's sense of imagination and suspense, which is always more wild than anything the game comes up with. Ultimately, to me, the game's story is about 2 damaged humans who are imperfect, navigating difficult lives. 

Worth note, I had several glitches where Henry got stuck on shrubs and I could not move the character so I had to reload the game. I never really lost more than a few minutes of progress due to it saving often though.

This is the sort of game that I really wish I could give a middling option to. On one hand, the dialog is well written and expertly performed, and traipsing around the mountain trails is a beautiful and relaxing experience. It's also a very short experience; even multiple playthroughs to hear all the different dialog trees won't take more than a few hours. This could arguably be a negative for some, but given that the game is all dialog and narrative, it doesn't really need more than that to feel complete.

The true negative here is in the narrative itself. An intriguing mystery is established early on and grows bigger and more intense throughout the game, but it completely falls apart at the end. I get the impression that the writer(s) started off with all these different threads and didn't know how to tie them together, and game's conclusion is incredibly weak because of it. It's possible that the blasé explanation for all the events was entirely by design, which is fine in theory, but the execution here makes some elements of it feel outlandish given the grounded mood of the rest of the game.

Tl;dr good atmosphere, great voice work, terrible ending. I don't regret playing it, but it's not something I can give an easy recommendation. If you really feel the need to play this, get it on a steep discount. Despite the myriad accolades and overwhelmingly positive reviews surrounding [b]Firewatch[/b], I managed to remain unspoiled about the game's narrative. Initially uncertain about my affinity for this style of storytelling, [b]Firewatch[/b] astounded me completely. The game exhibits a remarkable pacing, a distinctive art style, and introduces an utterly relatable and likable everyman – a character many of us can easily resonate with, as I certainly did.

Beyond the abundant acclaim the game has received, [b]Firewatch[/b] stands as a poignant ode to self-discovery, addressing themes of grief, shame, self-worth, and somehow the harsh truth over life's formidable challenges. Sometimes, all it takes to unravel one's thoughts is an unfamiliar yet sharply sarcastic guide leading you through the mundane aspects of daily life, offering purpose when you're unsure of where to begin.

It unfolds as a captivating journey, an adventure amidst lush forests and windswept mountains that characterize the arc of an audacious summer. [b]Firewatch[/b] fills your days with a blend of curiosity, courage, fear, comedy, and tragedy. I wholeheartedly recommend experiencing it, as it promises a journey that leaves you awestruck, perhaps prompting contemplation on the simple choices in life.

While I've noted that some individuals expressed dissatisfaction with the ending, I believe such sentiments reveal more about those players than the protagonist. The narrative, crafted with brilliance from start to finish, serves as a testament to the game's exceptional writing.

I got Firewatch on sale, and played based on the large number of positive reviews.  I played it through and enjoyed the story, finishing just today.  I won't spoil anything (alright SOME of my critique is a tad spoiler-ish.  You've been warned) but I will say that I left the game wanting a little... more.  I wish it was a bit richer - in just about every aspect.  

The world and effects are quite pretty and stylized in a cartoon-ish way.  The previews give you a glimpse of that, and it's pretty easy on the eyes.  It's relaxing and slow paced.  The controls are easy, and there were just a few glitches and screen stutters.  There was one Supply Box that just shoved me away about 6 paces when I tried to open it.  Never got that one open.

The world navigation is pretty linear.  Not open world.  There are definite boundaries that direct you in the game.  Some things where you are thinking "man I should be able to walk over that" you just get stopped.  Eventually you come to understand where you can and can't go.

The dialogue with Delilah is interesting... but ultimately sort of shallow.  Wish it could have gone a little deeper.

The choices in dialogue you get to make... they felt inconsequential.  Like the game wouldn't change much based on how you chose.  I might play again and choose completely different choices just to see.

The mystery was fun ... until it wasn't a mystery anymore and it was sort of just ... meh.

I wish the stakes had been a little higher.

I was not prepared for the salty language used throughout the game.  Is this how all games are these days?  (yes I have been away from gaming for a while).  I wish there was a way to "turn off" the profanity.  It's definitely R rated.  I am an adult - so I can handle it.  But I wouldn't recommend the game to kids or family members based on this alone.  Give me a way to make it PG and I would.

Ultimately, I got what I feel I paid for - (Winter Mid Week sale).  A quick diversion that was fun.

What this game and its makers really have is POTENTIAL.  This could easily have a far superior sequel.  Firewatch could be just the prologue in a far deeper and interesting story.  Devs could take this in any number of directions.  My biggest wants?  Not in order of importance... 

1.  Clean up or give option to play a profanity free game.
2.  Make it a truly open world.  I understand some barriers need keys and quests.  Make them real barriers - not something it looks like I should be able to walk or jump over.  Anyplace I think I can walk, I should be able to walk.
3.  Increase the peril.  I would have enjoyed a little more respect for the heights or hazards in the game.  Falling to your death is impossible in this game as it is, despite the high vistas.
4.  Increase the stakes.
5.  Make the threat to our protagonists more... of a threat.
6.  Make the relationship more meaningful.
7.  Give our protagonists the option for closure given certain choices.
8.  Make the choices you make in dialogue more meaningful, even if it means having the story go a completely different direction.

Overall - I am glad I played.  Maybe I thought it was something more ... but that's ok.  Overall a cool game.

If there's another one that promises more of... all of it... I'm in.

The gameplay, atmosphere, visuals, and sound are all good. My negative review is solely due to the story.
Firewatch has been talked about for years as a game with dull walking simulator gameplay and a phenomenal story. Now that I've finally gotten around to playing it, I was surprised to find the opposite: The gameplay is surprisingly involved, navigation and exploration are fun, and I would classify it more as an adventure game than a straight walking sim, albeit one with a low difficulty. The story on the other hand falls completely flat for me. My three main objections with it are that it's unsatisfying, morally questionable, and finally, it's one of the most stereotypically "Millennial" storytelling I've ever seen (speaking as a fellow Millennial). Which for a 2016 game probably makes sense.

Millennial trope No. 1: Right off the bat, they hit you with the depressing backstory. This being an "indie game narrative masterpiece," I already suspected this was what was going to pass for character development. However, not only did the absurd level of tragedy of the backstory exceed my expectations, it never really has anything to do with the entire rest of the game, except for maybe three throwaway lines of dialogue. I spent the whole time wondering how they would thematically weave the backstory into the eponymous "fire watch"--well, they didn't.

Millennial trope No. 2: While the voice acting is very good, about 80% of the dialogue has that typical Millennial snarky sarcasm. The two main characters are in their late 30's/early 40's and talk like sassy teenagers most of the time. It has that constant quippy mock-complaining and most lines would fit right into a Marvel movie or Disney Star Wars production. What makes this even more egregious is that the game takes place in 1989. While I wasn't alive then, I don't remember people talking quite like this even in the 2000's. Half the time I wanted to tell my male player character to just shut up, quit whining, and do the job he voluntarily signed up for. Some of it is endearing, but too much of it is irritating, at least to me. Your mileage may vary.

Millennial trope No. 3: There's quite a lot of "nerd stuff" and "you should touch grass"-type comments shoehorned into this game about a 39 year old man taking a fire watch summer job in rural Wyoming in 1989. Maybe this is nitpicky of me, but I don't think these present-day cliches would have realistically come up in this situation, especially tabletop RPG's  ... then again, this game did come out the same year as the first season of Stranger Things.

When it comes to the morally questionable parts, our "adorkable characters" have some pretty unlikable traits. They're more relieved at not getting in trouble than at someone not having died. The game has an obsession with alcohol consumption (if that's your thing, fine, but here the focus felt excessive and almost accidental. Even in something like Grand Theft Auto, characters in the story aren't constantly boozing or talking about booze.) And last but not least: the game goads you into cheating on your sick wife. You have the option not to, but it feels designed around that, and perhaps the dialogue trees I went with were less fleshed out as a result.

Not that any of this goes anywhere. Other Steam reviewers complain about the ending, but in my opinion the entire second half of the game was a dud. What initially builds as an intimate and unconventional character study suddenly becomes a weird, plot-heavy mystery story. What bugs me isn't so much that the ending is illogical (it is), but rather that none of the story's elements seem to cohere into anything--the tragic backstory, the two main characters, the fire watch, the reveal of the mystery. I don't see what any of these elements have to do with each other thematically or narratively. I thought the fire watch would end up being a big metaphor for the characters' struggles, or some teaching experience, you know, like in a good story? (Oh God, the Millennial snark, I'm doing it, aren't I?) Perhaps someone who's into parsing out really deep hidden meanings could make heads or tails of this, but to me it just seemed like a convoluted mess of a narrative. Not hard to understand, just messy.

In conclusion:
While I got some enjoyment out of the well-presented first half of the game (after getting through the, to me, pointless and forced opening backstory), I can't recommend this game as a package, not even on sale. Concerning length, I sprinted the entire time, didn't look at the landscape much, always took the optimal route, read every note, and listened to every call, and it took me around 5 hours to beat. If you don't mind the risk, check it out on sale, but 3 of those 5 hours could be spent better I think. Moreover, I think this game needs some negative reviews to temper the high praise a bit. Would I say this game is overrated? Yes. But I can totally see this being the perfect game for a gaming journalist to play for 45 minutes and then put up his 10/10 "Best Story of the Decade!"-review. Buyer beware.

P.S. One final trope about these first person indie games I'd like to point out (and I'm sorry if this ruins other indie games for you) is that I've been starting to notice you pretty much never meet another person. I get that character models and animation are hard, much harder than doing environments and landscapes. However, if you can't animate people, maybe don't make games that revolve around looking for people. It makes the fact that every last-seen-location is already abandoned when you get there really predictable.

Firewatch is like that really good TV show you accidentally binge-watch in one evening. I started playing, blinked, and suddenly it's over! Three hours well spent, let me tell you.

The story? Absolutely nailed it. Got me hooked from the get-go. It's like a mystery novel, but with fewer pages and more trees. The characters are surprisingly real for pixelated folks. Delilah, my radio buddy, felt like the virtual friend I never knew I needed.

The Wyoming scenery is breathtaking, or so I hear. I was too busy pretending to be a forest detective to notice the beauty around me. Plot twists were my focus, not picturesque landscapes.

The controls? Easy. Firewatch understands I'm here for a good time, not a complicated tutorial. It's the kind of game you play when you want a chill adventure without needing a PhD in button-mashing.

I know it's intentionally anti-climatic, but you can't just throw "we meant to do that" in the player's face and act like that's serviceable. You don't tell stories for them to have little to no conclusion. The whole game feels like it's made up to be something bigger, and then lets you down. What can I say I purchased this game today due to it being on sale and highly recommend to me and I have just played it start to finish in one sitting so I thought why not give my two cents on the the matter.

Firewatch kept me on the edge of my seat throughout the whole of the game, I will not be issuing any spoilers for those that have not played it, heard of it or seen it, it's one of those just buy it and play it. I was expecting you know one of those survival horror mystery style games and at certain points there were aspects that kept me gripped and stuck into the story and the diaglog thinking it was one of these games. This game is far more engaging then that. Although the game plays a relatively liniear path and direction of progression it still feels as if you have full direction on where and what path you want to take and no matter what path you take the ambience of the sound, the setting and also as it progressively changes is just incredible it's one of the first games I have been truly emmersed.

The story itself took me through twists and turns on a more emotional and physiological way also that I never knew I could even get from a video game especially one I paid less then £2 for at the time of this review, it's a wonderful insight to on how others react not just on your characters back story but the other characters who stories you discover while playing and how perfectly implemented into the game they are so you don't feel like you're forced into their stories and story lone. It's a wild discovery but wanting to find out more about each aspect as the game progresses adds to the mystery that keeps churning out.

The overall game play dynamic and genre of what the actual gameplay is in my opinion is what id like to call walking simulator +, as essentially the gameplay is a walking simulator similar to the Stanley parable however you have choice, you have ability to examine and take items and objects in the game, it makes you feel like a genuine humanbeing which adds to the game play enjoyment and the sense or realism despite the cartoonistic artsy graphics.

All I can say is Firewatch is a must buy despite its short story especially with the price you pay it is worth it, I finished it from start to finish in 4.5 hours this could be done even quicker I did get Abit confused at a few points while navigating, I liked to pick up everything for some reason to inspect and I also decided to see how long it would take me to do a complete loop of the whole area (don't ask me why I just felt the need.) But the game kept me engaged and kept me wanting more and the story line, the emotional trail it's worth it's weight in gold.

However...

With every load of positives there are a few negatives, The only negatives I could really say I had with this game is the duration I wish the game was longer and expanded on a few areas on the story some of the areas I felt had no need or purpose they were there just because. 

Replayability maybe an issue to some, with Firewatch it's very story driven, after finishing it you know the story and events, if you were to do a second play through it would be too predictable and would carry the same presence, I saw they had a free roam to explore at your own pace (which I was doing pretty much anyway during the story line) and play through with the developer/development audio but I don't feel this adds more playability maybe just more of an insight.

I also found a few bugs/issuea that may not effect everyone but it's what I at least experience once or twice on my playthrough. One being interacting with certain set pieces like doors and ropes made me walk into them on a weird angle and not open them rather just continue waking automatically towards the point but not doing anything or climbing on top of rocks partially I should be on. 

I also found a graphical issue while on the fenced area (not saying anything story wise due to spoilers) but at a particular point before you gain a new compass replacement I had graphical issues with the lighting outside. This could very well be subjective and down to myself playing the game on a steam deck however the game is also steam deck verified so would not feel this would effect the graphical videlity what did cause a slight break in emersion for me.

Overall I do strongly feel Firewatch to be an absolutely amazing story drive game that is a must have for anyone that wants to feel emmersed into the game and story and the character development and progression as you play and the personal and emotional attachments you can get from them. For the price there are now many games that can top this and I'm glad I have had the opportunity to play such a beautifully made game.

Compact with beautiful scenery and splendid voice-acting, this game is a wonderful treat to those that seek a temporary change of pace.

Gameplay-wise, nothing complicated. You don't need any set of skills to enjoy the exploration, so long as you don't turn off your brain mid-game.

Story-wise, the game offers an immersive experience as a fire-watcher. The pacing was nice, and so were the mysteries that accompanied the journey. So far no questions left unanswered. If you wish to partake in a temporary escape from your reality, this might be the perfect game for you. It provides you with a sufficient environment for you to feel calm, relaxed, happy, lost, panic, melancholy, and a tiny bit of anger. Note that the game also reminds you that no matter how big of problem or how difficult of a situation you are currently in, it's never a back idea to take a step back and escape for a little while, as long as the problem is not forgotten about. So basically a nice medium for escapism, but not enough to have you get lost into it.

Graphics? Gorgeous. As someone who studies art, I can imply say the game is delightfully beautiful. The colors are warm and cozy most of the time, much like sitting in a sunset as you set up a campfire by the lake. It changes depending on the situation you're in, but it fits in nevertheless.

As for the music, the devs certainly know what kind of music should be played, and when said music should be incorporated. It doesn't overwhelm you, it doesn't ruin the mood. It's just there, perfectly as it should be.

Voice-acting: arguably the best part of this game. They certainly knew what they were doing with Delilah's voice actor.

Overall, to those who are not constantly looking for teeth-grinding, jaw-clenching competitive games, this one is for you. Think of it as you literally going on a journey doing something entirely different than what you normally do.   Solid 9.5/10. Minus .5 points for a slight rendering bug that made me glitch under the map and falling into the abyss lol. The day could be restarted, so no worries.

Firewatch is an incredible experience. It's not a video game in the traditional sense, with a greater emphasis on the narrative than on gameplay. Take the branching dialogue concept from the Telltale games and marry it with a walking simulator to get Firewatch. Much of the run time is spent hiking the map while conversing with your coworker over the radio about life and about the day-to-day of keeping a look out for fires in the Wyoming mountains. The conversations are especially endearing because of how isolated the game world is, and I found myself really becoming invested in choosing the right questions and answers to keep up a positive relationship. I think the meaning of this is amplified by memories of pandemic-era lockdown, where sometimes a voice was all we had to keep in touch with people. There's a mystery at play too that I found rather gripping, and I didn't want to put the game down. The beautiful environments just add to the immersion -- accessible from the Special Features menu is an option to just hike the map without the story. I have 3.6 hours on record and intend to play through again for the different dialogue options and the developer commentary. This is far-and-away one of the more intimate video games I've played and the best $1.99 I've ever spent. I wish I could have bought the game at full price.

I had been playing a lot of Doom and Max Payne right before this so I thought this game would be a nice change of pace. I had it on my list for a long time but never got around to it. After finally playing, I can say this is a very interesting game. The story is a little strange and I will say, without spoiling anything, it didn’t really play out how I expected and when it wrapped up, it felt like it fell a little flat initially.

Though I do appreciate the story and I found it thought provoking, my one nitpick is that it didn’t really leave me with the gut punch that it set me up for. When the game started, I kind of expected to be in tears by the end but I just wasn’t…lol I know that’s a weird gripe and that honestly is one of my only complaints...The highlight of this game for me was the graphics and the environmental exploration. This game made me want to immediately quit my job and go work in a national park. The world you’re in feels so real and the sense of scale is just awesome. The actual area you’re able to roam free in isn’t actually that huge but going from place to place in this game feels so immersive..you get to know the different environments well and you feel as if you’re actually traversing through the wilderness. There’s something very relaxing and cathartic about doing these relatively simple tasks out in the quiet forest. The graphics are cartoony but amazing. And the voice acting is way better than most games I’ve played. 

I would love it if they could expand on this universe a little more and make a game where you could role play as a firewatcher a little more, set up your camp and add some survival elements…this game left me wanting more things to do, more story to uncover, and just more time in the world…sounds like a complaint but it’s really not..i just really enjoyed the universe this game created. The 4 hours with it was sufficient enough to tell the story but I didn’t want it to be over. 

If you’re looking for a slower paced, immersive, relaxing game with a cool little mystery element to it, this game is definitely a must play.

First off, let's address the elephant in the room: the game's ending. I won't spoil it for you, but will discuss it in the abstract.

The ending was quite disappointing to me, artistic license and the realities of life are the usual points brought up in its defense. Regardless, I felt cheated. This is not quite on the level of Mass Effect 3's rip-off ending, there is some level of consolation.

With that said, the choices you make in this game truly do not matter in the end, there is some different dialogue and so on but the actual, concrete outcome simply does not change.

I am convinced that the developer will claim this to be a feature rather than a mistake. As the person who played the game, I felt disappointed.

Now, on to the good part.

The game is good overall. The dialogue is superbly written and manages to make event he mundane feel engaging. Solving the mysteries of the wilderness feels rewarding and exciting. guessing the true answers is quite tough. Scenery is beautiful and not just for an Indie game, I found myself standing over a vista and just enjoying the views quite a few times. Characters are likeable and interesting, offering depth beyond a simple trope. Gameplay is fairly straightforward, and would likely be quite dull without the excellent dialogue to keep you engaged.

In conclusion - Firewatch is absolutely worth your Dollars, but do not expect a happy ending.

[h1]Left me scratching my head.[/h1]

I remembered that this game made quite a decent amount of fuzz a few years back and i've been slightly curious about it ever since, so when I saw it for an enormous 90% off, i spontaniously bought and played it.

In Firewatch you play as a guy named Henry. After a decade of marriage you discover that your wife is suffering from severe dementia and after she left for Australia to live with her parents, you take a new job as a firewatcher in Shoshone National Park and spend the summer exploring the park and doing...nothing much really.

And that's all the so-called gameplay is. It's the most barebones-basic walking simulator you can imagine. Each chapter of the game follows the exact same loop: You start in your watchtower, then get a certain task from your supervisor via radio and then just hike to the designated spot somewhere in the park. Navigating there via compass and map is basically the only remotely active part of the gameplay. Firewatch relies completely on its story and atmosphere. Admittedly, the dialogue is very well written, the voice-acting is professional and since the game is pretty vague in telling you what exactly is going on, it has a somewhat eerie and slightly suspenseful atmosphere. However, the plot goes ultimately nowhere. Some plot points that seem rather important in the beginning just fade into the background or remain completely unresolved and there is no big reveal or plot twist. In the end, what started out as a mystery turns out to be no mystery at all and the game just ends after roughly five hours. The visuals and artstyle are somewhat fitting, but everything has this weird yellowish-orange colour tone and overall the grafics just feel a bit flat, boring and lifeless.

As mentioned, I bought this on sale for only 2 Euros (instead of the 20 at full price) and still I thought that those 2 Euros were sort of a waste. It's always good when games take on some more mature themes and try something different, but Firewatch doesn't really do anything of that. Quite the contrary, it does barely anything and I've even played some mainstream games that are much more artistic, deep and rewarding than this, all while being a heck of a lot more fun and entertaining. Before buying this I checked out IGN's video review, they gave this a 9.3 out of 10 and after playing it myself I seriously have to question that reviewer's sanity. I mean, those people criticize Call of Duty's tube-levels but then praise this game where all you do is walking through the same areas over and over again at a snail's pace while talking to a woman on a walkie-talkie. To be honest, the extremely slow pace of it all was indeed kind of soothing and relaxing, but then again there are so many other much more engaging things you can do to just take a rest and chill.

I do understand that this is an indie-game made for a rather small and specific target audience, but to charge even those few willing people 20 Euros for an eight years old but only five hours long game with non-existent gameplay, average grafics, zero replay value and a shallow unrewarding story is more than a brazen audacity, it's borderline theft. Stay away.

All the different notes you were able to collect and read.

How your dialog choices different really effect the game what so ever.
How the randomly scattered supply cache only provide notes and map knowledge, no impactful items excluding the unmissable story caches.
How I am unable to drink the whiskey I confiscated!

A heavy, heartfelt, and tense walking sim that is at its best when it makes you question what is really happening to you in these woods. The start of the game immediately lays out the “situation” your character is in, and his motivation for taking a firewatch posting in the middle of the woods for a summer. You are then immediately thrown into the game where you quickly meet your coworker who you communicate only via walkie-talkie. The setup is isolating, yet fitting, and the game sets you on your tasks. Firewatch has tremendous voice acting and gives you the opportunity to make dialogue choices which really helps with getting in the headspace of the main character. You learn about your coworker, sometimes with light hearted banter, sometimes flirting, and even sometimes through an argument. All of it is a delight to listen to.

I don’t want to spoil much of anything here, but during your posting some odd things will start to happen. These little events build such a great tension throughout the game, as they lead the characters to consider some bigger implications, and really gets them “inside their own head”. I loved the feeling when this game had me questioning “I am alone out here…right?”. And what better location to mess with you than in a massive, middle-of-nowhere forest. The music perfectly matches the atmosphere created here: it feels so lonely, tense, and beautiful all at the same time.

The game’s artstyle is simple yet charming. The gameplay is smooth (I did get caught on the odd rock, but was always able to wiggle out) and  the exploration of the various wings of the forest is very satisfying. Yes gameplay is basic - but you will primarily be playing this game for its characters and story. And this definitely fits the category of: the less you know about it going in, the better.

Now I have seen some division on the ending. Most of the negative reviews here seem to reference the ending in some capacity. I personally liked it, but I do appreciate why some may not find it satisfying. Maybe minor spoilers here: [spoiler] I thought of this game more as a snapshot of this guy's life -  it wasn’t a full beginning, middle, and end. So I think if you are okay with that, you will be okay with the overall narrative structure here. [/spoiler]

So I’d recommend treating yourself to this journey out to the middle of the woods, all by yourself, with only a walkie-talkie as your lifeline. What could go wrong!

There are different types of gamers, and I'm sure there are many for whom this game won't quite work. I think it is a masterpiece in storytelling. I've played hundreds, if not thousands, of games in my life and have gradually refined my taste. In the end, I've understood that narrative is the main thing that counts for me. Everything else is an addition that can enrich the experience but is still only an outer layer of its core. Many titles have naive stories that pretend to be grand or convey something important. They are dressed in beautiful graphics and music, but ultimately, they fail at being relatable in any sense.

"Firewatch" is something completely different. It doesn't pretend, it's not overly complicated in what it tries to tell us, it's honest, and it looks pretty on top of that. Very few games in my life have managed to grab me by my feelings so quickly and effectively. One of those was "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter." Even though "Firewatch" is simpler than that little, beautiful gem, I think it's not wrong to compare the two titles gameplay-wise as well.

If you love human stories and feel that narrative is more important to you than action, don't hesitate. This game will give you everything you need in just about 4 hours. And what hours they are!

There are a few interaction glitches, nothing game-breaking. These are little annoyances that should have been fixed but can be ignored in the grand scheme of things.

Tl;dr: Highly recommend for sale-price (I paid $3.99), cautious rec' for full-price. Narrative with retro wilderness navigation elements (topo-map and compass only), and high-quality graphics for low-quality hardware. 

Overall impression:
Brief,  poignant narrative game, with immersive soundtrack and atmospheric graphics. Main plot is slightly tropey, but not cliche enough to ruin the game. Graphics run well for quality on even low-capacity hardware. Recommend to purchase on-sale, rather than full-price, for greater value for the money. 

Pros:
- Great visuals, even on low-quality hardware
- Voice actors really carries the narrative, which works well since the game relies on a heavy-isolation premise
- Immersive soundtrack and ambient soundscaping drew me in, so much that I felt I was being watched, even though I was alone in my home
- Set in 1980s, so technology is limited; navigation relies on an old-school forest service topographic map and compass, retro feel-good without being too complicated for utility.

Cons:
- Tricky spotting for interactive objects, sometimes have to back away and move in again to trigger the control
- Plot relies heavily on tropes (loved one tragic illness, running away to mountains to escape, more secrets and you don't know who you can trust)
- Minor immersion-break in late-game; the increased smoke and airborne embers were visual only, there was no voice-acting to enhance the experience. Would have felt more immersive if the vocal tracks had more labored breathing and even coughing fits. 
- Abrupt end-of-days, scene-cuts, and time-skips; might be better with a fade-out instead of cold-cut between

Let me start out with the good: 
The game LOOKS great. I love the vistas. I love how it does the distant object model like smoke rising from a fire. I've always been a sucker for what you'd call those semi-skybox models. They add some nice depth and distance to a big world. The storm from Sea of Thieves comes to mind.

In the beginning, the characters seem semi believable and I was starting to get a little invested.

And that's the end of the good. I wish to hell it wasn't.

The bad: 
This game is a bland, railroady walking simulator with dumb characters, and a lackluster mystery you're not even given the opportunity to unravel before the game slams on the brakes and commits a writing atrocity only a few steps removed from "everything was a dream."

Your communicator partner is charming at first but quickly gets annoying when they drone on and on about ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that is neither interesting nor has anything to do with the situation. 

Obvious traps set for you are completely avoidable, but your dumb ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of a character falls for every single one despite their obviousness and the infinite time you're given to think of a way to disarm the situation.

The story starts out with the cliche "you were happy, once" narrative that's literally given to you in text, paired up nicely with pointless "choices" to trick you into thinking you're actually playing a game instead of reading text on a background. It's a lazy ass attempt to tug at heart strings.

Also I'm convinced the development of this game was troubled. There's a specific beeping tool introduced that makes you wonder why the game even introduced it. I believe, at one point, this game was meant to be built in such a way someone was going to come after you and this tool would help you avoid them. But that was cut out and this beeping tool has since been turned into a glorified Skyrim quest marker.

----Spoilers beyond this point----
[spoiler]The narrative of the game proceeds to suggest there's either a killer out in the wilderness with you and has the tech and know-how to ♥♥♥♥ with you and your partner's communicators and listen in, taking tabs on your response time and the routes you normally take. Two campers you encounter go missing shortly before this discovery, leading you to believe this person is more than capable of killing others.

This builds into an even bigger mystery when you're lead to a "research station" and you find a ton of communication equipment that could feasibly listen in on what you two are chattering about, leading to the possibility that both of you are being used as unwilling subjects in some sort of experiment.

Eventually you find out you're being framed by someone when recordings of your conversations with key points cut out make their way to your lookout tower, making it seem like you've both either done something to the campers or started some fire at the research site.

Yeah, this game was never made for anyone who actually likes to engage. It's made for people to turn their brain off and accept ♥♥♥♥♥♥ narratives and mysteries with slightly pretty, and randomly timed, music that starts playing as you're walking about.)

And as it seems like the killer is finally making their move, trapping you in a cave, presumably to either take you or your partner out, you find out it's all because some kid slipped on some rocks a decade ago, died while caving, and his dad has felt guilty ever since. The game's main character is just like me- depressed and sad, wandering through a forest. Unlike the character, I don't live near a forest; instead, I take walks elsewhere :(

I recently bought this game at a whopping 90% discount and it was worth every penny. I stumbled upon some Reddit posts about this hidden gem when it went on sale. Before that I was unaware of this fantastic game and I absolutely love it.

The game is relatively short, lasting about 3 or 4 hours, but that's it. You wander inside the forest as a worker, do your job, and return to your place. Follow your boss's instructions, but the lady boss is cool and friendly—you'll love her. What makes this game special is the absence of gun violence or anything intense. It's just a calm and relaxing experience. The music and forest environment make you feel like you're in the middle of a forest, hearing birds chirping in real life. It's like an ASMR experience.

The lighting, music, graphics, and character voices are all perfect. I really enjoyed them. While it would be great if the game had more Steam achievements but it's okay. The voices of all the characters are top-notch, and I loved them. 

Overall, you must try this game. It's unique and different from all other games. If you want a calm and relaxing experience with realistic forest sounds, you will love this game. I wish I could play it again with the same first-time experience or at least find more similar games. Kudos to the devs who made this game.

Solid title; had fun even though there was no game in this medium known as a video game.

About that; in terms of actual gameplay, there's literally nothing. Unironically a walking simulator, but that's how Firewatch sold itself, and because of that, I think it's all fine. If you're gonna get this, walk in expecting an interactive movie, not a video game. If you set your expectations correctly, Firewatch will be better for you.


I had a great experience, fell deep into the role, and felt as if I was at the park myself. Henry's story hit pretty close to home in the sense of helplessness, pointlessness, and brooding sadness. It made relating to Henry easy as pie. A lot of my choices not only reflected what I thought was best for Henry, but what I would do if I were in Henry's position.

Story was very natural, lacking the artificial force felt in bad writing. Lots of situations where I regretted my choices, and also lots of situations I had no great answer for, but that made the experience all the more immersive. My Henry had a very sweet ending, and if I were to write him into a locked story, not only would I have picked the exact same things I actually did in game if he were a self-insert, but I would have picked the exact same things if I were a writer for the story itself. My end to Firewatch felt like an end to a great movie, and that's oddly rare in games with branching choices.


However, there are still some massive L's.

Biggest issue was softlocks. During my one-session 4 hour playthrough, I got softlocked thrice and had to exit the game every time. What caused these softlocks was very simple too. In order to be trapped in a softlock, all I had to do was interact with the environment, such as pushing through some leaves or climbing a rope. Once I attempted these interactions, the game would randomly decide to lock me into an endless walking animation, of which I had no viable answer to except Alt + F4. Really annoying, made me want to burn down an entire forest.
 
Luckily, the game makes resetting breezy thanks to the ever-so-quickly-loading save files, but any softlock at all is still a massive issue. The fact there were softlocks at all is unacceptable, especially for a narrative-focused game such as Firewatch. They seem easy to fix, so I'm truly dumbfounded by how these bugs remain in the game today.

===

So, my final review? || [B]7.5/10[/B] ||.

The game, apart from the atmosphere, fails to deliver in most of the parts it chooses to deliver. It hypes the player up, creates a bunch of different feelings all the time and gives clues for mysteries and tragedies just to deflate them every damn time!

I also experienced some bugs, some game breaking and some just immersion breaking: at several different points I was unable to interact with a stash box or other element, and my character would run back and to the right. Got this on sale for $2 and it's not worth a penny more. Found it lacking on story line and dialog quality with some frustrating gameplay mechanics.

Pros:
- Graphics have a Long Dark-esque, comfortable, low-poly quality. Nothing flashy but it does a nice job.

- Navigation was a nice touch and made exploring the world fun at first.

Story Cons (no spoilers):
- The story is pretty short overall, which isn't bad itself, but it covers a lot of time and some of the transitions in time periods and dialog are jarring and very forced.

- Throughout the story, you are presented with various dialogue choices. Many of them seem out of character, just plain irrational or borderline comedic, or the intensity of the actual dialog spoken doesn't really match the option you pick (i.e. picking a suggestion for why an event occurred and the actual response is an unhinged conspiracy theory).

- A lot of red herrings and completely unimportant lore and dialog throughout that just feels like a waste of time by the end.

- The story came to an unsatisfactory ending, IMO. There was an excellent build up in the first act, great suspense added by certain events, and....then it just ended. After 2 hours of build up you get the whole plot unraveled and played out for you in less than 5 minutes.

Gameplay Cons:
- What seemed like semi-open navigation at the start of the story (requiring a compass to move in the right direction) very quickly turned into linear paths with no actual ability to explore or chance of getting lost. 

- Eventually, you realize that you're basically just doing one long fetch quest running back and forth along the same paths to slightly more distant locations each time.

- Collision with most objects is frustrating. Things you would expect to miss by a wide margin just stop you dead.

- Sprinting un-toggles itself after an unknown amount of time when it determines you're no longer sprinting. Sometimes this happens after object collision, sometimes it doesn't but you think it does so you toggle sprint but you actually toggled it off, so you have to toggle on, then you run into the same invisible object collision box, then you reflexively toggle sprint again but you turned off, so you toggle sprint again, etc. etc. etc.

- The forced head bobbing and automatic camera direction resets when mantling and climbing are at times physically disorienting and I normally have zero issues with motion in any other game.
GG.

I think the biggest letdown is that the potential is there for this to be a great game, but I feel like they ran out of budget as soon as they started making it.  The story is pretty good, the environment is great, the ideas are there, but I agree with the comments that suggest this is a walking simulator.  There isn't really a whole lot that makes this a "game".  No logic puzzles, no survival skills, no real diverging story paths, just an interactive movie. Although I get that games like Raft, Subnautica and Portal 2 were made by bigger studios, this game seemed like it should have the same type of game-play, but it more or less felt like Portal 2 without the Portal gun. Without being too "spolierish", even the ending felt a bit rushed.  Everything sort of gets explained all at once, and then that's it.  Lots of questions remain, and you even have things you've collected and a camera that you've used all game long that just turn out to be for nothing.  If I had paid full price for this, I'd be really upset, but for the little amount I did play, I guess it was a decent story.

At first, I thought this was a game where your duty is to just stay in your tower or roam around the forest to prevent any fire disaster that will burn down the forest. I was dead wrong.

This is why I love games with story line rather than multiplayer games. The atmosphere is addicting. You get the feel. You get the emotion. You get attached to the characters. You're enthralled in the story. You feel like you're in the movie where you are the protagonist. But this is the character's story and we are just the silent observers. But most stories has a protagonist and an antagonist character at the very least. Firewatch? It doesn't have one. All you're facing with is just a human problem. A person who wanting to get out of his problem just to relax for a moment but ended up facing a new one. Makes him realize that no matter how hard he's trying to escape, his problem will always be in front of him until he work it out. And the characters? Don't get me started, the conversation is what you expect from any other people doing their daily activities in any other day. You get a rocky start at first, but then you realize how important you are to each other and that makes your bond grew stronger and stronger you wished it wouldn't last. You worked together to solve a mystery that somehow happened shortly after your arrival.

Firewatch is amazing; especially the ending. You don't get the happy-go-lucky ending kind of way. One word, bittersweet. I feel that most people that have played this game don't get what they expected; even myself. But we know that the characters here will go continue on with their lives, and it was sealed in the last conversation in Thorofare Lookout.

It is easily one of the most memorable experience I had in games. And I don't regret every single second of it. Thank you, Firewatch.

[h1]A Poignant Journey in the Wilds [/h1]

"Firewatch," developed by Campo Santo, is a first-person mystery that immerses players in the beauty and solitude of the Wyoming wilderness. Set in 1989, you play as Henry, a man seeking refuge from his turbulent life by taking a job as a fire lookout. This narrative-driven game is as much about self-discovery and coping with life's challenges as it is about the mysteries of the wilderness.

The game's strength lies in its storytelling and atmospheric setting. The dialogues between Henry and his supervisor Delilah, who communicates via radio, form the core of the game. Their conversations are adult, genuine, and often poignant, exploring themes of escape, responsibility, and regret. This aspect of the game may not be suitable for younger players, given its mature content.

Firewatch is a visually stunning game, capturing the essence of a wild summer with gorgeous vistas and an environment that begs to be explored. The attention to detail in the level design compensates for the world's relatively small size. However, the game's duration is short, offering only about 4-5 hours of gameplay.

One of the game's limitations is the impact of player decisions. While there are interesting responses to certain actions, like taking a whiskey bottle, these choices don't significantly alter the game's narrative. This lack of consequential decision-making affects the game's replayability.

The game's interpretation of dealing with personal issues is profound. Spoilers ahead: It poignantly illustrates how characters like Henry and Delilah use their jobs and each other as an escape from their real-life problems. Themes like alcoholism, denial, and escapism are recurrent, symbolized through various elements like the recurring presence of alcohol and the symbolic use of fire. The game culminates in the realization that running away from problems only exacerbates them, a message delivered with a blend of subtlety and directness.

Firewatch is not action-packed; its focus is on atmosphere, dialogue, and exploration. This design choice may not appeal to everyone, but for those who appreciate a narrative-driven experience, it offers a rich and emotional journey. The stealth gameplay, a point of criticism for some, is less about physical challenges and more about the internal journey of the protagonist.

In conclusion, "Firewatch" is a beautifully crafted game that tells a mature, thoughtful story. It’s a contemplative experience that invites players to ponder their own life choices while getting lost in the virtual wilderness. While it may have its flaws in terms of gameplay length and impact of player choices, its narrative depth, stunning visuals, and emotional resonance make it a game worth experiencing. "Firewatch" stands out as a poignant exploration of human nature and the complexities of escaping reality.

I finished this game in one sitting, it's brevity practically warranting it - the entire thing took 5 hours and I'm sure it's possible to do it faster. Overall, it was a fantastic adventure and a deeply emotional experience. It's been a while since I cared about the characters in a game so much. Suffice to say they are very, very well written and the voice acting is superb.

Both are deeply flawed in ways in which we can relate to, and both seek a sort of escape from the outside world that I reckon we wouldn't be playing this game if we didn't seek as well. And while they do get it, and we alongside them, at the end they have to come back to their lives and face whatever comes next. That's the crux of the matter, I think - it's a story about life, and not about watching for fires and solving mysteries. 

 For me the ending was fantastic, I couldn't have wished for a better one really. Yes, I definitely expected something different, but so did Henry! We both wanted, on some level (though myself probably more than him) to uncover a kind of government conspiracy, maybe even involving the supernatural. Alas, life is rarely written in noir and far more often the problems we face and the tragedies we witness are of simpler, though by no means less bleak, nature. The solution to the mystery was, in my view, sadder and more devastating than any conspiracy would have been. 

There is also the issue of Henry and Delilah. I wasn't surprised that she left like that, keeping in mind what she had said about her finding long-term committment scary and unwelcome, aware of what she was going through because of this entire situation in the park, all the guilt she had to be feeling. No, I'm not surprised, and I don't reckon Henry would have been either, though, of course, he would have feel empty and crushed nonetheless. Emotionally depleted, definitely, though, after some time, he would, I venture to guess, come to appreciate the experience, particularly his acquaintance with Delilah, as valuable and, likely, also life-altering, despite it ending with such abruptness. 

To the extent it's possible for a person sitting in front of a pc, partaking in this adventure through a screen, I share his sentiment thoroughly.

comment on story (spoilers);
[spoiler] This game in essence has 3 storylines. 
- The first one is Henry and Delilah recovering from their real world drama by escaping in this forest, away from civilisation, needing time to reflect upon their own scenario with infinite time to kill.
- The second is the one where there is people who are spying on Henry and Delilah and doing a psychological analysis on how this much alone time could change or affect individuals.
- The third and last is where we find a corpse in the cave, who is the son of a past lookout that died in a climbing accident. The father is still alive and hiding in the forest, who is listening to both of you, in a sad ironic fashion way where he is also in this forest to run from his problems.

Personally the ending made sense after thinking about it, Henry ran away from his life because of the trauma, but to truly heal it he has to go back and deal with it.
[/spoiler]

Knowing these storylines and seeing how many people complained about the ending falling flat, I would argue that that was the point. Sure escaping from your problems can be a temporary solution, but you eventually have to return to life and face those problems.

In all honesty, I mistakenly thought this was another lookout game when I bought it (Fears to Fathom Ironbark Lookout) so when playing I kept waiting for the more spooky and jump scare aspect to start at some point. That said, while this game wasn't the game I was expecting and while it's relatively short, there were several aspects I did like from it and overall it's a good game.

Pros:
* Good story line
* Several dialog options which do influence certain things within the game
* Fairly intuitive UI navigation
* Lots of places to explore for finding hidden gems
* I really liked holding up a paper map and compass for navigation, one not in a paused menu, to add to the immersion

Cons:
* Very linear in progression; many areas can only be accessed after certain chapters of the game have been completed
* Besides a buck you see in the very beginning of the game while hiking to the area, there aren't any animals so it feels like a very empty wilderness
* If you want to explore during the campaign, you essentially have to do so while your boss on the other end of the radio is waiting on you to go somewhere to do something
* I didn't like the cinematic, locked in action of climbing over obstacles, jumping gaps, climbing rocks, or dropping down from them. It seemed to artificially slow things down and gave a disconnect from the gameplay


Some advice for players, since the areas unlock progressively as the story progresses, unless you don't mind navigating to the same areas multiple times or waiting later in the storyline until you've at least acquired the ax, save the exploring for the Special Options in the Main Menu to do a strictly exploring game mode. There you'll have all the equipment (good rope, ax, flashlight, and pitons) laying out for you to pick up before heading out to explore.

Also, technically, there are 2 endings but one isn't so obvious...
[spoiler] At the end you can either get on the evac helicopter or when walking towards it turn around and walk away and it will eventually leave without you. [/spoiler]

All in all, I would recommend this game as it was fun, even if it wasn't the game I was expecting to get.

I rarely downvote games, especially if they are a labour of love. 

However, I really dont think this game is worth playing and I dont quite understand all the appraisal it gets. Maybe Im just too late, and this is just not so impressing by todays standards.

First of all: There is not much game in it, its a walking simulator. I knew this before, and this is fine, but you should still be aware of that fact. 
The real problem is most of the gameplay elements in it, doesnt really contribute to a good gameplay experience at all. They are just there because of ... Yeah, I really dont know to be honest. For the sake of having something to do I guess.

Like how is it important that I can pick up items, that have absolutely no use in the game world, and dont really contribute to the story development? Most of the stuff in the caches have no use at all. So how should the player be animated to go explore them? Right, they aren't.

Why do I have to jump over 5 blocking objects in a row, when there is no challenge (or puzzle) and you literally just press a button to do so? How does this contribute to better gameplay or story development? They are just there, because they stretch the gameplay time.

While there are multiple areas which are more or less explorable without any boundaries, the game world is still designed in a very linear fashion and its not that big. You rarely - need - the map or the compass that the game wants you to use. So why using it at all?

There is a single-use camera in the game, which doesnt really have a sense. It is not really a photo mode. A photo mode would be a real benefit in this game, because the game is gorgeous. Instead its just some kind of "toy" with no real usage in the end, despite having an achievement tied to it.

There is some seriously good character development, solely based on dialogues on a Walkie-Talkie. 
I liked that a lot. 
However, the dialogue choices dont affect the game in a noteworthy way, and this kinda makes them bad in the context of a "game". I just dont feel, that this is enough to describe this game as a "masterpiece", which a lot of people do.

While highly appraised, the story doesnt really live up to its expectations. 
The story has indeed a nice pacing, and you get very interested in how it turns out.
But what was good about the pacing in the character development between Henry and Delilah, was completely different for all the other side stories in the game.

The big revelation didnt strike me at all, because there was no attachment at all. (Dont want to spoiler here.) Pacing here was just very bad, as you didnt really got to know the persons part of that plot and therefore you couldnt relate to anything of it.

Seeing Delilah at the end was something I was really looking foward to while playing the game. Not showing her is as big a dissapointment for me, as it was for the games Protagonist Henry. 
A lot of people say, this is why the story is so great. Because the story leaves you with the exact same emotions the protagonist is experiencing. Its a depiction of real life, how we tend to run away from problems, and that not everything has a deep substantial meaning. However I really think this is a bad excuse for not having something to say at all.

In the end there is no message. It started out strong, depicting the struggles of a relationship with alzheimer's. But the games story didnt manage to pick up on that topic at all, actually showing how people might process those problems in the end, or how to overcome those struggles. There are a lot of set-ups in the stories development, and none of them got a concise ending - or any at all. I do like the fan theories. But its just not fair to justify the stories "greatness" based on some theories, that most of the people will never experience or even think about while playing the game.


It feels like that there is a good story between the lines - but it just wasnt told.

This game was such an emotional and interesting piece of storytelling. I absolutely loved this game, I would relate this game similar to SOMA's storytelling and this goes up there with my top story games. It was a lovely rollercoaster of emotions where you fall in love with the characters, relate to them in a deep way and cry together.

Spoilers:
This game consists of my own worst fears: Early onset alzheimer's, loving other people, moving on & life's big changes.

At the start of the game it tells a really emotional story of our main character and his wife falling ill to early onset alzheimer's and being disabled by that disease, it really hits hard and you can relate and empathize with the characters in sad way. 

The work starts and at start your supervisor may seem a bit nosey or weird, but days go by and you start seeing a new way of live from having to care for your love, which won't recognise or remember you, to loving a new woman who is sweet, lovely and humorous all at the same time. I believe it expresses insanely well about people changing in ways no one can ever predict, life happens and you have to make big choices, many choices are even something that you can't even full-heartedly do and you get pushed to making it (simplifying: Choosing and possibly loving and starting a relationship with Delilah rather than your own love, which isn't really there anymore). Of course our empathy tells us we have to care for our wife with alzheimer's and continue the same as it was before, but this experience brings well the reality of what that would be like. It wouldn't be easy at all.

In the end of the game it leaves the experience and story-telling back to where it started from, but with a lot of big emotions as a burden. You won't get together with Delilah immediately as there are big emotions from all the other life that happened in both your work. But also your own wife is still back home with alzheimer's and her family is taking care of them. 
I think this game symbolizes well of situations where you are stuck doing things you'd love to be different and you'd do anything for your situation to be slightly different but still with your wife. But at the same time it shines a light to what life can offer, even if we choose one person in our life to love for the rest of our lives, it still shows how just something can take that away from you. But as experienced in this, there is still life worth living for, it might not be never easy, not before or after making your decision, but at least there is always something to live for.

Whether you put your wife in a carehome for alzheimer's patients, let her stay with her own family. Continue living with her and caring for her, you will still need to do a big choice which will impact your life in a huge way. At the same time it's not just about your wife, it's also about what you are putting aside for caring for a loved one that could function better earlier in their life. With a disability they might not be able to love fully, remember their loved ones or recognise them. It might be a heartbreak everyday for the loved  one caring for the one with Dementia.

[b]Sights & Sounds[/b]
- I really enjoyed the (mostly) serene forest setting. Despite not having AAA visuals, the Firewatch is still very nice to look at
- The music is sparse but well-used when it shows up
- The voice acting from both of the main characters is excellent. Both leads put on great performances that really brought their characters to life

[b]Story & Vibes[/b]
- You play as Henry, a guy living in the 1980's whose life just took a major downturn. Given your dire emotional circumstances, you take a job in the Wyoming wilderness watching for fires
- All the while, you're frequently contacted on the radio by your boss, Delilah, who chats with you, helps move the story along, and gives you tasks to complete
- While working, you stumble upon increasing signs that point to you not being as alone in the woods as you initially expected. In fact, it seems like you're being watched...
- Despite the simmering mystery that boils over in the game's last act, there's a surprising amount of heartfelt storytelling and humor throughout the game

[b]Playability & Replayability[/b]
- Firewatch predominantly presents itself as a 1st person exploration and mystery focused adventure game. Some may even dub it a walking simulator
- Gameplay largely consists of trying to find your way through the forests, streams, and cliffs that make up the section of the woods Henry keeps watch over. Beyond simple hiking and rock climbing, you'll sometimes be required to solve minor puzzles
- Not a ton of reasons to replay the game if you got all the achievements. Once you've encountered the game's big twist, there's not much need to revisit the narrative (other than the fact that it's really good)

[b]Overall Impressions & Performance[/b]

Firewatch is the evolution of the walking simulators, the game that revolutionizes not only the gameplay of walking simulators but also the story as well. 

Without spoilers, you assume the role of Henry, a guy who works as a fire lookout in a national park. The only person you can communicate is Delilah, another fire lookout that gives you tasks and directions. Day by day you will investigate the events in the park and uncover the story of the game. 

The game shines in many ways. Visually it is beautiful, with clear art direction, although it is heavily stylized and not photorealistic. If you have an older pc/laptop/deck, it will play perfectly. The music and sound are amazing and convey the tension or the serenity of the scenes. The voice overs are top-tier with Delilah stealing the show. I mean she is a voice in the radio and Cissy Jones fleshes her out perfectly. The gameplay is essentially a walking simulator but it feels like a proper first-person game

Why it is revolutionary: Because it manages to tell a story somewhere between the lines. I mean at a first glance it is Henry's tale, but then there Delilah's dialogue, the notes, the stories within the park. The game utilizes almost every single narrative technique to tell its story. Because it combines open-world elements that make the walking simulation more bearable. It is more about exlploration of the park, than walk though a story. Because it is actually scary at a times, as the plot unravels. Because it manages to tell a story through radio, and by adding small gimmicks (like the camera or the flashlight), it makes it feel different and unique. Because although it is an open world game, you will never feel lost and the game does a great job to provide you with information without relying on UI elements. 

My only complain (and I can't believe that I agree with IGN on this) is that the ending is a bit disappointing, not because it is bad, but because the game set such a mystery along the way, that eventually the set up doesn't pay off. 

Still Firewatch is a great game and is definitely worth buying.

This was one of the greatest diasppointments I have had with games in the recent years. It has been a while since this game was released and I have heard only great things about it and its story, sadly the reality was not as bright.

Let us start with what Firewatch does well. The music and stylized graphics were a great choice and I am pretty sure this will be age very gracefully even in the future. The nature as depicted in this game made me sometimes stop my walking and appreciate the scenery, balm to the soul, absolutely beautifully crafted. However that is the issue, if I wanted to play and admire nature at the same time, I would have chosen some crafting simulation game, where I can explore to my heart's content instead of this visual novel only with different name. Games like this are usually played for their story and this where Firewatch is unfortunately very lacking.

First of all you choices do not matter at all. This makes this game even worse than a visual novel, where you can at least have some influence on how the story is going to end, even though the endings are predetermined. Not so much here. Everything part of the story here is predetermined, sure sometimes you may wander off the beaten path for several moments, but why would you, if there is nothing in it for you.
Second of all I had to suspend my disbelief so hard when I started playing through the story. There are just so many logical/internal inconsistencies I genuinely thought the plot twist is that everything is in your head and Delilah (voice in the radio) is your counsellor or the wife mentioned in prologue, when you overhear the suspicious call Delilah had when she left your line accidentally it only cemented my suspicion. When you find the girls' camp od day 2 is where I just had to know, because that whole thing was completely ridiculous when you find your bedsheets in their camp. How would they have time to thrash your place when you took the shortest path back and they had to dry themselves, dress themselves and be there before you and manage to thrash the place and leave? At that point it was obvious there had to be third party who just wanted you to think that it was the girls. Yet the MC does not mention that. Not to mention the cut pole that was cut approximately 20 meteres from the pole, what a feat of inhuman agility. So I looked up if that was the plot twist, because if it was not, the whole game is a ridiculous mess. And it was not and you cannot make me suspend my disbelief this much, sorry.

One more thing why would you make shift for radio and R for running as a default set of controls? Normally the control scheme is that shift is for running and R could be radio, I would see nothing unusual about that. Why did you try to reinvent the wheel?

I tried to think of circumstance under which someone could enjoy this mess of a visual novel, but I guess I am just not that creative. I genuinely do not know why this game was so critically acclaimed.

[h1] My Honest Reaction to [b] Firewatch.  (9/10) [/b] [/h1]
I didn't know how a game as beautiful and naturally 'human' as it is, could instil in me so much terror.

[i] Minor spoilers as this is something to play firsthand with no context. [/i]

At first, I was expecting a chill game and space out to a significantly gorgeous nature simulator, having to set out and accomplish minor tasks as a forest lookout volunteer. 
Then finding out I'm not so alone in these woods, did something to my gut that made me feel a ounce of fear than any other intentional horror game I've played (I usually never get vocally scared, but this game did slightly widened my eyes and increase my heart-rate by a smidge). 
I also want to give props to the realistic back and forth between Henry and Delilah's dialogue, whose realistic banter has only captivated my attention and intrigue for how this story will progress and what becomes of these lonely forest lookouts.

I totally resonate how fragile and vulnerable Firewatch portrays the experience of life through the glimpses and utters of Henry's life leading up to his job as a lookout. The specks of his downsides has sculpted what can only be described as a sympathetic human figure and I appreciate the game introduces our main character and plot's catalyst in the form of a stripped-down visual novel format establishes Henry's character to immediately feel sorry for and relate to (since we are playing him).
I also appreciate that the game [spoiler] doesn't lead to a happy ending, but instead leaves the player with a salty & bitter taste in their mouth; that they didn't uncover the conspiracy or save the forest from a ravaging wildfire, [/spoiler] whose entire summer job was not an escape, but a place to reflect how life's complications need to be fixed rather than reminisce on how to prevent it, which is what Henry probably needed to take from this journey.
The game's minimal provision of controls (running, interacting, compass etc.) only heightened the level of vulnerability that the player must've felt, reinforcing the fact that you are not an invincible, combat-proficient sleeper agent... but just [i] some guy [/i], which made the adventure so much more enticing.

[h3] TL;DR [/h3]
[b] Firewatch [/b] is a magnificently alluring outdoors simulator masquerading as an intriguing and life-resonating mystery thriller experience. [b] 9/10 [/b]

I mean, who knew pine-scented body wash could pair so well with a folk-inspired score? But now, the story. It's like a rollercoaster that promises twists and turns but leaves you craving a little more loop-de-loop action. It's good, don't get me wrong, but it's like ordering a pizza and realizing they forgot the cheese – still delicious, but something's missing. So, in summary, Firewatch is the game you never knew you needed, with a view that could make a mountain jealous, tunes that stick with you like a catchy jingle, and a story that's good but could use a sprinkle of storytelling magic. Seven out of ten – would hike and hum again. (8.5/10)
