Firewatch" is a marvel of storytelling and atmosphere. Set against the backdrop of the Wyoming wilderness, the game's lush and meticulously crafted environment serves as a character in its own right. The beauty of the Shoshone National Forest is both awe-inspiring and tranquil, creating a breathtaking canvas for the narrative to unfold.

The heart of the game lies in the compelling relationship between the protagonist, Henry, and his supervisor, Delilah, with whom he communicates through a walkie-talkie. The dialogue is expertly written and superbly voice-acted, drawing players into an emotionally charged and authentic connection.

The mystery at the core of "Firewatch" is a masterclass in suspense and intrigue, keeping players engaged throughout. The game's visual design, from the shimmering lakes to the sun-dappled trails, is nothing short of a work of art. The soundtrack, composed by Chris Remo, enhances the experience, perfectly capturing the mood and tone of the story.

As Henry, you'll find yourself engrossed in a narrative that's both introspective and thrilling, with decisions that shape the course of the story. "Firewatch" is a poignant exploration of isolation, personal growth, and human connection, and it's an absolute must-play for those who appreciate storytelling in games. It's an emotionally resonant journey that will stay with you long after the game ends.

If this is what you're into I have no doubt it's a great game but not for me. 

There's no gameplay as such, you walk around a fairly attractive open world (although outside of the plot there is nothing to interact with) and the whole thing is very much 'on rails' - there's no reason to go anywhere except where the plot takes you. Over time you pick up items that help the plot move along or open new areas of the map, and the only real input you have is the dialogue to change the nature of the relationship between the characters. I'd hesitate to describe it as a game, more like an interactive movie. The story mode takes about 3 hours and honestly I felt I overpaid for the game as I don't see any replay value. It's a little glitchy but not to the point of being a problem. 

That said - the story is good (I found the ending a little unsatisfying but that seems to divide people, I won't go into more depth for spoilers) and genuinely does elicit a sense of sadness, excitement and creepiness. From the descriptions I expected rather more. 

In summary, if you know and enjoy this kind of thing I imagine you'll love it. If you're expecting something more involved you'll be disappointed. It's a pleasant enough way to spend an evening.

Firewatch is an absolute gem of a game that manages to captivate players with its unique blend of storytelling, stunning visuals, and emotional depth. This first-person adventure game, takes you on a journey that transcends the boundaries of traditional gaming experiences.

The game's visual presentation is simply breathtaking. The lush, vibrant art style, reminiscent of a watercolor painting, makes the wilderness of Shoshone National Forest come to life. The attention to detail in the environment is astonishing, from the swaying trees to the changing lighting conditions that mimic the passage of time. Exploring this virtual wilderness is an experience in itself, and it's easy to get lost in the beauty of the game world.

While Firewatch is undoubtedly an exceptional gaming experience, it's worth noting that the initial price tag may be a bit on the higher side for some players considering the ~5 hours of gameplay. If you're budget-conscious, you might want to keep an eye out for discounts or special offers on the game. Firewatch has been available on various gaming platforms for several years, so it's quite likely that it will go on sale during seasonal promotions, gaming events, or in bundles. Waiting for such opportunities to snag the game at a reduced price is a wise choice for those who want to experience this masterpiece without breaking the bank. Rest assured, when you do get your hands on Firewatch, the adventure and emotional journey it offers will be well worth the wait.

Spoiler section discussing the ending
I've seen some ♥♥♥♥ given to the ending but I think it was the perfect way to send these characters on their way after the events of Firewatch. Reason why: [spoiler]First, the emotional impact was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ spectacular and right in line with the idea of being Henry. I was genuinely feeling vivid confusion, anger, disappointment, sadness, and regret, just as Henry would be in this moment. Second, the entire game is building up this tension of who Delilah is, what she looks like. I really like the choice to keep that card hidden for similar reasons to why horror movie monsters are best when they are hidden. There's just no comparison to that factor of unknown, mystery, and the kind of dreamy (or nightmarish in the case of monsters) quality to what is in your head. I feel like actually meeting Delilah would've invariably been a disappointment in comparison to the idea of her in the player's head. There could be a story told and commentary on that disappointment but there isn't, and I'm okay with that. That just isn't what the story is primarily about. I also can appreciate having just the idea of something. Sometimes it's better to hold onto the idea of something and not have to compare it with an inevitably disappointing reality. I feel it also helps Delilah to feel uniquely important to me as I've developed my idea of her, and will do the same for others. Yes, the ending is disappointing and bittersweet, but in all the right ways.[/spoiler]

It's a walking simulator (story-focused, no way to fail) with a lot of dialog between your character and a radio companion. The core plotline is fixed, but your choices of action and conversation along the way will affect how it's revealed and what relationships and goals you maintain through it. There's a good bit of subtle environmental storytelling and frequent opportunities to learn more about the setting and the characters through conversations as you go about your daily business. It occasionally reminded me of Soma, actually - though the dialog isn't set in stone here and there's certainly no stealth/horror aspects.

Anyway, I see two frequent complaints:

[b]1. The ending is disappointing.[/b] This seems to come from people who prefer not to use their imagination about one or two story threads, or how a character physically looks. Nothing is left as a cliffhanger in the end and it's important to the story and personal involvement that you don't have full-body artwork of every character involved.

[b]2. The game is too short.[/b] While I think the game lasted exactly the right amount of time, I will concede that $20 may be steep for people who don't intend to replay the game, or ascribe a higher value to the love that went into the art, writing, metaphors, etc. In that case, do like I did and wait for a 75%-off sale every few months.

[h1] Story (Spoilers Ahead) [/h1]
The prologue starts with Henry, (The player character) in university meeting with Julia after a bit they become friends and eventually they get married. After a while Julia develops early onset dementia which makes her slowly forget about Henry, after sending her to a full-time care hospital (or taking care of her yourself) Her condition worsens and you see an ad in a paper for a job which you take. This is the job for a Fire Lookout in the Wyoming wilderness. You take a hike to your lookout tower and before going to bed, meet Delilah, your boss. 
After waking up Delilah tells you over radio about what your job is and the equipment around your tower. Before even finishing the last bit of the first lot of equipment she is interrupted by a few teenagers illegally using fireworks. You are sent to go down and take care of them and after almost trashing their camp they run away and you confiscate the fireworks. The way back is blocked so you take another way home, through a cave. Once you make it out a silhouette of a figure shines a flashlight on you before retreating. This is scary because you are supposed to be alone out here. Delilah tells you it's fine because people can come in and out all the time but you still think a bit about it. You make it back to your tower to find it trashed and you think that it could either have been the figure or the girls whose camp you trashed. 
The next 70 days are mostly uneventful (and the game skips over a few days) but one certain day you see a massive fire that you cannot do anything about. Fast forward a few days you go to the lake to fish like normal but something, is... wrong. A clipboard stands upon a tree stump which shows radio conversation transcripts between you and Delilah, after looking around you find a radio which is muffled but a name is made out "Wapiti Station" after picking up the radio you get knocked out. "Wapiti Station" is this a station in Wapiti meadow? The next day you go there finding that your radios have been tapped.  When going to Wapiti Station it is mostly empty other then bios featuring you and Delilah and a device which can track signals. Delilah suggests you burn down the place but you decide against it. You make it out of Wapiti Station right before it blows up, merging its fire with the big fire from a few days ago. Once you make it back to your tower you find a cassette tape which is supposed to suggest that you and Delilah burned down Wapiti Station. 
One day you go caving and are exploring a cave but then you find a body a body of the child that was here before you you find out how to tell Delilah over the radio once you get out. Eventually the fire is too much and you have to escape. Before escaping the device you found starts beeping. You follow the beeping towards a cassette tape, this is from the dad of the dead boy you found in the cave. He says he has been the one who has been spying on you. He says he wants to go deeper into the wilderness and doesn't want anyone to know where he is going. Eventually you make it to Delilah's tower. You don't get to see her, Delilah had left before you in a helicopter. You have one last chat over her radio before going into a helicopter and escaping. That is it. You do not get to see Delilah. Your wife doesn't get better. You still have your own inner demons. That is it.

[h1] Final Review [/h1]

[h1]Title: Firewatch - Embers of Mystery Ignite a Riveting Adventure![/h1]

Hey there, gamers! We're stepping into the mesmerizing world of Firewatch, a game that's more than just a walk in the woods. Strap on your backpacks and grab your radios, 'cause we're diving into a narrative-driven experience that'll leave you pondering its enigmas long after the fire's gone out.

[h1]Graphics & Atmosphere:[/h1]
Let's kick it off with the visuals. Firewatch isn't about photorealism; it's about crafting an atmosphere that's as immersive as a thick forest fog. The art style, with its painterly strokes and vibrant colors, sets the tone for a journey that's both calming and suspenseful. The wilderness around you feels alive, from the rustling leaves to the distant mountain vistas.

Narrative & Mystery:
Get ready for a narrative that's as twisted as a thorny bush. You play as Henry, a dude who signs up to be a fire lookout to escape his problems. But guess what? The wilderness has issues of its own. As you exchange witty banter with your supervisor Delilah through your radio, you'll be drawn into a tangled web of secrets that'll keep you guessing 'til the very end.

Exploration & Solitude:
Firewatch isn't your typical hack-and-slash adventure. It's a slow burn, and I mean that in the best way possible. You'll explore the Wyoming wilderness, sifting through the debris of long-gone campers, taking in the views, and even climbing your way to places that'd make a mountain goat proud. The solitude isn't lonely; it's contemplative.

Voice Acting & Characters:
Speaking of solitude, let's talk about the voice acting. Henry and Delilah's voices feel like warm campfire stories, keeping you company even when you're wandering through the darkest woods. Their chemistry is like that perfect marshmallow-toastin' moment – just right. The characters might not be in the flesh, but they're more real than a lot of folks you'll meet in other games.

Atmospheric Music:
The music in Firewatch is like the subtle hum of the wilderness itself. It's there, weaving in and out of the scenes, enhancing the mood without ever stealing the spotlight. It's a soundtrack that knows when to whisper and when to roar.

Verdict:
Firewatch isn't for everyone, but if you're into deep storytelling, atmospheric exploration, and mysteries that'll tug at your brain, you're in for a treat. It's a game that proves you don't need explosions and gunfire to make a memorable experience. So put on your hiking boots, grab your trusty map, and embark on a journey that'll leave you both satisfied and contemplative.

There are a lot of great elements here, and the experience this game provides is unique. Unfortunately, in my experience, the game's finer details weren't as well-executed and kept the whole experience from meshing together for me. The themes of the game's story don't often get explored in games, and the character interactions are generally good, but there was always something that was annoying me or putting me off about the gameplay or the characters as I played. Sometimes it was the constant climbing cutscenes that just required you to press or hold one button and wait, or sometimes it was the bizarre dialogue trees, or sometimes it was the weird and unlikely details of the plot.

The story, the dialogues, and the overall plot are really nice! The vibe is also an 11/10!

However, there are some minor bugs (I got stuck in wooden and stone parts several times).
The game is kind of open world, but not entirely. There are specific trails where you can go and others where you can't. It was often confusing because I wanted to keep walking, but there was an invisible wall blocking me.

Anyway, despite these two things that could have been improved, the developers nailed the rest! Be sure to check out this game!

Firewatch is a short 4-6 hour slice of life game that offers insight into the lives of 2 characters, 1 who you play as, who work as lookouts for fires in a vast forest and mountainous area. The gameplay is mostly simple, moving from point A to B in a decently sized map, and selecting conversation choices as you move along and interact with the world around you. The story, while the ending might not be for everyone, is centred around the character you play as, Henry, and his need to get away from his life, where he ends up making a heartfelt bond with another lookout tower. Not all is as it seems though in the forest, and you'll quickly find out you aren't alone, and certain moments may have your hair stand on end. The voice acting is also top tier work and the graphics are rather beautiful.

I can see a lot of people labelling Firewatch as a "walking simulator," but it really is more than that. The game's serious, sombre opening sets the stage for why Henry, your character, takes on the role of a fire spotter in the Wyoming wilderness for a summer. It's an opening whose emotion and gravitas hit me hard, as the game's bright and cartoon-y art direction would later kind of betray how dark and serious some of the game's subject matter gets. Without getting into any spoilers, the story starts small and simple but begins to unravel the more time you spend hiking and climbing through the game's beautiful setting, ultimately taking some twists and turns that left me surprised.

The game's true bread and butter is its dialogue. Henry is mostly alone in these woods with (mostly) no one to talk to or interact with, but that's where Delilah comes in. She's your boss and veteran fire spotter, and the person on the other end of your radio day in and day out. Your only means of interaction with Delilah is over radios and walkie talkies, and though you never see Delilah in person the writing does more than enough to flesh her out beyond just a voice in the void. You learn about her past, her struggles, but will likely be won over by her witty sense of humour, which underscores pretty much all of your brief-but-meaningful chats with her. You'll frequently have the option to choose what to say to her, RPG-style, but this only has a small impact on how the story unfolds. For how natural the dialogue fees, there are times when it does seem unrealistic and scripted (as in, no one would actually say this stuff in real life), but most times you truly do feel like you're a third wheel to a private conversation between budding friends.

Gameplay-wise, you'll be doing a lot of walking in Firewatch. There's a rudimentary climbing system where you simply tap a button and can mantle most marked surfaces, but beyond that the game entices you with its environments, imploring you to look around and really immerse yourself in them. There's rocks, trees, water, hills, caves, and all manner of natural features for you to explore. I can understand why the developers may have felt limited in adding too much wildlife, but it could have been a nice addition to really make the world feel more alive. As the game goes on the environments will change in accordance with certain story beats, and by the end of your 4-5 hour playthrough you'll almost forget how it all looked at the beginning. The game's map is large enough to offer many interesting avenues of exploration, and you'll always have a handy map telling you where you are and where you can go. I do wish there was more to do, though, like little side quests here and there that give you more to do.

Overall, Firewatch is quite minimal in many regards, but that lends itself to the game's overall feel and atmosphere. You won't spend too much time with it, though there is a little bit of replay value in exploring more of the map and choosing different dialogue options, but the time you will spend will be enjoyable.

This is intentional, the devs are trying to make a statement about grief, how running away from your problems won't help you fix them, how life is mundane and trying to interpret it as anything but will only lead to disappointment. It could be any one of those, all of them or none of them but either way, when you beat the game you are gonna feel as if you have been ripped off.

Some will argue that the feeling of 'Thats ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it?' at the end of the game is what makes the 'game' good, art is designed to elicit emotion and it did just that. While I agree with the second part I disagree with the first, if someone took a ♥♥♥♥ on my plate I wouldn't applaud them for making me feel disgust.

Building up a mystery and a relationship only to rip it away at the end doesn't feel like a statement, it feels like I'm either being trolled by the devs or they couldn't figure out a good ending. Maybe if the game was longer Campo Santo could have slowly stripped away the mystery in a way that didn't feel cheap, but with less than 4 hours in the game I felt more of a 'lol u mad?' vibe. Your average player isn't going to watch the credits and think about the themes, they're gonna go 'This is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ lame' because it was lame.

Title: Firewatch: Where the Forest is on Fire and So Are Your Emotions!

Oh, gather 'round, gamers! Let me regale you with a tale about a game that sets your heart ablaze faster than a flaming marshmallow on a stick. Enter Firewatch, a virtual escape into the wilderness that will leave you questioning everything—especially why you didn't bring more bug spray.

Imagine this: You're a middle-aged man named Henry who, for reasons as mysterious as why socks always disappear in the dryer, decides to become a fire lookout in the picturesque Wyoming wilderness. Sounds idyllic, right? Well, buckle up, because this game will take you on an emotional roller coaster through uncharted forests, unexpected encounters, and enough suspense to make your fingernails beg for mercy.

Now, let's address the elephant in the forest: Firewatch isn't just about fighting fires. It's about fighting the relentless onslaught of loneliness, paranoia, and your own crippling self-doubt. Don't worry, though; you won't be armed with much more than a walkie-talkie and a dry sense of humor. And let me tell you, that humor is drier than a forest in the middle of summer.

The graphics in Firewatch are as stunning as an untouched landscape after a light snowfall. The developers have painstakingly crafted a world that will make you forget you're sitting in your underwear, covered in Cheetos crumbs. It's a sensory overload of vibrant colors, detailed foliage, and breathtaking vistas. Just be careful not to walk off a cliff while admiring the scenery. Trust me; it's not as picturesque as it sounds.

Now, let's talk about the story. Firewatch boasts a narrative that will pull you in faster than a bear chasing after a picnic basket. Henry's interactions with his witty and enigmatic supervisor, Delilah, are the highlight of the game. Their banter will have you laughing, cringing, and questioning whether your own life could be improved with a walkie-talkie romance. Sorry, Tinder, but I'm swiping right on Delilah's quick wit.

But don't be fooled by the charming conversations and picturesque landscapes; Firewatch will make you question everything you thought you knew. Is there something sinister lurking behind the trees? Are you being watched? Is that squirrel planning a hostile takeover? You'll soon find yourself more paranoid than a squirrel hoarding nuts for the winter.

In conclusion, Firewatch is a game that will ignite your imagination, burn through your emotions, and leave you yearning for more forest adventures. It's a clever and funny experience that will make you reflect on life's big questions while laughing at life's absurdities. Just remember to pack some extra bug spray, a dash of courage, and a spare pair of underwear. Trust me, you'll thank me later.

Firewatch is a classic! It is a pretty linear story that follows our Protagonist through his new job as a...well...Firewatch. His wife has recently passed. He is grieving and looking for a distraction, so he set's into the remote wilderness, with a partner, Julia, who is only there via radio chat.

You are prompted with multiple dynamic dialogue choices and have the freedom to approach the story path from a few alternate angles. The story is very developed and drawing. You get your emotions flustered by jumpscares and eerie moments. There are plot twists and dynamic events that can be triggered. There are missable tapes and critters. Fun little easter eggs. A lot more to a small storytelling game than you would expect.

After completion, you can free-roam the grounds. You can also extract any photos take via the in-game camera, to your computer! This game serves as an easy 100% completion for those fellow achievement hunters too :)

Overall, Firewatch is definitely worth a buy! It has a medium-length immersive story that will keep you on edge the entire time! Having plot twists and emotional key elements really makes you want to play it again and again!!!

Firewatch is a game that will stay with you long after you've put down the controller. It's a story of solitude, mystery, and human connection that will leave you feeling both moved and changed. And if you haven't played it yet, it absolutely belongs on your bucket list.

At its core, Firewatch is a game about a man named Henry who has retreated to the wilderness of Wyoming to escape the pain of his past. He takes a job as a fire lookout, spending his days watching for smoke and his nights alone in his tower. But as the summer wears on, strange things begin to happen, and Henry finds himself drawn into a mystery that threatens to upend his carefully constructed life.

What sets Firewatch apart from other games is its incredible attention to detail. The game world is stunningly beautiful, with vistas that will take your breath away. And the characters - especially Henry and his supervisor, Delilah - feel like real people, with all the quirks and flaws that come with being human. The voice acting is top-notch, and the writing is some of the best you'll find in any medium.

But what really makes Firewatch a must-play is the emotional journey it takes you on. As Henry navigates the twists and turns of the mystery, he's forced to confront his own demons and deal with the consequences of his actions. And along the way, he forms a bond with Delilah that feels both fragile and profound. It's a journey that will leave you thinking long after the credits have rolled.

In conclusion, Firewatch is a game that everyone should experience. It's a masterclass in storytelling, with characters and a world that feel both real and surreal. And it's a journey that will touch your heart and leave you feeling changed in ways you never thought possible. If you're looking for a game that will challenge you emotionally and stay with you long after you've finished playing, Firewatch is the game for you.

Firewatch is 1st person game, where you play Henry, a guy who is getting away from a difficult situation by taking a job as a fire watcher in the Wyoming wilderness. It is a short game - something like four to six hours - but tells a complete story. It is also pleasant to walk around the Wyoming wilderness, although it doesn't beat a real walk.

Henry is an interesting character, formed by some binary choices you make during the first chapter. I think no matter which option you pick, he ends up making the questionable decision to take this summer job as an escape from his situation. You further develop the character through conversations over the radio with Delilah, your supervisor, who has spent years doing this job.

The story is split into days, each with particular goals. The sun moves during the day as you accomplish the goals, so you can tell as sunset approaches that you are about done. Days are also useful stopping points, useful for breaking up the game into multiple sessions. Key items are used to restrict the map, so that you have a chance to explore an area before a new area opens up. By the end of the 90 days, I would have expected to be pretty familiar with my entire area, but I still needed to consult the map to orient myself. At the same time, by the end of the game moving around was getting repetitive.

I imagine the beats of the story stay the same, so I'm not sure if there is a huge replay value. I am curious what happens if Henry makes different decisions, both at the start of the game and in conversation with Delilah. There are a few more achievements to get. There is also a free walk mode, to get more acquainted with the map.
Expectations subverted successfully.

Firewatch is a really good game, it's a short story/walking sim game that has an amazing art style and some really solid atmospheric music. 

The general plot is very simple, you're a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness. You explore and wander the wilderness around you following the story. One of the main gameplay mechanics is the radio, it's the main story telling in the game and it allows you to choose from dialogue options to speak with your boss who provides quests and objectives for you. The core gameplay mainly consists of walking from objective to objective while using your radio to learn about your surroundings, other fire lookouts and the general history of the place. The game also tells a very interesting story that plays out between you the player and your boss. I won't go into detail on the story but it is extremely well crafted and meaningful, the whole experience is very gripping and detailed and I never felt bored or tired of exploring the environment around me. One really great thing about the game is how handcrafted the level is, it's crafted so you cannot often get too lost as long as you travel in the general direction you have been told to travel. The game also provides highlighted objects such as rocks and logs to signify that you are progressing in the right direction while also using shape composition to give you an overall understanding. The game also provides you with a compass and a map to make sure you are always on track. The game has plenty of things to interact with and discover which makes the general wandering around quite rewarding. The game is set in “days' ' which are specially set levels for you to play through, even though you are in a very open space the game is very nicely scripted, this might leave some players feeling trapped or disappointed however upon finishing the game you are provided a new free roam mode. 

The visual presentation of the game is outstanding and one of the biggest attractions of the game, it looks amazing. It is colourful, vibrant and packed densely with detail. The forests are dense with trees and foliage and the canyons are sharp jagged and built with large rock formations. The other spaces such as the cabin are also dense with small bits of environmental storytelling. The level also evolves and develops further as the story progresses and the weather changes which really makes the experience so much more unique. The music was also surprisingly good, there are moments of calm and quiet and then also times where the music ramps up to add suspense and mystery. All of the sound and visuals are excellent. 

As for performance, the game runs quite well, except for it to run on most modern machines quite smoothly. One complaint I would mention is the game lacks any FPS cap or settings such as dynamic resolution, this won't affect many average players but it would have been a good addition. As for bugs i had a couple small issues with collision which resulted in me getting stuck in areas that left me having to restart on older saves, i only had this happen twice which wasn't terrible, its not going to ruin your time playing the game but its worth saving often to make sure you can return to where you was if you get stuck. Generally I don't think many players will have that many issues when playing. 

Overall this game is definitely worth playing, if you are someone who doesn't often play games like this i think many people will be surprised with how engaging the game is. It's short and the story is deep and mysterious, however it is very easy to follow. An amazing walking simulator.

At this stage in my life, I am interested in games for the story and the experience.  I like being able to explore an environment at my leisure without the fear of dying or missing something critical to the game experience.  Firewatch was able to deliver on all of these points.

The theme of hiking initially pulled me into this game.  Firewatch was able to create a wonderful facsimile of exploring the great outdoors.  Sure a couple of things do look artificial here and there (like every climbable ledge has the exact same rock patterns), but the views you get are stunning.  Also, its great not worrying about getting ticks or falling to my death.

I found the prompts in the opening scene a great way to flesh out your character in a somewhat personalized way.  While this doesn’t change the outcome of the game, it does create more variety in how people will interpret the story based on who their protagonist is.  In a YouTube video discussing the ending of the game, the presenter talked about how [spoiler]the DUI that his character had[/spoiler] impacted how he viewed the ending.  In the comments, people talked about the different backgrounds their character had and how it affected the story meant to them.

Some of the criticism for Firewatch revolves around the ending.  There was amazing tension building throughout the entire game as the two protagonists tried to figure out what was happening.  Instead of a big reveal at the end, I can see how many people could feel the conclusion of this game was anticlimactic.  For me, however, the ending was bittersweet.  [spoiler]Our characters did survive, but there is still a lot of emotional pain that they will have to work through as they leave the wilderness.[/spoiler]

The only thing that irked me once in awhile was trying to figure out where I can and cannot go.  For the most part the its pretty clear where I need to be heading, but once and awhile I was trying to walk up a hill or a rock that looked like it was traversable.

If you are looking for a low stress, beautiful game, that tells a compelling and emotional story, than Firewatch for you.

[h1] Firewatch [/h1]

Developed by Campo Santo and published by themselves along with Panic, Firewatch is a single player walking simulator that tells a tense story surrounded in mystery that can be completed, start to finish, in an afternoon. The story this game tells will surely keep you at the edge of your seat, with bits and pieces here and there that will give you a chuckle and pull at your heart strings for good measure. Along with a pretty great story, this title boasts a very nice soundtrack and a world that is absolutely beautiful. The greatest strength Firewatch has is its dialogue and voice acting, which is easily among the best for a game of this caliber.

I found it was incredibly easy to let myself get lost in the atmosphere and story of this game. Typically I would be telling you about the setting, how the game starts and what the premise is, but all you need to know is that you are a man in the Wyoming wilderness trying to make it through the summer. It's best you go in as blindly as possible and experience the rest on your own.

It is worth mentioning that there is no real game play in Firewatch at all. There are no puzzles, no combat, no nothing like that. This is a walking simulator from end to end, with some item interactions here and there. Despite this, I really enjoyed Firewatch. The game is gorgeous and the music is spot on. I did notice that movement can be a little glitchey around frequently traveled areas, but it wasn't anything game breaking but any stretch of the imagination. Despite all of this, Firewatch is a great story and I cannot recommend it enough.

Even then, my GPU was still averaging at 85-90% usage.

Ultimately, I don't understand why this game is as highly acclaimed as it is. It's fine I guess. The story was interesting overall but it's just a drag to actually play.

The gameplay is essentially roaming through a beautiful wilderness whilst selecting dialogue between two characters via a walkie-talkie. The concept works surprisingly well! The story has a very strong emotional hook right at the beginning, but the rest of the story smooths out into an intriguing mystery that comes together really nicely.

It is surprisingly fun to explore this wilderness. I do think it was worth the $20, but if you're on the fence about pure story-based exploration games, hold out for a sale.

The voice acting is phenomenal, but that's where my praise ends. For a game with so many dialogue options, your choice doesn't matter at all. There is only one ending, and the story can only be progressed by following the given path so the choices we do have are all pretty empty. The conversations usually steer in one direction regardless of what you pick, and taking or leaving certain items at key moments has no impact.

The story was somewhat engaging at first, but there is so little payoff that it feels like I wasted my time. Most plot lines simply end and are very unsatisfying. The main mystery feels like it had its conclusion rushed and makes no sense. And the relationship you build with Delilah, your only source of contact, just ends, regardless of what you try to say or do, there is only one ending for the relationship, and it just felt so lazy.

The game is short too. Like really short. I beat the game in around 3 hours and I'm pretty sure I explored everything I could. For $20, it was just too short, and too small of an area to explore. There is a free roam which is kind of nice, but it isn't fun for long. There is also a commentary gameplay mode, but I don't see the appeal of that personally. Steam recommended this to me after playing Outer Wilds, and if you got the same recommendation, do not play this game. Outer Wilds is a masterclass in open world mystery, Firewatch is more like a demo by comparison.

TLDR: A first person exploration game with nothing but a narrative experience that is very chill, but manages to have moments where you feel pressured to act. It is short, like less than 5 hours and the ending sucks. 

Story: As a newly appointed Firewatch named Henry, a man in dire needs to get away from it all, you will be tasked to wander around your patch of forest to fix and prevent various issues, ranging from picking up a beer can to stopping a possible fire. Throughout your time spent there, you will often have exchanges of dialogue with Delilah, which is the biggest focus of the game and serves as the way to make the story progress. While there is a plot, the exchanges between Delilah and Henry is what remains with the player. Oh, that and the snapshots you'll take with the camera, I guess. Did I mention that the ending is also terribly frustrating?

Gameplay: You have a compass, a map, and a radio. So... You walk around with your compass, occasionally looking at your map to see how lost you are, and every now and again you will interact with something along the road or have something to report, or to chat about with Delilah, on the radio. 
You also have a disposable camera to snap some pics. It was a nice featurette imo. I remember getting my screenshots through my e-mail and being like... oh? Cool.... So yeah, there's that. Yeah, I was late to the steam screenshot party by over a decade, I know.

Graphics: While they are serviceable, they aren't great. They are very cartoonish and get the job done, but considering the majority of the game is spent walking and looking around, more graphical prowess would have been appreciated. Still, it does the job just fine.

Audio: The voice acting is top notch. There aren't many people to interact with, of course, but the dialogue between you and Delilah stays top of the line throughout, allowing you to simply sink deeper into it.

It's a nice short adventure, though somewhat expensive for its length. But if you play this game at a time in your life where you need to chill out, it might hit you in just the right way. If not, well it might a waste of money and time. Playing this in 2023 is a bit unfair to this game. To my understanding this was made by a rather small team and regarding a so-so time in one of the devs' life. Having said that, it doesn't excuse anything when it's time for a review. When it came out, this was a rather popular game due to youtubers giving it a full ''let's play'' which is both a good and a bad thing since it's a rather short story based game. A lot of people never even needed to buy it to enjoy it. That being said, going into the game a second time to see if it held up today, I'm still gonna say it's worth at least 1 playthrough.

"It´s a sleeper. It´s a scam. It´s the best writing in gaming. It´s boring"... A lot was said in 2016 when Firewatch was launch, so where´s all the smoke comming from if you forgive the pun?

Firewatch is, above all, a short exploration narrative game, similar to the so called "walking simulators". And there you have the first clue about why was it so divised when it launched, it´s simply put a "controversial" genre. Lots of them look gorgeous and sometimes the trailer may sell the game as something it really isn´t, so lots of people buy them without knowing what they are getting into. Firewatch particularly came out when the genre was not as popular and the trailers showed an amazing visual style, so it became natural for reviewers to give their oppinion on the title. That, in my oppinion, raised the awareness of the title in a way that was both good and bad for the title, but with time I think people notice what the game was and now people know what they are getting.

But what are they getting? Well, honestly, a true masterpiece in visuals and writing, that part is no lie. But also, a very, VERY, short game that even exploring and going out of your way it may take you around 5 hours to see everything. And that´s kind of like the mayor issue even for people who enjoy walking simulators with the game, it´s an amazing game, so well written, so gorgeous, it makes the part of walking simulators actually fun with the hiking equipment and different paths... but you will always would have expected more once you´re done. I dont get much into it but also plenty of people complain about the ending, I do not think it´s bad ending, and I theorize that such dissapointment generally comes more from how little does the character impact that ending or leads to it, as well as how you don´t really figure it out, the ending short of just happens suddenly and then it´s over. There´s a free roam mode that allows you to explore without the story, but there really isn´t that many secrets or point to it, you can hunt for the secret achievements you missed on the story mode (although they are all short of broken I should also clarify) and hear the soundtrack, but that´s about it.

So why give it a positive review when I just wrote gigantic blocks of complains? Because it´s still worth it. It´s overprice, yes, it will leave you with a "that´s it?" kind of feeling, yes... but also it´s an incredible experience, it looks so good, it´s so well written and realistic on depicting real characters, and the atmosphere is soo godd, that you have to experience it. Honestly I´m kind of shock there aren´t a thousand Firewatch imitators and the walking simulator genre didn´t really mimiqued some of the best features FW brings to the table, like hiking rather than just walking, sounds so small but makes the experience so much fulfilling. 

I give it 5 books dropped in the middle of the forest that you can´t take to control tower because there´s no real inventory system and you need both hands to go back out of 6. (So you can save the personal notes between 2 guys you don´t know for collecting but the books have to stay in the cache getting moister? C´MOOOOOONNN)

It feels a little bad to review against this game, because it does feel like it was made with some love. However, coming off of a dramatic high from Outer Wilds, the delivery of this game fell short. Mild, is what I would describe things -- the characters, the stakes, and the sense of space. The game is also at odds with itself in several respects.

It is story-driven more than anything else, despite limited gameplay and dialogue choices would have you believe, yet it feels more at home with a point-and-click game or mildly interactive movie, and could have been made just as easily as one of those -- it is at this juncture the game falls short because it does not stand up under those lenses. The choices don't seem to matter much, the dialogue is tepid, and after the [spoiler] attempted romance [/spoiler] it was difficult to identify with the main character. [spoiler] I played through with loyalty to the wife, Julia, who we were just made to be invested in during the introduction, but apparently that made for boring dialogue. It felt like the developers didn't want you to go that way -- why present the option then? [/spoiler].

I was excited when I hit the first trailhead of the game, and spent time looking around as if on a real hike, but the gameplay is at odds with the world presented; you feel as if you are on rails, both due to the structural pacing of the game and the clunky limitations on your movement, leaving you feeling discouraged to explore the world -- not that there seemed to be much to discover. So all the pretty trees and lakes and mountains go unnoticed because your character is unable to move past an invisible barrier made of a few trees and rocks. I contrast this to Far Cry 5 -- a totally different game -- but one that came with more of a sense of being outdoors and going wherever you wanted. 

For a game that seems to be recognized for its [spoiler] bait-and-switch plot device [/spoiler] in service of a "realistic" story, the goofy art style is again at odds. A very realistic environment, with realistic ecology and dynamics to explore would have made the "realism" set in a little more, but the art direction was more fanciful and encouraged more fanciful perception. I liked the poster hung with local vegetation and their scientific names. I liked the realistic trailhead sign. Give us a lesson in orienteering or something, to deepen the realism! Take away the GPS dot on the map, make us find our way through the mountains. The game introduces the Osborne Fire Finder, and didn't do [i] anything [/i] with that! What a cool lesson that would have been. The gameplay felt like a shallow premise for a story driven by "realism".

As for the big reveal [spoiler] yes maybe the situation is something that would happen in real life, because life is less exciting than media -- but that in itself is not interesting. Its commentary on escaping ones problems being tenuous and momentary seems like a lesson for anyone who hasn't lived much yet, and doesn't mesh with the emotional severity of Julia's illness. Are we to identify with Henry who appears to have only mild concern for his wife (at least in the dialogue presented to me, which I remind you was loyal to the wife)? Are we to cheer when Henry mildly acquiesces to Delilah's urging to see his wife again? We just developed (or at least were told about) a long relationship with Julia and she felt discarded in more ways than one. And the name -- Delilah -- a little on-the-nose, wouldn't you agree? [/spoiler]

I bet every one of us at least once had the time when we just wanted to run away from our problems or tragedies, forget about them for even a moment or at least rest from them. Well, that's what Henry, the character we play in this game, does when his life is falling apart. He departs to a beautiful nature reserve in Wyoming to take a seasonal job as a ranger. Welcome to Firewatch.

First of all, the landscapes of Shoshone, even if portrayed more cartoony, are simply marvellous. Hiking along forest paths, at any time of day, featuring well-composed, climatic music, felt comforting. I specifically liked strolls when there was a foggy, greeny morning.

But, of course, it isn't all only about going sightseeing in beautiful woods. The story, contrarily, doesn't belong to the category of relaxing. Day by day, as more of the dark mystery is unravelled, our hero Henry and his supervisor Delilah are more and more exhibiting paranoid tendencies. Soon enough, it also affects the player.

I saw many reviews pointing out that the ending was disappointing. While I agree that the final resolution felt kind of rushed, as if the creators had met a lack of ideas on how to wrap up the plot, I don't think I'm bothered, really. I didn't let this single shortcoming ruin my whole game experience when everything else was genuinely enjoyable.

Continuing on a more positive note, the fact that you're out there nearly completely isolated gives a fantastic atmosphere. I mentioned Delilah earlier but she's, in fact, far away in a different lookout and the only possible way to communicate with our boss is through walkie-talkies. And that ought to be the best part of the gameplay. Ever had or wondered what it's like to have a close friend you've never met in real life? Henry and Delilah's relationship feels so. In spite of the distance and no face-to-face contact at all, it is not long before they find common ground and grow attached in a friendly manner. I adored listening to all their conversations, whether casual or strictly work-related, and sometimes choosing how Henry would answer, although it barely had any influence on the story. Moreover, it is not a common practice in games to implement indirect devices as a primary or (heck!) the ONLY way of communication between characters. But when the creators can skillfully carry it out, it can do the trick. As in here.

[b] If you don't mind weaker endings and are able to appreciate other, better-executed aspects, I can sincerely recommend Firewatch to you. [/b] It is not the ultimate best title to pick out of all available games but worth a try. Just buy it on sale. When it comes to me, I am certain that one day [b] I'll be headed off to Ol' Shoshone again. [/b]

TLDR: [i][b]*NOT A GAME ALARM BLARING*[/b][/i]


[b][u]General Thoughts/Overview:[/u][/b]


Once again I find myself producing a slightly odd review. Once again I find myself looking at the boundary of ‘what it means to be a game’. Once again I find myself asking, ‘How much of why you play games is to appreciate them as a story telling platform, and how much is to master a set of mechanics and overcome obstacles based on those mechanics?’.

Firewatch is not a game, it’s a walking simulator. So I guess if you don’t like walking simulators you have everything you need right there. Firewatch is, however, better than pretty much any other walking simulator I’ve ‘played’.
You find yourself in the shoes of Henry, a man who’s life and love have unravelled in his hands (in a tell it yourself type background story), and so he has taken a job in a remote forest to, as the title very clearly states, watch for fires. (I am also happy to report that there are, in fact, fires to watch.) 
The main arc is one of the development of the relationship between Henry and Delilah, Henry’s boss, who is only interacted with through the radio Henry carries to report with. 
There are mysteries to unravel, as strange occurrences pepper Henry’s time at the outpost, all while he finds old notes and abandoned hats. Is he alone, or are there shenanigans afoot?

[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]
[list][*] Atmospheric. Incredibly so. The feeling of isolation, the vistas, the fear of that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ grizzly, scratching at the back of your mind. It all feeds in nicely to making the story extremely immersive. 
[*] The game had me guessing to the end. I hadn’t completely bought into the drama, but it [i]is[/i] set in America, and if anywhere, then there. I really wasn’t sure which side it was going to fall on, but I’m glad it went where it did. 
[*] The characters are fun to be with. They are well written, have a good dynamic, and are voice acted well.
[/list]

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
[list][*] The game is just tedious. Esp in the earliest portions where there is no investment. There is no hook, no reason to keep playing beyond ‘I paid for it so I’ll damn well play it’, and it’s just eye rolling. The entire game is in the development of those things, you have to want to get invested before it starts. 
[*] The responses you can give to Delilah do not always get reflected in the text provided, or are given with a very different tone to the one anticipated, making some of the dialogue feel out of character or out of place.  
[*] Lack of closure. I won’t spoil how it ends, which is natural and decent. But I will spoil that it criminally doesn’t tell you what happens after the story ends. I want to know what consequences my actions spawned, I want to know where the characters go and what they do next, I want there to be some kind of meaning to it all. And there just isn’t. It’s very disappointing. 
[*] There doesn’t feel like there would be any replayability. Having spoken with a couple of friends who played it, we all took different routes and ended up with the same ending… So I guess it’s a one and done.
[/list]

[b][u]Suggested improvements:[/u][/b]
 [list][*] This game would be massively improved if you could put stuff in your backpack to decorate the cabin with. It would also bring a little personalisation to the game.
[*] I want an Easter egg for bringing all those damned books back with me. Imagine my disappointment when my outpost is full of them and nothing happens?
[*] A debrief/what happens next thing after the game ends. What, if anything, is reported? Where do the characters go, what do they do with their lives? Closure, man!
[/list]


[b][u]Overall Recommendation:[/u][/b]


If you don’t like walking sims, it’s a hard no. If interpersonal drama isn’t your thing, it’s a hard no. If you’re not interested in atmospheric mysteries, again, hard no. 
It’s actually harder to say who Firewatch is for, other than folks who are just in it for a story…
Firewatch just isn’t a game. It’s an interactive story, and one done incredibly well. I thoroughly enjoyed it… but it isn’t a game. There are no challenges to overcome, no puzzles to solve, no enemies to defeat, no resources to manage. Just choices. I don’t think there is even a way to lose… so it may as well be a TV show. 
It also isn’t great value for money, though I bought it on sale when it was reasonably priced.
Ultimately, I can’t recommend this. It isn’t a game, it isn’t replayable, your choices don’t matter, and you don’t get to find out what the summation of your experiences were. If steam had an ‘it’s alright’ button, I’d have hit that, but it doesn’t, so it’s a no from me.

Much like Henry, the protagonist, this wasn't what I signed up for. Also similar to him, I was looking for a chill, relaxing escape. Everything about the description and photos implied this to me. We were both deceived by the ads. 

From the outside, it looks beautiful, it sounds like a thought-provoking game, and it appears relaxing. In reality, it's a bit more of a suspenseful, thriller-mystery type of game. (which is not my cup of tea) Because of this disconnect of expectations and reality, I was *not* personally upset by the ending. I kept worrying that it would be worse, even until the credits rolled. I am bummed that it wasn't something more akin to an atmospheric hiking simulator with an exploration focus and dialogue. There is an option to free-explore the world (maybe only after finishing the game?), but I don't feel that it lends itself to that. I may yet go back for that but I'm not sure. 

Besides these things, it was an interesting experience and it made me think about the importance of close friends. I really felt pretty vulnerable the whole time. I suppose it could have used more interactive padding as the game covers a couple months but only a handful of days are actually played, but I don't like thrillers, so I'm glad that it was short. I was a fan of the more thoughtful dialogue and that everything wasn't just sunshine and roses for the characters' lives. Having a bit more control over Henry's life choices would have been nice, to help solidify a connection. The other thing that bugged me is that the game seems afraid to show faces. I'm not sure if this was intentional or a time-saving measure. There are pictures of some people, but not of others. The voice acting was great, in my opinion. The music was excellent and helped the idyllic immersion, when applicable. The visuals are great, to be sure! It might warrant playing just for that. I just didn't like the story and felt mislead with my purchase. 

I really wish there was a "mixed recommendation" option, but I am saying "not recommended" simply because I feel that it is advertised as something that it's not. It's a mystery thriller that mainly exists to make you think about how people deal with issues. I feel that this could have been accomplished without any of the suspense, but then maybe people would criticize it for being boring. 

Overall, it's interesting, but know what you're getting into.

[quote] Almost a must-play for walking simulator fans. While some were unhappy with the ending, I felt as though it perfectly accomplished its mission and was a fitting end to the great narrative [/quote]

[b]In Firewatch, you play as Henry.[/b] Henry has a life that you’re introduced to in the beginning of the game. He’s married, with a partner called Julia, and for a while even has a dog. Their family may not be perfect, but it’s wonderful for them… until it isn’t. As it often goes in life, things eventually went awry, with Julia showing signs of early onset alzheimers at the early age of low 40s. Henry tries his best, but it eventually becomes too much for one person to bear. You can kinda influence, via choosing some options, what action he takes, but the final outcome is the same: [b]he leaves to go spend the summer in a fire lookout tower, looking out for fires.[/b] Obviously. This is where the escapism bit comes into play: he needs a break, and a wooded area mostly devoid of people is about the best a person can possibly find to fulfill that need to escape, especially if you earn money in the process.

Notice, however, that I said “mostly devoid of people”. While you barely ever see another human in your 4h journey through Firewatch, you will see some. Furthermore, [b]you will be interacting with one constantly. That would be your boss, Delilah. The thing is though, you only talk to her via the radio… and while it may seem weird to you, let me jump in your thought process and tell you to fear not, because this mechanic is easily the best part about firewatch.[/b] The dynamic between Henry and Delilah is incredible. [b]All their conversations are voice acted, and you can pick whatever options you want Henry to answer to her.[/b] In my playthrough, they ended up having a lot of banter back and forth, which I loved! 

[b]But I think what I like most about Delilah and Henry’s relationship and the fact that it builds via radio is that it gives you a sense of accompanied isolation, if that makes sense.[/b] And that on the other hand makes me think about all sorts of parallels to our real life, and how our internet relationships feel almost like the same thing. In Firewatch, you always have her to interact with, but at the same time, you’re always alone, as she’s in her own fire lookout tower, kilometers and kilometers away. Aside from the story's obligatory moments in which you interact with her, you can also find objects in your trek and report them to Delilah for extra dialogue. There is lots of this extra dialogue and I highly recommend listening to all of them, or as many as you can find. I will say it again: for me, [b]this relationship via the radio is the main element that makes Firewatch as special as it is.[/b]

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2908625847

And since I mentioned objects and your trek, it might be a good idea to talk about how the gameplay works. [b]It’s essentially a walking simulator set in the Wyoming wilderness.[/b] As a fire lookout, your job is to effectively deal with anything that might threaten the forest, as well as do whatever Delilah tells you to via the radio. It being a walking simulator, you can basically just walk, interact and run. That’s it. Throughout the story, you’ll find upgrades that will give you access to new areas, such as climbing ropes and an axe to cut down vegetation and dried trees to open up paths. 

[b]The movement and available controls might make it seem like the game is not very involved, but that could not be furthest from the truth.[/b] Aside from the dialogue options that you can constantly choose in your conversations with Delilah, you also have the added difficulty of navigating the terrain. That’s right, [b]the game has no map that hand feeds you a path to your objective or your constant location with extremely detailed drawings that make it super easy to locate yourself, no. You get an old fashioned paper map and a compass.[/b] While you CAN see your current location, it’s still up to you as the player to map out the best path to your next destination, and try not to get lost on the way. It’s a very cool mechanic, though I do understand that some people who might not have a great sense of direction will be put off by this.

[b]During your treks, you’ll also have plenty of sights to see and things to find. There are secrets hidden here and there[/b], including one of the best tracks in this entire game, Ol’ Shoshone, in a mixtape. Furthermore, you’ll also come across supply boxes that you can open. Most of them are optional and have some cool things inside like notes, but the main gain is in the form of an updated map. Every box has a map with markings that you can copy onto yours, outlining paths that you can take and making navigation a bit easier. It’s a really neat system. The boxes also often contain items you can talk to Delilah about, like a set of antlers.

[b]So while yes, the basic gameplay is quite simple, plenty of things make the experience very engaging.[/b] You really do feel like a sort of ranger navigating the forest without relying on technology and taking care of nature… mostly. See, [b]the game also has a kickass storyline that will keep you on the edge of your seat.[/b] As the steam store page so aptly puts: “When something strange draws you out of your lookout tower and into the forest, you’ll explore a wild and unknown environment, facing questions and making choices that can build or destroy the only meaningful relationship you have”. And that’s very accurate.

[b]The story here involves a mystery. I’m obviously not going to get into it, but I can say that it will constantly keep you guessing about what’s actually going on. Not only that, but the writing, and the way said mystery is presented, both do a really good job of showing the effects that complete isolation can have on someone.[/b] Just be warned, though: [b]while the mystery is well built, many people left Firewatch feeling unsatisfied with the ending.[/b] Again, I obviously can’t get into it, but I can ask you to not let that deter you from playing. The ending accomplishes exactly what it wanted to, and in my opinion is absolutely brilliant for it. I’m always up to chat about it if anyone wants to.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2902671250

[b]As for the other aspects, the game looks and sounds incredibly nice.[/b] The graphics don’t really reinvent the wheel, but they fit the vibe of the game fairly well. The soundtrack, though, is the stronger aspect of the two. I absolutely loved it! I actually played through this game back when it was released and again this month for this review, and since the release back in 2016, some tracks have been living rent-free in my mind. Ol’ Shoshone is my favorite - you can look it up on youtube. 

[b]In terms of issues, I didn’t really run into any. And in terms of flaws… While I was happy with the story, plenty of other folks weren’t. The choices, while there, don’t really influence the actual outcome of the story. While there is exploration, the experience also feels on rails, if that makes sense.[/b] You can’t for example run into danger of any sort, aside from whatever the script tells you to run into. No falling off a cliff and dying, no nothing of that sort. And while I don’t find the game really needed anything like that, it does feel somewhat unrealistic given the setting. 

[b]All in all though, I feel like Firewatch is an experience worth having for any fans of walking simulators.[/b] There is a reason why it’s one of the most well known titles in the genre, after all.

I recommend this with some caveats. It's a 6.5/10 or 7/10 game rather than a great one and I don't really have any major criticisms of it. It's a story-driven walking simulator with a really chilled out atmosphere and a pleasant way of losing yourself for a few hours.

The Good
-----------
* Gorgeous artistic graphics. Doesn't go for realism and this will age well, I think.
* Nice sound track. Music is sparse but well chosen, atmospheric / environmental noises are good.
* Good voice acting by both the main characters. The dialogue avoid becoming cheesy and I was fairly invested in the characters, who were both likeable.
* It really made me want to switch off my PC and go spend a summer in a tower in a national park.
* Gives you a map but no path-finder/GPS, which means you learn your way around quickly.

The Neutral
-------------
* It's a short game; about 4 hours long.
* The story doesn't really go anywhere. It's not bad but compared to other walking simulators such as "What Became of Edith Finch?" it's extremely light. At times it gives hints that you'll need to choose sides in a moral dilemma but any such decisions appear to be entirely inconsequential.
* Some of the game mechanics are completely meaningless (i.e., the camera)

The Bad
---------
* A minor point, but while the game allows you to rebind keys it shows the original key-bindings when displaying on-screen hints.
* Lots of invisible walls - and do we really need hints about which logs and rocks can be climbed over (would be nice to have a way of turning that mechanic off)

Firewatch: A Masterpiece of Atmospheric Storytelling

Rating: ★★★★★ (5/5)

Firewatch, a sublime creation by Campo Santo, is a game that transcends traditional boundaries, offering an unparalleled journey through the captivating Wyoming wilderness. From the moment the sun sets over Shoshone National Forest to the final haunting notes of the soundtrack, Firewatch mesmerizes players with its immersive narrative and stunning visual design.

The game introduces players to Henry, a fire lookout grappling with his own demons, as he seeks solace in the seclusion of his watchtower. The palpable sense of isolation is not just a setting but a character in itself, weaving into the narrative and shaping the emotional landscape of the game.

What sets Firewatch apart is its ability to convey a powerful and authentic human experience. The chemistry between Henry and his supervisor Delilah is flawlessly portrayed through the stellar voice acting of Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones. The dynamic and evolving relationship between these characters, communicated through radio conversations, is both poignant and relatable, making every choice and dialogue option feel weighty and significant.

Visually, Firewatch is a work of art. The stylized graphics, with their warm color palette and attention to detail, capture the essence of the wilderness in all its beauty and mystery. Each environment, from dense forests to open meadows, is a canvas for the emotional narrative, creating an ever-changing backdrop that mirrors the characters' journey.

The game's interactive storytelling is a triumph. The choices players make, the dialogues they engage in, and the discoveries they unearth shape the course of the narrative. Firewatch skillfully blends exploration with emotional depth, creating an experience that is as introspective as it is engaging.

The soundtrack, composed by Chris Remo, deserves special mention. Its haunting melodies not only complement the atmosphere but also elevate the emotional impact of key moments, leaving a lasting imprint on the player's psyche.

While some may find the conclusion open to interpretation, the ambiguity adds to the allure of Firewatch, inviting contemplation and discussion. The game's brevity is a testament to its focus on quality over quantity, ensuring that every moment is meaningful and contributes to the overall narrative.

In conclusion, Firewatch is a masterpiece of atmospheric storytelling that transcends the boundaries of conventional gaming. Its emotional resonance, stunning visuals, and immersive world make it a standout title in the genre. For those seeking a thought-provoking and emotionally charged experience, Firewatch is an absolute must-play, earning its well-deserved spot among gaming's finest achievements.

I will start off by stating that this type of game is not something I usually touch. I am very much into RPG style games with grand stories, multiple characters, and a large world to explore. Firewatch really isn't that. This game takes place in the Wyoming wilderness and while it has a ton of exploration, its more centric to the location the game is set in, and traveling far and wide is not really possible. You may read that and say "that doesn't sound fun at all", and honestly that is what I thought too, but after reading so many positive reviews, I gave it a go.

This game is not long. It took me about 4 hours to beat the main story and I did it in one sitting. Normally I would be opposed of even touching something this short, but Firewatch is different. You play as a man named Henry who is going through some tough personal things in his life. You take a job as a fire lookout deep within the Wyoming wilderness during the summertime. The main reason you are here (aka your job) is to observe the surrounding areas of the park and make sure you see no smoke/fires. You have no one to talk with expect your boss named Delilah, who you only can talk with through a handheld radio. You are bunked in a tall tower that sees over the entire park, sounds boring I know. Just when you start to get settled and moved in, you are immediately met with some rather interesting problems. These problems become more and more obscure and honestly frightening, and you work with Delilah via radio to get to the bottom of it. 

While I did state that I beat the game in 4ish hours, there is definitely more to explore that I have not. So keep that in mind. 

This is a game I truly do not want to go into full detail and feel it is better to just sum the story up and recommend it. It really does feel so different and refreshing to play - and if you want a more relaxed couch game that has a great story and narrative, give Firewatch a whirl!

I'd say this game skews adult, because it's an exploration of relationship themes that are weighty without being "dramatic".  If a 10 hour conversation with a stranger, slowly getting to know each other, doesn't sound exciting then this game isn't for you.  It's also fairly linear as a game, so essentially you're presented with a story where the only thing you can really change are how you respond to various conversation options.  Role-playing, if you will, but not the dungeony-type.

For me, this is one of the games that stays in your mind for a loooong time after you've played it, because of the exploration of emotions and because the park is a lot of fun to walk through if you're even remotely a hiker. 

Highly, but not unreservedly, recommended.

Firewatch made me angry, and it came from a very personal place. I can't do this review without some minor spoilers, so, you have been warned from here on out to stop reading if you don't want (some) of it spoiled.

_____________

"A Note: Firewatch is a video game about adults having adult conversations about adult things. If you plan on playing with a younger gamer, that might be good to know going in."

A woefully inadequate way to warn about and describe the premise of a game that involves someone getting early onset dementia and the main character running away from taking care of this person, his wife. I have lived through an almost identical situation. A lot of bad things happened that could have been avoided. It has left rifts in our family that will never, ever go away. Early on, when I got to the reveal about his wife, I was shocked, and then immediately got angry and flustered. I could not resume playing the game for nearly an hour. Had I known this was a heavy piece of the story, I would have never bought it. Obviously, it's not some developer's job to avoid triggering or upsetting everyone they want to reach. However, a description that accurately encompasses the basics of the gameplay and story? That isn't hard to do, and it honestly feels like they were intentionally misleading specifically BECAUSE of the content matter. 

"You are a man named Henry who has retreated from his messy life to work as a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness."

"Messy" is NOT the correct descriptor for his life. Messy is weird family drama, it's a bad break-up, it's an awkward past. "Messy" to describe what Henry is doing is wrong at best, and insensitive and hurtful at its worst. Someone abandoning their partner when they're dying of a degenerative disease is nothing short of awful. Understandable? Yeah, sure. Dementia and its related illnesses destroy so many more lives than the person affected by them. But a game based on someone doing it, and putting you in a position where you, the player, are supposed to sympathize with them doing it? No. It is still nothing short of awful. 

I don't really have anything negative to say about the voice acting, or the art, or the music. Cool stuff, decent stuff. But the lack of any sensitivity or research by the developers is unacceptable to me. What sticks with me most is how Delilah tells Henry he was "meant" to be out there in the wilderness and how she consistently stops Henry from feeling guilty over his choices that led to him absconding to Wyoming. I get that the ending of the story forces Henry to realize he cannot run from his problems, and that he (and in turn, all of us as human beings) sometimes just have to deal with what life throws at us. Getting to that conclusion, however, was not done in a manner I see fit for a game that somehow won 13 separate awards. 

At its core, Firewatch is a mystery and walking sim while effectively ignoring the harmful consequences of Henry being involved in said mystery. Misinformation about dementia is still wildly rampant in our society, reflected in inaccurate and cruel portrayals in all kinds of media. Firewatch fits neatly into that box. I do not recommend this game.

Review:
The game is short, you can beat it in about 5-6 hours. In those hours you come across some puzzles but it's mostly figuring out where to go next using your trusty old map (on which you can't mark anything, paths appear as you go through them, that's it) and compass. And ngl navigating through the game's world is more of a chore -for a couple of reasons including you can't run when you have the map in hand and weird (for the lack of a better word) borders that you face of the map- than a fun activity to do while you experience the story. But it's okay as it's a walking sim and what matters IS the story. Which brings me to my biggest gripe with the game that is the narrative. Throughout the whole game you communicate with the only companion you have in the game via a portable radio. This is your only way to experience the story except for the text screens at the beginning of the game that fill you in on the backstory of our character and how and why he ended up in this solitary land. And as I said, for the rest of the game you experience the story through the in-game dialogues and this would be okay actually if the story had anything to do with those dialogues. Without spoiling too much all I can say is for the whole game you go from one place to another at first to get some tasks done and then to uncover the truth behind all these, all while talking to Delilah about it (gal on the other end of the radio). But when it all comes to an end the game becomes about something else, like... all we've done was for nothing. Whole game we go after the 'truth' while talking about a guy with Delilah here and there but in completely different contexts from our goal, you know as a sidestory (just like we talk about many others throughout the game). But near the end everything kinda connects to this guy but completely inorganically, like the developers tried to merge 2 different stories into one (at least it feels like it). I know in the end it's a cohesive story and it makes sense but I never said I had a problem with the story itself,just the narrative. Bc they chose to tell it this way it feels dissapointing at worst and underwhelming at best. 

That leaves us with the characters and their interactions. The overall grim tone of the review is going to carry on to this section too but bear with me. The reason I didn't particularly enjoy the relationship between Delilah and Hank :) is bc i didn't get to enjoy it. I was so caught up in the story that I kinda neglected Delilah and put distance between us, didn't talk to her about my past, didn't choose the witty answers to her remarks and instead treated her like my coworker, my boss. And at the end of the game when I was left with the revelation I wasn't really happy about, there wasn't a good character development between them that I could hold on to (from what I've seen by watching some gameplay videos, you guys can get really close depending on how you choose to answer). But despite all these I enjoyed talking to her the whole time, it just wasn't enough to turn the game into a masterpiece for me

The game's graphics are stunning, with a distinctive art style that makes the forest and its surroundings feel both beautiful and dangerous. The soundtrack is also noteworthy, featuring a hauntingly atmospheric score that perfectly captures the mood of the game.

One of the most impressive aspects of Firewatch is its storytelling. The game's plot is intriguing and unfolds slowly, with the player discovering new clues and plot twists as they progress. The game also features some excellent voice acting from the two main characters, Henry and his supervisor Delilah, who communicate through a handheld radio throughout the game.

As Henry explores the park and its surroundings, he must navigate treacherous terrain, search for clues, and make choices that affect the outcome of the story. The choices the player makes throughout the game can have a significant impact on the ending, making for a highly replayable experience.

The game's themes are also compelling, exploring loneliness, loss, and the human need for connection. Through Henry's interactions with Delilah, the player is forced to confront the complexities of relationships and the difficulties of forming meaningful connections.

However, while Firewatch is an excellent game, it's not without its flaws. The game is relatively short, taking only around four to six hours to complete, which may be a disappointment for players looking for a longer experience. Additionally, some players have criticized the game's ending as unsatisfying or abrupt.

Overall, Firewatch is a beautifully crafted game that tells an engaging story and explores complex themes. Its stunning visuals, haunting soundtrack, and excellent voice acting make for a compelling gaming experience that is sure to leave a lasting impression on players.
