Overall i thought the game was pretty good. It definitely was not what i expected when i came into the game. I originally thought it was gonna be a sort of slice of life, fairly mellow character study. But in the end it turned into more of a mystery suspense plot. 

Graphics: The more stylized, cartoony graphics lead to a very unique, quaint kind of feel to it. Often these kind of visuals lead to aging much better than more photo realistic styles so i have absolutely no complaints about them.

Voice acting: The voice acting is on par if not better than most triple A games you see coming onto the market, leading to some very relatable, realistic characters. You can see the relationship between Delilah and Henry develop very well through the actors voices and mannerisms so overall give the voice actors, even the couple that only have a few lines, a 10/10.

Story and Writing: As i said in the preview, I was not expecting the game to turn out how it did. The starting text crawl where you choose what the basis of Henry's background and life is like is heart wrenching and fantastically written. It makes you genuinely connect with Henry and even with the idea of his wife in spite of only hearing her voice for a brief moment.  The story for the first act is pretty good, you spend most of your time familiarizing yourself with the games mechanics and the world you've found yourself in. The second act is still overall pretty decent where the tension and suspense begin to rise and you continue to wonder what the hell is going on. The third act, however is a little weak. The ending is pretty weak and predictable and genuinely feels like it comes too fast and rushed. The big suspense that permeates acts 2 and 3 really has no payoff and is completely wasted. The way much of it is presented is similar to a horror game where you expect some kind of major event but it never happens. You only happen to find a new clue or the one that's been stalking you leaves you yet another piece of evidence. By the time you really feel like something is happening the story drops off a cliff and the ending hits. 

TLDR: graphics are good, voice acting is fantastic, story is decent but falls short towards the end. overall score 7/10

[h1] Information / Review English [/h1]

Firewatch is a first-person adventure developed by Campo Santo.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2707516500

[h1] Gameplay / Story [/h1]

In Firewatch, the player takes on the role of Henry, a fire warden who begins work in a watchtower in the Shoshone National Forest in the summer of 1989 after his wife begins showing signs of Alzheimer's. On his first day, he is sent to an illegal fireworks display by two drunk teenage girls by Delilah, his superior fire warden, with whom he only communicates via radio. Henry rebukes them and is able to take the firecrackers away from them. On the way back to his "Two Forks" watchtower in the evening, he meets a stranger who, however, disappears as soon as he is noticed. When Henry arrives at his watchtower, it has been totally trashed, as if searched.

Gameplay in Firewatch is presented from a first-person perspective, so the camera reflects the point of view of the game character. With the help of the WASD keys you move Henry through the game world and you can rotate the camera freely by moving the mouse so that you can look around in all directions. Interaction with the game world is via a cursor that is locked in the center of the screen and changes shape when positioned over an interaction point by rotating the camera. The interaction is then initiated by a mouse click; For example, Henry can pick up objects and apply them to the environment elsewhere, open doors or flip switches. His only means of communication is a walkie-talkie, which connects him to his superior Delilah for exchange and advice. In order to speak to her, the player can choose from a number of dialogue options. This mostly happens when interactive objects are found and new areas are entered. The player's choices affect Henry's relationship with Delilah. More areas will be unlocked as you play. Objects found in the wild can be collected and used later, but there is no classic inventory. 

[h1] Per [/h1]

+ Beautiful comic look in a lively game world
+ atmospheric music and soundscape
+ multi-layered narrative about love, loss and responsibility
+ atmospheric, narratively believable staging of the wilderness
+ lively dialogues of two believable characters
+ frequent decisions about the course of the conversation or omission of information
+ Achievements and trading cards

[h1] cons [/h1]

- no playful challenge
- weak ending

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

Firewatch offers you an immersive adventure with a clever, layered narrative and lively interactive dialogues.

In Firewatch übernimmt der Spieler die Rolle von Henry, einem Feuerwächter, der im Sommer 1989 in einem Wachturm des Shoshone National Forests seinen Dienst antritt, nachdem seine Frau erste Anzeichen von Alzheimer zeigt. An seinem ersten Tag wird er von Delilah, seiner vorgesetzten Feuerwächterin, mit der er nur über Funk kommuniziert, zu einem illegalen Feuerwerk zweier betrunkener jugendlicher Mädchen geschickt. Henry weist sie zurecht und kann ihnen die Feuerwerkskörper wegnehmen. Auf dem Rückweg zu seinem Wachturm „Two Forks“ trifft er abends auf einen Unbekannten, der jedoch sofort, als er bemerkt wird, verschwindet. Als Henry an seinem Wachturm ankommt, ist dieser total verwüstet worden, als ob er durchsucht worden wäre. 

Das Spielgeschehen in Firewatch wird aus der Egoperspektive gezeigt, die Kamera gibt also die Sichtweise des Spielcharakters wieder. Mit Hilfe der WASD-Tasten bewegt man Henry durch die Spielwelt und kann durch Mausbewegungen die Kamera frei drehen, so dass man sich nach allen Seiten umschauen kann. Die Interaktion mit der Spielwelt erfolgt über einen Cursor, der in der Bildschirmmitte arretiert ist und seine Form verändert, wenn er durch Drehen der Kamera über einem Interaktionspunkt positioniert wird. Durch einen Mausklick wird die Interaktion dann eingeleitet; Henry kann so beispielsweise Gegenstände aufnehmen und andernorts auf die Umgebung anwenden, Türen öffnen oder Schalter umlegen. Seine einzige Kommunikationsmöglichkeit ist ein Walkie-Talkie, welches ihn mit seiner Vorgesetzten Delilah verbindet, um sich mit ihr auszutauschen und zu beraten. Um mit ihr zu sprechen kann der Spieler aus einer Reihe von Dialogoptionen wählen. Dies geschieht meist wenn interaktive Objekte gefunden und neue Gebiete betreten werden. Die Entscheidungen des Spielers beeinflussen Henrys Beziehung zu Delilah. Während des Spiels werden weitere Areale freigeschaltet. In der Wildnis gefundene Objekte können gesammelt und später verwendet werden, ein klassisches Inventar gibt es jedoch nicht

This game saved my life.

I am 27.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide.

After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.

Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ing minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay.

After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as.

Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends.

I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together.

Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

I don't usually play walking simulators, but I decided to play Firewatch just because... I dunno, this forest and the lonely tower vibe caught me, because I wanted to play something short and sweet. I liked Firewatch in general, it was a pleasant experience for me, but I won't ignore the drawbacks either.

What I like:
* Dialogues. Firewatch would not get so many positive reviews if only its core part - dialogues - was done poorly. The whole game is a dialogue.
* Music. There are just a couple of tracks, but the game does not play them over and over again, and this is good. Music here only emphasizes certain carefully chosen moments. I especially liked the "Prologue" theme.
* Story. My main fear was that some mystic line could start (I have a trauma after the game "Fahrenheit"). Fortunately, no - the story here is very real. The game will explain all the events, although there are some uncertanties about the characters motivation (which is good, it gives a chance to discuss and interpret).
* Atmosphere. Now, I want to become a firewatch.

What I didn't like:
* Poor gameplay. There is nothing you can change. You can't lose. You can't make things easier by doing something smart. Your choices don't matter. Just follow the story and press the buttons you are told to press. 
* Poor optimization. Low FPS even on a modern PC.

My personal opinion is that Firewatch would be more interesting to play if there was no navigation - only the map and compass (i.e. no player pointer, no player trail). In this case you would need to read the surroundings and match them with what you see on the map, and then use compass. Usually, I don't like such a mechanic, but here it would fit. Considering the small game world in Firewatch, players would not get lost and the experience would be more simulating a real firewatch guy.

Exploring the natural wonder of the great outdoors and solving a missing persons case are the only tangible joys you'll find in this game.

This is not a feel good game. It's grounded in a solid adult characterization based around weariness, selfishness, and inability to adapt. You're not a heroic personality; you're a damaged adult struggling to remain alive both physically and psychologically. The downbeat ending requires maturity to understand and appreciate because it's so simple and real-world.

The character you play is the standard trope of the grieving spouse escaping into the wilderness after a tragedy. The age old heroic journey of hopefully returning with a new sense of self instead of being consumed by the wild, literally or figuratively. Considering the kinds of people who inhabit this game world, living to limp in bandages another day is the best you can hope for.

In this case, you are a fire-watcher in a national park service tower, with only your boss in the neighboring patrol sector for regular company, and that only by walkie talkies. This is the Big 80s, where laptops and cellphones are still only for the super rich.

A major part of the game play is introspection of self. Your choices during game play don't matter at all except as a blank canvas on which to project your own feelings and thoughts. What you choose to talk about with your boss (who crosses over into possible romantic interest) only determines the topicality around which you deal with your own inner world.

Your exploration of the national park likewise is there to add implied subtext to the conversations and events when they happen. The physical challenges and puzzle solving are both tests of survival and a mirror to what is going on inside your psyche. Just like in real life, being largely alone in the wilderness leads to all sorts of eruptions from the unconscious, and pathologies can take root which drag you down into despair and petrification.

The game gets this stuff dead on.

As an experienced hiker who did some crazy stuff in his younger years, I found myself flashing back to those days while playing this game. The wilderness will kill you. It will make you careless and wear you down mentally. The climbing and scrambling, the treading over uneven terrain hoping you don't twist an ankle, the enormous time even the simplest of tasks takes, the constant need to be aware of your surroundings lest you walk into a physical dead end you can't get out of. 

The psychological stuff is true to life also. Without large numbers of people around to check your impulses, you go a little wild. People bond in the weirdest of circumstances. They grow inflated and reckless, and begin to act in subhuman ways. The devil inside is both dangerous and enjoyable.

Then there's the stillness of your true self that comes out in this savage environment. In a way, this is where poetry, compassion, and the grounding of your truth grow out of. The wilderness has been called the "sensible image of the infinite," and that's a good point to consider. The savage garden is beautiful beyond words.

Which makes the only real choice at the end of the game make sense. Do you stay and burn to death? Or do you take the implied growth through your activity in the game as a foundation of what is to come and escape? Only you, the player, can give it that meaning.

Most everyone who passed through this dragon's lair of a national park gets trapped in one way or another and adds to the casualty list. The hand up into the helicopter is the only shared gesture between two people that you see in the game. That's hugely symbolic, mythological stuff right there. The tarot card of Judgement is worth studying for extra credit.

Maze or labyrinth? Rise from your grave or fall back into darkness. It's your only decision.

Firewatch employs a fair amount of restraint in its design, delivering a surprisingly tight narrative that's elevated by [i]exceptional[/i] vocal performances. 

I'm returning after well over a year to share these thoughts as this was an experience that has really stuck with me. 

Many folks seem to have an issue with the story as a whole and, more so, the ending.

The mystery at play and its explanation will remain divisive, and may leave you disheartened as it rapidly unfolds near the 80% mark. 
If you set aside your own expectations for what is 'meant' to happen, instead remaining open to what ultimately does, there's a beauty to the reality of the events that take place. 

The aesthetic and general atmosphere of the world is something quite special. 
I really enjoyed spending time in the environment. 
Traversal was pleasant, with simple mechanics that are not overused or frustrating. 

Take your time with this one, exploring and uncovering details at a pace that you're comfortable with. 
Even if you waffle around, Firewatch is well-paced, guiding you through the sensibly plotted ~5 hour experience.

Firewatch, like other walking simulators, is not a game that is for everyone, but if you don't mind a video game that is without much challenge and closer to interactive art it is wonderful experience. The story is a highly personal one about a grieving man who takes a job as a fire lookout in a desolate American wilderness and the relationship he forms with another firewatch over the radio. It starts out casual and peaceful, almost like a low-key romantic comedy, but gradually transforms into a tense mystery that plays on deep psychological insecurities and fears. Most of the gameplay is walking around the streamlined representation of the forest in all its beauty, awe, and dread and interacting with a few items to get around the environment and uncover the mystery. It is a great journey through emotional experiences and human relationships and has rightfully in its placed in the walking simulator hall of fame.

While it is tagged as a walking sim, I felt it falls somewhere between open world and walking sim, without explicitly being one of either. The mechanics are a little clunky but it is not a big issue at all. The pacing of the story is fantastic and keeps you hooked from the start to the end. Perfect length. I loved playing it.

I have a hard time labeling Firewatch a walking simulator. It's true that wandering about and listening to dialogue are the main ways of interacting with the game, but the freedom to roam where you choose, the option to respond as you please, and the tools you'll find to enhance those abilities, give the game a level of agency usually absent from the genre. I didn't feel like I was being led around an already plotted out course, I felt like I was actively crafting it.

And what a pleasant course it was to craft! The Shoshone mountains may be more cartoony than realistic here, but they are still striking in the same way I would imagine that wilderness to be, producing some truly 'it was worth lugging this camera all the way up here' shots.

The natural beauty, freedom, and isolation inherent to a post deep out in the wilderness feed straight into the game's narrative. It's hard to say more about it without setting up player expectations that would stifle its intentions. Henry's going through something, and as much as you're allowed to choose what exactly it is he's going through, you still need to go through it with him for the story to be as effective. Firewatch is first person for a reason and I can't imagine you having as good a time with it as I did without first accepting that.

Firewatch (FW) is a first-person adventure game set in the wilderness of a forest. Part open-world, part walking simulator, it is a slow-burn story that focused on creating an emotional journey for the player. Does it succeed in this regard? Let’s dive in.

[h2]Pros[/h2]
- Beautifully-rendered woodland environments 
- Complex characters with excellent voice acting
- A branching narrative to create your own journey
- Engaging story filled with mysteries

[h2]Cons[/h2]
- The ending 

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
As mentioned above, FW is a unique mix of two genres. It is still mainly a walking simulator with a couple of action sequences sprinkled in. However, the places that you need to go are often far away from your starting area and you are only given vague directions on how to get there. Thus, you are provided with a map that covers all notable places with proper legends. As you progressed through the game, it will be gradually filled with more useful tidbits such as notable landmarks, hidden shortcuts or blocked paths. A thing to note here is that the map is a physical object, meaning you have to regularly consult it (with the help of a compass) to find your way around. There is no heads-up display, minimap or anything similar. This contributes to making the game feel more immersive, much like you would be hiking in real life.

If you are seeking for a game to spice up your computer’s screensaver, look no further. Every single scene in FW is jaw-dropping to look at, especially during sundown. The locations that you ventured into also varied frequently, from the luscious forest to a wide canyon to a gloomy cave. Clearly, a lot of effort is put into creating a life-like world full of amazing discoveries.

Speaking of discoveries, the details put into the environments are spectacular. Contrary to most walking simulators, almost every object can be picked up and inspected closely. For a clear-cut example, there are more than a dozen books hidden around the wilderness and all of them have their specialized cover and even a readable synopsis on the back. 

[h2]Story[/h2]
Our journey begins from the perspective of Henry (Rich Sommer), an everyday man that chose to work as a fire lookout in the Wyoming jungle to escape his troubled life. Being stranded in the middle of nowhere, his only form of socialization is with his superior, Delilah (Cissy Jones) using a small handheld radio. The job is simple: keep watch for any potential fire while making sure everything is nice and cozy. Seems like a walk in the park, right? Or so he thought.

These two characters ooze personality from the very beginning. Even though we never get to physically interact with Delilah, the conversations that we can engage with her are believable and three-dimensional. Not once do I feel that both of them are flat, uninteresting individuals; instead, I wanted to learn more about them. This is greatly helped by the voice actors who pour their strengths into bringing these people to life.

I would like to acknowledge the theme here, which I believe to be about relationships and isolation (while keeping the spoilers to a minimum). Henry’s broken past heavily involved a close bond and he used the job as a way to cope in silence. Apart from that, some of his talks with Delilah are about their former lives and what it means to care for someone. You can also find a couple of leftover notes detailing the relationship between two former lookouts; hell, even one of the books is about ‘the untapped power of the solitary mind’. It is a thought-provoking subject matter that the writers manage to present fairly well for the most part.

Using the radio, you can inform Delilah of any point of interest that you may have stumbled upon, and these are presented in the form of dialogue trees. These not only encouraged me to explore any secrets FW has to offer, but also expands their relationship further. While the responses that you chose will not affect the events that follow, it does impact Henry’s attitude and his overall stand with his supervisor. Therefore, the destination may be the same, but the journey will be personalized to each player.

And while we are on that topic, let’s discuss the destination AKA the ending. Truth be told, I do not like it. Not in the sense that it was despicable, but because it was a letdown. While it does explain all of the events you witnessed throughout the game, the answers are simply underwhelming (albeit realistic).

[h1]The Rest[/h1]
[list]
[*] Developers Commentary is available from the start if you are interested in learning the behind-the-scenes of FW.
[*] After completing the game once, a Free Roam mode is available where you can explore the entire map to your heart’s content. The only downside is Delilah is unavailable to talk to.
[*] You can find and pet a turtle. Truly the mark of a next-gen game.
[/list]

[h1]Stats[/h1]
[b]Playtime:[/b] It took me eight hours to complete FW, getting all achievements in the process. 

[b]Replayability:[/b] Minimal. Free Roam can be fun, but by that point, you probably uncovered everything.

[b]Achievements:[/b] Ten of them, which means ten percent per achievement. All of them are a piece of cake to obtain.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Campo Santo’s debut game is anything but forgettable. With a simple premise, basic gameplay and minimal characters, they successfully created one of the most memorable walking simulators to date. It is not an experience you want to miss. All in all, I recommend Firewatch.

Walking simulators like What Remains of Edith Finch or The Suicide of Rachel Foster among others have a more compelling story, have more interesting characters, and actually deliver a cathartic emotional ending to make the monotony of walking around doing nothing all game feel worth it. Conversely, the climax of Firewatch just made me feel like I wasted my time. 

On the technical side of things, the game runs like poo too. Constant frame drops/jitters coupled with a handful of insignificant but noticeable bugs. 

I often found myself lost, bored, or both at the same time. I cannot recommend this game at any price.

It's a fun experience, I loved seeing all that mountain wilderness, and I'm happy there's a free-play mode where you can just noodle around. (At least after you complete it.)

The plot is... well, don't go into it expecting high concept and you'll enjoy it. :)

-- edit, should add some more specifics:

- Art/visuals: A++ :D Loved it a lot. It really captures the feel of that mountainous backcountry.

- Music: Also really good, it matches the setting and mood, and blends into the background. I'm so pleased that, in spite of the music being quite good, a lot of the game has no music. It lets you soak in that backcountry ambiance and feel a little uneasy with the plot.

- Coding: Generally pretty good, though there are a few bugs (like a lock-up when trying to do a particular action, weird step-back when trying to do other actions, etc). Works pretty well on my m1max laptop.

- Writing: I thought the writing was really engaging, and the banter between the two main characters was really funny and real. I think my main disappointment here is that, like many, I have become too genre savvy, and I guess I was expecting something much bigger by the end. But no, this is a story that's very much about the journey. As could be expected of a writer involved with TWD, the story is about the people dynamics, not side gimmicks.

So yeah, go into it with all that and you'll have a good time. Cheaper than the price of a movie theatre ticket these days, and longer and more interactive.

[h3][b][u]Short Answer:[/u][/b][/h3] A really good narrative-driven game, often considered one of the best "walking simulators" for good reason. Artistic direction is stellar, the story is engaging, and the characters are the highlight of the whole experience; with only some mild pacing issues and a few minor glitches to complain about in my playthrough. Can be beaten in roughly 4 hours, and even as someone who typically dislikes walking simulators, I'd still say it's worth giving it a shot.

[h3][b][u]Long Answer:[/u][/b][/h3] [i]Firewatch[/i] is a narrative-driven mystery game that has you take on the role of Henry, who seeks to escape his tumultuous life by applying as a fire lookout, tasked to sit in a tower in the middle of the Wyoming wilderness and watch for signs of wildfires. Your only contact with the outside world is your supervisor Delilah on the other end of a handheld radio, and it's up to the two of you and your watchful eyes to keep the wilderness safe--but as you'll quickly come to discover, wildfires are not the only thing you need to watch out for. It's considered one of the best in the "walking simulator" genre; and after finally getting a chance to play it myself, I can see why it's so highly regarded.

Much like other walking sims, [b]gameplay isn't too complex[/b]: a lot of walking from one story-dependent location to the next interspersed with "dialogue tree" conversations over the radio about anything of interest you find along the way; but it's made a bit more interesting thanks to a light "open-world exploration" element. When tasked to visit a new location, you're not always given clear instructions on how to get there, often being told to just start walking in a cardinal direction or find things based on nearby landmarks. The idea is to regularly consult your map and compass while traveling to determine how to reach your destination, much like you would if you were actually hiking in the wilderness. [b]The most interesting part of the game to me, oddly enough, was the way the game uses your map.[/b] You don't get a traditional minimap, but rather a physical paper map--which you must equip like an item in order to read--that will keep track of your position as you travel (though you can turn this function off for a more immersive experience). It gives you the basic lay of the land, but supply cache boxes scattered around the park hold annotated pieces of the same map, which can then be recorded onto your copy to reveal available walking paths nearby; any story-related points of interest you discover will be automatically added in the same manner. The sense of freedom you get when you first view the sheer size of the map quickly fades once this process reveals how constrained travel can be; but the thrill of exploration can still be found in finding new shortcuts, the occasional secrets not marked on your map, and really anything and everything that will trigger new dialogue between Henry and Delilah.

Speaking of which, [b]the dynamic between the two main characters was fantastic[/b]. You can relay information to Delilah over the radio about nearly everything you find, and these are often accompanied with a dialogue tree to change up how you respond to her remarks. You can't change the outcome of the story through your choices, but they can affect Henry's background/personality and the relationship he has with Delilah in meaningful ways. Finding new things to trigger these conversations and learn more about these characters was a huge incentive for me to thoroughly explore whenever I could, and not just do the bare minimum to push the story along. Much of this is thanks to solid writing, but the high-quality voice acting helps turn the interactions between Henry (Rich Sommer) and Delilah (Cissy Jones) from "good" to "great". This relationship is only one half of the game's overarching narrative, the other half focusing on a series of events that coalesce into a big mystery story. [b]I don't really want to say much about the mystery story for obvious reasons, though I can say that I liked it overall.[/b] I've heard some say that the ending was underwhelming, but I honestly didn't mind it. [spoiler]Multiple times I was concerned that it would jump the shark in some regards, but it managed to ground itself in the end and make something that feels fitting given how true to real life (sometimes uncomfortably so) the story and characters can be.[/spoiler]

[b]It goes without saying how gorgeous the game looks, but I wish I had more chances to stop and take it all in[/b]. Each time you get the opportunity to go somewhere new, there's always this element of urgency that pushes you to go there. It makes sense from a narrative standpoint that things need to keep happening to drive the plot forward, but the only downtime you'd get were in brief scenes that had you locked into one location right before unceremoniously jump-cutting you into the next scene. I constantly felt like I was being rushed through to the end of the game, and I would've liked more opportunities to explore without needing to be as concerned with time management. You do get a "Free Roam" mode you can play with in a special settings menu, but unless you're looking to unlock some missing achievements, you don't have as much incentive to use it after you've already beaten the game; and since you're unable to talk to Delilah in this mode, using it before you beat the game robs you of what I feel is a valuable part of the "first-time player" experience.

Final side note, [b]you may run into some minor glitches during your playthrough[/b]. A couple times when trying to interact with something while still running up to it, my character would suddenly run backwards a few steps without my input, only to give me back control a few seconds later. One time I had triggered an event that was supposed to unlock an achievement but didn't, and I had to reload the game and try again for it to work--something I've seen people struggle with on several of the optional achievements in both normal and free roam mode. It's nothing serious, but it felt like something worth noting.

[b]It took about four hours to beat[/b], and I spent another hour getting the last few achievements I missed in my main playthrough. Firewatch is exquisitely beautiful and does walking simulators right. The player is given enough to look at that they're never bored, and the world is rather interesting. Honestly, it almost pioneered a new era of walking simulator, and it deserves lots of credit. As any game developer knows, a game this large takes years of hard work.

The beginning of the story hits hard, with some serious adult themes. It draws you in, and has you hooked. The voice acting is realistic and the world building fantastic. The color scheme is gorgeous, and the setting is just golden. Isolation with a singular voice as your lifeline? Wonderful. The graphics don't reinvent the wheel but they don't need to, and the game still has its visual moments.

If you've gotten to this point in my review, you're probably waiting for the reason for the first sentence. Honestly, the ending ruined the narrative. I'll avoid spoilers, but it's an incredibly controversial ending, The story arc isn't just incomplete, it's boring. All tension is just erased, and the player wonders the reasoning for the games narrative in the first place. The other reviews speak about the ending, and I truly wish I could talk myself into believing the ending was good. 

It's not.

If I were potentially buying this game, I'd say it isn't worth 20$. The story took me less than 4 hours, and that's very common. If it had a story to match the rest of the polish, it'd be worth it, but the narrative flaws are just too blatant. Don't let me scare you away! It's definitely worth it on sale.

I have to say - although it's an enjoyable experience - it's a bit short and underwhelming. The controls and movement are quite buggy, and since this is a storytelling game with lots of immersion, the moments where I slide around trying to get over obstacles and moments where I seemingly get stuck on nothing are a bit too often to stay immersed. They hurt the gameplay experience quite a bit, in my opinion.

The story is, also in my opinion, a bit underwhelming and short. You're working up to a climax and at points there are creepy vibes, but in the end nothing really happens, your choices didn't matter (much) and I was left with the thought: "that's it?"

This all made me vote no, I wouldn't recommended this game to other players. There are far better walking simulators, with better controls, movement and storytelling. If it's on a discount, this is worth a buy. But paying full price for such an underwhelming experience left a sour taste in my mouth.

I'd heard great things about this game but was left very disappointed. It had great voice acting and beautiful visuals, but the game totally fell apart at the end.

It's hard to describe how the game completely faceplanted in its final hour without going into spoilers, so I'll just make these two points:

1. The game's theme of healing and moving on from a devastating loss is completely contradicted by its sour ending, where a previously supportive character suddenly does a personality-180 and chastises the main character for having the gall to want to move on with their life after essentially losing a loved one

2. The plot is both extremely convoluted and underwhelming at the same time, with lots of events that seem important but then go nowhere. I really thought the "big twist" was going to be that it was all in the main character's head because the sequence of events is so nonsensical - think a character being like, "I really don't want you to find this thing!" and then giving you a key to where you can find the thing - but (minor spoiler) it's not. It's just a stupid plot.

I've read reviews saying the pointlessness of the plot and anti-climactic ending are the point of the game - to emphasize how bad things happen and you can't control them, or something. But with the last 5 minutes of the game contradicting the thematic message of everything that came before, plus the big plot reveal that makes no sense if you think about it for more than 30 seconds, the whole thing left a bad taste in my mouth. 

I'm not just underwhelmed; I'm angry with this game. Screw this game and it's "You can't run from your problems...YOU SHOULD HAVE THE BALLS TO STAY AND SUFFER FOREVER" message.

TLDR: Haunting tale of isolation and paranoia, with boilerplate gameplay

I'm not sure if I'd call Firewatch more of a narrative adventure or a walking simulator but I think it straddles the line between the two. The story concerns Henry, a man whose wife has descended into early-onset dementia and as he is overwhelmed with her care, she goes to live with family while he takes a job as a firewatcher in a remote national park in western America, to try and get his head together. His only contact is Delilah, another firewatcher at a nearby tower, though they only ever speak over their radios. Before long, they start to get the feeling they aren't alone in the woods ...

Gameplay is relatively simple, with the player using standard WASD movement, sprinting, collecting inventory items, etc, as they move through the woods and canyons. There is no combat and there are no enemies, and as near as I can tell, the player can't go off the rails and fall into something they shouldn't. Nothing about the game is hard or difficult to figure out and most of Henry's tasks and explorations exist just to move the story along. Travel paths are fairly linear but the environment is well-rendered and colorful. The game's art style is distinctive, without being overwhelming, and sound is good too.

Something unique about this game is that aside from catching a few glimpses of humans in the distance, and only by silhouette, the player never sees anything bigger than a raccoon until the very end of the game. Delilah remains a faceless voice over the radio, who gives Henry his "tasks," which help drive the story.

The thing is, that works. Even without some of the more haunting musical chords, the player can feel very alone and uneasy out in the woods--and after a point, very vulnerable. I found the deeper I went into the game, the more I came to look forward to the random bursts of conversation with Delilah, as she is the player's only human contact. It's an effective technique that amps up the feeling of isolation and sets the mood of the game as the story takes a more sinister turn. The emotional voice acting is outstanding; the actors nailed their roles and the dialogue is well-written, which is so important in this type of game. They story reaches a rather bittersweet conclusion as well.

On the downside, the game is *incredibly* short. I finished a 100% achievement run, with a lot of time spent on pause, in less than five total hours. I find that at the regular price, Firewatch is a bit overpriced for something that has very little replay value. I'd definitely wait for this one to come on sale.

While the game was basically stable, I did run into some odd glitches, such as the one that occurred when I tried to clear brush from the path at one point and my characters was thrown backwards and ended up levitating off the ground. A reload fixed it but it was weird. There were a few instances of clipping as well.

Steam achievements are a snap. Five will unlock in the course of normal play, but four of the other five require some exploration. Guides exist and none are hard to get. An easy game to 100% on, and without breaking the game's flow.

Overall, I have to give Firewall a thumbs-up, just on the strength of the emotional story-telling. Due to the short length, I do recommend waiting for a sale but when it's down to a few bucks, check it out.

Pros
- Haunting story and very atmospheric setting
- Great voice acting

Cons
- Incredibly short
- A few weird glitches

Final Score: 6/10

Firewatch is one of the better walking simulators I've played. It's fairly short, rolling credits at a little under 5 hours, but very memorable.

The game follows a middle-aged guy named Henry that took a summer job as park ranger to escape from his daily life. His only human contact is through a walkie-talkie with his supervisor Delilah. The story itself is mostly conveyed through dialogues between the two, complemented by some stellar voice acting and amazing writing, as you perform your duties around the park.

The navigation system is great, giving you just a compass and map to find your way. You can even increase the immersion by disabling your location on the map, having to use Delilah's hints and the area around you to determine your location. I may have lost my way more than once because I absolutely suck at navigating, but the breathtaking vista's and goregeous color pallets more than made up for that.

The ending left me a bit unsatisfied, but I absolutely recommend this game for the story, dialogue and amazing atmosphere.

-------

The Good:
- Amazing visuals, atmosphere, and audio
- Fantastic conversation system and voice acting
- Immersive navigation system

The Bad:
- A slightly disappointing ending

Story is short but there's some replayability like being able to explore the area freely and so on, would recommend it but mostly when it's on sale as some people may not find paying full price for 2h to be worth it.

The addition of stuff that enhances your immersion like ability to disable your HUD completely is a bonus + from me and this game is really best enjoyed without it in your face (although I wish it disabled all of it and instead incorporated your objectives on the map for example)

Overall, pretty good short story-driven adventure with choices.

Firewatch is not the game I expected it was. I thought it was a relaxing walking simulator set in the Wyoming wilderness that I could escape to and blow off some steam. Turns out it's actually a lot more linear than I thought, the story ramps up to becoming a thriller quickly, and there's someone in your ear talking to you (your boss, Delilah) at all times -- not the most relaxing or atmospheric experience, exactly. I say these things not because they're bad, but rather that from the start, Firewatch is subverting your expectations. Everything you expect this game to be it turns out it's not, and it's actually a stronger work of art for it.

Before discussing the game's biggest strengths (story and writing), I might as well get its biggest weakness out of the way: presentation. The actual forest looks fine (nothing mindblowing, but serviceable), but that's not the real issue: on my absolute monster of a PC, the game drops frames left and right. There's pop-in for trees when you're not even that far away. What's worse is that interacting with objects is quite buggy, making it annoying to quickly flow from one thing to another. The way traversing works is that it is a toggle to sprint, but if you ever stop or use an object you have to toggle sprint on again. Naturally, you'll forget about this little quirk and you'll start trying to move again but now you're slow as molasses. It ends up distracting you from the experience, and the game's worse off for it. As a side note, I wish the regular walk speed wasn't so slow. I'd love to have some speed that was between sprinting and walking; I felt like I was rushing past the sights but only because I couldn't bear the regular walk speed. I don't know; this is all to say that when you add these things up, the actual walking you do in this walking simulator isn't all that enjoyable. 

Most of the gameplay is navigating from point A to point B. I recommend turning off the feature that tells you your current location on the map, and using your own sense of direction to immerse yourself; I found it more engaging that way. You'll get lost but at least it's less boring. The setting is a wonderful idea (how many games are set in a national park!) and the devs almost get it right. Some of the scenery is beautiful for sure, but I'm surprised we didn't get any big waterfalls or cliffs. There's a lake, a creek (the nicest area, in my opinion), and a canyon. But the rest is pretty much plain ol' wilderness. You can't kayak, no fun rock climbing ... there's not much to do while exploring, truthfully. Just about everything you want to see is seen in the regular story, so you're really best off just doing as the game says and following that linearity. You aren't really able to or meant to take in the sights and sounds; the game turns into a thriller within the first 30 minutes of gameplay. Again, I actually like what the game becomes but it might have been more powerful if it took its time and let us settle in.

As a final criticism about presentation, man I am just not a big fan of Chris Remo (who also did Gone Home, another game whose soundtrack sucked). Like Outer Wilds, the game is quiet for most of it, and then turns the music on when something impactful happens. This is the right approach, but like, compare this soundtrack to Outer Wilds. It gets blown out the water. The music is plain, unoriginal, and doesn't even follow the themes or feel of the game. There is maaaybe two tracks (Thorofare Hike & Prologue) which are passable; the rest are wholly forgettable. Games like this live and die based on their music and his stuff just isn't that good.

Okay so that's a boatload of negatives. I must have hated the game right? Why am I still recommending it? Well, because Firewatch still succeeds at the core of what it's trying to do, and the story and message are powerful enough to make this game well worth your time. This is amplified by fantastic voice performances by the 2 main characters; just excellent stuff. The game makes you care for and relate to them quite well, and at times I was shocked at how much it had me invested. I guarantee you there will be a point where you won't be able to put the game down and you'll want to see how it all ends. It was to the point that when the game reached its climax, I kept getting lost because my mind was racing thinking about the story and I couldn't focus on navigating.

I'll have to spoiler text the rest of the discussion about the story, so beware: [spoiler]I felt SO deflated about that ending. It took me some time, but slowly I've come to realize that's the point: Delilah and Henry felt just as disappointed. Their voice acting near the end is perfect. Henry wants there to be more to this than the sad tale it becomes. He wants this mystery to never end and even though he feels guilt about it, he wants to meet Delilah and indulge in his new romance. The game gets you to a raging peak of emotional investment, and then boldly and deliberately pops that balloon. You're -supposed- to be disappointed and to actually aim for the player to feel that in a video game of all things is something I can't applaud enough. Bravo.

Ultimately, the game is about escapism and running away from your problems. Delilah and Ned have the same issues as Henry does: they don't want to face the music of their lives. Obviously this is deeply relatable, as that's usually what all of us do when we play video games, but it makes the final helicopter scene so much better. We never even got to see Delilah. She rejects us (a girl rejecting you in a video game, how's that!) and we have to sit on the fact that we were just a summer distraction for her. Henry goes into his helicopter and thinks the exact same thing the player does: "welp now time to go back to my normal, painful life I guess." It's that connection to Henry that shocked me about the game the most: when he felt paranoid, I felt paranoid. When he felt guilty about flirting with Delilah, I felt it too. Just an excellent job here.

Lots of fantastic, memorable moments strewn throughout. Infiltrating Wapiti, finding the boy's body, the final escape as the forest burns around you, the girls at the lake, seeing the shadowy figure of Ned for the first time, and my favorite of all: getting "cold-♥♥♥♥♥♥" by Ned. My jar was agape when that happened; that moment really heightens the stakes and makes the paranoia justified throughout. All of these scenarios are incredibly well crafted and acted so I've got to give the writers credit. This is good stuff.[/spoiler]

When it comes to Firewatch, there's a lot to say. Let's start with the bad. Firstly, this game is about quality over quantity. You can tell from the get go that the devs and voice talent were all very passionate about this project. However, the game is short. It took me about 6 hours (at a very casual pace) to finish the story and I was left desperate for more. Unfortunately with the studio's acquisition by our lord and saviors Valve it doesn't seem that anything in the form of dlc or the release of the game's spiritual successor (In the Valley of the Gods) are coming anytime within our lifetimes. And as for bugs I only ran into one or two throughout my entire play through. Nothing game breaking but it did briefly break my immersion at a pretty critical moment. 

Now on to the good (and there is A LOT of good). The story is gripping, mature, and REAL. I don't think I have ever come across more convincing characters in a game or piece of media before. Henry and Delilah felt real and their relationship developed in a way that felt refreshingly natural and their dialogue is written and delivered so damn well. The art style captures the tone perfectly and in a way that helps keep things lighthearted and removed from reality yet also immersive. I do also agree with the popular sentiment that almost any view in this game is screenshot worthy and the in-game picture mode is so well done that when my pictures were shown during the end credits it really felt like they were MY photos. The sound design is also top notch. I played with my surround sound system and I really felt like I was in the heart of the wilderness. 

If you're looking for a great narrative experience, Firewatch is for you. I picked it up at full price and don't regret a single penny.

This game has been on my pile of shame but finally I got around actually playing it and completed it within less than 5 hrs.

Things I liked:
- The story premise is engaging and deals with serious topics that do not feel video-game-y at all. At the same time it's also not artsy fartsy. I cared for my character from the start, so that was great.
- I liked the graphics even though for some reason I thought it looked better in screenshots than in motion.
- Both Henry and Delilah are wonderfully written and voiced characters.

Things I didn't like so much:
- I get it that this game is about telling a story, but in my opinion, it could have been a bit more of a game still in places. There's literally not a single choice of consequence in here, and that is a wasted opportunity in my opinion. For example the dialog choices seem to be mostly interchangable with no actual impact on how the conversation will continue. I understand that turning the story into a dynamically forking beast was probably beyond what a small team could have achieved with the resources available to them, but at least being able to influence my relationship to Delilah would have been cool.
- Navigating the world at night was annoying at times. Also the fact that possible interactions with objects are not displayed when you have the map up.
- The resolution of the "mystery plot" was a  bit of a letdown to me.
- I would have liked the game give a bit more spotlight to how wildfires are threatening nature and civilization as there were only very few very subtle hints to the increase in wildfires being connected to man-made climate change. I do think the devs had an opinion  here but chose not to advertise it. I think they should have. Feel free to step on people's toes. At the same time I also understand that this would have been a thin red line as having to much of an agenda in here would alter the games overall tone in a way that might not be aligned with the team's creative vision.

Overall I do recommend Firewatch. It's a relaxed story experience like an interactive movie. It has an interesting story that always left me wanting to know how it continues, even though I was not completely happy with the resolution. The characters of Henry and Delilah are top notch and make this game worth playing all by themselves.

I am actually astounded that I didn't like this game. I usually like narrative driven stuff, don't mind a slow pace, and I enjoy exploration and this game has a lot of good reviews, but to me it's just wasn't that great.

First of all the story starts painfully slow. Not much happens at the beginning and you're just sent from one spot to another doing boring stuff. I don't mind taking my time, if the game at least hints at some kind of mystery or plot element that can keep me intrigued until the story picks up pace, but here it takes quite a long while for the story to even emerge. Until that time you're interest hangs only on the backstory and dialogue between two main characters, which is - to be fair - decently written and very well acted, but didn't really make me invested for a long while in the beginning. 

After some time, when the story actually takes over, the game starts getting good. There are different threads to the plot, and it all starts to get pretty mysterious. Sadly this does not last long, as, whithout getting into spoilers, all those threads end up not leading to anything actually interesting. All this potentially cool build-up leads to a very dissapointing conclusion. The main plot twist is really surprisingly stupid, considering pretty decent overall writing, so my guess is it was done purposfully. 

Not long after the plot twist the game kinda... just ends. There is no satisfying conclusion to the characters, no interesting result, no one seemed to learn anything, no one ended up better, or worse, and not that much has basically changed, as the game just kinda faded away to the credits. 

A lot of people seem to really like the ending as well as the whole game. I read opinions praising it as brave, daring to go against the players expectations and so on. And maybe it is, but what does this bravery result in? What unexpected lesson have we learned? What brave statement did it actually make? I just don't get the artistic intent behind it. In the end I just kinda felt everyone's time was wasted - mine, as well as the characters.  

While there were some things in the game that I liked, like voice acting, dialogues, environment design, the overall feeling I was left with was negative, and so I will give it a negative score. I would probably reconsider if the game had a lower rating, but it's doing so good, that it probably won't do any harm, and I just wanted to share my opinion.

I played Firewatch at the end of June one year - oblivious of anything about the game, yet curious to see what it was about.

So it's a first-person wilderness mystery, but also a period piece, set in the late 80s. This really brings the great outdoors into focus - no digital gadgets to cloud the senses, just warm days and cool nights in a place removed from too much human intervention. Appreciating nature is possible at every step as you might imagine, but the game keeps a firm pace at developing the central mystery and it doesn't shy from the story at all. The plot itself is not overdone as to make it implausible, but it is also far from banal. Personally I found it wholly gripping!

However, the most amazing thing was the pretty wide range of possible emotional development (the characters and you) that makes the game breathe a different way for different playthroughs. The game presents you with dialog options that let you clue the game in on what you think is going on, and it goes to develop some aspects of what you believe or want to believe. The voice acting is truly superb and lends itself a lot to achieving this.

In fact, that's the real parallel between this game and actually being out in the thick wilds: it can be a magical experience that fills you with wonder for the natural world. It could be soothing and let you achieve that profound calm you can only get right there. But it could also activate those little primordial fears of things moving in the dark, little tiny sparks of an unreasonable fright that make you ask yourself: am I just imagining things, or is there something really out to get me this time? That's the fundamental excellence to this game: it relies on letting your imagination fill in the blanks. This is also why I feel Firewatch gives a different tone to the plot depending on the relationship you have with the outdoors.

Firewatch was, for me, an unforgettable experience. I would recommend it to anyone who thinks following a moderately paced mystery through the woods sounds like a great idea.

Firewatch is an interactive story where you play Henry, a man who’s trying to escape his current
life by becoming a Fire Watcher out in the Rocky Mountains. During the course of the game you
make friends with Delilah, a fellow Firewatcher who keeps you company throughout the game.
The gameplay mostly consists of exploring the forest and talking with Delilah as the story
unfolds and you unlock tools to help you explore more of the forest.

The scenery is beautiful, there are several sprawling landscapes and areas to explore in the
forest. The interactions between Henry and Delilah are very charming and I really enjoyed their
chemistry together. The story has a strong beginning and I quickly became invested in the
characters and the story. However, the second half of the game really fell apart for me. I feel like
they tried doing too much at once as more story threads began appearing and I felt like the
writers were trying to do too much with the story. The major climax of the story was lackluster as
it feels like all the plot threads get quickly wrapped up in a short time and leave an unsatisfying
conclusion. However, I really did like how the story concluded with Delilah and Henry, as it
wasn't something I was expecting, but felt like the best way to end their story.

Overall I liked this game, the world was beautiful, I liked the characters and even though the
climax of the story wasn’t my favorite, I liked several parts of the story. If you’re a fan of
interactive stories I’d give this one a try.

First, let’s start with the game’s positives. Firewatch is visually beautiful; almost every frame looks like a painting. Bright hues of red and orange, blue and purple jump out of the screen, creating a visually stimulating experience that players will not soon forget. This visual beauty allows for a more rewarding form of exploration as you traverse the national park. While the gameplay is straightforward – you mostly wander around the national park, talking to your partner over the radio, fixing a few puzzles - it lends itself to the game’s casual, relaxing tone. Instead, in the absence of a gripping gameplay sequence, you become enraptured with the game’s captivating, emotional storyline of loss and isolation. The relationship between the two characters is a fun dynamic from which the mystery unfolds, and is easily the game’s strongest part. These emotions are only strengthened and refined by the game’s exceptional soundtrack, which is one of the best I’ve heard in a video game.
   
There are, however, a few drawbacks that undermine Firewatch greatly. For a game that focuses on the interactive storytelling, there is a disappointing lack of choice in the dialogue tree. No matter what option you decide, the game’s progression isn’t massively affected, with only a few exceptions making a genuine difference. Firewatch also has a short runtime. Although it’s not short enough to not justify the purchase, it does leave you yearning for more.
 
However, most of these weaknesses could have been ignored if it wasn’t for the ending, which is easily the game’s weakest aspect. The language of the characters themselves seemed hollow—poetic, perhaps, but insubstantial. Although the cast of clearly talented actors made the most of the provided text, the ambiguity of their lines gave them no space to thrive, instead floating in the unfocusedness of it all. Uncomfortably open-ended, Firewatch seemed to ache for more substantial grounding, either to cement itself firmly as an interactive game or to delve deeper into the issues that it only touches upon.

Overall, I give Firewatch a 7/10. It's an enjoyable, relaxing experience that should be brought when on sale.

I had played 𝙁𝙞𝙧𝙚𝙬𝙖𝙩𝙘𝙝 a few years back, outside of Steam, and now I decided to replay it because I have fond memories of it.

𝙁𝙞𝙧𝙚𝙬𝙖𝙩𝙘𝙝 is a very emotional game. The atmosphere in this game is amazing, and the game looks beautiful. The voice acting is fantastic too, and it really drives this game, and the plot, forward — it is a major component of the game due to the fact you are alone in the wilderness, talking to someone else through a walkie-talkie, and most of the story is conveyed through these conversations.

The soundtrack is also a strong point of the game.

In terms of gameplay, it is very basic. You simply walk around, use a map and a compass and you occasionally use some special tools. All you do is walk, run and interact with objects. 

The main focus of 𝙁𝙞𝙧𝙚𝙬𝙖𝙩𝙘𝙝 is its story, and more importantly, its characters. This is a game that stuck with me ever since I first played it, and upon replaying it I realized why. It takes place in a heartwarming setting, with relatable characters that are written to feel real, and have real human conversations, hopes, dreams and flaws. In conclusion, 𝙁𝙞𝙧𝙚𝙬𝙖𝙩𝙘𝙝 is a beautiful game with an interesting plot and very well written dialogue and characters, and I definitely recommend it as it is a very introspective piece of media.

This is the game equivalent of one of those films that you don't feel the need to watch ever again, but which still move you ages after you saw them. It is sad and at the same time very life-affirming.
[list]
[*] The voice acting and character building is great. Without this, I have the feeling that Firewatch would be nothing.
[*] The character and object animations are solid and authentic.
[*] The map is beautiful. It's also large enough to make certain tasks feel authentically like a trek, but not so large that it becomes frustrating.
[*] The balance between tension and relaxation is carefully maintained. While the threat and mystery ramps up towards the end, you are allowed time to be alone with your thoughts and admire the views even as[spoiler]you're running to escape the wildfire.[/spoiler]
[*] While the opening is a bit slow, the plot progression is generally well paced. Fast-forwarding through days at certain points is a nice trick which adds temporal and emotional scale.
[*] The way dialogue works feels very natural. Your character's isolation combined with the walkie-talkie device really makes you weigh your responses in a way that you might not otherwise. Silence sometimes feels like the right choice, not a missed opportunity.
[*] I genuinely had to steel myself before some of the mystery scenes. The soundtrack does a good job of making the usually benign environment seem host to malevolent forces.
[*] You're never sure who, or what evidence, to trust. Even when you're sure something is a red herring, there are enough loose ends and allusions to withheld knowledge to keep you paranoid.
[*] The end credits really got me. Especially because[spoiler]at the beginning I used the camera to capture pretty landscapes, but as the story progressed, I increasingly used it to document evidence I thought I'd need to solve the crime. When the contents of the reel were revealed, going back through my own loss of innocence to the "before" scenes of the tragedy was very affecting.[/spoiler]
[*]I was also moved by[spoiler]seeing the contents of Delilah's watchtower[/spoiler]and felt that[spoiler]never meeting her[/spoiler]was a fitting conclusion to the story.
[*] A walk in the sunshine while listening to [i]Ol' Shoshone[/i] is one of those rare game experiences that has to be good for the soul.
[/list]

One of the top best video games, walking simulators, and phenomenal experiences of all time. Everything about this game is phenomenal. From the text-based adventure at the beginning to exploring the forest and finding secrets to Delilah's amazing dialogue, this game is so freaking good. As with all games of this type, it is always best to go in with ZERO knowledge. Don't read the description or look at the screenshots or reviews for longer than 1 second. I went into this game thinking it was going to be an actual park-ranger simulator, but that is NOT what this is AT ALL, and that is a good thing because what it really is is a lot better. The game starts off making you think that's what it will be but quickly diverges your expectations. The text-based adventure at the beginning was really really impactful and emotional especially when you are not expecting the story and twist. It was so good I would actually say it's worth the proce of admission alone. If the text adventure was all the game was, it would still be phenomenal. I would love more games like it. Exploring the forest and searching for anything and everything is so much fun. There are so many secrets to find off the beaten path and optional secret dialogue with Delilah to find and every bit of it is so good. The dialogue is the absolute best thing about this game. This game has some of the best and most realistic and compelling dialogue in any game ever made. Whenever Delilah and Henry are talking it's sooooooo good. Not only is their dialogue extremely well written and voice-acted, but the dialogue CHOICES are the icing on the cake. I did some counting and there are at least 6 or 7 different versions of Henry that you can play as and Delilah responds differently to each one. You can be happy joyful Henry, angry and depressed Henry, or silent Henry who is shy and reserved and rarely ever speaks and they are all consistent. The role-playing is very real and very good in this game. It is very fun to play the game multiple times as different versions of Henry making different choices. The dialogue in this game is actually some of the most REALISTIC I have ever seen in gaming, Henry and Delilah feel like such real people having real conversations, and the way their relationship forms and progresses is so good. All I'll say about the ending without spoiling is that I cried a lot because I really didn't want the game to end. The developers of this did such an amazing job with this phenomenal experience, thank you very much for this amazing game.

If the question was, "did you like this 'game'?" - would you have the time to read my answer?
Firewatch is not a game. Though, dubbed as a walking simulator, I've played games that build this aspect amongst other mechanics so you get the harmonious merger of meditative walking mixed with rigorous combat and puzzle play. Firewatch is void of any challenge other than exploring your surroundings and holding a conversation with your only lifeline in this wilderness. 

Without a means to fail and only wander aimlessly, Firewatch has no real objective other than to piece together a mystery that I was not invested in solving. The title of the media is "Firewatch," I was here to watch for fires. Instead, I kept hiking looped trails while wishing I was actually camping in the woods. 

Even with the graphics jacked up to "ultra," I was left unimpressed with what I saw. There were moments of simulated beauty walking through meadows framed with sunbeams illuminating dust motes and cotton floating through the air. But then I was met with flat textures scaling down escarpments.

Firewatch received a lot of hype since its release in 2016. Maybe I had to be there early on to get caught up in the wave of excitement for this IP but other games, from the same time, offer much more in the way of story, characterization, world-building, combat, puzzles, and graphics. To put it plainly, I was disappointed with Firewatch.

Ultimately, Firewatch is interactive media closer to a movie than it is a game. It's simplistic in nature, easy  to follow - if you know how to use a map a compass - and offers a limited escape for the gentle gamer. It is for them that I would recommend this "game." 

For the rest, go play Death Stranding; it'll change your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ life.

Firewatch is a "walking simulator." That is, it's a game where most of the gameplay is just walking around from point A to point B (like Dear Esther or Gone Home). The graphics are quite pretty, the dialogue is well-written, and the voice acting is very high quality. But for a game that has so few gameplay elements, it's a little hard to believe how badly they were implemented. I should not have to point my cursor at a one-inch segment of a rope to be given the cue to climb down. It should not be that hard to set a book back down on a table without throwing it like a monkey. Not to mention that at one point, my walkie-talkie just decided to turn invisible. These seem like minor gripes for any other game, but if the entire point of the game is immersion in the created environment (and that there is literally no other gameplay I could critique) then these are major pain points.

I could forgive these things quite easily if the story was compelling enough. I did not find that to be the case. Although the characters are well-written and well-acted, I did not feel that they matured, developed, or learned in anyway throughout the game. In addition, the events that occur throughout the game felt so disjointed from the main character's struggles, I could not find the relevance of any of it. It's true to life in that sense; things happen and there's often no meaning that connect events. But that's not what I expect out of a written piece of art. All in all, the questions that arise from the game all seem to lead to unsatisfying and bland answers -- that is, if any answer is given at all.

Amid all the serious topics that are covered in this game, I couldn't help but constantly look at my in-game body and feel like I'm Wreck-It Ralph.

A game about guilt, escaping, and self forgiveness.

Maybe it's only my interpretation, but this game pretty accurately depicted "life" for me in only 4 hours of play:

Something devastating happened in the past, it may or may not be your fault, but you were haunted by it. So you escaped. You know maybe it's not the best course of action but somehow you did. You felt guilt, for choosing to escape, or for the horrible thing in the past, or both.

In the new environment, you were alone, you felt like an alien, you felt you shouldn't be here. You were afraid of talking about your past with others, but deep down inside, you felt the urge to speak out. Fortunately, you encountered someone. You never met her, you only talked with her from time to time on radio, alongside work conversations. Only bit by bit, but you started to talk about the past that has been haunting you, you started to feel you found someone who understood you.

Life didn't become easy on you even in the new environment. You got new kinds of problems to deal with, new people to cause you trouble. Problems started to pile up and mysteries got more and more serious. You tried to solve the problems and clear the mysteries, only to find yourself in deeper water. You started to doubt if you have lost your mind, if anything is real.

In the end, everybody was on the same boat. We wanted to escape from the past that keeps haunting us, we felt exhausted just to deal with the current, we wanted to talk about our experience yet we fear not being understood. The few words made out of our mouths just felt so pale and tasteless.

So what should we do then? The game didn't tell me, I don't even know for myself. Maybe I should make peace with my past trauma, maybe I should focus on things at hand, maybe I should move on. Maybe, this is just what life is.


「罪悪感」、「逃げ」、「自分を許す」がキーワードのゲーム。

私だけの解釈かもしれないが、このゲームはたった四時間のプレーで「人生」を割と精確に表現してくれた：

恐ろしい事が過去に起きた。それは自分のせいかもしれないし、そうでないかもしれない。それにかかわらず、その過去が枷となった。だから逃げた。その行動が正しいかどうかは分からないが、とにかく逃げた。罪悪感を感じた、その原因は、逃げたことなのか、過去の事なのかは分からない。

逃げ先に、孤独を感じた、疎しさを感じた、自分がここに来るべきではなかったと感じた。他人に自分の過去を触れることが怖かった。でも心のどこかで、その過去を語りたいとも思った。幸いに、出会いがあった。面と向ず、ただ電波を通じて話すことしかなかった。それでも、少しずつだが、自分の過去を語り始めた、理解者があったと思い始めた。

逃げ先でも、人生は容易いものではなかった。新しい問題が起きるし、新しい人が面倒事をもたらして来る。問題は問題を呼ぶ、なぞも深まっていく。それを解決する事をを試みたが、もっと深く厄介事に飲み込まれつつあった。自分が正気かと疑った、周りのすべてが真実かどうかを疑った。

結局、みんな似たようなものだった。過去の枷から逃げたかった、ただ今を生きることでくたびれた、自分を語りたいが、理解されないことが怖かった。口に出る言葉は、無味乾燥に感じた。

それで、何をすればいいわけ？ゲームはそれを教えなかった、私自身にも分からない。過去のトラウマと和解するべきかもしれない、今に集中するべきかもしれない、過去をもう振り返らないことにするべきかもしれない。これが、「人生」というものかもしれない。

[h1]A Talking Simulator[/h1]

Firewatch is a great, albeit short, experience. There aren't many characters, but the few that there are all feel believable and, in a way, real. The best example of that are, of course, Henry and Delilah, which are incredibly well-acted and well-written, to the point where their conversations feel like they have no script sometimes. 

The story has many elements, notably isolation, loneliness, guilt, paranoia, and mental health, and all of them work together perfectly to provide a fantastic narrative experience which is unlike most games in its own special way. You will feel many different things as you play, and you will really get to connect with Henry, the protagonist, to the point where it feels like you become him for the duration of the game. 

The music is fitting and well-composed, and the graphics and visuals are outstanding; beautiful vistas everywhere will make you feel incredibly immersed in this virtual world. The gameplay is somewhat minimal: you won't be killing hordes of enemies or anything like that, but it's not like the game needs that kind of thing.

[b]If you want a good story with great characters, exploration and environments, this is the game for you. If you particularly want to hear two characters speak to each other in a way that feels completely believable, with dialogue choices that affect the outcome of the story, then this is the game for you, too[/b].

[h1]The Short Version:[/h1]

Sometimes in order to figure something out, you have to stop thinking about it for a while. Firewatch takes this mantra to heart. A beautiful wilderness, two fire lookouts, and a walkie talkie. It might appear simple at first, but underneath its exterior lies a compelling journey that will have you hooked from start to finish. 

While the trail may not end on a high note, the path leading up to it is filled with plenty of memorable moments that make it a must-buy for anybody looking for a great narrative experience.
