[h1]Escaping Isn’t Always Something Bad…[/h1]

Firewatch is a first-person, narrative adventure game taking place on a stunning stretch of nature somewhere in the Wyoming wilderness. You play as Hank Henry, a newly designated fire lookout assigned to an outpost in the area, who’s also trying to flee a troubled past.

The introduction to the story is presented through a visual novel-esque format, allowing you to choose between two different paths which ultimately lead to the same destination. This section is interspersed with brief gameplay segments of Henry making his way to his new home away from home. 

Through this beginning sequence, we learn that he has a wife, Julia, who he met at a bar a long time ago. You witness their life together, through the good, the bad, and eventually the ugly. Before long, Julia is diagnosed with dementia, and soon her condition spirals out of control, with her family taking her back to her home in Australia to look after her.

Instead of sorting himself out and going to Australia to see her, he joins the firewatch service, placing him at Two Forks Lookout. This introduction is great for a couple of reasons. Firstly, it immediately sets the tone of the story, and gives you a pretty good grasp of the topics it’s going to cover. Secondly, it quickly provides valuable insight into who Henry is as a character, as well as his motivations for being where he is.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2741412446

In all honesty, I could immediately relate to and sympathise with Henry. The game all but subtly plays into the escapist fantasy that I believe a lot of people share, - I know I certainly do - which is why I found myself fully invested in the narrative very early on. Sometimes a problem will feel so big, that all you’ll want to do is walk away; a choice that everyone has a right to. This is one of Firewatch’s most alluring facets, and it’s executed to such an exceptional degree. 

Despite being in the wilderness, you’re not quite alone. Enter Delilah, a knowledgeable, experienced fire lookout stationed in a nearby outpost, who acts as Henry’s supervisor. Through walkie-talkie communication, you’ll be reporting to her about pretty much anything of interest. This more or less sums up the first couple hours. It’s a slow start, but it serves as a way for the two of them to form a connection, of which is one of my favourite aspects of the game as a whole.

The authenticity of these characters cannot be understated. They feel like real people, thanks to their stellar writing and voice acting performances. Their motives are genuine and consistent, and even their smallest interactions feel like they have merit. It’s something that stays continuously great from start to finish. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2743822963

Which is why it really annoys me that the narrative ends the way it does. I don’t have a problem with the content of the conclusion, but the pace of it is completely out of left field. It’s a contrast that painfully conflicts with everything that came before it, and that I cannot help but think was written in a rushed manner.

How you experience this sequence can vary based on what dialogue options you pick. While Firewatch is very much linear, and does not stray from its set path at all, these options can give a sense of how Henry develops over time, but with the ones I picked, it didn’t really feel like he learnt anything at all after this. If given just a few more scenes, I’m certain that the ending could’ve felt less ham-fisted than it currently does. 

I will say this, it doesn’t ruin what comes before, at least not for me. The story as a whole has a lot to remember. It has charm, wit, intrigue, mystery, and suspense. I just wish there was more at the end. 

[h1]When the Sun is Down You Can Just… Get Lost...[/h1]

While the narrative may have a lot of depth, the gameplay has less to get sucked into, but I don’t mean that in a negative sense; quite the contrary actually. What appears superficial at first slowly begins to feel natural and fitting with the style of game it is.

In blanket terms, Firewatch is a walking simulator that provides you with a map and compass, then tells you where to go, but leaves it up to you to figure out how to get to your destination. Since you’re a fire watcher, you’re expected to maintain the area, making sure everything’s in good shape and isn’t on the verge of catching fire. 

You’ll sometimes be given a hint on how to get to a certain place, - go back to X, then head east - but it’s up to you to figure out the rest, and I loved that. Plotting and navigating your way around an area makes each trek feel engaging and challenging in their own way. It feels much less like a walking simulator in that respect.    

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2743817698

It helps that the place you are looking after is a treat for the eyes. The map is large and full of vistas to marvel at; screenshot lovers are in for a luxury here. The game’s fantastic use of colour makes each location you travel to a sight to behold.

Despite the narrative occasionally taking a creepy turn or two, exploring the wilderness is a rather relaxing activity. There’s so much to find, with plenty of things to talk to Delilah about, whether it be items in supply caches from previous lookouts, or various points of interest that have history or other interesting facts. It’s not something that will appeal to everyone, but I really liked it.   

If I had to make one slight complaint about the environment, it is that there isn’t really that much living in it. Where are all the animals? From memory, I found a deer, a raccoon, a tortoise, three ducks, and a few butterflies. Sometimes you can hear things rummaging through the bushes, but you can’t see anything. Just came across as strange.

[h1]In Conclusion[/h1]

Sitting at the heart of Firewatch is a deeply personal tale containing many relatable aspects. Despite having a bright, luscious appearance, it is not a happy experience, but it is filled with moments that will undoubtedly put a smile on your face.

While it didn’t conclude on the highest peak, the journey to it is something I wholeheartedly recommend. Its memorable characters, beautiful set pieces and charming gameplay make this a must-have for those looking for a great narrative experience. It’s a game that will stick with me for a while.

Firewatch is an okay walking sim.  It makes you get lost in the wilderness of Wyoming, and makes me want to get into hiking the Rockies.  The game play is mostly walking from point A to point B, with story happening over the radio.  The conversations build up the characters and introduce topics involving topics that older people might start running into in their 40s.  This part of the story doesn't go into much detail past the early half, it would have been better if the story did focus on the harder topics that we deal with as we get older.  I would have loved if the game punched you with those hard questions that would keep me up at night.  Sadly it never took off past introducing us to these points in the story.  Game play wise it was a walking sim that did suffer from backtracking but overall was really lean and I finished it in 3.3 hours. 

 I would recommend if its on sale, you don't know the story, and you like walking sims.  If not or want a better experience I would much more recommend getting into hiking.  I should do more of that myself.

Firewatch is a lot of things -- first and foremost of which is that it's hard to describe. From a purely mechanical standpoint, the gameplay is largely limited to that of a walking simulator. You traverse the area you've been set to care for and slowly uncover more of the story through your explorations and through conversations between your character and one another. It's a straightforward (and in some reviewers' minds, disappointing) gameplay system. But I don't think just talking about what you [i]do[/i] in the game does it justice. There are moments of sadness, or real tension and anticipation, or joy and humor as you climb, hike, and learn more about yourself and the world. The environment is absolutely gorgeous, too, and I could have walked around those paths for ages.

Even with all of those strengths, however, Firewatch is ultimately colored for me by its end. For those who were touched by the answer to the mystery, or who enjoyed speculating about what came after the credits rolled, good for you! I'm glad it worked for you. I wanted it to work for me. [spoilers]Unfortunately, the uncertainty and tension built in the first parts were compelling enough that learning that it all had such a mundane explanation was a huge let down. It's poignant, true. There's something to be said for a game that reminds us that sometimes, there isn't any conspiracy or secret on behind the scenes to give meaning and reason to senseless tragedies. It's just how life goes. But I, personally, play video games for a sense of magic: for the fantasies and escapism. No matter how much I appreciate the poignancy of the end, it doesn't quite sit right.[/spoilers] My feelings on the end aside, you should take the chance yourself to discover Firewatch for what it is. It doesn't shine for everyone, but it's worth giving it the chance to shine for you.

Firewatch is a walking simulator that is extremely atmospheric, not for everyone, but if that hook gets you in, I cannot tell you more without potentially spoiling the pleasure. 

All that I can say is that for me, it was worth it.

[h1]INTRO[/h1]

This is probably one of the games that disappointed me the most expecting very little from it.
I assumed this was one of those atmospheric games that it's better to go blind. I liked the aesthetics that I saw in "covers" and some screenshots so I didn't do much research. I wasn't hoping for a great story or fun and deep gameplay. All I asked for was a good atmosphere/ambient in the game.
I got none of it, it's just a walking simulator with only one gimmick: the conversations between the two characters.

[h1]REASONS WHY I DON'T RECOMMEND THE GAME[/h1]

- Gameplay is dull. It's a "fake" open world in the sense that seems like you're in a big forest to explore but in reality the map is divided in areas connected by pathways which makes the exploration really tedious. Mostly because you have to orient yourself since the looks of the graphics are so samey and when you pick your direction you often reach a cliff/rubble/vegetation which blocks your way and you have to make a detour to find the path supposed to lead you where you want to go (which might be disorienting at times because you'll have to go in the opposite direction to reach it). All you do is basically that: find places by walking around, use a walkie talkie to talk with another character and open boxes that all have the same password for the lock. No actual gameplay or puzzles other than that... Walking and talking.
- Characters are unlikable, at least to me. They're really bland and the dialogs can be extremely cringey at times. It's almost like an NPC writing a story about an NPC. Twice as uninteresting.
- The story is nonsensical. To make it mildly interesting they have to deceive you. Even if I don't recommend the game I won't spoil the plot, since it's all the game has, just in case people still buys the game regardless. But let's just say that this is not some deep introspection inducing game like Inmost or a game with great narrative like FAR: Lone Sails where the story tells itself within the background. It's just uninspired and mundane gibberish.
- The graphics are very disappointing. I really believed that, worst case scenario, I wold enjoy a nice game world even if everything else sucked like some reviews I read. That I could explore the game nicely and enjoy the artistic value of it. But it didn't capture that well. Games like Alan Wake have very enjoyable scenarios in the woods. Hell, even some free asset games are more interesting visually than this one. This is what really drove me to not recommend the game. It's visually tiring. [h1]Story[/h1]
The story begins with a short intro, which shows you how (and why) you became a lookout. After a long sleep, you wake up to your first day at work. Delilah, your supervisor, gives you a first task that isn't that interesting -- deal with a bunch of teens messing with stuff they shouldn't. [h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The map isn't that huge, but there are quite a few places you can discover besides the story. One of the main things in this game is manipulating with items. However, most of the collected items, that are not required to continue in the story, don't have any use, so what's the point of picking them up?

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The environment is absolutely relaxing, filled with pleasant colors and sounds of nature. If you are into making nice screenshots, this game will make it easy for you.

[h1]Soundtrack[/h1]
The music is fantastic, but it doesn't play all the time and you can't turn on any background music. It only plays when something story-related occurs, which is a shame.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
I wish the game had better ending and there was more stuff to do after completing the story, but I'm still going to give it solid 8/10.

the visuals are absolutely beautiful, the music is a treat, and the story is...well, i shouldn't spoil anything about it, but suffice it to say i felt pretty much every single emotion there is. i was initially skeptical and put off by the fact that it's tagged "walking simulator", and it does involve a lot of walking, but a lot of care was put into the landscape and i swear, every single frame of that game is a work of art. i was never bored or impatient while waking through the forest, and i often ended up taking the long way around to destinations just so i could experience more of the gorgeous landscape.

talking to Delilah was a joy too. you're given a lot of agency in your dialogue options, and the natural conversation, occasional small talk, and the superb voice acting made me feel like i was talking not to a bunch of scripted dialogue, but a real living person. the soundtrack is very well timed and heightens and deepens the emotional highs and lows of the game, perfectly dovetailing with the story. even though the folk-inflected guitar music isn't usually my thing, i could listen to the soundtrack over and over and never get tired of it.

the one difficulty i had with the game is that i got stuck on a few parts, but that can only be credited to my own non-awareness of my surroundings. so if you get stuck, take whatever items you see and leave no stone unturned, and you'll find a solution quickly.

long story short, this is a must-play. recommendation: get this while it's 50% off or more. $20 is a bit much for a three-hour game, but it's well worth $10.

"You can't just run away from your problems and life is boring". There, I saved you whatever you were going to spend on this. Except you can totally run away from your problems, but then you'd have to wait for the sequel: Watchfire. 

Firewatch is an interesting journey that, little by little, explains to you why you shouldn't care about it. In the end, it boils down to being an on-rails walking simulator with boring characters that you spent 4 hours on, left loose ends, and led you down false paths, touting red herrings as intentional game design. No choices you make in the game matter and it's supposed to be some philosophical reflection of yourself, which just doesn't work out. While with most games of this type you have memorable moments or satisfying stories that dilute boring gameplay, Firewatch is 100% boring all the way through. The way you flip between "days" is also disorienting, and it reduces the story to a specific set of events that discourages exploration  (Not that you can do much exploration when every other tiny rock is an impassable obstacle) and doesn't make you feel like you've spent X days in the wild.

I see some praising the graphics: If you are impressed by the graphics in this game, you should honestly try going outside. I'd rather recommend you go on a 4-hour hike than play this, ever. The graphics are simple and washed-out, and objects are common nature/household items and moderately detailed.

I wouldn't even recommend this game even if it was free and regret it as a purchase and time investment.

Edit: I should add, after looking some stuff up after I finished the game... and the (what would be) most memorable parts of the game seem missable. You can miss central parts of the story just by playing the game as intended. However, even *with* those moments I'm sure the game would still not feel worth it. So just take that in, if you explore you'll waste time finding nothing interesting, but there's a tiny chance you find the fun stuff in the game. It's like gambling, but with your time...

[h1] An Unforgettable Experience [/h1]

It's a game to play with on your own, with your thoughts, and maybe even Delilah.

Firewatch is best experienced blind; no spoilers, no walkthroughs, just slow-paced and methodical exploration across the vast Shoshone National Park. It's a rare find, and a must to try out yourself. What enamored me was just how well Firewatch brings nature to your fingers, it's honestly convinced me that maybe hiking wouldn't be too bad of an outing if it looked [i] that [/i] beautiful. Beset in the middle of nowhere, Henry dawdles across the wilderness doing odd jobs for his boss, whom you learn to treat as a friend amid the bellowing silence of being alone in the woods. Firewatch is honestly just such a nice change of pace from the games I'm used to: games trying so hard to keep your attention by throwing things at you one after the other to no end, no different from the fast pace of real life, at least here in the city. So I really appreciated the unique experience Firewatch provided me, and I'm certain you could too.

[h1] A Story About Responsibility [/h1]

Shoshone National Park is rich with backstory, you'll find notes here and there from previous rangers and fire lookouts as you explore and they really sell this game for me. There are mysteries, surprises, and neat little things that branch out from the main narrative, they helped make Firewatch a very memorable game.

Don't expect to go haywire, and don't go into this game expecting to be all sprinting around the woods. Take a step back, relax, and enjoy this game, maybe have a diet coke while playing.

This game is a solid 10/10 from me. If you are interested enough to start watching a playthrough of the game to see if it's worth your time, I highly recommend you just buy the game for yourself instead. I made the mistake of having the story spoiled for me and I can only imagine how much better my experience would have been if I hadn't watched a playthrough first. That being said, playing the game somehow made the story feel [b][i]more[/i][/b] captivating and relatable than it was when watching the playthrough and experiencing the story that way.

[b]Story and Storytelling: [/b]This is the reason anyone would want to play this game in the first place... Firewatch's story is perfect, or at least nearly perfect. It feels believable and it's told in a way that makes it feel relatable so much so that I teared up a bit by the end of the game. (This is a commendable feat as I rarely get emotionally attached to characters in fiction so I almost never really cry at books, films, games, and other forms of media)

[b]Gameplay: [/b]There isn't much to Firewatch when it comes to gameplay, but that's a good thing. Having minimal gameplay means that you can focus more on the story, which is the entire selling-point of the game. So, even though all you're doing is pressing W or using the joystick to move forwards (with a few other things occasionally), there really isn't more that's needed.

[b]Music: [/b]Remo did an absolutely FANTASTIC job with the soundtrack for Firewatch. The acoustic guitar and twangy, telecaster-ish sounding (I think?) electric guitar gave the soundscape an outdoorsy feel and matched the setting perfectly. The synthesizers give some of the tracks a sort of Minecraft feel and also provides a welcome contrast to the brightness of the guitar parts. An interesting thing I noticed about the soundtrack is that it seems to ramp up in intensity at a slightly slower pace than the story itself which provides this moment where the music is calm and serene but the story is starting to get a little bit more suspenseful and tense. The calmness of the soundtrack made me feel even more tense and anxious to see what would happen next. Remo's song "Ol' Shoshone" was written perfectly for this game; it gives a sort of '70s vibe which matches the fact that Firewatch takes place in '89, and its theme syncs up perfectly too. Every moment of the soundtrack is nearly perfect and easily puts it on par with the works of Kelly Bailey, Mike Morasky, Mick Gordon and Joel Nielson.

[b]Graphics: [/b] The art style of this game is beautiful, so much so that I found myself actually saving film in the camera just in case there was an even more amazing landscape that I might find later in the game. The game looks absolutely lovely.

This game is easily one of my favorite games of all time and I'd highly recommend it to just about anyone with a half-decent PC (or a console).

The subversion that people think the writers were going for appears totally unearned. There is a genuine unsettling external threat imposed on the MC--vandalism, kidnapping, stalking, assault from behind in the middle of nowhere, traps to lure you out into the woods. As that drama rises, the dialogue-heavy 'boring real life' angle recedes. So when the conspiracy turns out to be a red herring you consider if the game is REALLY about loss and the distance people try to put between themselves and facing those realities. But that is not conveyed adequately--for instance, compare the prologue sequence to the lack of choices or reflection in the ending sequence. In that sense, and more generally, nothing is resolved. 

So many video games feel like demos for bigger studios. In this case, Campo Santo was successfully acquired by Valve less than two years after Firewatch was launched, undoubtedly in light of the first part of this game and the scaffolding of different narratives they demonstrated they could possibly follow through on with sufficient time. Firewatch tells a story better than most games like it.

I've heard of these kinds of games referred to as "walking simulators," because you spend a lot of time walking from place to place to further the plot. Thankfully, Firewatch economizes the travelling: it tells you exactly where to go, you always have a map to help you get there, and unnecessary walking is eliminated (if you've done what you need to do on a given day, it ends the day instead of making you walk all the way back to your observation tower).

The entire focus of Firewatch is on its story. And it's a good one, about a man who takes a job in the wilderness to escape the sorrow in his life. He befriends the woman at the next tower over and they prepare for a calm summer, but then it seems they're not alone ...

For the most part, you'll never encounter another human being in this game. Voice chats between the two main characters are done beautifully well; Delilah's voice actor in particular imparts a lot of personality through her voice. The game makes good use of its area; it's large enough to be interesting but not so large that you'll ever get bored trying to get somewhere. Aside from a few easter eggs and hidden achievements, there's no 'collect the mushrooms' or 'escape within the time limit' or 'beat the boss' in this game; it's a casual walkthrough as the story is revealed. And I especially enjoyed how the characters will converse at various points while I'm walking, and how the time of day changes around me based on where I am in the plot for that day.  It's an interesting story and an effective way to tell it.

TL;DR: A few bugs, ending was meh, some animations were a bit stiff, and story is a lil too short (in my opinion)

Time to finish: The game probably takes around 4 and half to 5 hours to finish. I finished under 5 I and I even messed around in the game, left the game running while I went to do something, etc. 
Personally I don't like spending $20 bucks on 5 hour story game. That's $4 per every hour. Just doesn't seem worth it to me. Now of course this is completely subjective. Maybe you'll take longer, you could replay it, etc. 

Graphics: This game looks amazing. Of course it can be better but it was made 5 years ago (at the time of writing this review) and is an Indie game after all. So you can't exactly expect stellar graphics but it is still great. I mean I bet a majority of people the people that saw this game originally saw the views that this game has to offer. I personally ran the game at ultra settings on a 1660 super and experienced little to no problems. I couldn't be bothered to check how many frames I was getting but it was smooth enough for me. 

Bugs: There were very minor bugs. Though enough for me to mention them. There were some parts of the map where it was.. broken. There were flying boulders, your walkie-talkie not rendering, half rendered trees. You know those kinds of things. Nothing even remotely game breaking. I also want to mention I didn't go searching through out the map for these things, they just appeared.

Beautiful game, very well made, engaging story line and characters... but I can't help but feel it was set up for more. Other reviewers have also picked up on the fact that the narrative disappointing. I was fully ready to be gobsmacked... but it never happened. Just too many loose ends. It's like they included stuff to build tension, and just left it. Like.. 3 beds? Whose were they then!

Removing the narrative though, I was very impressed with the game. The voice acting was perfect! The map was very impressive; open world, stunning views and wasn't too difficult to find my way around. I commented to my friend how it was the perfect mix of low poly/stylised animation and realism. 

I did have one little suggestion; a pocket radio/cassette player with some relaxing, acoustic music that he listens to as he walks around. It could turn off when he radios Delilah, or when something serious is happening and he needs to focus. But for just walking around it would really compliment the scenery and I'm sure a lot of players can agree that when a game goes quiet you're almost anticipating something bad is going to happen, so some music would really help to cut the tension. 

Great stuff! I'll be watching out for what the developers make next :)

PS. Because of the length of it, and how the narrative is very linear, I wouldn't pay the £15 for it Wait for it to come on sale.

The game is also visually very beautiful and I enjoyed the dialogue back and forth between the two characters who have the most interaction in the game.  The music and sound design of the game was also very good at setting the tone and immersing me.

So onto the negatives -- I wasn't as let down by the ending as a lot of people were because by that point I didn't care anymore.  I just wanted it to be over after about the first 2.5 hours.  For someone like me, accessibility options needed to be much more expansive.  The first person view was nice for taking in the scenery, but it make me extremely motion sick.  I wanted to play the game in one sitting since it's relatively short, but had to keep taking breaks to try and settle the churning.  I also have a massive headache from all the camera motion from climbing up and down and up and down.  Oof.  The other major downside this game had for me was navigation.  If you took out all the time I spent wandering in the wrong direction, often straight into bushes and rocks, while trying to figure out how to go the direction the game said I needed to go, I'd probably only have 4 hours in the game instead of nearly 6.  It was so damn frustrating.  There should be some type of accessibility option that allows you to either fast travel to particular points or put up a minimap on your screen or lets you mark where you've left ropes, just SOMETHING so I didn't have to get so frustrated. Honestly I didn't go into this expecting a masterpiece, it was a random pick in a sale, but it came far closer than  I thought it would! The first few hours are really fantastic - even though much of what happens can be called mundane the character interactions between Henry and Delilah are extremely fluid and believable. When things start to get a little more creepy you get drawn into the paranoia of the characters and swept up in it. It really is extremely well done.

The ending, or perhaps the last 30 minutes, are very contentious. On the one hand many, many people have felt it feels like they rushed the ending and it doesn't deliver the emotional payoff that has been built up painstakingly over the previous hours. I've got real sympathy with that view. On the other hand there is a meta narrative about how the payoff is the most real part of the whole story, and I have sympathy with that view too. It feels a little contrived, but when you think about it the contrivances do fade away. I think there is a better payoff that could have been made, but this is the one they chose and it does work. 

I think for many the end of this game isn't the one we hoped for, but only because the story played with our hopes. There is a sadness and frustration, but those feelings are mirrored in the main character too. Was it rushed? Maybe - but it does stand on its own feet and is somewhat subversive in how it plays with the audience.

This game is a very firm recommend. Don't expect to be uplifted, but its a thoroughly enjoyable 4-5 hours. You can tell a good game when you really don't want it to end, and this definitely falls into that category.

Almost as an afterthought to this review - the graphics are really solid in a stylistic way. The music is minimal but highly effective. As a GAME it all hangs together really well, but first and foremost this is a story and a great one at that.

Things aren't always what they seem...

Set in the Wyoming wilderness in 1989, you (Henry) have taken a job as a park ranger to escape the real world and the problems that came with the life you had there. But as the days go on, you'll find that those problems have been right in front of you all along. On top of that, strange things are starting to occur in the park. Disappearances, conspiracies, one mystery after another. You're in complete isolation, save for your supervisor Delilah, who spends the summer in her watchtower keeping up with you via your walkie-talkie... so why does it feel like you're not alone out there? Why does it feel like you're being watched? An open-world game with an elaborately-simple art style, a compelling story and top-notch voice acting, you'll find yourself on the edge of your seat with every twist (whether it's a plot or a trail). Do you have what it takes to be a lookout? Then pack your bags, put on your hiking boots and get ready for an adventure!

NOTE: I like to make my writing look at least a tad professional, but in all seriousness, I've been wanting to play this game all the way through since like, 2016 and now that I have the time and money to do so I was able to sit down and play the game for 7 hours straight. I know, I'm a bit late to the party. Anyways, I couldn't leave my seat while playing through it; everything about this game was just phenomenal to me. It was cryptic and nerve rattling yet compelling and even heartwarming at times. It definitely makes you think- about the choices you directly have to make in the game or about the things that happened regardless of the paths you take. There are several minute details in the world of Firewatch that add an insane amount of storytelling without anyone having to say a word. For instance, the Vietnam Veteran hat that can be found in one of the caches scattered throughout the forest, or a red 20-sided die in a drawer in Henry's desk (without spoiling too much of course). An abundance of foreshadowing as well, in small encounters with certain people or places or even objects. So much storytelling in such a short game, it saddens me that there isn't more to it. What there is, however, is absolutely amazing. The game's soundtrack is a masterpiece. The visuals are breathtaking. I absolutely give this gem a 10/10, but my opinion should absolutely not determine yours. So play it for yourself. Give Firewatch a try, and it's a safe bet that you won't be disappointed.

I am going to start by saying that the experience of playing Firewatch is one of the best things I have played in recent memory. I am going to give a few spoilers for the early part of the game so if you do not wish to see these please do not venture any further.

The start of the game sees you advance a story through our main protagonist Henry’s life from meeting his future wife in a bar and through the rest of their relationship. Needless to say everything did not go quite according to plan and the game starts proper as you find yourself in the middle of nowhere having taken a job as a Fire look-out in Wyoming Woods to get away from everything.

This opening sequence is amazingly moving and really gets you invested in Henry as a character moving forward.

The game then takes place over the course of a summer with different days being treated as different chapters in the story. The location you are in is beautifully realised and an absolute joy to move around. But the main standout in Firewatch are the 2 voice-over leads. Henry is a heart-warming character who is relatable and you instantly feel for. Delilah who is Henry’s boss and must guide him through the summer is equally as well realised and pretty soon you care so much about these 2 characters in fact pretty much more than I have felt about 2 video game characters in recent memory. I will go out on a limb and say that the script in Firewatch is the best I have ever encountered and this game has as much in common with a fantastic written short story as a video game and could easily be converted to that.

For a man who is supposed to sit in his lookout and watch out for fires he doesn’t generally seem to do a lot of that. The game starts with you going to investigate some drunken teens setting off Fireworks and this sets the rest of the game’s narrative into motion. As well as the sublime voice acting the score in the game is also exceptional. The tension mixed with humour is beautifully brought to life by the excellent soundtrack.

While Firewatch falls into the walking simulator genre this is way more involved than most and you hardly notice the lack of certain types of conventional gameplay as you navigate the world and advance the story. As you travel around the area you often can pick up items that later appear in your Firewatch station. The game also has a little bit of Metroidvania in it by cordoning off certain areas until you pick up a certain tool to advance.

Another very cool moment is the disposable Camera that you pick up early in the game. As you play the game you can take up to 15 pictures and what is very cool is that once the game is finished for $15 you can actually get these photos developed and sent to you. I wish I had known this before I finished the game and I might have been more thoughtful on wasting them but I may very well play through the game again just to make and order a cool set of $15 prints.

The game is not absolute perfect. Navigating was often a little tricky using the map and compass and while I didn’t want a minimap or a big arrow pointing my way you at the very least could have let me still run while holding the map.

You probably have already heard by now that most people’s issue with the game is the ending… and while I will be the first to admit the ending was not my favourite part of the game It could have been worse. I guess it just wasn’t the ending or the big reveal I had expected or hoped for but this did not damped one of the purest and most enjoyable narrative gaming experience I have ever experienced.

Walking simulators normally cater towards player that have a very particular taste when it comes to gaming. And even though Firewatch is no exception, it sure sits on the top of the list as one of the best from the genre.

The graphics and sound come together nicely to create a welcoming atmosphere from start to finish. Add in the superb voice acting and the stage is set for your character's 'firewatch' in the wilderness. And even though the mysterious plot is quite gripping, it's the game-play itself that is the major draw. 

Yes, this is very much a walking sim in every sense of the word. But the conversations between the main character and his supervisor from another watch tower really adds a lot of flavour to the somewhat linear story. Linear as the story may be, the game encourages exploration within the enclosed environments to promote more options to open up these conversations. Hence, the heart and soul of the game is the developing relationship between the two firewatch character's that can shift and change based on your choices.

I think for those who are slightly curious, this is worth every cent because you'll be hard pressed to find another game just like it. Anyone looking for a fairly chilled out time within a game that presents a solid story, you can't go wrong.

I usually game in the evenings, and have plenty of other things I can be doing instead - this means games must catch my attention in order for me to stay awake and continue playing them.
While Firewatch is a bit slow at first.
I found myself dozing off quite a bit during my first play session, which took place during the first in-game day.
However, by end of day 2 in the game, the pace really picks up. Both speed-wise, and story-wise.
And in my last session I caught myself playing until 3AM, just to see what happens next, and how the game is going to end.
So as you guessed, the game becomes very interesting and engaging as they story progresses.


Graphics:
Graphics-wise, the game isn't something to write home about.
I know it boasts it's "beautiful graphics", but I did not find it that beautiful.
Certainly not compared to AAA games.
But not even compared to the better looking indie games.
I'd say it's similar to "The Long Dark".
It has it's beauty... But not something that people can describe as "amazing" or "top-of-the-line".
But to their credit I can say the game was basically done by 3 people, and the graphics definitely suits its atmosphere.


Sound:
The soundtrack is pretty good, especially in the sense that it suits the look-and-feel of the game.
When you reach scenic places, appropriate music is playing.
The Voiceover on the other hand, was simply amazing.
The voices and acting were AAA-game level, and done by professional who did TV and AAA games voices.
So that is top notch.


Look-and-feel:
The look-and-feel of the game is a bit inconsistent.
The Plot makes it feel like a mystery thriller, keeping you on the edge of your seat.
While between plot-progressing moments, it's more of a relaxed walking simulator, with appropriately placed background music.
Both are done well.
But for me, as a player, it was a bit confusing.


Story & Dialogs:
For me it was the strongest point in the game.
As soon as the plot gripped me, I just HAD TO know how it ends.
I've seen people write they are disappointed by the ending. I'm not.
Story-wise, it was very consistent, and folded the story pretty well.
It's not the typical Hollywood happy ending.
Nor is it a grand scale, earth-encopasing, alien invasion type of ending.
But it's completely consistent with the rest of the story as it unfolds.
And it's much more realistic than the alternatives.
IMO, making the ending with a grander scale, or happier, would actually diminish from the quality of the story.
Some of the best stories in the world don't have a happy ending.
Fight Club, The usual suspect, Seven... to name a few.
Because such is life. Life doesn't have happy endings.
You can only try to be better next time...

[b] Small summary: [/b] 
You play as Henry whose job is to look out for forest fires. And then there is your chatty boss Delilah who gives you various orders to do certain tasks in the forest. The whole game you are supposed to 'hike' in a very colourful and impressive looking forest. While you are just doing your job a lot of mysterious things happen in the forest and you are now supposed to investigate the incidents.

[b] My notes (pros and cons and some additions that don't come in either) : [/b]
1. I really like the design that they went for in this game. The game looks really nice. It doesn't look 'realistic' per say but the art of the forest game is really impressive. It makes you want to explore.  Props for that.

2. The game is a slow burn but picks up quick and I love it ! As it gives me time to explore around and appreciate the art and music of the forest. I promise that the story REALLY picks up exponentially once the investigation picks up.

3. However there are a lot of loose ends in the story. I definitely think that there were a lot of missed opportunities here where they could have connected the various plot points better. Some things just didn't connect well or at all. Also [spoiler] what's up with that broken down cabin of South Korean war vet ? There was not follow up. [/spoiler]

4. Edit : A day later I was thinking about this game. I don't think ending is bad at all. It justifies who these characters are and what situation they are stuck in their respective lives. [strike] The ending was a bit weird for me.  But what was even more frustrating was the interaction between the two main characters BEFORE the whole ending sequence. [/strike] 

5. Decent mellow soundtrack. Helps in the immersion and I guess "vibes" of exploration.

Whether you'll like this game depends very much on what you're after. It's definitely not got anything hugely 'gamey' about it; navigation is really the main mechanic. Most of the game I had my location in the map turned on - I recommend turning that off. It makes the environment more engaging, and I had a lot more fun when I'd turned that off.

The main character didn't draw me in at first, and sort of put me off the game. But I persisted. While I don't think my feelings about the character changed, the mystery itself drew me in particularly with certain moments - and the dialogue between the main characters was well written and acted. That said, the conclusion to the mystery felt somewhat underwhelming. 

A large amount of the small open world is blocked off to you, which is kind of a shame and it does feel fairly linear and hard to get lost as a result. However, perhaps due to this, the game pretty much always looks stunning and it ensures you catch some of the best views. For as much as it's not going for hyper-realism, it feels very real and immersive. And most of all, beautiful.

A lot of design touches were done brilliantly. The camera movement felt comfortable and realistic, and Henry's movements have real weight to them. It does a good job of making you feel like you are not just a person in the generic sense, but a specific person with his own ways of moving about the world. While providing dialogue options for you to choose, they do all feel like they make sense to the character. 

While the story, particularly in its conclusion, didn't blow me away, I can see the feeling it was trying to leave you on. I think it did quite a good job of building up to it. Even if it wasn't entirely my kind of story, I had an enjoyable few hours with it.

10 YEAR ANNIVERSARY UPDATE:

I can't believe that it's been 10 years already. As we indulge in this era for its anniversary, never forget that this soul is one of a kind. I guess the world was different back then compared to today... the children yearn for 2016. Whether you're diving in for the first time or taking a trip back to 2016 while blasting Kasbo's remix of The Little Things by Big Gigantic feat. Angela McCluskey, my original review stays the same; Firewatch was and always will be an impactful game no matter how far time passes. This game will always be cherished until the end of time. 

As for Campo Santo, I hope everyone is going great. I wish to see your name at the end of a trailer one of these days.

ORIGINAL:

Firewatch is a game that impacted my life so much in 2016 and even still up to this day.

I was going through a period of time where I felt lost in the world and uncertain about what's to come in my life and where to go...

The game has specific depth in its story that will make you experience so many emotions, ranging from happiness, all the way to fear.

"You are a man named Henry who has retreated from your messy life to work as a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness. Perched atop a mountain, it's your job to find smoke and keep the wilderness safe."

As simple as it sounds, there's more to this than what meets the eye. Many thoughts go throughout your mind as you explore this masterpiece of a game, not only visually but also from a storytelling perspective.

When the game begins, you get asked several questions with you answering all of them based off of your own personality. 

Afterwards, the story is set.

It is Spring, 1989, and you learn that your wife is starting to develop dementia... life spirals downward... you want to get away from it all... just for a little while...

You decide to get a job as a fire lookout in Shoshone National Forest, Wyoming.

After arriving at your lookout tower, you are introduced to your supervisor, Delilah.

You communicate with Delilah via a walkie talkie throughout the game. Keep in mind that this is the only piece of equipment you have to communicate with someone because you've left your old life behind for a while... literally and figuratively. You and Delilah develop a unique yet familiar bond.

Two months later, while scouting outside of your lookout tower, you see something that catches your attention... you leave your lookout tower to find out what is going on...

This is where the emotional roller coaster begins.

You go on a journey exploring mysteries in Shoshone National Forest and get faced with choices based off of what your mind wants to perceive... in the story's case, Henry's mind.

You're going to get ambushed by your feelings towards what is currently going on in the given situation. Every single emotion of yours will be challenged either by assumptions or facts.

As you start to unravel the main mystery, you realize that your emotions and mind made you believe what YOU wanted to believe.

The truth hurts... The truth is decisive.

You swear that you nailed this mystery on its head, but in actuality, this mystery's truth leaves you feeling empty inside. You could've sworn that there would be a big finale...

Firewatch is backed by an amazing soundtrack by Chris Remo. The music makes up 50% of the story because the emotions you feel each day in the game is being emitted by the specific song playing. The atmosphere, your emotions, and the music all work hand in hand.

If you needed a reason to experience this masterpiece, I would hope this review would be one.

This was not what I was expecting. I bought this game on a whim shortly after it came out. Mostly because everyone was talking about it and that's just how I treated my Steam account back then. If it was popular, I'd buy it. Didn't have bills and had a decent paying job, so money was rarely a problem. I then proceeded to let it sit, untouched, for 5 years. About a month ago I decided to start working through my enormous Steam backlog. This game was high up in alphabetical order so I just pressed play. I had no idea what kind of game I was getting into or anything like that. It opens with a bunch of text, which just coming off Ace Attorney I was fine with. You make choices about your life before the game, and then you finally reach your lookout tower. 

So at this point I'm already depressed as ♥♥♥♥. My wife is on the other side of the largest ocean on Earth with dementia and here I am watching for fire's in the middle of nowhere. But then stuff start's happening. You go stop some people launching fireworks and come back to a trashed tower. The mystery starts. I get more and more sucked in trying to figure out what's going on. And before I know it... the game is over. Everything is solved, but you never even see the person you've been talking to the entire game. It's a bit of a letdown honestly. For a game that kept me hooked for its entire adventure (I beat it in one sitting) and then ends so abruptly, it felt like it was missing more.

Story aside, the graphics are very nice. It's a small open world game. Not very graphics intensive but still comes off as vibrant. Not a lot of music, mostly ambient stuff. The characters, while not very developed (except for you), are nice and the voice acting is good. Controls are extremely simple to figure out, and the game points you were to go at all times. But it still feels like a world you can get lost in. 

I personally wouldn't pay $20 for it nowadays. I'd wait for a sale. $10 or less imo. But this is a must play if you like story. It's short, I 100%'d it in about 6 hours, but it's nice. Give it a try.

Firewatch is definitely a game to be played for its ambience. It feels like open world exploration while keeping the player very much directed towards small goals, but you don't get the big picture about the story until much later. The story does provide a lesson, and maybe gets a little philosophical at the end of the day. Overall the pacing is slower in some places than I would have liked, but the slow pace really allows for full immersion in the environment and helps cement that feeling of walking through the woods at different times of day. I like the transition from relatively quiet and relaxing strolls to sudden moments of tension where it's not clear exactly what is going on around the lookout tower. All kinds of theories may spring up in your head about what the truth of all the odd occurrences are, but the end result is startling. It's a fun simulator of trekking through forests and traveling, which is one of my favorite types of games to play. I would recommend this to anyone who like an atmospheric outdoorsy themed game with a rich story and a mystery at its center.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Overall, this game is a wonderful immersive (1st-person) story-rich experience. Worth the price for me, like a good movie, I would definitely recommend you to play it firsthand, without reading any spoiler beforehand

Here are the breakdowns of my impression;

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Visual Design[/h1]

It’s the first thing you’ll notice - the graphics and art style of this game are [b] gorgeous[/b] . The game is an enjoyment to simply look at, it pleases the eyes, even in the main menu. 

The colours, the nature, the objects and gadgets, the overall atmosphere, all beautifully tuned in to the experience. I particularly like the walkie-talkie and the signal detector, I have a thing for those little electronics

[h1]Story[/h1]

A good but short mystery-driven story. Grounded in realism, the [i]feeling of isolation & paranoia[/i] builds up gradually as you progress through the game. It isn't tagged with the horror genre, but like they say, the true horror is in the unknown anticipation - and in this case: the feeling that you are certain that you are being followed, listened, watched, analysed, and you don't know who and where they are.

[h1]Characters[/h1]

The voice acting in this game is [b]absolutely exceptional[/b] , vivid and convincing that it felt like these are real people, each with their distinct personalities and background past life, in a story that had actually happened. That said, it wasn't difficult for the game to get me emotionally connected to the characters and to the story. 

I fell in love with Delilah as I played. It's her voice, how she swear a lot, and how caring and flirty she is with Henry that got me interested. 
 
in this regard of character depth, this game is far more superior than some big titles.

But now that I have finished and watched some analyses, I think [spoiler]Delilah might have kept something from Henry the entire time, something about the Goodwin, about Brian's death and the research facilities. I had real bad paranoia, but I almost never suspected that she is aware of things and is lying to me - she knew about Ned Goodwin and kept communication with him from the very beginning.[/spoiler]

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Criticism[/h1]

- Ending Disappointment 
It was a disappointment that [spoiler]I can’t meet Delilah at the ending. One can argue that this might be part of the mystery, but given how the relationship between them has developed over months (or hours in playtime), it felt lonely and heartbroken that this person, who has been my only source of human connection for so long, wasn't going to meet me and maybe spend some time together off the radio.[/spoiler] 

- Short in Length
and there isn’t much value for replay either, except for sightseeing. I honestly wish it was longer, it felt like there was something more that was gonna happen to the final revelation of the plot, [b]BUT THERE WASN'T[/b] - and it just ended with the aforementioned disappointment 

- Emptiness of the Wilderness 
I get that loneliness and isolation is part of the intended experience, but wandering around the map, I rarely see wildlife, which, in a more realistic setting, would be ubiquitous in a forest like that in the 80s. The dev team really avoided much of the work lol - [spoiler]no character models, (almost) no wild life models[/spoiler]. Maybe more interactive locations & objects? but that would be dependable on the story
v short, buy on sale, but an amazing story and great voice acting.

As the story progresses, more and more focus is turned onto the mystery which is a detriment given the conclusion.  I actually see no reason for this story to have been a mystery at all; all the focus on the mystery does is distract from the game's aforementioned strengths.

All in all, if you can get through the game without expecting a satisfying resolution to the mystery it's an excellent game, although doing so becomes increasingly difficult as the game progresses.


SPOILERS BELOW:

To discuss a few threads I was personally unsatisfied with the resolution of:

1) Why did Ned trash the teen's camp?  This event was actually the first point Henry realized there was another person in the woods with him.  All trashing the teen's camp did was draw attention to him, something he clearly did not want.

2) Where did the teens go?  Ned had no reason to kill them, leaving them disappearing for unknown or unrelated reasons.  Although "it was a coincidence" is certainly possible, it's hardly a satisfying resolution to such a large mystery and it forces us to read the teen's disappearance's help in causing Henry's paranoia as nothing more than a plot convenience.

3) Why did Ned start the fire?  Henry made off with plenty of evidence of Ned's existence.  Burning down the forest was, again, nothing but a plot convenience allowing for a cinematic finale.

[h1]“I came out here for a breath of fresh air and some adventure.”[/h1]

[quote]This review contains no major story spoilers.[/quote]

The fire that burns between two people will sometimes face struggles, and if not handled correctly will be snuffed out. Henry, the protagonist, faces this struggle as a rift between him and his wife develops. With new marital issues arising and a need for an escape, Henry searches for an outlet until ultimately landing on a summer job. Finding himself deep in the forests of Wyoming, Henry will serve as a fire watch with his only source of communication being his supervisor, Delilah, via walkie-talkies. For the months to come a brand new flame will spark that will illuminate an unsettling shadow.


[h3]The Good:[/h3]
[list]
[*]Immersive world, everything felt like it belonged 
[*]Intriguing and lifelike dialogue
[/list]

[h3]The Bad:[/h3]
[list]
[*]Invisible walls impede real exploration
[*]Lifeless physics 
[*]Ending was underwhelming
[*]Timed dialogue responses 
[/list]

[h3]The Ugly:[/h3]
[list] 
[*]Had to adjust resolution before even playing, displayed ugly black bars on first launch
[*]Watched things render in and blocky textures smooth out while exploring
[/list]	

[b]Specs:[/b] OS: Windows 10 // CPU: Intel Core i7-7700K @ 4.20GHz // GPU: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070 // RAM: 16.0 GB


[h2]Gameplay Breakdown:[/h2]

💬 [b]Dialogue[/b] 
The conversations held between the two characters is where most of [i]Firewatch[/i] resides. While exploring Shoshone National Forest you’ll be constantly bantering with Delilah as she’ll tell you important information or radio you just to have a casual conversation. The game displays great character development as you’ll see the character’s bond gradually grow, till ultimately, they’re comfortable with each other and seek the other’s presence. With dialogue being such a vital part of the game I found it annoying and impractical for having a timer counting down on your responses. The timer often led me to rush my choice without reading all the potential choices. Even with the annoying timer the dialogue genuinely captured my attention, as I grew to love and appreciate the duo. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2548865943

🗺 [b]Exploration[/b]
Despite Henry’s best wishes, there's not much exploration to be had. The game constantly will force you along only set paths, and once you’ve gone through a couple days you will learn most of the major paths without needing the map. The scenery was gorgeous while walking about the Shoshone, but often you’d only need to visit a certain part of the map once and after that there would be no reason to ever go back. While exploring you would encounter multiple invisible walls that would restrict your exploration to only the set path which made the game's exploration feel so much more restrictive than it already was. 

🎬 [b]Story[/b]
From the beginning, I was pretty interested as the game has a consistent pace that continuously keeps feeding you with new pieces of the story as it unfolds in front of you. Each day would contain something new and interesting that not only would build onto Henry and Delilah’s relationship, but also give more into what’s happening at the Shoshone. Outside of the main story there aren't really any other side quests or lore entries besides the few you can find in the supply caches strewn across the forest. The story you can find and read up on in the caches are only there for some extra bits, and focus on two other fire watch members who write letters back and forth to each other. These two never really come up in the main story. While lacking any extras besides the main story, my interest was captivated by the events happening between the duo. Towards the end of the game the story starts to drift away and I started to lose interest. After spending so much time growing attached to each character the ending left me in an awkward state which I can best describe as: “blue balled”.

[h2]Sound:[/h2]
The sound was pretty basic. Nothing ever felt out of place or was intrusive to the gameplay. The end credit song was the only audio highlight of this game. Pieces of it can be heard throughout the game and at the end it’ll all come together giving you the full song. 

[h2]Graphics:[/h2]
This game is some great eye candy as it has one of the prettiest skyboxes. The color palette they went with in this game allows everything to feel alive and is generally visually stunning. Though some of the game's rendering issues were annoying to see, I still enjoyed the visuals. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2548866089

[h2]The Grind:[/h2]
There’s little to offer in the grind aspect, with there being no real challenges since everything is clear cut and follows the story. All the achievements are obtainable in your first run, with only a few being optional. There isn’t much reason to replay the story as once you experienced it there isn't anything else really to do other than experience it again. 

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[i]Firewatch[/i] is a beautiful game with some great dialogue, but I can't recommend buying this game. There really isn't much to experience outside of the main story, and that experience is easily achievable by just watching a no commentary video on Youtube. For $20 you're getting about 5 hours of gameplay, and using the word gameplay is being generous. This is a walking simulator through and through, and despite it’s great qualities it falls short in too many areas for me to recommend. Even in the areas it did well in, there were still some issues I had. I may have recommended a buy, but from where the game ends it only solidified my reason to deter anyone from purchasing.

Firewatch is...pretty good! The narrative of Firewatch is consistently engaging and mysterious, the voice acting is great, and the entire setting of the Wyoming wilderness looks amazing.

However, in some ways this game disappointed me. From the very beginning of Firewatch, the player is given choices that seem to affect what happens (as the first 10 or so minutes of the game functions as a text-only choose-your-own-adventure rather than a first person exploration game like the rest), and the player continues to make choices when choosing what to say over a radio for the remainder of the game. I don't have a problem with this in the least, and didn't think much of it when playing through Firewatch the first time, but as it turns out, these choices do not affect the story in any way. No matter what you choose in the beginning and what you say over the in-game radio, the narrative will progress and the story will end in the exact same way as any other combination of choices. The gameplay itself is similarly very linear, and doesn't allow for much out-of-the-way exploration - and even for those who wander around a bit during the game, there isn't really much to find beyond some picturesque spots on the map.

Would I recommend Firewatch? Yes. But for a game about exploration and making choices, the whole experience seems oddly linear and scripted. 6/10

I had first heard of this game through a video by Accursed Farms, a person who creates not only video game review videos, but most famously a machinima-like series called "Freeman's Mind". In this video, he listed games that he was rather excited to play eventually. This was one of them, and the game didn't strike me as interesting at first. After the while, the game released, and I watched some videos (thankfully very early in the story). I decided it wouldn't hurt to play it.

You play as Henry, a 30(ish) year old who has a wife that has early onset dementia, a rather touchy topic for some people. After deciding to abandon his wife to her family, he takes a summer job in a national park. As the name of the game suggests, you are a firewatcher, in constant contact with a woman in a separate part of the park named Delilah. Over time, you have to work with Delilah to solve a mystery brewing in the park.

Most of the game is centered on walking around in the park to various locations to perform tasks. Occasionally you can find boxes with information about trails and locations. You'll climb rock slopes, rappel down them, climb more rock slopes, and explore various caves. Don't be afraid of environmental lack, however. Every part of the map is naturally beautiful and, even though I am not a nature person, this game certainly stunned me with it's graphics.

What the game lacks is replayability. It attempts to make up for this in a free-roam mode where you can explore the national park without anything to do. However, most of the game's charm comes from the story itself. Any successors or expansions to the story would be heavily welcomed by people who love the story. The story also has a lot of questions open to interpretation, which if you're not a lore type person, is not your cup of tea.

Overall: 9/10

After coming back to this game 4 years later, i can safely say that this exceptional game still holds up!
The Story revolves around Henry, escaping his life problems and becoming a fire lookout in the Shoshone National Forest. His only form of communication is through a walkie talkie to a fellow fire lookout by the name of Delilah. While he may be trying to put is life on hold and clear his mind, Henry will soon encounter a series of events that will send him on an adventure to find answers to the ongoings that take place within the forest itself. The way the story flows is just exceptional with the way dialog is exchanged between the characters. The conversations between Henry and Delilah feel so natural that if i ever had the chance, I would always use the walkie talkie to pick a topic and listen to each of their thoughts and feelings. The voice acting is amazing with both characters bouncing from one another, coming off with their own quips, personality and making the whole experience more immersive. 
The setting of Shoshone National Forest is beautiful with each part of the map having its own personality and making it its own character. There are the open lakes, rocky hillsides, clusters of trees with streams running down them and a  massive canyon. Even the watch tower that Henry inhabits becomes an extension of himself as books, pictures and other items breath life into the world of Firewatch. 
Graphically, this game still looks gorgeous since its release back in 2016. Lakes and streams look realistic with the way light reflects upon the water, the trees feel alive with the way that sunlight breaks through the leaves and even different times of day and weather help make this experience more realistic. The art style is done in an animated-esque fashion which compliments and contrasts with the overall story and gameplay and i absolutely love it. It's most definitely a unique style that helps differentiate itself from other indie titles and makes it more memorable. 
The soundtrack for this game is just phenomenal due to the way that it simply accompanies the moments in the game rather than overpowering it. Its well placed with points in the game having no soundtrack to let the player be soaked in to their environment, but when it does play, it adds so much to the game. There are calming synths when walking to destinations, there are twangy guitars and low kick drums to add to the intensity of certain events. It is evident that the soundtrack had been well mapped out. The audio is again incredible. From the breeze that passes you by to the flows water in the streams to even the simple click of the walkie talkie. The sounds in here are authentic and add another layer to this already brilliant game. 
In terms of gameplay, it may not be for everyone. Some people may call it a walking sim but i think there is enough interaction with the world of Firewatch to class it as a story rich, adventure game. You will mainly be traversing the world around, using your compass, map and walkie talkie to get to destinations. The main gameplay mechanic is your walkie talkie as this is your form of communication to Delilah and how you are able to interact with her. There is always a selection of dialog choices for the player to choose from when talking to her and makes the players experience a bit more personal and immersive. There will be ropes you can climb down, an axe that you can use to chop down trees and bushes with and the previously mentioned map and compass to help you guide through the Shoshone National Forest. All of these, while may be minor mechanics (except the map and compass) the add so much to the immersion of Firewatch and makes it a really fun experience. There will be items and landscapes in the world that player can examine and discuss with Delilah that make the experience that more interesting, simply because of wanting to hear what each character have to say to one another. The main premise of this game is to sit back and take in the story that you as the player have to discover through Henry's encounters.
Overall, Firewatch is such an immersive experience with its top quality narrative and i would highly recommend for everyone to try it out and get as invested as I have.

what to say about this game… 
man, 98% of it was an amazing, 10/10, fantastic getaway experience that I thoroughly enjoyed. 

Excellent immersive ambience, great convincing voice acting, beautiful graphics you want to screenshot constantly, great functional gameplay that’s fun and doesn’t detract from the story, and realistic characters that you are fully invested in from the start. 

And the STORY! It’s allllll about the story. 
The gameplay design is so well done that you really feel like you’re there, IN the story. 
The whole thing is such a unique and well put-together experience that just immediately grabs your attention and keeps you gripped from beginning….to end.

The END though… therein lies the rub. The 2% of hidden worms at the core that almost ruined the whole apple for me… 

I’m not gonna spoil anything, but I will say that because you feel like you’re IN the story, you experience it very dramatically, from a very real, first-person perspective. 

And after hours and hours of analyzing it with my husband (who played it with me) and poring over reviews and possible explanations, not to mention playing the game again (and I take my time), going through all the possible dialogue options AND listening to the developers full commentary… 

I still just have VERY mixed feelings about the ending. As do most people, hence why it’s gotten very MIXED reviews. 

I think I understand what the developers were trying to do. The game explores real life themes in a very deep and real way that most games don’t even try to touch, and I admire it for that. 
The fact that I’m still analyzing it weeks later tells you that even as a kind of “virtual reality” it affects the player in a very real way, and I’m sure that’s exactly how the developers are measuring their success. 

I recognize that it’s not just a video game - it’s a piece of engaging literary art that manages to evoke and explore emotions with enough power that it can affect YOU, the player, personally.
The developers made the risky choice to keep the ending the way they did even though not everyone would love it, which makes it unique and courageous. 

HOWEVER, I still think there could have been just a few minor tweaks to the WAY they present the ending that could have made it a better overall experience for the player and measured up to some of their expectations, while ALSO keeping the integrity of their story, and what they were trying to achieve, intact. 

Your level of investment is up to you of course, but if you choose to invest all (and I still recommend that you do), just be forewarned that you may end up disappointed. 

The best OVERALL recommendation I can give is to play the game and see for yourself. 

Play the game and enjoy it for what it is because to ME, the experience really IS worth it.

Firewatch is a first person interactive story, featuring Henry, a man in his late 30s who, following his wife's diagnosis with early-onset dementia, finds himself working as a fire lookout in Shoshone National Forest in Wyoming, seeking to get away from the stress of dealing with his wife's condition.

As Henry, you experience the day-to-day tasks of working as a lookout, from telling partying teens that they can't set off fireworks in the park, to cleaning up trash, to maintaining utilities of the wider park. Throughout the game, Henry's boss, Delilah, communicates with Henry via radio, and serves as the deuteragonist of the game. The game's missions are represented through days, with each in game day being forwarded with a titlecard that lists the day's number, with days becoming more sporadically denoted as the game goes on.

Gameplay consists primarily of moving around the map, using ropes to scale cliffs, using a map and compass to navigate the forest, all the while communicating with Delilah, her relationship with Henry being forged and determined through however much you decide to reply to her, if at all.

I won't get too in depth as to the goings-on of the plot for Firewatch, but it's an incredibly effective narrative, relying on in-game cues to create an atmosphere of unease and anxiety that, for me at least, translates to the player's anxieties, strengthening the message and ethos of the title. If you enjoy story-driven titles, Firewatch is up your alley.

[h1] SYNOPSIS (Spoiler-Free) [/h1]

A game about Love& Loss, and a Mystery 'Who-Done-it?'.

Firewatch is a hiking simulator, that puts you in the shoes of a heartbroken man who takes a job as a Firewatch Ranger to escape the crushing thoughts and responsibilities of an old lover.  It's firstly a game about love and loss, but also a game with mystery, tension, and paranoia.

In Firewatch, you reside in a watch tower in the middle of a national park alone for 3 months.  You're only means of communication is a walkie-talkie that's used to communicate to a woman (Delilah) in another watch tower positioned across from yours in perfect view.

Throughout the game you're handed daily tasks from Delilah on the other side of your walkie-talkie, with the game also giving you dialogue choices that you can pick to further the story.  You're usually given 3 dialogues on how you can respond to her on the other side- Do you stay closed off?   Do you open up about your past relationship?  Or do you reciprocate as she attempts to flirt with you?  As the days go on, you two soon begin to develop a relationship which plays for most of the story.  

The back and forth between you and the main character turns varies from Sarcasm, flirtation, etc, with you being able to choose how to respond to your only lifeline of sanity.

[h1] MY THOUGHTS (Possible Spoilers) [/h1]

I actually cried playing this game.  
Firewatch is one of the most engaging stories I've ever played.  You really feel connected to the characters you encounter; and as if you exist in this games park as actual 'firewatcher'.  It's one of the games where I literally couldn't wait to play it again.  

The dialogue choices has me laughing out loud at times, with a huge grin on my face as the characters talked.
Your character also has to face the morality of deciding whether to move on from his wife or to stay with her, as she has fallen extremely ill and cannot take care of herself anymore.

It's a game about love and loss with a huge emphasis on mystery, tension, and dread.  The game is a hiking simulator, but at no point in the game, did it feel like a hiking simulator, or like a chore.. as the game always has something new for you to see and do.  The walkie-talkie conversations are front row in this game, and they're what kept me coming back.

One nit pick... Throughout the middle of the game, it turns into an eerie mystery of stalking, paranoia, and your character even doubting his own existence.  I was 100% let down with the ending of it all, however.  The game seemed to build.. build.. build.. tension for so long only to have it pop like a balloon in the end as if it didn't mean anything.

Despite the one flaw, I loved this game to death.  I loved the characters, the story, the dialogue choices, and especially the sarcastic back and forth between the two main characters (You and Delilah).

This games a straight 9/10.

What can I say about Firewatch that hasn't already been said? This game is the most beautiful, heartwrenching experience I've ever had the privilege to have. It makes me laugh, it makes me cry; every game I've played since has really just been in search of the same feeling of breathless nostalgia and love that Firewatch gives me.

Firewatch's number one priority is telling an amazing story and it succeeds in doing so better than almost any other game I've ever played. The gameplay is about as simple as can be but thats ok, this isn't sekiro, I'm not looking for deep combat mechanics or anything I just want a good story and nice visuals to match. And thats exactly what I got. The structure of everything and the writing for the two main characters is practically flawless in my eyes and the voice actors absolutely nailed it. having only two characters carry an entire game (especially one this dialogue heavy) is a risky move but it worked out magnificently. Henry and Delilah are so unbelievably interesting it should be illegal to make characters this good. throughout the whole game I was itching to call in every little thing on my radio so i could hear them chat some more. I'm kinda skirting around what the game is actually about because I'd highly recommend going into it completely blind if you can, and playing the whole thing in one sitting (i beat it in about 4 and a half hours) its a game that'll stick with you for a loooong time I promise.

In this game you play as a man named Henry. He is having some trouble in his life, and starts working in the wildlands of Wyoming protecting the people and the forrest from wildfires. In the wilderness of Wyoming you have a map, a compass and a stranger on the other side of a radio. I won`t mention anything else since mystery and not knowing everything is a huge part of this game.

---<Gameplay>---
The gameplay is really in depth and gives the player just enough freedom to feel like the forrest is an open world ready to be explored (which it truly is). I also love the fact that you have to use a map and compass to be able to navigate through the forest. This is by no means hard, but still a gameplay element that really emphasises the fact that you are totaly alone in the forrest, and can only rely on your own skills and intuition.


---<Story>---
Before i write about the story i have to mention the voiceacting. It might very well be the best voiceacting i have experienced in a game ever. Easy 10/10!

The story is what makes this game amazing. It keeps the player on the edge the entire time, and explores how imagination and isolation can impact both you as a player, but also Henry. My first reaction to the ending was that it could use a bit more time, and give us as players a bit more. After reflecting and researching the game more i must admit that the ending grew on me. It might still be a bit short, but that doesn`t really impact the game in a negative way.


---<Graphics>---
Best artstyle i have ever seen in a videogame. I ended up screenshotting everything.



---<Conclusion>---
This might be the best game to pick up during the steam summer sale (or any other sale). The game is pretty short, ranging from 3-4 hours, this is no problem since the game only costs around 4$ during sales. This game was a journey that i started, and ended the same night, and it quickly got a spot in my top 10 games of all time list.

Pick this game up during a sale, you won`t regret it.
