In Firewatch, one of your challenges will be going from point A to point B, finding equipment and other items in support boxes around the map, or even along your journey.
And that's really a boost, as the player only has a compass and a hand map to guide him. On the map, the only point highlighted is its location and the notes Henry makes as he discovers new observations. Otherwise, it's all up to you.
Talking with Delilah through Walkie-Talkie is a simple mechanic and very well explored.
Also interesting during all the trails, you can hear the silence of the forest. Seeing birds singing, ducks in the pond and even the howling of the wind through the leaves of the trees.
With each new location discovered, inspiring music takes over the gameplay and aids Henry's lonely experience.
Finally Firewatch has a unique, mysterious proposal that aims to capture your attention with an engaging narrative, beautiful graphic work and an exquisite soundtrack.

This game immerses you in the world of two middle-aged Fire Lookouts in the Wyoming wilderness circa 1989, who are trying to find a way to escape their misfortunes. With a run time of 3-4 hours, the story may be completed within one afternoon.

The most compelling aspect of the game is the narrative, which is delivered to the player via a series of walkie-talkie conversations with the lookout in the adjacent tower. How the player interacts with their conversation partner - if they choose to do so - allows for additional playthroughs, however the general path of the story will not change.

The environment is beautifully crafted and fun to explore, though there is not much extra to find. It was easy for me become completely immersed, and the free-roam mode allowed me to continue enjoying the scenery beyond the end of the story.

If this is the type of game you would enjoy, it is worth the full price. If not but you're curious, perhaps it's best to wait for a sale.

Worth it for the story alone, not to mention the graphics and soundtrack. Even though it is a short game, there is plenty of time to explore Shoshone National Forest before returning to the lookout or completing tasks. There aren't a lot of pointless tasks, since a lot of it is about reporting or exploring new areas on the map, as well as developing dialogue between Henry and Delilah. There isn't a big focus on achievements, and although there are a few hidden places or extra items to find such as in the cache boxes, it never feels dull. There is quite a time jump halfway through the game, since the game spans 79 days as a summer lookout, but the story remains fairly balanced through the calmer moments of casual exploration and the intriguing and tense moments where the player (and characters) face uncertainty and are trying to tie pieces of the story together. There is some great mystery in this game, as well unanswered questions and explanations that kept me as a player engaged. What I appreciate most about Firewatch is that it's not solely an adventure game, suspense or thriller. It may be cliche to say, but it admirably focuses on the surreal moments of isolation and the choices we have on how to move forward when we don't know how. The dialogue is realistic and shows a wide range of human emotion, with fantastic voice acting, especially as you try to uncover truths of not just your surroundings, but on why you took this job in the first place and what it means for the future. I think the developers did a good job of not going in certain directions that would change the fundamental nature/meaning of the game, and instead, sticking to a path (especially in ways of the ending), that simply comments on humanity and our options of whether or not we face what we've been avoiding. A memorable game for sure, that makes me want to be a fire lookout in the future, or at least visit/live by national parks.

[i]Firewatch[/i] is kind of brilliant. For starters, it’s appropriated the derisive term “walking simulator” into gameplay that literally sees players hiking the trails of a national park. Secondly, its understanding of and ability to manipulate its audience is almost eerie. The level design and premise railroad the player without revealing that they’re doing so, and the audio design and plot progression induce a constant paranoia with nothing but a few unexplained noises and errant lines of dialogue. All of this is in service to a hard-hitting message about the dangers of retreating from reality. The problem with resolving a mystery in deliberately anticlimactic fashion should be obvious, but it’s exacerbated here by the sheer number of red herrings and an ultimate explanation that makes less sense than any of the more fantastical ones I had in my head. Still, it’s the old journey-versus-destination adage, and [i]Firewatch[/i] will appeal to anyone looking for a second dose of [i]Gone Home[/i]’s magic or a less experimental, more meaningful version of [i]Dear Esther[/i].

This game is fantastic. It's a bit hard to review, because it has some very distinctive traits, that at first sight may seem off, and still felt totally right when playing it. 

I've had my fair share of exploration games (I love exploring), and yet none of them felt like this one. When I find exploration games that have huge open spaces, but very little to actually find, it usually bothers me, and leads me towards a negative review. In this case, there aren't many secrets, and the area is huge; but it feels sooo realistic, as if you actually were exploring a big national park, that it really doesn't matter. I think having lots of secrets here would even break how realistic it is. Terrain is never the same; it doesn't reuse stuff over and over; it's full of variety, and you really feel like you're hiking in the woods and mountains. You don't have out of place things you have to find, you just have (simulated) nature with a lot of variety and paths to take and things to check out. When one explores an environment in real life, you don't expect to find hidden stuff around or something like that; you enjoy exploring nature and finding natural "landmarks" here and there; and this is what the games feels like too. Now, don't get me wrong, you'll actually find stuff if you explore around, stuff that you may actually find in real life in those places (wildlife, for example), and the mechanics of talking over your walkie talkie about what you see, as you are seeing it, enriches it to a degree that's really quite surprising. On a separate note, animation of climbing, jumping, dropping off a high ledge, rappelling, and even just being tired and supporting oneself on a sign, are so incredibly realistic, that you can almost feel the effort and results of those actions (like the impact on your feet after jumping down a ledge). It's totally amazing.

The interaction between the characters is also very realistic. It makes you feel like you understand them, and what they say feels completely appropriate, just what you might hear if you were listening to real conversations between people who met over walkie talkies, and have a lot of time on their hands to just talk. 

Furthermore, you really feel like you have a [i] choice [/i] in this game, whether about how much you want to explore, what you want to do next, or what you want to say (or not say) to the other character. There are a bunch of possibilities. Even if the game doesn't offer you a specific choice of action in certain parts, you feel like it's totally warranted, because what your character does is either what anyone would do in real life, or he simply doesn't have other options. You don't get left with the feeling of "I would have done this totally different", because you either can choose, or there simple aren't many other options in that context. If you play it more than once, you'll probably find new stuff you missed the first time, even if you explore thoroughly and extensively (I've played more than 9 hours, despite what my playtime says, there was a problem with my connection during play, and I've already seen new stuff I missed on youtube). I'll probably replay this game some day in the future, to see what new things I can find, and where other choices would have led me to. 

I've had all of this to say about the game already, and still haven't mentioned the story. It is very intriguing, and realistic. It's really hard to say more without spoiling it, but I'll add that the ending is super realistic too, but in a way that is very rarely done in games (it's not your typical "realistic" explanation). You'll have to play to see what I mean by this :P.

All in all, it was an impressive, immersive ride, one I'll probably come back to someday to relive again. It's a great game, and I totally recommend it.

Perhaps streaming this with friends added some unexpected enjoyment, as I felt I had an audience as I performed my Community Theater version of the game.

About halfway through the game, the story was having to work harder as I started to realize I was just running back and forth. Eventually what seemed like a giant map started to feel like a Rat Maze of going up and down steps, and repelling down ropes. This would be my greatest critique of the game. 

For me, I was hoping the game had more of a puzzle adventure game element. Maybe not every box was unlocked with 1234 (granted one was different, but Delilah tells you the code), and you need to actually think about solving something, other than how to run back and forth from various landmarks.

Overall the game and narrative was beautiful and would recommend it to anyone who wants to feel something in a game, but doesn't really want a challenge.

As a person who doesn't play much, I adored this game. From the very beginning I got absorbed in the game thanks to its story, the visuals and the music. 
I felt like I was actually living this story, which left me feeling a little melancholic in the end, just like after a long and beautiful book. 
The game reflected upon topics that I felt I could relate to: loved ones fading away, the research of oneself, the contact with nature, and the relationships with other, in particular the one with Delilah, that I felt close and distant at the same time. 
The visuals and the music added so much to the story itself and I fell in love with the ambient I found myself in, and would honestly play it all over again and again just to be thrown into that world for a little longer. 
I appreciated that many things were sort of 'left' in mistery because it allowed me to just dive into the story as an individual with my own thoughts and experiences. 
I don't think I fully understood Delilha's character, because throughout the gameplay I felt like I was doubting her, couldn't count on her as I thought I would have. Till the very end she remains a evanescent figure, almost a dream? Something I (Henry) probably needed to fill the gap left by my 'lost' wife. It felt like I was creating her persona, and for a while I believed that the game was going to end showing how I had gotten not only physically but also mentally distant, lost, creating worlds and peeople I needed to find myself again. Almost a parallel to my wife's disease. 

Losing oneself and leaving everything to get in contact with nature has been a recurrent theme in our society and I like to think that the name of Henry may have been inspired by Thoreau, the author of Walden. 

I liked how everything was left unsaid not only to Delilah but to ourselves also, as if something needed to be cancelled in order to progress in the story. 
This was an experience os solitude, frightening at times, marvellous at others. Avoiding one's problems by being alone is something that not only Henry, but also Ned, Brian's father, does. 
Solitude may be a terrifying, beautiful,  revealing way to atone for our mistakes. 

The music helped me get even more absorbed in the game, accompanying me during the game, helping me dive deeper into certain situations. 

10/10 to a stunning game that I played at the perfect moment of my life.

A masterful work of interactive storytelling. Firewatch achieves a degree of realism and emotional poignance that few visual novels and other story-based games ever reach. While the game is foremost and fundamentally devoted to its story, it is neither boring nor derivative in its gameplay. The map is small enough to navigate easily but intricate enough to represent a realistic wilderness. The intuitive dialog and exploration mechanics help the game move along efficiently: the mechanics work so smoothly that I forgot I was playing a video game for a while. Like its wilderness Unity counterpart The Long Dark,  Firewatch doesn't try to create totally true-to-life graphics. Instead, it presents an idealized landscape of muted colors and simple shapes and light features that work together to give the game the appearance of a pleasant, half-remembered dream.  Where The Long Dark relies on its punishing survival structure and horror elements to engage the player, FIrewatch wins the player over with the charm of its two principal characters, with the relationship between Henry and Delilah defining the game and giving each playthrough its unique mood and texture. The voice actors do marvelous work with a strong,  cliche-free  script that's  full of edge, awkwardness, misdirection, and charm, just like conversations in real life. New players should not  become  overly concerned about the plot  itself  and the details of the plot: remember that story and plot are not the same thing. Firewatch is the perfect game for players who like to see how innovative game designers can tell compelling stories in unorthodox ways. It's  worth the price, and will probably be the most satisfying three and a half hours of your day.

If you're looking for a beautifully crafted, story-driven experience with memorable characters and a captivating atmosphere, then Firewatch is an absolute must-play. I wholeheartedly recommend it!

Firewatch is one of those games that sat on the back-burner in my library for months because it never seemed like the right time to install it and play through it. But I finally played through it (last night), and loved it. Firewatch is a beautiful, interactive story. The main characters are relatable and endearing, and their relationship proved to be emotionally complex for how simple it was: a two-way radio conversation between people who have gone through a lot, and now hide in the wilderness to escape the pain. The game takes you through their journey, and teaches you a lesson about facing what haunts your memory head on. Play it if that's what you're looking for.
 
Pros:
+ The voice acting was exceptional (Delilah was voiced brilliantly)
+ The visuals of the game are gorgeous (art style, world design, color palette)
+ The story's surprising twist wasn't a letdown, but rather proved to be the start of some reflection on my part

Cons:
- The game is relatively short (3-5 hours)
- One of the lead developers is a huge douchelord

* * Spoiler Alert * * A lot of reviewers seemed to have been agitated over not meeting Delilah at the end of the game. She looked after you, helped you over the radio. You shared emotional moments. You heard her voice when you were confused or feeling isolated. Yet you never meet her. But you can start to understand why if you take your time to explore her watchtower at the end of the game, and you can really understand why if you replay the game and select certain conversation options. (Hint: Don't ever mention your wife to her.) It becomes clear that Delilah is deeply troubled, and keeps your relationship with her to be a radio-only affair. You were just something to hide her feelings in, too. That's one of the key themes of the game.

On the second "Con" in my review: A few years ago a famous YouTuber (Pewds) dropped a gamer word on stream, and then apologized for it immediately after. A lead developer of this game (Sean Vanaman) decided to insert himself into the controversy by issuing a DMCA strike against the YouTuber, even though the Firewatch Let's Play (or whatever) video was older content and had nothing to do with the gamer word stream (PUBG).

Sure, take it easy with the game words, boys. We should all be mindful of how and when we use certain words. But devs --  don't inject yourself into an unrelated controversy for cheap PR or to virtue signal. Threatening to or instigating a DMCA strike against a streamer for a verbal mistake is immature and slimy. More recently, Vanaman abused his employment at Valve to manually punish a Dota 2 player for not following his (Vanaman's) recommend playstyle. Yes, he's a huge douche.

But don't let it stop you from enjoying a beautiful game. There are other, less crappy people involved with Firewatch. And it is definitely a beautiful game.

First off I completely recommend this game. This review doesn't have spoilers but its best to go into this game completely blind. 

Firewatch has always been a very important game to me.  I first played it on release day back in 2016.  I was relatively young and not somebody who really fits into this game's demographic.  The biggest thing I got out of it was the hiking.  It sparked something in me.  I was never really outdoorsy but after playing this game I decided to start visiting local parks and going for walks.  This evolved into a passion for hiking and backpacking.  I don't think this game is exactly what gave me a love of the wilderness, but it definitely played a role in encouraging me to get into the hobby.

Now I'd like to talk about the actual game.  I've probably played through it 4 or 5 times now.  As I grew up, I started to understand what the game was truly trying to portray.  Without going into much detail, I think this game has a great message even though it can be a hard one to comprehend and swallow.  Every time I replay it I find something new I had never noticed before.  By far the greatest aspect of this game is the dialogue.  The main characters are extremely believable and it is easy to get immersed in the story.  The soundtrack is also great.  I regularly listen to it while backpacking in real life.  The map is also beautiful and represents many of the biomes found on the west coast.  The artstyle still holds up to this day and probably will for a very long time. 

Overall this game means a lot to me.  When I first played this game, the community was huge.  Now a very tiny amount of people play this game.  The hype there once was for this game is nothing but a relic of the past.  Still, I see myself returning to this game for years to come.

It's hard to say anything about it without spoiling it, so if you don't mind Walking Simulators (though this one also has controllable character interaction by way of walkie talkie), then this is a great game with a lot to offer.
The way the game uses interaction to craft a slightly different story for each player and build additional tension, since everything that happens, good or bad, is ultimately made to feel like your doing, is awesome. Also the game very cleverly let's you transpose yourself onto the main character in the first few minutes of the game, by giving you a text intro, where you can choose some details of your backstory, to impose your morality and ideals onto the character.
A great deep dive into psychology, escapism and searching for meaning/distractions (depending on how you look at it) and a fantastic attempt at using the strengths of the video game medium to craft an enthralling narrative.

My only gripe is that I did encounter a few bugs along the way that had me restarting from previous checkpoints, so do save frequently, if possible.

There's always something kind of good about stories about people just going off into the wilderness to vibe. Maybe it's that modern culture is suffocating, maybe the thought of reverting to some 'pure' natural self is appealing, maybe we're just running away from stuff. 

Firewatch is legitimately engaged with that idea. All of the characters in it are trying to find something of themselves out in the forest, the only difference is in how far they've let themselves wander looking for it. I watched [i] Grizzly Man[/i] by Werner Herzog recently and I was struck by the similarities, not in the overall story necessarily but in the presentation. Both works love and value the natural world, but they recognise that it's not a substitute for society and it can't be, and by fooling yourself into thinking that you're only going to get yourself and others hurt.

It can be easier to form emotional attachments outside of society, to be someone you wouldn't be otherwise, someone you want to be, and sometimes that's just the way we cope with things. But there's a line between a coping mechanism being helpful and it getting in the way of the healing process and you living the rest of your life.

This is a short review of Firewatch. For a more in-depth review that covers the story/ characters more visit my website at: https://shutyourcakeholegaming.com/2021/02/18/firewatch/

I Feel bad for ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on a game that occupies a niche genre that genuinely tries to do its job well. Regardless of whatever I say, there is no doubt that there was a lot of effort put in, and very few areas are what I would consider lazy, or slapdashed. 
That being said, the game falters a lot in the narrative department, which isn’t so much a stumble as it is a fall off Mount Kilimanjaro, especially when you consider that the dialogue and character is the closest thing this game has to gameplay. 
You play as Henry, a man with a troubled past who tries to get over his wife’s dementia by escaping into the woods (in a forest ranger/ fire lookout way, not in like a moonshine making way). He meets a supervisor named Delilah and the two proceed to awkwardly seduce each other over the course of a summer as the world's most boring mystery unfolds in front of them concerning missing girls and dead lookouts. 
In the beginning, the characters were pretty great, with tons of witty banter.  Henry and Delilah act as great foils to each other, with Henry providing a dark, cynical sense of humor, and Delilah’s playful and sarcastic jabs. 
Over time, I started to despise Delilah though. Without spoiling things, she reveals that she's a truly cowardly and weak person, and it killed any empathy I had for her. The game also sets up a million different sub-stories, ranging from interesting to me wondering why they even bothered. The worst part is, they all lead to red herrings or dead ends, minus one. 

While the narrative is bland, the scenery is absolutely stunning. There's a mode after you finish the game that lets you wander through the park, collecting secrets and finding story beats.
The level designers, use a lot of deep colors, and well-planned level design, so it's never a chore to get to one end of the park or the other. The audio is fantastic as well, with a great variety of different woodland creatures, and decent music as well. 

If you want a good story-based game, I recommend Headlines:Novinews.

To the person who kept pushing me to play this game: there, I did it. I finished it. All of it. Top to bottom. All five hours of it, give or take. And honestly?

Thank you. This was great. Firewatch is a walking-simulator-radio-'em-up by Campo Santo. You've probably heard about this game by now. Alongside Dear Esther, it's seen as one of the two 'pioneers' in the walking simulator genre. Games with no real fail state where the gameplay consists of wandering. In Firewatch, however - and in contrast to Dear Esther - you do get to make [i]some[/i] choices and interact with [i]some[/i] of the world. The entire first part of the game is about choices. And, before I continue, I'll put this here: This is a [i]really[/i] good game, but the ending may leave you feeling unsatisfied. Or it may leave you feel incredibly satisfied. It did me. I loved this game. 

Do note: My review will be written from the point of view of the dialogue choices I made and what I heard. You can make many choices, including ignoring Delilah altogether. The call is yours. Your mileage may vary.

So, for the sake of brevity: you yell at teens, chase raccoons, and indulge Delilah, your boss, in idle chatter about crosswords, the boy scouts, and bush fires. If that seems like the sort of thing you'd like, set to an atmospheric soundtrack? Go for it. The rest of the review is a spoiler, so beware, stop reading here, and for God's sake, go fling money at Campo Santo.

[spoiler][h1]Life isn't meant to be satisfying[/h1]

That's...that's about it, yeah. This is a game about everyday people. It's a game about how, really, in daily life? There's no literary villain, no bad guy with properly evil motivations, not outside of the occasional self-serving ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and sociopathic autocrat. At the end of the day, the overwhelming majority of people either don't think about their actions as good or bad, or if they do, they see themselves as the good guys. 

Going into this game, I expected the usual from a walking simulator - a metaphor of some kind, an overarching point contextualised in a thematic envronment: Dear Esther's island, for comparison, as a symbol of isolation, grief, and detatchment. Firewatch has that. Shoshone National Forest is the perfect place for a man who is trying to recover from the loss of his wife to dementia. It's heavy, it gets heavy in the beginning and then it ticks up, to a sort of light-heartedness, a mundaneity.

Henry, the protagonist (or Hank, as Delilah likes to call him for kicks) is a kind-hearted, melancholy man in his middle age. As mentioned previously, his wife of many years - June - develops very early onset dementia. He copes through alcohol and isolation and, when things finally boil over, heads into the wilderness. away from all of it.

[h1]You can't run from your problems forever[/h1]

Through your choices, Henry can either become a stalwart guardian of the wilderness or a devil-may-care man with his own agenda, but no matter what you do, you will learn about your surroundings and become comfortable with them. The voice on the radio, Delilah, will only become nearer and nearer to you. Your choices will determine if and how Henry copes with his grief - and, as you play, especially early on, with each day you become aware that June? She's gone. Henry's wife is alive, but she may as well not be. And if that alone isn't enough to leave a knot in your throat, the rest of the game will. 

One of the paths you can take - and one which I see many users have taken - is one where Henry and Delilah become closer. They flirt, they exchange little quips, and they share a view of the fire. "Think of the things we could do if I were there..." Delilah begins, and thus, Henry stops wearing his wedding ring. You can choose to still have him wear it, but he can begin to move on. You have the choice of oblivion, and the choice of a new beginning - or the choice of both. And Firewatch covers all of them spectacularly. Honestly, I've never seen such an earnest examination of grief in a video game before. 

[h1]I'm sorry, Delilah[/h1]

The moment you become comfortable with Henry and his life post-June, his new routine gets turned upside down. Someone is watching you. You become aware of this, intimately. And soon, a line of intrigue forms. Henry, who came to Wyoming to run from himself, is now being actively pursued. The pitch of this pursuit increases steadily, as does the intensity of it. From broken in lookouts to cut telephone wires and finally, to a horrible discovery in a cave. It all begins to feel like a sudden, mad thriller. And just as the intimacy of being the only two people who are actively chased nears fever pitch, we learn that Delilah has a horrible secret. She's a murderer, but not by design - by kindness, of all things. And no matter what you do, it won't be okay. There is a gap and it won't be okay.

Delilah and Henry don't end up together. They can't. Their love is real, and you can feel that, but it is built on things which are too painful to speak. They'll never live a happily ever after. They'll never meet. Delilah starts out as a voice on the radio, and ends as the woman who Henry loves, whose personification is a hanging headset in a desolate lookout about to be swallowed up by the fire bearing her middle name.

Firewatch is a game about being okay with things not being okay. In the end, nothing turns out right, but the people this game is about? They cross paths elsewhere. They become their own people, and they learn from the deaths of their fragile and - from the outset - temporary routine.[/spoiler]

People complain about the lack of choices here, and whilst the outcome is fixed, the choices are there: they're just not satisfying ones. They're the dirty emotional maintenance of daily life that nobody wants to do, but the witnessing of which in someon else - Henry and Delilah, in this case - can be a very, very satisfying experience. 

Buy this game. Buy the soundtrack. And pray that we get Valley Of the Gods someday.

The game is pretty good. It takes between 4 and 5 hours to beat the game, based on how much you explore the forrest. You might replay the game with the developper's commentary and then add another 4-5hs for a total of around 10.
For that reason, I wouldn't advise buying the game full price. I got it for 5 bucks on Steam during a Sale but the game is otherwise around 25€, which is a bit much. 

Other than that though, the game's awesome. It's a classic Walking and Talking simulator. 
So let's tackle the walking first: it's good! It's amusing to see 40 years old Henry having unlimited stamina, as well as arms, kneecaps and ankles made of titanium. The man casually climbs stuff to get up and then yeets himself off ledges to go down, he jumps above gaps with ease but will take his time to vault over a wooden log, it's great. That being said, his legs when walking can be pretty meh, you will get stuck on the tiniest rock regularly because the game's like "no".
It's not that big of a deal however.

Now, for the talking part, that's when it gets awesome. Henry and Delilah are a great pair and their banter is very endearing. 
They tease and make fun of each other when the mood is light, talk seriously When the mood isn't for jokes. And there's this flirty mood between the two even though they both know they shouldn't. 
Which is something I really like in gaming. Both Henry and Delilah are their own characters, sure you can select the answers Henry gives (or chose to say nothing) but every choice possible is something that Henry could "realistically" say in the moment.

That's something I really enjoy and that I believe too many games get wrong. A silent/placeholder character in games is usually boring unless given many opportunities to express themselves in meaningful ways. 
Instead, here, Henry is a guy and you're going along his ride. He's riding the bike and you're in the Side-Car with the map telling him where to go, but you're not driving, and it's great.

But Henry isn't alone in this Ride, so is Delilah, and just like Henry, she's not a placeholder waifu, she's a person with a believable personality and reactions. 

All of this is helped with a fantastic voice acting from both Henry and Delilah. They're delightful to listen to. 

As a whole, the game's amazing. I was hooked on instantly with the characters and the story and was as invested as I could with Henry and Delilah. Sharing their happiness and their fear, their banter and their anxiety as adults that can sometimes be nothing but relatable.

Masked in beautiful graphics, this single-player first-person mystery game is an emotional roller-coaster that takes place in the Wyoming wilderness. You play as a man named Henry in the year 1989 who began work as a fire lookout a few years after his wife developed early-onset dementia and moved to Australia with her parents.

Strange and chilling events begin unfolding as you slowly unravel the mystery that plagues Two Forks. Your supervisor, Delilah, becomes a trusted voice on the other side of a radio offering a few bad puns and serious conversation. Firewatch plays on anxiety and paranoia, describing itself as an 'adult game' with certain aspects that may not be suitable to a younger audience. [spoiler] Such as the death and imagery of a small boy. [/spoiler]

The grim aspect of Firewatch aside, the story and world within the game is immersive. You can find a disposable camera along the way which invites the player to enjoy the simulated landscape and photograph it. While the game can be completed within five hours, it's well-worth the experience.

As a huge Valve and Half-Life: Alyx fan, I deemed it necessary to check this game out after hearing the involvement of Campo Santo in that title. And I must say, this game surprised me in unexpected ways: 

- The writing and voice acting is super high quality, and I grew to like both main characters very quickly [spoiler] despite all of their development being delivered through dialogue and text only; there are no traditional cutscenes where you see the characters moving, so this is a seriously impressive feat. [/spoiler]

- While the world has a slightly cartoony aesthetic, it feels very realistic and successfully creates an uplifting or tense atmosphere where appropriate, [spoiler] even though there is no combat whatsoever. [/spoiler]

- The narrative is really clever and successfully subverts the player’s expectations without feeling cheap; [spoiler] you feel like something bigger is going on as you would normally expect in video games, but the game decides to simply not go down that route. I think this is such a simple yet effective choice that makes it stand out by, well, not being bombastic in presentation like many other games would do. [/spoiler] 

- Like many people, the ending really confused me initially, but after sitting with it, it completely made sense given the direction of the narrative. [spoiler] I think the fact that many people seemed disappointed with it showed that the developers pulled off their vision successfully; we all expected something more substantial to happen, but the game’s final message reminds you of the harsh reality of the world, and that running from one’s problems can only last so long before it’s time to snap back to reality. [/spoiler]I understand why people wouldn’t like it, but at the end of the day, Firewatch is not particularly long so I don’t think it could really be said that it wasted anyone’s time, unless they completely despise walking simulators.

The game took me around three hours to beat, though if I was better with following the map and searching the environment in a couple of cases, this probably could have clocked in at about two and a half hours. This would be longer if you decide to not jog your way through the world, but I decided to do so throughout since the narrative consistently gripped me and I wanted to uncover the mystery surrounding it in good time. 

The game also offers free-roam after you beat the story, and there are a couple of extra achievements to track down if you want to squeeze the game for all its content, but aside from that there isn’t really much to do. It’s worth it at 75% off for sure, but due to its length I couldn’t really recommend it for anything above that since there isn’t much to do aside from the narrative. However, what is here is incredibly quality, and I’ll likely have this in mind when drawing up a list of my favourite games I played this year. 9/10.

I guess I am in the minority here because this game is simply bad. 

The aesthetics are the only thing going for it, but I got nearly 2 hours in and I just kept saying "wtf" at the dialogue options and the storyline. I let the dialogue choices time-out numerous times just because none of the options are good. Gameplay is boring, just a ton of navigating trails and walking around. *Apparently* you can choose the outcome of the game through the dialogue options, but already I expressed no interest in Delilah from the get-go and wanted to go through the game staying loyal to Julia. Even though I never told Delilah that I was divorced from Julia (because as far as I knew we were still married and I was still wearing my wedding ring), she still ended up using dialogue as if I said Julia was "my ex." The game basically forces you to be a cheater. Also, apparently there are no other ways to meet a potential lover than "at a bar." The obsession with alcohol and drinking in this game borders on adolescent fantasy. The mechanics of "girl on the walkie talkie" have been done 100s of times, I recommend Green Hell for a similar experience but much more exceptional gameplay and storyline. 

Plot holes. Apparently our protagonist hiked two days to get to his watch tower. So tell me, how did two teenage girls manage to hike by themselves with a full tent plus sleeping bags, what seemed like a 40 pack of beer, whiskey, and endless bundles of fireworks? How are they not dead after consuming what would be impressive to a chronic alcoholic and still be able to stand and speak? 

And when annoying Delilah wakes you up to look out the window and see your first fire in the night. She refers to it as "beautiful" which leads me to believe the writers have actually no idea how terrifying and devastating forest fires are. It completely sucked all the immersion out from that point forward and I rage quit. Come back to write when you actually look out your window and see a orange glow in the distance because that is real life for anyone living in a tinderbox state, and I am willing to put money that those in danger did not refer to the flames as "beautiful" especially in the dead of night as people are evacuating their homes. 

TLDR; its nice to look at. Everything else is pretty subpar imho. 4/10, 3 for the aesthetics and color palettes and 1 for the *somewhat* interesting mystery when it wasn't being completely soured by Delilah's annoying voice. Needless to say, I got a refund. Just watch gameplay through youtube and save yourself $20. Same experience.

[h1]Firewatch Review[/h1]
[i]**Spoiler Free**[/i]

[u]Quick Review:[/u] Firewatch is an atmospheric exploration game that’s light on gameplay mechanics but delivers a fantastic experience. The story and voice acting are top notch, and the atmosphere is inviting with its stylized art.  This game might be about walking through the woods, but it can be as intense and thrilling as it is peaceful and beautiful. I highly recommend you give this game a shot. Walking around in the woods can be much more interesting than you think. 

[u]Gameplay:[/u] As I said before, the gameplay is a simple atmospheric exploration game. There is no combat, no health, no platforming, and no upgrading.  Your actions essentially revolve around walking around this gorgeous stylized environment, interacting with items that you find, and using the radio to talk to your colleague, which gives you basic dialogue options when replying. You’ll also be taking out your map and compass often to orient yourself and figure out where you need to go.

With this sort of bare-bones gameplay, you might expect this to be a rather boring game. But to the contrary, this is one of the most interesting and engrossing games out there. That’s because it is heavily story-based, and heavily based on your relationship with your colleague. In fact, the simple gameplay mechanics actually [i]help[/i] to deliver that great experience because it allows you to focus on what the game does so well instead of distracting you with abilities, events or side quests.  This game can be really tense at moments, more so than other games I’ve played where combat and quick reactions are needed to survive.  

The gameplay is simple. The game is fantastic. 

However, this is where your own preference in gaming will have a big affect. If you want an RPG, open world, platformer, or whatever and don’t care about story and dialogue, then this game is going to sound like a turn off for you.  But even if that’s the case, I’d recommend trying out this game. It’s not that long and you might find that a good story can keep you hooked.

[u]User interface:[/u] The interface is simple and effective. Menus are easy to navigate and intuitive. The HUD is minimalistic, which I felt it was appropriate for this kind of game.   If you want to look at a Map or a Compass, you have to actually pull it out and observe it.  Mechanics like this, along with a lack of visual clutter, really helps to immerse you into the environment and story. 

The control scheme on a DualShock 4 is a little odd. You use the back triggers often, for actions like picking up items and using the radio.  I figured some of these actions would be mapped to buttons like the square button.

Instead, square is reserved for a toggle for running, which is pretty annoying. I’m not sure why running needed to be a toggle and couldn’t have just been implemented into pushing the joystick in a direction.  It’s annoying because every time you stop moving, it defaults back to walking. So you’re constantly having to toggle running on.  For an explorative game in the wilderness with wide open spaces and no need for stealth mechanics, I’m not sure why this decision was made. It’s a relatively small annoyance, but it’s there. 

 Overall the interface is straightforward, solid, and doesn’t get in the way. 

[u]Atmosphere:[/u] This is certainly an atmospheric game.  It’s how it’s advertised and it does not disappoint. The stylized environment can make for some very relaxing and serene visual moments. The level design often gives you opportunities to look out over vistas onto the background environment, which is a nice subtle artistic touch in encouraging you to appreciate your natural surroundings.

The sound adds wonders to the atmosphere too. Just the natural sounds of trees blowing in the wind, or birds chirping, or water running is enough to help you feel at ease during some of those long walks. The voice acting is top notch too,  and in my opinion is the true outstanding achievement of this game. It may be a peaceful wilderness, but the emotions, tones, and story that takes place between you and Delilah over the radio completely colors your emotional experience and investment in this world.  The verbal story progression, along with some haunting music, can turn the serene outdoors into a very tense thriller.  Honestly, it feels like the whole game is there to support the sound, and comes together in a fantastic experience. The sound is that good. 

This games atmosphere is so strong and so intertwined with the story that I promise you're going to get invested in this world.

[u]Accessibility:[/u] This game supports multiple inputs, which I greatly appreciated. You can change the controls to four different configurations: keyboard, gamepad, DualShock 4, steam controller. (FYI, changing the layout in settings doesn’t just show you what the control scheme is for that input, but [i]actually[/i] changes the type of input you are using. This is not made clear. So if you’re checking out a certain control scheme, and then your controls are all weird, that’s why)

For some reason the triggers on my DualShock 4 controller were not being registered by Firewatch. I ended up re-mapping the trigger functions to keyboard/mouse commands (right trigger = left mouse click, left trigger = Left Shift). It was annoying at first, and it’s possible I was not using the correct settings under controller figuration in Steam, but because of the multi input capability, you can see it was not a problem.

I was able to play this game using a DualShock 4 controller, voice attack, and a 3DRudder (keyboard or joystick modes)

[u]Conclusion:[/u]  I definitely recommend you play this game.  The gameplay, atmosphere, story, voice acting...just all of it comes together for a really great experience. It’s not super long, and priced reasonably so. Take some time and have some fun running through this stylized Woodland. You’ll be glad you did.

Action games will make you feel high on all the adrenaline while adventure/puzzle games will make you feel smart as they increase the difficulty of their systems.  Horror games will terrify you while narrative games will guide you through a coherent narrative in such a way that when you finish you feel cathartic.  

Firewatch won't give you any of that.  Firewatch's gameplay won't make you feel like a badass or a genius.  Firewatch's story is not interested in linear storytelling or making you feel like you accomplished something.  Firewatch is only interested in telling its story about a man past his prime who's most exciting time in his life involves running away from his problems. [h1] Pretty Game Good [/h1]

[b] Gameplay: [/b]
You walk and talk. You also pick up stuff and talk about it. And you also watch stuff to later talk about it. 
The traversal mechanics are good, although there are a lot of invisible walls that somewhat break immersion, but nothing game-breaking. You also obtain tools as the story progresses and it feels pretty organic; note that you can only use said items a couple of times. And you can also hop over stuff and not talk about it. 
The level design is a great aspect of the game, as the story seamlessly guides you thorough different paths that make the forest feel new and even exciting, at least for the first time. It kinda made me feel like an explorer among a mysterious big-ass forest.

[b] Art-Style: [/b]
It is a very scenic and beautiful game that I didn't get to fully experience, sadly, seen as my computer can't handle god-rays or something. But even on a downgraded version of the graphics, I can say it still looks great. Even the photos you can take in-game look very stylish. This game features a very detailed low poly style that meshes very well with the lighting and colors. The color palettes feel very well thought out and lived-in. Just looking at the landscapes and landmarks scattered around the map makes the free roam mode worth the while, for it is a very relaxed and nature-centric environment to fully be immersed in.

[b] Story & Characters: [/b]
There are two main characters that are heard through the whole game: Delilah and Henry. You play as the ladder, a man that is looking for a... distraction let's call it, in a very weird time in his life, time in which he meet Delilah, his boss as a firewatch employee. 
This is the central dynamic the game will focus on and it's very well acted, aside from some lines that don't sound as authentic as the rest of the voice work, but is good as a whole. 
You'll also meet other characters as a spectator, a feature I really liked as it makes the world feel like you are not the only one living in it.
The story centres around weird happenings inside the forest since the arrival of Henry, which will thrust you upon a mystery that culminates in what I consider to be a very human ending. The kind of ending I really like in stories like these.

[b] Achievements: [/b]
By golly, these have to be the easiest achievements I have collected so far! There are only 10 and most of them will be naturally unlocked with just one playthorugh, while the rest can be quickly collected in a matter of minutes without even repeating the story thanks to the free roam mode. I really do thank the developers of this game for making a good, satisfying and digestible game.

[b] TL;DR [/b]
Good, pretty, quick game featuring beautiful, scenic moments and satisfying characters. And a brease for completionists!

[h1]The Game[/h1]
Firewatch is a game that immediately draws you in, immersing you as Henry, entering into his life through what seems like trivial choices, each carrying consequences that shape who he is. However it always progresses and concludes the same way regardless. Multiple choice is not the aim of Firewatch, it's the characters and relationships.

The first thing to draw you in is the game's stunning atmosphere. Firewatch has held up exceptionally well for a game from 2016. While there are aspects that could be nitpicked over, it has stood the test of time visually. The story is gripping, beginning with Henry simply trying to escape his problems to the wilderness, only to be met with harrowing paranoia, speculative trust, and eventually tragedy. There are positive, almost romantic seeming moments that delay the ever pressing tension. Said tension transferred through the music, voice acting, and storytelling to the player is remarkably effective. Crafted expertly to make you feel just as paranoid as Henry and Delilah as they try to work out what the hell is going on.
Henry himself is a complex character to sit with. He is not always immediately likeable, but always understandable, which is arguably harder to pull off. His reasons for being there, the weight he carries from home, and the psychological stress of the unfolding mystery around him make him one of the more genuinely compelling protagonists I have played as in this genre.

Delilah is an interesting contradiction. She keeps Henry from feeling entirely alone out there, her insights and jokes throughout are genuinely funny, and her presence over the radio is what stops the isolation from becoming unbearable. Yet she always keeps her distance in ways that feel deliberate rather than accidental. [spoiler]Made most apparent on Day 77, when it is revealed she was capable of leaving her tower the entire time, having gone past Henry's tower entirely just to drop a radio at Cottonwood Creek rather than delivering it to him directly.[/spoiler] She flirts, she gets close, and then retreats. The game does lean into a slow burn romantic tension between them which I personally found weaker than their dynamic simply as two isolated people finding unlikely companionship. Their relationship worked better as a friendship forged under extraordinary stress than as anything more, and the flirting at points felt more awkward than entertaining but thankfully wasn't in abundance.

Navigation can occasionally be a little tricky and getting lost is not uncommon. That said I found myself appreciating it as part of the immersion, having to backtrack, misread a path, and find your way again made me feel genuinely like Henry venturing through unfamiliar wilderness rather than following a waypoint. It is one of those frustrations that paradoxically adds to the experience rather than detracting from it, further immersing me in the world.

[h2]The Twist[/h2]
[spoiler]The resolution of the mystery is not the grand government conspiracy the paranoia of the game builds toward, and that is entirely the point. What you find instead is far more human and far more tragic, Ned Goodwin, a former lookout and grieving father, has spent three years living in the wilderness hiding from the truth of his son Brian's accidental death, manipulating everything around Henry and Delilah to stop anyone from finding the body and exposing his shame. Every act of sabotage, every moment of harrowing paranoia Henry experienced, traced back not to some shadowy organisation but to one broken man who simply could not face what he had lost. For a game built entirely around characters running from their problems rather than confronting them, it is a perfectly fitting conclusion. The mystery does not end with a bang, it ends with something quieter and considerably more devastating.[/spoiler]

[h2]The End[/h2]
[spoiler]The revelation that Delilah simply left without ever meeting Henry in person was not surprising, her entire character throughout the game had already shown someone just as prone to running from her problems as Henry was in the beginning. Therefore the two never meet in person, and somehow that feels exactly right.[/spoiler]

Firewatch is a game that I first watched as a playthrough on Youtube upon release, fascinated by the beautiful scenery when I was younger much of the story got lost in my memory. Henry, Delilah, Jule, Brian, Ned, none of their stories really stuck with me, they didn't leave an impression on my mind back then. 
Now, this is likely due to youthful ignorance, but I find it hard to feel sad about the fact as it enabled me to go into this game with barely any expectations past the visually satisfying and beautifully designed graphics.

Even if during the prologue one doesn't feel connected to Henry yet, with every choice of dialogue there is a growing awareness that the man you're playing as is neither a hero nor a villain in the story. He's Henry, a guy trying to escape from his life, from his marriage and the painful truth of what awaits him back home, someone who is a little cowardly yet painfully aware of his situation, someone who, even if you pick the choices you think will lead him to the best possible result, is broken and hurt despite his best (or worst) efforts. And someone who finds comfort in the presence of another broken person, someone who is willing to listen and someone who understands what it's like to run away from your past, your bad choices and feeling lost in life.
Spending this summer with Henry and Delilah, listening to their conversations, learning what kind of people they are and what brought them to Wyoming and investigating the strange happenings in the national park, everything just a coincidence in these two people's lives. 
They are more human than I'd like to admit and their troubles seem so real that you really feel for them and at times find yourself enjoying the moments of peace and quiet while hiking through the park, briefly leaving the heavyness of it all behind you and just taking in the view, getting lost in the colors.

You're faced with some tough choices in this game, I found myself second guessing my own choices later on, questioning if there would've been a better way to do things, a better way to react to certain questions and situations, something I missed, something I overlooked. In the end, it doesn't really matter because when I made the choices they seemed right.

[h1] Firewatch is one of the best games ever written, and in a short time, will deliver you a unique and powerful emotional experience. [/h1]

Firewatch is one-of-a-kind and quite frankly nothing short of breathtaking. Before you buy, I recommend you come for a walk with me, let's talk.

Firewatch was never a game I saw myself playing, as a matter of fact, I still have failed to weasel into the genre it rests in. But astoundingly, today almost 5 years on, I still find myself desiring the opportunity to relive my first experience in this truly unique game.

When the game was first released I was 12. And as expected it did not cater to my First-Person-Shooter and Open-World preferences, so it still astounds me today I happened to punch its name into YouTube thanks to a unique banner that caught my eye (it was the watchtower one). Deciding to look it up on YouTube I was surprised to find more prominent names like Markiplier and Jacksepticeye uploading content surrounding the game, and take note, these were content creators I rarely engaged with. If ever. So the fact that Firewatch made its way to my library is still a shock in itself.

On my first play-through, I tackled the game in one sitting (~four hours of playtime). Almost instantly my interest was captivated by a narrative that was purely hiking, talking and sunsets—something no game had ever come close to doing. Taking an interest in a game like Firewatch at the age of twelve is rare, and I feel it has surprisingly little to do with who I am individually, and relies more on what the game is, in itself.

[b] My predominant interest in Firewatch, is through its [u]narrative[/u]. [/b]
Our protagonist Henry (the player) is introduced to Delilah; a US Forest Service (USFS) Firewatch—and Henry's supervisor during his summer of '89. Delilah is your sole communicate for the game. She will remain a bridge to emotion for your isolation, and a friend that to which you will develop a complex relationship of click and clack soon to be revered by a pursuing pressure. 
There is a clear purpose to your adventure, one that you (yes, you) will rapidly forget as you veer into a world of fear and complexity. The Ol'Shoshone is an escape (both in narrative and as a playing experience), do not try to fight either, they will (if respected) contribute to the quality of your experience. And in short; this story is player-driven, but it is linear.
The formation of the narrative will point you in a specific direction by letting you feel as if you are steering the ship. The connection developed between Henry and Delilah is what facilitates that directive and drives the anticipation, love and fear of every step Henry takes. So pay attention.


Firewatch and the detail in its art style deliver a true rarity. So when I say the game takes the top spot for graphical composition, I genuinely mean it. Not by its applicability to reality, but by its construction in tandem with the rest of the game. Every moment, every step and every minute you take in the environment feels honest; the intentional placement of flora and fauna, the use of daylight shifts and exposure rays, directed lighting and tone consistent colour ranges all contribute to a very unique visual experience. One that's hard to knock down too couple of words.
Furthermore, your adventure is accompanied by a remarkable Original Sound Track [OST]. Made by Chris Remo, your memories will form with some of the most emotive and powerful tunes you will ever know, my favourite, the subtle guitar strums of Prologue, the very first song you hear as you start your wander into the heart of Wyoming.

Now... 6 years have passed since I first experienced Firewatch. The very day I am writing this review I find myself coming back to this title—and in honesty, I can't tell you why. Maybe it was the trails that warmed my heart, the music that brought me to tears, or maybe it was the sunset's that made me stop... watch and wait. 

I can confidently say there has not been one title in my time playing video games that has [or will] ever been able to provide me with the comfort in the memories I truly revisit and admire from Firewatch. Nor has any game been able to suck me back in and re-create the way I felt the first time I launched it. This piece of art was an escape from pain, a distraction from sadness, yet today, the only things I retain are the plot twists, sunsets and lullabies that only ever bring me smiles. I truly find it ironic that despite such attention to the story, the two most vivid memories I retain—the sunset in Thunder Canyon, and the music that plays in your initial hike to your post—are of little relevance to it. And in transparency, once I'm back in, the rest follow suit.

Now to wrap up the game is set in 1989, and there are a few cute and hilarious easter-eggs that are dotted throughout the shrubs. But if you do end up reading this far and investing in the game I can only make one recommendation,

On your first play though, follow the narrative, your heart and above all else, [b]take your time[/b]. Soak in what a true masterpiece this award-winning game is, walk down the random trails, look behind the bushes, and sit and stare for a while. And yes it may be short, but Firewatch is worth whatever price may be placed on it because it will bring you memories I guarantee you will never forget. And memories that will not only remind you of the game and revive a desire to go back and play it but. But emotions that will revive the best memories of your life. Somehow this game is associated with some of my greatest adventures, and yet has no connection to their taking place.

I say one last thing like I did when I opened it. [b] Firewatch is unparalleled in its entirety. And it's the game that truly connects to my heart, and I hope it connects with yours. [/b]

Firewatch was a pure pleasure for the eyes to play. The visuals are stunningly beautiful and can easily join the ranks of gorgeous games like Eastshade or the Witness.


[b]Plot[/b]

We play as Henry who came to work for the summer as a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness while trying to escape from the troubles in his life. Our boss Delilah is the only contact we have with the human world. And we spend our days chatting with her about life or any questions we may have through a radio while roaming through the park.

There is one aspect in the plot that I found questionable, or maybe it was an oversight from the devs. At some point in the story, the park is covered by fire smoke, but at no time is it mentionned that Henry wears a breathing mask that would have helped him survived that part. I found that kind of strange.


[b]Exploration[/b]

Firewatch has been labeled a walking sim, but it has so much to offer that I would qualifiy it more to be an exploration game such as Infra but without the puzzles.

I found the exploration aspect in the game really interesting. While we will in any case uncover the very emotional game story, we don't have to follow the given path. We can in fact freely deviate from it, go the opposite way and explore every nook and cranny of the available game map. There are tons of objects and places to discover. I recommend reading all documents as they reveal more details about the plot and the game world.


[b]Dialogues[/b]

We are free to ask Delilah about anything we find, and are given several choices to answer her questions or we can just ignore them. I do not know how much our choices affect the game ending, but they do affect some of the later dialogues content.
Of course, there are still some mandatory dialogues to complete if we want to progress in the game.


[b]Screenshots & Camera[/b]

I took hundreds of screenshots while playing. And my favorites were the different possible views with the background sun, especially at sunset. 
Let's note that we can remove the central round pointer by selecting 'hide Interface' from the 'Settings' menu.
The game also has an in-game camera that allows us to take 18 pictures. I had no idea what it was for so I used it to take pictures of places (vista points, waterfall...) that had some unremovable in-game floating description. And we can actually find the photos inside the saved files folder or get a link by clicking on 'Camera Roll Upload' in 'Special Features' that allows us to download the pictures and optionally order a paid print of them.


[b]Free roam mode[/b]

The game offers a free roam mode where we can freely explore the whole game world.

This game ain’t a walk in the park. Well actually, it is.

Firewatch is an incredibly atmospheric, well crafted, story-driven game depicting a man struggling to grieve as he takes a new posting as a fire lookout deep in the Wyoming countryside.

I think what first captured my attention was the intro. How the story of someone’s life was told through little details and events. Reading about Henry and Julia’s conversation about having kids, or being mugged on night, allows us to picture who they are as people, as well as their relationship in a much more meaningful way than through events like their wedding.

Those first few days as a fire lookout feel like a walk in the park, pun intended. The brilliantly composed soundtrack accompanied some, not all, of your many treks throughout the wild. It feels incredibly peaceful, therapeutic even. The design of the world really feels like you’re walking through a national park. Most of the game there isn’t a clear “this way” or “over here” sign, meaning you have to rely on your compass and map, which is just brilliant game design.

Now, for the story. I had gone into Firewatch completely blind, and I’m so glad I did. I don’t want to spoil anything story-wise, but it certainly takes a turn you don’t expect, which I absolutely loved. The writers and developers were able to change the atmosphere of the game almost instantly.

Finally, my favourite aspect of the game just HAS to be the dialogue and voice acting. It’s practically perfect. The way Delilah and Henry interact, from when they first “meet” right to the climax, you actually believe these characters could exist. You believe their intentions, and root for them every step. Even side dialogue adds to their character. It was a joy to hear those voices, and the dialogue the evidently talented writers gave them.

In summary, buy it. If you are a fan of games like the Witness, or Gone Home (if you’re not then I don’t think you have a soul), then you’ll absolutely adore this title and it will fit very nicely into your library.

My Review Of Firewatch.

"Firewatch is a single-player first-person mystery set in the Wyoming wilderness, where your only emotional lifeline is the person on the other end of a handheld radio."

Pros & Cons

Pros: Amazing storytelling, incredibly immersive, perfect graphics.

Cons: Not enough to prevent you from playing this game.

Essay Time: I think many people enter a review section for a game and look for the person with the longest review with the most amount of hours. To be completely honest, I played this game once, entered the free roam mode for 20 or so minutes, and will probably uninstall this game now. Why? Because I've completed it, I've witnessed its charm, the mystery it offers, and the ending that is truly unforgettable. This game knows its pacing and keeps you on the edge of your seat. I was lucky that I could play this game surrounded by my friends, providing me with their opinion on how I should describe myself to the person on the other end of the radio. It contains some of the best moments of gaming I've ever had in my life. It's one of the only games that I can say I was truly immersed in for more than just a few seconds. The graphics and radio mechanics give it the infinite charm that won't allow you to forget this game. And that's a good thing. Firewatch is one of my favorite games of all time that I will never replay, and I think you should be able to experience it too. Pick it up when you can, and you won't regret it.

[h1] Firewatch- Spoiler Free Review | Not Just a game, it's an experience... [/h1]

[b] Firewatch is a rare and beautiful creation, that expands the possibilities for how a narrative game can be presented, without bombast or gimmick. It’s delicate, lovely, melancholy and wistful. And very, very funny. A masterful and entrancing experience. [/b]

A game about characters in their 40s is rare enough. To be about despondent, struggling people, without resorting to cartoonish crap about mid-life crises or outlandish unrealism, is a truly special thing. Henry’s [your character] specific situation is something with which almost no one in the game’s audience will immediately sympathize, but surely all will quickly empathize . That’s a huge part of the achievement here – to not aim to create a sympathetic analogue for the player, but like most great fiction, to allow the player to experience someone else’s life distinct from their own.

[h2]Story[/h2] Without spoiling anything, I don’t think the story was concluded – not in a satisfying way. Technically, the mystery was solved, and all threads reached their conclusion. And judging by the notes I gathered and everything else you could find in the last hour, there’s no other possible conclusion. you may feel disappointed if you weigh ending heavily but i'm not mad at the game, don't focus too much on ending. The journey is what matters and holy hell, what a journey it was.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2] mostly revolves around exploration and doing everyday tasks. But the story pace and the way designers smartly laid out quests around the map, you’re never doing too much of one thing. Even though, when you really think about it, they’re all mundane tasks that would otherwise be unnecessary distractions in other games. But Firewatch gives a certain splendour to even the most mundane of tasks, and it’s amazing how much well-realised character and atmosphere will let you get away with.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]

[b]Firewatch deals with love, loss, and how you put yourself together again after trauma. It does all this in a clever and engaging way that will have you emotionally connected to both Henry and Delilah.[/b]

The plot uses some strong emotional trickery (the dog dying is just the beginning of this country song), but that's part of writing a compelling story. I personally like low to medium poly assets with interesting artsy shaders which I feel completely negate any uncanny valley problems. The world was quite beautiful; for a small team the environment is really well done. The controls and pacing were sometimes frustrating, but usually good. For example, I was especially grateful for the automatic backtracking which spared any of it feeling like grinding. I appreciated the pretty accurate looking USGS quad sheet which was used for the map. I'm happy to give it a thumbs up and recommend it if you are interested in quality interactive fiction with a quiet outdoorsy theme.

[h1] Firewatch [/h1]

Independent developer Campo Santo's first game, Firewatch, tells the story of Henry, who wants to escape from the difficulties in his private life and keep his head for a while. Working as a wildfire watcher in Wyoming's mountainous and wooded area, where Yellowstone National Park is located, Henry's only contact is Delilah, on the other end of the radio. This game, in which the story of two people who do not know each other but who are connected to each other via walkie-talkies in solitude on the mountain will be the main actor, is also embellished with a mystery in the region. Promising a gameplay between Telltale games and Gone Home, let's see if Firewatch has met the expectations.

First of all, it is useful to open up the story and characters a little without spoilers. While entering the game, we experience Henry's meeting with his wife, falling in love, getting married, thinking about having a child, and finally getting sick of his wife by just reading the writings and making a selection with a very beautiful sequence. This marginal story sequence, which is divided by sections of Henry's trip to the desolate nature and his walk to the watchtower, offers a pleasant and powerful experience with a quick return to the elections and reminiscent of 80s text adventures. Thanks to this experience, we can immediately identify and connect with Henry. At times, while the contradictions and stress about his wife, who cannot recognize himself and can no longer take care of him, confuse his mind, Henry seeks the solution. The only person he communicates with in this process is his boss, Delilah. Delilah is as playful as he is mysterious, and in fact a deep character, and indeed, the lead role in the game is the relationship between these two.

There are many choices we can make in the game, but these choices do not affect the end of the game. Instead, it affects our conversations with Delilah, which could be a reason to play the game again. As I said, the main actor in the play is the relationship of this duo and when we make one choice in the conversation, we don't have the chance to make the other. We can also report the sights we see around or what we find to Delilah. However, we have a chance not to report them. So when we play again, the conversation goes on a completely different side. With these, we have the opportunity to deepen and differentiate this relationship by visiting many regions that we do not have to travel to and talking about that region and what we found there. The decisions we make in Firewatch, which we can describe as an "interaction experience", also affect Delilah's reactions to Henry or some common concerns in later chapters. At this point, we should congratulate Campo Santo who managed to present the same story with different experiences.

One of Firewatch's strengths is its visuality, which sometimes resembles a watercolor painting. The fact that they prefer an artistic and even fairy-tale visual instead of a photorealistic visual coincides with the theme of the game. Although it looks like a mystery game, Firewatch is definitely not a mystery game. The mystery in the game is always secondary. It acts as a tool for interaction and character development. This play is about a man's contradictions, escapism, and a woman he unexpectedly finds and connects to in an unexpected place. It can be said to be a literal human drama. Throughout the game, which will vary from 3.5 hours to 5 hours depending on how much you travel and your speed, the most memorable moments that bring different emotions to the top are always the moments of talking with Delilah. For this reason, instead of focusing on the detective direction with realistic images and throwing the characters into the background, they have managed to display a sad and sweet section of the days when the lives of the two characters intersect with artistic visuals. The atmosphere of Firewatch manages to reinforce its emotional and human story with the sounds of the forest, magnificent character voices and beautiful and peaceful music that supports the stage instead of coming to the fore.

Except for the dialogues and our choices at this point, gameplay is entirely based on exploration. We find our way around the map with climbing sequences that do not require skill. In the game, where we can open short paths by tying ropes to the rocks and hanging down, our progress process is based on acquiring items to overcome the obstacles that we cannot overcome. Of course, sometimes it is not enough to investigate in detail and the story needs to move forward. An interesting point about climbing mechanics is that while climbing rocks is automatic, hanging down from rocks with rope is manual. Usually, in such exploration and story-driven games, manual actions are done to increase the interaction with the character and the atmosphere, but here the fact that one of the two similar exploration actions is manual and the other automatic has distorted that feeling. So much so that one of the most important gameplay elements in the game is that unlike automatic climbing, the manual system hits our face.

The most common thing we use when traveling in hills, canyon, river, lake and forest is a map and compass. We are trying to find our way by opening the paper map in our hands. For the sake of convenience on the map, our carcass is marked as if there is a GPS, but the direction it is facing is not shown. We can attribute this to the character's understanding of where he is when he looks around. We understand the direction we are looking at and of course the direction we will go by looking at the compass. Also, the roads are not marked on the map. There are some food chests in the vicinity so that the village guards can be left with materials and communication between them, and there are details of the surrounding map on their covers. When we find these maps, Henry puts marks on his map, and when we look at the map again, we see hand-drawn paths on this physical map. This strengthens the atmosphere and allows us to progress in the game as a gameplay element.

Finally, it is necessary to mention the end of the game. The end of the game split the audiences in two, and the general criticism is that the story did not prepare step by step and then satisfy expectations. While this view is understandable, I disagree because Firewatch is a completely depressive game of human emotions and relationships. Although it makes you smile with a surprising bond that emerged during this process, Henry's experiences, the mystery element in the game, the nature of the story, and Delilah's own contradictions also proceed on the same theme. That's why I think this ending of Firewatch, which is not a mystery game, but a humanitarian interaction and drama game, fits the game completely. Frankly, the end of the game met my expectations.

Firewatch is one of the most successful "experience" games of recent times, a human drama that everyone can find a piece of themselves, and perhaps even not want to. With realistic and deep characters, incredibly natural and successful voices and wonderfully written dialogues, a fabulous conversation that you will want to never end is waiting for you. Campo Santo did such a job that Henry's escape turned into an actor's escape. The real crumbs sprinkled between the pleasant conversations with Delilah and the inability of both Henry and Delilah to escape the truth throughout the story succeeds in keeping the actor constantly on the toes and connected to the facts. In fact, the mystery element in the game can be interpreted as an unconscious escape effort of the characters. These round trips between escape and reality allow us to experience a special blend of emotions. For gamers who are not afraid of emotional experiences and enjoy interactive stories, Firewatch makes a powerful entry into the modern classics. If you like these games, try Firewatch. Have fun!

I needed to get this out of the way before I started my review. So many reviews tell you about how horrible the ending is and as someone who has had his fair share of disappointments with games I expected the worst.

It definitely isn't. The game delivers what it promised from start to finish: You follow two people and their conversation with a tiny bit of mystery sprinkled over their story. Their reactions feel good, interactions with other entities feel appropriate as well and all loose ties get tied up towards the end.

Be aware though that you are buying a story. 

Graphics are mediocre, there's barely anything to explore (though you will get rewarded for exploring), pathfinding is really good (I never got lost) and your decision's impact is limited to how characters react, not the story itself.

Which, to some, may be a plus. Maybe you want to read a story but some lines of dialogue feel subpar, maybe you felt like a character wouldn't or shouldn't do certain things in a book and you only wanted to influence that single element.

Additionally, you don't "feel" that your decisions don't matter, like in some other storytelling games. There is no hard break back to the plot. No matter which branch you pick the flow does continue to feel very natural.

If you are into that, you'll have a lot of fun.
