This game is rated at about 2-3 hours but I finished in 5 hours listening to a lot of radio calls but didn't explore too much. I'd say average playthrough would be 4 hours.

Now, this game is mostly a walking simulator. The story goes on while you do simple tasks. You can explore a little bit but generally the map isn't that huge and you'll see most of it by the end.

Storywise the start is very intriguing but it's let down by a kind of lackluster ending. It sets up some really mysterious plot points that the game will literally do a 180 turn near the end. But maybe that's just expecting too much of a simple walking sim game.

The graphics are alright but its not gonna blow your socks off. The player model looks like it came from the cartoony Team Fortress 2 world. The environment is nice to look at; the art design could be considered comic-book like.

There's something to be said about the setting. You're mostly alone in the wilderness with a person to talk to on the radio. Its sometimes relaxing. Sometimes contemplative. If you needed a break from general action game stuff, this could be good for you.

The conversations between you and the other main character in this game over radio are excellent. Though there's a lot of sarcasm and snark with both characters early on that doesn't reflect what I'd say in real life. Technically, they're really well acted audio recordings with crisp quality. Some of the best voice acting in a game no doubt.

The game tries to shoehorn a message for the player at the end which fell flat, given the incongruency of what I would personally do vs. the character in the game. But its a nice message nonetheless and I enjoyed my time with it overall.

There's little to no replayability to this game unless you want to listen to dev commentary so to me the game is maybe 5-6 hours of real gameplay content for the average user. I would pay no more than $15 for it, but personally got it less on sale.

The game didn't experience any crashes, but it suffers from a huge frame time spike everytime you whip your head around, or checkpoints, or loads a small new area. Frame time spikes are worse than getting low FPS. And in the main lookout tower area, the graphics barely looks good enough to tax a 1080 ti, i7 6700, 16GB RAM, but graphics on 1080p Ultra will go down to 50FPS so I settled on High.

Anyway, overall I'd give this 4/5 stars. Good short single-player experience, somewhat let down by anti-climactic ending and frame time spikes. =)

Honestly, comedy should be tagged as one of Firewatch's genres. The lines and voice acting got to be some of the most realistic ones I've ever heard in games. Authentic, genuine, and realistic. It's refreshing. I thought I was in for some cringy voice acting (judging from the trailers solely). And after completing the game, yes, there were cringy moments. Cringy, though, in an endearing manner. Like two friends who are used to poking fun at each other are commanded to hug affectionately kind of moments. Throughout, the flow in the conversations is exceptionally smooth (if you don't forcefully rush through their convos with quickly reporting what you see). It's like hearing two close friends bickering and jabbing at each other from time to time with playful insults yet you know that deep down, they both care for one another. It puts a smile on your face. 

The soundtrack is amazing. I love how it's not played continuously during the whole game but in certain (fitting) scenes which is great because it allows the players to immerse themselves with the natural music instead (the rustling wind, the quacking of ducks at the stream). Since the whole game is wonderfully optimized, it only elevates one's mood to explore into and beyond the woods undisturbed. Firewatch's all about the experience than getting through the day as fast as possible, really. Graphics-wise, it's EXACTLY like the thumbnails and trailers. You get what you see. 

The storyline is fantastic. Rather than immediately beginning the game with my character, Henry, stepping out into the fire lookout tower for the first time, it chooses to share a short yet succinct background of him and what led him to take this job in the first place. Firewatch's intro, I have to admit, is the best intro to any game I've played thus far. In the span of around three minutes or so, the intro gave me a solid, lasting excellent impression of Firewatch. It proved that words, alone, can do so much to invoke a range of emotions from a person. It's a summer with a twist. The whole story is beautifully pieced together like scenes into a movie or jigsaw puzzles into a picture. It all wonderfully fits. You'd be happy that it does, but sad that it is already finished. That's how I felt at the end: bittersweet. It's a wonderful ending, nevertheless. A fitting end to a summer story. 

Firewatch, in its entirety, is wonderful. It's wonderfully justed by its critically acclaimed reviews and awards. Definitely not overrated at all.

I thoroughly love this game. The story is why you play it. This is a game that knows how to tell a narrative. Beyond that, though, the game is good to look at, and it always flows well. This is more, in my opinion, of what a role playing game ACTUALLY is supposed to be. You play a ROLE in the game. Your role is not about getting an XP bar to the next level, you're a guy trying to cope with emotional trauma in his own way. 
I enjoy these types of games, especially when they are both visually appealing AND have a captivating story. 

I really can't find any more criticisms besides I wish there was more. When it was over, both the first time I played it and the second time, I wished so hard that there was more. I wanted to meet the lady on the other end of the radio. 

This game takes place over the course of a summer, with the prologue taking place over a lifetime. Even only playing for a few hours, it doesn't feel rushed. This feels more like a movie that you have an active part in, and I love every minute of it.

I want to say this might be one of the only games I've ever played that's made me cry. And not tears of frustration like some games. Genuine, heartfelt tears of emotional investment in the story. I'm actually getting a bit watery writing this up now. 

The game made me laugh, it made me cry, it made me feel alone, it made me feel helpless at times, it gives you the feeling of the total impermanence of everything. It makes you fearful for the characters, it imparts wonder and suspicion as the story unfolds. There truly is not a dull moment in the game. 

This isn't even to mention all the theories you could come up with about the game, I won't get into them as it's not appropriate for a review and might spoil the story for others, but there are certainly some tantalizing assumptions one could make about the main character and the story that make the game more interesting.

I think I got it for the full price of 20 bucks, it's worth that, but if you're seeing this on sale, like right now during the winter sale it's 4.99, absolutely it's worth it. In fact, I think I might go ahead and pick it up for my friend who has it on his wishlist as well.

I mean, just, wow. I really liked this game. I can wholly recommend it to anyone looking for a short, relatively chill game that is expertly paced and looks beautiful. If you are at all interested in what this game has to offer, just buy it already, maybe wait for a sale if you want, but I think that it is worth the full price. My advice is to go in with as little knowledge of it as possible. But if you either want more knowledge or want to read the review for some other reasons, here it is:

Performance wise, there was a bit of stuttering, but I was able to run it well and at a high resolution with a sort of below average rig. Aside from stuttering maybe 5 times over my 4.5 hour play session, the graphics were really quite stunning. The art direction and graphical style are phenomenal, one of the most picturesque games I have played in a long time. The attention to detail of all the buildings and flora is nice, it's heartwarming to know that people care enough about making a good video game to include all the fun details. The atmosphere is captivating. There were several moments where I completely lost track of time and didn't even realize that I was playing a video game until the 'day' ended. The music is good, I think that it fits the game well, and it's rare occurrence makes each time it fades in memorable and exciting. The times that the game got tense, I felt genuinely scared and worried, which isn't something that a whole lot of games have pulled off for me. I really liked that I could turn off the marker of my location on my map, and that the map and compass were actually inside of the game-world, not simply HUD or menu screen. I had to figure things out and solve my own problems. If I was stuck somewhere, you loop around and double-check to make sure that you didn't miss something. For example, there was one time that I needed to get across a ravine, so I thought maybe I can cut this tree down and so I had to go look for an ax where an ax might be and then I found it and was able to cross safely. If and when I would get lost, I would have to figure out where I was, how to get to where I was supposed to be, and then learn how not to get lost again.  It was just nice to not only be able to fend for myself and not have my hand be constantly held, but I get to treated like I know what I'm doing, which I learned by making mistakes and having to correct them myself. A welcome change of pace for most video games nowadays. 

But that's enough about game-play and user experience, now let's get to the story. I will slightly spoil some things, so, like I said, if you are at all interested, just play it and stop reading the review. [spoiler] The ending seems to be the most present part of this game's criticism's, but I think that everything was tied up adequately. There weren't many more questions that I had, and what I did were either minute or irrelevant. I guess I might have wanted a bit more of a 'reveal', but I couldn't ask for much more. The conversations were genuine, it really felt like two people (one of them being me) were just chatting it up over radios while wandering the Wyoming wildernesses. There wasn't a single time where I felt out of place, everything was just natural and smooth. I think the whole 'girls stole a tractor but they're okay' thing was a little bit shoehorned in, but it seems like something that could actually happen, so I have no quarrels with that. I liked how, by the end, all the mysteries that I had discovered had been solved and mostly connected together, and at first I would have never guessed that they would all have led back to Ned and Brian. It was a very tight story that didn't have any fluff and got done what it needed to. I never had to ask myself 'Wait, why am I doing this again?', it was all there. It said everything that it needed to and left me wanting more, wanting to keep playing to find out what happens next 'What could happen with Julia and where would Delilah go?' I asked myself. And that is exactly what I think a video game should do. I shouldn't feel like it is dragging on or just trying to get me to invest more time into it. It should respect me and allow me to do a little speculation and leave me wanting more, which is exactly what Firewatch did. [spoiler/] 

Firewatch treats the player like an adult, and doesn't waste their time on silly gimmicks. Everything had a purpose, and that purpose was solely to tell the story in an interesting way that only a video game can. This is a prime example of what video games have to offer as an art-form and a story-telling method. I'm not sure if I will play it a second time. I guess that's for a future me to decide. I think that, despite having only spent 4.5 hours with it, that I am finished with this game, and will remember it fondly, being able to look back on the beautiful experience that the developers cared enough to share with me. Thank you Firewatch, for embodying what it truly means to be a video game.

Firewatch was a fantastic and finely-crafted narrative experience which I recommend to empathic folks interested in a people-oriented experience. I might have played it for too long, exploring the environment and looking for tidbits I might have missed, but I'll happily recommend the experience for its price of $19.99. I know some people were disappointed at how short the game was and its ending, but for me, both of these points have been positives rather than negatives.

For one, I think I got a richer, more-lasting experience from Firewatch than most 50+ hour games I've played. In addition, for me the story, and the ending, in particular, felt very real--grounded--to this bygone place and time, and it made me engage with the main character's--and his disembodied companion's--experience and turmoil. The ending didn't necessarily satisfy me, but it made sense to me, which is pretty true to life.

In addition to it being set in a specific time and place (1989), the almost cartoon-like graphics and warm design direction in-game (almost like summer in the woods) will, I believe, lend to this game's cultural longevity so that people decades after its release could appreciate it.

Firewatch is a game about a concept that can either be very familiar to some people or very distant to others. The concept of loneliness is explored in this game as you get emotionally attached to the two main characters, Delilah and Henry. I think for an indie game that actually attempts to explore a concept as opposed to just providing gameplay, Firewatch can certainly be considered a great game.

Campo Santo's approach to the concept really allows you as a player to get emotionally attached to the two characters. The dialogue and conversation about almost everything interesting in the game allows for you to experience the thoughts of these characters like they were your own. Coupling this with the actual gameplay and art style, it truly makes for a great experience. The game isn't too long, making it short and sweet.

Would highly recommend this title for someone looking for a nice story-driven indie title.

It's important you know what you're getting when you buy this. You are getting around 3 and a half hours of story-driven gameplay which is primarily communicated via outstanding voice acting from Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones. Yes, there is "exploration"/"open world" gameplay of a sort, where you find a route from your watchtower to various parts of the beautifully stylised North American National Park using a map and compass. You can even snap some pretty pictures on the way. However, there is nothing that you particularly need to do other than walk from A to B and pick up a few things. 

The characters and story is where it's at and they are done superbly well: Henry (the player character) has taken a job as a fire lookout at Shoshone National Park in the summer of 1989 following the breakdown of his marriage. Delilah works at a lookout further up the valley and becomes Henry's mentor and, eventually, friend as they slowly get to know one another over the course of the game. The two converse over radio as Henry finds his feet in his new job, but a series of strange events suggests all is not as it seems in the Park and perhaps they are being watched... 

You can just play this in one sitting though I took a few. As long as you go in with your expectations set appropriately, you will enjoy this. The story and particularly the ending left a lump in my throat. I have a feeling I will remember this game for some time to come.

The research facility was just studying elk, and those teenagers were just drunk. Theres no conspiracy, theres no love story, we leave the game unsatisfied and disappointed, but that makes it real.

The good: 
The atmosphere was immersive and the voice acting was top notch.

The bad: 
The story. And that's why I can't recommend this game - because for me, that's the most important aspect. I understand the intentions of the creators and the meaning they portrayed at the end, but I just can't say it was all worth it. After everything that happened, I was on the edge of my seat, considering all the possible theories for the plot twist - but there was none. It was like that feeling you get when you watch a movie or read a book only to find out it was all a dream. After investing time and energy into the world and it's characters, you're rewarded with an anticlimactic ending that felt like all your efforts were for nothing.

This game has it all: Stunning art, the most charming dialogue ever, and...a controversial ending. The ending is why this is only *very* positive, I think. Some would call it anti-climactic. I would rather call it unexpected and sad, but also realistic. (My theory is that people dislike it for its preponderance of reality over typical story structure, but that's neither here nor there).

Regardless of what you will make of the ending, I can promise it will make you think. I hope it makes you feel. And I hope, hope, hope you give the characters trust. Digging around, I think every inconsistency has an explanation, sometimes in the audio commentary, even if events are not directly explained to your character. I think M. Night Shyamalan and his ilk have traumatized us a little, and it requires vulnerability to accept how some narratives play out. This story will benefit from your vulnerability, and it has some things to say about trust and love and paranoia, if you can see past the paranoia.

Funny, mysterious and heartbreaking, Firewatch is as good a story as I've experienced in a game. You feel intimately invested in the lives of the main characters thanks to some excellent writing and maybe the best voice acting I've heard in a game. 

The only drawback for me is that the game mechanics are a little clunky. You can get stuck on bushes and other laughably small obstacles, while in other instances you're able to scale cliff faces with ease. The stability of the frame rate can be a bit glitchy too, but, honestly, I don't even care. The story is that good.

I was bracing myself for the big gripe people have with the story: the ending. I understand why people would take issue with it, but there's a lot of subtext in that resolution that does the story justice. Even if you fall in the category of people who are disappointed with the ending, the journey that got you there will have been worth it. Big recommend.

I can see why some might have viewed the last hour or so as a 'let down', but I personally didn't feel that way at all. It felt realistic more than anything else, and I love it when characters respond realistically to high-pressure situation - without the 'and we came out on top better than before!' sugar coating.

It goes without saying that the game has little replay value, like any mystery - but the free-roam mode is actually quite nice for going back to grab achievements you miss, or just taking in the visuals again. At the time of this review I have completed the entirety of Firewatch in 22 hours, I held off writing a review until I completed it in its entirety including the "Free Roam" and "Audio Tour". I couldn't just write a simple review saying something tacky like "Oh I love this game" because I feel it deserves more, so I'm going to try and review a couple aspects of this game in separate sections.

[b]Set the stage[/b]

Firewatch is a game set in Shoshone National Forest in the state of Wyoming and takes place in the year 1989!

[b]Main Playthrough[/b]

The main playthrough was gorgeous! The graphics were stunning, I couldn't get enough of it! I took full advantage of my ability to screenshot so I could keep those beautiful photos forever. The dialogue was hyper-realistic, I could see this actually happening in real life. The game also includes many options for dialogue with thousands and thousands of different outcomes making your experience in the game truly personal as you develop emotional bonds with the dynamic characters. The controls can be a little strange at first but you get used to them relatively quickly, the game is mostly an adventure style type game with a world roaming aspect, with a bunch of little secrets for you to find on your own! The music (composed by Chris Remo) goes great with the locations and situations they go with. Chris did an amazing job on the OST and I thank him for these beautiful pieces.

[b]Free Roam[/b]

The free roam is unlocked after you have completed the main playthrough at least once, its not much other than what it says with having full access to the world. The main purpose of the free roam is to discover places you may not have checked during the main playthrough. However, in the free roam you have what seems to be a Sony Walkman that starts off with 1 cassette tape with 4 of the songs from the games OST, you can accumulate more cassettes by roaming around the world searching for them with there being a total of 20 songs and I believe 5 cassettes. Other than that there's not much to do in free roam.

[b]Audio Tour[/b]

Finally we arrive on the Firewatch audio tour which is a developer commentary version of the main playthrough with little booths scattered throughout the game as you progress through it with cool facts for how they made the game, came up with ideas, as well as little parts of the map with added props where you can test cool features. I highly recommend you do the audio tour if you plan on purchasing this game, it would be a huge waste to not include this in your playthrough of the game.

[b]Conclusion[/b]

Thank you for reading through my review, I hope I convinced you to either purchase this game or bring attention to some parts of the game that you previously did not know about and might wanna go back and check! Once again thanks for reading my review, I really appreciate it!!

I very, very rarely leave negative reviews for games, but I think one is warranted here. I bought this for £3 in the sale and even at that price I'm pretty disappointed.

This is not a computer game, but rather a story told using a 3D engine. There are no game mechanics to be found and no player agency. Choices appear to be purely cosmetic and make no difference to the world or the rigidly linear plot forged by the developers. There are no adversaries or challenges to overcome, nor any puzzles to solve. There is a form of exploration but it is pretty meaningless because the world is essentially a series of textured corridors and everything other than the intended path is impassable. This is really taken to the extreme when, despite routinely doing 20ft freehand rock climbs and jumping over canyons, the protagonist declares a 6ft chain-link fence to be an completely impassable obstacle. There are also no interesting things to find - even the series of supply caches rarely contain anything usable or worthwhile. The world does not feel alive and does not respond to you in any way. The graphics and voice acting are serviceable. 

I could forgive all this if the story was any good, but unfortunately it's tedious and poorly executed. The exposition immediately drew me in with the story of the wife, the dog and the early onset dementia, but these things were then essentially irrelevant to the rest of the plot. It sort of reminds me of when Lisa's mother announces she has breast cancer in The Room and it's never mentioned again. The story develops in a jarring and disjointed manner, including numerous events and motivations that don't make any sense at all and culminating in a cheap, disappointing and nonsensical deus ex machina. I suspect that what the developers were trying to do was create a mysterious atmosphere based on paranoia and uncertainty, but in this respect, as with so many others, they failed miserably. Despite her being the only other significant character, the relationship with Delilah does not develop in any meaningful way. It is inexplicable that she is presented as a mysterious voice on the radio whom the player never meets, given that her lookout tower turns out to be barely five minutes' walk away. This, like so many other aspects of this game, just doesn't make any sense at all. 

I enjoy a good story and I would happily play a game that was essentially just a good story, but this is certainly not it. I genuinely cannot understand what anyone sees in this game and find the positive reviews bewildering.

The characters are compelling.  They have depth, personality, and you can get really attached to them.  The voice acting was excellent. The so-so.
Firewatch is pretty much a linear story.  Sure you can choose different lines of dialogue but the story will still progress along the same ark.  So it goes.  It is basically an computer based novel.

Now the bad stuff.
As I said before the story up until the end was well done; however, the ending falls flat on its face.  It is always such a sad shame when I see developers put so much effort and creativity into a game but then seem to  either give up or rush through on creating an end that really fits with the high level of effort put into other areas.  A bad or disappointing ending will be remembered far more than any hours of enjoyment had previously.   And while the ending was not so much bad as it left a big "?".  Lots of loose ends. Lots of "Is that all there is?".  If there was going to be a sequel then having loose ends is fine providing they get tied up in said sequel. I came to Firewatch from Outer Wilds, hoping for the challenge of puzzling out the mystery plot. I was disappointed to find that thinking is unnecessary and unrewarding in this game, since every plot point is forced on you as the game directs you through the same sequence of events regardless of your choices. Firewatch feels more like a take-it-at-your-own-pace movie than a traditional video game.

The plot is exciting enough to keep you interested, but has enough contrivances and plot holes that I was ultimately left unsatisfied. In truth, the plot takes a backseat to the game's main agenda as it becomes the prompt and catalyst for the protagonist's relationship with the voice on the other end of the radio. And that's the one thing that Firewatch does really well: creating an ambiance of loneliness and driving it home with an alluring companion who's just out of reach.

Firewatch goes on sale now and then for $5, which feels like about the right price for a product that feels like a pay-per-view movie.

I went into this game thinking there was going to be some sort of weird twist, how quite early on the game makes it clear something is off. You find out you're being monitored so on and so forth, find a camp full of high tech equipment and are made to believe that there is something possibly of a social experiment going on. All of these "conspiracies" are laid out in the open pretty clearly to make you think there's something bigger at play.

What I don't understand is how the game sets up all of these troupes with the fenced off area, and all of that equipment with obvious government "research" at play to wind back the story to just be about some guy's kid that died in a cave and he can't coop with it. Not to mention how obvious romantic tension builds between the main character and D just to have her recluse and just leave. 

I wish they would have spent one extra day making the alternate ending just a tiny bit more interesting. Like being able to go back up into the tower one last time and call D and tell her you aren't coming back. Or for D to maybe call you on the radio one last time after the chopper leaves to say something to the effect of "I heard you stayed behind... Goodbye friend..." or just something. One tiny audio clip would have made this alternate ending far more interesting.

Or, even more interesting would be to tell Delilah something like "You know, I decided that Ned had it right, I don't have much to go back to. I really enjoyed my summer out here. Thank you Delilah, thank you for everything."

This would have been the most interesting. A small plot idea that I noticed is that in a way, Ned was a mirror of Henry. Ned had lost the one he loved most and had no reason to return to society without the one he loved. He lived out his days in the wilderness, knowing he will die there alone. Delilah helped Ned through the summer until Ned disappeared on her. Like Ned, Henry had lost the one he loved, Delilah helped him through it and eventually Henry disappears on her. While not identical, the emotions that drove Ned and Henry are almost the same. In fact I believe that the reason for Ned to leave the tape for Henry at the end explaining it all, was because Ned began to feel empathy towards Henry as he learned more and more about him.

If you ended with Henry choosing to die out in the wildfire, it would have a sense of Shakespearean tragic irony to it that would make for a fascinating ending as Henry decides to follow the actions of Ned, without ever truly meeting him, but all the while understanding Ned and what motivated him. 

I don't believe the game is ♥♥♥♥, or has poor story telling, because it is neither of those. The atmosphere and the dialogue were all very well done and pretty gripping and i actually was pretty interested in what was happening next. I guess I just wish the ending wasn't so bland, but what's done is done.

So this review is a couple of years too late which is when I completed it, but as I just saw it pop up in my library, I thought I'd leave a quick review. For me, Firewatch is one of the best gaming experiences I've ever had. I don't play anything that is too taxing on my brain or something that requires razor sharp reflexes these days - I much prefer a good story driven game and if it comes with great visuals then so much the better. This is what you'll get with Firewatch. 

The dialogue between the characters is the most authentic, witty, believable voice acting I've ever experienced in a game, and combined with the brilliant unfolding plot results in a truly unique and in my opinion, once in a lifetime experience. By that I mean that the team that developed it seemed to be a perfect coming together of people, time and place - exactly like a classic album or something similar. 

It really struck a chord emotionally for me and as I remember, I actually missed the characters after finishing the game and the overall theme stayed with me for quite some time afterwards.  I don't think I'll ever play it a second time as I think it would taint what I felt the first time around - some games are one off single play throughs and I'd put this game into that category, though you'd be forgiven for trying to find some alternate paths I suppose. 

Just to finish, the soundtrack is also superb and I'd listen to it on and off whilst working and would get transported back to key parts of the game. That is quite some praise for a game!  A masterpiece.

Ingredients:

1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter

Directions:

1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Intro:

Have you ever wanted to escape the troubles of your mundane existence? Chances are that we all have wanted to do so.  Firewatch tackles this premise well, a bittersweet melodrama about escape and recognition of humanity’s flaws.

Story:

What started as a fairytale romance turns into a tragedy for Henry, who can only watch helplessly as his wife's early-onset dementia consumes her.  Anxious to get away from this tragedy,  Henry gets a job as a fire watchman for a national park over the summer.  There, he forms a verbal relationship with his supervisor as both try to escape from their own lives.  But no matter how hard the two try,  life-like gravity has a habit of dragging reality back to our protagonists. 

Themes

The need for escape, I would say,  is the most prominent theme.  Shoshone National Forest becomes something of a sanctuary,  a means to escape from the character’s failures and problems,  a means of becoming someone else.  But much like any slice of heaven,  it is a merely temporary solution,  the fire (a metaphor for reality destroying the getaway) is always threatening our heroes with confronting their troubles and failures.  The fire gradually strips away the quiet sanctuary and protection Henry and Delilah have for one another. 

Exploring

I would suggest that you turn off map indicators when you play Firewatch.  Because with the map indicator there is very little challenge in getting from point A to point B.  As a result there the game can be a little easy.  Despite this, however, I love how the map is laid out,  there is always something cool to find,  some new mystery to solve, or another piece of dialogue to enjoy.

Then you’re given a mystery that you need to investigate and the game slowly unfolds into a thriller, leaving you in this constant state of unease and hyperaware of your surroundings.

I think a lot of "walking simulators" would be better terms "loneliness simulators". However interesting or beautiful the environment they put you in, the total isolation can gradually become oppressive and rather sad. In traditional games, the enemies trying kill you are at least company of a sort, but in first-person adventure games they're usually absent as well. These games often attempt to relieve this loneliness with a feisty narrator of some sort. But, of all of them, Firewatch succeeds the most for two reasons: Firstly, it leans into the sense of isolation. The protagonist has *chosen* to be alone, for specific, plot-explained reasons, and so when the player feels alone, it's because the *character* feels alone, thus helping you identify with him. Secondly, the isolation is undercut by the relationship between Henry and Delilah. While there are faults with how the plot developers and eventually ends, what definitely works is the interplay between the two characters. And it's enough to make you curse every game that puts you in the head of a silent, blank protagonist. *This* is role-playing, in my opinion: being put into the shoes of a memorable, fleshed-out character and being asked to reckon with who they are and the choices that have brought them to this point. And Firewatch succeeds in that more than any other game I have ever played.

A well told story with an unexpected ending filled with believable and relatable characters. Although Firewatch doesn't aim to achieve anything ground-breaking in its actual gameplay its ability to guide you into feeling what the protagonist feels so intimately is what made this game truly enjoyable to experience. The emotions, paranoia, questioning, helplessness, and fear of the unknown paired with the steady resolve and firsthand experiencing of disappointment both in your pursuit of some greater plot as well as in your (Henry's) own failings felt real enough for me to thoroughly enjoy this game.

Firewatch is nothing more than a 5-hour experimental journey of how you, the player responds to struggle and conflict through a fictional world as its medium. Do not go into this expecting internal revelations or character development that will leave you speechless. It doesn't matter what dialogue option you choose, or how you complete objectives, it makes no impact. This game prides itself on your emotional relationship with the protagonist, Henry. 

Firewatch is a beautiful game that is worth playing if it drops on sale. While the gameplay itself is simple and asks very menial tasks of you. It soon carries you away on this path where you begin to question your own morals towards relationship and love. It’s quirky, cliché and heartbreaking and you will walk away wanting so much more.

If you look at Firewatch on the surface, there are many improvements that can be made. However, at its core, the choices and dialogue within this game is there for a purpose. It’s brutal and you may not like it, but it’s simply a reflection of ourselves when we are at our lowest.

[b]Firewatch is one of, if not, [i]the[/i] best walking simulator(s) I've ever played, and one of my 2020 games of the year. Beginning to end it's just a beautiful story, and its only elevated by its soothing soundtrack, gorgeous visuals, amazing soundscapes, and [u]incredible[/u] audio tour.[/b]

I had seen the main trailer for Firewatch from way back in 2016, and despite being interested, never picked it up or read anything more. It wasn't until I went on a big Steam shopping spree this year that I decided I should finally pull the trigger and get it. Upon playing, I was surprised at the way the game played because it was so different than what I expected. But I was happy, as now I can't imagine it any other way.

Firewatch is the story of a man who, after an unfortunate series of events brought on by the worsening health of his wife, decides to take a job as a fire lookout in national forest to escape for a while. While working the job, he grows close to a fellow, more experienced, lookout through walkie-talkie conversations, and a series of strange events begin to unravel into a big mystery.

The meat of Firewatch isn't found in the gameplay, but in the story, just like in most walking sims. And while almost everybody I know enjoys the story as it plays out, I think many don't really [u]love[/u] the ending. Firewatch doesn't make a strong effort to tie up all the loose ends, or give you a strong sense of what's happening post-game, but for me it works, [u]really[/u] well. 

Unlike most games which are fictional and have no desire to emulate real life experiences, Firewatch makes a strong effort to do that, right from the prologue. So when all the right choices aren't apparent, when things are messy, and when you're not left totally satisfied at the ending, to me, at least, it feels like the most appropriate ending this game could have. Life is messy. Life doesn't always have a happy end, and sometimes you're left with regrets. That really struck a chord with me and Firewatch kind of reinforces this unforunate life truth in a really compelling way.

And the story is [u]told[/u] in two beautiful ways, both done incredibly well: world-building, and voice acting. Simply put, Firewatch has the best voice acting I've heard in a game, maybe ever. And the world-building is top notch. Every major location has so many wonderful details filled with world building that reinforces the character roles, their emotions, their thoughts, interests, etc.

And the game does a really good job  of mirroring these things through gameplay elements, too, by conveying that sense of struggle and turmoil in the tasks you have to perform as you go along. The conversations grow erratic or sporadic depending on the mood. The setting begins to shift as natural disasters begin to complicate things, and you go from hooking up carabiners often to chopping brushes with a fireman's axe and breaking into locked fence gates.

These amazing details and designs coupled with a, perhaps simple, but beautiful setting, a subtle yet impactful soundtrack, and an [u]absolute must play[/u] audio tour makes Firewatch just magic. There's not many games I can recommend more than Firewatch. It's the whole package and it's just so dang good. Please play it. It's a beautiful, interactive, cinematic experience.

This is really a "meh" rating, not a strong thumbs down. I knew that some people really disliked the ending, and was dreading for some serious "it was all a dream"-level of badness at the end. In fact, while not great, the ending at least makes sense and is somewhat plausible. My biggest beef is that when folks mean walking simulator they mean it. Unfortunately the story started to unravel for me around a third of the way through when the dialogue takes the form "but we have to *do* something!". Huh? Do we really? I think the most plausible response any sane, real person would have is "Screw this, whatever they're paying me it ain't enough." Essentially, the story forces several "Don't go in there!"-like moments because you don't have meaningful choice. Without real choice it felt much more like I was watching the story than participating in it.

The up-shot is, I am pretty sure you can enjoy the nice scenery, music, and story for *free* by watching a Let's Play video on YouTube to get basically the same experience as playing yourself. I would be pretty salty if I paid the full $20 price, but on sale at $5 isn't bad.

What a fun game that has mystery and adventure! Let's get down to brass tacks and talk about the pros and cons.

Pros
*AWESOME voice acting and dialogue - this by far is one of the best parts of Firewatch
*A creative and fun way to play a first person game - no shooting or running around aimlessly 
*Excellent story - refreshing to see a game with a quality story that pulls you in from the moment you load up the game 
*Game doesn't waste your time - everything you do pushes the story forward 
*Leaves you wanting more - What I mean by that is getting more story for the main characters OR just more from this developer, Campo Santo
*Reminds me of Telltale Games except better - you get full control over your character with a semi open world feel
*Worth the price

Cons
* Very short game - I know this wasn't advertised as long game or anything. Took my 4 hours to beat it, but I think there could have been more for the story. I feel like it ends abruptly. 
* This isn't really a spoiler but I wish dialogue choices influenced the story a little more then it does
* Weirdly this story takes place in the forest and there is practically NO wildlife, you do see a couple of things but those are scripted. I just find that it takes away from the experience a little bit, when it's kind of dull in that regard. 
*No replay-ability 

That's it. Honestly, not much wrong in this game. Not for the price. If you like story driven games with mystery and intrigue. This game is a no brainer. I enjoyed every minute of it. My biggest issue would be, I can't play it again and enjoy something new about it. 100% worth the full price, these developers deserve it! Thumbs up!

I was initially put off by the welcome. The game starts by railroading you through a totally ♥♥♥♥♥♥ life-experience, and you're not really allowed to handle it well.  The game depends on your character having some tarnish before you end up opening the door of your very own fire watch tower.

I was initially confused by the strange mixture of cartoony and realistic graphics, but they really grow on you. There's some great scenery, here, and you're going to be tromping through it repeatedly.  Fortunately, you've got an effective map, so at least you won't be getting lost.

The best part is the banter between the two characters.  With the lonely feeling of the game, I have to say that I was never sure if she was real or not, and that added to the strange atmosphere of the later part of the game.

I think that good art makes you feel things.  This game made me angry... worried... anxious... alone... and it did that in the context of my player-character.

Firewatch is a one of a kind game that has a unique setting, slow but meaningful story, simple controls, and the best part are the enjoyable characters.

Story: 9/10
The story is a 9/10 for me because of the slow burn (no pun intended) that it is. The mystery that gives the creepy feeling of uneasiness and checking over your shoulder because of what you see/hear, which brings me into the sound design.

Sound design: 7.5/10
Now the soundtrack isn't something that will stick out from other games but the music and forest noises really bring some life to this game. You can hear birds chirping in the day but then at night you hear nothing but the sound of crickets. The game was no way a horror game and not scary at all but when you hear the sound of a stick breaking while you are walking in the woods at night, it doesn't make you feel great.

Graphics: 8.5/10
The graphics are of my favorite parts of this game, I don't know what about it but it just makes me feel so comfortable with the warm skies and big trees. The graphics aren't going for realism but more of cartoony feel but still based in reality.

Characters: 10/10
The main character Henry is a calm and peaceful man most of the time but still feels real and isn't some fearless warrior, he is freaked out when something out of the normal happens. The beginning was... abysmal. Not because of the way they did it but because of the writing. It is not just the story but also the way you tell it that matters. The writer did the job very sloppy at the very best. Thus, the whole backstory of the protagonist feels just... meh. You can't establish an emotional connection with the guy nor feel his frustration.

Overall, the game feels pretty boring in the beginning. Almost Dear Esther boring. But what do you expect of a walking simulator? Fortunately, it gets better as the story evolves. Much better. Still, it is far from being great.

I do understand the idea: you are completely alone for weeks and the only connection with human being you actually have is a voice on the radio. It is really easy to like Delilah. Still, this love story just doesn't work for me because it feels completely out of the blue. I was looking for more to establish a strong emotional connection. A few more chapters/days could probably fill the gap but we have what we have.

And the ending could be disappointing. You realize that some things make no sense and were made just to get you believe that there's something strange going on. For example, [spoiler]why the guy thrashed girls' camp for no reason[/spoiler]? Also, there are even more questions. [spoiler]Why he tried to kill you in the cave? Yes, you were close to find Brian's body but the guy actually helped you to find the keys to the cave. It looks like a deliberate attempt to lure you into the cave to end your life, so he's probably a murderer who killed his son. But why he didn't kill you in the very first time when he had the chance?[/spoiler]

The rest is pretty predictable. [spoiler]You will never see Delilah[/spoiler]. Though, that's a good way to [spoiler]finish this flawed love story[/spoiler]. Still, in the end, it doesn't feel like you've wasted a few hours for nothing. So give it a go and decide for yourself.

A rambling tale was told, it was broken up. It started nowhere, and it ended nowhere.  So far as i'm concerned it was made into a game because it wouldn't make the cut as a movie. It has little to no choice on the player part, and literally no impact in the minor choices available. It relies on two cheap plot twists that are engaging on their own but really add to the scatter and pointlessness of it all.

I can understand a story that forgoes any positive themes, however this story is a tedious surface level device even with the themes that are chosen for it. The characters have no arc. They learn nothing about themselves, they don't really get challenged, and they hardly raise or fall in the end. All they do, is be present and learn a little bit more about the environment they are in. 

It's so bad that you as the main character could have the same effect if you had nothing to say at all. And there was only monologue instead of dialogue.

To truly grasp the meaninglessness of the narrative, you can have the same revelations and development if you remove the 2 active humans from it and substitute them for a single dog/raccoon/squirrel that goes around the forest and finds curious things to look at as it uncovers the tale.

Why do people like it? Because story-telling in games has deteriorated to often not even a sentence of meaning. Having some well voice acted characters connect to each other for a couple of hours, with a couple of effective plot twists is all that's needed to break away from the monotony of the usual gaming experience.

Some think it clever, to use the bare minimum of story and not really get fleshed out more. But really, you can get the same quantity and quality of narrative from segment in the 8 clock weekly news. The key motives are unclear. Most of the events are unclear. 

It focuses on continually fueling the curiosity of the player, but the means to do it are easily thrown aside one after another to keep it going. Even the key plot points have minimal development, they are rather dumped on you to keep the pace going. 

-Lets go fishing?! Shock plot-twist!!
-Lets get to the bottom of shock-plot-twist!
-Dump shock_plot_twist_1 and get shock_plot_twist_2, because why not.
-Shock plot-twists anyone?! Ah screw that, why bother, lets go home and forget about it...

To paint my dissatisfaction with it, in the end I expected the character to wake up from a drunk stupor and plot twist it into - he imagined it all, because his life is a mess and the escapism he tried is in vain.

There is a convenient emergency at the end to abruptly end it all, in the unresolved nothingness it dwells in.

There are large amounts of uncertainty injected into the middle. From this you can theorise about the connections between events in a number of speculative ways. However the events themselves hold little meaning, even if you connect them in all sorts of different ways.

Even if you scour to collect every scattered detail, you don't learn anything extra, nothing interesting happens. Having one ending is fine. Allowing for zero deviation from the small linear path even in the beginning and the middle is just cheap.

Essentially the developers provide an experience that doesn't bother to even offer anything to players who invest their complete focus and immerse in to every little corner the game. You can effectively play it with half attention as you watch a basketball game on the side, and you really wouldn't be missing anything. Yes you can use observation and critical thinking to figure out whats going on, but it doesn't matter because they dump the revelations on you soon after, and you regret putting any effort into trying puzzle things.

I understand that people can relate. But you can in the same way relate to nearly anything you see on television if you wanted to.

Overall, starved for growth, scattered and unsatisfying experience that last moment injects some drama to try and salvage itself. The developers just make utility of gameplay to cover for how ultra thin the tale is. Cut pointless walking around back and forth and this boils down to 5 minutes of voice chat.

I completely appreciate how so small a thing, has been inflated by filler to make a exceptionally well received title. Some expert craftsmanship no doubt.

I think its a testament of how crudely and badly games on average handle plots, that even such a deficient tale can succeed.

Firewatch Review

Story telling unlike anything else you’ve experienced before!

Some key points that this game offers:

1.	Gorgeous Open World
2.	Beautiful visuals
3.	Fantastic Story Telling
4.	Strong Mature game setting
5.	Thrilling mystery
6.	Choices that shape the narrative of the game

Gameplay & Controls:

Firewatch can be enjoyed with a keyboard and mouse or with a controller. Either method is comfortable to use, it comes down to your preferred playstyle. There are a few keys that the game makes use of, but the key mapping was done well enough that it is easy and commutable to use them as you go about exploring this beautiful world.

The game itself plays and handles beautifully, there is no delay in movement or responses as you go about exploring the wilderness. Everything is smooth and enjoyable. Great care was taken here to ensure that every step you take in this world is one to remember. 

Do Note: Due to the duration of the game and the beautiful and memorable story that it tells, I will avoid mentioning too much of the story itself. It is through and through a must experience. Firewatch is just best experienced without any spoilers for the sake of not ruining the beautiful story concept it tells.

You play as the character Henry; the year is 1989. Due to some unfortunate events you decided to retreat from your previous life and took a job as a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness. AS you hike up to your new home, you get introduced to Delilah, your co firewatcher and supervisor. She and your radio will be your only communication for the duration of your Firewatch tour.

Firewatch is meant for adult gamers. The story, the conversations you have with your co firewatcher are all adult based. The humour, the anger, and the sadness all touch subjects that you as an adult deal within your everyday life, and the way that Firewatch has incorporated it into the game makes it that much more brilliant.

Firewatch also features choices, right off the bat you have choices that can be made. These choices change the entire setting of the game and enhances the overall quality of the story progression and character build up immensely.

Graphics:

Beautiful doesn’t begin to cover it. The entirety of the wilderness has been beautifully created and illustrated to give us a constant piece of art to look at as we go about our business. The colour schemes that were used really brings this wilderness to life, there are numerous trees and other vegetation that all have distinct unique appearances and colours.

The day and night cycle are another remarkably beautiful aspect that really adds to the overall beauty of the game. The streams, lakes, and waterfall effects are another beautiful implementation. It adds to the liveliness of this place. There isn’t a single area that you explore that doesn’t look unique, beautiful, or absolutely captivating. Everything has a place and it has been ensured that that place looks beautiful and captivating at the same time.
Under the settings menu, we have some options to fine tune the game.

Sounds:

They did a really good job here! The voice over work is absolutely perfect. Both the voice artists and scriptwriters did an outstanding job to bring the characters to life. You can’t help but take everything in that is being said. The way the conversations are delivered and responded to is more than realistic and captivating. It is you here having an actual conversation with an actual person, that is the incredible work that the artists have done. 

Coupled with the amazing script puts the voice over the top and raises the bar for in game narration to a whole new level. The in game sounds and soundtrack further adds to the game and livens up the already living and breathing world. There are sounds for every part of the wilderness, whether it is the water lakeside or the canyons, you will never be alone.
Under the settings menu, we have full volume control.

Replayability:

Firewatch has one ending, but the method of getting there does vary. You have choices that you make throughout the game. Even though they do not always seem major, they change and shape the entire narrative of the game. You can end on good terms or terrible terms, the choice is ours.

This gives you the option to replay the game and experience an entirely different outcome.
There is also now the Free Roam mode where you can explore this beautiful world at your own pace.

MGR Gaming’s Conclusions:
Spoilers Ahead:

As close to perfect as they come. Firewatch is a short game, but what you gain from this game will stay with you forever. It offers a story that quickly changes from a casual exploration to, what the hell is really going on. As you play the game your own mind runs through possible solutions for what is going on and what all of it means, but I assure you, nothing that you think of is what is actually happening. 

That is how brilliantly the story telling has been done. It is further improved by the different choices you can make that adds to the overall theme of the main story. 

It is an absolutely amazing experience that you have to experience. It is memorable and will leave you wanting more.

[h1]So simple, yet so beautiful[/h1]
My first encounter with Firewatch was while I was in bed with the flu, suffering from a massive headache. Because I am a person that never can do nothing, I was looking for something to watch. Firewatch seemed to be the perfect game. Not too bright, wonderful nice colours and no loud noises. What I got while watching a Let's Play, was an experience that hooked me all day long. And although I already knew the story then, I chose to play it for myself afterwards. 

[b]Characters[/b]
You play Henry, who, for the first time in his life is a lookout inside the National Park in Wyoming. Not really because his heart burns for Mother Nature, but because he suffered a personal tragedy. To flee from it, he took a job, in which he only has to sit on top of a tower, watch the vast forest beneath him and do nothing. At least that was his perception of the job. The reality is quite different.

With Henry, the (at some points) quite naive, trustful, but also impulsive man, you get a main character who is just as likeable as Ezio from Assassin’s Creed II. Not because you are playing him while major things are happening in his life, nor because you condone his decision to become a fire lookout, but because you feel his helplessness. You sympathise with him and you both grow during your stay in the Shoshone National Forest.
Next to Henry, the only “main” character is not even physically present. Delilah, his lookout boss/colleague, is only contacting him via walkie-talkie. These contacts, these witty jokes and these serious conversations make a larger portion of why you like Henry. Delilah acts as a moral compass, guiding Henry (and you; as the player can determine the answers Henry gives) through Henry’s feelings of guilt and slowly opening up to Delilah.

The chemistry between Delilah and Henry is instantly there, hooking you as a player, leaving you longing for the next transmission of Delilah! The link between Henry and Delilah is astonishing. These conversations are so much fun to listen, for instance when you find the underwear of two teens near Jonsey Lake and report that to her, she playfully tells Henry to pick up his tongue of the ground and get his job done. Wonderful! The whole game continues through with these beautiful conversations!

[b]Environmental Story Telling[/b]
As because the only source of information is Deliah, the game relies heavily on environmental storytelling. You go to explore the wilderness and stumble upon stuff. A fence, a locked gate in a cave, stuff like that. Everything you see will come back at a later point. Two teenagers drink beer, you’ll find the beercans everywhere at the site of the *SPOILERS AHEAD* [spoiler]cut telephone wire[/spoiler]. Or your [spoiler]bedsheets[/spoiler] were stolen and you’ll find them in the [spoiler]destroyed camp of the teenagers[/spoiler]. Everything that happens is not explained by the game, but you as a player are motivated to explain it to yourself, getting creative in terms of what could be going on.

[b]Dialogue[/b]
As explained above, the only dialogue is between Henry and Delilah, taking place while on the walkie-talkie. You, as the player, are given three options of what to answer, having only a limited amount of time to decide. The dialogue is one of the best features in the game!

[b]Exploration[/b]
As this is a walking simulator, you’ll walk a lot. And surprisingly, the game is not an open world that has 5000 ways to one objective. Somehow there is only a straight way to your next objective, although the straight way is, in fact, a twisted, beautiful path.
And as a walking simulator, it doesn’t really give you the freedom of Skyrim or the combat system of the Arkham Series but instead gives you a map, that compares to a level of Call of Duty, with many areas being locked off or inaccessible until you get the right tool to do it and a story comparable to the likes of an Assassin’s Creed. And it works. It is no bad thing that a lot of areas are not accessible until you find, for instance, an axe. Because the story allows it. It grips you, you want to know what is going on, and that, compared with the environmental storytelling, really hits the nail on the head. Yes, you want to explore, but the game manages it to give you so much and so little to explore at the same time that you, as a player, are not even bothered by the fact that you cannot go into that cave right now, or possibly ever. (Losing the keys, honestly…)

[b]Graphics[/b]
The games’ graphics are not realistic, but so beautiful! As you are a ranger, you’ll walk a lot outside and see a lot of sunrises and sunsets. And boy, they are beautiful. You can see that for yourself in my screenshots.
A bright yellow afternoon, going into a nice orange-red sunset. That describes a lot of this game’s scenic moments. As for I am colourblind, I am not the one to tell you about colours and stuff, just that it is very, very beautiful. For me, this game looks a lot like Borderlands, just toned down a lot, but with the beauty of a Witcher 3. 

[b]Sound/Music[/b]
The music is so beautiful, I do not even have words for it. It is very relaxing and surprisingly turned down to a minimum. It only starts at certain points, for instance when *SPOILER* your tower is broken into. Or when nobody talks and you can just enjoy a hike through the forest, listening to a gloomy guitar playing in the background, catching yourself humming along and having such a good time, in this beautiful game.

[b]Controls[/b]
The controls are pretty straight forward, there is literally nothing fancy to it, no double bindings. It is, at the end of the day, a walking simulator.
The only thing I have to criticize is the weird animation when, for instance, climbing rocks. Henry doesn’t touch the rock, but his hands float a centimetre above said rock.

[b]Recommendation:
Completionist[/b]
Obtaining all achievements is fairly easy, as long as you explore everything you’ll see. Seeing as the game only contains 10 achievements and 5 are definitely unmissable, you’ll have not really the need of a second playthrough to get all achievements.

[b]Expectations[/b]
As explained at the beginning, my first encounter with Firewatch was while suffering from the flu, not wanting to watch anything with bright, flashing lights. Judging by the thumbnails of my favourite YouTube-channels, Firewatch was the game for me. And it was really a gem! I already knew the story when I began playing, but that did not diminish my experience at all. Seeing something is one thing, but experiencing that same thing, feeling immersed as Henry, seeing his story and the story of the game through his eyes, is just great and I can fully recommend it!

This is a short story - a good one - about the conversation and relationship between two lonely people and the mystery they uncover. But it's placed inside a first person adventure game. Find a map station, retrieve an item, get trapped, find a new tool, escape and unlock more of the map. Framing the story inside of a game leads the player to expect a less realistic end. You clash with the villain. You rescue the girl. Your multiple choices mean that your choices matter. So at the end, when the story takes you to a different ending, and you realize it's the only ending, you might feel cheated.

There is the argument that the journey is better than the destination. You can mold the conversation many different ways throughout the game, so you would think that you can shape the story arc or the final decisions of the characters. But you can't. Which makes sense from the very beginning - no matter what choices you make in the prologue, you still end up in that watch tower. You aren't truly Henry, you're just there for the story. Like a "choose your own adventure" book that always ends on the last page.

So enjoy the 4 hour story, no matter how you shape the conversation. Since this is a "multiple choice" but not a "choices matter" game, I didn't feel the need to replay it. So it might be best to wait for a good sale.

The gameplay is pretty basic. You have a map and a compass and you just traverse the land to wherever you've been told to go; climbing rocks and jumping gaps along the way. The only other mechanic is talking to your other lookout buddy (who is in another part of the forest) over the walkie-talkie. You get to pick between a small list of dialogue options that slightly affect characters actions and thoughts. It's like a telltale game only with less impactful consequences.

Overall, a very good game. short, but good. If you have 4-5 hours to kill and enjoy story-driven games, this is something you will most likely enjoy.

[h1] Firewatch is absolutely an experience I would recommend to anyone. [/h1]

You play as Henry, a man who retreats to the Shoshone National Forest to get away from his life back in civilization (you get to decide the important events of your life in the moments before the game properly starts). Your role is to be a fire lookout at the Two Forks tower for a summer. You quickly meet your supervisor over the radio, a woman named Delilah, who will guide you through the span of the game. 

At first, you are tasked with menial things but then you notice fireworks going off not too far from your lookout, and Delilah sends you down to investigate. This is where the story really starts. I wont share any further details of the story at risk of spoiling the game, but the story gets quite intense at times. The sheer amount of paranoia or uneasiness it can make you feel will push you to want to know more and more of the story and how things will turn out. 

The graphical quality is superb, yet manageable even on computers with lower specs. The art style however is a matter of preference, some people love it, some people not so much. Is it worth $20 however? Maybe, it depends if you feel 4-5 hours of play time is worth $20. I will note that I have played through the game 3 times over the past couple of years and the replay value is great, with each experience being just as memorable as the past with several options being available in ways to progress with Delilah.
The game does go on sale for cheap and it can be found at other places for less than $10 as well. For that price, it is absolutely something worth picking up.

Firewatch allows its searing embers to glow brightly within its picturesque woodland landscape through a taut, tense and personable narrative that beautifully accompanies its pedestrian walking pace.

WHAT I LIKED:
+ "I came out here for a breath of fresh air and some adventure". The story revolves around Henry, the husband to a wife suffering with Alzheimer's, who takes a summer job as a ranger at a national forestry park. Through communications with "D", stationed at a nearby watch tower, the two embrace a journey of reigniting passion, mystery and endearment. The sensational dialogue exchanges between both characters will keep you hooked until the very end, guessing the next suspicious plot detail as the central mystery progresses. Yet, underneath the compelling thriller, is a tale divulging in the human condition. Constantly relying on humour and empathy to develop Henry and his malnourishment for love.
+ Shoshone National Park looks absolutely gorgeous. Sprawling with dense woodlands, beautiful meadows, claustrophobic caves and glistening streams. Equipped with a map, compass and other necessary tools, Firewatch tests the player's orienteering skills whilst providing a lush semi-open backdrop to explore. The additional Free Roam mode after the story's completion adds to the vast beauty of the game world.
+ Whilst "walking simulators" generally last approximately 1-2 hours, Firewatch's average playtime exceeds that by an extra hour. The bonus is that the story is so compelling that it'll coerce the player into completing the game in one run. The branches of dialogue also result in multiple playthroughs utilising different conversational exchanges, therefore feeling fresh a second and/or third time.
+ Chris Remo, whom also designed and wrote Firewatch, gifts the National Park with a sensational score that both uplifts when necessary and produces tension during the more heated conversations. Truly captures that Wyoming aesthetic, to which the tracks can be collected and play in the Free Roam mode too.
+ You can adopt a turtle, if you can find it...

WHAT I DISLIKED:
- The ending. Ahhhh. It was *so* close to nailing the accelerated tension that Firewatch had been building up to. Regrettably, the final day at Shoshone was underwhelming, with a reveal that just missed the mark by a nudge. It's not necessarily the execution of the climax, but the artificial impact (or lack of...) it creates. Henry's turbulent summer grinds to an immediate halt with no sense of reward for either the character or player, a stark contrast to the exceptional buildup. 

VERDICT:
8/10 teenagers illegally lighting fireworks next to a lake...

P.S. Firewatch is undoubtedly my favourite "walking simulator" and I urge each and every one of you to play it.

Firewatch is a wonderful story. On the surface about forgiveness, regret, the role of memories and of taking time out to reflect, and the importance of reaching out to others. Especially when you've got things you need to reach deep into yourself to consider, much of which remains undecided.

Under the surface though... [spoiler]Firewatch is a game about psychotic, manipulative, and possibly murderous cuckholdry.

"Delilah" manipulates through sultry and playful flirting knowing well that people take the job to escape and are likely easily malleable.

Delilah's other half (Javier - pretending to be "Ned") sets up the "scenes" and Delilah maintains contact from the tower to ensure that you're following the carrot like a good boy.

There is a point where Delilah "leaves" the broadcast button on while she's talking with "Ned" (Javier). Listen carefully to both the tone and context of this conversation because it sets the context for all the later pretense.

If you choose to go to the research outpost once you've retrieved the fire axe Delilah is instantly angry, then realizes that this situation can be easily dealt with - "Ned" fixes the research camp discovery shortly after you leave...

Again listen carefully to Delilah's tone here. She is speaking first to you (because you weren't being a good dog) then to "Them" (telling "Ned" to burn the camp down through fake anger).

Delilah's manipulation is crystal clear from the beginning if you're paying attention. Throughout the story she constantly convinces you that you are her only contact, your only life line, gets angry when you do the unexpected, and plays the victim in the end -- even plays off any odd behaviour as having had "a bit too much to drink".

All said Firewatch is a beautifully made game, with some very extreme undertones. The suspense is immediate, and constant.

I'm surprised that people haven't seen between the lines more here.

"We all make choices, but in the end choices make us." Firewatch is a beautiful game about dealing with the past you left behind while in the quiet isolation of nature.

Firewatch consists of hiking around the mountains while chatting with your boss and friend Delilah through a radio, who will accompany you in an otherwise very solitary journey to unveil what secrets Two Forts, your surveillance area, is apparently hiding.

While the thriller story creates very tense and interesting moments for decision making, I believe the heart of this game is on its human interaction. The constant conversations between you and her, along with the options you're given as a player, reflect who you are as a person, how do you deal with grief, and how do you respond to conflict or danger. It is, at its core, a way to express you very being through a walkie talkie.

It is incredible the bond you make with the person on the other side just in the 4-5 hours that the game lasts, which in a way demonstrates how online friendships can run so deep even when the people involved have never physically encountered each other.

I recommend this game to absolutely everyone who's interested in deep narrative experiences. If you really care about your decisions and what they say about you, to put yourself in the shoes of the protagonist in the bizarre situations he finds himself in, then this game will not leave you indifferent.

I've watched a Firewatch letsplay back in 2016, which I did really like, and I've always kept it in memory. Now in 2020 I bought it and decided to complete by myself. And it was a lot better than watching the letsplay of it.
I think of this game as of one of the best quest game I've ever played. You will be playing as a man in his early fourties who ran away from his problems to work as a fire-lookout in the forest. The only person he will be able to talk with for this period is Delilah, the woman who lives in another lookout tower. Gameplay is really simple - you hike in a forest and speak with Delilah, gradually getting closer to each other. But despite this simplicity game appears to be really fascinating. Starting as relaxing, the plot gets more and more tense, some weird stuff happens and it makes the player willing to know what's going on. That's good, but the best part of this game is its graphics. I thought I would get bored hiking the forest all the time, but views are amazingly spectacular and picturesque, quickly I understood I really love to just walk in there. It does feel like you're on some forest trip - leaves are quivering, wind blows, sticks crunch under feet - graphics working together with soundtrack make the forest feel real. Another perfect thing is voice acting and dialogues themselves. You can see how the relationship between Henry and Delilah develops, how they are becoming friends and learn to care about each other despite the fact they have never actually met each other. 
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone. It has a breathtaking plot, a lot of touching moments about two man's hard lives and wonderful graphics working together with sounds - all this makes Firewatch an unforgettable experience. Hope you'll enjoy it and have a nice time!
