review:
[h1]The Cliffnotes Version[/h1]
[b]Very immersive story[/b] and [b]beautiful design (character AND environment)[/b] with a [b]great, fitting soundtrack[/b]. Game's primary drawback is the [b]short storyline[/b] and [b]relatively low replay value[/b].

[b]Overall score: B+[/b]
[b]_________________________[/b]

[h1]The Preface[/h1]
I'd been holding out on Firewatch for reasons I don't even remember. I think I caught it during the Summer Sale, and it was definitely worth it for me. Honestly, I don't know why I didn't pick it up sooner.

[h1]The Great[/h1]
[b]- Great attention to detail.[/b] The primary issue I have with a lot of lower-poly-style games is they're excessively detailed, or don't fit in. This is absolutely NOT the case for Firewatch. Everything is consistent, and even the radios are period-accurate (though coloured strangely for a duty radio).
[b]- Very immersive.[/b] It is extremely easy to just catch yourself admiring the scenery, instead of doing what it is you need to do. You might often find yourself stopping to take a break and take it all in.
[b]- Great soundtrack that fits in well with the game.[/b] The soundtrack, composed by Chris Remo, fits in very well with the tone and ambience of the game. It's also available as DLC, and I'm sure you can find some of it on YouTube if you want (if you do, I'd recommend 'Camp Approach' and 'North Backcountry').
[b]- The camera.[/b] While it's more of a novelty and a means to get an achievement, the camera is actually a pretty accurate and well-thought-out thing. It's a cheapo disposable camera you get early on in the game, and you can only shoot so many photos before it runs out of film. Every time you take a photo, your character stops for a moment to wind the film advance, as well. During the credits sequence, every photo you have taken will be shown to you, plus 3 or 4 you [i]didn't[/i] take, giving a bit more of a look into the events of the story.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
[b]- Story is immersive, but slightly nonsensical.[/b] I'm not going to get into it very much here because of spoilers, but during the height of the story (in the Day 70s) I was so engulfed in the story my heart was pounding. I was fully hooked, and I was scared for Henry and the events of the story. Why it's nonsensical is a spoiler: [spoiler]Had one of the mentioned-only characters not been so paranoid, the events of the story would not even have had to happen.[/spoiler]
[b]- The variety of radio responses gives you a bit of freedom to play Henry how you want to.[/b] One of the responses early on in the game, for example, is to name the cliff Henry encounters during Day 1, as it's not on topographical charts; the choices are "Cripple Gulch", "Widowmaker", and "My ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Boss is Going to Get Me Killed Hill". Whichever one you choose, it's marked on your map for the rest of the game, and the very next possible radio response (after Henry's rope breaks while he's rappelling) will reference the cliff's new name.
[b]- Open-world, with minimal roadblocks.[/b] You do need to pick up a grand total of 3 items to get past obstacles, but the first you can literally obtain on Day Two, and the other two items aren't even needed until late in the story. There's also no real death condition except for one (the [i]very last action of the game[/i]), and you have to deliberately try to fail for it to happen. Time does not progress until certain points of the narrative are met.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
Thankfully, there's not much to speak of here.

[b]- Short story, and relatively low replay value.[/b] I beat it my first time, taking in the sights and sounds of ol' Shoshone in roughly four hours. I wasn't even intending to do it in a single sitting, it just... happened. I thought the story would be a bit longer. In addition, while you're free to play Henry how you want to with the radio responses, literally zero of the decisions you make will affect the story in any way. Once you notice this, the major replay value comes in finding the different things your boss will say to you over the radio in response to different dialogue options, and exploring the Shoshone.
[b]- The flashlight is borderline useless.[/b] Though it's got its own funny cutscene when you obtain it on the first day, it doesn't output much light or for very far. Period-accurate, but useless. Guess the batteries were running low after who-knows-how-many days in storage - it does have a very noticeable amber hue to it, after all.
[b]- Certain notes differ if you're reading them by looking at them in the world, or in your journal view.[/b] One notable example is on Day 77, which involves very-spoiler-alert pieces of paper with some parts that have been circled in red ink - you're going to want to use the 'read' button to read those in particular.

[h1]The Verdict[/h1]
I don't even have anything I despised enough to put in the 'Ugly' section. I like this game, it's a good game, well-fleshed-out, great soundtrack, and killer story - but the replay value is 'once every few months' once you beat the story.

I'm going to have to give this game a solid B+.

This game is one I know has been talked to death in the past few years, but I feel it is important to share my overall experiences with the game. 

** Starting off with the Cons **
First off, this is a game that is monotonous in terms of exploration. You're gonna be retreading similar areas and you will be using the same tools from the beginning (apart from one or two) that are gonna be utilized later on. The game is not centered on a "meaty" play time with clocking in barely 6 hours (and that's with me doing minor exploration) which I know will bother a few.

HOWEVER!!!!!!!!!

** Getting into the Pros **
This game has a damn good soundtrack and the story grips you once it really ramps up. There's a central mystery that really drives the narrative forward and I found myself pushing past a lot of the walking sections simply to find out where certain events and decisions will take me. Music and beats hit at just the right moments and there's a lot of tension building once past the first hour of playtime. 

The story is primarily communicated w/ your radio that you will consistently bring up over the course of the story. As a matter of fact, the only other character with dialogue (other than another that i'd rather leave to your surprise) is Delilah, another look-out in the region with you. The conversations you have with her have some consequence during the story and she serves as a playful/fun figure that acts as your companion throughout the adventure. The voiceacting for her as well as your character are well done and there's moments of comedic relief between the two that I found really enjoyable in-between the tense scenarios. You can also replay the story once your first playthrough is over and you can explore some of the other dialogue options that you may have missed out on. Furthermore, there aren't really any "long cut-scenes" during the game but there are some segments where you are quickly watching events unfold. 

Beyond the main chunk of the story, I have to talk about the ending. I will leave it up to you to reserve judgement but I will say it's hit or miss depending upon how you view the overall message of the story.

I would recommend it for anyone who enjoys a good thriller, heartwarming/funny dialogue, and a good central mystery. Must buy on a steam sale!

Firewatch by Campo Santo is a first-person exploration/mystery game.  You play a man named Henry who starts his summer job as a forest ranger, intercutting with text flashbacks on how Henry met his wife, Julia.  Once at your lookout tower, your only lifeline to the wider world is your radio conversations with Delilah, your boss stationed at a nearby tower.  The voice acting and characterization is exemplary.  Delilah is very charismatic and the conversations happen naturally as you traverse the forest, but I could never shake some nagging doubts about her.  The story unfolds slowly, but picks up momentum.  From the beginning right up to the last moment, I never quite knew where the story was going.  What excitement!  Unfortunately, the intense build-up doesn't quite pay off--I kept waiting for one last revelation or twist, but it never came.  

Even with the game's lacklustre ending, I would highly recommend Firewatch.  The game takes place over one forest area, but you travel to and from different areas at different times of day and the variety kept me interested in the environment.  I don't know how much the dialogue choices change the game, but it helped me feel more like I *was* Henry, instead of *playing* Henry.  

This is the definition of a minimal interface--unless you're talking on the radio or have your map and/or compass out, there's no HUD at all.  No mini-map on continually, no objective markers.  It's wonderful.  You navigate using a map and compass and, while the map does show your current location and the route to your objective, you have to pull it up and examine it.  Even though the story progression is linear, you can take side trips and I never felt constrained by the world itself.  I also never felt lost as the paths are fairly well marked. On occasions where I walked too far and missed a fork, it was easy to correct with the map and compass.  Plus, the scenery and sound effects are beautiful and fit the game perfectly.  You can't die in the game, and your movements are realistic--you can jump over small gaps or climb up and down short, sturdy rock formations, but you can't slide down cliffs without proper climbing equipment.  

Aside from the story, the only quibble I have is that I sometimes got stuck on objects like rocks, especially if I was jogging and then stopped, but I was always able to get unstuck without loading.  Actually, I only loaded the game twice to play it again after taking a break; relying on the autosave for emergencies and never quickloading was another great experience for me. 

So if you like your games with rich characters, compelling stories, and have five hours to spare, do give Firewatch a try!

In 2016 a fresh faced indie team, Campo Santos rose to the gaming scene with Firewatch. Currently working on their second first person adventure title "In The Valley of Gods" but experienced issues concerning staff availability and some backlash involving a DMCA strike. Hope everything's okay but back to Firewatch- which I've heard many good things about. 

I admit I sometimes struggle to branch out from horror and so never got around to it (even though I had it for a while). Apparently a massive success despite being basically your run-of-the-mill walking simulator. Before you grab the torches and pitchforks, you'd be glad to know I'll be eating my words soon~


[h1]"When The Going Gets Tough..."[/h1]

[u]The Gist:[/u]
Henry is new to the fire lookout gig. Having only accepted the job to avoid dealing with the frustration and uncertainty of his wife's illness. Cut off from the rest of the world where the sole means of communication is over the radio with his supervisor, Delilah. He must set aside his personal life and not let it distract him from the job. But not before long, some troubles ensue and the past comes back to haunt him.

[spoiler] ! I know what you did last Summer...! [/spoiler]

[h1][+] PROS;[/h1]

[b](a) Keeping Busy[/b]
Firewatch plays out in a series of days, though in a linear fashion where time is beyond your control. Each day you are given a task that could involve scouting for firestarters and just being wary of troublemakers within your jurisdiction. This involves a great deal of running, climbing and other manoeuvres. There are also documents from past lookouts that detail their difficulties adapting. 

Other items of interest; several unique novels that you can examine in great detail but cannot read. Cannot tell you how many times I've fiddled with their arrangements. However, the most memorable mechanic is the radio and the chat- err reports to be had with Delilah about anything work-related. Nothing makes you feel pretty alive than bugging her when you are "lost".

[b](b) Emotional Affair[/b] 
By the way, I was taken aback at how much Henry connected with Delilah. Yes, these are witty banter and standup material but it's in line with their jokester personalities. I imagine it'd be terrifying to be isolated during a time where cell phones didn't exist. Even though Henry wasn't introduced to her properly or in person for that matter, the voice alone was comforting as if she's right next to her. 

This could also be attributed to the topnotch and human captivating performances by the two leads. How their relationship progresses is entirely up to you, but I always tried to stay faithful- there, I said it.

[b](c) Reality Check[/b] 
The story is excellently written- though not a horror game by any means, it still holds a few mysteries and some moments were disturbing. For one, the protagonist's job situation of being a caretaker of sorts is similar to Jack Torrance's (there's even a brief reference). Succumbing to cabin fever is stressful on its own, when you add it with the escapism he's knee-deep in from the circumstances surrounding his wife... 

But rejoice knowing that others have been in a similar situation, hence why they accepted this job at all! Uncovering all these understandably flawed characters' backstories was rewarding and depressing simultaneously. There's still a lush wilderness in mysteries as I haven't touch on the main twist~ 

[b](d) A Walk in The Park[/b] 
Would you believe I had no idea this profession exists? Anyways, the game, down to the design is based on Wyoming and the actual Shoshone National Forest. The graphics struck me as water color but the further I went in, those environments appear almost living. Some landscapes pack a punch to stop you dead in your track, appreciate and share via the radio. 

All these further captured- sold through the somber and rustic acoustic that always reminded Henry of his lonesome. Just the opening music drowned me in a sadness I couldn't really relate to but yet felt all of it.. There's a level of realism here that's on point it's unsettling! Its plot even the issues that plague the characters are so down-to-earth. The concerns of fire safety, animal attacks and disappearances. When you think about it, not much is fictitious.  


[h1][-] CONS;[/h1]

[b](i) Enough Baggage[/b] 
I know it's hardly a resource management game by any means. Still, I would have preferred it if we could maybe access an inventory of some type that's not just restricted to notes collected to peruse over. Perhaps you can put some things in it and have a carrying capacity. You will notice Henry shoves a few select things in there (where?) that's never to be seen again... 

Other items like the books I mentioned can only be carried by hand one a time back to the tower after a considerably long hike. Granted, these works of literature have no purpose (how dare me) besides scratching that inner OCD or bookworm within you- still I would have loved the option. Another tiny complaint, Henry doesn't get exhausted or show audible signs after running 10 minutes or longer, I'm not kidding. Yet after rappelling down a rope for about 10 seconds, suddenly gasp for air like an asthmatic? Once you see it.... ;)

[b](ii) Don't Got Time for This[/b]
Some design choices in how Henry gets around are a little peculiar. For instance, there's no designated key to jump whenever you please. Instead "space" prompts Henry to hurdle over and bypass manageable obstacles. However, the issue is that except for climbing sections, he can just as easily get past most. Henry could leap over several times in a lake area but I chose to run past. Should I engage in said prompts, they're performed slowly, clumsily (best to describe). 

Most troubling is Henry's movements as he can get stuck in objects and cannot break free so it feels like your time is better spent in the crapper. Similarly, conversations sometimes get bugged and responses pertaining to a problem (already resolved few seconds ago) remain so the two have another discussion and dance around the subject because why not. I guess I was a little too adventurous?

[b](iii) Is... That It!?[/b]
I would like to address two more immersion breaking matters. First, conversations with Delilah. Yes the choices of words do limit how you can respond but that's far from it. Sometimes (just one or two but enough to set off alarms) her replies invite more to be desired emotionally because hello, they're supposedly kindred spirits. Granted, she is still a stranger and work colleague so there's that. But it's something you'll have to listen for yourself. 

Finally, [spoiler]the "abrupt" ending. Personally, I've no problem with it because though it may come as a surprise- this whole story is not entirely about what Henry will do about his wife. I could talk about this game for hours - probably more hours than the 4 hour run time. And it'd be a mix of praise and criticisms. But I strongly feel that the criticisms outweigh the praise.

This game is visually very beautiful. The colors, the consistency of the shapes and shading, the altitudes, the views...and the ambient sound completes the feeling of being out in the wilderness. And the game has a very effective opening, with an emotional introduction told only through text, with the first hour or so a moving meditation on loss, moving on, and finding oneself.

However, once the story becomes a plot, that meditative quality disappears in place of figuring out a mystery. It's difficult to speak to the story's faults without spoiling anything, but in this player's opinion, the themes do not hold up under scrutiny and are not relevant to the deeper emotional quandaries we are primed for by the introduction. We are set up for a story about loss, self-realization, guilt, and moving on, and while those themes are voiced by separate characters, they remain separate and do not reach into the core of the storytelling, which is about wholly different emotions. The result for this player was deep disappointment.

Also, the game is really short - only 4 hours long. There's no shame in that if the story is solid, and I do commend the developers for not packing in filler for filler's sake. But in a game world as beautiful as this, it would have been better to have had more places to wander, more cool sights to see off the beaten path. Often, even if you wanted to do this, the radio would interrupt you to get you to advance the story with a sense of urgency. This is another strike against the meditative beauty established in the first 30-60 minutes. There is a "free roam" option, but that's not the same as experiencing that flexibility during gameplay - especially since there are very few things to find that you're not directed to as part of a regular playthrough.

I was very disappointed by this game - and not just the ending. BUT...take all this with a grain of salt, as the subreddit for FIREWATCH is small but active, and users there absolutely love it and think it's beautiful and deeply moving. They paint wallscrolls of the game's coloring, and so on. To each their own. So don't take my word as gospel.

The story of Firewatch kick-off after Henry M. our main protagonists' wife develops dementia. Henry takes a job as a fire lookout in Shoshone National Forest, Wyoming. The other major component to this game is the Radio. The radio allows you to talk to a fellow forest service member. Overall the gameplay is good, but as a walking sim, it's about the story and visuals.

The plot can switch faster than any E-Relationship ever. The plot twist hit me like a frieghtliner going 95mph on a salt flat. I don't want to spoil it but, pay attention to detail. 
Overall the plot is top tier besides the ending which was a letdown.

---Graphics---
At the time of playing I had a fairly budget graphics card, Nvidia GTX 1060 3gb. The game was running 60fps on the highest setting. The trees, rocks, ect were very detailed and beautiful. The visuals complement the plot. I really have nothing else to say.

First off, let me just get out of the way that the voice acting and writing are phenomenal. Easily the best I've heard in a video game, even better than most movies. So if you're tired of cheesy, stiff voice acting in video games this will be a breath of fresh air. The conversations between you (Henry) and Delilah feel jarringly natural and real. It doesn't even feel like a scripted dialogue sequence, it feels like an actual conversation. This of course raises the immersion factor immensely.

So about the ending. This is biggest area for complaints people have with the game, so I'm going to focus my review around it. Keep in mind I'll bock out any spoilers for those who have not completed the game, but it is difficult to discuss a story's ending without giving some details away. So with that said, please read at your own discretion. I really disliked the ending at first and felt robbed of my time, but after reflecting for a couple hours I ended up going down a somewhat introspective rabbit hole of thought until it finally clicked. The whole point of taking this job as a Fire Lookout for the summer was to escape from your life circumstances. In the case of Henry, it was to hide away from the reality that your wife is terminally ill and dying. Delilah has a dark past she's running from as well. The ending is basically a reality check; the whole mystery and friendship you've been wrapped up in all summer is nothing more than a distraction from what really matters in your life. Your problems are still there waiting for you, they haven't gone away. You don't get any closure in the end because that's how Henry feels about his life. His wife is still dying and his heart is still broken, and nothing else he experiences in the Shoshone Forest will change that fact. This ending is not exciting or satisfying from a narrative standpoint, however it is painfully realistic and something that most of us can relate to. Most of the mysteries and adventures we encounter in life don't have rewarding payoffs or thought provoking explanations. Life is not like the movies in that way. It's just different. You can't look to an adventure to give meaning to your life the same way an adventure gives meaning to a movie, or in this case, a video game. Reality isn't that simple. Life is a series of millions of seemingly meaningless occurrences in which we somehow have to discover our own meaning and purpose from them over time. This process is unique to every individual.

If you pay attention, throughout the game you are presented with potential plot points that suggest some sort of intriguing story is about to branch out and unfold, but it never does. The letters between the other Firewatchers that you find in the supply boxes ([spoiler]just a meaningless conversation and nothing more[/spoiler]), the two missing girls ([spoiler]turns out they weren't murdered or attacked by a grizzly bear, they just got arrested for Joyriding hence their "disappearance"[/spoiler]), the surveillance equipment ([spoiler]the government wasn't tracking you and there wasn't some grand conspiracy, it was just Ned keeping tabs on you[/spoiler]), the death of the kid ([spoiler]no murder conspiracy, just a climbing accident[/spoiler]), your ransacked watch tower ([spoiler]just a couple rebellious teens f***ing with you[/spoiler]), the potential love story between Henry and Delilah ([spoiler]it never fully comes to fruition[/spoiler]), the bear scratch marks ([spoiler]just normal bear behavior[/spoiler]), the random things you find in supply boxes ([spoiler]they're just that, random things[/spoiler]), when you overhear Delilah discussing your whereabouts with her superior ([spoiler]just a normal work related convo, no mystery here[/spoiler]), the abandoned snow mobiles ([spoiler]nothing ever comes of them[/spoiler]). There are hundreds of these occurrences littered throughout the game and they all lend credence to the main overarching theme. This is no coincidence, it is a deliberate decision by the writers to push the moral of the story. You, the gamer, are constantly trying to piece everything together to derive some kind of meaning from it all, but in the end everything is revealed to be a bunch of random, meaningless occurrences and nothing more (this is actually a good example of apophenia). Each of the potential stories are concluded with mundane, anti-climatic endings. It's a somewhat nihilistic tale, but also the closest to reality you can get in a fictional story.

The ending is only disappointing if you aren't paying attention, because it is clear that this is the message the writers were going for from the start and they have been non stop hinting at it throughout the game. In summary, Firewatch is a story of two individuals trying to escape their unfortunate life circumstances, before ultimately realizing that they can't outrun them forever and must confront them.

This review is unabashedly spoiler-heavy and is really intended more for the developers than for potential players. The TL;DR of it is that this is a decent game which I had a very bad first experience with. 

My first playthrough of this game was underwhelming, to put it charitably, but during the second playthrough (with developer commentary) I grew more appreciative of the experience. My initial experience was admittedly soured by encountering several bugs and design oversights which left me unimpressed, but the pacing of the game also felt off and somewhat rushed to me (i really disliked not knowing when a day would abruptly end because the narrative content of that day had been exhausted, cutting short all my exploration plans for that day). The pacing issues were partly my own fault, as I realized on my second playthrough; I had failed to find most of the notes/items which were intended to develop the story organically - though, in my defence, I am confident I would have found them had the game not forced me to advance (to the next plot-developing day) until I, the player, decided to go back to my tower and rest (if there were concerns about that level of player-freedom conflicting with the schedule of events an easy solution would have been to limit the number of in-game days the player was free to explore for before the game forced you to advance). Partly because I failed to find so many plot-developing cues, I felt very little emotional involvement when I came to the end of the game, and I recall saying out loud (in disbelief): "that can't be the end of the game, there has to be more than that." It left me with too many unanswered questions. Had it been (three) years since the accident, or was it just the previous summer - and either way how could there be no missing person's report of which Delilah was aware? Had I hallucinated the conversation with my wife, and why wasn't there more development of that narrative thread? Why was there a base at Wapiti if all the trouble was caused by a hermit? Who were Ron and Dave and what did they contribute to the story? How could Ned have had information about Julia which I never shared in conversation with Delilah? How did a story focused on Henry, Julia and Delilah become a story about some kid and a hermit? What was the moral of the story supposed to be ("and," I thought, "it has better not be that the pursuit of happiness is legitimate when it comes at the cost of marital vows, or that a 'person' is no longer with you when they have severe enough amnesia, Alzheimer's or dementia")? There are, of course, answers to (most of) these questions which i was fortunate enough to discover on my second playthrough, but I wish I had had the good fortune of discovering them on my first run; the game would surely, in that case, have made a much stronger impression on me. Even so, though, I didn't warm to the characters immediately; I loved Delilah's sass but was morally scandalized by the way she was clearly flirting with Henry (though, even here, if you flirt back by calling her sweetheart she admonishes you for it - and this happens whether you've turned down her advances or played flirtatiously with her, which felt like a scripting mistake). Even the jokes were hit-and-miss for me ("Turt Reynolds" was a stroke of comedic genius but the dialogue when picking up the trowel was cringy adolescent humour which felt genuinely painful to hear). 

Aside from those hang-ups, [i]playing[/i] Firewatch certainly would have been more fun had I not gotten so unlucky with bugs as well as running into so many environmental problems. For instance, during the intro sequence I noticed light cutting through the ceiling in the parking garage, and right when your character is supposed to slow down and look straight at a deer I ran into and got stuck on a rock, preventing me from ever seeing the deer (not until my second playthrough did I realize what had happened). I did get stuck on the geometry several times while exploring the world (e.g., on fallen trees and in the cave system) and I ran into a more severe bug which prevented me from grabbing the radio in the morning (I tried changing from controller to mouse and keyboard and back, verifying with the control scheme, disconnecting the controller, trying to pick it up with keyboard controls - there was actually nothing I could do to pick up the radio, and I eventually had to resort to quitting to the desktop and reloading the game). 

Even during the audio-tour of the game I encountered what seemed to me to be problems. One of the commentary booths by the lake had an interview tape which began with the (para)phrase: "so, there's a turtle here!" I began looking around for a turtle where there was none to be found; another mentioned that there was a stick "to the right of the gate" at Wapiti station, for which I scoured the area to no avail. The game hadn't loaded them into the environment properly, or, worse, the commentary was mistaken. Even when the game was working properly there were problems; the fact that Delilah's tower had the water cistern placed precariously on the edge of a cliff (not to mention that it was inaccessible to you, and, thus, presumably to her) seemed unrealistic in the extreme. I immediately walked around the base of the tower looking for a better place the developers could have placed it only to discover that the textures weren't all failed in (I could see right through a rock at the base of her tower) - disappointed, I gave up looking for a better place for the cistern and obediently marched up the steps of the tower to continue with the story. These experiences felt inexcusably typical. 

It was only after playing on Firewatch Audio Tour mode that I realized this was a good game, and it was only after playing on Thorofare Free Roam mode that I began to enjoy it. No one rushed me for a response and the game never abruptly forced me to advance to a new day. the game world felt tranquil, but the day-night cycle also made the world feel alive. Getting intentionally lost and disoriented in the forest at night also felt amazing; I'm aware that horror was hardly this game's intended experience, but there were lost opportunities here! Consider how much more engaging the story would have been had it included a section, after Wapiti station, where you were lost (perhaps robbed of your map) out in the woods in the dead of night, barely able to find your way with the aid of your flashlight, only to encounter a mysterious figure up to something suspicious. 

I am going to take a break from this game for a while before attempting another playthrough, and I hope the experience will be as good as I had initially expected from this game. Now that I'm familiar with the story, the layout of the world, and where several key items are located, I should be able to craft the narrative experience, to some extent, to fit my preferences. It occurse to me, though, that I shouldn't have to feel like I'm "gaming the system" - gaming the game itself - in order to squeeze the fun out of it. If the game is only really fun once I've played it enough that I become the director instead of the protagonist, then was it really that well written in the first place? On the other hand, looking back on my first playthrough after having gone through the game much more extensively, it seems to me that I may just be a victim of extremely bad (beginner's) luck. Either way, I will keep trying to have fun with it and I tentatively recommend it to others, especially if they enjoy similar games like What Remains of Edith Finch, The Fidelio Incident, and The Vanishing of Ethan Carter.

A man, in the woods, with nothing but his troubled thoughts, nature, and the only other emotional comfort is some unseen friend on the other side of a radio. What to say about Firewatch. This is a game unlike what I've seen before in recent years. From story telling, to soundtrack, to art style, to character development this work is phenomenal to say at the very least.

You start off with a short but effective choice making text narrative to develop your character Henry who has been going through some family trauma in recent years. To say that this method of introductory narrative is unusual is accurate but on the other hand it is very effective at accomplishing what it sets out to do which is develop your backstory very quickly and very well to the point where you are deeply emotionally involved with Henry by the first twenty minutes. As the story progresses you come to get to know a lovable character named Delilah whom you only ever speak to on the other side of a radio. Delilah is part of the neighboring fire tower and Henry and her get to know each other very well over the summer during Firewatch. Everything is fine for awhile except for some small forest fires and mischievous campers until Henry and Delilah start to uncover some deeper plots going on in the woods. As the plot develops the story unravels into something of epic proportions with a big twist and excellent story telling.

The soundtrack is simple but amazing. heart pounding and suspenseful at times but relaxing and somber at others. Never a failure to portray the proper mood. The soundtrack adds significantly to the games atmosphere and transports you to the world in a way most other games can't.

Firewatch takes the cake for one of the greatest and most unique art styles for a game in recent years. The mix of colors and abstract that they mix perfectly with realism to make gorgeous scenery that you could look at and explore in for hours and never get tired of what you're looking at. Every time you turn your head you get a new scenery to gaze upon. The scenery consists of dense forests and beautiful rocky mountain ranges that drop a jaw and could be used as wallpapers.

I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone looking to invest in a game that has replayability or will last longer than 5 hours at most. This game is strictly a linear story driven game that wouldn't be worth playing through no moe than a couple of times. However on the other hand, by combining this astounding soundtrack, art style, story telling, and character development, I found myself caring for these characters within only a couple hours very deeply and I'm very impressed with their ability to do that. If you're looking for a game that will allow you to escape reality with a very good story for several hours and transport you to another world then you've come to the right place. The under tones and messages and character development leave everyone with a message to decipher and a metaphor to take back to reality with them. This game changed me just a little bit for the better and has left me thinking about it day in and day out with a lasting impression. A story about friendships. A story about family. A story about not running away from your problems but facing them head on. A story about finding yourself in nature. But also all of those thrown into the mix with a deep conspiracy of being watched and spied on in the woods by secret government agencies out to kill them and burn the whole forest down with Henry and Delilah in it. Uncover the mystery, make it to the end, and enjoy the whole journey along the way. 

I rate this game a 9/10 for outstanding character development, outstanding world building, outstanding soundtrack, outstanding art style, and I refrain from giving it a full perfect score for the fact that once the story is done there is not much else to do other than finish collecting achievements and walking around looking at scenery.

[h1] I can certainly recommend this, regardless if it's on sale or for the full price.   [/h1]

I think we as gamers have begun to develop a stilted idea of what constitutes game and--more specifically--what constitutes a game story, particularly in the context of an adventure. Often, we start to think that "good" or (heaven forbid) great is only applicable when it ticks all the boxes of other games: it must have some intrigue, mysteries worth exploring that typically lead to a new way to see the world we explore, or--most apt to this review--revelations that make your jaw drop.

Firewatch doesn't fit neatly into those criteria. It's a slower paced experience, something we have developed to describe as a walking simulator in a negative connotation. While I don't necessarily think of these types of games negatively, I do absolutely think that there are issues that plague it as a sub-genre. They tend to be more on-rails so it feels as though all we're doing is pressing a button to walk forward and the story is the only focus of the game. I think primarily about Layers of Fear when I go for the most disappointing of what this type of experience has to offer. But when applied correctly, there's something incredibly fresh and interesting about these types of games that is really difficult to get anywhere else. 

I really enjoyed Firewatch. It is perfectly suited to the type of experience on display here. There's things to explore in an open world and the pace of it all seems to fit the type of summer escape that Henry has put himself into. And for as much as we might think we want there to be some big massive conspiracy, much like Henry's own eventual return to civilization, so too must the game be rooted in reality. 

This is a stellar experience, but not one that I would likely pay full price for. Thanks to the summer sale, I picked it up for cheap and feel no regrets for the short length--even if I think that game length is a conversation we as a community are not ready to have.

You will rapidly find your expectations turned on their head as what you may have regarded as a simplistic little game suddenly rockets off in an unexpected direction. The highlights of this game are the environment, the superb voice acting, and the aforementioned feeling of dread that hangs over you as you play. The downsides are the relatively lackluster sound design and the underwhelming ending. The writer puts too many plot lines into the air and doesn't satisfactorily handle all of them -- one plot line in particular lands on the forest floor with a resounding thud. Still, this is a title that is worth your time for the experience. Recommended!

First and foremost I think Campo Santo has crafted a beautiful and unique game that is well worth checking out if you're looking for a gentle mystery. However, for $20 there are games that will take you on a more satisfying journey which is why I ultimately wouldn't recommend it unless you know what you're getting or purchase it on sale. I want to go into this a bit more before I do a simplified breakdown.

The price point is tricky. AAA titles have been at $60 for years and we all know that they're under priced (we can debate whether AAA games are quality - my point is that the price for blockbuster games has stayed stagnant while costs have gone up to make those games). Here we have an indie game for for a third of the price which might seem even a little low for an indie game. If it's roughly 25 hours of content I'm expecting to pay $40-45. Firewatch is just six hours of content though. It's a well-made, unexpected game that you can finish in one sitting. I'm actually a proponent of shorter games, but I don't know if I would pay $20 for many of this brevity. However for a game of this quality I might because anything less doesn't seem sustainable for an indie studio. Ultimately, I find it's a difficult call to make. How much is $20 worth to you? I bought this at or near full price a while ago and don't regret that having played it through. 

Now on to the bite-sized review: 

The Pros:
- Gorgeous graphics that feel very original
- Immersion: I'm from Wyoming and grew up in its mountains. Campo Santo does a great job of capturing this region of the state.
- Excellent dialogue and voice acting
- The mystery and feeling of unease are really nicely paced. If you want mystery without killing stuff this could be a good option. 
- Solid interface and mechanics
- Time to finish: I think for the story they're telling 6 hours is appropriate
- Nice emotional notes

The Cons:
- Lack of consequences: even though this isn't really a choices matter sort of game, I feel like what the characters do doesn't ultimately have much impact on the story. Even if this were a book, where we have no control over what characters do, we'd still expect some repercussions for actions. There are repercussions for actions you're told about that happened in the past, but I don't think that's acceptable. It's too passive.  
- Tying into my last point, this might be why the ending feels a little lack-luster. I don't think I needed more game time, but I'm not sure it was a pacing issue either. 

If you're hoping for Allen Wake then you'll be disappointed, however if you like low-key mystery and exploration this might be up your alley. I felt like a boy Nancy Drew... The Hardy Boys. I just realized that's there is a boy version. Whatever. 

Final notes: if you go to Wyoming put you're f#%@#$@#ing campfires out.

Off the bat, it's art direction is fantastic and the voice work and dialogue exceeds any expectations for a video game. It's a walking simulator; the "gameplay" isn't intended to be punishing or complex, nor should it. While I understand others' dissatisfaction with the overall narrative, I think in its own way its story unfolds the way it should. There is something very poignant, yet humble, about how this game starts, tells, and finishes its story.

For full price? It's not much of a game. It looks like I've spent about 10 hours and that was running through once (I think in a single sitting) and listening to the developer audio diaries the second time around. I got it on a Summer sale for at least half off, if not more. This game is good if you want the equivalent of a park ranger slice-of-life film where you get some slight agency over aspects of the protagonist's personality.

First off, I would like to say that I appreciated Firewatch's ability to develop the protagonist, Henry, as a likable and believable character. The dialogue was well done, and the actors presented their parts well. However, I would not recommend the game because the narrative fell flat to me. The rising action of the plot occurred too slowly to get me hooked and create a sense of urgency and the ending seemed a bit too abrupt.

The pacing just felt a tad bit too slow. Much of the actions that Henry completes felt a bit pointless and errand-like. While I understand that a key tenet of this game is being isolated in a forest with nobody else around and doing simple tasks, I found little entertainment in the actions.

The artstyle was quite beautiful, but I encountered optimization issues and minor frame drops occasionally. Further, I felt as though the art could have been utilized more strongly in the forest setting by introducing more variety through wildlife, unique plants, or wind for example. I didn't feel convinced that I was in the middle of an active ecosystem.

Overall, this game was not bad and I don't regret playing it. I just was not satisfied and felt as though there was much more potential for a greater experience in both story and setting.

[h1] Fire in the Heart Sends Smoke into the Head [/h1]

[i] Firewatch [/i] is a psychological thriller with a capital P. Its compelling storytelling is reinforced with beautiful visuals and a phenomenal soundtrack. While gameplay is mostly limited to a ‘walking-simulator’, the game will have you on the edge of your seat, moving through all the emotions. The story and characters will make you cry, laugh, be scared and question everything, including your own sanity.
The game allows you some choices, but these have no significant impact on the plot. [i] Firewatch [/i] does not intend to be another many-webbed choice-heavy experience à la Telltale or [i] Detroit: Become Human[/i], but instead is certain of what story it wants you to experience, while allowing you some freedom to choose how you respond to what is happening. The story will progress and end how it was always intended to and that’s okay, because the narrative it tells is immersive and convincing.
Despite the fantastic storytelling, I wish the story’s pacing was somewhat more balanced. The game starts at a wonderful enjoyably slow pace and halfway speeds up like a Bugatti. The faster pacing isn’t a bad thing, but the first part of the game has some of the most fun memorable moments, so I wish someone had switched out the Bugatti for a diesel locomotive.

[h1] In Defence of the Ending [/h1]

I want to say something about the ending, as some players were disappointed by it. I understand their position, but politely disagree. My explanation could be considered a mild spoiler. [spoiler] Some player’s felt that the ending was anti-climactic. I understand this, as it is probably not the ending anyone was expecting. I too felt confused for a while after finishing the game. After all, the game has you doubting the truth for a good portion of the game and your brain refuses to stop speculating. But after thinking it over I really appreciated this ending. Though not really the ending the game seems to promise us, it is a very realistic ending for a psychological thriller, a commentary on the human mind. In the end [i] Firewatch [/i] is about the power of suggestion and what isolation does to our truth and who we trust. [/spoiler]

[h1] A Game like No Other [/h1]

This game is Campo Santo's first game and with it the small studio showed it was capable of grand storytelling. Sadly, with production of [i] In the Valley of Gods [/i] being on hold, [i] Firewatch [/i] will not only be Campo Santo's debut, but also its magnum opus for the time being.
I thoroughly enjoyed this game as I spiralled into the plot, becoming invested in the protagonist’s story while being immersed in the scenery. Sincerely recommended.

I would definitely play another game by these creators.

Firewatch is what's missing in modern game production. Firewatch creates a story where you develop an emotional connection with a character and forced to live his life, not your own in his person. In the end, as in real life, you are not always able to control your destiny. While this is aggravating to many of Firewatch's players, it enforces the harsh reality that the good guy doesn't always "win" and that while in some life experiences we may be the queen, in others we are just a pawn. Finally the game forces the player to decide what really happened, again a very needed aspect to many modern games. It challenges observant players to either accept the ending they have been fed or use pieces of the game to come their own conclusion.

There are many superlatives for this game - first off, it's one of the most visually beautiful ones I've played. I'm not usually one to fuss over graphics much, but Firewatch has a gorgeous pastel-like quality presentation that's winning, and creates a very immersive world to explore. This is also thanks to some lovely sound design, creating a believable forest setting that just begs to be wandered about in and taking in all the sights. Then there's the dialogue, which all feels very realistic and featured some very neat writing. Here, the conversations you have with your supervisor effectively become the main part of the game's story, although the overarching plot is also very effective, even if it doesn't quite tie into your character's backstory in a manner that I would have liked or expected. 

I loved walking and hiking through the wilderness, navigating through the area with the map and compass, and although there's no time limit or anything like that, there were scenes that conveyed a sense of genuine loneliness, and even abject panic. How things that happen in the area seem to conspire against you, or the feeling of being trapped and followed. Firewatch's gameplay may be fairly minimalist - even to the point where it possibly resembles some sort of highly atmospheric interactive story - but crucially you feel as if you're in control of the game and the whole thing feels a lot more meaningful than just a walk through the woods. I loved it.

So I picked up Firewatch in the 2020 Steam Summer Sale. I heard about this game way back when it first came out and I'd always been intrigued by it, despite not really knowing much more about it than you played as a Firewatch employee that looks out over a forest to prevent against fires, and that your only company was somebody on the other end of a radio. I didn't really know what to expect. Initially I had some ideas that maybe this would almost be like an emergency services kind of simulator, I had no idea, but being in a forest in a cool looking tower was enough to get me interested. On that particular point, the art style in this game is beautiful. I played on max settings and the forest, the mountains and the sunsets are beautiful. Even small little nuances of the tower are cute and homely. I almost want to pack up everything and live there myself. There's a certain romance that's conveyed from a life as simplistic as this. Admittedly the overall look of the game was one of the things that got me interested in the first place.

The minute I started up the game and the prologue began, I immediately changed my perceptions of the kind of game I was about to begin. For anyone who isn't aware, the game begins by asking you to make a few choices regarding the course of your (Henry's) life that led up to you joining the Firewatch service. What I though might start out as a lighthearted game (at least initially) changed immediately to a heavy story orientated game that had a lot of depth... and I was invested from the word go. Suddenly I viewed the whole reason for being in the forest and the forest itself in a completely different light and was plunged into Henry's mindset. There's a slight feel of the DONTNOD/Square Enix game, Life is Strange, that sets itself in.

The first few sections of the game are certainly relaxing and took on somewhat more of a casual feel that I initially thought I would be getting myself into with this game, all the while laying the groundwork for the story and developing Henry and Delilah as characters. The mechanics of the game are smooth and logical; it plays well on PC. My only gripe with the controls was that when rappelling down a cliff-side, you'd have to face a particular direction to begin doing so, you couldn't just walk up to rope and hit the space bar.

As the game progresses naturally the plot thickens. There's a lot that's presented to you in the first few days and little bits over time that certainly keeps you guessing throughout the game. While this is [b]not[b/] a horror game, if you're not entirely familiar with the game (as I wasn't), it does a great job of raising your apprehension and making you a little nervous, and in turn making you further invested you in the story. I guess in a way it's a bit of a psychological thriller. Personally I hate jump scares, so I found myself walking slower, giving corners a wide birth, and being far more cautious. So in a way I guess the game does a really great job of getting you into Henry's mindset. Don't worry though if you [i]really[i/] hate jump scares, certainly don't be put off buying this game, there really isn't that many and to be honest, I'm not even sure whether you can class them as jump scares, I think I'm just a bit of a wuss lol.

The main driving force behind story progression in Firewatch is dialog choices, most of which are timed. Sometimes in the time that you spend deciding what to say, Delilah will say something that usually either adds depth or comments on your silence which really adds to the realism. Additionally, I really like games in which your choices matter and have an impact on the game going forward. In Firewatch, it seems as though everything you say will have an impact on the game, your relationship with Delilah and the overall outcome. I've only played the game through once so far, however I think when I play again I would choose a bunch of different dialogue options just to see what would unfold. I have no idea whether the [i]whole[i/] game would change per se, but at the very least I'm interested enough to try playing the game through again and see what happens, even if those changes are small in the grand scheme of things.

The only major negative thing I have to say about Firewatch is the overall length of the story. From start to finish my first play-through it took me just 5 hours to complete. I would have liked for it to have been at least a few hours longer, even if that was just a few extra small bits in the introduction that seemed more casual, to develop the relationship more between Delilah and Henry and maybe add more mystery to the overall story, or a few extra section in the middle of the story to deepen the story even further. Having said that, I will be playing Firewatch through again at some point, so I'm likely to wrack up a few more hours in subsequent play-throughs. Additionally, I didn't spend a huge amount of time exploring, in fact there's a whole mode dedicate to just exploring without any story elements. The world isn't huge but I'm certain that there's things I haven't discovered. The game also lets you take pictures so if you're into that sort of thing there's another layer to the game for you as well. I also noticed that there's a developer commentary that you can switch on, so maybe I'll do a play-through with that at some point too...

Overall, I'd give Firewatch a 7.5/10.

At first glance Firewatch is just a walking game with a linear story line and an intriguing mystery. You are given tasks to complete and you have to complete each one before being able to advance to the next. None of the decisions you make will have any impact on events in the game or its final ending. However, the decisions you make [b]will[/b] affect how the other characters feel about you and how you feel about yourself, and therein lies the real heart of the game. The goal of Firewatch is to make you empathize with Henry, the character you're playing, to the point where the decisions you're asked to make have meaning to you and how you view yourself. Do you want to be the sort of person who would cheat on an institutionalized wife? Can you open up to others? Do you easily succumb to paranoia?

Firewatch does an excellent job of evoking a mood of somber reflection which goes well with Henry's story arc. The writing, voice acting, and sound design are all excellent. The graphics are well done and also play well into the mood of the game, particularly the lighting.

My only beef with the game is that the story line is [b]too[/b] linear. There may be multiple paths you can take through the forest to reach a given destination, but the outcome is the same for all of them. This leads to logical inconsistencies that tended to knock me out of the story. You can't climb back up that rope you just climbed down because the game doesn't want you to go back there. You can hop easily over a log half your height but not one a quarter the size because the game doesn't want you to go there.

The linear story line also means that the game has almost no replay value. There are a couple of achievements or easter eggs that you might have missed on the first time through, but nothing will change the game's outcome or its sequence of events. However, since I got a little over six hours of entertainment from it and paid a little less than six dollars for it, it certainly provided better value for my money than, say, renting a movie.

As someone who is relatively new to video games (I only started playing seriously about a year and a half ago) and who's majority of experience with video games was from watching let's plays, I wasn't sure what to expect from this game. I remember soon after the game came out, watching my favourite youtuber at the time play through the introduction of the game and wishing that I could play myself, but not knowing how. 

Right from the start, I could tell that it would contain a very personal feel with little choices that are brought up later, and a unique sense of humour and personality between the characters. I found myself radioing in to Delilah about every little thing, eager to hear more of the conversation between the two characters and to watch their friendship grow more over the course of the game.

The game isn't too heavy with music, and most of the time you will be listening to the sounds of the grass or the birds, which is nice, but can lead to the player losing interest as it can get a bit boring (however, this is a walking sim, so I'm not sure what I was expecting.) When the music does play, It is beautiful and simple and lets you know that you are going in the right direction, which can help if you're a bit lost. Similarly, The dialogue between Delilah and Henry is also a good indicator that you are heading in the right direction, which really helped when the game asks you to hike across the map.

Unfortunately, I was running the game off of a laptop, so I started off with about 7 fps (no joke) but after fiddling with the settings, the game seemed to run fine. The world is stunning, with a gorgeous colour palette of warm and cool tones that change over the course of the day, meaning that trails that you might walk often, never seem to get boring. I would have to say that at some parts where there is mist or smoke, it is very hard to see, and I found myself relying heavily on my map in the last chapter of the game, and still being lost for some time, however, this could be due to my inexperience as a player.

Overall, I found the ending to be slightly lack lustre, with the storylines being wrapped up pretty quickly in the last chapter of the game. I found the conspiracy storyline to be engaging and found myself at the edge of my seat when entering the fenced off area, (although, to my knowlege, this area was never explained- how could someone living in secret in the forest get all of that expensive equipment?)  What happened to Brian Goodwin was heartbreaking, and seeing his body in the cave caused me to mentally take a step back and I genuinely felt impacted, especially when remembering his play fort nearby and seeing his selfies in the credits. 
My main issue with the game is that I felt disappointed that you never see Delilah, although it is a very unique experience seeing all the easter-eggs from the plot in her watch tower (eg: Her drawing of Henry, and the Pork pond sign), which made me happy.

The BIGGEST advice I can give here is, like others have said, don't read or look up anything about this game if you haven't already. Just play it. Go in blind. It's well worth it. For anyone who wants a more thorough review, read on . . .

I was hyped for Firewatch as soon as I saw the first trailer for it. As someone who loves games driven by characters and narratives, I was very much intrigued by that first teaser. For me, it delivered, though not quite in the way I thought it would. This review will contain major spoilers, tagged as such. Don't click them if you don't want plot points revealed.

Visuals - Visually, the game is gorgeous. I love the simple look. Its much more focused on art over realism, which I very much appreciate. The setting of rural Wyoming is a gorgeous place, with varied terrain and beautiful views. I would genuinely love to visit the world in the game.

Audio - The audio is probably the biggest stand-out thing about this game. The voice acting is absolutely top-notch; Some of the best I have ever heard in a game. As I played Henry, I projected myself onto him and chose the dialogue options that most reflected what my real life choices would be, and by the end of the game I felt like I had made a strong and genuine connection with Delilah.

Gameplay - The gameplay itself is quite simple, and mostly consists of moving from objective to objective while expericening story along the way, mostly through radio dialog. It's nothing groundbreaking, but it serves its purpose. As someone who enjoys relaxing with a good "walking simulator" type game, and enjoyed Gone Home and Dear Esther, I found the gameplay fine. I really enjoyed the size of the game world, and the fact that you had to use a map and compass to find your way around.

Story - The story of the game is where most of its reviews are split into two camps. You either love it or hate it, and it seems like there are no in-betweens. Personally, it really took me for a ride, and surprised me in the end in a way I really enjoyed. [spoiler] At first, I was disappointed that there turned out not to be a big, grand conspiracy going on. I wanted aliens, or a secret government facility, or something. I wanted a Twilight Zone/X-Files ending. When I didn't get that, I was a bit disappointed at first. Then I realized that I had experienced EXACTLY what the main characters had felt. Delilah and Henry thought there was this big, strange, mysterious conspiracy going on around them. Reality is often much simpler than our expectations and hopes. It really made the explanation of everything at the end hit me in a different way when I realized I was guilty of the same paranoia as our characters. I wouldn't change a damn thing about it. [/spoiler]

Price - The price is a bit steep at $20. I bought it on sale for 5, and I think that's more than a fair value. I took my sweet time checking out everything, and it felt like I left no stone unturned, and overall it still took less than five hours to finish it. In hindsight, I would probably pay $20 for it, knowing how much I liked it, but I think for most people that's still too much, and I would say the average person shouldn't spend more than $10 on it.

Overall - I honestly think its one of my favorite games I have played in the past few years, and I could see myself returning to it again for another playthrough every once in a while. If you like story-rich, character driven games then I recommend it. If you liked Gone Home, I think you will love this. If you are more interested in complex gameplay over characters, it might not be for you.

This part of the game made me love it for its duration, the development of the mystery surrounding Henry and the Shoshone forest had me on my toes while playing and wondering while trying to sleep the same evening, wondering about details and hints the game throws at the player. I got so deeply invested in the mystery and anxious to get to the bottom of it, and suddenly the game threw everything out of the window and came up with a solution for the story that didn't make any sense and left a whole bunch of loose ends, a thousand of details and major parts of the mystery simply don't make any sense with the given end of the story.

During the whole last section of the game I was partly hoping and partly believing that something would happen or the game would present some other information to give some sense to the story. Up to the very last second and mouse click I was hopeful, and when the credits rolled up I felt terribly sad.

Firewatch has been widely praised by critics for its deeply personal and emotionally nuanced storytelling, and after playing it myself, I wholeheartedly agree. The narrative is a compelling exploration of loneliness, trust, and human connection, wrapped in the guise of a mystery unfolding in the Wyoming wilderness.

What sets Firewatch apart is how it balances intimate character moments with an overarching suspenseful plot. Many reviewers have highlighted the game’s ability to portray realistic dialogue and relationships, and this is no exaggeration. The conversations between Henry and Delilah feel natural and raw, capturing the awkwardness, humor, and vulnerability that define real human interactions. The story doesn’t rely on grandiose twists but instead builds tension through emotional resonance and subtle narrative choices.

Critics often commend the game for tackling mature themes such as grief, escapism, and personal responsibility without resorting to clichés or melodrama. Firewatch invites players to reflect on their own experiences and emotions, making the story feel less like passive entertainment and more like a shared journey.

The game’s pacing allows for moments of quiet introspection amid the mystery, which some may find slow, but these pauses deepen the emotional weight and create a genuine atmosphere of isolation and connection. The Wyoming wilderness becomes more than just a setting—it acts as a silent character, amplifying the story’s themes of solitude and discovery.

In essence, Firewatch is a narrative-driven experience that resonates because it feels honest and relatable. It’s a story about people—flawed, complicated, and searching for meaning—and that authenticity is what makes it memorable long after the credits roll.

When I played Firewatch for the first time, I got so hooked I did a full playthrough in one sitting. Granted the game is only about 5 hours long, however I found myself wanting to be able to replay it over again with everything still being a surprise.

It almost feels surreal how this game plays with your mind. One moment it's a comical game, with funny dialogue and silly tasks and the next you find yourself on the edge of your seat, needing to know what's about to happen in this ever so swiftly changing, tense to the bone adventure.

Many times I found myself smiling at the game, and the relationship between the two main characters, but there were several points that made my blood run cold with anxiety. 

It truly is a mystery as to who is with you and who's against you. You find yourself questioning everything, and debating whether what you just did was the right course of action.

This game is an absolute work of art from the exciting, 'new beginings' start, all the way up to the  bittersweet end. And if you're going to play this game, be prepared for a roller coaster of emotions.

[i]What is a good story?[/i]

You will probably never hear this question, but if you do, consider yourself screwed. A story can be good in so many ways that it takes a whole lot of thinking to put it into words and not sound like a third-grader with a speech impediment. 

However, all bad stories are almost always painfully uniform – they share a certain trait that you will recognise immediately. Bad storytelling revolves around problems that you, the viewer, the reader, the player, can easily see the solutions to. You sit on your sofa and get exasperated as none of the characters manifest even feeble remnants of common sense: they do stupid stuff, get in trouble which could have been easily avoided, and seem to make the most idiotic decisions imaginable just to keep the plot staggering forward, as one sensible action would take care of the majority of issues. Such a story is nothing but a pile of steaming rubbish and an absolute waste of your precious time; ironically, most modern novels, games and TV series suffer from it.

Firewatch does not.

I will admit that during the first half an hour I was suppressing yanws and looking at the clock a wee bit too often; but as the story picked up, which happened so unexpectedly and felt like a shovel landing on the back of my head, I was hooked and couldn't stop playing. The range of emotions this game makes you go through is unbelievable; you will experience everything, starting from being calm and relaxed to a tiny bit suspicious to straight up terrified. And there hasn't been even a single time when the solution to all problems was simple and evident; I was afraid to even think what I would do if I were in the main hero's shoes. This is a good freaking story; it grabs you by the neck and throws into the unfamiliar environment, making you feel helpless and incredibly vulnerable in your flimsy watchtower made of cankered wood and broken glass.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Firewatch is a short and charming game. A lot of people know it as the average walking simulator that is great for wallpapers, but I think it’s much more than that. The game is a beautiful walking simulator with great voice acting and writing. It is worth a playthrough, but not at the price of $20.

[h1]✅ Quick Pros and Cons List ❎[/h1]
[b][u]Pros[/u][/b]
[list]
[*] Great setting complimented by simplistic but beautiful graphics that give the game a unique pastel style.
[*] Surprisingly great voice acting for the first indie game by a small indie game studio
[*] Story keeps you on the edge of your seat, and makes the peaceful wilderness into a place of mystery and even horror.
[/list]

[b][u]Cons[/u][/b]
[list]
[*] Despite the great story, its ending falls a bit flat.
[*] The story goes by very fast, and the game is very short. You could easily finish it in one sitting.
[/list]

[h1]🕹️ In-Depth Review[/h1]
Firewatch is a very simple game, with not a lot of people you talk to as a firewatcher in the lonely Wyoming wilderness. The only person you talk to in the game is your supervisor: Delilah. The world is absolutely beautiful and the voice and writing is great, but the game just goes by too fast. It doesn’t help that there isn’t a lot to the game outside of hiking, climbing, rappelling, investigating, and chitchatting with Delilah.

[b][u]Gameplay[/u][/b]
The gameplay of Firewatch is simple. The game is notorious for being a walking simulator, which get a bad rep as barely being a “video game.” Despite this, I still think the gameplay was a nice change of pace from most games I play. Hiking, climbing, and rappelling through the beautiful Wyoming wilderness was relaxing and jaw dropping in the right lighting. There even is an option to explore the open world without the story. The exploration you’ll be doing is complimented by the game’s superb audio design. The calming wind, rustling of leaves, and the sound of displacing grass and dirt as you walk through it is spot on. There is also some pretty amazing music in this game. While there isn’t a lot of it, it always seems to come in at the perfect time during your adventures among the medium-sized open wilderness you explore during your time in the game.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2028813072
My main problem with the gameplay is that Campo Santo didn’t take more advantage of the atmosphere. There isn’t much beside hiking, climbing, and rappelling, and there’s not more to do outside of the linear story besides finding some extra dialogue. There’s almost no animals and no other activities you can do, like camping or fishing. The story just encapsulates the game too much, when there could have been much more to the game that could have taken advantage of the wonderful world and atmosphere Campo Santo has developed.

[b][u]Story and Writing[/u][/b]
The story is the game’s biggest strength. The protagonist you play as is Henry, a man who decided to take his break from his stressful life by becoming a firewatcher in the Shoshone National Forest in Wyoming in 1989. You quickly meet and connect with Delilah, the supervisor of all the firewatchers in the forest, who you can romance or simply befriend through your dialogue choices. As the game seems calm at first, it quickly takes some crazy, wacky, and terrifying turns. It also touches on some heavy topics, like the paranoia that can come from the isolation of being a firewatcher, PTSD, and being framed by someone you’ve never known or met.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2028808191
Despite loving the story, I thought it went by way too fast. I preferred the lighthearted and calm first hours of the game against the dark and intense later hours of the game. I wish the slow start of the game was longer, with more moments of lighthearted banter between Henry and Delilah before the story ramped up, so we had more time to see their natural chemistry. Campo Santo got me attached to them and had me wanting more in 3-4 short hours. Imagine what they could’ve done with 10+ hours of high-quality story and voice acting, with more balance between calm and intensity. I dare to say it would’ve been one of the best indie games ever made. The ending was also a bit underwhelming. I expected a big payoff at the end, but there was mainly some dialogue that wrapped up the story and some neat things that you discover. I think it felt underwhelming because the game was simply so short, which didn’t leave a lot of time to build up to a climax. 

[h1]🖥️ Technical Overview[/h1]
[b]PC Specs: i5 8600k, 16GB RAM, GTX 980ti
Played at 1440p[/b]
Even though this game is about 4 years old as of the writing of this review, the graphics have aged very well. They give the world a great cartoon-y and pastel feeling, and make the world look like a painting in the right view. Lighting, shadows, fog, and physics are perfect. I ran the game at 1440p with the settings maxed out, and stayed around 100-120 FPS, which is more than enough for this type of game. I ran into the occasional stutter when the game was loading the world during gameplay, but other than that, the game ran butter smooth.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2028809520

[h1]💳 Content-to-Price Ratio[/h1]
As of the writing of this review, the game retails at $19.99, and it can drop under $10 on sale. Despite all the positivity I’ve just spouted about this game, I think it’s not worth the retail price, because it’s simply too short with a lot of untapped potential and relatively low replay value. However, it’s definitely worth it on sale because it is worth a playthrough.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Firewatch is a small, charming, and beautiful game. This is the only game by Campo Santo as of the writing of this review, and I can’t wait to see what else they brew up in the future, because there is some serious talent behind this game. In fact, there is a Steam store listing for a game called [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/687440/In_The_Valley_of_Gods/]In the Valley of Gods[/url] that is being developed and published by Campo Santo, with no release date planned yet. I’m excited to see what’s next for this small indie studio!

An emotional masterpiece, Firewatch takes storytelling to a new and deeper level. What appears to be a simple tale of two young lovers turns into a wild adventure where Henry (you) uncover mysteries that lead to a much darker and disheartening truth. 

Pair this beautiful story with two wonderfully voiced characters and you have recipe for maximum empathy. I felt Henry's regret, his fear, his relief. Every choice I, as the player, made also felt morally weighted. It was easy to relate with Henry as I chose his every response to Delilah throughout the entire experience. 

Lastly, the visuals were as beautiful as the story. Very similar to 'Dishonored,' the landscapes felt like a painting that had come to life. Never did I find this game hard to look at, and if anything I found myself just taking in the valley I had been assigned to.

All the while, you are given a disposable film camera and the freedom to take pictures of whatever you want. Since I wasn't given any reason to believe this item was to be used for anything in specific, I quite often found myself treating the camera like a tool to acquire evidence. In this, I created my own game mechanic while exploring. It's only when the game ends that you find out it was just a way for you to relive the memories of the story you just regretfully finished. 

In the end, you're rewarded with catharsis and gifted your photos as a way to remember the experience; each photo available for download, and high enough resolution to use as a desktop background. 

Overall, a wonderful experience with little-to-no complaints. Highly recommend giving this game a chance!

I'm pretty picky when it comes to games.  I tend to stick to simulators (like City Skylines or the Sims), or open-world RPGs (like Witcher 3 and Skyrim). 

At first I was dubious about Firewatch since it's not exactly an open world.  But this game was really great.  I got it on sale for like four bucks and I think that was worth the price. The Pros:
-Story: I felt immersed and I cared about the characters. 
-World: I enjoyed how the map's atmosphere (literally) changed as time went on.  It got harder to see as the story got murkier.

The Cons:
-Some Mechanics: Most were fine and good, but the only thing that was a bit clunky was when hopping over/onto obstacles.  I felt it took too long for the animation to happen is all.
-Length of game: While the story was great, I felt the ending could have been tied up a bit better.  I only played through one time so I don't know if this is different in other endings (if you get a different ending, even), but I felt dropped at the end.  Like there should have been more to see before the credits rolled.  This didn't take away from the game experience, but it's just a small irk.
