Firewatch is a very short, calming game that I would say I ended up enjoying. While not an amazing, glowing recommendation, there are things I enjoyed and I could see a very specific audience loving.

The game is more of a story than anything, and that's perfectly fine for the creators telling a story that they wanted to tell, but I can't say there is much gameplay behind anything. It's mostly just walking, while trying to be immersive and atmospheric. It begs the question that, of all mediums, why does this need to be a game? Honestly, it could have been a very long independent film, or a short series, but I can't really pinpoint what made them want to make a game out of this other than a rather pretty map to explore. It lives up to it's definition of a "walking simulator". I can see that being most people's biggest complaint with this, and that is completely fair. I can see a ton of people finding this boring. The game even begins in a different style that lacks gameplay, where you just click text on a screen, it was even a little jarring compared to what I thought I was buying into. However, I can't say I disliked my time with it.

In terms of things I liked, the world you're set in looks and sounds gorgeous. There are many moments in the main story, and definitely in the free roam mode, where you can travel and reflect in silence, with subtle hints of naturistic sounds. It had successfully immersed me. It compliments the built-in photo mode very well. The ambience was very calming and sedative in a way that I can't really describe. While I think this may be the wrong entertainment medium for this story, the plot itself seemed to feel genuine, as well as the voice acting. I could feel the heart and soul that they were pouring into this. The theme of isolationism and long distance communication was sold to me as what the creators wanted you to experience.

I feel like the developers accomplished what they wanted, and it definitely isn't for everybody. If you're super into slow, atmospheric, methodical experiences, you'll probably really enjoy this. Even just hiking around in free mode without looking at my map felt like a nice day out on my own. It just felt sweet and non-confrontational, and I was mellowed by the whole act. However if you want a more exciting and eventful way to spend a few hours, stay far away.

I enjoyed Firewatch, and would recommend it to those who enjoy narrative experiences, but it isn't a game without its flaws.  It does have some very pretty art, and it's writing and voice acting are excellent, however I did feel a certain disconnect with the characters in the game due to an odd sense of 'illusion of choice' I experienced from the very start.

Without wanting to spoil too much, you start the game off with a short text adventure sequence where you get to make a series of decisions about the nature of your character's relationship with their wife.  It is ultimately of no consequence, as the outcomes of your choices all account to the same final conclusion.  This is where the disconnect happened for me; I am not choosing my character, I am playing Henry, and I am just piloting him around.  I expect it was intended to get us invested in his character, to give us a sense of him as a person so we could really play the role of Henry.  Instead I felt like the character I created, and the Henry we play as were two different people entirely, and it was a feeling I couldn't shake for the rest of the game.

Across the course of the game, we're only with Henry for a short period of time, chronologically speaking.  He keeps being Henry whenever we're not with him, and the world responds to him as that Henry, not the one you choose to be whenever you're in control.  It reminded me somehow of the film [i]Being John Malkovich[/i]; being inside someone's head, but never really being them.

[b]Major narrative spoilers follow:[/b] [spoiler]It could easily be argued that the whole narrative arc is about the illusion of choice, and how in running away from their problems the characters haven't actually chosen to do anything, merely delayed the decision to a later point.  The plot repeatedly asks us to make decisions that ultimately don't matter, as the course of the plot remains unaltered whatever we choose to do. This reinforces the idea that these decisions are not why we're here, we're merely avoiding making the one choice that actually matters.  However, I feel this message could have been much more effectively communicated if I felt like I was the character I was supposed to be playing as, not just some foreign observer existing in his head, at odds with the character presented to me.[/spoiler]

So, overall a fun game, but not as satisfying or cohesive as it could have been.

As someone who gets easily attached to a story, Firewatch was short and sweet. However, it also possessed it's own moments of sadness. The story was, as I said, short in length; but even with only a few hours of game play, it still managed me to encapsulate me, and this still stands as one of my favorite games.

There are many twists and mysterious plots that build up the suspense as you continue to play. As well as an unfolding relation between characters involved; and characters you have yet to meet. The environment you travel in is comical or cartoon-ish in style, but I find that the beauty shines through; as if you're looking at a beautiful landscape painting. 

If you are an achievement hunter and are interested in a game that is easy to 100% complete within just a few hours, I would say Firewatch is a good choice for you. You can easily obtain each achievement in a single run, especially with the help of an achievement guide.

Unfortunately, if you're looking for exciting game play or a highly evolved combat system, I would genuinely say that this game is not for you. Others have described Firewatch as a nature-walk simulator, which I can wholeheartedly agree with. Unless you are willing to spend a few hours purely for it's story telling, then I cannot recommend this to you.

The short and unsatisfying story that I experienced didn't hook me in and fell flat after the interesting introduction. While the game looks really great, i was never drawn into the world and never felt threatened by any of the 'spooky' elements that were introduced. 

The game makes you think it is a sprawling open world, but it's a VERY linear experience that doesn't feel as fleshed out as other narrative i've played. It also turns out none of the careful dialogue choices I made throughout the game made any difference to the story, which made me really think hard about why I bothered agonising over the choices I made in the first place. It made me feel like I was just along for the ride being dragged around by the art director to look at the pretty game they've made. 

I was waiting for the game to start, and then it was over. It felt like an introduction to a game, rather than the game itself.

It's a mundane trudge through a forest with a really unsatisfying conclusion that everyone seems to be in love with. I just feel like i've played a completely different game than everyone else.

This is quite possibly the game I've enjoyed the most in my entire life. I find myself replaying Firewatch over and over to listen to new bits of dialogue and rename my turtle. I play it to relax and to get lost -- literally, seeing as I'm terrible with identifying landmarks -- without the stress of not being able to find my way again. The music is calming and fitting. The plotline forces you into the mental state of the main character, which is soothing for someone with anxiety. The ending is appropriate, properly set up, and is as satisfying as it is infuriating, and every time I get near the end I find myself starting a new file and starting the game over again because I just don't want it to end. I don't want to leave Henry. I don't want to leave Two-Forks Tower. I don't want to stop talking to Delilah. This entire game had redefined how I see storytelling in this medium, and challenged what had once been a staunch disapproval of first-person games. I had gone into this game expecting to hate it, and the introduction broke me into little pieces and dropped me right into a world I knew nothing about, and as the music rose to a fever pitch and I joined this man through the woods as he hiked towards the starting point of the game... I realized I had no choice. I was going to love Firewatch.

This game is great. It's 2020, there are lots of positive reviews out there already; I'll stick to the points I really want to mention:

- Absolutely outstanding voice acting. This game got nominated for Best Performance in The Game Awards 2016 for the work of both Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones (Henry and Delilah), and personally I think it is [b]scandalous[/b] that they gave the award to Uncharted 4. 100% robbed. Same goes for Best Narrative. Oh, well.
- Visual style, and art direction in general. Great artistic choices make great immersion without resorting to higher degrees of realism.
- Great intro, characters are written so well since the beginning.
- I think at this point the self-isolation theme is a big trope ("I run away/lock myself in to avoid facing the past but eventually I learn that memories are always with me wherever I go and I cannot run away from them") but in Firewatch it works wonders. Gameplay goes along with this perfectly, and secondary plots enrich the protagonist's dilemma (maybe not subtly but very effectively).
- Overall great narrative, with amazing management of tension and calm. The player is easily hooked early-mid game and the story resolves in a very elegant and satisfactory way (at least for me!).
- I just found out there's a one hour long GDC talk about the art production of this game, so without further ado I'm out. Play this game!

[h1] I loved this game... [/h1]
A few years ago I watched a YouTuber playing this game and now I'm here, writing this review. 
As I saw the gameplay, I swore to myself that I'm going to play this game. I don't know why I was so hyped about it nor what hooked me so much, but I just really wanted it. 

[h1] Now... [/h1]
I'm not sure if I'd recommend this game full-price to everyone, but I, myself, would totally do it. It was one of the first visual novels I've ever found out about so it's pretty sentimental to me. Seeing it from the nowadays perspective, I wouldn't say that this game is for everyone. It could seem boring for some. It doesn't have lots of action or so. It's just you, wandering through the woods and caves, talking through the radio with a woman you never really met and discovering weird stuff [spoiler] basically strange equipment and weird signs from a disappeared child [/spoiler]. It's really simple, in my opinionl. But for some reason, I still loved it and I still do. 

[h1] Annoyances... [/h1] 
A nice thing, which can also be annoying, is the exploration part. You have a map and a compass and that's it. I've got lost a lot of times, took the wrong path and had to go back and forth again and again. The most annoying thing here is the running. It's not like you really run, it's always more like jogging. 

[h1] Cute little details... [/h1] 
What made every day of mine in the game was my wonderful [spoiler] turtle. Big up to Bucket Jr. [/spoiler]. Also somewhere in the game you find [spoiler] a camera [/spoiler]. You can actually [spoiler] take pictures with it [/spoiler] and at the end of the game you get [spoiler] a link that leads to a site whereto your photos were uploaded. If I'm not remembering wrong, you can actually email them to yourself [/spoiler]. I think it's pretty nice to finally see them, as you aren't able to do that in-game. There are more positive things that I could mention, but I'm leaving them to be discovered by others. 

[h1] In the end... [/h1] 
It's your choice whether you think this game would bore the F outta you or the exact opposite. It kept me entertained for a couple of hours (the hours you see I have in this game aren't the exact ones, as I also spent time in it after I finished it, whether if it was for achievements or for the extras). I do think this visual novel is pretty relaxing and nice. When you're wandering through the woods, the jogging gives a nicer vibe, a calm atmosphere. Of course, there are also some sad/alarming scenes, but overall the atmosphere is pretty calm. You could also add some slow music in the background while you're jogging and boom; it makes the time pass faster, it doesn't feel like you've been walking for hours anymore.

Firewatch is a story. That's all there is to it. There's very little in the way of challenge or gameplay (aside from finding your way around the park), but it's a game that manages to hold its own purely as an experience to be enjoyed.

The majority of the engagement revolves around your relationship with another character, a woman by the name of Delilah, who is often your only companion through the adventure. The story starts taking a turn, however, when the both of you discover events that cannot easily be explained. It's a good setup, which is, sadly, rather quickly undermined by the ending of the game, which leaves a lot unexplained, and a kind of unsatisfying black screen and credit roll.

Overall, I think the game could really have benefited from a lot more interaction with Delilah. After your first 2 days, the game skips over about 2 months of these characters getting to know eachother in only about 3 short scenes which offer very little choice, and allow very little of their relationship development to be shown to the player. As is, the game is only about 3 hours long, which is not all that much for a game with as little replay value as this.

Still though, I'd recommend it for the experience. It's a good and well-paced story, which rather sadly is in my opinion undermined by its ending, although I see what the developers were trying to do with it.

Firewatch

Developer: Campo Santo
Publisher: Panic Inc.
Release date: 9 February, 2016
Multiplayer: No

Time played: 16.5 hours
Completion: Yes 
Spoilers: Yes
Achievements: 100%

Steam description:

“Firewatch is a single-player first-person mystery set in the Wyoming wilderness, where your only emotional lifeline is the person on the other end of a handheld radio.”

Aesthetics:

Firewatch is a beautiful looking game. The devs have knocked it out of the park visualizing the Wyoming wilderness into a format both colorful and distinctive. Each area of Shoshone National Forest has a different feel that changes depending on the time of day. From the shores of Jonesy Lake to Wapiti Meadow the environments are vivid and atmospheric. The graphics are great and run really well.

Score: 20/20

Gameplay:

Firewatch is not a game in the traditional sense, you have choices but they have little impact on the world. Firewatch is an interactive, visual story where the player is more of a passenger than a driver. The gameplay is almost nonexistent, navigating is perhaps the only aspect of the game that would fall into this category. Despite this Firewatch wasn't intended to be gameplay heavy therefore its absence is not a fault of the game, it's simply a niche that the game was never meant to fill. As an aside the achievements for Firewatch are nothing special, mostly for completing sections of the story.

Score: 10/20 (N/A)

Storyline:

The story of Firewatch is easily one of the best in a video game. You play as Henry, a middle-aged man who has left his broken life behind to work as a fire warden in Shoshone National Park. Your supervisor Delilah is your only human connection for most of the game. Almost immediately you are plunged into a slightly unsettling, very compelling mystery, the plot of this game is phenomenal. The pacing is some of the best I have ever experienced whether in a book, video game or movie.
What astounds me is how the writers of Firewatch managed to get so much out of such a small plot. Some games are centred around enormous events, the invasion of a multidimensional empire (Half-Life: 2), or the return of a prophesied hero (The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim) but Firewatch’s story winds to a close with the most dramatic event being a potential murder. Firewatch is one of those few pieces of art that raises the bar for storytelling in its entirety and acts as an stunning example for writers of all creeds.

Score: 20/20

Characters:

The characters in Firewatch in my opinion are not as important as the story and its mystery. Don't get my wrong I think Delilah and Henry are well designed characters that have interesting interactions, I just didn't connect with them. What's genius about the game is how there are really only three characters, but yet each plays an integral part to synthesize an outstanding experience. 

Score: 18/20

Worldbuilding/ Immersion:

Even though Firewatch takes place on boring old Earth, the game manages to fit a multitude of tiny details into the world. For example a few books can be found in Henry’s lookout tower and around the world, each is labeled with an author but also has a blurb written on the back. Another great piece of world building can be found in the various supply boxes that litter the world. Past rangers at the park have left (often funny) notes to each other that tell a story for curious players to discover (as an aside almost every supply box has the PIN 1234, Delilah mentions at one point how confusing it was to have different codes to every box so she changed them. A great way of using the world to streamline player experience).
Some of the achievements can be gained from finding some of these hidden details around the world, such as a ranger's abandoned haunt or a dead deer with a high-tech tracking collar. Overall the minutiae of the world only add to the mountain of immersion and story that this game is.

Score: 20/20

Gripes:

As you would expect by now I have a lot of praise to give this game and not very much criticism. That would be accurate. 
Firewatch is one of those games that aims to hit a certain target and nails it on all fronts. This game fills its niche completely. There are few to no bugs in this game and it feels almost like a movie as opposed to a game. As mentioned before the characters are well designed but not very memorable and this game lacks in gameplay but for excusable reasons.

Conclusion: 

Firewatch is an excellent game despite the seemingly low score I gave it. My scoring system isn't perfect and this is my fifth review. If you love narrative driven games or just have extra cash sitting around in your Steam wallet, I cannot recommend this game enough. As always please leave feedback on the review and let me know what I could do better or your own opinion of Firewatch.

Final score: 88/100

Recommended at default price: 100%

Anyhow, in a nutshell: definitely give Firewatch a buy&try if you love interactive stories and amazing environments, you won't regret it!

Have you ever wondered if you own a pattern when it comes to dealing with the hardest decisions of your life? The ones you’re not most proud of, I mean. Is it shutting yourself down? Diving into other people’s stories in the form of books or movies? Everyone has their favourite pick here. Henry, the main character of [i]Firewatch[/i] is no different. And, oh boy, he’s truly had some of the toughest life decisions behind him already.

So he ends up in the wilderness. I won’t tell you much else not to spoil the joy of playing through, but I can promise you’ll enjoy it if you crave some premium outdoor experiences in this strange time of lockdown we're in right now.

These views and sounds! Beautiful graphics (a cartoon-like theme works very well here, and is executed perfectly), witty dialogue, and a bit of mystery. Or… maybe more than just a bit? The unfolding story makes you want to come back, but I feel these several hours of total playtime is just enough. And the most important part – a chance to self-reflect on the core psychological mechanics of our lives. Should we choose what’s the most convenient, or what is hard but deep down seems right? It’s only one of many questions you’ll be asking yourself once finished with this game.

The only downside for me, despite the world map being very open, were the [i]corridors[/i] in some parts of it. Just like the game taunted me I can’t go here or there because this would be too easy, and then I couldn’t move ahead even though there was no particular visual obstacle right in front of me. This, however, added greatly to the [i]puzzle[/i] character of [i]Firewatch[/i].

As for the ending, which seems to be the culprit of much whining among gamers – I think it is an ideal one. That is if you understand what [i]Firewatch[/i] is really about. Give me such ‘walking simulators’ any day! 7/10

[i]Firewatch[/i] is a pure and simple walking simulator. You receive instructions to go to a certain point in the forest, so you navigate there using your map and compass, and repeat this process until the game ends. 

There is no action involved like having to run away or hide from creatures who chase you, as is often the case with adventure games that are labeled walking simulators. And there are no puzzles to solve either, which is another element often added so as to create a game, meaning software that makes the player do something -anything- other than just walking from point A to point B and so on.

[i]Firewatch[/i] doesn't offer any incentive to explore its game world. There are no collectibles to be found, not even in the form of Steam Achievements, and there is no reason whatsoever to deviate from the straight line between your current location and your goal. The only reason why you can't just walk in a straight line to your target location, is because your avatar can't jump or climb even the tiniest rock, so you have to take large detours around rocky hills that anybody's grandmother would swiftly hike straight over.

I have no idea why so many reviewers praise the quality of [i]Firewatch[/i]'s graphics. To each his own, of course, but I found the graphics crude and not pleasing at all. 

So the only thing that's left is the story and the voice acting that narrates said story, which also gets a lot of praise. I really wish that I could recommend this game, but I'd like to save some folks from a similar feeling as myself. I started playing the game around 1am, and finished around 4:30am, so it's a fairly short game.

For those 4 hours, I'll start by saying that the graphics were fine, IMO not the most beautiful thing I've ever seen, but fits the rest of the game, I personally liked the voice acting, and didn't mind the walking all that much since there was often dialogue to keep your attention (though looking at the map starting getting very annoying). I really feel like the format and general basis of the plot had very real potential, but it wasn't fully utilized by rest of the story.

So, the story. I initially was rather invested in it, I thought it did a fairly good job at building some tension, and I know that there was points in the game I was looking around, somewhat expecting someone or something to jump out from the bushes. But... it was a lot of rising action, rising action.... but no real climax, I felt. The ending just felt unsatisfying and bland. It was kind of just like "OK, bye Delilah..." In a way,  I know there's some connections we can make between characters and the events in the story, but while that helps explain some stuff, it still doesn't give me that satisfying ending. 

I've seen too many people saying this is a "real life" story, and that the ending is supposed to be mundane... okay, so it's supposed to be a bad story? I don't play videos games or read fiction to be bored. That being said, the ending doesn't have to be what I expected, it doesn't have to end in Delilah & Henry climbing on board the helicopter together... but you can't butter me up the whole time and in the end just have them go their separate ways. There's other parts of the story that could have been explored as well, but I don't want to spoil too much.

Even with this information, I still _might_ have been able to recommend this if it wasn't $20... definitely for that reason it's a negative from me. If you have not seen the story at all, and can pick this up for a very cheap price on sale, I won't say it's the worst thing I've ever played, but please do not go in without expecting to be disappointed.

Firewatch is a nice little choice and dialogue driven game with mystery elements and absolutely no fighting. You talk to a person on the radio, you make your rounds, enjoy the wonderful scenery, and in the end make a report. Easy-peasy, right? Well, maybe not. In the end it is all up to you. 

I would say the only downsides of this game are the length and the depth. The conclusion comes far too quickly, and is far too neat. By the end of the game I was left with a sense of emptiness, because the existing game had material for a story at least twice or thrice as deep. That way it would have had the time to really wrap you in before unveiling it all.

After finishing the game, Firewatch has some re-playability value, but only in exhausting all the alternative choices you could have made. Beyond that, it is all about the scenery, and for some of us, imagining what could have been.

Overall, I still recommend it. This game is all about the walk. But once you arrive and look back, you'll keep wondering what all the fuss was about.

Sure, the ending left me scratching my head a bit, but that's part of the charm, isn't it? It's not about having all the answers; it's about the journey itself. And what a journey it was.

So, if you're looking for a game that's more than just pixels on a screen, give "Firewatch" a try. Trust me, it's worth every penny.

I was very excited to buy this game, only to be let down. It has a lot of redeeming values with an intense and exciting buildup to the climax, only to come metaphorically crashing down in the end and ruining what could have been a much better ending. 

PROs:
- Art style and visuals were absolutely gorgeous. By far the best part of the game. I don't think I've ever been this impressed with how a game looks. 
- Sound and voice acting. Extremely Immersive and created a fantastic atmosphere when combined with the visuals.
- Something close to a walking simulator,  and one done correctly. Never really a moment of boredom. 
- Very exciting buildup that was strong enough to let the devs take the climax into almost any direction they wanted while still creating an awesome story. 

CONs:
- The anti-climactic climax. The biggest letdown in the game. I've never had such an exciting build-up come crashing down as hard as this one. It was a story that could have been ended in an infinite number of ways, and one that was built up in such a way that it could have taken a 90 degree turn into almost any kind of twist ending. Instead, the millions of possible endings that floated through the mind as the story went on came to a sudden halt, leaving you hoping for something more - [i] anything [/i] more - fulfilling than what was given. In addition, the story seemed to buildup to a very [spoiler] exciting [/spoiler] ending, but instead decides to end with [spoiler] an unexpectedly depressing one [/spoiler] which was, ultimately, another letdown. 
- A story that feels unfinished. Not only was the climax disappointing, but there were more questions than answers at the end of the story that, although not necessarily important, still left the player hoping for something more - something that would have created much more closure for the player. For example, [spoiler] you never actually meet up with, or even see, Delilah. [/spoiler]
- Too short of a game for the price, but due to the obvious amount of effort that was put into the game, I don't want to give them too much sh*t for this one. 

Overall: 5/10. I really wanted to enjoy this game, and I did up until the ending, but the ending was one that was disappointing enough to almost make wish I hadn't finished it. There was definitely a lot of effort and creativity that was put into this game, but it was the bad decision-making on the devs part that was ultimately the downfall of this game.

I love a good story, whether told in books, movies, shows, games, campfire stories, or what have you. There's just nothing quite like being drawn in to a new world, getting to know the characters, and having mysteries unfold before your eyes.

If you're at all the same way, then good news, Firewatch is here to deliver.

It's a fairly slow game, often being called a walking simulator, but that's only partially true. Yes, most of your time will be spent walking around the beautiful forest, but you have items to use, blocked paths to come back to later, objectives to reach, and unlike the esoteric nature of most walking simulators, the story is told clearly and interactively.

It all starts off with a short, pseudo-choose-your-own-adventure section, where Henry's backstory is told, culminating in him taking a job as a lookout in the Shoshone National Forest in Wyoming (near Yellowstone). So, right off the bat, we have Henry's entire backstory. No sooner do you start the job than you get a call from Delilah, the sort-of-head-lookout in the park, who is brimming with sarcasm and wit. From there, you are tasked with various jobs around the park, the relationship between you and your only real confidant grows, and the fairly dark main plot creeps ever closer to you.

I'm not going to spoil the story, but I do have to say that this is not a scary game. It's not SUPPOSED to be a scary game, so it's best not to go in expecting that. It certainly tells an adult story, and there is quite a lot of foreboding atmosphere, but this is not one to watch your favorite Youtubers make themselves squeal at. Make of that what you will.

Since we're on the story, I will say that I felt like the developers did a great job allowing the player to feel involved in it. You have certain small choices you can make when interacting with the world, and even though that won't change the color of the end-screen from green to red or anything, it really helped make me feel like I was the person exploring the park rather than just Henry making choices and me watching them unfold. It's more about choosing how you react to certain situations than affecting their outcome, but I can definitely appreciate when a game is subtle.

It's a fairly brief game as well, clocking in at around 4 hours (unless you play the optional modes, or spend a lot of time basking in the sunshine), but I felt like that was only barely shorter than it should have been. There were a few small jumps in tone throughout the game, but it was only mildly distracting rather than alarming or confusing. One thing that helped with the brevity (one which I greatly appreciated) was how when you were nearing the end of the day and had accomplished your task, Delilah would say something like "go back to Two Forks, and we'll talk tomorrow", which would usually instantly end the day and start you back in your watchtower the next day. Rather than having to walk back yourself, the developers saved you the time. Since you're never stopped from exploring due to "narrative impatience" the rest of the game, I appreciated the devs not wasting my time there. Most other games do.

What you'll spend those 4 hours exploring is a cartoony but gorgeously-rendered park, filled with a fantastic variety of trees, cliffs, rivers, lakes, and wildlife. It never got tiring to look at, and there were quite a few moments where I said "wow" and pulled out my disposable camera to snap a pic. In fact, the only complaint I have about the visuals is that all of the various interact-able things in the world look identical. All the half-height blocks Henry has to jump over look the same (and play out the same animation), all the tall rock outcroppings Henry has to climb look the same (and play out the same animation), and all the trees Henry has to hop over look the same (and play out the same animation). It was a little distracting. It's also worth mentioning that the game isn't as well-optimized as I expected either, using quite a bit more of my GPU than I would have guessed based on the visuals. If you have at least a decent computer, though, it's a beautiful game.

The sound design is top-notch, too. The radio crackles to life when you pull it out, the wind rustles through trees and whistles through cave entrances, wild animals make various calls in the distance, and you can occasionally hear creaks and cracks in the distance. It reminded me of nights spent out camping in the forest, just listening to the sounds of Mother Nature doing her thing. Every once in a while, background music will swell up to match the tone at any given moment, but for the most part you're either left in relative silence or talking to Delilah.

Speaking of the characters, their dialog is done quite well. You're given choices in how to respond to certain things, and there's a perfect match between what you chose and how the dialog actually unfolds, which is always nice. The voice acting is pretty well done, too, although there were a few times it felt a bit over-acted.

Summing everything up, I found Firewatch to be a great game. It's beautiful, well-written, and while I wish a few things had been expanded just a bit, it's short enough not to outstay its welcome. I thought the way the story unfolded was perfect, and the tale it told was suitably dark but believable. Overall, I definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoys slower-paced, non-action-oriented, story-based games.

The game is stunning. Although you may have seen this said before I feel the need to reiterate: it is gorgeous. The colours are incredible, it really does feel like you're exploring a lush national park. 
The characters are flawed and nuanced: there are moments in this game where you're stuck between a rock and a hard place when it comes to decision making, and you can't always be the good guy. Firewatch forces you to play one of the most realistic fictional characters I've ever had the privilege of playing. I was so excited to learn more about both Henry and Delilah. 
The game does so well at building tension when it comes to the horror aspect. Suspense is such a key factor in this story and I adore it!
However, I did notice that when wandering around the woods, especially on paths I'd already used, it tended to drag. This game isn't bad, but it's highly overrated. I don't regret playing it, and I think I enjoyed myself overall, but it hamstrings itself in too many ways to merit a recommend.

     + Strengths +
It's beautiful, the voice actors are incredible, it's well polished, and it has a real story.

     - Weaknesses -
Exploration is discouraged -- events/dialogue will occur out of sequence or be missing entirely if you go off the intended path or discover something too soon.
This "on-rails" experience means it barely squeaks by as a game.
Choices in dialogue change nothing but how you feel about the characters. No outcome will change.
The story leaves one feeling vaguely depressed and empty. Now, I think this is a totally legitimate way for a story to end, but there's no message or sense of having experienced a change in or confrontation with myself. So it doesn't feel worth it.

Sadly, I think this game's popularity is due to people being dazzled by something that lacks the substance to truly be good.

Note: reloading the game fixed the issue. Overall my biggest complaint is Firewatch leaves you kind of unsatisfied with the conclusion - which is intentional, but it still kind of feels like a cop-out.

Let me explain:

Firewatch is a game with a good concept but that isn't developed, with lots of let downs.

Story:
You are a guy who leaves your life behind to become a ranger out in the woods, just for the loneliness. Weird things start happening. It's a good premise, and the tension is held for a good while. But over that it's just a huge disappointment. The ending is terrible and so many errors in the story line are left (purposedly?) unexplained. It's a huge let down the path the game will take.

Gameplay:
Although it wants to convey an open world environment the game is pretty linear and forces you to take the next necessary route. A handful of bugs were also experienced during gameplay.

Visuals: 
Kid like theme. If you like borderlands and such, that's somewhat what you'll find here.

Voice over:
Definitely the good thing about this game. It has very good voice actors and forces your imagination in a very good way. That's the only thing that would make me recommend the game, if deeply discounted (to, like, 1 or 2 euros maximum)

What a wonderful game. The story knows it's not some over the top narrative it has to deliver, but rather the connection and relationship between different characters. 
I really enjoyed visuals. It made me feel like I was imagining a novel I was reading, not playing a game. I also enjoyed the ability to pick things up from the ground and inspect them. I wish they had done more with that though. 
Of course, the main draw is the story. There's not much game-play here, and that's OK. 
The prologue will knock the wind out of you. I think it's the most powerful thing in the entire game actually. So sad, so poignant. 
The rest of the game you have this fantastic voice only relationship with another park ranger/lookout. Delilah. It's a great friendship. Being able to choose the responses is a big draw and adds to the replayability. 
Of course, your enjoyment of the whole game depends on how much you liked the ending. You may have heard a lot of criticisms for it. Me, personally, I liked it. It fit the scope and themes of the game. I'm not exactly sure what other people were expecting. 
Maybe they thought they would get a big confrontation. Something explosive. But Firewatch's ending is like a fire that burns slowly and quietly away at you. And you sigh inwardly thinking about it. 

But despite my praises, I would recommend getting this on sale. I'm not sure about the price in different regions, but do realize that you get around 4 hours of gameplay.

Firewatch is a walking simulator with quite nice story and beautiiful graphics.

I love these kind of games, they're relaxing and if there's a good story and world i enjoy most of them.
The story is about a man who decides to work as firewatch in the forest. Main character named Henry had some problems in life in decided to spend time alone for a while to think about everything and maybe make peace with himself. When Henry arrives to his outpost in the forest Delilah (another person who works there at another outpost) contacts him over walkie talkie. They talk about some stuff from time to time, Henry doesn't feel completely alone and the whole interaction between these characters is really interesting.
You explore the forest and one day you find some bizzare things and start investigating. There's some mystery in there, i must say i liked the story. And i'm probably in minority here, but i actually loved the ending, i think Henry finally found peace. The main story was about Henry, people tend to forget that.

Gameplay is very simple. You have a map and explore the area every day. You find some interesting and sometimes creepy stuff. There's a map which helps you to navigate.
I didn't like some parts of the game, they felt like time wasting, but overall it was a good experience.

Graphically the game looks great. Firewatch really has a wonderful artistic graphical style.
Voice acting is great and sounds believable, listening to them talking you start thinking how Henry feels.

What else to say? Buy this game if you love walking simulators/exploration games with some nice story. And it's easy 100% for achievements hunters.

I liked it. I don't tend to like open world walking sim type games cause usually set pieces are scarce and there's a lot of filler. But this was actually enjoyable. The game doesn't hold your hand. You have to find your objectives manually via a compass and a map. And you can just sit there chatting away at your boss.

I also liked the ending. People are saying they thought it was anti-climactic, and that all these mysterious plot elements build up to nothing, but...that's life. Not every experience you have is life-changing and dramatic. Sometimes you think something huge is happening but it turns out to be something mundane. You can work a summer job and leave completely unchanged. There's that saying, "it's the journey, not the destination." And I think that applies here. What I enjoyed was exploring the forest and having all this weird ♥♥♥♥ happen. Thinking there's this huge government conspiracy and a team of scientists performing a 'Regular Show dome experiment' on you. And then it turns out to just be a paranoid ex-military guy trying not to be found. I thought that was a brilliant twist.

And there's something to be said here about execution, too. In my review of To The Moon, one of the points I think I touched on is how [spoiler]the guy had a brother who died as a kid[/spoiler], and how poorly it was executed. It just felt hammy and forced, and I saw it coming from a mile away. In a way, Firewatch has the same twist. But the execution is so much better. I didn't see it coming at all, and it hit hard when it happened. Seeing a corpse in the cave and putting it together that...that's the kid. That's Brian. And then everything suddenly makes sense.

Edit:
The game is basically a walking simulator with a bit of story being told along the way. You can easily play through this game in 4 hours (if not even faster). The story is on the level of some random teen novel that tries to be spooky at certain points, but actually fails.

The game could be played through even faster if it didn't force you to walk the same paths over and over again and blocks paths at the beginning intentionally. Later on you will find additional tools to enter the blocked paths which sometimes also work as connections between paths you walked before.

You can't explore the map freely because of the design of the map which is a network of paths, paths and more paths. This is especially apparent at the beginning of the game when most paths are still blocked. Also the paths are narrow and some bushes or rocks block you from ever leaving the paths. There is freeroam mode, but the paths remain the same and you can't leave them and truely explore the map freely.

You never meet any other characters to have a true interaction with. Only on rare occasions (if the story requires it) you see dark figures in the distance that don't do much other than scream their one line at you or try to spook you before wandering of, never doing anything really to you. Yeah, the game tries to be "mysterious"... 

The only interaction you have with someone is via a walkie talkie (with a person that you never actually meet). You can choose between some predefined dialoge options when you find new objects that may or may not be relevant to the story.

If the game offers you several different dialoge options to react to an event, you usually can only pick one. If you want to hear the other options you have to reload the game or do several playthroughs. This might sound interesting, but the differences between the options never made me really want to hear them. Also what is being said is often very predictable. To me it wasn't worth a second full playthrough. The overarching story of the game doesn't change by choosing different dialoge options.

During your playthrough you find objects which have been left behind by other lookouts, visitors or rangers. These objects sort of give clues about what was going on in their lives or to what they did in the park. The goal of the game is to find those clues to uncover the "mystery". In the beginning that is sort of interesting, but after a while I lost more and more interest. The story is just too predictable and you can't really do anything wrong or die. You just follow the predefined paths and will uncover the "mystery" of the story.

There are some more or less funny and/or interesting achievements that you can collect along the way. After the first playthrough I had already finished 7 of 10. I finished the final 3 by looking them up because apparently I missed them during my first playthrough. But I never did a second playthrough and never will do.

After all the negative stuff, let me add some positive notes. The game is beautiful and very colorful. Depending on the time of day there are vivid oranges, blues, greens and so on. The views are nice sometimes and kind of invite you to take screenshots of the scenery.

If you are looking for a semi interesting walking simulator that you can't fail and have a "mystery" story on the side this game might be for you.

My personal conclusion is that the game isn't worth 20€ to me. The game is out several years now, but the price is still the same. For just 4h of gameplay it is way too much money imo. If you are looking to have a lot more bang for your buck you should rather buy The Witcher 3 for basically the same price, but hundreds of hours of awesome gameplay and story that has true consequences.

Oh, and btw don't expect that you have to actively watch for fires (as a sort of mini game or something like that). You will only "discover" them if the story needs/forces you to.

The game starts with you (as Henry) making some choices (Which have very tiny impacts in the dialogues) about your life with your wife Julia and then some stuff happens after which you decide to take the job at Two Forks region of Shoshone National Forest as the ranger to chill and sort things out. Delilah is your boss who is on another region of the forest and communicates with you via radio. Only person you can communicate with it is Delilah and the main purpose of it is so that Delilah can send you on different missions in your reigon if needed.

Now, as it can be predicted, the main focus of the game is on these radio communications with Delilah, and I'd say it is pretty succesful to a degree, as I know that sometimes I have  been searching around frantically so that I could find stuff around me that I can make a humorous comment about to Delilah and get an equally funny answer from her. Whatever I did, walking around in the wild forests, going towards a mission area etc I hardly cared about the environment and all I wanted was to have some more chit-chats with Delilah. The voice acting, humor, timing... All of these were perfect about these interactions. However, one downside I think there was, is the lack of information about their lives and backstories. For all the time I played, I had many small talks with Delilah but only a handful of our interactions were about our past lives (and Julia). As for Delilah, we have learnt even less about her backstory except for one (maybe two?) specific incident in her past. Maybe the game wanted to show that there is no need for backstories while creating characters and only the way they talk and react can be enough to portray them quite well. I believe they did it well enough too, to be honest. But if so, then what was the purpose of that tiny bit of backstory about Delilah?

Before going on with negative sides to the game, I'd like to list some more of the positives. The environment was really beautiful. Different regions had different terrains, different trees etc and all was nicely used to decorate your surroundings. There were different lightings through the game like morning, sunset and night and sometimes they changed through the day as you did missions. The audio of the game was also exciting, the musics becoming more clear and volume getting higher as you reach the mission area and it also reflecting the mood of the mission you have... Some of the said missions were also really exciting and eerie that speculating with Delilah about what is going on, swearing to your heart's content when you find something specificly peculiar things was so much fun. In a nutshell, this game did a very good job of portraying an interaction of characters solely through radio talks and without the two even meeting eachother.

Now, if we will talk more about negative sides, I have a lot more to say.

Firstly the gameplay. One of the very first areas in the game, the area that is around the Two Forks watchtower and the cache a bit to the west of it is definitely the most confusing area terrainwise. Many times I have lost my direction and ended up going towards the wrong sides when I wasn't looking on my map. There is a thick foliage around there and god knows how many times I have passed through it but ended up in the wrong place. And the game makes you wander through there many times that it might be a bit annoying, especially in the very beginning of the game if you are not that good with directions and can't be bothered with using the map.

Yeah, lets talk about the map too... Everytime I press the map button, I see a map on my hand and I suddenly can not even run and have to walk in slow pace. Yet, you still can't really make much of the map as you are not zooming to it so you should also click right mouse button and zoom into it to actually see where you are (Well, not to mention that you should also use your mouse a little more to wander through the map) and where you should go clearly. At this point even walking makes it hardly readable so you should stop. Therefore it is painstakingly annoying to check where you are via the map and kinda punishing. It could have been done so that at least you can run when you are just holding the map without zooming it. You can't really see much when you are not zooming anyway. This way you might at least possibly understand that you are on the right track if you have really good eyes.

Sometimes the walking becomes really repetitive... There are only a few easter eggs and achievements you can gather by walking around and thus it becomes incredibly boring walking the same truly long path you have walked at least 2 or 3 times before once again. Sure that the game tries to minimize it by ending the day after you finish some missions and not make you go all the way back to your watchtower sometimes but... I simply didn't feel that was enough.

And finally I'd like to talk about the ending.

[spoiler]It was... Super anticlimactic. Sure that this is a more realistic ending than a government conspiracy and pulls a vague parallel to Julia arc but all the bits about it left hanging like a loose thread or handled really unprofessionally made it very... "meh" in my opinion. I think in the way that it ends as quite anticlimactic, you can compare this game to "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter". And it was pretty fine in the case of tVoEC in my opinion, although it was a very cliche resolution. Because in that game, everything made sense to be that way and was perfectly explained. We didn't have anything that we can ask like "Then why was that so?" etc. But in Firewatch there are many of those. Firstly, why is there a government scientific base there that noone knows about? Why is it prohibited by fences surrounding a huge area? Why doesn't anyone care about the fires and try to put them off "especially" when there is a government scientific base there that is going to burn altogether with the Two Forks region yet upon one call helicopters can immediately arrive to take us? When I finished the game I felt like I got the false ending because of all those questions left hanging, although I knew there was only one ending and a small secret ending (The secret ending also felt pointless because it was very abrupt by the way. I expected at least one last dialogue in the secret ending with Delilah but no. It wasn't even bittersweet, I was only confused. Just like "Umm... What was the purpose of this secret ending?"). The lost teens arc was also used as a literal story bait to give a suspicious air through the game and resolved unprofessionally by simply telling "Well, they were bad kids and they stole a tractor and got lost."[/spoiler]

To sum up, the story sacrificed every branch it has introduced to assert a specific ending, without concluding them.

Yeah, it feels weird to still recommend this game after having so many negative things to say about it but... I still think that it was worth the experience with Delilah at least.

I hope you found the review insightful if you have read this far.

[h1][b]What is Firewatch?[/b][/h1]

Firewatch is a first person adventure game heavily based on story. It is an intimate experience, but also a journey into feelings and human relationships. Personally, I think the main theme of the game is "loneliness", not only literal, but more like an internal loneliness. From what I just say, seems like the game is too serious, grim. Not at all. There are also lots of fun dialogues, some of that they're really gold. The map is relatively open and you can explore (almost) every spot from the beginning. The game is rich of details and colours with many different areas that stand out.

[b]Is it a game that I should play?[/b]

You should at least give it a try. With time you'll start familiarize with the enviroment and the characters. And if you don't like it after a few hours, maybe you'll find it boring. This is a really slow game, based on dialogues and a lot of exploration. In fact, the map may seems small at first glance, but when you start exploring you realize that's a lot, and it is well crafted enough to have recognizable point of interests, so that you can oriented easily. There's a lot of backtracking, so if you hate it I can't recommend it. I personally loved the freedom that the game gives you from the start, sure you have "objectives" to follow, but it gives you enough freedom to choose your own personal path.

[b]Is it long enough? Worth the money?[/b]

Quality over quantity. This is Firewatch. I found it pretty entertaining so I didn't mind the lenght (I think 5-6 hours the first playthrough), but if you going for the 100% you can complete it in 10. Plus it has some funny easter eggs. When I completed every achievement, I immediately start a new game only because I wanted to explore freely, the atmosphere you feel walking in the forest has something mesmerizing, along with the stunning musics. I found it very relaxing and peaceful.

[b]Conclusions[/b]

When I started playing this, it really blew my mind of how the characters (i'm not gonna spoil you, but there are a few) feel so real, and you can actually feel lonely sometimes. The relationship and the bond that you're going to have with the other characters is another thing that I found enough real, that helped me immerse myself in the story. 
It is really hard to explain for me because my native tongue isn't english, but all I can say in conclusion is that Firewatch is a great "experience", that will move your feelings in some way, even if you don't like it.

Firewatch is a beautifully designed game with fantastic environments, stellar voice acting and an interesting narrative. So why the negative review after that first sentence? The ending was awful and many of the game's best parts fall short.

The game starts out with a fill in the blanks type story but with a linear outcome. You are a man who's recently found out his wife has early onset dementia and to escape his reality, takes a summer job as a national park outlook. The setting really pulls at your heartstrings, doesn't it?

You have one friend to talk throughout the whole game, your boss Delilah, on the other end of the line of a walkie talkie who relays you tasks. (I just want to remark here that both the main characters are fantastic voice actors who portray their characters with such charm. Also I got this game just for Cissy Jones' voice.) One day at work you stumble upon a mystery that sets the story in motion. A gripping tale of conspiracies and espionage.. until it isn't. I don't want to spoil the story for those reading this review but just know it is an underwhelming conclusion to the experience of playing Firewatch. 

Gameplay is simple, you walk around the park, sometimes attaching ropes to rappel down steep cliffs. There are a few tools to use such as the map and compass which makes up for the lack of an in-game HUD, adding to the immersion of being lost in the park. You can radio in to Delilah your observations of the park and ask questions, about what you're looking at or as personal chit chat. The earlier segments of the game were nice, getting the opportunity to watch the budding relationship between yourself and Delilah. Once you uncover the mystery, your relationship with Delilah diverges based on how you interact with her.

The national park is big and beautiful, while lacking in the actual appearances of other people and wildlife, leaves much space to explore in your own time. However, this is another aspect of the game I feel did not reach its full potential. The park is pretty big, but the story takes you through the same few paths over and over again without any particular incentive to explore the rest of it. What I mean by this is, for the entirety of the game, each day you are rushed to go do a task which leaves you little time to diverge off the path to explore the park. 

To summarize -
Pros:
[list][*]Great voice acting
[*]Story starts out strong
[*]Beautiful environments to look at and explore[/list]
Cons:
[list][*]Story's conclusion is underwhelming as hell
[*]While the map is large, not given opportunities to explore as you are rushed to perform tasks[/list]

If you do want to get the game at all, set your expectations low and maybe purchase this from a seasonal sale.

People aren't kidding when they rave about Firewatch being a sort of masterpiece. I came into the game expecting a walking simulator with pretty scenery, maybe with a bit of park ranger action on the side... Needless to say, when the main storyline started to take shape, I was just as ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up over it as the protagonist was.

You don't need me to tell you that this game is beautiful, with functional (although sometimes clumsy) gameplay and great sound design that gets you fully immersed in minutes. You also probably don't need me to tell you that the story is one of the most unexpected and gripping narratives you can find in a simple game like Firewatch. Although a bit hectic, I appreciated that the plot managed to keep both feet in reality from start to finish. Plus, although the story is linear, dialogue trees and free-roam give you just enough wiggle room to prevent it from feeling constricting.

Though the map is reasonably sized and designed brilliantly to encourage you along certain routes, it can be easy to get lost, and switching between the map and scenery can be nauseating. Additionally, I was faced with a handful of freezes that forced me to load previous saves - quicksaving frequently should spare you from some of my pain.

Really, this game gets its praise from its stunning creativity, chilling story, and all-around impressive air. I would love to leave this review glowing, but the longer I think about it... the more I think that it's not worth the price. With next to nothing interesting or exciting to offer in terms of gameplay, no diverging story, and zero replay value outside of achievement hunting, Firewatch is seriously more of a movie than it is a video game - and who the hell spends 20+ dollars on a movie this day in age? I bought it on sale, and would consider it a near scam to buy it at full price for the whopping four hours of gameplay it offers.

This game is beautiful, and wonderful, and gripping, and I loved almost every minute I spent playing Firewatch, but I seriously think it would have been a better deal if I'd just watched someone play it on YouTube; It would have been functionally the same experience, and I'd be a few dollars richer. For this reason, I'll give it a 3.5/10. While I don't think it's a waste of time, Firewatch is unfortunately not worth more than ten dollars at the very most. Watch a silent playthrough or something and you'll be just fine.

My favorite part of this game was how you can be able to process what is happening and come up with your own theory on whats going on. The objectives are a fair distance away sometimes and while walking through a beautiful nature park you are trying to figure out what is going on. In a movie, they cannot give you time to think or else the movie will seem boring. In a video game, they can do these long pauses without it getting boring and you can think about everything that is going on. You come up with ideas and you become more and more involved in it. 

However, this also had negative affect on the ending. You are given this giant conspiracy theory, you are starting to go crazy trying to figure it out, and then the ending happens and its found to be kind of a wet blanket on the whole thing, I feel like the writers were going into this amazing story, then someone told them to wrap it up. You don't expect it, sure, but I felt cheated. 

One other issue was the choices you made had no affect on the story. You are given a response choices; however, it doesn't feel like it really changes the story. The introduction part has no affect on the story and honesty was more frustrating because it doesn't have any choices that you actually want to do. Not trying to spoil it, but the options are like "Do you want to punch your grandma or your dog?" (Not an actually choice) I don't want to do either. Their was no moral question on right or wrong it was more like choice between wrong and wrong.

Walking simulator, the game genre that's not a game. You have to be a certain kind of person to enjoy this stuff. Coming off of Katana Zero and going into this. Man.. it's tough to defend these kinds of games. They're solely carried by their characters, and a game can have strong characters and still be...you know a game with gameplay.

To it's credit Firewatch has some pretty charismatic individuals. Flawed but enjoyable to be around. Hearing them talk back and forth about stuff in a light hearted manor is interesting and again to it's credit the mystery that starts to build has some serious intrigue.

But that's not the point of the game. The point of the game is asking YOU how good of a person you are. Your "decisions" from in game and dialogue options change the character experience you're going to receive. The ending will be the same, but the realization that hey...maybe you aren't as steel hearted against temptation as you think. 

For the record i absolutely threw that stereo into the lake. 

But...for me, these games only work if you are the character being asked the questions. Henry has a life, he has a personality. Henry is always going to make the same decision, he's just going to make the decision either calmly, or..not I guess. Not about specific things like the stereo, just in general.

At some point, it's pretty obvious that you and Delilah are getting pretty cozy with one another so it's asking how far does your eye wander. But that's the thing. Julie? Jules w/e, I've never met her. Even in the picture she's a blank face (not really, but it's covered). She is just text to me. It's hard to deny the character connection from delilah over text and a wedding ring. 

I don't know, to me the experience is akin of looking inside yourself, to really dark places and asking...What would my neighbor from 5 years ago do in this situation. It just doesn't work. I really appreciated how the subtle decisions you made in earlier dialogue sequences impacted multiple game elements later on: the actual script, landmarks on the map, artwork in the game, and the timing of side-conversations.

Navigating around can be a little frustrating due to not being able to freely jump over obstacles; you instead hit spacebar to "interact" with the obstacle, which triggers a custom animation depending on the obstacle. It does create an immersive experience, though, trying to stay true to what it would be like to be a firewatch roaming around a series of rough trails.

Overall great game! I would recommend a couple play-throughs just to experience what happens with radically different dialogue choices.

A short, sweet and for most parts relaxing experience. Firewatch is what most people would deem as a walking simulator with item interaction, and the short story (took me just under 5 hours) with limited dialogue choices doesn't give much in the form of replayability. The game is semi-open world but also limited in where you can go, things to interact with and overall very linear. 

Upsides:
- Very immersive. The game doesn't rely on HUD markers but a physical map you bring up in front of your character and a compass for navigation. You still have a map that you can fill in roads on as well as a marker showing exactly where you are so it's hard to get lost if you check it regularly.

- A compelling story which builds up into an intruiging mystery, although I felt the main characters were oblivious to obvious things at times but it did a good job of starting off as a relaxing experience that ramped up into keeping me pretty tense.

- Lovable characters that are well written and realistic.


Downsides:
- Very short with next to no replayability. It felt like the dialogue choices had very little if any impact at all, but it was fun to pick them in the moment.

- Few climactic moments, it's hard to say more without spoiling. 


Sidenote: This game follows the story of a man with a very specific background which is the entire foundation of the story, you will not be making your own character and while you choose how to respond to different situations he mostly has his own personality and traits. If you're looking to forge your own character this is not the game for you.

As a summary it's a short but polished game, maybe not for everyone but if you see it on sale it's a relaxing and compelling experience well worth to spend an afternoon with!

The trailer presents a bunch os scenes out of order and is kinda misleading about the story, which is okay to prevent spoilers.
But they do end up spoiling the scene where there's someone in your tower which completely undermines one of the scariest moments in the game.

The gameplay is kinda different and some of the default keybinds are unusual(like R to toggle between sprint and walk and the right mouse button to zoom). 
I decided to play it without showing my position in the map and it was a bit frustrating navigating around. Not just because navigating a forest with just a map and compass is hard, but also because the game doesn't really offer you freedom to walk wherever you want. You may think it does, but it is merely an illusion, you can only walk a bunch of trails and paths, but if you divert from it you'll end up facing a small rock that you just cannot climb(your character cannot jump).
The frustrating part is that sometimes you find bigger rocks that you can actually climb because they are part of a trail.
I kinda understand that simply letting you jump would open up the map way too much and cause a lot of work to devs(they would have to make sure you cannot go somewhere you're not supposed to), but in the end it kinda breaks immersion when you find a tiny rock you cannot get past right after climbing a 3 meter wall of conveniently positioned rocks.

Movement issues aside, the story keeps you hooked and the dialog is terrific.

Firewatch gives you a beautiful corner of America for you to explore. You're given everything from a map to a disposable camera to help you on your journeys. 

Freeze Frame. Record Scratch. 

Excuse me, I meant to say "your one journey."

I mean I already said the game looks good but not in a way where you'll want to walk 10 minutes to one part of the map, look at it, maybe take some photos, and then walk 10 minutes back to your original position where next you'll be walking 10 minutes elsewhere as apart of the story.

Nice mechanics, pretty good graphics, decent gameplay, awesome story. I bought this on sale a few months ago, and didn't get around to playing it until last week. I don't remember what I paid for it, but the story/atmosphere of the game make it worth ~$20, imo. Only complaint is that it's a pretty short.

THE GOOD:
The visuals are beautiful, the dialogue is human and earnest, navigating in the enviroment feels immersive and real. 
THE BAD: 
The ending is unsatisfying, the intro feels tacked on and clunky, and the rules for where you can and can't move feel really arbitrary sometimes.
THE UGLY:
Honestly I would probably recommend this game if it wasn't lacking a crucial final pass in terms of polish. There are trees that float in mid air, there are parts of the ground that clip through other parts or have gaps that allow you to peer into the void. The conclusion feels as though they changed it half way through and didn't go through a complete redesign which leads to some plot holes and pacing issues near the end. Because the game shines in its ability to immerse the player in this story, each of these little points becomes a glaring issue that takes you out of the experience. 

THE TAKEAWAY:
If you're more inclined to follow the beaten path you will likely enjoy this game more than I did. Similarly, if you don't like doing some "role-playing" to get immersed in a story with a protagonist who is likely dissimilar to the real you, you might enjoy the experience even less than I did.  Either way I think this was a super promising project that really deserved an extra 20% funding to fix all the little experience-breaking issues that compound to constantly remind you you're playing a video game.

Too peaceful for narrative-driven action games and too action-packed for exploration novels, as I like to call them, Firewatch is one of the most unique games in this genre. It is unique in a way that it does not just tell you the story but lets you experience a story unfurling around you. And oh boy a story it is! The characters are pretty well-written too - they feel like real people with problems of their own.
The wonderful soundtrack helps pass on the mood to the player pretty well too and scenery of a nature park is depicted pretty well, albeit in a cartoonish style, which I found quite charming. The included exploration mode that lets you walk the park and enjoy the scenery with all locations unlocked helps with the replay value of the game as the location is of quite noticeable size and you can easily find some new things to look at even after you think you've explored it to the fullest.
However, this game is not perfect. Model collision is a thing and I had to restart the game from the last save because Henry (the game's protagonist) got stuck in other models and I couldn't do anything about it. The ending seems rushed and not too fit for this game (in terms of quality, it fits the plot pretty well in terms of storytelling).
Overall, a pretty good game worth spending a couple of hours every evening for about a week on.

Firewatch is an example of excellent script writing and storytelling in video games. Firewatch is a "walking simulator" type game, where instead of taking an active role in the story through interacting with the environment, you largely progress simply by moving from place to place. Games in this genre typically have interesting stories, thematic music, and charming visuals, and Firewatch is no exception. That being said, where this game really shines is in the script and voice acting. Although you never see the face of your boss, Delilah, or even the MC, you still get a sense of their personalities and flaws through the way they communicate via radio. The banter, jokes, and occasional flare-ups lend a very human touch to the serene and isolated world of the Wyoming Wilderness. The world is vibrant and full of beautiful colors, but as other reviewers have commented, the game was somewhat lacking in animal life. A few encounters with raccoons, plus single encounters with a bee, an elk, and a turtle are all that happen within the game, which is a bit of a letdown considering the quality of the art styyle and strong level design. The result is a world that is beautiful, but somewhat dead, which has the effect of really making the player focus on the story and the radio communications, which is not necessarily a bad thing. The story itself is engaging and kept me interested for the entirety; at times I expected jumpscares or to turn around and find someone watching me, but that was fortunately limited to just one of said raccoon encounters. The result was that I was consistently on edge and found myself pressing the radio button to call Delilah even when no dialogue options were available. 


Overall, this is good game, great for eating up an afternoon or Saturday morning. I recommend it for people who like to explore the game world and get drawn in by the story. People who like active gameplay might be disappointed, but for those who can put that aside and just enjoy a walk in the woods Firewatch is a very pleasant experience.

At the end of the day, when I finish a game, I want to feel like I completed a satisfying journey and this one... it was a bunch of half-completed jaunts that ended with me still standing in the woods going...um. I haven't gotten anywhere, really. I guess I'm done now? Okay.

If you're new to walking sims, I've played Gone Home and Tacoma and prefer both. There's more to look at in either, tighter stories, and less confusingly developed characters.

This is honestly the most emotionally rich game I have played. The tension, anguish, and heartache that you feel just through engaging in periodic conversation with someone you never even meet, is absolutely astounding.

The amount of thought that went into the production of this game is very clearly evident, every aspect of it has been seamlessly sewn together to create a very unique and memorable experience. 

The gameplay is very simple, but yet still very engaging, not once did I stop playing due to being bored.
The voice acting and music was especially excellent, the way the developers were able to create subtle atmospheric changes that all pieced together in a way that created huge emotional cliff-hangers that sometimes leave you quite distraught, wanting to keep playing just to get that next slice of cake.

One thing about this game is that the story line seems to constantly change. Every new piece of information you uncover changes your idea of where this story is leading you. Pros:
- fun exploration since you're in the woods and you get to climb rocks and crawl around in the bushes and whatnot
- poignant story that honestly made me kind of sad at the end...maybe depending on your dialogue choices you can get a different ending though
- interesting plot that kept me playing consistently because I wanted to know what the big mystery was
- no combat/timed events but there were a few creepy bits which I enjoyed :)

Cons:
- I felt like the answer to the mystery was a letdown... [spoiler] they start it off like it's going to be a big government conspiracy but it ended up being much smaller and didn't make a lot of sense to me when it was all explained [/spoiler]
- a lot of the cut-scenes leading you into a different day can be triggered unexpectedly and you don't get to go back to explore the things you didn't look at
- when you pick up a note, it doesn't auto save into your inventory or anything, you have to manually decide to keep it which was annoying because I forgot to do this for a few of them and then I couldn't go back and look at them later when I needed to
- very few animals in these giant woods, none of which I ran into (I've heard there's a turtle and an elk or something but I didn't find them as I had no idea what to look for until afterward)
- the days/chapters were really inconsistent lengths, which bothered me and I think also contributed to my frustration about cut-scenes being triggered before I was ready
- the survival aspect was not as fleshed out as I wanted it to be; it would have been cool if you had to eat at certain times or grab more supplies from the cache boxes or something--even when you have to pack your bag at the beginning, it's essentially ceremonial because you don't end up needing most of it and it never comes up again
- there is no inventory you can look at, the items are just there or not
- why did we need to take pictures of anything during the game? Delilah asks you to take a photo of a campsite at one point and tells you that you can take one of another thing toward the end (which I'm not gonna spoil) but you don't really do anything with them
- there needed to be more explanation on one of the mechanisms/devices you have to use toward the end; I got confused and wasted like an hour trying to figure out wtf I was doing

Verdict:
Get this on a big sale and don't expect to replay it if you do. It's fine if you just like adventure/walking sim games with some light puzzle type stuff and you need something to tide you over on a rainy day. A lot of people like the graphics (I'm not a fan of the style but they're well done) and the dialogue is interesting enough to keep you from tearing your hair out as you tromp through the woods between one place and the next.

I was playing A Plague Tale and thinking about games that really affected my emotions in a meaningful way. And Firewatch immediately came to mind. People simply are going to have very different experiences depending on some key choices.  Given that caveat, if you like narrative driven games, Firewatch achieves something gaming as a medium struggles with; real investment in its characters.  I didn’t even realize how much until it’s conclusion.

At any rate, I thought I’d leave a quick recommendation for anyone who’s never played it and doesn’t mind “walking sim” type gameplay.  If like me, you think it’s refreshing when a game feels more like an immersive branching novel than a skill based “game”, it’s a must play.  It does some really interesting things that rely on your agency to make it all meaningful, but for that reason will offer differing experiences.  I’ll never forget the one I had with it.  I play a ton of games, and 2 years later it still stands out.
