Firewatch is tagged with perhaps one of the most unflattering and unappealing genre types listed on Steam. That of the ‘walking simulator’.

It’s true that walking about forms the core part of the experience and no doubt this single attribute has probably put a lot of people off from buying it. Yet if you ignore this – see beyond the fact that you won’t be reloading ammo clips, fighting off hordes of enemies or bringing an evil empire to its knees – Firewatch is a brief excursion into a brilliantly crafted yet slightly sombre world.

Without trying to reveal too much about the game, your character is a troubled soul. You pick through an array of story-based outcomes right at the start to dictate how and why he appears in the setting that Firewatch provides.

You take on the role of a fire-watcher – a live-in guardian of a mountainous region of forest in early-1980s America. Your home is a tall wooden tower from which you can survey many square-miles of woodland during the warm summer months. You have ample supplies, an outside toilet and as means to break the hours of solitary existence – a walkie-talkie to communicate with a fellow fire-watcher/supervisor in a similar tower across the valley.

Firewatch is beautiful to look at, but in no means stresses current hardware. The world is simply drawn - imagine a reworked vision of Team Fortress 2 to give you some idea of the slightly cartoony appearance that in this instance, works superbly. The background noises, from bubbling streams to the ambient rush of leaves and the functionally clever input method, all help to make the wilderness somewhere that you as the player, wishes to stay.

Both dialogue and story prompts progress well. Your relationship between the other tower dweller fluctuates between genuine interest, concern for your welfare and even the occasional dip into the flirtatious. Acting as another pair of eyes to the terrain before you, hints and clues from the occupier of the second tower assist in where to go. How you get there is down to you – with many trials and footpaths leading in different directions amongst the trees. I guess the underlying appeal to walking simulators is this ‘freedom’ that such games provide and given the well-crafted setting – you sometimes wander for no other reason than you can.

Firewatch cleverly taps into that nostalgic genre of the early 1980s that the likes of Stranger Things and other shows have made popular again. Having personally walked around some of the Rocky Mountains area of Alberta and British Columbia also, there’s a clear sense of realism and belief that has gone into the vibe of the game itself. That feeling of solitude has been conveyed well.

Firewatch is not a long game. I completed it within 5 hours and that wasn’t rushing through it at all. Yet out of 800+ games in my Steam library, it represents just one of three that I have all the achievements in. Granted, most are not difficult to obtain – but so welcoming was the setting that it provides, that I couldn’t leave any optional stone unturned.

A solid 9/10.

I've played at least a few walking simulators or games like it; The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, Life is Strange, Pony Island, The Stanley Parable, etc. So they can be done well.

Firewatch does not do it well. Even though they are just walking simulators, the crux of any game is that it must have some element of player choice, otherwise all we're doing is watching a movie except we have to do all the work. And Firewatch is work. The entire game you are lead by the nose by your boss on the other end of a walkie-talkie. It's a highly linear game where your only choice is to pick from a series of dialogue options. These options don't even rise to the level of Mass Effect as far as impact. Picking between three varieties of "yes" is not player choice. And when that is the ONLY choice you are given in the game it's a frustrating miserable experience, stymied even further by invisible walls and impasses in the environment as meager as a fall log. 
In order to progress in the story you have to navigate this large forest. It has a cell shaded style animation which looks good enough, but you'll quickly realize there isn't anything to do in this forest. Except pick up pine cones and sticks. And the eponymous fire? It's more like fog. This game could easily have been a text adventure for all the good the environment does you. You're given a compass and a map to navigate but going from point A to point B. I assume was supposed to be this cathartic experience of hiking in Wyoming but it's a bland slog as you guess which knee-high bit of terrain you can actually step over and which you can't. 

Walking simulators at least have to tell an engaging story or have decent characters. But Firewatch has just two characters; the player character and Delilah, your boss on the other end of a walkie-talkie. If this game has been getting any praise it's ostensibly in the interaction between these two characters.
And my goodness is this dialogue cringy. In the first 5 minutes I never wanted to hear from her again. Why is my boss prying into my personal life? Can't  i just do my Firewatching without her asking awkward questions? It is the most inorganic dialogue from a supervisor you can imagine, the kind of thing that in today's world would get you reported to the Labor Board. Delilah is a mix of Friends character and a breathy coquettish sex-chat line. The conversation gets so casual it feels like she's sitting in a bubble bath with a chardonnay talking to her longtime high school friend rather than her subordinate. She feels like a character written into some Lena Dunham Netflix original. Delilah swears profusely adding to the level of silliness, and sadly the option to throw away the walkie-talkie and never speak with her again is not offered. 

After the first 5 minutes I made it my mission to avoid all conversations with her. [h1]Underwhelming[/h1]
This is the first Walking Simulator I've ever played, so I wasn't sure what I was getting into. What I expected was essentially a story in game's clothing, but what I got wasn't much of either.

The game begins with one long exhibition about the troubled life and relationship of a man named Henry, who, after some personal tragedy, goes to work in a forest. He befriends Delilah, who also works in another area of the forest. Together they chat while Henry is tasked with a series of mundane tasks in keeping the forest safe.

There's much more to it, but I won't spoil things.

I will say that what we get as far as a story goes is a genuine mess. The writing is glib, hackneyed, and underwhelming. Banter between the characters is how this game unfolds, which unfortunately is its weakest link as much as it is its foundation. The two trade uncomfortable quips. Henry sounds impatient and dull, Delilah comes off as snide and patronizing. Neither have chemistry here, it all just feels by the numbers in execution. This isn't to say the voice actors were bad, but a weak script sold them short and undermined the overall tone and narrative.

Most of the rest of the cast is barely present enough to make a dent, though one I heard at the end of the story was convincingly troubled, and well played.

There really isn't much else here. The game play is very clunky, hindered by the need to go through very tedious rope climbing and walking through paths. I wound up visiting most areas at least three times by the end of the game, more than a few of them more than three times.

I went in completely blind and came out completely bored. While I imagine there must be an audience for this kind of experience, I know that I am not among them. Whatever Campo Santo does in the future, I hope they will invest in a better writing team, or make a game that is a little more compelling to play.

I should mention that this game did not play well with my Xbox One controller, causing all kinds of problems with menus and game controls. I could navigate well enough on foot, but button prompts were screwy, and some of the mapping was nonsense, such as using the right trigger to pick up items and use the camera, causing me to go into the camera mode whenever I grabbed an item.

This game was played with all settings maxed out using an Intel i7-8700k, 32gb DRAM, Samsung Evo SSD, 1080ti, running at 3440x1440. Some stuttering in parts, but overall no problems.

Firewatch is a story driven game set in 1989 that throws you helplessly into the vast and mysterious Wyoming Wilderness. Your only connection to humanity is through a small handheld radio and the remnants of history left behind. It can be found on Playstation 4, Nintendo Switch, Xbox One, Microsoft Windows, Macintosh Operating Systems, Linux and macOS. For the review this was played on steam, retailing at $20 USD.

I was going to wait a few days before I wrote this review for Firewatch but, I sit here at 6 AM, unable to delay the review. It's a very rare experience that I can be so captivated and moved by a video game, but Firewatch has moved me a million acres and I know it's going to be an experience that sticks with me forever. From the very beginning as you first delve into the story you are given a sense of wonder, beauty and sorrow. A mix of emotions that will have you laughing while leaving you in tears the next minute. This roller coast drives you through the game, offering a connection to the environment and characters that grows stronger as you progress.

Firewatch is a game about life, a game about exploring relationships and the connections we can develop to people we have never met. The story is rich and constantly seeks to impress, through stunning visuals, the orange colour palette and the unforgettable Delilah. A character who we grow attached to and want to discover more about. Behind every moment of titillating story is the breathtaking soundtrack. Perfectly suited to the story and environment, enriching the emotions we feel and sense of mystery and foreboding. As the player reaches critical moments in the story the soundtrack fits perfectly, as if it was moulded around the scene. 

Gameplay is superb, albeit it frustrating at times. Throughout the entire game we are travelling through a thick and beautiful forest, discovering new paths as we progress and developing the story. You will often find yourself lost and relying heavily on the map, which in itself isnt a perfect indicator of where you are or the direction you're heading it. This can cause some frustration and walking around in circles until we find the right path. This can be overlooked however by the impressiveness to the world and stunning scenery. 

Firewatch often rewards you for finding the right path by opening up new conversations between the protagonist and Delilah. Serving as a strong desire to follow the objective as you walk through the thick forests. This connection and sense of desire only grows as the game progresses and the story develops, leaving you unable to resist more. 

The user interface fits the general minimalist design of Firewatch, finding a perfect balance between ease of use and visibility. There are no separate screens during the game, accessing the map and other in game devices are performed through animations, stepping away from the commonly seen map screen.

Once in a while a story comes by that changes us and teaches us about ourselves, this is Firewatch. A game that I highly recommend putting on your wish list, every second takes your breath away. Firewatch is a game that I am glad played and I'm certain you will feel the same after having played through it.

TL;DR:   Firewatch is a “Walking Simulator”, meaning that you don’t actually do very much, but you are here to experience an interactive act of Story-Telling.
The world is beautifully crafted, the soundtrack is amazingly captivating and the voice-acting is excellent throughout (it would be a shame if not, the game is 70 % voice-acting).
The masterfully written story starts out slow, then gradually ramps up the pacing and finally ends a tad too quickly, so it might leave you behind thinking “Wait, that’s it?”.
If you do like these kinds of game (and not everyone does), you are in for a short, but intense ride through Wyoming…

6/10


"You two drink beer out on the deck. You drink beer just about anywhere. Life is good."

And indeed, life is good.

Grab yourself a few cold ones, pop on your headphones and begin your journey through Yellowstone National Park.

The Prologue consists mostly of a text-based “Choose your own Adventure” game, where you learn about Henry (the main character), his life, Julia (his wife), his choices and the reason why he took the isolated job as a fire lookout.
Ultimately the decisions you make (Henry makes) during this part of the game are pointless.
You get to choose your pick-up line, what kind of dog you want to get and if you want to fight or just scare a criminal, but you are powerless against the chain of heart-breaking events that lead to Henry taking the isolated job as a fire lookout.
Between the text-segments you get to control Henry and to experience some glances of what is to come: a beautifully cel-shaded environment, a subtle, but strong soundtrack and even the first few lines of dialogue.

To be clear: those first glances are technically everything there is to the game. For the next 3-4 hours you will wander through the landscapes, listen to either nature’s sounds or the music and occasionally talk to Delilah, your boss and the only person you get to talk to.
Sure, you get to experience a story with all its ups and downs, but all of that is told almost exclusively through dialogue.
If you are looking for a game that you actually PLAY, a game you get to DO stuff, a game where you CONTROL what’s going on, a game where you have any IMPACT, then keep looking.
You don’t play Firewatch, you let it play.
Which is pretty much the only bad thing I have to say about it.
In the end, your choices do not matter, anything you do or say will not change the outcome.
There are a few details that may vary (especially at the end), but eventually everything resolves in the same way.

Which leads me to the second point I have to speak against: the ending.
Specifically, the pacing of the ending.
The story starts out really slow, with you hiking through the Park, visiting a few key locations, so you really get to know the area.
During this exploration part, a few more dramatic and “quicker” elements are thrown into the mix, so you never get too comfortable and start to ask yourself a few questions, that you’ll want to find the answers for.
After you know your way around, the game slows down again, gets more serene and focuses on the relationship between you and Delilah.
Then, right as you think to yourself “Hey, this job really isn’t half bad” and the unanswered mysteries from before are half forgotten already, you get hit in the face (figuratively AND literally).
From there on, you don’t get to rest anymore.
You haste from waypoint to waypoint, always ready for something to happen.
No longer do you just stop and admire the landscape.
The environment transforms from this beautiful, calm National Park to a hostile and dangerous place, although physically nothing has changed at all.
Some questions from before start to get answered, but even more questions pop into your head.
And then, right when you are before the great climax and you think anything is possible, the game is over.
After the “Great Revelation” there are about 7 minutes of the game left.
This pacing really threw me off and I believe it is the reason why many people do not like the ending of Firewatch.

Personally, I think it was a rather fitting conclusion, as it was always meant to have a realistic and serene approach and all the stories that Henry and Delilah told each other and have made up are just that – stories.
In the end the whole game is one big metaphor about how people try to get away from their responsibilities, but they always catch up with them eventually, and the big, dramatic story that is starting to wind up between Henry and Delilah is just another attempt to run away.

Firewatch is a wonderful game with a beautiful, very unique artstyle and a gripping story that goes from slow explorative gameplay to thrilling mystery solving in a rather short time frame. On the one hand I'd wish there was more of it but on the other hand I feel like it is perfect as it is.

[h1] It's so beautiful game [/h1]

A fire burns in the distance. With the sun having long since disappeared below the horizon and endless acres of forest warding off the artificial light of civilization, its flames flood the night sky with incandescent hues. It's a natural brush fire, unlikely to do much harm, so for now I rest my elbows on the railing that surrounds my lookout tower and admire the view. A nearby transceiver crackles to life. It's Delilah, radioing from her own tower several miles away. She comments on the fire, how beautiful it looks, how it's all smoke and ash during the day but utterly resplendent under the cover of darkness. And it is. But over time, the fire spreads, and as its intensity escalates, so too does the tension of the narrative.

As with other story-driven, first-person adventure games like last year's Everybody's Gone to the Rapture and the seminal Gone Home, Firewatch isn't about gameplay, per se. There are no puzzles, no quick-time events, and no combat of any kind. Instead, it's about atmosphere, immersion, and exploration, both of an expansive Wyoming forest and a burgeoning friendship, one born of mutual isolation and built on idle radio chatter. Though its central mystery ends up feeling muddled and several major story beats are ultimately out your control, Firewatch's refreshing premise, endearing characters, and achingly beautiful world anchor a thoughtful, engrossing experience that succeeds in spite of its flaws.

The story follows Henry, a middle-aged, first-time fire lookout working near Yellowstone National Park in the summer of 1989. Because firewatch volunteers work in remote areas, you spend the vast majority of the game wandering alone through Firewatch's dense, detailed forests. There's not much to discover beyond the supply caches marked on your map, though the purely analogue navigation tools (i.e. an in-game, handheld compass and paper map that do not provide glowing way points or a fast travel system) add an immersive albeit occasionally frustrating touch. Still, because the captivating wilderness is so inviting, even just commuting to and from objectives can feel rewarding. The painterly art style imbues everything from the rocky vistas to the peeling paint on your tower's steps with a welcoming warmth.

The world also does an excellent job concealing its edges, making you feel as though the forest extends for miles in every direction. New areas always feel distinct, and the ever-present sounds of leaves rustling, birds chirping, and brooks babbling, make every moment spent in Firewatch feel like all the best parts of a real life camping trip. Soothing as it might seem, there's also a sort of profound complexity to it. When you stand still and focus on the blowing wind, it's equal parts ominous and enticing. Is the sound desolate or gentle? Foreboding or relaxing? As you work your way further into the campaign, your perspective may change.

Beyond solo exploration, the game's real focus rests on Henry's relationship with his boss Delilah, which manifests as an extensive series of walkie-talkie conversations with branching dialogue options. Unlike more dramatic games like The Walking Dead or Mass Effect that constantly place their characters in precarious positions, Henry doesn't need to make any intense, life or death decisions. It's more like, "Tease Delilah for her terrible joke or let it slide" or "Reveal more about your rocky personal history or keep her at arm's length." As a result, the game becomes not quite a character study but a patient, reflective examination of how two people grow to trust and care for each other. It's a bold and admirable choice. When you build an entire game around a single relationship, the experience lives and dies by the strength of the characters involved.

Fortunately for Firewatch, both Henry and Delilah are deeply relatable and human. Both are brilliantly voiced--with emotional nuance layered into every line--but more importantly, their dialogue gives them depth. Delilah is a bit mischievous, despite being slightly older and technically in charge. She's sarcastic in a playful way, yet passionate about her job and protective of her lookouts. Henry, on the other hand, is a bit more stiff and serious, but he's also fully capable of playing along with a joke. And when he does, you can't help but root for him.

Even as I describe them now, I feel as though I'm introducing my friends. I'm actually invested in you liking them, somehow. Their humor and vulnerability make both characters not only memorable but sympathetic as well. The fact that I developed such a strong attachment--and the ease with which I could write at length about the dispositions of these characters--speaks volumes about the quality of the writing. To direct the tone of their conversations, to shape the dynamic between them, to participate in the growth and evolution of their relationship--it's a unique joy, one that's nearly enough to singlehandedly carry the entire experience.

[u] The game becomes not quite a character study but a patient, reflective examination of how two people grow to trust and care for each other. It's a bold and admirable choice. [/u]

Unfortunately, the plot can't quite match the quality of the characters. Without spoiling too much, a central mystery gradually emerges as you play, and the stakes continue to rise until the story finally crescendoes towards the end. At first I got wrapped up in the characters' panic and paranoia and started to analyze all the little narrative threads that felt so much like clues. But once I learned the truth behind all the strange events, several story moments simply didn't add up or seemed a bit too convenient.

I also realized many of those narrative clues were nothing but smoke and mirrors, empty misdirection included solely to fool players (and, if you're feeling charitable, to flesh out the world). While dead ends and red herrings are common tropes in mysteries, the amount of focus the game devotes to certain storylines early on still left me feeling disappointed and almost cheated when they were casually cast aside later. Worse still, a few major plot points ignored my dialogue choices or didn't allow me any input at all because they came directly from Delilah. Even several of the items I'd collected while playing had absolutely no impact on...well, anything. Regardless of which decisions and dialogue options you select, it seems the plot is destined to unfold in a particular way.

This brings us to the story's culmination. If you squint your eyes and turn your head, you can just barely make sense of everything, but you have to make quite a few leaps of logic to get there. Yet, frustratingly, the characters react as if the truth makes perfect sense, which contradicts how authentic they feel otherwise. When you attempt to write a mystery, you need a grand revelation with a big story payoff to justify all the tension, but the explanation we get here comes off as muddled at best and forced at worst. The conclusion still manages to pack an emotional punch, but it's ultimately more confusing than it should have been.

It's a shame Firewatch fails as a mystery because it succeeds in so many other ways. Its world is captivating, its design is clever, and its characters are among the most well-written in gaming. Though it might sound counterintuitive, the plot is in many ways secondary to the relationship you build between Henry and Delilah.

It took me 3.7 hours to fully complete this game and oh boy did i have mixed feelings about it. First of all the game itself is like if you took an average episode of a ''slice of life'' cartoon and made a game out of it. The beginning of the game was really great! Exploring the forest and admiring the beauty was a really cool experience i enjoyed it. However the game quickly turns into one fetch quest after the other... And keep in mind you're stuck in the same forest for the ENTIRE GAME, so it's not like you're really going to be exploring a lot of new and exciting areas. Yes there are some areas locked off until you've obtained certain items that you get from the main story. This however is not an excuse in my opinion for all the back trachking that you'll be doing in this game. The story's climax is rather weak and doesn't interest me much. The last conversation you have with Delilah is rather depressing but somehow manages to just pass as a ''decent'' ending. Oh yeah and since we're already talking about Delilah, let me tell you she's the only thing that keeps this game even slightly interesting. Her personality is amazing and listening to her constantly cracking jokes can definitely make you laugh a few times. But her jokes and cocky voicelines doesn't excuse the borderline boring gameplay that the rest of the game is filled with. The trailer for the game sold it as an action/adventure story telling game which is pretty bad as well. I already knew before i bought the game that it wasn't filled with much action since a couple of my friends already own the game. I'm actually a big fan of games that just tell you a cool story and you get to pick a few choices in major events, but Firewatch did a horrible job at this. There's not even any pay off at the end, you're character is just the same as when he started this journey really.. Now if you're looking for a heart warming story and doesn't really care much about playing a ''video game'' then this might be the game for you. If you're someone who likes to look at beautiful textures slapped on top of somewhat decent trees and such then you might get more enjoyment out of this game than i did. But i as a gamer can and will not recommend this game to anyone. I even went the extra mile and tried to find all the secret events in the game that's supposed to ''wow'' you. All of these events felt cheap and pointless? I'd give this game a 3/10. If it wasn't for the talented voice actor who voicesDelilah then this game could easily have been a 1/10. There's also an extra game mode where you can just walk around the forest without doing any story missions or anything really. But seriously, why would you do that when you just finished doing a hundred fetch quests? If the game is on sale for 1$ sure pick it up, but anything more than that is a scam in my honest opinion. Call me bitter but this felt like a waste of time and potential. Wow, how to describe this game... I think the guy who said "screw this game, my heart hurts", pretty much summed it up perfectly. 

I cannot [i]not[/i] recommend this game as it was simply too well put together (the pacing was superb, the graphics fit perfectly, the voice acting and soundtrack were masterful) but at the same time I cannot [i]recommend[/i] it simply because of the depressing nature of the story. Without going into specifics...this game was like reading a great but terrifically sad novel where the carthetic element of the tragedy is replaced with just more negativity. The game starts out on a down note, the storyline builds a little but then leaves again on a downer. Probably because I am [spoiler]a single dad[/spoiler] the plotline hit me harder than most but as the credits rolled, soulful R&B music played and some poignant easter eggs from the plotline filled the screen, I was left with a huge lump in my throat, a pit in my stomach and I had a seriously hard time keeping it together. 

I've experienced this feeling before with sad endings (most recently with [i]What Remains of Edith Finch[/i]) but with those other games there was always some element of hopefullness that made the entire experience worth it, as if reinforcing an outlook that says "life is beautiful even in the face of tragedy". With Firewatch, it feels like the story was written by a cynic where the storlyine contains beauty but it expresses it in a colder and more pessimistic way. Even if you play the game with positive interactions, the basic plotline is a rough road. I would warn off gamers prone to depression. 

TL;DR - If you like a good story and can handle a tear jerker, this game is worth a go. Just don't expect a feel-good experience. Firewatch has been put together quite well but the story is achingly depressing.

This game is strictly a walking simulator, and it's all about the slightly interactive dialogue. I've only played the game once, but I reckon there may be a different way you decide to say things to get slightly different responses.

7/10 walking simulator, can be kinda monotonous looking at the map and trying to decipher your whereabouts and how to get back on a trail if you've left it; however it is not bad.
9/10 music, the best music was from story based scores, although the background music wasn't catchy. However, all the music of this game's OST is situational and extremely well placed.

Overall, I'd give Firewatch an 8/10. Fantastic dialogue, fantastic music, beautiful game and scenery, but the story could have been pushed through a little more. Personally, I like games like this that are laid back and you can enjoy an interactive story; it makes you feel more immersed into the game.

One of the greatest writing/voice acting combos I have ever experienced in gaming. Firewatch is a must play for people who are open to the "interactive movie" kind of genre of games. 

This is what games like Life Is Strange (a game I really enjoy despite its flaws) need to take notes from. The writing in this is on par with something you'd see in a good movie or book. The ability to pick your responses ranging from small little choices to seemingly larger ones ties into the writing so well. From the very beginning I found the story to be engrossing and emotional. I know that a lot of people aren't happy with the ending, but there's a reason why it goes in the direction that it goes and even though it can feel a tad disappointing it makes sense and ties into the themes. 

Obviously the "gameplay" is lacking compared to traditional games but that's just the way these kinds of games go. They focus more on story telling rather than a regular gaming experience, which is why I obviously don't recommend this to someone who is seeking a traditional experience. But that being said, it's designed pretty well, giving you what feels like an open world while being able to guide you just enough in the right direction. On occasion I got a little lost or found the map/objectives to be a little vague, but even that might have been on purpose to give a more realistic experience.

This is by far one if the best games I've playing in a long time.

I'm not normally one for single player games, and I'll admit that it was the art style that got me to buy the game, but Firewatch is so much more than just the visual art. Firewatch is like a movie that you're a part of and interacting with instead of passively consuming. There are so many clues that can lead you to multiple ideas of what's happening, but I, personally, was very caught off guard by the end; I just hadn't considered it a possibility.

This is a game that anyone who enjoys good story will love. I will admit that $20 for the game is a little steep if you only play through it once, as the story only lasts a couple hours, but if you either play it multiple times, or pick it up on sale (it's often on sale for $5 during the large sales of the year), I would 110% recommend picking it up.

Just finished the game and I thoroughly enjoyed it. Not only is the setting beautiful and tranquil (with particular praise towards the score and graphics), the story had me hooked from the beginning to end. The way that Henry (the main character) and Delilah interact is a nice touch. You feel like you can really determine the conversational flow and pattern through the various options you are given to chose from when talking over the walkie talkies. A fair bit of mystery and build up towards the final chapter but there in lies my only flaw in the game. The whole final chapter and build up towards the end was a bit underwhelming. Felt like the writers didn't put as much thought into it as the rest of the game. The mystery and build up of everything up until the end was absolutely epic (why is all this happening to you in the game, who is trying to set you up and what happened to the missing hikers and the two girls really had you thinking) but when it came to signing the game off the finale just fell flat on its ass. You felt like the entire relationship you had built with Delilah up until that point meant nothing and there the whole plot undermined itself and all in all the last 5% of the game was underwhelming...

All in all though it was a highly enjoyable 4 hours of my life spent on a very pretty and wholesomely fun game, would have bought it even at full price. Hope this helps!

First and foremost, I will recommend this game but only because I was successfully entertained for a brief time and the game is fairly cheap on sale.

That said, I am largely at odds with the resounding praise this game received. I do appreciate when a game attempts to offer character perspectives that are alternatives to the vast majority of games out there. It would be nice to play a non-heroic character and learn his/her story, or as in Firewatch's case, a character with questionable morals. However, I don't think it succeeds at this.

I think any person in this world, no matter how good and ethical they may be, can find it within themselves to commit evil or act out on poor ethics given the appropiate distressful scenario and conditioning. Firewatch attempts to have you experience this through our main character. I did not empathize with him whatsoever, though. You are given select choices in your dialogue choices throughout the game, rarely with anything positive or ethically appropiate to choose for significant decisions. This seems to be the origin of the game's noteworthy praise; you aren't forced to be a hero or at least to make good decisions. This is a good thing, however it only feels contrary to the "hero" problem we have in other games. I didn't really feel like I was making choices using Henry's history and intellect in mind, I felt that I was simply being forced to choose what the developers thought would get their point across.

That was my major gripe. Though, I also didn't think the plot was very good. It grips you in some ways but ultimately I was only barely-satisfied and felt that the story structure didn't lend well to the theme. Still, the game is well-made and I appreciate the developer's efforts. The voice-acting is superb, possibly some of the best I've heard in games. I liked the art direction as well.

I really enjoyed this game. The dialogue between you and Delilah feels unscripted and natural, and the story is incredibly good at pulling you in for hours. In fact, after you beat the game, i'd reccomend looking up a story breakdown on youtube because there's some really interesting stuff going on that you might not have noticed.

As for gameplay, it was pretty much a walking simulator while talking to Delilah. She'll tell you to go somewhere then you'll look at the map and find you way over. There's a few secrets along the way that change the way your tower looks and stuff like that. One thing I wish was implemented is a way to disable the dot that shows exactly where you are on the map. It would've been super cool to have to figure out where you were and navigate like that. It's not an overly big area so I think that would work well.

So overall, give this one a shot, but maybe wait for a discount. 3 hours for 20$ is a bit pricey, I paid 5$ but I think 10$ would be fair as well for the absolutely beautiful graphics, memorable characters, and captivating story. Seriously, the character development is top-notch on this one.

After playing Firewatch, one of the best words to describe the experience is "quality". Quality of writing, quality of acting, quality of art design, quality of structure. Everything that this game sets out to do, it does well. There's nothing else to say, really, but I will go into some more detail for the people who are interested:

Firstly, we'll discuss story. Because it is the main draw of the game as well as a clear focus of the developers: A lot of design choices are made in the name of pacing and story beats. As soon as the gameplay goes into "pointless" territory (for example, if the only thing left to do for the day is to go back home to sleep) it cuts to a new day, with new objectives that you are immediately supposed to set out to do. Not that the game is fast; in fact, it has pretty slow pacing, which the hiking mechanics of the game obviously support. The point is that a lot of care went into crafting the experience based on the story, and the developers did a great job as a result. 

The characters are great, brought to life beautifully by mainly Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones as Henry and Delilah. They are well written, relatable, complex and has some great chemistry between them. As they're trying to figure things out, you really get attached to them and as such you're invested in the plot. However, and it's a big however, I will say that they deserved a bit better. The conclusion is slightly anticlimactic, and it's supposed to be, but it also means that the characters end up having some unresolved plot threads. It's realistic, yes; but it's a shame given that the characters are so well written. It left me hungry for more with the knowledge that there probably won't ever be more, which is never a great feeling.

So, what will you actually be doing? Well, mainly hiking. That means reading a map, running and climbing. Oh, and interacting with Delilah, choosing dialogue options and pointing at things to talk about. That's pretty much it. It very much fits the game though, and the gameplay does flow very smoothly when it sticks to those mechanics. Unfortunately, it can get frustrating (I say "can" because I acknowledge that I'm a bit of an idiot when playing these kinds of games) when the game decides that you need X item to progress. When that happens, it gets vague in the information given and at the same time very specific in its wants. There were two or three times in this game where I went for 5-10 minute Benny Hill runarounds trying to find whatever the game wanted me to find (one of them being bear tracks that I wasn't even supposed to find, meaning that there were none to find. That was fun.). That's not most of the game, thankfully, so it's overall a pretty small complaint. 

Overall, if you like what you see in trailers and screenshots, you will probably like the game. It's not a game that reaches the highest highs that the medium can offer, but it stands as a game well worth playing nonetheless.

For starters, if you were unaware, this is a walking simulator. You play as a temp park ranger looking for an escape from the depressing circumstances of his life. You're guided from plot event to plot event around the park by your supervisor via radio, and how you get from location to location within the park is more or less the limit of the actual gameplay in this title. While it's fun at first to learn the land, eventually the game becomes little more than a "sprinting simulator" as the story's breadth outlasts the novelty of the park. You also have some control over your character's dialog, but I don't think you can actually change the events that unfold.

Of course, whether or not you will enjoy this game will depend on how you like the story -- especially its ending, which I will address but not spoil. The ending of this game appears to be very divisive, with some claiming it to be hugely anticlimactic and others claiming those who think that "didn't get it". I tend to lean towards the former, and it did sour the ~3 hour experience for me. After some reflection however, I would be lying if I said I didn't enjoy the experience regardless, even if I was ultimately dissatisfied with its conclusion. 

For me, this is a decent entry to the walking sim genre, which I tend to enjoy greatly. If you also enjoy the genre, I think this will be a worthwhile, but not high priority, experience for you. If not, I strongly doubt Firewatch will make a convert out of you.

That being said, I unfortunately cannot reccomend this game in all good conscience due to it's ending.

***POSSIBLE SPOLIERS AHEAD!!!! WILL TRY NOT TO RUIN THE STORY***


The story itself towards the beginning sets itself up to be something intricate, fresh, and emotional, but falls completely flat at the end. Keep in mind, this is not me saying "Ugh! The game didn't end the way I wanted it to, so it sucks!" What I mean is that the game could've gone in a number of different directions with it's storyline. The game could've gone the predictible route and said "Delilah was a traitor" or "Julia was actually the antagonist" and it would've made me just a bit more satisfied that I am now. Furthermore, the game could've explored Henry's relationship with Delilah more and it could've shown more of his inner conflict with being away from Julia or it could've gone in the direction of exploring the effects of isolation on Henry. 

Instead, the game sort of just ends after a VERY short playthrough, but I wouldn't even mind the length if it ended in a strong way (which it didn't). There's a particularly lackluster dialouge between Delilah and Henry at the game's finale, which is dissapointing as the dialouge throughout the rest of the game is so beautiful. Speaking of the rest of the game, it's exactly that which make the ending all the more dissapointing. The storyline in the beginning sets up a tone of isolation and fear mixed with real emotion so beautifully that the player is looking forward to a grand finale, yet it's as if the game snaps it's fingers and makes the height of tension fade from existence. 

Now I do understand that it is the creative vision of the creators and that perhaps they were just trying to keep things realistic. While I do appreciate this and the idea of keeping true to their vision, I can't help but think about what could've been.

In all, if you don't mind a short playthrough and are more interested in graphics and exploration over narrative, then by all means please buy this game as it is SO beautiful. However, if you are like me and are interested in an amazing narrative, then I can't recommend this game as the narrative is set up so beautifully that the ending is made all the worse.

Firewatch was on my radar for quite a while and I must admit I was not disappointed. At its core it is a walking simulator and you don't really have a lot of choice in the matter of what to do next. You walk as you're told and do what you're told and before you know it the game is over. It looks like an open world but if you poke the edges there's really just one way to go and one thing to do.

What makes the game is the story, atmosphere and visuals. The game looks really nice and it's just really pleasant walking around and looking at the scenery. There's something calm in this. They've really managed to capture the essence of what's best in the nature.

The story puts you in the shoes of a guy after a traumatic loss gets a job at the firewatch tower in Yellowstone park. That means being alone for a couple of months in a secluded place with no contact with the outside work. The only contact you do have is your boss stationed in another tower. But you don't get to meet her other than through the walkie-talkies.

And then you start watching a specific relation developing between the two characters and some things start to happen which makes you move around the area.

So why is the game so good? It has the ability to keep you guessing. As the story progresses and you're made to do more and more walking you're always unsure what's going on. I had at least a couple of ideas of what's really going on and how the game is going to end but was mistaken. But the suspense keeps you going hoping to discover answers to all the questions - and that what makes the game great and in a way it has to be experienced and can't be really described.

As for the bad sides. The ending had many people disappointed and I can see it now although I was absolutely fine with it. Also the relationship between you and your boss is not perfectly transferred to your perception. The story jumps between days in which we are made to believe that both start trusting each other and grow sort of bond. For player it's just minutes and because of it you never really start trusting the lady on the other side of the radio - I didn't at least.

Overall though it's a really good game. Probably the best walking simulator I've played and I highly recommend it.

EDIT:
Since my original negative review, I have learned that walking simulator games  are a thing. Existing as nothing more than an interactive story, where the tale unfolds as the player finds the next location or loosely hidden item. There is a following for this kind of game, and if you are among such, this is a good game. But they're not for me.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Yes, it's visually beautiful and the dialog between the two main characters is engaging. The mystery is bittersweet, but it unfolds completely without your help. The game lacks the most important element of gaming: gameplay. There are no choices to make, no puzzles to solve, no time trials, and the mystery solves itself.

The player only chooses where to walk. The game tells you where to go, and advances itself once you get there. A child with no gaming experience can complete this game. Ironic, because of how many F-words are in it. It's merely an interactive story. The player can choose how fast to advance it, but on a second playthrough, there is absolutely nothing different to do.

I played this game over the course of a few days and it had me gripped from start to finish. I read some of the negative reviews beforehand, which put me off playing it for a while, but I'm glad that I didn't listen and went ahead and finally got around to playing it for myself. The game is very cinematic, both in its sumptuous visuals and its intense storyline. It's also a nicely unique setting, and thankfully bereft of armies trying to shoot at you or other somewhat tired gaming tropes, which just adds to the mystery and tension. The dialogue flow system works smoothly and even though it's clear that the game is linear up to a point, it never felt like I was being forced to take a direction that didn't make sense to the storyline or didn't feel natural. I guess it's a game that would be enjoyed by more mature gamers who want some depth and substance to their gaming experience. I honestly don't understand what the haters were expecting from the climax, since as far as I can see, it couldn't have worked out any other way, except in an entirely illogical or fantastical one, which would have just made the situation seem trite. The characters are dealing with some real, dark issues, and the game manages to weave them in quite successfully. Perhaps the strongest part, however, is the voice acting, which is about the best I've heard in a game. The whole package makes for a vivid and highly satisfying experience. Am looking forward to exploring the free-roaming mode when I get more time.

[b]Firewatch[/b] is a walking simulator with a nice atmospheric story and charismatic characters. It starts off with a sad depressing tale about Henry, it is narrated in a way of text on the screen with some walking in between. It feels boring and not very interesting, though the game changes a lot after this introductionary segment. Henry takes up a job as fire lookout, he has to protect the forest from fire, by watching it from the tower and calling the firefighters, when fire starts. Even though this sounds like a really boring job, it is shown like something interesting and exciting in this game. 

Gameplay consists of you walking around National Park and talking over the radio with your boss. The park has a lot of secrets and even though the path is linear there's a lot of optional stuff, that you can find. Unlike most walking simulators, this walking gameplay expands on the story as you grow more and more attached to this park and its beautiful scenery.

From what I heard about this game, I expected a sad love story, but what I got was an adventure with thrilling mysteries and somewhat melancholic mood.

[h1][b][u]Review[/u][/b][/h1]

[b]+ Merits:[/b]

When you are surrounded by adversities from every corner, and the vicissitudes of life overwhelm you, it's either you stand up like a man and face your problems or surrender and escape to a different reality to live the rest of your fake, broken life with your defeat. Henry is a man who was happy with his love. He lived a colorful life until everything went upside down. Engulfed by sadness, he chose escapism as a solution. Henry ends up as a solitary fire lookout in a forest. The Wyoming wilderness is picturesque and a piece of Heaven; for Henry, it's the perfect place to work with peace of mind away from his tragedies. But soon, there will be a turn of events that will put him in a mysterious adventure in the woods.

Firewatch is an ocean of emotions. It's a peaceful walking and a sentimental talking experience. So don't expect any combat, action, or even puzzles. Firewatch's story is very gripping, but I did find the characterization and dialogue to be the luminous diamonds of the game. It's the first time in my life I feel that I am chatting with a real, live person in a game; it feels like Delilah—Henry's boss—is really interacting with you. Her voice echoes with emotional tones that resemble her soul and feelings; it swings from being sad, confused, fearful, seductive, funny, or happy.

Aside from the exceptional voice acting, the lively nature of the script has a decent influence on the overall conversation quality. Behind the walkie-talkie, you get to tease her jokes, share your past with her, or have a trivial chit-chat to pass time. The Wyoming forest's natural beauty is unleashed with Firewatch's ravishing arthouse. It captures nature's delicacy with its artistic, charming visuals. Its graphical setting makes the game look as if it was painted by hand. Firewatch's free-roam mode is a very appreciated addition. It's unlocked after finishing the main campaign, and it features a fully unlocked map with a 24-hour day cycle.

[b]- Flaws:[/b]

Firewatch's tale resembles that jackass friend who promises a lot and delivers nothing; it's an appealing story that's shattered by a shallow ending. I think the developers didn't know how to wrap-up the story, resulting in a rushed ending that upsets both the player and the protagonist. There are several frame rate drops, even though the rendered scenes aren't that intensive, and the game, in general, isn't that demanding. I recommend trying different builds of the game and see which one works best for you. It can be done in the BETAS section of the game's properties.

[b]> Verdict:[/b]

Campo Santo did a remarkable job in delivering a splendid walking-talking simulator that grants us a respectable mature conversational experience. Many people will relate to the problems both Henry and Delilah share; these problems are life troubles that most nowadays adults face in their life. Sadly, the game could have been phenomenal if there was a proper ending for the thrilling tale it had provided. Firewatch's stylish art combined with its calm soundtrack are enough to ease your mind and relax your nerves. It's a nice break from those intense games that burn your fuel.

This game is stunning. When it was first realeased I didn't understand all the fuss about the game but since playing it, I now do.

At a quick glance the game looks like your standard walking simulator with next to nothing in the game. A deeper look into the game will quickly prove that wrong. The games chapters are set by days and as time progresses (sometimes in larger chunks) so does the story. On the first day the game plays exactly how you'd expect it too, quite a bit of walking around, exposition and little happening except chasing off some youths who are misbehaving. From the second day on however you start to notice things are not as they seem and may require further investigation.

Throughout the entirety of the game your character will have a walkie talke which allows him to communicate with another firewatch tower lookout both for plot and for general chat. The voice acting in this game is superb with the two main characters talking exactly how they would in the current situation in real life. It doesn't feel like two voice actors reading from a script like robots and theres next to no over the top language to make it sound like a hollywood blockbuster, just two down to earth people getting on with their jobs out in the middle of a forrest.

As for the forrest itself, its stunning. The art style looks beautiful, the sound design is amazing and the lighting is fantastic and when all of that combines it makes for a perfect environment design. The forrest never fails to seem alive striking the right balance of emptiness at times and filled with nature at others. The game is also open world allowing you to explore wherever you so desire with only your map and compass to assist you and no clunky UI or HUD. Once completing the game you unlock the option for a sandbox mode which allows the player to explore this beautifully rich world at their own pace to capture some jaw dropping screenshots with an in game camera.

Overall this game is worth a play, especially when you have a quiet night in to yourself and are not in the mood for any loud action games. It doesnt take that long to complete story wise but this game has an emphasis on exploration and beauty of nature. I strongly recommend playing it for an utter unique experience that will surely stay with you long after you complete this piece of art.

The graphics are OKish but nothing to write home about in 2018. The voice acting is rather good. The character movement is sometimes clunky (only during climbing) and it can be a bit frustrating to figure out which areas are walkable and which are not. 

For some reason, one's responses/choices are time-out limited. If you are reading the map at the wrong moment, you may miss the option to respond/make a choice. There is no good reason for the game to deny one of making responses, just because one is distracted by something for some reason. 

Worst, however, your decisions during the game appear to have very little consequence. They do have some small impact here and there but nothing of significance. Personally, I'd rather not be given choices, if they won't matter substantially. 

A non-recommendation is a bit harsh for this game which employs very interesting concepts and had high potential but I finished it in one pretty short sitting and the ending ringed very hollow. Perhaps you'll love it, but in hindsight I wish there hadn't been that many positive reviews.

For fans of games that focus on a story I cannot recommend this one enough. Other reviews can tell you exactly what the game is about, but let me just make a few points.

* This is one of those walking simulator type games and will take around 4-5 hours to complete if you take your time. Keep this in mind considering the price and what you expect out of a game.
* Ignore the people who say the ending is bad, it absolutely is not! The story is very well done and nicely layered, I can see how people who blaze through Firewatch might feel otherwise though.
* Some say there's no replay value, but you totally SHOULD play a second time with the developer commentary turned on. There's a lot of stuff that gets explained with the plot that you may not have caught the first time through along with other interesting tid bits.
* Just about everything is important to understanding what's happening. This game doesn't just spell out everything for you. There are some things that are left entirely up to the player to figure out on their own. If you're not able to put some pieces together (like me!) just read up on the story after finishing the game. I can't stress how brilliant, deceptive and subtle the story can be at points.

I'm saying an 'old sory' here not so much because you know it by heart, but because the premise and the format are a familiar structure: middle of nowhere, nothing but mother Nature around you, and you only have one person to talk to, a person you can't even see. A
And of course, there's the Mystery. 
While this game is predominantly about storytelling, there is a fine ballance between how the game's design and the plot itself that makes it irresistible to just follow along and see what happens. I think the best part is how well portayed the element of lonesomeness (is that a word? it is now.) is. Sure, you have your radio companion, and you get to talk to them about what happens as the story goes along. But at the end of the day, you're all alone in the middle of the woods - and the mind can go wild when triggered by the smallest thing, or the wrong pop of a branch being broken. 
Last but not least - I've seen some people complain about the ending and I can see the reason why, but I definitely disagree there. The ending is just as good as the rest of the story, because, well, what did you expect to happen?

Firewatch places you in the role of Henry, a man trying to reconscile his past choices, to process regret, failure, and the uncertainties of life. Henry takes a job manning a fire tower in an wonderfully crafted rendering of the Rockies, with the player guiding him through sun-dappled aspen groves and steep canyons. The visual style and quality are immersive, and I was quickly drawn into the setting and narrative.

Henry is alone in his job, save for a handheld radio linking him to Delilah, his supervisor. The story unfolds in large part through conversations with Delilah. A simple but clever game mechanic of placing dialog choices on a timer mean ther are both more tense and flow more naturally; just as you can't pause indefinately to consider every implication when speaking to someone in real life, if you wait too long to select a dialog option Delilah will interpret your silence accordingly. The voice acting is extremely well done throughout, and the limited music in the game also serves the story well.

Firewatch is certainly an adult narrative -- not in the sense of violence or sex, but rather of emotional maturity and the ambiguities of life, where we all make difficult choices, doing the best we can. It gave me many things to think about, and also made me want to hug my family at the end. Players looking to feel clever by unraveling a mystery or be entertained by a twist or scare may be disappointed. Those looking for thoughtful, engaging storytelling will find Firewatch a great piece of interactive fiction.

I honestly just have a love-hate relationship with this game. I started this review as a good one, but the more I wrote the more I realized I didn't like a lot of it; I am so sorry, Firewatch, I'm about to tear you apart with a pulaski.

TL;DR
Fairly good game; dispite tearing it appart in my review, I actually liked it for the most part. Good graphics and a pretty good story. Just ignore the plot holes, rushed ending, and the fact that it has zero replayability.

***Beware of Spoilers!
[h1]The Good[/h1]
On one hand, the story is pretty good. I was really invested in the story as the game went on, though I had a few issues with it. I really liked the graphics as well, it's very peaceful, setting-wise, and you could have a good time just walking around and exploring I suppose. As the game got to the final few days/chapters, I felt excited to find out the conclusion to the story and witness the ending. Its a very calming game except for the few stressful bits, which kept it interesting and engaging.

[h1]The Not So Good[/h1]
On the other hand, this game is so much of just that: a game. Very scripted, no wiggle room unless you ignore Delilah, where she will then commence yelling at you. Your answers to questions don't change the way the storyline plays out,  [spoiler](You'd think that choosing to tell Delilah that Brian's death was her fault would cause a rift in the relationship, but hm.)[/spoiler] which was a dissapointment. What's the point of having multiple answers then?
Also, the amount of cursing in this game was very annoying and forced me to play with the sound down and subtitles on. I just don't enjoy that.
I also really hated the fact that this game is so non-immersive in the gameplay aspect. It's literally "Go to point A and do B" through the whole game. Not to say that I didn't rush from point A to point B to uncover more of the story, but that was a big downer for me; I expected to at least be able to try and do a little wilderness survival in a game where you're in the middle of nowhere for the summer. I mean, I get that it's a walking simulator. But at one point we go out to go fishing and end up getting side-tracked, which was super dissapointing. AND, probably the one thing that bugged me the most: Henry radios Delilah to tell her of a 'big overgrowth' in the path. He literally could have stepped right over it. Instead I had to take the long way around. What full-grown man can't step over a tangled root.

And then we get to the plot holes, unfortunately. There are so many weird little holes here. [spolier] Like who was Delilah talking to when we overheard her talking to someone else when she kept her radio on? Who trashed the girls' camp? [/spoiler] (Also, we're in the wilderness. Where are the animals. To be honest this whole game feels like the developers actively avoided making a model of any creature, which sorely affected the gameplay for me.) [spoiler] Why the heck did Delilah give the code to the cache box over the tapped radio (again with avoiding making a character model...)? How did Ned know all this stuff about Henry and Delilah that neither of them rold each other? How did Henry never notice he was being followed, as Ned was literally probably only a few feet away as evidenced by the cave gate slamming shut. How did Henry identify Brian Goodwin's rotting, mummified corpse so quickly? And last, but not least; Henry supposedly thinks that the death of Brian was an accident, but in his last conversation with Delilah, he labels it as murder. I digress. [/spoiler]

With the skipping around of the days/chapters, sometimes with huge gaps, it made it very hard to track Henry and Delilah's relationship, so that missed the mark for me. I also decided that I don't like Delilah as a character in any case; and I know It's a game about overcoming hardship, but good gravy so much of the dialogue sounded so scripted and fake. 


All in all, I might be uninstalling Firewatch. The game, as much fun as it was, has 0 replayability. I reccommend downloading if you are interested in a short, easy game with no real mistakes to be made, lives to be lost, etc, that you can finish in 5 hours. Enjoy the experience of it, it's a nice one. Not worth $20 IMO, but I got in on sale for $5, so hey.

It took me a few tries to get into this game, although once I did I played it all the way through in one sitting. They really tried to do something new here in terms of storytelling and I think they largely succeeded. The backdrop of the game is unlike any I've played before. Your character (Henry) has significant depth and is thoroughly grounded in reality. 

As the name alludes, you play as part of the Firewatch at a national park. You spend most of the game walking through the wilderness, climbing up and down rock faces, examining objects in your solitary outpost, and using your walkee talkee to advance the story with the only other major character, Delilah. Delilah is another Firewatch attendant, but she lives in another Firewatch station. The extent of the player-driven choices are to be had in your conversations with Delilah, fleshing out her background, yours, and how they might intersect in the epilogue. Delilah will also guide you with objectives as you begin to get sucked into a mystery thriller about missing teens and possible espionage. The story and dialogue are well written and engaging. Once you get through the monotony of the first few "Days" of the game, each new detail will drive you to know what happens next.

Firewatch is sometimes described as a walking simulator, which is mostly fair. I wasn't a huge fan of the interface, particularly that I couldn't map the butttons on my mouse to some of the commands. I also apparently missed a single piece of dialogue that prevented me from opening the supply caches strewn about the world, for which all of the lock combos are the same: [spoiler]1234[/spoiler]. The game largely plays itself as you walk from point A to point B and having extraneous items to interact with was annoying more than world building. Just enough times to be annoying, I accidentally picked up pinecones instead of items I actually wanted.

The game looks lovely and has a lot of character. The environments are pretty and the soundtrack is very appropriate and beautiful. I had some issues with audio crackling, but didn't find any others reporting the same.

Without spoiling anything, I found the ending to be underwhelming. Firewatch is unlike anything I've played before, but I'd be interested in playing something like it again. I think it's a great proof of concept, it just needs some polishing to make it draw you in more at the beginning and customize the experience a bit more. It's definitely worth picking up on sale if you've not played something like it before, or at full price if you enjoy adventure games, a good thriller, or the idea of walking through a national park without leaving your house.

"Firewatch" is yet another "walking simulator," where the player takes on the role of a fire lookout in a nature reserve. At first glance, the game world seems open, but its linearity is cleverly masked by the necessity to obtain equipment as the story progresses, allowing access to previously unreachable areas.

To immerse the player in the experience, the developers have added a lot of interactive interactions with the environment, as well as the ability to choose dialogue options in conversations over the radio with your supervisor. The game's graphics are fairly simple, but the artists did a great job creating beautiful views of the reserve.

The game is divided into "days" or "chapters," creating the illusion of changing times of day. I haven't tried standing still and waiting for the next day to come, but when I got distracted by exploring other parts of the map, I often ended up completing tasks in the dark.

The story revolves around the drama of each of its characters, who live alone in the reserve not for a good life, but to escape from their problems. As the story progresses, thriller elements are added, which enhances the player's interest, turning the meditative atmosphere into a tense one. This encourages the player to speed up and focus on the story tasks rather than exploring the world.

Personally, I didn't find the characters particularly sympathetic, but not because they were poorly portrayed. On the contrary, their behavior is very realistic. If you don't engage in exploring the world or strive to achieve all accomplishments, the game will feel very short. However, people who buy such "walking simulators" know what to expect from them.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Firewatch is a first-person adventure / walking simulator game and is the debut title from development studio, Campo Santo. It's getting a bit old now, having been first released in 2016, but it's been on my Steam wishlist for a long time. I picked it up on deep discount in a recent Steam sale and I am really glad I did.

You play Henry, a Colorado man fond of booze and tuxedoes (sorry; in-game joke). The game begins with a brief text introduction presenting Henry's adult past, setting the scene for his arrival at Two Forks firewatch station, around which the core of the story takes place. I won't spoil the backstory, as I found it very moving, immediately filling me with empathy for Henry and his situation. You're able to make some either-or choices through the introductory text, but -- as with the rest of the choices in the game -- the outcomes are really only skin deep; you can't change any of the major plot points.

The game proper begins with Day 1 of Henry's time at Two Forks, where he is introduced (via radio) to his new boss, Delilah.

[h1]Presentation[/h1]
Initially I was unimpressed with Firewatch's portrayal of nature. Many of the rocks and rock formations look far too blocky and I thought there was too much repetition of them -- though actually it turns out these repeated objects indicate places that you can climb, jump, or rappel up or down. But there's also very little animal life and flora doesn't seem as abundant and varied as I thought it should be; everything just seems a bit too sterile. The lake is rather bland, too.

After playing for a short time, though, I came to appreciate the unique aspects of each distinct area in the game world, from the lovely aspen grove to the burned-out fire break, or the rocky slopes near Beartooth Point. The excellent lighting effects that clearly indicate time of day and progress of any nearby fires, and the smoke and wind effects, too, add significantly to the ambiance, making the world and particularly the trees come to life. Though I still miss the dynamism of life I'd expect to see in a wilderness area such as that portrayed in Firewatch, by the time I'd played for an hour or two I'd come to appreciate what was here, too.

The game is fully spoken and the voice acting from the two main characters -- Henry and Delilah -- is brilliant. It's some of the best voice acting I've heard in a game. The excellent script doesn't hurt, of course, but these two actors really bring their characters to life, evoking a sense of understanding and empathy the likes of which I haven't felt since my time with Elika and the Prince in Prince of Persia (2008).

Music is sparse, but very well chosen and applied. You'll spend much of the game with only the sounds of nature, your footfalls and breathing, and Henry and Delilah's conversation. But particular moments of beauty, realisation, or suspense are expertly enhanced with some wonderful and non-invasive tracks that fit the events perfectly. 

Performance with everything turned up to maximum is mostly fine on my GTX1070-based laptop. The game does have a few hitches or pauses, though; I assume that's while it's loading in a new area. It's a bit distracting, but not too bad.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
On arrival at Two Forks you pick up a radio and you'll use this everywhere to stay in touch with Delilah, your boss, who also happens to reside at the nearby Thorofare tower. Your job, according to Delilah, is whatever she says it is. On Day 1 that involves finding out who's illegally letting off fireworks, but essentially you're there to keep an eye out for fires and monitor them when they break out. Other than your radio, you have a map and compass and, if you keep an eye out as you explore, you'll quickly find a flashlight, too. You update your map with notes as you progress through the story; "♥♥♥♥♥♥ Boss is Going to get Me Killed Hill" is probably my favourite landmark.

You control Henry using typical first-person controls: WASD for movement, space to jump, and the mouse to control which way Henry is looking and to interact with the game world. This isn't a shooter or action game, though; the core gameplay involves walking around the big, but not huge, Two Forks area of the national park, using your map and compass for navigation, and following Delilah's instructions over the radio. The basic gameplay loop has you hiking to different areas on the map, looking around or picking up or using something, talking a bit with Delilah, and then hiking to the next area or back to your tower. As with any most other walking simulators, the experience isn't the game play, exactly, but rather it's the story the developers tell you along the way.

The game necessarily has a fair bit of backtracking and covering familiar ground, as your only mode of transport is hiking and Henry spends every night in Two Forks watchtower. The developers have managed to reduce this in a few cases, though, such as by having you start a day already on your way to a spot of fishing at the lake, or sitting watching the sunset from a rock, or even in the middle of a conversation with Delilah, hiking towards some new mission goal. Though the story has Henry spending almost three months at Two Forks, the game itself is played only over a dozen days or so, spread across the Summer.

Ultimately, though you're free to wander the map and ignore Delilah's instructions and advice, the story will only advance when you go where you know you need to, and do what she's telling you, which makes the game feel a lot like an interactive movie. Your conversations with Delilah can usually take a few different twists and turns, but in the end the story goes where the developers intended; any choices you make only give you a few altered lines of dialogue here and there.

If the story weren't so well written and the characters so well realised, Firewatch would fall flat on its face. As it is, though, everything comes together just so, to make one of the best story-based games I've played in a while. It would be really well suited to seated VR play, too, but I don't know if that's ever likely to be an option.

[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]
Pros:
+ Superb voice acting
+ Great script
+ Interesting and believable characters
+ Pretty graphics
+ Great music

Cons:
- Short (3-4 hours)
- Choices are only superficial
- A bit too much backtracking in places

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Firewatch is good: very good. Some might say that its main drawback is that it's short, and thus doesn't offer a whole lot of bang for your buck. But I think it's just long enough to tell the story the developers wanted it to tell without overstaying its welcome. It has a good story with a well-written script, believable characters that you can actually care about, and some of the best voice acting I've heard, alongside mostly pretty graphics. It's a shame the choices you make in the game are only superficial -- I'd love to have been able to see different endings that depended on my decisions -- and I did get ever so slightly sick of covering the same ground over and over again, but for the most part the interaction between Henry and Delilah kept my interest even in these parts.

If you appreciate a good story told in an interesting setting, then I recommend you take a look at Firewatch. The relatively short story may just haunt you for longer than you expect.

Note: I should probably mention there's quite a lot of swearing in the game. It doesn't feel out of place to me, but I suppose some people may be offended by it.
