review:
I was hesitant to buy this game because it had so much potential and yet there were some very dissappointed reviewers. It turns out that this is one of the best games I've played in a long time. The immersive experience was better than expected, almost perfect, actually. The character you play is a novice to the firewatch biz which makes him completley relatable. They set the game up masterfully by including you in the decision making process as they back story is laid out. It's minimalist and yet emotionally pulls you into the character. The story itself unfolds at a perfect pace. As it does, you move threough a linear game in a way that feels organic, as if every thing that happens is a direct result of choices you make. The psycology used in the creation of these characters and the game itself is deep. 

If you have to have everything wrapped up in a nice package at the end of the game, you might be somewhat frustrated. If you like to have something to think about long after it's over, you will love Firewatch. I was a little sad to see it end, but only because it was such a great experience. There are some cool extras, though, including an open exploration mode. I haven't checked that out yet, but I look forward to doing so because the artwork is stunning from start to finish!

One thing that could inhibit your enjoyment of this game is motion sickness. I am prone to it, expecially on games woith a FP perspective. I managed to do okay playing Firewatch, but did have to break it up into a few different playing sessions. I quickly got used to it, though. 

I highly recomend this to anyone who loves immersive, story-rich, walking simulators. It felt like a great mystery in a beautiful setting.

Firewatch is a walking simulator that focuses on story and building relationships. This means you're not going to get a lot of gameplay, and at times the game will feel more like a movie, which could be either a good thing or a bad thing depending on the player. I've given this game a 'thumbs up,' however, if an option was available, I would've given it a 'mixed' rating. The game has many amazing moments, but at the same time there are a lot of negatives to be taken into account.

One of the highlights of the game is the visuals. The art style fits the enviroment so well, and certain views were breathtaking. At times my machine would struggle with the game, especially near the end, but these stutters would only last for a few seconds and wouldn't subtract from my playthrough too much. This game is also voice-acted, which made the experience so much better. The actors did a really good job and allowed me to establish a deeper connection with the characters. In fact, the sound in general is fantastic. One of my favourite moments in the game is an early morning hike with the sounds of birds in my ears. Music is not overused, but it's added in the right places and can really add to the suspense of the game. Overall, the game is presented extremely well and provided a very immersive experience.

Gameplay, on the other hand, was one of the more dissapointing aspects of the game. You shouldn't go into the game expecting much gameplay, because that's just not the point of the game. However, I felt at times that I was just a puppet in the game, and that I would do exactly what the developer wants me to do. I'm fed commands, I execute the commands. This means that most playthroughs of the game will be very similar. The game doesn't get 'boring', but a lot of the tasks do feel very similar.

Story is one of the most important aspects of the game, and it was good. I didn't think it was the best story in the world, but it was still a decent one. The game has an introduction which revolves around reading text and choosing a response to that text. The options you choose are mildly referenced from time to time, but most of them hold no weight. I would've liked this intro more if it were presented differently, such as in flashback form, but it didn't bother me too much. The story then just turns into the mystery in the forest and the relationship between you and Delilah. I won't spoil anything, but the mystery just kept me on the edge of my seat, and I found it to be really enjoyable. The same could not be said for the Delilah storyline, simply because there's not much of one. I didn't really get to see their relationship evolve, mostly because of the structure of the game. In this game there are 5 main days, yet Henry ends up being in the forest for 79 days. This means that we miss the long-term aspect of the game; relationships evolving, characters maturing, and little clues in the larger mystery. Everything happens so quickly, and I finished the game casually within just 4 hours (ignore my playtime). This doesn't give you much time to form deep connections with the other characters, or with your own character, which means that story just wasn't as good as it could've been. At the end, I didn't really feel anything. Sure, the ending could've been improved anyway, but just getting to know the characters a bit more would've made it a lot better.

At the moment on Steam, this game is £15 (full price). For most games this would be a fairly good price, but with this game that takes 4 hours to complete, and has little replayability value, I just don't think it's worth it. It's a good thing to grab if it's on sale, but at it's current price, it's something that can wait. However, if you do like slower paced games, and perhaps have less time on your hands to sink into video games, then this would be a good choice for you. Personally, I enjoyed my playthrough of the game, which is why I gave it a thumbs up, but I doubt I'll be returning to it anytime soon.

Firewatch is an aesthetically pleasing game, with good voice acting and dialogue to boot. However, its hampered by a vague plot and an underwhelming ending that is filled with a lot of monotonous walking which takes place in an environment where very little happens. 

The game starts off with a lengthy exposition where you get to decide some of the back-end story of the protagonist, Henry. This is only serves to provide additional dialogue options further on in the game which really don’t have any bearing on the game. Once you start out, you will be initially impressed by the beautifully designed landscape. The first day on watch you are indirectly taught how to use your compass, or rappel down slopes, and so on. You use your radio to talk with the only other person you can, Delilah. The conversations can be as amusing as you like, and add something to do on the walks. There aren’t any other gameplay mechanics to the game. Firewatch would have greatly benefited from adding 1 or 2 game mechanics to help fill the boring treks back and forth between places. Even as a 'walking' simulator it can get frustrating. Navigation is unintuitive and forces you to pull out a map and look at your compass. An optional HUD compass would have been a great addition to help ease navigation and reduce wasted time back tracking. Additionally, it seems counter-intuitive for a walking simulator to have a lot of invisible walls while in a forest. I appreciated that they include some side areas to explore, and you were rewarded with tapes and other interesting items, but they felt more like dead ends. During your walks you will also come across Firewatch caches which contain extra details of the area that the protagonist will add to his map. The locks on these caches are all the same, 1234, which makes me ask why even include a password if its all the same for every box, just give the character a key to open them. There was potential here to add something interesting. Finally, there was a lot to be desired from the sites you get to visit. As for the music, I never really noticed it until it starting playing ‘mid-walk’ for no particular reason at all. 

The story wasn’t really fantastic. Yes, my interests were raised by some strange and spooky happenings in the forest, and an interesting discovery towards the mid game had so much more potential. There just wasn’t enough rising action. By the end the climax just fizzles out and I was left confused if this was a story about Henry the protagonist or a certain character which was really not the focus of the story for about 95% of the game. After the climax, there was one final boring trek and some more chit chatting on a radio which by this point just felt unnecessary.

While Firewatch is beautifully stylized and the banter between Henry and Delilah is amusing, the game is let down by tedious treks in the forest, a lacklustre story.

Final Score: 2/5 Uninspiring
Pros: Beautifully stylized scenery, excellent voice acting and dialogue
Cons: Little to no gameplay, underwhelming story, monotonous travel

[h1][b]Full Review at [url=https://gamedragons.net/viewtopic.php?f=6&t=244]GameDragons.Net[/url][/b][/h1]

[b]Presentation[/b]
Firewatch is one of those games that manage to tell more in a few hours than most games do in a few dozen hours, it's a believable story full of intrigue, unknown and natural interactions between people, all wrapped with a positive message about life and finding the enjoyable parts in each sad story. The story follows Henry, a fire lookout in the Shoshone National Forest, hired following the Yellowstone fires of 1988 in order to increase the security and report any potential fire threat so it can be prevented before it's too late. Trying to escape the tragic recent events in his life, Henry decides to take the job for the summer in hopes that the silence and loneliness would help him reflect on life and move forward, but that silence only lasts for a little while, as the Shoshone National Forest seems to be a place where a lot of strange things happen. 

Joining him on the journey is his lookout boss, Delilah, to whom he is supposed to report any suspicious activity around his lookout as well as perform any tasks given to him by her, but as the summer goes by their relationship grows closer and the interaction between Henry and Delilah takes center stage in the game. Campo Santo's biggest achievement with Firewatch is presenting the story in a way that feels natural and believable, as if it came straight out of a classic novel, with the conversations taking a more relaxed and natural dialogue, instead of something that feels scripted; part of that can be attributed to the fact that Henry can answer Delilah's questions and interact with her in a bunch of different ways, either by being serious, funny or even flirting sometimes, but no matter which dialogue option you choose their conversation will always feel natural and that can be heard in the voices of the actors. 

Even if it starts in a more relaxed open manner, the story does get spookier as the days go by, but Firewatch is not a horror game and it doesn't even attempt to be one, because that's not what this story is about, instead the game uses the loneliness of the woods and the missing pieces of the bigger puzzle to always keep you on your toes and look twice behind your back, even if there will be nothing else behind you, except more forest. A few days in the game reaches its peek of mystery as you'll try to make up scenarios about what is going on before the game tells you and because that suspense is so high it does feel like a disappointment when the game does reach its conclusion, but that is something that I would rather not spoil for you, so you can find out what Firewatch is all about on your own, because truly the story is one of the game's highest points.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
Although it may seem like another walking simulator at first, Firewatch blends the lonely walking though the woods with suspenseful moments as well as freedom of exploration, as aside from the main objectives you can often stray from the path to find different supply caches, collectibles and even adopt a turtle. Even if at first your movement options will be limited, you will eventually find gear that will naturally unlock new areas of the map, as ropes will allow you to descent steep hills and the axe will allow you to chop through any trees blocking your way, and although those are your main and only traversal options, finding each gear piece as the time passes by makes it feel like you're never doing the same thing for too long and always finding something that may aid your adventure onward. 

Another thing that you will do a lot of is talk to Delilah on the walkie-talkie, as your conversations are seamlessly incorporated into the gameplay, allowing you to report any findings to her, ask for advice or just hear a familiar voice when you're out in the wild and feeling lonely. The way in which you respond to Delilah will also affect your relationship to her, as if you crack a joke she will remember to return the joke the next time the opportunity pops up, making the whole conversation feel tailored to the way you respond as Henry. 

[b]Graphics[/b]
Considering the fact that there isn't a lot of variety when it comes to the map and the locations you visit, since most of it is just forest with the objective locations being pretty obvious even on the map, it's quite surprising how drastically the map changes according to the time of day and the weather, as the forest will spark up with nuances of orange, bright red or clear sky blue depending on the day, the location and the time. The only missing thing that seems to have been overlooked is the lack of wildlife and plants variety, even if the area in which the game takes place is just a forest, it's disappointing to see that most trees look similar and animals or birds are nowhere to be found, except for your pet turtle. 

[b]Audio[/b]
Even if there are a couple of tunes that will play during key moments of the game, for most parts you'll be stuck with the sounds of nature, which isn't necessarily a bad thing since the silence of the wind blowing through the trees adds to the atmosphere, but once again it feels weird to hear the sounds of the forest without any birds chirping in the distance. On the other hand the dialogue is excellent, with the actors genuinely feeling like they're having an actual conversation, as both Henry and Delilah's dialogue feels natural, with occasional laughs, pauses and even angry outrages. 

[b]Extras[/b]
Firewatch is a quality, but short game, as the entire experience takes around 4 hours to complete, and since there are no additional modes or a reason to replay the game, that's pretty much all you get, so you either liked the story and the message enough to justify the purchase or you don't, but if you like environmental exploration games with the focus on storytelling you most likely will like Firewatch.

[b]Verdict[/b]
Firewatch tells an intriguing story full of mystery, suspense and wonder, the like of which you may only see in some more toned down Stephen King novels, but adding on that with great voice acting, superb, although sometimes repetitive, landscapes and gameplay elements that feel simple enough to allow anyone to play through this game. 

[u]Rating: 7.9[/u]

I'm incredibly torn about this game but I do recommend it.

On the plus side, we have great characters, great atmosphere, and an incredibly quaint environment, accompanied by an incredibly mellow and enchanting soundtrack. The voice performances are staggering and talking with your walkie talkie just feels incredibly alive and real. The latter I enjoyed the most.

On the other side,  you really feel the rails sometimes - even for a walking simulator. You have so many choices throughout the game but they almost always do not matter in any way (means: no achievements and only very mild changes in the game itself). The twist and turns are great, but during the game, this potential is simply not being fully utilized. Also - story wise and character wise the game misses a lot of opportunities to further develop the characters or adding more background info (in small doses). Also - 20 bucks for 4 hours of gameplay ... that's a little bit hard to sell.
But really - my biggest problem is with the end of the game. It is kind of ... slow - so to say - even though the path leading to it is designed quite nicely. I don't even have a problem with the ending being a bit anti-climatic - but for some reason, it feels like a weird mixture of relief and ... sadness (I guess?). While I really enjoyed the walk (no pun intended) - the ending also left me disillusioned and disappointed. Especially for the ending, it would be nice if all the small little choices that were marked out could notch it a bit in one or another direction.

Oh well - I guess that's just how real life can be sometimes. It's just different than how you hoped it would turn out (which - I guess - will differ for all of us). Or maybe that's just me. I still enjoyed it and I hope everybody else enjoys it as much as I did.

Firewatch is one of the more polished walking simulators out there.  Praise has already been rightly heaped on it for its beautiful artwork, compelling story, and superb voice acting—a rarity in this business—and all of which are probably the most important aspects of this type of game.  Likewise it appears to get, on Steam at least, its due criticisms of a lackluster conclusion and some tedious backtracking (for me the worst part).  This game is an experience, and one that won’t take more than an afternoon to have, and if it looks like the kind of game you’d like, then you probably will.  My wife found the game overhyped, the dialogue contrived and cringy, and the story uninteresting.  I however embraced the game and its role playing from the beginning, wanting to be shown this, wanting to really be there, loving the wilderness setting, the slow, realistic pacing, and accepting the quirky often unbelievably intimate relationship you build verbally through your walkie talkie--sort of like an alternate version of Cortana.  The game certainly has problems, but it does what it sets out to do very well.  If you want to jump into this world, then do it and you will most likely enjoy it.

This game is the best mediocre game I've ever played. The story and the way parts of this mystery are revealed to you the player, as well as your character, are amazing. The fact that everyone can have a unique relationship with Delilah is awesome, and the game's misdirection makes the story to this game a 9...but it can't be a 10. The ending of this game is...well...lackluster. When your character solves the mystery, and all is revealed, I'll admit I was a bit disappointed. And perhaps that's the point of the game. It's supposed to be a more realistic game, and maybe the disappointment of the ending reflects how this story may have ended in real life, if it were really happening. The disappointment of finding there is nothing else, but now face the consequences of your actions. There's no redemption to your actions, there's no antagonist that makes your character the good guy. You're just a man having to face the decisions he's made. And maybe that's how it's supposed to be. I would have preferred a more exciting ending, but perhaps that's not what this game was meant to be.
Unfortunately, the story is really all I can say is a 9. The gameplay is...mediocre. We are given a vast forest that seems eager to be explored, yet we are confined to main trails, with very little room for exploration. The character can climb over some objects and at other times cannot, even if they appear to be less difficult to climb than previous objects. This is all designed for the sake of keeping you on the path the story requires. While this is understandable from a writing perspective, from a game perspective this can become frustrating, as I would find myself wanting to make it to one objective going a certain way, but finding myself unable to simply because I had to trigger dialogue by backtracking a few miles. Not to mention the pinpoint accuracy that is required to interact with certain objects. The forest is beautiful, and the enviornment is captivating, but the clunky gameplay became more and more of an issue as the game progressed, and by the end I found myself less immersed in the world than when I began. 
Overall, this is a fun game. For 20 bucks I'd say don't buy it, as there's really only about 5 hours maximum you can play per walkthrough, and that's if you really take the time to look for Easter Eggs and such. However, on a deep sale, (IIRC I got the game for $5) it's a semi-fun, great story that takes you on a journey that is worth a few hours of your time.
Overall, a 7.5/10, I wish I could give it more. The story is worth experiencing if it's on sale. For less than a movie ticket I don't regret it.

Firewatch is an incredibly unique game with an unique setting, characters, and themes. You play as Henry who escapes his life to explore the Wyoming wilderness in the 1980s. There, you meet another "lookout", Delilah where you guys are tasked with helping rangers look for wildfires and other various problems around this national park. Overall, the story is fairly short (ranging from 3-4 hours on each playthrough), but has lots of twists and turns, adding to the adventure and mystery of the story. The dialogue is incredily well-written and all very realistic. Henry and Delilah are such amazing characters and feel so real.

The gameplay is perhaps the weakest aspect of the game, but I personally have no problem with walking simulators as long as the narrative is as engaging as possible. The interactions were spread perfectly throughout every "level" and exploration is fun. The dialogue options with Delilah are the greatest aspect of the gameplay though. There are some truly great moments of suspense, humor, and raw emotion that isn't rivaled in too many other games. The art style is absoutely gorgeous. I love the color and the "soft-textured" terrain and objects (much like an indie version of Dishonored's art style).

If you love unique, story-driven, interactive narratives then Firewatch is absolutely for you! Highly recommended: 10/10, one of my favorite games of all time.

TL/DR: Great story, well-developed characters, and smart level design. 

Beautifully-atmospheric, thoughtfully written dialog and well-structured level design makes Firewatch one of the best story-driven games I've played in a long time. Firewatch is a refreshing departure from the usual non-linear, open-world type games we've come to expect. The more structured approach to story gives a greater investment into the player's actions, with different choices highlighting the different facets of Henry and Delilah's personality, and continues to develop and shape their relationship.

The character you play, Henry, isn't a mute protagonist where a player needs to envision a backstory for. He feels and acts like a real person, with wants and needs, fears and desires, character quirks and flaws. All this and a meaningful backstory gives weight to the character. The dialog options you make, whether you decide to make them or not, showcases this and his own self-perception continuously shapes how he reacts to his job and his conversations with Delilah. 

What I really enjoyed were moments shared between Henry and Delilah about certain topics, and later on becoming a sort of in-joke between them. It made conversation choices seem more weighted and carried a real sense of character progression, not usually found in a lot of games these days.

I find that the game's length adequate, given the pace of the story. By the end, I felt that the story was answered enough questions for me to reasonably have a sense of closure.

Great indie game that will get you into it from start to the end. I would not say that it’s a total masterpiece, but it’s still worth a walkthrough and your time.  

Nevertheless, first things first: graphics – great, not a photorealistic one and mostly cartoonish, but with the lighting it creates just astonishing sceneries that you want to set on your desktop. Atmosphere – excellent both in terms of forest and mountains as surroundings and in terms of suspense and tension as story. However, the first one is a bit weakened by absence of any animals or insects in the wild but you get used to it after some time. Music is just perfect and I strongly recommend buying the soundtrack too. So, what’s about the gameplay?  

It turned out to be much better than I though. When in most of walking simulators you mostly can only follow the story path and sometimes examine items or notes lying around, here we will collect various tools throughout the game, which are gonna give us access to previously unreachable places on the map. The map itself is decently worked out, and you can easily forget about the goal and just start exploring. Also I was very pleased with dialog system: you can comment and discuss nearly every found item or observed situation and you usually have at least 2-3 options for answer. The only slight problem is small amount of time to choose an option in some situations, so you manage only to read all and have to promptly make a choice. 

And the main element of such games – the plot. I liked it for its development, dialogs and characters but it confused me by its structure. The thing is that we are initially given a long introduction during 1 and 2 day, so when you just start to dive into the story and feel that the game has begun, the narrative suddenly shifts to 5th gear and you get just a bunch of passages from the next 60 days and start to get complete days for walkthrough only when things go south. Yeah, in fact this is not a drawback and I understand why it was done like that but it still confuses you during the first playthrough. As for the plot itself, it’s very down-to-earth and close-to-life, for which it actually was loved by many and me indeed. It’s about usual adult people who have their own problems and quirks, made mistakes and choices. Despite the great denouement of the story, after the walkthrough I had a feeling of some ending looseness, though it could be caused by more or less open final.  

So, in the end we get a good game with wonderful graphics, music, atmosphere, nice gameplay and great story. Definitely recommend buying and playing it. 

P.S. Photos that you make during the game will be shown in credits, and you will be able to download them from the game’s official site or even order their developing and shipping (I’m not joking). So if I were you, I would not hesitate to capture local beauties. And, by the way, you will be able to use camera up to the game’s final, provided you still have tape.

This is a walking simulator and you must know that going in -  so don't expect to be firing guns, starting fires, and taking cover, because none of that is here.  

What is here is hands down the best walking simulator that has ever been made to date. It tells an incredibly intricate story about love and loss, faith and hope. 

The premise is that you Henry are a 39 year old man married to a woman named Julia who is in her very early 40s. You live in Boulder Colorado. Julia is suffering with severe dementia and has to be taken in by her family in Austrailia for 24 hour home health. You, Henry decided to take a job in Shoshone National Forest Wyoming as a Park Ranger from an ad you saw in the paper. You wanted to escape your life - your problems. And that's where this story begins.

You meet Delilah, your boss, and the two of you communicate over walkie-talkies for the next 79 days. You will have some of the most intimate organic communication I've ever seen in a video game. The conversations feel extremely real and extremely natural, and that is the highlight of the game. The dialogue is unmatched by any other title out there, and it will hit you incredibly hard. 

The writing here is outstanding, and the developers have paid attention to every single small little detail. 

For example: [spoiler] When you finally make your way to Delilah's tower at the very end of the game, look around very closely. She has many things in there that relate directly to conversations you've had over the course of the 79 day journey. And if you pay close enough attention, you'll smile so big. [/spoiler]

The world is absolutely beautiful, I took over 50 screenshots depending on the weather, the time of day, fire statuses, etc. It's very rewarding to explore the world as there are many great sights to take in. 

The gameplay is fantastic too! Outside of just walking you have to use your map and compass to navigate the world, as well as repelling gear to climb up and down terrain. You recieve an in-game camera to take pictures as well, and all of those images will be displayed in the credits, which was also very fun. 

Once you've beaten the game there is an option to play again with developer commentary, play sandbox free roam, as well as the ability to upload all of your in-game pictures to your email and have them developed in real life! 

All in all this game is 100% worth the $20 and you shouldn't think twice about it. If you get it on sale then all the better, but this game is worth its asking price, and provides an experience you will never forget!

Firewatch! What an marvelous thing. So beautiful it's impossible you haven't seen an laptop ad without one of the game wallpaper's in the wild, and one such deserves of a review.

[b]Pros[/b]:
-Beautiful, which salutates another of it's strong points:
-Easy to run! I could go on about the wonderful vistas, the excellent crated enviroment or even the dev's PHD on color paletes, but Firewatch just throws at your face on how a game being run even on a potato pc can bring such fidelity to the user's eyes. I mean, just look at Fortnite.
-Immersion, plot and gameplay. Everyone that played the Farcry games remembered on how they couldn't choose between Farcry's 2 "you in the game" thing, with how you had to bring your map on your hand and figure where to go, your character realistically with a health condition - which you had to obligatory progress the game to fix -, OR Farcry's 3 story (With a villain that seemed to come out of a Christoper Nolan movie) - which yes, was that good. Firewatch fixes that!
Not only the game gives you choices to make a background out of your character, since your character gets to comment on almost every interaction of the game, the game lets you choose how said interaction can happen. I'm not talking about the story itself, but the way the game delivers it is amazing. Literally the first 30 second trailer on the steam store page should give you an explanation of it.
What I'm saying is, I'm not particulaly fond of the story, but the way delivers it is amazing. Altough for me a personally not satisfying turn out of events, it still made sense, and the way each element was brought onto the player for the later plot was handled pretty well.

[b]Neutral[/b]: 
-Story: It's one of the love or hate things you do. As I said earlier, the game does a pretty good job at telling it (especially since you have control over almost any interaction of the game), but for me I was not really "ohhhhh" more like "oh." at the end. Some people might like it, some might not, especially considering almost every choice in the game only affects a drawing in the final moments of gameplay, I still got immersed, until the very second, that this was indeed an own unique world.
-Soundtrack: I liked it. Felt kinda weak though
-The style of the game: It's still, at the end of the day, a walking simulator. You won't fight any zombies or save earth from the aliens, but this should be pretty obvious by the very name of the game. You are a guy who works at a Firewatch station, and depending on the type of the player playing, that's where you will like or not. What I think? You should give it a try. Steam refunds exist for a reson.

[b]Cons[/b]:
-No additional plot points: relying heavily on only it's main plot, it doesn't have much forgiving traits if said story is not by the likes of the player. What could have been additional plot points? Hmm, maybe the cabin near the communications wires? You know, I actually wanted some optional backstory on that cabin, would have been cool.
-Runs like ♥♥♥♥ on high-end computers: I don't wanna brag, but Firewatch is a weird game. Playing on ultra on almost 200fps, (I use a stock cooler, but a lot of other players also reported this), the game causes a lot of high temperatures, even if I use vsync. A lot of other games have more dense/heavy graphics than this game and run cooler, especially on very high/ultra settings. It just doesn't make sense to me.
-Certain dialogue choices and the ending: [spoiler]Play the game before reading this. Certain dialogues with your partner can make the protagonist have a different view on his wife, especially the background choices you do at the start. The alternate ending where you wait 2 minutes and the chopper leaves, I presume is a joke from the developers for the "alternate endings" question from a news article. It could have represented on how the protagonist wanna leave his wife behind, or how he acquired some sympathy with Ned (they both have similiar problems). As a redditor said, literally one line of dialogue could have fixed this. Thankfully, the game has a lot of forgiving traits, but it's still pestering on some peoples nerves.

Another thing as to the main ending (where you leave with the chopper), it felt anti climatic to some. At the end of the day, you're just the guy watching the fires, and the forest burned down, but it is at the same time a rather forceful ending to what the game had been building with the whole Ned thing, the relationship between his wife and the protagonist, and how the player interacted with his partner over the radio. But as I said earlier, at the end of the day must they do outside of the dialogue is change just a picture.[/spoiler]

There's not much that can be said about Firewatch that hasn't already been said. The visuals are superb and the storyline twists and turns in unexpected ways. It can be funny and tragic at the same time and it talks about a subject that doesn't get a lot of exposure (early-onset dementia). While the game is rather short, it's just long enough to tell the story that the writers wanted to tell without adding a bunch of meaningless padding, which I appreciate. 

The game instills a lingering sense of wanderlust and one of its drawbacks is that exploration feels like it's on rails rather than open-world. I would love to have been able to tramp through the bush like you can in real life and explore at my leisure. Certain rock formations Henry climbs like a mountain goat and other small rocks that even I could hop over are insurmountable to him.

I wish a little more time had been spent on developing the hands that we see so often during the game, they had a slightly cartoonish feel to them that didn't jibe with the rest of the scenery. It's a small complaint, but it was something that broke immersion for me.

The music is beautiful and haunting and yet somehow feels like you've known it for years. It lends an ethereal feel to the landscape, as does the gorgeous variation in the sky as the game moves on: you get to explore Shoshone by day and by night and even during a raging forest fire. 

The conversations feel natural and I always felt that there was an option that was something I would say, rather than just choosing the 'best' option. I like the idea that Delilah is an unreliable narrator and you aren't sure whether or not to trust her, given that all the events are seen through her words to Henry and that at several points she mentions not wanting to speak to police, etc.

The game doesn't have much replay value: the free roam mode you can access would be better if the landscape were a little more Skyrim-esque and you could truly roam rather than stick to the tight constraints of the trails put in place by natural objects. That being said, the game doesn't [i]need[/i] much replay value because the story is one that hits hard and will leave you thinking about it: the motives behind actions and general human nature, for a long time afterward.

As someone who dislikes walking simulators, I can recommend this. Sure if you want action or gameplay you're not really going to find that here, but this is a slow burner that focuses on characterisation for its entertainment. While there is an emerging mystery in the story, this is a game you play because you want to interact with the characters (including the one you play).

People have complained that this game is boring, but that is only as true as you could say a generic FPS title 'has bad writing' or a JRPG is 'slow paced'. The genre of this game is not action, or horror, or even really drama. Its a story but one where the world isn't in danger, there are no bombs you need to hurry to defuse, and you don't have to protect a president. It's a kind of story where the highlights are deciding on a custom license plate for a motorbike, or helping a buddy name a weird pet they bought, or being pranked by your grandma when she put lottery money in a birthday card. It's about people and the small things, though the actual theme here is a bit of isolation, running away, and people just being human enough to mess up or enjoy stupid little things.

People have said the graphics are bad, but I found them perfect. They're not photorealistic sure, but they're deliberately stylised in a manner akin to TF2, with a mix of nice environmental effects but slightly cartoonish simplified geometries. You'll know the kind of style I mean if you just think of the rock faces and dusty rubble in Team Fortress 2 or certain Overwatch maps. I found it charming and fit the whole character of the game.

I had been waiting for Firewatch to be bundled forever, because I was curious about it but not quite interested enough to buy it over other titles during sales. I eventually decided to get it so I could play it during the more insufferably humid summer days here in the UK for a bit of dorky immersion, and I can safely say that this is a steal when its on sale. Sure there isn't really any replayability unless you want to hear the alternate dialogue choices, but it's a little relaxing experience that I think should be a little checkbox on any storytelling fans gaming bucketlist. I wonder how many people have this game in their backlog and are missing out, heh.

I just completed Firewatch, 4 hours. Not a really long game but I think by now we have to accept that these types of games aren't meant to be long. They tell a story that you shape with actions and choices. But was it interesting? Was it worth it? In my opinion, yes. I enjoyed the story. Some may not. Judging by others' reviews here, it may not have been their cup of tea. Myself, I like a game that tells a story, presents a mystery, and keeps you interested until the end.

Some here said the ending wasn't all that great. I have to disagree. If you paid attention to all the details throughout the progression of the story, the ending makes perfect sense. I think some may have been disappointed that it didn't end the way they would have ended it. And I don't want to spoil it for anyone else, so I'll say nothing more about that. Point is, everyone has different views and different things that interest them... so don't go by what others here say regarding their opinion on the story or ending. Just get it and judge for yourself.

As for the game itself, I thought the graphics were "okay". I say that because the lighting and colors can seem kinda saturated sometimes. They are like a "watercolor painting" I think; not meant to look too realistic, but realistic. Sound is fine, and voice-acting was well done and believable. Background music is also well done and does a good job of hinting at the mood of the situation or area you're in. 

Replayability... well, lets face it... most interractive story games aren't usually good enough to replay once you've seen how it ends and discovered the mysteries. Now, if it has various endings, that's a completely different story. I don't know if Firewatch has other endings as I've only run through it once, but I will replay it nonetheless just to see what happens when I make different choices.

This is a truly outstanding walking simulator, with an intriguing story that hooked me from the start, outstanding writing, and stellar voice acting.  Although the aesthetic is rather cartoony, it's gorgeous and somehow starts to feel quite realistic after playing for a few minutes,  

Like most good walking simulators, it's light on interaction (with no combat), but heavy on story and mood.  The interaction between the two main characters was realistic and drew me in - at least with the dialogue choices I picked.  I'm not sure how choosing other options might have changed the relationship between the two.

Speaking of realistic, I suspect the reason some reviewers were disappointed with the ending was that they wanted something more dramatic, more Hollywood.  I was pleased with the grounded outcome of the whole thing.  In fact, I think the whole theme of this game is to explore the way people approach the difference between fantasy and reality.  Almost all the characters run to various forms of fantasy when reality is painful, and the game itself teases the player with two forms of fantasy.  I think reflecting on the way one reacted to the mystery and its outcome as well as thinking about expectations the player developed regarding the interaction between the two main characters is exactly what the developers are hoping for at the end of the game.

It's rare that a game gets me waxing so philosophic. :-)  In short, if you are looking for a non-combat walking simulator that is heavy on emotional self-reflection, I highly recommend Firewatch.

Without being negative, Firewatch probably deserves the title of "Walking Simulator" more than any other game I've played. None of your actions actually change how the story unfolds (so far as I can tell) and while the scenery is thankfully pretty enough to be a pleasant stroll it's really just an slightly interactive walk on rails. Don't get me wrong, it's a compelling story despite a somewhat weak ending, but you won't be solving anything especially. You're just along for the ride.

This is probably all quite deliberate on the dev's part, as where your choices DO make a differences is how you choose to speak to, and build a relationship with, Delilah - the woman on the other end of your radio and this is where the real meat of the game is. There's no real replayability in the game, but on my first run-through (which took a little under four hours altogether) I kept Delilah at something of a distance, behaving as I probably would in real life. I'll probably have a go at some point at seeing what happens if I reciprocate her advances or just attempt to annoy her as much as possible.

I find music in these kind of games more effective when used sparingly and Firewatch certainly hits the mark there, dropping in some very atmospheric music at key points. It's the first time I've played a game where I've actually been tempted to buy the soundtrack DLC.

All in all recommended, as it's a very lovely game. Can't help but feel its short length and almost zero replay value doesn't quite justify it at full-price however, so maybe wait for a sale.

At the very start Firewatch began pulling at emotional strings, and a bit further in you start getting involved in some mysteries surrounding the main character. But by the end of about 5 hours of playtime, every single one of those mysteries resolved in a wholly anticlimactic way. I can't help but feel very disappointed, like I wasted my time.

On top of that, there were many times in the game that I felt the character was getting caught against small boulders etc. that realistically he should very easily have been able to step over; on occasion I even had to mash WASD to get him unstuck, since backing out wouldn't work. For a walking simulator, the walking part of Firewatch was sometimes extremely frustrating.

Most of the items presented in the game also don't seem to have much point... your character is told he can open random cache boxes around the map, which store equipment you can take. Some of them had some odd items such as a deer antler, and several pine cones. When your character questions it, your walkie-talkie companion tells you that after a certain amount of time in the outdoors, people get creative with the tools they use. This suggested to me that the more eccentric items were meant for some sort of puzzle. Turns out, none of it did anything. There is no puzzle aspect to this game.

On the bright side, I didn't experience any game breaking bugs in Firewatch, and true, the scenery is pretty and screenshots galore for wallpapers. Sometimes walking was annoying, but in all fairness, most of the game you won't encounter problems... but the times I did left a lasting impression. Combined with a lacking story, no puzzles, a lot of banter that I didn't find that funny, none of the good stuff is enough to make this game worth it for me. Given another chance, I wouldn't have purchased this.

Firewatch is a game following a man, Henry, who has taken a job out in the Wyoming Wilderness to escape from his problems. His new job, as the title of the game suggests, is on Fire Watch. Keeping an eye out for fires, preventing fires and calling them in when they occur. A simple concept driven by choices, discovery and interactions with his new boss - Delilah.

The story is filled with twists and turns and always leaves you with questions to be asked and answers to be found. The conclusion wrapping it all up into one nice little package. Firewatch is driven by exploration, the areas of the wilderness that you get to explore filled with various navigational challenges and sightseeing opportunities. Open Meadows, Caves and Cliffs are all presented in a beautiful visual style and each different area visited provides you with new items and story to discover. Firewatch is a walkie talkie game where you walk and talk. It does not sound very intriguing, but trust me it is, just let me explain. The game starts out with introducing our main protagonist, Henry's personal life and his releationship in 10-minute "Up!" style fashion which really makes us feel for this character. Then we come to the point where he joins the firewatch and meets Delilah his supervisor. But they never actually meet, they only communicate through a walkie talkie the whole game. And this is where it gets hard to make an emotional bond with a character who you never actually see, but Firewatch nails it. Through fantastic voice acting and writing, our two heroes have great chemistry which makes the game fun even just to listen through. The game is mostly a walking simulator with a linear but enjoyable story, with great dialogues and very soothing atmosphere where every moment of the day you can get beautiful screenshots (especially at sunsets). If you prefer story and characters over diverse gameplay I'd highly recommend picking this up.

Given the premise, I did not expect this game to be as tense as it was! Genuinely heart-racing at times, no doubt helped by the rich characterization of the main actors. I love the narrative arc of the game. The conclusion really ties the whole experience together in a way that adds to the lessons Hank learns (or doesn't). Tons of subtlety in the storytelling through strong sense of place and environmental cues. Some questions remained unanswered for me by the end, but I've learned from others that the answers can be found or inferred with more careful investigating, so this also still works for me. Besides, no good story should make it easy for you.

Just as a preface I hadn't played Firewatch until now completely out of spite. Back when I was making video game review vids on the YouTubes the developer acted like I'd get a pre-release press copy and just didn't deliver (which I assumed was because the game got hyped up to the point so they didn't have to rely on smaller reviews for exposure, who knows).  I am not a fan of being misled.

However, even with a bit of bad blood mixed in Firewatch is a supremely gripping story that I couldn't stop playing until I finished it.  It's not a hugely drawn out game with 100's of collectables and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ padding to deal with but it makes for a concise and interesting glipse into human nature.  The voice acting is great and everything feels fleshed out really well.  I didn't have any problems with the ending and I am definitely mulling over everything that happened now that it's over which I can't say I do often. 

The dialoge choices were a good call and really let your bead in on how you feel the main character's relationships ought to develop. The game constantly disarms you and lets your imagination take you to all the wrong conclsuions. You feel one way then the rug is pulled out from under your feet completely.  Its a subtlety that is lost on players that want everything explained to them and by the ending tied up in a neat bow; the subterfuge is masterfully executed.

Game looks, sounds and runs great.  No bugs or crashes at all which is always nice in smaller titles.  I was surprised at the cartoony look of the characters in farious drawings and what little you see of Henry but it's fine.  There is one jump scare that I thought was just a ♥♥♥♥ move and offered nothing of value to the game.

There were a few plot points that I'd file under missed opportunites but in the end it was all forgiveable. On sale this summer for $4.99 was a great deal and I'd say $9.99 is an appropriate price under normal circumstances.  $19.99 is a big ask for what you end up getting but that's just my opinion they can charge whatever they want.

TLDR Firewatch is perfect for people that want a gripping, interactive story driven game with great content.  Not for people that are looking for more action or hate "walking simulators".  if you don't like to read between the lines you'll be missing out.

This is a fabulous game and a definite steal when on sale. Firewatch features a gorgeous environment that isn't quite as expansive as some "sandboxes" but is certainly appropriate to the length and depth of the game. The story has considerable emotional impact; the world, and the characters, create an immersive environment that inevitably draws you into the mystery of this park. Firewatch has tremendous replay value, as well. I bulled my way through my first play and wanted to run through it again immediately. Somehow, knowing the truth of the mystery and having the power to represent my character's personality in various ways through choices and dialogue made the second play through at least as potent as the first.

Firewatch is also suprisingly scary. No, it isn't a horror game. However, the developers are very clever with the use of sound, or the absence thereof, to build tension. There isn't very "much" in the forest around you so any encounter with a living thing feels powerful. The absence of human contact (with the exception of your boss, Delilah, who is never physically accessible) builds heavy suspense at times, making you wish that aren't alone in the forest while also hoping that you are. 

Altogether, I do recommend the game. The voice-acting is natural and positively top-notch. The world, while not massive by any means, is a visual pleasure to explore. It is disappointing to discover that your choices have no significant influence on the story and despite living in the lookout tower for 79 days, you only truly play a handful of them, resulting in a very short playthrough. Still, if you can snag this game on sale, you shouldn't pass it up.

Firewatch is a first person exploration driven walking simulator that focuses on a character driven narrative. The beginning of the game consists of text based story options to determine the player character’s backstory. This is a great way to put the player in the shoes of their character. This was also super effective at getting me to care about and sympathize with the player character. After all, his life choices were the ones that I made.

The setting, gameplay, and character motivations of Firewatch reflect a theme of escapism. The way that the backstory comes around to play a role in the dialogue between the characters suggests inevitable failure when attempting to escape one’s own past. The characters are deep and complex. Both of the two leads in Firewatch are well written, well acted, funny, charming as hell, and believably tragic.

Plus the writing takes advantage of interactivity through the way dialogue is integrated into the exploration based gameplay. Since dialogue can only be activated upon using a radio mechanic to report new discoveries to the other character, I was driven to explore as much as possible just so I could see what the two had to say about it. The dialogue can also be affected by the order that the player experiences events which is some pretty impressive scripting.

Firewatch’s extent of optional discoveries and character interactions maintains a small enough scope as to not detract from the pacing of the over arcing plot. The pacing is also helped by extremely tight level design that cleverly uses terrain elevation to give navigation a sense of variety and guide the player’s line of view. Multiple pathways to and from each major point of interest provokes exploration and evokes a sense of non-linearity. The level designers have the player heading to exactly where they want them to go without sacrificing the world’s open ended feel.

The over arcing plot is totally captivating with interesting short term objectives as well as unexpected twists and turns. The lurking intrigue of Firewatch’s central mystery and the exciting ways that the plot developed kept me hooked until the very end. The ending of Firewatch is characterized by anticlimax which made it massively disappointing for me. But that is a more subjective complaint about a deliberate artistic decision rather than an observation of a flaw.

The designers deliberately cross contaminate unrelated environmental story details in order to create false implications of bigger conspiracies. The reveal of the actual mystery was intentionally set up to be a let down perhaps to suggests that reality can never compare with the stories we make up in our heads.

The stylized visuals are gorgeous and Firewatch thankfully rejects many user-interface conventions in favor of providing a more immersive and absorbing experience. For instance, there is no map screen. Instead, the map is an actual gameplay mechanic. The player pushes a button to hold up the map in front of their view in the same way “iron sights” work in a first person shooter.

The developers do something similar with the system for choosing dialogue options through the radio mechanic, but it is hard to explain. Though I will say that Firewatch has one of the most elegant and intuitive dialogue systems that I have seen in a narrative driven game.

To sum it all up; regardless of any criticism, Firewatch is great. Go play it.

[h1] Firewatch is NOT a GAME	[/h1]
When it comes to playing games I don't really have a lot of criteria. I want my experience to be enjoyable, or thought provoking, or I want my game to offer some sort of interesting design or feature. Firewatch does none of these things.
The Firewatch Devs had a story, they wanted to convey what they thought was a "deep" or "relatable" story. And it fell flat on it's ass.

[h1] "Gameplay"	[/h1]
As a game it has absolutely nothing to offer, choosing to rely on it's story to get you through, but here's the thing, if you're planning to make a "game" you've got to offer something for the player to actually do to connect all of the setpieces that the story includes. So what do you do in Firewatch? You walk. A lot. That is the only actual "game" part of Firewatch. Along with some contextual button presses. 

[h1] The World	[/h1]
Being set in the wilderness of Wynoming the devs had every oppurtunity to make the wilderness somewhat pretty to look at? Maybe have some varied wildlife or flora? Nah. You're gonna be seeing a lot of stones and trees. And you better get used to them, because in such a tiny map a lot of your journey is going to be back tracking and getting lost. With nothing but a compass and a map, and with every area of the game looking identical, it's a safe bet you're going to get lost. A lot.

[h1] The Story and the Illusion of Choice	[/h1]
Firewatch's biggest selling point is it's story, it's a narrative based game. And boy oh boy does it suck ass. Donkey ass. You start by making "choices" to decide your character Henry's past. You'd think something like that would impact the story? Does it ♥♥♥♥. The choices you make in dialogue have no bearing on the story what so ever. You may think that you may be making progress with the only other character you speak to, Delilah but the story's ending is a suckerpunch to the ballsack. It commits the sin of making the character think you're making an impact on the events of the game but you're not. Dialogue effects Dialogue and that's it. The actual story is a anti-climactic piece of trash that wouldn't pass for an 8 year old's school project. Without going into too much details or spoilers, you discover someone is listening in to your radio, and you have to discover who it is and what their motives are.

[h1] What it Gets Right	[/h1]
There are a few things that Firewatch gets right, mainly the performance of the two voice actors for Henry and Delilah, they make the characters believable and real, and their respective performances deserve nothing but praise. 
They're are a few moments that set a nice or tense atmosphere using meloncholic music which was a nice touch, however if you linger during any of these moments you'll discover the music loops.

[h1] Final Thoughts.	[/h1]
This game is poor. It presents a faux interesting story that would only appeal to hipsters or people lying to themselves. It isn't fun, it isn't pretty, your choices don't matter and the story sucks balls. This is the only game to ever inspire me to write a full fledged bad review.

tl:dr
The games ♥♥♥♥. Avoid it like the plague.

I was looking through the Steam summer sale for new and different games, and stumbled across this one. It looked promising; gorgeous visuals, intriguing locale, and convincing set-up for an okay story. I bought it and played it all in one morning. Descriptions of the unfolding of the plot may be considered spoilery, so you have been warned.

My first impressions upon the first part of the game was that it would be something of a Telltale Series game. That is to say, a game that would tempt you with the idea of freedom and a truly individualized experience, but deliver a forced story with minimal dialogue changes. That is partially true, but if that were it I would not have recommended this game. The story *is* forced. You can't do anything that majorly changes the story, and can choose to be a dumbass, a jerk, or a sensible human being with your dialogue selections (as with most of these kinds of games). But the "personalized story," or rather, the lack thereof, is not the draw. Instead, it's the way the story comes to be.

Your story begins simply, and ordinarily. After a brief prologue to get you invested in Henry's, the protagonist, life, you explore the mechanics of the game and the dynamics of your personality and that of Delilah, the only real connection you have out here in the forest. It's two standard people, who have had some awful things happen in their lives, but who hasn't had something awful happen? After simple teases of a mystery, while on the cusp of things seeming normal, you are unexpectedly and abruptly thrust into a more thrilling and confusing mystery than you thought.

Once you reach the end of the game, you find that the thrill, the drama, the peril, is mostly superficial. It was a lot of paranoia, a well-crafted atmosphere, and unsual circumstances that allowed you to foolishly believe this was going to be a dark drama of intrigue and deceit. Instead, the end was... simple. Anti-climactic. The ending isn't satisfying, because there wasn't this one, single person or entity who was responsible. The end was a culmination of everyone else's choices that resulted in you finding out about a tragic event, which you had nothing to do with. 

We are all satisfied with justice, with a story that tells what was wrong, why it happened, and how it was resolved. Unfortunately, this story tells something more human and real that we can all relate to in a sad way. Sometimes, people make poor choices. Sometimes they turn out fine, and don't change anything, much like Henry's-well, your-choices. Other times, like Delilah's, they result in unintended consequences. No matter how innocent and pure her intentions, she and another character in the game avoided what we all want; justice and someone to take responsibility. As we often find in our own lives, $#!% happens. And sometimes, no one is to blame. We can point fingers, or blame ourselves for something we couldn't have stopped or known would have happened, but in the end it happened because it did. It's truly unsatisfying, and ironically that's what made it such an interesting game to play.

Short Version:

Pros:
+ Beautiful art style
+ Stellar voice-acting
+ Intriguing, focused narrative
+ Great soundtrack
+ Manages to be funny, interesting, scary and thrilling

Cons:
- Tedious backtracking towards the end
- Disappointing ending
- Little to no wildlife

"Long" Version:

Firewatch is what some would call a "walking simulator" that focuses on storytelling instead of actual gameplay. Nevertheless, I consider it a beautiful looking game with great characters and interesting twists and turns. However, a disappointing, flat ending keeps it from greatness.

[b](I will keep this part of the review short and not too detailed in order to avoid spoilers - I knew no story points when I played and I truly believe it is the best way to experience it)[/b] The story revolves around Henry, a good man with a somewhat dark and flawed past and Delilah, his supervisor, who he meets when he takes a job as a fire lookout in Wyoming. It starts out quite simple but it soon evolves into a really interesting, tense and somewhat scary mystery. The story's build-up is outstanding and I found myself being scared to look back a bunch of times - however, all this build-up led to an anticlimactic ending. It isn't bad, per say, but I was not expecting something so... Underwhelming. On the other hand, it is a very grounded, realistic outcome and you still care deeply about the main characters.

Firewatch's soundtrack is great. Most of it is a really calm and soothing melody, but there are also quite a few moments where really scary music pops up - all of it is great. The tracks are used sparingly; usually, your journey is accompanied by the sound of the wind, leaves and birds.
Even better than the soundtrack is the voice acting. It is the best I have ever heard. Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones' performances are flawless - they are deep and layered - crucial to both the development and believability of the story. I seriously cannot stress how perfect it is.

Gameplay is serviceable. You can walk around and interact with several objects, but it is somewhat limited. Invisible walls, dense vegetation and big rocks; they all prevent you from moving freely and make sure you go where the game wants you to go. Everything is very linear too; which isn't necessarily bad, it keeps the story focused. Towards the end, however, all the backtracking started getting stale - luckily, nothing too dire. The absence of significant wildlife is also a bit disappointing.

The game looks stunning - throughout your journey, you will visit different parts of the forest and each section looks like a slightly different biome; it still feels interconnected though; great stuff!

Firewatch is a game I confidently recommend. Sure, the ending might not be the best, but everything else is up there. The voice acting is stellar, you care about the characters and the build-up is just too good.

Final score: 8 out of 10.

Minor Spoilers Ahead** Firewatch isn't a game in the traditional sense, I suppose it can be swept into the genre of 'Walking Simulator.' That isn't an insult of course, it's just a good way of explaining the genre. Firewatch is different to any other of these games that I have played in the past- it has beautiful looming acres of gorgeous Montana woodland as well as its own little story of heartbreak to tell along with a meandering narrative surrounding the characters Henry and Dellilah. Firewatch structures its narrative through conversation only and this is over a radio- there are only four voice actors in the entire game along with a couple of side characters but the game really benefits from the rapport shared between Henry and Dellilah. Firewatch offers the player choices- dialogue only without a meaningful path which would differentiate a second playthrough, all paths lead to Rome in this case. Nonetheless, the destination in Firewatch is only as important as the journey and the path you take to discover the truth about the national park and indeed the truth you find about yourself. The game is not without its flaws however, it is a bit of a buggy mess in places- I found myself trapped on rocks here and there and discovered some artifacting on some textures though nothing major. The only caveat I would really put forward about Firewatch is the price. The base game costs £14.99 or your regional equivilent and the game doesn't tend to last more than 4 hours for most people- even me, I explored everywhere- drinking in the art and story and I can't have gone more than 4 and a half. But- I did buy this on the steam sale for under £4 so I cannot complain. Do I think this game is worth £15 however? Yes and No. If you are stable with your finances and don't mind throwing £15 at a 4 hour game then go ahead, you could do much worse, but if you are on the other side of the spectrum you might want to spend your money on an experience which lasts longer and get the bang for your buck, because I'm not sure Firewatch is that. Overall, Firewatch is a solid story and uses its narrative masterfully, but what stops this game from being a true masterpiece is the direction and identity of the story. The beginning and end of Henry's narrative do not complement each other and his tragic story and relationship with his wife aren't wrapped up in a meaningful way, instead focusing on the issues in the present and choosing to forget about the real problems at home. But perhaps that's all part of the charm of the story, a commentary on human nature. You decide.

Spoiler Review: ( I MEAN IT, THE FOLLOWING PARAGRAPHS WILL SPOIL THE STORY FOR YOU, YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED )


The prologue is extremely depressing. You cowardly take a job in the remote wilderness after your sick wife is relinquished from your care by her parents, due to your inability to maintain the exhaustive practice of caring for her, or whatever sort of path you chose.

You start hiking toward this fire tower, and once you arrive, you "meet" Delilah, your ever-physically distant supervisor via radio.

Having played various walking simulators in the past, this game has the typical cutesy doodles or hand-drawn character photos to give you an idea of who you are, and what you look like, but then the slow but then sudden realization hits you that you will not see a single human face in the actual game. You realize that you will never actually meet Delilah, the mysterious figure, or any of the scouts, rangers, firefighters, what have you. In the end, you are rescued by a firefighter who is wearing a reflective mask, and you never see his face.

The voice-acting is absolutely incredible, don't get me wrong, but this at-times hot and heavy distant verbal relationship with Delilah loses it's draw at the consistently convenient avoidances and Delilah's uncharacteristic unwillingness to meet with you in any physical capacity. She even leaves things in places for you, but this scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ woman won't even come to your tower to try and decide what to do with the only person she can trust? It's cheap, and lazy. This incredible story is so obviously limited by the inability to spend the time on in-person character interactions, that numerous decisions are made to prevent them entirely, where they would normally be appropriate or expected.

Yes.  I mean it.

Firewatch is a heartbreaking story about loss, guilt, isolation, friendship, trust, and responsibility.

Story summary: protagonist Henry has taken a secluded job as a firewatching lookout in the deep wilderness to escape his real world problems.  Over the radio, he strikes up a friendship with his supervisor Delilah from the next tower over, and when a mystery emerges in the woods they work to solve it together.

Gameplay: this is not a "crunchy" game, but [b]is[/b] more than a "walking simulator".  The main challenge here is in navigation and traversal.  Learn to read your map, make good use of your compass, learn the names of different areas, find occasional upgrades to unlock new areas such as rope to climb down cliffs.  You won't brag to your friends about "getting good" at this game, but you can't simply press W with a beer in your other hand either.  Also see "Dialogue" below.

Atmosphere: simply brilliant.  Graphics and sound really "take you there".  This has all the beauty of your best remembered camping or hiking trip.

Characterization: perfect.  The two main characters are disarming, sympathetic, and compelling.  Henry's backstory establishes a firm foundation for his responses to the adventure to come.  His history is detailed at the beginning of the game through a brief "choose your own adventure" text, pulling the player in with small decisions about the tragedy that caused him to seek seclusion in the first place.  Delilah is a mystery at first, with a professional attitude, but as their friendship develops over time we learn some of her history as well, and more importantly her sense of humor emerges.  The growth of their relationship is the most unique and fascinating part of the game.  Performances are top notch.

Dialogue: again: perfect.  You have many small choices to make, which keeps you engaged, and your answers not only steer the immediate conversation but can have long-term effects as well.  To me [i]this is the real gameplay[/i].  The goal here is not to kill skeletons or collect coins, but to develop a relationship, and there is an everpresent sense of meaning to everything said.  Naysayers, crunch gamers, and "click-throughers" are going to miss out big here.

Story: good.  As excellent as the long radio conversation between two people is, there's more here than first meets the eye.  Some things are going on out here in the woods, and the drama that emerges is both strange and very human.  There's no "a wizard did it"; no robots, ghosts, or aliens.  I was pleasantly surprised.

Value: The game is short.  My playthrough was under 4 hours, and I played at a reasonably slow pace and got lost a few times.  If you're the kind of player who sprints everywhere and ignores distractions, you may find it even shorter.  (But don't do that.)  It's hard to recommend paying $20 for this, despite its quality, due to its brevity.  Grab it on sale though and you can't go wrong.  I paid $5 and got more than my money's worth for sure.

Cons: Dialog choices are strongly on-rails. Answering a simple yes or no can lead to your character going on a rant.

Boy, this game sure does have a whoooole lotta charm (and exceptional voice acting). What it [i]doesn't[/i] have is a lot of, erm...focus.

   In Firewatch, you play one of the dudes from Team Fortress, slumming it sans weaponry in the great Wyoming wilderness in the hopes that he might spot himself a Roadrunner. Things start out a little hectic for the first couple of days of his self-imposed exile: nothing violent, though there are a couple of mysteriously missing teenage misfits by the end of it all. For many a day afterwards you're largely left alone to discover your own mischief in the woods, while the story continues to [i]slowly[/i] unfold via a series of rather endearing radio conversations with a nice lady you happen to work with (albeit somewhat remotely). 

   Things then ramp up a bit towards a perfectly satisfying conclusion, but the whole thing sure does start to feel a bit rudderless around the middle. (And a tad frustrating at times, if your sense of direction is as flawed as my own. Getting lost trying to find the way [i]forward[/i] in a game is one thing; getting lost wandering around doing nothing-in-particular is another again.)

   Sure, the enormous map is beautiful to behold, but it's ultimately kinda same-ish. There simply isn't any great sense of reward for searching about extensively (though that cute little turtle I got to adopt was [i]almost[/i] worth it). What this all adds up to, then, is an impressive open world-ish map with a good story intermittently woven into it. (And an unGodly amount of backtracking, I might add.)

   I think this might be why I don't dig "open world"/"sandbox"-y games that much: I like a fairly tight story. Don't get me wrong...this game fully deserves its rep as one of the premier "walking simulators" on the market. Just don't expect as focused a storytelling experience as What Remains of Edith Finch or Gone Home, and don't forget to bring yer hikin' boots; you're gonna need 'em, especially if you find yourself wandering in semi-aimless circles as much as I did (hint to the wise: don't [i]ever[/i] put that compass away)!

   There's no doubting the love that was lavished on this project, and the talent behind it. Perhaps I wasn't the perfect person to appreciate this game's peculiar attention to detail, and I guess it just wasn't the great and revelatory "story rich" experience others had built it up to be (though I [i]was[/i] pretty moved, right at the end). Enter with lesser expectations, however, and you're almost certain to be pleased. It's a really, really good game - it really is - but the Second Coming of anything it unfortunately ain't. 

   Also, a final thought: perhaps there's a reason why walking sims tend to be under two hours long. Decent plot or not, this is one game that simply doesn't justify its running time, and I for one would have enjoyed it more if it was a good hour or so shorter. A strong recommendation, just the same.

   Verdict: 8.5/10.

I've been waiting to write this review. 

For an incredibly short, albeit fantastic, three-five hour campaign with arguably little replayability it’s hard to pitch this game as completely living up to its $20 price tag. 

That being said, Firewatch proudly displays an incredibly well written plot, remarkable voice acting, and gorgeous scenery wherever you look. If you’re the kind of person that doesn’t mind sitting down to watch a movie you’ve seen before, Firewatch is a great game to spend an evening playing when you just want to relax. I think it’s great to kick back in a recliner and play it on the big screen with a steam controller, but your mileage may vary. As mentioned, a lot of people complain that the campaign is little repayable; and it’s true. The plot is very memorable, so when you sit down to play it the second / third time it all rushes back into memory and some of the wonder goes away as result. Nevertheless, I hardly think this is a game to play once and shelf forever after—it’s more like a movie or a good book. We all know how that one episode of Star Wars, or Indiana Jones, or Full Metal Jacket goes, but we still revisit them every now and then.

Only other negative, and again this one will really depend on who you are and what you like, is the ending. To tiptoe around spoilers, many folks complain about the ending being a bit of a letdown, but I don’t think that’s what’s intended. This is a story for grown-ups, and you really can’t enjoy it if you aren’t able to relate to it. So many themes and wild ideas are juggled around throughout the course of the game leading up to the climax, wherein you solve the mystery at hand only to discover that all the drama and intrigue was simply coincidence. Henry leaves at the end of the summer with, in addition to one hell of a story to tell, a lot of reflection and perhaps a new perspective on life. The theme of all the games events is parallel to Henrys own personal struggles, how he’s dealt with them, and all the what-ifs. We see his youth, his family issues, and the repercussions of his life decisions echoed through the other characters and what they do in the game, and we see a lot of similarity to the characters own wife in his only direct peer and supervisor during the firewatch, Delilah. 

One might expect to uncover some conspiracy, or monsters, or who-knows-what at the end of the game—it’s easy to perceive a letdown when all that crazy ♥♥♥♥ is more or less explained away as just real-life, down to earth, crazy ♥♥♥♥ whose circumstances just happened to come together as they did. However, I never really felt let down. I think this feeling, whatever it is, after the end of the game is exactly what the writers wanted, and I find it refreshing. It allows the games plot to feel like the fantasy we expect from a game today, but also keeps things very down to earth, which makes the story relatable, especially for older audiences. Without leaving plot holes, just enough of the story prompts player to come to their own conclusions. As the credits role and the games over it leaves something to be desired, and I think that not-quite-empty feeling is just right to prompt the player to stop and have a moment of personal introspection. 

I’m normally not an artsy-fartsy person, but this game really does feel more like something between a stunning work of visual art and a good novella. Heavy stuff.

. . . 

Possible side effects: 
You may feel the need to go on a long hiking + camping trip after playing (at least I sure as hell did). You may also feel slightly depressed after playing if you find the games characters a bit too relatable.

This game is 100% about the journey, not the destination, and I'm not surprised the people beating it in 3-4 hours didn't like it. If you are the type who rushes through games to get to the end or tries to complete objectives using the path of least resistance, you will probably not enjoy Firewatch.

How long it takes you to complete it and how much you enjoy it depends on how much you go off the beaten path (literally) to explore, appreciate the scenery, ponder the story themes, and take in the atmosphere. 

There is a LOT of travel in this game. If you need to get to a place across the map, you will be walking there using a compass and a map. If this doesn't sound like your cup of tea, you may want to pass this one up.

PROS:
+ Mysterious story kept me interested for the duration
+ Beautiful visuals and atmosphere
+ Compass and map makes travel feel rewarding/meaningful
+ Strong character writing 

CONS:
- Ending may be disappointing to some
- No real choices that change the story
- Lots of time consuming walking A to B to A which hurts story pacing
- One really frustrating sequence in the forest at night
