I found this game to be slightly disappointing which in itself is disappointing because the game has many good aspects.  The premise is clever with the main protagonist isolated in a beautifully realised wilderness environment, his only contact a fellow firewatcher in another location. This is refreshing from a gaming point of view because you are exploring two people's emotions rather than anything more overt.  This aspect of the game is convincing and authentic. 

The games moves away from this as it proceeds and loses some of its intelligence as it does.  As a player you have little agency to direct the tale, so it is more of an interactive story than a game.  As the story becomes less about the people the lack of agency becomes more of an issue.  The conclusion of the game, which avoids a number of obvious endings, is in keeping with the tone of the first half of the game but by then I had lost some of my connection to the characters and so it had less impact than intended.

I wish the steam rating system was less binary but I have not recommended this game more to indicate an opportunity missed than anything else.  I also think there are better ways to spend your money if you want an interactive story.

In terms of genre, a lot of people have called it a walking/hiking simulator but that's just the game on the surface. If you like narrative based games, you will like this game a lot. The story and dialogue is really strong, and while you have different dialogue options that lead to different speech responses, they all sort of funnel through to the same outcome. And in this game, that's not a bad thing - it's a linear story based game and one thing it does really well, is make you care for the protagonist, Henry. 

Some people didn't care for the ending as it left a lot to be assumed, but if you think back on the dialogue, notice things in the environment, reflect on everything that happened, you can piece together the "mystery" at play here. It's a very strong story that doesn't hold your hand and yell in your face, but if you play the game with presence, you're likely to be able to piece together most of it. 

The art style is unique and the game is visually appealing; the soundtrack is excellent and there's really no reason not to pick up this game if you haven't. I picked it up for $8 during a steam sale which is the current historic low.

Firewatch is a beautiful game with most of its weight on the storyline--a majority of which is told through dialogue. There is mystery, suspense, and intrigue, all amidst a sprawling "national park" type setting. The art style works well for the game, and the story is compelling. That being said, I couldn't help but feel like things could have been pushed further, story-wise. The ending is sort of dismissive of some of the earlier plot points of the game leaving room for many unanswered questions. I also feel like the player choice could have factored in more with how the relationships are built up and what the potential implications are for the main character and their own personal journey within the main plot. 

That being said, it is a short, self-contained story in a nice polished package. However, like many more have reported previously, I too suffered from having the game freeze on almost every loading screen. This required me to force close and relaunch the game, which became quite tedious. However, in spite of this annoyance, the game is enjoyable and I do recommend it for someone looking for a short story and some lovely scenery.

Firewatch is a story-heavy, walking simulator with good humor and beautiful scenery. You play a new recruit to the forest service in Wyoming to look out for and report forest fires, but you really won't have a lot of firewatching to do. You'll be sent on different tasks by your faceless boss on the radio, things like checking for fallen telephone lines after a storm, chasing away teens with fireworks, etc. A mystery unfolds through mostly dialogue trees where your choices "matter" but really just affect the relationship between you and your boss, and how you are seen by one other character in the story (spoilers!). The scenery is GORGEOUS, even at lower resolutions and despite the cartoony overlay on the 3D setting, and you even have a camera to take pictures as you go along. The story is good, too.  Some cons: minimal music, which means sections without conversations between you and your boss can be very boring, walking across an enormous national park with nothing to do or hear. There's a lot of backtracking and lots of holding the run button just to make it less tedious. BIG CON: My computer crashed at nearly every loading screen, and if I didn't have a quicksave beforehand I'd have to replay huge chunks of dialogue trees because the autosave knocks you back pretty far.

Overall, despite some bugs and a lot of dead air/walking/backtracking, this was a very enjoyable game with a good story.

[h1]In-depth:[/h1]
So... where do I start. This game is a walking simulator. Which means, aside from walking and looking around, there's barely any gameplay attached to it. It also is a very linear walking simulator with no multiple endings or choices that actually matter. And it's also very short. The 4.6 hours on my record include some aimless wandering around and one ~30min reload.

Aside from that, this game is pretty, if you enjoy such visual style. It does, however, have quite a few bugs, with trees growing out of thin air, animals floating, fence not connecting to the floor etc. Not a big deal, but it is kind of a shame when such things ruin the picture.

So, why is this a positive review?
I'll be honest with you. It's voice acting. Plain and simple. This game is about two characters who talk to each other through the whole game. That's it. There's nothing else in this game. And it was a fantastic experience. If it was an audiobook I would gladly listen to it a few more times. Sure, half of the praise goes to writers, for creating the nice dialogues. But the delivery of both actors was fantastic. If it wasn't for them, this game wouldn't be even half as good. It just wouldn't be worth the time.

This game is also about the journey, not the destination. To be honest, the ending almost ruined it for me. It's not as bad as, say, "5 centimeters per second" ([strike]if you've seen it, you know what I'm talking about[/strike]), but it still felt like a huge downer, and really ruined the mood the other 75% of the game had established.

This is the game that I can only recommend if characters are the most important thing for you. Not the story, not the gameplay, only characters. And for how short it is, I would recommend you get it on a discount.

But I still consider it an overall pleasant experience and think that you should give it a try.

Now let me state that this game isnt bad game it's simply not a great one. When you first start up there's this little almost texting adventure style way of introducing you to the main character Henry; it gives you a little of his backstory about how he up being part of the fire watch. You're then introduced to the main character Delilah, you're supervisor and main point of communication. Now the voice acting and dialogue is great--alot of emotion and humor where it felt appropriate. The environment is beautiful to look and makes you want to spend time exploring all of it. There are interesting things to collect all throughout Shoshone such as trinkets from previous campers, missing persons letters, a turtle for a pet etc.

So why exactly wouldn't I recommend this game?

Simply put the ending to this games story is ABSOLUTELY INFURIATING. I'm not going spoil it for you if you're REALLY interested buy throughout this game it becomes more apparent that someone is spying on both Henry and Delilah--tracking their movements, conversations, and later on somewhat blackmailing them with a recorded conversation. It builds it up and keeps you guessing as to who is doing it to you, making you scared but excited at the same time. The soundtrack is also one of the major upsides of the game : it really adds up to the atmosphere, makes us feel the freedom of hiking in Wyoming, scares us when it must and just puts the player in the current mood of Henry. The characters are credible, quite complex and charming. But to me, the real gem in Firewatch really has to be the environment : it will wake something up in all of us : a memory of a summer going camping, a summer friendship or just that feeling of putting our lives aside just for a month, for a break. The landscapes really are stunning, and the details, particularly in the watch towers are of great value to character development and to the atmosphere. The game was so beautiful, i guess i'm not the only player wanting to visit Wyoming now.

It's so rare to find a game that so gracefully accomplishes exactly what it sets out to do. The thoughtful story, the narrative devices, the contemplative gameplay, the little flourishes of delightful detail, all come together to create an unforgettable experience: a straightforward examination of the psychology of escapism.

It's crucial to have the right expectations in order to enjoy the game fully. In terms of gameplay, I would classify it as a “hiking simulator": for the most part, you can hike to anywhere you want on the map at your own pace, but the story unfolds as it unfolds and you're just along for the ride. There are simple goals to move you along, but they are things to do rather than puzzles. The puzzlement comes from the narrative, layered over the gameplay via outstanding, understated dialog and voice acting. You have some control over the dialog choices, but they're there mostly to assist your identification with the protagonist rather than change the course of the game. You do not choose your own ending.

Speaking of the ending, you might see some reviews complaining about it. I woud like to complain about those complainers! In my view, the ending is [I]exactly right[/I] in mood, tone, and execution.

After all, working as a fire watcher is a difficult task: operating for weeks on end in remote, at times inhospitable areas without another person around for miles. What better way to re-inforce that sense of loneliness than with a walkie-talkie? How could the people engaging with each other through those devices NOT bond with each other?

Kudos to the folks who wrote the dialogue and the voice actors/actresses that brought those characters to life. It's sad to say those same people did their jobs too well. The dramatic tension that results from these performances feels... robbed by the games actual ending. Yes, the end is very real and utterly believable, which in itself is a welcome change. The end doesn't feel rushed, forced or disappointing, but it feels as though Delilah and Henry deserved... more. Not with each other, necessarily. And not with a longer game. Just... not what we got.

My issue with the game however, is the fact that the last third of the game comes up on you in about 3-4 hours, regardless of how slow you take things, and how rushed and unfulfilling that final third of the game ends up being. The way the first two thirds it written, you expect there to be a massive cresendo in the game's plot that takes place over at least the same amount as was required to get you to the "mystery," but the mystery ends up blasting through its plot points, wrapping itself up over multiple sometimes weeks long time-skips, and overall missing the Twilight Zone ending (that I was hoping for) and leaves you with a Scooby Doo ending (that everyone got).

Since there is virtually no story impacting decisions presented in the game, the linear story line could have certainly been longer. I am not aware if it was monetary or creative choices that truncated the plot in the way it was, but if it is clear from the rest of my review, I wish it was longer! Graphics: 8/10

Mechanically, the game is easy to run and use, but I do have one bit of advice... whenever you pick up something, especially notes, make sure you put them in your inventory before telling D about them. Many times picking notes up and telling D about them will trigger a cutscene and fast forward you to the next game sequence without being able to keep the note. So pick up and hold ("E" on PC) the note then tell D about the note. I lost out on a couple of notes I didn't read because I was talking about them before reading or saving them in my inventory.

The game really doesn't have much replayability, but it's worth a run through if you like casual, atmospheric games, and if you can get it on sale. I would have been really unhappy paying $20 for this, but for $5 it was definitely worth it.

Cons: If you're prone to motion sickness (I am), be prepared to take regular breaks. However, with the graphic quality turned all the way up, this aspect wasn't as bad as I have experienced on some games. In some cases, I would have liked other options available like [spoiler]just being able to confiscate the campers' fireworks, but not confronting them[/spoiler]. Of course, maybe this option was there, and I just missed it. 

What would have made it even better: 
[list]
[*]Changes in weather: It was always sunny or clear night. Some rain would have been nice. Even a particularly windy day would have been a change
[*]Book collection: With all the books lying around, the collector in me wanted to bring them all back to my lookout. It'd be awesome to see an achievement for this [spoiler]minus the books that you can't access until you get to Delilah's Tower[/spoiler], and even better if there were some way to carry the books back to the tower, without them having to be in hand, [spoiler]similar to the turtle you can adopt[/spoiler].

[*]This may be a result of some areas I missed, but I would have liked to see more info/backstory come of the notes left [spoiler]by David and Ron[/spoiler]. I don't feel that lacking this has a negative impact on the game (on the contrary, I feel that what we get is a more realistic outsider view), but my curiosity was peaked, and I wanted to know more.
[/list]

I highly recommend this game if you like:
[list]
[*]World exploration
[*]Games with some grounding in reality
[*]Games that don't tie ends up in a nice, neat bow

I can't recommend this game, but I'll mention some pros and cons.  

PROS

[list]
    [*]Nice production quality, good graphics & sound, really makes you feel like you're hiking through parkland wilderness.
    [*]Good acting & well-written dialogue, with a well-paced story
    [*]Intriguing mystery that really makes you think and try to guess what's really happening. 
[/list] 

CONS

[list]
    [*]EXTREMELY linear. You are on rails from the beginning to the end. There are no meaningful "choices" you can make, whether in dialogue or in exploring the world. No matter which of the narrow options available you choose to pick, the game ignores your choice and plows ahead with the predetermined storyline. The game decides who you trust and who you don't, it decides how you respond to danger, etc.
    [*]Characters make really, really dumb choices. Frustrating if you've already figured out the mystery to see them stumbling ahead like idiots while you're powerless to stop them. Example: if you've been attacked by some stalker creep in the middle of nowhere, stop broadcasting where you are and where you're going on the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ radio! 
    [*]Very short game. You can finish in a few hours, and the game has zero replay value.
[/list]

Firewatch is a story about people who try to escape their problems. It's about flawed characters in a world where nothing is clear-cut. 

It's a walking simulator. The dialog is well-done, and the voice acting is the best I've ever heard in a game. The story is well-paced, with clear themes that cut into some issues that I'd really prefer not to think about -- but that's exactly the point. 

You can't escape your mistakes by running away. That's the idea behind most of the story. Each of the characters has their own problems that they want to avoid, and none of them deal with it in a healthy way. 

The most poignant part of the game, I think, was the ending (speaking of which, spoilers!). In the beginning, Henry wears his wedding ring, and it almost feels out of place how much it stands out while playing. But in the final shot, when Henry gets in the helicopter after having one last conversation with Delilah, his hand shoots out so he can catch his balance. The camera pauses on his hand, showing his bare ring finger for a few seconds before he looks out at the place he's leaving behind. Henry has left his ring behind, just as he's left his heart. I'm not sure if he's ever going to work up the courage to go see his wife again. 

It's a nice game. I liked it. Get it if you think you would, too.

Finished [b]Firewatch[/b] on the 13.Feb.2016


[b]Who are the game developers?[/b]
Campo Santo ([url=https://www.camposanto.com/]Campo Santo[/url])


[b]What's the game about?[/b]
Homer Simpson has a walkie talkie. The forest is on fire! And while not at the bar, Homer decides to help Marge put the fire out. While in that, he gets a dog, some naked girls and goes spelunking. It's weird!


[b]General feeling after finishing?[/b]
Campo Santo did something very special here (the fact I bought the game 2 days after its release and not 1.5 years into it says a lot, for me), and I'm sure I'm going to miss these guys [well, I'm not, because I own the game, but really I would like to see more from this "universe"].


[b]Story?[/b]
Over the course of an entire Summer, Henry performs duty as a fire lookout in Wyoming. On his first day, Delilah contacts him via walkie-talkie. Later on, she asks him to investigate stuff.
Henry learns about Brian.
Henry also discovers a radio and a clipboard with notes from talks with Delilah. He is knocked unconscious. He discovers a tracking device.
Henry enters a cave.
The next day, the fire at the camp has grown out of control. Ned tries to scare Henry away (who is Ned?). Drama ensues!
[mostly copied from Wikipedia with some of the juicy bits taken out. If you're still not interested, don't buy it :D]


[b]Gameplay?[/b]
"Walking simulator"? It's short enough that you don't get bored, and compelling enough to have you finish it as soon as possible. And unlike most other walking simulator it really has a lot of different stuff you can do, but focused mainly on exploration.


[b]Graphics?[/b]
Along with the voice acting, and story, the best the game has to offer. AAA if I ever saw one.


[b]Sound & Music?[/b]
Memorable enough that almost two years after having played it I can still hear some of the songs in my head.


[b]Replayability?[/b]
Sure, just writing this 2 years after the fact has got me installing the game again.


[b]Time played?[/b]
Around 8 hours (I played slowly as I wanted to explore everything).

[h1] Status: [/h1]Finished
[h1] Recommendations: [/h1]Oxenfree, Night in the Woods

[h1] Introduction [/h1]
I feel that Firewatch isn’t a game for most people. There’s a lot of people and friends I would not recommend this game to but if you’re already looking to buy it, this review is for you. I’ll prewar that this is almost less of a review and more of a love letter. I think all parts of this game are great and as you play through it fully wraps itself up nice and complete. Every little detail in this game was handcrafted to the story they wanted to tell. From the moment I started the game til the moment I finished it, I viewed myself as Henry the entire time.

[h1] Characters [/h1]
There are two main characters: Henry and Delilah. Henry is the main character, you make his decisions and you talk for him. The person you talk to is Delilah. There’s a lot that can be said about Delilah and it’s hard not to say I grew an attachment for her. As a character she was sweet with just enough sass that you could enjoy. She seemed like the kind of woman to take no ♥♥♥♥ but when she was scared it made sense. She was clearly written with a distinct idea in mind and her flaws are probably what made her a good character. I felt that the voice acting only made the characters come out stronger. They had good emotional range and it never felt like I was talking to someone putting on a voice unless of course they were.

[h1] Story and Script [/h1]
The most important aspect of the game and personally the reason why there’s nothing in this game I would change. Every little exchange you have with Delilah adds to the story bit my bit and as you play, you can clearly see the characters feeling for each other. Everything about the interactions is fantastically realistic and I found myself drawn into every moment and every word. From the relaxed banter to the panicked mutters, it was all so real which was only aided by the fantastic voice actors. Each time Henry and Delilah would sass each other I could feel myself giggle and when they were scared I was too. Their emotions easily influenced me and I can honestly say that this is the type of writing one aspires to do. I haven’t really mentioned the story so far and I think it’s better to just play the game with no idea of what’s to come. I honestly could have sat there and talked to Delilah for the entire game but I’m glad they decided to have a story that really drew me in. It’s a bit more on the realistic side and I feel that a lot of gamers won’t really appreciate it but as an avid reader, it was really refreshing for a game’s story.

[h1] Environment [/h1]
This is a beautiful game. Living in Australia this isn’t the type of landscape I can see or explore. Being able to walk through the game as Henry and every so often stopping to take photos, I feel was a great experience. It feels like all the little details in the game are really lovely. Even though each area looked distinct enough, I did find myself getting lost and walking the wrong way but I strongly feel that, that’s a me thing. I think that the most spectacular part though was how they used the environment to section off areas for you to unlock later. It was a brilliant use of design and made perfect sense. I feel all in all that the environment, the trees, streams and canyon areas, really tie the game and story together.

 [h1] Soundtrack [/h1]
I will be listening to this soundtrack for the rest of my life. I think every song is perfectly atmospheric and add to the mystery that slowly amounts through the game. Each song made with the sole intention to truly sink the feelings you’re currently having in. They beautifully reflect what is happening or about to happen. All of the really peaceful songs set in as you walk into an area for the first time and it just makes my heart sing. You could almost say they use silence in this game far more then they use sound but when they do, they do it perfectly. I’d also like to make a little note that the choice of credit song was fantastic. While I’m pretty sure it was picked based on the idea that the people playing this game are on the older side, I still loved it. I grew up with this song and it really, for me, tied the game up perfectly.

[H1] What Makes it Special? 100/100 [/h1]
There’s not a single thing I would change about this game and sure there’s a lot of you who would disagree but this game was so well written. I loved every moment of it. I craved to play the game when I couldn’t and if I could go through again with fresh eyes it would be a fantastic experience. As I have stated again and again through this review every little thing was handcrafted. Each feature and idea they put their all into. This was a game made with love and while I was playing it, I felt that love. If you do like walking simulator type games, this is a must buy.

Overall, this is an amazing, beautiful game with an interesting and unique art style. The characters and story are engaging and the dialogue between the two main characters are funny, well written and at times very deep. However, I will say, two thirds of the game create this tense, creepy atmosphere and by the last act heading toward the less than climatic "twist" ending, the game left a little to be desired. So, even though the last third falls a little flat for me, the game is very enjoyable and shouldn't be ignored by anyone with $10 - $15  and a couple hours to kill.

Let me start by saying I hardly ever write reviews, for video games, products, or really anything, so excuse the poor formatting. This game had been on my wishlist for quite some time, and after seeing it on sale I finally decided to pick it up and check it out. The first thing that struck me was the delivery of the game, very pleasing and it made me feel involved. Then I was sucked in by the voice acting and visual aspects of the game. The dialog choices really made me feel like I had a choice, and I was actually out in that damn forrest. I have not played a game in some time that made me "feel". It made me want to go volunteer and run away and live a different life. It made me mad, and worried for the characters. If there is a thing as a video game novel, this game would take the cake for me. Before this I tried Vanishing of Ethan Carter and couldn't quite get into it so I was afraid of what this game might be, but all my fears were put to ease with Firewatch and honestly gave this type of game a new life for me. 

However, with all good must come bad right? You are absolutely right. My total in game time is 3 hours. Just three, and I finished it, while I have heard and read about its replayability I have zero desire to do anything again. It is sort of like those books where you choose your fate by going to certain pages, I don't want to change my fate. A game that sucked me into this emotional rollercoaster just seemed to end way too soon. I did get the game on sale, so I felt my money was well spent, however I am glad I did not pay full price for the game as I feel it would have swayed my judgement due to the short playtime. 

All in all I would recommend this game, if it is on sale. It was a lot of fun and I have not stopped thinking/talking about it to my friends, but that same talking about it comes with a warning. A warning that this game is very short. I wasn't looking for a 50+ hours of gametime game, but if I can finish it in 3 hours it feels a little like a college project that blew up, in fact even Stardew Valley lasted longer. It may sound like I am bashing the game, but I truly loved it, just wish there was more of it!

I want to avoid spoilers in this review, so I won't discuss any specific details about the plot and the specifics of what happens in the game at all since the game is very plot driven.

First, I want to get the positives out of the way. Firewatch is basically a beautiful-looking game. The screenshots from the store page is what it really looks like in game. Sure, it has more of a cartoonish artstyle, but it doesn't go overboard with it like some other games tend to do. Everything is modeled on real life things, but if you don't like that kind of art style then I totally understand why you wouldn't want to play it. Firewatch also runs very well. No frame drops, and no stuttering, especially on computers that are on the lower end (like when I played this game on my old PC). The sound design is also really top notch, with the voice acting and dialogue being perhaps one of the best I've ever heard from an indie game.

My main issue though is a couple of things. Tthe game is really short. I was able to beat it in under 4 hours. Now sometimes that can be to the game's benefit, as it never drags on for too long, since you'll beat it really soon anyways. I think that that aspect of the game works in part, however I do feel like there are questions that are never answered, or at the very least are left feeling very empty inside, and that's my biggest problem with the game.

The first half of the game is superb. It really builds up the suspense and atmosphere, however it does nothing to address any of those things by the end, as it doesn't feel like it ends correctly. Perhaps if they had taken a few more hours to flesh out some of the plot points, then I think that this game would be much better. I'm trying to avoid spoilers as much as possible, so I'm trying to keep it as vague as possible. The ending just felt rushed, which I think hurt the game in the long run.

The other aspect of the game is what will probably be the biggest turn-off for some people. This game is essentially a walking sim with an okay-ish story. The entire game consists of you walking from point A to point B, a little bit of dialogue, and then you move to the next area. While that part doesn't bother me too much, I do have an issue with the directions as to which your player is limited to. I think it would've been better if I was free to explore the park, instead of being forced on a limited path.

Again, I want to iterate that this game isn't garbage by any means. There are plenty of things to like about the game, and there are things that I really did like about it. Truly. However I think one of the biggest parts of the game, arguably the biggest part, didn't work for me, and when the whole game relies on the story, and it's only meh, then there's a problem.

I want to state that this is only my opinion. You may like the story, and that's perfectly fine. I just think, from a more objective point of view, that there was a lot of room for an incredible game, but the developers didn't do enough to capture the idea I think they had. But that's just my opinion.

Just finished this game in one sitting. 

Overall, a brilliant game with fantastic characters, voice acting, and atmosphere. 

I thought that both of the main characters, Delilah and Henry, were really well developed as people. The dialogue is written astonishingly well (for a video game). You really do get to see the way their relationship organically develops and the way in which they begin to trust (or not trust?) each other. Being able to pick certain dialogue options, and then seeing those options actively affect the narrative was satisfying as well as engaging. 

The voice acting was just absolutely fantastic. They got one of the guys from Mad Men, and the actor for Delilah was just great. There was so much dialogue in the game that had it been handled by VA's who were much less competent, it could have been really forced and cringy. Thankfully, this is some of the best voice acting I've seen in a video game. And the soundtrack was great as well.

The atmosphere was absolutely my favorite part of this game. There are some very beautiful and picturesque moments in this game. I don't think the game fully took advantage of the style it had at times, and wished it had allowed itself more often to indulge in it's unique look. I really liked the New Deal style of art that was going on in this game. They definetly could have taken advantage of that more. There are even times in this game where the atmosphere creates intense levels of suspense. Just play it and see.

I do sort of feel that the writing suffered in terms of the overall narrative. Without spoiling too much, I think that at times the overall pace of the narrative could have been better. Sometimes I felt like I really had to fill in the gaps in terms of my imagination in regards to the development of Delilah and Henry's relationship (I know I said earlier this was one of my favorite parts: it is, however I think they could have done a little better). On the whole I was not upset with the story like many are. I actually sort of appreciated the direction they decided to take. But it felt as though overall the narrative could have been stronger, because they had laid the foundation throughly to explore a lot of different avenues without really doing enough with it. 

Sometimes the map design could have been more inspired. By the end of the game, I had become a lot less interested in the sights of the game. It just felt less inspired than it could have been. 

The most glaring problem with this game is its technical issues. Buggy graphics at times when vaulting up stones or even walking across landscapes. Stuff like that. Which is dissapointing but not game breaking by any means. But for a games that heavily relys on immersion, this is a problem. 

On the whole, fantastic game. It went a whole different direction than I expected (I was a lot more scared than I thought I'd be!) but it was a very rewarding and worthwhile experience. Definetely recommend playing in one sitting. Have fun!

The first half of this game is phenomenal. Mundane slice of life about a middle-aged dude with huge personal baggage (and considerable actual baggage), in beautiful surrounds. 

 The second half strays from the grounded premise into 'tv drama', though. Never leans into the 'fantastic' but definitely breaks from the mundane 'human problems' setting of the first half of the game.

Dialogue is excellent, and makes up 70% of the game. Rest of the game is spent walking through beautiful but static and linear surrounds. The game is a walking simulator through-and-through. There's some really chewy dialogue choices but very little decisions to be made otherwise, and ultimately even your dialogue choices won't count for much (though the game does definitely pay attention).

Also don't expect to get a perfect happy ending at the end of this. I felt it was clear where the game was going given its tone but I have read a lot of disappointed reactions due to this. The entire game is really about how you can never really escape your problems - don't expect it to tie up neatly at the end.


The game is only about 4 hours long and has limited replayability, unless you play through again with the Developer's Commentary (which I haven't). There's also a 'free roam' mode but by the end of the main game you will have explored the whole park anyway.

But it all falls apart in the third act. The story loses its thread; it's almost like they were told to publish the game *now* and they just decided to end things where they were. They could have done so much more with the main two characters. As it is, there is so much potential wasted. I don't need a "tidy ending" in a game like this, but the mystery aspect of the game doesn't inform your character's motivation at all...and prevents the game from reaching a larger, more satisfying character development for him. If I had a magic wand to wave and could put this game back into development for another year, would the writing have turned out better?

I also wish the choices didn't railroad you so heavily into flirting, but I guess that's what the creators wanted.

Firewatch is a story that explores a trove of human emotions that aren't usually covered in video games. The game explores the regret, pain, tarnished hopes and the very nature of just running away from it all. Despite the depths of such emotions, you see a story of a relationship that blooms between the actors as they were set on a path from a series of mysterious events. If the game spoke to you in an emotional manner, that itself is enough for you to play it a second time to change the way your relationship played out. 

Props to the developers for developing an 'Audio Tour' DLC. I have never replayed a game to experience a different ending/story. This was the first. And it was largely due to the Audio Tour. [h1]Into the Shoshone[/h1]
http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1241247199
Walking simulator. In gaming as we know it today that term has a rather negative connotation stuck to it, normally associating the game with three things: that it’s going to be short, extremely linear, and almost entirely narratively reliant. The genre used to deserve this connotation, with the majority of its games containing extremely poor stories and relying wholly on their perception as “art”. As it stands though, I fully believe that the title of walking simulator is now as valid a genre as any other, and that it’s finally outgrown the previous negativity surrounding it. Now, in stark contrast to previous associations, recent walking simulators have more positive implications: that they’re going to have exemplary stories, gorgeous worlds, and some of the greatest characters and dialogue possible. Firewatch perfectly compounds all of that, and really is symbolic of these new walking simulators that focus on actually trying to create an unforgettable experience instead of seemingly playing the “games as art” card to excuse their mistakes. Firewatch wastes no time creating said experience and right from the get go you start forming attractions to the two, arguably three, main characters. First off is Henry, a gruff boyfriend-turned-husband with an extraordinary personality who you’re going to be playing as all throughout your journey. Second comes Julia, not a main character but included anyways since she plays an important part in the story as Henry’s wife. Sadly, before the game begins you find Julia is beginning to show symptoms of early-onset dementia, slowly killing her and stressing Henry out to the point he takes on a job as a Forest Fire Lookout in the Shoshone to get a break. Lastly comes my favorite character Delilah, your supervisory lookout who you never actually see, but can visualize better than any other. Again, there’s really only two main characters, as Julia is more of an idea used to push the game forward than an actual character, which might seem a problem but instead is a unique way to focus attention on character development. When you only have two real characters, it’s a lot easier to flesh out their dialogue and make every conversation have value. I appreciate that they didn’t become too ambitious and try to have a full cast, because there’s something indescribably serene about interacting exclusively with Delilah for something of four hours. It’s intimate. It’s personal. It’s Firewatch. 

[h1]A Trek to Remember[/h1]
http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1241224067
I'd argue that Firewatch’s two strongest features are the exceptional artwork and the absolutely unparalleled character development/dialogue, though not the only two strong features, these two were just the ones that stood out from my first playthrough. Artwork is one of the most critical aspects to a game’s success, though plenty of people would love to claim otherwise, and is intertwined with many other gameplay elements. For example, environment design and immersion are both nigh impossible with poor graphics, and if there’s no immersion or decent environment design then gameplay suffers, causing a catastrophic chain reaction. While there may be other games that have to worry about sub-par artwork, Firewatch is absolutely not one of them, having the most unique and attractive aesthetic I’ve ever seen. Artwork is an important part of building atmosphere and can heavily influence how you feel about the game, and I think Firewatch’s serene and peaceful air is built heavily on the fact that its art is so calming and beautiful. While this may have just been me, I found the game about an hour longer than expected, and I feel that can be attributed to me taking my time and genuinely wanting to just enjoy the scenery. I’ve never experienced anything like that before, Firewatch wholly immersed me in Henry’s character, as if I’m actually living in the Shoshone, with my only link to civilization being a small orange walkie-talkie. Looking back at my experience with Firewatch feels more like reminiscing on the past than it does playing a game, and I think that's caused by the various gameplay mechanics that pile even more immersion on top of what’s already there. My favorite one is the disposable camera you find about halfway through the game, allowing you to take pictures of the various parts of the environment. While that would be pretty neat on its own, the ability to upload your pictures online and to purchase high quality prints of them on the Firewatch website takes the feature from being neat to being unforgettable. What’s more, this literally gives you a physical way to remember and reminisce on your playthrough, an innovative idea that works well with how walking simulators tend to feel closer to experiences than games. I appreciate that, the small things put into the game to add detail and make this feel like a genuine world, I really do. 

[h1]All Adventures Have an End[/h1]
http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1241250035
Now story quality is irrelevant if you can’t experience it due to horrible gameplay decisions obstructing the narrative with pointless or poorly designed mechanics. Firewatch has none of this and maintains a simple method of interaction with your environment, really only requiring you to press a button to interact with whatever you’re looking at. I enjoy this simplicity because more often than not complex game design, especially in walking simulators, tends to focus attention on the mechanic instead of the atmosphere, shattering your immersion with mechanics that seem out of place. Firewatch however has an extremely minimalistic UI that borders on pretty much none, only really showing up when you interact with the world or talk to Delilah on the radio. The gameplay is simple enough to where it’s not like you’d really need any UI at all, it isn’t particularly hard to just go around pressing E on different things you find in the environment after all. I am however glad that they didn’t make this entirely devoid of gameplay because it gives you something to do, even if that something is just pressing E on a door or radio, it still makes you feel involved without breaking immersion. Gameplay isn’t really what you’re playing Firewatch for though and ,while it’s extremely well implemented, it isn’t the game’s main focus, that would be the story. Firewatch has a story unlike most others that I’ve seen, because it tries to avoid telling a story of aliens, heroes, or what else could have been, and instead focuses on being real. Firewatch has a story that, to me, feels like a retelling of a friends vacation, all believable and real, but with a few minor details embellished or twisted to sound better and build suspense. Many people have a problem with the game's ending and honestly I’m torn: on one hand, they really built the ending up in a direction it clearly never had any intention of going, but on the other it’s a story of Henry and Delilah’s real suspense, and real mystery. It’s not the satisfying conclusion that I was hoping for, but it’s symbolic of the whole journey, it may not be the greatest ending in the world, but I think that it still has significant merit to it and ties in well with the themes all throughout Firewatch.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Firewatch has the most intimately personal dialogue of any game I’ve ever played, with characters to match, and provided a beautiful, if short, experience I’ll never forget.

I don't normally do reviews, but I wanted to review this one.

To start, this “game” is a 5-6 hour story driven walking simulator … I’m not even joking.  BUT, with that said, I really didn't mind it at all.  It is important to realize that this is not a game in a traditional sense.  It is closer to being an interactive short-story than a game.

The year is 1989 and you play Henry who takes a job as a fire lookout in Shoshone National Forest for personal reasons.  Then slowly, things start to get a bit creepy.

I might be wrong, but I felt the developers were purposefully striving to make you feel like that you were actually in the story in a way… and for me, they succeeded.  I got a sense of hiking and being in the wilderness.  Plus, I got the occasional feeling of being vulnerable and confused.  I found myself looking over my shoulder a few times.  And honestly, I thought it was cool that I felt compelled to do that.

The story hooked me and ultimately left me feeling a bit melancholy in the end… like I had just watched the movie "Stand By Me" (if that makes any sense).  The story also felt realistic in a “this really could have happened” sort of way.  And much like real life, the ending will not tie everything in a nice pretty bow for you, but I had enough closure that I was satisfied and didn’t feel cheated.

The visuals and ambiance were great and the occasional background music set the tone when needed.  The pacing of the game was good.  And the voice acting was VERY well done and is simply what makes this game great.  I guess this is why I didn’t mind all the in-gaming walking.  The game simply never got boring to me.  The story pushed me, so the 6-hour playtime felt quick.

As for normal price of $20, I would say pass… and wait for a proper sale.  It is definitely worth a play through in my opinion, but not for $20.  I paid $8 during the winter sale and after completing the game that price felt about right to me.

[h1][b]Firewatch		* 9/10[/b][/h1]

Alone in a watchtower, guarding the forest and the entire park for fires and troubles. A quiet work, appearently, until odd things start to happen.

[h1][i]INTRO. What is Firewatch about?[/i][/h1]
It's 1989, you're Henry and you've just reached the watchtower of this park. You will be alone watching over the forest and your only human contact is Delilah, your supervisor that will give you tasks and advices. Job starts quietly with small trips from point to point, some nice chat with your boss and so on, but soon you will witness odd events and notthing will be the same.

Sounds generic, I know, but you will get to know Henry a lot more than it sounds, understanding the reason that brought him to this hermit life, the only human relation you're about to have will grow and evolve, and what you are about to see will involve you, make you suspicious, paranoid and worried. A story that seems incredible but not impossible.

[h1][i]GRAPHIC. Engine And Artistic aspects.[/i][/h1]
Made with Unity, the map (the park) is quite big, but you will obtain the necessary tools to reach all places along with your playthrough. The aspect is almost ALMOST cartoonish, with simple textures but no cel shading, yet the landscapes and places are simply marvelous. A canyon, a lake, planes, caves, the forest, everything is worth admiring for a second even though textures are quite essential. Locations have been realized with great care for details resulting in the beautiful park you can walk in.

[h1][i]SOUNDTRACK. Themes and Accompaniments.[/i][/h1]
You will rarely hear music during the game, but what you hear is simple yet very effective, simple movements, some classic guitar. Few tunes only during the right moments. Gives a stronger sense of loneliness walking through the park without hearing anything but nature and your own steps.

[h1][i]GAMEPLAY. How does it work?[/i][/h1]
Walking simulator. Nuff said. First person, you walk around, you can interact with specific objects and you can pick up a handful of items to use around in different specific occasions. The most interesting part however is the radio. You have a radio to communicate with Delilah. Sometimes she'll call you and lots of time you can call her... Mainly to report things and objects you find or need help with. And you can speak with her, chosing answers, or sentences according to the tone you want to use or the matter you want to talk about. In this lone place it's natural to be willing to speak with Delilah about as many things as you can. And it's made on purpose...

[h1][i]LAST NOTES. What doesn't work?[/i][/h1]
Nothing I guess. Unless you're looking for action but then I'd be surprised you're giving attention to a Walking simulator.

[h1][i]TL;DR. Pros And Cons[/i][/h1]
[h1]+++PROs+++[/h1][list]
[*][b] STORY.[/b] Harry's story, Delilah, and everything that is going to happen in the park. Everything is well written and so human. I can't say much because I don't want to spoil the core of the game, but it's worth it.
[*][b] THE PARK.[/b] It's, simply put, beautiful. There are Wonderful environments and landscapes to see and the paradox is that textures are so simple and almost cartoonish.

A poignant mix of walking simulator, explorer, and eBook, Firewatch pulls you in to a continuously deepening mystery with an emotional undertone, all whilst expereiencing the joys of forming a new relationship with a stranger via the radio.
The dialogue is repeatedly funny, appropriate, and the options usually cover all trains of thought - the one cavét being that you can never start a conversation, only respond to the messages you receive. 
You can, however, comment on what you encounter in your environment, and it is this aspect of exploring the world and discovering objects that brings Firewatch in to its own. 

Firewatch begins by giving you tasks to familiarise yourself with the world around you and how you can traverse it. As you progress, more of the world opens up through different objectives and tools which grant you access to previously cordened off areas. While this sounds unfavourable, the game is short (by modern standards) and the world is sufficiently detailed and expansive to the point where you never feel confined or bored.

As some have pointed out, the gripping mystery that unravels is what motivates you through your days on Firewatch which mainly focus on the begininng and end. While the ending may be anticlimatic for some, I for one believe we have become too used to twists, big surprises, and massive plot shifts in our media, and happily welcome a nice, neat conclusion that doesn't quite resolve the problem at hand theoretically, but does practically for the player.

Firewatch is well worth the ~5 hours of playtime and, combined with the art style and auditory accompaniments, will leave you happier for having experienced its world.

I had some performance issues, which is surprising considering the game doesnt appear to require real graphical power - it just seems the game loses focus sometimes (when reading/writing), bringing horrid low fps. Thankfully tabbing out and in fixes it (til it happens again...)

The game has a few more negatives. Actual gameplay is as simplistic as it comes, and there was some glitching on the landscape (getting stuck) which can break immersion. It didnt happen too often at least, and I never had to restart, just wriggle about a bit to get free. Its a real pity because these dings against the game mean I cannot shout to anyone who would care to listen to buy this gem!

Really enjoyed the game when I first started it. There seemed to be a good background story, excellent voice-acting by the two main characters, great environment to explore - atmospheric lighting and mist/smoke and ambient sounds and event/location-triggered music.

As time went by, game-play became a little repetitive and on the verge of being boring. But occasionally something unexpected would happen, or you'd discover a hidden 'treat', which would get you going for a while.

Much is hinted at in the way the plot unravels depending on the answers you give in radio conversations with your boss, Delilah - but I found this only seemed to affect subsequent conversation rather than the plot itself.

Having played it through three times (and once you know where the locations are, you can zip through the game in under 2 hours or so) -and taking different attitudes towards Delilah and my character's 'estranged' wife in the attempt to manipulate a different ending, or series of events, I couldn't. I think this is a trick lost by the authors, it would have made the game so much more interesting and made for very much better 'replayability'.

For example, travel throughout the forest and mountains could have been made more interesting with small surprises to break your walk - eg, glimpses of wildlife, interacting with other rangers or perhaps tourists.

And the tension could have been increased with even simple distant glimpses of shadowy figures, reflections off their binoculars in the trees... just something that made you feel you weren't simply yomping from one event or trigger-point to the next.

No harm of any kind (other than hard-scripted into the story) can come to your character - why not add a risk element that might hamper the character's search, or even put him in harm's way which might even end the game or level?

In the end, it played like an animated graphic novel, rather than a video game. Well written, well acted and actually quite poignant and moving. I enjoyed it admired many of the production values, but was left feeling it could have been just a little bit more. Having gone through it three times, I won't play it again.

My stint as a fire lookout was a masterclass in unparalleled excellence. It is every day that you come across someone with my unique set of skills, which are a bizarre mix of overconfidence and utter incompetence of breaking every record for incompetence and ineptitude.

The navigation was practically my playground. I would take a map and compass in hand, and then proceed to march confidently in precisely the opposite direction of where I needed to go. It was all part of my grand plan to explore the untrodden paths of the forest, and I did it with unparalleled gusto. I had a magnetic attraction to the opposite direction of wherever I was supposed to be. I would constantly wander off course, trampling through bushes and making my own trails.

When it came to maintenance, I brought a whole new level of chaos to the job. Repairs? The moments where I decided to rearrange the mess to make it messier? The nails and boards were no match for my "unique" approach to handiwork. The tower is still shaking its metaphorical head at my efforts.

As for spotting fires, I took it as a personal challenge to see how oblivious one person could be. The flames could be dancing merrily in the distance, and I would be entranced by a squirrel or mesmerized by a particularly scenic cloud. I guess my dedication to not spotting fires was commendable in its own absurd way. I would be be gazing at the serene forest, completely oblivious to the growing flames just a stone's throw away.

Communication was another area where I shone bright. Delilah would ask me profound questions, and I would respond with cryptic monosyllables, as if I was the guardian of a secret language known only to me. It was an art, turning meaningful conversations into head-scratching puzzles.

What is Firewatch? It's a first-person mystery adventure game. More than that Firewatch is a game which sets out to do just a very few relatively simple things. On a conceptual level, it sounds fairly unambitious and even limited. This is a game where the story is the draw and, while it is far more interactive than other games where that is the case, it is entirely devoid of what you might call challenge, at least in the mechanical senses.

Games like these have varied in success. With Gone Home being hailed a critical darling and a must own for any self-proclaimed gamer. While Everybody’s Gone To The Rapture being well liked by some and considered fairly bland by others. Firewatch shares traits with these games, but, I can honestly say it raises the bar. 

I don't want to say too much about the story so as not to spoil things, but Firewatch is much more of a game than some of these so-called "walking simulators" it is frequently compared to. While - as noted above - it lacks any fail states or explicit sense of achievement, this is not a game where you simply wander around the environment from point to point triggering non or minimally interactive snippets of story. You have agency within an environment which has a genuine sense of place and feels like a real location out in the wilderness. You have input into the narrative and you actively participate in it.

Firewatch will go down as one of my favorite games, an honor I think it completely deserves. It’s a beautiful piece of art that touches on notions and themes that few other game can say they have done better.

It's been called a "walking simulator" but in all honesty I'm not sure if I can even call this a game.  See to me a game has to provide some kind of obsticle to challenge the player to be called a game,  

While video games often resort to obsticles trying to kill you, a game certainly doesn't need violence to challenge a player, but it needs something.  This game really doesn't really have much in the way of such obsticles.  You pick things up and look at them, you talk to your supervisor, and you walk around, and if you come to what looks like a dead end, your supervisor will point you in the right direction.  So I'm not sure I can call this a game, though it makes for an interesting interactive experiance.  

The world is colorful, There are choices to be made in how Henry responds to Delilah that can effect their relationship.  Henry and Delilah feel like actual people and not caricatures.   

Furthermore the game does a better job making tragedy believable in the first 5 minutes of play using simple text, then most AAA games do  with visually dramatic opening sequences.  Even those who have never watched a family member go through Dementia will find it hard to fight the feels that the opening gives you just by text alone.  

Some who have played this find the ending anticlimatic, but then such is the way of life, and I think that's what the dev's were going for, real people facing situations in a realistic manner.  

In closing If your looking for a game to challenge you, you might want to look elsewhere.  But if you're looking for an well thought out and put together interactive experiance that won't make you want to smash your keyboard, you may want to give this a try.

Pros:
- Well illustrated
- Original idea for the story (being in firewatch towers, being isolated, not having much human contact)

Cons:
- Terrible movement system that forces you to watch an animation every time you want to climb over a rock, of which there are way too many put in your path for no reason.
- Extremely "on the rails", exploring is pointless, and paths of where you can go are super limited
- There is a whole system for choosing dialogue which seems like it's letting you shape the story/your character, but no matter what you choose, it's actually the same basic story. Pointless.
- Way too much running around for long distances for no reason
- Story has a great buildup, but falls extremely flat


Overall:
Would have been better as an animated show, than a game, there's almost zero reason for player input. The only time you're actually doing anything as a player is when you're running from point a to point b which takes up to 10 minutes sometimes. But if it was an animated show, I think people would realize that the story was pretty damn weak. People keep trying to give it a pass and explain around it, but if you think of this game as a show, I think it's pretty obvious that nobody would consider it a good show, and since it has literally nothing else to offer other than being essentially a show, that makes it a pretty lackluster piece of work. The concept was really cool, and original, I liked the idea that the main characters were out in the woods isolated and that the only way they had to build the story was through dialogue, but I think a LOT more could have been done with the framework they created. All in all I'd say...

Not worth it. But I'd like to see someone use a similar framework but write a better story.

The in-game world is really beautiful (I personally love the wilderness despite living in suburban Maryland). The backstory is quite sad but does serve to root the story from the beginning. 

Without spoiling anything - I can see the ending from both ways people are split (yes - I was disappointed and a bit angry at the ending...but I think after reading some explanations and analysis of it I'm a lot more "okay" with it than before). 

AS far as story-telling and unique games - I would give this an absolute 10/10 rating. However...given the slight disappointment of the ending along with the relatively short play time - I might knock it back to an 8. 

I think the storylines and gameplay of titles like Life is Strange is far more long winded and engaging. At the same time, for the amount of money paid for this game I cannot give it points off. 

I would even play this one or two more times to see if some of my decisions or responses on the radio would alter the story line at all (it will not alter the ending, however). 

It's worth picking it up if it's well priced.

Firewatch is an entertaining, albeit unsatisfying open world first person narrative game with a unique art style and minimalistic soundtrack. The story that it tells is one of a man who leaves his wife [spoiler] who is diagnosed with early onset dementia [/spoiler] and takes a job as a watchman for a parks service. 

The art style is what sets Firewatch apart from other games in its genre. It's animated similarly to the style of Fortnite or TF2 but also mixes a hand-drawn look into it too.  

Mechanically, the game's UI is average. It performs as it's supposed to, no more and no less. The controls are easy to pick up and use, with the only catch being the map and compass buttons, and constantly having to open and reopen the map. 

This game sounds good, but often has no music playing anyway. You might even be better off turning the music off completely and focusing on the nature sounds in the background of the game. I'm honestly not sure why the developers also sell the soundtrack, because I can't assume it contains more than maybe 3 songs, and they just weren't played that often. 

I completed the game in about 5 hours, which was a stretch to justify spending $20 on it. The story ended abruptly and in my opinion didn't resolve the story because [spoiler] I never got to see Delilah or my wife Julia in person after evacuating from the fire and also there was no end conflict with the two girls or with the man who killed his son.[/spoiler]

Looking at the game as a whole, it looks and sounds good, tells a moving but unresolved story, and is completed very early when considering value. Unfortunately I can't recommend it.

Lost Interest half way through, It is essentially a walking simulator with little gameplay or challenge. The Story is where this game is supposed to shine.  I will admit, It is well acted and the interactions between the two main characters are well written and does feel like two strangers trying to get along. But the problem I have with these interactions is how the game uses them. The game gives you multiple choice of how you interact with each other so I thought the character and games story would change depending on what your choices were. That is not the case; I found the story and characters were set on one  path from beggining to end with my doing little to no change, It also came to my attention after reading others thoughts on the game that the payoff to the story was disappointing for some and since I was already losing interest I dropped it. 
 Now gameplay wise well its a walking simulator you walk from point a to point b with no enemies and few obstacles to block your path. What few you do come by. Well. Just push the action button to watch a short preanimated action as your character does said action to get through. Such as Jumping over logs, climbing up small ledges, or using items you find in the game.  All while you walk around looking at your map ( and I mean stopping to look at a map not one in the corner o the screen) to find a certain path you can take to get where you need to be. All while interacting with the other character via walkie talkie about the scenery or whatever. 
Speaking of scenery this game is really pretty  sounds great and is beautifully rendered as most walk simulators tend to be. While stylized it definitely gives the feeling of walking through nature. A lot of effort was put into creating this national park landscape from the sound and flow of a stream. To the breeze and movement of grass it does not disappoint on that front. just watch a trailer or look at a screen shot. 
In conclusion I would say this game would have been better as an animated movie then a game. With a lot emphasis on the story and visuals, and with no real challenge in gameplay  unless you call getting temporarily side tracked cause of a high ledge or hill challenging. Clocking in at just over 3 hours  for most players. With a $21.99 pricetag  and no replay value since it will play out the same story. Hoo boy, lot I'd LIKE to say, but instead I'll try to be brief.
-PREFACE- This is my OPINION, and I share it so others might get a little perspective and compare it with their OPINIONS. i.e.; no whining, no crying, no arguing, no "fanboy" BS, if you found it helpful then thumbs up, if not then thumbs down. Simple.

While the game is well done, I feel it missed a lot of opportunities and had FAR too little choice and interaction involved. Firewatch looks pretty good, but the graphics are extremely animation-y/ cartoon-y/ low res. Firewatch sounds pretty good except for some of the random "forest noises", which do not sound like random forest noises at all. The voice acting is pretty solid, if extremely limited. The story is... well, it's just OK, really. Not going to spoil anything, but they could have done A LOT more with the story, plus it's short, short, SHORT.  Also, for a game in which your primary activity is moving around (walking/running) the movement system in Firewatch is TERRIBLE. Half the time it feels like you're not even moving and the other half of the time you AREN'T moving because you got stuck in a bush/rock/tree/creek/crevice/molehill/ YOU NAME IT, all because you dared to venture off the path and explore....Which... Hang on, I thought exploring was THE WHOLE POINT of these types of "games"?!??

My biggest hang-up and reason for the thumbs down? The entire premise of the game coupled with how it was handled. Maybe I just don't think that whatever genre this is should BE a genre, Idunno. I'll try to explain; Imagine you bought a new movie that you wanted to see. You get home, stick it in the player, press play.. watch 5 minutes... then it pauses... and you have to press play again...watch ten more minutes... have to press play again... Come to find out that the ENTIRE movie is that way. Watch a little-press play, watch a little-press play. This is what "playing" Firewatch feels like. This is NOT a game by my standards, this is a full on movie that keeps stopping (SOMEONE CLEAN THAT DISK!!). Also it's absolutely one of the MOST linear experiences I've had in front of my computer in a long time. You are on rails, the ENTIRE time, you cannot leave said rails, you can look around, but very quickly don't want to because, A) not much to see, B)you are just prolonging the overall time you will be forced to be on rails, and C)you're probably gonna get stuck in something. Honestly? I wish I had just watched someone play the whole thing on Youtube. I would not have missed out on anything (linear, set ending), I would not have wasted my time, and I would not have wasted my money.

Would I recommend it? Sure... For 3-4 bucks. That's about the value point I would attribute to this.

Are there good things? You bet. Are there bad things? Yup, plenty. Honestly, if you enjoy whatever type of "game " that this is, you'll probably enjoy this. If, however, you think that a game should have some game elements in it, then this may not be for you.

With the sun having long since disappeared below the horizon and endless acres of forest warding off the artificial light of civilization, its flames flood the night sky with incandescent hues. It's a natural brush fire, unlikely to do much harm, so for now I rest my elbows on the railing that surrounds my lookout tower and admire the view. A nearby transceiver crackles to life. It's Delilah, radioing from her own tower several miles away. She comments on the fire, how beautiful it looks, how it's all smoke and ash during the day but utterly resplendent under the cover of darkness. And it is. But over time, the fire spreads, and as its intensity escalates, so too does the tension of the narrative.

Finished my fourth playthrough. Yes, it (almost) ends the same way every time, but that's not the point. Playing Firewatch is like watching a favorite movie again and again: because of its atmosphere, its actors, its scenery. It doesn't have a lot of cutscenes, though. Most of the time, what you do and the way you behave is absolutely up to you.

I really liked the way dialogue options were presented. The different choices along with the timer really make you think about what to say next, and the conversation can take completely different turns. 

You can also find some nice gadgets, like the camera or the turtle, which aren't really necessary for solving the game, but add a personal touch to your experience.

All of these things help you feel "at home"; it's your time in the lookout, your summer in the Shoshone.

But what makes this game so exceptional in my opinion is the way it makes you care about the characters – and that's amazing considering you hardly ever meet anyone. Henry and Delilah are not your typical stand-ins, but people with a real personality, and their chemistry is remarkable. The voice acting is superb, but like in a good movie, a good book, so much that's important is left unsaid, however you can feel it right under the surface. The only thing that maybe doesn't work for everybody is that some plot points might be hidden too good; it all makes perfect sense if you spend enough time in this world, but it's possible to miss some explanations when you rush through the game. Which you shouldn't, because it's too beautiful.

Firewatch is a single-player first-person mystery set in the Wyoming wilderness, where your only emotional lifeline is the person on the other end of a handheld radio. Yes, it's a walking sim.

So let's get the obvious out of the way first. Firewatch is a walking sim. No running and gunning, no arcade elements, some dialogue choices. I have to say I luv me a walking sim. And this is one of the best. Dealing with some personal troubles you take a job far away from civilisation, summer spent in the middle of nowhere, to clear your head and deal with current worries.

The game is short, at around 4 hours, during which you'll travel around the beautiful environments, deal with your traumas and uncover new mysteries while having only one other human to talk to, a fellow ranger - Delilah. I read a lot about this game, and I expected a good game and a poor ending. I got excellent game and ok ending. I understand how some poeple might feel everything is leading to a climax and then nothing happens, but to me the ending was in line with all of the game.

Anyhow, if you like walking simulators or adventure games in general this is one of the best walking sims I experienced. If you like the genre even a little bit and/or like slowly told human stories just play this. You will not be disappointed.

[b]Story [/b]

[b]Mechanics[/b]

It's disappointing that, even as Generation X moves steadily into middle age, the games designed to appeal to the First Video Game Generation are still saddled with the campy, melodramatic conventions of comic books, B movies, and television.

Other than Kentucky Route Zero, Portal and possibly Dear Esther, there isn't much to recommend in the interactive experience category if one is a well-read, well-watched adult with little ingrained patience for complex control schemes and video gamey tropes.

I was really getting into Firewatch. There was some interesting meat there. Two strangers, separated by space, getting to know each other over the radio, possibly the subject of an unethical study, lonely, rough backstories full of mistakes and regret, good characterization, decent voice acting...

And then suddenly there was all this pseudo-thriller drammuh - property destruction, violence, missing teenage girls, a dead kid, a survivalist loner, and a bunch of strained emotive voice acting that sounded like two people trying desperately to overcome constipation.

Why is it that video game audiences demand Big, Dumb Thrill Rides? Firewatch could have been a really interesting, branching, gorgeous love story. Instead, it had to hang on to a rickety scaffold of Dramatic Conflict to sell itself to the perpetually bored, adrenaline junkie crowd and the games reviewers who pander to them.

I found the "thrilling" aspects of Firewatch to be a distracting annoyance from the gorgeous scenery and budding friendship of Henry and Delilah. The title's insistence on inventing stuff for the player to DO, spoiled character building and a setting that should have been allowed to just BE.

In the end, I was just pushing through the actiony, fetchy, double backy bits of the experience in the vain hope that there might be some kind of emotional payoff for the two main characters. There was, kinda.

I'm really don't mean to dog on Firewatch. I asks a fair price for a very polished few hours of time. It pushes the art of the possible further into adult territory for interactive experiences. It's the fact that it comes so close to greatness that makes it a bitter disappointment for those searching for something that isn't shootybang idiocy.

Why? Because if you look at the reviews people, people complete the game in 3hours. 

I did mine in 4hrs 20mins (blaze it), but I STUCK WITH IT, and these days I don't usually stick with a game if it bores me. So it kept me interested enough to play through it.

The game its self is basically run from point A to point B using a map and compass, in a visually pleasing world. You are in a forrest and the scenary is beautiful. Your reason for being there...is interesting. Working alone in the forrest and talking to a woman in a control tower who is doing the same.

The game opens up beautifully depressingly. It creates an emotional attachment, in which means that running from point A to B seems wothwhile. I was constantly getting lost thinking 'this is the right way innit m8', but no m8 sadly it wasn't and then I had to check the map and actually make sure I'm going in the right direction.

After the opening scene, the game remains interesting and visually pleasent... but after the first hour and a half, it just tapers off into an unsatisfying ending. 

I wonder if in creating this game the dev's had deadlines that were too strict? Something seems missing, or cut, from what was a beautiful opening and interesting story...into something that is as if the writers just lost any sense of care or interest and working on this game became 'work', rather than a brilliant optimistic thing it was when they first started on it.

I finished Firewatch about 1:30 a.m. this morning (spent 7 hours according to Steam, but part of that time was just me examining and reading/studying things). I've been reading the other reviews--particularly the negative ones--and can't really relate to much that was said (except maybe the price, although I purchased Firewatch when it was on sale). Aside from that, though, I didn't see any faults in the game, although it was short and the ending was kind of abrupt.

However, I've been thinking a lot about my experience...read some articles written by other people about the story...and I have a deeper...understanding? I guess that's the right word. Or maybe appreciation, like a work of art where the interpretation is usually subjective, particularly if it's abstract in nature.

For me, the storyline--while feeling like a mystery thriller most of the way through--was pretty unique. It was unique in the sense that it took a setting and characters that could have easily been based on a true story and simultaneously evoke that fear of the unknown. As the game came to a close it became clear that the fears and paranoia were unfounded, much like a lot of conspiracy theories in real life. It also brought childhood memories back of being afraid of the dark.

In addition--and this came to mind just a few hours ago before typing this review--I see parallels between the timeline of the game and the timeline leading up to Henry taking the job at the Two Forks lookout tower. Just like Henry felt an ever widening gap between himself and Julia as she succumbed to her illness, there was also a gap (albeit physical) between himself and Delilah. As Henry got to know Delilah over the course of the game I could tell there was an attraction and a desire to see each other. However, it never was meant to be as she decided to leave her lookout tower before Henry arrived, just like Julia who left Henry to be with her family in Australia. Physically he was able to go see Julia, but emotionally/mentally it was a great chasm. It was one of those "so close yet so far" scenarios; it's quite sad, actually...

Anyway, I liked the game and do not feel my money or time was wasted. Would I have preferred a more cinematic approach to the introduction?: Sure. Would I have preferred a happier ending?: Of course. Unfortunately, though, real life does not ever guarantee a happy ending, so in that light I felt the ending was apropos. A small chapter in someone's life--Henry's--ended and he had to start a new chapter. Whatever that was is irrelevant since, I feel, it was outside of the intent of the game, that being to cherish every moment you have with friends/relatives/significant other, both the good and the bad.

I understand that to some extent the developers have tried to maintain a level of realism within the story and it's characters, but I have to say that the majority of the key points in the storyline (and in particualr the ending) added up to what I would consider to be one of the most disappointing and lack-luster story of any game I've ever played.

After 4 hours of gameplay and really investing in the characters/story but still being let down more than once, all I was hoping for is a strong and satisfying ending that provided both closure and potential for a sequel. Instead, you are left feeling that all the decisions you have made throughout the game (which at the time feel subtle, but still significant to your character) have been completely pointless and that the developers have just simply ran out of ideas.

It really is such a shame that a unique game like this can possess such amazing visual and audio elements, but be let down by the actual foundation the game is built on, the story. Truthfully, there are 5-6 moments throughout the 4 hour story I can think of immediately that the developers could have changed to send the player deeper and deeper into the storyline and it's characters. By making the story more exciting throughout, they probably could have both extended the game's length (and therefore satisfy the player that think the game is too short) and vastly improved the ending, leaving the audience happy with the outcome but also longing for a second game to continue the story.
