Firewatch feels like the lull in the middle of some larger untold narrative. The choose-your-own-adventure style opening text unveils a backstory with more plot potential than the game's actual narrative, and the ending of the game implies consequences that have yet to be fully realized and could still conceivably come to a head if events were allowed to continue on. The main bulk of what you actually play is something of a muted thriller which morphs into an aborted murder mystery before abruptly ending. It's both more and less exciting than it sounds, largely due to the campy writing and clumsily disorganized structure of events.

Outside of the story, the game is a strange mash-up of early 2000s linear, corridor shooter design. You might imagine an open world, from what little marketing material there is, but it's actually just a well-crafted series of tubes that are surprisingly difficult to get lost inside of. All of the usual tropes are here too, inexplicable canyons, cliffs everywhere, heaps of impassable terrain, and mini-mountains shaping obvious paths around thick underbrush.

There's a surprising amount of gameplay here in sending out and answering radio hails as you hike along with a compass and a map as your guide, but this starts out about as challenging as it's going to get and becomes completely trivial by the end of the game. The term "walking simulator" feels a bit off here, as the game has got you doing a lot more than its competitors in that space, which is usually nothing, but it's ultimately not an irrelevant label either as you'll spend most of your time just hiking from one end of the game world to the other for arbitrary story reasons.

Really I wish I could recommend Firewatch, because the game is filled with the kind of potential I’d love to see fully realized, but the team behind it just didn't pull any of it off. It's simple, it's uncomplicated, and it ultimately doesn't give you much to walk away with. If you want to kill 4 hours doing something slow, then this is the game for you. 

It just probably isn’t the game for most people.

Firewatch is an unique experience. The story is all about the past of the character you play and the characters you interact with (wheter they are around or not). It is done beautifully, but also in a very liniar way. You can try to figure out who people are and what they are about, but you really only get bits and pieces of a puzzle, with a lot of missing or misleading pieces. Not every player is going to enjoy that.

But here is the thing with this game. The main protagonist, isn't you, but an average joe, who steers you in the direction he sees. I don't think this is neccesarily a flaw, but a lot of people will see it as such. A lot of players want to investigate and try to confirm their suspicions about this and that... but the character you play, just don't really go there. Sure he will investigate the obvious, but he doesn't think in between the lines and his dialog reflects that. He doesn't know what to make of most of the things he discovers.

I do recommend this game, but only to people who like the kind of story where you need to fill out the gaps and ponder upon what is really going on, in between and after game session. I also think you need to relate to the characters, in order to like this game. I, myself, loved the fact that I was playing an avarage flawed middleaged man, who had a rich and complicated life to look back upon. You are not playing a hero. You just play a guy, who gets into ♥♥♥♥, and has a hard time dealing with it. So yeah, not for everyone. But an old fart like myself liked it :)

This game is probably one of my favorites. Artistically, this doesn't really try as hard to create something unique and deep as Braid or Hotline Miami, but just on many levels it was more satisfying to me personally. This game is not for everyone: it really is basically just an exploration game with very little additional gameplay. But unlike "To The Moon", the gameplay is not annoying, and I feel that this really took advantage of the interactive element of gameplay (whereas "To the Moon" may have worked just as well, if not better, as a movie).

One of the most interesting things is how the developer really involved the player in the narrative. In the beginning, you make choices about how you met your wife, and these choices come up later in dialog. Also, while some choices are made, the character acts on their own based on those story choices--in ways I wouldn't, but the fact that I had made key choices made me feel complicit and emotionally attached. Even beyond the intro, this carries through--what is said during dialog and small actions in solving the puzzles are referred to later. All these things create a real sense of presence.

They also accomplished this by using various techniques to keep players from backtracking and to keep them moving forward. For the radio, they made it very easy to respond while doing other things (I only wish I could use the map and radio at the same time), and there was a time limit on response. This caused me to fairly quickly make a dialog choice rather than carefully choosing one. It was awesome because the dialog became more natural and less strategic. In addition, they only allowed the game to be saved to the save file it was started with, preventing backtracking. Overall, this helped to make the story feel unique and special to me. Normally I would backtrack and reload to optimize the outcome, with this, my choices became my life. None of the choices were particularly significant in a global sense, but they really added to my feeling of ownership.

What I liked:
- I love the outdoors and hiking and have visited many national parks. They really got everything right. Furthermore, I love how the trails were branching and yet subtle and didn't always follow the map--just like in real life. Hiking really felt like hiking, so I was really amazed by this.
- Art: they have a really great minimalist art that really goes with the nature scene
- Adult plot elements. I don't mean violence or sex. I mean the dialog was consistent with an older person, and the themes of alcoholism (subtle--it was a constant undercurrent, but never really called out), abandonment of the wife, the discussion over messed up fire-lookouts, flirting, etc. This dialog really sounded like two adults.
- Interaction and feeling that I controlled the story (see above)

Things I didn't like
- The nature of the game meant that I was mostly alone, but they really went to extraordinary lengths to prevent direct human interaction. Sometimes that really didn't make any sense. I understand this is probably due to budget, so it's forgivable, but it was still very annoying.

Overall, I highly recommend this, especially to people who love nature and the outdoors (but are going to stay inside playing video games instead).

The game is a story telling game and the story starts out quite good. Maybe a bit overly dramatic for my taste and the main protagonists behave very american and there is quite some stereotype stretching involved, but it's all for the story, so that's still ok. Then things get quite thrilling and at a certain point you start to become really suspicous of everyone and don't know anymore who's on your side and who isn't. Very good building up of the "arc of suspense". And then ... POOF!

The whole story collapses back upo itself like a souffle that has been taken out of the oven at the wrong time. REALLY, that's what you make out of it ? Honestly ? Did it needed to be finished fast for Xmas sales, or what is the excuse for such an uninspired ending ? I don't want to spoiler anything, just in case somebody really wants to play it, but man was I disappointed! And don't get me wrong, it's not because everything isn't nice and cosy at the end, that's not the point. But the profanity of *SPOILERALERT* [spoiler]"well, that was it and everybody goes their way" [/spoiler] ... no, that story had deserved more. That's probably what a creativity crisis looks like.

My advice, save your money and watch a letsplay. It's about as entertaining and you don't get the feeling to have wasted 10-20 Euros. If you need to buy it (for whatever reason), make sure you don't pay more than 5 Euros for the 3 hours of gameplay you get with that ending.

P.S.: Actually, after I did watch a lets play, I feel outright betrayed. Not only that the whole game is totally linear in terms of walking and result (just one possible end, regardless of what you do or say), but additionally the conversations are totally linear in themselves. This means, that even single conversations have exactly the same outcome, even when you choose options, that are totally differing in content. And you will be FORCED to say things, even if you don't want to, like talking about Julia or not reporting to the police the full truth about the girls.

So the game feels quite immersive and emotional the first time you play it, because you get the illusion of free will and that your decisions led to THE ending, but actually anything you do will lead exactly to the same conversations, the same string of events and the same ending. And this is not due to a philosophical approach on the existence of free will, but due to the mere lack of content!

P.P.S.: Writing my first game review was actually an enlightening experience with regards to the STEAM mechanism of sorting comments in the terms of "helpfulness". While I do understand, that STEAMs main purpose is to sell games and positive comments probably sell better than negative ones, the "hiding" of negative comments in "the most helpful"-section is so obvious, that it actually is a shame. There are almost only positive comments on top in the different time categories, some with ZERO percent helpful votings and a whole bunch of negative comments wayyyyyy further down, with helpful ratings of 80-90%. This is ridiculous and gives me a totally new perspective of the comment and ratings system on STEAM, that I used to rely on quite a bit. In the future, I'll have to rely on other sources as well, since this seems to be manipulated for whatever reasons ...

I enjoyed my time with Firewatch. I love the art style and the voice acting was amazing. 

As an adult gamer in my 40s, themes such as mortality, fidelity, depression, loss and the stresses of life resonate far more with me now than they would if I was 20 or 30 years younger. While I was certainly drawn in by the suspense of the game's narrative, the only fear I felt was the idea of actually living in the protagonists' shoes and facing losing my own wife. That, my friends, is called empathy. And if you can create empathy, then you're a damn fine storyteller.

I've seen criticisms about the game's length and it's value. While I certainly understand that $20 means different things to different people, I've never fully agreed with the benchmark of hours per dollar equating to value. With Firewatch, for example, my time playing the game came in at around four hours. But my time thinking about the game afterwards has easily tripled that. 

Similarly, criticisms of the game's abrupt ending puzzle me as well. While it's true that games and stories on other mediums often follow very clear, complete arcs, life doesn't work that way. Things happen unexpectedly. Lives end abruptly. We're always planning for a tomorrow without realizing tomorrow is never a guarantee. After losing my own father both abruptly and unexpectedly this year, I can attest to that.

In the end, how you feel about Firewatch, and how much you are able to appreciate its story, may depend greatly on you. If you lack the context of personal life experiences, then the maturity of these themes may be lost on you. For those players, maybe all they see is a "walking simulator". (Personally I think that descriptor is overly-reductive, and says more about the person using it than it does the game they're playing.) But for anyone like me who has had to state some of these things in the face in my own life, the game is far more than just the sum of its parts.

I highly recommend it.

I was going to buy Firewatch no matter what it turned out to be. I've been a listener of the Idle Thumbs podcast since shortly after it started, following Chris Remo from when he was an editor at Shacknews. I love the insightful discussions the Idle Thumbs crew has every week. When the bulk of them joined together to form Campo Santo, I was instantly onboard for whatever game they would make together. "What is Firewatch?" was never a relevant question to me. I'm glad to report that, now that I know what Firewatch is, it's rather good, if a little pedestrian.

You play Firewatch as Henry, a volunteer fire lookout in Wyoming in 1988. You're in Shoshone National Park to look out for fires (obviously), and get away from your life for an indeterminate amount of time. Your boss, Delilah, is in the next tower over, and you communicate with her through your walkie-talkie over the course of the game.

Let's get this out of the way first: Firewatch is a first-person, narrative-driven adventure game. A "walking simulator", if you must, comparable to Gone Home, but set outdoors with more walking to do, but not necessarily more to see. The game is to listen to and talk to Delilah, "solve" a mystery, and get lost in the woods. You have a map, so getting lost is on you, and the mystery is revealed in whole by the time you get far enough in the game, so the bulk of the game rests on Henry and Delilah.

What it does best is that interaction between Henry and Delilah. Over the course of the game, you learn a lot about each other and it's wonderfully voice acted and well written. As Henry, you have a little bit of control over your voice. Many of your responses to Delilah are multiple choice, some with wildly different tones. There's a multiple choice prologue that sort of acts as a mad libs for your own Henry, but your choices don't necessarily change the story in radical ways. Some dialog might be a little snark-heavy, but that's also a choice of the player. Delilah and Henry are great, and Firewatch is non-existent without them

Though it's a short game (3.5 hours by my count), it's difficult to put down once you start. I didn't intend on playing through it all on release day, but as soon as I stopped, I would think about getting right back in to see what the next day brings. The game parts are a little anemic, and the ending abrupt, but the storytelling, character building, and the environments are all fantastic. It's a game that will give you something to think about for at least as long as it takes to play.

I try to remember the summer (it's getting into a rainy British autumn now), and the first thing I think of is Firewatch. It has a gorgeous, memorable palette, that just gets more and more beautiful as the summer in the game wears on.

Players take on the role of a park ranger, during the heat of an American summer. They have a tower, a map, and that's about it. All around, a gorgeously laid out national park, to explore at your leisure.

There's a plot and a decent mystery to it too, which you will have to solve piece by piece, but the main draws are by far and away the experience of navigating this forest wilderness, which isn't dangerous at all, but just has this look that sears into you heart, particularly towards the end of the story. Some entertaining dialogue crops up throughout between the player character and the major NPC, one watchtower away, and keeps the pacing of the game flowing well.

In terms of negatives, asides from choosing dialogue options, and also navigating (as best you can) the park itself, which is possibly one of the most appealing mazes ever constructed, there's not much else to do, but that's not really what Firewatch is about - it's all about the peeling back of a mystery, both concerning the park, and the people you encounter. And above all, it's about exploring the forest itself, which has the same kind of unique character as a location as Dunwall did in Dishonoured, or Rapture in Bioshock. It's just that memorable.

A disclaimer, I haven't played the steam edition of Firewatch that I own, mainly because my laptop at the time could not handle it. As of now I've played the game multiple times, but exclusively on Playstation 4. I felt secure in purchasing the game twice because I adore this company and like to offer my support, but also because Firewatch has become a very personal game to me.

In May 2015 I lost my aunt, who I was very close with. She died after a long battle with dementia and mistreatment in a nursing home we would not have placed her in if given the choice. I was there by her bedside when she died, around a week before my birthday and moving into my first apartment/starting my first job. I had very little time to grieve for her, and after helping my grandma and family watch over her and help her, issues facing people with and families effected by alzheimer's and dementia has become a very important thing for me. Because of the fast pace at which my life was changing, I bottled up my grief and went on with my life.
My boyfriend introduced me to Firewatch later that year, telling me that it was coming out in the upcoming year and he knew it would be something I'd love. I watched the website and news regarding the game like a hawk, eager to see more about it. When it went up for preorder, I immediately bought it on steam. Once I realized that my dying laptop would struggle to even boot it up, I preordered it on my PS4. It may have been silly, but I believed in this game.
The day it came out I was incredibly excited. And then, almost immediately after starting the game, I had to stop. I was unaware that the protagonist had a history with dealing with a similar issue, watching helplessly as a loved one succumbs to dementia. I broke down on the spot, every bit of grief that had been kept inside came swelling up all at once. I pressed on, and found that the game was not only therapuetic, but everything I had wanted it to be and more. It has become one of my all time favorite games, and I'll still play it every so often just so I can wander the forests and mountain paths. It's very soothing if you've had a stressful day.

The gameplay is solid, though there isn't much to it. You walk around the park and interact with things, it's one of those games that are narrative driven rather than anything else. I liked throwing things around the watchtower at the start of each section.
The graphics are beautiful, stunning to look at wherever you go in the game. The only issue I ever had was if the environment was too dark in the caves, it made manuevering through it a bit difficult at times. This wasn't a frequent issue, and mainly a problem with my television settings. 
The voice acting and character writing is fantastic. You get a real sense of who these characters are and their motivations and dreams through the game. You start to really care for them which, surprisingly, can be a difficult goal to obtain.
The story was seen as controversial when this game first came out and, while I understand why, I thought it was perfect. I was ready for a round of park ranger the simulator, but what I got instead was *SPOILERS* lonely people who fall into conspiracy theories, only to be jarred back into reality and the fact that sometimes things are a lot more simple than what you may hope for. The soundtrack at the climax really holds the moment up well, and I was forced to sit in stunned silence as everything sank in. This was very divisive for many people who wanted an ending more fantastical, but sometimes reality just ends up this way. Endings in the real world can be sad and plain, unremarkable, regardless of the journey you took to get there.

I wholeheartedly recommend this game. I know that many people avoid "walking simulators" but that term is often used negatively and I personally wouldn't attach it here. Firewatch is a narrative driven experience that has moments of adrenaline mixed with moments of serenity and is something I'd love for all to enjoy at least once. I've played through the game multiple times and I expect to continue doing so for years to come.

However, that right there is the bigest problem with this game. I'm fine with walking simulators, but the areas have to be interesting and have things to interact with. The plot had some good twists, but the final one was a bit of a letdown. I felt like the reveal of the Big Secret That Explains Everything was built to much too quickly, and by the time you're supposed to be experiencing the shocking reveal you've already figured it out.

Bottom line, Firewatch either needed more varied environments and more things to dig up (perhaps literally) in them, or else should have been a visual novel. In the latter case it could at least have had a lower price point. Or maybe it should have included a strong puzzle element. I dunno, point is it's just not a satisfying experience at the end (which, again, you will reach in less time than it takes to get through an airport paperback) even in the things it does well. An unremarkable walkie-talkie simulator by an anti-free-speech developer. I am not providing a negative review solely as backlash, however. These are my actual opinions on the game, and I simply feel more inspired to say them when the developer establishes himself as someone who likes to block the things he doesn't want to hear.

Firewatch has not aged well. It's a member of the earlier era of walking simulators where they still tried to trick the player into thinking there were choices to make. This is especially evident in the dialogue. In nearly all cases you have three dialogue lines to say, and while there are some mild differences that can change the implications of some character relationship, by and large there's no difference. 

This is especially evident, unfortuantely, if you do a "radio silence" playthrough, never talking to your walkie-talkie friend and making them come across as desperate and you as a bitter social outcast. This could have been amazing, but the game really doesn't change much in response to this behavior and seems to have been unprepared for it. It honestly had the gut-wrenching potantial to be a more realistic, down-to-earth version of the Undertale genocide route, where the player causes lots of emotional anguish for another person just because they can, inviting introspection upon themselves.

From a pure game standpoint, there's also little that Firewatch offers as an interactive experience. I can think of all sorts of ways that old-fashioned landmark and boyscout-knowledge woodland navigation could be made into an engaging experience. For instance, imagine that toward the end of the game you lost your map and needed to race to the helecopter at the end, deciding whether or not to stop and spend some of your limited time finding the truth. I offer ideas like this because there's a real lack of tension at the ending, and it becomes too obvious that there are no fail states or bad endings for making poor decisions. The player is never disempowered or challenged which makes investment in the story difficult. The fact that you can pick up items and interact with them a little just highlights what more could have been done.

Finally, we have Firewatch as a story, a narrative to draw the player in. This was a success in micro moments, but not as a whole. Your walkie talkie friend is sufficiently vague and well characterized as someone as lonely as your own character. She's mysterious, but gradually opens up, and the game's final location really feels as personal as meeting her yourself. This kind of thing doesn't knock my socks off, but it's good enough. It just doesn't invite multiple playthroughs or much after-play discussion. The main issue is the phony mystery plot, which has the most bare, tangential connection to any of the actually present characters.

All in all, this game could have done a lot more to live beyond its novelty as a walking simulator in an open park map. It mostly sells a single experience, what it's like to be this guy living in this place, and in that respect a lot more could have been done. If you're really fascinated and haven't been spoiled on the story, consider getting it on a sale. For full price, I can't recommend it.

Alright, what we have here is a classic walking simulator. It's the narrative story of a man who had to face serious downers in his life, and therefore decided to apply for a firewatch-job in the wilderness of Wyoming, far away from everything and everyone. He moves into his watch tower to spend months in almost total loneliness. Only with his radio he keeps brief contact to other members of the firewatch. 

Our boss on the other end of the radio sends us out to "missions". Like early in the game, we have to find a few hiker teens that left their trash eveywhere and started fireworks, which in the dry woods is far from a good idea, of course. A routine mission, as it seems, but while we are out there surrounded by nature, strange and mysterious things happen, and we got to find out what's going on. I'm not going to spoiler any more of the story, as it's a relatively short story of roughly 5-6 hours.  The game lacks any kind of "action". Pretty much like "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter", we walk around, discover and explore locations and follow the narratively told story. Sounds a bit boring, and well, for players who seek action, it probably will be boring, but for story fans it's a really nice little gem. A lovely game for a long, rainy weekends day. Besides the story and dialogs, I really liked the graphics. Firewatch uses a graphics style that is almost comic-like. The setting is really beautiful, with warm and lovely light moods, and still many objects, like rocks and clouds, are lacking details. Still walking through this simulated nature somehow feels right and natural. Hard to describe. I hope you get what I mean. Anyway, I've had a good time playing this game, and can clearly recommend it to fans of story-driven walking simulators.

I played this game months ago, and the experience has never left me.

This is a visually stunning, emotionally mature, big-picture-of-humanity game. It won't be for everyone - action fans will probably lament the amount of time spent just walking around and the lack of a big payoff at the end - but playing this game left me feeling not only as though I'd just spent months in the great outdoors instead of 5 or so hours at my laptop, but as though I'd read a really profound novel.

2017: As much as I'd like to recommend this game, after watching how the co-developer decided to Witch Hunt PewDiePie I lost all desire to have this in my library. I don't think I want to support this developer anymore unless they fix their faulted mindset.

2024: Editing my review but keeping the old one here to illustrate my change in mindset. Firewatch is a beautiful game with a heartbreaking story that I played through in one sitting. Keeping in mind with the tone of my original conclusion above, I recommend this game to anyone who wants to sit and enjoy a story unfold before them. - Very good atmosphere. The graphics are 'unique', and it give it a good feeling of how the nature would look. The music and voice-acting wasn't bad too. You could really 'experience' the feeling of being there, while still looking at a 2D screen.

Cons:

The actions were very 'hollywood' like too, it didn't matched the realism the atmosphere gave me. The thing about making your own decisions with your radio and the actions was very bed too in my eyes. There wasn't much space to create your own story, I think it would have been way better if you could drasticly change the story by what you do. Like not reporting the things you do to Delilah would change the story. I tried to say nothing about the situation of entering the camp and radio of the guy that was tailing us, but the story still went on with her knowing I broke in that camp, but I didnt even told her I was inside. So much possiblities but the result was horrible. The ending was very 'vague' too, you expect to see delilah of something but the action put in the story results in disapointment...
- Exploring wasn't very good. There were a lot of edges on the paths, but in a real world, everything would be accesable. I know that would be a lot of work to do, but:
- The price is way to high for what it gives. 20 euro for 3-4 hours of gameplay !? I expected something very good, so my expectations were high. I wouldn't recommend anyone to buy this for the full price, 5 euro at most. (your choice)

It wasn't a bad game if the price would be much lower. 20 euro for 3-4 hours should be something perfect, instead of this dissapointment that could have been way better.

I don't usually write reviews of games, but after the recent brigading of this developer I think it is necessary to do my part to make sure people do not get the wrong idea about this game.

Firewatch is a first-person story about a man who spends a Summer volunteering in the woods to get away from some tragic circumstances. Without going into spoiler territory, some intrigue starts to happen and he finds that his job isn't all it's cracked up to be.

This game falls into the ever widening genre of walking simulator, a game where you walk around in a first person perspective and experience a story, like an interactive movie almost. This places it among other such games like Dear Esther and the Stanley Parable, although I would liken it more to Gone Home. I say this because, like Gone Home, there is a lot of emphasis on the personal drama, as well as an aspect of piecing together what exactly went on to others who have roamed these woods before you. While not quite the coming-of-age story told by Gone Home, Firewatch's theme of dealing with mistakes and hardships in life are no less relatable.

Other reviewers have complained that the game is short, and I have to agree with them on that point. I took my time with it an only spent a little over three hours to beat it. However, I would not agree that this is necessarily a bad thing, as the game is a story, and had it been much longer, odds are it would have overstayed its welcome. Instead, Firewatch gets in, says what it needs to and leaves quietly, leaving you, the player, with all you need to understand its world.

I recently purchased this game in spite of the mixed reviews (a result of the review brigading from folks with 0 hours played in the last two weeks.) I don't regret the purchase at all!

Firewatch is akin to an interactive, 3d story/adventure/mystery game. The player, upon starting the game, makes a quick series of decisions defining their background. Then, it's off to to the watch.

The game takes place over a course of several days, and the player is always in contact with Delilah - your supervisor at a neighboring watch. Without spoiling it too much, the player must investigate a series of incidents in Wyoming wilderness with Delilah's help.

Gameplay wise, it's mostly walking and interacting on the radio. There aren't difficult puzzles to solve, but the world is filled with details for you to explore. The dialogue is some of the best-acted and best-written dialogue I've encountered in any game. The graphics are stylized and beautiful, and the sound direction is amazing! I highly recommend playing this game with high-quality headphones so you can truly immerse yourself in the awesome environment.

The player makes a series of dialogue choices, but the plot is mostly on rails. It doesn't seem to really effect much when you choose one response versus another.

I'd recommend this game if you want a tense, but also relaxing trip into the Wyoming Wilderness and a world to explore.

What is Firewatch? That was the question that was so often asked leading up to the games release. There were also many answers that fell into the camp of its not a game or it is a game. Some called it a walking simulator. Others called it an adventure game. For me it was a game with film like properties. It told a wonderful story as my wife and I sat together and played. I more or less watched her play this one than actually played but I feel the experience would have been the same. You come to care about the protagonist Henry and his friend Delilah. The mysteries that unfold working in the park are page turning if this was a book. The less i say about the story the better but I will say this is the story of a man. He is not saving the world nor is he in some grand adventure. This is a story of a man that inthe grand scheme of things seems rather insignificant. I think that is the beauty of it. We can all relate to personal struggles that feel so important but only to us and perhaps those around us. The rest of the world will pass us by and not give a thought to what we do or where we are going.

This is a great little game. While short, it covers everything it needs to in that period of time. Henry and Delilah's interactions work well, and while I would say that the story is overall linear, your reactions to events in the game do add color and personality. A moment that got me in my original playthough was the beginning of a day where your wedding ring is sitting on the desk in front of you. While there is no real gameplay effect for putting it back on or leaving it off, the presence of the choice alone, and how it affects no one but yourself as a player, is fitting for the atmosphere of the game. Visually the game is beautiful. While often a personal preference thing, I love the stylized realism paradigm that many games have taken these days, and Firewatch delivers the beauty of the outdoors excellently.

I *love* Firewatch, so much I bought it on PC and PS4.

I bought it on Steam last year in the Summer Sales, and of the 10 or so games I bought in that sale it was the one I was most eager to play.

I knew very little about it going in beyond the name and that it was a narrative based game (my jam), and I think this really enhanced the experience. I won't go into plot details here because I don't want to ruin it for anyone else but if you're into mystery, solid narrative, amazing characters and interaction between the characters then you're going to love Firewatch.

Speaking of the characters, the voice acting in Firewatch is incredible. The characters feel so real, and it made it so easy to become totally immersed in the game. When I first played it through I actually didn't think I'd play it again, because I knew everything that happened. I've lost count now but I'd guess I've played it 5 or 6 times now if not more. I've seen it criticized for your "choices" not really having an effect on the plot but I think those people are kind of missing the point.

Again without too much detail, the "mystery" in Firewatch (at least in my opinion) is there to serve as the story and to give you something to do. The actual choices in the game that do have consequences are the dialogue choices. I've played through many different ways now, the way I wanted to play it, then picking all the worst possible dialogue choices I could, then picking as little options as I could, and it felt like a whole new story/experience each time. That's incredible.

My other favourite thing about Firewatch is the compass/map system, especially the option to turn off your location on the map. It's a very specific thing to love but I was a scout growing up and did a lot of hiking/orienteering, and Firewatch perfectly captures that experience.

Lastly, I think it's fantastic that the developers have chosen to take a stand against the racism that occurs way to often in the gaming community. I enjoy playing a game that much more knowing that the people who made it share the same values and commitment to making the community and industry a more conscientious place as I do.

While the art style is really nice, this 3-4 hour game is fairly monotonous and boring despite its attempts at injecting suspense and mystery into the incoherent story it's trying to tell. With many of its early leads, the game has tremendous potential that is all wasted by the writing which abruptly squanders all the side-plots in order to advance... I'm not even sure what - it's not really a story; one could with careful measure call it a feeling maybe, so the tag "Atmospheric" can to some extent stand - but the climax and resolution just feel sloppily slapped together. The extremely linear plot provides a small illusion of choice but fails eventually to sustain its early clumsy stabs at mystery and thriller and occasional humor: what could be behind the fence, is there some sort of monster about - the answer to both is of course "hey, let's get back on the actual storyline" - and the actual storyline is pretty weak. One could say the journey is more important than the destination of course, and the game is actually decent as a whole, voice acting definitely a shining counterpoint to the mundane story as noted by other reviews as well, I found the mechanics to be well made and just out of your way enough that you don't notice them too much and there just enough to help when they are needed. All in all, it might just be worth to get on a sale or maybe as part of a humble bundle, but 4 hours of linear story with no real progression just a forced and fake character development arc leading into a meaningless void not unlike a certain forest burnt to ash by the titular fire. And should we accept that the game is indeed more about the journey, it's really just as well if one watches a playthrough stream; maybe even at 1.25x speed.

Today, I finally started and finished Firewatch Game from studio Campo Santo after being on my list for a while to play. Now I feel stupid for not playing until now. 
It's a relatively small game (about 5ish hours) which plays out more like an interactive fictional book, but it's about a man named Henry taking a job as a fire lookout after having been emotionally drained and shouldering guilt after his wife Julia gets Dementia and moves away to Australia to be with her family for care.
The only other person you have contact with in the wilderness is another lookout and your supervisor named Delilah and through Radio Walkie Talkies.
A bleak but sometimes brilliant tale of avoiding responsibilities, conspiracies, geocaching, revelations and reconciliation.

Firewatch is quite refreshing and different.

Playing this offers a fresh perspective on your own humanity, and that of others. It's an interesting experience to go through, and may give you a fresh view on guilt, escapism, and resolve. 

4-5 hours. Play it for a night or two for a fresh break from the usual. Enjoy!

Firewatch is a first person adventure game in the style of Gone Home and Dear Ester, where by inspecting and exploring the environment as well as absorbing the dialogue of the two principle characters are your main interactions with the world. The story centers around a man named Henry who's temporarily left his life to become a fire lookout for the summer. The games graphics and aesthetic are gorgeous, making the setting of '89 Wyoming a more than pleasant place to explore with beautiful vistas and a decent variety of wooded areas (all of which were quite easy to run without much or any FPS stutter or lag). The sound design along with the sparse use of music pair well together to create a naturalistic atmosphere (as someone who enjoys hiking, this made the game immediately more engrossing). Although interactivity is on the minimal side, per the games archetype, the narrative definitely picks up the slack where the gameplay may be "lacking" to some, and at about three to four hours long doesn't have the opportunity to outstay its welcome. It's paced well and maintains intrigue entire runtime. At twenty dollars I definitely wouldn't regret purchasing Firewatch, however my personal recommendation would be to wait for a sale due to its length. At a discount, it is a must buy.

Firewatch is an absolute masterpiece of gaming and storytelling. It may just be the best written game I've ever played. The characters are likable, yet shrouded in just enough mystery to keep you wondering what their motivations are. It's easy to dismiss Firewatch as "just another walking simulator," but it just isn't. It's an exploration game. Rather than stick you in a house with some photos, papers, and no motivation or direction to continue, Firewatch has mastered when to guide the player and when to let them discover elements on their own. Yes, you're walking, but that's where the similarities to walking sims begin and end. The world itself is graphically stunning and filled with precisely placed details which bring the park to life. Nothing is ever just "there" without some cause or effect. The sound is perfect, as is the soundtrack. As is to be expected, given the hollywood-caliber cast, the voice acting is top-notch, as well. I can't recommend Firewatch enough.

Honestly I'm coming back to replay this game over a year later because I've had the insatiable craving for something like it. That is the only problem with this game, and the only thing that will frustrate you after its over. You WILL want more.
There are so many things I could compliment the studio on. The amazing, half-cartoony, half-watercolor visuals. The incredibly realistic sound design that immerses you fully. (DEFINITELY WEAR GOOD HEADPHONES, TRUST ME) The most believable and compelling voice acting I have ever heard in any game, or other medium for that matter. Or the sheer originality of the dialogue progression and story through the use of the walkie-talkie. I'm sure if you are considering this game you've been privy to the acclaim this original mechanic has gotten them, but rest assured it is merely the vehicle for an insanely addicting story that unfolds in the second half. This game will leave you hoping for some continuation, something to bring you down off the edge of your seat that even it's resolution fails to ease. But most of all, this game will entice you to go out and go for a hike in nature, something that a great many of us probably need more of us in our life. 
The greatest stories will always leave us wanting more, but not diminish themselves in giving it to us.

In that regard, Firewatch's plot was successful from beginning to end. That seems to be a break in the general consensus, but I found the narrative about two people connecting in a strange place in their lives to be cathartic and resonant. Firewatch is a... curious game. It's a story-driven ambiance exploration title (aka. "walking simulator") with a both simple and complex premise. And most of the game is mostly about having conversations about everyday tough choices with the partner's voice over the radio. With the more or less open map and some optional exploration being just a backdrop to the story, something to go along the idea of escaping the situation you are in via incredible adventuring, but never really going that far from it.

And the game is great at it. It always tries to hook you up with promise of something exciting, while keeping things grounded and, in the end, might very much manage to surprise you with mundane. Yet, that is also one of the reasons I couldn't help but feel slightly disappointed with it while playing, since it never felt truly going anywhere. As is, it's a great story-driven game that's worth checking out. But don't expect it to be more than what it is after the opening minutes. To be up front in this review, I haven't seen storytelling that stuck with me this much in recent games. I bought the game because I figured I'd be going on a big nature hike, maybe report a few fires, and dodge a bear or two. Instead, I got an opening that nearly ripped my emotions out of my body with heartache and dialogue throughout that made me feel like I was dealing real life characters in a realistic situation instead of a madeup one, and an ending that left me with more questions than answers.

The characters: Henry (The player) and Delilah are so brilliantly well-written as characters; so well in fact that you'd almost think they were people you've already met, or could see yourself meeting in the real world. Sarcasm, wit, and humor is shared amongst them, and it's never too far-fetched in what they say or do. It's not like meeting a fairy princess of a space empire as a muscular brute with a sword; you're an average bearded guy in his 40s just setting out to do a job with a chatty coworker. Just another day on the job as a fire lookout.

The setting: You're Henry: a man who has had a rough time dealing with some troubles back at home, looking to find a temporary escape from all of that to clear his mind. You find a job as a fire lookout in Wyoming and travel there to start your routine; upon which you meet Delilah: a goofy, smartass, down to earth woman serving as your lookout supervisor that communicates with you only through radio. You'll find that not only will she always have a job for you, but will gladly talk with you while you perform these tasks. Saying anymore would only be spoiler-filled.

The atmosphere: Firewatch is beautiful. Graphics-wise it is very pretty. The environment has just enough detail to paint you a clear picture of your surroundings, but not too much to where you're focusing on every nook and cranny instead of the experience you're going through. While you are playing a story mode instead of a free-roam, you are in fact free to explore the surrounding area of the forest you watch over. It's not a clear path either; there's paths blocked off, there's cliffsides you have to climb down, and rappeling areas to hook a rope to for a safe journey down. It's calm, peaceful, and you can lose yourself in the setting listening to the radio conversation between Delilah and Henry while sweet music plays in the background.

The overall conclusion: While I didn't play many hours to complete this game, I felt like it was a satisfying experience. My only real gripes are the ending (for story reasons) and the free mode being the nature walk I was wanting, but having so little to do that it gets boring quickly since I've experienced the majority of my freeroaming in the story mode. Along with that, no use of the disposable camera in freeroam bites. Guess I'll have to start a new save to get my glorious nature hike pictures taken.

If you're looking for a heavily action-based game with guns and explosions or a terrifying game with jumpscares all around and bears chasing you through the forest, Firewatch isn't for you. However, if you're looking for an engaging, calming experience with some realistic and believeable story-telling, then I would recommend picking it up (However, I did get it on sale so I am a bit biased there).

I hope this review shed some light on your curiousity of the game; although I really wanted to avoid major spoilers if possible. Try it, see what you think. If you don't like it, refund within 2 hours. No loss there.

Watching the trailers for Firewatch and reading the comments I was expecting, metaphorically speaking, a satisfying dinner of steak and potatoes with most, but not all, the trimmings. Sure, the commenters warned, the portion size is small (i.e. 3 hours), but well worth it. So I ordered one. Thankfully I got this on sale because: 

Firewatch is not steak and potatoes; Firewatch is a chicken wiener slapped on a piece of bread and handed to you as a hotdog. They do add some condiments in an attempt to improve the flavor, but it's still just a wiener on a piece of bread.

To be fair, Firewatch could have been that metaphoric steak and potatoes. The concept and storyline have great potential. Unfortunately, character backgrounds and relationships are not woven into the story, in-game events have no real meaning, the few toys they give your character are mostly irrelevant, the few objects you can interact with (and ‘inspect’) are also irrelevant, and the ending … no easy way to say this: the ending sucks. It’s not even a cliff-hanger, it’s just bad and lazy writing. I want to love you Firewatch, why are you acting like this!?

If you must buy this, buy it on sale. I don’t often say that because I believe in supporting game developers (my steam library is, metaphorically speaking, well endowed) and most deserve the full asking price. But not Firewatch; it’s a gorgeous game to look at until you get to know it. I beg you, Firewatch developers, re-do this game: it could have been incredible.

Update (2016/10/26):

I've read a few of the recent reviews and see that there's some unhappiness regarding the depth of the story and how the options affect the end product. I beg to differ. I believe that Firewatch is a vanguard for future games with the depth of interesting dialogue and relationship building. Most games lack continuity with their dialogue options and it often leaves me looking for a 'skip' option as there's no real relationship development. Furthermore, the plot does leave you lingering for that satisfaction, but I feel as though that's what makes it unique - there is no definitive ending. Lastly, and probably the most important point, is that you need to remember that this is in-fact an indie game. 

I would easily recommend this beautiful mini-story and have in the past.

Beautiful game that feels like a living, breathing world. Lots of desktop wallpaper screenshot opportunities, as most of you probably have already seen on others pages. Light rays are a nice feel without overwhelming the senses (think Dying Light for this example of too much). 

In terms of story/lore I feel like it could have been better. My playtime noted above is indicative of how long the game took me to complete from start to finish (mind you I didn't collect all the things, but that's not my cup of tea in every game). 

The voice acting is spot-on and the characters feel believable (+1 immersion), however like Destiny 1 (in my opinion) it only scratches the surface of the lore and leaves the player begging for more. Given, I could have went around looking for all the little bits and bobs to piece together a better story, but it probably wouldn't have been as in-depth as I'd have wanted (based on past experiences). 

The mechanics used to navigate/climb/etc. were easy to learn and master. I used an xbone controller and didn't have any issues (if anyone was wondering). 

Without spoiling anything, I found it disappointing that regardless of the choices you make throughout the game, the ending never reflects this. Nothing hurts (to me) more than feeling like all those choices I carefully picked were meaningless. My character should be a reflection of my choices and experiences, right?

TL;DR: Sorry for rambling this one was a lot of fun but like said before left me wanting more. Like Fruit Stripe gum if you know the brand.

This is my first review, I was so touched by this game I could not resist writing about it.
This game is gorgeous and absolutely immersive. You are convinced by its pallette of colors, by its music, by its sounds. but it is also an utterly convincing, psychologically and philosophically deep story. It regards escapism, fleeing from your problems in the hard, real life, and that even applies to playing the game in first place as a form of relief. The ending was shunned by a lot of people because there is nothing epic or a real closure with it - as is with life: your reality comes back to haunt you. It is high quality literature we're talking about, not a simple game. Something to touch you deeply.
There are a very few technical issues like lots of invisible walls and a few uninteractive objects which should be interactive. Nothing that screws up the immersion though, and the controls are responsive and well thought out.

Pros:
* Deep and philosophical story, high quality literature.
* Amazing visuals, pallettes, sound, music and pace. Convincing and immersive.
* Good acting and dialogue
* Educative: it teaches you to orient using a map. In the beginning you get lost a lot, after that you make your own mental map of the locations. It is worth to play a second time turning off the map trails!
* Very "human". The plot is focused in human emotions and idiosyncrasies, not technology, idealist quests or stuff that's too abstract.
* The plot has a lot of mysteries that make for good discussion on the internet afterwards. Was Delilah lying? Was she talking to Ned? What happened to Ron and Dave?


Cons:
* A few awkward uninteractive objects and invisible walls. Nothing excessive.

TLDR: 

Firewatch is a visually pretty "casual adventure" game with strong immersion aspects that ultimately leads to a largely unsatisfying - if not aggravating - conclusion. I do not recommend it to the general player, and would recommend fans of the adventure genre wait until it goes on sale. 


Review:

If there is one sentiment to sum up Firewatch, it's that the journey is sometimes more important than the destination. That certainly seems to be where the designers of Firewatch placed their focus. 

The game starts with a narrative that helps you define certain aspects about yourself through a series of, "in this situation, would you do A or B?" questions. This, in turn, seeds the way that your interactions are going to go with main interaction you have in the game, your boss, Delilah. Your interactions with Delilah are where most of the gameplay resides, as you tromp around the wilderness of Wyoming basically going from a start point to and end point that triggers further interactions with Delilah and moves the story along. There is some mild orienteering you have to do in order to figure out how to get to this end point, but I wouldn't necessarily call that gameplay, as it's more an element to help immerse into the game. 

And from an immersion standpoint, Firewatch does a very good job; the game is visually attractive - albeit going for a cartoonish reality (a la World of Warcraft), rather than a photo-realistic reality - and music is used sparingly, but to good effect, and the voice acting is adequate. The building story is effective in keeping you riveted; there's so many plot threads going on, so many unexplained mysteries, that this game definitely fosters a sense of both isolation and paranoia in the player. 

The interaction system is also rather interesting; rather than a dialog wheel where everything freezes and you have time to ponder your response and make a selection, here the dialog selections all happen in real-time, with a short-fuse timer; not responding with an interaction within that timer counts as ignoring Delilah, which in itself steers the interaction between you two. So yes, it is very clear that the interaction is the chief gameplay here and the genesis of replaying Firewatch.

But this game has some very significant flaws. To wit:


1. You only have the illusion of control

What I mean by this is that, while it appears that you are playing in an open world sandbox, the game decides when it's time to move on, not you. One of the bigger pet peeves I had was when I would be heading towards something I wanted to check out, and the game would start an interaction with Delilah, where - on completion - the game would fast forward to the next chapter, without any say from you. Once I was literally ten feet from my objective when the game decided the chapter was closed and put me back at home base. 

You also experience this in your interactions with Delilah. You will be confronted with ethical dilemmas and asked what you think you and Delilah should do, with the assumption on your part that whatever you respond to Delilah with is the direction that the game will go. But that's not necessarily the case. Sometimes Delilah just ignores your response and does whatever she wants. Now, some may correctly observe that this makes her more "human," in that she's not going to automatically do as you dictate, but there is nothing that makes you feel like your choices do not matter faster, than this kind of strong-arm tactic. 


2. Too much "ghost in the machine" to drive the plot forward

Treading carefully to not give away spoilers, almost every major event that happens in the game comes as the result of "unseen forces" in the background acting against the interests of the player. But the problem with that it's just a little *too* convenient how these actors always seem to be in the exact right place, at the exact right time, to foil you. There's one incident where the "unseen actor" would literally have to get by you in plain sight in a one-way-in-one-way-out section in order to commit their action, and yet somehow they do so, and act within seconds of you beginning to exit the area.  While you're playing the game, it's not that bothersome, because you don't know what's going on - if anything, your imagination is concocting all these possible paranoid theories - but once the big reveal takes place, you can't help but to begin to ask questions about how all of this was accomplished with perfect timing, perfect location, and perfect execution to foil you...and that's part of the reason the ending is so unsatisfying


3.  That ending

Again, treading lightly as to not give away spoilers, this was a real punch in the groin. That's really the only thing you can call it. And there were three punches, really:

Punch-in-the-groin #1: 

All the threads of the mystery you're trying to unravel magically unravel themselves without you doing a single thing. That's right. You don't *defeat* the antagonist; the antagonist just decides to leave. Done. Bye now. Got tired of "ghost-in-the-machine" teleporting around to mess with you, I guess. In fact, you would never even have gotten to the "big reveal" if the antagonist didn't specifically lead you *by the nose to it.* Nothing you did positively led to this conclusion. (And no, this wasn't the "bad" ending; all of the endings except one go this way.)


Punch-in-the-groin #2:

This is a corollary to Punch #1, but when the "big reveal" happens, you're just dumbfounded. Wait, what? *That's* what's been going on all along? Are you kidding me? And it's around this moment you start thinking about all the "ghost in the machine" moments I describe above and you're trying desperately to understand how this could possibly be the "big reveal," just from a *logistical* standpoint. Noooo, you say. Noooo, this is a false ending, you say. Noooo, the *real* reveal is around the corner, I can just FEEL IT. You almost had me, Firewatch, but this ain't my first rodeo.

Nope, sorry. That was the real reveal. Ha ha.


Punch-to-the-groin #3

After spending the entire game with Delilah as your sole source of interaction and companionship, when the end finally looms large and your life is in danger....she doesn't give a fig what happens to you. I grant you, that is a bit of a spoiler, but it doesn't really effect anything since it happens right at the end, so I'm letting it slip. In a word, she bolts. Stay, you plead; wait for me, you plead. Nope, she says, I'm out of here; hope you actually live. Good luck.

Now, from what I've gathered, no matter what relationship you have crafted with Delilah, she always does this. ARE. YOU. KIDDING. ME. To be fair, some have speculated that this was done to conserve budget that would have otherwise had to be spent creating an in-game representation of Delilah for you to finally meet, but still...you spend all this time building a rapport with this person, dealing with her BS on multiple occasions, and the pay-off is: never actually getting to meet her. If your groin wasn't already throbbing in agony from the first two punches, this one's just icing on the groin-agony cake.


So in summary, this is a game that let's you forget the world for a while, and is interesting and immersive enough to keep you glued for a couple of hours. And for some folks, that alone would be worth the price of admission. But this is the rare media where a fairly enjoyable experience is quickly forgotten by the sheer ham-handedness of the way the game is concluded, once you realize that nothing you did, nothing you chose, nothing you said, ultimately made a lick of difference, and now you wish you'd never played to begin with.

Every now and then there are games that manage to merge both the movie medium and game mechanics into a well thought out, engrossing whole. From the first few minutes in Firewatch you just know this is such a game. This is one of those games that makes a presents a shift in what the future can hold in store. The game is set in the 80’s, without spoiling too much of the story, you end up taking a job as a fire-watch in a forest. A very emotional start of the game, which after a while turned into this ‘Stranger Things’-like mystery adventure. 
I have read that the choices in dialogue you make shape the game, and this was just my first game through. So I don’t know how much the story can deviate from the story I went through.
I found the story well written, it keeps you going, wanting to know what happened. It’s not easy to put down half way through, just like a good movie keeps you hooked for the next plot reveals. I’ve read some comments that the ending was too sudden, that it didn’t make much sense. I don’t agree with that at all. It’s not a long game, that is correct. But it costs about the same as a movie ticket, and since this is  basically a playable movie, I don’t see the problem. Once finished, you can still replay it again, try other dialogue paths, or just plain explore the forest.

That brings me to the graphics. These are just plain wonderful. They have a cartoony look, which suits the game just perfect. It will keep the game fresh and good looking well past its release date. 
With the story being the main focus it is important to have characters you can believe in, and the excellent voice acting does just that. I think we are well past the time when the voice acting in games was an afterthought and sometimes was so bad, that the game would have been better of without. A game like Firewatch really sets a standard. They manage, through the actors, to make you care and feel for the people in this game.

As great as it may be, there are also some quirks in the game, for example while exploring the forest it is possible you bump into invisible walls/boundaries, for example if there is a rock or some bushes. The annoying part is that your character is able to climb rocks and fallen trees just fine, even though they are higher. This is a common problem with many games, but here it’s a pity because it temporarily snaps you out of the whole experience.
Another problem I had, certainly as the game advanced was that I would lose my way in the woods, some parts also look so similar, it’s easy to get lost. Luckily you have a map, but it was still frustrating none the less. You could argue that this is realistic, as it is probably just as easy to get lost in a real forest (and you’re probably right).

The game runs without a problem on Linux/SteamOS and poses no problems to control using the Steam Controller, although the on-screen instructions don’t match the buttons on the controller, it’s not really difficult to figure out or remember.

Firewatch is a game about leaving home and venturing the wilderness. It's a walking simulator where one explores the beautiful landscape we are presented. We follow the life of Henry, a middle aged man going through a very rough time who has decided to take a job as a Firewatcher during the summer of 89 (if I'm not mistaken on the year) in order to run away from his problems.

The game has an interesting concept and a very nice presentation. Depending on how your computer handles this, it can come as a very detailed and beautiful landscape (for me it was a middleground). The objective is  very straightforward: you stay on your watchtower looking out for fires and having a female colleague, your boss, as company over radio who guides you on what to do when certain events happen. You are also encouraged to explore your surroundings. 

Being a story driven game, the beauty of it comes mostly from the relationship between the 2 main characters: Henry and his boss Delilah. Much effort is put in the dialog which sounds very convincing and interesting. You get multiple ways of interacting with your boss, either trying to get to know her and coming off as an opened extroverted guy or you can do exactly the opposite and watch her reaction. The most interesting part of this game is by far interacting with your boss over every single thing and creating some hilarious moments. 

However, I do believe the game falls apart a bit. For a game that focus on exploring the wilderness so much, I felt that there was very little exploration to be doing. The paths seem all too linear and sometimes it's not clear at all if a given trail is indeed a trail or just part of the decoration. You get a map and a compass for orientation which is a neat detail that adds to the exploring part but then again, it's just a matter of choosing which trail on the map to take, and given that most areas of the game are accessible through one trail only, well... it doesn't add much variability to it. The interaction you make with the few little objects you find, is also on the poor side. You either collect it, when you can, or toss it. Most of your interactions accomplish nothing which is also a thing that frustrated me much. Your interactions do not matter. For the dialog part, you are given the option to give different inputs and receiving different outputs. But overall, your decisions do not affect any major points of the plot which wouldn't be exactly a bad thing if it weren't for two very big reasons: 
1 - The game keeps raising your expectations and making you believe otherwise.
2 - The exploration part alone is not enough to keep me motivated through the game.
MINISPOILERS The game tries to keep you hooked with this mystery kind of thriller thing going on and by the end of the game, after the mystery is solved, the plot just becomes plain boring and leaving many many questions in the open. Since the exploration part wasn't truly fulfilling, you get but a bitter taste in your mouth /MINISPOILERS

After spending one captivating morning playing and finishing Firewatch, I felt compelled to share my thoughts on this unique, narrative-driven game. Developed by Campo Santo, Firewatch offers an immersive experience with a good story, superb voice acting, and breathtaking visuals. It may not be groundbreaking, but it certainly leaves an impression on those who venture into its beautifully crafted world.

Engaging Story and Characters

Firewatch's story, set in the Wyoming wilderness, revolves around Henry, a fire lookout assigned to watch for potential forest fires. The game's narrative may not be groundbreaking, but it effectively pulls players into its world and keeps them engaged throughout. This success is largely due to the game's strong character development, particularly between Henry and his supervisor, Delilah.

Their relationship unfolds through radio conversations, which are brought to life by exceptional voice acting. Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones deliver performances that capture the emotional nuance and humor of their characters. These conversations, as well as the choices you make as a player, shape the story and create a sense of genuine connection.

Visuals and Atmosphere

Firewatch's stunning graphics are one of its standout features. The game's art direction, led by Olly Moss, presents a world that is both vibrant and atmospheric. The lush forests, serene lakes, and sweeping vistas invite players to explore and become immersed in the game's environment. The day-night cycle and dynamic weather system further enhance the sense of being in a living, breathing world.

Exploration and Pacing

The game's core gameplay focuses on exploration and navigation, with an emphasis on environmental storytelling. As you traverse the wilderness, you'll uncover clues and information that add depth to the narrative. Firewatch strikes a good balance between exploration and storytelling, ensuring that players never feel lost or overwhelmed.

While the game is relatively short, lasting only a few hours, it offers a satisfying and complete experience. This allows players to become fully engrossed in the story without the need for excessive filler content or repetitive tasks.

Conclusion

Firewatch is a beautiful and captivating journey that pulls players into its world through engaging storytelling, excellent voice acting, and stunning visuals. Though it may not revolutionize the gaming landscape, it offers a memorable experience that is well worth a few hours of your time. I wholeheartedly recommend Firewatch to anyone looking to lose themselves in a gorgeously crafted world with a well-told story. My final rating for Firewatch is a solid 8/10.

[h1]A Beautiful Journey[/h1]

A cursory glance over the negative reviews reveals that most people who were left with a negative impression of the game enjoyed it until the ending. Undoubtedly, the ending of a narrative is important – it is the part of the story that the player will remember most keenly after completing the game, when writing a review or recommending the game to a friend – but it does not negate all that happened previously.

Firewatch is a walking simulator set in the backcountry of Shoshone National Forest. You play as Henry, a middle-aged man who took a job as a fire lookout to escape from personal problems in his home city of Boulder. While navigating the beautiful but overgrown trails of Shoshone, your only link to the rest of humanity is your supervisor, Delilah, who you converse with over a walkie-talkie. As the summer wears on, a series of increasingly bizarre incidents cause the pair to suspect they are the target of a conspiracy. 

Firewatch has some adventure game elements – there are trails you cannot traverse without certain equipment – but I would still classify the game as a walking simulator. While I enjoy walking simulators, there is a sizeable group of gamers who don’t. If you are part of this group, Firewatch may not be the game for you.

[b]Positive[/b]

[list]
[*]The game's dialogue and voice acting are top-notch. Unlike many other games, which employ exaggerated archetypes, Henry and Delilah both feel like real people. This is not to say the conversations are boring. They are witty and charismatic enough that I spent a large amount of time looking for interactable objects just to see what dialogue would result when I mentioned them.
[*]The game looks incredible. The graphical fidelity is high, but everything is slightly stylized, giving the game a memorable aesthetic. Additionally, the environmental design of the open world is beautiful, with memorable landmarks and stunning vistas.
[*]Chris Remo’s music is very good. The soundtrack only becomes noticeable at poignant moments, but in those moments, it really contributes to the atmosphere.
[*]The little text-adventure at the beginning was a clever and cost-effective way to make players emotional invested in the character of Henry.
[/list]

When people describe walking simulators as non-traditional games, there is some disservice to people who find story-driven, immersive and interactive experiences what they enjoy the most about games. There may not be tangible long-term choices, challenge, replayability, etc. that can be easily more satyisfying to create gameplay; the sole quality these games rely on to a fault is if you want to play it for yourself.  However, this does not make these games any less of a game because they focus on interactions to immerse you rather than challenge you, although it is difficult to be objective when discussing a walking-simulator's merits and flaws. 

Firewatch is perhaps the first walking-simulator where I felt the interactions were intentionally made to immerse the player with these mechanics that are often lambasted as padding or the illusion of choice from other games. This is the dividing line of your enjoyment; it depends entirely on whether you find the means of interaction a way to engage with the story or appears as filler meant to excuse a shorter experience.

[h1]A Hitchhiker’s Guide to Get Lost[/h1]

The best means to play is to let the forest overwhelm you by forcing you to rely on the navigational tools provided after turning off the default settings. As someone who lacks direction, it’s important here to let yourself be vulnerable to its scale. 

Backtracking is often a dirty-word that means people do not enjoy feeling lost or the slowdown of pacing. It often is meant in action games to keep the player from exhaustion as the purpose of quiet time allows players to contemplate what is next while they catch their breath. Firewatch understands this as the narrative relies on you taking your time to explore in finding your position as you traverse the Wyoming forrests. Markers, points of interest, etc. are penciled into the map to help build your mental map with time, so you never feel totally lost if you use all the tools given to you.

One minor criticism I do have with navigation is the the lack of using tools to scale the terrain organically rather than the roadblocks of “Bethesda mountains” and sectioned off areas of the maps to let the forest feel more like a real place. This is perhaps the only complaint about its gameplay that I find lacking immersion for the story, which the story relies on the details you see, the tools/environments you interact with and the lies/truth you manipulate to tell its narrative. 

[h1]Lies Like Wildfire[/h1]

Games are the ideal breading groups for sadists, cheats and lairs to manipulate systems in their favor, and ultimately in games it’s rather the context to use these actions that define the situation rather than the input itself.

Firewatch excels in the usage of lying for a narrative. It taps into the tendency for players to make Henry tell the truth as well as the various lies to make Henry tell passive-aggressive half-truths to avoid discussion or to outright fabricate the facts for self-interest. The main drama is centered around a relationship between a supervisor, Delilah, that stretches her truth with puns, missing details and lies and the player avatar that can be as jokingly dishonest, truthful and distrustful as her. Events happen with gaps in memory for the player or for Delilah that may pit them against one another, establish mutual trust with each other, or leave both confused which one is telling lies. The feelings and thoughts shared between these two are unknown to the rest of the world, so whatever occurs has no relevance on what truly was said or happened in a lonesome part of the woods. 

This is a quality the game deliberately plays with to get inside the mind of the player with questions upon questions as you never get to see another person other than mere figments from afar, photos, documents and the details you discover about them in isolation from the person. Even the player’s avatar is not something the player knows for sure as there are no mirrors, reflections or outside camera shots—only an old photograph of you to tell someone what you look like now. Even if you could describe Hank as you think of him, the result is probably always choosing to tell lie in some small way.

Decisions made are treated as such where the player could get away with doing something they shouldn’t and then setting the record straight with no repercussions. To most gamers, the lack of consequences other than superficial flavor text/dialogue options may sound like the game undermines any lasting weight behind the emphasis to lie but it’s more so about what you choose to do in the moment that is far more important to consider than the outcome of that one decision. This is perhaps something a lot of people who didn’t enjoy Firewatch felt when they finished the game.

[h1]I Know What You Did Last Summer[/h1]

If you felt disappointed of Firewatch because of its ending, then you have first-hand vindicated the purpose behind telling it as a game rather than a movie, though perhaps had the game been made into a novel the same effect could have been done to a lesser degree without the immersive benefits of the gameplay and player-influence on the narrative. This is perhaps the only part of the review where I would consider it delving into spoilers because it will shape how you think about the game after experiencing it for yourself. 

As someone who has read books like A Cat that Walks through Walls and Starship Troopers by Robert Heinlein, there is a common trend to end his stories by deflating the narrative and leaving an impression with vague answers and with many questions such as, “What was the point?” This unconventional means of resolution is something I think Firewatch is also guilty of doing for a story with an ever-increasing demand of higher expectations to bring closure. That dissatisfaction after the final conversation and “choice” with Delilah was rather the water bucket moment the game needed to avoid becoming another instance of a story ending with no purpose like LOST.

Players who found themselves invested in the chemistry between Henry and Delilah were also the same people who were becoming more easily susceptible to Henry’s wild imagination, and the game went along with Henry’s ideas of an ever-prevalent government conspiracy spying on two Firewatchers mingling over a summer job and the disappearance of hikers over years in a national park because… When you describe the storyline in this manner, the ridiculousness of the idea is rather more apparent that it makes more sense why it was not true. Examining any piece of Henry’s dialogue as well as his personality as a writer, the books he enjoys reading, and his thought-process of arriving at conclusions with leaps of logic gives a picture of someone prone to exaggeration.

Why then did it seem so believable in the moment that we did believe a conspiracy would be resolved? It’s rather because the game uses the relationship, whether friendly or serious, as the focal point as well as utilizing its immersion to reinforce that narrow view of the story as Henry to create the mystery itself. Only when you know the full story do the facts show that both characters are as much as on the sidelines as the other Lookout rangers or the other major characters of the story; these two are given the most exposure for players to get caught up in their drama. The real protagonist is the setting itself that showcases all the major and minor characters the park affects and that the lasting effects of “a pause in the hallway of time” will remain even when the truth is burned away from memory.  

In the end, it does not matter how insignificant are your choices or what other characters decide to do after one summer compared to the entirety of their lives; the moments of happiness, confusion, sadness, guilt and terror you created are what matter from experiencing the story you shaped to make it your own, and no one can take that from you.
