That is not what Firewatch is trying to do.

See, everything in Firewatch wants to be realistic, the story is realistic, the way you hike, the way your character is kinda old and can't go everywhere, the voice acting feels legitimate, you don't have a mini-map but a compass and a map to navigate, and most of all: the ending is realistic.

Most of the time it goes that way: there are odd things happening and naturally we think crazy things might be going on, conspiracies or danger but in the end, it's nothing. Well, nothing compared to what we were imagining.

TLDR: the story was good. The ending really ruined this game for me. If you really want to play, purchase the game when it's on sale. 

DR: I can honestly say that this ending was by far the least satisfying ending I've ever played in a story base. They put too much weight on a character that really didn't effect Henry's life or character development, and then made that not-important-character the severely-important-character in the ending??? I would have been content with a "life gives you lemons" ending (which would probably be a weak but at least satisfying ending), where Henry had to deal with his own life and had to learn that he can't run away from his problems, but this wasn't the case at all. This character remained the same, there was no growth in his part (I tried to stick to the faithful route where he still cared about his wife), I felt like this character should have at least developed SOME, because he went through a couple of months of some extreme loneliness and the only communication he had was with Delilah... Didn't he have time to reflect on his past (which was so wonderfully described in the beginning, which is why the story, to me, was so powerful)? I feel like the game should have continued more, but it didn't and I feel like I'm missing something crucial to the story's plot. 

 I don't know, maybe it was just my play through, but I found this game overhyped for what it is. I'm glad I got this on sale instead of the actual $20. Please play though it yourself if you want, but I really felt like the ending ruined everything for me.

[i]Firewatch[/i] is easily one of the most enjoyable games I have ever played.

In the game you play as a watchman for forest fires in a natural park. You are Henry, a mid-aged man seeking to escape from his problems  in life. In your solitary life in the forest, There are barely any characters that you can interact with, with one exception -- Delilah, another firewatch. The two of you communicate over the radio, and Delilah is your only comfort in the two months you spend in the woods.

Everything about this game is amazing: the graphics, the environment, the controls, the plot, the ambient, etc. There are no notable downsides of this game. The game has a big map, but it is designed so that the sceneries are not at all repetitive, and with the help of a compass and a map, paths are often easily found. 

Don't worry if you are not good with roads; I am the worst at recognizing roads. A few years back I moved. The day after that when I came home, I spent half an hour wandering around the neighborhood, looking for the building where my apartment was. But in the game, with a compass and a map, I never spent more than 5 minutes looking for where I needed to go. Also, I felt immensely rewarding when I found the path by myself; it is the same pleasure you derive from hiking in the real world.

The plot is cleverly designed so that the player can relate to the feelings of the characters very well. The plot builds suspense over time, and even though this isn't a horror game, the thrill and the nervousness at certain points really match what you would feel in a horror game. The game is very realistic is how its story develops: the ending makes sense while not being too dramatic. To some there is a conspiracy involved, but how you look at the game is completely your freedom.

After you finish the game once you unlock the free roam mode, where you can explore the map at any pace you want and go anywhere you want. In the story you really have the freedom to go wherever, but you still need to follow the plot line. You also unlock the option to play with developer's commentary.

I think one of the reasons why [i]Firewatch[/i] is great is the same as why [i]Breath of the Wild[/i] is so great: free exploration. Nothing in the map inhibits you from going any corner of it. The beautiful art style and the fresh natural sights keep the player from easily getting bored. 

You are also offered an impressive amount of freedom over your action. [spoiler]Early in the game there were two college girls who lit fire, threw trash, and took baths in a lake with a radio making noises. I picked up the radio and turned it off with the girls still in the lake, shouting insults for interrupting. And then I saw the radio in my hand and the water in front of me and drew a link. I walked over to the water and threw the radio in it; sparks sputtered and the radio went silent. The girls screamed in overwhelming anger.[/spoiler] This is the moment that I fell in love with the game.

There aren't many elements of the game that can be really considered groundbreaking, innovated or unprecedented. Nonetheless, the game does best in everything it does, making a game that is mostly refreshing and relaxing, sometimes thrilling, and truly enjoyable. 

Strongly recommended to everybody, especially if you like stories and vivid characters in games.

This game is amazing, and I don't really think I need to explain why. I picked it up during summer sale, having heard about it before. If you enjoy video games and video games only, this isn't for you. If you appreciate good writing, character design, and interactivity, then you'll love this. 

But you've heard about this game, it's been out for over a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ year. I wanted to talk about the ending of this game briefly. 

[b] *SPOILER WARNING FOR BASICALLY THE ENTIRE GAME* [/b]

[spoiler]    If you've read any review of this game, then you've heard about the anticlimactic ending. No matter what you do, you don't get to meet Delilah, and you don't really get to see what happens after the events of the game. It's an ending that doesn't really conclude such a great story in very grand way. Many have sought out to find that huge climax hidden in the game's dialogue, however. The most common theory that people have made is that Delilah is a huge liar and conspirized with Ned just to ♥♥♥♥ with you. I don't really think that this is true, but I'm not going to touch on that. I think this game's ending is actually one of the best ending's I've personally seen. It concludes the experience in a way that fits the game's nature, not in the typical "Grand finale" or "happily/sadly ever after" that we're all used to. I've heard it described as a very "human" ending, and at this point, I can agree with that. 

    Something that this game does best is put you into the shoes of the main character, Henry. It does this while also perfectly making sure that you have enough control of the character that is necessary in a video game. In the beginning of the game, both you and Henry are extremely depressed about Julia's condition. As you go through the game, however, she starts to slowly fade away from Henry's thoughts and feelings, as well as the player's. That is until Delilah abruptly brings her back up at the end, reminding you that Henry has to go see her. 

    Henry gets so caught up with the mystery, with Delilah, with the missing teens, and making sure that the whole ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ forest doesn't burn down that he eventually forgets about Julia entirely. When he finds out that the "Secret organization" listening in on them is nothing but a hoax, he's underwhelmed. The fog clears and he finally realizes (with the help of Delilah) that he still has his own problems back at home to deal with. The mystery he was chasing was nothing more than a distraction from his life. He says near the end that they must have missed something, that there must be something else to explain all the weird occurrences, But there really isn't, and if there is, then it doesn't matter. He has to go back to his wife, no matter how much he wants to, and no matter how much more there is to the mystery. 

    Basically what I'm getting at is, the ending [b] is supposed to be disappointing. [/b] Henry's life will just return back to what it was. The job and the events of this game were just a method to get away from it, but only for a finite amount of time. Now that I'm writing about it, it feels like the story was cut short by the length of the job. Anyways, the same things apply to Delilah. She has to go back to her ♥♥♥♥♥♥ life without Javier (Yes, I'm pretty sure that she is, in fact, broken up with him) and just deal with life instead of running away from it. The reason why she has an easier time going back to life than Henry is because tragedy and sadness finally caught up to her in the woods, as she finds out Brian Goodwin is dead. Delilah leaves the forest depressed, and Henry leaves underwhelmed. And because of the reasons that I explained before, the player also leaves underwhelmed. This is the reason why the game has gotten so much criticism for the ending. 

    However, though, I do feel like a [b] tiny [/b] bit more effort could have been put into the ending. Here's my best, but simple, idea. WHAT IF...if you go through the game without taking too many pictures, then during the credits, you'll see pictures taken by Henry back home in Boulder with his wife? I think that might make the ending just a bit more satisfying, as you'll get to see what happened to Henry after the job. But it will also maintain that underwhelming and inconcluded ending. Alternatively, what if you could somehow leave the camera for Delilah to find, and then in the credits, you'll get pictures of what happened to her after the job? This is just a small idea, but honestly now that I think about it, maybe it might make the ending a little bit TOO satisfying.

    One thing that I believe FOR SURE should have better is the "secret alternate ending". For those who don't know, if you walk away from the helicopter at the end and go back towards the forest, the game will end. No alternate dialogue, pictures, or anything, just end. You could say that this is an easter egg, but someone at Campo Santo openly tweeted saying something along the lines of "I'm surprised nobody has found the secret ending". Like, 2 lines of dialogue could have made this better. The screen could just cut to black and you could hear Henry say "Delilah, I'm not going back" and Delilah say "What?" and that would have been WORLDS better. Once again though, just my thoughts.

    One last thing I wanted to mention is that Henry and Delilah most likely DO end up meeting, just after the game. In the end she says that she's right next to Henry's truck. Since the helicopter drops him off at the same spot, then it would be difficult for them NOT to run into each other. Additionally, if you ask Delilah to come to Boulder with you, then she'll decline, but promises to come down and visit sometime. If you do this, then one of the last options of dialogue you can give to her changes from "Goodbye" to "See you soon", indicating that you guys eventually meet up.

    All in all, I think this game is one of the greatest I have ever played, and it gives me a conclusion that makes me think not only about Henry's life, but also my own. 

TL;DR: This game's ending is purposefully supposed to be brutally realistic and underwhelming, and although it could have been done a little better, I believe it fits the game very well. [/spoiler]

First 'walking-sim' I've ever played but I picked up based on a good review. So in-turn, here's mine;

Story-
The story is tight with not much wiggle room or player choice. That being said, there is a bit here and there which adds a bit of depth and weight to the situations and how things resolve.

Narrative/Dialog-
I found both how the narration was presented and the dialog was written to be done well and they flowed smoothly. At no point did I feel out of character, nor did any of the other characters, nor did the narration. At times things are witty, sarcastic, or even emotional and they all came across accurately and correctly.

Sound/Music-
Overall the sounds in game were well done to the point I knew when something was happening or where a particular animal was before the HUD informed me of such or I saw them. The few tracks in the game were good and composed well but I found them sparse enough that I wished there were more earlier on.

Gameplay-
The game is pretty straight forward with only a few basic key inputs needed, but is intuitive and new features are explained well when they are introduced.

Pacing-
Overall a short game that keeps itself concise with room for the player to explore but when things get going, you feel compelled to push ahead and not stop to smell the flowers.


In summary, a short game, as a walking-sim should be (from what I'm told) but well crafted and worth the $30 I spent on it.

 John Keats once accused Isaac Newton of destroying the poetry of the rainbow by describing how it exists and why it appears to us the way it does us using a physics and maths-based explanation. *Firewatch* isn't a bad game per se. The writing is rather good, the graphics are beautiful it's just...there really isn't much of a game here. While much has been said about the improvement of storytelling in games and some people have pointed to *Firewatch* as an example of a game with a good storyline, I feel that is somewhat missing the point.

In my oppinion, a game isn't a game unless there is some kind of challenging gameplay, and there is none of that in *Firewatch*. As long as you can successfully move your mouse and press the assigned keys to perform actions, there is no challenge in this game.

Let me be clear, "challenge" does not nessicarily mean combat. Or platforming. Or really even obtuse puzzels. But for something to trully be a game I feel it needs to have something that you need to put your mind to, that you need to figure out. Throughout the game there are several fires, but not at any point to these impeed you at all. If something as simple as those fires preventing you from travelling a certain path so that you had to figure out an alternate route was in the game then, sure, that's a gameplay experience. Sadly, there is nothing like this in *Firewatch*. Yes, there are some things you can miss if you don't expore the whole area, but again that isn't really gameplay, that's just more simple button pressing.

The story in *Firewatch* IS good, although I found the ending the be a huge anticlimax. But without the elements of gameplay there all you're really doing is "playing" an interactive story with, really, not that much meaningful interaction. So, as a *game* I feel *Firewatch* fails. If you are really into *only* story in your games and don't care about being challenged then you'll probably enjoy this. Myself, I want to experience some kind of gameplay experience when I play a game. If I just want story I have novels or comics or film. In my opinion a game is meant to challenge, even if that challenge is a casual one a la *Botanicula* or *Machinarium*, both of which I really enjoyed.

Is *Firewatch* an example of good story telling? Sure. Can I recommend it as a game? No, I can't.

Firewatch is a first-person point-and-click adventure released in 2016.

[b]Story[/b]
It tells a story of grief and loss that will appeal mostly to people aged 30 or more. The main story is told through a series of radio conversations between Henry, a man in his early 40s, and his supervisor, Delilah. The game does an admirable job in having both Henry and the player quickly form a bond with what is essentially just a voice on the radio. This is in no small part due to the excellent voice acting. Suspense keeps the story moving and makes sure it doesn’t become stale. There are several interesting story lines throughout the game, but unfortunately the ending doesn’t manage to conclude these properly.

[b]Graphics[/b]
The game’s cartoony style works surprisingly well for nature, and the lighting is excellent. The environments you encounter are also quite varied: you’ll spend time in the forests or by the lake, hike through a canyon, go spelunking in caves, there’s something here for everybody. The engine can be a bit choppy at times, but it’s not so severe that it breaks the magic.

[b]Controls and UI[/b]
The controls and interface are quite barebones, which allows the player to focus more on the story. You’re eased into the controls, but the game sneakily withholds telling you that you can run until later on, once you’re already used to the more laid-back pace of walking around. You can even hide what little user interface you do have. One thing I’d recommend is turning off your location on the map, this makes the game much more immersive and realistic.

[b]Sound[/b]
The sound design is excellent in its minimalism. There’s the occasional subdued guitar at key points in the story, but really it’s mostly wind, birds and silence.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
The vast majority of the game is spent walking from one place to another, and that’s exactly the point. Walking through the woods and enjoying the way the light plays through the leaves is what it’s all about. Firewatch embodies the journey being the destination. You just walk, occasionally consulting your map and compass. You might stumble upon supplies, or if you’re of the lawful good alignment, the game even lets you clean up other people’s trash.

Unfortunately, exploration both in the physical world as well as through dialogue options is rather linear. While you can sidetrack, wander around a bit or change how Delilah responds depending on what dialogue option you chose, ultimately the game always shepherds you in a single, preset direction. Many people expect to make meaningful decisions and that is something you just cannot do in this game.

[b]Verdict[/b]
Both the games industry and its audience have matured to the point where a story about grief and loss in a package that is mostly devoid of any action can still turn heads. While the game has its flaws, the graphical style, excellent voice acting and general atmosphere of the game will make sure you’ll revisit the forests of Wyoming more often than you’d think.

Firewatch is a fascinating adventure game with plenty of flaws.  If you are not prepared to put on headphones and let yourself get lost in the great outdoors and the gradual freakiness of the storyline, this game is not for you.  However, if you are a fan of games like Gone Home--where the sole focus is figuring out what is going on--this game is worth a try.

[b] Story [/b].  I played Firewatch over the course of about 7-8 hours in the course of a single weekend.  I seriously doubt it would play well in 30-60 minute increments since the story builds upon itself.  From the very start, Firewatch presents itself as a game of options--much like Life is Strange.  But, as things progress, you will find that the storyline is actually fixed.  Although you still feel like you words and choices have meaning, they don't.  It's unfortunate, but it don't detract from the overall feel of the game as much as you'd think.  The mystery of Firewatch presently itself so gradually that you will be sucked in.  Sadly, the conclusion does have plot holes.  Not big ones, but they are there. 

[b] Gameplay [/b].  I struggled getting comfortable with the blurred look of the surrounding as you move through the forest.  After 30-60 minutes, I got a good feel for it.  I rarely ran in this game (unless I was scared something was behind me) because the scenery really is quite beautiful.  The addition of the disposable camera was ingenious.  It forces you be aware of the beauty of your surroundings and stop for a minute here or there in order to get the perfect shot.  My only complaint with gameplay is that there is a bug that happened 3-4 times.  It happens when you are clearing a bush usually--the game just start moving your character for you and suddenly you are running in the wrong direction until you find a way to interact with something else.  I was usually able to fix it in a couple of minutes.   However, once, it was in the middle of central gameplay and forced me to restart a day.  

[b] Atmosphere [/b].  On Steam, this game comes with a soundtrack option.  Don't get it.  To be perfectly honest, it's not all that great.  It seems like they relied on someone with a sound mixing program rather than a real musician or composer.  However, this doesn't detract too much from the game since it focuses more on the sound of nature.
Achievements.  I got eight out of the ten achievements through the natural course of the game.  With the help of the internet, the other two came quite quickly.

[b] Replayability [/b].  Honestly, there is almost no incentive to play this game beyond the end or the quick platinum.  By then, you have explored the map nearly in full.  You technically could try different dialogue tracks, but since they have little impact on the game, I have no desire to do that.

[b] Price [/b]. I abide by the $1.00 for an hour of gameplay rule.  This game falls barely short.  Steam tracked me at 8.7 hours.  I bought Firewatch at the Summer Steam Sale 2017 for $9.00.  However, I did leave the game open an running for at least an hour.  I would say the normal course of Firewatch is 6-7 hours and the normal platinum is 7-8 hours.  My only advice, do not buy at full price.  Although Firewatch is good, it's not $20 good.

[b] Overall [/b].  This has to be your genre for this game to be worth it.  The flaws are obnoxious but not game breaking.  The lack of good music is frustrating.  Make sure to buy this game on sale.  And make sure you have enough time to dedicate to it within a short time--much like reading a short novel.
Don't think of this as a game, think of it as a 4 hour book.

The story of Firewatch takes place at the end of '80s. Our protagonist, Henry, is tasked to be a lookout in the Shoshone National Forest. For me it makes the story more interesting that this is not a made up but an actually existing forest along with the references made to the fires occurring in the Yellowstone park years before. During the gameplay we walk around and complete tasks assigned by our superior, Delilah, who's sitting in another watchtower not that far from ours.

The game's atmosphere is excellent. It is great listening to Henry and Delilah going back and forth conversing via a walkie-talkie. Dialogue options are picked by us by pressing shift and scrolling by our mouse. They do not affect the outcome of the story, still, it is an interesting concept. We can be rude to Delilah or, for instance, use different options to describe ourselves (her drawing found later in the game will match our dialogue lines).

So, we see a column of fire and Delilah tells us to investigate. We see some fireworks and we need to go out and find the culprits. And this is the life of Henry, the lookout. We have a map, we can find hidden caches, go to special locales, find a rope to assist in climbing and all the while wonder how great the graphics are in this game. As the days pass the seasons change slightly so the same spots look a bit different - best example when we approach the same meadow and we can see the small fog above it (Henry does mention it to Delilah that early mornings can be cold).

The game has great music, a free roaming mode after story completion and an interesting story. While we complete some easy tasks we come across a mystery that slowly unfolds. For me the ending was a letdown (but this is just my opinion) as I did not find it satisfying enough. Also, do note that the game begins with a text telling us the background story of Henry; details about his girlfriend which can be very emotional. This is an interesting concept and even here we get to pick from 2 options we are regularly presented with.

Firewatch is a must-have first person exploration game. It has a relaxing gameplay and great voice-acting that all help with the immersion. I did 2 walkthroughs in quick succession as I liked the game very much. I believe this game is on par with the likes of Vanishing of Ethan Carter and the Old City Leviathan.

If this was released in, say, 2012, it would be a groundbreaking mega achievement. Vanishing of Ethan Carter or Mind: Path to Thalamus later, it's just an amazing game, but not groundbreaking. Plot is down to earth (i.e. all of it could happen in real life) and very mature (kids will think it's stupid), graphics are absolutely sweet (and not overly demanding), gameplay is very next gen, i.e. it is accessible to people who do not play games and have very little experience with them. And writing is of a good movie quality, easily, which helps, because there is a lot of dialogue.

Now, it has to be stressed this is NOT a walking simulator. I repeat, not a walking simulator. Sure, it hasn't got what gamers call "puzzles" and what supposedly must be present in all adventure games, but how often in real life you have to figure out the lock code by counting pigeons in a painting and adding seven because that was, I don't know, a name of the black dog you met an yesterday (and the lock is black, getit)? No such nonsense in this game and, I must say, this is how adventure games should be built. All these stupid puzzles are only required when you cannot come up with more meaningful and interesting things for the player to do, imho. 


BTW, it took me 5-6 hours to complete (steam counter is useless when you play offline). Completing it in 3 hours is like watching a two hour movie in an hour, imho. To do that, you will have to always do what has to be done, letter to letter, which is not interesting. You will also miss a lot of dialogue. I dont' understand people who brag about completing this game in 3 hours or less.

Firewatch has been described as a “walking sim”. It is. And it’s also a complex story about real feelings, and people, and emotions, and pain. And it’s a story about trust AND paranoia (because that’s what life is.) It’s not just a walking sim, it’s a “life sim”.

Henry has found love, and as result, has suffered loss. He chooses to go into the wild of a mountainous national park to experience the wilderness and do good in the process, in an attempt to purge some of his very real demons. He meets a co-worker, Delilah, who he comes to know and trust as little more than a voice over a two-way radio, but a voice understanding of demons. And their tasks are to protect the wilderness from fire, AND each other from themselves, while finding that there are larger mysteries in the wildness.

I suspect that many gamers playing Firewatch expect both more…and less. The graphics are perhaps not of the quality long-time gamers have seen evolve over this new century. The game is more linear than a “true” sim typically is. And the attention to game detail that has become expected is substantially absent in Firewatch. But once those issues are encountered, and understood, they become pluses, not flaws. Yes, there are more places one CAN’T walk than CAN, but this is a larger world than many, and lines need be drawn for practicality. It takes getting used to that details that so typically ARE the game, can mostly be disregarded in Firewatch. Going from day to day is pretty much the only task of importance (at least in the first half or more.)

Firewatch is filled with amusing detail, which goes far toward balancing out the very real sadness that Firewatch often comes close to bogging down in (yet is so crucial to the story.) If you play, be aware of just how the radio is intended to be used (but also that much of that use is not crucial, if you find yourself in the unfortunate need to rush the game.) There are many dozens of choices that feel critical to story development, yet I suspect rarely are. Feeling to be a controlling game element is what matters more, and Firewatch succeeds in that aspect admirably.

There’s not a lot that can be said about Firewatch without saying too much, so I’ll stop. But if you like the outdoors, or mystery (mostly the mystery found in the human heart) there’s an excellent chance you will like Firewatch very much.

Except it never came. All the build up, all the suspense, all the mystery was thrown away and the plot was revealed to be much smaller than anticipated. Even up to the very end, I was convinced that something would turn around, that there was no way it could end like this. But it did. And after a fairly disappointing final dialogue with your supposed "friend", it ends. No epilogue, no cliffhanger, nothing. 

At the end of this riviting and exciting journey, I experienced an ending that made all the mystery and wonder vanish as quick as it came, and made me feel like the only other character who I actually was able to become attached to didn't give a sh*t about our hero in the end at all. I faced the credits feeling as if I failed. That maybe I screwed something up. That somehow there was more than the disappointment I had experienced. But there was nothing. That's all there was.

So to conclude my review, I will say this: the journey was amazing. I have never played a game that drew me in this much and made me care about all my little actions like this game did. So in that regard, it was a success. But the ending was a failure. No other way to describe it. I'm not saying I need a happy ending, or one with a bowtie that makes everyone happy in the end. I just want an ending that lives up to the hype the gameplay created. You cant have an ending that disappoints the players. I want a ending that makes me feel as much excitement and thrill as the gameplay did. But it simply did not deliver.

So after careful thought, I would recommend this game to anyone who knows nothing about the story. But keep this in mind: enjoy the journey. Don't fantasize and ponder about how all this could add up. Just enjoy the moment, enjoy the character development, enjoy the scenery, put yourself in the characters shoes and live the ride. And when the ending comes, don't expect a grand ending to it all. Just look back on the story and remember the parts that made you laugh, made you sad, or made you just happy. Thats all I can say. Just enjoy the ride.

Whenever I can't decide if I like a game enough to replay it, I wait a day, start it up again, and see how the title screen makes me feel. I did that just now, and seeing it made me feel excited to play it two more times and hear every subtle difference. That feeling is very irritating, because I know that will take ten more hours of hiking and I am very lazy.

This is very much a slower game, but there were moments of genuine fear & anxiety & upset. I can honestly say I couldn't predict what would happen next. During the (sometimes too long) time I spent hiking to the next area, I'd try to map out the plot but it was never quite what I expected by the time I got to where I was going. It was more of an interactive experience than a traditional game. The graphics are gorgeous and the music is pleasant and natural. The ambience is not at all forced or overdone.

I spent years living in the woods hiking all over the US as well as doing parts of the Appalachian Trail avoiding society and deodorant, and this game really touched on the beauty and joy of nature and the sheer isolation you feel. That is counterbalanced by your lifeline on the radio, and the snowballing build of the plot. The amount of think-time in this game is intentional and frustrating and wonderful.

The ending was a hard pill to swallow, but if you look at the overall tone of the game I think it matches perfectly. Sometimes things aren't what they seem. Sometimes the idea of a thing can be more powerful than the thing itself. Sometimes you get less than you wanted. This game left me wanting more, and not because there was less.

The story really builds up hype as you go through it but in the end, it gives you something unexpected, something different and something that really makes you think all the stuff that happened. 

When it comes to gameplay, this one offers a refreshing touch of openness, whilst incorporating a well-though amount of direction and coherency. You feel as if things come to you naturally as you explore the map and proceed along the story. If the beautiful, large and well engineered forest of the Shoshone wants to lead you somewhere, you will get there feeling like an explorer. Encountering obstacles, areas and plot items feels more like a true adventure rather than a deliberately planned, restricted route. The map has so many sights, places and secrets to explore, that coming back to it in free roam after your first playthrough feels just as intriguing as the story and characters themselves.

If you're considering to buy Firewatch, go for it! It offers something truly unique and for many people, something different for a story based videogame. And now after playing it I'm not even shy to come to the conclusion that, [i] Firewatch isn't a game, Firewatch is ART. [/i]

It's June 25, 13:30 and the Grand Prix of Azerbaijan is about to start. Max Verstappen is on pole 5 and my wife is already in front of the TV looking at the warming up. 

Two days earlier I bought Firewatch which was already a long time on my Steam wishlist. I'm thinking to myself: "I'll play half an hour and then watch the Grand Prix." I start up my laptop on the kitchen table and start Firewatch and immediately get some very interesting and real life questions. One really hits me in the stomach and makes me wonder what kind of game poses these real life questions. 

Then the game begins. My wife calls that the start of the Grand Prix is almost about to broadcast. Reluctantly I get up and watch the start. Nothing special, so I get back to the game. I am completely mesmerized by the graphics, the voice acting is phenomenal and the story pulls me in completely. I am Henry and I am a Firewatch and my only radio contact is with Delilah. This is done so brilliantly that I forget everything around me. Although I am playing without a headset, somewhere far away I hear my wife yell: " That bloody Vettel just crashed his car deliberately into Hamilton's car, mother******!" Annoyed I watch the TV for a second, not even seeing what is happening as I already turn my head to my laptop screen again and play on. 

I walk through canyons and woods, solve puzzles, finish tasks Delilah gives to me and unravel the mystery behind the story. And that story is so intriguing that I keep playing and playing. This game is ART and easily one of the best games I ever played in my 45 years of gaming.

Five hours later I look up from the screen realizing that I finished it and my wife is in the garden. I didn't see her leave. 

Only on the eight 'o clock news I hear Daniel Ricciardo won the Grand Prix...

I'm a huge fan of story-driven, atmospheric experiences and this is a game I really, really wanted to like.

I was immediately intrigued by the prologue, which seems a simple enough choose-your-own-adventure type portion, but does very well to invest you in your player character, Henry. After doing some research I discovered this game was made by the same people responsible for The Walking Dead Season 1, which I adored and consider one of the best written games I've played. Walking Dead Season 1 had characters that you ended up growing incredibly attached to, and the same ended up being true of Firewatch. Unfortunately, that did just enough to get me to finish the game, because I was disappointed with pretty much every other aspect of Firewatch, including the story's resolution.

Firewatch looks really good for an indie, but it didn't run so great on my system (i7 4790, gtx 1080, 16gb RAM). I would experience pretty regular frame drops through my nearly 6 hours of play. And while the game looks very good, I never felt much drive to explore after the first couple of hours simply because there just isn't much to find. Aside from some notes in caches, I never found anything more interesting than a slightly larger tree or a nice viewpoint, and soon I began avoiding any exploration altogether because the characters and the dialogue had grabbed me so much. Any actual "gameplay" (ie. "walk here and then click the radio for a dialogue option") became a chore, a barrier behind which the game would reward me with some more bits of dialogue from these two characters that I had really grown attached to. There was a specific moment about 2-3 hours into the game where I was informed that I had to cross the entire map in order to find somebody to help me through a fence, and I came very close to just quitting because I almost didn't feel driven enough to take the next step. That's how dry and unfulfilling I felt the actual gameplay was in Firewatch. But I ended up doing it anyway just to hear more of Henry's and Delilah's story. I was fully invested in these two characters.

And that's really saying something considering how short this game is. The ability of these writers and the voice cast to grab me so quickly is pretty impressive now. The big problem I had with this game is simply that nothing else even came close to being as compelling as the relationship between Henry and Delilah. There's an overarching mystery that drives the plot forward, but once you actually begin to uncover what's going on it just felt too hokey, too clumsy, and just not believable enough despite being pretty grounded in reality. One of my issues with this mystery was that I simply wasn't feeling the isolated paranoia that my avatar within the game, Henry, seemed to be feeling. His actor seemed close to completely losing it, whereas I was just making my way to the next task and hoping for some interesting Delilah dialogue. The game failed to impart any sort of anxiety due to the setting and the isolation, possibly because it was so short, or that it had to skip days in order to keep things interesting due to a lack of any real gameplay systems outside of walking to an area indicated to you and pushing a button, or reporting back to Delilah via your radio.

Firewatch reminds me a lot of Gone Home. Both games offer an interesting setting and premise with some well-written characters, both try to impart a feeling of creepiness which succeeds at first but both ultimately fails to amount to anything substantial and becomes overly hokey after just a couple of hours. Additionally, the resolution of both games' mysteries are wholly unsatisfying, and the endings in general are not very good. Firewatch, in particular, really dropped the ball and left me feeling unfulfilled; like I had wasted my time despite really enjoying the characters and dialogue. It's the type of experience that will you have you saying, "Really? That's it!?" as the credits roll. If the ending had been a fulfilling conclusion for these two characters then I believe I'd have recommended this game just on that strength alone. But squandering the story of two compelling characters left a sour taste in my mouth, and for that reason I can't recommend it to others until it begins selling at a sub-$5 price point.

[h1] Firewatch [/h1]

[b] An Enjoyable Walking Sim That Is Grounded In Reality [/b]

On the surface, [b] Firewatch [/b] appears to be just another walking simulator that is mainly focused on its plot while sacrificing its gameplay. Well, it pretty much is just that. However, unlike many other games in its genre, it succeeds in teaching the player a valuable lesson in escapism and expectations, an important topic within an entertainment industry that has begun to stray away from representing the realistic complexities of everyday life.

Firewatch follows Henry, who is running away from a once perfect life that has now begun to crumble around him. He takes up a job as a fire lookout during the summer of 1989 in the Shoshone National Forest as a way to take his mind off of his life that hasn't turned out the way he thought it would. Through meeting a fellow lookout named Delilah, chasing off a few rambunctious teens, and dealing with an assortment of strange occurrences during his time as a lookout, the player learns a lot about Henry and his situation. Without spoiling the story, the player learns that many of the events occurring throughout the game may be merely coincidental, and Henry and Delilah happened to be caught up in it all.

What this game teaches the player is at first difficult to determine. While many may dislike the endings' lack of drama and emotional catharsis, it actually shifts the focus more to the reality of the situation - his entire experience at Shoshone was a way for him to escape his real-life issues. Everything he experienced may matter in the moment, but there are bigger issues that he is trying to avoid confronting.

Lastly, [b] Firewatch [/b] manages to be a good abstract commentary on the current state of not just the gaming industry, but entertainment in general. Most people who consume entertainment are looking to distract themselves from a life that may not always be filled with positive experiences, and during those times, the mind being able to wander is good, if not natural. Additionally, [b] Firewatch [/b] ignores doing what most players want the game to do in favor of serving as a hybrid between escapism and reality. The dialogue isn't overly dramatic or wacky, its human and endearing to the player engaging in it (while also feeling like some of the most natural dialogue EVER to exist in a video game). By its finale, the player is aware that they played this game to escape, even for a moment. While nothing in-game changed Henry's life, the game brings awareness to the simplicity and purpose of entertainment - to serve as a meditative tool to take one's mind off of the stresses of everyday life. It's a bit of a stretch, I know, but this is MY review so deal with it!

I would [b] Recommend [/b] this title despite its simplistic gameplay, only because it provides an interesting plot with some great performances. It doesn't do anything particularly new and fresh in the gameplay department, but in terms of narrative and dialogue, it will keep you playing until the end.

[h2] Final Verdict: 7/10 (Good) [/h2]

Spoiler Free Review:
Nothing happens. You're forced to walk around constantly to no end; the "narrative" falls completely flat. You'd get a better experience from watching one episode of a daytime soap opera: only 30 minutes long and you don't have to hold forward the entire time.

Ultimately, Firewatch is a game about conversations between two lost souls, which you can shape to a certain extent. It does a very good job of this, and then wraps a beautiful, but ultimately shallow experience around it. 

There aren't really any puzzles, or action sequences, or anything similar, and I wouldn't mind that ultimately... except that I felt like the story was leading me in that direction. I also don't mind subverting expectations, but the reveal felt rushed compared to the significant build-up, and I think it took the wind out of the last act of the game to a certain extent.

Still, as an attempt to broaden narrative interaction in adventure games, Firewatch is worth a play. Just be sure to take your time and appreciate the attention to detail put into the world; there's all sorts of fun stuff that a fast playthrough will miss.

Whether you replay this game or not will probably depend on how much you liked the first playthrough. I personally felt like I got everything I needed from it, but I might go through once more just to try all sorts of things I didn't do the first time through.

Overall, Firewatch is a good game. It has great core components, such as the over all premise of wandering in the wilderness with only a walkie talkie for communication, and the simplicity of it which really makes you focus on the story instead of get distrated by small, inconsequencial aspects, such as an inventory. However, I'm not able to give this game a perfect rating because there were some aspects that, had they been different, would have made the game much better.

First, the game starts off as different colored backgrounds with some writing on it, setting the stage, explaining the story of the main character, Henry, and why he's eventually going to end up in a firewatch tower in the forrest. However, as the game is set up now, the credits that usually role (such as the producers and what not) as the game is starting up in general, role when you start a new game file, and when clicking through these credits, I accidentally clicked through a few pages of the story. It didn't ruin anything, I was still able to understand what was going on, but there was no way for me to go back and read the skipped story without starting a new game file.

Second, the map of the game was a bit of a bastard. There is no "off roading" in this game, which doesn't upset me at all, but you start the game with no trails on your map. So, you can only walk on trails, per the games mechanics, but you don't have any trails marked down... because of this I spent about the first hour of the game fumbling around, stuck on only my second mission because I couldn't figure out where I was going. It gets better as the game progresses and you unlock trails on your map, but the start of the game was tough and very annoying because of this, especially as not all the trails in the game are intuitive.

Following that, my only other real qualms with the game are nit picking the story line. The ending, will include spoiler text, was disappointing. [spoiler] You spend the whole game talking and forming an ambigiously platonic/romantic relationship with a fellow lookout named Delilah, whom you anticipate you will get to meet at the end of the game, but you never do. Not only that, but at the end of the game Delilah acts in a way as if the relationship was strickly platonic and you, the player, seemed to imagine the romance. I found this frustrating, especially considering you board a helicopter after this and do not even get to learn what happens to your steadily declining wife either.[/spoiler] Over all, not the ending I had in mind.

In conclusion, this was a great game with some minor kinks. It took me about 5.5 hours to complete this game, and it was cute and I did enjoy the story. However, I did get this 55% off during a sale at the price of $8.99 USD and couldn't see paying the full $19.99 USD price tag for it, for what the game was. I would recommend waiting until this item is on sale to purchase it.

Firewatch is an immersive first person mystery with an absolutely amazing soundtrack and gorgeous visuals to suit. I didn't think I would enjoy the game as much as I did but the story was far too interesting to not completely immerse myself in. The suspense at each turn, the character development coupled with the ability to direct most conversations, I found myself falling deeper in love with not only the characters but the place as a whole.

Firstly, the visuals are absolutely gorgeous. I found myself almost wishing I was outside in this beautiful place. The art style paired with the colour palette used is perfect; gorgeous orange, yellow and red hues are what greet you in the introduction and as the game goes on the palette only continues to expand. As each day went on I found myself wandering around just to enjoy and explore the beautiful surrounds on offer, at times forgetting that I had some set tasks to complete.

The game is surely one to move you. As you connect to the characters on a deeply emotional level through their dialog; I found myself tearing up and even relishing in their joy. The introduction to the game really sets you up for this. Not only was it simplistic in its execution but it really pulled on the heartstrings, making me feel for the characters I would never actually technically see at all. I have to admit that a lot of this is thanks to the absolutely stunning soundtrack. I honestly cannot talk highly of the music enough. It is absolutely perfect with the setting and not only made me tear up several times but even made my heart race as the story progressed. **SPOILERS -- DON'T READ IF YOU HAVEN'T PLAYED YET!**

I consider myself very lucky as I came into this game completely blind; it sat on my wishlist for a long time pending a sale and free time to invest until just last night when I banged it out in a long continuous session. I didn't even watch any gameplay footage or any in-depth reviews, and it was only on my wishlist because it was lauded as something spectacular when it was released awhile back and occasionally I'll bite when games are universally praised. (I still haven't played Last of Us and I know that's one I should get around to based on it's pedigree).

Well, now that I've digested Firewatch I can say that it does some things splendidly (voice acting, tone, keeping the player on edge who hasn't read spoilers)... and other things rather poorly,  (with the beginning and ending and your in-game choices not effecting the game's conclusion beyond some slight dialogue being the biggest disappointments). To put things in perspective, that last fact alone basically means that unless you desperately want to hear some random radio dialogue about a snail or signpost or stone circle you may have missed off the beaten path somewhere during your first play through, there's no point in replaying the game: you will end up in the SAME EXACT (sullen) PLACE at the game's conclusion. Flirt with Delilah, ignore Delilah... it doesn't matter: she won't wait for you, and will always blow you off during the end sequence. Gather evidence against Ned? Doesn't matter... you can't do a thing about what happened. Even if you piece together the most likely events that happened during the game's story, again... it doesn't matter as you can't act on it while playing the game. It's fairly soul crushing when you realize your fate is sealed the second you hit play with this (well paced and voice acted) game, and I'll never play it again because of that fact.

TL;DR -- I'd say as a Visual Novel (with fairly pointless running + climbing simulations tossed in since you can't die) it's very good, but as a satisfying story it falls rather flat. It truly needed to have multiple endings depending on what you chose as a backstory at the start and how you proceeded, and to give the player choices to make instead of just pushing you along on rails.

↓ SPOILER ↓

[spoiler]We start the game off finding these teenage girls. Their tent gets ripped apart and they leave behind lots of their stuff. They go missing. We hear a strange signal by the lake, find that walkie-talkie from the research site, get knocked out.
We find out we're being listened to. Find transcripts of our characters, in a place with tons of expensive equipment. Soon after we arrive there, the whole place gets set on fire. Someone's implying that they could blackmail us, having recorded our conversations, making it seem like we lied to the police and caused the fires ourselves.
And in the end, it was a crazy father who accidentally killed his son and then decides to just disppear, the teenage girls turn up out of nowhere completely fine, and Henry and Delilah (Who are the main characters)  just get evacuated from the area. We get a short, awkward goodbye between the two and that's it.
They had the set-up for a fantastic mystery story there, and it had me intrested all the way through. But when the "twist" turned out to be that Ned caused his son's death, it just felt like a cheap cop-out. The entire final act of the game felt pretty rushed, to be honest... there's no real payoff. It's an ending that leaves more questions than it answers, and it feels shallow and disappointing. While making my way to the evac point, I was convinced there was some kind of swerve coming, turn the story around, but that moment never came.
Don't get me wrong. I've enjoyed my time with Firewatch. But it feels like the writers set up this huge intresting mystery and then just... fumbled it. Failed to make anything out of it.[/spoiler]

I still recommend this game tho!

If you only plan on buying one story based game, you should buy Life is Strange. If you plan on buying two story based games, then you should buy Firewatch. Firewatch is a game about the human mind. More specifically, it is about how we often get so wrapped up in our perception of events that we ignore any signs that our perception and assumptions are wrong. The ending is dissapointing, but not because of any fault in the game. Rather, the fault lies in us players for falling into the trap of assuming our perception of events and of others to be correct. The game ends with a slow fizzle rather than a bang, but that's how most things in life end.

Firewatch is a narrative driven game that put you into the shoes of a newly hired fire lookout in a Wyoming state park.  A brief prologue before the events of Firewatch kick off sets the backstory of our main protagonist Henry and his motivations for taking this job out in the middle of nowhere.  Once the game starts, you are let loose into the wilderness and your journey really begins.

The initial reaction I had when receiving my map of the wilderness was how big the world was, but it became apparent after the first couple of days that the world is far more linear than it seems at the outset.  However, the world never felt small and was structured in such a way to keep the story moving at a fair pace and to avoid confusing the player with a large world that would otherwise serve no purpose to the narrative.  Eventually, you'll begin to recognize paths and trails but when the game sends you to someplace new, you'll likely need to make good use of your map and compass to navigate.  The actions and tasks I was assigned with never felt repetitive and while it does make you pass previously explored areas, you're often sent to a new area that you likely haven't explored yet.

The main hook of this game is the narrative and it is convey almost entirely through a two-way radio you get soon after you arrive at your watch tower.  Your boss, Delilah, speaks to you through it at key points and initiates a dialogue that you can choose responses to.  Outside of the scripted dialogue, there are tons of opportunities for you to initiate them just by exploring and examining things.  I've only played through once, but it's clear your responses have an effect on shaping the developing story.  The story obviously being the main purpose of this game, is not only very well written, it's voice actors are also perfect for the roles.

The story is very carefully crafted and well written.  It has a lot of different emotions that it dips into with seemingly effortless command and it works very well to create the changing atmosphere as the game progresses.  One day it can be lighthearted banter and simple 'getting to know you' type dialogue, to serious and more depressing chats, to seriously creepy and distributing dialogue.  At one point, I was legitimately feeling scared being out in the dark wilderness by myself, constantly looking over my shoulder.  This game focuses directly on the narrative and doesn't try to be anything more than that.  It effortlessly pulls you into its world and its two characters while continuously pushing you forward to not only discover whats coming next, but to get a chance to further your relationship with Delilah.

The game world itself is a beautiful piece of work and its attention to the detail of the world itself as well as its keen eye for atmosphere and color really sets the perfect backdrop for the narrative to unfold.  This is also where my only real complaint comes in, and it's more of a technical one than anything else.  For some reason, the frame-rate jumps around while out exploring and sometimes while standing still.  I don't know if it's streaming in data or has other background functions that are causing the drop, but it just seemed random with no real correlation with what was happening on screen.  It happened often enough that I was slightly annoyed towards the end but it ultimately wasn't a deal breaker.  Still, it would be nice if such an issue could be fixed because it can pull you out of the experience momentarily.

I've seen a lot of polarizing views on this games ending and while I won't spoil anything, I feel that both views are valid.  I would say that this game is more about the journey than it is the destination but to some, that's not acceptable and that's fair.  Narrative games like this take a risk because while it's a great story, it has to end and the writers have a very specific ending in mind.  That ending may be wildly off base with any given players expectation of how they feel it should end.  While I feel the ending was the logical conclusion to the story, that won't be the same sentiments from everyone who plays.  What I think is the real treat here is examining the story after the credits roll.  Much like similar narrative based games, there is a deeper narrative than what one would think if just taken at face value.  When you really start to examine the dialogue, the timing of it, and the events that unfold, it opens various avenues that just beg for a replay to truly discover what is happening.  However, it should be noted that this game and the subjects it deals with lend itself to many various interpretations and I think that's the hallmark of a great story.  Some may see a story with a deeper mystery that needs deeper examination while others may see a story dealing with grief and depression.  It's because of this that I believe the ending can be polarizing because depending on what your personal experience with the story is, your expectations of the ending will vary.  If this is at all concerning to you, then waiting for a sale might be the way to go.

The technical issues with frame-rate aside, I think this game is a great piece of work.  It's short, sweet, and a must buy for anyone interested in narrative based/driven games.  It's choice driven narrative and underlying mysteries offers enough to net some replay value and I can see myself coming back to this game from time to time, just to enjoy the story again.

So if its story is, in the end, inexistent in itself and didn't affect the characters either, what's left of a story-driven game? Yeah, graphics and voice acting, I guess... let's say the storytelling was very good but the story itself was so underwhelming :/


--------------------------------------------------------------------
SPOILERS and other thoughts about the flatness of this ending:

Of course the "conspiracy/experiment" was not going to be real (Delilah and Henry (or Just Henry?) were not the brightest folks when they came up with that science experiment theory, and actually there were not very bright a couple other times either...)
Still, there was room to manage a big plot twist, something else hiding behind the surface.

There are plenty of theories out there, about what was going on, in the background, between Ned and Delilah, because the game is full of hints in that direction. And those are really masterfully done, tension rises, you look behind your back all the time and starts doubting everything (even you own sanity), etc...

This tension builds up until we reach Delilah's tower, which would have made a revelation particularly striking at that moment. We could have seen something in there that would have turned the whole story around, connecting the dots together...

But nope, nothing at all, just a shallow talk between the two main characters, a totally underwhelming goodbye and the credits. Btw, even without changing the content, just a change in the form would have helped this ending: at least show us the landscapes from the helicopter as we leave, maybe we could witness those familiar places burning or anything that gives the moment some kind of intensity!

Clearly the game (the storytelling) was well done though, and this huge deception is a good illustration of the disproportionate importance of an ending in a story!

Concisely put, Firewatch is a masterpiece that game developers would do well to learn from.

The longer answer is that, while a rather short experience, Firewatch has breathtaking visuals combined with stellar voice acting. It's set in Wyoming, a place where few storytellers, let alone game developers, would dare go...and is represented incredibly well. This is perhaps one of the most gorgeous interpretations of Wyoming's wilderness that I've ever seen and the game flawlessly succeeds at capturing the atmosphere of the wilderness.

In addition, the developers expertly shifted tone throughout the course of the story, causing me to feel exactly what they wanted me to. When they wanted me to feel at ease, I felt at ease. When I was meant to feel scared, I felt scared. There were several moments throughout the game that I expected a jumpscare to pop up and, although it never did, the developers successfully made me tense up at the proper time, nonetheless.

If I had to nitpick anything, it would be that the game will only take about 5-6 hours to complete at the most. While I'm perfectly satisfied with my purchase, as those 5-6 hours were crafted with extreme care and every moment felt enjoyable, some people might be less willing to spend 20 dollars for such an experience, all the same. If you're already curious about the game, the 20 dollar pricetag might still be worth paying. For those who are a bit more apprehensive, if you wait until the game is half off, you'll definitely feel that you got your money's worth, and then some.

I recommend this game with reservations. First up - the good stuff. Obviously the visuals of Firewatch are spectacular, and I can report that it even looks pretty good on mid-range hardware. The visuals are a balance of cinematic cartoonishness and naturalistic designs, and the sound design especially works overtime to create an all-encompassing sense of atompshere in this surprisingly wide-ranging open world. Your character's interactions with the environment, from scaling cliffs and sliding down ropes, are some of the most tactile I've seen in any videogame. 

The downside, however, is the story - it felt very predictable to me, and the characters, Henry and Julia, far too dumb and inclined towards paranoia. While I understand that this is the story the developers want to present to me, I always felt a little offended by how dumb the characters are - it took me out of the headspace of Henry, who you play the game as, and never trustworthy of Julia, who you only communicate with over radio. Perhaps this was deliberate, but regardless I felt like more could've been done to make Henry, at the very least, a bit more believable and reasonable. 

That said, the game is one of the more unique "walking simulators" out there - there's actually enough interactivity to the game that the term "walking simulator" almost feels innapproprirate. For instance, the open-world is quite sprawling, and reaching objectives requires puzzling out your position using a map and visual clues in the environment. It's much more in the vein of an adventure game - and with the multiple choice dialogue branches, I suppose it's most approprirate to describe it as such.

EDITED REVIEW:

I thought about it a bit more and wanted to go through some issues.

What bothered me most, although I was also disappointed with the story as well (it makes almost no sense to me), was that from the get go things seem to be designed to extend play time artificially. Slow texts, slow everything really. All the numerous items in the map you want to find, pick up, and explore, but actually mean absolutely nothing and have zero gameplay value. I wonder what these pots and kettles, books and notes, drawings and typewriters and generators and friggin pine cones can be used for? Well, nothing at all. They were only interactive to make you click on them and waste as much time doing random meaningless stuff as possible. They could have been static, because it wouldn't have changed anything, so clearly they were made this way on purpose.I spent time cleaning up the beer cans as I wanted the character to be responsible and take the new job seriously and thought it might have an effect, and while I appreciate that not every action needs to have a consequence in a story and often the journey is the main point of it, those actions were entirely pointless in the end. I took pictures thinking maybe I might need those pictures later as evidence or something (I know, a bit complex but something like that), and it had absolutely zero meaning, and actually I was meant to just take pics of landscapes and such even when dialogue suggested otherwise. These things, to me, are very clear pointers to a design which tries to bait you in to going slow, doing extra things, going through every item in the game carefully (as said, this is sometimes encouraged by the dialogue) when it actually has no gameplay or story effect at all whether you do or not. Showing other characters was clearly avoided, very likely because it's infinitely easier to develop a game with no actual interaction and animation, AI etc done at all. It's all just a bit disappointing, and specifically that it so clearly affected the game design. And it seems a tad lazy and makes questioning the value and pricing more important. I like world building and lore, but in a game with so little content and the way this was designed in the game, this really has a bad taste to me. 

The gamplay felt clumsy, and like said, just felt constantly like they are trying to slow me down on purpose. So much just walking from a to b, with beautiful art, but that's it. No other point to any of it. I felt like they must have been so tempted to push the day changes even further. 
In the beginning I was going to the lake, and was supposed to pick up an item along the way, but since I was exploring, I went a different route, and so when I got to a certain point I couldn't actually proceed in the game. I had to go all the way back and go the "normal" route to be able to then go further. This was simply waste of time, and annoyed me specifically because it immediately told me that you better not go off the beaten path or you might have to reverse a huge deal, yet some other paths are offered and lead to nothing at all. Similar thing happened when I checked a poster in the watch tower and figured out where I needed to head next based on some dialogue, hiked all the way there, only to discover that I hadn't clicked on the last bit of dialogue and so the game didn't yet progress with me and I had to go back again, or start the day over, to get the game to move forward with me. This is clumsy design. 

The character moves unbelievably slowly, and running is easy to only discover after a while of gameplay, and it's also put on a key which isn't intuitive at all and doesn't follow suit with pretty much every other game ever made. Not a huge problem, but stinks to me like trying to force us go slow, for no good reason other than making the game longer in duration. No jumping, getting sort of glitched with the environment whenever trying to find different areas, slow routes on purpose etc. The exploration is rathr bad honestly, and if you try and find different paths and look around corners to find cool stuff, there's nothing there to be found, and you soon get annoyed by the terrain and the incapability of your character to move through it in any other but clumsy and slow manner. Btw, just remembered I found a flashlight in the game too, which I never once had to use. Another example of a waste of time prop for the sake of it (and an easy addition development-wise btw, which I suspect is the reason it's in the game. Add something, why not, it's easy. Who cares if it doesn't have any use). 

Anyway, I don't mean to say it's a horrible game, but I do think it stinks a bit of greedy sales program and strategy, and slightly lazy developing. I want to support good games developing and sales strategies, like the team and strategy behind witcher games, or Titanfall 2 (which did a 180 from the first game because of criticisma and push in ambition development-wise). I reckon it's important we don't just accept whatever qualityand pricing from indies either. It's still a half decent game / experience and worth a sale price.

More an interactive movie than a computer game (in its genuine understanding), Firewatch deals with a very important topic for people beyond 30 (ehm, like me): how far and how long can you run from your problems and when will you stop doing that. Like any remarkable piece of a thinking man's modern fiction, Firewatch does not give any precise answers, only hints. There's definitely something to ponder on here after the game ends.
And it does end very quickly, even abruptly, just after 4 hours of gameplay, yet leaving an aftertaste for another 10-15 hours to savour. Anyway, given such modest game timeline, the few protagonists manage to unfold themselves in full blossom. I'd say I haven't seen characters so alive and complete yet complex for quite a while in computer games.
Get this game NOW if you look for some easy-playing yet touching game experience.

To get down to earth, here are some pros and cons I've spotted (will be interesting mainly for those, who have already played the game):

+
* Absolutely well-developed and self-standing characters, as if people were taken from the real life and uploaded into my PC. Brilliant voice acting only adds to their vibrance.
* Some really good graphics and depictions of American landscapes for quite a low-budget indie game.
* THICK atmosphere of romantic loneliness and seclusion. Something I dream about too often, but will never have.
* A plot with a slight twist.
* Short playtime: add another hour or two in the same setting and the game would possibly get old quickly.
* Living in a lookout tower! (really, all my life's dream)

-
* You don't actually have to make any choices and cannot change things. The game just flows on as prescribed by the writers (like I said, it's good for a movie but not too god for a computer game).
* The forest you can never get lost in. With all natural beauty, the map has a limited number of paths you just cannot stray far away from (I understand that it's not the point of this particular game, but guys, it's a forest after all!).
* Short playtime (again): there are definitely places where the plot could be made more elaborate. I mean, firework hunting was fun!
* Too few adventure components to make this game really a game (not an interactive movie).

To sum it up: very recommended for pleasant passtime on a lazy day. But don't get too surprised when the ending sets you pondering on life's trivialities even more than you expected when the game started. After all, better spend some cash on this "film" than on another movie theater flop.

Exploring Firewatch is tremendous fun, and the game is all about that adventure. Your character has run away from a tough real-life situation (the nature of which you define as the game opens) to spend the summer watching for wildfires as far away from other people as he can get. He's pretty successful, too; your only daily contact in the game is the voice of your supervisor, Delilah, radioing in from the next outpost with daily objectives and your daily dose of snark. 

At least, you think you're alone.

Firewatch distinguishes itself in that it can play very differently in different hands. Every choice you make in your conversations and explorations contributes to the story, which is hemmed in by only a few key plot points. When people say games can't be art I'm going to point towards this game. What an absolute gem. It's a 'walking simulator', as the phrase goes, and for people who dislike such game this is going to be a tough sell, but if you don't mind something outside the paradigm of what is generally considered a 'video game', this is an instant buy. The game is about a man named Henry, who has had a troubled past, signing up for the job of a firewatch in the forests of Wyoming. Upon arriving there, he strikes up a relationship with his boss Delilah, whom he can only interact with via a walkie talkie. It's this relationship that is the central focus of the game. There are no characters whom you meet face-to-face, and the only person you can talk and open your heart to is just a faceless voice on the phone. She's your only link to humanity, so to speak, and the times when she stops talking to you (either because of scripted events or your own behavior), the solitude is almost stifling.

Delilah tasks you with numerous jobs and keeps talking to you almost endlessly. You can interact with her about anything: find a Missing poster and talk to her about it, and she tells you a story. Find a deer antler and she schools you about the difference between antlers and horns. How this relationship evolves, how you grow to trust, suspect or love her is what the game is about. You have multiple choices in how to reply to her, and different people will come off with different opinions of her depending on how they talked. You can cut off her sarcastic comments and she'll get upset, you can laugh at her jokes and she'll throw more at you and she'll open up. Her dialogs adapt according to how you reply, basically. This feeling of being lost in the woods is amplified by a stellar soundtrack, and the graphics are gorgeous. In the course of being a firewatch you stumble upon a mystery which seems to grow more and more ominous and your relationship with Delilah starts showing different colours as a result, and while the resolution of this mystery might or might not satisfy you depending on your tastes, the story of how two people bond with each other in absolute solitude, the quality of voice acting and the stark realistic way the characters and their stories, motivations are portrayed makes it one of the best games to come out in recent times.

And so begins the crushing prologue to Campo Santo's debut game, Firewatch, a first-person mystery/adventure game.

Firewatch tells the story of Henry, a middle-aged man, whose wife begins to show early signs of dementia. Unable to cope with the impossibly hard circumstances, Henry decides to get away from it all and take a job as a fire lookout over at Shoshone National Forest. There, he gets acquainted with his supervisor, Delilah, and the two of them keep in constant touch using walkie-talkies.

Then, slowly, but in increasingly disturbing fashion, certain uncomfortable events occur, leading Henry and Delilah to believe that something sinister may be going on in the woods...

I'm going to have to talk about the presentation first, not only because it's the very first thing you notice in a video game (or in anything, really), but also because, in the case of Firewatch, it's just [i]so damn good[/i]. The beautiful cartoonish-like art style is supplemented with vibrant warm colors, and you could grab a screenshot of pretty much any part of the game and frame it like a glorious painting. The soundtrack is low-key, but on point: at turns relaxing and haunting. And the voice acting; well, we'll get into that later.

If you've heard of such titles as [i]Gone Home[/i] or [i]Everybody's Gone to the Rapture[/i], you have a pretty good idea of what sort of game Firewatch is. It takes no interest in providing you with some form of gameplay or challenge, so I guess one could describe it as a "walking simulator"; though it does give you just enough freedom of exploration so as not to feel like an on-rails experience (I'm looking at you, [i]Dear Esther[/i]).

Essentially, you follow whatever orders you're given from Delilah: go check out that power line, or confiscate those illegal fireworks, for starters. At times, you may need to take a look at your map and compass to get your bearings, and/or try and find all the goodies-filled Cache Boxes scattered around the relatively large map. There's also some choice making here: you get to decide how Henry responds to the events unfolding before him, but that's about it. Whatever choices you make only serve to offer a closer look at Henry's temperament, rather than have an impact on the game's overall narrative.

So in terms of gameplay, there's not really much to write home about.

Firewatch's power lies elsewhere. It's in the story and the characters. And boy, does it deliver on story and characters. Does it deliver big time.

It's vital for a narrative-driven game such as Firewatch to be able to hold the gamer's interest throughout, despite the lack of a challenge in terms of gameplay. It's all up to the writing, and the writers have a consistently sure hand, effortlessly shifting the tone between mystery, comedy, and even horror. They slowly ratchet up the tension, until the game's final moments, of which you may have heard a thing or two (the word "anticlimax" is thrown around a lot).

I have various thoughts on this - but for now, let's just say that the answers we finally get are much, much smaller and grounded than we're initially led to believe. Whether they're satisfying, I believe it's a matter of personal taste. I, for one, am sure that I was satisfied.

How could anyone do justice to Firewatch's main voice actors? The line delivery (and there are a lot of lines to deliver) rests heavily on the shoulders of Rich Sommer (Henry) and Cissy Jones (Delilah) and they both pull it off with ease: their chemistry is believable, their relationship constantly evolving (and thus requiring the actors to evolve accordingly). The marriage of the top-shelf writing and voice acting that's present here is truly something to behold.

It must be noted that Firewatch is a short game, clocking in at around 4 hours, and I'm kind of skeptical about whether it's worth the 20$ price tag. But it's concise, perfectly paced, and, at the end of the day, has something to say. Think of it as buying a good, if expensive, book. Plus, there's always the Free-Roam mode, which boosts the replay value (but let's be honest, not by much).

If you are not into walking simulators, Firewatch is probably not one to change your mind. But for those of you who are up to do some hiking, and learn a thing or two about human guilt, and escaping from your problems, do pick Firewatch up.

If anything, it's a memorable experience.
