Nearing the end of my time with Firewatch, something strange crept over me; the dawning realisation that instead of exploring it’s rendition of the great outdoors, I could actually… Well, go and explore the great outdoors. I was playing a form of escapism whereupon I could easily experience the real deal, if only I could bother to get up and make an effort to actually reach it. It was a weird little moment, to say the least.
 
There’s a good reason for sticking with Firewatch instead of heading out my own front door, however, with that being that it’s hard to draw yourself away from the striking world that’s on offer here. The art style is the first thing you notice, with its minimalist design style and simple colour palettes creating something that looks pretty unique. Yet then you also notice how good the map design is, taking in all the wonders of the American national parks that form the game’s setting – from shady forests and great lagoons, to narrow mountain valleys and wide open vistas. It’s a world that you want to keep exploring just to see what new sights might be around the next corner, and one where it’s hard not to keep yourself from tapping your screenshot key every few minutes.
 
The way you explore and traverse the area is also interesting. There’s no arrow pointing your way, no big on-screen hints pointing out the right direction for you. Instead, you’ve literally got to whip out a map and compass, and carefully plot your route towards your next objective. Then, as you go, you have to keep checking and adjusting your direction, paying close attention to the distinct possibility you might wander off course and get hopelessly lost. It feels as if you are actually hiking, that every endeavour and successful journey is a result of your hard work. It’s an incredibly satisfying experience.
 
Firewatch’s world isn't perfect, however. For one, it isn’t the biggest out there. From about the halfway point onward you’ll be stomping through a lot of old ground, the charm on exploring the unknown being lost, and your relatively slow travel speed making things feel a little bit of a chore. Additionally (and just like real life) getting lost isn’t exactly fun, and having to consult your map constantly to make tiny course adjustments in such situations can get tedious at points. Still, for the most part the game’s approach to navigation works, and praise has to be given for it being brave enough to actually try something new in the first place.
 
The world itself is only half of what’s on offer, however, with the other half coming in the form of the story itself. It's one that grabs you from the very start – before things even begin proper you’re greeted with a text-based tale that tells the story of the main character’s life in miniature. It’s poignant, it’s well written, and it’s honestly one of the parts of the game that stick in the mind the most. Beyond that, things pans out in what is essentially a two-person plot – your character, and a woman whose only presence throughout comes in the form of a voice coming from the other end of a radio. As time passes, you slowly uncover mysterious going on, and struggle to get to the bottom of the mystery – with only that lone voice to help you on.
 
It’s an interesting premise, and it works, mainly because both characters are so well written and voiced they feel distinctly… Well, human. They bond slowly over time, learning more about each other, cracking jokes and telling stories about their lives. Then, when thrown into an intense situation, they panic – not always making the best decisions, freaking out over what might happen to them, and so on. It’s so expertly crafted, it’s hard not to become invested in what’s going on; you’ll want to keep on going just to find out what the eventual outcome will be.
 
Shame, then, that the actual closure to the story falls so damn flat. This is incredibly frustrating on two counts; firstly, many of the plot points get written away with remarkable quickness and ease, negating a lot of the impact that they may have had previously. I’m obviously not going to spoil anything, but there’s a particular thread to the story that honestly feels like it’s a big part of everything that’s going on - and then it suddenly gets brushed away via a few throwaway lines.  Secondly, the game does a remarkably good job of building up a lot of suspense and tension, only to whittle it away on a simple resolution that never even gets close to justifying all the gravitas that had gone on beforehand. The end result is that you’ll probably walk away from Firewatch feeling a little let down; a distinctly disappointing note to finish upon, especially after the rest of the game was crafting things so expertly.
 
On a final note, it’s also worth noting that Firewatch is a very short experience as well – it took me just over three hours to complete, and I don’t particularly think I was rushing through it. Yet don’t let this necessarily put you off, because there’s certainly enough done right here to at least mostly negate the game’s faults and short playtime; indeed, exploring the game’s world is almost worth the entrance fee alone.  In the end, Firewatch is a unique little title that sticks in the memory – and one that makes hiding indoors on your computer infinitely more justifiable.

Firewatch is a wonderful story, told through the medium of a video game. It's difficult to call it a game though, it's more of an experience. In the 3 hours and 20 minutes it took me to run the software for the first time to completion, I was really awestruck by my emotional investment in the characters and by how immersed I was in the wilderness that made up my home.

As the story unfolds through your radio contact with Delilah and your own discoveries in the wilderness, you can feel the panic and tension growing in ways that few games can accomplish. While this is not a horror game in any way, I felt there was a curious similarity to Amnesia: Dark Descent in how I felt so vulnerable and exposed at the right moments. 

To call it a game still isn't fair though. It's an interactive story, but one that your choice of dialogue with Delilah seems to directly affect. I'm pretty sure that after my single play through, there are no alternative endings, but I couldn't tell you for sure. The detail to the dialogue and voice acting is on par with the best of the best.

The only flaw with the game is that you'll sometimes find yourself stumbling to find the right way around a ridge or past a bush. Getting lost felt somewhat annoying because my immersive map showed my exact location as though it we're GPS, and I could infer that it was my fault as a player I was lost, and not a challenge of the game. The only improvement I could give the game would be a light survival aspect that requires me to figure out exactly where I am, rather than showing me.

There's a problem with that desire though, survival features would turn this tightly knit story into a more lackluster game, rather than an engrossing tale of adventure and discovery. As such, it may be perfect as is.

Firewatch puts you in the shoes of Henry, a man who recently joined the Wyoming Firewatch as a way to escape his personal problems. You are introduced to Delilah, another Firewatch and your supervisor at another tower. The interaction and dialogue between Henry and Delilah feels authentic and reactive based on the choices in the conversations you made. The voice acting for both Henry and Delilah are superb. The developers had put a lot of thought into how conversations branch and accounts for what the player did or didn't do in the game. 

Another thing that stands out with Firewatch is how the natural scenery is absoultely gorgeous. The lighting, environmental effects, and ambience sound effects come together make the forest truly immersive. 

There are some reviewers who despised the ending of this game, which is understandable from a gamer's perspective on expectation and reward. Personally, I think the game ended perfectly based on the narrative and the story that the developers are trying to tell. 

There's a neat commentary playthrough that is unlocked once the game is completed once. There are various audio tapes in the game world in each game day that offers more insight on the developer's development process and game design choices as you play the game. One gripe that I have with the commentary playthrough is that it's easy to miss certain tapes and there's no way to go back to them once the game moves on to the next day. 

Overall I would recommend this game if you are interested in narrative games with interesting characters set in a unique wilderness setting and don't mind the relatively short game time (I clocked in at 18.4 hours because I played the game twice: second time I was listening to the commentary; one can finish the game in ~3-4 hours if exploration is kept to a minimum).

Highly recommended. This game was my first step into the "walking simulator" genre, but for those of you who haven't yet tried something like this, it is so much more than what it sounds like. Firewatch was a unique gameplay experience for me, one where you step into the life of your character and sympathize with him even if you don't relate. The game starts off with a surprising amount of backstory, and throughout the game you are able to look at your character's journal and find information about others in the world, but much of it is extra. They're not collectibles; they're purely there to add to the atmosphere and to enhance your immersion. The story is the same for everybody who plays, but there can be differences that may end up adding to your experience. My friend and I played through the game around the same time, and he managed to find a little treat that I missed, that being a pet turtle that he kept through the end of the game. I found myself being rather disappointed that I didn't poke around more. Games like these are not about action, they're more interactive stories than they are games. You are offered small choices, and whether or not these choices make a difference, they feel personal. The strong points in the game are the story, the characters (namely your character and the voice on the radio), the immersion, and the setting. The game won't take you a long time to complete, but it will be a rewarding experience.

“Firewatch, then – on the strength of its gripping story, brilliant branching script, wholly convincing voice-acting performances, and stunning art direction – is easily one of my favorite and most memorable game experiences of this decade.”

Firewatch is a story of a lonely man in a big country, presented as a series of prettily frescoed spaces, strung together for the player to explore in exacting chronology.

The player strolls along narrative paths in the first person, gazing at passing tableaux of gorgeous nature, while investigating a mystery parceled out in discrete, bite-sized chapters of the authors' devising.

Inside its confining corridors of cottonwoods and aspens, boulders and ravines, Firewatch delivers a deft story about loneliness and paranoia in a world of deceptively far horizons and dreamy vistas. It's a pace-y series of scripted scenes that amount to a graceful and entirely beguiling illusion of agency.

The story remains gripping for almost the entirety of its five hours. It's only in the final sequence that the illusion begins to blur and disintegrate as the drama's converging arcs fail to entirely yoke together.

Firewatch is about solitude and space, a first-person journey through the massive wilderness of America’s Shoshone National Forest. It’s a space of such magnitude that it almost unavoidably conjures mysteries and conspiracies of corresponding size. But in this game, we are drawn back down to the essential and human.

You are Henry.

This is how it all starts, in the second person like a choose your own adventure book, although the opening prologue is more like a multiple choice quiz sketching the history of Henry’s heartbreaking early adulthood. You meet a girl. Life happens. There are moments of extraordinary joy, giving way to an overall theme of devastation. Henry decides to escape, to a job as a fire lookout at Shoshone National Forest.

I absolutely loved the first half of this game. It got me right at the beggining: I hadn't read much about it, just a short review in a "best indie games of 2016" list. I expected the protagonist to be silent, without any personality, one of those characters you project yourself on. Of course, that's absolutely not the case. The game gives you small choices on your life before the actual game, not meaningful in the sense of having any impact on story or gameplay, but they get you emotionally invested on your character. 
The voice actors are amazing. Dellilah is delightful, I was frustrated that my character didn't want to talk to her on our first conversation and so I couldn't keep it going any longer. Henry didn't catch my attention as much until later in the game, but I won't tell what did it in order not to spoil.
There's not much in way of gameplay. There are no enemies, no health bar, no ways to die, you just walk around, but it's not an exploration game either, there's not much to see besides what is connected to the story and the invisible boundaries can be really annoying sometimes. This is not, however, a problem. Not at all. Firewatch is much like an interactive movie, you're just bringing your character where it needs to be for the story. 
Now, what I didn't really like about this game is the solution to the mystery. I get what the authors were trying to do, but it felt underwhelming. The explanation was a bit convoluted for me, I didn't really buy the reasons for what happened to have happened. I also felt it lacked closure. Some people may like this about the game, in this sense, it's much like real life, but I think if that's what they aimed to do there was no reason for the whole mystery thing, I'd be more than happy to be just Henry, doing some chores around the park, trying to deal with my past and developing a relantionship with Dellilah.
Now, of course, it's important to talk about the lack of choices in this game. I have absolutely no problem with it being an interactive movie, but if that's so, I needed to have a lest a few choices on what'll happen. No mater what you say, your relationship to Dellilah will be the same. You'll go to the same places, find the same clues, have the same problems. And if falls short on that. Having such wonderful voice actors, why couldn't they focus more on the characters, let your decisions affect, if not what happens, how they react to it?
Though most of the reviews are very positive, I don't think this is a game for everyone. I think it has very clear problems and, depending how much they bother you, your experience won't be pleasant. Everything I love about it is in the first three hours, but this was enough to make my experience worthwhile. Still, don't pay the full price, wait for a promotion.

The story itself is mostly conveyed with dialogues between the protagonist and his superior via walkie talkie and the voice acting is on par with big budget productions, if not better, and again the writing proves its quality

Those 4 hours I've played were incredibly dense and intense

Yes, the game is short and yes, the game costs a bit much, considering you can get more bang for your buck these days, but I don't think I have ever played such a compelling game

You go back home from a normal working day. A day of grinding makes you eager to sit in your warm chair, and you switch on your computer, hoping to find some games to relax your brain and body. Then you see Firewatch. 

You listen to the conversations, you read the dialogs. It sometimes just so reminds you of the life that is somehow real. Your bills, your friends, unfinished love stories. 

Walking among the trees doesn't feel relaxing at all, sometimes. You thought you merely wanted to play a game. You don't really like this game, probably.

But you keep playing

I really liked that this game gave you a map and compass and expected you to simply navigate, so many games give waypoints that take away from the exploration and discovery aspect.

I beat the game in under 4 hours, and do not expect much in the way of replay value. There are some story choice elements, but none of them seem to be relavent to the oucome of the game in any real way (so far as I can tell).

Some people here are criticising the story, but I actually enjoyed it. I don't think it ends too soon, and feel that it provides a window into the tragic life of a regular individual. There is realism in the story and not much in the way of the fantastic. That being said, the game does keep you wanting to know what is happening and to keep exploring.

As a hiker, the trail system and terrain are about as good as you can get for a semi open exploration game. At no point in real life would a lone experienced hiker deviate from known trails to scale a mountin rather than walk around it like I do in Skyrim.

I found the game to be very relaxing and cathartic. $20 is a little steep for under four hours of gameplay, but reasonable if you view this as an interactive story. Go see a two hour movie for $20 or go play this game for the same. The price is not unreasonable when you really consider the value of other forms of entertainment. And, this truly is like going to a long movie. There is nothing to do besides explore plot and the world.

Completing the game unlocks free explore mode and allows you to simply explore the map unhindered. There are many things to see and discover, though they are all realistic in their presentation. The game leaves it up to the player to find beauty and wonder in the world.

Some mechanics are not fully explained in the game, such as the camera, and as such were wasted on me expecting to need them at some later point.

I would recommend this to anyone who wants to explore a human drama for a few hours, and to get a small taste of what it means to wander the wilderness in isolation.

As far as the story itself goes, it is somewhat derivative. I guessed the plot very early in the game and expected no surprises. I was satisfied with the level of depth, and with the level of realism (no sudden lone action hero mechanics). I was also pleased that the developers didnt feel the need to wrap up the game in a large unrealistic crescendo of action. The ending is exactly like real life, things just go on never really changing all that much.

I don't think this game is for everyone, but it is very satisfying if you are looking for something that allows you to empathize with a very human and heartfelt story. If you need action, look elsewhere. If deep down in your heart you feel the need to be alone in the woods admiring nature, give it a try.

There are games convincing people in offering massive multiplayer action, stunning special effects and lots of blood and gore...
Firewatch ... is not one of these games.

In case you expect a mind-blowing open-world-BF-style-FPS killing spree, you will be disappointed. 
In this game, you won't kill anyone. You don't even have a weapon. Your main tool in the game is your walkie-talkie.

To be honest: Its not even a real open world game, since you are following a VERY linear story and you are only able to move within fixed paths and areas. 

Firewatch is a pure Adventure Game, comparable to those point & click 2D Adventures like monkey island in the 90s ;-) 
You're moving around, collecting items,enjoying the atmosphere and experiencing a short but interesting Story.
The hell no, there aren't even riddles in the game (despite of the story itself, of course).
Bad minds would say: Firewatch isn't even a videogame. It's more like reading a book or watching an interactive Movie. It's what's called a walking simulator nowadays.

So what is it, making Firewatch so interesting?

It's the atmosphere, it's the dialogues between the two protagonists, and its the story itself.

Although the story is really linear and really short, the players' restrictions in his freedom of movement sometimes are pretty annoying (you can't even jump over a stone),
The developers know how to catch you in the game. Is there a mystery here, in the wilderness,
far away from civilisation?

It's fun to try out various dialogues and seeing what's next.
What's the story behind the warm, sympathic voice coming out of the radio? 

what happens, if you simply don't answer. or what happens, in case you don't do what you are expected to do by your boss? 

Unfortunately, it doesn't affect the storyline itself but it affect the realtionship between you an your boss.
The voice actors of the game did a fantastic job, and its easy to identify yourself with one of them.

The developers managed it maintaining a light, creepy but not scary atmosphere throughout the whole game.
The soundtrack and the comic-style cell-shading graphics are pretty nice too, the light-effects know how to underline the games setting.
Unfortunately, unity's performanc- hunger is also very big, so an up-to-date computer is very recomment

This Game also offers a very unique special, you'll usually only find on DVDs: 

You may play the story along with the developers commenting the game.
that's really cool, especially if you are interested in game developement, and their comments are pretty entertaining.
It's very fun listening to them

So, as a result: 
The developers really put in a lot of love in the game. You will regognize it everywhere.
Since the game is really affordable: Get the game!

[b]Firewatch: A game without a Genre. A SPOILER FREE REVIEW!!![/b]

When this game came out I heard lots of hype from people. Calling it a fantastic tale of emotion with amazing atmosphere. A story driven narritive with very limited gameplay. I put it on my list of games. I felt that the price for the game was a bit high for the amount of time it would take to beat the game. So when it dropped to $10 on sale I picked it up. That still might be a bit to much for some. For me I was okay with it. Because of the amount of love I have for its story.

Now there are tons of "Games" these days that are "Walking Simulators" that are more of a story that is unfolding before your eyes, then a game that you control your every move. Where the player has very limited controls on how it all unfolds. The Taletale series for example does a fantastic job of connecting players to characters and telling these players they have choices. In the end almost every choice won't effect the story as a hole. These "Games" are basically for the player to sit back and enjoy a story with just enough "Gameplay" and "Feedback" to make them think they are doing something. Firewatch does almost all of these things, BUT BETTER!

Firewatch instantly from the start connects you emotionally with a character.  You are thrown into a life of a person who is struggling with some very tough life issues. You connect with this character because he could be you. The first thing I thought was "What if this was happening to me? How would I handle this issue" 

I instantly wanted to know more, I wanted to continue because I was sucked into how this characters life pans out. How his story unfolds. There are basically no choices in Firewatch.  You have options but all of them lead you down the same path. (Just like the map LUL)

My problem with the game (And yes I have a few) are with its trickery. It makes you think you are a small object in a big living world. The first time I set off into the woods I was looking at my map every few seconds. Worried I would go off on the wrong path and end up lost. It quickly became apparent to me that this world was very small, and instead of being one big forest, it actually was a series of paths that lead to points of interest. There are only a hand full of them and by the time you finish this (Short) game.  You will be rushing through just to get to your objective. The game kind of loses you right there. The immersion and atmosphere are the two things that make this game great. Once you look past the stunning lighting and beautiful forest and mountains you are left with just plain old paths and a lonely forest with nothing much to interact with.

The only real gameplay in the game is pressing the walk button and clicking on certain objects , leaping over things. Very limited exploration.

As for the story, its a wonderful experience that by the end it makes you feel what the main character is feeling. I won't say what that is, because it will spoil the story. The story gives you great perspective and you would be doing yourself a favor by giving this game 3 hours of your life and experiencing it. 

In movies they do editing to trim out parts that aren't advancing the plot and hold little or no purpose to make a cohesive story that doesn't feel weighted down by non-sense. I felt this way while "Playing" Firewatch. It felt at times the "Game" (walking around from one point to another) was just holding me back and wasting my time. Other than that I would recommend this game on the grounds that its story is strong enough to waste your time pressing the walk key. I think wiht a bit more interaction and a more open map or the exact oppisite as maybe just a visual novel Firewatch would be a much better overall product. 

Either way pick it up when its on sale. Set aside 3 hours or so of your life and let everything you experience in this "game" soak in. It is a wild ride that throws your emotions all over the place in a good way.

This is one of those games where it's best played completely blind; that said, all I knew about the game going in was that it was a walking simulator with dialogues that you can choose to (and how to) reply. The story isn't so impactful that it'll change your life, but it's significant enough to get you thinking.

What kept me wanting to finish it in one sitting was how each segment of the story resulted in new open-ended developments that keep me wanting to know more. It's a very mature-themed story that I would expect younger audiences to find rather boring and uninteresting, as implied by the game's description.

The gameplay is as you'd expect; it's a walking simulator to the core. If you expect Firewatch to be a traditional videogame rather than an immersive narrative story, then you're just setting yourself up for disappointment. One of my favorite things about the gameplay itself is the use of the map and compass to find out where you are. It's very intuitive and makes it feel like you're really hiking; you have to actually navigate the world instead of being spoonfed where to go.

I would highly recommend Firewatch for someone who just wants to bunker down and lose themself in a good plot.

I really liked this game, but I am going to have to give it a downvote.

On the plus side, the art and world is beautiful, and it was almost completely bug and typo free. The characters a lovingly created and seem real... even making real, heartbreaking mistakes. The story was engaging and you cared about the characters. As I went along, I grew more engrossed in the mystery - how did the [Spoiler] two "murdered" girls [/spoiler] fit into the plot? Why were they [spoiler] murdered and their camp destroyed? [/spoiler]. Was it some sort of framing job? What were the [spoiler] scientists studying? [/spoiler]. Why wasn't delilah told about the [spoiler] giant fenced off area? [/spoiler]. Basically, who was behind what was [spoiler] an obvious consipiricy? [/spoiler]

But the downsides are vast. I got lost, sidetracked, checked out the view... and the entire story took 3 hours total. This is the length of a long movie :/ The world is also almost completely lifeless - a few very rare wildlife enounters in an area that should be teaming with rodents and birds. The game's short duration also left me with the chance to reflect on the story. Which does not make a lot of sense the more you think about it, as you unravel the "mysteries" above. Specifically, there are a number of serious plot problems:  

First,  [spoiler] the scientist camp springs up out of nowhere, very close to the characters fire tower. And yet Henry doesn't notice and Delilah isn't informed about it and can't get any information about it. Is it really a secret hush-hush government experiment? From what we see, it is a research project relating to earthquakes, or weather, or elk tracking. So WTF is the secrecy about and why can't Delilah get any info? Even if, somehow, Delilah was not informed, then surely she would find out the instant she called in to HQ. Also, again, how TF did someone put up a mile of chain link fence without the character ever noticing? [/spoiler]

Second, [spoiler] why did the sad dad mess with the lady hikers? There was no reason for him to do this, and every reason for him NOT to do this. Consider if a specific area of the forest suddenly has a problem where a mysterious force is regularly attacking campers and hikers. Maybe this would cause an investigation, no? Of course, in the story, it becomes a plot point that Delilah doesn't report this and it looks bad because the kids are missing, and you think they maybe died because their camp is messed up... which really ratchets up the tension. But really the two girls are just in jail?!? If so, all the worry was for nothing, and the sad dad's attack on their campsite only revealed to everyone that there was a mysterious force operating in the park. For. No. Reason. Whatsoever. And remember, this dude had hidden out sucessfully for *years*. What broke his excellent concealment? Was it stolen food? A cook fire? An airial spot of his hidey hole? No - he fricken attacked a campsite like a crazed axe murderer. Guess he failed his stealth roll, huh. :/ [/spoiler]

Third, [spoiler] Delilah goes to all this trouble to smuggle a new radio to Henry. And in the next "act" of the game, sad dad records and remixes the audio of their radio *immediately*. So, the new radio didn't work to protect their radio security even once, as far as I could tell. Sure, this could happen IRL - maybe the sad dad guy was a former military signals guy and found their new frequency. But its just one more improbable coincidence added to the pile of "things that needed to happen for the story but which are very unlikey." Or - and this is arguably worse - it is essentially "filler" in a game that is only 3 hours long. [/spoiler]

Fourth, [spoiler] maybe this one is on me, in terms of me missing story elements, but there is a serious problem with the cave part of the story. Either the sad dad wanted Henry to find the dead son (because he left all of these clues, and the key, etc) or he wanted to kill henry, because he locked henry in a cave with no apparent way out, no food, no water, and no signal. Sure, Henry happened to have a fire axe, and there happened to be a rubble filled way to escape. But if there had not been, he would have died. And the rubble filled the hole, so no one else had used that escape route as far as we know. So, is this schitzophrenic character motivation AND improbable escape, or something else? [/spoiler]

TLDR? This is a lovely game that is really engaging, but is too short and too expensive... and the more you think about it the less sense it makes. A shame, because being in the story for the short time I had was truly great.

Ok how to start this review, I'm going to be thorough throughout but also trying to make sure that I don't miss a single aspect, because firstly, this game is beautiful. It recreates the atmosphere of a semi open world "survival" game. Although not really survival, very much story based, it still hints at that aspect of gaming. And quite frankly I haven't played a game this good in well over 4 years. The only game I can say comes close to giving me this feeling is Fallout New Vegas, with the story being interesting and fun for many many hours on end.

Story: To start with, the story is perfect, it leads up well, everything is a mystery and honestly, it makes you question the actions of yourself and Delilah at some points. No spoilers however, I'm very glad with that. Curiousity takes the better of you when you wander into the wilderness and for example find a camp. My first instincts as Henry would be to do my job, prevent a fire. But after wandering for so long you get lost in this feeling of serenity and tranquility, it's the most fascinating feeling imaginable. In comparison to Fallout New Vegas, I feel so much more immersed in this environment than my now beaten favourite game. Not to forget however the possibility of the story constantly changing if you choose different dialect options. Just the icing on the cake there, well done guys!

Environment: One thing to mention before we continue, the Developers of the Graphics Team involved in the making of the environment, Bravo, you guys have out done yourselves here! I hadn't heard of you before, but now you will forever be stuck in my mind, the work you have done here to not only make the scenery look beautiful, but for it to run so well on any hardware, I applaud that. You have done a fantastic job, I would happily pay triple the amount for this game than what I did just because of the environment. Although, I do wish that maybe in the future there would be more areas to explore, It felt slightly small for me, taking a mere 5 minutes to cross the map, I feel like it could be bigger, but there's always room for improvement! 

Characters: The build up to the main protagonist (Henry) I thought was perfect, couldn't have been done any better, not only do you outline his abilities and the path he chooses, but you also aid in the development of his relationships and you really get to bond with the character before the game even begins. This is excellent, it gives the player an imagine to the character before they even begin. I honestly feel like Henry could have been me, simply because I created his background knowledge. Delilah on the other hand is interesting. She is the opposite of Henry, you learn about her in reverse, you don't know the full extent to her until the game ends. Her story is unfoolding at the same time as the main story, un-disclosed for obvious reasons.

Dialogue: One thing I will never forget about this game is the dialogue, the reason I even purchased the game was watching the videos outlining the chats between Delilah and Henry in the cave. When Henry was banging on the gate and he screams, makes a sarcastic remark and getting that sort of feeling immidiately that I knew the game would be of excellent quality. I did giggle at that cut scene however, I was sold instantly. I don't regret a thing. Throughout the game dialogue was consistent, very high quality but most of all, the voice characters deserve a medal, the conversations felt so real, the emotions felt very real and quite frankly no other game compares to how well those connections were. Nothing will ever come close in any current game. Well done once again!

Finally to conclude I will go over a few things which I feel could have been done a bit better. Firstly as I stated above, I feel like the world should have been expanded, but not only that a bit more open, I just felt through some of it a bit constricted to choices, only one path and only one option especially while exploring. On another note I feel like the story should have been extended, was there room for side missions, for example "There's campers out again lighting fires, do you want to go tell them off or leave it to another station" And let Henry (The Player) have the option of choosing whether they should go tell them off or not. I'm not sure if this would clash with the main story line so I guess it should be kept to the free roam aspect of the game. But otherwise, this game was spot on, I would like to thank you for the hard work you have put into this, it truly is a masterpiece, thanks for the perfect experience!

一幕幕回忆在眼前展开：我如何与我的妻子相爱、我的妻子患上AD、我选择远离人世成为一名看火人...

你让我看“六月之火”，你说你喜欢看它们在夜间的样子，在白天，它们只是烟雾，但当太阳落山，你就根本无法无视它们的存在。
你说你想和我一起坐着，喝着冰镇威士忌，还可以做些什么。
我说我也想和你在一起，看星星月亮，看云海、沐浴阳光。
我醉酒，朦胧中把你当作我的妻子，你顺着我与我道晚安。
有人在监听我们的一举一动，我们陷入了危机，你差点成为“纵火犯”，我说别担心，有我在。
因为我妻子的悲剧、你不堪的往事，我们变得更加惺惺相惜。
今天我们要离职了，意味着我们不会再用大哥大聊天了，我们还没有一起坐在瞭望塔上看星空。
难过地打包着自己的东西，“小木桶”、我和妻子的合照...

终于找到了奈德的老窝，奈德坦白了一切，我们“纵火犯”的嫌疑终于洗清了，我兴奋地告诉你这里的情况，被盗物资、检测器、工作台....奈德其实很爱布莱恩，到处是布莱恩的漫画书、玩具。还有布莱恩的照片和他送给父亲的贺卡，他长得真可爱。
你却渐趋沉默，你开口，抱歉，我不知道要说什么，我不知道你想让我说什么。你劝我赶紧离开。
我取下了布莱恩的照片，我想带给你。我知道你会很难过，但我不希望布兰恩没有留下任何东西在这世上。

灼灼山火鼓起灰蒙的烟雾，我一次次迷失在路上，我以为你会在无线电的另一头 像往常一样鼓励我、陪着我。
我只是始料未及，你说你想先走了，你无法面对我。我很失落，其实我并不担心直升机不会回来，只是有些话还说不出口。
在我可怜兮兮的请求下，你说你可以等等我，让我加快速度。我急得一直在奔跑，我心里喊着，你等等我，我想和你一起离开，一起在直升机上聊聊这两个月的点滴，一起看六月之火最后一眼..
我把照相机带来了呢，我还想跟你合照呢，还有小木桶，它很可爱。
我一边跑，一边想，这就是你天天走的地方啊。

终于到了缆车这里，对面就是你的瞭望塔了，我习惯性地跟你报告着，“Delilah?...”没有回应，好吧，或许你在和救援者聊天呢..

第一次来到你的瞭望塔下，高兴又平静地拾级而上，既熟悉又陌生，就像你一样..
扭开门把手，你不在里面。我很少拍照，但这次一进来就先拍了两张你小屋的全貌。我想了解你，我一样一样，慢慢地翻看着你的东西。瞧，你真的给我画了画像，还贴在了窗户上，可是没我本人帅气呢。
红白灰相间的床单、挂在墙上的白净的衬衫、纯白的碗碟整整齐齐地摞成一叠，很像你的风格呀。
床边有两本填字游戏，就是上次我想抓小浣熊却被你吓走的时候的帮凶吧。
海报上挂着个牌子，写着猪肉水塘，哈哈，看来你真的很喜欢这个名字。

碟子上有切好的苹果，我想你是特地为我准备的，很好吃。
我坐了下来，戴上那副耳机
“Hello，Delilah...”
你说我们可以给对方做未来的选择，我鼓起勇气追求你，我说你应该来我身边，你却劝我回去看看妻子。
我的妻子已经傻了，我一个人很累。你勉强同意来年路过我家时会来看看我。
飞机来了，我们的通话该结束了。平静地走出你的房间，下楼梯....
我看见你的木椅，在房间外，上面还有一副望远镜，当时你就是坐在这偷偷看我的吗？
下了瞭望台，我忍不住打开了你的户外厕所，里面还放着鲜花。

我真的很想和你在这过一辈子，我想和你一起喝着冰镇威士忌，陪你做数独，天气好时爬爬山，我钓鱼回来你做给我吃。
本以为我们还会在一起很久，没想到就这样断了联系。
我对你的感情，或许就像“六月之火”一样，白天只是一缕缕若隐若现的烟雾，到了晚上，却无视忽视。

我失了魂似的上了飞机，还想着问问救援者你的样子，你好不好。

Firewatch is a compelling and memorable experience centered around the elaborate fantasies that two lonely, isolated people can create to explain what they cannot understand.

In order to escape depressing circumstances at home, protagonist Henry takes a job with the Forest Service as a firewatcher in an isolated Wyoming forest.  His only other point of contact is a follow firewatcher, Delilah, an unseen woman in a distant fire tower.  The game takes place over the course of Summer in 1989.

The gameplay mostly consists of exploring the forest using a compass and map.  Walking is broken up by contextual actions like climbing and rappelling.  The conversations between Henry and Delilah are the focus of the game, which you navigate using dialog trees.  Eventually, the two become embroiled in a larger mystery surrounding the forest and what is happening there.

It goes without saying that the game is beautiful, with a very unique art style.  The acoustic music fits perfectly, creating a sense of melancholy that permeates the whole game.  And, of course, the voice acting is executed very well.  All the characters are believable.

That said, the game is very short at 3-5 hours and the $20 asking price might be a bit steep for some.  But, let's face it, people will pay that much to go and see a movie these days.  That said, I really wanted to see more reasons to replay the game, like multiple endings, because given its length, it's the kind of game I would happily replay if there was an incentive.

Still, it's very much worth playing.

Without spoiling much of anything, I completed this game twice within two days:

1.  My first go-round was long, drawn out... I explored everything at every opportunity. I crept, checked, and did, just about everything. I disregarded all objectives if the mechanics would let me go to another area, and only once I was satisfied that I had seen and found what I could, I would proceed through the day. I played Henry as the "good guy", the devoted lookout, and the troubled husband. I had these major experiences:

[list]
    [*] There was a fair amount of things to find, and a lot that can be easily missed.
    [*] Within the mechanics and story I smiled and laughed, was paranoid or nervous, and I also felt sad.
    [*] There's enough to wander around and do, but at the same time isn't a sandbox timesink. You have to progress.
    [*] I found myself constantly preparing and second guessing anything before I did it. I always took the whiskey and fireworks.
    [*] You aren't meant to collect everything. While we may never know if the books unlocked a secret, things tend to just glitch or disappear forever, and randomly reset within the world.
[/list]

2.  My second turn, I played Henry the "bad boy" who said what he wanted and asked you to "take it or leave it". I collected almost nothing, and having known the ins-and-outs and limitations of the story and the mechanics, I played it very care-free. I found myself going so fast, sometimes, that whole sections of known dialogue just wouldn't happen. Whatever choices I made the first time, I did the opposite the second time. I had these experiences:

[list]
    [*] You can breeze through the whole story in a matter of two hours. Start to finish, Henry can get things done and over with really quickly, which may make you consider if the cost of the game was worth it.
    [*] The game leaves a lot to be desired sometimes from a logical standpoint, and is more about the story you're supposed to find for yourself, than your every whim within the mechanics being fulfilled.
    [*] Jerk Henry was a lot more fun to play as. [spoiler]Talking to D with the stolen boom box in my hands, and taking ALL of the food was my favorite parts of his dialogue.[/spoiler]
    [*] A lot of the choices I thought would really make a difference, kind of didn't.
[/list]

[b]So here's my final take:[/b]
--Firewatch was a good game, for what it was. I did what I wanted, what I really set out to do, and I never really felt upset at the game for any reason (not even the mechanics or lack of them, sometimes). The achievements are obtainable, and the price wasn't so off-putting that I would scoff at my purchase afterwards wondering what I did.

--The story, whether explored entirely, or rushed... it works. The ending may not be as big a pay-off as you would hope, but it does the job of, well... feeling like it mattered a little bit. Good or bad, you get a small, tiny reminder of what makes you, you... because you're going to develop an opinion of something rather than trying to rack up a high score.

--I would have liked a little more from the "collecting" aspect. I find it entirely unreasonable I can clean up every beer can, but cannot find room in my inventory to tuck a book away in my pack (seriously... I found a cache with three books in it and had to make the slow journey back and forth to keep them in my lookout). When I bring back the boombox, my only choice is to throw it on the ground or on a countertop and then it disappears anyways. Then I get teased with the possibility of "what could have been" when it comes to this gameplay aspect as I collect the [spoiler]pieces of evidence surrounding the Goodwins[/spoiler], and everything is saved like it all matters. I wasn't asking for full personalization in my lookout, but I often felt almost no connection to it sometimes, like it wasn't really Henry's. 

--I said before, a lot of the choices simply don't matter as much as I thought it would. All too often, I discovered the big impacts some of my choices had was a fill-in-the-blank in a line or conversation. The game still went the same way, and everything "happened" as it would have all along. 

-- I was a little disappointed I didn't get to experience every little bit of dialogue, and I find myself after almost 8 hours of gameplay wondering if there was more I was missing. Some branch of dialogue, some combination of choices that would reveal a new word, phrase, or quip that  I would enjoy. Knowning that on certain days, in certain areas, things could happen unexpectedly... did I miss something unknowingly? After two playthroughs, I'm content with the experience I got out, but there's still a small piece that just continues to imagine what could be.

--The big payoff was the end, seeing [spoiler]the picture that D drew[/spoiler]... that part was nice, like a little personal easter egg. I saw two of them [spoiler](1. nice clothes, happy eyes, beard) and (2. tuxedo, steely eyes, and long scar/thin mustache... a fun dialogue about a Bond villain)[/spoiler], but probably wont play to see the third option. The camera tries to live up to this as well, but was more of a "meh" thing to me.

There is SO so much to love here, there really is.  There's also an enormous "BUT..."  I seriously waffled back and forth between thumbs up or thumbs down.  The visuals are gorgeous, the dialogue is amazing, the paranoia and tension over the course of the game is so tightly wound, it's glorious.  There will be serious emotions felt in this game.  Compassion, sorrow, fear, suspicion, humor, romance.  It's incredibly well done, and it's what made this game get a thumbs up from me.   Firewatch delivers a beautifully rendered National Park for you to explore, breathtaking weather effects, and a lot of fun little details throughout.  The journey of the game is absolutely worth the price of admission, as brief as it is.

However the huge "BUT" is the ending.  I'd be okay with the game being only 3 hours long (I beat it in two sittings) if the ending delivered on the buildup of the rest of the game, but it doesn't.  The ending is such a huge letdown, and not even in a rage kind of way, but more of an "Oh...well, okay I guess..." kind of way.  I wasn't even mad, I just felt like this finale had been built up for me and then stolen away.  The ending was like being a little kid and getting socks for Christmas.  I felt robbed.  You spend the entire game with the tension being ratcheted up more and more, only to have *nothing* happen.  And I don't mean that in any kind of like, cliffhanger, unanswered questions kind of way.  I mean nothing really happens.   It kind of soured an otherwise excellent gaming experience for me.   

So definitely play this game, but take it with a grain of salt.

Firewatch is basically a movie presented in the format of a walking simulator. There's some limited interactivity, but the effect of your choices on the outcome of the game, beyond simply determining how quickly the different scenes are presented to you, seems purely cosmetic. The difference between different dialogue options seems limited to the responses you get right after speaking, or *occasionally* to responses you get an indeterminate time later. Sometimes it's fun to see the echo of a dialogue choice much later, but it doesn't change the story itself.

So how's the story? It's not bad. It's not great. It feels kind of a like a second-run Raymond Carver story, by which I don't mean to insult the storytelling (Raymond Carver is a high mark to aim for), only to say: the story wouldn't stand on its own, outside of the context of the game.

And, as I mentioned two paragraphs ago, the game really isn't much more than a clunky, occasionally-buggy way of presenting the story.

Which is kind of a conundrum.

But the strength of Firewatch is really less to do with the gameplay, or with the story, than with the fact that the world of the story exists, all around you, as the narrative unfolds. You can wander off the paths. There are stunning panoramic views worth a bit of a hike out of your way. The graphics are excellent, and the sound design is immersive (the voice acting, too, is standout, and does a lot to carry the story).  The Shoshone National Forest of the game is a lovely place to spend some time.

It's a flawed game, sure. But it tried for something impressive, and it came close, and I'm just glad game designers have set down this road. I look forward to seeing the next game made in this sort of mold.

(Oh, and if you find a camera, use it.  Take nice pictures when you find nice views.  Don't let the fact that you've found a usable object in an "adventure" game trick you into getting all utilitarian about it.  Cameras are for preserving memories, chowderhead.)

The price of videogames and the value you get out of them is often compared to going to the movies. You can spend 20 bucks on a 3D flick with some popcorn and a drink or use that to get a game of the same length or even more.
I think that deep down we still feel the need to justify the medium, even though I understand the argument, but Firewatch was the first title that made me reconsider that comparison and where it immediately made sense to me.

Firewatch is a [i]walking simulator[/i], with Telltale-esque dialogues, that tells the story of a man that chose escapism as his life went downhill and became a fire lookout. 
The prologue is only told with text and some accompanying soundscapes, but I already felt deeply moved and instantly invested in the story, which tells a lot about the writing, where other games struggle to achieve this level of immersion even with access to all the artistic tools videogames offer.

As soon as you're thrown into the actual game you can't help but be amazed by the breathtaking vistas and goregeous color pallets. Definitely one of the most beautiful games I've ever laid eyes on.
The story itself is mostly conveyed with dialogues between the protagonist and his superior via walkie talkie and the voice acting is on par with big budget productions, if not better, and again the writing proves its quality. 

Those 4 hours I've played were incredibly dense and intense. [i]All killer, no filler[/i]. It's an emotional rollercoaster.

Yes, the game is short and yes, the game costs a bit much, considering you can get more bang for your buck these days, but I don't think I have ever played such a compelling game. 
And if this wouldn't have been a christmas gift I probably would've waited for a steep discount, yet after finishing the game I think that those 20 dollars are more than justified. Just like going to the movies.

If you are looking for a good adventure and an exciting story, this is your game!
More games like this, please ;)

[h1]Walking simulator?[/h1]
Not in a bad way. The way the map has been designed is clever, as it means you never really have to walk the same path twice (your tower is in the middle, and your objectives rotate around the edges of the map). Each destination seems to have two paths that lead to it, so you can go a different way home (or you get teleported). 

Despite not knowing where to go a few times, I really enjoyed the experience of Firewatch. The storyline is gripping, and although the ending might seem brief at first, I'd recommend looking up the conspiracy theories on youtube afterward to tie up any loose ends. It all makes sense now ;) 

It's also worth noting that the playthrough is different each time. Debbie's responses are randomized, and going to places in a different order causes a different chain of events (judging by youtube playthroughs being completely different from my experience). Despite what people are saying in the reviews, the choices you make in game do have an impact on what Debbie says. Admittedly, it doesn't change the storyline in anyway.

The game only has ILLUSIONS of choices and possibilities, but nothing actually changes any outcome (aside from a secret ending which isn't really worth anything beyond reading about it on a forum - you'll see why). 

The Firewatch world is full of seemingly-interesting things that seem like they could be collectibles that lead to hidden achievements, or things that could lead to additional intrigue or puzzles, but no, they serve absolutely no purpose except to populate the world so you can pick things up, look at them, and drop them. 

What's that, you say? "Surely, if I collect all of the numbered books and put them onto my bookshelf, that has to unlock something..." Nope, sorry. You've just wasted an hour or two of your time. I'm not particularly crazy about collectible-hunting, but I'd rather not be presented with false possibilities. It seems like the developers wanted to expand the game and they set the stage and maybe ran out of time. But instead of removing these meaningless objects from the world, they just left them so you can pick them up for a few seconds and wonder, "What do I do with this?" (The answer: nothing - drop it and move on).

Replayability is also existent in the sense that while your actions and choices don't really influence major plot points nor the ending of the game, they do influence the interactions you have with other characters. If you've ever played Gone Home, and wished the story and graphics had been equal to the game's stellar atmopshere and voice acting, then you need to play this title. It's everything I wished Gone Home was.

If you haven't, then prepare for an emotionally-battering tale about a man named Henry, who after being dealt a particularly terrible hand by life, takes a job as a Fire lookout in rural Wyoming during a particularly dry summer, and subsequently gets caught up in an exceptionally well-told mystery that takes him all over the forest.

As with Gone Home, the game relies heavily on the general atmosphere it generates to tell its story - a combination of a wide-open Unity 5-powered forest to explore, an art style that sits somewhere between Studio Ghibli and Pixar, and some of the best audio and voice acting I've come across since the Dead Space games work together to serve as the platform, while the story itself is told via the strange relationship between Henry and his boss, Delilah, who Henry communicates with over radio. Henry and Delilah's voice acting is practically perfect (in case you're wondering, Henry is voiced by the same guy who played the bespectacled Harry Crane in Mad Men).

The specifics of this relationship (and Henry's general demeanour) are set by your dialogue choices. Play him as an honest, grounded guy leads to an odd friendship where these two people bounce their issues off each other. Play him as an angry man of few words results in an icy relationship. It's up to you, and the closest thing I've seen to this kind of thing is the dialogue system in the later Bioware games (Dragon Age 2/Mass Effect 2 onwards). 

At times the story feels like its channeling the paranoia of the X-Files... other times it's more like the mystery seen in M Night Shyamalan films like The Village and Signs. If you're a fan of these, I'd wager you'll love this.

It's not all perfect - while the sheer size and detail of the wilderness is awe-inspiring to begin with, you soon find that the game can be a bit clumsy in keeping you on path. When required by the plot, Henry is capable of some quite admirable feats - jumping off crumbling bridges, climbing up and down hills and rock slides... but when there's no plot reason, Henry is stumped by a small rock or a bush. I get that Henry is just a normal late-30s guy, he's not Lara Croft or the Doom Marine, but this weird disparity between plot-acrobatics and normal restrictions can be a little jarring. 

The game also has a weird feature which allows you to initiate a conversation about an item before actually examining it - this can create a strange effect where Henry starts reacting to something that the player themselves isn't aware of - sometimes Henry reads into things I didn't, sometimes I spotted something that Henry didn't, and sometimes stuff is glossed over entirely to an extent that you can't understand why Henry didn't question it at the time. It creates a weird imbalance in which you're not sure whether the game wants the player to think of themselves as the viewer of a story or Henry himself. 

This is all nitpicking though. It is very much a 'walking simulator' (a title I hate, but use because no better title exists for this kind of game) so if you're issue with things like Gone Home and Dear Esther was the lack of traditional gameplay then this won't convert you. But if you love a good story with amazing atmosphere, I'd say this is one of the best choices on Steam.

Length-wise... expect about 3-4 hours (I've ran through it twice). Personally I feel this is the right length - longer and it would have been simply padded. Whether that computes with it's price depends on how much you value story vs gameplay time, but I purchased it for 40% off during a sale and I feel like I got bargain.

FWIW, the soundtrack edition is worth it - the included soundtrack is [i]great[/i].

I just finished Firewatch, and all I can say is wow. Be forewarned though: the actual gameplay is entirely based around walking through a forest, looking at things, and talking to a voice on the other end of a radio. If you're looking for an active gaming experience, you'll definitely want to search elsewhere.

If, however, you are looking for a rich story fueled by excellent voice acting and artfully created landscapes, pick this thing up. It's short (I completed the game in a little over four hours), but it is absolutely worth the price tag. The opening is simply text with small decisions here and there on what you want to say, and I found myself crying by the end. Of the first 10 minutes of the game.

The characters are beautifully developed, the landscapes are gorgeous, and the fluidity of the gameplay keeps you fully immersed in the world. Plus, it has a killer map system that both guides you and forces you to take an active role in keeping an eye on where you are. Sort of like actually hiking. This was of some relief to me, having played Henry as myself in this situation, and having to reflect on the moments where it felt like things could work out differently. (I would understand this being levelled as a serious critique of the 'game,' after all, where are our multiple endings, where's the harem ending?)

What *did* actually irk me was the volta, where paranoia jumps into high gear and time jumps ahead. If I were writing this story, I might actually let things get tedious, to an extent -- not much happens in the park, Henry goes on patrol, Delilah shoots her mouth off... rather than the sudden acceleration into a B plot that doesn't *really* link into the established motifs (though certainly isn't un-interesting, and casts an interesting light on the earlier portions of the story.)

Presentation wise, there's not much to critique -- it's a lovely game, with a lovely soundtrack, top quality voice performances and a simple interface. 

Still, it made me feel some feelings and I'm glad I played it. Definitely a good game to grab during a sale (it was a gift, so I've got no qualms with the $20 tag, though in a $/hr rating system it doesn't come out so favourably.)

Firewatch is not for everyone, but I did greatly enjoy it. A game that I didn't quite understand when I first finished it, but after thinking about it a great deal, I think I understand it's purpose. 

It is incredibly well written and every detail matters, just not in the way you think it will. Every character and line of dialogue is purposeful and, when it's all said and done, makes a very real and interesting point about how we as humans tend to deal with life's hardships. 

My interpretation:
*SPOILERS*
I think this game's purpose was to show that some people choose NOT to deal with their problems at all. Henry and Dililah try to escape their mistakes and their real-life problems. Henry is unable to properly care for his sick wife. He goes out drinking in order to escape his responsibilities. Eventually Julia's family takes her in to care for her. Henry takes the firewatch job to escape his failure and the pain that comes with his wife having dementia. 
Dililah got dumped by her long-time boyfriend because she couldn't be there for him when his family member died. She works out in the forest every summer to escape her mistakes. Throughout the game it is made known that she also uses alcohol as an escape, just like Henry often does. Alcohol is a reoccuring symbol of attempted escape. Even the teenage girls use alcohol to try to escape. But in every case, it never works. 
Henry and Dililah spend most of the game pursuing answers to what seems to be a conspiracy. This also serves as an escape. They keep finding clues and it leads them to assume more and more dramatic possibilities. Is the government watching them? Are they being studied or set up? In the end it is just Ned, another character who is escaping his responsibilities. He caused his son's death, and chooses to hide in the woods instead of face what he's done and give his son a proper barial. He was only trying to keep henry from finding his son's body. 
Dililah is also an escape for Henry, and vice versa. They sort of fancy each other and flirt quite a bit. You even find Henry has removed his wedding ring and set it on the table at one point. They use each other as escapes from their own romantic issues.
Even the fire is a symbol. Dililah talks about how last year the authorities thought they could let the wild fire runs its course. No. She says Yellowstone almost burned down. You can't ignore fire (the problem), it will only spread and do more damage. The deer Henry sees in the beginning of the game flees just like he did. The teenagers steal a tractor and go to jail, they were running from their problems. Julia and Henry choose to take a different path for walking the dog after they almost got robbed. 
The point of all this is that every attempt at escape fails. There is no conspiracy, all the clues lead to nothing. Just coincidental occurences, and Ned trying to cover his tracks. Dililah tells Henry to go see his wife in the end. She knows they can't be together, and that he should face his responsiblity: Julia. 
I know a lot of people might think the end is disappointing. No conspiracy, no romance. But that's the point. That's life. You can't fix things by running away. There was no big twist or secret, just Henry and D letting their imaginations run wild. Trying to ignore their responsibilities. It is simply a very honest, real human tragedy.

One of the best story-driven experiences ever. [b]Firewatch[/b] has this crazy way of sucking you in with its charming characters and narrative, making it almost impossible to put down. 

It's a first person linear-open world experience with a big focus on story following a broken man named Henry and the relationship he has with his cohort, Delilah. Players will experience a really well-written script between these two characters through radio communications as part of the Wyoming wilderness firewatch.  

The core gameplay is simple and streamlined with the main focus centering on dialogue choices and how the player advances the relationship between the characters. This ends up being the game's strong point however, seeing as the voice acting and writing offered here is superb. 

The main issue [b]Firewatch[/b] struggles with has to do with its length. While shorter narrative experiences can be every bit as impactful as longer titles, [b]Firewatch[/b] ends up faltering because there's just not enough time for the characters to fully open up and develop. 

When essential character development starts to take place the game already reaches its end, making a lot of the dialogue feel like filler - seeing as most of topics discussed between Henry & Delilah are never revisted. 

Other than that, [b]Firewatch[/b] still offers an excellent experience, giving players with a beautiful game world to roam around and explore in coupled with a really touching story line. 

[h1]Verdict:[/h1] 

Offers a story that will definitely tug at your heartstrings and will leave you dying for a sequel. Despite its short length it's still more than worth your time if you enjoy story-driven games.

I bought the game on a sale for $14.99 and it was certainly money well spent. The scenery is absolutely gorgeous and the game is so well written with genuine suspense. I would advise caution to starting the game on a day you have stuff to do because you'll likely play straight though. The world is big but they do a great job at not wasting any time with hiking. It's all for a purpose and is such a beautiful game that hiking isn't a drag. The map is very detailed so you never feel lost. The game itself plays like a movie and you're just guiding it from point A to B. You're not making any decisions that affect the game and there is no challenge so be aware before spending your money if that's something you're looking for. What you're getting with this game, is a sensationally rendered world with a genuinely suspenseful (and a bit scary at times) story that you'll keep playing until you figure out. The standard $19.99 price tag seems a little steep since the game only takes a few hours to complete, but if you can catch it on a sale I would recommend without a doubt. There are also special features such as a commentary where the developers annotate as you play. I haven't dove into them yet but I'm excited for the opportunity.

Pros
- Greate atmosphere
- Great story
- Outstanding voice acting
- Great graphics, like a waterpainting
- Cool places to go, realistic story (everything done is believable)
- A great mix of mystery, exploration and dialogue

Cons
- Limited replay value: I might play this game one more time through, but definantly not soon. There's about 2.5-4 hours of content here.
- Weak ending, yes I know I said the story is good. The ending just felt abrupt and quite underwhelming. Many people give this game a thumbs down for this very reason. I would've given it an easy 9.0+ if the ending wasn't like it was.
- (*SPOILERS*) Continuing on that last point I wanted to meet Delilah, or at least have ending text that explains you future with Julia and meeting Delilah at that bar (that's the last thing I asked her, there are other options). 
Also, it was never clear whether or not Ned murdered his son (unlikely), was a bad parent (i.e. let him climb when he should not have), or Brian acted on his own and it caused Ned to become a paranoid hermit. It also never explains how Ned got all his fancy equipment at Waipiti Station much less how he put up that fence. The only thing I can predict is that he was using some equipment that some briefly mentioned scienctists left behind (which still doesn't make much sense). 
(*END OF SPOILERS*)

(Personally, I did not enjoy the rest of the game either.  There are lots of small things that all add up to make it a bit disappointing.  Every single pile of climbable rocks looks exactly the same, for eg.)

This game kept me involved with enough balance between what I have to do, yet following a fairly linear story line.  So, I didn't feel I was JUST mechanically following the story, I had to go to place and navigate my way, and would see surprises there.  Yet, while not feeling like an automaton, I never felt 'lost' in a game sense, of not knowing what to do next.  It's this fine balance between being a game and movie (or visual novel).  Firewatch is my favorite of this type of game, at this time.  If you find the visual novel too 'lock step' and therefore boring, try this.  If you want play a game with essentially no fighting or killing (i.e., essentially no violence), try this.  If you want to plan an action game, don't try this.  Note: it's not a lengthy game. I didn't really read anything about Firewatch before jumping into it, aside from people saying how great it was, and you shouldn't either, but I do hope this review at least gives you some idea of what to expect.

At first the game kinda made me feel like, hey, this isn't what I signed up for... and then you take your first step, aside from the few sneak peaks you got in the introduction of the game, into the world and you just get blown away by the amount of detail in the world. The sun in the sky shining through the trees and just... the amount of attention to detail in every inch of the world. I know people say this all the time these days, but this game has gorgeous graphics. I'm not one to claim that graphics is a key factor in whether a game is worthwhile or not, but in this case it certainly is! It's not the same as picking up a triple A game, but it stands out artistically.

Firewatch managed to make it feel rewarding to search every nook and cranny and as you progress through the story all the places where you couldn't go at one stage or another suddenly become accessible and things start falling into place which, to me, was a very rewarding feeling. (I'd say more, but avoiding spoilers :))  There's no real combat in Firewatch, and death doesn't really play a strong part in it although I did kinda feel that it had to be coming at some points in the game. It's more a game about listening, reading, making choices and taking in your surrounding. It's an experience more than anything else. Most of the plot is revealed through the conversations between Henry and Dililah and for a relatively short (5 hours for a playthrough) game there seems to be a lot of replay value here as it's not really clear how your choices effect your final outcome of the story with one play through.

Another thing about Firewatch that really caught my attention is the attention to detail. Almost every object can be picked up, twirled around and inspected. Notes on walls can be read. The books have covers and a description at the back and I could go on, but you should experience it for yourself.

The music is good and increases the suspense when neccesary, though the sound design fell a bit short in my honest opinion. Eg. each time a character starts saying a new line all the audio (music, ambient etc) stutters which can get a bit annoying after a while. I'm not sure if this was just an issue my side, but I figured it's worth mentioning.

★OVERALL★
Firewatch is not your typical 'walking sim.' At first, it seems simple and beautiful. But things take a quick turn for the strange as isolation and paranoia take their toll. This is one of those games that's better the less you know about it, so I'll keep it vague. It's a short game- about 5 hours long and only 10 achievements. Honestly, $20 is a little too rich for what the game offers, but keep it on your wishlist. Once it goes on sale, snatch it up and enjoy an evening of mystery.

★STORY★
You play Henry, a man trying to escape his complicated life and spend a simple summer enjoying the Wyoming wilderness as a lookout for the national forestry service. It's your job to keep a constant vigil for signs of fire and preserve the natural beauty of the forest. With just a handheld radio to communicate with another lookout miles away as your only company, the loneliness of the woods can drive a person mad.

Your responsibilities become more than you bargained for when you realize you're not as alone in these woods as you thought. Or are you? The forest can play tricks on you. Try to stay calm.

★GAMEPLAY★
The gameplay is simple. You can walk and run, you have a map and a compass to guide you through the forest. There are various tools to help you navigate the natural barriers provided by the landscape. The game is fairly linear, although, you're generally allowed to go where you please. But the story will only progress when you go where you're pointed.

The landscape is large enough without feeling too massive or empty. There are enough landmarks to make getting lost easily overcome. The heart of the gameplay is done through dialog between you and the other lookout via your handheld radio. You are provided 3 or 4 options when responding to conversations which shape the general mood between you and your only other contact in the woods. But the dialog options didn't feel important enough to change the flow of the story. It ends the same way every time, with only a few details being different.

★SOUND & MUSIC★
Lending to the backdrop of isolation and loneliness, there isn't much music except during important scenes. Even then, the music is hushed and only there to encourage the given mood of the scene. It's well done and sounds good.

★BUGS & BOTHERS★
I didn't experience any bugs with this game, which was a welcome surprise. That being said, I do have one thing that stuck in my craw.

The ending. It made me feel... disappointed. I was hoping for something a little more science fiction-ey, or frightening, but that wasn't the case. Now, that may just be me. I have high expectations and a wild imagination. All this doesn't take away from the enjoyable experience I had during the meat of the game. The ending wasn't *bad* it just wasn't what I was expecting, that's all. It's a good game and I still recommend it.

Firewatch is a short, beautiful game that pulls on the ol' heartstrings with two endearing lead characters that communicate via radio. The majority of this game is fun (although the idea seemed boring to me at first, I was persuaded after all of the good reviews it had) and very tense. Unfortunately the ending had less to offer than one would hope. Everything you want the ending to be, it is not. It feels as though the game is a successful TV series that got cancelled and had to wrap the show up quickly, causing the game to end with a bitter-sweet taste in your mouth. Despite the poorly paced and strange turn out of an ending, the game really does make you feel a lot of emotion in a strange way and I would recommend it to anyone.

I want to like this game. I really do. I think Firewatch is really trying to do something that is very rare in games, and that's exploring a very complicated relationship. In Firewatch, that relationship is between Hank, who is married to his wife who has early onset dementia, and Delilah, his boss that he only communicates through the radio.

The game gives you various things to say to Delilah with prompts from items, settings, and responses when she contacts you. It's up to you to choose what to say, and a lot of options are to flirt with Delilah. 

All of this is fine, and it's hard to say anything about this game without spoiling it, so I'll tread lightly here. There's a big tonal shift in the game about halfway through, and I was honestly surprised by it. The game started referencing characters that were only mentioned in passing, and now suddenly they were a big part of the story. It left me scratching my head, wondering if I was just not paying enough attention. 

Look, I don't really know what else to say about the story, but I will say that it just left me extremely underwhelmed and slightly confused. The game is executed well; the voice acting is some of the best I've heard in gaming, it's really stunning to look at, and it really is fun to explore the Wyoming wilderness as a Firewatch person-guy.  But in the end, I think it dropped the ball. 

I don't want you to not play this game because of my review, because I think a lot of people will find enjoyment from this game. I don't think any of my problems that I have with it are especially damning. It's not like the game doesn't work, or isn't fun or whatever. It's just that I don't think it succeeds in what it specifically sets out to do, and I think that's why I'm not recommending it.

The music added wonderfully to the atmosphere, and every rustling bush left you wondering if it was you that made the sound or if you were being followed.

Let's just get what everyone knows out of the way: even with the graphics settings turned pretty much all the way down (maybe it's time I got a new computer), this was still a stunning game. Visually, it's a true delight. It's like being in (a more stylized) Yellowstone without actually being there, and I have actually been to Yellowstone, so I can confirm.

While it is primarily a walking sim - I will not deny that at all - there is definitely a solid and engaging story at its core. You build a relationship with someone whom you can only speak to over the radio, and yet it still feels real and honest. I often found myself wishing I could talk to Delilah just so I had someone to talk to, although the game wouldn't let me just call her whenever I felt like it. And isn't that a hallmark of a genuine relationship? Enjoying someone so much that you want to talk to them for no real reason other than wanting to talk to them?

I admit, when I started, I was not prepared for the horror. But being alone in the wilderness with no one to keep you company but a voice gets pretty freaky, and being followed by... [i]someone[/i]... does not help. Eventually, every rustle of the trees, every cracking of a tree branch, every sound of nature becomes something to jump at, and you constantly are turning your head wondering what the hell that sound was. Be prepared to realize that sometimes, [i]nothing[/i] is scarier.

Finally, let's talk about the ending. Yes, it's controversial. Yes, it's anticlimatic. Yes, you may come away disappointed. But honestly, I didn't mind it that much. I totally understand why one might dislike the ending. I felt that the buildup and the reveal didn't quite equal out. But honestly, you should play it for yourself and decide. Besides, if you finish it in under 2 hours and within two weeks, you can always get a refund.

You're put in the shoes of a man who's life has  gone astray. His personal relationship has fallen apart due to circumstances out of his control, and he is immensely troubled. He decides to escape into nature for a summer, only to find himself in the midst of mysterious events that test his sanity and his convictions as he develops a repertoire with his supervisor, the only contact he has.

Yes, it's a walking simulator, but one in which you're in charge of how your character responds to the supervisor on the other end of the walkie talkie. And it's one in which you constanly guessing what will happen next, all alone in the beautiful, desolate nature of Wyoming.

Firewatch is an exceptional indie walking simulator. The voice acting, the art style, the atmosphere, and the relationship between the main characters is top notch. I enjoyed the entire time I was in this world. 

However, the mystery that drives much of the game play falls short of the standards set by the rest of the game. I understand that the "real" story isn't the mystery, it's the relationship, and the character arc of the main character. However, the mystery does play a key role in the game as a game, so it should be as high quality as the rest of the work. And, it simply isn't. It isn't just the big reveal of the mystery that falls short, but also the manner in which it is presented to the player, and the somewhat false tension it creates in the other dimensions of the game. It is a bit contrived, in my opinion. 

I think the writers/developers could have had a little more faith in the power of their creation and the core inter-personal dynamic they established between the main characters to carry the player through the game. The kind of players who are drawn to this sort of game don't need sensational bait to draw them in and keep them playing. Had the game wholey committed to it's strengths, I think it would be truly great, not just exceptional.

Having said that, I can recommend this game without reservation. It is worth the time, and is a wonderful experience, despite the slight flaws. It certainly flags Campo Santo as a developer worth following.
