A very exciting and engaging game from the onset. The prologue is clever in that it repeatedly flips between the backstroy of the main character, Henry, and the beginnings of his journey in the present day. The choices at the beginning are not game changing but are reflected in certain dialogues further in the game (for example the name of the dog you choose to adopt) which is a nice touch.
The main story itself is very well written and cleverly builds up from the humorous adventure at the beginning to the mystery that eventually defines the game. 
Certain strange events that occur begin to play on your mind and you find yourself consistently intrigued to go on further and uncover the truth behind the happennings. I honestly found myself on edge with my heart racing as I became a little creeped out by the eerie development of the plot - the humorous banter shared between the two main characters is a welcome relief at times. I do believe that a lot of the suspense comes from being on your own for the entire game with nothing but a voice on a radio to keep you comforted. The world is wonderfully designed and the way the player must navigate with a physical map and compass adds more realism and appreciation for the world as you really have to 'discover' it as you go and find your own way around. I really liked the whole setting of it too, the role of a lookout in a forest/wilderness was well thought of and was perfect for this genre of mystery/adventure.
I only have one criticism for the game - Despite the brilliant storyline and building of suspence, I feel like such a strong development was let down by what happened to be a pretty 'nothing' ending. By the end I felt like all the effort and time had not been rewarded enough. The great mystery behind it all was disappointing. I hoped for a last minute plot twist or maybe a cliffhanger for a follow-up game but unfortunately it never happened and the ending felt very final - I understand many would like this but I personally appreciate a good cliffhanger to finish.
However, this criticism does not outweigh the many positives of an outstanding product (and at under £10 it was well worth the money!). I would love to see more games like this in the future and I would happily recommend it to others.

As far as interactiveness goes, this is basically walking simulator 2016. As far as story telling, this is one of the best games I've ever played. I can't comment on how your dialog choices affect the ending, though I don't think they do, but they do affect the short term. There are two main characters in here and never in my life have I ever seen such natural dialog between two characters.

But the above isn't enough to make someone like me, someone with ADHD and an affinity for action games, to play through the whole thing in one sitting (which I did). What kept me going was the suspence, and the pacing.

 First off, the story is a thriller(imo) and it's great. I won't say too much besides the fact that the ending supprised me(and it will you too) (It didn't end the way I wanted it to but thinking back on it, it was the best ending) and it kept me on edge but not to the point to where it became spooky. This game made me feel emotions I haven't felt in a long time and while some of them were sad the way the whole story is executed and put together plays off of the shallow stereotypical story we(the public) are used to in order to red herring the F*ck out of the player and elicit emotions. It's not how I would have written it, but it's how it was supposed to be written.

As for the pacing, the majority of the game is walking from place to place while talking to this person on your radio. The talking point is crucial because without it there would be no story and more importantly, the game would be boring as hell. As such they managed to space out the conversations so that the player never gets bored. And furthermore, there are dialog choices and they do create different responces. But it's more than that, some how these choices and thier responses create the characters in a way that is very natural and real.

Really, if I had to make a top ten list of games, this would be on it. All that praise you see. They deserved it for making one of the best story games I've ever played. 10/10

I only roamed long enough to get the remaining achievements as there wasn't much to do.

My only real complaint is that the story is pretty short. I finished the game in about 4 hours and thought I explored quite a bit along the way. I would have liked a longer story or maybe even a few non-story related side tasks to keep me busy awhile longer. I was able to complete the game a second time in about 2 hours once I knew what to do and where to go already, there really isn't much re-playability.

A bigger map would have been nice and could have led to some additional locations and tasks to increase the length of the game. This could have also allowed for tasks to be used in free roam so you had something to do. Maybe this can be added in a later update.

Overall I really enjoyed Firewatch and would recommend it to anyone who enjoys these types of games!

The camp was just studying wildlife even though Delilah explicitly said that wildlife biologists never fence off areas that large? Ned was spying on Henry and Delilah just because he was bored? Ned was sneaking transcripts of radio conversations into the wildlife camp and no one noticed? Despite the  large open area to walk around in, there was no real "choice" on where to go or what to do next--areas were blocked off until it was time to go there, and so on. There were notes and other things around that ended up having no use, and there was never an opportunity to use any of the things collected in inventory. I found the characters rather unlikeable and underdeveloped as well.  The whole plot with the wife, Julia, never went anywhere, and the ending didn't provide much of a resolution to the characters' individual story lines.  As a walking simulator it's pretty, but it was ultimately forgettable in terms of story.  The mystery at the center of the game had moments where it was compelling, but then it wrapped up very suddenly with little fanfare. This game is worth it if you buy it on sale and don't have many demands of an adventure/simulator game beyond pretty visuals.

This is a really great game worth checking out. If you don't know the story, it's about a guy who works as a fire lookout in the forest. You (the player) will be hiking around the forest doing various things throughout the day. The only person that you will talk to is Delilah (via walkie talkie), who also works in the forest. There are a couple of different 'main' storylines that you will get caught up in during your time in the forest. The dialogue throughout the game felt very natural to me. I have only done one full playthrough of the game, so I have no idea if choosing different dialogue options will influence your game outcome in any way. If you choose to, you can spend a lot of time just wandering around the forest. The game is very beautiful. The ending left a little bit to be desired in my opinion, but other than that, it was great. Like I said, I don't know if it's possible to get slightly different endings for the game by trying different dialogue. The main character has his funny moments and is definitely likable. I personally did not care for Delilah and just wished that she would leave me the hell alone sometimes, but that's just my personality. One last thing that I will say about the game is that you will probably be able to get through it pretty fast if you put your mind to it and don't wander off too much. It may not last very long, but it is definitely worth it.

As long as you go into this understanding that you are basically walking through a story and NOT playing a game where you get to make decisions you should be fine. It was a beautiful game that was very well written and voice acted. It only took me 5 hours to complete and that was taking my time. I got it 40% off during the Winter Sale and, even though it doesn't meet the whole one-dollar-per-hour-of-entertainment benchmark, I don't feel like I was ripped off. I did miss out on a couple of the achievements because I was too busy enjoying the story. I think I will come back and play this game again, kind of like re-reading a book that you really enjoy.

Actually, I did replay the last scene of the game and made a different dialog choice. While it didn't effect the actual "outcome" of the game, it did leave me with a different sense of how it ended. It's kind of difficult to explain without giving it away. I also forgot to mention that the soundtrack REALLY contributed to the atmosphere of the game. Also, Delilah has a sexy voice, and that is nice too.

Again, go into this expecting a semi-interactive story, and not a "game", and I hope you will enjoy it as much as I did.

OK, So the good of this game is that in its simplicity lies a story and two characters that develop as good as any page-turner of a book you will ever find.  It is on par with literature and film; beautifully done and executed goregeously.  The pacing brings you back for more and after each chapter you feel both satisfied in the development but nowhere near sated to where you can just walk away from the story.  

The bad is that with the incredibly well done build up and development the resolution is a let down.  Not just a let down, but more along the lines of being frustrated because of major holes in it.  Its like you let accomplished authors write 95% of a thriller novel and then let "Timmy" in the 4th grade wrap it up in the final chapter.

As a whole you will spend 90% of the game enthralled by the story.  Unfortunately the 10% is what you walk away with.

Still, even at that, it's an amazing game with compelling characters and near flawless execution up until the end.  It's totally worth your time.

I read a small article in a Hungarian blog about the best games in 2016. At least according to the blogger. I was happy to see unknown titles not the usual AAA ones. One of the titles was this game. Read few sentences, watched the trailer and looked for Firewatch on Steam.

CONS:
- The play time/price factor is not very good. One can purchase a game with much more play time for that amount of money.
- I'm quite a fan of role-playing games. Although this is not an RPG, but it's mostly dialogue driven and I cannot play a lawful-good character. There are many choices but all point to almost the same direction and you cannot be, cannot play the good guy in shine armor on a white horse. Even when you try to act as good as possible the story does not let it happen. I understand that the developer tried to minimize the characters, events, interactions but dispite of all that, I missed the opportunity.
- The story is written. No matter how hard you try to change the main narrative, it remains the same.

PROS:

All in all, I liked the game, I recommend the game even if you could purchase it on a sale. For me it is like a point&click adventure game in a charming, fascinating environment. Do not expect complex riddles, just live the life of a not-completely-ordinary man in the wilderness.

I bought Firewatch fully expecting to play it for half an hour, not get into it, and request a refund. Boy, was I wrong. This game creates a story in a way I've never seen before, with the player character only ever seeing four other humans for the duration of the story, and all of them for less than 30 seconds.

The story is at first told through text-based flashbacks that lay the framework for the story beautifully, even if it is a bit boring. After the exposition is done and over with, the story is told entirely through your radio conversations with Delilah and the things and events you happen upon while hiking around your lookout. This is a kind of storytelling that I have never before seen in a video game, and it works wonderfully. Over the course of the game, you really bond with Delilah as a character and feel as if you perhaps know her personallly, all without ever actually laying eyes on her over the course of the entire game.

The soundtrack fits the mood of the game perfectly, and accents moments of tension and stress. Overall, this game is one of the best I've played in a long time, and even though it is quite short, only 4 hours long, I feel that it is well worth the money, and I'll come back and play it again soon.

I disliked Firewatch and was surprised how disappointing the story was. I knew it was a mystery and not a game, but I refunded it on the basis of it being a disappointment solely on its merits as a storytelling piece. The story was so uninteresting to me that I'm confused that others would be captivated by it or find the dialogue compelling in such a setting.

As a firewatch in a Wyoming forest, I would expect to feel a sense of responsibility for the safety of others first, and a sense of adventure second. But I found neither in Firewatch. I felt little sense of adventure going through points on a map at the command of my supervisor. And I felt no responsibility: the story puts me in charge of a character who took a firewatch job without any interest in it or qualifications, just to escape from the harsh problems of reality. Not shoes I would want to fill. Worse, I'm expected to believe my character's supervisor would immediately shirk her responsibility in a life-or-death situation just to avoid talking to authorities, and that my character would be okay with that and continue to converse with her in a friendly or even romantic way.

The conversations and connection between the player's character and his supervisor play no role in the mystery except to present conspiracies that you know won't play out.

The introductory videos on Steam try to build up suspense, drama and humor that don't really exist in the game. I believed the story was going to pick up as certain factors were presented, and that my character was going to learn to deal with the conflict or have to figure his way out of something. But in fact as the mystery "unravels" I found my character was all along having a sort of pointless non-encounter with someone I knew nothing about and cared nothing about. So there was no arc. Then the story ended even less dramatically, punctuating the weakness of the main discovery with nothing at all happening with another character I cared nothing about.

The graphics and audio were great, especially for an indie title, but I did not buy the game for graphics and audio.

I see a missed potential. I may have enjoyed the interactions if this had gameplay rather than just storytelling, and I had been given some challenges performing duties as a firewatch with some risk and reward. With the environment that Firewatch has (minus the invisible collision meshes that prevent scaling over anything 10 inches tall), I might find some enjoyment discovering and locating fires, calling them in, and even fighting the flames as the story unfolds. But Firewatch is not intended to be a game at all, and the story failed me on its own.

A couple of other notes: (1) I considered the walkthrough format, being commanded to go from point A to point B to point C in the order prescribed by the storytelling, to be an abuse of my time in this context; (2) any indie can do better than a 55 degree FOV that can only be changed by a registry hack; (3) when changing controls, a previously mapped control should be removed when a new mapping is made, rather than preventing a new mapping, and Firewatch not only prevents the mapping, but apparently has no way to remove a control mapping, which is a disaster.

[h1]BLOT[/h1]
Good game, but very short. I'd give it a solid C, with the recommendation to hold out for a sale. Taking my sweet time, I was able to complete the game in the first play-through in under 5 hours. Considering its so short, I think the current price tag ($12 at the time when this was written), is a bit steep. My recommendation is to wait until its under $10. (Details below)


[h1]The Good[/h1]
[list]
[*] Graphics - in particular the color palette - makes it feel like a watercolor painting.
[*] Dialog - Great jokes and commentary. Got a few solid chuckles out of it.
[*] Writing - They cultivate an amazing sense of paranoia. The game is scary but it isn't clear whether your fear is rational or you're just psyching yourself out. I kept second-guessing myself whether or not I was blowing stuff out of proportion.
[*] Voice acting - very believable, sincere, easy-to-listen-to, great delivery of the lines
[*] Music - Great for delivering the atmosphere. Haunting at times, soothing at others.
[/list]

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
[*] Short - and I mean VERY short. I took my time when playing this. I read every note, the back of every book, I stopped and took a few screenshots here and there, I listened to every voice conversation and tape that I could, and I still completed the game the first time through in under 5 hours.
[*] Story - Without getting into spoilers, I did feel like the story was a bit of a let-down.
[*] The last section - Once again, without getting into spoilers, it takes FOREVER to get to your destination with crap visibility. It becomes less fun and more straight-up annoying.
[*] Minor glitches - I did have a few minor glitches. Birds getting stuck in their air (not flapping or moving forward - just floating), some ground becoming invisible if I turned around quickly, stuff like that.
[*] Movement flow - I realize this isn't supposed to be like assassin's creed or anything where you can seamlessly vault up onto stuff or drop down, but it did get a little annoying to have to stop and do the up / down / climb / drop animations, especially when there was a sense of urgency. Its not that these animations take too long (they're actually quite short), but in some areas you do them [i]a lot[/i], and it would have been nice if it felt more fluid.
[/list]

Thanks for reading!

The story itself is a believable mystery adventure that explores the difference between solitude and loneliness. Like the game as a whole, there's nothing bad about it - just nothing outstanding either. 
 
Ultimately, if you live in the city and want to escape into a non-threatening wilderness at the click of a button - this game is for you. If you're looking for an interesting narrative-driven game that truly utilises gaming as a medium: [i]The Stanley Parable[/i] is a better choice.

Why give it thumbs down?" and I can easily reply to that: Imagine you are watching a thriller like Shutter Island, Identity or The Sixth Sense and instead of the plot twist or at least a proper explanation for all the mysterious stuff, you just get hit with an ending like "Who was flickering the lights? Aw never mind, my light bulb was defective!". You probably wouldn't like that too much, right? It destroys every bit of tension and atmosphere the game has built up over 3-4 hours. It's a shame, because this game would deserve every bit of critical acclaim with an ending that actually fits the game.

Firewatch puts you into the shoes of Henry. He has problems in his life which he tries to escape by taking a job as a firewatch. His solitude doesn’t last for long, as his boss and a firewatch in the neighbouring tower, Delilah, starts to keep him company through a walkie-talkie. She gives tasks and teaches about the job but they also start to develop a personal relationship.

The dialog between Henry and Delilah is the focus of Firewatch. Their characters are really believable with faults and strengths. They are confused, frightened, but also show courage and determination. They feel like humans. It’s an absolute delight to listen to the conversation. 

Firewatch has themes of losing loved ones and guilt, but also mystery. The game starts to hint at a big conspiracy and i got thoroughly into the mystery and was on the edge of my seat. It’s great stuff. Without spoiling anything, the ending could divide opinions but personally I thought it was just perfect.

Other than talking, gameplay is spent mostly by walking around. The gameworld is open and you can go anywhere, but it is a series of paths. The paths are surrounded by canyons or bushes which you can’t go through. It’s a bit irritating at times, especially when you have to go from A to B but you have to trek around C and D to get there, because of an invisible wall. You can pick up items which have very specific uses and it's always clear what to do next.

You have a map and a compass which shows your position in the gameworld. This feature can be turned off which I recommend. Without a guiding marker the game requires actual surveying of the environment and navigating. This makes the game much better since it’s easy to get lost in the forest and further emphasises the feelings of loneliness.

Graphics have a cartoony look which is great. Textures are not super detailed but the use of color gives an excellent mood to the game. It’s a treat for the eyes. The framerate was not consistent on my machine and I could not see a clear reason why. The graphics have a similar style with games like Team Fortress 2 but feel much more demanding on the system. 

Music is really strong and fits the mood and the world. The soundtrack is a great listen also outside of the game and I recommend the soundtrack edition. Other sound effects are a little plain. Voice acting is some of the best I’ve ever heard in a video game.

This game is beautiful. 

I could leave the review at that and that would almost be enough - the star player is the environment (of course, as you barely see another human for the duration of the game) with its crisp colours, sunset-illuminated vistas, and its unforgiving paths. That said, there's beauty in the script too, with an introduction that crushes your feelings to a pulp before you do anything but click a few times and a warm dialogue between the protaganist and the co-worker in the neighbouring tower. 

I felt the pacing was perfect - any time it was getting a little dull or samey, you'd get a wisecrack over the radio. Walking around and exploring never felt overwhelming but never felt too constricted either. This was helped by the map (THE MAP!). I really love this game's map - it feels like part of the game in ways that other game maps just can't seem to grasp. Whereas most games have either a tiny always-present minimap or a map you can only access via a pause menu, Firewatch gives you a physical map that your character scribbles all over. This gives it a personality that other game maps lack, avoiding the grim sameness that a computer generated map with a key just can't avoid. I also liked that it didn't hold your hand - to work out which way to go always required a few moments' thought and occasionally checking the compass.

Overall, I'd highly recommend this game. Despite its reasonably short playtime (I got four hours out of it, according to Steam's stats), it's an immersive experience that really packs an emotional punch.

You start off with some dirt, you dig a little more and you see traces of gold and then you hit the jackpot. This game has a beautiful soundtrack, breathtaking views, and a theme that connects with me at this exact moment in time. The theme is about (in my eyes) running away from your problems, the forest being isolation and the fires you have to snuff out being the confrontations. Until a giant forest fire occurs you mostly enjoy the bliss of being alone. But the giant forest fire is the final confrontation, you can run but you can't hide.

This game came out a while back and I’ve only just now picked it up and played.

From trailers I knew it was going to be a indie game that featured storytelling and visuals over gameplay and constant action. The game held up that expectation pretty well, and that’s a good thing. Firewatch is another varied storyline, choice driven game but it isn’t another telltale game. If Halo is a pizza then Firewatch is a homemade sandwich, it’s a good change from the typical and proven video game.

In the game the characters felt real, like you could take them out of the game and put them onto the street and nobody would think twice. The choices you were given in conversations ranged from one to four options but it never felt like the game was imitating telltale and their four option strategy that is rarely deviated from. The visuals were very good but the game also had story to back it up. For instance the game Brothers had visuals, but no real story and no quality gameplay and no constant action, which led to it flopping despite its goty nomination. (which was probably bought by microsoft to market the game) Another thing that made Firewatch better than pure visual games is that it didn’t force the visuals onto the player. The player has to stop and look around to see how pretty everything is. And the player is enabled to do so by being given an in-game camera. In terms of the story, it is very intriguing I think I sat down to start playing and stayed for the entire game (~3 hours) so it was a very good experience and well written. This also means I didn’t get annoyed by the game and felt a need to take a break.

One of the first critiques I have for the game is copy and paste obstacles. These are fairly common in most video games really, even from major studios that have the manpower, time, and ability to avoid them but that isn’t any excuse for smaller indie game devs. Additionally like many choice driven, multiple storyline games, there is the obvious damned if you do damned if you don’t scenario. Really these senarios would be so much more okay to encounter if you couldn’t see them coming from a mile away. It’s like being told, “shoot this character or poison them” when you don’t want to have to do either option. Technical aspects that fall short are sometimes you walk over some terrain and the game gitches on you and you’re a bit stuck until you go back from where you came. (while this falls under acceptable shortcomings from indie studios it is still a shortcoming) In the game you have a map and it felt a bit clumsy to have to zoom in and locate where you are on it or not be able to understand any of it. Finally I had heard the game described as a walking simulator and that isn’t too far off. Sure you could run but it is a pretty big game area and you have to stick to the paths. (no side-strafing up mountains like in bethesda games.)

In the end I really enjoyed the game and I give it a 7.5/10 would recommend.

Firewatch is not simply a game, it is a work of art with a lot of effort put into it: the dynamic weather system, the real recorded sound effects, the voice acting, the music, the 3D layout, the props and everything else fit together perfectly and just make you love this game. Hopefully there will be a sequel.

This game is bland.

It begins with a gob of exposition. Thankfully, the descriptive reading is interlaced with some slow action and scene building.

The main body of the game is exploring a linear path in a small forest, doing fetch quests for a disembodied voice named Delilah.

There is no real gameplay to speak of, other than walking back and forth and retracing your little sand box. Each day ends when you complete an objective.

There is no story.

There is no character progression. There is no resolution to the character issues or conflicts. There is no climax or denouement. 

This is basically a playable vignette about two broken people. 



SPOILERS AHEAD.



Hank is a broken man. We are told he loves his wife and, with sad music, we follow along and find out that she is in early dementia. Her family steps in to provide care-giving that he, apparently, does not want to do himself. His response to her family stepping in is to flee to the forest and forget about her.

Hank is a decent character study. He is selfish and looking out for number one. He doesn't need to be a saint – but for the audience to empathize, he has to have some redeeming traits. Thankfully, he has a fun voice and the dialogue is strong enough to move the story along.

Delilah is grating from the get go. Over cheerful and pushing dumb dialogue that just keeps going. She is designed to be off putting when Hank first talks to her. But she seemed to be stuck on annoying for far too long. Once she starts getting a little less salty, we find out what a deplorable person she is. 

Delilah is a broken woman. She hides in the forest to escape people. She refuses to believe Hank when he says he has been jumped by a mystery stranger. She gets drunk when Hank is working and wants her help. She lies to save herself, even when it could harm others – and eventually does.

I could not find a place in my heart for either of these people. 

I appreciate that these two were fleshed out enough to make for a decent character study, but there was nothing gained from this. Hank does not grow as a man – as far as we know when the story ends. Delilah disconnects at the end, she no longer cares about Hank or his path, she just wants to leave the forest and moan that she cannot come back and moan that the death of a little boy has endangered her firewatch job.

There is no story. The death of the boy in the cave and his sneaky father are a subplot of sorts – but they do not constitute a story. They can be removed entirely. Hank and Delilah have nothing going on, other than their radio interactions. The teen girls – subplot. The research station – subplot, and not really resolved.

The art direction and dialogue are the pluses in this game. But both are not perfect. Delilah starts off so badly I wished I could mute her. And the art had so many limits. I knew when the text started at the beginning that the game was stuck inside a limited narrative. I knew I was not going to interact with humans. I knew I would never meet Delilah. I knew that I would never come across another human. I was surprised to see the dead boy – but not surprised at how poorly designed he was. The game is great at showing off the forest. But it is stuck in neutral when it comes to interacting with others. I was surprised to actually meet the rescue fellow in the helicopter – but he was rigid and cloaked in firefighting gear – so, they did what they could with what they had, I guess.

I enjoyed becoming emotionally attached to a character I ultimately never had the hopes of developing, let alone encountering, and I would recommend this title to anyone eager to throw themselves into a story without an interest for mental development. Not to suggest this title doesn't include puzzles, it certainly does. Simply put, however, the puzzles one will encounter in Firewatch aren't on par with the sort of puzzles that would essentially create a puzzle-game. To rephrase, if you're a fan of story-driven games with linear plots that still allow wiggle room for the sake of immersion than look no further.

Cons:

If you're looking for action, adventure, romance, puzzles, running from scary axe-wielding maniacs with a flare for hockey, Firewatch isn't for you. The term “walking simulator” gets tossed around quite a bit, and it's technically correct. Henry (the character you play) just basically strolls from one part of the map to another while talking over the radio to his boss. There's no puzzles to sort out and no bears to wrassle. You just do a lot of walking, climbing, jumping down from rocks, and more walking.
However, that being said, the experience was far from boring. In fact, it was wonderful. It wasn't until I finished the game that I realized just how little I had actually done, and I was okay with that. It was a story that kept me gripped and entertained the whole ride.
Henry's conversations with Delilah were witty, well thought out, a ripe with emotion. The voice acting was stellar and it was hard not to get drawn into the story. The developers took a great deal of time and care when it came to designing the conversations between Henry and Delilah. And while it has no impact on the plot, what you're looking at, holding, and interacting with will change the words and responses between the two. That's some awesome game developing, in my opinion. I'm extremely curious what a longer, more in-depth game would be like with this style of character interaction. How immersive would it be if the world and its characters could react to everything your character is doing – such as holding a random poo-shovel for way longer than a normal human would? Little things like that which make the game draw you in like a trap. I'm excited to see more, I'll say the least.
Back on topic, though, Firewatch wasn't perfect. My first run-though took just under 5 hours – which is short for a $20 game – so snag Firewatch when its on sale. The ending also left a little to be desired. Without going into detail, Henry and Delilah are sorting out a big mystery, and it's stocked full of suspense, confusion, and high-strung emotion. And just as it's starting to hit the peak, when some answers might be given – WHAM – out comes a curve ball and you're left going “wait, what?”. The developers do tie it all in, but it left me feeling as though this impressive story they were designing fell flat in the end.
The biggest flaw was with the chain-link fence. No barbed wire – no electric current – just a simple fence with a padlock. How, oh, how will Henry get around this obstacle? Henry decides not to climb the fence (who knows, he might rip his shorts) and decides not to use the terrain to get a boost over (there's a rock next to the fence that ran up the fence to the point where all he had to do was step over and drop down) but instead comes to the conclusion that he will hike a bazillion miles to see if he can find a tool to smash the padlock. In the end, this was more humorous than game-ending, but a flaw nonetheless.
Despite anything wrong with the game, I enjoyed it and I recommend Firewatch for anyone who wants to get drawn into a beautiful game with a nice story. Grab it on sale and take a long evening enjoying it.

First, let's talk about what this game isn't.

This game isn't challenging, difficult, fast-paced, or action-packed. You don't fight, solve puzzles, and you can't die. In fact, you never come face-to-face with another soul throughout the entire game. A cynical or easily bored person could dismiss this game as being simply "push button to make story happen." 

And really, it is. But that's not at all a bad thing. This game is immersive, suspenseful, and overwhelmingly beautiful. As the game progresses, you explore the beautiful park, unravel your character's backstory, uncover a decade-old mystery, and develop a friendship with another lonely ranger whose face you never see. This isn't a movie that requires the occassional press of a button; you become fully immersed in the story and are quite free to encounter the story on your time, taking breaks to explore the forests and cliffs. Oh, and take some great pictures. Don't neglect that camera, you'll kick yourself if you do.

With almost 20000 review here, I probably won't bring much to the table, but I simply have to share my opinion.
[i]Firewatch[/i] is [u]phenomenal[/u] experience.
Some might argue in terms of gaming, there isn't much to it, and that this tittle would work better/same as movie, maybe a book, TV show even, with basic consensus that being a game does't add much.
I, on the other hand, would argue, it actually add significantly more - at least for me. I felt more immersed in the story. I felt more emotions. Laughs were more sincere, intense moments more intense, because you play for charismatic character acting on your behalf, with sidekick character who is is even more awesome.

Characters in this game are surely the strongest part. Writing felt like true conversation between two people, not fabricated, it felt [u]real[/u] - so characters also felt real. And it was only amplified by [u]spectacular[/u] voice over. I would listen to any podcast, with Rich Sommer & Cissy Jones at this point, just to get more of them, and their voices. Thanks to them these characters came to life ...

... in story that might not be the best story ever told. But they are together in story that, again, feels real. Yes, we might get lead to different conclusions as we progress, it might be misleading at times on purpose, but it never give you the idea that story is actually about something else, it just let your fantasy and inner mathematics play out and taking advantage of it.
Because of that, revelations have bigger impact, and it brings honest emotions, that are underlined by characters and the sadness, anger, or whatever state of mind they are currently in.

From technical stand point, it is really simple tu judge [i]Firewatch[/i].
Beautiful visuals. Stunning sceneries. Music fitting in every occasion, and sounds which develop further the magic of the forest under our protection. Controls are smooth, so walking simulation, or hiking simulation if you wish, could be even more pleasant.

[i]Firewatch[/i] on space of almost four hours left significant mark on me; and became a tittle I would love to get back into one day. This game was a great experience, fantastic story, very engaging characters and certianly pulled me in emotionally. Exactly what you want in a game like this. Because of this, I have no choice but to recommend this game. HOWEVER, I want to list here the reasons I DONT think the game is worth the current price, or more than $5 or $6 in my opinion (given comparable games on Steam) - 

-The game lasts a MAX of around 5 hours. I can't say that I explored everything possible, but I certainly uncovered most all dialouge lines and secrets in this game in around 4 and 1/2 hours, left the game running for around an hour while not playing which accounts for the extra hour. I simply can't recommend a game with that few hours of play at $12 - the price I bought it at ON SALE.
-The ending was quite disappointing. I'm sure it was a great artistic statement, but for me it felt unfufilling and was a shock when I realized the game was really ending - I assumed I was simply triggering another plot of the storyline, one that would extend the game for another 10-15 hours.
-I have seen the graphics noted as a major selling point for the game, and I certainly liked the graphics, and the feel of the game was done masterfully, especially with the intermittent soundtrack. However, the "motion blur" (which I set to low) was somewhat of an annoying mechanic, and the game lagged and was slow to respond at several points during my playthrough.

This being said, I loved this game, and while the ending doesn't sit well with me and left me unfufilled, anyone who is looking for a game that plays out with a good, intriguing story, has a powerful envirnoment and mood that sucks you in, and character development at an emotional level unheard of in such a short span of time and with the level of interaction you actually have. 
At a minimum, I would expect to at least get an equal amount of hours out of a game as that at which I paid for it, but I enjoyed Firewatch enough to give it a positive rating regardless. I hope this review is helpful to any of you considering this game.

Game description:
As the story is the game, I don't want to tell too much about the story itself. The game is an interactive story. There are no real puzzles, you can't die, you can't do anything wrong. Instead, you follow the orders your boss tells you over the radio, exploring the area, trying to solve the mystery. Or, instead of solving the mystery, you just play along and want to know what happens next, like reading a book. It's a bit like those old books, that said on each page "do you want to go down the road? Flip over to page 99. Do you want to enter the old house? Read on on page 45." Something like that.

It has limited replayability. The general gameplay ad story will be the same. However, you can choose different options in the dialogue, resulting in different reactions of the other character, different dialogue and as such a slightly different story. There is also an option to play the game while listening to developer commentary, and there is a free roam mode as well.

Verdict:
The game is a great experience. I really loved playing it. It would have been nice to also see some regular Firewatch work in the game, but that's ok. The game wasn't that long, but I think it's better to have it like this, than artificially drawing it out. It reminded me a bit on Dear Esther, but giving you more choices. Or on SOMA, without the horror aspect.

The voice acting and scripting is some of the best I have encountered in any game, and the mechanics suit it perfectly. Where it is let down is in 3 areas. Firstly the game is far too linear - it forces you from section to section in a way that does not feel realistic and is immersion breaking. In some places you can climb up rocks twice your height and in other places you can't even get up something higher than your knee. For an exploration game this breaks immersion. Secondly whilst you have to traverse this linear path the other characters are seemingly unimpeded. Again this breaks immersion. However most importantly the game plays like a King novel. The start is atmospheric. The middle is incredibly suspenseful. But the end just feels flat and rushed. You don't discover or deduct what has happened, it is literally put on a cassette taped to a rock with your name on it. It is not like the ending is even bad - it will leave you with a strong emotional feeling one way or the other, it's just getting there is like when a TV show has 3 minutes left to wrap up and you are then just told everything in a dialogue. Very unsatisfying, and for a game primarily about the story a sadly unforgivable mistake.

Wow. I just... wow. There hasn't been a game this clever in a long, long while.

Right from the get go this game will draw you in with its superb writing and touching introduction. The intro does a fantastic job of painting the back story of the protagonist Henry. By the time you finish the intro segment you will truly feel for the trials Henry has gone through which is a fantastic way for the player to immerse themselves into filling Henry's boots. However after the introduction is over and the player starts to get into the meat of the actual game they may find that the story starts to peter off towards the second half. The back and forth banter of the two main characters does a decent job of building up the plot and does get you curious as to what is going on and what is going to happen next. About half way through the game I did start to get excited to get answers for the questions the game was posing.  Many mysterious happenings start going on and you really do start wondering who or what is causing everything. There is a big build up to finally get the answers you're looking for in the climax however by the time you get there you may find that the story starts to fall short near the end. I found myself saying "really, that's it?" at the games climax. I was hoping for more of a thrilling end or even just a happy ending but instead just found that the game just well, ends. It left me wanting more out of the characters I had spent 4 hours learning about. I have only played through the game once at the time of this review and I do intend to visit the game again at some point in the future to try and do things a bit differently in my second play through. This game however, like many games in the genre, I believe just gives you the illusion of choice and I am pretty certain that no matter what dialogue choices you make in your play through it will still result in the same climax at the end. Many of the dialogue choices are optional,  it seems as though you could just run through the game and not say anything if you really want to. Though I doubt it would affect the plot in any significant way.
As for the actual game play it's basically a walking simulator with a little freedom in what path you take to get from point A to point B. There is some mild exploration aspects. The exploration part of the game is actually what drew me in to buying the game.  However I found it to be underwhelming as the map  really isn't as big as it originally seems and there is little to actually explore and find outside of some seemingly useless collectables. You can pick up and inspect just about any item in the game and you can choose to "keep" many of these items too, however few have any use in the game and there is no inventory to track what you have picked up along your journey. Some key items you may choose to pick up may appear on your desk after a day passes but other than seeing them sitting there they don't do anything. The game has a day cycle that triggers after you reach a certain point in the dialogue. While I didn't hate how that worked it did slightly bother me that there is no telling when the day will just end and go on to the next.  You could be out exploring or taking in the scenery and having a conversation via walky talky while you're walking and the day may just abruptly end because you reached a point in the dialogue that triggers it. Also you do miss a lot of days that you just don't see probably because the writers had nothing important to say about those days. It'll jump from day 15 to day 30 and with no explanation as to what Henry was doing in that time. I thought this kind of broke the immersion for me.
The game's graphics look good. Nothing spectacular but good enough to let you enjoy the scenery around you. I did run into a few performance issues in my play through, most notably some stuttering and clipping. There was one instance when Henry clipped through a ledge while trying to hop down and got stuck, I simply turned around and climbed back up the ledge, re-centered myself and hopped back down. The stuttering seems to be from somewhat poor optimization as my rig far out classes what the recommended specs are for the game. I have a friend who purchased the game on PS4 and he complained about some stuttering as well on console. It's nothing game breaking and won't ruin the experience at all just a minor annoyance. The voice acting is top notch, I give kudos to the voice actors as they all did an excellent job. The sound design in the game is also very good, I found  the music that plays during the intro sequence to be very memorable and does a fantastic job setting the tone. 
My final verdict for Firewatch is a 6/10. A good short story to get into for the right price. If this game is on sale for $10 or less and you enjoy walking simulators with a strong narrative I would recommend picking it up. The game is somewhat short and should only take 3-5 hours to complete. This doesn't hurt the game as I feel that If it carried on for a whole lot longer I probably would have started to lose interest. Overall not bad I just wish there was more exploration game play and maybe stronger character development after the intro.

[Minor spoilers from the introduction to the game]

We all expected Henry to be escaping from something, and the trailers give away already that there's something up with his marriage. But I wasn't expecting it to be early-onset dementia. Suddenly the game got all too real. My grandfather was a cartographer. He last held a job when he was 35 before his strange lapses in concentration became too much. He was diagnosed with it a few years later.

(I like to think there's a map of Somerset out there somewhere with a road that goes to nowhere, and everyone is all confused about if there was ever a road there at all and where did it lead, but actually it was just my Grandad being scatterbrained one day)

It's always been a big, big fear of mine that this is genetic and I only have ten years left to be myself before I begin to lose my ability to communicate effectively. I live a pretty stressful life right now with not much sleep, working three jobs and doing a PhD - I also have dyspraxia - so forgetting things, lethologica and being generally scatterbrained is a normal part of my life. But there's always a voice in the back of my head reminding me of how my grandfather used to burst into tears because he couldn't explain what he liked about a TV show he was watching. Or his anger at being unable to read books.

Despite all this I sympathise strongly with Henry, and I don't think his choices are so bad given the situation. He hasn't really abandoned his wife, though maybe his self-care routine isn't as healthy as it should be. Dementia is a life-limiting disease, and Jules is going to die sooner rather than later. He should spend time with her, but he also needs to spend time with himself to try and come to terms with this.

I've read a few reviews calling the big reveal disappointing, but I don't agree. It was strange for sure, to be given such a mundane (if you can call it that?) excuse for the events that happened. What's important, and what people are finding so hard to come to terms with I think, is that it was never about you. You basically play as Henry, guy with a tragic backstory, who signs up for firewatch in a National Park in the late 80s. You're alone in your outpost but for a walkie-talkie that lets you talk to the next lookout, Delilah. That's it. A dialog-driven interactive story in scenic views around a beautiful National Park.

The gameplay is alright. You'll wander around the park on a few fetch quests that will guide you through the narrative. Like I said: it's more the trip than the achievements in this game that makes it worth playing. There's not much to actually play, you can't be killed, you can't do whatever you want ... it's quite linear. The terrain is quite challenging mainly because the navigation isn't that easy. But it works good enough. The main device is the dialogue, and they mastered that perfectly.

All in all I enjoyed Firewatch a lot, but thought it was a bit too short for my taste (5hrs). The story could have been denser and definitely a bit longer (= could have used more story), but it still was a very interesting and immersive experience. Loved the overall feel, graphic art & amazing voice acting.

[h1]VISUALS - 8/10[/h1]
Let's just get this out of the way first: Yes, the visuals are great. They decided to go with a hand painted style which served them quite nicely and it's the one reason why I stayed for the first hour of the game, which I'll get onto a bit later. Everything is vibrant and pretty, the textures looks really nice (even up close), and all the models looked nice and smooth. Outstanding job in this department.

[h1]SOUND - 6/10[/h1]
All I really have to say about the sound is that the music was very nice and the sound effects were quite solid, but there's was nothing overly special about it.

[h1]GAMEPLAY - 5/10[/h1]
This is where it starts to fall apart a bit. Now given I wasn't expecting much from the gameplay since one of the tags for this game is literally "Walking Simulator", but the walking between places got boring pretty quickly especially towards the end since you just know where you're going and the trek from point A to point B can be really long without something to keep you occupied. The worst part though is definitely when you go off the correct path and you don't know that, cause by the time you realise you're going the wrong way you've just reached the other end of the map and you have another huge trip all the way back. Maybe if Delilah (the woman on the other end of the radio you carry everywhere) checked in more frequently during these dull moments to see that I'm doing alright then it wouldn't be so bad, but it is what it is. I do want to get it out there right now though that the gameplay was not all that bad, discovering new areas was always good fun and talking to Delilah was actually my favourite part of this game.

[h1]STORY - 2/10[/h1]
This was such a shame, really it was. I wanted this story to be awesome, hell for a good portion of the game it WAS awesome, but then the ending happened, and it killed all of the magic for me, every last bit of it. Now, I won't spoil more of that for anyone because that would be unfair to anyone who legitimately wants to play it, but do know that I actually really enjoyed the mystery that was unfolding over the course of the game and it may be enough to let you enjoy the story, but for me the ending just dragged it all down.

[h1]OVERALL - 5/10[/h1]
So would I recommend this game? No, but also yes? It's unfortunate Steam only provides a binary yes or no system for these recommendations since I consider this more of a maybe. If you're into walking sims that's rich on story and art then this game may be for you, but if you're new to walking sims you may want to try something a little more involved such as a point and click adventure like Oxenfree or Life is Strange before you try this. If you're hesitating to buy this game, it's probably not for you anyway, and if arty games such as The Vanishing of Ethan Carter or Everybody's Gone to the Rapture don't rub you the right way then this most definitely isn't for you. If you're intrigued, buy it on a sale and give it the 4 hours it takes to complete, maybe you'll get a better experience than I did.

Firewatch was a surprise of this year. Up until a month ago I had no clue what it was about. I heard a lot about how great it was from reviews and decided I would buy it. Even when I bought it I was skeptical. It wasn't the type of game I was used to. So I launched it and was instantly greeted by the nice menu screen. Lit up with daylight. As if to represent the gleaming presense this game has on you. Although it is bright from the menu, after playing through, I can tell you that this is barely the case.

Firewatch is a psycholofically thrilling, story-driven game that exceeeds in almost all areas. This may be one of the best games of this year. It is short-lived but never the less perseveres. It challenges your mind to withstand its challenges and does it beautifully.

Good:

The Story: The Story in Firewatch is perhaps one of the best I have seen in years. Every turn is a mind game that twists how you percieve the game and characters. It starts out fairly average and then builds to a point where the human fears of Isolation and Paranoia begin to not just affect the characters but the player themselves. It is short but sweet and although there is really only one character the voice acting is superb. Everything about the story is superb, though the ending is a little lackluster not to spoil.

Graphics and the World: Now it isn't Witcher 3 Graphics but the cartoony like graphics were really a nice fit to this game and the world around you was beautiful. You began to enjoy the world and how you went about it. Every turn a new rock to climb over, a new unique area... well not every corner but you get the idea. Enough to make you interested. The Forest itself is crucial to how this game flows. A Man alone in the woods with nothing but another person on a radio to be your only hope for sanity  in this isolated environment. The Graphics make this world vibrant and pristeen beyond what I first expected.

Characters:
Although I discussed voice acting earlier on and how they all fit nicely I figured I would explain it a little better here. The Characters and of course their actors were unique and satisfying in this story. Although there were only really 2 important characters. the way the story shapes these characters through common occurences and how people react to situations was masterful. Every time the chracters went through a twist they were affected in ways that left them distrought and in shambles. Every sentence that was uttered sounded appropriate, like it should have sounded, It wasn't the bland commentatry you see in other games which is why this game has great characters. Even if it just two of them.

Negatives:

Travelling: This is not a very big issue but I felt like addressing it. Unless you get all your turns right you will be annoyed when trying to travel around to your locations. You have to carefully manage the environment if you want to get through this without wasting a good 20 minutes throughout the whole story backtracking to go the right way. This might just be me but I thought I would just leave it out there.

Ending: This is more a mixed perspective. The ending was only satisfactory, It was a great story but like many of the people who played this game, a great many people will find this ending rather bland but at the same time it is perhape the only way this game could have ended. Whether you are satisfied with the ending and this game's story depends on how you take it all in.

Conclusion:

Firewatch has done something that hasn't been done by a game in a long time. It surprised me. It took me on a ride that I thought would never end. It was shortlived but at the same time, worth all the things money could buy. It was something a lot of games haven't givem us in a while. Quality. Now be warned however. Not everyone will like this game but even if your skeptical. Take the risk, It is worth it.

Score: 8.9/10

[h1]Great characters and interaction, but not much else[/h1]

I found Firewatch a pretty decent game, but did not like it as much as I thought I would. While the character interaction was indeed amazingly well designed and written, and made me enjoy the game throughout both my playthroughs, several other elements felt underwhelming to me.

Let's start with the good stuff: A lot of the game consists of talking to your supervisor via walkie-talkie, and these conversations are brilliantly well written and acted. They always flow naturally, the comedic moments are well executed (especially the frequent sarcasm), there's also drama, panic, a good deal of flirting, and more. All of this is extremely well done. Additionally - as you will notice on a second playthrough - the game does an amazing job managing all the little bits of information that you may or may not have talked about in previous conversations, and reflects those frequently in the later ones. It has become very rare for a game to be so adaptive in its dialogs, not only because it's one hell of a task to juggle with all these different game states - it's also incredibly hard to make all these nuances work seamlessly in a fully voice-acted game. Firewatch tackled this task and excelled at it.

However, no matter what you say in these conversations, none of it will change the actual game. The story follows a completely linear plot. You may skip parts of it, but you can never change the outcome. So while there's a lot of adaptivity and freedom of choice in small details, these details are embedded in a fairly rigid framework. Your choices may have a lot of emotional impact on you (both as a character and as a player), and they may change your _perception_ of the plot, but never the plot itself.

While the game handles the relationship between Delilah and you spectacularly well, the same can unfortunately not be said about the other main story line, which deals with several mysterious events in the area. The story _does_ succeed in building up suspense and suspicion, but the actual 'solution' at the end felt implausible and lackluster to me. After listening to the developer commentaries in my second playthrough, I now understand better where the devs were coming from and what they were aiming for, but I still think that this story line could have been executed better to make it more believable.

The actual gameplay is fairly minimal. There are no puzzles, no action sequences, and no challenges. You simply walk to various destinations, find things which you report to your boss, choose dialog options, and the plot then progresses.

Unfortunately, even though I like many so-called "walking simulators", I disliked the walking-around aspect in Firewatch for several reasons. Even though the game technically offers free movement in an open map, in practice any attempt to leave a given path and actually go exploring, gets stopped very quickly by impassable walls, vegetation, or slopes. There is only about a dozen of available paths, which you keep hiking back and forth on. This makes a substantial part of the game feel very repetitive, especially since these paths are fairly long, and they often contain several unskippable animations of you climbing up a wall or rappelling down a slope. Many parts of the area are impossible to get to until you receive tools, and even then the game sometimes blocks areas off for arbitrary reasons (e.g. it literally tells you that "you cannot rappel down here before you search for bear tracks" at a completely unrelated location). As a result, I never felt like actually exploring a vast wilderness - instead, I felt like put in a very gamey artificial environment with lots of "smart" roadblocks to keep me reigned in.

The game's graphics are beautiful - a bit cartoony, but that allowed for low-footprint assets, which made the game perform fluidly even though it's not using the most efficient engine. The lighting is spectacular at times. A lot of attention was given to ambience sounds and occasional (very atmospheric) music. Sadly though, while you can clearly _hear_ a rich wildlife, you will never see any animals apart from two completely scripted raccoon encounters, and a somewhat hidden turtle. For a game that advertises "a spectacular wilderness experience", this made the environment feel surprisingly lifeless for me. As someone who's done a bit of hiking, I know of course that there aren't deer around every corner as some games have you believe, but usually you see at least some birds, and perhaps a squirrel, fish, or frog - none of which exist in this game.

The game is fairly short. I took about 6h per playthrough, and I like to play slowly. If you want to spend scarce funds on a game that lasts you a long time, this is not it. But if the limit is your spare time rather than your wallet, then you may appreciate Firewatch as a full experience that can be had in one session.

[h1]Recommendation: If you like well-written stories about the human condition, with believable characters and a mystery-driven overarching plot, absolutely buy Firewatch. If your main draw is the "hiking in the wilderness" experience, then you may want to wait until it gets higher discounts. If you want action, puzzles, or meaningful interactivity with the environment in the games you play, then you may want to skip this one.[/h1]

I first saw this game one or two days before its release, since I've always enjoyed games with beautiful music and absorbing stories, the love was instant. Usually a walking simulator is heavily relied on the script and the conversations of the characters, because unlike other games such as a First Person Shooter or an RPG, the only way of telling stories is through those conversations you will be having and it's highly possible that it is also the only experience of gamepaly in the whole process. You won't be dashing crazy, chopping down hollows or darkspawns or the whatever-the-name-is bad people, the only thing you can do is walking around, listening to people, and with a bit of luck, solving problems. Sounds boring, no? It's quite the opposite.

After finishing the game I couldn't help but trying to remember every touching moment and difficult choices I encountered. As Henry, who was not so lucky in his "old" life, we were able to explore a beautiful forest and experience the life as a firewatch. Then this runaway turned out to be quite eventful. The only person you can talk to in the game is a woman called Delilah, she's also Henry's supervisor. As the story progressed, I found myself becoming more and more attached to her, emotionally, even if I could only listen to her voice through a walkie-talkie. The disappearance of the young girls, the dilemma, the "June Fire", all these things added to the determination to not having her harmed. It's just like Scarlett Johansson in the movie [i]Her[/i]. She played as a self-aware AI and only by her voice, yet leaving an unforgettable impression. And in the final part of the game, Henry and Delilah discovered a shocking secret lying in the forest that beneath this peaceful look, someone was trying to take advantage of them and hide something that was meant to be known. Delilah brought him comfort every time when he needed it. 

This is not only a story about watching over the forest, but also a modern life simulator in a more natural way. It's beautiful, insightful and unforgettable. Shame we couldn't see Delilah in person, hopefully she'll finally move in with Henry at the Boulder, as all of us would tell her in her very own Firewatch.

Having finished Firewatch a few days ago, I can't understand why it has such favorable reviews. If you're on the fence, heres my .02 cents.

Good things:
--The game worked on my computer without crashing
--For a fleeting moment you feel that you're a part of some kind of story

Bad:
--The story is on rails. You decide the responses but it has no appreciable influence over the story. I went to play it for a second time and discovered no matter what I said, most of the times Delilah's responses  were EXACTLY the same. You CANNOT change the ending or any other parts of the story. Why even offer multiple choice dialouge if it literally has no impact on the game? 
--The story is dull and left no impression on me. After reading IGN who said this was one of their most memorable gaming experiences ever, I am at a loss for words. The best word I can use to describe the entire game is unremarkable. I highly doubt I'll remember any details of it a year from now. I honestly love the 'slice of life' style of writing but it was too poorly executed. There aren't enough details. There is no free will. This game corrals you.
--Its not an adventure game... obnoxious rock formations, trees and brush create a obvious and boring maze that you must walk through. 
--The enviornment colors are odd and too harsh. A lot of tearing/judder when looking left and right, with or without vsync

My final impression:
Firewatch is an unremarkable game. Its well polished but seriously lacking a story and ability to influence the narrative and world around you. I can't reccomend it.

Very atmospheric game. Realtively short at 5 hrs to completion, but elicited a range of emotions like a great movie. From suspense, to humor, and great sadness this game drew out the feels in a big way.

In the synopisys they give the warning: Firewatch is a video game about adults having adult conversations about adult things. If you plan on playing with a younger gamer, that might be good to know going in.

That's no joke. The themes in the game are adult in nature not because they are about taboo content like sex, drugs, or violence. Indeed there is very little of any that in the game. Rather, it seems targeted at adults (30-45yrs) because it can be difficult to appreciate the gravity of the story without some real life experience like dealing with the serious illness of a loved one, loss, depression, *real* responsibility, and the evasion there of -- which is the most essential theme of the game.

The very beginning of the game is a little bit rushed. It's told via text as a minimally interactive story rather than being visually engaging, and I think it accelerates too quickly. It should have been integrated as a real prolouge to the game that required you to play through it and interact with the other characters involved to generate more emotional entanglements before delivering the gut punch that is the motivation for the game's setting, very much like how Fallout 4 executed it's prologue. Of course, this is where the "life-experience" aspect comes in because if you've actually expereinced anything similar you don't need to play through it to "get it", and it can generate some very surprisingly raw emotions right off the bat if you've suffered in life. ♥♥♥♥ gets real, real fast.

One area that I think was a real miss in this game is achievements. There is a series of books spread out throught the game world that I went through a lot of freaking trouble to collect and return to base, only to not be rewarded via what seemed like an obvious achievement mechanic, because why else is this even in the game? Trolled 9/10.

Lastly, take a lot of pictures. There is no consequence to using (or not) using the camera than an achievement, a credits scene with your photos, and a menu option that allows you to upload your photos. Anyone old enough to play this game will have used one of these at one point 20 years ago and should get the anxiety at not using the limited number of pictures on trivial things vs the practically unlimited pictures people can take these days. Another subtle way in which this game is so eloquently geared towards the 30-45yr old crowd

Voice acting is 7.5/10, which is to say very good, but could use a little polish.

Sound 8/10 Great, atmospheric tracks, but too few of them over all.

Visuals 8/10 Nice cartoony/artistic style generates some really good vistas, but also a lot of repeat use of very similar textures all over the map. A bit more of individualized attention would have gone a long way.

Story 8/10 Short and slightly rushed, but full of a lot of emotionally significant elements that are entirely worth the experience.

All the questions I'd had were answered and things were resolved in a non-infuriating way, which is certainly more than can be said for a lot of games. I found the two flawed main characters very likeable and believable, the dialogue very well-written, and their interactions with each other enjoyable. It's not the best walking simulator I've played, but after playing more arty/abstract ones like 'The Stanley Parable', it makes for quite a nice change to play one that's more grounded in reality, i.e. the characters are real, the world is real, everything is how it appears, and if it isn't then it's because some character in the game world is messing with you, as opposed to the game itself deceiving you at every turn, regularly spinning things on their head, breaking the fourth wall, and leaving you to guess what it could all be a metaphor for, what post-modern artistic statement the game is trying to make. As you will have gathered, I'm avoiding going into too much detail as it's always best with this type of game to know as little as possible going in, so I'll simply say that if you don't like this sort of game then don't bother as it won't convert you, but if you do then I'm sure you'll enjoy this one.

[h1]Firewatch Review[/h1]
[i]A walk in the park...[/i]

Before I played this game I had already heard a lot about it. Mostly good things and a couple of negatives that I will address in this review. Overall I feel that most of the information out there is valid I think a couple things need some clarity brought to light.

Firewatch is a beautiful game to look at. The artist Olly Moss created some amazing mimimalist promotional posters for the game that capture the aesthitics rather well. As you wander the wilderness of Wyoming you will see changes in time of day and weather that really set the mood of the story.

Many people claim they felt the game was too linear and your choices do not carry enough weight. The game is comparable to something in the vein of Gone Home. I personally felt that having a more linear story allows them to present a more meaningful plot that you can take the time to really understand. What choices you do have do impact the dialogue and make you feel more involved with your role in guiding Harry. Ultimately it is not a story about you but about Harry and what you take out of it is up to you, so with that in mind I appreciated the more linear nature.

Some felt the game was too short for the price and it is rather short. I finished it in less than 5 hours and while its not the cheapest game I have purchased on steam it did not cost too much. The way that I see it is that if someone is willing to pay for the price of entry into a movie for 2 hours and this game is about twice as long and the production values are fantastic then the price is adequate. You are not paying a AAA title price for this and I think the asking price is alright for the entertainment value and story telling it provides.

One of the biggest complaints other than price that I came across before playing the game myself was the games conclusion. I don't want to get into any spoilers but what I can say is that many felt the games conclusion was underwhelming in comparison to the rest of the story. I personally can understand why people would feel that way although in my own opinion it was a great ending. The story overall is a rollercoaster ride of emotions and keeps you guessing as to how it will tie it all together. While no loose ends are left it does do so in a way that may not be as exciting as you would expect but is believable and grounded in reality. To me the ending shows that the game is more about personal relationships and something deeper then just delivering a typical Hollywood feel.

[h1]In conclusion:[/h1]
The game was a thoroughly enjoyable ride and with the added audio tours in a recent update I expect I will play the game again. It is a wonderful universe to explore and one that will stick with me for a long time. It emotionally hit me to the core at some points and I would recommend to anyone to sit down and play it. It is accessible to all and the length does not require much of your time. Definitely worth experiencing if you are interested.

At its core, Firewatch is a glorified walking simulator. Sure, it doesn't have great mechanics, or Bethesda-worthy plot, but that's alright; that's not why I play walking simulators. Firewatch is exactly what I wanted from it: a beautiful game, with a beautiful setting, soundtrack, and story. I'd caution you from buying this game if you're looking for a Skyrim; but if you're someone who wants to take a 2 or 3 hour break from life and just watch the beauty of nature, this is your game.

In Firewatch, you play as Henry, a new fire lookout in Shoshone National Forest (in Wyoming). You spend your days doing fire lookout stuff, including looking at just how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ beautiful this game is. It kinda makes me want to take a trip to Yellowstone just to take a look with my own eyes. Anyways, along with this, there's a plot (that I won't spoil). It's mediocre, but there are definitely some sad parts, and some happy parts. But, along the way, you'll look at the beauty of the entire map, and listen to great atmospheric soundtracks, and generally have a good time as you explore the forest and everything it has to offer. In addition, character development is pretty nice: I love the personalities in this game, and you really feel like you're Henry and going through the ups and downs of life. Plus, this game isn't mechanically intensive; it's supposed to be a relaxing game, which is great if you're looking to take a break from fast-paced anything.

I have very little criticisms of this game: unlike some other players, I don't really feel duped or anything. I will say that it's a short game (2-3 hours), doesn't have much mechanical or plot depth (counterbalanced by amazing visuals and audio), and the ending is a bit... wonky. Regardless, if you're looking for an awesome experience, I'd definitely recommend Firewatch to you.

This game follows a set story which the player can influence slightly by making different decisions. It is played from a first person perspective in the Shoshone National Forest in Yellowstone National Park in the United States. You take a job as Firewatch and you take assignments from Delilah who only talks to you through a radio. Basically you are alone. The graphical style is stunning although cartoonish and the sound track is relaxing and quiet. The story develops as you go along and you get to see many parts of the Forest as you navigate the map. There is little action, no guns but a comfortable dose of suspense. 
After finishing the game there is a "free roaming mode" which allows you to explore the entire area without any missions or goals.
The game controls well and, unlike many other games, has a setting that allows you to set a controller AND ignore all other controllers. A setting that would be welcome on many more games.
You play through the game in about 5 to 7 hours and is well worth playing through again.

However, for the price, the game is very entertaining and will provide you with a couple hours of enjoyment before you leave it in your steam library for good.

Firewatch is definitely a game I would recommend for those who enjoy good writing and great narrative pacing. It's funny, endearing and also intriguing as it progresses. Ultimately the pay-off story wise is not as earth-shattering as you may expect, but it's completely appropriate for the game world. It may be one of the best character studies in the medium of games so far.

Gameplay wise:

This game is mainly walking around a lush national park with the occasional obstacle and a small set of tools to aid progression to previously inaccessible areas. Getting around is largely fun, but takes time. Initially the park seems huge on the in-game map but you quickly learn that traversing it is not a headache. Luckily the gorgeous visuals help with this and everywhere you look, you'll feel like taking a photo (which, handily, you can do!). In terms of exploration, there are places to go and see absolutely, but the reward is just extra dialogue - which I always enjoyed but some may feel a bit cheated by this. Frequent radio chats liven up the walks from place to place. Your navigation is with map and compass which takes about 30 mins to get into but becomes second nature.

Performance wise:

No issues on a modest PC build running this game. A few little animation hiccups and body parts clipping which breaks immersion a little, very minor though.

Story:

It's absolute strongest point, although don't expect a dense and thrilling plot - the pleaure here is derived from character moments and getting to learn more about your character and his counterpart Delilah on the other end of the radio. You help to shape a complicated backstory for Henry (the player character) and hear someone react to those choices in a realistic way. Delilah too gradually divulges more and more about herself and I became incredibly invested in their relationship going forward. The superb voice acting helps tremendously with this.

Sound:

The music is inobtrusive and fits well with the game - the perfect companion to your wandering.

Overall:

This game is fantastic fun for a short character piece that doesn't overstay its welcome. Don't come here looking for action or excitement, but if clever and engaging writing holds your attention, then it's a great way to spend 4-5 hours. For me a 9/10
