Firewatch has a lot going for it. It's visually fantastic, just short enough to feel satisfied without dragging on, great voice acting and character development, a great sense of expanse and exploration, and overall fantastic immersion. They carry the theme of "self-imposed isolation" throughout the entire story and it was very well-composed. The explored those emotions and implications thoroughly. 

The major con that everyone keeps addressing (which I will rehash here, spoiler-free), is the ending. It's not a BAD ending, per se. It's simply lackluster. It falls flat. The entire game is spent building tension, making you care about these characters and what's happening to them. They build 4 or 5 smaller stories within the main storyline, and they're all incredibly tense and interesting. You begin to craft possible explanations in your head as to what's going on with these mysterious plotlines, and it's fantastic. At one point my wife put the controller down because she was literally scared of what could happen next. For anyone who has ever tried to write narrative before... that's INCREDIBLY difficult to achieve.  Amazing job. However...

Here's the problem. They never did anything with it. They took those 4 or 5 micro-stories, full of high-stakes, fear, and tension, and they ALL didn't pan out. They just fizzled. It's like spending hours making bread dough, letting it rise, resting it, seasoning it perfectly, and never putting it in the oven. YOU'RE SO CLOSE, FIREWATCH. You did the hard work! Now just close the deal! I'm on the hook, reel me in! They never satisfied any of those high tension moments, they just explained them away. Every conclusion left me feeling like, "oh, that's it? Okay, I guess."

So I'm very torn. It's really quite an experiential game, my wife and I completely enjoyed it for what it was. However I feel there was a lot of lost potential with the ending. They just sort of ended it, not taking advantage of the hard work they put in developing the tension. The payoff is the easy part, I feel. But the didn't give us that.

On other minor con is that I felt the illusion of choice with my dialogue choices, however after finishing the game, I learned that the hundreds of dialogue choices you make have very little to no substantial impact on the actual progress of the story. At most, it slightly changes the tone of your relationship with Delilah, and some minor easter eggs here and there.

Pick it up on Steam sale. It's worth a play through. It's very unique. I'm just still not sure about the ending.

[h1] Take a break from the usual games out there and give firewatch a try. It offers an incredible experience. It's nice to be able to play a game knowing that it doesn't need a lot of my time to finish it. Sometimes you need those. [/h1]

That wasn't a problem for me personally because Firewatch also has a relatively low price point (11.99€ with discount), and I think I got my money's worth. They did well with what they had. 

The developers weren't aiming for photo-realism. Firewatch has a slightly cartoonish aesthetic, but there are some beautifully rendered landscapes. The voice acting is top-notch, and you really do feel like the two main characters forge a relationship of sorts, even though you're mainly talking to each other over the walkie-talky. I have noticed that there is a bit of disagreement on the ending and whether it accomplished its goals. Without going into spoilers, I will say that there is a discrepancy between the first two-thirds of the game, and the last third both in terms of pacing and story. That being said, I didn't have a problem with it. The game is, at the end of the day, more a meditation on isolation, as well as coming to terms with one's mistakes and the past. 

If you approach it with an open mind, you will probably walk away with an appreciation for this title. As far as this reviewer's past experiences with this genre, the only other "walking simulator" that I have played is Dear Esther and Vanishing of Ethan Carter. I enjoyed those games for a variety of reasons which I won't delve into here, but I found Firewatch to be more palatable, probably because the writing is witty, at times humorous, and you don't feel quite so alone when you're playing. 


*RECOMMENDED*

Firewatch is a gorgeous game that utilizes a compelling story and excellent voice-acting to create a real experience for the player. In brief, you play as Henry, whose life so far is given to you in text vignettes that you have some choices in - in the present day, you take a job as a lookout in a Wyoming national park. Your job is to protect wildlife and report forest fires, but soon enough you're plunged into a series of bizarre encounters and happenings that seem to hint at something more sinister at play in the wilderness. With only your supervisor, Delilah, to talk to over walkie-talkie, the game gives you a sense of isolation that feels almost as beautiful (and at times, eerie) as living in the real wilderness. It's a story about finding the mysteries in life and how people deal with loss and difficulties.

PROS:
+Beautiful art style: Taking place over a series of days during the summer, you get to see the park at all times of day - early morning, afternoon, evening, night.
+Music is situational and adds to the ambiance well.
+Voice acting is top-notch, with enough emotion to make you connect with the characters. Dialog feels witty, yet realistic.
+Compelling, thought-provoking story that also tugs at some heart strings
+What I like to call "little touches". If you find a turtle at some point, you have the choice to adopt it and give it a silly name. You also get a camera that you can take pictures with. They don't serve a purpose, but it makes the experience feel more believable. (Plus, you can order prints of them after you finish the game!)

CONS:
- Controls/movement is somewhat buggy. The most insignificant things sometimes act as full-on stops that make you walk around them, which can stall you if you're in a hurry.
- Occasional framerate bugs.
- Ending is polarizing to viewers. Some love it, some hate it.
- Little replayability value, unless you want to explore the environments more thoroughly or just pop in to see the view.
- About 4 hours to complete the story. It's pretty brief and honestly could have had a LITTLE more added to it. However, it's nice as it is.

I just finished my second playthrough of FIrewatch, so I thought that I'd describe each of my experiences with the game and then provide a general overview of pros/cons.

1st Adventure (Februrary, game release)
Total Time: 7 hours

     The first time you play Firewatch you can expect a plot with suspense, paranoia, and the possible jump scare. By no means is this a hardcore thriller though, I spent most of my first playthrough exploring the gorgeous environment in between working toward the main plot. The backbone of this game is the relationship that is developed through dynamic dialogue with Delilah, an off screen character. As you may have read many folks were disappointed with the "lackluster" conclusion of the plot, but I found the openess of it to be liberating as a player. In essence the conclusion leaves you with more questions than answers, and in doing so forces you to think about the characters and their motivations even once you've finished the game (an objective that every game should aspire to, I think).

2nd Adventure (November, 10 months later)
Total Time: 3 hours

     The second playthrough was possibly more enjoyable for me than the first, even though I knew what was going to happen in the main plot. Going into this run I planned on enjoying the scenery and taking more pictures in game, the artwork is really that good (I now use these photos exclusively as my desktop backgrounds)! It was really gratifying to know the layout of the map based on past experience, the game feels more emersive when you intuitively know how to get around.  Once again though, it was the dianamic dialogue and subtle plots that made for superb replay value. What you choose to say as a character directly affects which subplots you have access to, and I discovered many clues and stories this playthrough that I had assumed were simply unanswered/unfinished the first time. 

I look forward to revisiting this game in 4 or 5 months, via a playthrough with developer/voice-actor commentary.

Pros:
-Artwork/scenery
-Dynamic dialogue
-Emotional character plots
-Judicious use of suspense and tension
-Ambiant music that enhances mood
-Open world
-Special features
-Replay value (occasionally)

Cons
-Short highly structured plot
-Limited endgame

[I]Firewatch[/I] is one of those games that I feel went through a tad few too many reworks. The world is fine, artstyle terrific, music pleasing, and I think it's definitely worth a buy, but there's lost potential here.

Delilah and Henry are overall both written terrifically, and I have nothing but praise for the dialogue and performance of their VAs. These two were organic, convincing, and overall just [I]human[/I] in a way that many game characters fail. During the first few days their relationship developed in a sweet way, and I'd be content if the game focused on that the entire time. Nevertheless, the story presented always had a feeling of that there was supposed to be something more, past the point of an intentional red herring and into where it seems that the last arc especially was altered with not much time left in development. 

What made the characters so great was dropped at the end - they no longer remained logically consistent and failed to behave as an emotional person would. The game spent a huge amount of time building up to a seemingly certain climax, only for it to never come. Events occurred, sure, but the reaction to them by both Henry and Delilah fell completely flat. The last scene suffered from the same issues.

Regardless, [I]Firewatch[/I] succeeds in both developing and keeping player attention, and while I'd have preferred a different ending I also wouldn't say that the current spoils the game entirely.

Overall a nice experience, not quite a complete adventure game. 

As a true adventure game, Firewatch is heavily depended on the narrative. However, the narrative (especially towards the end of the story) seems like a game design course narrative assignment than a finished product. On a personal note I would like the narrative to exploit the background that it sets early on (wife, dementia etc.) without taking everything too literally. You can read the justifications behind the creators' choices here: https://quarterly.camposanto.com/the-end-of-firewatch-8a7d334a9586#.muhqnina2 I would like for the creators to treat the story more like a game narrative and less than a lesson of high value. After all, it is a serious adventure game and games of this kind usually have to be firstly fun and then deep.

The narrative is also linear and the world quite closed, thus the player does not have many choices for real exploration of the game and, ultimately, does not really allow the player to make the choices for the character.

The game also has a very short duration for its price, making it look even more like a course assignment (the project team would score a good grade nevetheless). Most of the game's duration is spent on moving around and try to get from one side of the map to another and not with actually interacting with game elements. 

The music soundtrack is short and the music too generic, it sets the scene nicely but definitely not worth the money as a separate DLC. 

The graphics and the art of the game are very good-looking and colourful. A minor issue: too much emphasis is given on the shadows, thus burdening the performance of the game for some older systems. 

Finally, the game is too overpriced for what it offers but - especially at the beginning - it is a nice experience and sets up a nice mystery story, despite the late disappointment (LOST-like style) and the short duration (appr. 3-4 hours for playing it once-twice, 6 hours for people playing it over many days).

I would recommend the game just for the experience and for you imagining how good it could be with a slightly different narrative. 

PS. I read the news that Firewatch is being made into a movie. It would be interesting to see how the production team will address the narrative issues since it is not going to fit into the Cinema or TV medium with such a mediocre narrative.

I originally played Firewatch in 2016, which now feels like an age ago. With little else to do, I chose to replay the game that I had once completed in 2.7 hours.

In my second playthrough, I had a vague understanding of the story from my first playthrough, yet somehow I managed to get more immersed in the story this time than before. The story, paired with such gorgeous graphics and incredible atmosphere creates a world where you truly feel a part of Henry's story, and the world he's living in. The game is relatively short, and can range from about 2 hours if you really speedrun it, to 5 hours if you take a bit more time with it, though if you were to explore outside of the tasks presented to you, you may well take longer.

(perhaps a few minor spoilers ahead)

The story is a well crafted experience, which is linear in the sense of what you have to achieve, but is presented in a way that is makes it so it doesn't feel like you're being pushed down a path, as every next event feels logical, in order and further piques your interest and curiosity. The game may seem as a walking simulator from a distance, but for the most part there are very few occasions where I felt it to be tedious or annoying; exploring the forest is more of a pleasure than a chore. With cleverly placed, beautiful views at points in each day, it makes using the disposable camera satisfying, especially when you view all of your photos from your journey at the end of the game. Dialogue feels varied with mostly 2-3 options, each opting for a slightly different response to and from Delilah. The dialogue may not directly effect story outcomes, but it is very effective in creating a believable and almost entirely seamless relationship between Henry and Delilah.

On the topic of these two, I have seen many reviews criticise the game's ending, claiming it was disappointing. I too felt like this when I first played it, but having revisited it, I wouldn't change a thing. The game shows the harsh reality of Henry's life, in which he simply can't leave his past for the sake of the charm of a woman he's only met over a radio. The game allows you to craft Henry into someone who is trying to move on, or live stuck in his past, with fears of Alzheimer's, where he doubts his own thoughts and thinks "it's happening to him too". Subtle things such him waking up with his wedding ring off, with the option to put it back on again, are very interesting ways of portraying this. With these different approaches, it changes the ending slightly, not in terms of content of the game, but in how we perceive it. [spoiler] Delilah's decision to leave can be more harsh based on what dialogue you've chosen thus far, and begging her to stay vs telling her to go means, despite really being the same ending either way, based on how you've created Henry's personality, the ending hits differently. [/spoiler]

Overall, Firewatch is an incredible game, and a journey I urge anyone to experience. If you have even an ounce of curiosity, this game will catch your attention immediately - since ultimately it is a playable book experience, albeit a short story at that.

Not only that, the story makes you feel curious to find out the truth about the mysteries that lie ahead of you. This story makes you want to keep playing until the end of the game in order to fuel your curiousity that this game bestowed upon you. Basically this story line is like a drug (sorry for all those who are actual suffering from drugs), you are addicted to it and would keep on wanting it, till there is no more.

Basically at this point, I have like listed a lot of positive things about this game, making this game seem to be the perfect game in this year. But there is one aspect to this game that impacted greatly what this game can achieve. Which is Gameplay, something that wasn't really present in this game....

Cons: 
Lack of Gameplay: 
This game did not contain alot of options to interact the surroundings such as the objects around you like even the simplest of objects such as your mug or even your typewriter. Even thought, this seems a bit dumb to be so particular about something so miniscule. But this is basically what is needed in this kinds of story mode type of games. In addition, the option of Hiking out on your own away from the story mode is usually never taken, since the story mode is what keeps the player going. (most likely). This is why nobody picked that choice as the gameplay was too low for a lot of people to enjoy since it would bore them (atleast this is the case for me). If this game had gameplay, it would have been as good as Life is Strange.In an exploration game like this, it has to have action and a lot of gameplay value. (imagine an Indiana Jones game with a lot of rock climbing but no action like dodging traps.)

Low Replayability (not really a con):
It is expected that story Based games have low replayability because there would be no suspense the second time you play the game since you already knwo the story.

[u] Final thoughts on the game [/u]
Overall, I would recommend buying this game at a lower price, to make up for the lack of gameplay to it. BUT, the good storyline and Graphics covers for it. If you are a person who gets bored easily when there is no action or events. Then this game might bore you. But for those that do not get bored when no action, then this game shouldn't be boring to you. This review is a bit subjective (basically personal opinion), so do not take this review as a general review for everyone since everyone has their own opinions.

I've been playing video games for as long as I can remember and it seems like the virtual experience we are usually offered is a violence ladden death tour.   I wanted to try a game that wasn't about violence or completing commando missions so I tried Firewatch.   While this game puts you on a linear story and gains the descriptor a "walking simulator", it does allow you to roam a stretch of forest with just enough sense of danger that adds a sense of urgency.  There are no missions requiring you to bludgeon zombies to death or "shoot and scoot" thorugh an ambush.  If that's what you are looking for you will be dissapointed as there are no weapons in this game.   An axe for completing mission goals is about all you get in that regard.      The story was short, casual but interesting with an interesting but sad twist.    I won't talk about the story because that is what this game is all about.  Telling a story.   The game is the story and plays like an animated/narrated book.    You don't have any real choices as the game progression is based on the next linear scripted event.  However, I covered that already.     The graphics and soundscape are cartoonish but detailed enought to draw you into believing you are hiking a mountain trail. The game duration was short and you can complete in a few hours if you don't take time exploring the limited access terrain.   The map feels like an open world but it isn't.  You have trails that lead to open areas but you are restricted to where you can go.   Which wasn't a problem as the terrain is the backdrop for the storyline.   I think the storyline duration was just about right as I was getting a little bored of the tedious back and forth hiking in some parts of the game.   If the story went any longer I would have got bored with it and gave up.    You play the plot from a first person perspective and it works.  It was entertaining and I this was just what I was looking for.   A high quality, bug free, non-violent escape from reality playing out the plot of a mild unexpected mystery novel.   Very enjoyable for those looking for a casual non-violent escape.

Quick as this is on sale at a price which I believe is commensurate with its value.  The pros are that for those of us watching with wonder the evolution of video games, this is definitely a step towards interactive novels.  In this case you are playing a first person (named Henry) who is unraveling a mystery while on a respite from the world in the mountains of Wyoming.  His backstory is nicely told in the first few minutes.  Other pros are the gameplay ease and little Easter eggs such as the camera (which you should use and use the entire roll, no spoilers but just do that) and the implied recommended reading list based on all the paperback novels (alot of Richard Sturgeon books) strewn around the cabins and supply drops.  Henry's only human interaction is with Deliah, his supervisor whom he communicates with through a radio.  Ostensibly, he's in a remote firewatch looking for, well, what else fires but also keeping tabs on park visitors and wildlife but soon they find they are being watched and they uncover things that don't make sense until the area is fully explored.  The negatives about this game is that it ends all too shortly and there's a bit of "is that all there is?" but it does fully emcompass a story line - however, you can play the game again (and get slightly different dialogue based on your responses to Deliah) with the game-maker's dialogue and someday I believe I will do that.  At any rate, if you like to see the evolving possibilities of this video game medium and it's potential to strive towards great works (and yeah, I'll say it - ART), this is one to check out.

Firewatch is one of those games that I wish I could forget....so I could play it again as a newcomer! This game's story is fantastic! You play as Henry, a man trying to escape it all as he goes to his new summer job, a job in Fire watching. While at the park, you meet Delilah, a seasoned fire watcher there to show you the ropes (well, tell you the ropes) and to keep you from being lonely. 

I won't reveal any spoilers, but as the game goes on, the more mysterious it gets. Like I said before, the story's extremely good and you'll want to play through all of it in one sitting. Another great aspect about this game is the graphics. I've heard the artstyle being compared to TeamFortress 2, and I do agree that it's pretty similar. The graphics are beautiful and the artstyle really adds to the game's charm. There are some truly beautiful views.

The game is a walking sim so, you'll be walking everywhere, which is pretty fun. You have a map and compass, just in case you get lost. Also, along the way, you'll get some more gadgets to help you in your endeavours. The map is pretty large so, you can explore and find some new stuff whenever you want. It's a great game to relieve stress if you don't have a place outside where you can go! 

Another thing I really liked was the bond that you form with Delilah. I've never really experienced anything like it in any other game. Sure, there are some that are close, but this game blows it out of the water. In the end, Firewatch is a great game! Some people are complaining about the price because the game only takes about 3-5 hours to complete, but think of it like this, you can always come back and replay this game. I know I will! I did get the game on sale, but I definitely would've paid full price for this game. It's kind of like playing through a 4 hour movie.  I definitely recommend giving Firewatch a try.

The ambiance was strong and captivating in the beginning and got just more intense as the story progressed. The story deals with dark and serious issues and handles them with sadness, fear and humour. Especially the humour. Being a relatively short game, it does a great work building the characters, so that they feel real, are sensible and relatable.

The game world gives an impression that it's completely open-world but has confined paths and areas that'll eventually lead the player to the next marker. Interaction with the surroundings (such as climbing rocks) makes the playing more engaging and interesting while traveling from one place to another. The graphics, lightings, colours and sounds are very lovely and it's easy to just wander around in the woods and look around. The game has a limited use of music and I found it quite effective to the emotional impact.

I saw the trailers for this game before it came out, and I thought it looked interesting.  Funny dialogue and the animation style made me think that it was a light hearted tale of someone watching over fires.  I didn't really know what to expect, but I was still wrong.

It's an great tale of what can happen when someone is alone with their own psyche for 3 months.  I loved the little bits and pieces that personalized the game to me, although I did find that not all the choices are things that I would have said if it had been me.  Some of the decisions felt a little bit forced, and I really don't see the story being all that different depending on the choices I picked.  They all seemed very minor.

One thing I didn't like about this game, is how it skips vast periods of time.  It jumps weeks at a time, and you're just expected to pick up from where the story wants you to, as well as ending days when you're done with your daily objectives, not even giving you a chance to get back to your post.  I felt rushed to get the story done, and not enough time to fully explore the vast beautiful world that was created for us.

I had some technical issues with this game.  I played on an Xbox One Gamepad, and there are options in the Settings for this, however when I chose gamepad, it disabled my D-pad, which is essential to playing the game.  I would either have to play in keyboard mode and guess what the controls are, or play with the dual PS4 controller settings, which is what I ended up doing.  I also lost the ability to do anything other than look around when the game bugged out on me during my first attempt at a play through.  It was fine after I restarted the game, however.

Okay, so I just finished Firewatch, and I found myself torn. Here is why:

Pros:
- The story is immediately immersive. You get drawn in very quickly. The writer(s) did a great job of making you care about the protagonist. The supporting character is interesting, as well.
- The graphics work well. This title has a certain style to it that lends itself to the overall feel of environment. It's simplistic while simultaneously being quite beautiful.
- The voice acting and interactive narrative is top notch! There is nothing more to be said here, they did a great job.
- The sound effects, audio ambiance, and musical scores enhance the experience and never get in the way. Well done.
- The controls are simple and basically standard for a first-person title. Easy to learn and remember.

Cons:
- Very short. It took me all of 5.3 hours to complete this title, from start to finish. That time includes moments where I paused to get food, listen to my girlfriend tell me about her work day, and perform assorted other real-world tasks. In the end, I probably spent about 4 to 4.5 hours actually interacting with this title.
- Very linear. While you are technically free to explore the environment as you see fit, there is really no point or reason to deviate from the path of the story.
- Decisions seem to have little to no effect on the long-term experience or final outcome of the story. More on this point, the only real decisions you make are what dialogue option you'd like the protagonist to respond with to the supporting character(s). All physical "decisions" (actions) only support the linear aspect of this title. For example, tieing off a rope so you can decent a steep incline isn't really a "decision" so much as it is an interactive plot device intended to give the user the feeling they are in control, but this device really only serves as to advance the linear story or change up the buttons you are pressing.
- Tools. There are a few "tools" you acquire as you advance this story.
-- Camera: There is no point to this. ***SPOILER ALERT*** Take whatever pictures you like, they have no impact on the final outcome. You get to see your photos during the end credits. That. Is. It. The camera is pointless.
-- Flashlight: At no point in the story is this tool ever necessary. Even when you are in the cave, the environment is never so dark as to necessitate the use of the flashlight.
-- Axe: You may be thinking "Oooo! Finally, I have a weapon!" Nope. The axe is a tool. You absolutely "need" to use this tool a total of 2 times. I used it 4 times. You can probably squeeze out another 1 or 2 uses, if you try REALLY hard.
-- Compass: While this tool is useful for getting your bearings, there is no time-based threat in this title, so you will eventually get where you need to be with or without the compass. It saves you time. That is it.
-- Map: The same as the compass, only it saves a little MORE time.
-- Radio: If you NEVER report anything you find... the story will still advance.
-- Miscellaneous Items: Throughout the course of your trek, you will discover a number of items that you can keep. With the exceptions being the axe, rope, and pitons, absolutely none of the other miscellaneous items (hat, bottle of whiskey, assorted notes, cassettes, etc.) have any use or impact on the story.
- There are no risk elements in this title. Nada. None. Zero. Zilch. Zip. The title is impossible to fail.
- Antagonists: ***SPOILER ALERT*** There are no actual antagonists. You only ever see a total of FOUR other characters: The silhouettes of 2 teenage girls, the silhouette of one man, and a corpse. You never really see yourself, the main supporting character, or the protagonist's wife! And the only character you see that isn't a silhouette is a freaking CORPSE!
- Dropped the ball: At about the halfway point in this title, it starts to get intense. The designers could have done a LOT with the story at the point where ***SPOILER ALERT*** break through the chainlink fence and discover all the surveillance equipment. Is the government investigating aliens? Is there some crazy cover-up conspiracy going on? Unearthed ancient ruins? NO! Instead, it was an elaborate diversion from something much more mundane and lame. Dropped. The. Ball.

* * * * * * * * * * ZERO REPLAY VALUE * * * * * * * * * *

TL;DR: This is not a "game". At no point in my above examples did I refer to this title as a "game". This is an interactive story with only one outcome. There is no combat, whatsoever. There are no survival elements. There is no platforming. There are no quicktime events. There are no timed action scenarios. For that matter, there are NO action scenarios. There is are no risk elements. There is absolutely ZERO chance of dying, failing, or losing. If you NEVER respond to your timed radio dialogue options, the story will still progress.

If you're looking for a good, immersive, interactive story... This is a great title. Get it on sale. I paid $12 at 40% off, and I think I paid too much. $10 or less seems more fair, and only IF you want an interactive story.

If you are looking for a GAME with immersive story... SKIP THIS TITLE. This is NOT a "GAME". For you, this title is worth maybe $5.

In the end, I cannot recommend this title. And I definitely don't know how a 4 hour interactive story is worth more than $10. The story was engaging, but that's all this was; an interactive story.

PROs
-Graphics are well suited to the game
-Gameplay is fairly intuitive
-No bugs that I noticed, fairly polished
-Top notch voice acting
-Good story

CONs
-Ridiclously short game.  It's over in 5-10 hours.
-ZERO replayability
-Not at all worth the price, this is a $5 game.  I got 40% off and I stll feel a little ripped-off.
-ZERO depth.  There's nothing to really discover, the ropes and axe you discover are only used on rails, 99% of items do nothing, etc.

Summary?  You're basically playing through someone's novella.  And I don't mean like a choose-your-own-adventure novella... just a straight story.  A short one.  Don't buy this until its 80% off the normal price.

Ok, this is my first review of a game on Steam.
I knew as soon as the credits rolled I would be writing this.
I've never bothered before. I even have over 2500 hours clocked on other games yet I've never bothered.
(What is a measly 9 hours compared to that? Well I aim to explain.)

I'm lazy by nature but when something moves me, sometimes, just sometimes, I want to shout from the rooftops about how great it is.
- This is one such time.

>>A little forward reading, just skip to the ----s for the stuff directly related to the game<<
((There are ZERO spoilers in this review))

I inadvertantly came across the game on steam sale. I watched the trailer and thought, yeah, this looks like something I'd like to play. I was a little reserved at first however considering many of my recent purchaces...

I then, as I usually do, fired a message to a friend who already owned the game looking for some real number insights.
Unfortunately he was busy at the time but would later reply just as I alt-tabbed from the game after the credit sequence had rolled.

I resisted the temptation of jumping onto youtube or google for more information, knowing that the game was definately of the story driven type and I didn't want any spoilers.

I grew up on Lucas Arts point and clicks, Broken sword, all the old favourates.
Back when games were games, a good story was a good story and small furry creatures from Alpha Centauri were real small furry creatures from Alpha Centauri.
I haven't delved very deeply into the world of contempary indie games, I've seen a few. 
Some I liked, some I loathed. I just hoped my punt would pay off.
I was not dissapointed.

Well, that's enough about me.
Let's get to the meat of it.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

>VISUALS

The game graphically looks nice. A sort of mixture of cell shaded overtones in a mostly realistic backdrop.
Maybe subtlety stylised would be the best way to describe it?
It is cleverly done, reminiscent of some older games but with the polish that's expected now-a-days.
Some of the scenes and vistas are breathtakingly detailed while other animation and flourishes are almost akin to the hand drawn feel of epics like Flashback or Another World.
Think the beauty of The Forest or Stranded Deep (An insight into the engine used possibly?) fused with animation from adventure game royalty.

The theme and feel remains consistent throughout.


Now, I have a lower to mid range PC. (That's probably a generous estimate)
AMD FX @4Ghz, 16 Gig RAM, a 770 and a 256 Gig SSD.

I ramped everything up to full right off the bat, I knew the game would probably involve long walks through nice looking scenery so I wanted to enjoy it.
(If you don't already turn off motion blur in games religiously then shame on you, but for this game I really do recommend it. The effect seems to be on the aggressive side. Not the worst I've seen by far but it's just as strange (but not quite as vomit inducing) as most.)

I can say, on full settings with my build the game ran *almost* flawlessly.
There were definite frame drops at times, probably as new areas were loaded in but they really were minor and didn't really detract from the experience at all.
(I assume that people who worry about this sort of stuff will have bought themselves a better system anyway.)
So on that front the game runs nicely. I also see it scaling well although I haven't actually tested that.

>AUDIO

The audio fits the theme well, I definitely recommend playing with a decent pair of headphones.
The game plays on the senses. Shutting out any external noise takes you right into the story.

There is a tremendous amount of dialog and I feel it's best not to have subtitles turned on unless you have to for whatever reason. You don't want to spend your time reading what's said as it's being said.

I didn't notice any significant 'sound track' during play, just a little bit of suspense stuff here and there.
If anything, any tracks playing fit so well or were in the background so much I rarely realised they were there.
That's how I like it.

As I mentioned before though, the dialogue is really what makes this game.
The writing and voice acting is spot on.
Funny, dark, sarcastic and even emotional. All pulled off exceptionally well.
(Even as a non-North American the humour and language is believable and fitting. This often doesn't translate well, even to UK English. I don't think I can report even a single 'Cringey American' moment. (Sorry but it's true for so many things).)



>GAMEPLAY MECHANICS

Controlling the character and general interaction with the world is pretty intuitive.
I could bring up one or two things like slightly strange button choices but really, you can change anything around yourself so it's a moot point.
There aren't really many controls to worry about anyway.

I will say that picking up and dropping items seems a little on the reckless side but for the mainstay anything crucial to the game is easily manipulated and fairly straight forward.

There was no instance on both play throughs where I found myself confused with how I should do something or felt that anything was overly complex or redundant.

There are also no random game mechanic puzzles thown in to clutter the story. Which is nice.



>THE STORY

This is what you buy a game like this for.
The story in it's self isn't a great epic of adventure, rather it focuses on the protagonist and his absent companion.

Firewatch features excellent adult writing and phenomenal voice acting. It's a story of people experiencing life events beyond their control, and how they deal (or don't deal) with them. Woven around those themes is a compelling mystery story with many twists and reveals. The art style and music are fantastic, complementing the story and furthering a mood.

Some will complain that the game is fairly short and doesn't have a lot of replay potential. Indeed I took my time and finished in about five hours. Compared to $10 for a movie ticket I think it's well worth it, only because the quality of writing and acting here make that a meaningful comparison. The compromise you make for the excellent writing is that the game funnels you into a single storyline despite what appear to be choices along the way. The funneling is subtle and done in a number of ways, and while I knew it was happening it didn't bother me because the writing and presentation work so well. As much as anything this is an interactive movie, or a first-person narrative experience.

If the aim of art is to evoke emotion, Firewatch succeeds brilliantly. Like Red Dead Redemption or The Last of Us, it conveys something more complex than the usual game and likely to stay with me for a long time.

Playing Firewatch, I found the game's highlight to be its characters. I think people were let down because of the ending because they came into it with their own preconceptions about the story. But it's not about the characters' story, it's about the story's characters. You really get to experience the setting through Henry's eyes, understand his thoughts, and see his back-and-forth with Delilah. Honestly, in the end, I didn't care about the story. I cared about the characters. You get relatable, believable characters, with superb voice-acting and very well-written dialogue. The game expertly flows between light-hearted joking and playful teasing, into paranoid anxiety and somber melancholy. I cannot speak highly enough of the writers, their dialogue and characters kept me and the girlfriend enthralled the whole way through. (She actually sat through the whole thing with me, from beginning to end! I don't know how many games can boast that kind of third-person retention!)

One of the other reviews I read put it pretty succinctly, the story has a bittersweet ending. I think other players went through it all, expecting some big payoff at the end, "solve the mystery, get the girl, save the day." But real life isn't always like that. Remember when I said I'd get to the part about this being a "game"? I get that games should be an escape from real life, but this is sort of what makes Firewatch special; it's [u]not[/u] a game that's meant to be [u]played[/u], it's a [b][i]story[/i][/b] that's meant to be [b][i]experienced[/i][/b].

Exploring the Wyoming wilderness, getting attached to the characters, and getting immersed into their world. That's what Firewatch is about, and I think it achieved its goal admirably.

Firewatch is a fantastic, lovingly designed game with a beautiful art style and an incredibly nuanced, down-to-earth story. 
It is a walking simulator, but with an impressive open-ended design that allows you to approach the game in many different ways, and to even skip some objectives throughout the game. 
The attention to detail in this game is incredible. The music is atmospheric and a perfect fit for the game and is generated somewhat procedurally to fit your adventure. The voice acting is absolutely top-notch. The world is lovingly crafted and wildly beautiful. This is the sort of virtual experience that I could see myself wandering aimlessly around after a stressful day at work, taking in the feel of the place.

The story is very well told. Some people may not enjoy it all the way through but I believe that it actually has something deeply thoughtful to say about dealing with grief, human relationships, and time, which might have been impossible if they had tried to please everyone when writing.
The game is also not actually that short. People were throwing around estimates of 3 hours. It took me at least 4.5 on my first playthrough, and I felt that if I had gone slower I could have had a better experience. Walk, don't run. Take in this beautiful game slowly, at your own pace. Explore and enjoy the reflective, lonely, and occasionally intense feel of this wonderful game.

In summary:
9/10. Well worth full price, and a steal at 40% off. Like Gone Home, this is an indie game with something thoughtful to say, and you won't want to miss it.

Being a hiker myself, I was attracted to the idea of a game with hiking as the focus. For what it is, Firewatch does a good job capturing the isolation of the backcountry experience. With that said, I feel like there was a lot of squandered potential here. I understand that this wasn’t intended to be a hiking simulator and I am fully aware of the fact that I only paid $12 for the game. For what it is, it’s a nice short story without a lot of nuance that does an excellent job utilizing ambient sound and music to ratchet tension throughout the game. However, I would have absolutely loved it had it incorporated a few changes

I loved the fact that the story stayed grounded even though it felt at times that it was going in a completely different direction. It’s great because by the end, you kind of feel like a schmuck for overindulging in your own overactive imagination. With that said, I don't feel this story needed the exposition it gives right at the outset. In fact, I believe it detracts from the tension as it gives you enough information into your character’s past to keep you grounded to reality. I also would have liked to have seen the story expanded to incorporate player selection. Forcing everyone into the role of a 40-something man, which I believe was the sole purpose for the expository narrative at the beginning, definitely limits player emersion. It would have been nice to see how the interactions between everyone in the game changed depending on race, sex and age of the player character. I realize that is a lot to incorporate into a game like this, but perhaps if Campo Santo intends to release a sequel, this element could be incorporated.

I absolutely would have loved this game if it were more a hiking simulator. While nothing compares to the real-life tension you experience going out on a lengthy backpacking excursion, it would have been interesting to play a game that challenges you with the reality of how improper planning can lead to your unintentional death.  I recommend this game for the story, but I don’t think a lot of younger players will identify with it. It’s definitely refreshing to play a game that defies convention, but this subject matter definitely had me yearning for more depth.

2) Having to pick a choice and thinking "Umm... None of the above????"

3) Short gameplay. I will add to this that the fact that you can't go back and do more in certain situations or investigate further the next day when a day abruptly ends sucks.

4) The top reason I will say I can't recommend this game: the ending- there are just so many ways it could have ended - SO many - and I think I would have preferred almost any of them over the way it ended. It just fell totally flat. I was totally bummed that I spent the money I spent to play the game for an ending like this.

If they did something to change the end- make a mod, an add-on, an alternate ending - anything- something -that did more to wrap up/ finish the story, I would totally replay it and maybe even change my rating. 

Bottom Line:

----It is kind of like a story you wrote one time in school. You were all gung-ho at the beginning, really excited about it, it was really well rounded and you were putting in so much effort... then you realized it was taking too long to write, ran out of steam and gave it a quick end just to get it turned it in on time. -----

This is a bit of a weird recommendation.  I went in expecting this to be a pretty short, story driven game and that's what I got.  It lasted about 3 hours, and even though I payed around $15 bucks I feel like I got my moneys worth.  First off, the game is beautiful -- it's certainly not the best looking game on PC, but part of the enjoyment of the game is being in a beatiful environment.

The voice acting and dialogue are top notch as well, both of the main characters have a ton of personality, and as many other people have said, the dialogue seems very realistic.

Now for the gripes -- I though the story was overall very good, but it shifted in focus in the second half of the game towards something I wasn't crazy about.  The ending wasn't very good either.  Also, the gameplay isn't amazing, you aren't living the life of a fireguard, you're mostly just trekking from point A to point B.  It's also a pretty short game, and don't expect to want to play it again, since I don't think there are any branching paths in the story.

That being said, I was ok with it being short, as it didn't overstay it's welcome.  As well, despite the shift in the story and the disappointing ending, I still really enjoyed parts of the story and the banter between the two characters (once again, excellent writing and voice acting) and because of that I would still recommend this game.

"Walking Simulator" does come off as a derogatory term, and though Firewatch fits squarely into this genre, it's a great example of why such labels do not do games like this justice. 

Firewatch delivers narrative in a way other media could not. The time spent walking through the wilderness, trying to figure out where to go, knowing where to go and simply having to travel there, and noticing things underfoot you must have passed a dozen times without realizing is a huge component of this story that you could not get from a movie or a book or a poem. The time meditative time spent moving through the environment is part of the narrative. 

Spectacular aesthetic, well written and well delivered dialogue, and a plot that gorgeously compliments the aesthetic and gameplay, Firewatch is something anyone interested in video game storytelling should try.

Hyped higher than a towering inferno, Firewatch is a modern take on the old school adventure game ethic as seen through FPS eyes.  There's no fighting.  You can't succumb to the elements.  So thusly, you interact your way the Wyoming frontier with only your boss Delilah to lift the fog of solitude.  Playing as troubled transplant Henry, you've uprooted yourself from Colorado and the chains of a sick wife to start anew.  Henry has also of the checkboxes marked in terms of a classic brooding protagonist; he's a misunderstood alcoholic...a writer trapped in the past...capable of twitchy moodswings...the works.  Even though he's not the guy you'd typically always root for, the expertly handled script and fantastic voiceover keeps you in his corner.  Delilah is equally well-played and thanks to the writing/delivery of the lines the emotional impact hits like a sack of bricks to the temples.  

The big question here is Firewatch actually worth playing?  That answer would be yes, as long as you keep your expectations grounded in reality like the tale the game invites you into.  Firewatch is broken up into a series of days in which you will explore the surreal Wyoming woods via the game's daunting world map.  Truthfully, once you've done a decent chunk of the exploring the location isn't quite as sprawling as you would imagine.  Pressing farther, you'll discover numerous places blocked off by jagged rocks, craggy cliffs, lush treelines and numerous other boundaries set-up to keep you fenced in.  Still, what's there is brought to life thanks to dazzling graphics with several key landmarks, awesome use of light and shadow (day and night are represented here) and the bewitching mystique of nature.  Even though the story offers bits of desperation, this is truly a relaxing work to play.  It's a touch cartoony but this works to Firewatch's advantage in the end.  This game has its own personality for sure.  Sadly, you will encounter very few animals during your journey which does dial down the immersion a bit, but hell adopting a turtle was cool!    

Even more impressive than the graphics is the sound.  You can tell the designers went to great lengths to capture the vibe and they've succeeded here.  As stated the two leads are professionally acted; rivaling movie quality throughout.  Hell, the acting is probably better than a lot of the mainstream drivel that's pushed into theaters these days.  To my knowledge field recordings were used to represent the flowing rivers, breeze blown leaves, realistic footsteps that change with surfaces, booming thunderstorms and helicopters whizzing overhead.  The entire package is just above n' beyond the call of duty for an adventure game.  

Some folks are complaining about the gameplay, though it's hard to understand why if you know that this is primarily in an old school adventure game with a new dressing ontop.  You can run, walk, cross ravines using downed trees, rappel down rock walls, equip tools like a flashlight and axe, jump certain gaps, etc., with all actions controlling reasonably well.  Navigation of your surroundings is done by using a map and compass with realistic utilization of both.  The more you explore, the more areas you will mark on the map and you'll triangulate the same way you would with a roadmap.  There are no arrows or prompts pointing you in the direction you need to go and it actually makes getting your bearings a fun experience.  It's not quite as true to life as Miasmata or Near Death but it's realistically implemented.  Firewatch isn't full to busting with interactivity though and it's labeling as a walking simulator isn't off the mark.  There is enough that you can do to keep it interesting thanks to the walkie-talkie.  Using the walkie you communicate with Delilah frequently and since you're given the option of numerous responses it's impossible to hear the dialogue all in one playthrough.  I enjoyed Firewatch enough that I'm giving it a second one.  I'm not sure at this point that the outcome itself is affected, yet it's cool to develop the relationship with your new friend in different ways and see how these options play out.  

At its core, the relationship between Henry and Delilah usurps nearly every other gameplay element.  It's a bit of a missed opportunity thus far on a second playthrough because events really aren't altered at all by selecting varying options.  You will hear bits of information that you missed the first time around, which does give the game a dash of replay value if not a serious reason to go through it again unless you want to take the ride with characters.  That's where Firewatch is strongest because I certainly WANTED to take the ride again.  Between the screenplay and the acting you really do feel for these two and hope they form an unbreakable bond.  

Of course the game's ending has been the subject of much criticism, perhaps unfoundedly.  Personally, I found it fitting if not earth-shattering.  In fact Firewatch's main folly is the fact that the plot itself and the arc that it takes just simply isn't very exciting.  Loose-ends will remain untied, red herring will nip at your knees and you'll be rather shocked that a few of the revelations will incite a basic, "So, that WAS it," sort of reaction.  It's also an odd development decision to exclude certain days from the story, which often jumps several weeks at a time.  An expansion that includes some of the missing days would be a fantastic idea...even better than a sequel.  This choice in pacing gives the game a feel that you're on rails to the conclusion and things pretty much keep going hyperspeed even when you don't want them to.  The score loses a few points because of it but such a stellar script ensures that the entire game isn't flattened by a shaky plot.  Though $20 is a steep price to pay, adventure gamers should definitely check out Firewatch.  Just be sure not to overcook your expectations...  

Pros:

-Rich graphics and fantastic sound design.   
-Superb script and voice-acting.
-Characters that you really care about.  
-For the most part, vintage and engaging adventure game play (basically an upgrade of point and click).
-At its best the game evokes a feeling of mystery, enchantment and subtle dread all at once.  
-Map/compass navigation feels fitting and eliminates pesky arrows/prompts simply showing you the way to your next destination.

Cons:

-As short as everyone says it is.  
-Shaky plot with too many half-baked subplots.  
-Too many days skipped in the story without explanation.  
-Lack of wildlife in the woods.  
-Even on a high-end Alienware PC the game sometimes hiccups and lags (not often, but it can get you briefly lost).  

Overall:  7.5/10

Firewatch is a great game, but more importantly, has one of the most profound narrative experiences I've had from a game.

Graphically, there's a lot to love, The art style is fantastic. It gives the world such a beautiful, rich and colorful feel. And my goodness, is the world incredible to look at. The lighting effects, the varied scenery in form of trees, grass, water, rock, all gel together to form a beautifully scenic visual experience as a medium to experience the rich narrative of the game. Nothing to complain about the visuals of this game, simply splendid.

As for the gameplay aspects, there really wasn't much in the way of anything interesting. Exploring is enjoyable because of the rich visuals and dialogue, but gameplay is rather uninspired. It mainly takes the form of walking around and button presses to one-dimensionally interact with the environment (such as tap a button to chop a tree, open a supply crate, grab an item, open a door, etc). Simple traversal through areas is really the main form of gameplay. The best thing I can say about the gameplay is how much it evokes the sense of actually experiencing a nature hike, given the beautiful environments and just the organicness of using a compass and map to navigate. That just makes it feel so much more real It's a really immersive exploration experience.

I absolutely loved the character building of Henry and Delilah. One of the most amazing and meaningful developments of characters relationship I've ever seen in a game. The dialogue was fantastic. Fun, witty, extremely well voiced acted (probably the "most real" I've heard in any game I've played), and most importantly incredibly natural and immersive. But even more so than the dialogue, both of these characters simply bled depth and their relationship was given one of the most complex and well thought out stories I've ever experienced. 

It's amazing how well Henry and Delilah complement each other in the story. Both characters are clearly flawed, but more specifically, are shown to be running away from their problems. They are both in the same boat. Henry was unable to handle the situation with his wife (who has dementia) and took a firewatch job to escape the pressure. Likewise, Delilah had left her behind relationship with her boyfriend after his brother died, failing to be there for him and being afraid of facing him. This puts Henry and Delilah in a position to really understand and connect with each other, which can be seen happening as they get very close with each other. The truth is, they've found comfort and solace in each other as they share their past experiences and find out just how similarly they deal with their problems: running away, alcoholism, isolation, and avoidance. Their relationship blossoms because of this, and this makes the dynamic between the characters truly meaningful.

What is interesting as well, is the development of each character differs in how they deal with their problems throughout the story. Delilah is shown to be undoubtedly still running away. She speaks only through a radio with Henry, seemingly reluctant to meet him. She lies about having involvement in the incident with the missing girls in the police report, hoping to avoid the police. Most importantly, she decides not to wait for Henry when evacuating, despite his wishes to see her. She's been avoiding and running away from confrontation her whole life, and it really shows in the progress of the game. Now take Henry, who develops differently. Henry makes an effort to stop running away. He takes the initiative to investigate the strange events occurring around him. He tries to fix his problems. He even seems to stop drinking when he's on the job. The fact that he is the one doing the work really goes to show that unlike Delilah, he's really trying to change himself. Although these two characters come from the same position and grow close because of the connection they share, the difference in how they deal with their problems in the course of Firewatch really shows just how much they contrast each other as well.

In the end, the evacuation really reinforces the idea that both characters are still running away. But this time they are running away together instead of alone, as they've grown to understand and connect with each other. However the difference in how they are conveyed is that Henry is shown to still be trying to tie loose ends, by making an effort to meet with Delilah when they evacuate. It's easy to see that Henry is trying to stop running away. Delilah in contrast however, is unwilling to wait for Henry, and simply wants escape from her responsibilities, instead of looking to face them.

As can be seen, the relationship between Henry and Deliliah is really the centrepiece of the game. It's so much more complex and intricate than what most people who play the game give it credit for. 

I've heard a lot of people call the ending disappointing, because "nothing really happened or was resolved". But I think people give it flak for the ending because they judged the game as a mystery-suspense story. It's not one. It's a drama. The mystery arc was simply a plot device for the development of Henry and Deliliah's story arc. The mystery car was not meant to be resolved because that's not what the game was focused on. People were expecting it to be, and felt empty when it wasn't, which is likely a prime reason for why there was an air of disappointment surrounding the ending. But it's not about the mystery story. It's all about Henry and Delilah and the progression of their stories and characters. It's about showing a bonding between two people, born out of the similarities between who they are how they deal with problems. It's about studying character interactions and development.

If I had a complaint, it would be that the game didn't really seem to fully "complete" Henry and Delilah's character arcs, as they didn't progress as characters all that much and never really "resolved" any of their problems and flaws. But I couldn't honestly expect a full character narrative, given that this game is only $20 and has only 4 hours of gameplay. It was simply meant to *show* character and relationship dynamics and how characters deal with problems and provide a thoughtful perspective on human interaction, thought, and behavior. Definitely a game I enjoyed more when I took the time to really think about it.

[h1][url=store.steampowered.com/app/383870/]Firewatch[/url] is best appreciated for its maddeningly beautiful art style, appreciably simple gameplay and intriguing story line. Its only major flaw resides in a final segment and conclusion that disappointingly peters out after an otherwise nicely executed ascension, but the journey is absolutely well worth it.[/h1]

The game looks fantastic from the onset with its unique color palette and perfectly executed art direction. Impressive hue shifts accompany different times of day and weather conditions. It's all very serene and peaceful. The pacing is also just right, allowing you to pause at any time and contemplate every scene.

Soothing occasional music and impeccably voiced characters add further credibility to the world. Everything feels appropriate and is very immersive.

Your primary form of interaction is to communicate with your distant partner on the radio, from which you will be given simple tasks to perform, informed where to go, and learn more about every little thing you discover. This feels great thanks to well-designed conversation mechanics and engaging dialogues. Game mechanics as a whole are simple and fun to use. Although you can pick up objects and examine them, this is rarely necessary or even useful.

This game is short and easy. It is entirely about discovery and storytelling, it is not meant to be challenging in any way.

Exploring the environment is genuinely rewarding. The expertly designed world is very intuitive to navigate and gracefully guides you where you need to be with minimal consultation of the map and compass. It is made to look like a vast, open world but is really not that huge, with only a few main paths to choose from.

I didn't like the unexpected choose-your-own-adventure type of text intro, mostly because I didn't appreciate many of the available choices and the initial tone, but it quickly offers needed context for the game at an understandably low production cost. Thankfully this is not representative of the overall experience.

Your character Henry can be a bit of an idiot at times and I often did not like the way he responds. In fact I initially really disliked the guy but I eventually warmed up to his personality as the story developed. Henry is visibly under-qualified for the job, while Delilah is infinitely more pleasant and complex.

The story interestingly gets progressively weirder and takes unexpected turns, leading to a mild state of intense excitement that can border on paranoia. It is generously filled with contrasting humour and suspense.

However, the conclusion can appear unfulfilling at first glance as it turns out to be infinitely more intimate than you'd be led to believe. The overall writing remains incredibly excellent, despite a few inconsistent plot holes, and it only loses steam drastically towards the end when certain revelations are made in an unsatisfying or questionable manner. Everything makes sense if you bother to piece things together, but it nonetheless feels a bit disappointing, and marks the game's only negative point.

[h1]If there was ever a game that I both loved and hated, it would be Firewatch.[/h1] 

I think of what this game could have been and it pains me that it never went there. I really wanted to like this game. Even now, I wish I was writing a totally positive review but my conscience won't allow it. 

And yet, credit has to be given where it's due so here are the things that I liked:

1) A beautifully designed game world, where all you mostly do is hike. Go from Point A to Point B, investigate and get back. But this part of the game is still enjoyable due to the pretty landscapes. And the fact that you have to navigate using a hand-held map! 
2) That your only other human interaction is with someone over a walkie-talkie. 
3) Voice acting and dialogs. This should probably be top of the list. Both Henry's and Delilah's voice work is top-notch. And probably the only thing that will stay with you post-game.   

I'm struggling to come up with a fourth point and I guess you can see the problem with this game already. 

The game starts off as a go-there-investigate-this adventure. But there's only so many times you can walk through the same bushes before it gets boring. Fairly, at this point, the game throws a mystery in. Something strange is brewing, there are some unexplainable events, and you are somehow the target - very LOSTesque, rite? You wish. You wait for the big reveal, a payoff - and it never comes! All you get is an anti-climax. And the developers fervently hope you feel empty after the game ends. But I felt more dissatisfied than empty. 

And that's a shame, because had this game left me with a "Wow!", I would have probably called it the greatest game in the recent times. But no, like I said the game never goes there. 

So what this game is then, is a fairly enjoyable walking simulator which could have also had a great story, if only. For $20 and roughly 6 hrs of gameplay at max, the price-to-fun ratio is just off. 
If you still want to get this, wait for a sale. 

P.S. I'm giving this a thumbs-up because I still want people to experience this game, despite the flaws. But in effect, my recommendation is both a Yes and No, depending on you.

Firewatch is definitely a unique game in the sense that it gives pretty environments, solumn quiet moments of interacting with nature and the exploration of human behavior and interaction.  The back and forth between Henry and Delilah is involved and deep, and that alone makes the game pretty awesome.

The bad part is the plot.  The game has a fantastic set up.  Wife with early onset dimensia, two girls getting "taken" in the woods, threats of blackmail, a mysterious figure showing up, burned research centers, bugged comms... It was a great start.  Then the ending came.  And it was just an awkward goodbye between Delilah and Henry and we find out "oh the kid fell and the dad didn't want to deal with it".  No conspiracies, no elaborate plots, just playing with the human mind.  And while sometimes this is nice (after all this is a game about human interaction) that much build up leading to almost nothing is very disappointing.  I beat the game in 3 hours, and the price at the time of purchase was $20.  Maybe if this was an $8 game, I would be ok with this.  But the game is far too short and the ending sucked.  

With that said, it is still worth playing if it goes on sale, because the journey up to the end is quite nice.  Just don't expect there to be anything at the trail head once you reach it.

Here's the thing about Firewatch - if you're not looking for a glorified walking stimulator, it isn't the game for you. Which isn't to say the game's not good - I thought it was fantastic. But the whole thing's just a bunch of walking, checking your map, checking your compass, looking around, pressing a single button to interact with something, and occasionally talking over the radio to your supervisor and fellow lookout Delilah. 

Impossible not to notice while criss-crossing through the forest is its overwhelming atmosphere of mystique, which only adds  to the enigmatic - and, in my experience, creepy - tone of Firewatch's story. Rest assured, this isn't a horror game; there's only one moment in the game that could be considered a jump scare, and its shock value is far from purposeless. Similarly to Gone Home and The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, Firewatch's narrative is overwhelmingly sinister without ever actually being outright scary, and it definitely works. Even the unavoidable tedium of having to (often seemingly endlessly) trek across the Wyoming wilderness is significantly lessened by the chatting of main character Henry and Delilah as well as the gorgeousness of the graphics - although the former could change depending on how you interact with your supervisor, as your relationship shifts according to the responses you choose to Delilah's comments. 

TL;DR: Really great narrative. Gameplay was uber-realistic in the sense that your face is constantly buried in your map and compass and yet you are still constantly getting horribly lost. Gorgeous graphics. Realistic and satisfying dialogue.

I suspect that the negative reviews for this game relate either to its length or its relative simplicity which, while understandable in one sense, is blatantly unfair in another. Firewatch is not a long game, I've beaten it in its entirety, including wandering around a good bit to pick up missed stashes and such (I'd forgotten the combination for the locks at one point) in under 5 hours of play. With that said, I don't feel the slightest qualm about having paid $20 for the priveledge of venturing through this masterpiece.

It is best advised that you approach Firewatch not as a game, which it is in only the most technical of senses, but instead as an interactive movie. The vast majority of choices you make in the game will have only the most minor of effects on the story, and many don't have a meaningful outcome at all, and that's okay. Firewatch is immersive in a way that few other titles are, In many games, you are empowered to shape the main character into anything you like or not at all, but not in Firewatch, In a bit of masterful design you are not left without choice, which would have served to detach you from the story as a mere observer, but instead provided just a bit of choice, the exact right amount to give you investment with the character and his story without requiring a vastly branching story tree to accomodate each choice and its' outcome.

This sense of investment, coupled with the beautiful artstyle creates an experience like none other. It pairs the best features of video games and movies to create a triple-feature-length tale that draws you in and leaves you wanting more. Henry is (most likely) not you, his story is not yours, but because of the small choices you are allowed to make along the line you are emotionally invested in his story and that is what makes Firewatch so brilliant. You are left hanging on the edge of your seat as the mystery unfolds and wrapped up in the tale on through its inevitable conclusion. I paid full price for this game I would be glad to hand Campo Santo another $20 and another $20 and another $20 for future stories like this one. Compared to going out to a movie, for example, there is no competition, Firewatch wins hands-down and, even better, it's cheaper by far if you factor in concessions. You won't get a thousand hours of gameplay out of Firewatch, and its replay value is limited for the most part, but if you treat it as an interactive story, not a game, you won't be disappointed.

Firewatch was one of these games where I've visited the store page for the very first time, watched some trailers and ranked the game to number 1 on my wishlist. Literally it was love from the first sight. Short summary of a long text: This game is amazing, it even exceeded my expectations and will maybe forever have a special place in my heart.

People complain about many things: The game is way too short, it is a stupid walking simulator, there is no real open world, dialogues are boring, the story is too linear, the ending is bad. I don't want to argue too much, everybody has his own opinions, I just want to share some of my impressions. 

The main reason why Firewatch got my first attention was the graphics. I don't care too much about texture quality, shaders etc. What matters for me is that this game is by far the most beautiful game I've ever played. Firewatch has an awesome graphic style, colors and illuminations create an outstanding atmosphere in a very well designed environment with lots of little details to discover. While it is possible to do this in 3 hours, personally I've never understood why people buy and play games in order to rush through them. This is a wonderful exploration game, so take your time, pace yourself and enjoy. I visited many places, watched the sunset, took many screenshots, looked at the books and information pieces lying around and had fun for around 10 hours. If you have an eye for details 5-6 hours should be viable at least. People are right when they say that Firewatch is some kind of walking simulator with simple interactions. You don't need skill to play this game, there is no challenge, no puzzles, everybody can play through it. And this is great. Because It is so chillfull and allows you to focus on the real package: the nature, your map, your compass, your walkie talkie and you. If you disable the location marker on the map it feels even more realistic. Yes, there are borders limiting your open-world experience, I did not care about, everything else was just so good. Voiceacting is the best I've ever heard in any game, no exaggeration, and the music is also very immersive. Boring small talk? C'mon, this 'boring small talk' is absolutely fantastic and one of the reasons why this game is so authentic and emotional. This is what makes you feel like being a part of the game and not just being the audience of a hollywood blockbuster. It is about small and ordinary things, things we like because we are familiar with them. Do you like french movies? Maybe you know what I mean. While the story builds up tension during progress you should not expect and action-packed survival game, expect heart-touching dialogues and an adult story about people dealing with their feelings and problems instead. Firewatch is unusual mature and honest for a game and for me it did far more than just scratching the surface. I also can't think of a better ending, in my opinion it is perfect because it is refreshing realistic and consistent. Everything is said, there's nothing more to explain.

Seriously, nothing has been really negative for me. Sometimes I've wished there would be a bit less talking, a bit more silence. Also there could be more animals. Often you hear but don't see them, for example at the lake. I have not seen the turtle however, another reason why I need to play the game at least once again. Possibilites for hiding the HUD or crouching for better screenshots would be sweet. Regarding the price it can be reasonable to say that there are cheaper games out there in relation to the pure playtime. But that depends on your viewpoint. For me this gaming experience was really revolutionary and I don't regret a single cent I've spent.

I think there should not be a question if Firewatch is good, because it undoubtedly is, there is just the question if this is a game you would like to play. If you are not totally scared by walking simulators in general and the game appeals to you, you should give Firewatch a go. For me it was certainly one of the best games I've ever played.

The intro was moving, the feeling of isolation was indeed powerful, but by the end I couldn't wait for it to be over.

Firewatch is a very pretty game. Unfortunately, that's about all there is to it. Whilst some of the dialogue is amusing or involving, most of what you will be doing is selecting which bit of smalltalk you want to say, or you'll be jogging back and forth between waypoints. 

The story starts out well enough, but in the end falls a bit flat. Untimately that's a metaphor for the game as a whole. At the start I was impressed with the beautiful scenery and the attention to detail. From the lighting effects, to the way you can flip a book over in your hand and read the blurb, the designers have put a lot of love into the world of Firewatch. 

But after a while the whole place starts to feel like a tech demo. The forest is devoid of life. There's birdsong, but no birds. It's an illusion. Much like the impression of choice and freedom. What starts out as an interesting way to shape the narrative, talk choices quickly become a little tedious as you realise most of the choices lead back to the same path anyway. The same issue exists in travel. Firewatch looks like a huge forest, full of caves and canyons and rivers. But the game is very much on rails. You can't brush bushes aside. Instead they get in your way. I lost count of the amounts of times I got stuck on rock scenery, or found myself lost inside a forest of tough shrubs. 

This would all be fine were there a way to quick-travel. But you can't. Gone the wrong way? You've got twenty minutes of hiking ahead of you. And whilst I was impressed with the realism of having to look at a map to get your bearings at the start, I actually found having to stop and open up the map (which you can't run with while holding) and then having to put it away every two minutes a very tedious affair.

Like Everybody's Gone to the Rapture, I'm not sure that interactive storytelling is in any way improved, and in fact likely greatly diminished by the removal of most of the gameplay elements. 

5/10

Pros

Immersive first person perspective elements, such as seeing your own body, being able to manipulate objects.


Cons

Barely any interactivity with environments.
No real 'wow' points, both in terms of story and gameplay visuals.
