Firewatch is a beautiful little walking sim. The story is mostly quite simple with the addition of interesting mysteries. The strength of this is added to by pretty strong voice acting and a real sense of involvement in the action of the story thanks to the isolation of the characters.

Firewatch is an all-round great game with stunning graphics and brilliant voice acting. I really enjoyed by time as a Fire Lookout in the Wyoming wildnerness and there were times within the game where I felt quite alone and vulnerable. However, I was never truly alone as I had Delilah, my supervisor, on the other end of my trusty radio. Something I liked was the ability to just wander off track, not following Delilah's instructions. There are a few points I've found in the game where I can go off and do my own thing. Unfortunately, this causes Delilah to become rather irrate. I especially like the little "Choose Your Own Adventure" introduction to the game which definitely contrasts with the rest of the game, and this allows a slightly different narrative through the game. However, nothing is truly perfect, and there are some downsides.

1. It's not long enough!! I finished the game in about 6 hours, which is nowhere near what I wanted. I would've loved to spend more time in the game, exploring the woodlands. A great day to wander around is Day 3, where you get free run of the place for all intents and purposes, without receiving any instrucion from Delilah. I've played through it twice, and I'm currently on my way through it again, trying to discover more ways to annoy Delilah.

2. The ending. So, the ending was slightly anti-climactic and wasn't really what I expected. There was such a build up throughout this game and I expected a lot more from the ending, but it was a bit of a disappointment. However, it wasn't THAT bad and isn't really a deal breaker for me.

In conclusion, although the game is rather short, with a bit of a disappointing ending, I highly recommend this and if you enjoy exploration games/walking simulators with a rich story line and dialogue, then I highly recommend it.

It was a truly memorable and powerful gaming experience, operating around a unique idea, and is therefore one of my favourite games of all time.

- The length was dreadful. I don't mind short games, but holy hell. I finished it in almost 5 hours, and I was going slowly I think. Midway through I felt the story wrapping up and I didn't want it to end abruptly.
- That ending man, ugh. Everything that was interesting about the story just fell apart. How you do mess that up? - The illusion of choice really bothered me. Pick a side! Either commit to player choice with  ones that actually AFFECT the story or give you options for a different ending, or remove the choice element all together and allow me to experience who this man is with a solid story driven game. You get all these choices in the beginning and through your conversations with Delilah, and nothing to show for them. It's annoying.
- The game is way too linear. You are given lush environments, beautiful landscape, and the works. But, it's a lie. You really can't drift far away from the set paths the map gives you.

So having just finished the game I'd like to write a review while it is still fresh in my memory.  Over the chunk of a couple days (evening), a week break and then another day, I finally finished the game.  While there is much to say I'll do my best to keep it brief.

_Visuals_
The game is absolutely gorgeous.  The artwork, execution, or overall atmospherics are absolutely breathtaking; to create realism is one thing but to create a strong visual aesthetic is the work of a true artist, and honestly I wouldn't mind having a screencap or a poster up on my wall.  Though beautiful it often feels like you can't really enjoy it.  Moments of beauty and adventure are present but as the game progresses it becomes secondary to the story.  While it would be fun to explore, the Wyoming wilderness it isn't as huge as your map intially suggests and the story pulls you along always giving a sense of urgency; so perhaps the small map size was designed with this in mind.

_The story_
The story is the main driving force between all that you do.  Your frequent radio chatter and the looming mystery keeps you moving in this beautifully isolated world.  There are times when going from point A to point B may seem like a chore but it's just another excuse to take it all in, it never once felt frustrating or irritating.  The buildup, character interactions, and the bond you form over the radio are superb.  At the height of the suspense I often found myself checking every corner like a horror game, expecting to find something around the next corner or over the next boulder.  I was totally immersed.  It got to the point where even at work I couldn't help fathom how it would end, it occupied my every thought until I  could come home to play it, even if it was only for an hour or so.  That's a damn good setup.

So you can imagine my disappointment when it came to the ending.  Not because it had to end but because it seemed to end even before the game was over.  You sort or reach a point where all these clues start falling into place and then the game just reaches a plateau and you ride out the final moments.  ...I think there is more to the ending than I'm giving it credit for but my brain is still reeling with all the possible outcomes I had envisioned, some I liked much better, but maybe that's a testament to what the game is what the game isn't.  It definitely is an experience and maybe it's just not a concrete one...I don't know.  I was going to shelve it but I think this game warrants another playthrough.  Some dialogue choices I would have made differently and now knowing the outcome, maybe it would give me more time to reflect on the larger whole.  If I do I'll be sure to update my review.

TLDR: A fanatastic game with great atmosphere, story, and character building.  It leaves you wanting more while the spellbinding suspence keeps you guessing up until the end, it's seriously that good.  The ending isn't what I envisioned but maybe there's more to it that I can take from the first playthrough...maybe with time I'll have more to say.

Firewatch is an interactive mystery story. Although first person, there is no shooting, and there are no guns. It's only you, a radio and the voice on the other end out in the wilderness.

The opening narrative is a lovely touch: chronicling the tragic events that led you to escape your old life, with you making the choices that write your own backstory. Like the opening scenes of the Pixar film 'Up', it works wonderfully, and in only minutes you are deeply involved before the game has even started. Instead of bullets and guns, you fire one-liners and witty banter back and forth. It's funny, it's personal, and the voice acting is great; probably one of the best scripts I've seen in a game.

The game is beautiful. Vegetation sways in the breeze, colours are vivid and the light is gorgeous. Deep red sunsets cast crisp shadows over the landscape and shafts of light spear through lush forest. Think Borderlands' comic book style crossed with the brooding realism of Dear Esther. You can run, leap, rappel and climb your way through the landscape... but... here's my gripe: the game only gives the illusion of open world and you are are funnelled down certain paths to ensure that you stumble upon the right things. The short, linear story dictates where you go.

And that is... it.

This game is not for those with short attention spans, nor for those expecting lots of things to happen. There's a lot of walking, and a good deal of talking. The pacing is slow (sometimes too slow), and there's a lot of criss-crossing over familiar ground. It's just a plain old mystery and that's... refreshing.

As long as you accept these things, then you'll love it for what it is: a beautifully crafted piece of story and art.

The Way I Review (and why you should care): In these reviews I will always disclose any info that colored my gameplay experience, as well as any outside information that could influence my opinion of a game one way or another. Fully objective reviews are a difficult goal to achieve, and the last thing I want is for my opinion to color the presentation of fact I'd like to think these reviews strive for. That said, I will strive to review these games as objectively as possible regardless of my personal opinions and gladly welcome any polite feedback or constructive criticism. 

My ultimate goal is to provide information fairly and accurately so that you, as an individual, can decide if the game I'm reviewing is something you would enjoy. They may be a bit wordy as a result, but my goal is to cover all key elements fairly and accurately, so sometimes it's an unfortunate necessity. In these instances I will attempt to condense the key points, though those should be seen as a well-intentioned simplification of my arguments, not a distillation of their essence. If it is EVER necessary for me to discuss a "spoiler" element of a game, I will do so with prior warning and will take all appropriate precautions.

[b]I have no affiliation, financial or otherwise, with any publisher, developer, journalism outlet, etc. I have to work to earn money and time to play these games, just like most of you, so I thought I should use my limited platform here to provide an honest and independent look at games that I've bought and had some sort of opinion about.[/b]

THE REVIEW ITSELF:

DISCLAIMER: I'm aware there are some divided opinions about this game, and I will disclose my biases before I go into my review; to do otherwise would be dishonest. A relatively important plot point was spoiled for me accidentally as I read an article about this game while trying to decide if I should buy it. Knowing that piece of information colored my perspective, and steered me towards the favorable opinion I have of the game. I understand the issues raised by the other side and can certainly understand why they would feel the way they do. My enjoyment of the game is not meant to imply their concerns are in any way less valid; these are just my opinions.

I'll start out with the things about the game I either did not enjoy or felt were in some way a little bit lacking. FIRST, I know this is a necessary limitation but I feel compelled to mention it because it has been my gaming pet peeve for most of the last two decades: invisible walls. In a game with such a beautiful environment and such an emphasis on exploration, it could be frustrating trying to find which roughly meter-wide gap my character was supposed to go through to progress. 

SECOND, though it's loosely related to the first: moving around with the map up is kind of a pain because your character (realistically) lowers it so he can keep his vision focused on where he's going. Nothing wrong with that in and of itself, but  with rough trails it happened enough that it felt a bit like padding. I certainly wouldn't advocate for quest arrows or the glowing trail from Fable in a game as realistic as this, but a middleground solution seems like it would be doable without breaking immersion. 

NOW FOR THE GOOD STUFF! I'm sorry I spent so much time on the negatives, especially since as I said they're all relatively minor and none had any bearing on my choice to recommend the game; I put them there because some people may weight those aspects higher than I do when they're considering this game. I try to include the good and the bad about games for that exact reason; in pursuit of objectivity I mostly just try to bring up everything I think someone might consider important. For games when it's hard to explain what's good about it without spoilers, I tend to go into more detail on the negative aspects simply because they tend to relate to elements of games unrelated to the story (usually).

Uuuuunfortunately, I cannot discuss the plot of this in any meaningful way without giving away many spoilers. As this is a game some may which to enter without hearing any plot elements, I have marked it as such below.


VERY MINOR SPOILER (Pre-title screen info, setting only) You spend the first few minutes establishing through text prompts and similarly delivered choices the nature of your relationship to your girlfriend (and then wife) Julia, as well as some minor details about your home life in Boulder Colorado. An unexpected illness drastically changes Julia's life, and her family becomes more involved and you must decide how you best fit into these drastically changed circumstances. Seeing and ad for a fire lookout in Sheshone National Forest, your character takes the job; you'll be out there all summer. Did you do it out of guilt? Were you just trying to catch your breath and re-orient yourself for the new challenges presented by your wife's illness? Or is the stress of it all something you just need to get away from? That, and a multitude of other important questions are up to you to decide. POTENTIAL MINOR SPOILERS END HERE

That, in truth, is the core mechanic of this game. Throughout your time in the Sheshone National Park you will encounter and interact with other people; their opinions and actions are influenced by what you do--the plot, mostly, is not. This is a game about the exploration of the characters and their circumstances; while you can affect people around you, the history and the future of the larger world will largely be unaffected by your efforts. In my opinion, this was a good thing for reasons I'll explain in a moment. For now suffice it to say that I enjoyed the realism of it; people can live and die and forests can burn and kindness or cruelty only exist on interpersonal levels; life goes on regardless of what happens in your corner of the world. 

That being said, one should not undervalue the ability to affect the lives of the people around them. The voice acting and writing have gotten a lot of praise, and in my opinion it is absolutely well-deserved. But something I've seen lacking in a lot of the reviews is the reason for why we find the dialogue so "authentic" or why the relationships between the main characters seems so real. 

[b]Firewatch does a lot of things most media seems (In my opinion) unwilling or unable to do; accurately depict normal people.[/b] No cartoonishly evil villains or impossibly pure paragons of morality: [b]At its core, Firewatch is the story of a group of broken people; they are noble and they are base, they are wise and they are fools, they are corageous and they are fearful. They are flawed and imperfect and because of that they are beautiful. As the game transpires you will come to your own conclusions[/b]. You are given enough info to unravel the mystery, but the morality of the events is honestly something every player will probably feel slightly different about, even if they played the exact same game.

I think major studios could stand to learn a lot from what's presented here.

Firewatch isn’t really a game in the conventional sense; ostensibly, it’s a kind of interactive, dialogue-heavy… ‘experience’. It isn’t a game, insofar as you can’t win, or lose. No choice you can make within the game will affect the final outcome. In fact, there aren’t any real choices, aside from those you make with regard to dialogue, which itself, has no bearing on the final outcome either – at least not any outcome you can perceive on the screen, or from your speakers.

Yes, so, it’s linear – like a film – but certain dialogue options provide pleasingly circuitous routes back to the main narrative. 

In essence, Firewatch is a first person movie. But don’t be misled – although the nineties and early noughties were awash with interactive movie type games, none of them did it like this does. Through its stylish and immersive art direction, spare but sensitive use of intelligent incidental music, and knowing, human dialogue and script, it managed to completely captivate me. It’s short – only a few hours’ worth of gameplay – but what a few a hours they are.

The story manages to strike a unique balance between whodunnit, suspense, thriller, romcom, and abstract tableau, without actually being any of the aforesaid. The lasting effect, and the level on which it works best, is that despite the rails you find yourself on, the story telling is so good that your first person viewpoint only serves to make you internalise everything that happens. Most of the time, you do really feel like you are Henry, and you are there, feeling and experiencing what he feels and experiences – which is quite an achievement. 

The way your path through the Wyoming wilderness is handled isn’t perfect – often, I found myself thinking ‘But I could just jump over that log – why can’t I just go over there?’. I understand very well that the game isn’t Skyrim or Fallout 4, and is not meant to be open world – and as good a job has been done, and with appreciation for how challenging it must have been – little things like this broke immersion from time to time. 

This said, Firewatch ultimately demonstrates how effective a first person movie can be – but does so on the strength of its writing, dialogue and acting. It bravely straddles some line between drama and gaming that to this point, to my knowledge, has remained a wild and untamed frontier. The result is a new sort of thing, if you can approach it without expectation. Campo Santo have made the look, feel and atmosphere of the project totally their own, and despite its flaws, Firewatch goes down in my top twenty memorable experiences - of any kind - at a computer.

I loved Gone Home.  I want to explain why in relation to Firewatch, really.  The reason why I loved Gone Home is because it was like discovering someone discover themselves.  Sure, the influence you had on the story was limited, but it wasn't really about your influence at all.  It was about trying to figure out what happened, where everyone was, and you do that in the story.  The point of the story was discovery.  There's no changing the fact that no one's there and you aren't given opportunity to do anything other than explore or any reason to try to change anything.  You can't say, hey I don't want her to run off, let me stop her.  She's already gone.  You just need to figure things out.  And that's fine.  You can't really influence things if people aren't there to influence them.  I get that.  And that's ok to me.  The discovery part of Gone Home was what to me made it a good game.  A purposeful game.  You were experiencing it.

But FireWatch is different.

On the surface, if it were a novel, I'd be fine fine with it.   I'd think it was deep, it would have some meaning to me.  But you don't interact with novels, you are passive in the entire thing.  You don't feel like you can direct the characters.  You aren't put in a situation in a novel where you feel like you should be able to influence the outcome somehow, typically.  Gone Home didn't give you a situation where you can influence it but it walked that balance, you discovering and finding out what happened, still participating but not being able to choose to change anything.  But it was ok, given the parameters and situation you were in.

FireWatch, on the other hand was an excercise in frustration.  Here I was, playing this character who has options. He's got an entire forest to explore.  He and his radio girlfriend are being messed with, but he literally has a whole forest, a whole forest and items in his tower that he could be able to do something with to stop that.  It was horrible.  I was stuck playing this dumbass character, who just let other people marionette him.  At one point I'm like, let me head this dude off, why am I letting this guy just direct me wherever he wants me to go, I'm going to go over here.  NOTHING.  I have no choice but to let this guy do his dumbass things.   I appear to have a choice, but no, I really don't.  They even stuck the fake ranger behind the outhouse. I'm like let me prop this up here  in the tower because someone's watching me.  But no, my character is too stupid to have that option, because it's not written.

Bottom line is - Gone Home successfully limited your options in a believable way and at the same time let you ramble around and experience things.  This game limited your options in a totally bogus way, by making you unable to actually act, but letting you think you might be able to.  The restriction is that character an absolute dumbass.  I wanted to like this game so so much, but I just can't.  It's just frustrating and stupid. And I'm sorry if you don't agree, but that's my opinion on it.

What can I say?

Firewatch is a brilliantly made game. It features a fantastically gripping story line with likable characters (although few). The content of the game is short, but in a small space of time it raises questions about morals and personal experiences between Deliah and Henry than most games can in 9 to 10 hours of play. It was compelling throughout and I was (literally) on the edge of my seat while playing. 

Graphics wise, this game is beautiful and surpasses my expectations of what a story driven game would usually have to offer. It tends to keep things simple but shows how the simple "things" can make a vast and eye-opening view. 

The best comparrison I can make to Firewatch is Life is Strange. The art and look of the game gives me the LiS vibe to it, which is an extremely good thing because I was hooked on Life is Strange, even doing a second runthrough. However, the content of the games are similar, except Firewatch's decisions do not impact on the story. As far as I'm aware it all ends in the same outcome, but gives you different ways to approach talking between characters. It is not your story in a sense, but the way that you feel it and react is. 

Overall, I give this game a superb 9/10 because I feel like there could have been more to the ending of the story and that the options you chose impacted the way the story may have been played.

Firewatch is a game that ends up being less about it's gameplay and more about it's experience. You play as a man who's had a bit of a rough life and decides to get a job out in the middle of a national park to get away from everything. His role is to just watch over and make sure there aren't any fires that spin out of control during the summer. Sounds boring? Perhaps ... but there's actually a lot to like about it.

Firewatch is very atmospheric, has tons of voice acting and character building, great pacing, tension building, all with excellent use of music cues and ambient sounds to top it off. I'd highly recommend playing this game with a headset so you can hear the ambient sounds as you go along.

As far as gameplay goes, you'll mainly be hiking all around the area you're suppose to be watching over, while talking to your boss friend over a walkie talkie. Some other things pop up like making sure hikers aren't getting into too much trouble, or checking out communication lines that have gone down for example.

Now, I don't want to give too much of the storyline away as that's the main point of playing this game. The story unfolds in a very interesting way though, trust me!

I could step into Henry’s shoes, embodying him fully.

You are let loose on the wilderness of Wyoming with just a map and no ugly waypoint markers or handholding. The sense of being able to explore away in any direction in a very realistic way using an unmarked map was exhilarating. There are some invisible walls of course but despite this, the game successfully created a sense of vastness of the wilderness.

Although most of the story threads are tied up, the ending was anti-climactic. Though I tried to justify and rationalize the ending, it only left me disappointed and unfulfilled.

This game provided a great, tightly knit, focused experience. Don't let some of the other reviews fool you, this is much more than a "walking simulator." Sure, you'll do a lot of walking (and running) in it. But it's more of an open world adventure game without fighting and weapons and all that sort of stuff. The pacing is fantastic, there were rarely moments throughout the entire experience where I felt bored. You're kept on the edge of your seat for a good portion of the game, with it's fantastic writing, dialogue, and storyline (for you Madmen fans out there, Rich Somner who played Harry Crane is the voice of the main character). And at the heart of it all is this really intriguing relationship that develops between your character, who is quite a broken man, and your other lookout buddy, via radio, who also happens to be a fairly broken woman. You pick each other up when you're feeling down, you joke, you flirt, there are hints of potential romance. But like the flames of the forest you are trying to watch out for, everything is quite fleeting. I took extra time to explore a lot of nooks and crannies and got lost a few times (use that map!) and discovered wonderful little hidden extras that the devs through in, so my playtime was around 8 hrs. A straight go of it would probably be around 5-6.

Also a warning to those of you using Steamlink via a Mac, I had a miserable time using the Xbox 360 controller with this game. It worked fine if I plugged the controller directly into my Mac, but when using it via Steamlink, certain buttons became almost completely unresponsive, in particular the button which lets you use your radio, which drove me crazy because there are numerous timed dialogue responses in the game and some of them I wasn't able to select because the damn button wasn't working at that moment. Very frustrating. Also the mouse cursor wouldn't disappear on my TV when using Steamlink, but on my Mac it went away like normal. Very weird. So I would avoid playing this game via Steamlink on a Mac, unfortunately, because it is so beautiful and deserves a big screen to really get immersed in the wilderness atmosphere, the colors, light rays, and so forth. Not sure if there are the same issues with the Windows version as I haven't tested that out, but I have noticed that there are TONS of controller problems in general reported on the forums for this game. So my only beef would be the developers stating full controller support with Steamlink which is totally not the case.

Firewatch is a unique game for me and not something I would usually pick up. It is a hiking simulator mixed in with a little bit of mystery. It was honestly a great experience. The voice acting is 10/10 and the game itself is very immersive, I found myself truly lost in the world.

The game looks beautiful and there is nothing in there the were no bugs that broke the illusion. It's a 3 hour story and it is up to you how you value your time. I think I picked it up for $10 - $15 on sale and have no regrets. But if $20 for a 3 hour experience is too much for you pick it up on sale.

Firewatch is a great example of storytelling through a first person narrative. While the story has a few stumbles towards the end, the narrative driven by Henry and Deliliah is compelling and highlights some of the best dialogue in a video game. The game is at it's best when you're given room to explore and let the world breathe, you won't however find much in the way of puzzles or action. 

The art direction and look of the forest is stellar and it was hard for me to not take a moment from time to time to just sit and look at the scenery, and the game often rewards you for taking time to just explore down different paths, and even has a camera for you to capture some of this beauty.

The story is where things get a little sticky. Starting off, the story focuses where things work, the characters and the exploration Henry and Delilah are delightful to listen to and seem so much more like relatable people than the all too common cariactures in video games, and the exploration and choices you make along the way really pull you in. However the overarching story is perhaps a little weaker than it should have been. I won't delve into for the sake of spoilers, but it felt as though they forsake some of the games strengths and the characters for a lackluster story ending

All in all, Firewatch is a stellar narrative experience like Gone Home or Dear Esther, but with a little more fun and lighthearted dialogue to draw you in.

Very good as far as these types of walking simulator adventure games go. The conversations between Henry and Delilah feel very natural, and the pleasant naturey graphics give a good backdrop to their relationship developing. An outdoorsy game with plenty of dialog, it made me forget I am sitting at home alone in the dark. 

Overall no complaints, the ending is not for everyone and personally not how I would've ended it either, but I can see why they did. A good way to spend ~4 hours and would recommend.

This game is wierd. At first you begin as with a mystery about who you are and what you are doing here in the wilderness. You start to put the peices together but there are many gaps that you need to work out yourself, nevermind the mystery of a mysterious girl on the radio. Slowly you realise why you are here, but also who else is there with you. [spoiler] Baby turtles and violiot racoons [/spoiler] . All jokes aside. This game is somewhat like Keemstar, it can be confusing and two-sided but it ends up shocking you with what is really inside. 

The exploration of the game is mediocore at best, and i know people will disagree. The game is revolved around exploration (as it is advertised as a camping game) but in my experience, the map was small and when you looked on the map and saw where the [spoiler] mysterious signal [/spoiler] was coming from, i thought "Oh my goodness, this is going to take forever!", when in reality it took 10 minutes to scale the map, half of it taking screenshots. 

On to my next pro of the game, the screenshots. Oh my god are they good. The amount of insane opportunities you have for amazing screenshots is uncanny and i can only think of one other game that is similer, which is 'The Binding Of Ethan Carter'. The games are so similar, but also so different. One thing to keep in mind for screenshot lovers is that the crosshair can not be removed from the options (although there was talk about doing from the devs so this may have changed) so the only things i found to remove the crosshair was mods,  SPOILERS!!, or to take your disposable camera you find and as you lower the camera the crosshair is not there for a split moment, and this is how i took my screenshots. You can check them out for an understanding of the game.

I really enjoyed this game, and recommend it to anyone who likes story-driven walking simulators. It is similar to Gone Home, where you walk, read things, and try to figure out a mystery. It is a shorter game (playable in just one or two afternoons), but it was the right length for the story.

There are a few things that set it apart from the standard story-driven walking simlulator. 

First, it does have a fair amount of typical normal video game elements to it. You do get new gear that lets you explore new areas. Hiking through a national park ads more depth to the walking. 

Second, the story. Even video games with good stories rarely compare to the story quality you see in novels, films, or TV. (Seriously, where is there a Breaking Bad level story in video games?) This is one of a very very small list of games where I think the story holds it own with the top novels of the year, I would have enjoyed it if it were a book. 

Finally, I love the way it handles dialogue in the game. In the introduction, your character has some choices, and some times when the choice is made for you. There is more depth in what you choose to say than the standard paragon vs renegade. It's really how you are responding to your backstory, and how you envision your future.

This game is very story driven and some might complain about that and how there isn’t “much content” but the content comes with the multiple choices of dialog between the two characters and the beautifully written story and the voice acting of both Henry who is voiced by Rich Sommer and Delilah who is voiced by Cissy Jones. In the short 5-6 hours you play in Firewatch you feel like you know these characters and you really care and feel for them and when it ends you just feel like you want more of this game which is a great for a game to establish a feeling like that in someone. The downside is the ending as you are left with some questions unanswered but it doesn’t affect the game too badly. Overall I do recommend this game as in my opinion it’s worth 20$ and the time playing it. The overall score for Firewatch is a 9/10.

P.S. This game actually influenced my future career path as a Fire Lookout and Park Ranger so if a single game can do that that’s pretty awesome in my opinion!

• Investigating a mystery surrounding you both. 

Believe me, the intrigue of the world rubs off within 20 minutes as almost all in-game assets look the same, but interestingly enough the creators do try their very best to disguise this by -admittedly- deploying beautiful varying lighting across the world. Be that as it may, do not go into this expecting a huge world of wonder with much to discover and fawn over. There isn't. Much of it looks the same, and this isn't aided by the lack of 'gaming' you can do. Mechanics are limited to 'interact' (opening boxes and climbing ropes) and 'sprint'. 

Ultimately, from a content point of view this doesn't hit high marks. So, what about the story? The characters? Well...

They aren't really characters. The dialogue between them is fun and engaging, but their 'backstory' which is shoved down our throats from the offset isn't relevant to the story whatsoever and I sat there scratching my head at the end wondering why I needed to know any of it.

Imagine you go to a cafe and ordered a coffee. The person who brings you it then goes on to tell you the origin story of said coffee. You'd just sit there with your mouth open wondering, how does this make me enjoy it further? Stop! Stop!

Sadly the creators didn't think about that, so friviously throughout the game they drag up the dregs of the characters past to add 'interest' to the game. Why? Because Firewatch is so bare bones that they have to try everything they can to keep players engaged. This game is worth perhaps £3, certainly not £14.99 that it's marked as currently. What were they thinking?

The mystery holding the game together has some of the widest gaps I've recently witnessed, unexplained red herrings are treated as main selling points to this game and we are expected to swallow them all as a part of this supposedly 'emotional' experience. 

The ending, as most have highlighted, is not good. It. Just. Ends. Like. This. Review.

A good adventure game. It's good. 

It's good at telling an interesting, albeit sad story of loss wrapped in a good mystery of personal-discovery. It's good at visual and artistic design, and it's good at its voiceovers.

It's good. Good buy worth your good earned money.

[b]Firewatch[/b] is a first-person, narrative-driven adventure game. The player adopts the role of Henry, a regular guy who takes a summer job as a fire lookout in Shoshone National Forest as a way to escape his personal issues. Gameplay involves watching for fires, wandering around the Wyoming wilderness, and performing park rangery tasks assigned to you via two-way radio.

The visuals are very well done, colorful and heavily stylized. The core gameplay is smooth and streamlined: exploring, examining random things, simple tool use, chatting and reporting over the radio. The story is engaging and deeper than I expected.

Despite having enjoyed the experience overall, there were a few things that bothered me:
[list]
[*]Although ostensibly open-world, the terrain is carefully arranged in such a way that the player is forced to stay on a handful of discrete paths. While this makes sense in terms of helping players navigate the game area without getting lost, it does detract somewhat from the Wyoming wilderness experience.
[*]The few types of interactive obstacle (logs to scramble over, rocks to climb up/down, rappelling areas) are all visually identical, and give a cookie-cutter vibe to an overall varied and well-constructed terrain.
[*]I would have liked a wider variety of ways to interact with more of the nonessential objects, other than the standard: look at, talk about on radio, use to advance objective.
[*]The game presents the player with a lot of choices, but I feel as though they only superficially affect the narrative.
[/list]

I spent about 4 hours completing the story, in "role playing mode". I.e., I wandered and explored a bit when the objectives weren't urgent, and remained more objective-focused when it was in line with occurring events.

I would recommend Firewatch to people who are looking for a relatively freeform, story-oriented adventure with uncomplicated gameplay.

The two major critiques I hear of Firewatch are its almost singular ending and how you can finish it in only a few hours--both of which are missing the point. Firewatch isn't about having a long, extravagent game or an extraordinary, ♥♥♥♥-your-pants ending.

It's about the details, the little nuances in the game you interact with and discover by chance or curiosity. It's about the spectrum of human emotion, trapped in between a gorgeous, surreal environment and a slowly-creeping unease, left only with the voice on a walkie-talkie keeping you company (and possibly a turtle or wooden cutout). It's about how you relate to the characters, and how they relate with you. And for what it's trying to do, Firewatch is just the right length.

The people, the dialogue, the fear and uncertainty and relief--it's just all so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ -real-. That being said, you may  need to be in a certain mindset while playing. An excellent and fairly immersive story about a middle aged dude who goes into the fire watching profession for a summer in order to escape his life's problems. 
The gameplay is simple enough: using navigational tools to follow directives. There is no combat, as it is a relaxed environment, which I personally enjoyed. It's very easy to get turned around and lost in the forest, so frequently checking your map and compass is highly recommended. The forest ambience is fairly realistic albeit minimized, probably for the sake of emphasis on dialogue, which enabled character development of both the protaganist and his unseen companion.
The plot is very engaging, allowing your mind to wander to various possibilities, likely enducing anxiety or paranoia if you have the inclination.
The visual design of the game is very unique and minimalist in an attractive way. Without much in the way of settings, the default imagery is quite gripping, almost as if it were painted. The lighting is fairly accurate, I found, aside from inside caves, and made for a very warm feeling to the environment.
The only qualms I have with the game is its length, easily completed within 3 hours, and a lack of visible life in the forest, no wildlife or bugs or rangers. I think if they had added more than just a single instance of a deer sighting, I would have been more inclined to take my time and explore more, as opposed to focusing on the directives.
To summarize: A beautifully presented story with an engaging plot.

For those curious about Firewatch, it should be said that it stretches the boundaries of what is considered a game. I've read tags such as "walking simulator" and while I jokingly agree, there's a high level of quality to this game that needs to be acknowledged. The prologue draws you in and gently pulls on your heartstrings in just a few minutes, and when you've finally reached the lookout tower, you feel right there with Henry.

 What amazed me about this game was how deeply I felt drawn in and immersed. The unfolding mystery plays with your head if you let the game get its tendrils into you, to the point of peeking around corners, keeping your head on a swivel, and questioning the sound of your own footsteps. The further along you go, the more invested and careful you become about your interactions with your radio partner Delilah. I was questioning the tone of everything I said, thanks to some superb dialogue writing and voice acting. As much as Firewatch loves to build the tension, it also finds a way to draw out other heartfelt emotions. Anger and sadness, laughter and wonder all have their place in the vast nothing of the wilderness, with a bittersweet culmination.

Firewatch is by no means a traditional game, but for an adventure meant to draw you in and involve you, it's polished, well written, and on top of it a beautiful game to get a bit lost in. Sure, you might finish it one session. In fact, I reccommend doing just that!

So this game's been getting some rad reviews from very notable sources and with good reason. The game is fantastic. Coming from only ever playing one other narative game (Life is Strange), it's not hard to believe that I was kind of hesitant getting into the game. This is also due in part to the pricing. 

So let's talk about it. If you're debating whether to get the game or not, you have decide on what is most important to you:

If the hours/dollar spent is a dealbreaker for you, don't get the game. If replayability is a dealbreaker for you, don't get the game. If you're not into narrative games, this game's not for you (that's not to say that you shouldn't try it). If you're expecting action 24/7 from the game, look elsewhere. 

However, if the price doesn't bother you too much, if you're not too keen on ultra-high-tech graphics and textures, if you're prone to getting drawn into a very strong narrative, I'd say pick it up during a sale. Pricepoints should never be a deciding factor on the merit of a game. While it can be used to drive away potential customers (that's entirely on the publishers), reviewers should be critiquing the content of the game and not how much the game itself cost. That's where most of the negative reviews come from. 

The game defines the walking/hiking simulator genre. It's daunting to think that you're in the middle of the vast Wyoming forests and yet there isn't an animal in sight. You seldom every see another living human being. The only saving grace in this vast wilderness is your female companion, Delilah and you're not even sure if she's real. 

It says volumes about gaming nowadays where multiplayer is such a norm and you need interactive interactions every living, breathing moment and yet, Firewatch is able to reduce all of that into nothing but simple textures, beautiful lighting and beautifully crafted banter and dialogue. Now, I don't plan on playing the game again so I wouldn't be able to tell you if the choices you make throughout the game have any effect on the outcomes but what I can tell you is that the responses you get to them feel.. real in a way. It's as if the dialogue was taken from a real-life conversation rather than a scripted one made to make you feel a certain way. It's as if the developers got the voice actors, said "GO!" and they just did their thing. 

It's not all great though. The game does have a few flaws. Not mentioning the price-point, there are some spots in the game where the game and dialogue jitters. It's as if it was loading in the background and couldn't make it in time. That really took away from the immersion. Another thing is the fact that you're in the vast wilderness, and yet there's not a single animal or living being? It's a bit odd and unrealistic to have that sort of expectation or that you'd be so lucky. Although, I can forgive that because the game is isolative in nature so I can understand the dev's making that decision. It's also rather sucky that you can't access any of the contents in your pack. When given the option to fish, I put away my fishing rod thinking I'd be able to bring it back. Nope. No way to access your items. 

This last gripe is a more personal one and might contain the tiniest spoilers. I don't know why the developers decided that they needed to make a shock-value twist in the middle of the story. Why do narratives need to do this? Why does every narrative need a villain? Someone to collectively hate on? It came so out of left field I had a hard time following what the hell was going on. Because of this, the ending seemed... unwrapped? Rushed? Out of place? A bit of a non sequitur? I don't know. I was really hoping to hash things out with Delilah towards the end, sort of get some closure but because of the "twist," everything fell apart. It's like everyone wants to be J. K. Rowling but also wants to be M. Knight Shyamalan. Just.. stop. There's no need. Keep to the original narrative. You're not getting any extra points with the players by shocking us. 

In all, it was a fantastic game with some flaws here and there. Would I refund it if I had the chance? Sure. But I'm happy to say that this is the first game I've perfected and I have absolutely no shame in it.

To summarize: a tightly delivered narrative experience that knows exactly what it is -- AND knows who you are.

So, details.

If one of the first questions you're asking about this game is 'what is the gameplay like', then you might be recommended to walk away now. There's exceptionally little in the form of true 'gameplay'. I've often said that while video games are their own type of medium, they can also serve as an evolution of other mediums as well, and Firewatch is best described as an evolution of graphic novels, or even ordinary novels. It's a narrative experience and nothing else. If you're going to ask about controls, aiming, or tactics, then this game isn't for you. Different strokes for different folks.

If, on the other hand, you spent a vast majority of the Elder Scrolls or Mass Effect games simply talking to people, enjoying the dialogue and characters, then you might want to keep reading.

I dislike labelling games as 'Walking Simulators', because that term carries a certain level of stigma with it. I'd rather describe it as an 'interactive narrative experience'. The goal of Firewatch is to tell a story, pure and simple. The great achievement of video games that do this - where they surpass their conventional counterparts, like novels - is in their ability to place you within the story itself. It's not some protagonist walking along the creek, it's YOU. Firewatch stands apart from many other narrative games in taking full advantage of the fact that you are invested and integrated with the game and its story. In fact, it depends entirely upon that very concept.

I would recommend this game for anyone, but I would ESPECIALLY recommend it for seasoned gamers. Why? Because the game knows what you expect. It knows that you've played dozens - maybe hundreds - of games before, and have sort of begun to know what to expect, even from games you've never played before. Sort of like how watching a lot of T.V. makes you able to predict plot twists on brand new television shows - not because the show foreshadowed it, but because you understand how people write shows. Firewatch knows that you understand how people write game narratives, and it's ready for you. It USES that to further its own ends. It's breathtaking in its execution. You can't just drop a gamer down in the middle of an idyllic setting and expect that gamer to actually believe everything is as peaceful as it seems, and Firewatch damn well knows that, and uses it ruthlessly to deliver an atmospheric setting and fascinating story.

I paid $14.73 CDN for the game (Steam summer sale) and it took me four-ish hours to beat it. Some might look at that metric and call it poor. I would contend that four hours of edge-of-your-seat quality storytelling is far superior to eighteen hours of filler side-quests to round out an otherwise empty open-world game. Total playtime is one metric to measure a game, but it's far from the only one. For fifteen bucks I got an extremely enjoyable afternoon. Concerts, movies, sports events... they all cost more and last for roughly as long, or shorter.

The story does a good job of keeping you tense and making you care about the characters ('yourself', the protagonist, and the person you communicate with via radio). The only thing that could disappoint you is the ending. The storyline is definitely a mystery, and clear answers are few and far between until the end. It's easy to imagine all kinds of crazy explanations for the mysterious goings-on, your mind taking you to X-Files and beyond, and when you reach the ending and find it to be quite... mundane, you may be disappointed.

So. The story is excellent. The playtime is short but that's no issue. What about the rest?

The graphics, from a sheer technical perspective, aren't amazing, but that's masked very well by a fantastic art style. The music is gorgeous and used sparingly, to great effect. A couple times I was frustrated by invisible walls even where it seemed like I should be able to walk, but not often.

In summary: a great game if you want to sink yourself into a great narrative experience with fanstatic atmosphere that comes ready-made to play with your expectations, with an ending that could be seen as a bit more mundane than you might be hoping for.

Simply put, it plays like a book. A book with gorgeous visuals, and in which you play one of the main parts. You really don’t need any “gamer” skills–there’s no button mashing, no combat, no crafting, nothing really “traditional” in the gameplay mechanics of Firewatch. It’s part of a genre labeled “walking simulators” because, to be honest, a lot of the mechanics of the game revolve around going from place to place, talking, and picking up stuff. Sound boring? Far from it.

Firewatch is a first-person story-driven game set in 1989 in the forests of Wyoming. You play as Henry, a middle aged guy who has some really painful stuff in his life–real, heartfelt pain. I won’t spoil the introduction for you, but it’s a masterfully choice-driven component of the game that really makes you invest in Henry as a person.

As a way of escape from his life, Henry takes a summer job as a fire lookout in Wyoming, where his only human contact is a women named Delilah, his boss, to whom he talks through a handheld radio. The tale quickly dives into a gripping mystery, but its true beauty lies in the conversations between Henry and Delilah (honestly, it really says a lot about a game when the left and right triggers on the controller are mapped to the radio/dialogue control). Delilah frequently chats with you, and you, as Henry, can radio Delilah over a myriad of large and small things, and the branching dialogue gives you satisfying control over how Henry approaches those verbal encounters. The writing is spot-on, the voice acting is perfect, and the interactions feel so genuine and real. It’s an emotionally refreshing experience, because unlike many female game protagonists, Delilah, even as a disembodied voice, feels like a real person, with agency and depth (similar to Ellie from The Last of Us).

Firewatch contains M-rated content (primarily in the form of strong language from the two protagonists), but it is truly a mature game in the best possible sense–that is, emotionally. It’s a game about messed up humans, loss, love, loneliness, and responsibility, and it deals deftly with those themes.

Some people were disappointed by the resolution of the mystery and the end of the game, but frankly? They were actually pretty much perfect. The ending hurt. It really did. But it felt right. It fit.

Aside from the brilliance of its story, dialogue, and voice-acting, it’s a distinctly beautiful game with rich, stylized landscapes to explore, and a simple yet exquisitely beautiful soundtrack.

So if you’re in the mood for a deep, beautiful, heartfelt journey–whether you’re a gamer or not–I’d highly recommend picking up this game, particularly while it’s on sale. It clocks in at about four hours, so is certainly on the shorter side for its price, but the developers nailed the timing and it’s worth every cent.

My first thoughts when playing this was, "Hey its pretty similiar to Gone Home". If that statement and the "Walking Simulator" tag this game doesn't sounds good to you, then this might not be the game for you. To that I'd say while the game is short, you get out what you put in. There's tons of little things the game does with your minor desicions and exploration to make you go "Oh, that's kinda cool" and while these are small moments they ensure you have a more unique playthrough each time. I probably will play through this game again, sometime in the future, because of how interesting and engaging it was for the short time I played it.

Video Games are generally thought of as forms of escapism; where you witness fantastical worlds and plots for your own enjoyment and escape from the real world.

However firewatch twists that trope and tells a story *about* escapism; and you the player are not the one escaping from reality. What you see and play in this game is all just more reality; the wilderness in this game is not designed for you to craft items or survive, but just to hike in. It is the real world, where a forest trail isn't likely to have any hidden traps or loot, and where circumstances that may seem crazy probably have a really unexciting answer. It is the character's in this game who are escaping, not you the player.

(minor spoilers ahead but nothing specific)
Through the 3-4 hour playthrough the game is subtley telling a story about you; chances are when playing the game for the first time you were doing it to escape. You got sucked into the conspiracy plot and forgot about anything else; much like practically all games you forget about reality or expect situations to be more exciting and meaningful than reality. And so when the ending comes and completely puts a stop to the fantastical plot it is used to force you out of the immersion and escapism, in the exact same manner as Henry, as he too is finally getting pushed out of his escape.
So when so many people complain about the game mechanics or the lackluster ending I really think it is that they are looking too much for the escapism that this game is actively fighting against; I think looking at it from this point of view makes the game a lot more meaningful and interesting than looking at it as just another game.
All in all, I had fun playing the game, however for the price you're paying it isn't worth it. Story is very short and with little replay value.

I greatly enjoyed the fourish hours I spent playing through this game. The near-walking-sim gameplay can be boring if not monotonous at times, but this isn't Rocket League. The gameplay isn't the focus, and the story is well capable of carrying the game. It's a twisting tale of spying and deception worthy of a mystery novel. A novel, however, would have lost two of Firewatch's greatest strengths (besides the story, of course).

One, it's gorgeous. It looks and sounds simply amazing. The visuals aren't gunning for photorealistic, and they don't have to. The game simply looks awesome, the sort of game where nearly any screenshot looks like concept art. The environment is pretty and well-designed, full of rolling hills, green plants, and rugged cliffs. The atmospheric effects combine with the haunting soundtrack (which plays at major plot points, Half-Life style) to bring the tense story to life, and the sound effects bring a surprising amount of realism to the slightly cartoony style.

The real reason to buy Firewatch, though, is the simultaneous isolation and connectedness brought about by its premise. You're in the deep woods, so people are few and far between. However, you have one connection to civilization: your radio, carried with you at all times. It is through this radio that Firewatch's story unfolds, and your developing relationship with the person on the other end is where the game really shines. Nearly every dialogue offers you a choice of words, and those words have a deep effect on your developing relationship, if not on the game's core storyline (which is fairly linear on its own). Every single dialogue choice is elaborated by some incredible voice acting work. The voices are relatable, believable, and really bring the two characters to life. And on the rare occasion that your radio fails you, you truly begin to feel alone.

I have only one real complaint with this game, and that is that it suffers from a few technical issues. The game's FPS varies wildly, and some scenes are quite obviously not optimized. I also managed to get into a situation where the game ceased to respond to keyboard inputs, forcing me to return to my previous save.

My last statement is one of cost: Firewatch has a very low price to gameplay ratio. I got it on sale, and well I thoroughly enjoyed it and would pay full price, you may not find 4 hours of gameplay to be worth $20. There is some replay value, but the story itself doesn't respond much to your input, only the subplot of your relationship with the one at the other end of the radio.

All in all, Firewatch was an enjoyable experience, and I highly recommend you try it. If you're on the fence about the price, go for it! You won't regret it.

Controls get a little confusing, as each function is bound to a different key on the keyboard and I mixed them up a time or two.

I was surpised to find that my orienteering skills came in handy on this game; there is a marker on the map to show where you are and where you've been, but you really should know how to use a map and compass IRL to take full advantage of the map.

I liked the story as well, (still no spoilers) it was a little short but there's plenty of things to do. The game does skip over the 'boring work days' so you only have to deal with the interesting stuff. There's also plenty of comedic relief right at the beginning.

Essentially this is a walking sim with strong characters and a solid story that does a good job of transitioning the player through different moods.  There's plenty of casual, relaxinga and humorous moments that balance nicely with the growing sense of paranoia and tension as you drive deeper into the conflict of the story.  

The visual style is definitely pleasing and draws you in, and the sound design is very good as well.  One of the subtle accomplishments that I really appreciated was how the developers made a point to subtly remind you of your physical limitations as a character.  Little moments of hearing your character get winded as he hikes helps to escalate the sense of danger in moments of tension, as it becomes ingrained in your mind that your character is clearly not some godly athlete or fighter that's going to be able to easily bust himself out of a bad situation should he encounter one.  It was a nice touch. 
|
Some will be dissappointed with the ending, as a number of reviewers have expressed.  But I actually appreciated it, and I think it works well with the overall style and setting of the story.  

My biggest gripe is the fact that they put a timer on your ability to reply on your radio.  I think this was to ensure the dialogue always flowed and seemed natural so as to not remind you you're playing a game.  But still, considering the game is entirely driven by its dialogue, as it s a walking sim, it kind of sucked when I didn't get a chance to reply here and there. 

The game took me about 5 hours to complete. And yea, as others have said, its not the best bang for your buck in terms of game hours to dolalrs - even having gotten it on sale at 13 bucks.  But then again I've spent 13-20 bucks on a movie tickets, and this is essentially an interactive film. So viewing it that way, it seems more reasonable. 

Bottom line: if you're ok with games driven entirely by story/dialogue

I guarantee you that all the 'negative' reviews on this are from people who:

A) Don't like games with lots of walking

B) Don't like games that are mainly about story more than gameplay

C) Are telling you it's not worth $20.

And to adress those issues, I say:

To both A and B... Why even buy the game, then? It should be pretty clear by the videos, trailers, and description that this game is mainly about story telling and environment. Not gameplay. Negative reviews written because of that purpose hold no water, as they're biased right out of the starting gate.

To C... Eh. It really depends how much you like story and environment-based games. If you really, really like them, this is definitely worth the $20. It has a good amount of replayability, as most of the chat options you choose are pretty obvious choices between being a total ♥♥♥♥ and being a good friend, so you can replay all you want to change your relationship with Delilah.

Look, I'll be blunt. There's no multiple endings. I don't want you to buy this game if you're in it for finding all the endings. But the different dialogue paths are certainly intersting. You can restart any day, so you don't have to play through the entire game again to change one dialogue option (Although some days are pretty long, so you might have to play through a bit if you're changing a dialogue option towards the end of one of them...).

Is the dialogue, environment, and storytelling good?

Yes. In fact it's some of the best I've seen in any game, really. I'm not exaggerating. The reactions seem very real, and at times I would think or even say something the characters were going to say in a couple seconds because, well, the reactions are very human and not faked at all. If your character sees something horribly unsettling, he's not going to be all heroic like, 'Do not fear! I will... yada yada", he's going to freak the ♥♥♥♥ out.

Like I said, it's sort of a walking simulator. But don't mind that. Please don't take that as a negative at all, unless you really, REALLY hate walking. The environment is so beautiful, you'll totally forget how long it took your to walk one place to another. There's also a jogging toggle without a stamina limit too, if you're not the type to want to stare at painstakingly crafted, beautiful landscapes (you monster).

There's not many characters either, which is good if you ask me. It helps the game really develop all of them, although I will say some relationship statuses are sort of forced on you through huge time-skips, where things sort of happened without your consent. And some of the dialogue options can be variants of the same thing, making you say something you don't want to, one way or the other. But those are basically the only bad things about it. No map glitches or texture bugs to be found.

Oh and last bit of advice, there's no way to get a game-over. No way to die or anything... Which kinda helps actually, since it makes the characters' reactions to dangerous scenarios more realistic and less 'Oh, well, if I die its no big deal anyways'. So if you want a game where you have to worry about dying now and then, and have the tension of danger over your shoulder... Look elsewhere.

Overall, 9/10. It's a bit short and is really only a great game for the people who are really into the genre of environment/narrative-based storytelling games, but believe me, for those people, it's a must-have. Please don't pass this up because of a few harsh words if you're really into the genre.

Firewatch is good. As in "Stay up to twenty to three because you want to stay in this world" kind of good. You play as Henry, a man who becomes a fire watchman to escape his troubled past. You gain a rapport with Delilah, your boss from a neighbouring tower. The chemistry between the two actors is superb and by the end of the game you understand both Delilah and Henry like real people. It is this dynamic which differentiates Firewatch from other "Walking Simulators" as you are given options as to how to respond. I am keeping this vague as the story relies on subvering your expectations. Ryan McCaffrey from IGN compared Firewatch to a good book, but unfortunately this book is more of a novella. It is annoyingly short. I would have liked more time to get to know the Wyoming wilderness without the story taking over, as make no mistake; this game is beautiful. The story feels over surprisingly quickly and despite all loose ends being tied uo (or, at least, enough of them) there's a sense that the story is not complete. When everything is revealed, it makes sense but you (or at least I) wish you never learnt the truth as I wanted more time to explore this world and hear the interplay between the two leads. While there are a lot of branching dialogue paths, there is not much replay value to be had due to the linear narrative.
Firewatch has changed my perceptions about what games can do and I look forward to what Campo Santo do next. We're also going to have to coin a new term for "Walking Simulator" as this game, despite its short length, doesn't deserve this disparaging title.

Firewatch is a nice story driven game that I would liken to a Talltale game like The Walking Dead series.  Much of the game play revolved around timed dialogue response events.  I didn't really like that mechanism in The Walking Dead and it wasn't much better here but I can understand the impetus behind it and why it can sometimes be effective for story telling.  Most of the time, it just feels like a timed quiz or a more boring version of a quicktime event from an action game.

What I really liked about Firewatch, however, was that the voice acting and character development were a little better and less cliche than the Walking Dead Telltale series.  I found myself caring a little more about the people themselves.  The other development here is that the game takes place in a 3-D first person environment which is just a way better interface than what you had to deal with in the Walking Dead games.  The graphics were a little cartoon-like but beautiful and the action animations were really well done.

In the end, I feel like this game is a good purchase when bought on sale.  There isn't a whole lot of content here but what is there is very promising and I really like supporting new developers that look like they have a bright future.  I found myself wanting more out of the game which means they did something right - the audience should want more out of a good game.  That said the content was a little thin.  I could've used some more side quest like achievements - easter eggs for collecting pine cones or getting all the books or more things to collect to personalize the watch tower.  It would've been cool to see things that you physically did in the environment affect the storyline of the game (rather than just the timed verbal responses).

In the end what you have here is a good solid core of a game that plays out more like a nice playable book.  Looking forward to what these guys do next and hoping for more depth and breadth in future installments.

Perfect until the end. The end was very anticlimactic but it starts off perfect. I was so involved in the story, I found myself actually holding my breath and feeling an intensity.

This is the strongest part the game had. It has amazing dialogue with maybe good and technically consequential choices. It's sort of like Sword Art Online (season 1, although not as awesome).

The story had me guessing and trying to predict what was happening. Right after a high level of positivity, I have a very mixed feeling.

*Spoilers from this point*

You could easily argue that Deliliah might have been mostly lying all along. What if she turned against you or came out about other lies she didn't tell you?

Another guess was that there was a team of scientists conducting psychological research, but there was something aside from that which no one could know about (probably a murder or something). This guess was sorta close.

It still doesn't make sense why Ned had to be so paranoid and scared that he tried to put negative evidence on Henry and Deliliah. I mean that's literally the reason the story exists.

I would be much happier with a less anti-climactic that extended the game a couple hours. I would be even less annoyed if we got to see Deliliah and Henry actually meet, and maybe get some additional information and future perspective of them. If that happened, we could see a Firewatch 2 and end the story with episode 2 about a mystery they may not have noticed before in the park with a less anti-climactic ending.

Overall, this is worth buying, but only on sale. It's a great story up until the end where everything falls apart, your hopes are torn apart, and what was such an amazing piece of work is now shattered because someone rushed the end or lost interest in the script or whatever. Regardless of whether it's about financials or being lazy, there is no doubt there could have been a way to work through it, because the reason this isn't so popular is the annoying ending.

There could easily be a second (and final) episode if the ending was changed, and therefore more profit driven.

I still recommend this game because it represents some of the best writing I have ever experienced (I will keep shunning at the end). I just became so attached and involved. I love everything except the end if I haven't already said that enough.

Just finished and it's hitting me like a ton of bricks. It plays like a movie, but an interactive one. Beautiful and cohesive scenery and well written and incredibly complex characters. That means that excitement fiends may not enjoy it...it's walking, and talking, and looking at things. I love shooters and I still enjoyed it.

My favourite part was the beginning half, it had a good pace, a little mystery, and amazing dialogue. I felt the last half was weaker, I found myself getting lost a few times and feeling stressed by the situation more than I would like (but it's immersive, which is probably the point).

I think the 'level' designs are very clever; they lead you towards where you are supposed to go without pushing. When I found the cave I went towards it without even trying to go back the way I came, even though I could have. Many times I found myself just 'wanting' to explore or return in the exact direction that the story required, and it felt seamless. The environment felt expansive even though it's not (further exploring will run you into places you cannot pass), but the detail in the backgrounds expands it to seem as if you could, but don't want to, explore the giant national forest. 

Soundtrack is good, perfectly placed, and doesn't overwhelm the lovely sounds of nature that speckle the environments. 

I would recommend it if you are open to a different style, to the characterization and look of it. If you do not like games that aspire to anything other than COD levels of gaming, then you won't like it and it's fine. I personally will likely replay the first half because I loved the mood and environments, and want to soak in the amazing art.

-It has a great story which is great in the build up even if the ending was a bit lacking

Bad points:
-The game does feel a bit padded out at times with long treks through the wilderness but exploring that beautiful scenery makes it less of a chore

Firewatch was a pleasant surprise...I really can't say how much I enjoyed this game! I'm not saying that it's without flaws but it was really well done. I'll start by telling you what it isn't...it's not an open sandbox, it's not a 100+ hour game, it's not violent, it's not explosive, it's not packed full of needless tasks...but what it is is a game that's been well thought out, it's a story driven game, it's a game that doesn't waste your time running around doing pointless things trying to level up your character. This game is very straight forward with pushing the story along...in fact it only took about three hours to complete it which show you how intuitive the game is! I won't say much about the story plot because that was one of the things I most liked about getting this game, as I was playing it I didn't know what to expect and this deepened the excitement every time there was a twist or turn in the plot of the story. I highly recommend this to anyone that loves a good story although it is from a male perspective so it might not be that engaging for a woman to play, this is one of the things that I would like to see them put into an update...having it so that male or female could enjoy the story...which would actually be very easy for them to do. The graphics are really good in a cartoonish look, not unlike Team Fortress II. The atmosphere of the game vamps up as the story progresses which really adds to the tension! In the end I felt very satisfied with the money I spent on this game and could only have wanted to have a little more backstory to the relationship of the people involved with the main plot point...which is my only gripe. So...if you want to sit down for a few hours and be in control of an animated film from a first person perspective then this is a must have!

Firewatch is a game about a man named Henry who took on a summer job to watch for fires in a national forest in Wyoming to temporarily leave behind some frustrations of life back home, who's only emotional and human lifeline is a female called Delilah on the other end of a radio.

Wow. Besides the flora rich environment, and the great pacing, this game packed some serious punch in the three hours of gameplay in its storyline. Henry is trying to escape some trouble back home with his wife who was diagnosed with a form of dementia, and he was no longer able to take care of her. His boss Delilah is the only other person who he has contact with throughout the game constantly. Feelings begin to fly and the two form a great relationship and friendship. Frelationship? I don't know. I digress.

What makes this game so great is the storyline. Many people were upset and could not get over the end (myself included) because it did not feel proper. It felt cut off, short, and very anticlimactic. However if you sit back and think about the process of the game and how Henry and Delilah progressed together and put two and two together about events that occurred ([spoiler]H and D were paranoid about the potential Government employees spying on them, tapping into their radios frequency, listening to their conversations, which apparently was solidified when they thought the biologists camp was a monitoring station spying on them, but once H found out Ned was simply covering his end because of the death of his son, and making up everything as he thought they were out to get him, H and D suddenly realized everything they had done was out of human feelings of paranoia, and ultimately, for nothing.[/spoiler]) you realize that it was simply basic human gut reactions. The final knife in the heart so to speak. We see ourselves in Henrys shoes, doing the exact same thing, and when everything we worked for was taken away ([spoiler] Delilah leaving us and not staying, never meeting up like she wanted when she told you over the radio when she was flirting[/spoiler]) we feel hurt, and betrayed, and confused. Almost like a "Real life simulator 2016". 

Campo Santo really drew into human feelings and interaction in this game and really hit the nail on the head. I'm still not over it and I feel an emotional pull to this game, which is very hard to come by these days. I absolutely recommend this game. It will put you on the feel train even if you didn't buy the ticket.

You could easily sit down and play through this entire game and be on your way in just about the amount of time it would take you to go see a movie and grab a coffee with your friends and, if you're frugal, wouldn't cost you much more either.

But, if you're like me, you would rather play this game instead. The developers did a fantastic job of really capturing the situation that the main character Henry (you) finds himself in and had no trouble of transferring that situational feeling to the player, which just gives it an invaluable sense of authenticity. If you play games for the story or you're afraid that you might not play this game very much, then don't worry because the story is good and you really don't need to play it over and over. This game is like a movie that you buy because you liked it so much or a good book that you'll never forget; you don't need to buy it to enjoy it and reading it once was enough, but if you were to read any book again or buy any movie, it would be this one.

$20 is $20 but a truly enjoyable and beautiful game is priceless these days. Buy it, install it, play it, enjoy it, and support the developers along the way. Maybe, if we're lucky, we'll have another good game on our hands before too long.

I bought Firewatch because it hits on one of my favorite story tropes: two people who are alone together. But I've left Firewatch being amazed at so much more of the game! 

First of all, ignore what people say about the ending. I finished Firewatch and thought that the ending was satisfactory but also had a sense that I was missing something. There are glorious fan theories that cover all of this on YouTube and I would highly recommend checking them out after you play. 

Secondly, I'm not someone who likes walking simulators or first person games. However, Firewatch uses everything I don't like about first person walking simulators to build up an incredible experience. The creeping feelings of panic and fear would not be the same if you were not playing first person. Similarly, the emotional connection to what is happening would not exist if you were not actually acting as Henry in the game. This is not a violent horror game, and yet it was easily the most scared I have EVER been in a game. To me, that takes incredible work and story telling. 

The potential to change Henry with each play through is enormous as well. This to me is amazing in a story driven, atmospheric game. There are a huge variety of options throughout every step of the game, opening up the possibility for a completely different version of Henry in every play through. 

Finally, there is so much to think about in this game and after playing it. It really drew me in and has given me so much to think about as far as what happened in the game, but also including things like how this experience might be different for a male player than a female player and so on. 

Overall I am stunned. I played this in two days and have thought of little else since finishing it.
