This is a good first person perspective suspense-thriller personal drama story. Though very linear and relatively short, this was still interesting and humorous enough that I played it through 3 times (mostly to ascertain how much (or how little) freedom this game actually gives you). Ultimately, Firewatch is more of a mildly interactive story than an actual game. Indeed, there are places in the story where this "game" almost seems to play itself out and there are no choices you can make which have any great, ultimate effect on what happens in this game or on how it ends. You, the player, are essentially just along for the ride. It's an interesting (and at times, extremely tense) ride though.

The good:
+Good Graphics throughout, especially outdoors (which is where most of this game takes place. This game has a nice, well thought out cartoony, graphic novel style. One may think this graphical style would be enough to keep the game feeling humorous throughout but surprisingly this game depicts some increasingly tense and suspenseful situations. There are wonderful graphical flourishes throughout and a great attention to detail. Also, when you look down you can see your character's body, unlike many other games. Your character's hands do look a bit too pudgy and odd though.

+Great sound. Perhaps perfect sound actually. The sounds are realistic and excellently detailed. Crickets chirp and birds sing and bushes rattle mysteriously while strange metallic tinkling can barely be heard in the exact places where you should hear it. Every sound is meaningful and intentional. The sounds are vitally important to creating the tense atmosphere of this game and succeed brilliantly. The music works well to increase tension even further but wouldn't make a great soundtrack in itself. Voice acting is outstanding throughout and the script writing is excellent as well with many witty exchanges and jokes.

+The game controls well (it feels like you are playing as an out-of-shape but muscular guy which is exactly what your character is) and the controls mapped very well (and very easily) to my keyboard and mouse using the control settings menu. The controls are also fairly simple making this an ideal game to use if you want to learn how to play a first person perspective game and are uncertain as to how such game's should be controlled or are not yet very good at it. It is a bit odd though that you can make your out-of-shape character sprint around (including up hills) as much as you want to. It was also a bit overly difficult to figure out how to operate the radio and select dialogue choices (Odd considering what a vitally important element of gameplay this is) but I got used to it.

+The environment is big but not so big that things get boring if you enjoy being in the real-life great outdoors. It is big enough to get lost in but small enough that you can easily find your way back again. The environment feels like a fairly realistic outdoor area as well (especially if you were in some sort of state park). It is a bit grandiose for a mere national forest but that's a minor issue which is easy to overlook.

The Mediocre:
+/-This game could have had better pacing. I sometimes felt as though the game was trying to hurry me along through its plot. I particularly wanted there to be more peaceful moments wherein I was not encouraged to hurry but instead encouraged to explore for the sake of exploring. There's lots to see and have your character respond over the radio about but mostly you are busy with some more pressing matter (like trying to make sure someone doesn't set the forest on fire). There's no actual time limit on completing objectives (perhaps there should have been though) but wandering idly along looking at every little thing that catches your interest while someone or other is setting off fireworks in a high-danger fire area seems really strange, particularly after your boss has just told you to hurry (but doing just that kind of thing what you must do in order to get the most character and plot development out of the dialogue in this game's story. The game does give you an opportunity to go exploring on your own before the plot fully winds up but it doesn't seem like its encouraging you to do so at that point.

The Bad:
-It's almost impossible to figure out just how nasty or sarcastic your character is going to be before you select a dialogue choice (if I wanted the character to say anything at all). This encouraged me to want to play through the game again and again in a very frustrating way because, after the game was done the first time, I had yet to really see what would happen if I had responded in a way I wanted to. I had responded to several plot-critical situations with sarcasm or with nasty remarks wholly on ACCIDENT because the game won't tell you whether you are about to say something sarcastic or nasty. It only gives you the first few words of what you might say and nothing more. It's hard to choose one dialogue option over another based just off of that. All Dialogue options should have been labeled with easy to understand emotional labels such as "sarcasm" or "angry" or "depressed" and so forth to give the player a heads-up on what they are about to make the character say before they let the character say it. The dialogue systems in Deus Ex: Human Revolution and in Fallout: New Vegas and Fallout 3 are head and shoulders above the one which this game is built around.

-Regardless of what you say or don't say and regardless of whether you have your character respond at all (even to direct questions being repeatedly screamed at you), the same basic plot occurs and the same basic situations happen each time you play. This game is very linear and (sometimes as sheer luck would apparently have it) nothing you say or do really makes much permanent difference to how the plot develops. This is totally unrealistic. If I refuse to talk to anyone at all, there will be ramifications. If I act insulting on a constant basis, other ramifications will ensue. But in Firewatch? The same thing happens each time. Some of the same dialogue will be spoken NO MATTER WHAT YOU SAY OR DO. Your relationship with the main character will seem different to you but that does not change whether or not the forest burns down and nothing you say or do can change whether or not you prevent it. After playing the game 3 times in a row this inability to affect the game world in any meaningful way left me with a feeling of mild frustration. This game should have been more like a choose-your-own adventure story with multiple different endings. Instead it's like a normal suspense-thriller novel. It's fun the first one or two times but it wears thin far too quickly. 

-I could more easily accept the fact that this is a relatively short game if it had a plethora of potential endings but it doesn't. It has just two endings and they both seem a bit anti-climactic.Despite it's flaws though, I'm still glad I played it once, twice, even thrice (to see and hear everything the game has go offer) but I will not play it a fourth time. Now that I really have seen 90% of what this game has to offer, playing it yet again would just be repetitious and boring.

While this is a fun game to play I heavily suggest waiting for a sale. $20 for a game that takes 4 hrs or less to complete is simply overpriced. Much of my playtime is simply being lost as well. It was an enjoyable game with an interesting story and an interesting presentation style but it lacked the necessary content to pay a full $20. With a sale I believe it is worth it.

Firewatch is an adventure game, developed and published by Campo Santo that was released in February 2016 on PC.  The core team behind this game have got a plethora of experience, with some coming from big titles such as Mark of the Ninja, Brutal Legend and Bioshock 2 so I went into this game with high expectations. 

You play as a middle aged man named Henry, whose wife has sadly got dementia, a crippling illness which tears people’s lives apart. Doing what a lot of people do in this world, Henry runs away from his problems to become a woodland ranger in a national forest. Your job is to mainly look out for signs of a fire in the dry woodlands and help prevent them spreading across the rest of the forest.  This should be a calm and relaxing job for most, but you soon become the centre of a massive conspiracy plot as the story unravels. 

Gameplay consists of hiking across rough terrain in order to reach objective points, loot supply crates which contain key game play tools such as ropes or walkie-talkies as well as notes left by past rangers which form part of the history of the park and give you some back plot to the story.   Another core element to this game is the interaction you have with the only other human you have contact with throughout, Delilah – you maintain contact with her through your radio and talk to her every day. The two develop a relationship depending on how you respond to her in dialog and actions throughout the story.  The dialog was probably the most compelling part of this game; the hiking between objectives did actually grow a little tiresome at times and grew very repetitive towards the end of the game. 

The story is what carries this game hands down, I’ve been on a bit of an adventure game binge lately and this is by far the most interesting and gripping story I’ve played in recent memory. The relationship and bond between the main character Henry and Deliaha develops throughout the game and you really find yourself becoming completely immersed in this story. The game will leave you asking yourself moral questions too, and of course the ending will allow you to decide yourself on how everything works out in the end. You’ll probably finish the game with more questions than answers, and normally that would point to a case of bad storytelling, but in this case it is simply amazing that a story such as this can bring out so many emotions and questions regarding certain subjects. 

Whilst the game isn’t the most graphically enhanced, it does have a nice art style that is pleasing to the eye. The game is ran using the Unity engine so we do get OK looking graphics but some of the texture quality and graphical effects are lacking which let Firewatch down sadly. The voice acting and sound effects are all really good though, again the dialog between characters is spot on and I cannot fault it even for one second in that department. 

The forest in which you are situated is huge, although the game has set objectives throughout the story, you are allowed to roam around and explore anything you want. You will come across certain areas of the map that you can’t explore just yet as you won’t have the right equipment, such as axes or climbing gear, but you are free to check out every nut and granny if you please. You will find a handful of those supply crates I spoke about above scattered around the forest, along with a few points of interest too. 

Due to the fairly linear overall story line there may not be room for more than two playthroughs of the game; yes you can choose to respond differently to Deliaha and that will result in different dialog between the two characters but I personally don’t see any other reason other than achievement hunting – to play more than twice. A single play through of Firewatch took me just over five hours to complete. 

I had minor technical issues whilst playing, you will get some stuttering when you enter a more graphically heavy area such as near a large mass of water, or looking over a cliff with a long draw distance; I was a little disappointed in this as my rig is more than capable of playing this game on high settings according to the specs recommended. I was able to get a little bit of a performance boost by using an SLI profile for my graphics card and thankfully was able to get a steady 60 FPS with the odd stutter throughout my time playing. I did also fall through the world a number of times which did become a huge annoyance as it kept repeatedly happening but this was fixed by reloading the game. 

My conclusion of Firewatch is that it a stellar adventure game, which whilst it does have faults with average looking special graphical effects and minor technical problems; it is still a joy to play through. The story kept me gripped right until the end, and the relationships that you form between the two characters are brilliantly executed.  The price tag of £14.99 is completely fair and justified given the production values on offer for this title. The game has very rarely been on sale up until now so we might get a heavy discount in the upcoming Steam sale, so keep your eyes peeled.

I will go into more detail about how the ending of the story I felt was a let down, so consider this line your spoiler warning:

While I am not entirely opposed to the way they went about it I felt the ending wasn't quite what I was expecting, and whats more, doesn't make a ton of sense to me. There are too many loose threads the story just trys to sweep under the rug. And issues I would think would be cool to resolve never were.

To start (And is somewhat hinted to in the trailer) there are two girls you have a bad encounter with and then go missing. To start the game should've delved into that more. Instead we have the dread of being implicated in there dissapearance just being resolved by "Oh nothing happened, they ran off on their own and were found later" and just got sweeped under the rug. 

Furthermore the actual culprit behind alot of the mysterious events was, while not a terrible pick, not really answering any real questions. The high tech camp inside an enclosure that wasn't supposed to exist wasn't built by our antagonist the father. It was built by someone. Someone who had been keeping tabs on our character and partner. Not only keeping tabs, but keeping tabs on how easily they could be manipulated. And the hidden scanner we found in that camp tied into a trap that was left by our antagonist, and he himself had set fire to the camp to further frame us after we left it. 

Yet he had nothing to do with that camp. We knew three people worked there but were not present. The father was by himself, hiding, hoping to never be found and ensuring no one could find his son's remains. In the end nothing of real note happened yet there was more that could have been done. And this "games" selling point is story, narrative and what have you, so for that to be a let down ultimately lends itself to a negative review. As far as the story is concerned, I generally disagree with the boys at IGN or whatever review comes up on youtube first.  They got all hot and bothered by the ending.  Let me try to describe it without spoiling anything: I think this game would make an excellent book, one that would involve vivid descriptions of Shoshone National Park with its lonely beauty, piercing that peacefulness with the lives and conversations of the two main characters.  You have to be open to what the author, in this case authors, want to tell.  While video games are different from books in that they place the reader/viewer in the action, games sometimes ask us to step back and examine a tragic situation much akin to the catharsis of Greek tragedy.  While we often wish to be the agents of the action, sometimes it's just as interesting to be a pawn or someone who is unaware of what is happening.  I think some reviewers missed the cerebral nature of those who play games like this one.  It's not always about the finale, but how resolution is achieved and this game does it masterfully, evoking a number of feelings in the player while challenging us to simply view something that happened before we even arrived for a summer of fire lookout duty, to view it and have a response, rather than create that response ourselves.  The game makes the viewing great, though.

While I have to say that I enjoyed this game and it was an endearing experience, I can't really recommend this game due to the fact that I don't feel like I enjoyed it any more than I would've just watching a playthrough on YouTube. The characters are well written and relatable, the scenery looks nice and pretty, and the story starts off kinda nicely. But any decisions you make have extremely little if any real effect in-game, making different playthroughs essentially identical. 

While the setting looks nice and soothing it also lacks any real 'soul', there's not much exploration, and I feel like that wastes the map design. Wherever you go you're running into trees and rocks you can't cross, paths that go all over the place, and all of that only really serves to get the player lost and maybe extend the playtime a bit, making the player resort to pulling up the rather clunky map system every 10 steps. There's nothing much to see in this game aside from the trees and rivers, etc., and the game suffers from the gameplay consisting entirely of "Go from Point A to Point B". While this is a "Walking Simulator" as you might've heard, the game really relies on okay-scenery and occasional funny banter between the characters to keep you from falling asleep. 

The story also eventually devolves into a "mystery" kind of ordeal, which seems like a rather sharp turn from the tone of the game before. Not only does this "mystery" kind f come outta left field, it also lacks a satisfying conclusion, much ike the game itself. The ending is agreed upon by many to be rather disappointing, which some argue is on purpose, leaving the player empty and wanting more in some kind of artsy way. 

Another thing to take note of is the pricetag to playtime ratio here. There are games out there worth $10 that could keep you playing for dozens of hours. This game, however, falls a little short in that respect. It carries a heavy $20 pricetag despite the fact that players will not take more than 3-6 hours to finish this game, depending on how often and how badly they get lost. With different choices and options making really marginal difference, it causes this game to have EXTREMELY little replay value. In fact, the first minutes of the game are you making 'decisions' (as many are you just clicking from single dialogue option to progress), with the whole section having such little impact that it could've just as easily all been a textbox and the game is simply trying to fool you into thinking it's anything different. I can't in good conscience recommend a game of this price when it lacks so much in the entertainment value. 

I say you should only consider purchasing this game if you feel strongly about supporting the developers, and even then you should wait for a sale to come around.

I'm an avid reader.  I like reading fiction because it brings me elsewhere.  Somewhere I can't seem to get anywhere else.  That is until developers, who just happened to also have great writing or a writer with them, decide to weave a story pretty seemless into their videogame.

Some people might call it a walking simulator, or they might think it's boring.  They might even complain about the graphics or the lack of hours in the game itself.

I can't tell you whether or not you'll like the graphics (I did), or whether or not 4-5 hours of gameplay is "long enough" for you, but what I can tell you is that the story and the mechanics in telling that story are very well done.

You can jog through the peaceful yet haunting landscape, or lose yourself staring into a setting sun over a nothern lake.

The story is as real as one can get, with a very nice twist to get your excitement up.  I found myself constantly circling and looking for someone, knowing no one will ever be there.

If you've ever dealt with or worked with someone ill, or cared for a family member who suffered; you will immediately relate to the content of this story.  The struggle of the protagonist.  The arching theme of mental illness does an incredibly great job at pulling you in, and pulling on your emotions.

The reason I write this review, and why I prefaced it with my love of reading, is that I wanted to congratulate the crew behind this game and let them know they'd brought me to gasping at my game.  I had to make a decision.  I [b]chose[/b] to not make a decision.. Not answer someone's question when I regretted it later.

This game made me.. [i]feel[/i] something for the character and I haven't felt that since Frodo losing Gandalf and Roland losing Oy.

If you're looking for a great story that will make you second guess yourself, making choices for a fictional character that could otherwise be fashioned after yourself or a brother/friend, then I invite you to take the plunge and support this game.

I felt this game was very polished, had solid voice acting and demonstrated what simplicity in gameplay will do, just as creative storytelling can captivate you.

Firewatch focuses on real people and their very, very real problems. The dialogue/voice acting in this game is superb. Henry and Delilah quickly become extremely relatable characters, with their constant flow of dialogue ranging from witty to funny to philosophically deep. The storyline can be controversial, but give it thought and you begin to appreciate exactly what the game developers aimed at doing. It's funny, yet sad when it needs to be. It's a serene playing experience, yet intense when it needs to be. All in all, just a fantastic narrative.


As a side note, the graphics in this game are stunning. It's a unique art style that works, really capturing the beauty of the wilderness and immersing the player into the atmosphere.


From the stunning, immersive environment to the endearing characters who we grow so attached to, Firewatch is an artistic masterpiece in its own right. It's a very thought-provoking game that has kept me thinking about the game for hours on end.

So I have never written a review here on Steam, but this game is so good and its ending is so divisive that I feel like I need to put in my two cents. But first, I need to get my prejudices out of the way: I'm an aspiring English teacher, a writer, and I love studying narrative craft and over-criticizing even the smallest details of any story.

Since I won't be able to write a review without spoiling some elements of the story, I'll give my verdict right here: If you love narrative-driven interactive experiences, buy this game. The dialogue is impeccable; the lead characters are both lovable and memorable; and the experience is quite immersive. If you prefer escapist, mechanic-driven games, then this probably isn't for you. The story is real and often depressing, and the narrative depicted is intended to make you think.

And with that, here comes the spoiler-y section...

***SPOILERS AHEAD. YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED.***

I guess there's not much to say about the presentation as a whole that hasn't already been said. The art style is brilliant and Henry and Delilah's performances excel. So instead, I'll be attempting to answer some of the common complaints about this game.

1. "This is pretty much a movie where you hold down W the whole time."
If this anonymous commenter means that Firewatch is a narrative-driven experience much like a movie, then I have to agree with him. If he is faulting a game for having a particular button designated to go forward, then any first-person game can fit under this complaint. If he is stating that this game would function much better as a movie, where interaction is taken away, then I must disagree. Though the player may not know it, every choice in this game is designed to draw him or her into Henry's experiences. This is most apparently seen in the text-based Prologue, where Henry and Julia's life together is summarized. The text makes the player synonymous with Henry by only using the second person pronoun "You." The player is manipulated to not only identify with Henry, but to feel the same way he does. But this manipulation isn't a bad thing, without it, the moral and major themes of the story would partly be lost. The game succeeds by making "you" Henry, something a movie rarely can do (though if you want a good example of a movie that succeeds in doing this, watch the first scene of Farhadi's "A Separation").

2. "The ending sucks."/"The ending is disappointing."
I would posit that many players feel this way because players, as they are supposed to, identify with Henry. The game is about our incessant desire, as both gamers and people, for escapism and our eventual, inevitable return to reality. As the prologue sets the stage for the story, we are given a dulled, blue and purple, grief-laden text, then we are dropped into the bright, red and orange fantasia of the Two Forks region with the potential romance of this mysterious Delilah. We are thrilled--exhilerated, even--and when the potential for espionage and conspiracy comes to light, the isolation and escape drives us to what we hope is greatness. Of course, this dream is ultimately shattered when we discover that it was all a sham, and we are hit with a double-whammy when Delilah leaves us. This is the point of the game. We want to escape--be it our relationships, our sorrows, or the mundane--but reality is always calling. We need to face it.

3. "We never get to see Delilah!"
Exactly. Just like with any story, we are given only what is necessary. The remaining blanks are left to the imagination. Now, with Delilah, we are given many more blanks than the average character, and this too is intentional. Because we never get to see her, we get to make her what we want her to be. Regardless of how sexy, quirky, or sensitive the developers made her external features, some, if not all, of the players would be disappointed or put off. And if the players are not completely enthralled by Delilah, her ultimate rejection would not provide the emotional impact that the developers wanted. Again, if we saw her, the themes and moral of the story would be entirely subverted.

4. "Well, I just didn't like it."
That's totally fine. Everyone has their own tastes and opinions. No matter how great a product or piece of art is, it will never appeal to everyone. I, for one, despise horror films, but that does not mean that there have never been legitimate, well-crafted films in that genre. No matter how much I defend the artistic merits of this game, I can never force you to like it. I can only attempt to justify the choices the developers made. Might there have been better endings? Sure. Were there enough clues in the story to make the ending feel justified? Totally. Did the ending uphold the morals and themes the developers wanted to get across? Very much so. Therefore, is it a good ending? Yes.

Let's avoid spoilers here and get right to the meat of it.

Firewatch bills itself as a mystery game, and while it does have elements of mystery mixed in, I feel like that's an inadequate description of the content you're going to experience. Firewatch can more appropriately be considered a narrative adventure. What this means is that you will spend a lot of time exploring and interacting with the world you're placed in, and you'll have a lot of dialogue to listen to.

The gameplay itself is intentionally simple, and in many ways plays a bit like Portal. You'll find yourself collecting a reservedly small number of tools, completing tasks given to you by a faceless overseer, and learning about your environment and its past. You'll have plenty of time to sandbox, wander, explore, and so on, but ultimately you're still following a narrative, and the game will gently nudge you along towards your goals.

Unlike in Portal, you'll never encounter complex puzzle mechanics, and interactions with others are limited to, more or less, handheld radio. This is where Firewatch reveals its true colors as an adventure and suspense game rather than as a pure mystery. Firewatch is a pure, old-school adventure game smashed together with the visual novel genre -- just, replace visual with audio.

Much like in the Monkey Island, Ace Attorney, and the vast assortment of, "escape the room," games, you, as the protagonist Henry, will be collecting various objects from within your explorable environments, then using them to interact with the world in meaningful ways. Henry might find some rope and attach it to a climbing anchor, unlocking new passages... or he might find himself in possession of a flashlight to help him see in caves or at night. In this regard, Firewatch more than demonstrates its genius as an adventure narrative.

What you should know going in:
-- The primary focus of the game revolves around Henry and his relationship with his supervisor, Delilah. The nature of this relationship can vary depending on the choices you make during the game, very similar to how Bioware treated dialogue in games like Dragon Age and Mass Effect.
-- This is not an action game. Unlike Portal, you will not be training yourself for a final showdown against a big bad evil guy. This is a narrative adventure game, with a focus on Henry's exploration of both his environment and himself.
-- The ending is foreshadowed early in the game and is pretty much a foregone conclusion, but what's not quite as obvious is how Henry and Delilah will interpret events as they unfold. Remember that this is basically a visual novel game in many ways, and that the point and focus is on the evolving relationship between the characters involved.

Should you buy Firewatch?

Do you like adventure games? Yes.
Do you like suspense games? Yes.
Do you like visual novel games? Yes.
Do you like games that provide heavy immersion? Yes.
Do you like action games? No.
Do you like strategy games or puzzle games? No.
Do you like games with easter eggs or that reward thoroughness? No.
Do you like to gloss over the story of a game in favor of its mechanics? No.

Firewatch isn't for everyone. It is an adventure narrative with elements of suspense and mystery. It plays, start to finish, like an adventure narrative, and its conclusion is extremely similar to how many Hidden Object games (adventure games in their own right) wrap things up.

The pure adventure genre has been predominantly catered towards a female audience for some time, and many female gamers who enjoy such games will likely enjoy the rare male perspective in their otherwise female-driven genre. For male gamers, you'll find yourself able to relate to Henry and sympathize with his isolation. The game is presented well enough that any male players that enjoy it should seriously consider picking up another adventure title and playing as a female protagonist -- many adventure games are just as good from the female perspective, and if you liked Firewatch, then you deserve to give them a chance.

Overall, I rate Firewatch a 9/10. It loses 1 point as I feel as though the disposable camera Henry discovers could have ultimately been put to better use by the developers -- you'll understand once you complete the game.

This game is brilliant. The reviews will be mixed, and there is a very good reason why, but it is absolutely worth your time and money to play.

What is the (singular*) major problem?
- The overarching plot is a fantastic build-up to a terrible let-down (it is fragmented / non sequitur)
- The game is very, very, very short (3 hours)
- I concluded that they had a perfect design up front, then ran out of budget during production

* Three bullets to describe one problem - the first is the problem, the second is an effect, the third is a cause.

Why is it good despite these problems?
- The micro-level dialogue is super fun to listen to, and most of it isn't about the overarching story
- The environment is beautiful to look at
- This is possibly the most relaxing game I have ever played
- The character backgrounds are well done
- The smaller story arc in the first few days is well done
- The ending sequence is well done

If you're still on the fence after reading this, please consider the following: while this game does have a couple of major shortcomings, they are obviously logistical. I maintain this game is worth your time, BUT EVEN IF IT ISN'T,
it is clear that whoever made this will churn out something brilliant given the proper resources (e.g. revenue from this game), AND EVEN IF THEY WOULDN'T,
this game has an extraordinary potential to start an entire genre of amazing imitators, AND EVEN IF IT DIDN'T,
there are still a ton of things to be learned from what it does well.

In the best case, it is a flawed masterpiece.
In the worst case, it is a tool for pushing our industry forward and inspiring other developers.

Fireatch is a walking simulator with adventure game elements developed by Campo Santo. The player takes control of Henry, a middle-aged man who decides to take a summer job as a firewatcher at the Shoshone National Forest in Wyoming, in order to escape his tense family situation. Firewatch is about following Henry as he goes around the woods dealing with various issues as he's guided by his senior watcher, Delilah, via radio.

Your main goal is to guide Henry through the woods as you follow Delilah instructions, with some help from a map and a compass and report to her anything you find interesting till the next day is triggered. At several points you are free to choose what answer you are going to give her and collect the objects you come across. Henry can also find a camera to take photos of the environments, althought the thing doesn't have any impact on the game proper.

While Firewatch's artistic direction and voice acting are good and can hold the player's interest for a while, this game has two serious flaws that seriously compromised my enjoyment of it:

1) The whole plot department of this game is unremarkable at best and downright annoying at worst. Firewatch's story doesn't seem to be able focus itself on a single point and just goes on till the ending, where nothing is resolved in a definititve manner and the time you spent in the Shoshone National Forest feels wasted. Not helping matters is the fact that the promised interactive storytelling angle is also completely absent from Firewatch (the choices you make are esthetic at best and only change the tone used by Delilah during conversations. Nothing you do alters the game's story in any significant way)

2) The pacing of this game is downright schizophrenic. The first two days have a nice pacing where you, along with Henry, get to know the setting and are led from point A to point B by things happening to you as you walk by. During the following days, however, you have either to sit through really short sequences where you get to control Henry for some minutes at best, then the screen fades to black and you are off to the next day or walk through huge distances to reach your next objective in very familiar surrounding at that point.

I think someone is entitled to expect something better from a videogame like Firewatch, even if it's a walking simulator

This game finally prompted me to write my first review. I have over 300 games in my library.

Firewatch. Wow. The wonderfully constructed virtual landscape carries this intricate visual novella, and in the process, takes you though every conceivable human emotion. This game's true challenge is purely a mental one. Despite the fact that this game is physically paced with consistency, you will go from having your heart racing while feeling like you are running for your life, to a sense of drearily monotonous hiking, as if you are going nowhere. You will feel completely lost one moment, and then feel joy at making what seems like the biggest discovery a minute later. You'll feel safe and comfy in your tower one day, and obvious and exposed the next. You will not be able to resist Delilah's charm and witty conversation, yet your temper will flare with anger at her more than once. 

The deeper down the rabbit hole you go, the more that Henry experiences, the more you will wonder whether anything you do is important or not, or if anything you say matters. But by that time you have been cast on the path, you will be too emotionally involved, and you will learn everything you need to in time.

The virtual world set forth in the game is wonderful, as is the simple ways in which you interact with it. Yes, you could even call this a "hiking simulator". Any experienced gamer will have no trouble navigating this world, although you will be checking your map and compass frequently. This game is visually appealing. My one small teeny tiny complaint has to do with getting "stuck" occasionally on certain textures, which take about 10 times longer to get out of than fall into, but don't let this sway you (this is just how I play games, trying to go everywhere, I'd probably drive people crazy if they watched me play Skyrim, but I suppose in a game where all you do is walk around, that I could have at least taken better care to be careful where I was going.)

Debating how and when and why I want to replay this.

What I have started to discover more and more lately, is that I am a sucker for a great trailer; A great trailer and a great thumbnail. As such, I had very high hopes for Firewatch, maybe a little too high? I can't tell just yet. It certainly didn't blow my mind like The Cat Lady, or Sword & Sworcery, but there are definitely aspects of Firewatch that make it stand out from the crowd. The critic in me mourns for opportunities missed, but then the optimist in me is left with a series of images and feelings that have really stuck with me from playing Firewatch.

Cissy Jones' voice acting, to me, is the backbone of this entire game. That may cause cringes for some people, but playing Firewatch reinforced for me that the quality of the voice acting plays a MASSIVE role in how immersed I can get in a game. Throw in a good, original story, as well as plenty of opportunities for screenshots, and you basically have all the reasons I play story-driven games. The quality of the protagonists voice acting doesn't even come close to that of the lead female character unfortunately, which left me feeling like I wasn't the star of the show, rather just some Dev's Brother who does commercials for men's incontinence pads, and would do this job for $37 and a case of beer. But to be fair, there are VERY few male protagonists voices that I haven't found off-putting, so play on I guess.

Firewatch is short. Normally I'm okay with that, but in this case I was left with a little bit of a bitter taste in my mouth, and for once it wasn't because I'm a tight arse and expect AAA games for $15. No. In this case it's because the story itself is absolutely full to the brim with potential to flesh out the experience further, and provide a positively exceptional psychological thriller title. All the plot hooks are there, 90% of the items and locations are there, but unfortunately underutilised. Capo Santo have all the bones for such an excellent story in Firewatch, and I was totally sucked in to be sure, but I always had this niggling feeling like more should be happening. I don't know, maybe I'm subliminally comparing it to stabby-stabby-murder games and I've missed the point?

The beginning of the game uses a very interesting "choose your past" kind of mechanic, and includes some pretty weighty emotional themes that set the tone for the entire game, and immediately had me sitting up to pay attention, and I really would have liked to have seen that mechanic used more often throughout the game. Not only would it have given the game a better sense of coherence (The film style in the 2004 version of Dawn of the Dead comes to mind), but it could have been used to subvert some of the uneventful walking throughout the game.

What Firewatch has managed to do is get me very interested in Campo Santo. It's very obvious from this game that they are extremely capable writers, able to deliver original concepts. The "Girls at the Lake" scenario absolutely enthralled me, and was beautiful in its simplicity. In the future though, I think I will definitely be expecting more from the gameplay in their games: How they make me go from one excellent plot thread to the next. Simply because with Firewatch they have shown a world of promise for future releases.

First off, NO SPOILERS.  I'm going to talk around story stuff but not about it directly.

Whenever I'm on the fence about picking up a story-driven game, and multiple reviews say it has an "incomplete" or "non" ending, I get intrigued.  In my experience, people often respond this way to games that leave their endings open to interpretation, or leave you dwelling on a theme, and I like that a lot of the time.  That might just be me.  But I liked the endings in Soma, and Life Is Strange, for example, so maybe you can use that to calibrate how useful my opinion is to you.

Anyway, I got exactly what I wanted out of Firewatch: Honest Hearts-style (the Fallout: NV DLC) exploration that uncovers a story, plenty of chatter with interspersed dialogue choices that affect the story in unpredictably large and small ways, and good commentary on some core themes.  It doesn't hurt that the game is very pretty, either, although I'm unapologetically a story-oriented sort of gamer.  I just don't want game devs to feel like they have to put exclamation points at the end of statements they're trying to make with a game.  This game is about exploration, in themes as well as environment.  The ending is fine the way it is.  I just wanted that out there in the morass of opinions.

Just finished the game. It really is something else. It is unusual and quite short, that I have to admit. I finished it in 5.1 hours in two sittings.

I was genuinly spooked more than once and the odd twigs breaking here and there behind me sure didn't help to make me feel safer... You have a front row seat as the story turns from a nice quiet hike in the woods to something a lot more mysterious and less serene.
Some reviewers have criticised the ending, though I found it fitting. Yes, I was expecting something else, especially after the build-up, but it does fit the story. What I really loved was the sense of urgency on the last day. I won't spoil what causes it, but if you play it, you will know what I mean. 

The graphics are unusual, but lush and bright. The surroundings are beautiful and offer many a picture worthy scene. Some stunning screenshots have been shared on the community page. Hiking through different terrain feels natural and fluid. Yes, it takes a while, but this is a game that you can take your time in, there is no rush. The map and compass help if you get lost (which will happen occasionally), but some trails you will know pretty well in the latter half of the game. 

You get very used to hearing the voice on the other end of the radio, but beware, you can make her angry, which will lead her to step away from the radio for a while. There are several dialog tree options, though I presume the end will remain the same, no matter which option you choose. Chatting with Delilah is entertaining and the only connection to "civilisation" you have in the game. The dialogue is well written and gives you the feeling that a real person is on the other end. Both characters have their own share of secrets and chips on their shoulders and it only makes them more human. You start to genuinely like both characters early on. 

All in all I had a lot of fun and will play it again just to explore more, take my time to enjoy the scenery and to try some other dialog options. Definitely worth getting as it is a unique experience.

I've been eyeing this game for a while and, due to a recent sale, finally snagged it. From the art direction to the semi-eerie, yet totally fitting soundtrack to the intricate story telling, this game is a masterpiece. The visuals are often stunning, except for the overbearing reddish yellow hue that occasionally plagued the evenings of the Wyoming wilderness. The strange tint tended to feel too artificial for me, though this is just my opinion. This game is very detailed. The posters are worth looking at, every book has a cool cover (probably designed by Olly Moss), and the landscapes are vast and varied. The graphics look similar to Team Fortress 2, but I'd say they surpass the graphics of most indie games.

I just played through the story in one fell sitting, so to speak, as I think that gives me the best impression of the story. Taking breaks relieves the tension, and boy was this game tense. Don't confuse intense for tense, however. Firewatch is very relaxed for a good half of the game. Heck, the only thing you really DO in the game is walk around. What makes the game so tense is the backstories given to the two characters and how they relate to the main plot of the game. Upon completing the story, I was left wanting more from the fantastically voice-acted characters. I felt that the characters were so well fleshed out that I simply wanted more of them. The dialogue that takes place between Henry, the protagonist, and Delilah, your boss, makes them truly feel like real people. They have their flaws; neither is a paragon of virtue. This, however, only makes them more relatable. While the mystery aspect of the plot felt a little underwhelming come the conclusion, the real story lies within the real/witty/tense conversations the two characters have. 

In the end, if you're willing to spend time maneuvering the game world (which is well designed, I might add. Very rarely got lost.) and are all about great storytelling through narrative exposition and personal experience, this is your game. Give it your time, attention and patience, and you won't be disappointed.

Firewatch seems like something built around the conceit of trying to capture the dissonant alternation between the vast scale of nature and its intimacy. It's really remarkable how, in this vast section of the Wyoming wilderness, you come to tie emotions to specific locations. 
That, more than anything, is the game's achievement, but that's not to say it slacks off elsewhere: there's an intriguing, twisty story that works both on a high-minded metaphorical level, exploring themes of alienation and denial, and also just as an unsettling mystery. It's sold by a pair of fantastic voice performances (including Mad Men's Rich Sommer) and the aforementioned beautiful, intimidating environs (courtesy legendary pop-artist Olly Moss.)
Those looking for a wilderness-survival game, in the vein of, say, Rust, may want to look elsewhere. Firewatch does have some fun orienteering elements, but it's much more of a story-driven experience--no crafting here.

Firstly ignore my 9 hours playtime, I accidentally left the game on pause for several hours, this game takes about 4 hours as other reviewers have noted. There are a ton of reviewers that hated the story, or enjoyed it until the end. I was a little bit worried about playing this game and a really terrible ending ruining it for me, so perhaps it was my expectations leading up to the end of the game, but I was really satisfied with the ending. During the game I was quite immersed in the environment and the relationship between the main characters. I found that the building and release of tension was really well done, and I feel like the resolution was totally appropriate for what this game was. I can accept that people didn't like the ending, but I don't think it was a bad ending. A bad ending is one with Deus Ex Machina, or characters doing things those characters wouldn't do, or countless loose ends that remain untied, or something completely unrelated to the story elements changing the narrative entirely. This game doesn't have any of those problems, it just doesn't resolve as completely as I guess some people might like.  That doesn't make it bad, it means they didn't like it and that's okay. I personally really appreciated how the story ended, so don't let that be the thing that stops you from playing it.

This game is f---in' awesome.  If that kind of language offends you, then this is not the game for you, as it primarily involves two adults engaged in adult conversations and using adult language.  If your fine with that sort of thing, keep reading.


*MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD*


Before you get to even get to really see anything you are presented with a series of emotional choices - several of them are HARD choices - that set up your character and his personality.  Whatever you choose, you, as an average joe named Henry, are made to spend 14 years watching your relationship with a beautiful and intelligent Aussie woman named Julia grow, flourish, and then die in the most horrible of ways.

Then it is May of 1989.  Julia has been taken away from your care.  Your dog has died.  You take a summer job as a firespotter lookout with the National Forest Service, and wind up hiking to your post in the beautifully recreated wilderness of the Shoshone National Forerst, just east of Yellowstone, in Wyoming.  You are tasked with watching for fires, dealing with campers causing fire hazards and whatever else your supervisor, Delilah, tells you to do.

Delilah has been doing the job for ten years.  She's an alcoholic.  She has issues.  She sees you as a potential friend, or maybe more?  The choices you make in your talks with her will determine how far that friendship goes.  You can be standoffish and cold or open an engaging, but the more you open up to her, the more she opens up to you.  This can have consequences as you work together and unravel the mysteries of the Shoshone.

(These chats, by the way, are all done over a walkie-talkie, you don't see her face-to-face, since her lookout tower is six miles away across an impassible ravine.  And your reaction time with answering her questions may end up determining your answer, or if you answer her at all.  If you screw up with an untinded response you may have to reload your last save point to get it right. Or just run with it and see what happens.)


*PROS*
 - Gorgeous scenery:  I can not gush over this enough.  Every every tree, branch, leaf, and blade of grass sways with the wind in a perfectly natural way.  The canyons and rock formations all look like they were carved out by God himself, rather than a graphic artist.  Hiking and climbing your way through this landscape - something you have to do a lot of - never feels like a chore.

 - Deeply immersive and emotional story:  By the time the forest starts to burn (the game's not called Firewatch for nothing) and your view of the wilderness is blocked by smoke and ash, it doesn't seem to matter, because by then the story has ramped up the tension enough to keep you hiking toward your goals without the need for scenic distractions.  Delilah's voice on the radio, alternating between skepticism, whimsy, paranoia and near-panic, is ample distraction on its own.

 - Great voice acting:  Every conversation comes across as completely natural.  Nothing sounds phoned-in.  Both main character's voice actors are alumni of succesful television shows, one of which is the same show the game's writer worked on.  They don't treat this like a step down in their careers.  They are completely on-point with every piece of sharp, witty, poignant and frantic dialog.

 - Simple, intuitive controls and interface:  What do you need to navigate in the backwoods country?  A well-marked map, a compass, and nothing else.  So that's what you get, aside from a helpful "you are here" marker and the last hundred yards or so of whatever path you walked to get there traced out for you, to help you backtrack and find the trail if you get yourself lost.  Basic WASD-Mouse controls and a few reconfigurable command keys in mostly easy reach complete the deal.  I remap R and LCtrl to Radio, LShift to Jog, Map and Compass from M and N to X and Z, and assign MsWhlUp/Dn to be alternate dialog selection controls so I don't have to use the arrow keys.  This brings all the controls under my left hand or onto my mouse.

- Replayability:  As mentioned, your dialog choices can completely change your relationship with Delilah and even some minor plot points.  You can be a complete jerk to her the first time through, then the next time you can form an open and trusting friendship.  Then you can play around with different answers and see how they affect the dynamic and the game, or discover new things out in the Forest, which prompt new discussions with Delilah.  Or just hike around and find new and interesting vistas to photograph with your camera, which you can upload to twitter or facebook and people will be convinced they're pictures of the real world.  I've played the game through twice now back-to-back.  I'm trying other games now but I'll be back soon, if for nothing else than to pay another visit to the beautiful woods and canyons of the Shoshone.


*CONS*

 - The game is too short:  It's taken me about seven hours on each of my playthroughs, but others (who obviously are not big into exploring) have done it in four or five hours.  It seems to me that there could be a lot more for the player to do before things start to go bad; build a fishing dock on the lake, clear brush in advance of the fire, round up campers and help them evacuate, etc,  And then the mystery story felt like it could get drawn out further too.  My gameplay time could have easily been doubled, and to a lot of people, paying $20 for a game that wraps in five hours - even a game as good as this - feels like a rip-off.

 - I honestly can't think of anything else.


*BOTTOM LINE*

If your the kind of gamer who just mindlessly completes tasks and asks "okay, what's next?" kindly move along, this game is not for you.  But if your the sort who can take the time to explore this world and the relationship with Delilah and appreciates the intricacies and attention to detail, the payoff cannot be measured nor expressed.

Firewatch is a 4-5 hour adventure through a heavily forested Wyoming park. You never really see other people up close, but you do have a radio buddy that keeps you company. The game styles itself "an adult game about adults having adult conversations" and that's a pretty apt description. Sadly, the ending is incredibly simplistic and fails to tie together any of the storylines or themes.

The best part of Firewatch is the writing and voice acting. The main lead is Rich Sommer (you know him as Harry Crane from Mad Men) and he nails this role. Cissy Jones is a video game mainstay and she delivers wonderfully as well. Put them together and you have a legitimately funny yet poignant conversation that basically continues for the entire length of the game. The same story without them would've been a shadow of itself.

The graphics are simple but well executed and consistently styled. The music, on the other hand, is amazing. Some of my favorite moments in the game would have been boring walks through the woods without the music. Each track managed to transform idle time into something serene and precious.

The mechanics are largely like any other "walking simulator." I've had such good experiences with that moniker that even though I know it started as an insult I'm beginning to think developers should take it as a complement. The single biggest problem with Firewatch's particular implementation is that there is a minimum distance to interact with objects. Watching someone struggle with trying to climb a rope they are right next to is painful. "No you need to back up. You need to be farther away from the rope to climb it." That's advice anyone playing this game should take to heart, but it's stupid that it has to be given in the first place. There's also a bizarre bug where the reticle can be partially on an object, but then pressing shift to bring up the radio moves the reticle off the object. Talk about frustrating and unintuitive. Though other than those complaints the game plays like you would expect.

If you're looking for a game where the focus is on the journey instead of the destination then you should pick up Firewatch. The ending is truly disappointing compared to what it could have been. It's almost like the developers had less of an imagination than the people playing their game. I'm holding out hoping for some alternate, apocryphal interpretations to gain traction. Until then, the journey alone is well worth the price.

I grew up a gamer, starting with Infocom text adventures on a C64. Through middle school, high school, college, two marriages, two children, many jobs -- I have played thousands of games on many consoles. Along the way, life changed me. While I enjoy the occasional FPS romp or a convoluted strategy game, the older I've grown, the more I've skipped off of the surface of most games I've tried. They are mechanics or they require twitch or they have a shallow, predictable, and/or uninteresting story. I don't put those games at fault because they often are good at what they try to be. I just chalk it up to changing tastes and move along.

Firewatch, to me, is a deep breath of clean crisp air. Here I finally was exploring some of the emotions I've grown into and playing a narrative that reflects nuanced struggles of a life well-lived. Firewatch is an adult game, not for nudity, violence, drugs, etc... but for emotion. The story is engaging; simple dialogue choices reflect nuances in emotion rarely seen in interactive media. And they bind together into an emotional narrative arc that should allow considerate players to engage with the characters in an uncommon and powerful way. Here we get attached and we think about the meaning of love, happiness, abandonment, and discovery. And the characters build up small concerns into large problems and work through issues of trust and doubt, culminating in an ending that embraces all of those emotions. I've read the gripes about the ending and I understand why some people feel the way they do. For me, however, Firewatch is about embracing ambiguity and establishing boundaries of normalcy in times of emotional turmoil. The ending placed me, as a player, on a pedestal where I could review and consider the narrative arc as a unifying experiece between characters. Ultimately, it is a story that has no physical payoff, so to speak, so I'm glad the developers avoided trying to include one.

Most of all, I hope Firewatch signals the beginning of an age of games that explore the complex layers of emotions and decisions we experience as adults. It was a powerful 5 hours for me. I'll always remember Firewatch as the first game that treated me like an adult by respecting and realistically playing to my emotions.

Well finished the game in just slightly over 3 hours, and felt I needed to add a review on this.

Firstly I would like to state with a simple fact that most people would come into a game like this thinking that somehow, and somewhere your decision and the way you play this game will have some impact to the outcome…. Well…. It doesn’t... from what I can see (and certainly willing to be corrected there).

I have avoided spoilers as much as possible, but I will give a warning that this might contain things which might make you think I have told you too much – so please do not read if you fear that.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Firstly the things I liked about the game:

* The voice acting is amazing, and the humour and communication between the two main characters in the story is well done and give the story a great "real life" feel to it. 

The quality of the voice acting, and how much you can believe their dialogue would be like that in real life was more a testament to two very good voice actors than to good story writing. 

It saved the game from less than 30 minutes of game play, and helped me finish the game to just hear the two characters banter away like they did - was just (again) amazing!

* The graphics were "good". It is a type of graphic style that you either get right, or very wrong. 

I have been disappointed in the other "cartoon coloured" games (and the like)  for example I really didn’t like the artistic type feel of Game of Thrones, but in this game it felt like an Animated Movie, and worked well because it didn’t make everything feel “this is attempting to be realistic” and thus giving it that "creepy" vibe, but instead gave the game the feeling of being an interactive animation movie.

But, sorry to say, that was pretty much all I could say positive about this game. While the above was (again) amazing they were shadowed by a lot by some fundamental flaws that made me overall disappointed on the game.

* Firstly the pacing of the game was all off. 

3 hours to complete a game at the price being asked is just insane, and especially since most of that time is walking (or running) around a few limited locations to get from point A to point B. 

They do add “caches” to get along the way which contain some items that spark off conversation between the main characters, but there was no apparent relevance to them, and to be honest I think you could play the whole game without opening them, so they were time fillers.

I believe that if you removed all the walking (running), and no-point collectable things (like finding all the caches, you would be left with probably an hour or maybe an hour-and-half of story content.

Ultimatelly it felt like going to an expensive resturant, waiting three hours for your meal and getting a single pea with a plate full of sauce.

* And the story was a let down. 

And to follow on from the resturant, you found the pea and sauce tasted like week old stale bread... 

...Because that is how the story made me feel.

I will give it its due however, the story started strong(ish), and did really build the characters, and even built up the suspense on what was happening. 

It then got more interesting as it went along as you started the suspense being built more, you not really knowing what was really going on, and it was starting to get into being a a triller worth all the time I was putting into it, and then.... it ended with probably the biggest let down I have felt in my gaming history. 

It wasn’t a hugely bad ending, and some would probably say it was "realistic", but for the amount of time building up to something exicting, and then getting an ending that was so left field and so mundain, it felt like a massive disappointment. 

It just felt like the developers (or story writers) just ran out of steam and said, “okay, well… let’s just end it now and make the whole thing ...... "

The biggest insult to injury here is that the story did sudden things which just made utterly no sense, and they all seemed to happen just because the creators wanted to railroad you down into a quick end of the story instead of putting a more thought into the story where you had to find the clues yourself. An example of this is when you find the Cave key… this was just randomily done, with no real answer, and when you do find out the answer you are just left feeling WTF!

To be honest if they had just made it an animated movie wthout the interactive parts you would have less than an hour to watch, and at least you wouldn't have felt like you had wasted 3 hours of your life running around and getting what added up to a slap in the face for an ending. 

* The value for money is pretty low. 

I understand that making a game takes time, and also they need to recoup costs – however – having a 3 hour game cost so much, and most of that time is just walking (or running), it really felt like I wasted my money. Even on special this game wasn’t worth the money when compared to other games of the same type, and better quality, and longer game play.

* No real fire watching, alerting or anything. 

You are introduced to tools on how to report a fire, and yet there is nothing to do in the game with that tool. 

There are two fires that comes up, and each of them are found and reported before you get to do anything about it. 

To be honest this was probably one of the biggest disappointements because the developers lost a great chance to give more context to the game, and not just around the force feed - pretty weak - story that was being done.

* I felt there appeared to be limited value of the options and communication you have, and it felt really like you were railroaded through the story. 

Don't get me wrong here, the actions you picked in converrsation did have some impact to the way in which they interacted, however there was no long impact to the game play.

I cannot fully validate this since I would not really want to live through playing this multiple times. However, having read on Google and other reviews this also appears to be a valid observation.  

And then the ending on how to relate to Delilah (one of the main characters – supervisor) is just totally taken from you and just…. Well again, it feels like you (as the player) just add no value to the game.

In the case of this game, I can say that the hype to me was far more than the delivery. Maybe the hype just made me blind to what the game was, but, be sure to read the reviews yourself and decide from them - unlike me - stupid me :)

But I will state again that the the voice acting and the dialogue between the two main characters was (again!!) amazing and certainly what saved this game from what I would have been an utter flop to me. However, you can get pretty much a fair idea of that by just watching the trailers, or even watching youtube play through. 

To me it holds nothing against other games of the type and they just didn’t add enough to the game to make it feel worth the money or the time I invested into the game.

I hope that the developers do another game but this time add more to the contents of the “GAME” so that you feel you get more value from the experience, and in fact... well get a game!

I initially thought I would wait to play Firewatch, but ended up breaking that resolve early on in the game’s life. In retrospect, that was an excellent decision as Firewatch is a quality game well worth your time. I felt the mystery and intrigue surrounded by lush scenery and an interesting interplay between the protagonist and his never seen mentor/supervisor made for an exceptional experience.

[h1]Story[/h1]

Although a walking simulator at heart (a genre I particularly enjoy), the dialogue in Firewatch was outstanding and as close to natural as it possibly could have been. You really feel as if you are taking part in something that is at times sweet and sensitive and at others tense, foreboding, or simply mysterious.

You play as Henry, a man who has taken a summer job as a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness to get away from the turmoil and tragedy surrounding your personal life. In a sense, you are placing the world on hold as you leave to catch your breath and simply be away from society for a spell. Your only human contact is with your supervisor, Delilah, whom you only interact with over a handheld radio.

In every way, Firewatch was a thoughtful journey through mid life crisis and dramatic change in a pair of individuals lives, the way in which they tried to escape their realities, and the way they started to sort through their issues via communicating with each other over walkie talkie. The subplot, presented as the main plot throughout, was a mystery surrounding a stalker and possible murder(s). Although at the forefront, as I said, this was really the subplot. The main plot being one of self discovery through adversity and communication. A catharsis of the human spirit if you will.

The presentation of story in Firewatch is both many layered and brilliant. This is a game that pulls at all your emotional strings at various points throughout your playthrough. Some things are relevant to the mystery you are investigating, others are specific to the relationship you build with your unseen supervisor, and yet others are completely unrelated to any of that, but serve to add life and luster to the setting.

One major complaint I have heard and read about Firewatch was with regards to the ending. It is my opinion that the ending served as a masterful conclusion to the game, and while it did leave some things to the players imagination, I think the topic of the ending is quite overstated. I felt it could not have ended in any other way, and it made complete sense when you factor in the character development and interaction between Henry and Delilah. Without revealing any specifics, I would just say that I think people let their hopes for a certain type of ending cloud their observations of what was made quite obvious throughout. Firewatch had to end the way it did in my opinion, or the journey to get there would not have been nearly as relevant.

I found the story to be touching and sincere. A true examination of humanity and the soul such as it is. Not many games can claim to possess as much depth in their writing as Firewatch can. This is an easy 10 out of 10.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

Gameplay in Firewatch is fairly standard walking simulator/exploration fare. Walk, run, jump, pick up and examine items. There are areas where you will need to tie off a rope and climb, or will simply have to hoof it up rock shelves and such. The majority of your time will be spent walking around the national park, investigating the aforementioned murder mystery, trying to find some vandals that have been littering and some possible arsonists as well, or simply wandering around taking in the sites in a far more mundane fashion. When not doing all that, you will be in your tower, sleeping or chatting with Delilah.

There is a photography feature offered about half way through the Firewatch. That was a nice feature in my opinion. You can take pictures in game which also are featured at the end, and serve to add depth to your personal experience.

I found nothing too revolutionary in this regard, but the gameplay was solid and I experienced no technical issues whatsoever.

This is a solid 8 out of 10.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]

Visually, Firewatch is also a beautiful game, but in a more muted way than you might expect from a game that released within the last year. It was evocative, and really added to the story without getting in the story’s way. Although muted, the world was alive and vibrant in every way possible. This was a unique presentation that I think will be copied many times in the future. Truly a backdrop for the story being told without ever trying to seize more attention that is demanded of it.

Understated brilliance. 9 out of 10.

[h1]Sound [/h1]

The ambient sounds in Firewatch were much like the graphics. Present and relevant, but only as much as was necessary to help convey more depth and meaning to the story. However, the voice acting is probably the single most important aspect as a method of conveying the story in Firewatch to the player, and the voice acting in this game was done to perfection. You can tell the actors really took the time to understand and allow themselves to become fully invested in their characters, and that fact was in evidence throughout. Without the fine work done here, the story in Firewatch would have been a shallow shell of its magnificent self. Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones as Henry and Delilah truly deserve recognition for such excellence, and voice director Jared Emerson-Johnson should share in that credit as well for getting so much out of the cast.

Also an easy 10 out of 10

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

All told, the game weighed in at about 4 hours, and I don’t really feel that there is any replay value. However, Firewatch was easily worth the asking price of entry for a single 4 hour experience in my opinion, so strong was the writing and the character development.

In an attempt to come to grips with the hardships in your life — your wife has late stage Alzheimers and can barely recall who you are — you take up a job as firewatch in a remote forest location. This game is quite on the cerebral side; there is little direct interaction with the world around you, and your sole lifeline is the radio contact you have with your unseen colleague and supervisor over in the next watchtower. 

This is absolutely not a bad game, and I did enjoy it.

But, I am torn on whether or not I should actually recommend it. On the one hand, this game does have a very immersive story that takes place in a beautiful setting. The premise of the game is excellent, and for the most part the execution is great as well.

On the other hand though, my leisurely play-through took no more than four hours. I am not in the habit of rushing games, and I feel that I've thoroughly exhausted the majority of (radio) conversation options. The world, while serenely beautiful, may seem open ended at first glance, but the paths you'll take in the order ordained by the narrative become apparent quick, breaking the suspense of disbelieve, and making the world feel artificial.

Story-wise the writing is good, but it feels as if there is so much more to explore and achieve. As it stands, it is hard not to get the impression that the writers had to wrap things up in a hurry, deciding to just [i]torch[/i] the unresolved threads of the story. What disappoints me is that the protagonist spends three months as a firewatchman, but the game just skips days at first, and weeks later just to get to the days where the main story progresses. This would have been a superbly interesting game if it could make you experience the utter loneliness and introspection of the character you are playing at a suitable pace, but there is just not enough content for that (both in terms of conversation and world).

There is potential here, but Firewatch just falls short of hitting that high mark.

This game has many technical aspects that make it excellent, including immersive environments, good lighting, and a great soundtrack that fades perfectly and never gets boring.

But what makes it really stand out is the delivery of the story. It presents questions that intrigue and involve, but doesn't become weighed down with loose ends. It builds plenty of suspense through plot alone, without having to rely on jump-scares. The story itself is fresh. Most engaging of all is the dialogue that takes place between the protagonist and the other main character of the game.

Some have voiced disappointment over the lack of alternate story paths, and I do agree that a little diversity in player choice would be welcome. While the player can approach events in several different ways, these decisions only really impact the dialogue, and have no real bearing on the development of the plot. This does limit replayability significantly, though, for those who are willing to hunt, there are many rewarding secrets hidden throughout the game.

Another common criticism is that the ending is anticlimactic. I agree that it is disappointing, but I felt that it was absolutely satisfying and was "right". To me, this as a game about the moments and relationships in life that sweep us in, churn our world on its head, and, just as abruptly, come to an end.

And those are the ones worth remembering.

This project is more of a "The Stanley Parable" type. i.e. it explores using "games" as a new media for expressing your creativity. This is rather a very immersive movie than a game. You don't make any plot choices, you don't get different endings (maybe there is something hidden, but I hope not, because it feels very solid the way it is). Voice acting is amazing and visuals are obviously done with love and care. Game pace makes sure whenever you pass same area - it's in different time of day, so it looks and feels different. By no means it is a "walking simulator". It is much more mature and solid than e.g. Dear Esther. And that's probably why some people don't like the ending - because it is mature. It's not detective thriller for teens when you find out "gardener murdered her" on the last page. It's about enjoying the experience while it lasts, not rushing to the end for the plot,
If you enjoy good books, movies and music - this game is for you. 
Of course, it's not perfect: you can find some plotholes if you want, you can pick on absence of animals to spy on etc. etc. Btw, someone mentioned "meaningless interactions" like fishing rod, I think it was a good touch to the game.
Even the way it is, Firewatch rises standards on games in this genre, which aren't so many out there.

There are other reviews here that give a very good account of the game, so I'll just mention a few things that I especially liked.

• The character interaction between the two main protagonists is the meat of the game. This is a "talky" game, in that what they say is what matters most.

• What is expected of you next is sometimes pre-empted by other goals, which is something I like. You may think you have to hike back to your tower, only to run across something that changes the goal and the game shifts accordingly. I found this eliminated the sense of "I know what I have to do next and I don't want to do it" sort of dread I get in some games that get repetitive.

• The environment of the game is gorgeous. I'm not a particularly outdoorsy person, but the landscape is so thoroughly rendered and detailed that I found simply being immersed in the scenery to be very satisfying. Strangely enough, it also gave me some appreciation for what hikers get out of doing what they do.

• The sounds are wonderful. The voice acting, the music, the atmospheric noises, the background sounds of birds and wind and brush ... the audible experience goes hand in hand with the visual experience.

My advice: if the above appeals to you at all, buy this game and enjoy it!
