While there were some parts of the game I did not like, I can't not recommend Firewatch.

Before I start, let me just say that if you want any semblance of gameplay outside of the story, go to the options and turn off the tracker on the map. With that off, the game actually does have a challenge in the form of orienteering your character based on landmarks and directions.

When the closest a game comes to a challenge is finding your way to a place where the plot can develop, you know you're playing a walking simulator. But let me say that, for the most part, the rest of the game more than makes up for it.

[b] The Good [/b]

In the game, you play as Henry, a 40-something man who takes a Firewatch job in a national park for the summer to clear his mind after [spoiler] his wife has to live with her family after he's considered unfit to take care of her after she gets dementia [/spoiler]. After making some choices as to some specifics of Henry's past, the player controls him from here on out. The story does a good job of getting across the themes of escape and isolation.

Henry and Delilah are great characters. Their voice actors did incredible work getting the traits across in voice alone, and the dialogue was so well-written that they feel like real people. When Delilah, a character that you never see, has more depth and personality than most main characters in big-name titles (let alone [i] female [/i] main characters), you know a lot of effort was put into making the dialogue between her and Henry believable. And while the player does have a choice in what Henry can say, the choices, along with his delivery, still give him a distinct and consistent personality. No dialogue option feels out of place. The [spoiler] implied relationship Henry and Delilah can develop [/spoiler] feels real despite it being entirely over a radio. You would just be doing yourself a disservice if you decide to stay quiet most of the time, as many dialogue options branch out. The game leaves room for some replayability if you want to hear alternate conversations. Not much replayability in other aspects, but I'll get to that. 

One particularly memorable experience in the game for me was when [spoiler] Henry starts to have a breakdown, thinking he also developed dementia, and that everything from Day 1, including the conspiracy to spy on him and Delilah, is just some elaborate punishment he made in his own head for abandoning his wife because of her illness. Listening to Delilah trying her best to calm him down was one of the most touching moments I've heard in a game, and almost made me tear up. [/spoiler]

Also, the game looks gorgeous. The stylized forest is beautiful, and seeing the varied environment at all times of day just enhances the hiking experience. I was able to recreate most of the screenshots you see on the store page. I know some people didn't like the acoustic guitar that comes out of nowhere at times while you're walking, but I'm a sucker for ambient music, so I liked it. If you let yourself get lost in the game (metaphorically and literally), it feels like an experience.

[b] The Bad [/b]

Aside from the orienteering, there's not much in the way of gameplay. Most of what you do is go to a place and interact with something. This game is firmly a walking simulator, and anyone even slightly outside of the circle of people that enjoy that genre is going to get bored fast. 

Since the gameplay is more of a framework to hang the dialogue and story on, the game has to really bring it when it comes to those two things. And for most of the game, it does. Henry and Delilah's relationship gets developed on a steady pace, there's a lot of things to see and have them talk about, and there's an air of tension over the first few days. And what's essentially a montage in the middle of the game gets across the passing of time over a few months. And let me just say, for me, the game provides one of the biggest letdowns I've ever experienced in a game's story.

On the tail end of the summer, they discover [spoiler] some conspiracy to spy on them when Henry finds a clipboard containing highlights of their radio conversations. The last few days bring the tension right back up when the two of them try to figure out what's going on with the very small amount of information they have.

Do not get your hopes up that the big conspiracy has any kind of substantial payoff, because it doesn't. It essentially amounts to a facade of conspiracy that gets taken away in the form of a minute-long tape that you listen to while you get to the conspirator's hideout. One major hint at the conspiracy (a fenced off area with a research station in it) turns out to be something mundane, and should be common knowledge to a person in Delilah's position, but isn't for seemingly no reason other than to add to the mystique.

The relationship gets no payoff, either, since the two never meet, and essentially go their separate ways regardless. The circumstances also mean that both of them sound so down at the end of it all. I can see what the game's going for: trying to escape your life to find some new excitement only results in something equally sad or mundane in a different way. But I wish the game didn't reveal its key theme at the very end. Maybe a series of connected mysteries with mundane solutions over the course of the game would have worked instead of this. [/spoiler]

All I can say is that how the story is resolved seems both rushed and disappointing.

[b] Summary [/b]

If you're interested in beautiful stylized scenery, great dialogue, as well as a game centered around the interaction between two characters with great chemistry over the summer, then you'll love Firewatch. If, however, you want involved and action-filled gameplay, or the dramatic tension and conspiracy is all that drew you in to the game, don't get it. Firewatch feels very human and has well written dialogue and is, overall a good experience. But it should be bought [i] just [/i] for that experience, and not for the complexity it alludes to.

I bought this game a couple months ago, and am now getting around to reviewing it. 

It's fantastic. It's tough to find the language to describe this game, because Firewatch isn't about the challenge of gameplay as much as it is about experiencing a story. This genre has gotten the moniker "Walking Simulator" and I think that's pretty dismissive of the great things this game offers. Whether you play games regularly or not, if you're a fan of suberb storytelling, Firewatch is for you.

I love the outdoors, and the prospect of playing a park ranger was incredibly appealing to me. You use your map and a compass to navigate your neck of the woods to deal with things a park ranger deals with: teens setting off fireworks, downed power lines, overgrown trails. Your watch starts off fairly routine, mundane and isolated except for another firewatcher who you talk to over the radio. She's a veteran of the job, and you're a rookie and she guides you through the life of a firewatcher.

Just as you're getting used to a largely uneventful stint as a firewatcher, a mystery starts to unfold. You start to find clues hinting at something mysterious and potentially dangerous happening right under your nose. You no longer feel as safe up in your tower. You start to lose trust in your only lifeline. As events start to unfold, the story reaches Hitchcockian levels of suspense and paranoia. 

This game filled me with joy, scared the pants off me, and broke my heart several times. It's stylistic art direction is gorgeous, and brings the Shosohne National Forest to life. The voice acting is absolutely stellar. The small cast of actors in this game are incredibly talented and make the difference between what could have just been an enjoyable story, to an overall wonderful experience.

I strongly recommend playing Firewatch.

This game is not for everyone. 

            This is a fact but that does not make Firewatch a bad game. In fact, the game itself is artfully executed with a lot of love and care from the developers with wonderful environments, well-crafted characters, and a lovely build-up.  With hints of the art style of The Long Dark and the tension and wonderful dialogue (and slightly misleading) from Gone Home, Firewatch has a lot of factors which make the money for the experience- but once again, this game is NOT for everyone and many people would not feel that the game is worth your time. 

MY RECOMMENDATION: If you do not mind an emotional story about two people’s internal struggles with some great atmosphere, induced paranoia, beautiful graphics, and well developed characters that don’t involve as much external struggle, like fighting or shooting, then I recommend this game to you! 

Pros:
+ A beautiful environment bursting with color.
+ An atmosphere fitting any scenario the game thrusts you into.
+ Branching dialogue and impressive voice acting.
+ Emotion inducing in some parts.
+ Henry is a badass middle-aged guy and is a likable main character and is very human.

Cons:
-	NOT A HORROR GAME (could be misconstrued as one, not the fault of the game).
-	Easily disliked by those who do not like dialogue driven stories with more emotion driven themes than an actual threat.
-	Easily lost, even when following the map and a lot of back tracking. 
-	Getting from one point to another takes a long time, more so annoying when retracing steps BACK to a place you’ve already been. But the visuals and dialogue were interesting enough to keep me entertained. 

** SPOILERS **
The most complaints that I have seen regards the ending, which I felt turned many people off to it- expecting a government or secret organizational conspiracy but ending up with a normalized story about a man who becomes a hermit due and is an individual watching both Henry and Delilah and tapping into their walkie talkies. While I did not mind this ending, I felt that there were some unanswered questions in the end and a lot of facts used to make the player believe in the potential, large conspiracy that were not answered or solved.
The story is NOT about the conspiracy, it is about the individual people involved in solving his conspiracy- Henry and Delilah are our main characters with flaws and are attempting to decide what to do with situations in their lives and the story inevitably is meant to help the player guide these characters into a decision about their lives. It is an internal struggle, being driven and changed by an external struggle, for both of these characters. 

** Also to the reviewer who complained what Henry looked like and called him ugly- please pay more attention because his face was in a photograph and drawing since the beginning of the game **

Long Review (Some spoliers)

Firewatch is everything an indie game should strive NOT to be.  It’s short, has no replayability, no game mechanics and a bad story.   

It's a slice of life tale that is fed to you from the start as a man whose wife develops Alzheimer's in her 30's and is ultimately taken by her family to live in Australia.  The protagonist is Henry a tortured man that takes a job as a lookout for the summer to watch for fires alone in the wilderness.  This is explained all by unvoiced text at the start of the game.
  
Thus begins the story in where you are greeted by Delilah(head lookout) over the radio who will be the only other character this in game.  The game is really linear so you are pushed on to immediately tracking down people setting off fireworks.   Overall a decent start, you get down there and you fine 2 drunk college girls skinny dipping in the lake.  You return home and catch a glimpse of mysterious man making the player curious.  

At this point the game does a fine job of building tension and suspense.  The main problem the story some scenes exist purely for setting a tone of suspense or danger.  The player doesn’t realize this at first and is only made aware of it at the very end.  

For example, a lot more happens with those girls(supposedly) and they vanish from the story after they are reported missing.  No follow up or anything, all of tension and suspense around them vanishes and they become so unimportant the devs didn’t even mention their fate, yet are made out to be potential players in the mystery.  

The worse crime the devs committed was the ending, it totally ruins the story in so many ways.  To the point it poisoned the whole game for me.   After playing the game, I wish I had never played it….it was that bad.  It cheapens the whole experience which was the length of a long movie.  The game should have been way cheaper and the reviews are deceiving.  I’d be happy to go over my thoughts in detail on the game/steam forums but they appear to ban topics of criticism of this very flawed game.  

Don't get me wrong, there are good things about the game such as the dialogue and voice acting but that isn't enough.  That doesn't make the game.  

TL;DR?
Firewatch is the MOST overrated game I’ve ever seen based on the reviews and has one of the worst stories of any game I’ve ever played.

Relaxing 'story'-driven gameplay; exploring a scenic wilderness, reading notes, and chatting via radio with your new best friend. Places and objects can be somewhat interactive, though Firewatch is definitely a walking-simulator or interactive novella rather than a puzzler or platformer. I found the character and narrative elements to be touching, amusing, and thrilling in turn. 

Much of the interaction comes from getting to choose the protagonist's dialogue options. This succeeds in making you more emotionally invested in the constant character interactions, which are almost exclusively between the protagonist and someone he's in communication with over radio. However, these and the other few choices you can make do not seem like they have much impact on anything beyond immediate dialogue responses. Also, the multiple choices, and the fact that you may simply not find some interaction-triggers or even cause dialogue to cut off by moving along too fast, means you miss out on many entertaining moments. You would have to replay the game several times to experience everything, but I feel that's too much of a time investment for the few extra minutes of content it would equate to.

So, i'd like to start this off by saying that i bought this game on a discount.

Firewatch is not only a game about a man in the woods taking a summer vacation.
It's a journey of self dicovery, of realising one's inner flaws and rectifying/copping with such flaws and their related choices. The "cast" of characters is woefully complete with details, with a characterization that takes point in remembering the time of ambientation, through the things it put's in the open, and the tiny details about them. For instance, you may wonder if character A and B have a romantic relationship, you may wonder if the fact that they're a same sex couple is indeed a fact, but you can also just say "what if they are?". It sets your mindest on a third person view on other people's lives. All while maintainning a prospect of your own conflicts.
Henry isn't perfect, nor normative, neither is no one really.

As for the scenery, it's marvelous, the cell shadded enviroment, acompannied by the amazing acoustic soundtrack makes for a perfect experience, that takes "immersion" to it's core. Beign that not it's similarity to reality, but it's capacity of creating one of it's own. Firewatch is worth playing for the pros, I think. The problem is that it tantalizes the player with it's central mystery, but doesn't pay off in the end. I'd say "don't go into it expecting some shocking revelations", but the game seems to [i]want[/i] us to think a big revelation is coming - it's hard not to fall for it. Indeed, even though I had read remarks about the ending being mundane prior to playing the game, I had a hard time believing those remarks [i]while[/i] playing it, and I found myself very drawn in by the game's mystery. I have no problem with games that deal with more mundane and intimate subject matter, but it's when they put up a pretense of being about more than that - as if they're ashamed of being mundane - that bothers me, and which is ultimately detrimental to the experience.

I also think it would have been nice if the game had more of a "simulation" component to it. I kind of wish we got to stay in Wyoming for longer, and that there were more things to do, more ways to interact with the world. I would've liked if Campo Santo had included a binoculars for example (seems like a no-brainer), and some wildlife would have been nice. Maybe even an option to have a picnic wherever you wanted or something. I know these things take time and they were working on an indie budget, but I just can't help feel that Firewatch's true potential wasn't realized.

Nevertheless, there's a lot to love about the game, and it certainly has merit. I've ultimately got to recommend it just because of how beautiful and atmospheric it is. However, unless you can't wait, I'd suggest waiting until it's a little cheaper or on sale.

I normally enjoy this style of game - The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, and Life is Strange to name a few. I realise games that deviate away from traditional gameplay have their  flaws but I am happy to overlook them as long as there is a good, gripping story. Having seen the artwork months ago I had been eagerly awaiting this title. The environment looked amazing and the premise and user experience seemed top notch from the trailers.

The story of Firewatch sees the player as a new employee of the Parks and Wildlife service. You are alone in your watch tower with no communication with the outside world except from your two way radio.  On the other end of the radio is Delilah, an experienced firewatch ranger in another far away tower. Through this radio you recieve tasks from her while engaging in frequent banter. The developers of Firewatch have tried to incorporate the same 'time' based response as made popular by Telltale games. However they don't pretend that any of the decisions you make really matter. And unlike in Telltale games it seems dialog does't really affect much in the short term either. I ended up find this mechanic a bit annoying as there was no real purpose for being rushed and just instead it became an inconvenience.

The core gameplay revolves around 'walking'. The idea of hiking around the wilderness sounded appealing and really tingled my sense of adventure. However, Instead of wandering  around the environment and finding cool secret areas or perhaps spotting wildlife, the player is instead stuck on fairly linear paths. I spent a lot of time trying to find my own path but  would end up being blocked by a small rock. This really destroys the illusion of the game and makes it feel claustrophobic. Additionally as you spend most of the game walking, the linear paths make the  mechanic of walking feel like a chore. It brings back the horrible memories of "shooters" where you would trapse across half the map to get a key, then have to find your way back again. I found myself wishing for a teleport option. Of course if they did that this game could be completed in twenty minutes.

The tasks the player is issueed is fairly standard fare and follow a "go and investigate over at X" which requires bring up the in game map and compass to navigate the paths. As the player progresses mysterious events occur that creates an intriging atmosphere. [POTENTIAL SPOILERS AHEAD]

Any repoire with Delilah seems to just fizzle out into nothing. There was no personal discovery. It left me with a rather pointless and hollow feeling. I had hoped that something small like picking up rubbish might lead to some reward but there was no such luck.

In the end this game initially promises so much yet delivers so little. The gameplay mechanic is based on the worst aspect of games, and is not improved in any way or utilized to good effect. The visuals are great but the linear pathways break the illusion of wilderness. Finally the the story itself, the crux of the game, really fizzles out and destroys the inital good work. Very disappointing.

Despite the overwhelming response of the game being disappointing and short, I gave this one a shot and decided to really take my time breathing in the smoke.

At first I thought it was a `choose your own adventure` style game, and picked my dialogue carefully. Chose my interactions carefully. However, after reaching the end so abuptly, I realised this isn't true. It didn't matter what dialogue I choose, the outcome would have been roughly the exact same (with a few easter eggs apparently). Pity too, because I was ready to replay and try different things.

The story was quite clever and dark at times, but others it just made no sense looking back on it. The scenery you should stop and look around at it, even when you feel rushed to more onward by your companion, as there is very little time for exploration in the game on your own. Though to be fair, I think I saw about 90% of the map throughout the story.

Somehow I woke up and still wanted more. I want more style games like this. The dialogue was well written. The graphics had some awesome rendering. I also felt the UI was quite clever. And thus, I'd recommend this game.

Suggestions to Game Developer for next time: 1) Make a `choose your own adventure` game based on the actions and dialogue. You came close here, but it was limited. OR, 2) Make another adventure game very similar based on a true story. If this had been a true story about 2 Fire Watcher's in Wyoming in the 1980's, it would have been so much more powerful and satisfying, and then having only 1 possible outcome would have been okay.

Firewatch is not your usual type of game. I've read some of the negative reviews, and I believe they stem from people who just would never like this type of game. It's not a game for everyone, but that doesn't make it a bad game. In fact, I loved the game so much my wife and I played it for 7 hours straight just to see what happens with the story!


This game is very narrative driven. You won't be ambushed by 50 people trying to rip your throat out. You won't be speeding through a busy city with 100 cops chasing you with sirens ablaze. No, instead you will have a suspenseful story that gets more and more on the edge of your seat the longer you play. It can get genuinely creepy at times. It can also get very emotional.

As far as plot and voice acting goes, it is phenomenal. I would easily give the game an 8/10 for story and a perfect 10 for voice acting and dialogue. The ending of the game is a little bit of a let down, which is why I can't give it a better rating than 8, but it's still a very good plot and I really enjoyed the experience.

The graphics take some getting used to as well. They aren't super realistic. In fact, they aren't realistic at all. They are more water color like, similar to Borderlands. While certainly not a style for everyone, I liked it.

Overall I would give this game an 8/10. As much as I enjoyed the game, I don't see a lot of replay value, and I was a bit disappointed with the ending. That said, I'm good for a good second playthrough, maybe a third. The game is only 20 dollars, so it's affordable, and provides a very memorable experience.

Would I recommend this game to everyone? Hell no, but if you don't have to be having someone try to kill you every 5 second or decapitating something every minute to have fun with a game (which is honestly where a lot of the negative reviews comes from), then you should give this game a try.

- PLOT was fantastic, obviously the primary focus of the game, not just an afterthought for superficial depth.  It was like reading a good book as opposed to racing through a script in search of something interesting.

- VISUALS, while not photorealistic, have a pleasant, surrealistic quality to them and even near the end of the game I was still stopping to look around at the scenery, which is something I don't tend to do even in those 'AAA' games that are always praised for their gorgeous graphics.  The game is a little heavy on the saturation at times, but I really didn't mind all at much.

- MUSIC was excellent!  Nothing fancy, just soft and atmospheric.  I'm listening to it now, and will be adding the tracks to my music library.

The bad:

ORIENTATION was difficult.  With VR I imagine it would have been perfect.  I was excited about the option to turn off the locator icon on the map and rely solely on gameworld features and my map/compass, but although I'm great at finding my way in the real world I've always had trouble in computer games...such as this one.  Luckily, the entire world is designed from scratch with plenty of unique objects in the landscape.  Beware, though:  getting around is a HUGE part of this game, so pay VERY close attention to your surroundings.

INTRODUCTION, although well-done in terms of story, felt a little thrown-together.

Features:
- Not a 'fighting' game
- Plays out in 'days' (like chapters); there are plenty of good stopping points so you can get to bed.
- Semi open-world, organized in a somewhat maze-like fashion (picture a huge network of tunnels and chambers, like an ant nest.)
- Engaging storyline
- Mainly for guys:  The main character is a guy, and the dialogue plays out with respect to that (G-rated, from my experience).
- Timed, multiple-choice responses to dialogue; I'm not sure yet if they affect the storyline or mood.

Maybe it’s because some of Firewatch’s themes feel, in a way, personal to me, but this is the game whose narrative resonated more strongly to me. Towards the ending it suffers from a slight case of wall-of-text-ness, and the mystery side of its tale is probably more contrived than necessary, but overall its pace, and the way it plays with your emotions and imagination, is truly masterful. When I reached the end I felt drained. This is a game that you not only watch in awe—because its graphics are wonderful, visually and narrative wise, and its direction is beautiful since the very first minute—but that you truly experience.

Your co-protagonist is your boss, a woman in another far lookout. You never see her, and only talk to her via radio. Well, it really works, and is a statement to the power of subtraction and imagination (on the contrary, I was slightly annoyed by your own character being so strongly defined from a physical point of view, and I would’ve preferred that to be more vague too). You’ll spend a summer with her voice, and with the gorgeous solitude around you. With its mysteries, its melancholy, its vastness, its wonder, its infinite sadness. Firewatch is after all a tale about loss, about how it can shape the world around you and reverberate into other people’s life, even when you think you’re actually avoiding it. And it’s told with such a beautiful pace.

While the game was well narrated, and had a solid story line, be cautious: It is *extremely* short. I beat the game in under 3 hours, which is very little playtime for an $18 pricetag with limited replay value.

I'd definitely reccomend purchasing, but only if it's on sale.

So, as with many walking simulators, the verdict tends to split people quite harshly 
But here’s my honest take on Firewatch:

It was good, I liked it.

Not much to say right? – well let me explain myself;
The first thing to note – the visuals are stunning. The low-poly art style is executed superbly (you know the development team have faith in their creation when they literally give you an in-game camera to take photographs with whenever you want)
Second off – the sound design is beautiful, and the voice acting excellent too (as demonstrated in the trailers) 
Mood and tone is captured perfectly at times, (maybe not-so-perfectly at others) but the game has (just) enough dialogue options to keep the conversations interesting. 
The third point seems to be the most polarising among reviews – the story.

***Mild spoilers below***

I understand where people are coming from when they say the story is far too anti-climactic, especially for what it builds you up to throughout the main portion of the game – don’t expect any fancy mech fights or explosion-filled chases through the wilderness here, it just fizzles out in depressing realisation for the characters’ own inadequacies and failings in life. However, I still felt the ending was quite well done: there was something very… human, (I guess?), about it – and despite the kind-of empty melancholy it leaves you with, I’d be lying if I said it didn’t resonate with me in many ways. 

*****

I’ve heard a lot of people taking issue with the price, and yes – for what they’re charging versus how much playtime you get out of it – it probably isn’t worth paying full price for, pick it up on sale. 
That said, with the amount of craft and polish that has clearly went into making Firewatch – I have no problems in having paid the development team that little extra if it means they can continue to bring us more things of this standard in the future.

In short; give it a shot – it’s only a few hours out your life, and at its worst – it’s still something nice to look at.

I really liked Firewatch. It's got a great visual aesthetic with very visceral lighting ranging from sun bleached dayscapes of midday to the soft orange hues of late afternoon to a calming navy blue night sky. The only other thing besides a desolate forest is your player character rendered in a semi-cartoon style that I don't see nearly enough of and I'd seriously like to see more. It gives a sort of light fun texture to the otherwise strikingly evocative visuals.

This lighthearted fun carries over to the characters as well. While your character, Henry has a somber back story of his wife suffering from early onset dementia, the back and forth banter between Henry and fellow lookout partner Delilah softens the blow with that bit of fun. Some of my favorite parts of this game were finding the cool little trinkets, landmarks, and other things to tell Delilah about to hear how she reacts. Delilah made a real impact on me because her dynamic with Henry seemed like a really nice friendship with fun jokes, sarcasm, and sharing little intimate moments like watching a fire from afar in the safety of your watchtowers as the blissfulness of night washes over you. 

In fact, if the game's narrative just revolved around Henry and Delilah snarking at each other while walking through the forest, I would have been completely fine with that. That isn't to say the narrative we have in the game is bad per se, but more that it didn't fit tonally with the rest of the game. While the forest is calm with no danger in sight and the characters are at their best when they have sarcastic banter and quiet, serene moments that develop their relationships and characters, the narrative plays out like a mystery. I don't have a problem with mystery in itself and if it took on a more lighthearted approach, it would have been great. Instead what the narrative does is drop the characters into a paranoid conspiracy. It works because the characters are endearing and they're the kinds of characters you'd be willing to watch do anything and be entertained, but it doesn't mesh well with the rest of the tone of the game. 

I hear a lot of people say that the mystery aspect of the narrative was akin to that of Scooby-Doo but I can't help but disagree. The mystery in this game was played too seriously to evoke anything like it. If they took on a pulpy, Scooby-Doo style, lighthearted mystery, I think that would fit the game a lot better even if it seems outlandish. It would take the focus away from the main story and focus it more on the interplay between the characters which is where the game is at its best. 

One more point before I close. The music from the jukebox early on in the game is rad as ♥♥♥♥. I liked it so much to the point where when I came across it, I took the jukebox for myself and listened to the song on the way back to the lookout tower. For those interested, the band that made that banger track is Cheap Talk and their album “Let's Get Electric” is chock full of that synthwave radness.

Firewatch is a great game for what it is. The narrative is a little off putting but if you look past it, the characters, visuals, and jammin' music is a definite hook. I hear lots of people complain about length and while one playthrough doesn't take long, this is the kind of game you'd want to come back to because of its amazing charm. Stop.  Don't watch any trailers, look at any screenshots, visit the forums, or read any articles.  Firewatch takes place deep in a beautiful mountain wilderness over the course of a summer in the 80s; knowing any more than that will greatly diminish your experience with it.

WIthout any spoilers, the game is a good example of how a "walking simulator" can capture that vibe of the classic point n click adventure game while bringing it into today's technology.  Clocking in at about four hours (about $5 per hour, which is a better deal than most Hollywood dreck out there), you will be treated to a beautiful, stylized view of American wilderness coupled with some truly delightful voice acting.

The only caveat, then, is that Firewatch is very much about the experience, meaning that at least for me, it fell a little short in its conclusion.  Up until that point, however, it's just a terrific ride so while I wouldn't give it a full-blown recommendation, I'd say you can't go wrong for $15 if it ever dips to that point.

To say any more about the game, as I stated before, is to just take away from what you'll get out of it.  It's difficult to talk about Firewatch without spoiling its charm because every single piece of it is lovingly-paced and presented to you.  Unlike other walkies, this one is quite interactive, even if the plot in its entirety is deterministic.  I suppose that the best thing I can say about it is that what you get from it depends on what you give it.

With that in mind, I say give it a shot if you can get your hands on it.  Whether you play a friend's copy, get it on sale, or simply have a $20 laying about, I can't say there isn't potential for disappointment, but the ride Campo Santo has worked so hard at building is a fine example of its genre.

Pros:

-Excellent characters

Cons:

-Seriously disappointing ending that did not answer any of the questions I still had
-Antagonist revelation is incredibly anticlimactic, not even a confrontation
-Still had minor framerate issues on my decent laptop and running low-quality settings
-$20.00 is incredibly stupendously steep for an indie game that literally took 3-4 hours to complete, finding most of the secrets and not rushing
-I enjoyed exploring the world, but that map is the worst. There should have just been a toggled mini-map in a corner. I liked the idea that my character literally had to navigate using a paper map in his pack, but it was so clunky and I missed so many turns. How hard is it really to just put an arrow on my dot so I know which direction I'm facing?

Overall, I liked the game. I thought that there were many great ideas implemented very well. My main complaint is just that the story seemed to end too abrubtly. I felt like we were just started to uncover the mystery, and then it's over. It wasn't even a set-up-for-sequel ending. It was a figure-it-out-yourself ending. Like they didn't want to help you enjoy their game. I finished the game, was like "wtf I still have so many questions" so I went to the YouTubes and found videos explaining the intricate details and how they related and revealed all this stuff about the story and the characters. It was really interesting and made me appreciate the story quite a bit more, but then I realized, "I seriously had to go have someone explain how the obscure details come together in order to appreciate this game." That's not a very good thing to think about a game. 

My advice to you is to play this game if you enjoy walking simulators, story adventures, detail-rich stories, beautiful environments, and great characters. Do not, DO NOT, take this game at face value like I did originally. Pay attention to the details, put together the pieces that the game isn't telling you to put together. At the end, the main character mentions that he felt like they had been missing something this whole time. Trust me when I say that he's right. There is quite a bit to be uncovered, and it really is satisfying, but it's hidden so deep I have to wonder whether the developers should have made it more obvious.

 This makes for great replayability, and although you can't change the overall story or ending, the dynamic between Henry and Delilah can vary greatly with each playthrough.

I have not played a game like this before. Firewatch is mostly about exploring the wilderness and occasionally chatting over a walkie talkie with Delilah, your boss who's stationed at a nearby watchtower you can just make out in the distance.

It works because the landscapes are stunning, the dialogue is well acted and well written, making me curious about these characters, and the story reacts in subtle and mostly effective ways to your choices, making me feel that I'm actually influencing this world. I did not replay the whole game to find out how much difference choices actually make on the overall story, but it's fairluy obvious that your choices leave small marks in the world: a place on the map is marked with the name you jokingly give it, and so is a fire. A sketch of yourself is based on the description you chose to give, and the choices you make about your character's past in the intro leave little ripples throughout the story.

There were a couple moments when the fiction broke down because of small timing issues (like a piece of dialogue triggering before I had actually seen whatever it was about), but mostly the game manages to uphold the illusion, and in some moments managed to actually surprise me and move me. It's immersive in a way, because there are lots of little realistic details in the world, but at the same time the character I played as was not me: from his physical appearence to his way of talking to his background, Henry is a distinct person, like a character in a movie that I happened to be moving around as.

The issue of the playing character's physical appearance is also interesting: though you often see Henry's hands and legs you never see your own face, except in sketches or photographs, and the first one of these instances was suprising both because of Henry's distinct physique and because I'd read about that sketch in the introductory section, before I acutally saw it. It was a queer moment of disconnect, because at the same time it made the prologue "real" it pushed me away from identifying with Henry.

From a practical perspective, it took me 7 hours to finish the game. I had to play on medium settings because my laptop could not keep up, and even so there was some stuttering so I didn't get the best experience of the visuals, but I don't recommend playing on low settings as without some of the effects the landscape then becomes "flat" and loses the sense of magic that it has even on medium.

Finally I'll finish with a little spoiler to describe what was for me the most memorable moment in the game. In the middle of the night you get a call on the walkie talkie, and Delilah passes you over to your wife, Julie, who is on the phone. She has an australian accent, and we just exchanged a few words, and I suddenly found out Henry's nickname for her, nothing much happened but it made the whole situation between Henry and her real all of a sudden... and it felt like a dream, as it must have for Henry, I just had to search for this moment in somebody's playthrough on youtube to be sure I had not imagined it.

(Narrative is the most important part of this game, and I’m just going to have to spoil key parts in order to properly talk about and critique them. You have been warned.)

When first I started really looking into this game, I’ll admit I was sold pretty quick. I was in love with the idea of a game exploring a true thriller narrative. And for what little it’s worth, it hits some of those classic thriller beats like an experienced drummer. But ultimately I just find myself rather disappointed in that things hardly ever get as exciting or pulse-pounding as the trailers would have you believe. 

Now, let it never be said that I’m opposed to the walking simulator subgenre. Some walking sims have come around that are great, such as The Stanley Parable. But so very often, games of this type act as a glorified narrative delivery system, giving the player absolutely nothing to actually do. A good way to avoid this off putting stigma is to at the very least give the player some modicum of narrative influence in the form of branching story paths, so they aren’t completely stripped of any agency. Going back to the Stanley example, sure all you can actually do is walk, but you get moments of choice about where to walk, changing the narrative path of that particular playthrough. Firewatch, however, for its heavy handed focus on dialogue options, doesn’t even offer players that much. And its explorative nature is exceedingly lackluster. Sure, you can walk whereso ever you please pretty much from the word go, but nothing will ever actually happen until you go to designated points so you can wait for the plot to happen around you, turning the open map into a sham of linearity. 

But hey, I’m obviously focusing too hard on the gameplay side, and things like player agency. When I play games, I hope that two things engage me: the gameplay, [i]and[/i] the narrative. Usually though, if one is good enough, I’ll excuse a lack of the other. And to be fair, there is actually a market out there these days for games with no gameplay. So since narrative is all Firewatch has to offer, let’s talk narrative. 

At best, Firewatch is a really good character study for our main two characters, Henry and Delilah. Both are pretty good, well-rounded, fleshed-out characters, with a really enjoyable chemistry. Just listening to the two of them chat was fairly engaging; I laughed at times, I felt bad for them during others, the whole nine. But then there’s everyone else. The other characters are just kind of there, flat and uninteresting, serving as platforms for Henry, or Delilah, or both of them to have their poignant, introspective moments, or to add tragic backstory elements. I know that I was supposed to feel bad when a sleep addled Henry started deliriously talking in dream to his dementia ridden wife, but I just didn’t. Because Julia isn’t really a character, she’s but an element; a facet of Henry which exists purely for the sake of his own impetus leading him to where he is in life now. In fact, she matters so very little, that the player gets to decide a grand portion of Henry’s life with her up till now. The story has all sorts of moments like this, none of which have nearly the impact of a somewhat drunken Delilah wistfully admitting she wants to be there, next to Henry, to hold him, and the hesitation over whether or not to have Henry reply with mirrored desire. The main characters are literally the only ones that matter. All others feel hollow and pointless, typically being described by little more than occupation or hobbies. And this is kind of a major problem when one of the hugest reveals in the story is that one of the other characters mentioned is discovered to have been dead all these years and nobody knew. But the game honestly fell so short of getting me to care, because it’s nice and all that this person liked D&D, but that’s not going to have me in tears five minutes after learning that and not much more. 

As I said earlier, Firewatch does hit some pretty classic thriller beats. A communications wire gets cut clean, some rowdy teens go missing, and a mysterious figure is spotted rummaging around in Henry’s tower. All the great things are featured prominently in the trailers, and the game even goes a few more steps. A good chunk into the game, I felt like I was practically on the verge of falling asleep, when someone coldcocked Henry in the back of the head and put him under for five minutes. I jumped back awake, my excitement for the game suddenly rejuvenated. Plenty of great, pulse-pounding moments that really set the mood and do wonders for the tone. But the biggest shame of all is so much of this energy just sort of peters out. So very many narrative threads end abruptly and often flaccidly. For example, those rowdy teens that go missing early in the game? Yeah, halfway through, Delilah calls you up and unceremoniously informs you they simply got drunk and wandered off into jail in the next county over. Or hey, what about this fenced off area nobody knew about? Turns out it had nothing to do with anything and was just a red herring. And how about the big reveal about who’s been behind all this? Could it possibly be literally the only other person the characters mention living in these woods at some point? Wow, it turned out to be literally the only other person the characters mention living in these woods at some point. It’s predictable to a fault, and most of the tension isn’t so much cut as it’s released in the same a partially inflated balloon lets out air through a wet, sticky nozzle. 

It’s a divisive point, but I feel I’d be remiss if I didn’t at least address game length. This game is three hours long. Some equate a game’s length to its inherent value. Me, I’ve always been a quality over quantity kind of person. But even I have to admit the brief playtime feels like a minor insult on top of an already lackluster product. I say minor, because it’s roughly 6.67 usd per hour of content, which honestly isn’t as bad as worse movies on the new release rack at Best Buy or something. While some of those movies might be bad for about the same price, really, Firewatch is just bland. It starts off with so much energy and intrigue, but falls asleep at the wheel. 

I guess at the end of the day, part of me is glad games like this are even getting this much attention and success. Variety is the spice of life, and it gladdens my heart to see the horizon of gaming getting broadened by entries like Firewatch. I just wish Firewatch was better. Not exactly terrible, but it’s boring. I can’t say I didn’t get some enjoyment out of it; as I said earlier, Henry and Delilah are a delight to listen to. But I didn’t foot the bill for a glorified screensaver while I listen to a really good script reading just to be underwhelmed by a story that stops caring about most of its own narrative threads halfway through. And neither should you.

Firewatch showcases some of the best possible facets of storytelling, allowing you to fully comprehend, interpret and forge the backstory for that character, and how they respond to scenarios and people. Many complaints about this game are due to the length of it compared to the price, and at $20, that's understandable, but when compared to a film at ~$15, this experience is far more fleshed out and comprehensive, displaying such a beautiful understanding of storytelling and intrigue that other games actively disappoint me at their lack of attempting to expend that much effort. 

The aesthetic of the game allows for even the most mundane of sights to be wonderful experiences, with many humerous and interesting things hidden throughout the rather large and fluid map. For a "Walking Simulator" the game teaches you alot of mechanics, and uses the radio and your own observation as a genius supplement for a tutorial, as it revels in you finding new things to talk to Delilah about, with some of even the most minute details being well fleshed-out discussions that tell you more about not only your only companion, but yourself.

All these thoughts of pseudo-isolation are aided by the fact that you never actually SEE anybody else until very abruptly at the finale, allowing for an incredible amount of tension to be built during the mid to late area of the story, in which a mystery presents itself and is constantly elaborated upon, and evokes feelings that I personally have not felt since Lost, with the sensation of discovery being the most satisfied I've felt in a huge amount of time.

The music is the as the one that composed the music from Gone Home, which shows not only in the music, but the setting, as they are both set within the same time period and deal with the same themes of isolation and pseudo-horror. But, anyways, the music is incredible with a country-esque theme to it, being mixed with the 70s-80s synth, allowing for an incredible range to be achieved and atmosphere to not only be built, but amplified.

Another thing about this game that has brought a large amount of flak to it is the ending, being criticised as too sudden and not closing every topic brought up, when for me, (Though most certainly not for all) it closes itself just as it started, by using you, it has you think about all of the possibilites and results of the ending via providing no definitive one, hell, if you want to, you can even refuse the ending and allow it to resolve in one singular way, via doing nothing.

And to revisit the earlier topics in a TL;DR format, the Art Style is outright beautiful, with an incredible amount of thought being poured into it, the story is one of 3 that have permanently stuck with me (The others being Bastion and Transistor) due to just how well and intelligently made it was, and this game even excels in the area of game design itself, even though, due to the medium of the game being a "Walking Simulator" isn't even close to being held back.

All in all, I would recommend buying this game, downloading, turning your internet and lights off, and then taking a few hours to allow this game to dazzle you. (And I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ refuse to give a numbered score, because that's just really stupid.)

My experience of this game can be broken down into three pieces.
1. The opening act
2. The game
3. The ending

1. It seems as if the opening act serves as a way of both taking ownership over Henry and establishing that he is not just an avatar of you. I think it was one of the most emotionally stirring parts of the game and succeeded in setting up the rest of the game in a profound and unique way.

2. The game itself is beautiful and rich with detail. The main mechanic of moving from point A to B and getting to know Deliah is executed with so much personality (though I can only picture Henry looking like Rich Sommer). There are a ton small details that add to thoughtfulness too. They've accounted for a silly amount of actions that players testing the system might do, but the issue is that there is a sense of urgency in many of the tasks asked of you. When a hidden feature exists within these tasks, going easter egg hunting can really break the immersion.

I really enjoyed the story laid out in front of me, but I felt the contrast of the opening act and the main game was a detriment as a whole. Despite the intent of the opening to set up Henry's character, in the grand scheme of the world presented to me, it made the story of the game seem more like a side quest, or filler episode of a serial TV show. That's not to say that it was not strong on it's own. Despite the contrast, without the opening, the player would never be able to properly speak with Henry's voice while interacting with Delilah. I think the problem lies in the pacing. The very short opening act covers years of Henry's life, while the main game covers a much smaller period of time.

3. The end is all about pay-off. A bad ending can lead to a retroactive "bad taste in the mouth" for the whole experience. You'll read a lot of negativity about the ending to the game, but whatever your opinion is, the rest of the game is worth experiencing. I feel there is no need to review it beyond saying that it is not objectively BAD. One's opinion of it has more to do with how they experience stories, storytelling, and video games a medium and how much they have emotionally invested in the characters.

An outstanding game, or rather, an interactive story.

Especially in terms of atmosphere and dialogue, I can hardly imagine a better adaptation. This game truly captivates you; you constantly find yourself pressing the talk button on the radio, hoping for another conversation with "D." Unfortunately, the playtime isn't very long at around 4 to 5 hours, but those hours are incredibly intense. There are also no alternative endings, which would make multiple playthroughs more enjoyable. Technically, I really like the game; the visuals are simply beautiful, making you want to take pictures constantly. The game is rounded out by the fitting musical score and the excellent conversations between the protagonists (a full German dub would detract from the experience, I think, but German subtitles would be a sensible and sufficient addition). The Unity Engine seems to occasionally reach its performance limits with a relatively large open world (even though it's manageable and not truly open), but the game still runs smoothly on my PC at Ultra/High settings (XEON E3-1280 v2 / GEFORCE GTX 750TI / 16 GB RAM).

Comment on the story (warning: some spoilers ahead):

Many are a little disappointed by the story and its resolution, as major twists and supernatural elements are often expected. However, the ending fits the game perfectly, and all side quests and theories are explained (e.g., the whereabouts of the two girls, the strange station behind the fence, etc.). Anyone with unanswered questions clearly wasn't paying close enough attention or only skimmed certain clues and conversations—and these are what make the game so compelling.

I got this game because I love adventure games, am crazy for exploration & atmosphere, and even like walking simulators that other people are bored by. I do recommend this game but with some caveats.

First things first: Firewatch is an absolutely [i]beautiful[/i] game. It's a pleasure to look at from beginning to end. The scenery is top-notch. Likewise, the atmosphere is wonderfully done. There were moments where I simply walked around and enjoyed the wonder of it- I always wanted to see what my exploration would turn up next. This part of the game is so well done that, as the climax of the game approached, I felt a genuine sense of dread about what was happening.

So, if you're a gamer who lives for the "mood and feel" of a game, you will like this aspect of it.

Now for the area where I feel conflicted: the story. A "walking simulator", of course, lives and dies by its story and how well that story is crafted and presented. I feel that the story had a lot of promise, but ultimately disappointed. You come to truly feel for Henry and Julie (however, I found the character of Delilah more obnoxious than anything). But... there's something lacking. I don't know how to say it any better. The story feels empty on the inside, and not in an intentional way that reflects Henry's personal problems! There are too many instances where it's obvious the developers didn't want to make too strong of a decision regarding the direction the story took. Everything is open to the point of feeling unrealistic. Henry's decisions are vague, his friendship with Delilah is vague, the ending... is vague.

After playing the game for almost 8 hours (I took longer than necessary cause I wanted to go everywhere and look at everything!) I felt a bit cheated. It was sort of like reading a long novel that ends in the middle of a chapter. I realize that life isn't always neat and tidy, but in fiction having your characters go through too little character development comes across as poor writing. In a game genre that [b]needs[/b] an excellent story, this one left me feeling like the characters wasted my time.

Oh, and a minor nitpick: there's a bunch of anachronisms in Firewatch. If you're old enough the mistakes will stand out like crazy. Like, no one used the word "burn" to mean "insult" in 1975. Also, there were no Victoria's Secret supermodels in 1981. There's some other dialogue options that do not fit in the '80s as well as they should. Not a dealbreaker but it pulled me out of the game for a moment, and again- a walking simulator needs to avoid that at all costs.

So yeah. Play this- it's beautiful, it's something different, and it will scratch an adventure gaming itch if you're into those sorts of games. But don't expect to get too much out of the story except some 'feels', I guess.

*An explanation of the ending without spoilers.*

Now I’m not one to usually write a review about one, but seeing how this game has gotten so much hate because many felt as though the ending was abrupt or lazy. In the next paragraph I hope to explain that in my opinion of why people disliked the ending, and how that resulted in so much hate towards the game.

I want to first start off saying that it can’t be denied that the developers at Campo Santo made a beautiful game which you can’t deny even if you think the ending sucked for Firewatch. Now onto why I think many people thought the ending sucked. From the first day Henry showed up at the Shoshone National Forest in the Wyoming wilderness for the firewatcher job, he was asked an bizarre question by his supervisor Delilah, which was “What are you escaping from”. Now to keep it spoil free I won’t mention why, but through the next day’s Henry will start to get more bizarre questions that he will both ask himself and Delilah. Now throughout the game there starts to become this one big problem that Henry and Delilah are trying to solve, this problem has you guessing, and questioning so much. This problem is what I think was the cause to many hating the ending, because throughout the game the as you’re getting closer to solving this problem, the rising action increases ever more, until you reach the climax, which is the answer to that problem. Now during that rising action there becomes many speculations on what this problem is which leads to the player overthinking it and becoming frustrated when it wasn’t what they hoped it would be. The same can be said about the ending where things didn’t go the way players wanted it to go, but to think that certain events would play out in the way you hoped were not possible. Because if you remember what I mentioned about day one, that this place was an escape for Henry, that he was carrying weight from his place back home, and that while he was here in Shoshone National Forest he could feel free, but once he leaves he has to return to the world he once left. Now some of this might not make sense since you haven’t played it, but I’m telling it this way so I don’t spoil it for you.

Now I hope I was able to convince you that Firewatch is a great game, that should not be rejected because some players felt it didn’t go the way they wanted to and that Campo Santo has given us a masterpiece for only a mere $20, while many AAA developers out there charge us $60 for something they can’t even deliver on now a days.

But we forget that, like movies, games also have character development. There is more than what happens in the narrow scope of the game- and that is why the ending proved to me the acting (and more importantly, writing) finesse and supreme character development.

Firewatch is a beautiful atmospheric adventure that has some mystery elements, and plays like a walking simulator with amazing dialog.

In Firewatch, you play as Henry, and you are looking for an isolated escape from your regular life. You spend a lot of time hiking, and climbing through the terrain to complete your objectives. You can explore different areas, and interact with different objects. With just your backpack and a few items, you are practically alone in nature, and the only other person you have to talk with is on the other end of a walkie-talkie. While talking on the walkie-talkie, you will have a finite time to reply, and sometimes have different choices in dialog selection. Different dialog selections prompt different responses, but none of which will impact the outcome of the game.

The story is a linear. The dialog and circumstances throughout the game are very realistic and believable. There are some mysteries in the story as well, and it added a nice touch on the game overall.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list][*]the controls are fully customizable, and the game has full controller support
[*]immersive and beautiful graphics - nature is absolutely stunning, and everything feels so alive with the grass and trees moving and swaying in the wind
[*]background music, and ambience sounds of nature are really well done
[*]believable characters with dialog and voice acting that are incredible[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list][*]the story is too short for the price tag
[*]the ending was done well, but I have mixed feelings about how it ended (it was what I expected would happen, but not what I wanted to see happen)[/list]

The game took me just under 4 hours to complete. After I finished it, I went back and played it again to experience the different dialog choices, but other than hearing a few new lines here and there, there wasn’t any other reason to replay it.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
I really liked the game, and I would definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoys an immersive experience with really great voice dialog. It was a wonderful game, but the price is too high for how short it is, so I would advise picking it up at a sale price.

[u]DISCLAIMER[/u]
This review is subjective. It's a review of the game in general, and not a review of it as a linear walking simulator. This is done in order to show a broader range of points.

[u]PROS[/u]
+Great graphics
+Brilliant voice acting
+Can get a pet turtle

[u]CONS[/u]
-Predictable twists
-80% of the game is just the gameplay mechanics, and the gameplay is just alright
-The big map is actually very restrictive (4 canyons with some small open areas where paths split)
-Disappointing and abrupt ending which isn't well explained and makes little sense
-Developers claimed '6-8 hours of story minimum', 3-4 hours in reality
-Dialogue provides the illusion of choices that will stick but in reality there is one ending (There is also an ending if you don't do 'the thing' at the end but it's a very minor change and was probably only made by the devs as a side thing)
- linear
-The 'funny' bits you see in the trailers are the only funny bits
-You will end up paying around £3.75/$5 per hour of gameplay (assuming you spend 4 hours on it).
-Story seems rushed
-No replay value since there is only one ending
Overall, the game was very over-hyped, on the surface, this game seems amazing, but once you've gotten more than 2 hours in, you realize that there is little more than climbing up and down stones and being prompted to radio in everything. I would not recommend you buy this game, unless it is well discounted during a sale.

[u]EDIT 28TH NOVEMBER[/u]
Since the big update which added free-roam, I've gone back to the game. One complaint about this update is that I'd really appreciate some way to change the time, and perhaps pause it, as I'd like to be able to explore the entire map at a specific time

While I would still give this review a negative rating overall, the extent to which it is negative is reduced with the newest update.

Firewatch is an adventure/exploration game set in the Shoshone National Forest.  While there, you're confronted with a very disturbing set of events, that you ultimately research and flesh out.  This is a review of how it felt to play it on day 1.

Value: $15.  The game is very, very short.  Other reviews will tell you this.  There is not an unenjoyable minute for fans of the genre, so I feel like it's worth it.  There is a purpose to every minute you spend on the Park, and I think it's designed to be a single-serving game.  However, I feel the $20 sticker is a big ask for a game that is admittedly cut in half for a playthrough when you use the run function.  An extreme bias of Quality over Quantity.

Gameplay: 4/10.  There is literally nothing to do.  You walk around and play out what is an extremely linear path to solving a mystery.  However, you didn't buy this game for the gameplay, you bought it for the visuals and the story.  Fans of games like Gone Home are going to find a lot of fun here, but anyone expecting an RPG that's more of a life in the wilds experience, or some sort of a survival game, are going to be very disappointed.  You absolutely cannot die or fail, and that's something that needs to be mentioned.

Sound: 10/10.  The ambient music is flawless.  The voice-acting is probably the single best script in recent memory.  It's utterly breathtaking to hear the real chemistry between the actors.  Again, for fans of Gone Home, the real pathos of the main characters comes through right to the heart.  It's beautiful and you feel acquainted with these people in a way that's frankly too close.

Graphic Presentation: 9/10.  Superb.  The forest feels alive, and it feels like you're in it.  The sky is beautiful in the way that a distant, unrecognizeable backdrop is daunting and alive.  The changes caused by the fire are well-articulated and presented cogently.  The styling is immaculate, down to the inking and shading of the backdrops.  Some of the assets put in the game are incredibly funny.  It's a great styling and so enjoyable that I wish that the publisher would sell additional content using the same scenery.

Replayability: 5/10.  It's absolutely worth finishing, but you will never get more than six hours out of this game.  I almost feel like this would have been a genre-defining animated movie if it was done entirely as a graphical render.  It really is a beautiful and satisfying story, set in a lush and enjoyable location with immaculate voice-over work and background.  The first playthrough is stunning, and it's legitimately a better game than something like Gone Home.  It's pretty similar overall to a game like "The Wolf Among Us" where if you enjoy the source stylings (remote wilderness here as opposed to fairy tale city in Wolf) you'll find the game to be enchanting and immersive.

Overall: This is a tricky review and I'm not going to assign a score.  For what the game is, it's very very good.  For what the game was hyped to be, it isn't that at all.  I don't think anyone who is approaching this game with the hype in mind can get what they expect or hope to get out of this game, and that's a very relevant criticism in an era of misleading Greenlight games, bad betas and overhyped games that won't work on Day 1.  I will say that this game will be worth anyone's time on the very first occasion one finds it on sale.

The outstanding success and popularity of Firewatch seemed to come out of nowhere when it released in early February of 2016. The game itself seemed to just one day exist, and then it became some magnificent indie hit; just one month after its release, the title has sold over half a million copies. With many worried that the game is nothing more than a cash grab, and an equal amount of folks skeptical about paying $20 for a proposed walking simulator, what is it exactly that has so many people enchanted by Firewatch?

Without a doubt, it is a combination of the captivating storyline, ensnaring characters, and superb dialogue. Yes, it is true... Firewatch is little more than a glorified walking simulator set in a national park of the Wyoming wilderness. However, the aforementioned attributes make the experience worth every penny of the pricetag, although there are a few things that could've made the game even better. Set in the late 1980's, you will take on the role of Henry, a man who has taken a job as a fire lookout to escape from his troubles at home. Throughout the game, you will have your choice of dialogue options, each that will impact your immediate relationship with your supervisor, Delilah.

Things start out good enough, lazy summer days that quickly escalate into a bizarre mystery which will keep you from putting the controller down for the entire 4-5 hour length of the game. Sadly, Firewatch does only last for a few hours, and that is one of its major drawbacks. Even with getting lost as much as I did (I really suck with maps), the event will only last a maximum of 5 hours. However, in defense of the game, I do not believe that the mystery could've been prolonged much further. While it lasts, the air of suspense and undying necessity to find out what is going on is unrelenting. Likewise, each interaction with Delilah is deep and connective; there's an undeniable chemistry between her and Henry that lasts right through until the end.

The game is filled with sarcastic and crude humor, spontaneous wit, and even the occasional bout of depravity that makes us all human. The voice acting is the best I've ever heard for an indie title, and the soundtrack is just as impressive as it is immersive. The graphics are simple, yet somehow amazingly detailed; even when you get turned around or lost in the wilderness, you won't mind since you'll be taking in some astonishing views, be it deep in the forest or on a ledge overlooking the horizon. However, do not expect to explore a plethora of areas; Firewatch is incredibly linear, and while the game might look like it is open and spacious, there are narrow trails hidden within the sandbox illusion.

While I didn't encounter any game breaking glitches or bugs, I will note that my framerate dropped from 60 FPS (the games cap) to the lower 40s at some points; now, this could've been due to the fact that I was streaming on Steam for some friends, so take this for what you will... it was a mildly rare occurrence. There is also one particular place on the map that if you stand in a certain spot, the ground textures from the previous area disappear. I played the game using an Xbox One controller, and with that you use down on the D-Pad to pull out your compass, and left for the compass and map; this function did not work and left me to rely on the keyboard, but pressing up to bring out the in-game camera did work. All minor issues, but they are still present nonetheless.

Firewatch has not only set the new bar of standards for walking simulators, but for indie games overall. It's hard to explain in a review just how captivating and immersive the character interaction between Henry and Delilah becomes, and the player will find themselves emotionally invested in each one as backstories are learned. There's a slight replayability factor, in that there are a few dialogue choices to pick from for almost every interaction. While the story is a great mystery that will keep you guessing, the ending is sadly lackluster and feels close to being a cop-out; but don't let this deter you from taking on the experience. The graphics are extremely pleasing to the eye to boot. If you have a spare $20 to throw at a game, lay it down on Firewatch; if you get it on sale, that's even better, but Campo Santo are one indie developer you should consider funding in full.

Firewatch is an atmospheric, narrative wrapped in a walking simulator of sorts.  If you like games like Gone Home, Dear Esther, and, to a lesser extent, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, then you will appreciate this game.  

For the most part, Firewatch is an engaging and compelling experience.  There are times where decisions are made, but I don't feel that those decisions would really have much of an effect on the overall story.

It's hard to really critically review a game like this without spoiling the story, which is one that I enjoyed.  So here comes the spoilers.  

[spoiler]I found Delilah's character to be very flat.  Tongue and cheek dialogue aside, she just didn't work for me.  Predictable, hollow, and at times more of a storytelling device than a character.  

I felt that there was much more that they could have done with many of the arcs of the story.  It just seemed like they really could have fleshed out the girls at the campfire more than just "they were found and they stole a tractor and they are in jail".  It was a sort of deus ex machina that could have made the entire game less of a linear story and added a more compelling subplot than 'drunk teens act like drunk teens'.[/spoiler]

I could really elaborate a lot more about the story, because I really think they were onto something there, but it felt like either time or budget kept it as a good story rather than allowing for a more immerve experience.

tl;dr: game is good, but not great.  buy it because these types of devs and games need to be fiscally supported so we can see more of this in the future.

Summary first: The game looks great, well written dialogue, and good voice acting. Unfortunately, it feels a bit unpolished. It does not feel as if it's worth the $20 asking price.

------The remainder of this review will contain some spoilers------

Graphics:
The game looks good, but is also utilizing a very simplistic art style, and thus beauty isn't terribly hard to achieve. It does have confusing variation in the quality of the textures. Some textures are blurry and pixelated while others are very, very detailed. But otherwise, the game looks good.

Story:
The story, I personally find rather lacking. I like the banter between Delilah and Henry, but at the end of the game, everything simply resolves itself. Two teenagers that you confront early in the game go missing for weeks, but near the end of the game Delilah simply says "oh, by the way, they found those girls." The game leads you to believe there's some strange conspiracy going on, and that you're part of some social experiment, but it ends up being Ned, a character mentioned earlier on in the game. I won't get into how Ned's story goes, as it's not really relevant, but what I will say is that his actions do not make any sense at all. Why he's monitoring your conversations, why he's tracking your movements, why he's trying to frame you for arson, etc. It's never really explained. When you look at the evidence, he's even the one responsible for leading you to figuring everything out! At the end of the game, I didn't feel like I figured anything out, or solved some mystery, I simply walked from point A to point B and the game took care of itself.

Voice acting:
The voice acting is very good. Everyone involved did a great job.

Dialogue:
Mostly good, with some portions that felt...out of place. At one point, after finding a monitoring site behind a chain link fence, Delilah panics and says "burn the place down!" It's completely out of character for her, and it's obviously only said as a set up for something that happens later. It didn't sit right with me.

Game feel:
The game feel is good overall, but does fall short in some places. The movement system specifically. I often found myself frustrated with my inability to climb over waist high obstacles. They have a system in place to jump over things, but only the things they've placed there to be jumped over. You can't do it without a prompt. I also found myself getting hung up on objects sticking out of the ground, like fallen trees, etc. And I don't mean I was walking and ran into it, I mean I ended up on top of it and couldn't move. I was usually able to free myself by going back the way I came from when I ended up getting stuck.

I also found myself frustrated with the level of interactivity with the game world. There's a dozen books in the game, all strangely written by the same person more or less, and you can pick them up and turn them around, but you can never look inside, find a bookmark with something written on it, find a hand written note on one of the pages, etc.

Inside your tower you can pick up a coffee pot, a thermos, a dish soap bottle, all of these things, but you can't do anything with them! So frustrating for me, personally. It reminded me very much of SOMA and Cradle, only in those games you can actually use those in-game objects with each other. In firewatch, they don't do anything, and it felt very unfinished in that way.

Conclusion:
Overall, I felt like I had very little impact on the game. I was more of an observer than anything else. And while the game hands you a number of choices to make, in the end they all felt very inconsequential. There's also next to no real resolution to the game's underlying issues (your relationship with Delilah and Julia). Having said that, I still found the experience enjoyable, but I feel it would be more appropriate to price the game closer to $10, maybe $15. There's simply not enough gameplay there to warrant the $20 asking price, in my opinion.

Firewatch 

Impression

	In a world full of triple A titles demanding the spotlight, games like Firewatch tend to get overlooked. Gameplay, in the modern sense of the term, may be scarce here but there is a lot to like nonetheless. What game mechanics do exist work fluidly and feel realistic in nature. Whether swinging an axe or using a compass and map, you feel the immersive realism this game thrusts upon you from beginning to end.

	The art direction is absolutely gorgeous. Cartoon like in its appearance doesn’t hinder the serene feeling of wonder you get when just looking up toward the sunset in the distance. Watching a fire burn miles off in the dark forest instills both a captivating scene of beauty and a primal fear. What if the wind changes direction? What if it engulfs my tower in my sleep?

	All of these dynamics are compounded by the most engaging narrative driven game to come along, at least in this console generation, so far. The characters are not only interesting but they feel like living breathing people. By the end of the game I couldn’t help but be invested in them. Incredible voice acting breaths sarcastic and sometimes dramatic life into a world devoid of physical human interaction. The tones and inflections of both characters convey even more complicated emotions like annoyance, caring and anger in a way that is believable. The story hinges on these vocal interactions and the actors do not disappoint.

	Although my entire playthrough was a total of three hours and fifteen minutes, I feel satisfied. Episodic games like the new Hitman series, offer significantly less in terms of satisfaction for the same price tag. By the time the credits rolled all I wanted was more to play. But I do feel the story fits its length well and dragging it out would only diminish the game as a whole. 

	Replaying the game doesn’t offer a lot of value, but the same could be said for reading a novel a second time or even rereading this review. There is a point where a game transcends just being a game and becomes something else. An art. For me, this became a hidden treasure among all of the loud obnoxious titles boasting hours and hours of gameplay and multitudes of levels (cough, The Division, cough). This game is a masterpiece in its own right. Not for innovative gameplay or mechanics, but for a story that is so much more. It truly shows us that video games can be art. They can be emotionally compelling. I don't want to put down the controller so I can shoot more people in the face, but because I want to immerse myself in way that is unequivocally unique to gaming.
