Let me first start by saying I believe myself to be qualified in writing this review because I have played a fair number of narrative-based exploration/adventure games and consider this genre to be my favorite. I typically don't play blaster "pew pew" shoot-em-up games.

I'll start with the positive: I really enjoyed this game's beautiful environment. The setting was very nice, the graphics style was unique but well done, and I really felt like I was walking through a forest...most of the time. The games story premise was decent as well. I wouldn't call a stellar box office hit, but I think it was at least compelling and suspenseful such that it kept me playing. As some others have said, there was more they could have done, but it is clear that they were limited on time.

Now for the negative: It really is a shame that I have negative things to say about this game. It had so much potential. I'll mention the most frustrating element of this game first. The swearing. Good grief! You claim that this is "a game of adults having adult conversations" but I feel like the characters in this game were more like high schoolers. All those F words? You really couldn't come up with more intelligent language to express astonishment, surprise, grief, fear, disgust, sadness? Immaturity is everywhere these days. ADULTS know how to use words other than F-Words to express their feelings, and it sounds like the folks at Campo Santo have a good deal of growing up to do. SO disappointing and irritating to have to hear that word so often. 
I was anticipating this game from the moment I heard about it's development. It promised to deliver a stunning environment, which it certainly did. What frustrated me is the lack of ability to really explore this environment. Yes, there was some ability to explore, but the game was so focused on the narrative that it detracted from the players ability to explore. The trails were far too limited, and I had to stick to the path far too often when I really just wanted to explore the environment. With as restrictive as the story line and invisible barriers were, I would probably have more enjoyed actually being in the Shoshone (I have spent some time there myself). If I'd had more opportunity to explore, I would have put in more hours in this game.
The story was intriguing, but somewhat linear and anticlimactic. I would have liked to see more involvement in decision making into the stories outcome. There was also no real resolve to the backstory of Henry. 
As others have said, this game is rather short, and it didn't need to be. There were plenty of days in the game that went by with one simple dialog. For example, why couldn't I have have hiked to that rock precipice to eat my half a sandwich, before talking with Delilah? It seems like the product was designed by a group of very talented artists...but not really game designers. Campo Santo might even have known that from the beginning since their picture screenshot taking thing was a way of featuring their artwork. There was little creativity to player interaction like puzzles, challenges, or other aspects to keep the game fun. 

In summary: The game art was great, but that was almost the only thing that this game had going for it. Notice I said almost.

Firewatch is a beautiful game, but not for everyone. It is said, that it is a walking simulator, but in my opinion this the walking is only used as a trigger for the dialog between you (as Henry) and your supervisor Delilah. Both of you are about 40 years old and have some serious personal problems. And that the reason why this game is not for everyone. You should be of same age and experience in life (at best you are in some relationship) to understand the feelings and thoughts of Henry and Delilah.

The story of the game evolves very fast to something that seems to be a great conspiracy, but in the end, all is very normal, no aliens, no conspiracy, nothing special or unusual at all. You can think of it as a boring end, because your expectations gets quiet high on the secret you think you will find, but this story is so normal that it can real happen, perhaps some aspects of the story are not fiction.

The game mechanic is very simple, not much to learn about it, but you sometimes must decide very quickly your dialog answers. Also it was not easy for me (as non-native speaker) to fully understand some lines. The game give you goals to reach, but the map has more than these goals and if you do not leave the paths you will miss some beautiful places and their story (told you by Delilah). As far as I experienced there is no pressure to reach the goals in a specific time, even if there is a fire burning in the woods. So take your time playing the game and do not rush through it.

While I concede that this game likely speaks more to me and my demographic (heart-broken, male, thirty-something, fan of dad jokes) than what I guess it would to other people; this was nonetheless a type of game that I feel I've never experienced before.
It's kinda funny actually, because unlike most "genre-braking" games one encounters, this one doesn't innovates in a technical or mechanical way. Part of what makes it unique in fact, is how 'restrained' it is on its gameplay, taking a minimalistic approach to it, so to speak. It's easy to imagine for instance, the same story and concept being done by another studio using tons of quirky mini-games and other gameplay gimmicks related to exploring the wilderness. And yet, the developers wisely restrained from going into that direction.

Instead, what makes Firewatch so different and unique to me is how... 'adult' it is. I've been thinking for a while about this, and I can't find a better word to describe the core essence and feeling of this game.

It kinda puts upside down the connotations we usually put to "mature games". We usually relate this tag with violence, edgy social critizism, high philosophical concepts that require at least some high school knowledge or, more commonly, we connect "adult" with blood, sex or upsetting drama.

Firewatch however, goes into a whole different path. A path that I feel very few titles explore succesfully. Rather than being edgy, Firewatch is subdued. Instead of big explosions and high stakes to save the world, Firewatch is small and careful were it places its feet. Controlled and calm dialgoues rather than big displays of emotion. Hints of humor transitioning smoothly (and realistically), with serious exchanges between the characters.

More thoughtful novel than summer blockbuster. More conversation by the porch with beers than grandiose speech at a crowd. Not bigger but smaller. Not extensive but deeper.

This is my first review ever after many years of gaming. I like a wide variety of games but I feel compelled to share my thoughts on this one. First of all I think the people giving this negative reviews didn't really grasp what the game was, or simply wanted it to be something else.

What this game does is provide a fantastically realised narrative and a gorgeous backdrop to explore various themes. What it ultimately highlights is the stark truth that you cannot escape the realities of your life. The ending has real meaning and poignancy BECAUSE it was bittersweet and hard to swallow, not despite this. Life isn't all happy endings and rainbows and this is why Firewatch provides a welcome break from the everyday; the beautiful surroundings and budding relationship between the protagonists serves to provide a temporary time out from ordinary problems (isn't this what gaming is all about for some?). This mirrors the time the main character spends in this new environment, before ultimately facing up to what he left behind (or not if you choose to stay!).

The sense of wit and honesty in the dialogue is fantastic, and it is simply a well-written, thoughtful discussion piece that deserves your attention. Enjoy this game for what it does, not what it doesn't, and you will be taken on a very memorable journey.

It’s 1989. Your name is Henry. You’re standing in the elevator going to the underground garage. You’re about to take a trip to your new job: a fire lookout in Wyoming wilderness. The reason you took the job will be explained promptly. There’s nothing left to do other than get in the van. In a few short sequences you’ll arrive at the lookout tower. First trips out will be mundane, nothing much happens  yet, you have time to get accustomed to traversing cliffs, opening storage boxes, using the compass and the map. Quite soon though some weird and creepy stuff will begin to happen. Two trespassing teenagers will disappear, somebody will raid your tower, wires will be cut preventing communication with the outside world. All the components of the classical horror are here, but is that really it?

It’s easy to draw parallels between Firewatch and Gone Home, to focus on what’s conspicuous. Both games make you spend a fair share of playtime walking, both have soundtracks composed by Chris Remo, both even have enclosed continuous worlds with parts that are initially locked. And yet these two are very different. Gone Home explored the possibilities of a static installation engulfing you in thousands of ordinary household items mixed with the occasional important note or a peculiar artifact. Firewatch dismisses such disjointed freeform approach in favor of directing. The beginning is sliced and mixed like a good trailer: a few seconds of looking around in a serene and lonely environment are followed by a story premise retold with nothing more than a text. The game even is generous enough to let you pick a more personalized version of happy memories. The horror that destroys them afterwards is as imminent as it is calculated. And then it fades to black and cuts to the next scene, and fades to black again and cuts to the next scene again. The increasing speed of these transitions isn’t supposed to erase protagonists’ problems or your memories of them. It’s just a reminder of lesson learned long before: running away doesn’t work.

Lush and colorful wilderness that you’re supposed to traverse with map and compass in hand is deceiving. Gigantic national park disorients at first (especially if you turn off your position display on the map), but after a few hours of running various errands you start to see right through it. You get accustomed to it, like Henry got after living in the cabin for days. It’s your home now, and it’s nothing more than a set of corridors loosely connected with shortcuts that will become available in time. Firewatch exploits metroidvania mechanics in a straightforward way: all those overgrown bushes will remain impassable until the very end when you finally lay your hands on the axe. The sequence is unbreakable and all that you’ll get from wandering too much around is an occasional easter egg or particularly scenic view of the sunset.

Small yellow hand radio is two things at once: your agency and director’s will. It tells you what to do next with the voice of Delilah, your supervisor. It lets you to react to the unfolding of the story and game’s world by selecting a remark from a list. The choice of words serves seemingly no purpose other than letting you feel the attachment to your bodiless guide. You don’t have a choice in what to do next, but at least you can express your opinion (or at least select one from a predetermined list). Dialogs are the beating heart, the rhythm of the game. There’s just the right amount of jokes and witty remarks to make you feel at ease and become attached to the invisible partner. And just enough guiding to go forward with the story.

http://coub.com/view/bcuea The good amount of humor and bantering gives this story a human side. 

Delilah tells you what to do, you try your best to not let her down. She relies on you to know what’s happening, you rely on her on what to make of it. You both struggle to make sense of what’s happening and both wait. It is your job after all to watch. It’s in the title. And of course it happens. The fire. The inevitable conclusion to your waiting, the backdrop to the mystery that you’ve been trying to solve and the catalyst for the final stretch to the finalé. It forces you to retreat from your temporary shelter back to the pain of the unsolved problem that you’ve ran away from.

The fire burns away not just trees, but the fabric of the game itself. You lose access to most parts of the world. Most importantly it destroys all the red herrings, that distracted you. The Truman Show atmosphere, the horror movie scares fade out in the smoke. The irony is unbearable. There’s nothing left but guilt, sorrow and emptiness. The single jumpscare (which is actually pretty hard to find) turns out nothing more than a joke. The explanation for all the disappearances and other mystical events is simpler that you would’ve prefered. The ending is anticlimactic, there’s no point to it other than sad truth that you’ve known right off the start. It’s time to get back to the city and move on.

Firewatch does not feature heroes, but rather ordinary people with a rich past and powerfull present day desires, and you get taken on the rollercoaster drama ride of their summer in Wyoming wilderness. It's a mysterious, suspenseful, well crafted light novel, not particularly happy or sad and yet deeply emotional and reflective experience.

The gameplay is simple and the game does not have a lot of action -it's about walking around taking in the sights and doing your firewatch job. The fun begins though, when a little bit of creepy and a little bit of unkown starts happening around you, leaving you feeling powerless but curious. The way that the story progresses and that characters are presented, only by what they say, what they do or where they live, enhance the feeling of loneliness and fragility throughout the game, wich in turn resonates with the main character's personal story.

In my opinion this game is about making the player connect emotionaly with the characters -not to change anything, not to make anyone's life better, but simply to feel and understand. To me, that is equal parts powerfull and meaningful and beautiful.

Most negative talks about this game speak of it's ending, and i understand them. We are culturally wired to expect big BOOMs and adrenaline shot payoffs of any outside driven experience. Everybody wants mystery stories with poison daggers and cops and killers, but Firewatch fails at that. It gives you people with stories, with a mystery to get things moving, instead of Hercule Poirot and a crime scene. Beware of this and don't get this game if you rather play the role of the latter.

To wrap it up I want to strongly compliment the overall design of this piece. The graphics are dazzling in a way that you can just sit there with it, and the narrative is so tense and well put together that i have not once failed to advance nor felt boredom while playing.

All I can say is wow. Firewatch is one of the greatest games I have ever played. With a magnificent story and amazing graphics, this is one to be remembered. The dialogue was so good that I, at times, was laughing out loud - not chuckling - laughing.

A quick bit on the cons: The only cons that I could really think of were the natural barriers, which at times were a tad frustrating, and the fact that you cannot jump. The second con is very easily overlooked, as the gameplay style does not really need you bunny hopping around.

I can definitely say that I plan on playing this game again, as soon as possible! I want to choose different dialogues, read up on some easter eggs, and explore areas in the game map that I haven’t seen yet. The reason why? I have never felt like I wanted more, and to follow the characters of a video game more than with this one. I wanted to know what happened to the characters, what they did next. I can only relate this feeling to when one finishes a damn good book and wishes that the last chapter is one page longer, or that there is an epilogue. This is clearly because of the (no spoilers) well thought out and well written ending. It tied up loose ends, of course, and provided a sentimental feel for players. Like I said before, I wish that I could “keep going” in the game! I can’t wait for the next game made by Campo Santos!

[b]Overview:[/b] [i]Conversation simulator, but in a good way -- really well-done interactions, writing, and voice acting. Having a Wallpaper Generator like this makes it worth the $20. Runs well on low-end computers.[/i]  

If you enjoy Life Is Strange or Telltale games but hated how restricted gameplay felt, Firewatch is a good bet for you. 

The gameplay is more liberal though still linear, in the sense that the game gives you [b]a lot of breathing room to let you do things[/b] between plot points. [b]You're allowed to explore,[/b] and look around, and take everything in. The game's not going to let you jump off a cliff and die (or at least I avoided it well enough), but you can see some cool stuff if you wander around. 

Wandering around is definitely worth it. You can have some [b]pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gorgeous views[/b] -- even on low graphics. And they set the atmosphere really well. The way they use nature to frame each day/night's events is brilliant. 

Speaking of graphics, this game has a [b]nicely low threshold in terms of computer requirements,[/b] which is wonderful for low-end gamers like myself. [b]Everything loads gorgeously regardless of graphics settings,[/b], but if you have the privilege of being able to load it in Ultra settings, you're in for a treat. The game even lets you take a limited number of photos -- limited likely because they store it in an online server, which lets you share with friends and buy prints if you're feeling up for it. 

I have to say, though, while the physical gameplay of the game is solid, as are the graphics, [b]the plot-related gameplay centers around your conversation with another ranger,[/b] who describes herself as a veteran and talks you through the ropes. It's pleasant conversation, really. The writing's great in that sense. 

What really got me was [b]how naturally your conversations are integrated into the context of the game.[/b] In other games, the "jolt" of reaction from the game is usually more obvious, or they'll exaggerate it: "Riningear will remember this." "This action will have consequences." Part of what makes Firewatch so great, though, is how subtly the game itself will pick up what you've said. Sometimes it'll point out things that your character observes in terms of reactions, but mostly obvious things. When you return to replay or watch the game through someone else's perspective, though, sometimes the unique dialogue makes it feel like you're playing a completely different game.

[b]The voice acting and writing really make the game, though.[/b] The two characters, Henry and Delilah, make hilarious, entertaining banter that doesn't shy away from their characters and situation. When they need to be serious, they're serious. And mixed with the way the game is designed to react to you, it's all absolutely persuasive.  

I do agree that the ending left a bit to be asked for. I personally don't think it's a [i]bad[/i] ending. Bittersweet, maybe, and a little awkward. But it's realistic, in my honest opinion, and I don't dislike it that strongly for that reason. 

[b][i]Is Firewatch worth it?[/i][/b] To put it into perspective, a movie is about $9, and that's about 100 minutes. It took me about 3.5 hours to get through this game. And I personally liked this game. [b]So yes, I'd say it's worth it.[/b] $20 is a good price for this neat experience.

With the difference that, in a movie or a book, you can't have feelings for a random piece of junk you go past every day on your way to work, until you walk past it for the last time, knowing that it won't be here tomorrow. And you can't walk, climb and absent-mindedly look at stuff for several minutes, lost in thoughts about tough stuff the characters go through and how weird life is. And you don't get attached, say, to a certain silhouette of a building on the horizon, silently greeting it when it shows momentarily through the clearing in the trees.

Also, the game contains arguably the best written set of "found documents", found so often in countless other games. Actually, the whole material world of the game tells you something and means something, which is amazing if you think about it. It's ordinary life, so ordinary objects (like detective novels, an apple or empty beer can) are not decorations for shootouts, but meaningful objects that people use, like or dislike, and that sometimes mean a bunch to you and your character.

The best way I can describe Firewatch is that it is the grown-up version of going to camp for the summer. It's about the kind of relationship you can forge with a person when being so far away from your real life and the kind of mysteries that seem so grand and terrifying when you have nothing else to do but dwell on them. Above all, though, it's about the feeling you get when the summer comes to an end and it's time to go home. Do you feel disillusioned? Did the bonds you form mean anything? That's for you to find out.

Firewatch is a narrative experience that lasts roughly five hours, and it's not something I'd particularly want to play again. However, I loved this game and my experience with it will be something I'll talk about and think about in the future when I think about how games can do things that books and movies cannot. I highly recommend it.

Firewatch is a first person exploration game. There's not much interaction with the world besides picking up and examining some items. You play as Henry, a volunteer fire lookout at the wilderness of Wyoming. You keep contact through a radio with your supervisor Delilah. And this atleast for me was the best part of the game, the well written dialogue between characters where you can make choices how to react and what to say. These choices won't affect the actual plot of the game, but ofcourse will shape the relationship between Delilah and Henry. The voice acting is magnificent. The actors make everything sound so natural and real. I wish there were even more dialogue choices to make, too often there were no options at all. 

The world looks beautiful and is quite fun to explore with a map and a compass at hand. Unfortunately the world has very little if any wildlife. I suppose it's ment to highlight the feeling of isolation, but it would have made the world less static and bit more interesting. The music in the game is used very sparingly, but always adds to the already great atmosphere.

Because of the short nature of the game, around 4-6 hours I won't talk about the story and plot points. It's all better left for the player to discover. There are big tonal shifts throughout the game, it starts with brilliant heavily dramatic text based intro and goes to jolly first day at the job. There's bit of a romance and suspense. There has been complaints about red herrings and dissapointing ending. But in my opinion, the game did really good job of putting me in Henry's shoes. I felt paranoia, joy, remorse and also dissapointment with him. It wasn't dissapointment about the game. The story, just like the characters felt real and mature. There's also have been people pointing out plot holes, but that's mainly because they weren't paying attention or were excepting something different. Though there is one thing I personally can't explain but nothing too major.

Firewatch is a good start for Campo Santo as their first game. I know they can do even better so I will be getting their next game day one also. Ofcourse this game is nott for everyone, since it could be called as glorified walking simulator. But personally, im open for more narrative driven even quite short experiences when the price matches that.

Warmth. This word that comes to my mind when I think of Firewatch. You know, this kind of warmth that comes from hands of your grandma which you visit once or twice a year, this warmth that comes from candles on your dinner table on the Christmas night, this warmth that is radiated by the bonfire you and your father made one cold summer night beside a calm river. This "game"... Forgive me but I can't call it "a game". It is not a game - it is an interactive story. So this INTERACTIVE STORY from the very beginning with its visual style, music, setting, even the animation and gameplay makes you feel comfortable, cozy, peaceful. Campo Santo created a beautiful place where you want to come back to after a stressful day and just walk around that dream-like forest...alone. Kind of. You have your colleague: Deliah. This is where the game shines the most - the characters are developed beyond any praise. The dialogues are one of the best in history of videogames. The voice acting is on top notch. From the very beginning Deliah feels like a real person and Henry isn't just a character - you become Henry after some time thanks to the great job the creators made in the beginning by introducing Henry's backstory and giving you a chance to play your role in that as well.

Though it is a story-driven "game" the plot here isn't something phenomenal so don't expect to be blown away by some crazy twist that turns everything upside down. But that what makes it special, in my opinion. In the end of the day you realize that all what happened actually could happen in real life and that makes the whole experience more relatable and believable. Conclusion: This game isn't for everyone - this game is for those who are looking for escape from their chaotic and tumultuous lives. Firewatch is a story-driven walking simulator set in a stunningly beautiful rendition of the Wyoming wilderness. Unfortunately, Firewatch is not without its issues. While I understand what they were going for, the revelation of the plot’s big mystery will come as something of a let down, and the game continues on just a little bit longer than it needs to after the main plot is resolved. And though the game does feature a variety of dialogue options to choose from, these decisions are truly meaningless in terms of their ability to have any effect on the game’s plot. It’s great for immersion, but the decisions you make will have literally zero impact on the plot itself.

Firewatch is also a very short experience, and though the value of a game is something that’s extremely hard to tackle, I consider an average of 3-5 hours to complete to be underwhelming for a $20 title with zero replayability (due to the aforementioned lack of impact of choice). Ultimately, this may be one to wait on until a Steam sale dips it below $10.

Firewatch is a beautiful and gripping experience. It's smartly written, with well developed characters and some of the best dialogue and voice acting I've came across in any game.

It mixes genre well, with genuinely moving moments and characters you're drawn to invest in, while keeping you consistency gripped with incredibly tense thrilleresque sections. The vast and stunning natural environment around you contributes to a feeling of eerie isolation as the game goes on, and you share your characters increasing anxiousness and paranoia when it becomes apparent that you are not alone. 

Firewatch's other great success is how this all draws you to invest completely in the central mystery; and ultimately this is also where the game disappointingly falls a little flat.. From the moving and poignant introduction, through the consistent building of tension, and suspense at the unravelling of the games main mysteries, to an urgent ending as the forest fires rage and close in around you.. there comes a suspenseful expectation which is not met by the far more understated (both in tone and event) and somewhat anticlimactic ending. While in some ways I do actually like the ending in terms of those characters and the games themes, due to the build-up it inevitably makes the experience feel a little confused in tone in the end, and just a little unfulfilling.

On the whole I really enjoyed Firewatch. Recommended.

This review is an open letter to one of the developers, Jane Ng, the lead environmental artist at Campo Santo.

Jane recently made a very thoughtful post right here on the Steam Community Forums...

-----------

"hey there.

I thought about not responding, because normally ppl who want to refund are rude and unpleasant and I choose to not engage and dwell on it.

You seem nice and I figured what the heck, why not have a conversation about this, now that I have read it and it's right here in front of me.

So here is what I think. As the developer. Sorry if it's a bit stream of consciousness because I want this to come from the heart.

The 11 of us all took a lot of risk to make this, and sacrificed financially to give Firewatch a chance. We all could have had much better paying jobs elsewhere, but we all thought this game idea had potential to be something special. We seemed to like each other ok, so we all took a big leap of faith. Two years, we say. Let's give this a go, worst outcome is we all hate each other and go back to various money jobs, but we all could say, WE TRIED.

Two years +. We are all crammed in a tiny office, sharing one bathroom. It is not a glamorous thing, making an independent game. It is just a small room full of computers and a used microwave and $10 office chairs we luckily got from craigslist. Life happened during those two years: there were big breakups, profound illnesses of loved ones, a baby, etc. The dev team got to be like family, because that's how making an indie game is, you are all in it together, through thick and thin, supporting one another bc if you don't, there is no way in hell this game would get made, let alone any chance of it to be worth more than a bucket of ♥♥♥♥.

We were excited, but terrified. We felt free, but were constrained. I have been in this industry for 15 years almost, and this is the hardest I have ever worked. We all gave it our all, to make this weird thing, and we had no idea if it was any good to anybody else. All we could do, was try the damn hardest to make something we are honestly proud of. At the end, if this was a commercial failure, all we have got is what we have made. Nobody could take that away.

So yes, I am sad when people think this game is not worth the money we asked for (which we thought was a fair ask). It makes me feel like I failed them. It is ok if people don't like the game, but it affects me personally a lot, when people feel like it was not -worth- the time they engaged with it.

But do I blame you for wanting to get the most out of your $18? No. I don't know your financial circumstances. $18 might be a lot. Or even it isn't a lot, why shouldnt' you try to get the most out of it? That's a fair desire. That's why we asked for $18 too, because money is something we could all use more of.

So I supopse in conclusion, if you do refund, I am not upset. It's on me to learn not to care too much. All I ask is that maybe sometime in the future, when the game goes on mega dirt cheap sale, you could gift tthe experience to someone else you think will enjoy it like you did.

Sincerely,
Jane"

Okay, this is the first time I've ever reviewed a game here. 

I'm a career Wildland Firefighter, so you can probably guess that I was attracted to this game from the videos and pictures. 

Now that that's out of the way, the only real cons I had were just a couple of details that weren't quite right [Slight spoiler, sort of] -the FF on the ship at the end, during evac... We don't wear SCBA in Wildland. The flipside of that, is that there is a lot of authenticity in this game. Many of the brocures and documents you find along the game are *almost* exact replicas of RL things, such as the fireline handbook (which even went as far as adding NWCG standards), fuel model publications, USFS prints and logos -hell even the terminology was for the most part correct. I was initially twitching a bit when he calls the pulaski an "axe", but pleasantly surprised when he was quickly corrected. 

Many aspects of this game are pretty realistic, even with the stylized graphics. Some others -not so much. 

That's the technical stuff. 

As for the actual depth of the game? ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Legit first time I've ever played a game that was so emotionally involved with the player that I'd get that tingling, hair-on-the-neck-standing-up feeling. It felt super believable, yet keeping you on the edge of your seat guessing. 

I'm sure I know where this story is going. Okay, maybe not, but I have a good theory... Well, that theory just got shattered all to hell. Damn, this is some crazy ♥♥♥♥... Maybe it's one of those good stories turned bad horror flick? Nope, and then the heartstrings. 

I honestly feel that the creators did their homework on this piece. Are there technical things that weren't 100%? Sure. But then again, I've never played a game that's... well, a simulation of my career. So that's a first. Going into it, I expected a lot of mistakes and some of the more common misnomers to fly right up in my face, but was shocked when I started to notice just how much care was taken in creating this work of art. 

The music is on par, the scenery is awesome, the story is amazing. 

Do yourself a favor and buy this. Best money I've ever spent on steam. 

Bonus: The ending credits remind me *so* much of some of my fondest memories, going on western fire detail. That little addition was the icing on the cake. Campo Santo just HAD to make me all nostalgic. I'm not going to ruin it for you, but when you get to that point, you'll see what I mean. 

Short and simple: Buy it.

I think this is a gem of a game.  The story, voice acting, dialogue, and artwork are all excellent.  Some particulars:

 - The landscape is truly beautiful.  You get a camera in the game, and I actually found myself wanting to take pictures with it.

 - Your movement -- whether down the staircase that wraps around your fire tower, over a rocky trail, or rappeling over a cliff -- is pretty authentic.  I'm a fan of hiking, so I was really happy with all of the little kinesthetic things that make it feel like you're actually a person moving through a textured space.  There are so many fine touches -- one of my favorites is how sometimes while you're descending your fire tower, your character will brace an arm against a wooden beam overhead and skip down the next few steps.  It feels like something I would actually do.

 - The story feels like something out of a literary short story anthology.

I can see how it wouldn't be for everyone, but if you like the outdoors, or you like stories with a heavy psychological focus on the characters, or you like both, you will probably like this game.

After completing the game I think the reviews are a little too much in favour of the game. First thing when I fired up the game, I set all setting to ultra and 4K resolution. To my suprise the games frame rate was all over the place. Once I was getting 60fps, then I would move forward a little and it would dip to high 20s. I decided to change the resolution to 1440p and 90% of the time I was running in locked 60fps with occasional drops to 40fps and couple of times to below 10fps. Seems poorly optimized as the game doesn't look to be graphically demanding (I'm running GTX 980 Ti).

What I trully love about the game are its voice actors. Seriously, they did a great job at conveying emotions, humour and sandess. It is among the best voice acting in the games I played and without showing their faces or any cutscenes, is an even better achievement. They add so much more life to the story and seems more engaging.

There are few moments in the game where you have a break from the missions and can go and explore (you can do that on the missions as well). This is where the game falls short. I was really dissapointed by the dead world of Firewatch and its emptiness. There is absolutely no wildlife except of one deer and a turtle. As a game set in the woods that's a big minus. Then you start to notice that there is nobody else there with you. There are two moments where you meet other people but you never get to interact with them except telling the girls off. That combined with the fact that you never see Delilah makes you feel very alone in the game. Also, prepare to get lost and taking wrong turns a lot as the game doesn't have a proper map and navigation. Without getting lost or exploring the map I probably would finish the game in 3 hours.

There are very little things to interact with in the game, there are few cases here and there, couple of trees to chop down and couple of overgrown paths to clear. There is nobody else to interact with, no animals, not even any collectibles. I think that this kills the whole idea of having an open world, it's just emptiness and lack of content. I really was looking forward to exploring this beautiful game but felt really dissapointed after finding out how boring it is. This makes this game something that once you complete once, will probably never play again, unless there is Firewatch 2 coming out in couple of years and you want to remind yourself the storyline before playing sequel.

Then there are bugs. I have encountered multiple times trees flying in mid air, objects appearing out of nowhere and even areas of the map not loading properly. There weren't any game breaking bugs but just something that would break the experience a little.

I really enjoyed the story though. It was really emotional and I really got attached to the main characters. I was expecting a little more from the ending however I didn't find it as dissapointing as other people say.

In the state this game is now I think it deserves a 6/10. There was so much more potential in the world created that it makes me sad the developer just didn't use it. There's no "neutral" button for reviews. I'm on the fence about Firewatch, but don't want to discourage people from buying it. What you'll get out of it depends on how you value games - It's not bad and there's a lot it does right, it tells a story that can leave an impact, but be aware that it's only about 3-4 hours long, linear, and with few gameplay elements.

Firewatch is more like an interactive movie than a game, with beautiful visuals and decent voice acting - Although despite that, after getting halfway through I realised I wasn't really enjoying playing it. I bought it blindly on release without finding out more about it first - I was hoping it'd be a survival timesink with a story. Instead it turned out to be a very short walking simulator, which isn't want I wanted from a game. After refunding (and swapping it for Subnautica) I watched other people play it - The story was good enough for me to want to see how it ended, at least.

Short game as it is, you actually get out of it what you put into it - Although many of the plot points are only explained if the player throughly explores some rooms. It's also dependant on how the player responds to the dialogue, despite that not changing where the player goes or the plot's events - And IMO this makes the plot fall a bit short. Also, the game seemed as if it should've been longer and wraps up far to quickly at the end, almost as if the devs ran out of budget or something. 

If you don't mind that then go ahead and get it - Just don't expect it to charm your socks off. IMO, there are many other games out there which tell better stories while actually being fun to play at the same time. This makes me think that perhaps Firewatch should've been an animation or a film instead, especially considering the linearity of its plot. It'd work better as a game if the player's actions had more consequences.

Stories in gaming vary from light-hearted, to dark in tone, and anywhere in between, and many take twists and turns in order to surprise the audience, subvert expectations, or to keep things fresh and intriguing as the player progresses. Firewatch certainly changes its story arc and expectations partway through, but it ends up doing so in a confusing and flaccid manner that acts as a betrayal of its original intentions rather than a heightening of interest. This ‘hiking simulator’ could’ve been a pleasant character-driven experience, or a tale of an eerie discovery which leads to paranoia-inducing consequences, but Firewatch refuses to commit to one or the other, instead mashing both together into a poorly realized affair.

Firewatch has a lot of hiking and climbing to do and the patch of wilderness that Henry is stationed in is certainly sizeable in scope, but thankfully Henry, the main protagonist, doesn’t dawdle when you need to get him somewhere in a jiffy. Getting lost is something nigh impossible due to mechanics twofold: the handy map that has a limited tracking of your movement, and how traversable terrain is structured likes ‘lanes’, rather than open ground, that you can tackle however you see fit. Henry can move through the environment in three ways; on foot, by climbing or dropping down at specific context sensitive places, or by rappelling - And that’s it. How limited your interactivity with the environment is becomes a bit laughable, but it could be argued that exploring the wild is only a secondary thought to the progression of the story. Not being able to just reach up at a random ledge to hoist myself up for a better view of my surroundings continued to be an awkward, though minor, bother for me throughout the game.

The game is clearly advertised for its story, writing, and the pleasant, warm visuals that would look great as a photo print no matter how you angled it - Not its dynamic gameplay. The story is, for the most part, about Henry and his escape into a job out in the forest to try and escape issues plaguing him at home, along with his supervisor, Delilah, who also isn’t in the greatest condition  concerning her homefront. The duo are clearly unhappy and confused with their lot in life and the hands dealt to them, though they combat it (and each other) with wit and sarcasm via walkie talkies, which are their only means of communication. The radio system is very basic but it’s what pushes along the dialogue and story between the protagonists; in many cases it’ll be Henry reporting something on his hikes and Delilah continuing the conversation, or sometimes she’ll strike up a chat out of nowhere resulting in a handful of replies Henry can resort to - Or he can not respond at all. Your choices of replies isn’t comically night and day like Mass Effect’s response wheel, as Henry is already a tired, worn down man who’s quite dry and straight forward, and many of his responses revolve around his nature, not trying to make him to be a paragon of goodness or an utter jerk. The conversations between Henry and Delilah are often comical, with their sarcasm bouncing off one another resulting in humour that is very dry and snarky, which is an understandable turnoff for some.

While the writing is solid and it’s relatively believable that two people could get so sassy, it’s the continuity that impresses me the most. I’ve never really been able to see continuity or consequences for decisions be capitalized on in a game before, excluding a lone decision that has a major sway in future events but was executed by a lone button press. Firewatch has many small things that are referenced to and brought up later on that you and I probably forgot, but the game certainly didn’t. Should Henry dodge a question about his personal life, Delilah will ask him again later. If Henry vandalizes personal property, he’s later held accountable for it. Finding an item in a cache box is referred to when a different cache is opened. It’s these small acts of continuity that puts Firewatch a great leap above other games that boast the impact of player decisions, and that makes me respect and commend the writing.

Henry and Delilah are good characters that are unfortunately stuck in a story that, while I hesitate to call bad, certainly subverts expectations, as mentioned earlier. Without going into spoiler territory, the tale of Henry’s escape to the wilderness goes from personal drama to mystery and conspiracy only to run its course and return to personal drama in the final act’s fleeting moments. If the story focused itself entirely on Henry and Delilah’s dilemmas back home while he’s sent out to perform duties for his job and explore along the way, that would’ve been just fine. If the story focused itself entirely on this mysterious plot and how two lookouts ended up getting wrapped up in the mess and their desire to uncover the truth, that would’ve been just fine. Instead it mashes these two angles together into something of a limp, soggy mess that I can only assume was written in order to both fill game time and introduce enough intrigue to keep players going past the original personal drama. Quite frankly it just falls flat, especially when in moments of duress the protagonists continue to make quips and pessimistic gags in the face of looming dread, doubly so when clues are discovered, only to find out later that the ‘villain’ takes on some laughably implausible means in order to get their way. Near the finale this menacing story is more or less ‘solved’, but it’s an empty resolution that brings nothing to the overall conclusion of Firewatch and is practically gleamed over before the credits roll. The game has an identity issue in what kind of story it wants to tell with these two characters the player can have legitimate interest in, which ended up dragging me down to the point of dragging Henry’s feet along just to complete the game.

Firewatch’s writing, continuity, characters and visuals are the biggest positives I can levy in its favor, but the disappointing turn of the story and its conclusion makes me realize I could’ve enjoyed Firewatch much, much more if it had a better head on its shoulders. I would be able to look past the inadvertently limited movement in the environment, but traversing it while pursuing a plot I ended up losing all effort to care about only made its completion a chore rather than a joyful chase. Firewatch is a difficult game to review.  On one hand, I liked it personally, but on the other hand, it definitely won't appeal to everyone.  Some people will even go as far as to consider it a "walking simulator" similar to Dear Esther, as the game generally consists of you walking from one part of the forest to another while chatting with your supervisor over the walkie-talkie.  However, there are still some mild adventure game elements present; you will need to obtain a few tools to reach certain areas that would otherwise be inaccessible, and you will need some orienteering skills to navigate the forest using a map and compass.  Furthermore, you are constantly presented with multiple dialogue options during the radio conversations with your supervisor, which subsequently influences each character's tone when speaking to one another - although it has no effect on the major events of the story.  I believe that it can actually be beneficial to maintain a certain degree of linearity in the plot because it becomes difficult to tell a compelling story when there are too many branching paths for the player to take.  That being said, the game still presented an adequate amount of interactivity to keep me engaged.

The biggest criticism most people have of this game is that they were disappointed by the ending.  You will often hear people say that the whole game maintained an aura of suspense leading up to the finale, but then the ending fell flat since they were expecting something crazier.  You will also hear that, while the ending resolves the central mystery of the plot, it raises even more unanswered questions that are left open to the player's interpretation, and people wanted more of a sense of closure.  I personally think that the developers intended for the game to end this way; Firewatch has a very strong theme of realism, so it would only make sense for the ending to follow suit.  However, I will say that I sensed some budget difficulties as I witnessed the ending.  I won't spoil anytihng, but I'll say there were certain elements that could have easily been added to the ending if the developers had either more time or money.

Speaking of realism, the voice acting in Firewatch is nothing short of excellent, and it makes the characters very believable.  No matter which dialogue options you choose, you can always see why the characters respond to each other the way they do.  To top it all off, the environments in this game are absolutely gorgeous; you will feel as though you are walking through a real forest in Wyoming.  You can clearly tell that the development team poured a lot of heart into Firewatch, despite consisting of only 11 people.  Still, I think $20 is a lot to ask for considering the game is only 4 or 5 hours long.  It might be best to buy it during a sale, but I'd still say it's worth your time.

Firewatch is the story of someone who takes the job of a forest ranger for the summer in order to escape the problems of his life.  During his tenure, the only person he has to talk to is the dispatcher named Delilah who keeps him company over their walkie talkies.

A couple of strange things happen which lead them to investigate what appears to be a conspiracy going on in the park.  

First of all, the dialog between Henry and Delilah is probably the best part of this game.  They have a natural rapport that is absolutely believable.  By the first 20 minutes of the game, they seem like real people.

The graphics are good too.  It's presented in a first person perspective in a cartoony graphical style that reminded me of Team Fortress.  The way they show your hands as you climb up rocks and ropes reminded me of Mirrors Edge.  

As for the story, well, just understand that this is not a horror game.  If you're looking for a slasher film payoff, you might want to save your money.  This is more of a human story and what isolation can do to people, even when they're together alone.  This is the part I was sort of disappointed in, but fortunately I can shake that off and appreciate what was presented.  The paranoia that the game builds up through story and subtle changes in the environment was well thought out.  

One other con that I should mention is there is a lot of back tracking in this game.  It got to the point where I'd see on the map where I neede to go, and think, "Oh man!  I need to go all the way over there?!"  Even with the ability to run, climbing rocks and ropes takes forever...and there aren't really any shortcuts.  You'll find two routes you can take, but each of them  are about the same distance. 

Finally, I did encounter a bug where there was an invisible wall placed right in front of an open area you had to walk through.  It had no business being there at all, and it made me find an alternative route just to get passed it.  It took me a few minutes to figure out if it was a bug or if the story suddenly took a science-fiction twist.  :)

So overall, if you like walking simulators with good stories, give this one a try.  If you're looking for the next scarefest, I'd look elsewhere.

And with the writing and voice acting put forth here, getting to know Henry and Delilah is as simple as turning up the volume and listening. The dialogue of Firewatch might be some of the best I’ve ever heard in a video game. The characters are real, fleshed out people. Too many characters in gaming before have been one trick ponies. If the character has had a sad life, he or she is nearly always moody and bleak. The tough guys are always tough guys. The happy ones are always happy ones. Firewatch is a unique game, a heavy emphasis on story and the interaction between two people who never meet face to face and the lives they are trying to escape from.  

Gameplay wise there is not a great deal of interactivity with your environment, instead if focuses more on navigating from location to location and interacting with your boss, Delilah over the radio.  As such, this game might not be for everybody, it is more a receptive experience rather than an interactive one.  

Visually I love it, I really like the art style and colours they use, quite breath taking in my opinion.  

Story is for the most part excellent and compelling, fantastic voice acting between two characters that are flawed and feel very human.  As others have noted the ending is perhaps not as strong as it could have been, but it should be noted perhaps part of the reason is the start and middle portions work very well.  

As mentioned, voice acting is fantastic and the music, while sparse is very well done as does a great job of conveying emotion. 

Length wise I clocked in over 3 hours to complete the main story without really treading too far off the beaten path.  Considering the amount of things to do in the game, this felt about right, not too short but it doesn't drag on either.  There could be some replayability, making different conversation choices, although I am not certain these will have a dramatic affect on the overall story.  

Overall I recommend this game to people looking for a good emotional story between "real" people.  Those looking for an interactive experience (i.e having lots of things to do) might want to consider if this is a game for them.  

It left me quite satisfied and was a different experience than that I usually have. 

Price wise I think it is fair, it costs just a bit more than a take away pizza here (to put things into perspective) and far better value for money.  

Pros
+ Strong Characters that feel real
+ Relaxing game for the most part
+ Outstanding voice acting
+ Beautiful visuals
+ Strong story overall
+ Nice music


Cons
- Ending feels weaker than the rest of the story.  Story builds up suspence only to fall a bit flat. 

Other
- Not a lot of interactivity in the game, meaning apart from walking, talking, a bit of rappelling and the odd item pickup and tree chopping (twice for me) there is not a lot to "do".  For me, I am completly fine with this, but people looking for lots of things to actually do might want to watch some Youtube vids to see if this is for them.

Firewatch is a game whee you play as a man named Henry. Your wife Julia is sick with Dementia and moves back to Australia. You want to escape from everything and you decide to become a volunteer and become a firewatcher. When you arrive at your outpost you meet a woman named Delilah who is gonna be the only person you talk to through the entire game. You never see her and the only way to talk to her is through your trusty radio. The game also has a sub plot, but I'll cover that a bit tad later.

The dialogue between Henry and Delilah is my favorite part of the game. It feels very natural how they talk between each other and I feel like that helps a lot with the game. 

Firewatch is a walking simulator and a very bare bones one at that. The game takes place over a period of 79 days ( you don't play through all of them) where you explore the forest. When you explore the forest you can sometimes find stuff that have an icon of a radio next to them and you can talk about that stuff to Delilah and maybe spark up a conversation that will reveal the more about Delilah or Henry. The game also lets you explore the entire map at your own pace, so if you want to wander off and explore you are free to do so, but Delilah will drop in once in a while to remind you what you're supposed to be doing.

The graphics are absolutely outstanding. The entire environment looks absolutely gorgeous and it's breathtaking just to go to the highest point in the map and look around at the sights which are all just amazing. The entire forest feels alive as the trees sway with the wind and the sounds of the wilderness help to build the perfect atmosphere.

The soundtrack is also amazing, when you explore the music sometimes changes to somber music to stuff that will creep you out a bit, it's all very good and definitely worth owning the soundtrack.

Alright now I'm going to the territory of stuff that I thought were really bizarre and downright poorly executed. 

The texture problems in later sections of the game really are just not good and break you out of the game as soon as you see them. Also the frequent frame drops happen quite often in the end game section. Also the ending is very out of place and happens way too soon.

The game took me 3 hours to finish and I took my time off and explored the forest and not to mention I got lost quite a lot during my play time.

Alright here is the problem I had with the plot so *SPOILER WARNING*

Alright the two subplots with the missing girls and the stalker are very mediocre. First the missing girl subplot has one of the worst wraps up I have ever seen. The game sort of expects you that the stalker did something to them, but it later turns out that they were messing around somewhere else which I thought was cheap.

The stalker storyline has a very nice buildup, but the ending for the subplot felt very out of place and very weird with in tone of the rest of the game. Thinking you will end up with a satisfying conclusion the game lets you down right at the end.

*SPOILER WARNING OVER*

Overall, I enjoyed my time with Firewatch. While I don't think it's worth the full price at a discount I can safely say you can check this game out. 

Final Rating:
7.5/10 - Great game, but only on a discount

Firewatch is principally, a mystery story. It takes place in the wilderness of Wyoming and you are Henry. You come in control at a crossroad in his life as his wife has an early form of dementia, and he's had some recent trouble involving his drinking problem and the law. He escapes to the Firewatch post as he can't quite come to grips with his situation and the solitude might have done him well.

After a two-day hike to the watch tower, you 'meet' the boss, Delilah, via handheld radio. This vehicle of communication is literally your only means of any sort of social interaction as you're quite alone with only the trees and wildlife to keep you company. Or, are you?

The game allows you to respond to situations and dialog with several choices, and playing through, there's that personal touch like you're making a difference.

Your first day is a bit tough as you have to deal with some skinny dipping college girls—I said tough didn't I? Though the interaction is never face-to-face, you shout empty threats at them across the pond in an effort to get them to stop being litter bugs and shooting off fireworks. With the addition of a far-off interaction with another hiker, the day was rather uneventful until you returned to your watch tower. It was very clearly trashed maliciously.

From then on, when Henry isn't enjoying his summer solitude in the woods, there's an air of mystery as strange things happen. It is all brought to a head when he discovers a clipboard with transcripts of his and Delilah's radio conversations out by the lake! Shortly after, he's knocked out and the makes of a conspiracy start to unfold.

Much of the gameplay was running errands for Delilah up to this point, but it quickly escalates into investigating an unknown fenced region in the middle of the woods and the eventual abandoned caves.

So much of what you find points strangely toward a human experiment involving two people left in isolation for an extended period of time. Even more mystery unfolds as those girls were reported missing and suspicious calls, claiming to be Henry, report that Delilah knows what caused the forest fires that quickly swallow up the area. 

The conclusion comes all too quickly, and it honestly, left something to be desired. 

The story-crafters did an excellent job in building it all up as I was hooked in wanting to know more. Once those final credits made their crawl across the screen, it then left me wanting more, actually disappointed since—this—was it. 

You're given a disposable camera mid-game and it seemed like the perfect opportunity to document the strange occurrences. Even more so when evidence began to point at your character's guilt! Those photos' ultimate purpose was a bit of a slap to the face as it really makes you feel foolish.

I could only think of all the strange things that had happened to Henry.  

In gameplay, I found charts with character traits written in. Indicating that whomever the author was, specifically believed that Henry was gullible. Even knew his history prior to joining the Firewatch program. 

On those charts, Delilah was also mentioned to still be in a relationship despite her tale of how she came to be at her post. She seemed to be just as innocent, but she admitted to fudging a report to avoid talking to the police. 

Things weren't adding up. 

Regardless, the ending was so simple. 

I enjoyed the game and was engrossed in it's execution. Running from one end of the forest down to the lake front, and back up to my tower as quick as my feet would carry me. The character development between you and your only emotional anchor, Delilah, is effectively the main attraction next to the mystery that surrounds the woods.  It was so engaging, I really liked the snarky wit and chemistry her and Henry shared. The visuals were beautifully cell-shaded and the ambiance really immersed the player into the environment. From the first person perspective, scaling cliff walls during those intense moments, there were several opportunities I was sure something dangerous was going to be waiting for me. 

It was the equivalent of a good book in terms of entertainment. Being able to choose my immersion level meant I could look at everything, or just follow the objectives. It was neat reading and investigating whatever I could put my hands on.  Putting together these details into this side-narrative next to the one built into the game.

Ultimately though, it was a book that ended in such a way that it actually made me angry. 

Not so much at the journey, as it was great ride. But at myself for being so invested.

It's a "life is tough" tale, and really, that doesn't bother me. It's the fact that my choices may have warranted different responses, but played no part in the ending at all.

Games made by Telltale like "the Walking Dead" series make your choices matter by potentially losing favorite characters and changing the outcome of the story. Whatever that may be, your crafted it with your own morals and values. Firewatch fell flat in that regard, and it should have been evident to me early on with the prologue choices.
Plus, I don't think it was worth the $20 price tag. I knocked it out in 3 hours of gameplay and there wasn't much 'playing' besides running back and forth while making superficial choices. If it had had more substance, or it hadn't skipped in the number of days, and just allowed me to explore freely in the mean time between chapters; maybe I would have felt more justified.

I walk away from this game conflicted that it could have been better, but then I remember that it did it's job of engaging me. It had me with the little adventuring prior to the great mystery and the with the interactions with Delilah. I didn't want to miss a single one. Oh, and Turt Reynolds, too.

The mystery, despite not meeting my highly imaginative conclusions, was something so simple I had dismissed it early on in favor for something grand. Accustomed to other story driven games where there are always aliens and secret societies in the background, it ruined me for Firewatch's epilogue I think.  

Delilah beckoned to the hopeless romantic in me. There was an authentic and convincing nature with the voice acting. Even though in hindsight, she may have been behind it all, in some way—says the conspiracy theorist in me.

This story doesn't wrap up neatly the way you might want it to, but it does in it's own way. It really was an experience. It would be worth an afternoon play through to learn about these characters and delve into the shady nature that looms in those Wyoming Woods. [i]Firewatch[/i] is one of those interesting games where I definitely enjoyed it and would wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone still on the fence, but am still a little ambivalent about awarding it "best game of the year". The visuals are certainly stunning and the storyline, while simplistic, is in my opinion well-written.

You play Henry, a man at a sort of crossroads in life. His past and the events that led up to his taking a job as a wildfire lookout in Wyoming are revealed in a sort of choose-your-own text adventure intro. The visual aesthetic is very reminiscent of [i]The Long Dark[/i], but if you're expecting a survival game, Firewatch is most definitely not that. In fact, it's a little bit difficult to place [i]Firewatch[/i] in a particular genre. If I had to, I'd describe it as a sort of 3D audiovisual novel. 

The core of the game is your interactions with Delilah. While I admit that [i]Firewatch[/i] suffers from the same problems as Mass Effect and every other "choose your own dialogue" game in that the main character doesn't always express how you feel, Delilah is a very believable and understandable character.

I think what frustrated me most about [i]Firewatch[/i] wasn't so much what was in the game so much as what [b]wasn't[/b]. As I wandered the map, I was constantly thinking ahead, waiting for the shoe to drop or expecting something big and perhaps that is [i]Firewatch[/i] falls flat in a way that is entirely not its fault. I had some unfair expectations of [i]Firewatch[/i] and while I feel it's a game that everyone should play, it perhaps comes with a recommendation that you buy it on sale.

Considering how I had picked this game up on little more than a whim after having heard it mentioned on a podcast that I frequent, I've gotta say that this was quite the fascinating and interesting experience. 

First of all, this game is very pretty. Its mix of stylized realism (as well as the gorgeous lighting) made it quite the pleasant experience to explore the world and consume the story. 
Perhaps, the most notable note is the voice acting. While I struggle to find the words to describe how it is so, this game has one of (if not the) most realistic and natural voice acting delivery that I've come across. 
The music is quite nice, too. While I didn't have any particular piece get stuck in my head, it did enhance the atmosphere quite well without ever becoming grating. In short, it did its job quite well. 
While the game's mechanics are simplistic and can be cynically described as a mere hiking simulator, that's not the insult that it may appear to be. In my opinion, the game’s delivery of its story is just fine as it is and would likely be hampered by more complex mechanics. 
Finally, we have the run button. It's always so nice to have the run option (Unlike some other games). Yes, there were times when times were tense and I preferred to walk. And then, there were times when I walked up the wrong path and it was even nicer to run back and not have the game waste my time. 

Those positives aside, I do have a couple of quibbles. Amusingly, they are all consequences of the game's phenomenal visuals. 
One, the game, sometimes, doesn't do a fantastic job of telling you just where it intends you to go at times. For instance, there was one point where I had spent several minutes circling an area, just because I was told to go to a creek, but the next set of instructions wouldn't trigger until I had arrived in a particular place. 
And two, despite the art style's suggestion of open and free world design, the game is actually quite linear and chock-full of invisible walls. Now, as I said, I did find the world to be very pleasant to explore, but... At times, it did get quite annoying when I'd be trying to enter an area that looks easily accessible and be unable to step over a fallen log or continue going up a large rock. 

Edit: So, I've talked to a friend about this game and realized there's a ton of stuff that I missed that I couldn't have seen in a single playthrough. 
Here's the thing. If you didn't like the game because you didn't like the story or the characters, keep going as you were. However, if you didn't like the game because of length, you're overlooking quite a bit. For instance. Go back and play through the game and try not responding to Delilah a single time. I guarantee you'll be surprised at how different the experience is. And, that's just one example.

[h1]Summary[/h1]
Firewatch is a beautiful, emotional, deeply atmospheric game that will leave you thinking about its characters long after the end credits have rolled. As you can tell from this opening sentence, I thorroughly enjoyed playing it. Let me give some more details (without any spoilers!) on why.

[h1]The Game[/h1]
One of the games I've been looking forward to coming out the most, Firewatch had been on my wishlist for a while. When it finally came out I couldn't wait to play it, and it didn't leave me disappointed. Campo Santo did an excellent job setting up the premise and immersing the player in the story from the very beginning. All elements are balanced perfectly, the beautiful visuals match the impactful storytelling, and the music underlines and emphasizes the atmosphere of the game perfectly.

[h1]The Story[/h1]
I won't spoil anything! I was deeply impressed with the story of Firewatch. Finally another excellent adventure game that puts storytelling first and uses elements of suspense and atmosphere to enhance the story, not hide the lack thereof. I'll agree with what others have said: The story is probably not for everyone, especially younger players might not be able to relate to the characters and settings. To me that made it even better, because it feels like Firewatch is written by adults for adults. It's not trying to satisfy everybody out there and hit as many player points as possible. Instead it chose a storyline that will appeal to certain more mature audiences, but in that it excelled in every aspect. Just like there are certain movies that will only appeal to certain viewers while turning others off, this is a clear, deliberate choice, and one that I applaud.
Another important take-away is that the story left me wanting more. I wanted to explore more, find out more, learn more about the main protagonists and their stories, and to that point I wish and hope that Campo Santo is already working on a story for Firewatch 2, or a completely new setting that brings the characters back together for another adventure.

[h1]The Characters[/h1]
There have been quite a few games recently that have done an excellent job at bringing their characters to life. Game developers have come to realize that the backstory of a character has become more important as the games have become more realistic, more life-like, and characters are more identifiable. All the main characters in Firewatch are brought to life in a wonderfully realistic way. How they talk, react, think, is like "normal" people would do. This isn't a game about super soldiers in the future trying to save the world from the umpteenth alien invasion. This is a game that takes a story and its characters out of our world, and as you get to know the characters better while going through the game you really feel like they could be you, or a friend, or neighbor, or someone you know. These characters are not perfect, they make mistakes, they screw up, they have feelings, they have a part of their lives behind them and made experiences good and bad, and all of that is reflected in Firewatch. Just like I said in the previous paragraph, I can't wait to see if Campo Santo will send our (non-)heroes on another adventure, hopefully sooner rather than later.

[h1]The Dialogue[/h1]
This deserves its own paragraph. I have not played a game in recent memory that has excelled at natural dialogue and voice acting as much as Firewatch. Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones deliver stellar performances that really help bring the characters and story alive. And they talk like normal people! It doesn't sound like reading from a script, but just how someone would talk in a normal conversation. They swear (as pointed out above, this game isn't for young players, there is occasional strong language here), they hesitate, they laugh, they get mad, there is real emotion that I could feel through my headphones, and the very distinctive voices of these actors breathes so much life into Firewatch. I hope they come back for more.

[h1]The Visuals[/h1]
One word: Beautiful. Just look at the screenshots and videos out there. The environment in which you walk around is not some procedurally generated map slapped together by an algorithm. Everything here has been hand designed and every tree and rock manually placed with a purpose. There are endless details to explore and take in, and Firewatch uses different times of the day and sun settings to generate different atmospheres depending on where you are in the story right now. The VIsuals enhance the story, and everything looks so great it makes you want to strap on a VR headset and explore everything even more immersed. In fact, I hope Campo Santo is working on a VR update (if it's not already compatible? I don't know actually) once the Oculus Rift and HTC Vive hit consumers.

[h1]The Music[/h1]
Great soundtrack, atmospheric, with music cues along the way as you progress through the story, it is clear that Campo Santo has spent a lot of effort in matching the music to the game and making it a seamless element that help immerse you even deeper into Firewatch. The music never overpowers and doesn't get old, and at the right time adds suspense and triggers a response in the player. The final song during the end credits is perfectly matched as well, great job all around!

[h1]The Bad?[/h1]
After paragraphs of nothing but praise you must be wondering if there is anything wrong or missing in Firewatch? The obvious thing would be, as pointed out by others, that it feels too short. But only in the same way that you say a really good movie is too short, because you want to see more of the story and not have it be over yet. It's certainly not as short as Gone Home, but short enough that it made me want to play through the entire game again. However, people complaining about Firewatch being too short are probably too spoiled from other non-adventure games whose main concept it is to keep you playing forever with never-ending online matches and procedurally generated infinite universes. However, that isn't what Firewatch is. Firewatch is a story-driven adventure game, and once you completed the story, the adventure is over.

Other than that, I wish there were more choices in how you want the story to progress, and really significantly alter the storyline to the point that you get a completely different ending (or at least parts in the middle). There are small elements where that is possible (again, I won't spoil anything), but they are mostly smaller side details and nothing that affects the overall story. When I play through it again, I will deliberately try to alter the story and see what happens.

[h1]The End[/h1]
This isn't about the end of the game (which I won't spoil) but about the end of this review :-) If you've read all the way to here then what are you waiting for, play the game yourself already, and have a blast! Darken the room, put on some headphones, get comfortable in your chair or couch, and play through the adventure that is Firewatch!

Games shouldn’t all be open world fill-in-the-map-icon simulators, linear experiences are great for conveying meaning and adding artistic credibility to the gaming medium as a whole. Firewatch is an incredible experience, so long as you're not going in with the wrong expectations.  This isn't a role playing game, a survival game, or some sort of Sherlock-inspired Half Life prequel.  This is a game that wants to tell a story, and to that end it succeeds marvelously.

Most of that story is told either through documents you find out in the woods or through conversations with your trusty wildfire watch supervisor Delilah.  When you spend a significant portion of the game talking with someone on the radio, it makes sense that this game has some of the best dialogue and voice acting of any game I've ever played.

It helps that it's easy to immerse yourself in the Wyoming wilderness.  Firewatch looks drop-dead gorgeous.  I found myself constantly stopping and taking pictures of the landscape.  The soundtrack and sound design are top-notch.  The game also adjusts to your playstyle, so the choices you make along the way will affect your relationship with Delilah and a number of other small but noticable details.

The game does have a few faults.  For being set in the wilderness, it's frustrating that you're forced to stick to specific paths.  You can wander away from each day's task, but you're still stuck to the provided trails.  Going along with this: just about everything in the game is linear, almost to a fault.  A lot of people also had issue with the length.  Even if you're walking everywhere, reading absolutely everthing, and otherwise taking your sweet time through the story the entire game shouldn't take you more than five hours.  If you're rushing, I wouldn't be surprised if you could complete it in under two.  The length is a good fit for the story the developers wanted to tell, but it's a bit short for a $20 title.

If you enjoy story-driven games, I'd highly recommend picking up Firewatch.  Though you might want to wait until it gets a bit cheaper.

Ah, Firewatch - where to begin?

Having since followed Firewatch's development on their blog, and since admiring Olly Moss's artwork, I was already very much look forward to playing playing the game.  I was stoked.

Then teaser trailers were unveiled, and more and more hype started to be generated, and I was left slightly unsure as to what to expect from the finished title.  As with film trailers nowadays, sometimes a whole two hour story can be given away in just a trailer.  It's safe to say that Firewatch leaves much to be enjoyed and discovered in time, and I think it will be a story that I go back to enjoy in years to come (or so I hope).

Of the newer games that I have played and enjoyed in recent years, few have left me with such a huge set of feelings as after completing Firewatch.   For the time invested (as many people have pointed out how comparably short it can be to complete) it gives a lot in return.  

I would put it in similar places to 'Her', 'Lost in Translation', 'Norwegian Wood', and many other stories that leave you with an uncertainty, an almost overwhelming sense of sadness, and a huge craving to find out the answers to 'what if' and 'why' things begin and end as they do in life.

It's not going to be a game for everyone, but I'm almost certian that everyone can take something away from Firewatch.  For the sentimental farts like myself, well it's just gold.  I would whole heartedly recommend this, even if you enjoy it (as I have) in just one sitting.
