Firewatch is a forest-strolling conversation video game. There's a few racoons in it. It's very pretty. And while the few trailers will successfully get you wrapped up in its mystery and escape to the world of the game quickly, the real heart of the story is in why you get wrapped up in said mystery, as well as the main characters. If you are observant, and take your time, you will realize that this is a stunning game about some very well written characters given a real world to live in and experience. You'll probably feel like it's not long enough, you'll probably feel like the mystery plot is sub-par to what was possible, and you'll probably feel like the developers could have spent some more time polishing the game (I've noticed some oddities and areas of the game the devs didn't think the player would look). And yet, the important things in this game really do outweigh the bad. Not enough games are about the subject matter in this game, which I won't spoil for you. Life is Strange [i]could[/i] have been a game about the the complexities of time travel and the impact of changing the known "should be's" of the time travel continuum. Instead Life is Strange is about the strength of friendship using time travel and confronting life scenarios with the ability to undo mistakes you don't like.

Firewatch, in that manner, is similar to Life is Strange. It's not about the mystery.

And that doesn't hold the game back from greatness, in fact it helps push Firewatch towards it.

Okay so there seems to be a lot of discussion around this game and if it's worth the money. I myself bought this game without any idea what I was heading into, which might be what causes most to reconsider buying it after reading/watching negative reviews about the game. So here's my thoughts:

[b]Is the game short?[/b]
Yes, the game can be beat in 2-3 hours if you don't have any intention to explore. On my first run through it I simply followed the "story". Which lead me to beat it listening to all dialogue in 3 hours.

[b]Is it open world?[/b]
Yes and no. You can run around the area freely, but the way you're being presented with the world you will often find yourself following a path even though you think you're running around on your own. The game presents you a path through dialogue and atmosphere. It's so well made and barely noticeable, I really only noticed it because I was on the watch for it.

[b]Does it have any replay value?[/b]
Sadly, no. I don't see any replay value to the game, you can get some other responses out of things by choosing other paths in the game. It may or may not lead to a different ending, you would have to buy the game and figure that out yourself.

For a semi-replay value spoiler you can [spoiler]take photos with the camera you get at a point in the game, you can get these photos printed and delivered to you as well as saved.[/spoiler]

[b]Should I buy it?[/b]
Yes, you should buy it for all these reasons. You can simply not miss out on a great story. There might not be much replay value right away, but I see myself play this game again in some months or a year when it's been dying in my memory. Think of the game as a movie, not an action packed game. You play it for the story and atmosphere, not for thrilling adreneline rushes.

But now after playing it, I'm split down the middle. The dialogue IS great and the voice acting is very good in my opinion, I wasn't let down by that aspect at all. But is that enough to carry the whole game? After having just finished it in 4 hours, I'm at a crossroads in my mind. There were certainly enjoyable moments to it, the banter between your character and Delilah is very charming at times, and fun to listen to. The feeling of seclusion is very real also, and the graphics are definitely above average.
But the MEAT of the game... it's just not there, sadly. The "story" of the game seems a little hamfisted, like it's supposed to be this huge mystery to what's going on, but it turns out to be quite normal in the end. Is it a comedy on how we always perceive things to be different than what they really are? Is it an artistic depiction of impending dread that we are supposed to feel throughout the game, that something truly bizarre is going to be the endgame?
I don't think so. 
The end result we get, is some huge opportunity for character development and friendship through dialogue during many many days of seemingly mundane responsibilities, that is ultimately cut short. The game misleads you into thinking every day will be as long as the first and second, before rapidly fast forwarding a week or two for one dialogue exchange, before then fast forwarding another few weeks. It feels forced and a bit lazy. Instead of actually getting to experience how these characters end up talking in the way they do, we are forced to ASSUME what happened. This would be fine in a sort of "non story centric" game, but in this one, where this is the main attraction; it falls flat, sadly.
I don't feel like I wasted my money, however. The quality of what IS there is very good, and the work behind it is evident. It's just the sum of all the parts that doesn't quite come together in the way you want it to. I'm not going to bash the people behind the game, as what is here is certainly competent. It's just not the "greatness" the critic reviews would have you believe.
I definitely hope this developer learns from this experience and makes more games like this in the future, though. There is a ton of potential here, but my ultimate feeling from playing the game is that that potential was not fully realized.

The climax, to me, was when you solved the mystery. I was ready for anything. All the info I gathered, clues, associations I constructed, scenarios I considered, predictions I made, patterns I observed. My brain was firing on all cylinders, and I frantically craved answers. I looked at the mystery as one powerful experience in a real man's life, that I got to see through his eyes. From that point of view, "life moves on" isn't a cop-out, it's just a logical conclusion to it all.

My one and only criticism is this: I wish I could have interacted with [spoiler]Ned.[/spoiler] There could have been a lot more done with him. I realized early on the game wouldn't have animated face models, so no face-to-face with him. But he did have a voice. And he did essentially hold my life in his hands the entire game. There could have been some super tense threats and negotiations between us via radio or notes at the end.

But all I would have asked for, if I had the chance, was one final opportunity to speak to him. 3-4 dialogue options where I lay out what Henry thought of the whole thing, forgiveness, blame, fear, etc. Because I personally forgave him 100% for what he did. The only thing I felt was pity, and I desperately wanted to let him know. That was unfortunate. But it took nothing away from the rest of the game for me.

This is a very uneven game. It is trying to tell a story and to create a spiritual atmosphere of loneliness and vastness. And it does so, mostly. Occasionally it does something brilliant. But... but there are an awful lot of buts. And they rather upset my experience of it.

What I particularly like about it is its aesthetic. Its light (its light, its days and nights and so on, is astounding), its chunkiness and physicality, its aesthetic coherence (the people fit into the world so well, the voices fit the story, the sounds fits the landscape, etc.), the music (which is very sparse but excellent and perfectly-pitched), its voice-acting and script. The rest of this review will be critical, but I don't want to suggest by my brevity here that I don't like the game: but I think its failings are more interesting that what comes off wel.

I particularly disliked two basic things about. First, its lack of ambition. Second, lots of details. To the second criticism first. Graphics: Although the lighting is great, the textures and other graphics points are quite poor. The game is so minimal that the little details all matter (as in minimalist architecture the grain of the wood matters), and so it's very annoying when rope physics look silly, or the character models look like they're from the alpha build, or there is no detail on the trees and leaves. And the pacing of scenes often isn't great: cuts can come too quickly, upsetting the slowness of the characters' lives. Physicality: how your character is connected to the world is important, so it's frustrating when he sometimes feels like he's gliding across the landscape rather than tramping across it in his heavy hiking boots. (I wonder if first-person was a good artistic choice: one doesn't see one's character, so one's sense of embodiment is weakened.) The sound of his walking can be unconvincing or quiet, there is no sense of there being a difference arising from whether he's walking forwards or backwards or sideways, and, worst of all, he often doesn't physically connect to the landscape very well. Flying over rocks, unable to walk across a plain, this kind of buggy stuff.

I've gone on about this because I think it's really important to get this stuff right when you're not trying to do something big. (This game is far worse than Metal Gear Solid 5 in all these respects, but these respects are so much more important to it than to MGS5.) But to the other criticism: this game is small in every way. The plot is short, as has frequently been noted, but it's also shallow. I can't imagine replaying this game - it would just be the same - and its mysteries are more or less wrapped up by its finish. One can't change how it unfolds except in the most trivial of ways by exploring outside the beeline the game places you on. One can't even go to many places that one doesn't have to go to for the plot. This means that the sense of openness suggested by the size of the landscape is lost, because you feel that there's nothing to this game apart from the plot, and so you feel rushed to just get through it. It's hard to just wander the world. This in turn undermines the atmosphere of the game.

So, all in all, a very well-written, well-acted, well-coloured game, hampered by a myriad infelicities in its details, and by a littleness of vision.

[strike]Firwatch[/strike] Firewatch is an enjoyable "first-person mystery" by a small team of folks who know what they are doing.

Applying the "walking simulator" is not inaccurate, but that may be too dismissive of the refined experience Firewatch offers.

Much walking through a nicely realized, highly stylized forest environment is involved, but the most notable ingredient of the game is your character's interaction with the other main character via portable radio - one of the finer examples of such interaction in the video game medium.

The game starts by building a backstory of your character via text, allowing you to make several choices - an effective technique to help you identify with your character. These choices are later reflected in dialogue (although they do not, as far as I know, have a significant impact on the plot). The dialogue mechanic, the control over dialogue responses effectively facilitates immersion and the dialogue is very well voiced.

Firewatch does a good job at pacing, at maintaining suspense. Although, you can choose at times to wander off on a few detours and delay story progression. There's a decent amount of optional secrets and details to discover, but not very many - if short on time, don't worry about them and just stick to the goals at hand, as you won't miss much. The game can last about 4-8 hours depending on how much you stray/dawdle.

Perhaps the most questionable aspect of the game is the hype and marketing that emphasizes the mystery. There certainly is mystery, and it's pretty good, but many, perhaps even most, might be surprised and perhaps disappointed that the story progression doesn't match quite the expectations they had. Although I did feel a mild sense of being the victim of misdirection, I liked the story, and the game.

The other perhaps surprising but astute design principle here is what isn't explicitly shown. The (visual and auditory) presentation is such that much is left to the imagination and exposition is trickle-fed. A cynic might accuse this paradigm of being a cost saving measure. And maybe it is. But, it is effective at engaging the player's mind.

I recommend Firewatch as a short but good interactive mystery experience, especially if it's on sale.

Clocking in for me at a little over 5 hours, Firewatch packs a lot of emotions into a small, beautifully crafted, package. Firewatch differs from most video games as it lacks any sort of combat mechanic, this is more refreshing than you might think. I truly enjoyed just walking around the wilderness, talking on my radio, and enjoying the occasional reminders of humanity in the form of discarded beer cans. I made it a point to collect every piece of garbage I came across, as far as I could tell this didn’t have any impact on the game, but it felt like what Teddy Roosevelt would have done in the same situation. I also channeled my inner Smokey the Bear by ensuring that I stomped out every smoldering campfire I encountered. 

The game has been designed in a way that effortlessly guides you through the story, while rewarding those who prefer to take the road less traveled with scenic vistas and an opportunity for reflection that is usually reserved for great literature or film. If the game was nothing more than an opportunity to walk around and explore while doing your best to prevent forest fires, that would have been enough; However, Campo Santo studios has more ambitious plans for their debut title than simply walking around collecting garbage. Firewatch does a great job of lulling you into a sense of complacency with just enough excitement sprinkled throughout the first half of the game to keep you focused on your main goal of keeping watch for fires. The game’s second half takes a sharp turn and plunges you headfirst into a very thrilling mystery set against the backdrop of the ever expanding June fire.

There is an immediate and obvious chemistry between Henry and Delilah, they very quickly cling to one another, as if they are both running from their own lives but are afraid to go it alone; Henry needs Delilah just as she needs him. Firewatch explores loneliness from multiple angles and forces you to confront complicated emotions. Henry is a man running from his past and Campo Santo has done a fantastic job of making you feel that it’s up to you to use this time in Henry’s life to influence the course of his future. The dialog choices available feel like what someone might actually say when put in a similar situation, I didn’t have any trouble trying to find the choice that would best reflect my actual feelings at that exact moment. 

Firewatch is not so much played as it is experienced, It doesn’t feature any difficult platforming or puzzle solving elements and much of the conflict presented is internal. The ending left me with more questions than it answered, but I think I prefer it that way; the player is left to make their own interpretation as to what happens next.

Dive in: there are few experiences available right now that challenge your emotional fortitude in the way that Firewatch does. It’s visuals are stunning and the voice acting and writing are superb.  

FULL DISCLOSURE: My Firewatch experience may have been influenced by the delicious notes of pine and citrus that were present in the Dogfish Head 90 Minute IPA that I was enjoying during the second half of my playthrough.

Feeling a bit obligated to throw in my opinion of the game at this point because it is getting a lot of criticism. Without a doubt this is very good game. Is it a game for everyone? No. Does it have problems? Absolutely. Is it worth $20? That is debatable and will vary on who you ask. What about $10 to $15? Yes. Now before I go any further I want to say that this completely my opinion and not objective facts about the game. You are free to agree or disagree. The people who don’t like this game have good points and opinions.

          Let me say this about the price as it seems to be the main source of the dislike of this game. I got almost four hours of gameplay from this game and I was moving quite quickly through it. Its full price is $20 and a movie is a little over $10. Say you go see 2 movies that are 2 hours long and you get 4 hours of entertainment for $20. Same as this game. Another way to justify the price is comparing it to the price of The Last of Us which was $60 at launch for about an average of 14 hours of gameplay which is one of the best video games of all time and virtually loved by everyone who played it. One third of $60 is $20 and one third of 15 hours is 5 hours. So when comparing the two they have virtually the same price per gameplay time. Also people really loved the Stanley Parable which has about the same price and gameplay time, but it never got a whole lot of criticism for that. So I really don’t understand why people are hating this game so much. If you don’t want to spend $20 then wait for the next sale and it will likely be $10. At that price you should really buy this game if you have doubts about it right now. Look the game should be longer and cheaper, but you need to understand why it is this length and price. This is the developers’ first game and they made it under bad working conditions with little money. Yet they put in as much effort as they could. They could really use this money to support themselves and future games they are planning on making. So I really think people should cut them some serious slack for the price. Camp Santo (developers) has a lot of potential and I am looking forward to what they produce in the future.

          People are really upset at the middle part, final parts and final ending of the game. They are unhappy with the direction the game took. Now I am going to be as general as possible to avoid spoilers so bear with my vagueness. First off it is a very sad game overall and I think most of the issues with people not being satisfied come from that. Yet I really enjoyed the game and I knew exactly why Camp Santo made the decisions that it made in regards to the story. If you have beaten the game and are feeling distraught at what happened try to understand why the story went the way it did. Really think about it. There is a very deep meaning to this game that I think a lot of people are missing. 

          Now let me move on to what I liked about the game then I will talk about what I did not enjoy. Okay graphically speaking this game did an amazing job. Even on the medium settings (which is what my computer could handle) it is a gorgeous game with a minimalistic art style. Yet the game has an amazing level of detail in many parts of the game. The soundtrack to the game fit the scenes and feelings of the game very well. Despite what people say about it I really enjoyed this story. Again I will say that there are deep meanings to this game. I would say more about it, but again I want to avoid spoilers. If you want me to go into detail as to why I liked the story I can post it in the comments of this post or I can send you a message with my interpretation. Great voice acting that really added to the overall experience and pulled you into the story. The characters in this game have really great interactions that flow well with the overall storyline. Felt a lot of emotions playing this game, happy and sad ones. The game dealt with a lot of the issues I am dealing with in my own life so it really was touching and moving to me.

          Now what I did not like about this game. If they were able to, this game could have been much better with a fleshed out middle part of the game. It would have added satisfaction to the ending of the game and the overall feel of the story. So the length is a problem, but not a huge one in the end. Really wish they didn’t block off a lot of the map to your access. If the game had a bigger open world with less blockades the game would be a lot better. The story is quite linear and the choices you make don’t really alter the story that much. Mostly just future dialogue options and a few areas in the game. That being said the story was really good and the lack of choice doesn’t take too much away from the game. No significant glitches or problems. The foliage pops in and out depending on how close you are. The game is beautiful, but not detailed enough to justify the demand it put on your graphics card. My card is getting older, but had the game been better optimized I should have been able to run this game at 60 fps on high rather than 40 fps on medium. The game was kind of a big build up to nothing at the end. Again I understand why this was done, but I wish it could have ended another way. The game starts out really depressing and ends on a depressing note. Perhaps it could have been done better? The saddest part is that no matter how much I wanted the story to end my way it really could not have ended any other way.

          So final thoughts. I am feeling a 7 out of 10 on this one. Please buy it. It is worth the money now and will definitely be worth it during the upcoming spring and summer sales. It is a unique and important story. Camp Santo I love you guys! Keep up the good work.

Firewatch is a first person exploration game. The game is about atmosphere, immersion, and exploration, so do not expect puzzles, quick-time events or combat of any kind.
You are Henry, a man who has retreated from his former life to work as a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness. It is your job to keep the wilderness safe. Your only contact is your supervisor, a woman named Delilah, who is in contact with you at all times over a small, handheld radio. Soon you will find out that Henry is not the only person in the forest after all. It does not take long until strange things start to happen and it is up to you to uncover the mysteries.
Unfortunately, Firewatch takes approximately only 3 hours to finish.
The graphics are beautiful.
The game offers a great narrative, Henry and Delilah are brilliantly voiced.
The soundtrack fits perfectly to the game.
I enjoyed the game overall but I missed a bit more interaction with the environment. Besides of the short duration, my only problem with the story was that the finale seems a bit too rushed and I asked myself: "What that's all?"
The price of 19,99€ might be too much for some people because of the short duration of the game. If you are a fan of exploration games you should get Firewatch as soon as it gets a discount immediately.

This game is...confusing.

I don't mean that the storyline is confusing or that the gameplay is perplexing. The game itself, as a piece of art or literature or just as a game, is enigmatic. Hard to pin down. After finishing it in a little over twice the time it takes most folks, I am sad, vexed, upset, and still in awe. 

It's a rail shooter without any shooting, a mystery without any distinguishable question, and a bit of an open world game, but in a very strict environment. It looks like a choose-your-own-adventure, and it certainly behaves like one for most of the runtime. But it's not quite that either. 

Many reviews have been playing up the mystery angle. Saying it's similar to Myst or the Witness. I'd say it's closer to Twin Peaks: the mystery is there, and yet it's somehow beside the point. 

Firewatch is about the relationship two people can form in the face of loneliness. The intro starts you out filling in the blanks of how the protagonist, Henry, got to his current place in life. He's got a rocky past filled with love and heartbreak, and his journey to the park is the culmination of growing anger, fear, and uncertainty. This place is an escape. Letting you mold that path is a good way to both introduce players to Henry and allow them some tinkering to make him more their style. The reasoning is that you'll identify more with a character if you've made some important choices [i]with[/i] them rather than in place of them. The choices you can pick from are still Henry's, you're just sharing the responsibility.

After the lengthy but not unenjoyable intro sequence, Henry gets to his watchtower, a place you won't spend much time in despite the typical nature of the job. Over the radio, you'll meet your co-star, Delilah, supervisor and fellow firewatcher. 

Now, the game let's you continue making some choices. Most significantly, when Delilah speaks to you over the radio, you decide which responses (if any) you throw back at her. I've played by myself, and I've played with a friend. For the most part, these choices only affect the remainder of the conversation. I had a feeling that they made some vague impact on later convos or minor actions you can take, but that's not the point. The conversations are the point. The whole game is about talking to this person, or not talking to them. Every day spent wandering the vallery was more about her mood, her personality, her questions than it was about the valley itself. There are two things that I know will stick the most in my memory of Firewatch: the gorgeous vistas of the Wyoming wilderness, and the sound of Delilah's voice when I've actually gotten her to laugh at one of my dumb jokes or when I've pissed her off for inexplicable reasons. That very human connection, and the uber complex emotions surrounding it, are a triumph and the true centerpiece of Firewatch.

While the rest of the game has some issues (glitches, mostly - some miniscule, some glaring), it'll be hard to forget my trip to Wyoming that I took with Henry and Delilah. Thank you for that, Campo Santo.

Firewatch is, above all else, about placing you in a picturesque, remote environment and letting you live a short story. Like a book, you may enjoy the experience or you may find it to be a terrible waste of four hours of your life. Either way, it's fine. Everything is fine. Life will go on.

The experience is indeed on average about four hours, with a bit of sight-seeing included. $5/hr of entertainment if you want to be shrewd about it. Cheaper than a movie for two.

The voice acting, imagery, controls, sound were all on point. Simply beginning to think about the art style gets me giddy. The fact that style doesn't "strive for absolute realism" is a breath of fresh air and fits perfectly with the environment you are placed in.

A minor critism is the set choice itself. One gets the impression that Firewatch is here to experience and be awed by - not to explore (in the current gaming sense of 100% completionism). New areas with distinguishing features are opened up as the plot progresses, but they are true-to-life: a remote wilderness/national park simply doesn't have tens of amazing unique attractions to check off your list. It's about the whole, not individual parts, where Firewatch excels. The story spans months in the wilderness - the fact of the matter is expecting every day to be jam-packed with capital-A Adventure is unrealistic.

In regards to the plot and specifically the ending: [spoiler]Perhaps why some find the plot so mundane is that [b]it is[/b]. There are no aliens, no government conspiracy, no true bad guys lurking around the corner waiting to kill you when your guard is down. There's some bored kids and a few adults trying to escape from their decisions instead of facing them. There is no escapism here. I found the smash cuts to be appropriate as they spanned days or weeks of the protagonist most likely [b]watching for fires[/b] and doing his job. The ending was fine. Characters were introduced, a couple conflicts met their climax, the situation resolved. Roll credits.[/spoiler]

I hope that Campo Santo enjoy success from this title and use it as a springboard for a long and fruitful stay in the industry.

Firewatch is a really interesting concept. It's entirely story - that's not to say there isn't gameplay, but the gameplay definitely takes backseat. Or, rather, is the vehicle for the story itself. The voice acting is superb, the environments are gorgeous, and the writing is genuinely witty. The last couple chapters of the game are incredibly tense, and all the while, you'll be on the edge of your seat waiting for what happens next. The ending really plays with your expectations in a unique way.

However, there is a bit of a flaw with this game: the price. It's not full-price, and I can appreciate that (especially given its length, and relative lack of replay value - it is, after all, a mystery story), but $20 seems just slightly too high. It took me nearly four hours to play through, and I was being thorough. However, I wouldn't have had any issue paying that much for it in another form of media (novela, short story, etc), which probably says more to my expectation of what games are than anything else.

I'd recommend it pretty highly. Good game, great story. You won't regret it, unless you're looking for an action game.

Edit, November 30, 2017: So, I recently heard that Firewatch got an update that included developer commentary, a la the highly informative commentary tracks for Portal and Portal 2. I decided to check it out, and this has honestly improved my view of the game. Hearing about the technical underpinnings, the writing process, and the opinions of those involved themselves was fascinating. It also allowed me to flush out different aspects of the game that I hadn't found before. 

I also want to retract what I said about the pricing. In thinking about it, movie tickets are often quite pricey, but we don't complain about them as being "not worth" it. Firewatch is absolutely worth its price, and then some.

The only flaw to Firewatch is that it isn't longer.

My only real complaint is, yeah, that it isn't bigger. I could've spent hours, hell, days, more with Henry and Delilah, without getting tired of them. I wouldn't even have minded if more of the time was just... casual forest stuff, pretty much busywork that gave me an excuse to wonder the gorgeous environs, to get farther away from home, to climb more cliffs, walk through more canyons, look at more pretty vistas.

Eventually, I think I'll play this again, just to see if different dialogue choices change anything. I'll be somewhat disappointed if they don't, I'm not expecting a whole second game to unfold, but some of the dialogue options are diametric opposites, so... they should change something.

In any case, this is a game I will happily recommend. Perhaps not quite at full price, because it really is relatively short... but I'm not going to say I regretted playing it.

Be ready to experience an atmospheric if not short and compelling drama about isolation. Firewatch is a character driven game where you live out the feeling of isolation with only a friendly voice to help keep you sane. Starting off in an almost innocent and funny ideal, the game quickly grows as a feeling of gloom seems to cover all of your actions. Small moments exist to heighten tension and, many times, you may find yourself wondering if the only thing causing you fear is your own paranoia. This is definitely a game to play with the lights out, speakers up, and all attention on it.

However, no game can be truly perfect and Firewatch is no exception. There is a genuine feeling early on in the game of artificial blocking: being limited by a lack of equipment or simply requiring plot tickets to open up. While the game grants players tools organically, exploration oriented players should realize that their journey may be limited to later in the game. Likewise, the game's tension comes from the feeling of isolation and the dissonance that occurs naturally while playing, meaning that if you're an individual who enjoys listening to music or distractions while gaming this may be a game to skip. Finally, and easily its largest weakness (though truly subjective), the game's ending can be easily seen as a sour note to the entire game. Despite it making sense from a literary standpoint, it's easy to see how one would feel cheated out of an ending.

Firewatch is a game truly experienced by yourself. While watching a Let's Play would allow you to see the story, it's very likely that the experience would fundamentally change. Only buy this at full price if you want to experience an immersive story that is not afraid to explore literary and adult themes. For those looking for a quick or fun story, wait for it to be on sale.

Firewatch is a mystery. A good mystery, at that. So what makes a good mystery? Interesting characters. Interesting setting. A sense of tension that grows until the catharsis at the end. A story that keen minds will unravel just in advance of the plot is revealed.

It's as replayable as a favorite movie or a loved book; you will almost certainly remember what happens once you get into it, but it's so beautiful and engaging that you won't mind. Henry and Delilah will feel like old friends, or enemies, the next time you see them. 

PRO
Art - It's beautiful. Like playing a painting. It pays attention to how light and motion color the world around us, like an impressionist painting, but with the beautiful colors and emotional bias of expressionism. 

Voice Acting - The voice actors for this game are phenomenal, and there's an incredible intimacy in communicating by radio or telephone. It's like being in bed at night, phone cradled to your ear with a friend or loved one on the other end.

Story - The game has a story it wants to tell and an emotional impact that it wants to make, and it succeeds with both.

But what about it being...
Short - If you're expecting a long AAA title, this isn't it. This lasts about as long as a long movie, and you should treat it as such. If the price point bothers you, check out what a theater ticket and a beverage would cost you.

Directed - Because it's telling a story, it wants to direct you from point to point and not give you a lot of time to explore the scenery. If it gives you an indication to use the radio to report you are ready, resist the urge and explore. The game will take you to most of the locations, but there are some fun things to explore.

Cons:

There is also at the time of this reveiw a flaw in the first shale cliff you encounter where you're shadow does not appear and the rope's shadow has an odd spike in it where you are holding it.

2. Cussing. A minor issue in my mind, as you encounter a similar amount of cussing playing games like Team Fortress or Rust, but I think it is worth mentioning. If you have sensitive ears, this game is not for you.

There are other minor errors in the gameplay, but none especially worth mentioning.

(This section of the reveiw contains spoilers pertaining to the end of the game.) As mentioned above, the plot resolution leaves you with a lot of questions. What exactly ARE the scientists doing in the park? Why is Ned monitering you're and Delilah's actions? What exactly was Ned's relationship with his son? Before I start - yes this game is short - it took me 3-4 hours to complete.

The game follows a man called Henry who takes up a summer job as a fire look out in a Wyoming forest. The game sets itself up as a thriller of sorts as Henry gets to know Delilah, a more experienced look out, in a near-by tower. The pair communicate only through their walkie-talkies and a majority of the dialogue is between the pair of them.

The thriller aspect comes the pair notice weirder and weirder happenings in the forest. Problem I have now is that Firewatch is a very story driven game, so going into anymore detail would be ruining a majority of the game.

I really enjoyed the story through the game, it's presentation through a very complimenting artstyle and the character development - however, I do feel the ending was... well, it tied too many loose ends together. Not that I want every game to set-up for a sequel, far from it. But nearly everything that happened during the game was answered on the last day. 

If you're not the type that enjoys a story driven game, walking around in a beautifully made Wyoming forest then this probably isn't for you. For the record as well, the thriller aspects are more or less "anticipation" scares - leaving an idea in your head for you to create something scary.

Either way, I did enjoy the game and it's story. Like I said, the ending was a little poor compared to the rest of the game but it was an enjoyable experience none the less.

I wanted to like this so much and there are a wealth of great things about it, but it just doesn't pull everything together and the story fizzles out to nothing. Like many mysteries, the resolution is its undoing. 

The visuals are nice (though performance is questionable on a 3 year old Macbook Pro), and the world nicely realised, however even here there are many missed opportunities with the almost complete absence of any animal life leaving the world feeling a little lifeless. The moving about quickly gets boring, especially when moving from one side of the map to the other and although there are times when plot devices add tension, too often I found myself twiddling my thumbs.

The voice acting is pretty good but not half as great as some of the reviews make out, and you never really feel like anything you respond is changing the course of the characters' relationship. The script is generally solid with some good laughs and nice twists and tension-building, but in the end the narrative arc leaves it floundering.

The music is fine, but pretty unmemorable and sounds rather synthetic. It often seems to appear out of nowhere and disappear without any obvious purpose.

This game will undoubtedly sell many copies and win many awards and there are certainly worse ways to spend 4.5 hours and £15, but anyone looking for something genuinely deep is ultimately going to be disappointed.

This is honestly one of the best and most thought provoking games I've ever played. The two main characters in Firewatch, Henry and Delilah, are well developed and the choices you make as Henry will affect his relationship with Delilah. This is very important as the story progresses and tensions begin to rise.

Without giving away any spoilers, Firewatch is about how isolation can lead to paranoia and mistrust. Your only point of contact is on the other end of a walkie talkie. You, as Henry, are completely alone except for this person miles away that you talk to every day and get to know through your interactions over the summer. You put your trust in this person you have never met, and depending on how you interact with Delilah, this trust may or may not be genuine.

Firewatch is also about escapism. The type of people who take this job are trying to escape from the life they had before they retreated to this isolation, as Henry is. You get caught up in a mystery that is more exciting than the life you left behind, and you get swept away. You forget what ordinary life is like.

I knew a lot of people were disappointed with the ending of this game when I started it, but I didn't look into why that was because I wanted to experience it for myself. But now that I have finished the game, it seems to me like those people obviously didn't get it. I thought it was the ending the game deserved. It suited the message that the whole game was trying to convey.

Overall, Firewatch is a beautifully crafted game. Here are my pros and cons:

Pros:

Stunning graphics and environment
Engaging and thought provoking story
Witty and diverse dialogue
Well developed characters - you genuinely care about them

Cons:

I got 4 hours of gameplay. Not worth £15 - get it on sale if you can
Could get a bit boring if you're into more action based games - a lot of walking around
To add to the above point, you could get lost fairly often - map and compass skills are useful

I thoroughly recommend this game.

This game... It’s hard to put into words how I feel about this game.  I bought it shortly after I watched [url=https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLMBYlcH3smRzvljKjxfsPCM6ibjr6ox-0]JackSepticEye's[/url] whole play through of it.  The game really stuck with me after I had watched the entire play through from start to finish.  I found myself contemplating it quite a bit and so I had to experience it for myself to know for sure.  Quite honestly, I'm glad I did.

Having watched the ending over the lets play I originally felt the ending was lack luster and anticlimactic, however now having experienced it for myself and having to make some of the tougher choices I find that the ending is actually very apropos.  I found myself feeling for the 'antagonist' of the game (I put that in quotes because he's not really an antagonist but I lack a better word for him).  I understood how his character was written and why he did what he did.  Even though I knew the ending of her story, [spoiler]I found myself whispering "Please wait for me, Delilah" as I rushed Henry to the cable car in the final sequence and actually felt hurt and disappointed that she didn't.[/spoiler]

I've seen a lot of complaints about the length of the game, that it’s "too short".  True, they could have padded the game out by sending you on other random tasks that took place during the time when the game skipped several days, however the game [i]really[/i] doesn't need it.  The story alone keeps this game engaging and makes the game really stand out for its genre.  Granted it’s very "walking simulator"-like but it’s by no means boring.  Yes, it's only about three to four hours but I feel that it’s honestly as long as it needs to be, any longer would have made the game have less of an impact in my opinion.  And yes, the game has a very linear story, but in this age of games that are bursting at the seams with survival mechanics and multiple endings its actually rather refreshing to find a game where the plot has a definitive end and where the developers focused more on the journey than the destination.

The music in the game is beautiful but used sparingly which I feel adds just the right amount of tension, relief or effect when it needed to.  The rest of the time you are left with the ambiance of the forest which adds a nice peaceful contrast to the tension the story starts building upon.

The art style for the game is truly fantastic.  Every single frame feels like a painting, be it looking out over some of the games beautiful vistas or focusing in on specific objects.  A lot of care went into building a world where everything is unique and fascinating.  The world is full of vibrant colors that draw you in and really help with immersing you in the rich story the writers built.

Far and away the best thing about the game is the writing.  The interaction between the main characters, Henry (your character) and Delilah, is very beautifully crafted.  From witty banter between them to the serious and frantic moments the dialogue feels very natural and unscripted no matter which option you choose.  I found myself reloading my save file from time to time because I either wanted to relive one of these interactions and listen to them again or to choose a different option to see how the characters responded.  Both characters are incredibly three dimensional with their own goals and flaws which makes them both relatable and believable.  They undergo what I consider is some of the best character development ever put forth by a game.  It’s very easy to find yourself invested in these characters, wanting to know what happens next in their story.

Despite the shorter story than what modern gamers are used to and despite not having multiple endings I really must recommend this game.  Honestly I'm glad I bought it at full price to help support the developers, testers, artists, writers, musicians, and voice talent that put a lot of heart and soul into building this game.  It's very obvious that the team at Campo Santo were dedicated and passionate about putting out an amazing game with a fantastic story and superb dialogue.

If you are looking for a game with a rich story with three dimensional characters backed by amazing art then look no further and get this game.  It will be worth every penny.

Firewatch is very much a cross between a Metroidvania and a walking simulator - and while I enjoy these games a lot, I have to recognise that aside from unarguable sheer craft on display in the product, the 'story' content of these games can be seriously divisive.

W/out extensive systemic goodness, these games tend to lean heavily on plot, characterisation, prose and quality of narration / vocal performance, and usually they're fairly meditative affairs as far as core content goes. Firewatch is a visually SPLENDID game (emphasis on art direction and level design rather than technical achievement), but the visuals are strictly in service of the narrative and atmosphere. So how does it do?

From a plotting standpoint, Firewatch manages to dot it's 'i's and cross MOST of it's 't's (the influence of THE FUN TRAIN is visible at one or two moments) - it plays fair with it's audience and rewards a close reading of the work. That said - the quality of the game is not to be found in it's narrative plumbing, but in the quality of characterisation and the nuanced approach to the central themes of the game; of times in your life where there are no good choices, of encountering events too overwhelming to find the strength to face.

Firewatch is the story of Henry, a middle-aged man who runs from the mundane horrors of his life by taking a job of fire watchman in the Shoshone National Forest in Wyoming, in 1989. His only regular human contact is Delilah, his supervisor - who's based in another watchtower and talks to you by your radio. For the first few weeks, things seem peaceful - but eventually the tale takes a turn for the dark, building into a story of paranoia, stalking and the bleak outcome of consequences avoided for far too long.

It's beautifully written (funny, sad, thoughtful) and built by some of the creators of Telltale's Walking Dead (Season 1), along with a veritable super-group of modellers, animators, musicians and graphic designers (and the supporting media of the game is as sumptuous as you would expect from these developers).

I highly recommend the game - it takes 2-6 hours to play, depending on how much you engage with the content. Just don't expect anything SUPER EXPLODO EXCITING YAY - the mood is much more in the vein of something like Gone Home... Quality, low-key tension, humour, characterisation.

I'll get this out of the way up front: this game is short. You have probably seen posts about refund requests or the developer response and maybe you're not sure who to listen to so I will be as honest as I can. This game is disappointingly short. When it ended I desperately wanted there to be more. I watched the whole credits sequence hoping for more game to play. It ended. Nothing. I took my time and meandered around and read everything, searched every corner of the map and still managed to finish in under a little over 4 hours.  It really was that short.

But the more I thought about it I realized that I had never been more engaged with a story. I have never had a game truly mess with my head to the point that when the twists came it didn't just happen to my character; it happened to me. I felt confused about what was happening to me. I felt lost and alone in the woods. I started to distrust my only friend.

The way you might read your favorite book or watch your favorite movie over and over, you will want to play this game again. Even if you think you've figured out all the secrets (or even if you actually have) the story is great. PC Gamer says the game has a genre problem but they are wrong. The moments where you aren't sure what type of game you're playing are intentional. The feeling that the next twist could take you anywhere makes the story powerful and emotional.

That's about all I can say without spoiling anything. Best written game I've ever played and that isn't just the dialogue being spoken, it's the way they make you experience the story. If you want a game that will take you 100 hours to beat and explore then look elsewhere. If you're looking for an engaging storytelling experience that is impossible to accomplish with a movie or book, this game will not let you down. 10/10

For $20 with an incredibly linear 4-hour story and no replay value I would not recommend this game right now.   The story itself is fine for about the first three hours.  The opening  minutes actually had me cry a little when you're piecing together the protagonist's back story.  Unfortunatley the story does not deliver, and in a game that is clearly story-driven this is a big deal breaker for me.  

Most of the other reviews on here all point to the fact that the story feel like a thriller by around mid game and it gets you all anxious and excited to see how it unfolds and see what happens to your character.  The thriller story line is killed right around the climax and there it turns into a sappy drama with a little social commentary that most people would agree with without needing to play this game.

Mechanically the game plays and looks nice.   The "boring" walking around gameplay was quite relaxing for me; I pretty much walked the whole game without sprinting because I really was in no rush to get to the next objective.  The voice acting between the two main characters is very good and lends to the feel the game very well.

That being said I just can't honestly recommend this game to anyone, at least not for $20: the payoff to the story in this story-driven game is just too much of a let down, and without the story there's not much going on for this game.  Walking around the park is nice but it's very linear and there are clearly places you can go and places you can't go.  If I wanted the wilderness feel I'd play The Long Dark for the beatiful atmosphere and sandbox exploration while listening to an audio book or podcast.

TL;DR This is a 4-hour long, heavily story-driven game that either gives up at the end or succumbs to maybe not the best writing team for tying things up.  Also, 0% replayability because ultra linear.  Only buy when 50%-80% off, and only if you don't mind getting a lil disappointed.

Firewatch combines all my favorite things about games. It has gorgeous visuals in a creative art style, interesting game mechanics, and a thoughtful storyline. You may hear people complain about the length of the game, or how the story doesn't end the way they wanted it to, but I think it is important to consider Firewatch as more of an experience than a game. The length is just right for what it is, and it doesn't take much critical thinking to realize the deeper morals that are taught by the seemingly lame ending. The character development pierces straight to the heart from the very beginning, then the impressive voice acting leads you with them, side by side, as they process their own problems and are faced with new and mysterious ones while alone in the wilderness. The descisions your character must make about his life are reflected with curious symmetry to the big reveal near the end, which pulls the development of the well-crafted characters full circle. It leaves you wanting more, but I think it should. I highly reccomend this game.

An emotional journey that will have you on the tip of your seat. It's a roller-coaster of love, sorrow, hope, loneliness, tranquility and terror when you realize the implications just beneath the surface. There isn't a single emotion in the human spectrum that did not manifest within me while playing this game. Make no mistake: This is a very well crafted emotional experience. Don't see a Let's Play. Don't read spoilers. Experience the story for yourself in a single sitting. It's a damn good ride. It begins great, then falls into disjointed tedium before rising to an amazing second half. Graphically the game looks amazing with very few bugs. I encountered more bugs in five minutes of Dragon Age Inquisition than I did with six hours of Firewatch. That said..

              The Bad:
This is not an open world wilderness survival game (which I assumed, going in blind). This is a very strict narrative experience which often hits you with jarring and sudden time skips to days or even weeks later. You won't miss out on any exploration, but in terms of pacing the game randomly slaps you in the face on occasion. The story lacks the tight tension of Gone Home or the narrative tranquility of Dear Esther, but for what it is Firewatch is a good experience. Just go in knowing that this is not a survival/exploration wilderness game in any sense of the word.I also experienced a glitch at the start of both Day 1 and Day 2 where my character couldn't get out of a chair. I couldn't even open the menu with escape and was forced to exit the game from Windows. This happened once on each day and never again. Still, it's worth mentioning.
The biggest issue I have with the game is the price. Get it on sale, it's not quite up to the asking price of 15$. 


            The conclusion:
This is a great game. But the price is the main sticking point. Don't buy it at full price. It's a six dollar kind of game, get in on sale and play it once. Or twice. This is an amazing experience usually only found in great novels, and I can't wait to see what else the studio has coming next. The game is poorly paced and too expensive but beyond that it's a damn fine game. It won't be game of the year, but it just might find itself on my top ten of 2016.

Firewatch is the debut title from Campo Santo, a recently founded game studio. I'm glad to say that Firewatch proves to be an excellent debut from them.

The initial most striking thing about Firewatch was the way that the game looks and sounds (I guess the overall aesthetic package). The game has a sort of cel-shaded feel to it graphically, but with really beautiful lighting that casts shadows on the ground in front of you and peeks through the trees as you wander throughout the wilderness. There are plenty of moments in the game where I found myself take screenshots (both using the hotkey and the in game camera), just because of how incredible it looked. The games music is provided by the same composer who did the music for Gone Home, and it shows: the music is kind of droney/ambient, but it fits really well with the general melancholic mood at points in the game itself.

The narrative of Firewatch is relatively simple: the player assumes the role of Henry, a man who decides to take up a job watching for forests (and ultimately other happenings) in a forest preserve. He does this not only for monetary reasons, but also to search for himself (think Walden or any Thoreau, I guess). Things quickly become more complicated as the player sorts out Henry's various emotions. If you'd care to read more about that, my review above goes into more spoiler-y detail regarding the games actual plot.

I can't recommend Firewatch enough. It's a game that does an outstanding job on all fronts and makes me incredibly excited for what Campo Santo has in store next.

Firewatch isn’t really about watching fires, but it is. It isn’t really about the vast Wyoming wilderness, but it is. It certainly isn’t about throwing a boombox in a lake while skinny dipping teens taunt you about how you are a lonely loser, but it is. Firewatch is about life and how we all deal with the sad, terrible, heart-wrenching things that can happen in it. It doesn’t wrap everything up in a nice, neat bow like we are used to with most video games, but is also doesn’t have guns, blood, and zombies. What Firewatch does best is put you in the boots of a man who’s trying to escape a once happy life that fell apart faster than flames sweep through underbrush, a man alone and fearing it.

You play as Henry in Firewatch, and through a very clever introduction sequence, paint a backstory that is both bitter and sweet. The results of Henry’s past lead him to take a job in the forests of Wyoming, one that essentially means he’ll be alone for months on end watching for wildfires. The game gives you control of Henry just as he is first approaching his watchtower, thus beginning his (your) 79 day journey.

Henry is alone in body and mind, but so is Deliliah. Delilah is Henry’s boss and the soul person he can talk to while on his assignment. The first thing Delilah asks him is “What’s wrong with you?” But in truth, Delilah has just as much “wrong” as Henry. Throughout the game you will forge a rather intimate relationship with Delilah who you only communicate with via walkie-talkie. The conversation system allows you to be as talkative or reserved as you want, as open or closed as you want. I have to say that the vocal performances by both Henry and Delilah are what makes this game work. If one of them had missed their marks, the entire game would have fallen apart. That said, if you happen to be turned off by either of them it may be a deal breaker because you will hear them talk. A lot.

Their relationship and trust of each other is what leads to the central “mystery” of the game, but I won’t spend too much time talking about that as it only serves to move the story and conversations forward. A four hour game where you just talk and look out a window would be a disservice to anyone who played it, so there’s a mystery that gets you out of your watchtower. It feeds on the loneliness and isolation of the two characters, and does a fantastic job of showing how much they come to trust each other over the course of the game, despite never physically meeting.

While your conversations with Delilah push the story forward, the gorgeous realisation of the world around keeps the conversation grounded. Firewatch uses a slightly cell-shaded style that is pleasing to look at, while not being totally detached from reality. The lighting effects are particularly great; sunrises look hazy from the evaporating dew, and evening sunsets are breathtaking. Late-game environmental effects completely change the way you see the world, making you feel lost in places that were once familiar.

Music is sparse, but used to accent important moments. Most of the time all you hear are birds chirping, water flowing, and wind blowing. Unfortunately, there is almost no visible wildlife. This was the only immersion-breaking thing I noticed. It is a very minor complaint and may actually help strengthen your sense of isolation.

Gameplay is fairly simple and you can classify this game as a “walking simulator”. You can interact and inspect various objects in the world, some of them have lore attached to the them, others are just rocks. Henry moves at a brisk pace, and none of the canned animations you do when scaling cliffs or opening caches get in the way. The only real gameplay complaint I have is that you have to press a button every time you need to climb over something, like a log or low ledge. I would have rathered Henry just do that automatically, as it would have made walking around smoother and less cumbersome. The gameplay is really just used to propel you through the story, similar to games like Gone Home and The Vanishing of Ethan Carter. Firewatch is one of my favorite games ever. 

First, since it seems to be a contentious point: I don't agree with any of the myriad criticisms against the narrative. To me, it was a deep, nuanced, excellently-paced experience with lots of subtext that still has me pondering what was really going on, and what the events really say about the characters. People who say the story "fell flat" or didn't have enough of a climax are missing the point--this storytelling style isn't about the concrete plot points, it's about offering moments / themes / questions to explore and reflect on internally. That said, there's still a lot of subtle plot points that complicate the surface-level story (you can already find a bunch of fan theories online arguing what was *really* going on in the game). Sometimes the minor stories (such as the ones told through notes) are just about quietly witnessing a human relationship, and I like that simplicity.

The main characters are amazingly fully-realized, and their dialogue (as you've heard) is one of the best parts of the game. So much depth comes out of these characters and their conversations throughout the story. One of my favorite parts is actually the conversation system itself, though. The things you can say aren't options to roleplay as different characters (good Henry, evil Henry, neutral Henry, etc) but different thoughts in Henry's head, and you choose which ones get spoken aloud / embraced. I felt like I learned a lot about Henry from the conversation options I saw but didn't choose, not just from the ones I chose. There's not really any way to be out of character in this game and I think that's a bold and beautiful decision for a first-person game. It also highlights what I think is a common misguided approach to the narrative--this is about empathizing with another, fleshed-out human being, and the story is set up to give you opportunities to empathize, it's not necessarily supposed to be a bombastic roller coaster going for maximum entertainment.

I also personally really enjoyed the light game-y aspects. I know some have criticized saying it's not game-y enough but can't we all agree that that's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ criticism at this point? I don't care whether it's technically a game or not, I care about whether it was a meaningful worthwhile experience. For me, the simple world interactions were just enough to help me engage with Henry's character and situation a bit more immersively. And I'm glad they didn't pad out the length with menial side quests or daily tasks. (Though I confess that I have fantasized about a mod that turns the gorgeous environment into an actual ranger simulator where you just have randomized tasks to do each day, along with a bit of survival sim-style resource gathering. Just to have an excuse to be in that beautiful world every day. c: )

While it's not right to call this an "open-world" game, there is a lot of opportunity (especially early on) to explore the environment with virtually complete freedom. Yes, the paths are a bit linear / corridor-y, but not oppressively so, and there's still fun little things to discover and lots of humongous vistas, so for me it still created the sense / atmosphere of a vast natural environment. The real-time paper map-and-compass system ads to that vibe of being in the midst of a huge undeveloped natural area, too.

To all of the above, add the obvious stuff: the visual design is stunningly beautiful, the voice acting is some of the best ever (and funny!).

Overall, if you're looking for a fantastical escapist narrative or exciting visceral mechanics, this is not the game for you. You shuld play this game if you're interested in stories with pacing rather than padding, and nuanced subtext that encourages reflection and empathy; gorgeous stylized renderings of lovely natural environments; light interactive elements that enhance engagement without being distracting; and voice acting / dialogue that is disarmingly human, even when it's also hilarious.

Sigh... I've seen people claiming having cried during the first 10 minutes of the game. That might be the case if you're overly sensitive, but anything can spark the inner emotional inferno for some. For example, let me tell you a short story about my pet gold fish Jeremy. Jeremy had cancer. Jeremy died... Bravo, best emotionally striking story of the year, 10/10.
 
The initial sequence atempts to do the same. Succeeds in some respects, but let's be frank, as far as gaming goes, there are much more creative ways of emotionally investing the player than text fading in and out with sad music playing in the background. You're better off putting on Beethoven's "Moonlight Sonata" and reading an article on animal abuse.
 
The game gives you only an illusion of choice. No matter what choices you pick - you'll end up with the same results. Everything's linear. Invisible walls everywhere, some sections are blocked off until you get a hold of the means required to pass through, for example an axe to cut down a tree and create a bridge over a canyon, or a rope to descend down a mountain.
 
Controls and interactions are very strict, you must be in a very specific position to interact with objects. Would be great to run around and jump around at your own will. You are restricted to only one straight path towards the objective. Pretty much everything you find in the world has no practical use whatsoever. You can pick up those props, inspect them and throw away. I remember picking up a pair of antlers. Delilah said I'll find a use for them later. Well, I never did. Also, at one point I went fishing. Well, at I least carried around a fishing rod by the lake. At this point, a fishing mini-game would present at least a small amount of gameplay "depth". Nope, the "fishing" sequence was made only to lead to the scripted event by the lake. 
 
Storytelling and character development is done via a walkie-talkie and you have to report EVERYTHING. See a nice tree - report to Delilah. An oddly shaped rock? Report. An outhouse - discuss how you would feel feel taking a dump in there.

Story is disappointing. Not really a mystery. Nothing to solve. The story unfolds by itself and the "striking finale" makes you ask a question: "So what...?".

Someone complained that there wasn't enough back-tracking. I found that to be plentiful and that's in itself infuriating - same path, no interaction with the world, no encounters, just walking.
 
Optimization is not good, occasional frame rate drops. Overdone with bloom and saturation. Aesthetics is a very subjective matter - I personally wasn't too fond of it.
 
One of the few positives: Music is calming and dreamy. Voice acting is great and the dialog is pretty well written - feels very natural.

 
All in all, I'm really disappointed, I wanted to love it. I gave in to the hysteria and even pre-ordered it. The length is just over 2 hours, 3 if you're willing to "explore" every single inch of this small map.
 
Boring, linear, uninspired, badly optimized, too pricey for the amount of content you're getting.
 
I can see why fans of walking simulators would like this, but I, personally, wanted more interaction and a better pay off in the end.

No, the flawed part is mainly that they did a fantastic job of building the tension to a climax (hair was standing up on the back of my neck when I was exploring the scientific research area), but then the denouement just failed to satisfy. Its like they rushed it at the end despite coming so close to perfection. I wanted something more complex/multi-level to be going on (as was hinted at) And what did come to light was a little poorly explained, felt instabstantial somehow.  Still not sure why the 'villain' went to so much trouble to misdirect and confuse. Did I miss a key plot point at the end or something?

Conclusion – the fact that I am spending the time to deconstruct the story in a video game is a huge complement. It is by far the most sophisticated and mature narrative I have even come across in a game, and one of the most moving, though-provoking and poignant story games I have every played – on a par with Gone Home. 

Though it frustratingly failed to hit its final mark for me, I would recommend it without hesitation to my friends and I hope it sets the narrative bar for future games to aspire to. A great story stays with us far longer than cool graphics or a fun game mechanic.

This game greatest strength is also it's greatest weakness: it breaks genres. Until the very end, you're not really sure what kind of story you're being told. Some people find that very challenging, even to the point of labelling the ending a "disappointment". Other people (e.g. me) find it refreshing and entertaining. The ending is... what it is. It's neat little story, and I like it, and the ending, though unexpected, is not an M. Night Schyamalan-style "twist". 

Twisting genres, and telling a powerful emotional tale is something Gone Home did too, arguably more successfully. This does well enough though, and I think we should be encouraging developers to do more of this sort of thing.

Also, the visual design is transcendently gorgeous. I could just traipse round Shoshone National Park for hours, ignoring Delilah and any need to advance the plot.

Firewatch is a game made, in part, by some of the awesome folks over at the Idle Thumbs network who host a bunch of gaming podcasts that I frequently listen to. So being somewhat familiar with some of the folks who made this game had be very excited to see this game released. Director Jake Rodkin and writer Sean Vanaman previously worked at Telltale on The Walking Dead game, so that's the kind of high caliber writing I was expecting from Firewatch. And it delivers - kind of. Firewatch is a narrative heavy exploration game where you the player character take a summer job as a park ranger to escape and diconnect from your own life for a while.

For most intents and purposes, Firewatch is another Walking Simulator, except for when choosing dialogue responses when talking to Deliliah, a fellow park ranger who keeps in contact with you via radio. The dialogue interactions between Henry, the player character, and Delilah are very well written, charming and geniuine in a way that sells the evolution of the relationship between two middle aged people who don't know each other and whose relationship grows only through conversations over a radio. Picking up or looking at certain objects in the game will sometimes generate a prompt to question Delilah about what you're looking at which can be informative or humorous or reveal aspects of Henry or Delilah's characters. Firewatch can hit a range of emotions from quiet and metitative to tense and suspenseful. It's a game that has you pondering events of the plot, or mulling over things Deliliah is saying all while exploring the wilderness.

The excellent characters and writing had me hooked and this seemed like it would be a game I would fall in love with up until I got to the ending. The ending to the game comes rather abruptly and leaves a lot of plot threads unaddressed or explained unsatisfactorily. It appears as though Campo Santo ran out of time during development and possibly weren't able to include some of the content that would have neatly wrapped up these story threads. But as it stands, these threads don't end up connecting or leading anywhere and the ending of the game feels abrupt and unsatisfying. Still, the first two thirds of the game are engaging and well written, so if you're up for a walk in the woods that you know won't take you anywhere, check out Firewatch

From the get-go, Firewatch pulled my attention unlike any video games has ever done (except probably "The Last of Us"). I understand why many people grumble at it for the lack of replay-values and the linear story-tellings, but this game is not meant to be compared to Fallout 4 or Skyrim. The beauty of Firewatch lies in its narrative, in its seamless rendering of complex emotions. Imagine playing it in a third-person view. I can't imagine it. The idea is to see the world from Henry's eyes, to experience the human emotions from everything in the environment, and the soundtrack just killed it.
   I am a big fan of exploration games that do not shy away from telling difficult stories. Life is full of choices and contradictions. In a way the choices we made doesn't impact the game that much, but that was what the life was like. We are vulnerable, we make mistakes, we lose people we love. After the credit rolled, my first instinct is to call my parents and say how much I love them. Rather than pulling us into digital fantasy like most of the mainstream games do Firewatch taught us to step out of it and cherish the real moment we inhabit.

In a world where many pundits shout the death of the single player experience, here comes another great indie title to prove them wrong.  There will always be great experiences meant to be played in the tradition of the single player campaign, but as our community of "gamers" grow, so does its diversity of gameplay.  

Firewatch is simple in its elegance, but deep and rich in its content.  What I mean by content is a richness of storytelling, the type that only games provide.  Since the game is short, I won't spoil anything for you, but I will give you a bit of insight as to why I really enjoyed the title, and why it deserves your attention.

Firewatch follows a man named Henry into the wilderness to.... you guessed it, watch for forest fires.  Your only point of contact is with your boss, over the radio.  As you pick apart each other's lives, you begin to unravel a mystery that is engaging, and really propels the player forward.  

What struck me about the tone of this game, is that it has great art appeal, and isn't afraid to show a more adult perspective on life.  There is a lot of truth to these characters, and that is at its heart, what makes this game so special to me.  Perhaps it's because I've played games since I was old enough to use a controller, but this game challenges the players notion of control, and delivers some unexpected elements that really add to the story's realism and suspension of disbelief.  Top that off with solid writing and great voice acting and you have a really good title that says something about an ever aging demographic of gamers (and developers) longing for content that has a more mature edge.  I'm not talking about sexuality necessarily, or about gore and violence, but rather the intangible space that we all reach after we've seen life take its tole. When reality has set in, and we must make choices on behalf of our loved ones that alter our interactions with others for the rest of our life.  This is a game for people wanting more truth in their games.  A game that doesn't always cater to the player's every desire, but rather tries to have a dialog with the player, and show them a glimpse into the lives of some well defined characters.  

I've read several reviews where people are disappointed by the ending.  I don't fall into that camp.  They took a few shortcuts that would have been nice to avoid, but ultimately it didn't change my mind on how I felt about this game after finishing it. There are a few issues with the title in my opinion.  The controls could be a bit smoother, and I found myself constantly challenging the collision meshes to see where I could and couldn't venture.  Sometimes the boundaries felt ridiculous, but the storytelling was engaging enough to keep me invested.  The rock jumping and dropping felt like it could have transitioned a bit smoother, and I think other aspects of the gameplay could have been finessed a bit to feel more streamlined.  The design is fantastic, it really comes down to the implementation of some of the controls that leaves a little to be desired.  Lastly, some of the items you get throughout feel underutilized.  It would have been nice to see reactions or more functional uses for a few items in particular, but I won't mention them so nothing is spoiled.

It's far from perfect, but what game is.  Campo Santo  made a great title, and if you like narrative storytelling in games, I would consider this a must play.  8.5/10

Take a deep breath. You're going to have to go against a lot of what video games have taught you. Ready?

Turn off your map location*. Spend time learning the forest. You don't have anything 'to do'. No, really. Sure, you're given an objective at each turn in the narrative, but go collect books instead. Yeah maybe D is asking you to go check something out, but I think you should be hunting down the perfectly lit set of trees to photograph. A lot of people will focus on how it isn't a game that demands you rush around and get ♥♥♥♥ done. They will find the pace to be slow, maybe 'boring'. I argue that I want other games to let me slow the hell down. Frankly, I find that wandering around finding notes of a story, of two guys I'll never know, so much more engaging than collecting herbs or ♥♥♥♥.

I will first preface this review by saying that I went into this game knowing that people were disappointed/unhappy with both the length of the game as well as the ending, however I was not. I will do my best to be as spoiler free as possible! 

Firewatch puts you in the shoes of Henry, who after suffering a personal tragedy decides to take a position with the Forest Service in Shoshone National Park in Wyoming as a firewatcher. Over the course of the ensuing 79 days, you develop a close relationship with Delilah; (who is both your boss and the only other person you have direct contact with during your employment with the Forest Service) as you both try to unravel the mysterious incidents which begin occurring when Henry takes his post. 

The game itself is strikingly beautiful, the character voicework is absolutely top notch, and there is a fantastic story Campo Santo has told here if you can just get past the "but it's only 3-4 hours long!" part. I understand that $20 is a steep price for some people to pay for entertainment that lasts only a few hours, but you also have to appreciate what Campo Santo has done here by creating something as unique and intriguing as Firewatch. By the end of the journey, I found myself connected to both Henry and Delilah and wishing that the story went further. These are some of the best voiced characters I have seen in a very long time. The music is also fantastic, and the tunes are spaced apart throughout the journey for maximum effect versus something you hear in the background at all times. The absence of music throughout much of the game really emphasizes the isolation and loneliness of being out in that vast wilderness.

As far as the "walking simulator" tags - I would agree that the game is a walking simulator of sorts. Aside from pushing a button to climb some rocks, pushing a button to hack through some brush or open a supply cache, you will find yourself mostly navigating your way through your section of the park using your trusty map and compass to complete the various errands and tasks that Delilah sets for you. Along the way you will discover supply caches and items left behind by past rangers that give you a bit of backstory to the area and the past individuals who held the post before you. No guns, no platforming, no inventory management - it's all very simple and straightforward. This is a game you play for the atmosphere, setting, and the story; not the action. 

While I was initially somewhat disappointed at the ending, after a bit of reflection I found myself really liking the way they tied things up. This is a game about love, loss, and that no matter how far you try to run from your problems eventually you will have to turn back and face them.
