Having watched some pre-release footage, I went into this game expecting a pretty-looking mystery with an interesting premise and setting backed by some snappy dialogue writing, with the vague hope that it might be something that could come close to the phenomenal PS4 game Until Dawn. 

Upon starting a new game, however, you are immediately greeted by an absolutely vile text-only intro written in a second person narrative style that is equal parts superfluous and pretentious. It immediately confirms that yes, Firewatch was indeed spat out from the infernal orifice that is the San Franscisco indie developer scene. The game *clearly* wants us to focus on the story by omitting silly things like, I dunno, gameplay and other archaic concepts like that.

Once it gets going, the dialogue writing is actually charming for the most part. The voice acting is competent, but for a game that essentially foregoes any semblance of gameplay, the story just isn't good enough to hold it up. It goes through a lot of buildup and dangles several red herring plot threads in front of the player that are never followed up on. For a moment, there is even some immersion and a sense of tension, as the mysteries seem to ramp up towards the climax. It all soils the bed very quickly at that point, however. The 'twist' is literally that nothing out of the ordinary actually happens during the game.
 
It doesn't matter whether the writers were out to prove a point about how isolation drives people to start imagining things out of paranoia and how it's a reflection on our collective existential ennui or whatever interpretative drivel you can come up with. It's essentially a glorified "it was all a dream" type resolution. And hell, if the writers thought this twist was clever, original, or even a remotely good idea, doesn't that make that worse than if they had written it like this out of ignorance?

The visuals, although probably one of the games' strongest aspects, lose their luster pretty quickly too once you realize that the map actually consists of a series of prettified corridors rather than an actual open world as one might be tempted to assume given the setting. Outside of the chubby protagonists' body, character models are conspicuously absent. I'm sure that was a deliberate choice as well in order to underline the protagonists' isolation and not just cheaping out on animators and 3D modellers.

The sad thing about this game is that it could have been so much more. The potential for gameplay is absolutely there. There could have been more adventure elements, or a greater focus on day to day survival. Even simple menial tasks would have worked. But nope, you just walk around and listen to people talk.

Stay away, even if you like games with a strong narrative focus. Get something by Telltale instead or hell, get a PS4 with Until Dawn.

Firewatch is gorgeous, breathetaking, engaging... and slightly overpriced, but I don't regret buying this.
In Firewatch, you play as a man named Henry who is at a difficult stage in his life. He finds an ad in a newspaper for a Fire Lookout at Twoforks Park and takes the job to get away from his problems. Along the way, he's greeted by Delilah, a very chipper woman who runs you though the ropes in being a firewatchman (that's probably not an actual word, but I'm rolling with it regardless). Together you explore the forest, report any misshaps, and discover many secrets... Not all of which are pleasant.
Gameplay-wise, there isn't much to talk about since it's a very story-oriented game. You hike, climb, spelunk occasionally, and inspect/talk about nearly everything you lay your eyes on. This isn't a bad thing, however. Controlling Henry while walking through the forest is an awe-inspiring experience. From the amazing view from the watchtower to the lush, green fields and woods to the burned-down sections of the forest, you get to take in some of the most amazing visuals I've had the pleasure of witnessing. There was only one moment when I saw the end of one of the utility wires suspended in the air, but it didn't distact me for long.
There's a lot to say about the story but not without spoiling anything. The story was a joy to sit through the entire way and you come to care about these two characters who just want to have their own lives out in the wilderness but can't shake the feeling that someone is watching them...
In conclusion, this game was well worth the $16.50 (I got it on sale). If you're curious about the story but don't want to spend the money, there are plenty of YouTubers (I know Cry and Markiplier are nearing the end since writing this review) who will play it for you so you can see the story for itself. However, if you're anything like me and wants to experience a story rather than simply watch it, I highly reccommend picking it up.

Do yourself a favor and try not to listen to the (largely misguided) criticism for this game.  Sure, to each his/her own and all, and that's perfectly valid.  But above all, this is a game that is most certainly worth experiencing, despite whatever apparent setbacks others have brought to light.  It's difficult to try and review/rate an experience, as opposed to simply commenting on gameplay and playtime and graphics and such, but know that's exactly what you're in for with Firewatch.  It's an experience through and through.  And one that I'd highly recommend - so much so that this is my first review ever posted to Steam.  I finshed the game no more than a few hours ago, and can't stop thinking about the narrative and dialogue and visuals and themes and... well, I can't stop thinking about the game.  It's a perfect example of what a story-driven, deeply personal, gorgeous walking simulator can aspire to be.  It may not be a perfect game, but it's certainly one of my favorite in recent memory.  

Pros
- Incredibly believable, authentic voice acting (conversations feel natural; Delilah and Henry feel real)
- Gorgeous art direction and design 
- Visceral, engaging, (at times) hilarious dialogue
- Story (Many seem to disagree, but I feel the story most certainly pays off. perhaps just not in a way most expected)  
- Atmospheric (This game is a testament to the validity of games as art)

Cons
- Upon completion it may leave you feeling empty, yet somehow full, inside, emotionally drained, and intensely pensive
- Could be the only game you want to play ever again
- There's no sequel immediately available

Bottom Line
This is an experience worth playing.  It's short, yes, but in a way that never overstays its welcome.  Rather than focus on time, embrace the incredible experience and play a game relatively unlike anything else available.  Highly recommended.

Short review: I recommend Firewatch. BUT ONLY if it's on sale for $5 bucks or less.

The game starts out with nothing but text on screen. Nothing wrong with this, but you never revisit this mode of game play, and so it feels a bit out of place looking back on it. You make a few superficial choices that really don't make much of an effect on anything after the first 5 minutes, and are pretty pointless in the grand scheme of things. You are introduced to your character Henry, as well as your wife, Julia. Again, none of your choices really matter, and after a few clicks, you will be swept off into the wilderness to take on the lonely job of a forest outlook, whether you want to or not. 

The Firewatch world appears huge at first, until you actually get to the forest floor and start exploring it. It's about as linear an experience as you can get, and so calling this an "open-world" game of any sorts is pretty false. It's a linear game, with restrictive choice options that don't allow you to be your own character, but simply make you choose different ways to be selfish. I get it, "You are Henry", you aren't yourself in the real world. But if that is the case, more effort should have been given to build up the backstory on who Henry is and why he is the hard headed, poor decision making person he has become. You're given choices, but your choices really don't seem to matter much at all in what happens. Maybe that's true in life in general, but in a game, you'd like to have some control over what it is you're doing. Otherwise, you might as well just watch a movie.

Once you get to your ranger tower, you quickly get in touch with your main counterpart in the game, Delilah, who is really the only person worth playing the game for. She is voice-acted brilliantly, and you actually start to believe that she's a real person. 

However, by the time Firewatch feels like it is just getting going, it's over. There's a great build up sequence, where the suspense starts to really get going, but then it just abruptly ends. The entire experience is simply WAY too short. In certain areas, there's really no exploring to be had. I was excited to get to an abandoned camp, for instance. Once there though, there was nothing to do other than look around a little bit. One scene starts with your character holding a fishing pole. I thought maybe this would lead to a mini-game of sorts, but no. You stash it away and never mention it or see it again. More interactive content could have made this into a lasting franchise, but as it is, it's just kind of a "meh". 

FW is something to do for 3-4 hours when you have nothing else going on, but nothing really more than that. It's too bad too because I could pretty easily envision a follow up game or a 'part 2'  where you "re-visit" the forest/Delilah, but how it was ended was pretty finite and final.

As time has passed since I completed Firewatch, a maturing bitter taste has been growing in my mouth about it. I keep seeing more and more positive reviews of the game around the web, and with that, I become more annoyed with my experience and what was lacking from it. I love to immerse myself in story games, this one included, but the substance just wasn't there. And as a big fan of story driven/atmospheric/walking sim games,  I so desperately wanted it to be.

In my opinion, the Firewatch hype has been greatly exaggerated in the average review online. The game is a maybe 6 of 10 at best, mostly because of the superb voice acting. Compared to other atmospheric games it is simply dwarfed in comparison due to it's lack of depth. I hope to see more from this developer, with an emphasis on MORE. Want a good story driven game that immerses you from the get-go? Check out Life is Strange.

The one complaint I've heard others voice is that there are plot holes and the ending is a disappointment, but I don't quite see it that way. There were unanswered questions, and a few points that straight-up should have been explained FAR better than they were (which was not at all), but many of the "holes" people talk about are really "fill in the blanks." For example, Delilah's character never reveals a particularly rich history, but it's about what she doesn't say, and what the player interprets that that makes Delilah especially interesting: she can be a very different character for each player.

I guess everything about this game has been said already, so I'll just recap:

 * Gameplay is, let's say, ascetic. Atmosphere of the game is build mostly with dialogue. But game also offers distinctive visual and sound experience (fabulous landscapes in intriguing palette - looks a bit comic, but not completely unreal) with discreet, but very good music to complete the mood.
 * A big applause should go to writers and voice actors - they did [b]awesome job[/b]. As said above, dialogue between two main characters is core of the game, and it's done perfectly. Firewatch is tagged with “the walking-simulator games”, like the game Gone Home. (which unfortunately I did not find engaging) But I have to say I had a very good time playing the Firewatch. The game has fully lived up to my expectation despite its relatively short playtime and to me, Firewatch resembles a [b]post-modernism novel[/b] in telling people a story and unfolding the plot and the ending. Here are my thoughts.

         The game started with a script-choosing prologue, providing the basic background of the story (basically about the early life before our protagonist, Henry). I found this part very immersive for the simple dialogue choosing mechanism and the relaxing background music, the characters are all very relatable and the twist in Henry’s early life made my tears welling up :( It is just ordinary people’s life, but it proved to be moving, especially when this initial part only took up about 15-20 minutes to present Henry’s whole life before he went to the wilderness to be a fire lookout. It was such a climatic experience and after this initial part the gamers should have a basic, yet ambiguous understanding of why Henry took this job.

         The main gameplay of the game is fairly good, first the mechanism of walkie-talkie is really brilliant idea, as the name puts, it allows you to report many thing you see to your supervisor, Delilah, which you do not feel lonely while exploring the wilderness. To make this mechanism work, the voice acting is essential and it is just fascinating. The navigation system---the map and the compass combination is very interesting and works well. The major problem I have with this game is the performance, the game has glitches during the autosave when you move to the next region, and the game requires high spec for its grass&trees rendering and shadows. There are many invisible walls in the game, which breaks my immersion sometimes.

         To the end of the game, some people found it “anticlimactic” and frustrating about the [b]short 4-5 hrs playtime[/b] to “complete” it. Personally I disagree with these opinions. [b]The longevity of the time never justifies a game when the quality is below average.[/b] This game is all about imagination, people nowadays are easily become disconcerting when something strange happened, especially for gamers (or Hollywood movie fans) who has taken it for granted that---there has to be a climax, many conspiracies and lots of twists in game’s story. The fact is, what the developers want to tell is a small episode of life involving only several character(Actually the number is 6, according to the cast list) and I think they have done a good job. [h1]There is no survival mechanism (like the one we have in The Long Dark), there is no death or failure penalty. Yet I found myself overreacting to some thrilling elements and then it turned out to be just my imagination.[/h1] 
   --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     [h1]<Spoiler Alert>[/h1]

     [spoiler]As for the ending, yes you never actually get to meet Delilah, which is acceptable in my opinion, in the game, when you get into her tower in the end, you can found her sketch of you, which was completed only by the descriptions of how you look through radio times ago in the game. I definitely think that everyone has his/her very own image of Delilah, and so again this is a game about creativity of human thoughts, which is imagination. So I do not think the game has a mundane ending.[/spoiler]

     [h1]Personally I may play the game for several times in the future, Firewatch is more like a good book of fiction to me.[/h1]If you are into readings, you shall find that the style of story’s beginning, unfolding and ending is quite close to the post-modernism. In this category, we have Murakami Haruki with [i]1Q84[/i], Lisa Genova with [i]Still Alice[/i] Jonathan Safran Foer with [i]Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close[/i] and so on. These books, they all offered readers a basic yet vague setting, people [b]HAVE TO[/b] use imagination to understand, to engage. The ending will not surprise you that much, but that is the [b]real life[/b]. In the Firewatch, the same applied, maybe you can be sure to expect the ending exactly in the middle of the game, but there are still many things remains unexplored, many choice to reply to the supervisors I would like to try out. [h1]Firewatch is the very game for the late night reading time, it is immersive in the first playthrough and it shall be more of a casual journey from then on.[/h1] I have already decided to close the captions in next playthrough for more immersion :)

If you're looking for a fully story driven game where it requires you to walk from Point A to B to progress, then you've found the right game. If you require something more to keep your attention, don't even bother reading the rest of the review yet alone buying the game.

Plot: 
You are Henry, a middle aged husband whose wife got sick and was moved away for her health. Now all alone, he takes up a summer job as a fire lookout for a national forest in Colorado. A solitary job with only his supervisor, Delilah, to give him jobs and company via walkie talkey, they tackle a mystery involved with the forest and it's connection to an approaching out of control fire.

Gameplay: 
As I said, this is a walking simulator. Which there's little else to do but go to the designated spot on your in game map and follow the story. And this is not a bad thing as it forces you to soak in the nature of the world of game. The lighting is pretty spot on too. There was a point during approaching sunset that was so bright it literally almost obscured my map (you're going to be pulling that thing out often). There's no inventory wheel and the map is brought up in real time to keep you in the experience. I love this mechanic in games and wish it would be implemented more in non stressful environments of course. Dialogue choices are present as you talk to Delilah on the radio. To me the best part of the game was the Dialogue and two top notch actors are probably the only people who couldve pulled it off.

Characters: 
The characters of Henry and Delilah are practically the only characters in the game and thankfully their likeable. Henry is weary and tired from his wife's illness and Delilah is likeable, yet quirky. Their dynamic is the highlight of the game and other than the main mystery is what kept me playing.

Conclusion:
This is a game you should not pass up, sale or no sale. Everyone's finances are different but in my opinion 20 dollars is a more than fair price for this game.

Firewatch Review

Nearly A Burnout

• Platforms: PS4, PC (Reviewed)
• Publisher: Panic Inc., Campo Santo
• Developer: Campo Santo

Firewatch is a compelling experience that is ultimately a victim of its own ambition. While it promises to offer a memorable narrative, it's mainly the result of an elaborate bait-and-switch, as the developers write a check they have no hope of cashing.

--Story--

Firewatch puts you in the shoes of Henry, a big, bearded, middle-aged guy trying to escape his crumbling life at home by coming to work at a National Forest as a Fire Watcher. Upon arriving at his lookout tower after a 2-day hike, he receives a call on the two-way radio from a fellow Fire Watcher, Delilah.

Delilah welcomes Henry, teasing him and explaining what tasks he needs to complete. As the game goes on, Delilah and Henry form a very strong connection. Henry begins to put his troubled past behind him, as his new relationship with Delilah continues to blossom.

However, bizarre occurrences begin to happen in the forest, occurrences that make Henry question everything that's transpired while he's been employed there. As the game continues, Henry works together with the only human connection he currently has in order to figure out just what the hell is going on.

And sadly, this is where the game stops being remotely interesting. The follow-through on these "bizarre occurrences" is so disappointing, it literally made me angry. And that's before we get to the hilariously abrupt ending. An ending so depressingly awful, it evokes laughter, rather than any kind of meaningful contemplation.

...Look, maybe I'm being too hard on the game's ending, but that only highlights how deeply invested these developers got me in their narrative. The writing in Firewatch is quite possibly the best I've ever seen in a video game. It's so human, and believe-able; it's the kind of writing that makes you want to hold this game up as an example of how mature and artistic the medium can be.

Henry and Delilah have the most complex relationship I've seen in a video game in quite some time. The way this game explores how relationships develop is just incredible.

And all of this nearly becomes invalidated by the ending. It may seem over dramatic to place so much value on the ending of a game, but in a "walking simulator" with no real gameplay to speak of, it's really all the game has to offer.

--Gameplay--

N/A

--Presentation--

Firewatch is a pretty game. With a unique, aesthetic somewhere in between cartoony and realistic, the game is certainly pleasant to look at. Add to that the gorgeous forest that's open for you to explore, and you have one of the best looking games of the year, thus far.

There are minor graphical glitches, such as Henry's meaty hands clipping through environments, or his legs clipping through the rocks he's climbing, but overall the game runs wonderfully on PC.

Unfortunately , the same cannot be said for the PS4 version. I played the game on PC, myself, but as I understand it, the game is borderline unplayable on PS4, even prompting the developer to encourage people to seek refunds if they're having trouble.

--Arbitrary Score--

Firewatch could have been something utterly phenomenal as a work of art. Unfortunately, the game's final chapter ruins the overall experience. While the game explores human relationships on an impressive level, the narrative just isn't worth getting invested in.

Excellent, believable characters with well-written dialogue, and beautiful visuals make for a game that you could spend hours on just walking around, enjoying the view, and talking on your walkie-talkie. Which is great because that about sums up the game. Walking and talking.

Shame about the story though.
It builds atmosphere like it ain't no body's business, but it ends both suddenly, and disatisfactorily, utilizing none of the atmosphere it built, and the characters just seem to stop caring about each other, in sharp contrast with how they have otherwise engaged with each other so far. It almost seems like they planned at least 4 more hours of classic slasher-isolation horror, but then ran out of time or budget, and decided to write a half-assed conclusion and rush the release.

I am pretty torn on whether or not I would recommend the game, because aside from the disappointing ending, my experience with the game has been overwhelmingly positive. I really want to recommend it, but there is just no excuse for ending the game in that manner.

Gotta say though, I do love their approach to NPC companions: A person on a radio who rarely contacts or engages with you, except when important plot points occur or else when YOU choose to contact them. You choose how much -excellently written - exposition you're willing to engage in, and you don't have to bother with some NPC running around, getting in your way and ruining your immersion with shoddy pathfinding or glitches.

Firewatch is a great, self-contained, impactful story, about when you decided to run away to be a park ranger. It will take somewhere between 2-5 hours, depending on how long you spend wandering around, taking in the gorgeous scenery, atmosphere, and the trinkets that other hikers have left behind. I didn't really feel any of that with Firewatch. I didn't really get attached to the characters. I felt the whole plot twist at the end was hard to believe. Firewatch is an extremely addictive game that pits you agaisnt the Wyoming wilderness and the people there. I would consider Firewatch a mystery thriller while also putting in some horror aspects. Ever when you first figure out people are watching you I found myself looking behind my back or checking around corners to make sure I wasnt being followed. I found myself extremely intrenched in the story line and itching to find out what happens next. However after about an hour I experienced an awful headache I would assume from the more cartoon like graphics, however this may have just been coinidence, so Im not counting it agaisnt it. 

GRAPHICS/ANIMATION: 9/10
Firewatch is an extremely beautiful game and has the world progress with the story line, for example, when you first start off and make it to your tower, you are set in a humid Wyoming forest. But as the story goes on a massive forest fire will start to spread and by the end of the game it is very smokey and orange out. I adored the cliff sides you could look over and just take in the vast landscape. The animations were great as well, you can actually look down and see your feet move! (lol) However you do see other people in the game, and they are just silhouetted agaisnt the wilderness, however they do move in a believeable way for a human.

AUDIO: 6/10 
I absolutely loved this games audio and soundtrack as where ever you were corresponded to what you were hearing. You could hear fireworks go off in the distance and the closer you got the more detail you could hear. I loved walking near the lakes or ponds as you could hear the vast wildlife come alive and make out different animals. When you were in a cave your feet would echo and you could hear wind swooshing through. However the music, while building up suspense, would go off in places you wouldnt expect it to, letting you know something was ahead.

GAMEPLAY: 6/10
I loved how realistic your movements were in the world, how you couldnt sprint everywhere like in other games. However I often found myself stuck on little rocks and such just because you couldnt "drop down" to places, so whenever you stood on a rock that would just be a little step over you would have to go back and walk down or else you would be stuck. I also found it annoying that whevener I picked something up in my tower, and attempted to put it back down, it would be flung to the floor and time after time I had to try to position my character in a way that he would chuck it onto the table. There were also no waypoints, which while annoying, was realistic and really made you think to where you were going next, and forcing you to seek out caches where you could update your map with any trails nearby. This was also a very short game, taking me only 2 hours to beat completely.

STORYLINE: 9.5/10
The storyline in this game kept me on the edge of my seat every minute playing it. I always was so curious what would happen next or who the stalker might be. The characters were extremely thought out and gave you many options to change the story. The ending was dissapointing and reminded me of Emily is Away by the fact you never get to really meet Delilah. However it left me hoping for a second one. Firewatch 2 PLEASE!

This would be a great game if it cost <$5, but at $20 (currently $17 with a sale) save your money. Clocking in at just over 3 hours long (with no replay value), most of the game is actually spent running through the woods while very little happens. The game is driven by the narrative of your conversations with your fellow firewatcher in a nearby tower, but too many periods of radio silence permeate your wandering through the woods going from objective to objective without anything to occupy you but paper-and-compass navigation. The story was interesting, well-written, and engaging as I was going through it, until the ending. It's a game built on a well-crafted mystery, but your choices through the game don't matter much and the ending is an abrupt and ultimately unsatisfying resolution that leaves too many questions.

If you want to feel like you got what you paid for, don't buy Firewatch unless the price is VERY low.

Firewatch is a great concept that does not go far enough. The game is about a guy named Henry, who meets a girl and gets married, only to realize down the line that she has dementia. Henry starts drinking and then gets a DUI and has his wife taken from him by her family. In an effort to find an escape, he takes a job as a Firewatch Volunteer at Shoshone National Forest. During his time there he notices many strange happennings in his territory, which turns into a suspenseful mystery that many will find must be played until the end. 

One playthrough will last you about 4 hours, which for $20 bucks seems worthwhile since it is more than just a movie, it's an interactive experience where you really get to be engrossed in the details. Let’s start with what is great about this game, the graphics are absolutely gorgeous. Early on you are given a camera where you can take pictures of the game. I knew where this was going the moment they gave it to you. And it’s cool that they allow you to do this. As I was playing the game I thought the camera would become a central gameplay mechanic, where you needed to take pictures of things that you saw as evidence to defend yourself later, sadly this is not the case. 

As I continued playing, I kept on wanting this to be one of those fluid choose-your-own adventure books, where you could play and make decisions and things would end in a very different way, much like the Stanley Parable or Who is Oscar Lake or even Myst. Nope… And here in lies the absolute disappointment with this game. Rather than this game being a linear narrative, it really could have gone one step further and create random encounters with different outcomes. 

Do I regret spending $20 on this game? No. Considering that an IMAX movie in my area costs $18.59 for a single IMAX ticket, I think that this game definitely pays for itself. This game offers way more value than an IMAX experience as it is more interactive, where you can take pictures and it takes place in a first person perspective, where you, the player has the ability to look around and really take in the environment.

The sound design in this game is excellent. The voice acting makes you believe you are there in the moment. The interactions between Henry and Delilah are amazing and feel completely real. As you explore the game you hear your footsteps through the wilderness and the sound of the stream. I guess the only thing that took me out of it were the slightly repetitive noises when Henry would jump down long casms. But this is forgiven because of all the radio chatter and excellent storytelling of the game. In a way it is what I wanted Alan Wake to be. 

Honestly, there is not to much gameplay, and the visuals, sound, and the way you interact with your environment really lend themselves well to that escapism feeling you get from a book or movie, and considering you play Henry from a first person perspective, I think this game would be the perfect way to showcase VR done right.

If you are really into narrative experiences, you should definitely check this game out, however, if you want more puzzles, and exploration gameplay, this game may not be for you.

There's little I can say to convince people to at least try this game that won't spoil important story events, so I'm a little handcuffed to describing the quality of the production. The world is vividly, colorfully recreated with history in every inch of its design. Animations are fluid and evocative and wonderfully serve the interface of interacting with objects (and friends), usually by picking them up and rotating them (yes, including your friends) for inspection.

What hazard I approach is in describing the story too much, so I'll leave that to the trailer.

Now, my thoughts on that I can approach without giving anything away:

So, this is what a game for grown ups promises to be: interesting choices that change narrative and relationships moment to moment, superb voice performances and exceptional dialogue. For all of the mature approaches to love, conflict, and survival I have played until now, it's kind of amazing to walk away from something that feels enduring, a story well told in its own sake using the medium to surround and engage you not just with the weight of discovery through the eyes of a character but with the gravity of making choices and finding clues on behalf of that character.

This is honestly an exceptional bit of fiction, and I can't express too much about it without revealing the ending or any twists along the way, partly because that ending and your perspective on it will be your own as you make choices throughout the story and uncover clues that provide new insight to you and the characters within.

------Now, technically, the game becomes a little stuttery in the final stretch and some of the alternate paths you can unlock become superfluous by the time you can unlock them, making me wonder if there's some content or secrets that were withheld from the final product. It was a little distracting to go back over my steps to delve deeper into the world and find a shortcut that cuts about 10 seconds off my travel time. Kind of disappointing. Also, the journal is buggy as hell. I found it impossible to go back and read old journal entries once I'd picked them up. That's not a game breaker, but it's a hell of a problem.

Highly recommended, though, 8.2/10.

I took a lot away from Firewatch.  After my first playthrough, I wasn't quite sure what to think.  I ruminated on the story a lot and ended up coming up with a lot of conpiracy type theories (this is a game you can REALLY dissect if you're into that kind of thing).  My second playthrough is when I really developed an appreciation for it though.  I read every note, examined every item, listened to every conversation and explored every area wanting to find everything I possibly could.  I wasn't let down by the ending like some people were; after it I found this profound feeling of sadness; it might have something to do with the amazing voice acting. I related to Henry AND Delilah's characters.  I also loved playing detective and trying to figure out the true narrative.  There's a lot of navigating, but I don't notice it too much or find it too daunting because usually there's a dialogue tree going on and I was trying to find stuff evidence and items, and I was very engaged the majority of the game.  I found the gameplay itself somewhat unique; I liked being able to choose my dialogue while having nagivation objectives, WHILE a mystery also unravels.  I wouldn't call the game overly depressing, but I do think that like myself, a lot of people will connect with the characters or want to examine every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ item they find to learn more about the situations presented.  If you don't exactly like having to think during a game or like even remotely sad narratives, this isn't going to be your cup of tea.  I think it can get tedious, but for people like me who like to study narratives like this, it's pretty great.  Some people think it's short, and you CAN get through it in a couple hours if you stick to the paths, but I found myself spending a lot of time looking around and taking notes about the things I found.  I went around literally reporting EVERYTHING I could find.  If you fly through it, you're probably going to miss some cool/important things.  It's not a scary game but it does like to play with you; I would say it provides more of a vunerable feeling. My anxiety was spiked during certain times, and the game knows how to play with suspense and tension.  The game also inspired me to read up on Firewatch towers and some of Yellowstone's history, and there's a lot of accuracies and interesting references to ponder.  The game is actually impressively accurate in a lot of regards.

Here's a video I did that talks about some of the things I found really interesting: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V-kJek00O0Y

As someone who came into this title not knowing what to expect, I felt an overwhelming sense of joy as I progressed through the intro. There were no big sci-fi/fantasy twists and the world itself never really attempted to be anything more than normal. And it's the words "normal" and "average" that actually struck an incredibly strong chord with me. So many games nowadays strive to be big action adventures or paranoia infested thrillers, Firewatch however, is no more than the tale of a man trying to escape his guilt after a series of rather emotional events turned his life upside down. It's a human story, right down to replicating the very feelings of the characters within the player. When the characters expect something terrifying, they're normally let down (and relieved) by the reality of the events that take place around them, and we feel this same relief when placed in their shoes.

 And that's what makes this experience all the more poetic. The story never really amounts to anything because it's no more than a projection of the protagonist. What really shines is the interaction between characters. Henry's (the protagonist) communication is limited to nothing more than his supervisor, Delilah, through walkie-talkie. Throughout the game, you really get the sense of a blooming relationship between the two and it feels so fascinating and heart-warming with every small piece of dialogue, a massive congratulations to Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones for their fantastic work!

Another small detail that I myself fell madly in love with, are the scenes in which nothing really occurs. Some days you will spend your time just staring out at the scenery, whilst others you're just nailing down some boards. It's another human aspect that just hit me right, and whilst I agree that this aspect is incredibly niche, I do applaud Campo Santo for integrating these everyday exercises into the game, as it just gave it this extra layer of humanity and realism that not many other titles really strive to do. Couldn't recommend this title more!

Firewatch Review:

For those unfamiliar with Firewatch, It’s the first game developed by Campo Santo studios. It was announced in 2014 giving audiences a glimpse at what the game had to offer without disclosing any major concepts behind the game. It was the game that had people asking, “What the f*** is Firewatch?” And with the wait finally over, the game is out and we get a chance to see it in its true colors. I have to admit, I was really excited for this game because it looked like it had so much potential, but it ended up being a dissapointing game.

Gameplay.
Gameplay-wise it is what I feared it would be, a simple and mundane walking simulator. This might be a contreversial opinion to have since some people might catergorize it as an “Adventure” game because it allows you to interact with and collect items, but let me explain myself and where I'm coming from for a sec.  To me, a traditional adventure game enables you to collect random or specific items that generally have a purpose in the grand scheme of things; solving a puzzle, accessing an area, main and minute plot progressions and so on. Whereas Firewatch, the only purpose to interact with items, is for dialogue or commentary reasons between your character and his supervisor. Technically, with the exception of 2 or 3 things, you don't even need to collect said items. All you have to do is highlight them with your cursor to bring up a dialogue option. And yet, aside from plot-related journals, the game gives you an option to take or interact with things for no apparent reason. A bottle of liquor that has no purpose, fireworks that have no purpose, a bar of candy that has no discernable effect. And that's probably 20% of the items you will interact with. The other 80% is nothing short of just admiring things for the sake of admiring things. Sound familiar (See: The Order: 1886)?

This game is also short. Most people could probably finish it in under 3 hrs. Normally, I like to place quality over quantity, but I was hard pressed to find either in Firewatch. And it becomes even harder when you consider that it’s priced at $20.00. As short as the game is on its own merits, it is made even more painfully obvious by the large amount of time spent backtracking through the same areas over and over again. Adding a bit of variety to the gameplay would have gone a long way towards cushioning the repetition. Running into a dangerous wild animal, solving puzzles or having to flee from a wildfire before it engulfs you are just simple examples that could have been implemented without having to compromise the overall essence of the game.

General gameplay aside, I did encounter technical problems, most of which are negligible but The one that stood out to me was the save management mechanic. While the game allows auto saving and manual saving, they unfortunately share the same slot AND, you're allowed  only one save slot per game. This is problematic because if you unknowingly save in a glitched state, you'll have to start your adventure from scratch. I was deep into my first game when I decided to save my progress, only to find out that I was standing on a small tree stump that I could easily step on, but could never alight. The only solution was to start again from the beginning and losing two hours of my progress.... and that was the only time during my entire play-through that I appreciated how short the game is.

Plot/Writing
And for a game that skimps heavily on gameplay, the hope is that it would inundate the player with compelling and robust plot points that engage on several levels. That hope is rightly justified and it is apparent that people behind this game had it at the forefront of their minds. Right from the get go the game entices you with a glimpse of options and consequences using a textual tree of choices that are similar to your standard emotional quotient tests. And as you make your way deeper into the game, you encounter several different plot points that range from simple letters you find in lockboxes to larger geographical areas shrouded in mystery. It’s all thrilling stuff that will keep you cycling through to see how things will unravel...but that's where it starts going downhill. As you slowly approach the conclusion of the game. All potential mysteries and plot points are tossed out and the game relies on a poorly presented discovery that marks an abrupt and unsatisfactory ending that tries to tug at your heartstrings. Which is a HUGE shame because the game really goes out of its way to threaten you with a good time, but never really delivers. It’s tempting to try and justify the nature of this game's plot by analytically approaching it, but When all is said and done, when you sit down and ruminate over your experience from the beginning to the end of the game, the realization that this was mostly an exercise in sarcasm between your character and a disembodied voice will creep in.

Audio
And this is where I can feel comfortable throwing some good points at this game. It has some of the best voice acting I've heard in a long while. That goes a really long way in making the mostly nothing that you do in the game tolerable. The conversations that occur between your character and Delilah, your supervisor, is extremely organic and, although contextual, it's believably adaptive. There are moments where you hold a long conversation with each other, and moments filled with quick, dry remarks when one character gets fed up with the other. And as a testament of how great and well thought-out the conversation are, it’s the moments of silence that really haunt you and make you feel vulnerable.

The game also does sound effects very well. From the sounds of the wind blowing to rustling bushes in the background. There are also several animal noises that are extremely convincing but unfortunately, that's broken by the lack of animals you encounter in the game. I think there were only two animals I saw throughout my entire play-through. A raccoon and an elk. Which, brings me to the visuals:

Visuals
It’s a vast Wyoming wilderness. An “open” world with intertwining paths that will leave you lost or moving in circles if you don't use your provided map and compass. And that's where most of the fun is to be had. Trying to move around and exploring the area by yourself is very fascinating. The design of the map is cleverly done and almost maze-like and every once in a while you run into a historically relevant site or landmark that make you feel like the next big explorer. The geography itself is beautiful and has a lot of breath taking sites like canyons, lakes, rivers and dense forests that lead seamlessly into each other without breaking your immersion.
The map surprisingly gets even more beautiful as the sun begins to set and casts a shed of amber around you. The mornings are often foggy and project a sense of eeriness, and where there is wild fire, the area becomes enveloped in smoke and destructive beauty.

Conclusion
So that's pretty much it for the review. This is probably the shortest review I've done, but I can only work with that the game has to offer, which is not a lot.
And although I've been critical, I don't want you think that this is a horrible game. I just wouldn't recommend it since there's hardly any meat to the bone. There's some fun to be had here, but it quickly wanes at the two hour mark. And for $20.00, unless you’re excited about the prospect of meandering back and forth around a map to no satisfactory end, you're better off waiting for a sale or using your $20.00 on a game that has more to offer.

As you have read from literally every other review, the ending is lackluster. To explain why would spoil the events, but the jist of it is that the mystery that takes up most of the game does not resolve in a very satisfactory way, which some people are very unhappy about. Personally, I found it lackluster, but I didn't hate it. I understood the point, I just wish it was executed better. To end the way it did was unsatisfying - which may be the point? - but that doesn't make it good. Part of the problem may be the pacing. The game jumps rather quickly from Henry just chilling out doing his job to BIG MYSTERY in way that makes the way it slowly turns into the ending section jarring. My two cents, but I feel the game would benefit from being bigger, let the player get more into the feeling of being Henry out in the woods (mostly) alone. More menial tasks like yelling at the teenagers in the beginning. Actually observing and reporting potential fires. Warning some campers about their smoking. Firewatch suffers from its linearity because, like an unfortunate amount ofd the story based games, it doesn't benefit from being a game. Firewatch as a movie or short tv series or a book would have been the same experience. That said, it didn't ruin the experience for me, and I certainly won't be seeking a refund for a game I played to completion.

Some graphical and technical issues, nothing major.

Sometimes you are met with what the characters describe as an impasse but in a way that only makes sense in the context of the game's controls. Henry could easily finagle his way past that downed bridge. And, most egregiously, the concept of CLIMBING a fence is never brought up. It breaks immersion when what the characters percieve and what the player percieves are not in line and in fact conflict.

Again with the really bad portrayal of teenagers. Yeah, real life teenagers talk weird and are jerks, etc etc. But with how well written and acted Henry and Delilah are, it is very out of place for the two teenage girls to be the standard cliche Teen Slang and Not Caring About Mean Adults!

In writing a review of this game, I find myself in a real tough spot. There are two competing and equally reasonable viewpoints about this game, and I still don't know which side I find myself on even still.

On the one hand, this game is immensely polished in its graphics, gameplay, voicework and interface. If you read the comments from the team members who worked long nights for years building it, you really get a feel for the passion they put into the game and how much they cared about it all this time. For a freshman effort from an indie studio, this is an immensely impressive game, and I think our saturation with cheap AAA titles has led us to expect the world from these tiny teams.

On the other hand, I agree with many who say that the retail price seemed a little steep to me for a game with about 4 hours of total play time and not very much replayability. The storyline is quite linear, and while you can occasionally wander around off the beaten path, there isn't enough of that side material to justify playing the whole game through again.

So the question has to be, is this worth $15 or $20 or whatever to you?

If you're like me, without a reliable stream of income, it hurts the wallet a little more to think that I only got 4 good hours out of this, and I probably won't pick the game up again. Years of Steam sales and Humble Bundles have spoiled me by giving me dozens upon dozens of hours of replayable entertainment at pennies on the dollar. This game doesn't make that same value proposition, but once you realize that it's coming from an indie studio, it makes more sense why they're asking that amount for it. They've gotta keep the lights on, after all.

Consider it a compliment to the game and Campo Santo that it's so well-polished in so many respects that, at first, I assumed it was just pushed out by another big name publisher who wouldn't care about one refund in the big picture. You might get that feeling after playing it, too, but remember that this isn't a product put out by a giant, monolithic company, but rather a small and hard-working team of people. I wouldn't dare ask for a refund knowing that.

The characters and the writing in this game are as phenomenal as the voice acting and the direction. It's a beautiful game in pretty much every sense of the word, and in so many ways the visual successor to the interactive fictions that were my first-ever computer games. 

I think it's probably important to stress that it's interactive fiction, though. For some reason, the ending and the payoff are causing a lot of mixed feelings, but I wasn't one of the people who had them. I was relieved when the resolution ended up being precisely what it was and there wasn't any [spoiler] vast conspiracy or goverment hubdub or any of that other tired and over-worked "game plot" reveals [/spoiler] in everything else that uses a first-person perspective. 

I think this might be the first game I've played in a long time that was so immersive, and might be the first game since I was a teenager that felt like a great paperback on a beach. I found it to be well-plotted, creepy when it needed to be, charming when it wanted to be, and with one of the most difficult-to-read characters I've ever encountered in a game. I was thoroughly twisted up about her by the end. 

I think you need to approach this game like its characters and setting suggest: ready to lead a simpler life. You won't be playing a master detective or a resourceful adventurer. [b] You'll be a guy in the woods for a summer. Some stuff is going to happen to you. [/b] How you're going to react to it when it happens and when it concludes might say more about you than it does about the game.

First, before i even start my review please consider if you buy this game turning off the player's position on the map. Hell, it should be turned off by default if you want to appreciate this game as a game. That might be too harsh on Firewatch but its a deserved criticism of the fact you could get a completely different experience from such a simple option. It'd be boring.

First off, the game is gorgeous. It's artistic style is very minimal, feeling like something ripped from Team Fortress 2. That should be evident from any screenshots,footage or the artwork that you've seen on this game. What i didn't expect was this game to improve upon the current formula of "Walking Simulators" as they are so dubbed. This game is very much like Dear Esther,Gone Home and many of the others you are associated. The difference between those two and Firewatch is that you never feel strictly gated to objectives as it is a completely open world experience, i always felt inclined to go off on my own and have a good look around the area. I found quite a few things and conducted quite a few theories during my time with the game and that improved the overall experience. The quiet time between moving from location to location always gave me a time to either let the environment sink in, take in it's details or conduct theories on what exactly is going on in the plot. Which wildly go over the place. This is a no spoiler review, so i'll leave the ending to you.

The whole game's plot functions around a very very small cast. Henry and Delila. The game setups the background story as you wish it to be and you can mix it up and it will defintely have reprecussions later on in the story among other events that do so as well. Firewatching is the Backdrop of this woodland setting as you'll be investigating, going about your day,discovering secrets and hopefully stopping fires as Henry, with Delila acting as a welcome voice in this incredibly isolated landscape. You defintely feel that you are inheritantly alone for most of the game and when you aren't it's unsettling or comforting, Delila does well as a companion character. Much better than i've seen from most Walking Simulators. Nothing as mind wrenchingly entertaining as the Narrator from the Stanley Parable but you feel like there is character in her words and not just a voice actor reading her lines. The hallmark of a good cast, Henry is a little spotty but nearly all of the time he is just fine.  The plot structure feels very sectored off into acts, it's nothing revolutionary but having the freedom that you do during the whole game stops the game from feeling linear like Gone Home, which to this day i haven't replayed. I can see myself digging through Firewatch again, as i absolutely feel that i haven't explored other avenues of the plot or that i might have been able to advance certain aspects or interact with certain characters in a particular way.

The Music is rather minimal, popping in occassionally when it suits the mood. Usually during the downtime between moving from location to location. It's not obstructive to the overall experience and its actually rather soothing in certain places.

There are defintely a couple of shaky issues towards the end of the game in particular that i didn't like, but these were minor to the overall experience of the game. For it's current price at £15, for me it's a fun experience that you can casually play through and unlike previous titles i actually want to have another go at it to see what changes and what doesn't, something that the Stanley Parable mastered. If i'm putting you on the same tier as the Stanley Parable, you're actually pushing this new genre somewhere. It's defintely better that Gone Home and Dear Esther, i'm excited to see more games work with their environments the way that Firewatch has.

Recommended, for the price it's at and maybe even doubly so if it'll evitably go lower but i digress it's a great game if only for how it's used it's environment. A shame about that default navigation setting though.

Despite a few plot holes, Firewatch succeeds in creating an incredibly immersive and aesthetic game. The character development across the game is on point, with the ending taking it into account. Though some may find the end unsatisfying (I don't want to spoil it!), I found it to be a good resolution to the story. 

The game is largely built upon atmosphere and dialogue. Henry, our protagonist, is in constant contact with another lookout named Delilah. The game centers around their interactions and around the mysterious happenings surrounding Henry's lookout tower. The mysteries built up are a little conspiracy theory-esque in nature, but fortunately the game doesn't run too far with that. It's just enough, and far enough in to the game, that it's not overwhelming. 

Delilah initially came off as a bit... try hard, to me. As a woman myself, she very much came off as a woman vying for the attention of a man. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it felt a little fake at first, until some of the real plot started in. She is, in most ways, a fantasy - but the fantasy felt self aware. It was written the way a woman would write a woman who was attempting to be a fantasy in real life, if that sentence isn't too obtuse. Therefore, I wasn't overly bothered by it. She had nothing else to do up there, found someone interesting, and put some effort into becoming something men would want.

On the subject of atmosphere, the soundtrack, colour choices, and stylistic graphics completely sell it. The views in the game are lovely. I highly encourage everyone to make use of the disposable camera they're given during the game! It pays off at the end. I'll be adding the game's soundtrack to one of my ambient playlists, as well. 

Given that this is essentially a walking simulator game, what little gameplay there is was actually quite good. It doesn't suffer from feeling as though you're going too slowly and it doesn't have too much "empty" padding without dialogue or purpose. The world is large enough to feel exploratory, but small enough it's not frustrating to get from point A to point B. 

If you're looking for a game with a story with emotions and that run true-to-life, this is a great game in that regard. The story has a mature feeling - no one necessarily gets everything they want, but at the end, you're left with the thought that everyone had at least SOME closure and has a hope for a better future. I'd say it was well worth full price, to me, at least.

Now for why I recommend it

Because if you are doing a walking simulator, do it like this one. This game has seriously best written and dubbed dialogue I have ever seen in any game. The dialogue between you and your supervisor is what carries this game. Without it, it would be nothing, not even something in pre-alpha build. When you choose your response the response from Delilah, secondary protagonist, feels like said by a real person not just a bot with written lines on a paper that she has to read. I found myself in sections of the game where I turned off my flashlight and slowly was walking by the side of the rock to another corner so nothing can jump on me. I was making in my heads connections between every little thing that grew in my head into some large government conspiracy which was a cause of a mystery behind the game and my character did the same because of what I choose to tell to Delilah. I literally just finished this game from start to finish, in one sitting, and immediately had to write this review. I bought Firewatch in a heartbeat aftering seeing part of a let's play on YouTube, thanks to Markiplier. Boy am I glad that I did. There are so many good things I want to say about this game. 

First off, Firewatch is an absolutely breathtakingly gorgeous game. The environment felt very real and natural. Secondly, the story is so enthralling that I couldn't bring myself to stop playing until I completely finished the game. The story kept me guessing and on the edge of my seat the entire time. And thirdly, the voice overs are well done and the dialog felt real, not scripted. The characters spoke like real people with all the sweaing and sarcasm, which only added to the immersiveness of Firewatch.

My only gripe about Firewatch is the ending. It didn't give me the payoff I was hoping for. Despite this, however, Firewatch is a fantastic game that everyone should buy and experience for yourself.

This is not a very good game. And no, it's not because it's a hiking simulator. I excepted that. The only good thing in Firewatch is the dialogue and the voice acting. That's it. (The story is disappointing as well.) 
The main problem—by far—is how the game tells the narrative. A good example of everything wrong with it, is at the very beginning, in the Pixar's Up inspired opening. In Up the opening was told entirely through pictures, no dialogue, because that's the main asset of movies. Here the opening is told through text. Fucing words on a black screen! In a 2016 game! One might say you have different dialogue options to choose from, but the choices make absolutely no major difference to the plot. It's basically a long backstory told through text instead of interactively with the player’s investment. Sometimes, between those texts you press the "W" button to move forward in some forest and then more text follows. That is the opposite of a gut-wrenching opening like Up. 
The rest of the game is the same, but thankfully the text gets replaced with actual good voice acting. Yes, the choices make no big difference, I know, but the developers obviously wanted to tell a specific story. I get that. 
Other than that, you’re forced to go on one boring hike to another, so you get rewarded with dialogue and plot points. The gameplay and narrative aren't connected at all—never does the game try to tell it's story through gameplay. You’d think, this being a product of indie super-stars, they’d know how interactive storytelling works, but nope, I was wrong.
And let’s not even get into the story itself. We’re supposed to feel bad for a kid who’s never in the game, and is only mentioned in conversations? The payoff is disappointing, and the main character learned nothing of value, nor was he shaped by the events of the game. Everything he learned on what to do with his wife, and the advice he received, he could’ve learned just the same, even if nothing would have happened all summer. The events of the game were completely unrelated to his personal struggles, both directly and metaphorically. 
Overall, this is a piece of dog turd you pay 20 bucks for and finish in an afternoon then forget you ever played it.

The main complaints about this game is that it's too short and many find the ending disappointingly anticlimatic. After my own playthrough however, I really dont think these two drawbacks are that dire. It seems that most of the people who complained about it being too short weren't actually fans of walking simulators (which this game obviously is, so it's unclear why this clashed with expectations) and just sped through the game, and those who were disappointed by the ending I think didn't really understand what the game was really about. 

First of all, Firewatch can't be that open because it's a short indie game and it follows a pretty tight, well-written and well-acted script. If you guys felt that Firewatch would have made a good first installment with a series of followups, it pretty much is since the studio is relatively new and pretty small. Rather than rating the game down and not recommending it because you think it's a good game but not worth the full price, it would be better to actually pay a little more so that the studio can start working on longer and larger installments. After all, the general consensus seems to be that Firewatch is one of the most beautiful games ever created and definitely an admirable first attempt, so it would be a shame to not support the studio that made it. 

Regarding the ending, I feel like a lot of people were disappointed because the mystery and terror that were being built up throughout the game ended on a quite mundane note, but the game and its script outlined and connected everything pretty well! I think the ending was actually really surprising because not only were we misled by the clues, but also by the two characters. By the time the final act was coming along, I was so invested that I became as paranoid as Henry felt, even up until the end I was expecting something terrible to happen--but what was truly terrible and tragic was what had already happened before the beginning of the game, and the kind of lives that Delilah and Henry have to return to after experiencing the events of that summer. Firewatch functions not only as a escape for us, the gamer, but also for Henry/Delilah, and i think it rewards players who are willing to think of the events during and after the game from the characters' points of view, which it easily encourages by creating terrifically realistic characterizations with great voice-acting. In the end, the lesson is that the past catches up with us all, and even the choices that we feel are inconsequential end up being pretty damn important, in shaping both our own lives and the lives of others. In a way, our restricted choices in dialogue and their consequences reflects the trapped feeling that both (or actually all) of the characters experience in regards to their personal circumstances and the responsibilities that they're supposed to shoulder, before, during, and after the events of the game. Firewatch really captures the essence of our common, mundane, human experience, with its miserable lows and exhilirating highs, all over the course of one summer in Ol' Shoshone.

First of all, I recommend this game but only to people who like this unusual genre of in-game storytelling. I personally was looking for something else, so I'm writing this review to tell others what they can and cannot expect. The graphics is my opinion high end for an indie game but cannot match AAA titles. Anybody who expects beautiful depictions of wilderness, open world and realistic graphics will be disappointed. The graphics is nice looking but with cartoon shaders and not very realistic. The game itself is an interactive story with lots of conversations and some mystery. It is best described, in my point of view, as a serious short novel turned into a video game. It is essentially about people who somehow got stuck and need to find a way to get on and find a new life. If you like the idea of putting such a plot in a video game, you might like this game. 

If on the other hand you expect a large open world wilderness game with survival elements, as for example a totally misleading review at Arstechnica has suggested (which is why I bought the game in the first place), you will get none of this and will be disappointed. The wilderness is only a setting for the story that unfolds in the conversations with Delilah and by some things that occasionally happen. The game is also relatively short, around 5-6 hours of gameplay maximum.

Back to the story: The beginning is kind of horrible and there is some annoying psycho-babble later in the game, too, but overall I found the story interesting and well-executed. There is also some mystery and suspense in it. So I recommend the game although it's not the kind of game I'd usually like to play. It's worthwile and serious entertainment.

Sigh, I bought this game because I adore all podcasts on the Idle Thumbs network.  Specifically, Idle Thumbs, Idle Weekend, and Three Moves Ahead.  I also love adventure games with a mystery as the central narrative.  So I figured this game was perfect for me.  The game is certainly a very beautiful walking simulator, that is the pinnacle of this type of genre of games, but the lack of any puzzles or choices is a real burden on this game.  This game is just not good.  It really pains me to say that as I love all the people from Idle Thumbs, but despite what basically every single review of this game says the narrative is just abysmal.  Maybe if this game had been longer the narrative problems could have been solved, but it’s 3 hours long.  3 hours for $20, that’s unacceptable to me.  I just don’t believe a videogame can manage a strong narrative in 3 hours.  Mainly, because if a game is 3 hours then the studio clearly didn’t have the budget to craft a strong enough narrative.  Sure a 3 hour movie can tell an amazing narrative, logically a videogame should be able to as well.  But…it just does not work that way.  A 3 hour movie has the budget to tell an intricate and complex story, a 3 hour game means they have no budget and have to cut narrative corners to fit the budget.  

This game certainly tries it’s hardest and probably could have pulled it off, but the narrative just utterly falls apart in the end.  It’s so terrible that it quite ruins everything that came before it.  A lot is good about the game though so I’ll start their first.

The art direction is just outstanding here.  Olly Moss and Jane Ng have outdone themselves.  The forest feels alive, but more important literally everywhere you look everything is just framed perfectly.  There is probably a reason they give you the ability to take pictures in the game, every single direction you look is a perfect photo.  I found myself just starring up at the skybox they created.  It’s very stylized, definitely not real life looking, but that doesn’t matter when everything is this stunning.  Care clearly went in to every detail of this forest and make walking around a joy.  My favorite had to be the approaching storm, you just feel dread but also wonder while you watch it roll in.  

Chris Remo’s score to this game sets the mood perfectly.  He makes the silence of the forest as pleasurable as the most suspenseful moments.  As the game continues the silence turns from pleasurable to paranoia, as you constantly feel that someone is always watching over your shoulder.  When the actual music comes in it always hits the right beats between wonderment, suspense, and solitude of the woods.

Then there is the narrative.  Sigh, Sean Vanaman…I just don’t know what he was thinking.  The characters of Delilah and Henry are expertly crafted as is the dialogue...but the overall narrative just is bad. The game has other narrative problems that come from the fact it feels like you should be able to change the story through dialogue options with your companion (who you never see), but definitely can’t.  If this was 3 hours long, but literally every single word you said had an impact on the game and changed how events played out then this would have been worth $20, but it’s a very linear experience.  This would have been fine, albeit frustrating, if the narrative had been good.  It just isn’t though.  

Spoilers ahead:  [spoiler] So the narrative is great basically until the last 20 minutes.  I literally could not put this game down.  It was such a tense and pleasurable experience, I just had to keep going.  It felt so much like reading “The Magus” by John Fowles, that I can only assume Vanaman was influenced by that.  If it had followed that novel to the logical conclusion, I probably would be recommending this game.  The central mystery is that a person is stalking your character, constantly stealing your stuff, listening in on your radio conversations, trying to terrify you, and a few times probably trying to get you killed…not on purpose, but more through placing you in such dangerous situations that you could have easily died.  Halfway through you realize there is a science camp in the area and discover they have been keeping massive notes on you and the other rangers.  It’s also very possible they have been murdering people such as two teenagers and perhaps the previous ranger who had your job and his son.  

Now I really really hated this twist in the story, because it would have been just stupid if it was true, if this was all some weird govt experiment and they were just trying to drive you insane.  However, since I figured this was following the plot of “The Magus” I expected this to all be a red herring…which  in the end it was…but the final twist is so mind numbingly terrible that I literally would have preferred it to have been a govt experiment.  In the end it turns out the pervious ranger who had your job accidently got his son killed in a climbing accident and decided to hide out in the woods this whole time and decided to terrorize you, going to insane lengths to plant evidence to hide his involvement.  

This conclusion basically means everything else was red herrings throughout the story.  The missing teenagers, the science camp, Delilah acting weird the whole game, the cut comms wires, the notes between the rangers.  The game basically has far too many red herrings.  They can all be explained of course, they aren’t necessarily plot holes.  However, the explanation is always oh the previous ranger is insane because he got his son killed.  He has no real motive for what he does.  The game tries to wave it away by saying, oh he was just trying to scare you off so he can have free roam of the forest.  Ok…well he starts a fire that basically burns the forest down, and he literally sets up blatant clues for you to follow him so you can find his son.  If he was trying to hide his actions setting it up so you literally find him makes no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sense. So why he felt the need to fake a shadowy science experiment being conducted on you by the government makes no sense.  Also why Delilah who apparently supervises the rangers/lookouts knows absolutely nothing about a major science experiment being conducted in the park is actually a plot hole…or I guess she missed the memo. Also, why were the police not looking for the previous lookout and his son?  Literally no one cared that they never returned? I guess it was the 80's...

In the end this story is about two miserable and selfish people who spent a summer together, they clearly deserve each other, because no one else should be stuck with these cancers on society.  Throwing in this suspense mystery is literally an afterthought, it was poorly thought out and I can only assume they were originally going in another direction before they realized they had no budget to add any other characters. [/spoiler]

Just go buy Life is Strange instead.  It has a far stronger narrative and is 15 hours long.

Deeper, possibly spoiler-ish followup thoughts, which are necessarily vague (trust me, you don't want to spoil the experience):

[spoiler]The conclusion of the game may have been a letdown, but that's at least in part because we've been conditioned to expect incredible, life-changing, over-the-top wrap-ups to our drama, and life really isn't like that. And this is a game about life. It's about ♥♥♥♥ happening to you, and running away from it, and learning - maybe - that no matter where you run to, there will be somebody there with their own ♥♥♥♥ happening to them. 

My heart ached at the beginning. Hard to say why, except that I've had a very peripheral view of the sort of loss that instigates the game, and its re-creation in Firewatch was unhappily vivid. But then adventure ensued! Henry's connection with Delilah was as real as any I've encountered in a videogame, and whether his slow climb into happier days resulted from healing or simply forgetting didn't seem to matter. Even the mystery was exciting at first, before spiraling into a surreal sense of frustration, anger, and fear. And then, at the end, my heart ached again. Differently this time, and no less palpably, but tinged with a sense of focus, purpose, and maybe even hope. I don't know if Henry is going to be okay. But I think he might be.

I've had my eye on Firewatch for almost a year, and I've been interested in this game. It looked pretty, the characters were interesting, and the overall story had a lot of potential. Does this game live up to the hype?

Somewhat.

The game isn't worth $20. I would recommend buying Firewatch when it's at least $10. It's a flawed game, but what it does right, it [i]excels[/i] at.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]

This is one of the categories that Firewatch (obviously) does right. The graphics were done by an artist named Olly Moss, and they're absolutely gorgeous. Firewatch is definitely one of the prettiest games I've ever played. The screenshots (if you haven't seen them already) further justify my point.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

I don't play walking simulators (or in Firewatch's case, a hiking simulator) very often. I'll get into more detail with the dialogue when I talk about the story, but they all lead to the same conclusion, and your choices feel like they're just there to give the characters some depth. I did like the fact that there was no HUD, so you have to rely on a map and compass to get you to your location. One other thing I noticed is that there were minor glitches lurking around every corner, and although none are game-breaking, they can kill the mood sometimes.

[h1]Story[/h1]

This is where Firewatch is getting most of that negative reception if you looked at the Steam store page. I can understand where they're coming from. The game starts off great. Once you start to get further into the game, you'll see the mystery begin to unravel. The suspense building is amazing, and I was hooked.The dialogue options give Henry and Delilah more depth as characters, and as a result, they feel like believable and relatable human people. However, where the game fails is the ending. While the suspense was amazing, the execution felt rushed and the ending was abrupt. After I finished the game, I stared at the screen, thinking there had to be more after the credits. The ending really killed the buildup, and I was disappointed by how the story played out at the end. 

[h1]Audio[/h1]

Another spot where Firewatch exceeds, the voice actors for Delilah and Henry played their roles amazingly well. I've already mentioned this a few times, but they both feel like genuine human beings. The voice actors make this feeling ten times better. I can easily say that Firewatch has some of the best voice acting I've heard in a video game, if not the best. One problem I did have, however, is that there was a lack of everything besides that. There was music, but it only played occasionally. There were sound effects, but not many, another reason why the audio falls short of perfection. However, the good definitely overshadows the bad here, so that's all made up by the phenomenal voice acting.

[h1]Replayability[/h1]

The game is really short. It's only about 4 hours long if you take your time. I wish it could've been longer because the story ended so abruptly, but at least it didn't last like an hour. The choices don't really mean much in the long run, so you'll probably do one playthrough of this game and move on. Maybe you'll see how Delilah reacts with different dialogue choices, or maybe find some easter eggs, but that's about all of the replay value I see the average player getting.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Although the game does have a really weak ending and a pretty high price of $20, Firewatch is still one of the most realistic games I've played. I would recommend picking this one up when it goes on sale for about 50% off. In the end, Firewatch is not the magnum opus of storytelling or anything like that, but the experience was still really good for the most part.
