Okay, let's be honest, this game seems to have created a bit of a split in the gaming community as to it's cost to length and replayability alongside the plot. One thing just about every reviewer accepts though is that the graphics, script and voice acting are beautiful and, for the script and voice acting especially, some of the best you'll find in any game. There are endless reviews praising these points so there's little point in going into detail. So, on to the controversy . . .

The largest complaint I've seen about this game is the playtime and replayability. Going through at a steady pace, looking at every item I could clearly see and not taking time to explore away from the current objective I finished up in 3.5 hours. Here in the UK the current price is £15.00, $20.00 US. Would I play the game again any time soon? No. Due to the linear nature of the plot I see no reason to replay it, albeit maybe to explore a little more, but maybe in 6 months or a year I'll see it in my library and consider watching it again, just like a great movie. In my opinion that's the way you have to look at this, and other narative driven games, like movies or other older styles of media. 

When I played the game I hooked my PC up to my TV, grabbed a controller and lay on the sofa with my girlfriend with the lights off and the speakers up loud. After the first half hour or so we had forgotten we were playing a game and became absorbed in the plot. The reason I didn't explore much, in honesty, is that the plot was so gripping we wanted to speed to the next plot point as quickly as possible. At the end of the night we talked it through and were both happy with the purchase. Where I live a couple of cinema tickets puts us back £20.00 and we'd got almost two films worth of time out of £15.00. Would I like the game to be longer? Of course, it's a great game, but, for me at least, this is a reasonable price for the experience.

In short, if you're after days or weeks of gameplay then stay away, you'll feel disapointed. If you go into this game thinking of it as a night in for £15.00 then you'll love every second.

With that out of the way I'd like to breifly mention the complaints I've seen regarding the plot. Almost everyone agrees the first 2/3rds of the game are fantastic and gripping and that the end is . . . disapointing. To avoid disapointment I advise the same as before, go into this thinking of it like a book or movie rather than a game. Don't expect explainations to be obvious and think about what concepts the game is trying to explore. If you're strugling to come to terms with how things progress then remember that this game was made to explore the feeling of paranoia.

Would I reccomend this to someone who exclusively plays games for their replayability due to PVP, changing landscapes or challenging difficulty? No, this game isn't for you. If you're up for experiencing a look into what I hope can be seen as a new(ish) art form comparable to movies an books, grab this game and a friend or two and have an exciting evening with some thought prevoking questions to be discussed at the end.

While it's always recommended ignoring the price when reviewing a game and review it on it's own merits, it ignores that when that game goes on sale, it's competing against other games that could be better and is also available to the consumer. 

Firewatch however challenged that notion for me. It took me about 3 hours to beat and that is including time spent wandering around the map albeit it was due to me trying to find a path and not actually "exploring" the map. Some would consider that bad for a $20 game, but the strengths of Firewatch are very strong.

The biggest one is the dynamic between Henry (voiced by Mad Men's Rich Sommer) and Delilah (voiced by Cissy Jones). Henry comes out to work at a Firewatch tower due to tragedy in his personal life and his boss Delilah helps him not only on the job, but gives him a human companion to talk to out in the open wilderness of the Shoshone National Forest in Wyoming. Both characters have a witty temperment and it comes out in the dialogue. Like in Telltale games there are different responses (including not responding), but most of the choices are very interesting especially if you want to play a smartass. Sommer and Jones also do a fantastic job in communicating various emotions in the dialogue, especially when the characters are afraid and/or furious.

The story itself is another strength although it has flaws. The intro starts of like a text-based prologue about Henry and at times you get to choose different choices in how to respond to scenarios. While it was jarring at first, I can't imagine not doing this section, it gives you alot of emotional buildup with Henry and you'll understand why he decided to work as a Fire Watchmen, even if you don't agree with his decisions. 

If there is one word to describe the story, it's very atmospheric. The developer did an excellent job in getting the aesthetics of 1989 down, even with the small objects you pick up. The visuals were reminiscent of documentaries I seen about the American wilderness. 

The forest is very beautiful, but the story will introduce several elements that make that forest feel sinister. There'll be times where you walk/run through it and feel both vulnerable and trapped in this open landscape. I won't say what it is, but there is one moment in the game that is very shocking and ramps the tension up to 11. There is a mystery that you need to solve and I felt compelled to solve it even if it meant putting Henry into grave danger.

With that said, there is a giant flaw with the game: the "reveal". Again, not going to spoil it but the end point of the mystery may underwhelm you. I certainly was emotionally moved by it, but I have to admit the buildup overhyped the ending I got. It wasn't dramatic, it was low-key and that will put people off. The way the game ends too is anti-climatic and some will feel that it's not a satisfactory conclusion to the big mystery we went through. 

I was one of those people that came out of the game very mixed because of those flaws and while I don't excuse them, I slowly came to accept them. 

Overall, I found Firewatch a short game that has a interesting story and very compelling characters. I felt my $18 (bought it when it was 10% off) was worth it to see what Camp Santo's debut game was going to be and I didn't feel cheated out of the experience. With that said, if you don't like games that are very short, are "walking simulators", and don't have branching plot trees, this is not the game for you.

Firewatch is a new release on PC and PS4 developed by Panic Inc and Campo Santo. It's a wonderful RPG/Adventure/Story game that is based in the Wyoming wilderness. You play as a protagonist, Henry, who finds himself in the mountains after what I could describe as a mid life crisis. The game is wonderfully executed and has many moments that made me have a case of the feels. Yes. I just said this game gave me the feels. Many times. *sniff* 

The game is divided between "Days" (episodes or missions) in which you go on "quests" to advance the story. It's actually really well done. The pacing with the "Days" is really balanced. I did not find myself wondering, "Dear God, is this thing going to end soon!?" No, rather, I found that each "Day" left me wanting more. It was hard to stop playing once I got going (almost like binge watching Breaking Bad episodes). 

Admittedly, I have not made it to the ending (reasons below). I've heard that the ending is predictable and somewhat of a letdown. Please keep that in mind when reading my review.

Personal Enjoyment (9/10)

I loved the crap out of this game. Truly. The story telling and the overall artistic design of the game are beautiful. There's nothing quite like standing on a ledge overlooking the red hues of a Wyoming sunset. I derived a lot of satisfaction from the time I played this game. 

Will others enjoy it? (9/10)

Yes - probably. The game isn't filled with action. In fact, it's fair to call it a walking simulator. However, if you like a good engrossing story, then yes, you'll like Firewatch. If you want a survival RPG with a story, I suggest you check out something like The Long Dark.

Developer Honesty (9/10) - Fairly Honest

I had a hard time scoring this section. Honestly, I feel like Campo Santo and Panic were pretty honest when it came to the presentation of the game. The graphics match the trailers and things were pretty well communicated. I do have one gripe, though. The minimum specs were off. My gaming laptop should have been capable of running the game.

The specs listed on steam are as follows: 

Processor: Intel Core i3 2.00 GHz or AMD equivalent
Memory: 6 GB RAM
Graphics: NVIDIA GeForce 450 or higher with 1 GB Memory
DirectX 11
4 GB Storage Space

My PC exceeds these requirements. Yet, the game had frequent framerate drops - even on the lowest graphics settings (we'll get in to this below).

Performance (6.5/10) - Needs to be Optimized Badly

In short, performance was spotty. When it was good, it was bloody good. The development team should pat themselves on the back for this. However, the frequent frame rate drops and spotty performance issues are a huge nag and detract from the overall pleasant experience. 

The game is really poorly optimized to be considered a full release game. I'd expect the same level of optimization from an alpha or beta stage game. From a full release? It's sophomoric at best and utterly shameful at worst. I expect patches to fix this in the future. However, my review is of the game at launch, not how it will be fixed down the road. 

Bugs/Glitches (1/10) - Game Breaking

The game ran beautifully for the first two hours or so before it crashed into a glorious fireball (no pun intended). I loaded up Day 77 and the whole game froze. I reloaded the save and found out that it was corrupted. Two hours later of research about this issue revealed that many other people were having the same issue. The game would randomly corrupt saves and crash. Okay, seriously, what the actual hell? Is this how we release games...? With bugs that destroy a user's experience? Totally unacceptable. That's two hours of my life flushed away because someone couldn't code a save game file correctly.

I read threads that claim that the developers are deleting threads in the Steam forums about these types of crashes and save corruptions. While I did not find evidence of that (if someone points me to it, I'll edit this whole review), this accusation is disconcerting. If Campo Santo and Panic knew that the game was broken on release day then why did they release the bloody thing at all? 

Users suggest saving often and in multiple slots in order to get around this issue. While this is an acceptable fix for the time being, it does not excuse Campo Santo and Panic from creating the issue in the first place. This solution doesn't work for everyone, either.

As of today (Feb 10, 2016) there has been a patch to fix some of the other issues regarding save corruption/crashes on other Days in the game. However, they have not patched the issue I found. Again, the day after the game is released and they have to issue a patch? Really? This is not an alpha game. This is a full release title. Fix your bloody game!

Overall Score: 7/10 

The game is good and I do recommend checking it out. The artistic design, voice acting, and story telling are superb. But, the game is freaking broken for a lot of people. Campo Santo, shame on you for not fixing a huge game breaking bug before release. You had to know that these issues existed before you launched the game. I give this a cautious 7/10 only because the quality of the game (when it's freaking playable) is great. If Campo Santo fixes the bloody bugs with patches, I'll gladly give the game a solid 9/10. It deserves a 9/10 - it really does. But, when you release a game with such horrible, game breaking bugs and really poor optimization, you deserve to be given a poor rating.

My review for this is going to be a little different to my usual and I apologise if this comes off more as a rant but I think this is the sort of game that's very personal - this review is pure opinion! It contains spoilers (marked, don't worry!) - not specific story spoilers, but general spoilers that may give hints towards what will happen and change expectations. If you like to go into things completely blind, please don't read the following. If you don't mind some general impressions that hint at how things end but without going into specifics, read on.

[spoiler]Imagine that you're reading a book or watching a movie, and someone hears a noise in an attic. There's a lot of atmosphere, and potential for problems. Spooky things have happened. The power is out!  This noise is scary. The tension builds. Something is up there. What is going on? You don't know! No one knows. You have to find out! You're reading a ghost story. There are expectations. Now what if, after reading that entire story, giving that book several hours, investing your emotions into the characters, the end just said "And the cat jumped down and it turned out that he'd knocked a few things over during a power cut. The end." This is pure analogy - I don't want to give out specific story spoilers in such a short game, so all I  can say is that if you go into a genre with expectations and don't receive them, it can feel jarring and disappointing. In the case of walking simulators like this, I do believe they should be considered more like a book or a movie, since there is essentially no gameplay.

Now Firewatch isn't a spooky ghost story - but my point is, the most obvious, boring, dull things don't make it into books, movies, or games. I had expectations for the writing; and this wasn't delivered on.

"But it's about the experience, the journey, the characters!" you might say, and you would be absolutely right. Those are important things - but at the same time, the writers should be going somewhere and I felt like there was so much that this game could have delivered and it simply didn't. You shouldn't just be wasting peoples time and at the end say "Well weird things don't happen to normal people, if you hear hooves, think horses, not zebras." I don't invest my time into entertainment and media for the mundane. It is a demonstration of good writing to be able to hook people into a story and keep them gripped - but by the end this felt like half a game, like something was missing, as if development had ended too soon, and a DLC called "The Real Ending" would be announced (I wish!)[/spoiler]

If you didn't want any suggestion of spoilers, I can sum it up by saying I was disappointed by the ending, and the general story of this game. I loved the art, the setting and much of the dialogue. EMPHASIS -  I do not think this is a bad game - in fact, I think it is a very good dialogue driven first person adventure, with amazing graphics and a wonderful setting. But for me, that's just not enough to recommend it. In this type of game for me, the story is the most important aspect and in this regards I felt it fell short. But after every plot point, the game just kept going on as before and I was left observing and not really acting. The "missions" all follow the same formula:
1) Walk to the thing.
2) Have a conversation about the thing.
3) Walk back from the thing.

Ooooohhhhh boy. So let's get this started the right way: this is not really a "video game". It's more of an interactive story. I mean, if you're a grown man with emotional ties to anything you will probably sob your heart out by the end.

When you put away your expectations that this is going to be a thrilling-jaw dropping-adrenaline pushing adventure, you will learn to love it.

[b]Plot[/b]You play as Henry, a man who leaves his life behind because of family issues and becomes a fire watch. You become best friends with your boss Delilah (voiced by Cissy Jones). Aside from a couple of other minior characters in minor scenes, she is really the only person you will talk to during the entire game. Jones really did a wonderful job voicing Delilah... you feel the relationship building over the course of the game.

You start out doing mundane tasks, but eventually start to discover some strange happenings in the park. This is where the story starts to take off and get very interesting. You feel the tension between D and Henry as they try to figure out what is going on.

[b]Graphics[/b]: The graphics are wonderful. The "painting" style didn't really match up with the seriousness of the plot... but they looked very crisp and the draw distances were very nice.

[b]Music/Sound[/b]: The soundtrack is great! Going back, I wish I would have bought the soundtrack bundle for the extra few dollars. It's not consistent music... it just comes up during integral plot points (example: ending a day, discovering the mystery) As mentioned earlier in the review, the voice acting is top notch. 

Overall, I'd highly recommend this game at the original price point of $20. A lot of reviews seem to complain that it's "too short" and to wait for it to go on sale.. but... I disagree. Any longer and I might have become disinterested. There's no need to stick more filler in a game just to artifically extend it.

Do bear in mind though that this is more an interactive story than a 'GAME-game'. While there still are a few game elements in this title, the meat of the game is spent navigating the forest you are stationed in (as someone who watches for fire. Hence the title.) and talking, by radio, to another firewatcher one tower over. People looking for combat or anything like that are not going to find what they're looking for in this game. 

For people who like story- and character-driven games with less action, however, this game will be really good. (Think Dear Esther, but much more involved. In Dear Esther, all you do is walk. In Firewatch, you actually get to DO things, and the dialogue is much more meaningful. Correction, there IS DIALOGUE)

One last thing that might influence your decision to buy this game: I got through the story in approximately 3 to 4 hours. Exploring the wilderness is, if it appeals to you, an infinitely enjoyable task. It's what I loved most about this game, even above the heavily praised performance between the two starring voice actors. Being out in the wild, just walking around with a compass. This is accompanied by a lot of good interaction between enjoyable characters, and this keeps up almost entirely throughout the game.

There are times when the game presses you to proceed to an area significantly more than it does in the early game, pushing you back through areas you've likely sufficiently explored at your leisure, and often just not giving you enough chatter to fill in the gap. This isn't horribly common, but given how the game is more than willing to make harsh cuts, it's a shame that the exploration that initially feels free and fun begins to feel like unrewarded busywork. When things do change, there's plenty going on around that. But most of the time it hasn't, and this slows down the faster pace the story begins to take on in the last couple hours.

It's worth mentioning that I was lucky and had made a save backup after interacting with an item clipped me into the world and locked me out of actions until I did a quick save and load. While a jarring issue, it wasn't unsolvable. Shortly after, a scripting error occurred which resulted in radio sequences playing out of order and the game redirecting me to complete the objective I had just completed, which was no longer there. Saving and loading kept me stuck in a broken gamestate, and if I hadn't been lucky enough to have a save backup on hand I would have lost hours of gameplay on a broken save. This only occurred to me the one time, but it would have completely ruined me on actually completing the game due to autosaves locking me out of restarting further back.

Despite my issues with it, I definitely enjoyed Firewatch. Many people have said the ending is something they enjoy, and I strongly suspect my encountered issues with said game-breaking script error as well as extremely poor player collision in a late-game area spoiled the magic for me as a sense of frustration began to build up. But even if the game had only been the first couple of days, I would have still enjoyed it immensely. Hopefully patches can be quickly applied to fix the major issues people are having, and it's likely you won't run into the same issues that left me with a bad taste in my mouth.

A $20 romp through the forest that just barely lasts a little over the two hours you can get out of a game before refunding it. The third most popular tag for the game at the moment is "Walking Simulator", and while I'm sure there's no mistaking the game for anything else but that based on how it was marketed, be certain that you know that before buying it and expecting something entirely different.

The length of Firewatch isn't even the issue. If the game were much longer than it was, I'm afraid I would have never been able to force myself through to the very end. The characters and story are uninteresting, and yes, while I did know I was buying into a walking simulator, the gameplay's uninteresting as well. They marketed this game as something I wanted to watch the first trailer of, and then go on a news blackout for. They told us there was some big underlying mystery. Maybe I thought it would turn into some sort of horror game. Maybe even if not some mysterious creature prowling through the woods, watching, waiting, something at least interesting enough to slog through the repetitive objective of walking from point A to point B, then back to point A so you can acquire something that will allow you to get to point C.

A majority of the three hours it took me to complete the game was spent watching mountain climbing animations, and walking around because during particular segments your character forgot how to run. And that's just if you can make it past the frustrating opening of the game, wherein the game tricks you into thinking you're playing the role of a character, rather than simply viewing the world through his eyes. The game repeatedly refers to "You". It says that "You" did this. That "You" said this. When in fact the options to choose from play absolutely no part in anything that happens, and likely aren't even decisions you would make as a real person in real life, because the character is stuck-up and has a completely unrelatable personality. 

In the end, you're left with 3 hours of walking around in the forest, anticipating a decent conclusion to make up for the rest of the game, and finding out that because the entire game was based on a single painting the developers happened to like, whoever was responsible for writing the story never actually knew where they were going with anything. This feels like episode 1 to a Telltale game, where they were told near the end of its development that it wouldn't be receiving any further episodes, so they had to wrap it up as quickly as they could while still pushing the game out the door at the date they had originally promised. 

[h1]The Good[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Visually appealing.
    [*]Sometimes interesting dialogue between the two main characters.
[/list]

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Uninteresting story that wraps up more poorly than any recent story-driven game I can think of.
    [*]$20 for 3 hours of gameplay. Even a single piece of DLC for The Witcher 3 was half that price, more than 5 times the length, and a thousand times more interesting. Can't think of another game I recently bought that had a worse price to value ratio. And yes, while comparing anything to The Witcher 3 will likely leave you disappointed, Layers of Fear, an early access title for the same price, with the same general concept of being a walking simulator, was also a lot more interesting in its current unfinished state than Firewatch will ever be.
    [*]Performance is lackluster, especially because the game, while visually appealing, isn't doing anything above and beyond in the visuals department. It uses Unity Engine, and the performance is likely the result of that combined with the fact that developers behind the Telltale Walking Dead games had their hand in this. Telltale games are well known for shoddy performance.
    [*]Gameplay is boring. Get told where to go. Go there. Do thing. Screen fades to black. Wake up sometime in the future. Repeat. I'm not asking for guns. I'm not asking for a leveling system. I'm asking for a game where I'm not actually worried about whatever's rustling the bushes behind me, because I know the developers couldn't be bothered with modeling and texturing anything but environment assets.
    [*]When it isn't stuttering along, there's various glitches like the audio cutting out randomly, and at one point I was faced with a glitch I've only ever seen in Minecraft where a large portion of the forest decided to not be there anymore, leaving a massive void of empty space.
    [*]I legitimately have to launch the game and idle it in order to get the rest of my card drops out of it, because the game isn't long enough on its own to drop them all for me, and has absolutely no replay value.
[/list]

When I played this game back in 2016 this is what I wrote for my review, typos included: "This game was great but i felt it was to short for the price. I was also very disapionted by the ending." I find it really fascinating that despite the fact that I did not enjoy the ending (which is the entire crux of the narrative) I still enjoyed the game back then. Ever since it has had a special place in my heart as a game that I remember very much enjoying as a kid. Sadly, on a replay I found Firewatch to be uninteresting and just unremarkable. The narrative doesn't do anything interesting with its themes and presents a stock-standard mystery with a *Spoilers* subversion-of-expectation style twist ending that was ironically what I found to be the most interesting part this time around. Overall I was just bored and did not buy the pseudo romance between Henry and Delilah. More often than not their conversations had this grating sarcasm that wore thin quickly. It is always disappointing to revisit a childhood favorite to find it lacking, but despite the blandness of my experience playing it today, I still have fond memories of the first time I played Firewatch. I remember being entirely sucked into the mystery and absolutely chomping at the bit to know the resolution. This year I have come to the opinion that there is no way to have any sort of personal objective assessment of a game or piece of media. I used to think that replaying a game or re-watching a movie was me "updating" my opinion on that piece of media. Nowadays however I see it more as creating a new assessment which does not impact the previous one. Each experience is it's own individual snapshot of where you are in your life at that moment. Even if you revisit media in the future and find it not up to par with your current standards, it does not mean you cannot still cherish that original encounter. Back then Firewatch was still in the first ten or so games I ever completed, and back then It did not take a lot for a game to impress me. everything was still novel as compared to now when I am really feeling the diminishing returns on video games coming in strong. In some ways I wish I were still that easy to please, I think life would be more enjoyable that way.

Let's go ahead and get this out of the way: if you don't like walking simulators,  you almost definitely won't like this.

Now, for the rest of us: I'd classify it as more of a hiking simulator. Still a walking simulator, but with far more interactivity and exploration potential than a lot of games in that category will provide. An appreciation for exploration is very important here, as there is plenty to see if you're willing to look. That includes everything from plain scenic vistas to little humorous and referential tidbits scattered across the region. However, there isn't really any external incentive to see much of this, so be sure to bring a healthy sense of curiosity. If you do, I'm confident you'll come to appreciate the idyllic atmosphere that's been captured here so well. It's truly unlike any other outdoorsy game I've seen.

Now, story, characters, writing, all that. It's narratively driven, but don't expect anything truly brain-bending or even supernatural here. The story is a light mystery, since there's clues as to what might be happening, but lots of little red herring's that strike some interesting psychological notes, occasionally bridging nearly into psychological horror. That's the situational side. The character building side is probably one of the stronger elements of the game, as you never truly "meet" another character face-to-face in-game. Despite this, you're given a believable cast of characters that are easy to care about, whether by way of outright dictation, radio communication, visual storytelling, or conversational storytelling. I'll let the game show you more of the details there. Again, the story is grounded squarely in imaginative realism, so expecting a twist ending or some melodramatic climax will only set you up for disappointment. Fair warning.

As for technical and surfacey stuff, it ran well, looked nice, excellent range of colors, gameplay was a little obtuse to start off but became more natural feeling as time went on, sound was great, if a tiny bit too sparse, and runtime was too short for my liking. That's actually probably my biggest issue here; I wish there was some more variation to the gameplay and extended sections for character building to make the game longer (especially at the $20 price point). I don't really know how they might have done this, but it would have been appreciated.

I'll try to make it short, since I really doubt that anyone will even read my ramblings here.

So first of all, no, I was not following Devs during the development process, neither was I sitting on the edge of my chair in the anticipation of the release. I just noticed that there's a new game on Steam, and I kind of liked the overall synopsis.
Plus, in my region it's only 420 RUB (which is roughly $5), so yeah, I just grabbed it, because why not.

Normally I would not go to Steam forums or read reviews or google the heck out of the game if I am not closely following it. So I just hooked up my controller, launched the game, and crashed on my couch with my headphones.
And tell ya what - it was a great experience playing this little game.

Maybe it is because I was not watching every single teaser, or reading each and every press-release out there - I was not overly demanding at the start. And therefore, for me, it was a struggle of a middle aged man whose rather stable life of habit was just torn from the foundation and sent flying in the nothingness. And, in a way, for me this trip to Wyoming wilderness was exactly what it was for Henry (the protagonist) - a getaway.

Aesthetically, it was a threat. Heck, I even got up from the couch a few times to take some screenshots! Soundtrack was really great (I made sure I have a copy of it). And yes, the voice acting is tremendously great.

As for the gameplay - I honestly can't say that it is bad. I mean, it is basically a novel. You know, saying that gameplay here was mundane, or that it's a simple walking simulator - it's just like saying the The Wolf Among Us was a clicker game. [b]It is a story. Your interaction with it - is merely a mean of advancing it, much like turning the pages in a book. You don't want to solve some finobacchi-sequence puzzle each time you turn the page reading a book, do you?[/b]

And as for the plot - [spoiler]I would say it was quite solid. Because no. This is NOT a detective story (unlike TWAU) it is a story of a man, who spent a good part of his grown-up life with a woman, derailed from the tracks and left shattered. It is a story of him getting away (from the old way of life, from the responsibility, from the pressure). No wonder he bonds with a stranger on the other end of the radio - primarily because Delilah is running as well. But to think that their relationship is what this game is about - is just wrong. In the end, for Henry it was a three months breather. And he has to return to his old life in the end. And this is precisely what you get in the end. For better or worse.[/spoiler]

Can I recommend it though? If you are looking for Shyamalan/Nolan-esque kind of a twist riddled mystery with over 20 hours of gameplay and four possible endings - No. You will be disappointed.
If you have few hours you are willing to spend following a story of loss, guilt, responsibility and other grown-up stuff,  cast among fascinating landscapes, accompanied by a stellar soundtrack, and incredibly good voice acting - Yep, go for it.

If you feel like discussing something above, or asking some questions - go for it and comment.

[h1]Firewatch is an intriguing narrative experience with untapped potential[/h1]

Firewatch is a game about a man named Henry, who volunteers to be a lookout in the wilderness to escape from his difficult life. This narrative driven first person experience is enthralling, beautiful, and at times, suspenseful. On the surface, Firewatch can be easily percieved as your standard indie walking simulator. Vibrant aesthetics, non engaging gameplay, and a severe lack of depth. For the most part, this is true. 

The game is visually stunning. The exquisite illustrations are remarkable and are simply marvels only capable of acheiving in a video game, as I constantly find myself breathlessly immersed in the beautifullly crafted environment. It was the game's aesthetics that sparked my initial allure to Firewatch. 

The story of the game is quite interesting, exploring the life of a normal man, Henry, and his decision to escape his daily life by retreating into the wilderness. The relationship between Henry and Delilah, his boss, is fascinating as the charmingly written dialogue paired with superb voice acting left you wanting for more. The narrative itself was initally compelling, however, as the story progressed, the narrative began to diverge and stray into various scattered subplots. These plot points were then hastily pasted together and labeled as finished, leaving you feeling unsatisfied with the game's ending.

I initially found traversing the terrain as refreshing as most walking simulators don't allot you the freedom of being able to travel to your destination your own way. Whether you want to walk the long way round, or climb some rocks, or cut through a cave, you can choose the way to get to your destination. However, as I progressed through the game, traveling became more repetitive and the varying paths to reach your destination grew more linear. 

Many people have complained about the length of Firewatch, and that 3-4 hours of a walking simulator is certainly not enough. To a degree they are correct as $20 is a steep price to pay for a short narrative experience, especially one with less than adequate replay value. 

Firewatch is definetly a fun game, and I am grateful for the opportunity of having played it. I reccomend that this game should at least be played once through, just not at the current price. Firewatch is an intriguing narrative experience with alot of untapped potential. Despite it's shallow gameplay and lack of depth, it is definitely worth picking up if it ever goes on sale.

I feel like Firewatch is an observation on how we react to loss, in its many forms.

My review does not contain game experience/gameplay based spoilers, but does contain plot spoilers. This game is a subjective experience and below are mainly my own thoughts having just completed such a thought provoking game.

[spoiler]By the end of the story the two main characters ultimately reach their resolutions, and as the player, we witness this first and second hand. First hand, via Delilah and Henry, and second hand via Ned and Brian.

Delilah openly (if a little nonchalantly) admits that she is out there because she has been running away over the loss of an old relationship. She returns to the Park summer after summer, putting off having to deal with her loss and move forward with her life. However, as the story progresses and events unravel, i felt as if her mind was put into perspective. It could be argued that she just runs away all over again, from the Brian and Henry situations respectively, but that is subjective. The narrative ultimately seems to point to the fact that she returns home to take care of some stuff and perhaps get closure on her past. A resolution perhaps?

While Henry is a subjective character, as it is us who play through his eyes, he comes across as a man who is trying to deal with the devastating results of his wife Julia's Dementia. He tried boozing in bars all night, but that just made things worse and seemed to compound his frustration at the situation, leading to his Firewatching. An unwilling passenger to the events in his recent past, Henry comes across helpless, empty and at a great loss. Delilah rekindles Henry's spark somewhat, and as the story progresses, he too is shown the true perspective of things. Of living life, of the beauty of life, of what love truly means, and ultimately of his promise to his wife. The shortcomings of Delilah and her relationship with Henry, and of how Ned treated his Son seem to underline the right choice and resolution for Henry even more.

In Ned & Brian we see a Father and Son relationship that is slowly unraveled over time. We hear that Ned was a veteran and later discover that he didn't find being a parent easy (who does). While so much of Brian and Ned are left ambiguous, we know the most important things to the story, that Ned had a focus and drive to be out in the park as a Firewatcher and that Brian was just a normal innocent boy who loved his dad. Over time, as the player, we uncover more and more truths behind the theories, which provoke the mind and develop the characters of Henry and Delilah further.

The narrative deliberately puts a negative connotation on Ned as a character, which leads us to wonder if he is behind a bigger and nastier chain of events. However, as certain things come to light, we discover clues that tell us things aren't as extreme as we feared, Ned 's reaction to the loss of Brian manifests itself in quite a profound way. It shows him to be a man transformed into a bitter and reclusive hermit, obsessed with the intimacy of others and perhaps, with the guilt he bears for bringing his son out with him when he shouldn't have. He lets his loss and his greif overcome and consume him. Ultimately it is unclear what happens to Ned, does he stay and die in the fire? Does he get eaten by mama grizzy? Or does he live out his life in total isolation? There is Poetic justice in the unknown.[/spoiler]

On conclusion of the story and on further examination of the plot points and characters, you can't help but reflect upon how we all, for better or worse, react in different ways to loss. Importantly though, it highlights that loss is such a strong emotion, and one that has the potential to cause problems. There is no solution to or 'best way to deal with' loss. There are however, stories from which we can hope to learn and better understand it, when it inevitably lands at our own feet. 

Firewatch touches on some moving topics but does so in a very mature, charming and enchanting way. When you pair a rich, complex and cerebral narrative, with a fantastic script, incredile voice acting and beautiful artistic style, you get story-telling at its finest. Firewatch forges its own genre of novella, providing a kind of - forrest walking, trail hiking, adventure seeking - escapism you simply cannot find in any other game.

Ahh, yes. I've been really looking forward to Firewatch. When I finally got to play it. I found that I was both pleasantly surprised and a little disapponted. This game is absolutely beautiful, not a detail out of place. The shadows are as shodows should be, the trees and grass move in the proper direction with the wind, and the lighting allows for some of the best scenic shots I've seen in a videogame. 
The audio does not miss a single step, each step you take provides a satisfying crunch of the leaves underfoot, you can hear the wind whistling through the trees. The music comes in at the perfect moments and adds tension to the air, but doesn't force it down your throat. The diologue, oh the diologue is phenominal. With the voice-actor for Henry predominantly from Mad Men and the one for Delilah from various other games, they make an already amazing script feel natural and human, more than I can say for way too many AAA titles. 
Seems flawless, right? Well, maybe. A tag you will notice this game has is "walking simulator," similar to other games with that tag like Dear Esther, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, Gone Home, and The Stanley Parable to name the most well known. The one thing all these games have in common is the generic lack of true gameplay. You know, shooting stuff, solving puzzles, collecting hidden items and the such. Dear Esther and Gone Home failed in to execute this well because at the end you were left with no real reason to have played. With Ethan Carter  you at least felt like you did something and with Stanley you experienced something relatively new and unexplored, and you left feeling like you learned something new. Firewatch is above Gone Home, Ethan Carter and Esther in that you leave feeling like you've discovered and learned something, that you were moved and felt real emotions that weren't forced by circumstances. The different choices in diologue can lead your relationship with Delilah down one path or the other, depending on the kind of person you are. What truly drives you through this game is the anticipation of hearing the next bout of diologue, and for some people the space in between is too much.
Of course, a lot of people would not consider "Walking simulators" true games, as you don't interact with them as much as you "should," and this will defintely push people away from this $20 title. If it was cheaper or more overall content I don't think there would be near as much complaining, but for how it is now you either come for the visuals and stay for the script, or avoid altogether for fear of wasting $20. I am left with mixed feelings about Firewatch, although those feelings for the most part are positive.

Here are the two greatest negative criticisms—and note that one of them is a spoiler, although I'll do my best to make it relatively generic:

1. The game is short and for the most part, I think, lacks replayability. Playtime clocks in at about 3-4 hours. There may be some possible alternate conversation paths that could be worth playing through to experience but other than that, the main story is wrapped up in a relatively short amount of time for a game currently priced at ~$20.

2. The ending of the game leaves you with a desire for a sense of closure that it doesn't deliver. The primary antagonist escapes, your reasons for beginning the adventure in the first place are left mostly unresolved, and your relationship with the secondary protagonist is left up in the air as well.

Despite all that, I actually got a sense of fulfillment from the game that actually STEMS from its lack of closure. Life simply isn't always as simple and neat as we'd like to be, and the sense of not knowing exactly where to go, or what is going to happen next, echoes perfectly the state that Henry (the main protagonist) must have been left in.

Part of me wants a happy ending for him anyway, and the fact that things are left open lets me write that ending in my head without it being dictated by the game's creators.

Overall this was an enjoyable experience. The game itself is gorgeous, the soundtrack is both peaceful and haunting in equal measures, and the voice acting and characterizations are both believable and touching. I would honestly hesitate to call Firewatch a game; it's more of a playable narrative, an interactive movie that forces you through its sense of isolation and solitude to really connect with the main character.

The one thing I didn't really like about the game was the length. I beat it in about 4 hours. Now 20 bucks isn't a steep price by any means, but I've paid 20 bucks for games that have a lot more content and replayability. 

Overall, I think if you're on the fence about getting this game, you should wait until it's on sale.

I wouldn't let these negative views affect my play so I choose to first see what might be the problem here. In the end I found an amazing and beautiful story about two people who are alone but aren't in a national forest for the duration of a summer and the ending was a fitting conclusion to the psychological mind game played by everyone. 

We as people love a good mystery, we love to know about the wizard behind the curtain or the monster under the bed but when it comes down to it sometimes those mysteries are as mundane as the day to day existence that many of us experience. To say that the ending of this game is disappointing offers extremely little credit to the commentary on human psychology that it expresses and belittles the characters that we develop over the course of this game. For me the only negative part about this game is the short amount of time I spent immersed in it's world. I would love to return to the Wyoming wilderness someday and to Henry and Delilah, and I would love to spend more time with them, but overall the story told here is in no way short. It tells it's story the way it wants to, and it plays out it's events to you the way it is intended. I know that the time put into this game and it's world and characters was all done with love and it truly shows in the end. 

If you truly love a good story, and a beautiful immersive world, and well thought out and developed characters, then buy the game. $20 honestly isn't that much for it, and we have all spent a ton more on games that have given us so very little in return emotionally.

I just completed my first playthrough of "Firewatch", a first-person perspective adventure style game by Campo Santo, though calling it a game hardly seems like an accurate description.

Firewatch is virtual wonder of scenery and exploration enrobing a heartfelt human story, and shines brightest in the voice acting of the two main characters, Henry (Rich Sommer) and Delilah (Cissy Jones).  The envrionment is beautiful, with brilliant lighting direction for sunsets, late summer afternoons, and mid-morning adventures, and top-notch stylized modeling of the landscapes and forest scenery, but each and every radio conversation between our two cast members, while you take in the majesty of the Wyoming parklands, is stimulating, even during the seemingly mundane, everyday dialogues that would be just as normal at home, in the city, or over even the phone with your best friend.  It's these little touches that help humanize the experience as you hike around a little piece of the Shoshone National Forest.

Without spoiling any of the story, I can say with absolute sincerity, that I was emotionally engaged from the very beginning, and was curious to see what direction Firewatch would go every step of the way.  Having been a computer gamer for over 30 years now, my instincts had me expecting a lot of plot devices to appear whenever the story put seemingly familiar situations in front of me, but each time I was pleasantly surprised, all the way through the end of the game.  And though it is a singular storyline, I intend to playthrough it again immediately to see how subtle changes of my dialogue choices effect the experience.

The full playthrough only took me about 6-7hours over the course of several sessions, but this is actually a plus in my opinion, as time is a precious commodity, and I'm glad for a chance to have a complete story-driven gaming experience that won't take me weeks or months to finish, which is usually what I'm in for anytime I play a quality RPG.

In short, I highly recommend this purchase (I pre-ordered it at the discounted price, but I'd have paid full price) for anyone who wants to have a short, but complete story experience in a fun, unharried exploration of the wilderness.  I do support the recommendation that game is aimed more at adults (partly due to the time period), but overall I think it's probably appropriate for young adults with parental approval.

Firewatch tells the story of Henry, a temporary ranger working within the Wyoming woods to stop fires from happening (taking place after a major forest fire). He is almost completely alone, apart from his trusty walkie-talkie friend Delilah, two mischievous party girls and a mysterious figure that only appears once in the entire game (I'm not kidding). The genius through the mystery surrounding the game is what you don't see. Who is the person watching Henry's waking moment? Why are they ransacking camps? etc. The Henry and Delilah relationship is very believable, and admirable to a certain extent; though quite disappointing when you don't eventually meet her (I know this has to do with lip synching and team size). Admittedly, it is more of a walking simulator, and can be finished in a Sunday afternoon (and I disagree with the current price). I found the mystery unveiled plot underwhelming, as it would've been great to have this large conspiracy, but I digress. Firewatch managed to keep me interested for the four and a half hours I played it for. A few nitpicks here and there:
- Henry can't walk on clearly walkable surfaces
- Constant little jumps made on ridges to bide for time
- Fairly accessible routes to get out of the game world
- Often difficult solutions, requiring further exploration
Despite all that, it still holds up. And the soundtrack... Listen for yourself, you'll know what I mean.
An interesting, albeit time-demanding, and connecting story, interwined with the Atlas-Jack relationship from BioShock combined with a exploration/walking sim. game; and you've got Firewatch. Despite being a little short, and some of the tasks being a pain from time to time, Firewatch will please anyone with an open mind, open sense and open view.

[b]"Safer in the Forest"[/b]

[b]Firewatch[/b] 
It is the first game from [b]Campo Santo[/b], and it's a solid first entry into their catalogue. 
The Wyoming wilderness stretches before you, painted in beautiful colours of fire and dusk. The trees whisper in the wind, the crunch of dirt beneath your boots grounding you in a place that is both breathtaking and isolating. It is a journey through solitude — one that is equal parts mystery, melancholy, and self-discovery.

[b]A Living Postcard[/b]
The first thing that struck me was the sheer artistry of it all. This isn’t just a forest—it’s a living oil painting, shimmering under the golden light of the setting sun. The visual design is stunning, each frame worthy of a postcard. The soundscape completes the immersion: the rustling leaves, the distant calls of unseen wildlife, and the soft hum of the wind against the fire lookout tower. Every detail pulls you deeper into this lonely, yet strangely comforting world.
 
[b]The Weight of the Watch[/b]
Getting around the map proved to be a bit of a chore sometimes, simply because of the vastness of the environment. Getting lost is tedious, but lets be honest, hiking feels exactly like this feels. You get desperate to find the path to where you want go, and albeit to my annoyance, it makes total sense in creating tension. The field of view was fine for me, but I understand how subjective that can be. The UI is wonderfully minimalist, leaving only the essentials, and I often found myself navigating with the map in hand like an actual back-country ranger, rather than stuffing it away for convenience.

[b]Voices Over the Airwaves[/b]
Being the Henry you want to be is entirely up to you, and the voice acting does not suffer whether you choose to be vulnerable or outspoken.
I appreciated the quality of the banter between Henry and Delilah, she fills the emptiness with sharp wit and genuine warmth, making the vast wilderness feel smaller, more intimate.
There’s a quiet sadness in its unraveling—a reminder that some questions don’t have satisfying answers, that not every mystery is meant to be solved. As the summer wanes, so too does the illusion of escape. Perhaps that’s where Firewatch stumbles; the final moments feel like an exhale that never quite fills your lungs. A few more words, a lingering pause—anything to soften the abruptness of goodbye.

[b]The Echo it Leaves Behind [/b]
I always gauge an "interactive narrative" game's quality by how much time I spend pondering about it after I've finished it, and this game has been doing exactly that. Coming to my own conclusions as to what exactly was going on, the intrigue, the mystery. Going on forums to find answers. And in the end, isn’t that what stories are supposed to do?

Totally worth $20, because it stays with you for a long time.

So first of all, all reviews who mention they completed the game in 3 hours or less didn't play it correctly. If you're someone who is into action games, or has to compulsively complete objectives to unlock acheivements and all that primordial stuff, move along. If you care about story, are willing to immerse yourself, don't mind a little roleplay, read on.

Firewatch is a first-person narrative. Playing it feels like reading a book and imagining yourself in the book. But on top of that, it provokes genuine feelings. I fell in love with the characters, and found a lot to relate to.
At the beginning you are forced to read. So if you absolutely hate reading, it means you probably won't immerse. So give up. Slow down. Read. Let yourself be washed over with Firewatch's story.

In many ways, the plot itself reflects life itself. There is so much to relate to. To both Henry and Delilah. You can imagine Delilah's face and the longing to see her. But as you play, this longing becomes more than wanting to see what her 3d mesh looks like, because if you've been playing it right, you just want to meet her. She's become a friend. The characters feel very real. The story is poignant and great. Like all great books, you'll be thinking about it weeks later.

I can't wait to see what, if anything else, these new age storytellers will come up with.

I got into this for a few hours and will be going back shortly, but just wanted to get an early review in noting that the experience has definitely been worth the money already.

Firewatch is a 'walking simulator' to an extent, in that you explore an area and find clues with very little in the way of problem-solving, but the thing that sets it aside from others in the genre is that it's less about being a puzzle-solving archaeologist, picking over the aftermath of something more interesting that's already happened, and is more about being some guy going about his job while the excitement kind of happens in close proximity - all with some company who you can interact with.

The dialogue (and its delivery) is fantastic and would be great even if you weren't offered options on how to respond.  But there are options and that increased level of involvement had me fully-engaged for hours, hunting down any excuse to get those two kids talking again.  Choosing different options to see how it changes their conversations is probably something that will have me doing another playthrough or two.

In a similar way to how I felt like conversations with your ship-mates were the best parts of the Mass Effect games, I felt like the character-driven dialogue is the best of this game (impressive visuals and authentic-feeling sound aside).  And it slathers that special sauce all over its otherwise pretty-but-simple walking/exploring base game.

A few hours of exploring and I'm hearing that I might be either at the mid-point or even close to the end, and it doesn't really feel like it... but knowing that I might almost be done really just leaves me hungry for anything else these guys might do in the walk-and-talk genre.  The talky... I need more.

I'm seeing a lot of negative reviews of this game, and for the first time ever I felt the need to write a review so that others don't get the wrong impression of what this game has to offer them. And LOVED it. I played through twice, and am contemplating a third run.

If you're looking for a combat based game, look somewhere else. Do you love minecraft? Nope, this is something different. Enjoy puzzle games like The Witness? Ehh, that's not really what this is about.

But are you the personwho had to explore and click on every square inch of Final Fantasy to make sure you didn't miss anything? Yup, we're getting closer to what this game offers you. Did you constantly quicksave/load in Mass Effect so you could listen to everything a character had to say for every interaction Shepard had with them? Bingo, now we're getting redhot here. Do you pine for the days where Myst was fresh in your mind as the most beautiful world you've ever seen in a game? Gamer, you should buy this game. If my last paragraph resonates with you, you'll love Firewatch.

But if length of time played is what you're after, that's not what this is. And others seem to not understand that these characters are written like they're real people - warts and all. They'll make poor decisions and say mean things. That's what people do in real life. That's what make characters like Henry and Delilah so rare in modern games.

So spend 20 bucks. Get lost in this world. Enjoy these characters like I did.

Overall, I liked the game and will recommend it. I just finished it, so the below points are what stand out most in my mind.

1) Length: A number of people have said it's too short. I finished in just shy of 6 hours[spoiler], and it turns out I missed a few secrets along the way. Whether I go back to experience them firsthand remains to be seen[/spoiler]. Price point on release is $19.99. Is this 6 hours of beautiful art and voice acting worth the price of two movie tickets? Yes, to me.

2) Plot: Initially, the story sucked me right in, and I think I owe that to the fantastic voice acting and unique premise[spoiler], but as time wore on, the plot holes got bigger. For instance, the walkie talkie Delilah leaves for Henry. The location made absolutely no sense. Additionally, we never even get to see Delilah, no matter what choices you make in the game, so I really don't feel like my decisions of what to say and how to talk to her made any difference whatsoever. This is the biggest disappointment to me[/spoiler].

3) Voice Acting, Visuals, Interface: Voice acting is top notch. The two main characters are voiced by well-known and talented actors, and Henry and Delilah really come alive. The visuals are spectacularly done, with lush forest, rocky outcroppings, and star-filled nights. The interface is point and click, and is a little persnickety in some places, but overall it's fine. 

The game does a pretty good job of holding your hand, as well, so you're never stuck somewhere without knowing what to do.

I've been following this game for a long time, ever since the original poster dropped and I saw an article attached to it describing what the goal was. For a small team to have put this experience together is quite an accomplishment. 

I'm not going to get too deep into the controversy about the ending. By now you've all heard about that, as well as all the hemming and hawing about the story's length. I will quickly touch on these two subjects and move on.

The game took me 4.8 hours to go through, and I felt that was a comfortable pace where I wasn't rushing, and yet I was able to explore a little. I didn't spend much time exploring off the main path, as I was confident that each mission I was tasked with would take me where I needed to be and give me a chance to look around a bit. Looking at the whole map now that I've finished the game, that's exactly what happened. In this game, it's safe to go where you're told and explore as you go. 

The game is not really as much of an "open world" as it is a big map that you're steered through. I did feel a bit like I was being led every step of the way, but I sort of expected that going in and didn't mind that. If you're a fan of the Walking Dead Telltale games, this is very similar. However, don't be misled into thinking that any of your story choices really matter in the long run. I don't think they do, but there isn't enough replay value for me to go back and play this again to find out.

As for the ending, yes, the game just kind of ends. And while I'm not necessarily the type that needs a button-down Hollywood ending, I will note that the reason we play stories, the reason we read stories and the reason we watch stories is because we usually want to see a character undergo some change during the course of a story that gives some added meaning to the rest of their life, even if they have to return to that life at the end of whatever happens.

While I have seen specific references from the forums to points in the story where I may have missed some imparted meaning, I would argue that if the writer of Firewatch really meant for those points to have true "movement" in the character, it was so subtle that it was too easy to miss. I think the arguments against those complaining about the ending would have been a lot easier to formulate had some extra attention been given to the story in regard to showing more clearly what each character might have learned from their experiences over this summer. 

As it is, if you can accept that the summer spent here was just an escape for both characters from some drama in their lives, and that's all it is, then you'll have no problem with this game. The scenery is gorgeous, the sounds immersive, and it's just a joy to walk through. As it is, it was a 5-hour escape for me from my life, and an enjoyable one at that, so I think that's "enough" for my $20. 

The voice acting and banter between the two characters was spot-on, although I felt at least at a couple points, the hysteria came a little too quicly, but that could have been because of dialog choices I made that weren't seamless when branched. Only the developers know.

Overall? It's a game I'll remember very fondly, even if I don't go back and play it ever again. I enjoyed my time in the park, and would gladly pay another $20 to spend another five hours with these two people to find out what happened after the events of this summer.

What captivated me as I watched footage of Firewatch was its honest and witty dialogue, great voice work and breathtaking art design. I bought it despite the average completion time falling between 4-6 hours. If €60 Call of Duties can get away with it, then I don't see a reason why €20 indie games shouldn't. Ignoring multiplayer for the sake of argument, which I have very little interest in if a single player campaign is included. My time with Firewatch fell just under 4.5 hours, which was still surprising to me, cos normally I'm the one who takes their time. If there's a world to explore, I'm likely to get lost in it, hopefully for the right reasons.

Firewatch's structure takes longer jumps between days the more you progress, the quality of the dialogue, voice work and a thirst to solve a mystery will compel you forward, rather than have you explore every nook and cranny. The world and its characters are completely in service of this mystery, so it's unlikely you'll find yourself wandering in Skyrim-like wonder. The days in Firewatch often end without warning, sometimes offering you the choice to call it a day, as you discover the next clue or trigger. I've only played it once, so I can't say how deep or shallow the choices and its consequences are but at first glance there doesn't seem to be much replay value. Considering what cinema tickets cost nowadays, Firewatch is not overpriced for its length. If you thought Dear Esther was worth it, then Firewatch has little explaining to do for the added interactivity and length.

What I would've liked to see and experience was some of the more mundane aspects of the job of a fire lookout or a security guard. After a certain point in the game I felt a desire to clean my lookout, but picking up and placing down items (books and such) is the usual clumsy affair. I can't help but wonder if a Viscera Cleanup Detail type of gameplay would've worked here, something to ground your character better and have you spend more time in the game, however meaningless compared to the story. You don't spend a lot of time in your tower, which is a shame. I would've generally liked more night time discussions with Delilah, my feet on the table, whiskey in hand and you just stare at the moon or a forest fire while you chat. Like I said, the game has a plot and it hurries you along, but what use is a beautiful wilderness if you're only there to look for your car keys, so to speak. The writing does a superb job in pumping you up for something grand, but I'm not sure the payoff is appropriately matched. I didn't find it underwhelming necessarily, but it allowed our fantasies to take off more than it should've.

Maybe I'm at fault here, cos I hurried myself along faster than usual, instead of taking in more of the sights and sounds, reporting more findings to Delilah, reading more of the notes I found and generally just taking a bigger interest in more backstory. Your conversations with Delilah is the essence of Firewatch, so you should savor those moments and break the silence any chance you get. You're in the wilderness after all, not chasing down collectibles in a big city or doing the next mission. Slow down, talk with Delilah, report what you find.

While my setup exceeded the minimum requirements, I had to play on Low settings to get a steady 30 fps, so it could use some futher optimization. That's just me and my old laptop though. Since I wrote this it has received several small patches. Despite the team members being experienced, this was Campo Santo's first game. While I haven't played The Walking Dead yet or finished Life Is Strange, this felt like a hybrid of the team's past projects, but the choices you make don't feel as impactful as in other games. Ultimately it boils down to being a the bad guy or the good guy, so it's suitable for two playthroughs at the most. This would be fine if the the mystery were more weaved into those choices, making the ending carry more weight. I wasn't expecting someone's head in a box or the entire thing being an elaborate birthday present, but even a solid X-Files episode would've sufficed.

I still recommend it though, cos it delivered on what I saw in the footage and I had no expectations beyond that. Like watching a good indie movie. Many of the short games released in recent years are ultimately experiments in creativity and exploring the paramaters of a what a video game can or can not be. You can label them as walking simulators or something else, but it's important to put something out there and test the waters. Dear Esther was nothing but walking for 2 hours, but I'll never forget it. Firewatch is compelling enough to see what Campo Santo has to offer in the future.

In order to review Firewatch, I will attempt to compare it with other games in the same genre. 

There are two types of walking simulators. The first takes form in Dear Esther and The Beginner's Guide. You hold W until you reach the end of the story and then you quit. Calling this type of walking simulator a 'game' is generous. 

The second type of walking simulator, which is a game, revolves around discovering art or narrative by exploration. The two best examples of this are The Stanley Parable and Firewatch, which give the player options and then respond to those options in relatively simple ways. 

Where The Stanley Parable allows the player to explore a physical space only, Firewatch allows for exploration of both a physical space and a dialog tree, adding a layer of depth. 

In both cases, the character is motivated by some mystery, and the player is motivated by the fantastic writing and voice acting. While the world of Firewatch is beautiful, the real draw of the game is in exploring the main characters, Henry and Delilah. I was able to finish this game in 2 sittings (I got tired and had to sleep) because I wanted to learn more about the characters and I found that ultimately, the mystery was  a secondary concern. This is actually the case in The Stanley Parable as well. Ultimately everyone in the office disappearing is just a catalyst for Stanley to stand up from his desk, and everything that happens thereafter is completely irrelevant to the mass disappearance. In Firewatch, the mystery is primarily a source of tension - a conflict for the two characters to overcome - more than a key component of the game.  

One feature unique to Firewatch is that navigation is a mechanic. You occasionally have to slow down and pull out a compass or look at a map to get your bearings, because it's 1980's Wyoming and those are the tools available in that setting. I didn't mind the navigation, especially with the little "You are here" indicator on your otherwise paper map. 

The main caveat is that it's short for the price. I completed it in about 3 hours and I don't really feel a need to replay it. I believe the quality makes up for it, but $15 might be a better price. To be fair, before playing I thought $10 was probably a better estimate for a 3hr walking simulator, but I really was impressed by the game's art and writing.  

Some people didn't like the ending,  but I thought the ending was human and real and for it to have been more than that would have been rather jarring when juxtaposed with the very human and real relationship developing center-stage.

9/10 Exceeds expectations for character building and pushes the boundary of its genre without simply adding elements from other genres. Game is a little short for the price and for some people the mystery pay off would not be grand enough.

[h1]A great premise, fantastic voice acting and a beautiful setting, sounds like the perfect game, right? Wrong. [/h1]

Firewatch is a “single-player first-person mystery” otherwise known as a walking simulator with dialogue. In Firewatch you play as Henry, a middle-aged man who has volunteered to be a lookout in the Shoshone National Park, Wyoming during one summer in the late 80s. The beginning of the game sets up his story in the form of a ‘text adventure’ in which the game describes a few key events which you’ll need to know to understand Henry. Once you get to the Shoshone part of the game you begin speaking to your supervisor, Delilah, who talks you through your summer job as well as chatting to you about a few things. You’re usually given three dialogue options when talking to Delilah which will change the path of the conversation (though not the game as far as I can tell) though sometimes you’ll only get one option, usually if you’re reporting something. Having been excited about Firewatch since the first trailers of it were released I was incredibly excited to get my hands on it but unfortunately I’ve been left rather disappointed.

Please note: The game took me three hours to beat, any game time further than that has either been spent getting the trading card drops or going back to unlock the first two achievements which were broken when I started the game.

Firewatch has two main strong points, its appearance and its voice acting. First up, appearance. Firewatch is positively beautiful, even on low settings as I played it on. While it’s not a unique aesthetic, as some have said it looks a tad similar to The Long Dark, it fits the game well and when there’s something like a sunset it can be quite breath-taking.

Like I said, the voice acting is also fantastic. The actors who played Henry and Delilah did a fantastic job at making two believable characters and a lot of their dialogue feels real. There were a couple of bits here and there which were a bit weaker but nothing major enough to take away from how good it was. 

Moving on, we have gameplay, or in Firewatch’s case, lack thereof. It is, as has been said by others, pretty much just a walking simulator and if you’re a fan of walking simulators then that’s great, sadly I’m not. There are a couple of things to do other than walking, for example there are certain places were you need to repel down steep slopes, but the vast majority of the game is taken up by just walking around. This is made worse by the fact that there are a few points in the game where you have to backtrack or walk through an area you’ve already been through, it just makes walking through said areas even less interesting. While the bigger areas are pretty dull, especially the familiar ones, there are some areas in the game which are pretty cool and actually enjoyable to explore, they’re all tied to the story so don’t worry about missing them. Admittedly I’m not sure how they could have added any real gameplay to the game but I do think that Firewatch would have been more suited to a different format, i.e. a novel. The interactions between Henry and Delilah are definitely the best parts of the game, the longer interactions anyway, but these interactions are usually on either side of a chunk of walking in silence, which is as boring as it sounds.

Firewatch’s story starts out strong, really strong and for the most part it’s very well-written, made even better by the voice actors. Even the little text adventure at the beginning is great, it sets up the character of Henry incredibly well and it’s also like an emotional punch to the gut. The story carries on strong as Henry eases in to his summer job with some simple tasks given to him by Delilah. Sadly things take a turn for the worse when Henry discovers something he probably wishes he hadn’t and Henry and Delilah are catapulted into a rather worrying situation. The story actually remains pretty strong until you get to the end of the game at which point I found myself presented with one of the most disappointing endings I’ve encountered in story-driven games as well as in novels. There’s simply no pay-off for beating the game, I honestly think I would have enjoyed the game a lot more if they’d just cut the last twenty or thirty minutes from what is already a disappointingly short game for the price (just for the record I would have been happy with the six hours the devs said it would be before release but three hours is too short for £15 in my opinion). Without any plot spoilers I’ll explain why I don’t like the ending a little more: [spoiler]the problem with the ending is that it feels forced, like the devs ran out of time so they just threw something in there to tie it up nicely. Except, it doesn’t tie it up nicely, it ends with so many unanswered questions that even the characters, who have just gone through this pretty alarming experience, don't care about. In the final interaction between the two before the credits roll they act like nothing has happened at all and it made the three hours I spent playing the game feel so pointless. I didn’t get the sense of closure I want from story-driven games. [/spoiler] There is also a pretty major whole in the plot. Once you get to the end of the game and piece things together there's one thing in particular which just doesn't make sense, something that should have been addressed in the game.

[h1]Verdict [/h1]

At the end of the day, Firewatch is little more than another overpriced walking simulator. While the story is great for most of the game the ending completely and utterly ruined the experience for me which just made it harder to look past the distinct lack of interesting gameplay. Grab it on a deep discount if you like story-driven games and don’t mind a disappointing ending but at full price I can’t recommend this game.

Firewatch. One of the most beautiful games I have ever had the good fortune to view. But is it a good game?

The story is a few strange mystery occurrences which spring up during your stay in the Shoshone wilderness. Your job as the only one around for miles, is to explore and to try and solve these mysteries, with your only communication being a woman (let’s call her D) on the other end of a walkie-talkie. There is a certain text adventure-esk intro but I won’t spoil that. It basically sets the story up to you getting to the Shoshone, although it seems a bit lazy, as if they didn’t want to create any gameplay or visuals for it so they simply just thought up a simple intro. Potential was lost here. 

The gameplay is pretty basic. Think of it more of an interactive walking simulator with beautiful scenery. You walk from point A to point B communicating with D trying to solve certain issues. It’s not bad gameplay assuming you don’t go into it expecting CoD and go into it with a cup of Tea, a couple of biscuits, and just relax (although there are some tense moments which get you going, as well as some very depressing ones which were 10 out of 10 for making you feel empty inside).

The voice acting is something else. It is fantastic and, for all of you who get the reference, it’s a whopping 5/7 (AKA a 10 out of 10). It is brilliant. It really makes you feel everything the characters feel. If every game had voice acting like this, gaming would have just moved up into the god-like levels. You feel the tension when your characters fall out, feeling isolated in the Shoshone. You get angry when D decides it’s a good idea to get drunk when you’re trying to solve a mystery and need her help. Fantastic stuff. You can tell no expense was spared here. 

However. Now to explain why I thumbed this game down. I really enjoyed it, the visuals, and the voice acting. I didn’t mind that I couldn’t shoot and roll and such like other games. The reason I thumbed this game down is because its £15 for 3 hours of gameplay. I really wanted to love this game, I did. I wanted to get deeper into the story and have deeper mysteries that I could unfold, really get immersed in the story, except this is cut short by the devs. Maybe because they ran out of budget? I don’t know, but I feel betrayed by the company as they made it out to be so much more in the trailers, only to drop a 3 hour game on us which is absolutely not worth £15. If it were longer or maybe £5-8 or maybe even episodic, I would’ve thumbed this up, but as is it, I simply can’t.

Overall, it is a good game, but too short to be worth £15. Save your money and pick it up in the sale. It had the potential to be something fantastic, but fell short (in more ways than one). If you do pick it up (hopefully not for £15) enjoy it, but know what you’re getting in to, a 3 hour game.
