Oh boy, where to even start... The story begins with [i]you[/i], who you are and that one girl you've met at the bar. That cliche ends up following you over the years with all the happy/sad things we all come to expect in life. At some point, things change dramatically and you find yourself in a watch tower overlooking stunning vistas and beautiful wilderness. Welcome to Firewatch.

Out here, your only contact with humanity is through your radio, which you use to talk with Delilah, your boss - and maybe even friend - situated in a tower just like yours. Over an entire summer, you go through quite the experience, which I most certainly will not be spoiling here.

Firewatch is a game made [i]for[/i] adults [i]by[/i] adults, exploring grown up themes. It's a surprising, liberating breath of fresh air among so many shovelware out there. This is a "walking simulator" in the best possible meaning of the phrase and I couldn't be happier to have experienced it.

The ending however is [b]very disappointing[/b]; now there might be some alternate ending but after reading other forum posts and watching others it appears there is only one. The voice acting is excellent; it's one of those games where I wanted to hear every piece of dialogue just because every scenario was done so well; both characters feel natural - The voice acting doesn't feel forced, cheap or cheesy. It can be witty, serious or depressing depending on what you choose in-game. It should be noted what you choose in no way affects what actually happens in the game, you will just get different dialogue - All outcomes are the exact same, unless there is a secret ending but as I said there probably isn't.

A lot of people complain this game is quite short and I can see why; many users are reporting 2-4 hours (which seems to be the average) - It took me 4 hours, mainly because the map in this game is so annoying to use and navigate with, I got lost all the time. Combined with the awfully confusing map which sometimes just seems to change at random this means it can take 10-20 minutes just to find a certain area or navigate back to your tower. I like the voice acting, and the story did show promise but I cannot recommend anyone to pick this game up right now - Watch it on YouTube or wait for it go get really cheap in a sale; if a friend has it ask for a family share but it simply isn't worth the asking price - Especially considering most will beat it in 2-4 hours (speedrun record is currently 1 hour) and there isn't any replay value; not unless someone does find some secret ending or extra story stuff comes out.

First off I really liked the aesthetics; the game world looks really nice with its style and I enjoyed exploring it. The gameplay itself is quite simple, and while there is some minor player choice I find the game runs its course more like an interactive novel. Perhaps the downside with Firewatch being mostly about story and not actual gameplay is that I'll probably not play it again. Some people have an issue with the game length (~4 hours) but at this price I'm okay with that.

Right off the bat Firewatch surprised me by putting the game in a rather heavy context, but I'm glad it did as it provided some depth throughout the game. What really makes the game however is the dialogue, which feels natural and entertaining. You build a relation to the characters and the voice acting mainly by Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones is excellent. Because of them, I found myself quite invested in the story and their characters.

And the first thing you should do when starting the game is toggle off "Show Location On Map". This'll make the game much more enjoyable.

There seems to be some talk of the story's ending being of no significance or value, and being disappointing. However, those same people say that they were engaged and riveted to the end, this tells me that perhaps they are missing the point.

The game was a brilliantly crafted journey, with excellent voice acting and an incredibly engaging story. There were lulls of saftey and enjoyment, and peaks of uncertainty and concern. Nothing gave away the storyline along the way, leaving the mystery hanging in the air, allowing your imagination to go wild, and letting you contemplate what might be going on.

The game didn't resort to any tropes or deus ex machina like circumstances in order to make it feel like a blockbuster movie, it simply made sure to tell the story it intended to tell and stayed authentic and true to that goal. It was an incredibly refreshing journey, and just because the ending didn't have you diving off a cliff into a helicopter or being chased by an axe wielding murder, does not discredit the journey you took.

There were definitely lessons to learn along the way, but if your focus is on the ending then you may just miss them.

Ostensibly Firewatch is a game about a guy who goes into the woods to escape his problems and finds mystery and excitement therein. But the first part of that: the escaping into the woods part is what Firewatch really focuses on.

The game gets a lot right when it comes to presenting a narrative and environment to explore. Its world is fleshed out and there is no doubt of who you are or where you’re going. 

Where the game falls short and where a lot of review negativity surrounding this game comes from the game also having a console release.  I believe the marketing for this game was sort of presented it as an action/mystery game. Trailers showed things like falling down a shale cliff or a stranger shining a flashlight in your face with a panicked voice-over. If that action/mystery is what you’re here for, you may be disappointed.

This game does have elements of mystery, it does have elements of action but it is neither an action nor a mystery game. Its core experience is the relationship between people who want to be left alone but can’t ever escape their need for others. 

Most players won’t find this experience worth the $20.00 price-tag. It’s well written and beautiful and considering the size of the studio and the stunning graphic and voice work I felt the price was fair but for those who are merely curious I suggest getting it when it’s on sale at -50%.

The game suffers significantly in its final act; it ultimately felt as if the creators had too many balls in the air and dropped 90% of them. That said, some of what they achieved and their unique take on the genre is definitely worth a play-through. The design is beautifully done, evoking a sense of paranoia and slipping sanity that hinges on the unreliable narrator. You can't trust yourself, and that's really interestingly done here.

Was it a let down? Yeah. I'm not sure what I wanted to happen but I know I wanted it to have more meaning, more impact, something. I want to know what the burned down cabin was, why there were bears, why would he have faked an entire research site? Ned's actions don't make sense within the story, and it's waved away with the explanation of PTSD. I wanted to meet Delilah, to know more about my wife, to run across other people or have a chance to explore different cave systems. I think a collectible system would have improved the game significantly- a reason to explore the wilderness would have been fantastic, and could have fleshed out the bare bones world. The game has the illusion of choice, but very little reason to venture off the strictly set path. 

There may be some value in a replay- different choices, different dialogue options- but without significant reworking or the release of new content, the ending would feel the same way. I wish this game had lived up to its promise.

Pros:
- Amazing graphics, the art style with the lighting and everything else makes for a unique and beautiful world.
- The landscape itself feels real in the sense that it doesn't feel like the map is built around you and instead you are exploring this world put before you. (If that makes any sense)
- FPS was stable and performing well, no drops or underperformance. This game has been optimized well.
- The ambient sound and the soundtrack itself fit the game perfectly and none of them feel out of the place or forced.
- The voice acting is believable and it feels like the protagonist and other characters are actually talking to eachother and not reading lines off some paper. Feels very organic and that helps build to the emotion of the game.
- The story for the most part is well told and realistic and gets the player very invested in the lives of the main two characters, making choices a thing of importance. There is plenty of backstory and mystery embedded into it as well.
- The game mechanics are simple and easy to use, can very easily pick up this game and just play. 

Cons:
- I have finished the game and done most things inside of it you can do, and only racked up 5 hours. With little replayability this means for a $20 price tag I might get 9 hours out of it overall. In my opinion this game is worth around $10 and I advice any cautious buyers to wait until this game is down to around that price.
- Like I said a majority of the story is actually really well told and intriguing but it starts to fall short near the end. I was disappointed as they could have done so much more with this, it's not completely terrible but in comparison to the excellent story previously displayed it didn't match the same caliber. 
- There are still a few bugs around as any game does, but I did encounter a few more annoying ones such as world not loading walking on nothing to being stuck on top of objects that are difficult to get down from because there is no jump mechanic.
- There is a lot of walking in this game, a majority of this game is just walking from location to location. Now this is a minor con because the world is stunning and just walking through is fun, also the person on the radio is usually talking to you and there is story being unfolded so you get distracted, but in some points in the game it can get repetitive and I was just groaning at the fact I had to trek so far through already explored parts of the map. Also for some missions it will just make you backtrack the exact path you took to go back somewhere, where in other missions it would just fast forward time for you and put you there or close to there to save time and I just wish they had put more of those in.

TL;DR: Graphics and atmosphere are amazing, story is gripping but lacks at the end and there is only 5 hours max of gameplay per playthrough.

Many people pose the question, "What is this game life?" and the answer is very simple. The game is akin to the Text-Based Adventure games from the 1970's and 80's, where you explore your environment, solve simplistic puzzles and experience a story heavy experience. Text-Based Adventure Games have been coined as Interactive Fiction and that really is what Firewatch is. You explore a vibrant and colorful world, uncovering a mystery while interacting with another watchperson via a walkie-talkie. The most important thing you need to know is if the story is good and if the characters are engaging. The answer to those questions is yes. The story is engaging. I have heard critics say that the story has a lackluster ending and I disagree. There are themes and elements that leave the ending open to your interpretation and that always sparks controvery. The reality is that the game is a delightful mixture of emotions that tug on the heartstrings in a variety of ways. If you are looking for a story-driven interactive fiction, then the game is for you. It isn't for everyone, I understand that, but for those looking for this style of game, it will not disappoint.

Going to start off by saying NO SPOILERS *Safe review*

Where do I even begin? This game is a first person, mystery, "walking simulator." I do not like that term however, as it seems like so much more once you get into it, at least it did for me. 

As far as character developement goes, the developers did a fantastic job of creating enough back story and information to invest yourself into the main character, his motives, and the supporting cast. Rarely do I find myself playing a game, with the mindset of actually being the character I play. This game in my opinion gets a 5/5 for this category.

Musical score is up next, and it does well. Not the best, but it's up there. Music matches well to your mood and the story. I feared going into this game that you would have the typical "spoiler music" that gives away upcomming events, but I was happily disappointed. The music just seems to flow with the story. In my opinion 4/5.

Visuals, are always important for me. This game did not dissapoint. The graphics are wonderful on the eyes, and have a depth in places you would not expect. During your time, make a point to look up into the night sky whenever the oportunity presents itself and you will see what I mean, 5/5.

User interface, is one of the rough areas for me with this game. Sometimes you will find yourself finding just the right angle to interact with something, which can become frustraiting. It is also very hard to use gear sometimes, but that might have been due to the fact that I ran through almost the entire game with the keyboard mapping in the options menu, but was in fact using a controller. You can change the on-screen cues for interactions however by adjusting the settings in the options menu. For this I give it a 3/5.

Plot, was freaking amazing!!! (In my opinion.) It kept me going until the very end, and kept me really thinking about my every decision. Looking back I don't feel as I would have played it any other way, but it still keeps me wondering "what if I did this." I give it a 5/5.

Last but not least as this is a "mystery game" I would include thrill/suspense in my categories, and boy does this game deliver. I didn't figure this cookie out until almost the end, and that might be my way of thinking or the fact that I completely fogot about the fact that this was a mystery game while playing it. Definately a 5/5 for me.

Overall this game did not dissapoint. I question it's replay value, as at the time of this writing I have only gone through it once. I might go back and do things differently to see if it affects any outcomes, but for now I am simply enjoying the game for what it just gave me.

Firewatch is an excellent addition to the genre, and (largely) succeeds in what it sets out to do. It certainly isn't for everyone, but it's a very unique game in terms of it's narrative-driven gameplay, beautiful art direction and impeccably-delivered dialogue. Firewatch is really all about the story; gameplay, while not at all bad, is minimalist and certainly takes a backseat to the interations between Henry and Delilah, the two main protagonists. 

Most of the game is hiking around through the wilderness near Henry's lookout tower, while choosing how--and sometimes when--to interact via radio with his only human counterpart. Much of this entails walking or jogging from point A to point B in order to accomplish X, but the plot and dialogue that develops caused me to hardly notice what might otherwise be seen as menial tasks. The relationship that develops between the two throughout the 4 or 5 hours of gameplay will mostly be a consequence of your choosing, and this system is really something that I have not seen employed to this extent in a video game. I must say that the effects of my decisions, while subtle, seemed incredibly realistic and satisfying.

In short, Firewatch is gorgeous to view, and emotionally impactful to watch and play. The story may not leave all completely satisfied, but the journey is definitely well worth it.

Firewatch had such potential, truly.  But unfortunatley much of it went to waste with dangling plot points and a very anticlimactic ending for such a suspenseful buildup.

Pros:
-Amazing atmosphere and art design.  Proof you can make games look beautiful and engaging without having a AAA budget.
-Great voice acting.  The two main characters, Henry (you) and Delilah are a joy to listen to and you never really want them to stop talking.

Cons:
-Story sets up a lot of interesting points that seem to end up going nowhere.  Potential conflict and mistrust between the two characters gets brought up and then immediatly forgotten.
-Of all the ways the story could have gone, it felt like the creators chose the most banal, leading to a big anitclimactic letdown of an ending.
- Compelling backstories don't really seem to matter.

Neutral
-Linear: Yes it's a linear story.  So what?  Not everything needs to be an open-world, choose-your-own-adventure.  If the story is a good one, telling it the particular way the creators envisioned is fine.  The problem was this story was not that great.

The game starts off with an interesting text based scenario where you (the player) get to decide how exactly you want to start your story. Then you get put into the forest. I can describe how beautiful the scenery is and you start to believe that everything is real. The sounds, the dialogue, and movement is so realistic I actually feel like I'm not playing a game, but rather living the protagonist's story. The dialogue used in the story is mostly between you and a person named Delilah. She's basically the only source of communication through out the game and the conversations you are able to have with her are rich and sometimes quite intense. You have choices to pick to see what to specifically say to her and no matter what you decide to choose, they are all great. I kept looking towards my radio as I always wanted to see what was next. I constantly wanted to speak to Delilah.

The story is captivating and gripping. I found myself getting paranoid (at best) being in the middle of the forest and occasionally looking back and around me to see if any monster/freak/pervert was following me. Although the story can be easily decrypted and you can predict the outcomes, it was still suspenseful and I kept on wondering what was going to happen next. The only real downfall for me was the ending. I wish it had a little more of a bang. It felt unsatisfying and I just sat in my chair wondering "that's it?" Regardless of the ending and how short of the story is, I still felt like they did a great job at retaining the player's attention.

So here's my review of Firewatch: it's a pretty damn good game. Started it last night and finished it in about 5 hours. It's relatively shorter than most games in that aspect but it's only $20 so it's a pretty reasonable price for the content. At the same time it doesn't overstay its welcome with sidequests, things to collect, or achievements. You play as Henry, a fire watcher employed at a national park in Wyoming. You have little to no physical human interaction as you spend the entire game talking over a handheld radio to your fellow firewatcher, Delilah, who is stationed on the other side of the park. This, in my opinion, is one of the best things about the game because it allows the player to emotionally connect with the two main characters without knowing anything but the sound of their voices. It tells its story in a quirky, down-to-earth narrative that has dialogue options making you feeling like you ARE your character. Seriously, the dialogue in this game feels so natural and unscripted that it's like I'm talking to one of my friends. The graphics are pretty decent for games these days but what really stands out is the color schemes. The oranges, yellows, and reds of the Wyoming landscape beautifully contrast the azure sky giving it a nice, warm feeling as you hike throughout the park. The game has a linear story and although the park is pretty large there's a lot of hiking between areas that will quickly become familiar, which is cool because it makes you feel like you've worked there a while. Even so, backtracking is never wasted since the story continues as long as you are headed the right way so hopefully you have a good sense of direction. I won't spoil any of the plot but as you progress, you find out that you're being watched by something or someone and things go south from there. Overall, the game is beautifully crafted for one so short and its simple controls and linear story make it an enjoyable experience. The only gripes I have are the occasional bugs (game crashing, getting stuck on terrain, etc.) and the mildly disappointing ending (maybe I was just expecting more closure). For all it's worth though, I give this game an 8/10. Bravo, Campo Santo!

So a big gripe off the bat I have with this, is the false advertisement on the main store page. The Developers state:
"A tailor-made story: the choices you make shape the narrative and build relationships."
However this is false, while you can change your responses on the radio, it only effects the immediate conversation, all the plot points have a stock responce and there is only one "real" ending to the game. Any choices you make when talking to Delilah won't factor into the ending save maybe one small line of dialogue, tactfully choosing responses on the radio to try and get different outcomes never works as the game will then force you into saying certain things to progress the plot for the ending the developers intended.
This removes a big chunk of re-playability as nothing you do will have any real impact on the plot, which brings us to the next issue with Firewatch.

Despite being a narrative heavy game, it fails in the story department, the first hour or two in the game are great, it played out as expected with spooky events happening to our hero, however the issue is, the game is only three to four hours long for the average play length, so only about half the story is any good.
Parts of the game hint at a bigger, more interesting story that was cut for budget or time constraints so instead you get a nonsensical plot by the antagonist to scare the player away in the style of a Scooby Doo villain before letting you in on the secret he was trying to hide anyway, when speaking to Delilah if the player makes sensible decisions on informing the authorities on what's going on. Delilah always brushes it off as you being paranoid or fails to report an event, meaning she is either very poorly written or is in on the conspiracy, which never gets brought up despite some foreshadowing again hinting at cut content. As a result I felt like someone who was self aware in a horror film but was being forced to make stupid choices despite knowing things would go badly.

Before the plot goes off the rails we're lead to believe the antagonist might be a serial killer and later a Man in Black trying to cover up a MK-Ultra/Shutter Island style experiment being conducted in the forest.
But it suddenly just becomes a upset father who's trying to scare you away from his kids body but instead draws more attention to his Machiavellian plot and goes to stupid lengths when he could have just buried the corpse or thrown the keys to the mine away.

The ending is also a let down, as mentioned earlier, none of your choices really matter. The game feels as if it should have three or so different endings but only has one "real" ending as well as a choose to die "false" ending. Regardless of how you talked to Delilah (or didn't) during the game, you will always get the friend zoned ending despite on my play through non stop flirting and having implied phone sex with the protagonist.

I really wanted to like this game and there are redeeming features, the visuals are lovely, sound design is excellent and the game is genuinely interesting until the plot nose dives into absurdity near the end.
I'd recommend it when it's on sale for £8 or less but buy it being aware that for a narrative driven "Walking simulator", the story isn't all that good.

When I sit down to play a so-called walking simulator, I try to keep the following question in mind: Will the money spent equal what I would spend on a movie of the same length? In the 4.4 hours I spent with Firewatch, I found the experience to be engaging and entertaining. The dialog (which is the main form of interactivity in this game) was well-acted, and fun to listen to. The number of F-bombs dropped (while natural, given the circumstances) may be off-putting for some players. The plot did have some unanswered questions, which given the ending will remain unanswered (barring a sequel).

I was fortunate enough to purchase this game at pre-launch price, which helped make the “ticket price” of this interactive movie easier to swallow, since I may not play it through for some time. 
One way to have increased replay value was to open the model, allowing Hank the ability to jump, scale, and hike his way through the Shoshone wilderness. This would have opened the possibility for the player to open new vistas and sights, providing pictures worth printing. From a gameplay standpoint, I did experience some frustration by the enclosed surroundings. I should be able to walk over a fallen tree without having to put away my map and compass, followed by pressing the space bar. 
This leads me to the other issue: If the idea of Firewatch is to provide the user with an immersive story-driven experience, forcing the user to press the spacebar for even the mildest obstacle takes away from that experience.
Experiences are what drive a game such as this. Thankfully, the story and voice-acting helped overcome the gameplay issues, helping to make this an enjoyable experience. Given the closed nature of game (the inability to wander in a wilderness setting is unnatural), I would have to consider Firewatch a few steps away from being a great interactive experience.

TL;DR: I got my money’s worth, but the lack of freedom took away from a wilderness which could reward wandering.

Firewatch is a beautiful game with incredibly engaging characters and a plot that really sticks to you. Pros:
+ Game looks great.
+ Story starts our really really nice. Wish more games would do that kind of thing to get people involved in the story.
+ Very good dialogue.
+ It experiments with feelings of isolation and paranoia in an interesting way.

Cons:
- The experiment with feelings of isolation has very minor impact because the game is very short (which we expected anyway).
- The story starts strong and keeps up a good pace, but at about 70% through the game it becomes fairly predictable.
- The ending of the game is... well not bad but a bit of a bummer. Forgetable.
- Dialogue choices are meaningless. Normally, I am not in the habbit of bashing games for allowing choice but have the endings focus and limit the long term impact of that choice for the sake of the narrative. But in a game this small, implementing different consequences to some of the choices (even just cosmetic ones) would have been fairly easy.
- Leading on from the previous point, the fact that regardless of whatever you chose to do or say the outcome will really be the same, gives this game pretty much 0 replayability.

Final thoughts: this game is really nice, and I liked it, but now that I finished it I must say, this game is not worth the 17.99 EUR I paid for it. I don't regret it, but most people will agree that this game is really barely worth half that price.

Some people will moan about "walking simulators", and dismiss these kinds of games as though they need a challenge to be wroth investing in. Firewatch has a lot of walking, but it isn't as if there is no game here. The only difference is that the gameplay takes place in your head, rather than on the keyboard. Did you find a weird out of place clue? Did someone not answer your question quick enough? You are constantly cross-examining and second-guessing every little detail you pick up, as the story funnels you into an ever expanding intrigue plot. A lot of that is down to the lack of face to face human interaction; with only a walky talky to communicate, you find yourself incredibly suspicious of any ambiguity in conversations, and tactically trying to craft the best response. I've been reading a lot of the reviews here on steam and on other websites as well and while there are various reactions I am more interested in the gaming community as a whole. 

First allow me to say the facts about this game first so that there isn't any misunderstandings. The game lasts about 4 to 6 hours, depending on how much you explore and how many conversations do you respond or engage. 

The main game mechanic would be the conversation aspect of the game. There's no action or much in th way of puzzles. 

There are lots of choices and conversation trees but at the same time there are several plot points that will always occur and while how they are approached can vary depending on the conversations you have, they'll play out the same. So there aren't wildly different endings in this game. 

In my opinion this probably going to game of the year for me. Let me explain.

Video games, for a while now, have been fighting for the right to be labeled as an art form, like film and literature and theater for example. However what is most interesting to me is that a significant portion of the gaming community is still thinking in an old way. A lot of people have called this a "walking Simulator", it's almost as if a lot of people don't know what to do when confronted with a game that focuses on telling a story versus what score do you get, or achievement you earn. 

Let's call this work what it should be called. It's a Thriller. And if you desperately need to remind people that it's an electronic medium then Interactive Thriller could work. 

The community can't function without trying to out this game in the typical "game" boxes which is why you'll still hear, *it's too short" "It's too linear" "There aren't any side quests" "where are the achievements" "no multi-player" etc. 

To those who would argue it's too short and too expensive for the money. $20 for 4 to 6 hours of well written and acted content isn't a waste. If you'll pay that much for a movie ticket that you can only view one time then this is definitely justified in price. 

I am curious how can people complain about how it's too linear? It's clearly telling a story with a beginning, middle and end. While the conversation choices add variety, it is a story and it doesn't need to have giant multi faceted story possibilities. 

The gaming industry, in comparison to the other mediums, is still very young. And we still have a long way to go. I can tell you that Firewatch is one of the few games released so far that is trying to make the statement that an interactive medium is just as powerful as a way to tell a story as a passive one. We need more games like this. 

This game is beautiful visually, a very well chosen  art style. 

The voice acting between the two characters is so well done that if it were for an animated movie it would receive such high acclaim. 

This game would have made a good book or film in its own right and it knew how to keep me continuing on. 

Play this game if you want to support good story telling in video games.

SUMMARY: A very personal, narrative-driven game with great voice acting that brings the playable story to life.  A great purchase for people that want an intensely character-focused experience.

Firewatch can be best summed up as "a playable indie movie."  Like many good character-driven small films, it focuses on a small cast, who they are, and what they experience.  The fun is being immersed in the intimacy of the world.

You're Henry, a man in his 40's needing a break in his life (which you get a role in defining).  He's taken the job of keeping a watch for fires in a park, his only real contact being his supervisor Delilah.  Being alone, in the middle of nowhere isn't easy, and it's made worse when some mysterious happenings complicate Henry's attempt to get away from it all.

Game play is a mixture of dialogue choices and going to different locations to do things, mixed with wandering whenever you want to.  Dialogue choices affect your relationship with your supervisor, but the plot is largely on rails - the goal is to explore characters first.  This actually works because the character conversation is a  vital part of the story (in a way, it is the story), and because even if there's specific plot points, you get to them your own way.  Little tasks and elements add to the sense of realism.

The result is an interesting story and an experience that feels like being there.

The visual presentation and the voice acting are worth calling out as both are spectacular.  The park looks gorgeous, sort of like a painting that moves.  The cast are entirely human and believable, and the writing comes to life.

One caveat on the game - this is a $20 game you'll finish in about 4 hours.  Its replayability is probably limited to one more time, if that.  It's not a game who's value is in duration, it's one whose value is in a sene of being there, emotional impact, and thought-provoking experiences.  It's not for everyone - or for every mood.

But who is it for?
* People that want an immersive story.
* People who like character-driven tales and good dialogue.
* People who want the above (or don't mind the above) in a game that's play is more interactive adventure than challenging mechanics.
* Someone who want a more laid-back game. (for some, this game may be an excellent break from other fare)

Leave it to a small studio to make a hiking/mountain movie simulator that really submerges you in the role of a lookout guard with a decent luggage on thi back both literally and mentally.

The pleasent and sarcastic conversation with Delilah keeps you interested and although there's no real traditional gameplay involved other than looking, looking for clues and "puzzling" your way around the environment.

The choices you make in the game are mostly conversation based, and they swing the mood from sarcastic, light to dark at times. But sometimes you can also explore areas off the main quest which will give you meaningful information about the story and the area you reside in. 

The cool thing about this whole game is the way you explore the environment. There's no waypoints, you only have your  eyes, a compas and a map as tools to use and this makes it a very immersive exploration experience molded into gameplay. The environment isn't also enormously big, and some paths are more linear than the other, offering some choakpoints that lead you down areas of the game. This makes the experience not intimidating and overwhelming. It's just right and you can relax and play, find the solution without eternally getting stuck somewhere.

This game is more of an experience like dear esther, home alone, with some faint hints at metroid: which means: you can only pass area X when you find Y and then areas start gradually opening up.

I really enjoyed playing it and it gave some feels that I rather not have felt at the end. That ending hit  home in a very personal way so that's good. If a game can do that, even if it's "just" a hiking simulator, that means it hit a nerve. Firewatch is probably the best of the "Walking Simulator" genre I've played yet.  While there is a mystery plot that provides some set dressing, the real meat of the story is about two characters who have found themselves at a turning point in their lives, and deciding which direction to go.  Each is informed by the events they experience in the woods of Wyoming.

Unlike a lot of scary, tension-filled games, Firewatch digs directly at real-life fears.  Running from zombies or hiding from space monsters can be tense and scary in the moment, but the characters in Firewatch are coping with real problems that may yet strike me or my loved ones.  At its core, the game asks "what would you do?" in a somber and direct way that makes you wonder what your values really are.

Firewatch isn't targeted at hardcore gamers, or casual gamers, or even any audience we would normally thing of as a market.  It is targeted at people who have reached the stage in life where the thought of something happening to your spouse or life partner is far scarier than the thought of it happening to you.  It isn't a story about the people struck by tragedy, but about the people around them, who have to cope with the aftermath.

If you're in that category; if the most frightening thought in your life is having to find a way to go on after your happily-ever-after has been brought low by disease or disaster, pick up Firewatch at any price.  It will be an experience you might not necessarily enjoy, but you'll appreciate.  If not, give it a miss; if you just come for mystery and adventure, you're likely to be disappointed.

Firewatch is an absolute triumph. Beautiful and grand, you exist in and explore vistas that will take your breath away. Details abound that will captivate you in this world, some you may not even notice at first (like how your character, Henry, has a difficult time scaling rock faces at first, heaving and dragging himself up, but becomes more proficient with time).

Then the story starts to unfold, and it is absolutely gripping. The atmosphere in Firewatch is spellbinding, and I was left at the edge of my seat with tension and a feeling of impending doom more often than almost any other game I've played in recent memory. There's a certain vulnerability to being alone, in the woods, with only one tenuous link to another human being. Campo Santo plays this solitude along with incredible art and music to deliver a complete package and exhilarating experience.

There's the oft debated question "Are games art?" If you're still on the fence about that, Firewatch will make you a believer.

Oh, and a lot of folks seem to be complaining about the ending and the interaction with your supervisor at the end. I, for one, appreciated it. Because it was a real ending, not a video game ending. I won't spoil it, but I think us as gamers get used to common tropes and, eventually, get dissapointed when a game doesn't fulfill these things. Sometimes the climax isn't something that would be found in thousands of other games. Sometimes things don't work out the way you want them, even in this virtual space.

It's not bad, and plays well in its niche. If you consider it an "interactive novel", [i]not[/i] a "choose your own adventure book", then you're on the right track. I didn't mind the linearity - it works as an extension of the world that movies and books inhabit. The viewer/reader can't really influence the outcome much and that's ok. Especially since that's pretty much [i]exactly[/i] how a situation like this would really work - really, how much impact do you think someone could have on the outcome in this sort of situation?

I approached it pretty much like I approach the paperback mystery novels you pick up in beach houses on holiday (not unlike the many books scattered around the watch towers and supply caches in Firewatch). They have plots that are a bit melodramatic and sometimes it's difficult to suspend your disbelief, but in the end they're books about people and relationships - and the plot is really just a vehicle to explore that.

The mystery was presented well, I thought. The details, red herrings, and interpretations by the characters were all pretty plausible. 

As for playtime, I savoured as much of the world as I could. I picked up and read all the notes I could find, and explored all the branching paths on the ground that I could find. Oh, I also turned off the "show location on map" off, which made navigation a bit more immersive too.

I got 6 hours out of it and that wasn't too bad. The people who blitz through in 2 to 3 hours are the equivalent of the people who read a couple of words at the beginning of each chapter and the last page of a book and then complain that it wasn't very engrossing. They're probably missing the point?

FWIW, I also enjoyed (and preferred, actually) SOMA. But you'd have to be open to some decent sci-fi concepts to have a crack at that one.

One-line-game-description:
Firewatch is a story-heavy suspense-walking-simulator with a unique atmospheric graphics-style and excellent voice talents in a fresh setting.

Comparable games: The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, Gone Home

I’m not a huge fan of the the so-called walking-simulators, most are just plain boring (Dear Esther, The Stanley Parable) and offer just too little interaction. A few stand out however, be it by story or presentation (like The Vanishing of Ethan Carter).

In Firewatch you don’t see much more interaction: besides picking up and examining stuff you can jog around (hey, it’s a Jogging-Simulator!), climb and jump, rappel down some rocks, chop some wood. That’s about it – basically it’s all another mouse-click or press on the space-bar – no skill involved (or intended). What sets the game apart from other walking-sims is the natural dialogue and its dense atmosphere.

You’re Henry, an average guy from Boulder with some personal problems who takes a seasonal job as a fire loukout in Wyoming - for a change, to clear his head. For the next three months the only human soul around you’ll have (radio-)contact to is your supervisor Delilah. She introduces you to the job, helps you around and chats with you about pretty much anything you’ll see and encounter.

Thanks to the two extra-ordinary voice talents the dialogue is always convincing. You have quite some choices and whichever you make, it feels like a natural conversation (like a Quentin Tarentino movie... just without the blood and violence).

I love the art-style, the game’s graphics prove that you don’t need ultra-crisp textures & hyper-polygon meshes to create a beautiful, immersive landscape. And I really enjoyed the orientation part: a topological map and a compass to orientate in your surroundings – no mini-map here. If you’re an iron-nose like me you’ll find your way around quickly. Else you might struggle a bit and have to regularly consult the map which luckily shows your current position.

Another pleasant surprise was the clever scripting: the game spares you uneventful and boring back-tracking once you completed your given task. As with a book the narration jumps to the next chapter respectively the next eventful day in game. If you have to backtrack it either means you lost orientation ;-) or it’s connected to an event. This helps holding up the tension and spares you meaningless travel-time. It’s an honest and adult approach and good game-design: no artificial game-lengths here.

The luscious graphics with the illusion of wide space, the great voice-acting, and the well-paced narration lead to a very immersive game-experience that held me up well past midnight. Oh, and I liked the ending – it kept true to the game’s ideas and protagonists.

If you like well-written and -performed dialogues and a down-to-earth adventure for a change, this is the thing to buy. It’s one of those rare Indie gems.

TLDR version - frustratingly linear non-explore-'em-up.

I'm not really sure why Firewatch rushed to the top of the Steam charts upon release. Maybe everyone was thinking the same as me - this looks different, fun and pretty.

Well, it turns out the game isn't really much different, and the "fun" is quite limited. Firewatch is one of those "experience" games, so maybe I was playing it wrong in expecting there to be more. Perhaps I was supposed to be entranced by the prettiness, and the by the whole idea of being isolated in a remote tower.

I would have loved to start a collection of the things I found, but whilst there are things to find there is no collecting to be done. I was looking forward to exploring the wilderness, but more or less everything was on rails. There isn't even a jump button, and no way to step over even small obstacles unless there is a button prompt allowing you to do so.

The single level contains multiple locations connected by what are effectively corridors, steering the various gameplay tasks in a frustratingly familiar way. Various mechanisms (such as obtaining an axe) allow deeper exploration, but others (such as the torch) seem entirely superfluous.

The game seems to believe it is a work of literature. The story and setting are both quite original for a game, but that only served to remind me why most games are the way they are. The conceptual realism contained within the design was central to the whole idea, and because of that the two main characters are nicely rounded and quite human. But don't we already know what human beings are? Don't we have plenty of media to present that idea to us?

Games should be about what we as players do, giving us choices and changing the outcome.

There are interface problems too. Responding to Delilah on the radio is a timed event, so if you are using the map, or tardy in any way you will lose the chance to respond. But having watched others play I couldn't see any branching caused by dialogue responses. I think everyone is going to get pretty much the same experience.

I found the walk/run toggle to be a bit glitchy. I was using an Xbox 360 pad, and I frequently felt as though I was running through mud. Watching someone play it with M&K they seemed to be getting about a lot faster.

I picked up a whole bunch of notes and letters, but was never able to read them later because the list in the menu would not scroll (again, a controller issue?)

If Firewatch is available in a sale then you might enjoy a couple of hours wandering about in the woods, but if you like a challenge or you enjoy exploring in an open world I'd steer clear even at a knock down price.

I've been waiting for Firewatch since its announcment a few years back. After finishing the game, I really wanted to give it a review, so I've laid out some positives and negatives from my experience.

[h1]POSITIVES[/h1]
[b]• A beautifully crafted world.
• Good writing with charming comedy.
• Fantastic voice acting.
• Very atmospheric.
• A nice soundtrack which adds to the atmosphere.
• Great concept.
• The ability, despite it never being hinted at, to collect things and bring them back to your tower.
• Very relaxing.
• Choice that affects conversations (but not the plot).[/b]

[h1]NEGATIVES[/h1]
[b]•  Despite its message, an anti-climactic ending.
• The game pulls you out to get you to progress with little to no warning, making it hard to explore after you've completed an objective.
• The world doesn't feel very open. It's mostly made of straight paths with locked-off walls, meaning that over half the map is just forest that you can't walk in to.
• Short length of 5-7 hours, with little replay value. It ended at what I would have expected to be the mid-point.
•  No long-term effects from your dialogue choices.[/b]

While the long list of negatives will turn many people away, I will still defend this game. The positives outweigh the negatives to make an experience I very much enjoyed and was excited to come back to. I'm glad I didn't let the hype get hold of me as it appears many people did. While there was a lot of potential here for what could have been, I was delighted with what Firewatch is regardless. If you have a lot of stress in your life at the moment, Firewatch is an excellent way to get rid of it without actually going to a fire-lookout tower in the middle of nowhere.

So, there are a lot of people criticising this game for it's length, ending, and "branching plotline". Despite what these people say - though some of it may be true - it is still an amazing game in my opinion. The plot was really really well done. In a sense, it's like a movie or book that you're playing out on the screen and it really engages you. The amount of detail put into the characters, the plot, it can be overwhelming at times. There may not be a lot to do, but there's PLENTY to see. For a debut title from two indie companies, it's extremely well put together. Well worth the price in my opinion. For as much criticism as this game receives, it delivered in each department that counts I think.

Firewatch. Where to begin?

Panic Inc. and Campo Santo deliver a first person, narritive-driven story that'll grip you within the first 10-15 minutes of gameplay.  You play as Henry, a witty, relateable, and charming man in his late thirties who works as a fire lookout in the Shoshone national forest in the sun-baked state of Wyoming.  Like many, Henry leads a life that he feels he needs to escape; A life many actually find themselves facing everyday..  Henry soon comes into contact with Delilah, his boss and trusted companion.  After what appears to be an easy summer gig, the duo is unexpectedly thrown into an unusal and paranoia-inducing mystery that'll keep you hooked...

Gameplay is simple, straight-forward and easy to pickup.  It may take one some time to find out how to navigate the lush landscape, but with just a few minutes of playtime, you'll be just fine.  Henry can pickup objects, inspect them, and even engage in entertaining dialouge with Delilah about ongoing events.

Firewatch is beautiful.  WIth a unique art style some would find similar to Team Fortress 2; Firewatch easily delivers stunning color pallets, jaw-dropping contrast, and complimentary colors many triple A games even hope to achieve.  Campo Santo knows this, and they push it to its full extent.  Hot colors for daytime and sunsets, and colder, more relaxed colors for night.  Bright orange canyon rocks compliment clear blue skies perfectly in a way that simply made me stop and admire the hard work put into it.  You could take a screenshot anywhere and it would fit perfectly on any desktop.  Godrays coming through tree leaves as I hike alongside a small, flowing creek gave me a sense of gaming euphoria that graphics have never done before.

The story is on a different note however.  Firewatch does an amazing job at pulling you in with conversations voiced perfectly by Rich Sommer and Cissy Jones; Firewatch's main leads.  Chris Remo's soundtrack creates a sense of peace and the thrill of being alone in the woods.  It plays at just the right time, adding more to the games sense of progression throughout the narrative.  Sadly some things are too good to be true.  As if reeling in the biggest fish in it's life, Firewatch does an amazing job with the hook, but the line snaps as soon as the prize is at hand; Leaving the player with a rather anti-climax feel towards the game's final 15 minutes.  You're left with a feeling of sadness (dissapointment being too strong of a word to use) at how the game could've had the great, awe-inspiring ending that you wished for.  That is unless you really enjoy the ending; For which if you do, even better!

Overall Firewatch, is a beautifully crafted, character-driven narrative that left me with overall great memories.  Some mostly enjoying the engaging dialogue while hiking through the gorgeous world Campo Santo has made.  Replayability may be low for some as the ending was not quite what they have expected, but that doesn't mean that this is not a good game.  Please do not think that.  I myself wanted more from the 4-5 hour journey, but as I look back on it, I found myself enjoying a game that truly filled me with a gaming passion I had once thought long lost.  Even though 20$ sounds like a good chunk of money, know this.  Firewatch is a game that you should not look over.  If you don't want to spend money now, wait till a sale, but please, don't pass this down.  I loved it and see myself going through it again soon enough.

Walking Simulator 2016: Now with climbing, rappelling, and the prettiest environments you've ever seen.

It's just you, your tools, and your radio to your boss, alone in the Shoshone National Forest. Except when you're not alone.

Firewatch adds some menace and mystery to typical walking simulator fare and tries to make the Wyoming wilderness feel more real. Your UI is you literally holding up a map and compass; your dialogue requires you to hold radio buttons like you might in real life. It makes slight concessions to accessibility by adding text readouts of notes you'd otherwise have to squint at and giving a real-time "you are here" marker on your map, but for the most part, Firewatch tries to eschew artificiality and really immerse you into the role. For the most part, it succeeds. 

Where it doesn't succeed as much is story. Oh there's great characterization and wonderful moments that evoke powerful feelings. But the story itself feels strange and disjoint, and by the end of Firewatch's scant 5 hours, it feels like frankly very little has been resolved, and the stuff that has isn't necessarily resolved to satisfaction. There's a really excellent allegory tied up in the whole thing about fire management, forest fires, etc. and how they reflect on protagonist Hank's reasons for being in the Shoshone National Forest, but a really well-executed allegory in a story that feels rushed on its nuts and bolts is a strange thing. One can't help but get the feeling some much more satisfying story threads were in the works and when a release was just around the corner, they kind of got tied together into one of the *less* compelling story threads just to give it all a clean end.

I don't mean to bust Firewatch's balls too hard. It's fundamentally a good game with beautiful visuals, a really nice sense of peace and solitude early on, and it's wonderfully immersive.  I just can't help but feel like these characters, these mechanics, and this fantastic setting could support quite a bit more than we got.

What is this other than art? A story with which many of us can relate: fear of the future, resentment, the need to escape the present, and the discovery of some glimmer of meaning, a thing which puts all else in a different, much-needed frame. As a game, I doubt Firewatch will explode expectation; as a work of masterful storytelling, and visual gravitas, Firewatch is exactly what all of us need: perspective.

Ever since Firewatch was announced at last year E3 2015, I was quite intrigued by that game. It seemed to delve into the mysterious forest watching inside of "the watcher being watched" kind of game.

[b].

... builds up for nothing. Nothing supernatural, no serial killer, no alien or whatever... but being stalked by some lonesome hermit scientist father (NED).

But the fact that you meet Ned fairly early (flashlight figure) and then a few other moments, you don't meet much anyone else. I did expected something to happen in the woods... a bear attack... more pranks from the naughty teens.

But that's that. I understand the direction this game went and maybe, we don't require a frickin' monster in every game!

Thinking past that, I enjoyed this game. I took my sweet time to explore, read stuff... but beside that, you don't have much else to do. And unfortunately, there is no replay value as any conversation choice you choose, no impacts are laid out in the end. Disappointing...

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
[b]+Outstanding visuals and very good use of colors.
+Soothing to stressful atmosphere (but honestly, you don't have to stress for anything as nothing happens to you!).
+Decent soundtrack.
+Excellent voice acting.
+Engaging story from the start till midway in the game (mystery builds up... for nothing!).[/b]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
[b]-Misleading premise. Thought it was kind of a "watcher being watched" kinda story, where more mystery would unfold but alas, it turned out very "normal". As a gamer, I might be too spoiled and used with monsters/aliens/demons/ghosts in a game setting! But you aren't even in any danger!
-No consequences (that I could think or seen) of your dialogue choices. 
-No replay value. Since conversation choices doesn't really matter and the game is very straightforward, I wouldn't replay it anyway.[/b]

[h1]OVERALL:[/h1]
If you really dig walking simulator games with "some interactions", get this game! You do have "some" exploration to do, for your own gamer benefit although, nothing ingame speaking. But as much as how walking simulator games go, I was still very enjoyed by Firewatch. Ending was as "normal" as it could be and I was surprised by that. I do hope on their next project, please, make a similar game but with more interactions, more dread feeling and heck, even supernatural events! I'd love to have more interactions with other characters too... like you lost contact from another tower and you gotta investigate with the help of other watchers! Just pointers here and there!

[h1]RECOMMENDATION:[/h1]
You really have to enjoy walking simulator games or you'll just be bored out of your mind!

Firewatch is a damn good game. It is the first game where I made sure I had gotten everything else I needed to do finished before I began so I could play with not interruptions. Firewatch kept me enthralled the entire way though; had me laughing, frightened, even verbally exclaiming at my monitor when something happened, which is a rare thing from me in a narrative-driven game. The story is very well presented and wrapped up in a nice package so you're left feeling satisfied if you made sure to go out of your way to find secrets. Olly Moss and Jane Ng deserve a massive shoutout as well for creating a unique and beautiful aesthetic for the game. I often found myself simply exploring the wilderness and taking pictures with a camera I had picked up along the way, and then found myself taking screenshots once I had run out of film. The soundtrack is sparse, yet beautiful and adds appropriate mood to the game throughout. My only complaint about the Firewatch, if I had to make one, is that I wish there was more of it! The big twist at the end seemed like a bit of a copout (I was hoping for aliens) and the ending was lackluster and left me scratching my head until I replayed it and chose some different options which led to a far more satisfying conclusion. My advice to people who didn't like the ending: Consider your options as much as you can with every dialogue choice. How you two interact most definitely affects the nature of the ending. I will be keeping a very close eye on any projects from Campo Santo in the future. Boy was I wrong. After thinking about this for several weeks, I've come to realize that this is a fantastic game, twists and all. At its core, this is a game about running away from your problems, and depending on how you play the game will determine how you perceive the ending. I was anticipating a relationship with Delilah that never came, and was disappointed as a result. However, after thinking about it, I realize now that Delilah was an unhealthy influence on Henry. Her overreactions throughout the game caused Henry and her to concoct this fantasy of them being spied on and there being some massive conspiracy against them. Really, it was all in their heads, mostly caused by Delilah convincing Henry that there was something more than there really was. In the end, Ned was running away from what happened with him and his son, Delilah is running away from her problems of a lost lover, and Henry was running away from a terrible situation at home with him and his wife, leading him to go into the wilderness for an unforgettable summer. After going back home, presumably back to his wife after a failed attempt to convince Delilah to come back home with him, I felt disappointed. Now I see that Henry had to go home and face his problems, lest he never fully come to terms with them, like Delilah and Ned never did. This game is perfect for what it is, and if you're okay with sitting down afterwards to think about the open endings this game offers, then it is a must own.

Yes, I get the metaphor of the tower/escapism/reality vs. hopes and dreams/etc. etc.  I already understood that from watching trailers of the game.  Having said that...

I have mixed feelings.  I don't the mind the short length of the game, as I understood going in that it was a narrative focused experience.  The problem is that experience did not pay off in the end.  I'm able to tolerate cliff hangers of all kinds (I have read all of George RR Martin's books without having  multiple strokes).  But, this game, as beautiful as the visuals were, took little advantage of the possibilities the story had and completely fell flat at the end.  I literally sighed and thought "surely there is more" even as the credits rolled.

Considering the raging fire at the end, and the "tying up" of the father/son story bit, the ending took little to no advantage of these circumstances.  There were so many great climactic possibilities there but instead...they just ended it with a sort of "Well, that's life" message.  No kidding, I'm fully aware that life can suck, hence the use of video games like this to escape it.

It's really ashame that so many are hailing this as "deep" and "insightful" when in reality, if this were the narrative of any novel in a bookstore, it wouldn't sell 1000 copies.  The story was building and building and building, only to end with no payoff.

Visually, it's stunning, and I kept thinking how great it would be to have an open world, multiplayer game in such a beautifully crafted world.  The light shafts through the trees, the color schemes and contrasts were amazing.  In fact, the visuals are about the only reason I don't feel completely cheated with this purchase.

What story purpose did the camera serve?  Why did I board up the windows after the break-in?  Why did I explore the child's fort?  Why collect any of the notes and letters?  On and on there were experiences that felt like they'd build into something.  Instead, they were just "rest stops" in a story going no where.

The voice acting was great, but again, the story didn't live up to the talent those voice actors gave it.

If you like a beautiful walking simulator then purchase it.  If you are hoping for a real story, you won't find it here, no matter how many fanboys tell you so.  There are 3-4 different major plot lines in this game, and none of them come to any real closure.

I never felt like if I went and replayed a section of the game I would get a wholly different outcome.  It sort of felt like a choose your own adventure book where all the choices lead to the same ending, so that at first glance it "feels" like you have a choice when you really don't.  

Basically you should think of this as more of an audio book with pretty pictures then an actual game.

That said, would I recommend this game?  Yes, but not at its current price point.  It's abosutely worth the same as a short audio book and I'd be happy to pay half price for it, but not full price.  There are just too many other games with very strong stories, very strong voice acting *and* very strong gameplay in and around this price bracket to reccommend first.

I quite like the walking simulator genre. I loved Gone Home, loved Among the Sleep and also enjoyed playing Soma and Everybody's Gone to the Rapture on PS4. I also enjoyed narrative heavy titles like Life is Strange and the David Cage games that I also finished on my Playstations.

So you would think that Firewatch would be right up my street. Right?

Well actually No. I was left feeling really disappointed. I can only say what you have all seen in many a review: that being that it starts off great, the mystery builds and builds...........and then it is all quickly resolved with a pretty lame ending. I don't mean the literal end (the last 5 minutes) but the last 30 to 45 minutes.

Compare that to the ending of Soma that absolutely blew your mind and sent you on an emotion rollercoaster. Also Gone Home had a terrific ending that left you with a real positive feeling. I thought the ending to Everybody's Gone to the Rapture didn't quite live up to the rest of the game (although I still loved it) but the resolution to Firewatch was a ten times bigger let down.

I've come away feeling really let down.This game could have been epic if they had only completely torn up the final hour and replaced it with another two hours that leads to a more exciting/thrilling/terrifying conclusion to all the very story arcs. 

So my advice really is to avoid this game and spend your money on all of the titles I mentioned above.


Final score: first two thirds get 7/10, but when dragged down by the final 35 minutes I can only give it 3/10.

Edit: I've since played Tacoma that suffered from an almost identical problem with the ending crippling the game. Another game I'd recommend is What Remains of Edith Finch. Spend your money there.

EDIT - My view of the game changed significantly on my second play through. My original review is below but I feel much more positively about the game now.

All the mechanical and technical problems remain, but the atmosphere of the game -- what brought me back, despite my original lack of satisfaction -- overcomes it. Now that the shape of the game and its story is known in advance, and there are no false expectations of serious branching narrative or anything remotely complex in the mechanics, the sheer beauty of the world and the relationship at the heart of it takes centre stage.

And it really works. It's haunting, winning, eery, lovely -- it leaves you heartbroken, it gives you hope... It's hard to put into words. I started making the same choices as my first play through, until I could no longer remember what I had chosen; at that point, the playthrough took on a life of its own.

I still couldn't abide all the backtracking and navigating. The world is constructed like an open world game on the N64 -- a huge open space fenced in by a million invisible walls cloaked by impassable bushes and logs that are almost indistinguishable from passable bushes and walls. The sections where you have to hike to somewhere far away were barely tolerable on a first play through and probably mean my third play through will be in a few years.

But the music, and the dialogue, and the way the world looks -- the way it makes you feel -- it's a thing of wonder.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:

I really wanted to love this. But I just couldn't.

- I never felt like the dialogue options made enough of a difference.
- The plot points essential to the story's main twist weren't conveyed clearly enough, so that the surprise reveal was more confusing than surprising.
- Technically, there were some major issues that constantly wrenched me out of the game: a noticeable audio cut out before dialogue played, lack of working Xbox One controller support, textures that looked bad at high resolution (2560x1440).
- The world felt strangely fake: getting stuck on bushes and invisible walls quickly got old. And where were all the animals you would find in Shoshone in real life? 

The visual direction was second to none - all the Olly Moss book covers were superb - and the audio was great too.

But all in all, a strange, compelling, beautiful letdown. I think it's something everyone should experience - but with tempered expectations.

First and foremost, this game is short (~3 hours) and it does feel like you're not getting enough game for your money, even at the current sale price of $18.  With that said, the absolutely wonderful voice acting and stunning, though stylized, graphics create a memorable scene.  Without spoiling anything, this game does not re-create the adventure genre except for showing how good voice talent and a novel locale can create a great and interesting story.  While the game was only 3 hours long, I was completely enthralled in the story from start to finish.  The character's feelings - paranoia, loneliness, love, regret, anger - were not just communicated well, but you literally feel the same emotions as you play the game.  Couple this with the truly beautiful location and the uniquness of the location and theme (the idea of an isolated firewatch tower is amazing!) and you have an absolutely wonderful story from a new developer.  But... the game does leave you wanting more.  All in all the story has a sad ending and leaves you a little underwhelmed, as the ending focuses more on the mystery within the game rather than the relationship built between the two main characters.  The gameplay could also be more in-depth and choices do feel empty other than changing the banter over the radio, especially since they do little, if anything, to impact the game's ending.  With all that aside, it is the story that makes this game and if it were a move, it would be a box office hit!

Firewatch is a beautiful game in more than one meaning of the word. It looks very good as well though. If story-driven, narrative-focused experiences are even a little for you, try this game. If not, you should probably try it anyway. 
Firewatch puts you into the Wyoming wilderness as a watcher in a lookout, whose job it is to report problems such as fires. Hence the name. Suffice to say, this is not, where the story ends. The game will draw you into an engaging story told only via environmental story-telling of the best kind and conversations you as the protagonist have with your chef in another tower not too far from yours via radio. The voice-acting is brilliant throughout the whole experience and easily counts as one of the best I have ever witnessed in a videogame so far. Firewatch is a game that sold itself to me primarily on the amazing aesthetics, and I ended up going into it almost entirely blind. This turned out to be a furtunate decision, and I thoroughly enjoyed playing it over a bit less than 4 hours, having had few expectations going in. And for the first time in a long time, I did another playthrough of a game very shortly after finishing it (clocking in another 3 hours), in order to see what I had missed the first time around.

Briefly, Firewatch is a narrative game centering around two people, one of whom is the protagonist, Henry, who has taken the job to monitor for the presence of fires in the Shoshone National Forest, from atop a guard tower. The main gameplay element, and the major draw, is the radio that Henry carries during his duties, which connects him with the second major character, his supervisor Delilah. Delilah not only gives Henry tasks to complete, typically involving longer or short trips into the wilderness, but also grows to be a close and familiar presence to both Henry and the player, and their interactions form the backbone of the game. During their interactions, the player has the option of choosing between various responses, or even no response, shaping the narrative between the two. I found this aspect of the game to be incredibly well done, thanks to a great script and the fantastic voice acting performed for both characters. The game is further underlined by an incredible soundtrack, which I found to fit the story and the setting very well, and which makes for great listening on its own.

However, as the narrative is the backbone of the game, more gamey elements take a backseat. There are very minor puzzle elements, and some minor "collectibles" which allow you to learn about some secondary characters, but these take the back-seat to the narrative between Henry and Delilah. Fortunately, I would argue, as the game would not have been any better in my eyes had it included an abundance of such elements. If I have to make one criticism, it would be that the game could have benefitted from a bit more time spent fleshing out the relationship between Delilah and Henry, before the plot gains steam.

Finally, while some were apparently disappointed by the ending, I will say that I am not among those. In fact, now that I know the full scope of the story, I was eager to play the game again, to reshape the narrative (in some ways) compared to my last play-through, and to see what hints, clues, and [spoiler]turtles[/spoiler] I missed the first time around. Indeed, playing the game again provided answers to several questions that I had missed during my first playthrough, and revealed additional background information thanks to different dialogue choices, though I did find that this also revealed that certain parts of the conversation were not as flexible as I had hoped. Still, for me, both the game and the soundtrack was worth every cent, and worth playing through twice.


A final recommendation before I finish: By default the game will show your exact location on the map, and pop up notifications when your objective changes. It is, however, possible to turn both of these features off, and I would strongly urge anyone playing Firewatch to do so, as this makes for a much more immersive experience. Furthermore, I would also recommend playing with head-phones, to enhance the already great sound-design, both in terms of the environmental audio and the music.

After having tried and subsequently dropped several gaming podcasts, years ago already I came to the conclusion that Idle Thumbs is second to none. Their unique mix of thoughtful silliness is a joy, and after playing The Walking Dead: Season One (with two regular Thumbs hosts handling the writing), I became convinced they could make great games as well.

Since leaving Telltale Games behind, Firewatch is their first shot at a true independent title with characters of their own creation. I carefully kept myself unspoiled of all but the most general information about the game, and waited. One of the biggest questions in my mind was, why would anyone take a job as a fire watch in the middle of nowhere in the first place?

Fortunately, this is the question the game is most interested as well. Taking place during a hot Wyoming summer during the eighties, Firewatch focuses on its characters. You play as Henry, a newcomer to the forest preservation job. You get to know him and his boss Delilah, who has her own watchtower miles away, through extensive discussions held over the ether via Walkie-Talkies.

Or rather, you might get to know yourself. Firewatch is mostly a story-based game, and only fits the adventure genre in the loosest, non-puzzley definition possible. Like a few other indie games such as Kentucky Route Zero and Oxenfree, Firewatch gives you a lot of freedom over the direction of the discussions, mood and the general relationship between the two main characters, but the story beats always stay the same.

In other words, there's no right or wrong way to play. The way you handle conversations is really more of a reflection of yourself than choosing the "correct" answer for every situation. The game tackles some weighty subjects such as guilt and responsibility, and has an unhurried, melancholic vibe running throughout. In the end, it's more of a character study than anything else.

And I have to say, the writing, graphics and music are all really good here. However, despite its beauty, techically Firewatch isn't the greatest and you can really feel Unity creaking at its seams at times. Some of the gameplay mechanics, such as picking up and examining objects, also feel completely superfluous and can only be explained by the developers' irrational and misguided love for Far Cry 2.

Overall, I quite enjoyed Firewatch. I wouldn't call it a masterpiece by any stretch, but it is a really strong first effort from Campo Santo and a game that could only have been made by an indie studio. After the credits rolled, the foremost feeling I had was a strange, lingering hollowness. But I think that's the point.
