I began playing the game thinking it was not as good as The Long Dark… because of the scenery, you know? The scenery is great, but TLD is more so. But, as I played I soon realized it was nothing like TLD. Firewatch is unlike any game I’ve played. It is not like the text-based choice games I’ve played, and as one of my friends said, it’s not like the Tell-tale games. And, that reticle! It’s in your view from the time the game starts, until the end.
I’d classify it as an adventure mystery game. It’s totally uncontrived. Everything you do and explore involves real-world exploration activities you might find in that environment, like in Stanley’s Parable. Instead of contrived puzzles, most of the game is spent using a map and a compass to navigate around a series of paths through a State Forest in Wyoming. 
The dialogue is sensitive, and besides the f-bombs sprinkled throughout, various topics such as suicide are discussed. So it is not really a game for younger players. The dialogue uses quite a bit of foreshadowing. Their world is outside the real world, disassociated and cut off from phone lines. At times you are not sure whether to trust either character. But, you soon realize they both feel cut-off from the world; Henry by his wife’s loss of awareness, and Delilah by her inability to attach.
If you like mysteries, if you enjoy dialogue and rich story interactivity, if you ever took trips using a map and compass, or just wish you could; this game is probably for you. However, the game has numerous issues that may be problematic in the eyes of some “gamers.” I will be giving some spoilers, so you may choose to not read the rest of my review until after you’ve played the game. 
Henry’s wife is a college prof diagnosed with early onset Dementia. For various reasons he runs away from dealing with this, and ends up in the forest watching for fires. It seems he can’t deal with the loss of self-identity more than anything. While there, he falls into a routine of a radio conversation/romance with Delilah, another Firewatcher. It’s a definite source of comfort to him. But, he’s dealing with a lot of guilt over his wife who is living with her family back home. Ultimately he abandoned her. He has a run-in with some college girls/teens who are shooting off fireworks and skinny-dipping in the lake. One refers to him as just “a sad old man in the woods,” which hurts his feelings and tends to lead you to believe the girls are grad students and are recording their conversations and studying them. That never panned out in the ending I got.
I felt the graphics were very well done, the drawing was beautiful, and the game played well, though it was quite linear. The mechanics were fun, and not forced. But most of the issues I found related to the story. Actually, I saw what I thought was a spoiler in the forum before the game was released. Some guy randomly announced that everything that happened was a figment of Henry’s imagination and that Delilah was not real. I was disappointed to have it spoiled before I even played, but soon found out I came up with a very different ending than that. I asked a few friends who played the game, and they all got the same ending I got. It certainly seemed to me that there were certain “collection points” where regardless of how you chose your answers, you were pulled back into the same story line with everyone else. 
Sometimes, things happened the opposite of what you had chosen. For example, I told Deliah to go ahead and go when she asked if I minded. A friend told her to wait on him. In both games, she was gone when we got to her tower at the end of the game. It didn’t really seem to matter what you chose to say to her.  In the words of another friend, it seems that little things change, like how you describe yourself or dialog. (Thanks James!)  I would have preferred choices to make major changes in the endings.
Another issue I had with the story is that everything points you to conspiracy theories… the allusion to JFK on the cover of one book; the whole idea of government sponsored tests using radio signals, like with HAARP; and the mentions of Ronald Reagan’s policy of dealing (or not dealing) with forest fires.
So, there are a lot of easter eggs “littered” throughout the story… literally. Primarily, there are books skewed about everywhere you go, and the titles seem suggestive, if not a little familiar. But, only one had a name that I recognized for sure… Jane Eyre by Charlotte Bronte. I believe most of the others were fake books to give hints the storywriter wanted to use to lead your thinking in a certain direction… toward conspiracy theories. 
There were a number of books around the map by a Richard Sturgeon, who I’ve never heard of, but they all have numbers in their titles. Death Strikes at Two, Eight Rolled the Hard Way, The Fourth Estate, Terminal 7, One Chance to Die, Three Blind Rats, and Five Degrees North. 
Of course, the 4th estate is a term used in America to describe the media. Eight rolled the hard way would be rolling eight in a game of craps without getting doubles. It’s considered a hard roll, because there is only one way to roll it. The rest, your guess is as good as mine. 
Other books found include: The Singular Mind –Jonas Allard, Glory – Michelle MacManus, The Birds of Wyoming – George Sinclair, The Patriots – Donald Anderson, The Accidental Savior – Terrence Greenbriar, Jane Eyre- Charlotte Bronte and Black Band Comics. 
Notice that Jane Eyre is definitely a real book, though I’m not sure about the others. In Jane Eyre, the lead male character has a “crazy wife” who he has locked away and basically abandoned. He is trying to remarry, and experiences much guilt over this, much as Henry feels guilty over abandoning his wife in the game. Also, Delilah seems slippery, much like Jane Eyre, seeming to turn Henry away in the end, suggesting he go see his wife. 
There were other things scattered throughout that seemed suggestive, but were certainly loose ends. The “Escape from Two Orcs Map” seemed to lead you to the idea that some evil force lurked in the forest. The Polyhedral dice (d20) similar to those from Dungeons & Dragons games only showed Bryan liked fantasy stories. Like the FireFinder  and Medicine Wheel, they just seemed to be included for atmosphere, perhaps to lend a reason for loving the forest, which goes up in blazes in a very dramatic conclusion. 
Many of the days are skipped automatically. To thoroughly explore all the items found in every location, you have to ignore the mission mentioned in the map until you are finished looking at everything. Otherwise you will jump ahead to the next day in the sequence.
It has a sad ending, and feels hollow. But, it plays beautifully, and you feel engaged throughout. There are a few additional features, like an in-game camera that will provide actual prints of the photos you take. I did not feel the need to buy the sound track in this game, though the music is nice.  I just felt it wasn’t used in the game very much. The sounds were mostly nature ambient sounds. 
I felt like the pieces were left unresolved. But, I would definitely play it again, simply because it was a lot of fun playing, and the conversations between characters (who you never see) are so real and personal, in a way that few other narrative games approach. It is certainly not an “Answers” story.
With all of that said, I do highly recommend the game. I loved it and spent a lot of time playing it. Most gamers seem to be completing it in just 3 to five hours. I spent over 20. But, I do not consider myself the average gamer. For all the reasons I mentioned, I think Firewatch may be more of a niche game with awesome graphics.

Firewatch was a truly powerful journey for me thanks to how easily and quickly I became invested into Henry, his life and feelings. The day Firewatch came out, I watched the first 15 minutes of gameplay that IGN put out with my little brother. I immedietly fell in love with the look of the game and bought it when I realized it was out.

So, let's preface this review with the main thing I see other people criticizing the game on: it IS a short game, I got through the whole game in about 4.5 hours. If I new what do do and just did it as fast I could, I probably could have done it shorter than that, but there were also times when I just wanted to explore the area's because I thought it was very inviting.  A lot of people would have issues dropping ~$20 on a 3-5 hour game, and I definitely understand that, if I knew that before going into the game I would have been very hesitant to get it as well.  However, after buying and playing the game I would 100% recommend playing through it.

This game has such a fantastic atmosphere about it, the graphics combined with the magnificent soundtrack make for a very very calming hike through the forests during the day, and a stressful spelunking session when you're deep into a cave.  The voice acting was better than I've seen in a lot of more recent games and I thought the dialogue, and it's choices, were fairly well written.  The interactions between Henry (yourself) and Delilah (the other lookout), range between semi-witty banter, bad puns, and deep conversations.  It does feel like there is a connection between the two characters.

I won't go into the story a bunch, since it is a story driving game and I don't want to spoil it for anyone. The story is interesting and captivating and get's very suspenseful.  The game takes you through this entire make trying to solve what's happening all while you have to look out for fires during the hot and dry Wyoming summer.  The story isn't extremely complicated or anything like that, but it's captivating and well thought out and worded and that's really what drew me into the game.

There isn't much I can say negative wise about the game, other than it's length. And honestly that isn't even a huge deal to me, just to some other people.

TL;DR

All in all, Firewatch is a fantastic game for people who want a game that is strongly story driven, has great voice acting, features no combat, and lets you explore the world; or any one of the four.  If you've got the money and it's available I would highly recommend getting it and playing through it, and if you're a little hesitant on buy it just wait till it's on sale.

Most games are about gameplay, action and/or violence but there a few games that attempt to make the story the main focus; this is one of those games. If you mix that up with some fantastic art and visual design and add up to that some of the most credible, realistic and better performed dialogue ever on a video game, you get an amazing game that can stand on it's own, even if the gameplay it's not innovative at all to the point of just being there to not make this game another 'Telltale-esque' game. To provide some sort of dynamic interaction with the player.

Performance-wise; I ran this game mostly fine with my GTX 970M laptop 1080p at ultra settings. There were some specific areas with some fps degrading always ocurring. Most of the time though, the game stayed at 60 fps. The game isn't as light on the hardware as you might think, the sound of the vents on my laptop while playing it are a sign of that. Also, during the last hour of the game, I experienced this issue when the audio was lagging when a new radio message arrived or a new line of dialogue was starting play. It was like a less-than a second lag, it didn't really ruin the experience but this should definitely be fixed. I restarted the game from the beginning after finishing it and the issue was not there. When I loaded my previous save from my first playthrough, the issue occured like it did before. All of this after 2 patchs in less that 3 days. 

Firewatch is a game aimed mostly at adult gamers. People that are expecting scare-jumps and extreme violence can pass up this one. The plot tries to be as realistic as possible. Sadly, I enjoyed the whole trip but not it's conclusion. They made everything so credible and real, including the ending; that when the credits roll it felt that the way they ended things was  mundane and just completely passive. The commitment to keep that neutrality towards violence and paranormal elements probably was what leads to this ending. Probably I'm used to big endings with explosions and incredible revelations. It's not that the ending is bad, it's just that the trip to get to it was so good that the way everything concludes feels uninspired.

The 4 hours, and around 30 minutes prior to the conclusion of the story though have to be some of the most memorable hours I've spent playing a videogame in recent memory. Yeah, the game is short, that's a fact. How long is the longest movie you've watched? 2 hours at best? Which was the longest not MP game that you have played? Hundreds of hours long, isn't that right? Hundreds of hours repeating gameplay elements again and again. Firewatch grants 5 hours of originality that become precious time that will be gone in a flash. 

I would definitely recommend this game to everyone that's looking for a mature game. Although, like I said before, the ending didn't impress me, everything else did, and a lot. Props to the developers for trying something different and succeding at it. The game isn't perfect by any stretch, but it is indeed an excellent game that deserves to be played. Just... Firewatch is a beautiful game, if judged by it's artistic craft alone it's the best in years at delivering great environmental feel.  The visuals and audio tie together so well it really brings you as close as you can be to video game wilderness outside of a VR headset.

The voice acting is well done, Henry and Delilah bring their lines to life and speak with a great cadence of back and forth banter.  Henry is a believable rookie while Delilah is a seasoned veteran of professional firewatch crew.

The place where this all unravels is the narrative.  The game funnels you to multiple story beats through its four hour experience without the grace or natural feeling that the visuals and voice work provide.

Great little game unlike anything else I have played.  I was a little hesitant to buy it after reading many reviews criticizing the  length of the game and the ending.  I think those two points are valid to bring up, but I don't necessarily see them as negatives after playing through the game.

The overall visual and audible design of this game is fantastic.  As someone who has spent time in various national forests in the NW corner of the US, the designers really nailed the overall feel of a hot forest in the middle of summer.  The environment of the game becomes another character in the story, and it is dynamic and vibrant.  The homebase of the watchtower was really detailed well, and there always seems to be something to look at.  It didn't feel like a lot of indie games where environments are sparse and minimally populated with objects; it actually feels like a digital snapshot of a real place.  I also enjoyed the "collector" aspect, where if you decide to gather various objects during gameplay, they show up in your tower on subsequent days as though you placed them there.  While the visual aspect of the game is somewhat stylized, somehow it is also very realistic, which I don't quite undertstand how they pulled off.  The voice acting is just about as good as it gets, and the dialogue is really well thought out.

The storyline is where some users have a problem, and I can kind of understand.  I am comfortable with the fact that this game is going for a realistic story as opposed to a fantastic action-packed thrill ride which we are used to in games.  This is not that, it is a well-written mature story.  I don't think the audience for this sort of thing will be as huge as that for a Just Cause or Fallout, but it definitely has a strong place in gaming as the first and second generation gamers find themselves with graying hair and less of an interest in beam weapons and levelling up.  I still love those games, but I also love this one.  This game has its moments of excitement, but don't expect an edge-of-your-seat experience.  It is understated and realistic.  I hate to equate it to "mumblecore" films, as that is a polarizing genre, but I appreciate it in the same way I like some of those films.

The game is short, no doubt about it.  $20 may be a lot for some to spend on a game that can be completed in several sessions.  I will probably not play through the game again, as I took the time to check out everything I could on my first playthrough.  I know there are some things I did not see, and the developers have said that you will not see everything on the first playthrough, but I feel satisfied with my brief journey through this world.  As far as the price, I am alright with dropping a 20 on a game like this as I see it as an investment in both the company that made this, as well as a kind of new branch of gaming that I hope to see expand in the future.  

So, I don't think everyone on Steam will enjoy this game, but I do think it should have a large enough audience to be a viable game, and hopefully a viable genre.

[b][i]Firewatch[/i] is a great walking simulator. So great, in fact, that many gamers (including myself) at times wanted it to breach the walls and actually have more 'gaming' elements.[/b] This game really has the whole package; the artwork, music, voice acting, animation and atmosphere are all expertly crafted. The storyline is moving, to say the least.

[i]The two major shortcomings in my mind are 1) the game is quite short (3 hours to 'finish' the story), and 2) there is little replay value.[/i] I will elaborate on both.

Although the twenty dollar price tag has become fairly standard for quality walking simulators (a la [i]Gone Home[/i] or [i]Dear Esther[/i], among others), you only get a measly few hours of enjoyment out of it. The hours are top quality, though. After I was done, I kept asking myself why they couldn't have added in more achievements or side quests to fill out the time and add more incentive to replay. Sure, there are little 'easter eggs' of sorts littered throughout the map, but its certainly not enough for me to justify the large-ish price tag. [b]Achievements would incentivize this; for example, I earned all the achievements in my first 3 hour playthrough.[/b]

[i]Beyond that, everything is great. The story is wonderful and the experience is divine. [/i] Just realize that this is a walking simulator proper. They may tease you with finding an axe, but there is no game here. Thats ok, but I think some of us wanted it to go to that next level.

It was most likely created to be a short experience on purpose, though. For example, while the map feels large and sandboxy at first, it quickly shows that it is quite limited. Once again, thats ok, but it merits being mentioned. The map is not as open-world as it may have us think. Its a series of 'tunnels'. Very beautiful tunnels.

Yes this game is short (about 3-4 hours give or take depending on how much exploring you do).

No there's not any replayability - unless you want to hear every dialogue combination choice.

Yes the ending is very anti-climactic and very limited.

But the journey is amazing!

-  The dialogue between yourself and Delilah is very engaging and eventhough you never see her and she's just a voice coming from a handheld walkie-talkie, she comes across as a very real person.  When you're in your tower talking to her over the radio you can't help but look over to her tower too and imagine that she's looking back at your tower as the two of you converse.  And given that there are no other characters in the game to interact with (except the two girls in your first "mission"), for Delilah's voice to be enough to make the game feel "populated" just shows how excellent the dialogue and scriptwriting between yourself and her really is.

-  As the mystery deepens you find yourself not wanting to stop playing because you just [i]have[/i] to know what happens next, you [i]have[/i] to find out what's going on.  You're fixated on the story all the way to the end (which is probably why so many people find the ending so unsatisfying - they were [b][i]THAT[/i][/b] hooked into the story).

-  The environment is beautiful.  Lighting and shadows feel perfect.  The wide open space, the great soundtrack, the solitude...it really does feel like hiking through a national reserve.  And the colours...when the fire breaks out and the entire environment is an orange hue, I really did feel like the air was scorching dry!

And despite its failings (with an ending that really went nowhere, a very short game, lack of replayability, and a lack of multiple endings where your decisions matter), I really enjoyed experiencing this game.  I really think the developers would have learned a lot with this game and definitely look forward to what else they produce in the future.

Would I pay $20 for game that offers no challenge, is quick to finish, has a flat ending in relation to its story, and offers no chance to play again to try other things?  Probably not.

But would I pay $20 to watch a 3-hour long mystery story with tension and emotion, with engaging characters you empathise with who have witty, intelligent banter between them?  Yeah I think I would.

Longform review:

Firewatch easily reminds me the most of Gone Home if you approach it purely from a technical aspect. The entirety of the game consists of moving place to place, examining objects and easily runs less than 3.5 hours if you're trying your hardest to speed throught it. The idea isn't that it's a game, but a story you minorly shape. Through literal choices in the opening to dialogue between Henry and Delilah, you affect who Henry is as a person, and what type of relationship he forms with Delilah. But this isn't a roleplaying game, you don't choose branching paths, and some people might take issue with this if they're expecting something more. If you want a well written story about adults dealing with adult problems, you'll enjoy the game and most likely get your money's worth. For everyone else, just avoid it.

On a technical aspect there's some minor framehitching, shadow resolutions are horribly low in quite a few areas (even on Ultra) and you'll need a decent rig to play above 60 FPS on all the max settings. If you need frames desperately, SSAO should be the first thing you disable. Personally I turned it off even though I could afford it, mostly because I'm not a fan of the effect anyway. There are a LOT of issues regarding keybinding, you cannot bind a key already bound (so customizing them is a chore) and there's no confirmation upon selecting them making it more cumbersome than it needed to be. Other than these issues the game ran perfectly fine with no crashes.

If you like story games, buy it. If you don't, pass.

VERY MINOR SPOILERS BELOW

[spoiler]There is one thing to note, I've seen a LOT of complaints about the ending and while I don't think they're entirely unfounded do NOT go into this expecting a huge payoff. Part of the game's story is revolved around this, so if you're expecting something groundbreaking, don't. I found it a perfectly fitting ending, and while implausable (like, really implausible) the payoff was more than enough to satisfy me, but I can see people getting dissapointed because of how well the game builds up tension.[/spoiler]

My take on the first game by developer "Campo Santo" 

Since its initial announcement, I have been pretty stoked about giving "Firewatch" a try. And that is not because of the impressive developer cast behind the game, but because of the idea. After finally getting the chance to step into the hiking shoes of Henry, I was instantaneously blown away by the visuals. The way the Unity Engine is used to simulate the wilderness is something to behold. But don't let the beautiful cartoony exterior of the game fool you! Underneath it you will find well tuned gaming mechanics, which allow you to traverse the Wyoming wildes with ease. So far from a visual and navigational standpoint "Firewatch" is solid, but what about the story? 

The beginning sets a special tone that does not slowly ease you into the life of our protagonist, but on the contrary - it throws you in! While you are still trying to assimilate the predicament Henry is in, you find yourself atop of a watchtower in the middle of nowhere. As the player and the hero take in their new surroundings, the immersion intensifies itself by giving Henry a handheld radio with a voice on the other side - your supervisor Delilah. At this point you learn that not only does she speak, but your character does as well. This initial moment sets up the stage for the upcoming performance by the protagonist and the disembodied voice, as they try to protect the the wilderness from forest fires. This is immersive, because of the incredible voice acting by both actors portraying Henry and Delilah! During their talks the player controls the direction these conversations take and so he shapes Henrys personality, thus turning the player into his own version of the protagonist! 

The developers at "Campo Santo" have fused movement and storytelling mechanics with the visuals excellently, allowing for an immersive and emotional adventure, where you become your own unique Henry, while also forging a unique relationship with Delilah! Sadly we reach the ending quite abruptly, leaving us unsatisfied with the length and the conclusion to the story! 

This is a game that is all about the journey, not the destination! I suggest playing the game more than once, so you can experience different conversations between Henry and Delilah as you make your way through the Wyoming wilderness. During my second playthrough I found new and exciting areas I had missed, and managed to develop an interesting new relationship between our heroes.

In conclusion - I give "Firewatch" a very high recommendation for all fans of interactive storytelling games (or oldschool fans of the choose your own adventure books, like me).

Firewatch is a beautifully crafted narrative-driven game, where you are wandering around in the woods, explore the scenery and follow the story.

You are playing Henry, a man struggling with what happened in his life (which gets told via a short, multiple choice story at the beginning) who is "escaping" to a summer job as a fire watcher on a lookout in the woods.
After arriving, you get to know Delilah, your boss, via walkie talkie, who then sends you out to check on some happenings in the woods.

The story itself is nice to follow, it's very grounded and doesn't contain any supernatural stuff. But after around half of the game, it get's pretty suspensefull and thrilling.

The dialogues between Henry and Delilah and how they react to the happenings around them, is what breathes life into the game. They exchange humorous, sometimes sad or emotional stories and are very likable characters.

Often, you'll get to choose which answer to give to Delilah, or if you want to say nothing at all. Depending on that, the dialogues might differ and/or you'll hear something which you wouldn't if you had chosen another answer.
Though this won't change the outcome of the game, the story is very linear, but you'll also have time to walk around and explore every corner of the woods if you like.

Gameplay-wise there is not much to do, there are some objects throughout the game you can inspect, some others you can take with you (and very few of them are actually necessary to advance the plot - but those are not missable).
Even exploring is not always that interesting, of course, sometimes you stumble upon something you can talk to Delilah about, but there are few things to interact with/talk about with her.

Though i liked the beauty of nature and the atmosphere quite a lot.
Which brings me to the graphics: They are pretty colorful, beautiful and comic-like and the created atmosphere is sometimes breathtaking.
The paths through the forest and canyons are rather linear, with different trails to walk or climb, mixed with some more open areas where you can stroll around.

Overall it doesn't take that much time, to finish the game. If you go through the game with rather little exploration and run from time to time, i'd say you'll need around 4 hours to finish.

I'd recommend this to you, if you like games which have a focus on characters, atmosphere and story, rather than gameplay mechanics.

[i]Firewatch[/i] will not be for everyone, but I loved it and would recommend it to adult gamers who are interested in good characters and stories. I would also recommend it to people who usually prefer books. Clocking in at about four to five hours of gameplay, [i]Firewatch[/i] is a walking novella and feels a lot like the game equivalent of a [url=http://www.britannica.com/biography/Raymond-Carver]Raymond Carver[/url] short story.

Understand that while there are things to do in this game, it is not a "doing" game. People looking for tons of action and the ability to explore an open world should look elsewhere. It's a "thinking" game—not in a puzzle-heavy sense, but philosophically. It has similarities to other novella-like games, such as [i]Dear Esther[/i] and [i]Gone Home[/i]. (There is even [url=https://twitter.com/iamfantastikate/status/697261856432361472]a nice little [i]Gone Home[/i] Easter egg[/url].) [i]Firewatch[/i] is all about—maybe [i]only[/i] about—the beautiful world and the story within. 

* People who "get" and like literature will appreciate [i]Firewatch[/i] more than those who don't.
* The story is small, almost a [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slice_of_life]slice of life[/url]. It's meant to be. It's not a mistake. 

[h1]Story and Setting[/h1]
It's 1989, and Henry (voiced by [url=http://www.imdb.com/name/nm1360860/]Rich Sommer[/url] of [i]Mad Men[/i] fame) and Delilah ([url=http://www.imdb.com/name/nm4047315/?ref_=fn_al_nm_1]Cissy Jones[/url] from [i]The Walking Dead[/i], [i]The Wolf Among Us[/i], and a host of other games) have taken jobs in Wyoming's Shoshone National Forest as an escape from their individual realities. In the lonely quietude, they find in each other an acceptance that isn't always easy to come by. It helps that they have no real responsibilities to each other outside of their jobs. They don't see each other face-to-face; a radio is their only regular form of communication. In the wilderness, there is no one around to judge them, and they can focus on each other and the tasks at hand. It's a deliciously selfish reprieve from "real life"—much like gaming, actually. And yet their tasks become increasingly unnerving as mysterious things start happening, deep in the forest. 

* The music is great, and I enjoy how it only plays on occasion. It's fun listening to the nature sounds. 
* The world is gorgeous, and the way Campo Santo directs players is clever. [i]Firewatch[/i] is a very closed world, but the wilderness environment makes navigation feel oddly natural and open.
* The opening to the game is a nod to text-based adventure games and sets the literary tone.

[u]A "Mature" Game[/u]
[i]Firewatch[/i] is one of only a few games I would call "adult." (I'm inclined to include games like [i]The Talos Principle[/i] in such a list, but they're of a different gameplay style.) By adult, I don't mean the game has swear words, though it does, or innuendo and nudity, though it has those things, too. I mean that nearly all of the characters mentioned are well over the age of 35 and—without spoiling anything—have dealt with Real Adult Sh^t. 

This makes [i]Firewatch[/i] different from similar games like, say, [i]Gone Home[/i] or [i]Life Is Strange[/i], which have young adult, coming of age stories that adults can certainly relate to, but only, to some degree, by looking back on their past. I don't mean to say adventure games or stories that focus on young adults aren't "deep." They can be. I [i]like[/i] some YA fiction. I just mean they're focused on feelings and conflicts specific to adolescence and early adulthood. They are not often about issues found in adulthood, like relationships between individuals with decades of baggage between them, the difficulties of parenthood, or what to do with a loved one who falls ill. But [i]Firewatch[/i] is such a story, which is refreshing. 

* I suspect people who are 25 and older will appreciate this game a lot more than teens and dorm dwellers. This is okay!
* With regard to the ending: [spoiler]Not every story has to be prettily beribboned with a happily-ever-after or even an unhappily-ever-after. Not every story is here to coddle its readers/players.[/spoiler]

[h1]Sacrificing Replayability and Player Freedom to Create Complex Characters[/h1]
There is probably little to no replayability to [i]Firewatch[/i], but I don't count this against it. Not every game must be replayable. Part of what I really like about this game is that it [i]doesn't[/i] go for the bigger story that might allow for replayability. Some will always want that story—no matter how many times it is (awkwardly) fed to us—and will be upset when they don't get it here. But by choosing the narrative path they do, Campo Santo is able to offer much better characterization for those who are interested in it.

Choices do not make much difference in [i]Firewatch[/i], other than to add some (very) limited personality alterations to dialogue exchanges. The fact that the player doesn't get to tinker with the characterization too much is why the characters are good and, above all, [i]sound natural[/i]. The thing about those bigger, replayable games with more open worlds, harder choices, and additional dialogue options is that it is difficult to control characterization in them. Games like [i]The Walking Dead[/i] do an admirable job of it, but you'd be hard-pressed not to laugh when a dialogue tree doesn't quite go as planned or when a character does something completely contrary to the characterization selections you've previously made. By limiting options and foregoing some or all replayability, games like [i]Firewatch[/i] and [i]Dear Esther[/i] are able to delve more deeply into their themes and characters. To some, that will mean [i]Firewatch[/i] isn't really a game or isn't worth what you pay for it. To others, it will seem like a work of art.

[h1]Price[/h1]
[i]Firewatch[/i] takes about four to five hours to play. In other words, each hour of gameplay costs about $5, give or take a little. It's not a bad deal, so it's sad to see people complaining about it. If anyone wants to know why creatives "starve," it's because some people think they should get hours of entertainment for $5-10, max.

The game puts you in the shoes of Hank/Henry, a man who's wife was diagnosed with early onset dementia. You attempt to work through it, take care of her, but the burden becomes too much. The game is all performed in a first person perspective, full body for maximum immersion. You look down, you got legs. You're greeted over the radio by your boss Delilah, who you end up forming quite the emotional bond with. You will laugh, you might cry, you'll feel the tugs a normal relationship comes with, including possibly upsetting her and causing her to step away for a few. Let me start off by saying that yes, asking £10-15, $10-20 for a game that lasts no longer than 5 hours, is a little much.
But I prefer quality over quantity, what this game gives, is most certainly quality.
I have seen disastrous games that have cost more than the asking price of this game.

Now let me highlight the Pros and Cons of this title.

Pros:

-Graphics:
It is not the most stunning looking game ever made, but it is still beautiful nonetheless.

-Music:
The music that accompanies you throughout your journey does make the experience all the more enjoyable, all music relevent to the game style. It's relaxing and soothing to your ears. (I also bought the soundtrack and am currently listening to this while writing this review.)

-Voice Acting:
I hope the voice actors for this game got paid good enough, because honestly, the voice acting is one of the best I have ever heard. The voices were clear, some of the dialogue is extraordinary; funny, childish, playful, emotional, sad, happy etc. I think this is one of the keypoints that make this game remarkable.

-Ambience:
From the music to the little whistles of the wind blowing between the trees, every sound gives you the feeling of being in the game, from the echos in the cave to the sounds of your footsteps. This is also one of the keypoints of this game. 

-Storyline:
It was well thought out and implemented, every new discovery left me wanting to keep on going and carry on until I finished it. Again, without the voice actors, the storyline wouldn't have been as interesting. I never felt lost with the storyline.

These are only just some of the Pros.
Now for the Cons;

-Length & Price: (THE MAIN CON)
Again, this game lasted only 3-4 hours for me and that was a HUGE drawback. If they had increased the length of the game, it would be absolutely sensational. But they either ran out of budget or ideas. Also It's priced too steeply for what it is. 

-Graphics:
Like I said previously, this is not the most visually stunning title to date, but it is still beautiful nonetheless. For example. Every object (or mostly every object) in the game has a beautiful and realistic shadow, but then you look at your characters shadow, just a mere blob on the ground.
And sometimes I'd see the occational screen tear (with v-sync turned on)  

-Gameplay:
Some points in this game had me questioning was doing this (or that) really worth it? Or was it something they just included to lengthen the gameplay by another 5 minutes, for instance, my curiosity got the better of me and I opened every cache box and some of them had either nothing or nothing of relevance. The flashlight, for instance, was not needed AT ALL. I had the brightness set on default for the entirety of the game, it was bright enough for me to see without the flashlight, I used it when I first entered the cave and noticed I didn't need it, so I kept it off for the rest of the game. 

Those were only some of the drawbacks I could think of.

Conclusion:
It's a well designed game that had serious, SERIOUS potential, but the length of it let it down.

Would I still recommend buying it? Depends, do you prefer a voice acted driven short storyline game with beautiful, yet simple graphics? Yes, by all means purchase it. Or do you prefer a lengthy storyline game, accompanied with tedious side quests that have no relevance with the main storyline, but play it purely because of the hours you can pump into it and it's replay value? Then no, avoid at all costs. 

But let me say again, for the last time. The voice actors are the main attraction of this game. Where ever they are and if you happen to read this, you did a f****** FANTASTIC job. And I pray to god that they release a sequel or something after the events. Because after finishing the game, I almost had tears to my eyes. I want to know what happens to Henry and everyone else in the game. 
But please, for the love of all thats holy, make it longer than an episode of mythbusters. 

PEACE!!!!!

The game is a "walking simulator" mystery set in an absolutely stunning national park: each day seems to have a different colour to it, and the mountains are a starkly beautiful backdrop. Henry and Delilah are entirely realistic people who you find yourself caring for, and the story is one you will want to see through to the end.

It's true that your actions are almost negligible to the story - this is a narrative experience all the way. The story weaves itself as you wander around, and the actions you take are just a way to be a part of the story and immerse yourself into Henry's character. Do you pick up trash left by visitors to the park? Do you retaliate when people are rude to you? Do you respond to Delilah's sarcasm with friendliness or detached silence? It's all about shaping your experience of the story.

I see a lot of people complaining about this game. "It's too short" or "Its just a walking simulator...". I feel that the people whom express these opinions are the same kind of folk who buy a V8 Mustang for the performance, and then complain about the gas mileage, and build quality. 

Lets put this out on the table right from the start, between press for the game, and what we've heard from Campo Santo this game from day 1 was very blatantly marketed as a story driven exploration game. This isn't Call of Duty, nor is it ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Destiny. There is, nor was there ever a mention of a multiplayer, so if you want to bicker about the lack of replay value you might want to re-evaluate the kinds of games you play.

Campo Santo, I applaud you for taking the chance that you did with Firewatch. The older I get the more I begin to appreciate games that are written so damn well. Firewatch is the latest, and I'd certainly say one of the best in the genre of "walking simulator" adventure/narrative games. I'd very easily put it up there with other standouts like Dear Esther or The Stanley Parable. Though, as with any game, it has its share of shortcomings.

The visuals are incredibly impressive, with endless screenshot opportunities that would make for beautiful wallpapers. The voice acting is about as good as I could possibly expect, and it along with the writing make for what is probably the most natural dialogue I've heard in a game. The two main characters that do the brunt of the talking in the game are really believable, have great chemistry, and will really draw you into the game. What will also draw you in is the great atmosphere. There's a lot of potential for optional exploration on the fairly large map, but the game is a largely linear affair, with a pretty clear point A to point B objective at any given time. Even still, the game world is beautifully realized and the story so well presented and so intriguing, that you can very easily get completely absorbed in the whole presentation. 

However, I'd honestly say much of the intrigue the story builds into actually does the game a disservice on the whole. You'll see many reviews criticize the game for two major things: the length (which is short, with my completion time sitting around 5 hours, with a decent bit of exploration and sight seeing, though not exceptionally so for this genre), and the ending. I fully agree that the ending is not nearly as satisfying as I'd hoped, but I think much of the reason for that is that I feel the story takes a wrong turn midway through. The mystery and intrigue is very satisfying and very well presented, but the game's ending falls flat as a conclusion to that mystery. 

The thing is, after being initially let down, but reflecting on it a bit, I think it's pretty clear that the game was always intended to be, from start to finish, a deep character study of a man and a woman, who had been through some hard times in their lives, and came to a remote place to escape from their problems, and to that end, a detailed look at their relationship with one another. And in that sense, I'd say the game is a huge success all the way through. The mystery sub-plot is really just that, a sub-plot. Unfortunately, it's one that was maybe given too much attention and I'd say written and presented a little too well, as odd as that might sound. It ends up overshadowing what feels like the actual intended focus of the story, and thus, makes the ending feel hollow and disappointing.

So, Firewatch is certainly not a perfect game, and isn't totally successful, but all things considered, I'm extremely happy I played it, and definitely hold it in high regard as far as narrative games go. I look forward to what Campo Santo has in store for us in the future, if this is their first attempt as a studio.

Summary (TLDR): Firewatch presents a fantasitc interactive story of sorts driven by vivid writing, voice acting and gorgous art direction worth the $20 (or less) purchase.  

Graphics: Stylized eye-candy everywhere, this is the first thing that hooked most of us that have played it by just looking at the screen shots and trailer alone.  

Gameplay: certainly in the "walking simultor" category which may not be for everyone.  It involves lots of hiking to various locations to progress the story or dialogue between Delilah and Henry.  There are some subtle varied tasks that occur to break this up such as climbing and decending tasks, attaching a rope to repel or searching an area for clues.  

Audio: The audio is superb from ambient sounds to the score that ocasionally pops up or the often mentioned spectacular voice acting.  The dialoge flows naturally leaving the player feeling highly connected to the characters, for me it even lead me to want to radio in every chance I had.

Writing(story): The narrative is engaging and well thought out, there is a fairly steady flow to the events and it has enough twists to leave you wanting to finish the game in one sitting.  Many have complained about the ending, in the big  picture of things I felt it was fitting because of how diverse the dialogue experience may have been.  (I didn't do a second play through to know about variety and choices in the larger scale of the story).  

Value: I purchased this game at the pre-order discount of 10% off for $17.99 USD.  I think this is a fantastic price for the quality of content even though the play through time is roughly 3-4 hours depending on how much you choose to explore and read/investigate.  Making a game is a far from easy task, nor is it cheap, especially for a small team so anything in the $20 or less range is typically a steal.  

So in a nutshell: if you don't mind games that are shorter and take the approach of an interactive store this is a great game for your collection.  If you like games like "Beginners Guide" or "Dear Ester" this is a perfect match for your interestests.

Four things to note, no spoilers:

1) The pictures you take with the camera you find can be retrieved later after the game. You don't need to use the camera to collect evidence; you just use it to remember your run after it's over. 

2) My favorite feature of the game was the radio control. You can only speak to your boss, who is the only other character in the game you ever interact with, by holding down the left Shift key and scrolling with the mouse, just as if you were holding down a button on a two-way radio.

3) You control how your relationship with your boss, Delilah, develops based on what you say to her and if you choose to talk to her or not. I suspect that players can work out a few different endings based on which conversation tracks you choose, or if you choose not to say things.

4) You only have so much time to respond to Delilah - and the amount of time you have changes depending on how sensitive the subject you're broaching is. If your hands are busy when you're rappelling or holding your map and compass at the same time, you'd better not ALSO be trying to have a serious conversation, or else you'll miss stuff.

OK, now for my actual review: I was transported by this game and immersed right from the start. It's very well written, the dialogue felt authentic and the voice acting was excellent. I felt that the story was powerful, moving and the ending was entirely appropriate.

Some have commented that they didn't feel the various elements of the story (particularly Henry's backstory and the events of the summer) had any real thematic connection, but I have to disagree. The character's dialogues were scripted perfectly and executed perfectly as well. I hope the voice actors that played the two main characers, Henry and Delilah, have a big future in the business. Back to the dialogue, the conversations between Henry and Delilah seemed like real, down to earth conversations that anyone would have with someone they've never met and are spending a period of time with. The two characters start to grow chemistry as the story moves along and become more and more comfortable with eachother. So to sum up what I'm saying, The characters just feel human. The conversations you have with Delilah seem so real you start to care for both characters and really hope that they achieve what they are trying to do. But my favorite part about this game was how it left you with so many questions after almost anybody said anything. There have been questions flowing through my mind since I finished the game, and I think that only time, and super fans who explore the lore and secrets of the game, will answer my questions. 
     Now I don't have the best PC so I had to turn down the graphics a lot (and by a lot, I mean everything on the lowest settings). But even then the art style of the whole game was amazing. It was a prettied up TF2 with a more polygonal look, and it worked, really well. The one problem I had with the video apsects of the game is the Motion Blur being on by default. As soon as I started I turned that off real quick because I was already feeling nauseous. Game devs stop putting motion blur in your games. The human eye hardly notices motion blur in real life. 
     This game does give you some travelling to do every now and then but its not too bad. The map is pretty small, which it should be because its a linear story, but even when you need to travel there is always something to find on your way there to report to Delilah about and hear their interesting conversations. The game was very exciting throughout until the ending. Now we all know the ending of a game can make or break it but I think they just played it cool. The whole game you're being thrown all these plot twists and turns and then the end just didn't bring that *BANG* every one was expecting. It wasn't a bad ending what so ever, it just wasn't at the same level of excitment that the rest of the game was at. 
     I feel like this game, if the devs allow it, can be WAY more worth it if they add a Workshop section for it. Custom stories, mods, skins, all mae by the community and fans themselves. If this is added that would make it the true selling point, because a 3 hour game is not worth anything over $5, but if there are thousands of custom stories to play by hundreds of different fans then the playability is almost limitless because every story will be different in its own unique way. But for now, not worth $20.
     Regardless, the game delivered where it mattered most (the story) and did what it wanted to do, make a game where the story excites its audience, and make that game very pretty. Would I recommend this game? Yes, but not for the $20 price tag. As you can see, I beat the game in less than 4 hours and for that low of a play time, a $20 price tag is defintely not worth it. Espacially a linear story that ends with the only one outcome, maybe 2, (I looked up on a steam forum and never got a clear answer but correct me if I'm wrong) but most people aren't going to play through a second time to see. They can just look up on Youtube in 5 minutes instead of playing through the game again. So get the game when it goes on sale during summer sales in a couple of months, or watch someone interesting stream it. Either way I think you should experience this game because it gives you a real look at lonliness, abandonment, relationships, and just life as an adult. I could keep going on and on and on about this game but I won't even though most people have stopped reading by now.

As we begin our first day in the Forest protection service, we are introduced to a delightful character aptly named 'Delilah' this benevolent and rather sarcastic 'tongue-in-cheek' character is our only source of communications to the outer world. 

Which directly influences the 'isolated' feeling one receives whilst hiking about the absoloutely breath-taking forest. 
(We will come back to this point) 


The hype for this game was phenominal, to be honest, I only became aware of this game, a month before it was to be released. Was the game as exceptional as the hype had made it out to be? Quite so, infact more-so I personally believe due to the quality of the voice acting, the atmospheric and often quite tense scenes, and of course, the ending. 


Many people have complained that the ending was 'Lackluster' that they had expected more, I think not, I think the ending was superb, the game plays out, as a mystery, as a 'whodunnit' style of game, which you will find out, is no more than a lie, your characters are merely becomming paranoid, and for good reason to, who would not feel greatly unsettled by discovering that someone as followed you about and recorded your conversations? 

Which is why I tend to look at this game as a playable metaphor for 'Occum's Razor' "It states that among competing hypotheses, the one with the fewest assumptions should be selected." 


You begin to wonder as to whether this is a Military opporation, or a morbid scientific encampment that are using you as Guinea pigs, for isolation tests. 

But no, that is not so, the truth is much less stranger than fiction, I will admit that there were several aspects of the story that left me quite confused, but perhaps I am merely inept and when I replay this game, perhaps I shall understand more. 


Would I recommend this game to the average everday normal guy? Perhaps not but would I recommend this to any fans of the 'adventure' and 'story rich' genres, this game takes little skill to complete; once you have the paths mapped, you shall never become lost, everything is clockwork.

Imagine life as a secluded fire lookout in a national forrest. There is nothing around you for miles, except nature and gently-cut trails. Your job is simply to identify, observe, and track wildfires as they move through the area. Sounds pretty mundane, right?

Well, you're not wrong. There isn't much action aside from the occasional rock-climbing. That said, this game isn't about action. It's all about the story.

Firewatch is an interactive story, more than a traditional game. Thankfully, this is Firewatch's strength. It is well-written, and the voice-acting is excellent. There are times when you can get absorbed with taking in the scenery, and others where the scenery is blurring by as Firewatch dials up the tension. Even the casual controls help keep your mind off what your hands are doing, and focussed on what you're experiencing.

I've seen a lot of complaints that it's short (I finished in just under 5 hours), but there's no point to dragging it out. The narative is what is presented, not the mechanics. Would I say it's "a fun game?" Maybe not. But it's definitely an enjoyable experience, even if it's only for a few hours.

Oh, and the graphics are gorgeous. I love the art style. I almost feel it's what the Borderlands games could have/should have been.

[b]TL;DR:[/b] Loved it. A great experience, from start to finish. But if you want to really enjoy it, you'll need to let go of expectations of testing your survival skills in the wild, and just let the story guide you through the experience.

[b]Pros:[/b] A well-executed story, beautiful visuals, really engaging
[b]Cons:[/b] A few dialog continuity hiccups, seems like some areas are wasted opportunities for exploration (but that could be a throw-back to traditional expectations)

On the other hand, if you enjoy things like Dear Esther or Gone Home, then you will find there is a lot to love about Firewatch. I would recommend waiting if you are not sure if that sort of thing is your cup o' tea.

Also don't expect Firewatch to be some epic tale like The Walking Dead. This is not the zombie apocalypse. It is a summer job where you walk through the woods and make sure trees are not on fire. There is a sort of mystery involved, but don't expect it to be a fast-paced and suspenseful Sherlock Holmes type of mystery.

I would equate Firewatch to the movie Stand By Me. You just sorta... go for a walk. With a friend. Through the wild. And you see some interesting things out there. Some mysterious things out there. And that's all it needs to be.

It's a relatively short game. You can complete it in just a few hours. As little as three-ish hours if you are just blasting through the story. But if you are a more leisurely player that likes to stop and examine things, enjoy the vistas, smell the flowers (mm! smells like computer monitor!) then you might be looking at close to 5 or 6 hours. Keep that in mind when deciding if the price works for you.

Strictly speaking I do recommend that this game is played, but a giant thumbs up at the top of my review would misrepresent my position. The game is short (not that that in itself would be damning), its interesting plot points are wasted or discarded, its ending is abrupt and unsatisfying (which many will argue is the point, which it probably is, but I do not appreciate it). The gameplay, not that it is the point of the game, is uninteresting and in my experience runs the gamut from clunky to mildly glitchy.

However, the atmosphere is absorbing, the interaction between the player character and Delilah is vibrant and believable, and the setting is beautiful. There are also very intense points that are emotionally affecting in a variety of ways, with palpable mystery and paranoia being more prominent in this game than any other I can readily remember.

Overall, this won't go down as one of my favourite games, or even one that I particularly like as a complete package, but that is only because what the developers were going for does not resonate with me. I have minimal if any fondness for the ending; others aboslutely love it, and by no means do I wish to dispute that with them. It's very subjective. If you're like me, you'll be disenchanted, if you're not like me, you'll adore it. The game is worth experiencing for its high points, and the chance that you're in the latter camp.

[h1]Firewatch in a nutshell?[/h1]

An over-hyped well-narrated FPS-style point-and-click adventure on rails.

[h1]Would I recommend it?[/h1]

Unfortunately, the answer is a definite no due to a multitude of reasons:
[list]
    [*]the game is completely on-rails; none of your choices really matter in the end
    [list]
[*]exploration awards you with... extra wasted time
[/list]
    [*]despite being very short (can be easily finished in 4h), there were some clear immersion-breaking bugs that should have been fixed pre-release:
    [list]
[*]physics can be easily broken and stuff can stay mid-air
    [*][spoiler]Delilah completely ignoring your silence and acting like you said something[/spoiler]
[/list]
    [*]despite giving the illusion that your dialogue choices matter a lot... they really don't
    [list]
[*]they only matter for one or two following sentences or until you "complete the objective"
    [*]after that, it all follows the same narrative line
[/list]
    [*]while it is well-narrated, the story is very bland
    [list]
[*][spoiler]you're basically some guy trying to escape your harsh life by working a very boring and isolating job for some 80 days[/spoiler]
    [*][spoiler]during that timeframe you are made to believe you are in the middle of a conspiracy[/spoiler]
    [*][spoiler]... yet it's just a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and the game is over[/spoiler]
[/list]
    [*]very poor value at the "promotional" price of 17,99€ given how short the game is and the above issues
[/list]

There are some good things:
[list]
    [*]the graphics and styling is nice and clean
    [*]atmospheric (when no bugs)
    [*]very good animations
    [*]great music and used artfully to create tension and add to the atmosphere
    [*]great voice-acting
    [*]interesting concept
[/list]

Just finished playing Firewatch, here are my thoughts. The game features some of the most beautiful stylized graphics I have seen in a very long time and I would love to see Campo Santo continue to use this style. The story was alright, but I have to admit that I was a little let down at the end. It wasn't the ending and outcome that the whole game really played up. I was hoping that there was going to be this dangerous confrontation that made you feel really on edge or that there was some kind of eerie-creepy ending. I say this because the game does a REALLY good job of creeping you out in multiple different parts. The soundtrack, sound effects and narrative direction all take you to this headspace of feeling really uneasy and very tense....but you just can't wait to unravel the whole mystery, so you have to keep going. I loved the immense sense of urgency that I felt while running all around the map, trying to find out the whole story! My favorite parts were the special graphic style that the team used and the emotional and relational elements that really made you feel invested in the characters. I just hope that on Campo Santos' next game that they really push the danger envelope and deliver on all the spooky and tense build-up. I know you guys can do it, because Firewatch is an excellent first game and you should all be proud!! 4 stars out of 5. (4/5)

Up until that point I was quite absorbed in it all and looking forward to the ending, so it was a bit disappointing to see how it played out. 

If you can overlook that annoyance, the game can be very atmospheric and generally does a great job at giving you natural looking environments to wander around in - it reminds me a lot of "The Long Dark" in some respects, giving you the sense of being alone (or mostly alone...) in a vast wilderness. The beginning of this game is very interesting.  The visuals are gorgeous, the atmosphere is light and airy, and the sound design is stellar.

The problem with this game has to do with both the promises made by the developers and the actual delivery of the game's story.  This game was advertised by the developers as being a 6-8 hour experience, with 6 hours being the low end.  Without rushing, I completed this game before logging 4 hours.  I read everything I could, explored aimlessly for a while, found some interesting things, and completed the game in this time.

The beginning of the game is paced very well.  You're slowly introduced to Delilah, growing a relationship and learning more about each other.  Then, around a third of the way into the game, the story rapidly picks up pace and feels extremely rushed, leading me to believe that the developers of the game either ran out of money or ran out of effort.  The ending feels extremely rushed, leaving the player with effectively no closure regarding the events of the game.  Without spoiling, the game asks one very large question with its plot, and when this question is eventually answered, it is done sloppily and in a way that doesn't make the player feel like they've actually achieved anything.

The taste I had in my mouth when I finished this game was, predominantly, buyer's remorse.  I feel cheated by the fact that the game is only ~3 hours long, cost 17.99, and that Steam only offers refunds for games with less than two hours of playtime.  I feel like the developers had this 2 hour limit in mind when creating this game, as it feels like a lot of effort went into the first two hours, then rapidly dropped off after the developers realized that they'd entertained their players just long enough that they won't be able to refund the game.

I quite honestly loved the beginning of this game.  I feel I've been scammed by the developers of this game and therefore cannot suggest this game to anyone.  Quite frankly, it's a ripoff.  It will also make you feel like you've wasted emotional effort and time on a story that fell flat at the end.

Oh, and your choices don't matter.

Edit: Steam has refunded my purchase of this game even though I played more than 2 hours.  Good guy Steam.

Like a lot of the other reviews for this game, I really wanted to love this game. The atmosphere and scenery were really well done. It reminded me a lot of that isolated feeling you get when playing something like The Long Dark, and I appreciate the consideration that went into trying to create an immersive experience like that. The voice acting was well done, but Henry could have had a little more life to him. Delilah was the one character that was well established, even if there were a lot of unanswered plot holes about her past. I'm not sure why certain things like her sister, her boyfriend, etc... were brought up very briefly and then never explored again. Then it takes a turn for the weird with how attached she is to a certain character, and how the game goes from Henry struggling with his past to all eyes on Delilah. The ending was just abrupt, and the story seems like it was done by two writers; someone started, and someone else finished.

I even feel a little cheated by the intensity that the game starts with, like it was used to drawn me in quickly and get me emotionally attached, and then the sincerity and severity of the first 5 minutes are just discarded for booze jokes and sudden paranoia. 

And I was really aggravated by the way things ended with Delilah. This woman starts their relationship by prying, and almost relentlessly probing Henry's past. She draws him. She starts building this relationship with him very aggressively, even pushing romantic notes, and then at the end, Henry is made to feel like he's crossing the line and she treats him so coldly? Very poorly done.

If you're looking for a story that will leave an impact, go play To The Moon.

I want this game to have an "overwhelmingly positive" review,. The thing is,  Firewatch is a divisive game, because it is peculiar in how it contains its narrative and how it lets you explore it. Many people will hate it, but that's because this game is not what they thought it would be, not because it's a bad game.

It's hard to explain why you may like this game or not without spoiling the surprises of it has, because, while many compare it to Gone Home, I'd say it's more like The Stanley Parable or The Beginner's Guide in that it plays with your expectations but it does so in a more subvertive way.

So I'll give it a try and tell you first [b]what Firewatch IS NOT:[/b]
[list]
[*]It's not a fully open world adventure game
[*]It's not full of action
[*]The story is more akin to a Jon Kazenbach thriller than to a J.J. Abrahams or Stehen King fiction-fantasy novel (take that as you will)
[*]It's a slow burn semi-thriller (despite what the trailers may led you to believe)
[/list]

Firewatch doesn't give you a lot room to bend or shape the story. The characters are pretty well stablished and know what they want and who they are. You sort of help them pick reactions to some stuff but you're mostly a passanger in this unfolding story. You've been warned.

[b]What Firewatch is is...[/b]
[list]
[*]A very human story
[*]A self contained story with an open-ended ending
[*]A game that let's you explore in the same way Mafia II does: You can deviate from the path and see what you can find, but the story pushes you in a very specific direction
[/list]
All in all, Firewatch is a very unique game, one you can honestly love if you know what you're getting into and let yourself be indulged by its mesmerizing views and involving script. But, like some of those cozy books one reads under the sheets in a cold and lonely winter, it is a game you need to go into in the right mood.

I hope I've given you an idea of what Firewatch is and wether you may find it as amazing as I did or just not worth your time. I also hope I did so without spoiling all the fun it might give you!

Another great entry into the narratively story driven exploration genre.
The story sucker punches you in its prologue and puts you into the shoes of an everyman struggling with an unavoidable conflict who decides to find serenity and take a break in the position of a fire lookout operator in Wyoming national park circa late 1980's.

What starts as a routine set of tasks and daily occurrences quickly turns into something that appears more sinister and throws the protagonists into a mystery to uncover. With only a radio and a voice on the other end of the line to a fellow tower operator, the feeling of isolation and helplessness reigns true as you delve deeper into the goings on and emotions start to shape and form what they perceive as the truth at the end of the rabbit hole.

Special mention has to go to the dialogue and voice acting as a whole for the two characters (The player character Henry - and Delilah, the voice on the radio) as they do a superb job and have some of the most believable and down-to-earth deliveries that I've seen in a game. The conversations flow quite naturally and make seamless references to other things you've talked about or seen, or in some cases stumbled across beforehand out of sequence. Plenty of genuine laugh out loud moments through this banter in the early portions too and the range of emotions varies as topics such as Henry's home life and reason for being here surface.

Has some beautiful scenery and lighting effects that I've stopped and admired at times, and an eerily somber soundtrack that picks up and backdrops during certain plot points or after particular revelations that added to the experience nicely.

A lot of people are concerning themselves with the length as if this were a replayable RPG or third person shooter to speedrun, I valued and enjoyed this for the story experience and clocked in at 4.2 hours personally. While there are a few optional side areas to explore and more notes/radio conversations to uncover, it does have to be stated that it is more of a linear narrative experience first and foremost. 
At the end of the day a movie ticket for me would cost a similar $17.99 and provide about half that in length of storytelling and narrative, the quality of each comparatively obviously being subjective based on a case by case basis. So to me I have no regrets and found it justified, this is certainly going to be a point of contention and a turn-off for others though I gather.

Simply put it's not a game for everyone or for people who aren't into this particular genre and I can't for the life of me understand why non-fans of this established genre would even be so vocal and hate-filled that they appear to be on the message boards. But if you *are* a fan and did enjoy similar styles of art such as Gone Home or Dear Esther etc. as much as I did, then this should definitely be on your wishlist.

I was really looking forward for Firewatch. The trailers they released made me so very hyped for the game. The game looked amazing, the characters looked full of personality, and the story sounded very interesting. A day before the game was released, many websites released their reviews for the game. The reviews were all praising the game for being amazing so, I took their word and took the plunge to buy the game.

I started the game and instantly I saw the slick menu. The options menu is lacking of a FOV slider but I didn't really get too bothered by this but, I know some people who will get bothered with this. I launched the game and it started off with a very well written backstory. Even though this was only about ~10 min long, I really got intrigued to continue  with the story. 

After the starting is over, you start the main part of the game you meet a girl named Delilah. She talks with you through a walkie-talkie. She's a really big part of the story. Hearing the main character, Henry, talk to Delilah is probably one of the best part of the game. The connection they have and the conversations are really fun to hear.

You're probably wondering why I gave this game a "No" after writing all these nice things. Despite all of this, the gameplay is piss poor. The whole game is very linear, you can't take other paths to get to each objective. Places that look like you can go are either blocked by rocks or invisible walls. This whole game is beautiful and all I want to do is explore the forest and take paths my way. I think this game would be better if this could be done. I also find the speed you walk/jog quite slow. 

[b] TL;DR [/b]
Firewatch has a beautiful story, visuals, and very live characters. All of this is hindered due to the fact that the gameplay is just a slow paced and linear walking sim. 

I won't give this game a score since I didn't finish it. I think just marking this game as a "No" is good enough.

Pros:

-Beautiful environment
-Intriguing story (beginning -> mid-game)
-Great animations and artwork assets

Cons:
-Terribly short (3-4 hours) - Overpriced in my honest opinion
-Terrible story mid-way through - gets you extremely hyped up then the hype drops instantly with lowsy conclusions!!
-Minor bugs and glitches - getting stuck on a small rock, on loot cache, etc
-Terrible ending - felt extremely rushed and put together to get the game out quickly and no real closure
-Character choice glitches - chose what to say, then chose another option right after and it never got said
-No real difference in choices made - played intro twice with no real changes in the different choices I've made

One of my most anticipated releases of 2016, and sadly I bet it'll end up as one of my biggest disappointments. 

Firewatch focuses on a very grounded and human story, about a man named Henry who's just trying to get away from life and get some perspective on things. As the story develops you as the player get to choose what kind of man you want him to be, through the conversations you have with your watch partner Delilah. This is where the game shines the brightest and it was pretty much the only thing keeping me interested throughout the game. The dialog is well thought out with great voice acting to boot. There were moments I found myself grinning like a complete idiot because of the friendly banter between the characters, and there were also the heavier darker moments which made me genuinely feel for them as well. Add to this a beautiful woodland setting and a great soundtrack and you've got yourself one heck of an immersive experience.

This is pretty much the only good I have to say about this game though, sadly. When it comes to mechanics it falls short in pretty much every department. The hiking around is teadious and I found myself having to bring up my map way more often than I'd like just to see that I hadn't gotten turned around. And while we're on the subject, there really isn't any point to exploring becuase most of the areas are locked away until the game tells you it's ok to progress down the storyline. Most of the areas you explore are just big empty spaces anyway (albeit pretty spaces, but vast and devoid of content nonetheless), so in the end I just found myself plowing through the story just so I could get to the next section of dialog.

And to adress the elephant in the room: this game is short. As you can tell by my game time I beat it in two sittings at around the 4 hour mark. For a 17 pound game this is not ok, no matter how great your characters are.

At the end of the day though, I advice you to get this game, just not at full price. And I genuinely wish the devs the best of luck. Its been a long time since I felt so invested in the relationship between two videogame characters and I'm eager to see what Campo Santo can cook up in the future.

I'm honestly not sure how to rate this game.

Well, let's start at the beginning; calling it a 'game' is a bit of a stretch.
It's interactive fiction, no more, no less.
The story is very linear, and you have absolutely zero impact on how it progresses.
Walk here, trigger the event, walk there, trigger the next event, and so on.
Now, there's nothing wrong with that as such. Plenty of other games out there that offer the same experience; Telltales offerings and Life is Strange springs to mind.
But if all you have to offer is a story, you have to come up with something better than this.
Not only is it very short (the 3.7hrs on record was the playthrough), there are some gaping plot-holes in it.
And the ending will leave you thinking: "Was that it? Really?"
There simply isn't enough meat on this bone to make it worth it.

Having said that though, there are some very good aspects to this game.
The art is absolutely stunning. Wyoming has never looked this good.
The voice-direction and dialogue-writing is top-notch as well. You never get to see any of the two main characters, the only interaction you have is through a walkie-talkie.
And yet, it's one of the most interesting relationships I've seen (well, heard).
One of the reasons I'm a little sad the game was so short is that I wanted to spend more time with these two people and see where they'd go from here.
But that apparently wasn't to be.

Had this been Episode One of a series, I'd have whole-heartedly recommended it.
But as it is.......
Well, I still recommend it for its art and voice-overs alone, but wait for it to go on sale.

I was intrigued by the slick styling and presentation and once I found out it was written by some of the same people as Telltale's Walking Dead Season 1, I knew I had to check it out. I went in almost totally blind and played through the game in a single sitting because it was impossible to put down.

Firewatch is the walking simulator that actually deserves the praise that was lavished upon Gone Home. It is richly detailed, thoughtfully designed, the narrative is creative and well executed, and it has probably the best voiceover work that has ever been done in a video game. Seriously, the banter, writing, and delivery in Firewatch is some of the most enjoyable I've ever experienced.

It is a mystery game, and fairly linear. Probably the best way to think of it is like an old point and click adventure game or the modern Telltale games, except with a gameplay engine that has you hiking through the beautiful territory of Wyoming in between plot points. The gameplay is very slim, in service to the story. It explores themes of grief, regret, responsibility, and isolation. I found the story to be deeply engaging and did not have the problems with it that I am seeing come up as common complaints looking at reactions around the web.

The total amount of gameplay is between 4 and 6 hours, which I think is fine, but has earned some backlash from the plebeian internet masses who don't understand the difference between a tight, short narrative experience and a complete failure of design like The Order 1886. Portal is about 4 hours long and linear, and it is a classic of game design. Firewatch is a similar experience that I cannot imagine having been better if it had a branching story or multiple endings or collectibles.

Bottom line: definitely recommended if what I just said about it sounds interesting. Definitely check it out sooner rather than later, avoiding as much discussion about it as you can. It is a mystery so the less you know going in, the more effective the story will be.

P.S. I adopted a turtle and named it Shelly Duvall, 15/10 would retreat to the wilderness again
