I have some mixed feelings on this title, and they pretty much mirror most of the reviews you've probably already read.

PROS:
1. The gameplay and story are great. I was much more emotionally attached to this game than any others in recent memory. 

2. The graphics are beautiful and remind me of a more realistic version of The Long Dark (which is a huge compliment). 

3. You can get lost in the overall experience of the game and just wander around. There aren't as many places to explore as most other "open world" games, but you still get the sense that you're out in the middle of nowhere.

4. The ending was a little anti-climactic but definitely not a "bad" ending as other reviewers have claimed. It's a reasonable ending given the storyline and I think that makes it a more immersive game. There really aren't many places in the game where you need to suspend reality to enjoy the story.

CONS:
1. For $20, the game is much too short. It's a great story but I finished it in about four hours without rushing. I expect that I'll play it through again to see if I missed anything interesting, but even if takes me another four hours to finish that playthrough, it's still only eight hours of playtime. I don't think it's unreasonable to expect about twice that from a title that costs $20.

2. Although you can direct the flow of conversation in the game (and that's a big part of what makes the story interesting) I don't get the sense that the outcomes of any of the events are actually changed by your actions. There are no important decisions to be made so it has limited replay value.

3. There is no DLC planned for the title. To me. this seems to be a HUGE waste of an opportunity. You have this beautiful environment and excellent dialog system. Offering additional DLC with new stories, new characters, and additions to the map seems like a no-brainer to me. I really hope the developer reconsiders this decision.

4. You know that feeling when your favorite TV series ends, or you read the final pages of the six-book set you've been lost in for the past few months? That's what it feels like when you finish this game. You want more of it, you know you can go back and play it again, but you also know it won't be the same.
The game was an enjoyable ride till that ending... Pick it up for maybe 5-10$ at most.

There is a lot to like about this game.  Fantastic, realistic, adult dialogue & storytelling, which makes the experience worth having just to be a part of it.  The graphics are also gorgeous on the high settings.  Unfortunately, It's kind of short, and has little replay value.  The most unfortunate part is just how slow your character moves.  

It's a fairly large "open world" type of environment, and some of the things the game asks you to do involve trekking quite a distance, and the character walks excruciatingly slowly, and doesn't sprint much faster.  It can take what seems an absolute age to get from one point to another sometimes.  For me, as a naturally-inclined explorer in these types of games, it was a little crippling because I would get myself far away from where I was supposed to while trying to open up shortcuts that didn't really need to be opened, or because I wanted to look for hidden things, etc., and it would take forever to get back on track.

It took me only 6 hours to beat the game, and at least 1 full hour of that was unnecessary wandering that I had done and discovered frankly nothing that wasn't on the path I was supposed to be traveling but had deviated from.  The relationship you develop throughout this game gives the illusion of a lot of choice, but it's not immediately recognizable to me how it's really influenced by the things you do and don't say.  There are some subtle differences here and there that I noticed by restarting the game and playing for about an hour and a half (through the first few days of in-game time), but overall it seemed like the game was going to take me down largely the exact same path and story as the first time, even though I was actively trying to make as different of decisions as the game would allow me.

So all those minor disappointments aside, the game is still well worth playing at whatever price you would personally deem fair for about a 4 or 5 hour experience that's very much like an interactive movie with GREAT writing, characters, dialogue, etc. and a fairly fascinating story.

This game opens up, I think, better than any story I've ever heard. It puts you into a scenario, and tells you that you experience certain things. Of those certain things, you can decide certain outcomes to determine future narrative in the story. And honestly, that part, the connection that the beginning had with me personally, was great. The scenario described is something I've had a certain deep lingering fear in the back of my mind as if, what if this were to ever happen to me, to my family. It scares me. It honestly does; indeed, I could even imagine myself taking similar courses of action as to those which are in the game. However, as far as that segment of the story goes, that's it. I mean, it will be brought up in conversations, sure, but the entire purpose of the story from that point on, is how disconnected you can get from that. The beginning of the game is by far the most emotional point of the entire game, which traditionally, is kind of odd.

My real pet peeve in regards to this game, is that the climax comes almost out of nowhere, and then it's gone. There was no real rising action leading up to it either. All of a sudden, there's something going on, there's more stuff going on, there's a bunch of even weirder stuff, both that you find, and are told about. And then, in the end, half of all that you found out, half of all that had peaked your interest, and really made you question what was going on, is seemingly completely and totally irrelevant. What?

Firewatch is a heavily narrative-driven, short, scenic trek through an open area with great characters and a mystery theme. This game has been getting some flak for being short and not having much in terms of gameplay, which I don't understand since that's what it has been showcased as since it was announced. As long as you know what you're buying, you won't be disappointed.

The primary focus of the game is story and dialogue. You play as Henry, a man in his late 30's who takes a summer job as a forest fire lookout in order to get out into the middle of the woods to escape from issues he was dealing with in his personal life. The only other character that you have direct contact with is your boss, Delilah, who communicates with you via radio to instruct you on your job, and just to kill time. Odd things start happening to you while out in the woods and it becomes apparent that you're being watched by someone, at which point you add figuring out who else is out here besides you two to your list of duties.

In terms of gameplay it's incredibly barebones. You navigate the woods using a map and compass, occasionally open supply caches to mark things on your map, attach ropes to rocks to navigate certain cliffs and drops, and inspect things that you find. Normally I'm not a fan of this type of game. I'm someone who hated 'Dear Esther' and thought that 'Gone Home' was one of the most boring things on the planet. The way that this game manages to keep walking around interesting is the conversations.

The voice acting is nothing short of incredible. At certain points while walking around various areas Delilah and Henry will just start talking, as would be expected of two people isolated in the middle of the woods with nothing else to do. You'll figure out things about each others' pasts and use a multiple choice dialogue system to guide the direction of the conversation. This game implements that dialogue system better than anything I've ever seen it used in. Between the lines that the characters say, the choices that are available, the additional lines that are used to prevent jarring silence while the other person waits for you to make a decision, and the voice actors' great chemistry makes the whole thing about as close to an actual conversation as you can get in a singleplayer title. From the funny bits, to the frantic, and everything in between. This game's dialogue is virtually flawless.

Visually it's easily one of the best looking games made with Unity that I've seen in a long time. Lots of warm, summer colors. Plenty of foliage and trees. A nice overall atmosphere wrapped up in a highly stylized package. The framerate was pretty stable at 60 with the occasional dip when the game needed to render a new area.

PROS:
-Incredible voice work
-Fluid dialogue system
-Unique visual aesthetic
-Stable performance
-Solid story and development

CONS:
-A few minor bugs (One of them has already been fixed and the other one was an area not loading correctly which only happened once and didn't impede my progress regardless)
-Very short (I finished the game in around 4 hours)
-Gameplay is shallow (Even though I expected it to be this way, I still would've like a few things to set it apart in this department)

Overall, I like the game a lot. A was a fun, well made, unique little experince that I'll probably play through a few more times in order to see how my dialogue choices shape the relationship between the two main characters. I consider the game absolutely worth the $20 price tag assuming that you know what to expect going into it. If the things that this game does well are things that appeal to you, I strongly recommend it.

[h1]Overview[/h1]
[b]Skip to the end for pros, cons and a quick summary.[/b]
Firewatch is a fairly short, story-driven adventure game by Campo Santo.
Playing as Henry, you head to Shoshone National Forest in Wyoming, having taken a summer job as a lookout. Your job is to spot fires and report them, but of course, you wind up doing more, thanks to your ever present companion Delilah, your boss. As soon as you begin your day, you’re tasked with finding people setting off some fireworks, and after that, your journey begins.

Let’s get it out of the way: Firewatch is short. If you take your time, explore the wilderness, talk to Delilah about pretty much anything, you’ll finish the game between five and six hours. If you rush to the conclusion, and only talk about what’s necessary to advance the story, you could probably do it in a couple hours. While the game is short, it is priced accordingly. If this were a $60 game, you’d have every right to be mad. But as it’s under $20, and with Firewatch being known to be short, you’ve no reason to argue about value for money, or being misinformed.

Throughout the game, you’ll explore various locations. The wilderness is “open”, but it’s also restricted. You’re blocked in by rocks, outcroppings, thick brush. Some of these will open later when you come across certain items, but not all of them. And don’t let the map size fool you. When you’re viewing your paper map, the wilderness may look big, but hiking from the north end to the south doesn’t take much time at all.

The story starts off really well. It maintains its intrigue throughout most of the game, but starts to falter at the end, and winds up not being as good as you had hoped. The story is pretty decent, and I did not expect it to end the way it did, but the ending seemed like a bit of a copout, unfortunately, and did not have the oomph I was expecting.

That said, the dialogue between Henry and Delilah is astounding. It’s very smooth and flows naturally, thanks to excellent voice acting by both people, as well as a very well written script. While the main story doesn’t change much throughout the game, the little touches are what make it fun. Naming the first hill you come across is reflected on your map, and slightly changes the dialogue. Telling Delilah how you look determines something you see near the end of the game. Even the introductory sequence with how you met and lived with Julia changes dialogue options later on in the game.

The game looks beautiful. The sun shines and reflects off of the environment, the environment is a joy to explore, there are nice details everywhere. Henry looks a bit odd when you see his hands, they look oddly sized, but the rest of the game is astounding. Campo Santo has crafted a fantastic version of Shoshone National Forest.

When it comes to sound, the game is great as well. You can hear rustling in the bushes, water rushing, leaves underfoot crunching, and various environmental sounds. Music is very limited, but works well in what it does. It cuts in at story moments, crecendos when it needs to, and works well within the story of the game. As mentioned earlier, it really is the dialogue between Henry and Delilah that is the selling point of Firewatch.

Unfortunately, Firewatch does not have much replayability once complete. It’s definitely worth a second playthrough to hear the alternate dialogue, but aside from that, nothing else changes. Since it’s short, a second playthrough will take you half the time. Maybe instead of having the beagle, you’ll have bought the other dog with Julia, Mayhem, and you’ll talk about him at a later point.

When you do find the camera, you’ll notice it’s already been used. When you receive your developed photos, perhaps they’ll explain a bit more of the backstory. I purchased my photos just before writing this review, so I’m interested to see what will arrive in two to four weeks.

Firewatch is a beautiful walking simulator, wrapped around an engaging growing relationship, wrapped around a pretty gripping mystery. And you can steal people's alcohol.

The graphics are gorgeous and a big selling point. It seems like everywhere you turn is a work of art, and I had fun pulling out the in-game camera to take pictures of sunsets and vistas. I love games such as Borderlands which are stylised in a unique way, so this really stood out. It looks almost painted.

The conversational system was a good idea, and felt pretty natural -- instead of getting locked into a conversation screen, you pursue branching conversations while walking around the environment, and you can phone up your radio buddy to start conversations about most of the things you find. The dialogue is well-written, well-acted, and often hilarious. The main characters' relationship did seem to develop depending on what I said -- I'm looking forward to playing again as a huge jerk and seeing what's different. Even inconsequential-seeming dialogue choices sometimes paid off later on in small ways that made the world feel a lot more immersive.

The story kept me interested and guessing, and broke my heart in a couple of places, and I really came to care for the characters. There's no combat or puzzles, but the mystery and characters keep pulling you along, and it's easy to grow fond of the environment you're hiking around in. My one gripe is that travel sometimes got frustrating when I found myself lost off the side of a trail, and had to double back. But I've never had much of a sense of direction.

Firewatch is a visually stunning, single-player, mystery game and the breakout title from freshman video game studio Campo Santo. You play as Henry, an average guy with a sad past who takes a job as a forestry lookout in the middle of nowhere to get away from the unfair hand life dealt him.

The game opens by alternating between scenes highlighting Henry's trek into the Wyoming wilderness and flashbacks explaining why he chose to go in the first place. These flashbacks provide the player with choices which seem to impact Henry's personality and other aspects of the game (such as objects you interact with) later.

Once Henry makes it to Wyoming he befriends a fellow lookout named Delilah. Your interactions with Delilah, all made via radio communications, help shape their relationship as Henry investigates mysterious issues around the park and opens up about why he took the job. 

I highly recommend this game. Firewatch delivers top-shelf story telling packaged in what is one of the most beautiful virtual settings I've ever had the pleasure of exploring. Despite its relatively short length Firewatch delivers in more ways than I could have hoped. This game has heart!

Hopefully we can expect more of this from Campo Santo. I'd love to see more of Henry in the future. Nicely done!

Let's get started with what the game is not, because I think a lot of people expected based on previews more than what it's offering. It is not really an open world game. Yes, you have access to most of the map at all times, but the objectives are linear and mostly punctuated by taking you back to the tower once you complete them. The world is pretty, but there isn't anything in it. Aside from a few lockboxes you find and objects specifically related to your current objectives, there's nothing you can interact with in the world or see besides trees and ♥♥♥♥.

This game is also not a choice-based story in the vein of Life Is Strange. While you do have dialogue choices, they will not impact any in-game events or the game's ending in any meaningful way. It only affects the dialogue you hear back from your dispatcher.

This game does not have challenges in its gameplay. There are no puzzles, no combat, no way to "die" or fail your objectives. You are simply going through a story in first person.

While none of these things are by any means requirements for a game to be good, it leaves us only with the story, which unfortunately isn't as good as I had hoped. The idea of the game is that you're alone, and because of your past you're emotionally unstable and susceptible to paranoia, and weird ♥♥♥♥ starts happening that you have to figure out. The game does an amazing job with the setup, and an amazing job of making everything feel creepier and creepier. But the big discovery about what's happening is super disappointing and anticlimactic (though I'll give that it's interesting and unexpected). I think they had a great opportunity to take it a step further and they didn't. And then everything that happens between that and the ending is really dull and unsatisfying.

Most of the time the game gives you the feeling that you are actively exploring with a goal, and the game does not forces you in a direction.

You will feel very connected with the main character, because his background story is well thought out and narrated as if you watched a movie about a person's life decisions.
The game is beautiful and has a nice sense of humor. 

The pace of the game is very relaxed (I never used the running function except for the last 10 minutes), but the story kept me nervous until the end. The whole experience took me 7 hours.

Negatives: 
- The replayability is very low.
- This game seems tobe bug-free, but I got stuck in a rock or a tree three times in 7 hours. Each time I could free myself by very slowly moving around.
- Fans of action games will not like this game, because there is no action that requires dexterity.

First off, let's get it out of the way and say that yes, the game is extremely short. It took me about three hours to play all the way through the story. With no incentive to replay it, the game might not be worth the asking price for many people who read this review. If you don't want to pay $20 for a 3 hour experience, then that is fine, and respectable.

However, the experience that you're buying here is something unlike other games you've played. Firewatch, no matter what all the naysayers believe, is a very groundbreaking game. It did something no other game has ever done for me: make me feel like I was talking to an actual human being when I had conversations with Delilah as Henry. The connection you build with her is something unlike anything you'll see in another game. It just feels so... real. She feels like a real person. I believe that the feeling is amplified by the fact that you never really see a physical representation of Delilah in the game. You only ever speak to her through your handy walkie-talkie, which means the only thing I ever associated her with, was with a real, breathing human.

The story that Firewatch tells is also an extremely believable, heart-wrenching, and yet heart-warming one. I'll not go into details or spoilers, but let's just say that the story is a very human mystery, and has a few twists that leave you pondering every single thing you ever did in the game, and wondering how it was all connected. The story wasn't something that will completely blow your mind and make you rethink your life, but it is just that hint of subtlety that makes it so enjoyable. It just feels so real, man.

I believe that the price tag on Firewatch is worthwhile. The beauty of the landscape in which the game is set isn't really comparable to very many other games. The world is exquisitely detailed, and the art style does a lot for the overall atmosphere the game is going for. Photorealism wasn't something that the developers were going for, as the art has a very cartoonish, animated feeling - and yet all of the finer details in the world are still there, such as print on the back of some of the books found in the game that can actually be read. The environment will immerse you in your surroundings, and if not for your map and compass and Delilah's guidance, it would be quite easy to get lost in the extensive wilderness in which the game is set. On top of that, the voice acting in the game is probably some of the best you'll ever hear. For such a small title, it is astonishing how well voice acted it was. The voice acting certainly helped to add to the immersion of the world, but it also helps justify the price of the title, as quality like that can't come cheap.

In the end, if you're looking for a quick, hearty game that you want to make you feel something, then this game is definitely worth your time, and your money. If you don't have the cash to fork out for a game you'll probably only ever play once, then I don't think this title is for you.

However there's not really much dialogue, not much of anything at all to be frank.  There are a few cute diversions, such as digging through ranger bins or finding a turtle or a burned shack ( which literally nothing is said about...no back story, no point at all from what I could tell )...but by the end, all these little nuances that I had been filing away for the end to see how they measured up instead began to give me a stark, depressing realization...they had no point whatsoever.

What should have been factoids that added to the overall story instead, at the end of my 3.5 hour journey ( I paused and took an hour for dinner ), felt like just enough added weight to hold me over the 2-hour refund limit.  No, I'm not being overly dramatic...I honestly think most of the extras in this game are just there to make sure you cannot get your money back.  The story climaxes in a very oddball, unoriginal way with a paltry plot point and an abysmal ending that just sorta...happens and leaves you there with nothing to show for it.  I paid 20 dollars for a 3.5 hour game that gave me nothing in return, not even a good wrap-up of the meager story I had invested in.

You can literally go onto youtube and watch a full playthrough of it that ends at somewhere short of the 3-hour mark and get all the story, all the ambiance, and miss absolutely NOTHING in the process except a 20 dollar bill...I hate sounding petty, but I am reporting this to Steam and petitioning for a refund.

review:
The game is pretty good. It plays likea good novel or short film. Definitely an "artsy-indie" game. There is a lot of walking, but it's full of talking between Delilah and Henry (the two main characters). It is funny at points and sad at others. It is just the right length (4-5 hours), because any more and I think the game would have gotten a little boring. 

The only problem I found had to do with scripting and navigating. At a couple of points, the game describes where you're supposed to go, so you leave your firewatch tower (or another point you're supposed to be at) and hike to the location, only to discover that you can't advance the story because you forgot to respond to a dialogue sequence back at the firewatch tower. The only way to get the game back on track is to hike another 2-5 minutes back to the original location and que the appropriate response. 

Navigating was an issue only a couple of times. It could be difficult to find the path in a line of trees, for example, or sometimes the game will tell you to "reenter the cave" (for example), so you return to your most recent exit, only to discover that the exit is an exit-only, so instead of doing the "easy" thing and jumping back down into the cave, you have to walk around a mountain and go back to the original entrance. 

Those are minore blemishes in an otherwise fun game. Get it, especially if you're like me and believe games are the best medium for artistic and narrative expression and want to see more games like this be made.

The thing that infuriates me about Firewatch is that it has so much going for it, but fumbles with its content that barely fills three hours to a predictable end.

Opening with a text-based sequence that knocks the emotional appeal of the game out of the park, coupled with a simple tutorial sequence that furthers the story and shows off the game's aesthetics: I was impressed when I started playing Firewatch last night. 
Rounding off that intro and getting through the first day of protagonist Henry's new job, I was stunned by the immensely appealing aesthetic qualities of the game, which you can clearly see in the screenshots for the game. As I continued on, getting stuck into an intriguing mystery and some great voice acting, I found myself only being drawn further into a story that seemed to slowly expand over time and could seemingly spring in any direction unexpectedly. The paranoia and honest moments of fear that emerged were great, really amping up the beauty of the canyons and forests into a fearful wilderness.
But as each day of the game passed, the story narrowed itself down in a way I had already spectulated for myself and I increasingly saw through each day of the game as less of a continuation of the story but more of a level of playing the game - very simply moving from place to place without feeling anything more of that space. The story became more so a string in the forests to be picked up and followed, trivialising the agency of my character and discouraging a more organic and free exploration of the space.

The colour palette and visual appeal of Firewatch is genuinely extraordinary. I don't think I've seen anything quite like this before in a game, wherein I look at my surroundings and this environment and really feel that I'm there: one man in all this nature. The singular lighting, the intense colour through the trees, the distant horizons and lush fauna: Firewatch is a beautiful game. Even if the appeal wears off over time, the beauty and finesse with which the environments have been composed is great and should be commended as one of the best features of Firewatch alongside its voice acting and soundtrack.

The story of Firewatch is very much so the Hitchcock-ian thriller, deconstructed in part. The lingering notes of people missing, things left in precarious places and "that can't be right" moments that fall down to you give a great sense of mystery to the story and fit the bill quite well. The issue is that they only expand so far, in the end ultimately being given up for sake of a rather predictable pursuit of characters that we don't feel connected to. Likewise, Firewatch lets go of its emotional bedrock that starts the game off very quickly and only ever returns to it briefly in order to reassure some kind of feeling that I certainly didn't have halfway through the game.
A disappointing aspect is that whatever you find will ultimately be relevant to the central story in a way that diminishes the overall effect of the game. For example: there is one cave in the game. Just the one. And something is in the cave because you found that one cave. Nothing gets left lingering or tying itself up. Everything falls down to this ending that really isn't that appealing: the conversation from which it comes up in originally just rolls off like every other conversation you have in the game. It's disappointing to know that the game world, although feeling big, is actually just as small as any other nowadays. It diminishes its appeal massively and in the end throws the majority of it away.

The voice acting is grand, despite treading the convoluted story over time. Given more time, I'm sure the true emotional range of these characters would blossom in a way that fees more developed and mature for the story's themes. But instead, Delilah tells you of cripplingly stupid decisions she's made that make zero sense in such a small timeframe. The to and fro that her and Henry engage in is wonderful but unfortunately often lacks the depth that I feel it aspires to with its emotional backstory.

I wish Firewatch was longer. After three hours, I didn't feel like I had gotten £15/£19's worth of an experience. In parts it felt rushed and painfully so, sacrificing its mystery and isolated veneer for story progression and clumsy, forceful character development. Firewatch is a beautiful game, but an empty one also, in the end falling down on its seemingly meaningless story (what the hell did it happen for?), which cannot be redeemed despite its aesthetic strengths.

So I am going to break this down into the four main aspects that in the trailers and pre-release articles seemed to be the focus of the game:
Art
Dialogue
Story
Exploration

First off the art of the game was absolutly stunning. The environment was beautiful.

Second off the Dialogue was really great, you had several options and the voice acting sounded very real. You could really make Henry however you wanted him to be. The only down side on this part I think is that in the end how you speak with Delilah doesn't change your relationship with her.

Third is story/mystery. The story of the game is gripping, it really does pull you in and you really begin to feel unsure. Campo Santo did a really good job of making you feel like Henry did in the game. Two things that I think could have gone better here: 1st is that I wish that there were side-plots! There are so many things that you find in the game that go unexplained and aren't part of the main story line! There are other things that are mentioned is say a note or flyer that you don't find that would have been cool to find too. I was going to say that the second was that it wasnt open ended, but I changed my mind. I think that the point of the game and the story was really supposed to be about how what happened changed Henry. That the ending isn't to be about what happens to him but how the whole experience changes him, in a subtile kind of way.

And last but not least was exploration. And this is really the part that I was disappointed with. They made the world so stunning and beautiful but the area of the game is a lot smaller than expected. And it doesnt feel so open, yeah there are a few ways to go to get to each area but you end up going each way probably at least 4 times. And there isnt anything beyond what is needed for the story, that is the real kicker. I wish that there was more content that is outside of the story. Cool things that you can do or find and interact with that arent part of the story. That was the real disappointment.

All in all I think that the devs did what they said they would do and most of what I had hoped for. I do really hope to see updates that add more things that you can do in the game between story points.

The story starts out pretty strong to be fair, setting up and establishing a lot of Henry's character. This gives a lot of framework for the conversations between Delilah and Henry, as well as his motivations. It's downhill from here though.

We're cycled through locations and asked to go from A to B repeatedly to fetch things. I recall one item took me 20 minutes or so to run around and grab, only so I could open a door. That's 1/9th of my 3 hour experience spent fetching an item to open a door... Most of the game isn't fetching items but at the end it felt like I had been through a museum tour. Please make your way to the next exhibit.

I don't hate the game but I also think I would never recommend it to a friend. It's just a game I will never boot up again... Because without the element of mystery there is very little left to drive the story. It's basically a scooby doo adventure in the woods. You could argue that the game has some pretty vistas in it but if that's the criteria I could list off dozens of other games that are both pretty and worth playing.

Really the only thing I'll give the game props for would be the dialog / banter between Delilah and Henry, it feels natural. The plot points / what they do is far less natural... But even that doesn't ruin the relationship they have. If the intention was that their relationship would carry the game though, that was a mis-calculation by the devs. It is a driving force for the player but not enough to make me ignore the deeply flawed story telling.

- Zero replayability.

Okay, let's just start with the good stuff: The writing and voice acting in this game is absolutely stellar, and I adored the art style. The story was somewhat intriguing at first but it was actually very light, in that I think most of the game shines in the dialogue between you and the woman you're speaking to on the radio. It kept me on edge, though. There were some genuinely tense and suspenseful moments in this game that had me uneasy.

I guess the main reason why I'm let down is that I wish the story was a little less... simple, I guess? Yes, simple stories can be wonderful, but throughout the game I kept expecting that there was more to what was going on, and the theories started swirling around in my head. But I was disappointed that the big "twist" wasn't really all that big at all, and I just... wasn't that invested in it, to tell you the truth. And the game also isn't as choice-heavy as I was expecting. You don't really get to make any huge decisions, and none of the choices that you do make seemed to matter in the end, and they were just there to mask the game's linearity that lurks underneath.

Another thing I'd hoped was that I wish there was more to DO in the game. The area you get to explore is huge, and it would've been more enjoyable to explore if there'd been actual collectibles or secrets to find. The closest thing to that are the various caches that you stumble upon, but they're all pretty close to the linear path that the story takes you, and are hard to miss. Heck, they all even have the same padlock code. There's not really any replayability with this game, and it's pretty short. Should take you 3 hours or possibly less to complete it if you blitz through it. Took me longer than that cause I tried my best to really look around and get the most out of it, but like I said, there's really not much TO explore.

I don't know if I would recommend this game, I'm sad to say. The good things in it are good, but the lackluster things in it are exactly that as well. Maybe my hopes were too high, I don't know. Overall I was just let down by this game. I understand the kind of narrative experience it was trying to give, but it lacked the extra oomph that a game like, a most recent example would be OXENFREE, had. It left a lot to be desired, and was pretty linear despite its illusion of branching pathways.

I wouldn't stop you if you wanted to experience the game for yourself, but otherwise a playthrough on YouTube would suffice, I think. This game is a 5/10 for me. The art style, voice acting, writing and soundtrack are all great, but everything else sadly doesn't live up to the hype, and I don't think that it's worth the asking price.

I was so excited for Firewatch. I'm a forest firefighter, and seeing a game in this setting was unusual, and really got me interested. I watched every gameplay video and trailer that came out, which got me insanely hyped for it. I even preordered it, which served as a healthy reminder for me to go back to my personal policy of not preordering games.

I'm pretty disappointed, to be honest. 

The trailers gave the impression of a creepy thriller set in the wilderness, and probably the first hour and a half (if that) lived up to that hype. I was on the edge of my seat, blood pumping, jumping at loud noises. The plot had grabbed me, it was creepy and interesting, I was suspicious of everyone, even Henry himself. 

And then it just fell apart. It's like they were writing the plot outline on a friday arvo, thought "♥♥♥♥ it, let's wrap it up so we can head to the pub for beers," and hastily wrapped it up into a very tidy package. No mystery, no puzzles, nothing to solve. Once it started to wrap up, i lost interest. I wasn't scared, I wasn't curious. I finished it in like two and a half hours, and that's reading every document, taking it slowly. 


Don't get me wrong, it's got good points. The design and aesthetic is awesome, great setting. very basic gameplay, but that's not a bad thing in every case. in this game though, it feels like a tool so you can wander through the bush and collect items. 
You can adopt a tortoise. Dialog is witty, well written and well voiced. Too bad it seemed like the options had no impact on the outcome of the game, which honestly in hindsight makes the dialogue seem so useless.

I wish I was defending this game, because i waited so long for this to come out. If the plot was deeper, or choices had impact on the outcome of the game, or the game was longer, then maybe I would be recommending it. But for 20 USD (more in AUD), I can't. that's like 10 dollars an hour! If it was 10 bucks or less, maybe I'd recommend it. Wait for a sale or something if you want to play it.

tl;dr:  buy when cheaper
cons: Shallow gameplay, short unfulfilling plot, choices have no impact on outcome of game, too expensive, conclusion was weak and disappointing. 
pros: witty clever dialogue, great setting, nice aesthetic, you can adopt a turtle, first hour and a half is gripping and thrilling
buy when cheaper

I have to preface this by saying that I really, really don't want to dislike Firewatch in any way. The voice acting was great and so were the characters. The graphical aesthetic was colourful and immersive. The music was subtle and excellent.

The problem lies with one specific important element that Firewatch is missing: it's not a game. I never felt like I was actually doing anything or participating in the story in any meaningful way. None of my choices seemed to make a difference - which is the entire point of telling a story through the medium of a video game. If this were a movie, it'd be a fairly decent movie. However, it isn't a movie. I spent about 50% of the game running from point to point while staring at the map. 30% was spent doing stuff that the game wanted me to do (click this. break that. pick that up. radio that object in). 20% was making small talk over the radio (arguably the best part of the game). This game suffers from 'tutorialitis.' I felt as though I was on rails and being babied every step of the way. It becomes an absurd experience when I realise that I'm a robotic function of the game. That is to say, I'm not controlling the game but the game is controlling me. It's like doing a series of QTEs but without the 'Q'. 

With that said, I didn't expect challenge from this game. I did expect a story focused experience, which it was. Yet, the story was disappointing. As other reviewers have pointed out, nothing seems to be of any consequence. The stakes are raised in the middle of the game and then immediately fizzle. Every bad thing that could happen to the protagonist is reversed with absolutely no input from the protagonist. Imagine this: The rebels are about to take off in their spaceships to shoot the Death Star core, when suddenly the Death Star just blows up on its own from a malfunction. What's the point of creating obstacles that solve themselves? Is it some sort of message about futility or is it just lazy writing?

This game's fan base seems to almost entirely revolve around people who think the voice actress is sexy. She has a great voice, but that's not enough to make up for a mediocre story and a terrible ending.

The main characters Delilah and Henry are not broken people with a strong interesting story. They're broken people with a maybe interesting story that implodes in on itself when you reach the end. In some cases, I could jump across wide gaps but couldn't step across narrow ones. In other cases environmental barricades (trees/bushes/rocks/fallen trees) were passable and other times they weren't. 

The map was not aligned in all places to the paths. Sometimes I needed to be "on" the red line of the path, other times I had to be to the left or right of it. Time of day was calibrated to reaching certain story points, so it was hard to use the sun to track direction. Holding up the map and compass blocked the interaction symbol for most items, so I used them as little as possible. With a bad sun, bad map, bad compass, and bad environmental barricades, I spent most of my play time wandering in pointless circles (or restarting after getting stuck, and playing the same conversations again and again). 

This was just a bad game. I'm sorry to put it in those terms, I'm sure the development team worked hard on it, but it was not worth the money I paid for it nor the time I put into playing it.

I stayed up late and played this game from start to finish in one session last night. But I only realised this games true genius when this morning in bed my wife asked me what it was about. I explained the story in 10 seconds and I just couldn't get the magic accross to her.

The beginning is simply beautiful. And you're invested in the character before you even begin. It's an interesting step, as most games reveal things about your own character as you go on, which is exciting but leads to a lack of immersion. This unorthodox approach meant that I was already bonded with and understood the character, and had a tear in my eye, before the game even began.

The world is beautiful, and perfectly sized. I knew my way around quite quickly, which was nice, I felt like this was my patch. But at the same time it never felt small either, and there always felt like bits I hadn't fully explored.

But the true point of this game is the presentation. The world and the dialogue are beautiful, and the tension it builds is simply incredible. It feels very believable, very real. The only violence is when you get hit over the head, and yet you feel like you're in danger a good portion of the latter half of the game. But because it never breaks from an experience that you believe to be absolutely plausible in your real life, it feels that much more tangible. Like it could, and often like it is, happening to you.

And that's what sets it aside from other games. I feel like I actually played through a snapshot of someone’s life last night. And while at four hours it will never win any awards for duration as a game, if you take the amount of dialogue, which felt nearly constant, and it's general experience, it feels more like a film that I have been fully immersed in. And with that in mind at fifteen quid it's the same price as a DVD, for twice the length.

In conclusion, the reason I couldn't explain the games magic to my wife this morning, is because I had experienced it. I was immersed, and I was there and I couldn't convey that. So if you're an adult wanting an immersive narrative experience over a night or two, pick it up, you won’t regret it.

Firewatch is pretty brilliant, pretty smart, and pretty in general.
From the begininning, youll be quickly led on to the fact that this is a "feels" game, And damn does it "feel" good.
You play as henry, a man trying to escape an incredibly complex and unfortunate past, but luckily none of the game is really about your past. No typical cliche story thumbtacks involving a man with a shady past, It's simply there to get you out at your new job.

You've taken a job watching over a large section of forest, reporting any fires that start, and dealing with rowdy kids disturbing the laws of the trail. It's a secluded job, but from the first day you reach your tower, you will be in near constant communication with one of the most pleasant people you will ever come across in a video game. This person is your sanity, your drive to keep going, and with a system in place that you can talk to her about just about anything you find in the forest, it feels more like a person rather than an extensive dialogue tree.

I can't say the game is perfect, but it does a lot of things perfectly, and I have no doubt that someone looking for a nice game to enjoy their alone time, would be nothing but satisfied with this 2-6 hour journey (depending on your pace).

The only part I don't like (semi-spoiler):
[spoiler] For such a well thought out and well executed single player experience, the ending really isn't what you'll be hoping for, it's not a sad ending, or a terrible ending at all, its just not the satisfaction you will be entitled to. [/spoiler]

Small and perfectly formed, a story telling gem of a game!  9/10 (no spoilers)

A game that reminds me of the strong script writing of titles like The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, Firewatch is like a good page-turner of a book that you just can't bring yourself to put down. One, in fact that I didn't, seeing it straight through in a most unintentional single sitting. And in a similar fashion to the aforementioned; short, but oh so very sweet! 
There are some very clever decisions your protagonist, Henry has to make along this ordinary man's journey into the extraordinary, which does everything a good story should. The game embraces you on an emotional level in clever and engaging ways you might not be aware of until you pause for thought once it's all over.  It will certainly test your moral compass more than once, and you might just surprise yourself at the choices you make. 

The visual art style is a little cartoony for my liking but nonetheless beautiful and immersive. I was pleasantly surprised to see it running flawlessly on my 21:9 monitor in its native 2560:1080 resolution straight out of the gates.
 There are a few performance issues which seem to be scene-loading related which can cause fps spikes, but nothing a patch or too can't sort and certainly nothing that will break immersion. Audio is largely focused on atmosphere and drops in subtle and effective passages of music in just the right places, the kind of detail I would parallel to a movie production, an effect which only further pulls you into the game world. 
Although Firewatch does have its linear moments, and at times cumbersome controls (XBOne controller)  the game does feel very open-world, and the map is huge. So much so when you start the game, armed only with a compass and a map, it can seem a little daunting given its scale. Having said that, by the end the whole place felt familiar, with enough character and diversity in each area that you quickly familiarise yourself with your surroundings. I think the only thing I would have loved to see was a change of seasons, just to squeeze even more beauty out of this majestic environment. 
If you love a good story (and they don't come around too often in video games these days!) and you have a soul, you will love Firewatch. It's gems like this that restore your faith in how great games can be when the end goal isn't mountains of money and their predictably disappointing hype train we are all shoveled into leading up to it's release. And at this price? You owe it to yourself to pick this up immediately.

This game is slow at some few points, but for the most part it is well paced. The voice acting is amazing. Same with the characters. I knew from how they talked about the game that it was a mature game, but I did not realize how upsetting I would find it. In a game this well done you can't help but be drawn to the characters. And the pain they are going through. And the unknown you, and the characters are faced with at the end of the game is really upsetting. I honestly don't think I'm going to sleep a wink tonight. But I tend to be sensitive to this kind of stuff. 
Please, if you are interested in the game, pick it up. It's less about the mystery, and more about the interactions between the two main characters. If that sounds like something you'd like, then please, get this game. 
Now, Cons?
-Holy crap that one jump scare. Was not ready for it. I'm a jumpy guy though.
-Had a fear at the end of the game. Really really unerving. Lot worse then any horror game has given me. I was scared of what was coming up. Thought something awful might happen. But it was also a fear of saying goodbye to the characters. Having to break away from these characters that felt so real in the past few ours I spent with them. 
-Some parts feel like you can easily get accross/over something that it doesn't allow you to. Some. Otherwise more open then I thought it would be.
-Big problem with it being open, I, out of my own stupidity, got lost multiple times. Perhaps make a time function or something where if the player is not heading in the right direction or is taking to long they have an option to skip to where they need to go. 
-Second time I opened the game (and last seeing how I beat it then) I would get pauses in the sound when I would talk on the radio
-hard topics covered 
Despite that list, if you care about story and characters, get this game. It really is amazing.

Rather than a traditional "game," Firewatch is more of an interactive story. 
It's...fun. In the sense that I really enjoyed learning about the characters (who are incredibly well written, I might add) and just progressing through the story.

 Is it worth $20? Maaaaaybe not for everyone. I love story-driven games, so I think it was worth it, but you might not.

However, 
That's not to say the game wasn't good, it was amazing. After about 15 minutes of playing I was fully immersed in the story and quickly lost track of time. The story here is amazing. The environments are done in an extremely beautiful art style that suck you into the world and make you want to stay. But the gameplay is very limited. You click to interact with things, but that's about all you can do. 

The story is more or less what you make of it. If you like speedrunning through games just to get the required bits, you'll miss so much. I highly suggest you explore everything you can to get as much detail as possible about the world. That's where I found a good chunk of the fun in this game. 

Pros:
-Great story
-Awesome visuals
-Believeable characters
-Great soundtrack 
-Large amount of detail 


Cons:
-Limited Gameplay
-Some minor graphical bugs, and rare but noticable frame drops (I have an i7-4790K and a GTX 980, for reference)
-Relatively low replayability

Do I recommend this game? 
At its current price, it's a maybe. If you really really like story-driven games like me, then I'd say $20 is a very fair price. I feel like I got my money's worth.

If you don't, and you just want something to kill time, I'd wait for a sale.

Firewatch is an amazing experience at the start. There is a great setup, tremendous innuendo that hints at a great mystery, and a world that quickly sucks you into the story. The problem is that the game cannot sustain this for the final act. And the grand reveal is - unfortunatly - underwhelming. 

The game spends a long time setting up conflicts that are never actually explored. And at the end, i was quite convinced that  i hadn`t seen the "true" ending, because all of the conflict and mystery i was invested in was tossed aside.

I wont spoil the story. When I read reviews that complain about story i often find that super subjective. If anything, i take statements like these as challenges to see the story myself. And if you are a skeptic like me and do play it, i think you will agree the setup is amazing. You wanna see the end of the mystery, There are these weird unexplained events, and the things you say trap you in the unwraveling mystery. But i warn you, the ending does not do the story justice. There are plot holes everywhere at the end. 

And its such a shame! The VO work is great, and the walkie talkie mechanic really grounds the characters. There are tons of little treats to be examined everywhere you look, and its such a pleasure that they feed into the mystery and suspense of Firewatch. The world is beautiful, and the exploring mechanics - especially early on - fire off all of the good brain chemicals.

But i cannot stress this enough: the ending takes all of the goodwill the game builds up for three hours and betrays it. It doesn`t accomplish it by making the characters do something without choice (a la Mass Effect 3 forcing you into a set of choices) or by an ending that disregards the players choices (a la bioshock infinite). Its not a cliche or even a nonsensical twist.

The ending is just deeply dissapointing. 

Play it yourself and see. If there turns out to be a true ending, i would be totally willing to reconsider. But for now, its a character study that portrays itself as a mystery. The ending is not bad in a subjective way, i think. Its bad in how it sets up the characters and our relationship with them in a way that is deliberatly manipulative.

------------
tl;dr 
Great Setup, Great Characters, Great VO work. Ending makes those great qualities irrelevant,

You play as a rookie fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness during the dry summer season. Your only other human interaction is through a two-way radio with your supervisor. On your first day, you spot some careless campers setting off fireworks, and head out to set things straight, which starts the beggining of a rather engrossing story.

The gameplay is very, very bland. It's a walking simulator with lots of dialogue. While the atmosphere is very peaceful and beautiful, it serves as a pleasant distraction for the fact that this isn't really a typical "game". There's no dangerous wildlife to defend yourself from, or hunger/thirst mechanics. You walk to various checkpoints to trigger story events, and sometimes find new gear to unlock new areas to wander around in. Several times I found myself getting turned around and trying to travel somewhere, but invisible, or non-logical barriers often kept me from doing so (Beacuse I wasn't walking on the "intended" path).

The game LOOKS pretty, and cleverly calls you out on some of your actions. I found a small, abandoned shovel that my character was informed was for burying your crap. My character was disgusted, and asked himself "Why am I still holding it?!", and after a few more moments after I didn't drop it, asked again "I'm still holding it!!"

My other main complaint is that the game is INCREDIBLY sparse. Aside from the odd butterfly, I only encountered two animals, both of which were just scripted events. Theres no deer, or bunnies, or foxes running about and the world feels very empty.

After finishing the game (In around three hours), I felt very unsatisfied. The story didn't pan out quite as interesting as I'd been lead to believe it would. Some sources claim that there's multiple endings, which is not really true. There IS a second, alternate ending that triggers if you simply wait around for five minutes or so and don't walk to the object you're instructed to. The only difference is about five seconds of cutscene.

In conclusion, it IS a fun game, but the pricetag is absolutely ridiculous. Get this game when it goes on sale for AT LEAST 75% off.

Firewatch was my most anticipated game this year and I finished it in one sitting in about 4-5 hours. It is a very good game, and very much of the type that I wanted it to be. We are talking about a "small" and down-to-earth story elevated by great dialogue and voice acting. You take the role of Henry who after several problems leaves wife and home behind for the Wyoming wilderness. Once there he is contacted over radio by another fire-watcher, Delilah who will supervise him over the summer. 

Here I want to squeeze in that another major strength of Firewatch is it's strong world building. Having grown up in the 90's this is perhaps more of a personal preference, but just as in the superb adventure Gone Home, or open world-RPG Shenmue, the developer manage to evoke a "cosy" 1980-1990-feeling, for lack of better words. It's there in terms of the technology that is available for the explorers, what items they scatter around them etc. Very nice, and not that easy to pull off I guess since quite few games revolves around this time to my knowledge.

I ran the game on Ultra preset settings and then had occasional problems with frame rate drops. There are several beautiful vistas to see but I felt that the environments looked like I had hoped, as in the beautiful artwork, only when viewed from a larger distance. The soundtrack kicks in on selected occasions and manage to further enhance the mood.

The most tense parts are midway towards the near-end and many have already expressed they felt let down by the ending. I did not really think in that way, even though I might have over-hyped Firewatch up until a few weeks ago, before I started The Witness. I always expected and really wanted; a short and well-written game with good environmental design, relaxed game-play and realistic story. That's what I got more or less. Personally, when ranking games, I lately tend to favour game-play over story, which is why Firewatch will not be my no.1 of 2016, but it will probably be high up on the list. Before Firewatch I did not know there was such a thing as fire-watch-towers and now I would really like to go to the U.S. and rent one for a night or two (yes, you can do that!). No matter how you see it, the artwork is lovely and I look forward to receive my prints in a while (btw, you can order print-outs of photos taken in-game if you want "personalized" artwork).

Like any game, it is not for everyone but it is quite unique and charming. So prepare a thermos with coffee or a chilled beer, maybe a light snack, and go for a nice relaxing experience as a fire-watcher in Wyoming.

There are two reasons this game stands above other "walking simulators" or adventure games:
-The dialogue
-The choices

And when that's basically the whole focal point of these types of games I consider that a huge selling point.  The dialogue comes off as so natural and sincere and the voice acting itself is fantastic in its delivery.

On top of that are the choices...nearly every single piece of dialogue you say has SOME impact on the story.  I'm not going to spoil how or why, but it feels fulfilling to the extreme.  In the end you feel like the character in the game, having lived through all the stuff he did and done it as both yourself and him.  If I were pompous I'd call it "the pinnacle of immersion" but in all honesty its just really, really, really good game and story design.

It's only about 3 hours, give or take some time to dawdle or speed through, but I can already seeing it being pretty replayable.  I highly recommend you buy this and play with friends or watch a friend play after doing it yourself, its very accessible and interesting to see what people would pick and do.

I echo the sentiment of others. At the end of the day, this game has only 3 hours of content with little to no replayability. Buy it when it's on sale for $5-10. At that price, it's a [strike]game[/strike] [i]interactive story[/i] worth [strike]playing[/strike] [i]being part of[/i]. At $20, it's alright at best.

Price tags shouldn't [i]really[/i] influence how good a game is, but in this case it does. For example, a AAA title with only 20-30 hours of gameplay (the low end) at $60 is still worth it if the hours are fun (Shadows of Mordor is a good example). In this case, however, I can't seem to justify paying a third of a triple-A title with only one tenth of the gameplay, if that. Something just doesn't feel right.

Anyway, price rant over, here's the actual review, with a warning that some of this may be considered minor spoilers given the nature of a "mystery" game:

Without getting too involved in the plot, the story starts off with an almost text-based choose your own adventure style RPG about the romance, life, and love lost, leading up to your taking a job as fire watchman. You end up wedding a "Julia", and life is good, but some things aren't so good. Eventually, things are pretty bad, and you run off to do manly stuff in the forest. I'm exaggerating points here, but basically no matter how you try to "choose your own adventure", you still end up having to deal with this depressing plot premise. None of the text based intro ends up being relevant to the game except to set the stage for some of the quirky dialog later on. And to tell you what your motivation is. Really? You needed to give me a whole cliché backstory just to justify why I would want to move to Wyoming to be an awesome fire watching person? Oh well, at least we made it to the watch tower! Now we can do fun watch tower stuff with this mysterious radio voice girl!

The game is very linear and story based. It's basically a 3 hour interactive movie. That's not a bad thing, it's actually kind of refreshing, because it's NOT told through ridiculously frustrating cutscenes. Instead, the game is the cutscene, if you will. That said, the story itself is fairly anti-climactic, as others have pointed out. You might have guessed it from the vague trailers and concept, but you're in the wilderness doing one of the most mundane jobs ever. Your expectations should be set around this fact. This is one of those "take joy in the little things" indie type stories that you would see premiered at Sundance. It's [i]Wild[/i], in game form.

As for the artwork, it is nothing short of glorious. The game looks great and that is what sells the game. It's why you will probably buy this game anyway, even after reading this review. And guess what? You can take pictures! And order real life prints of the pictures you took in game! Yay!?

As you may have guessed in the lead up, the thing that bugged me the most about this game is the dialog and character choices. I simply had a hard time empathizing or identifying with any of the characters, and I found the "witty" banter between you and Delilah (your firewatch boss) to be awkward and forced. There were some relatively heartwarming moments, but for the most part, it felt like they were ad libbing half of the conversations, and poorly. The interactions with Delilah did little to advance the plot or relationships in the game except for 2-3 key moments. Everything else I probably could have done without. I get that they were trying to create a Portal-like relationship with this "ominous voice", but I felt like the execution was off. Especially since (major spoiler) [spoiler]she was about a 10 minute hike away but you two never ever meet over the course of 3 months being completely secluded together. And there is one notable "scene" that calls this arrangement completely into question.[/spoiler]

Anyway, moving on. The controls were easy enough to use, so there's really nothing to say about them, though I kind of wish the game had a button to turn off the walkie talkies so Delilah would stop bugging me every 2 minutes. 

To conclude: as a fun little interactive movie to sit through when you're relaxing on a lazy Sunday, this fits the bill perfectly. The selling point is the art style. As a game that's worth $20, it's no barn burner.

This is one of the most beautiful, emotional, and immersive stories I've walked through in a very long while. Where as Gone Home was a story from an outsiders standpoint, reading about what was going on in the home while you were gone. FireWatch is a story where you play as a character, experiencing what it's like to be him while facing a difficult trial in his life, in a time where he felt the need to escape the life he had for a summer. 

You get placed into a very beautiful forest (yellowstone?) and your story unfolds as you learn about the life you're escaping from along with the life of the person on the radio and the former watchers that stayed in your tower before you. Meanwhile learning about the mysterious events that seem to be following you. There are also a myriad of things to find and collect along with a Disposable camera that at the end of the game you can get the photos you took in game developed and mailed to you IRL.

Although the game is short, very short (Too short for most peoples tastes. But as my grand-pappy always said, "it's not the size of the ship but the motion of the ocean" and this story, although short has a lot of motion.). It's important to note that this isn't a "game" as much as it is an interactive short story. [u][b]Anyone who wants to buy this game thinking it's going to be fast pace, rush through, full of action, heroism, valor, etc. Should probably turn away and not buy this.[/b][/u] However if you're going to take this game slowly, explore and let yourself be immersed in the character and his surroundings and truely experience the world that Cammpo Santo create, if you want some time to spend on a story that will have you ponder life choices, give you many hard feels and leave you shocked, then this is a game I reccomend. (Basically if you liked games like Dear Esher, Gone Home, Lifeless Planet, Stanley Parable - to an extent -, The Beginner's Guide, or Dream you'll enjoy this. However if you didn't like that style don't get it, you'll dislike it.) 

[h1]In Conclusion[/h1]
This story is potentially going to be one of the best interactive story "games" that will come out this year (and perhaps for the next few years). Also is quite possibly my favorite of these interactive stories to be released yet. [b]Though I cannot emphasize this enough because I can definitely see this happening; [u]if you're going to buy it, do it knowing it's a short story. It's not a point and click, action, or puzzle, it's not a game you want to speed through.[/u] It's a story that you want to take your time with, get immersed in it, explore, collect, and experience what it's like to be Henry during this time in his life.[/b] I enjoyed this story very much and I look forward to seeing what these developers release in the future.

First and foremost, I would like to say this is in no way a bad game.

For those who want a quick review 

[h1] Good stuff[/h1]

Well made graphics ( if you like cartoonish style )
Fairly good story
Intriguing enough that you want to know what's next
Walking around didn't feel like a chore
NO BACKTRACKING ( I think once you need to explore the same area again), something new for this game genre

[h1]The not so good[/h1]

No replayability
Performances issues ( FPS drops for random reasons, quick freezes ... )
Gameplay sometimes feel dull when nothing's happening
For the content included in the initial release, it's overpriced
No closure in the ending

[h1]Full review[/h1]

I finished the game twice ( took around 4.5 hours each time, but I did pause every now and than and wander off, it takes between 3 to 4 hours to finish it ). 

What I would like to say is that first, the game has no replayability ... you finish the story, and even with different ''dialogue'' choices, the story barely change, sure you get to hear the voice acting, but that's about it. The game also has some performances issues, I was running the game on an AMD fx-8320 & a Nvidia GTX 960, which is more than enough to run demanding games like Starwars: Battlefront 3 on medium/high but still got FPS drop / shuttering & some quick freezes every now and than.

Another bad point is that you're just walking around listening to the story more or less, you go from point A to point B with barely no interacting except dodging some obstacles or finding your way in the wood, for people who dislike games where you walk a LOT ( for most of the game pretty much ), avoid. The gameplay is pretty dull like most ''walking simulators''.

There are good points tho, the art style is pretty good if you like stuff that look like cartoons ... the game does a good job at making you want to know what's happening next in the story, but does it make up for dull gameplay ?

The ending leave you VERY unsatisfied, I felt like it was rushed if anything, lots of hole not closed yet in the plot, maybe they want to make a second game following this one ?

For what it is, the game is fairly good, but I can't recommend it for full price, either buy it on sale ( 5$ is a good price I think ) or go watch a let's play, it's be the same as playing it.

I'll start with a note that chilling experiences like this game always get me from the word 'go.'

I bought Gone Home and Dear Esther pretty quickly after seeing their gameplay in action, just like I did with Firewatch, and while they were short, they were always interesting. This game takes those and dunks on them hard by adding the narrative mechanic of the radio. Hearing your character talk, not to you as the player, but to another human being in the game world is an extremely compelling way to enhance all of the feelings surrounding the adventure in this game.

The social aspect and the radio options felt reminiscent of a visual novel, or a Telltale adventure game, but the first person walking around complimented this in an strange way. I was able to slow things down, stand in one place as I spoke to Delilah or keep moving forward as the conversation played out naturally. The game allows you your preference. The first-person view also built the tension of the game, constantly giving me feelings of paranoia, not being able to see my character's position made me wonder what was watching me outside of my field of view.

Despite how much I enjoyed it, there are small things to complain about. The game uses a positively arcane hotkey layout with the keyboard, furthering my panic in certain situations when I tried to remember how to use my map or didn’t realize that I had a radio conversation to activate. The ending of the story fails to tie together some of the threads that it starts weaving in the bulk of the adventure, leaving them to flap in the wind and causing me to ask what they meant. These things can be forgotten easily by the experience of this game on the whole.

Absolutely recommend. This game offers something different from most other modern games. It's hard to capture it correctly without spoilers, but in the just about 5 hours it takes to beat, you will experience a wonderfully written story and an emotional rollercoaster. If you ever play games for the story, this is 100% the game for you.

Firewatch has proven to me once again that dialogue driven storytelling is still very much alive and well.
Intrigue, tension, mystery, exploration and a dash of provactive writing combine for a game that will be one to remember for quite some time.

Pros:
+beautiful artstyle means exploring never feels repetitive
+voice acting is superb, dialogue options feel genuine
+pacing is just right, slow building but fast enough to keep things moving
+story is very well written, even if it's steering you towards a specific direction it never feels like you were forced to do anything you didn't want to do

Cons:
-Control scheme is decent (for mouse/keyboard) but some might have issues with it
-no fov option. Fov is pretty tight in this game and there really needs to be an option to adjust it for those who may get motion sickness, especially dealing with the sometimes jarring rock climbing sequences
-lack of visual options to adjust. It's extremely basic, the game still looks fantastic but again, us PC gamers need more options to tailor it to our needs/performance levels
-ending can and probably will leave you with wanting more closure. I understand why it ended the way it did but after getting to involved with the characters lives I felt as if I was cut off so abruptly without getting the explanations or conclusions I wanted out of the investments I made

Overall I can honestly say that this is one of my all time favorite games in recent memory. Camp Santo should be proud and I hope they learn and grow because of this because they have the makings of creating even more special and truly memorable games just like Firewatch.

A character-driven narrative game disguised as a hiking simulator, Firewatch tells a story that is compelling until it attempts to resolve itself. While the plot's climax may subtly relate to the game's stellar (and deeply sad) intro, it can't support the weight of the events leading up to it.

Firewatch is beautiful, the art style is striking, the voice acting is superb. A few rough edges are present, but forgivable. It can be completed in four hours or so. There are no challenges or traditional gameplay to speak of: your choices are entirely narrative in nature. Time advances as dictated by the story. Exploration is rarely rewarded.

Sadly, through no fault of its own, the game's narrative is shackled by the near-total absence of animated human beings. Being a small studio, it seems Campo Santo determined that they didn't have the budget for animated people, and designed Firewatch around this restriction. While their attempt should be lauded, the character-centric story they are telling ultimately suffers from it.

I'd recommend this to people that like narrativist gaming or are craving a survival-free first-person adventure game experience... but I'm still mad about the ending, so this gets a red thumb from me.

Just many coincidences that add up perfectly to equal..... nothing. Even from a character standpoint, not a single character in this story undergoes any change, they left the same way they entered.

In closing, the individual parts of this game are expertly crafted, from the scenery, to the characters, to the build-up for the mystery. The problem arises with the game's ending, which renders the last three hours of your life pointless. If you were to stop before playing the games final segment, you'd have a better experience than I did.

[url=https://medium.com/@FUTURTOPIA/firewatch-a-review-analysis-7ca61aa4a3ee]I have prepared a definitive review for users whom aren't afraid of spoilers and are looking for an analysis or specifics on the game.[/url]

Firewatch is a first-person adventure game about a man named Henry, who retreats from a messy personal life to take a job as a firewatch in the woods where his only emotional connection is a woman on his radio named Delilah at a nearby lookout tower. However, Henry's state of peace is shattered when he becomes embroiled in a mystery and discovers something more sinister than he had originally imagined.

Overall, as a person who has been waiting for Firewatch since it's release, I am conflicted with two different emotions: the feeling of happiness, and the feeling of disappointment. I reckon I should delve into those details:

[h1]The Good[/h1]
[b]Firewatch is a beautiful world filled with beautiful things[/b]. It combines timely and effective storytelling, beautiful world designs, and some other great factors to make a one-of-a-kind experience. People have been quick to compare the art design and narrative style to games like Gone Home and Life is Strange, but Firewatch is definitely a unique one that - although similar - deviates from the industry standard.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
I noted that the storytelling is 'timely', which is perhaps where the most distraught fans have caused an uproar. The reality is: if you plan to play this through quickly with no extra exploring and all the assists turned on, [b]you're going to finish this game in 3-4 hours.[/b] However, there is plenty of content on the map to make this game a 5-6 hour gameplay. This is both a blessing and a curse. Some aspects of the story are really fast, but other parts are left devoid of attention, and this is something that I feel is kind of regrettable considering the potential.

I must also acknowledge the conclusion, while not spoiling it: [b]In short, I've seen a lot of people griping about the conclusion.[/b] It's being described as, "A steady escalation of plot, only to fall flat." However, it is relevant to acknowledge that this is just one perception of the ending to the game. I will acknowledge that the ending is quick, and some users are left sort of distraught by its rapid manner. I will repeat what I've told others: [I]give it time.[/I] I reckon people who hate the ending today will be feeling it this time next week.

[h1]Is It Worth It?[/h1]
If you're patient, artistically-minded, and enjoy some fairly interesting narratives, [b]I would highly recommend Firewatch for you.[/b] However, I will stress that this game truly isn't for everyone. If you're a person who finds it hard to appreciate games of this style that are more story and artistically driven, you will not find Firewatch to be an interesting experience. In fact, I might contest that you'll be trying to escape it within your first days in the game.

[h1]The Extra[/h1]
If you have already played Firewatch, or aren't afraid of spoilers, [I]I really do recommend the definitive review for you.[/I]

I'll open up this review by stating that I have not technically finished the game, due to a game-breaking bug that occurs thirty-three minutes before the end of the story. Yeah... Make of that what you will.

That being said, I opted to uninstall the game and finish the story by watching a playthrough online. I believe my four hours of gameplay, combined with 3/4 of the story is good enough to let you know that you should probably wait until this is on sale for, say, $10. The characters in this game are some of the most well-acted characters you'll hear in a video game, and that's going to be the main thing you'll hear about. Sean Vanaman has written some fantastic dialogue that made me laugh, and tear up just minutes into the opening. The tension builds, and builds, and builds to a level of near discomfort, and that's a great thing. Then the ending arrives, and you're left to ponder whether or not the game was worth it. In my opinion, it was. Without spoiling anything, I thought the not-knowing how it would end, even to the last second, made the arrival of an all-around anticlimactic ending feel comforting.

A typical movie ticket costs $12 in my area, on opening night.
