Was looking forward to this game for a long, long time. Really wanted it to be good. And it is good, at certain things. The first hour or so of the game is wonderful, thanks to the chemistry between Henry and Delilah. It's some of the best writing and voice acting I've seen in a long time.

Then it turns into an episode of the X-Files, and all the chemistry between the two leads vanishes. 

I'm not going to spoil what twists and turns the story takes. Instead, I'll point out that the story starts out great and ends up falling flat, largely because of two things:

1. The pacing. The game starts with a slow burn. You're learning about the two characters, about the world, and occasionally a weird thing here, a weird thing there. That's fine. Then, all of a sudden, there is an abrupt turn into crazytown. I felt like I was just starting to settle into the groove of Hank 'n Delilah, when all hell breaks loose. Suddenly Hank and Delilah are bemoaning [spoilery thing I won't mention] plaguing them ALL SUMMER LONG, and I'm like "Wait, what? All summer? It was Day 2 of summer ten minutes ago. Then you jumped to Day 30 something, then Day 40 something, and now we're here." The game doesn't actually build a solid foundation between Hank and Delilah; it pulls the equivalent of "Two months later..." and expects that time to add weight to the proceedings. It doesn't. You can't just skip months of time and then have the characters say "Oh, all that time we've spent together" as if it means something. It doesn't. 

2. The quality of the writing. The first hour is phenomenal. Hank and Delilah have charmingly awkward conversations about their pasts, about the job. You have opportunities to press a little, or hold back, and you begin to shape your relationship with this total stranger who is also your only lifeline. Once the game takes the aforementioned sharp turn into crazytown, though, every conversation basically becomes:

Hank: I found a thing.
Delilah: You found a thing?! What the hell? Are you sure it's a thing?
Hank: I am certain it's a thing.
Delilah: I can't believe it's a thing. I don't like this, Hank.
Hank: I don't like it either. I'm going to keep looking.
Delilah: We've got to find out about the thing.

Relationship building? Basically gone. Character development? Not so much. Sense of humor? Vanished. As soon as the plot kicks in, the core pillar of this game - the relationship between Hank and Delilah - is sucked dry of everything that made it interesting. As soon as the story takes center stage, they become a *stunningly* boring pair.

I don't even care about the actual plot. Weird stuff happens, more weird stuff happens, you're given a seemingly plausible explanation for some of it, the end. By the time the credits ran, I couldn't have cared less about any of it; I was still just wondering what had happened to those interesting characters I met in the first hour, and why they were replaced with Blandy McBlanderton and the Blandtime Band.

What a waste. So much potential, and the developers clearly know how to write compelling characters; I just can't understand why they would abandon those characters to focus on a completely run-of-the-mill story instead.

I was excited about this game months ago, but I would be lying if I didnt say I was underwhelmed. Its hard to explain, but Ill give it a shot. 

It almost feels like Campo Santo decided to lay down a basic outline about how the game was going to be developed... and then decided to just stop there, as if the first draft was just fine. The gameplay, the level design, the storyline were all borderline basic. One example is how they force the player into a "point of no return" in which the player must find an object to progress in the game ( the axe, the piton). This is okay at first because it teaches the player the necessity of these items the next time they encounter such obstacle later in the game. The problem is that those obstacles are never encountered EVER AGAIN. You wont ever have to use the axe, nor the pitons to any further extent. The mystery about the two girls vanishing is well established at first becuase it gives the player the sense of consequence from his actions (throwing the boom box into the lake, telling Delilah what she should say to the police), leading the player to believe that there are repurcussions in the future. To my dissapointment, no matter how you interact/ what you say, it does not affect the plot in any grand way. This mystery was only an element of the main mystery. 

The main mystery itself hooks you in because it adds the sense of danger and vulnerability for someone who is wandering alone in the woods, who can only interact with a stranger via radio chatter. It sets up the expectation for something extraordinary, something dangerous, perhaps even something life changing. But after discovering the truth behind all the strangeness it kinda leaves you saying "oh...okay then". I can only assume that the the mystery was an element to move or advance the development between the two characters: Henry and Delilah.

Its without a doubt that the characters and how they interact with one another is the highlight of the game, and perhaps whole the point. The main protagonist, Henry, after a troubling history in managing his relationship with his afflicted wife, escapes into the wilderness to run away from his relational issues. Delilah, to a certain degree, is in the same boat as Henry. They interact with eachother throughout the story, each one flipping through the other's story, almost as if they were trying to solve eachother's problem. They are stuck in this internal state of limbo (metaphorically speaking their isolation in the park) not knowing where to go next in their lives. For a breif moment they find solace in eachother because Henry and Delilah understand eachother, but through natural events (the convergence of the two fires that threatens to spread in their area) they are forced to act once again. It subtly acknowledges the severity of being forced to a difficult decision in life, even though most of the interaction in the game leads to nothing consequential. (Funny, isnt it?)

Maybe Firewatch wouldve been better adapted as a novel. I would like to believe that the character interaction and introspection is the true purpose of this game, because if  not then this game is simply lackluster in every single aspect. Unfortunately, Campo Santo decided to advertise this game as an exploration-filled, vast open world mystery title. Im afraid this title will receive the same fate as Gone Home, but with less controversy.

I'll keep it brief.

Firewatch is the first game out by the studio Campo Santo. My playtime (3.9 hrs as of writing), was the time it took me to finish this game, doing minor side exploration. I made a lot of use of the in-game jog function as well.

First of all, let me get this out of the way. Firewatch is NOT:

An action oriented game of any sort, if you can't capture that from the trailer, then get your eyes checked.

A fully open world experience. What I mean by this is that certain areas of the game are story-locked until certain events happen. Each "Day" in Firewatch you get more and more tools that allow you to explore the world. By about the mid game you are entirely unrestricted and free to wander.

A game that will go out of its way to show you things. The game will gently lead you places, but by and large it is up to you, the player, to explore. I've seen plenty of things in the trailers that I have not encountered in game on my first run.


Now, what Firewatch is. Firewatch is:

A "walking simulator". Much of the game you will spend walking from to and fro on a very detailed, very beautiful scenic space. If that is not interactive enough for you, then Firewatch may well be not in your tastes.

A mostly linear goal-oriented game. There are no side quests apart from any you assign yourself (explore this, do that, go exploring, etc.). There are obviously main goals that progress the story, but they are left mostly for you to reason out and discover.

Heavily focused on the dialogue between Delilah and the player. At my count only five other characters directly appear in game, three as silhouettes, one as [SPOILER]a dead body[/spoiler], and one as a fully detailed and animated model. They all have minor dialogue.

A story-heavy game. The primary enjoyment of Firewatch comes from following Henry's story. In fact, without the main story thread the game is very bare on content, but what do you expect for $20.


Now, if you're on the fence still with this; if you've got 20 bucks to spare, I'd say go for it. At worst, you're out one day's lunch at a chain restaurant and you can go on with your life. At best, you'll enjoy this game as much as I did.

Also, a bit of an interesting twist. The photos you take with the ingame camera can be saved and uploaded to various social networks. For $15, you can actually purchase your photos and have them developed and mailed to you.

I know that Firewatch doesn't have a bear in it.

Well, probably.

Well, maybe.

I [i]trust[/i] that Firewatch doesn't have a bear in it. I trust this because I don't feel I've been effectively equipped to deal with a bear. And I trust this because I know that modeling and animating and programming a bear is a lot of work, and if Campo Santo had put a bear in Firewatch then there would probably be a bear in Firewatch's trailers.

But an hour ago, my offscreen boss Delilah asked me to keep an eye out for bear tracks in the area, and now I'm inching through a cave, terrified that I'm about to come face to face with a horrible grizzled grizzly.

---

Firewatch is a tricky game to describe. It's not exactly a Gone Home, not exactly a The Walking Dead, and not exactly a Far Cry 2. But all those elements are in its DNA, and they combine to create something intriguing, memorable, and extraordinary.

Don't listen to anyone who says Firewatch is a walking simulator. If anything, I'd call it a talking simulator. The core mechanic—communication with an unseen colleague via a handheld radio—functions something like a combination of The Walking Dead's timed conversations and Dishonored's Heart, and serves not only to advance the plot but also to provide color and humor and a degree of player expressivity.

I won't say much about the plot here, as it is hard to do so without treading into spoiler territory. It's a mystery story, and a story about the relationship between a man and a woman. In both regards, the worldbuilding is exceptional: the principal characters play off each other well, and there is a real tension while the mystery is sustained. The worst I can say about Firewatch is that I wish I could spend longer in this remote part of Wyoming. The first half of the game feels like the greatest TV pilot in years, and the second half is like fast-forwarding to the series finale.

---

I loved everything about Firewatch. The gorgeous art, the stellar voice acting, the beautiful yet disquieting soundtrack. Highly recommended to anyone who enjoys narrative-driven games.

Just watch out for that bear.

What is Firewatch? Firewatch is a video game.

Over the past year, I have heard a lot about this game called Firewatch, and until about two or three weeks ago, I knew nothing of it. My decision to buy Firewatch was caused by one simple thing. I watched a Giant Bomb video titled "What is Firewatch." If you're on the fence about this game, I highly recommend, you head over to Giant Bomb's website, or their youtube page and check it out.

You play as a man named Henry. Henry's life isn't going the way he had planned, and due to circumstances revealed at the start of the game, he decides to take a job for the summer as a fire watchman in Wyoming. The entire game takes around 4-6 hours, depending on how much exploring you do.

The story this game tells is one that feels familiar in some ways, but is told so different from anything I've played before. It's familiar, but its conclusion was entirely unexpected. This seems to be a point of contention with a lot of folks, but I really feel the game's ending is one of its charms. Plus, there's a lot of neat little easter eggs and little references to other games, some of which I didn't even catch right away.

The game looks gorgeous. The graphical style used is one that will likely hold up over time. Realistic styles tend to lose their pizzazz as newer and better graphics are introduced, but Firewatch will likely look beautiful for quite a long time. The atmosphere and scenerey is stunning, though I wish there was more wildlife to see scurrying around the wilderness.

Firewatch ran flawlessly for me at max settings, but from what I've read some people were having problems with frame rate issues, and field of view cannot be changed from the game options. These problems are fixable, though one involves a little bit of work, and the other involves editing a registry file. The fixes are there if you need them, but I wish they were a little less complex.

As far as replayablility is concerned, it's a little hard to say. If nothing else, I believe video games and movies share a common theme when it comes to replayability/rewatchability. Some movies you watch once and put away to never watch again, others you can watch over and over despite the story never changing. The same can be said for video games. There are plenty of games out there, even linear ones that you can play through again and again, and it never gets old. That's how I see Firewatch. It's one of those games I could go back and play again.

The normal price tag for Firewatch is $20, and I think that's worth it. The game took me a little over 4 hours to beat, and if you want to do the whole price per hour thing, it's roughly $5 per hour, but that's a horrible way to look at things. Sure, the length of a game is a key factor when deciding whether a game is worth buying, but it's not the only factor. A $5 pie and a $15 pie are the same size. You get the same amount of pie, but the $15 pie is made with real fruit, and the $5 pie is made with wax fruit. You'll probably finish the $15 pie faster because the other one is made of wax, and that stuff is kind of chewy. Not only that, but you could get another two $5 pies for the price of the one $15 pie! But do you really want to? Sure, the $5 pie is cheaper and lasts longer, but it's also wax and probably not good for digestion. 

What I'm saying, is Firewatch is a short game, but it's a really good short game. It's worth the price, and I highly recommend it. I'm also saying you shouldn't eat wax, and should probably think about taking some probiotics if you do.

Firewatch is an intersting game that a lot of people have some beef with. So let's get the cons out of the way. The game is worth $20 and for its length it's a fair bit overpriced. The other thing people can be sour about is the ending. There are no real spoilers here but to say the least it ends a little abruptly. But the old adage rings true here: It's not the destination, it's the journey. 

Now the messy part is over, I can drool over the game with all its good things. First, the writing. It's a mystery game, so it's the most important genre to keep interesting and the viewer engaged. They do a very good job with Firewatch. It's a slow burning tale of two people figuring out what's going on that isn't quite normal. The characters are expertly written by the two writers for Telltale's The Walking Dead and so the two main characters have a naturally interesting relationship throughout the game. As a normal man doing a normal job, the introduction of the mystery into this normal enviroment keeps people intrigued enough to explore the story. As well as the story, players will like the slice of Wyoming wilderness that you are stationed in. It's large enough to make each place feel different enough, but small enough so that each place is familiar enough to you as you play.  Firewatch is so chock full of things from its world that it feels like a real place. Every lake and forest has its own name, there's a mascot akin to Smokey the Bear, and it's more real that it's based in a real place. Small elements in a story like this makes it on par with Alan Wake and even Dark Souls for setting a tone for it's lore.

Firewatch is an indie adventure title that tries harder to break the mold of that genre than any other before it. Involving you in virtually every single aspect of your character's path, FW takes bold steps to ensure that you never feel like you're not a part of the action.

The graphics are stunning. Whether it's blazing shafts of light pouring through the individual branches of trees, or the realistic motion of a raccoon foraging for food, or simply the tiniest flap of wings of a butterfly gliding inches overhead, this game takes notice, and doesn't let such an insignificant detail go unseen. Blades of grass sway gently, and leaves dance against the skyline. Though there is a slight bit of stutter, it remains to be seen if that issue is due to the game engine, optimization challenges, or simply launch errors. I ran with hardly any issues, but there was once I had to relaunch the game due to a low framerate. It immediately fixed the issues.

The sound is fantastic. The musical score for the game is well worth half the price of the game from the start, and I am heavily considering upgrading my copy of the game to include the soundtrack this time. I can say with absolute certainty this is the first game I've kept the music on for since Rocket League. It's just too good, and provides an ambiance that I'm not sure could be replicated elsewhere. It just fits, and that's something you should care about.

The story is amazing. Hands down, one of the most engaging and thrilling tales I've been party to in over a decade. I was thrown into melancholy minutes in the beginning, just to be met by the parallel tale of hiking out to the middle of nowhere, an act of escapism that instantly sets you up for the isolation and uneasy feeling of not knowing where you're going or why. Henry is living minute-by-minute, and you're along for the ride. A snarky and quick-witted counterpart, Delilah gently coaxes you out of your safety zone for adventure games, being led by the hand through narrow corridors, into Firewatch's sprawling wilderness, where you can go where you want. I found that out the hard way, when I went wondering and she just started questioning me at every turn. I eventually realized I had been going the wrong way the entire time, and I never even realized it because I was so immersed in the intriguing tit for tat conversation that took place between our main characters. It kept me playing without pause until the end of the tale, and when it was over I wished for more. I have to know what happens next, and if there's anything I want more than Firewatch 2 right now, I just can't think what it is.

Should YOU buy this game? Absolutely. It would be a tragedy to never become engulfed in this world that is teetering upon the edge of destruction. However, if you can't survive on story and the substance of dialogue alone, I would consider waiting for a sale. I wouldn't want you to be disappointed, and with adventure games seemingly "tricking" people into buying them these days, I wouldn't want someone buying this thinking they'll be able to take a firehose and spray down the entire Shoshone national forest themselves. You can't do that. However, you can feel free to explore and discover a corner of the wilderness in Wyoming.

Conclusion?

You know all those people saying it's really short? Well, they're 100% correct. While my time played says two hours, it's probably closer to three hours give or take, but I finished it in that time anyway.

Gameplay wise, it's a first person, naritive focused walking simulator. There is still plenty gameplay to be had here with different means of traversing the beautifully crafted landscape, but to it's core, it's a walking simulator. The game has set paths that you will have to follow, meaning your range of exploration is somewhat limited. Half of the map you can't explore because of this. If you're looking for an OPEN world game, this game isn't going to satiate you I'd imagine. 

Presentation wise, the game uses a cell shaded artstyle, making it all look like a very well made cartoon. The graphics are pristine and the enviroments are beautifully made. The animations are smooth as all hell, they make the main character feel that bit more alive inside the world and also do a good job of showing his character from time to time. Where this game shines to high heaven is the sound design, which is arguably some of the best I've ever heard in a video game. The voice acting is phenominally done, making both the main characters feel extremely believable. You can trully tell how both character's feel, even though one of them comes from a walkie talkie. 

This is a story game through and through, it lives and breathes for the story; but is it anything special? I'd definately say so. There is little that can be said that wouldn't expose the game's plot points, so excuse me if I sound vague. The game hooks you from start to finish, the opening alone made me feel like I just got punched in the gut. Midway through the game, stuff starts to get real as both you and the other person in the walkie talkie begin to get paranoid. The game's story eventually makes you feel uneasy, like you're always being watched, like any corner you turn might result in a swift rock to the head. There is a huge pile of mystery sneaked into what I thought was going to be a game about dealing with forest fires. 

Personally, I didn't mind the ending. [spoiler]Although I do feel like it kept things way vaguer than it should have done, leaving you feeling like there was something else you missed on your journey. [/spoiler]

Despite it's short length, I do recommend this game. It's an amazing experience, one that tells you the story it wants to tell. While it's length and ending may be questionable, I still believe this game is something special to be had. I'd say it's overpriced just a bit, so I'd wait for a sale first before purchasing.

You get to choose your responses that build your backstory as well as choose how you communicate and build your relationship with Delilah as you explore vast forests that all have a strange eerie feeling to them.

For 20$, its safe to say that I got much more enjoyment out of this than I would have from watching a movie at the cinema which is the exact same price, and I recommend it to anyone who can appreciate the value of an endearing story that you can feel like you're a part of. 

Honestly at one point I was crushing hard on Delilah, and it made the situations that you encounter feel even more real because you feel like there is a rapport that is built between you and your eagle eyed friend instead of just railroading off through a mission.

It has suspense, mystery, adventure and exploring. Now I know some people have mentioned that it felt strained, or that the story was cut too short, but if you take it for what it is, it really is something special.

Ever since Firewatch was announced, and I saw the first 15 minutes of this game being shown off by the developers, I fell in love with what looked like GOTY potential. The voice acting was natural, the hiking looked seamless and free, and the story looked like it would blossom into something really worth investing my time and money into. 

When I finally loaded up my game after giddily waiting for a solid day for it to release, every expectation was met as I happily hiked around the beautiful forests of Wyoming, seeking ferocious fires and confiscating beers and fireworks from rebellious teens. There is no question that Campo Santo put a lot of effort into creating a stunning environment to lose yourself in, with the colourful canyons and trickling streams along with the incredibly fresh dialouge from the games protagonist and his lookout counterpart. 

So why in the WORLD would I not recommend this game? 

Firewatch lights a match at its beginning, throws it into a bundle of kindling and by the half way mark a raging bonfire stands before you, hurling paranoia and interesting plot developments that leave you gagging to know what comes next. But before you can huddle around the flame to envelop yourself in what feels like what's going to be a gut wrenching journey of conspiracy and mystery, the fire dies and leaves you cold and confused. 

While the storytelling is superb, the execution of the conclusion is left to be desired. It frustratingly falls short in the end and I felt like the REAL ending would jump out at me when I least expected it... but it didn't. I had to sit there and ponder "is this it?".

Maybe that's the kicker. Maybe that was the goal. Maybe I was meant to feel the paranoia of the characters in the game and that it was all in my head too, but it was such an uninteresting ending I just felt like there was some serious wasted potential with this title and it really, really disappoints me after the first two thirds are almost perfect for the set up of something that seemed so much bigger than the characters; a real thrilling mystery to be solved. 

If the game was more around the £8 mark, I would probably just say go ahead and get it, but with the story falling short for me it was also only around 5 hours long (I'm even seeing people completing it in 3). It's a shame.

This is *exactly* the sort of game which doesn't fit neatly into Steam's Yes/No framework. In short: it's a unique experience clearly lovingly made by a small, dedicated team, but it's way too short with an extremely narratively lazy ending.

On the plus side:

1) The game looks beautiful. It has a Dishonored-esque sheen, which allows the developers to eschew high resolution lifelike textures and poly counts and instead present a heavily stylised aesthetic that could easily pass for a fluid painting. I barely even noticed the low-poly models for the most part because everything works well as a visual whole.

2) The voice acting and dialogue writing is superb. Henry and Delilah are relatable and believable narrators who say and do things that make sense according to their characters (something all too rare in game writing), and I genuinely cared for their safety and welfare.

3) The story - until the ending - is well paced and interesting. I played through it in a single sitting just so I could figure out what was going on. For the most part, it was extremely captivating.

On the down side:

1) There is a *lot* of walking around and staring at a map/compass. This was a mildly interesting game mechanic for the first couple of hours, but it really started to drag after that. It began to feel like a chore rather than a fun activity, deliberately placed in the game to pad out the relatively sparse narrative. 

2) The story ends pretty abruptly, and with no real emotional payoff. I don't want to spoil it, so I won't say much; but whilst the ending makes narrative sense, it's probably the least interesting ending they could have used given the context. It wraps the story up neatly (which is nice, I guess) but in a pretty dull way. I was expecting something much, much more given the quality of story telling up to that point. 

3) The game is very short. Steam says it took me 5 hours, but that was an extremely leisurely 5 hours with a couple of large breaks where I got some drinks and made some food. If you're focussing all your attention on the game it can be completed *fully* (i.e. seeing everything) in 3-4 hours.

Despite these issues I still genuinely enjoyed the game. It's a unique and memorable experience which will probably be a gaming talking point for some time... it's just that - sadly - it's not the game it could have been. For these reasons, I definitely recommend it, but a) only at a sale price, unless money isn't an issue, and b) if you go in not expecting a groundbreaking experience. It's unique and compelling in many ways, but lazy and perfunctory in others.

This will be a generalized review that is spoiler-free.

I really like these kinds of interactive-narrative games, and I have played quite a number of them in the past few years. Firewatch is a title that is definitley a little more interactive than some of the more popular titles such as Dear Esher and mabye even Gone Home, but as beautiful as those games are I feel that Firewatch accomplishes exactly what it sets out to do and may appeal to a broader audience within that genre. How you take that experience in hits home more than just an interpretation of what did or didn't happen in the story; but instead has greater potential to affect you on an emotional level, and the decisions you make can perhaps allow you to observe your own life through it's lens. I would even argue that this interactive narrative, actually interacts with YOU the player.

Talking about the more tangible features of the Firewatch;

The pacing of the story is brisk with a number of fresh and concise plot turns here and there. The game also lets you play around a bit in it's world, and take it in at your own pace. You can observe the enviornment and whats in it, or consult your Delilah over the radio if you want more advice, insight, and story. It's up to you, and this makes it easier to craft a very unique interactive experience. There's crisp humor, some mystery, and even the feeling of inherent spookiness that just sort of comes with being isolated in the woods. That maybe you yourself are always being watched, an ironic spin on the game's title.

You come into this story knowing alot about your character from the start, and I feel that this allows the you to focus on how he might be thinking at this very moment, instead of being concerned with his past. Because of this, I feel that the intent of the developer was to set up the decisions you make to have more emotional weight to them for you, the player. Additonally, The external world itself changes as the game goes on, which I felt to be sort of a figurative display of how the characters are feeling internally, and how you might be too. 

At any rate I'd highly reccomend picking this one up. It's price tag is more than reasonable considering the amount of work that went into it.

Firewatch is, overall, a good game.  It executes well on its core gameplay mechanics and has interesting characters, but is significantly shorter and less fulfilling than expected.

I finished Firewatch, from "new game" to the end of the credit roll, in just 3 hours even with my fair share of getting lost and sight seeing.  When I was making my purchasing decision, I looked into the length the game was projected to be and I found 6 hours being quoted by numerous sources.  While I don't exactly feel tricked, the game being just half of the length I was expecting is disappointing.  To help put that into perspective, the gameplay that has been shown of the game is a roughly 20 minute segment near the beginning of the game.  That 20 minute segment, when compared to my 3 hour playtime, shows over 10% of the total game.

At its core, Firewatch is a game about conversation.  You talk to Delilah, another fire lookout, throughout the game via a handheld radio about things that are happening and things around you.  Whether you're talking about a noise, a fire, or an interesting landmark, Delilah is always there to provice insight and a fresh perspective.  Throughout the game you develop a strong relationship with Delilah as you work through the story.  This relationship between yourself and Delilah is, more or less, the core element to the game.  The rest of the game's scenery, story, and tasks are, more or less, disguised reasons to talk to Delilah and have a conversation with her.  This part of the game is very good and is something I would love to see applied to other games.  Questions can go both ways, conversations can spark to life at unexpected times about unexpected things, and you have to choose carefully what you say because you can't have that conversation twice.

While  won't include any specific spoilers to the game or story, I will add a spoiler tag to this next section because it may include information that I might not want to read about the story before playing the game.

As for the story and reasons you're talking to Delilah, I'm left feeling unfulfilled.  [spoiler] Throughout the first hour and a half of the game, I genuinely had no idea where the story was going.  I was doing mundane things in the woods and talking to Delilah over the radio and that was about it.  The story wasn't doing anything or going anywhere.  After what turned out to be the first half of the game, the story very quickly began picking up and the mystery I was sold on the steam store page was finally beginning to pick up speed.  There was intrigue and mystery and I was getting excited about all the possible avenues the story could go.  After about an hour of deeper investigating, heated conversations, and mounting tension, the mystery was solved all at once in a very unfulfilling way.  There was, in fact, little actual mystery of note and the entire balloon of tension and suspence just deflated.  Then for the last half of an hour I was just wrapping up the remains of a story that I was suddenly uninterested in. I packed my bags, had a last conversation with Delilah over the radio and left the forest as though the entire mystery and game never happened.  If someone were to ask the player character "What happened in the forest this summer?" and he were to respond "Nothing much", there would be a significant amount of truth to that.  In the end nothing was lost and nothing was gained.  
[/spoiler]

It is very possible that my lack of fulfillment with the story was due to my missing the content that would've fulfilled me because of conversational choices I made.  Unfortunately, due to the nature of this game I have no way of knowing without replaying the game and trying every combination of choices.

Overall I would say that Firewatch is a fun game, an absolutely gorgeous example of the unity engine done well, an interesting and well executed conversational mechanic, and a very mediocre and short story with the price tag of a significantly larger game.

Also, [spoiler]You never see Delilah at all.  Like the "they didn't make a model for her" kind of not seeing her.[/spoiler]

[list]
    [*]Graphics/Art Style (The cartoonified or TeamFortress style of graphics can be hard to find in games and firewatch does it amazingly well)
    [*]Conversations/Jokes (The game constantly relies on small talk and jokes which makes it feel alive and makes you feel like your actually involved with the game more than just playing it)

When I first saw this game at E3 it had me intrigued right from the beginning. I didn't really know what to expect when I first picked it up. But within minutes the game has you hooked on it's excellent writing style. I was surprised how quickly it pulled me into it's world and didn't let me go until I had beaten the game 3 hours later. The art style is beautiful and the worldy interactions with things make it feel like a very lived in place. I'll admit, in terms of gameplay, there is not a lot too it. Most of the game you are walking around and occasionally you find a new piece of gear which only acts as a gateway into the next section. But the game does it so well that it often doesn't even feel like you are repeating the same cycle again and again. 

But as many people have already said as well the real magic comes from the interactions between your character (Henry) and your co-firewatcher (Dillilah). Seriously, some top notch voice actors were brought in to fill these roles and they performed beautifully together. Yet all of that stellar writing adds up to a very disapointing ending. Just when things started to get intense and had me thinking, the game just decides to call it quits and tie up it's own loose ends out of no-where. This game would be so great if it were an episodic series but unfortunately it seemed to finish the story in one of the most underwhelming finale's I've ever seen. Which is an absolute shame too considering how good the rest of the game was. For $20 I don't feel completely justified with the 3 hours it took to finish the game, but I am fine with it because I have hope that Camp Santo will learn from that mistake in the future with their next project.

Overall though, I was mostly satisfied with the game. I would give it a 9/10 if it were and episodic series, but due to the length of the game and the underwhelming ending I am content with calling this game a solid 7.5/10.

Firewatch is a game about Henry, a person whose wife suffers from a terrible sickness, and he decides to take a job as a Firewatch in Wyoming in order to escape reality, collect himself, and decide how to proceed. There he meets Delilah, his boss with a sexy voice who guides him through the entirety of his adventure.

In true fashion for my reviews, I will go through the good and the bad.

The GOOD:

1. Beautiful park to explore, consisting of caves, ravines, forest areas, mountainous landscapes, canyons, you name it.
2. Exploring the park gives you this awesome zen feeling of relaxation and puts a smile on your face.
3. The witty jokes and jabs between the two main protagonists are so fun to listen and respond to.
4. An extremely pleasant soundtrack.
5. The game is more of a walking simulator than a mystery adventure experience. It is a damn good one though.
6. You get to take pictures that would remind you of your adventure.
7. You actually have a compass and a map. I was expecting another long dark... Thank god it is not.

The BAD:
1. The story is very subpar. It has a nice buildup and it's as if they wanted to make something epic but... got scared or fell short of it. You get prepared to this big event... and nothing much happens. Saying anything more would be a spoiler.
2. The story is extremely predictable. I was sure what's going to happen, and was waiting for the big punch... which never came.
3. The soundtrack, albeit great, seems to few and far inbetween. You will be hiking for a while without any sound.
4. The game is short as hell, clocking at about 3.5 hours even if you're not running.
5. There are no multiple endings from what it seems. I have tried to approach some situations differently, and all Delilah does is change her lines and still get back to the main point.
6. Even though you get to make some pictures... that's all there is to it, and the game doesn't even tell you that you should (apart from once). I took pictures of all the suspicious things I found in order to deal with the police if necessary... Just to see them all in the credits. Thanks, but no thanks. As I said in my post on the steam forums, I even opted not to upload them, because all of them would have been huge spoilers!!!
7. The ending was not satisfactory for me... I so wished there would be more, and I hope they release some free dlcs to round up the story. There is simply no CLOSURE!
8. The replaybility seems to be all about playing again as Henry being a jackass, saying bad things to Delilah, or saying almost nothing, and so on...
9. The price tag is very high. I would totally pick it at 50% off though.
10. I tried to follow the suggestions of some people on the forums to ignore the story and just have fun. Sadly, all I found was walled off areas by bushes or thickets that you need to clear with an item that... was behind the wall of bushes. I am sorry to report that this type of exploration isn't there - at least until you go halfway through the game and a certain event.

Conclusion:

I am giving this game a no with a heavy heart. I know I had awesome time for the first 2 hours, laughing at the jabs between the the main protagonists, and having a blast exploring the the park. But then... it just pettered out. I was waiting for this huge showdown, but I was treated to just tapes and pieces of the story. There is so much buildup for nothing. No, I just have to get this out of my chest - I even brought my freakingly inferoir laptop to work for the night shift just to go ahead and finish the game! I was so looking forward to the endgame story I wanted to see happening, and didn't find it. The early game got me stoked, the midgame got me absolutely hooked and the endgame doused me with supercold water. As I said in the comments, Thing is, I don't want much :) If they have put just a simple a text screen before the credits saying what happened with whom and how they went on with their lives, my review would have been positive, but they just ended the whole thing... On the positive side, there is a lot to like about this game, and as I said in my other reviews, something or someone that puts a smile on your face is priceless. But overall, with the bad outweighing the good so seriously, I can't really recommend it.

[b][h1]Firewatch -  The Flagship Of Awesome Per Second[/h1][/b]

Firewatch is one of those gems that is rather a hit or miss. Personally, I enjoyed it. It is extremely short, (2.5-3 hrs long)
But the experiences you will have in those hours are the most memorable hours you will have with any story-driven game.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

Firewatch is like a Telltale game, but you can move around and interact with the world semi-freely. You can pick up objects and examine them LANoire-style, and piece together story dialouge. If you are the type of the guy who rushes in and likes to blow things up, This probably not for you. If you like taking things slow and steady, observing every little detail, this game will be your soul mate.

[h1]Story[/h1]

The story of firewatch is voiced, written, and delivered excepionally well. You can feel and hear the emotions in any character's dialouge, from the teeth jittering of realizing how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ you are, to Delialah (Did i spell that right) understanding she asked too many questions. It takes a new stride in a type of storytelling, and im too afraid to spoil anything. But spoilers tho:
[spoiler]Dummy, i said i'm not going to spoil anything. Besides, if you already played the game and know the spoilers, why the hell are you reading this?[/spoiler]

[h1]Asthetics/Atmosphere[/h1]

Firewatch has a unique artstyle. from the indigo-smothered nights of mystery to the orange-baked rocks of Thunder Canyon, the atmosphere is very immersive. Your immersion may be broken a couple of times due to glitches, but you can glide past them.

Graphics aren't the new XXX_MLG_COD3_ADVANCEDFISHAI_GWAPHIX_XXX, But they are just enough to support the game. It's soft, warm, and likely won't need a monster computer to run.

I’ve seen some reviews complain about the duration of the game. I think it is a complete narrative without a lot of filler content. The game could have been padded with some more non-plot content: you could have had to report fires or use the fire finder in some mini-game or go out and do maintenance work. But they would have simply been padding and it wasn’t at all really needed. 

The story continuously moves forward and is engaging to the end. If you think about the game in terms of something like a movie, TV show or book and less like a typical game, I think you would be satisfied. Though, much like with a book, there is limited “immediate” re-play potential.

Firewatch is a story-driven adventure game in which you play as a troubled man attempting to escape from the troubles of life in the wilderness of Wyoming. Although short, it is thrilling and emotional, and worth every second.

Take some butter. 





Now play the game.

Playing Firewatch has been the single most intensive single player experience of my life.
Played it at a friends house in one sitting and bought it right after I came back home for myself, just so I could write this review - and hope for more stories to be told in such an immersive and affecting way.

I have never felt so attached to a video game character before - be it in my relation to the player's character Henry and his very sensitively told story, or to Delilah, his only anchor in his solitude. Both the narrative and the gameplay compliment each other to an extend that it creates an experience of true aesthetical beauty.

Even now a lump in my throat remains.

If you want to see how interactive story telling - or in fact any kind of story telling - should happen, play Firewatch!

Firewatch is quite an emotional rollercoaster, with a very good mystery to boot. The back-and-forth between you and your boss over the radio keep things interesting, although just the environment itself could easily stand on its own. For the first time in a long time I really felt immersed, like I was actually out in the wilderness with nothing but a map and a compass, and it didn't even take hyper-realistic graphics to do so. Something about the sound, the lighting, everything just comes together and feels right.

The game has a sort of progression system in it, where you acquire various tools throughout the story that allow you to traverse certain terrain. Fortunately coming across these spots before having the proper equipment marks them on your map so you can come back to them later without having to memorize half a dozen locations (one of my least-favorite parts of games like Metroid). Finding your way around is easy with the help of your GPS-like map and compass, provided you either have a decent memory or don't mind looking down every few steps (I did the latter). Supply caches scatterd about will add trails and POIs to your map, and may provide some extra goodies every now and then. 

I have very few problems with the game. The occasional invisible wall tends to break the immersion a little, but you probably won't come across them unless you search every nook and cranny like I did. It's also a little tough getting the prompts to pop up for certain actions, like walking across logs and climbing down ropes. If you like your games to be full of action, Firewatch is NOT for you. It's basically a video game version of a choose-your-own-adventure mystery book, which may sound bad, but it does it very well.

I'm not sure what else I can say about Firewatch without spoiling the experience, it's a very solid game and worth a try! The game lasts approximately 3-5 hours depending on your level of exploration.

Firewatch is a combination of mystery and an immersive wilderness/walking simulator with a killer story.  That sounds like a mouthful but let me explain.  The first 10 or so minutes is a visual novel style game that sets the pace of the story.  You come to find out that you play the character Henry.  Without giving away too much, your spouse, Julia, was showing signs of dimentia at an odd age, and her parents took her away to Australia.  Henry attempts to cope with this by running away to a job as a firewatcher in a Wyoming state park.  For those of you who don't know, a firewatcher is a real job in places like national/state parks (in America).  It's as uninteresting and terrible as it sounds: You watch for fires and report them.  

Sounds easy-peasy right?  Well not for Henry.  It was already difficult enough to cope with Julia, and now he has to cope with being thrown into the deep end that is the Wyoming wilderness. Not to mention his partner/supervisor/guardian angel Delilah, who continously pries around in Henry's business and gets drunk.  As your relationship with Delilah develops, you find out more history about firewatchers in the area.  

Before you know it, your life becomes a backcountry noir while Henry and Delilah become stuck in a pickle.  The mindless summer job becomes a riveting case of murder, arson, and stalkers coming together as one.  The game kept me on the edge of my seat and it honestly made firewatching for a summer my dream job.  

A few final notes.  This game is simply amazing, and my only complaint is that it was too short.  However a game being too short is only a sign of a masterpiece.  My playtime is how long it took for one playthrough exactly, barring a few minutes of idle time for water breaks, food, crying, etc. I used both a controller and keyboard for different parts, and I found the keyboard to be better, but that's just preference.  Also brush up on your map/compass navigational skills before playing.  It will save some time.  This is also a game where I would recommend to stop and smell the roses because it's a wilderness game, but make sure not to get lost (save often at places you know are on track to prevent this). Enjoy.

From the stunning graphics that can be compared to Hinterland Studios' The Long Dark, or an upgrade from the graphics of said game, to the relationship Henry had with Delilah, Campo Santo did a fantastic job with this game. The music composition was perfect and how it was used in timing with the mood had me on my seat. When it was a serene moment or a moment of concern or terror, the music kicked right in, setting what the mood should be.

Although the ending was.... well, I'm not sure how to say it, so I won't say anything really. Just a single word could spoil it, and I'll leave it at that. However, what I can say is that in a way, I'm curious about the story afterwards, and I would love to see what happened in a follow-up game or perhaps even in some sort of free online comic. And what I'm really curious about is what happened in the days we did not get to play as Henry? What were his and Delilah's conversations like?

On the note of the voice actors, specifically for Henry, he didn't really seem to fit the "man in his 40s" age, but even then, Rich Sommers was still a great choice for the role of Henry, and the character itself felt more like a real person than one made of pixels and digital art, despite having a body that could be comparable to Wreck-It Ralph.

Honestly, I've rambled at this point, so I'll leave it at this: 

Firewatch was a fully enjoyable experience from beginning to end, leaving me wondering what would happen next when the plot got interesting. The graphics were enjoyable, the humor between Henry and Delilah was fun to listen to, and I do wish there was more to this story. If you buy the game, great! If not, then that's your choice.

Edit on 2/20/2016:
I should have also pointed out that the music, which was made by Chris Remo, really did add to the wonders of this game. Every bit of music that was made was beautifully composed and made all the important bits of the game work perfectly, definitely giving each moment the right tone that you should feel.

 Like a lot of other people, I was a bit let down with the ending, feeling as though it didn't fit with what the game was leading too. Maybe the intensity of the story was artificially inflated by the reactions of the characters. Maybe the story was just too realistic. I dont want to give anything away.

Either way I would give this game an 8/10. I feel as though most would be happy with the $20 they just spent. If you are on the fence, it might be safer to wait for a sale.

So I bought and beat this today. Below is a brief review: 

Basically, Firewatch is a first person exploration game that puts you in the shoes of a man named Henry. Once you answer some questions, Henry takes a job as part of a firewatch team in the wilderness. The bulk of the game revolves around Henry and the one companion he converses with via radio--Delilah. Delilah is Henry's boss and the one who gives you your objectives. 

Employing a dialogue choice system, based on the way you respond directly effects how Delilah responds to you and how your relationship grows over the course of the game. The story is fairly simple in the beginning, but the twosome are soon thrust into a mystery which compels you, the player, to push forward to the end. The graphics are nice enough and stylized in a manner similar to cel-shading--they're nice and colorful to look at.

The gameplay is mostly walking from place to place--i.e walking simulator--completing whatever objective you're assigned. The enjoyment comes from the natural conversations you have with Delilah. The voice acting is excellent and the topics of discussion are appropriate and genuinely interesting to listen to. You don't really notice the tedium of simply walking around since there is so much conversation to be had. In the end you realize the tasks you had were very simple, but the strength of the acting really carries the game. 

The one glaring flaw is the navigation system. You use a map and compass to get around, but the map can be a bit difficult to decipher and it's not always easy to know when you are near something contextual because you have to be in the exact right position in order to activate things. Adding to the frustration is the amounts of backtracking required to progress. You move faster in this game than in games like Ethan Carter and Everybody goes to the Rapture, but that doesn't take away the annoyance of having to go back and forth to the same places. The forest is samey looking as well with barely any unique areas within so it can begin to grate after a time.

Thankfully, the game is only 4-5 hours long so by the time you do start getting bored of scenery, you're just about at the end. Speaking of the ending, I won't spoil anything, but please don't get excited for something groundbreaking or revolutionary. I will admit it can be emotionally resonating if you allow yourself to get immersed, but I personally found it to be disappointing considering how drawn into the mystery I was. 

Overall, Firewatch is an above average experience, but I would not pay the full price of 20 bucks or even the sale price. I think this game is worth about 10 bucks for the length, but it SHOULD be played at least once. Despite my grievances, it says something that I played this game straight through with almost no breaks. If you're on the fence, wait for a price drop. If you're confident you won't feel ripped off, dive right in.

A very pretty game that very, very narrowly gets a recommendation.  I wanted to like this game, but it's not entirely what I expected.  Despite being set in the Wyoming wilderness, there's no real exploration to be done.  All the locations feel close together, and are arbritarily walled off by story, hamfisted item progression, or invisible walls.  Despite this, due to the game keeping you almost always on the low ground, navigation is almost impossible without the map.

All of these are minor compared to the story mechanics.  The time limited chance to respond to radio messages is crippled by disallowing radio responses while the map is up or the player is examining some items.  Since responses drive the story, this was a pretty huge oversight by the development team.  To their credit, the characters seem well enough written, and they have reasonable backgrounds.  Unfortunately, the story amounts to: even out in the Wyoming Wilderness, with mysterious events transpiring, the human condition shows up to miserably wipe all that away and substitute it with "yeah, people suck."

A huge question remains up in the air.  Or, possibly, I missed the chance to have the characters discuss it correctly (possibly due to the bad story response mechanic), and the writing down that particular path ignored the elephant in the room for the rest of the game.  [spoiler] Even after the story turns to Ned monitoring radio communications to cover up the fact his son died, there is no good reason for the Wapiti Station documentation to exist.  Are we really supposed to believe Ned created and filled out forms that included the susceptibility of Henry and Delaila to manipulation and discovered history they hadn't even discussed on the radio???  In my game, once it was revealed that Ned had been stalking the player, concerned about Henry making a discovery at the cave, this subject never comes up again between the protagonists.  It seems like the writer forgot what they wanted to do with this information, and it just got swept under the run.[/spoiler]

It could be that I wasn't able to progress the story or make a discovery that brings this into better focus.  Perhaps the main characters were both misled in my game, but the fact neither of them brings it up ever again, even questioningly, feels sloppy.

Also I took photos expecting I would need them to back up the story the characters would have to present at the end of the game.  Instead, they're just fluff for the gallery, so you may as well take just the prettiest pictures you can, or better yet take more and better ones by pressing F12, because this game is on Steam.  Sheesh.

So, why even call this game a positive experience?  I like the visuals, I like the characters, the voice acting is really good, the gameplay does mostly what it needs to (I only experienced one bug, falling through a log crossing), and for a few minutes there things were pretty tense.  It's just unfortunate that the main storyline leaves the player feeling "damn, that sucks" rather than "Whoa!  Mystery solved!"

Even though there is only about 3 hours of gameplay (if you strictly follow the story), it is probably my most favorite game.  If you like good plot, this game is DEFINITELY for you. I would like to see a DLC where the story continues (in the wilderness of course, I feel as if Henry's story is not complete). I will definitely buy that without a doubt.

There are a couple of good points about the game but the rest of the stuff is BAD.

Let's start with the good points:
Excellent voice acting
Great dialogue

Now, for the rest:

The beginning is really very strong. First minutes are quite emotional, then when the game actually starts there is a really good buildup. Then it gets spooky and mysterious; however, after a while it kinda just flatlines and starts going downhill from there. Only at the very end it felt a little exciting again but that was just me thinking there's more to it than there actually is.

The game is split into days. Many days are skipped but I guess that makes sense. Some days are just tiny flashes, which I didn't really like. I guess that was the point, to make the player feel paranoid. The solution of the mystery was very meh. There is no substance behind the mystery, nothing that would justify its existence. It made no sense after it was revealed. It's there just for the sake of there being a msytery, and that's bad.

The relationship buildup is interesting, and it really pissed me off that there was a disappointing ending to this. You can also look at this as a good thing - emotional reaction from the player. What I dislike here is that the game was fooling me  all the time. From the dialogue between Henry and Delilah, I got the feeling they might want to meet. And then she just ran away. This makes me want to try to play again, just to see if there is a different ending, if there's a chance she waits there at the end. But here's the problem. I am not willing to spend another 5-6 hours of my life hodling down the W key and occasionally pressing spacebar to find out. Alright, alright, you get to press Shift pretty often...but that doesn't help. One more bad thing here is that we don't get to find out anything about what H and D actually do after the game ends.

Another major problem with the game...there is no wildlife, like none whatsoever. There is one raccoon. I also saw a butterfly. I assume there were birds I didn't notice. That's it.

There's also a pretty big hole in the story. There's this research place in the forest. It's not on the map, and Delilah doesn't know about it. This makes no sense whatsoever, since it's a university research site and Delilah has had the job for years. It should be on the map and she should know about it. Not worth the full price. If you want this game, get it during a sale when it's at a massive discount.

I’ve actually been looking forward to Firewatch for years now, long before it was announced. Firewatch didn’t disappoint me at all.

Firewatch is a narrative driven adventure game that has you play as Henry, a man working in a national park looking out for forest fires, seemingly trying to get away from his normal life. His only real contact to anyone else is his superior, Delilah, who’s stationed in another outpost miles away. The game focuses on how you develop your relationship with them, as well what kind of guy Henry is. There’s also some good amounts of exploration as well. The dialogue is fantastic and reactive, and you will probably make a habit of calling in everything to Delilah just so you can have more of their interactions. It's overall a fantastic character piece video game and the first ten minutes alone illustrate this from the get-go.

While the plot is set in stone, their relationship and who Henry is is not. The plot is also engaging and has an air of real mystery to it. The ending is ultimately quite satisfying and bittersweet, practically all loose ends are tied up and it can end on a melancholy yet hopeful note. It also has really good pacing, people may whine that its short, but some gamers just don’t seem to appreciate tightly-paced games. (And really its not that short, it took me almost five hours to complete it, also give me quality over quantity any day.)

Also the game is gorgeous and walking around the forest is great. The soundtracks is also really good too and adds to the atmosphere.

Overall Firewatch is a great adventure game and while I’m still mulling it over if it’s one of my favorite games of all time, its most definitely going to be one of my GOTY.

First, if you're the type of person who really cares about this sort of thing: I played this game slowly, and it took me about 4 hours. I'm not assigning any moral component to that opinion, but I know a lot of people care and figured I would lead with it.

That said, I can't speak highly enough of this game and what it is. It is a finely crafted, compact story about people in Shoshone National Forest for a summer. Very minor spoilers (no specifics) ensue below.

The game opens on a slow emotional crescendo for about the first ten minutes, which I think is a really good picture of what the game is going to do throughout. Before you even get to the forest, you may have tears in your eyes.

From there, the game explores human relationships in a way that feels like it has a tremendous amount of relevance today, though it takes place in a pre-internet era. Just how well can you get to know someone online, or over a walkie-talkie? Firewatch argues that you can get to know them damn well.

Its setting is absolutely gorgeous, the soundtrack is sparse though very effectively used, and the story beats it hits are really well executed. The story in this game feels real.

Based on the initial reaction I have seen online, this seems like it will be a game that is divisive (like Gone Home, for instance) because it is short and some people disagree with narrative choices that the developers made. I disagree with that backlash and hope that when the dust settles the greater portion of those who play this game see what a beautiful piece of artisanship it is. 

I can't recommend this experience highly enough.

This journey I went on with Delilah by my side was one filled with thinking about Henry's situation in life, and whether or not I connected with him as a character. I am ecstatic Campo Santo has presented the player with Henry's backstory that is filled with grief and tragedy. It builds such a rocky foundation for Henry as a character, that it is easy to get swept into your own methods of dealing with hardship. Do you talk about it with Delilah, or do you hide it, make it seem better than it is? Again, extremely important methods of storytelling unseen in most, if not all interactive experiences.

For those claiming Firewatch is a glorified walking simulator are unfortunately tied to the notion that a video game must have it's story dictated to the player in a straight-forward manner. This game is steeped in choices that will reveal the true qualities of our two main characters and in them, a story of Henry's summer getaway from his pretty ♥♥♥♥ life.

I have written three paragraphs about the story and have not touched on the breathtaking visuals, the gripping acoustic-guitar soundtrack, the incredible pacing of the entire experience, the metroid-vania like path-taking. I do not feel the need to comment deeply on these established and extremely polished pieces. 

Firewatch in my humble opinion is a must play game. I encourage everyone to take it slow, not rush through it and soak in the details of the relationship between a troubled man, and a distant lonely park ranger.

Playing Firewatch doesn't feel like an interactive movie, it feels like a book. It's a cool feeling, but it's a short book, which is actually why I would recommend buying it on sale. Another downer was that nothing really "happens" in the game. I don't just mean with the story or events, I just mean in general. The game establishes controls and settings, then skips SO MUCH story time to the point that you only play through days where something MAJOR happens. A few days here and there of random activities would really have helped build atmosphere, and would have been a great chance for dialogue.

The good things: there are few games like this, and the story is at least very unique. It only became predictable for me in the last 30-45 minutes, and I still wasn't 100% sure I was right. I love that the main character is a character and not just the player. Even though you guide his dialogue, Hank is a human being in his own right. The atmosphere is good as well, I never really got tired of running around through the park, I could have stood for more of it. I was let down a little by the climax, but even the moments afterwards while the game was winding down still felt poignant.

If you want an experience that is immersive and has more thought in its writing than the average game, go for it. If you're interested in gameplay mechanics or you're looking for something really active, it's probably not for you. Having just played Gone Home (another interactive storytelling experience) just yesterday, I immediately preordered this game, and pre-loaded it. I may or may not have also called out of work to play it on release...
No, I was actually sick, and didn't have much better to do.

And, may I say, it was most certainly worth it.

Now, despite being of the same genre, unimaginatively titled "walking simulator" by some (which i think is biased and has a negative connotation out of the starting gate) and having the same musical composer, this title and Gone Home are succinctly different. 

By the way, that composer, Chris Remo, really knows how to create atmosphere with a limited but soulful instrumental palette.

Anyways, Firewatch is beautifully rendered and colored, and does a bang-up job capturing the midwest with an art style that isn't too samey, even as you walk through trees, trees, and more trees. Its environments are built well and I found that it was fairly easy to navigate if you've read a map before, (I turned off the player indicator for ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles/to test my navigation skills) though I am not a fan of only contextual jumping. Let me jump on things that look jump-onable, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
That being said there is a reasonable amount of environmental obstacles that you need to traverse, and they are perfectly reasonable and flow well with navigation.

Now, if you read my review of Gone Home, you will know what matters most to me in this interactive story experience is just that: the story.
I found myself easily falling into the protagonist Henry's shoes as he is a bit like me, though considerably older, (and in terms of hobbies I'd probably be more like Brian Goodwin). I found his story at the beginning heartbreaking, but enough to bring you up to speed, and the dialog/story options were and interesting feature, though I have a feeling all roads lead to Rome, so to speak.
I really felt the connection between Delilah and Henry as well, very well acted and the amount of dialog choices was plentiful enough to feel like you are actually influencing the conversation. In fact, early on I made a comment that made Delilah annoyed and leave her radio for a second, and I felt genuinely bad for having reacted the way I did.

I felt the story arced well at the beginning, but once it hit the turning point, where things got weirder, it lost its stride. Soon weeks and months were passing, and everything was a rush, and I needed to run all over the map to chase a mystery I didn't really feel was pulling together all that well. It was a lot like putting together a puzzle with no idea what the outcome will be, and being spoonfed pieces that don't fit together, and in the end it came together into something you wholeheartedly didn't expect and didn't really feel satisfied with.

The big reveal, the climax, wasn't really much of one. It left me depressed mostly because the ending to Henry and Delilah's relationship plotline ended in a somewhat lazy way. The mystery started out like it was Scully and Mulder exploring an enigma in a remote location in one of the better early episodes of The X-Files, but ended like one of the crappy episodes without Mulder in the 8th season, where the two cynics leave things completely unfinished.

Now, despite my complaints, I do think if you loved Gone Home, or enjoy interactive storytelling games (or *spits* [i]walking simulators[/i]) you should play this game. It is more of a game than Gone Home, as I didn't find myself bored, or running through locations just to unlock the next story bit. Its also a lot more engaging to play with the conversation with a living voice, which you choose your words for. But, unfortunately, I don't think it is worth the price. I would disagree with the price of Gone Home as well, but I got it in a humble bundle, and this is coming longer after I finished that game than my review of it. Hindsight is 20/20 and all that. So, buy it on sale and play it. Love the characters and the location and even the gameplay.

But don't expect a [i]great[/i] ending.

9/10 Brilliant Game but can be classed as a short game with it providing around 5 hours of gameplay

The gameplay is like Gone Home except with; person-to-person with Telltale-style dialogue choices, less emphasis on studying the environment, and a larger environment to navigate (pro: variation, con: back-tracking). 

I found the writing entertaining - if the dialogue in the trailers appeals to you, then it'll likely appeal to you throughout. In terms of narrative, the stucture feels rather episodic, visiting new locations around the woodlands, and after the first few days, the narrative skips forwards by weeks at a time, until the last few days. 
The first hour starts very strong, and there is a fair amount of intrigue as the plot progresses, (MILD SPOILER/ OPINION:) however I found the conclusion rather unsatifying. The game itself is also a little shorter than I was hoping (I finished it in roughly 4 hours, though I've seen people reporting they finished closer to 2.5). I understand there's always limitions of time and resources, but if there was an extra fleshed out day or two, either expanding on the protagonists' relationship or the events towards the end, I think I'd feel more satisfied. 
Regardless, I'm still recommending this game because there's still plenty of high points throughout, and I don't think a weak ending should undermine how those moments made me feel. I don't often get emotive when consuming games, moives, etc., so when a game is able to make me genuinely feel something (be it glee, dread, guilt), then it earns a gold star, and FireWatch has several of those slapped across its head. 

On a technical level, this game is a little jankey. Everythings works - there's no bugs which ruin the game. The framerate is well below what it should be for a game like this (on max settings, it was sub 30fps using a 980ti). When I was running around the environment, I'd sometimes get stuck on foilage, and since there's no jump, it was up to fate whether I'd be able to squirm myself off or not. I also noticed some unpolished areas (e.g. the character's feet clipping through the terrain when rock-climbing, and boulders which weren't lined with the environment properly). These points (besides the framerate) are really just nitpicks though - at worst, they just broke immersion momentarily.

Overall, it's a worthwhile experience. I wasn't particularly blown away, but I found the overall experience enjoyable, and there were certain scenes and themes which I felt are under-explored in video games, so there's that. If you're the kind of person who loves narrative heavy games with minimal gameplay, then buy it. If you're someone who's interested by some aspects of this, but are put off by the length, wait till it's around half-price.

Firewatch, if you haven't already seen a description or gameplay video basically plays like Gone Home, if you've already experienced that. You explore an area and investigate things left around by other people. The big difference is that here, you're given an agency. You're involved in the story. You're not just observing, you're commenting on what's happening. Really, it's a clever update of the "Look" command you would find in point and click adventures. Instead of your player character breaking the third wall and making a snarky comment to no one in particular except maybe the player, here you have an actual person, Henry, talking to his boss, Delilah. And it works splendidly. The game feels alive, the voice acting and writing are absolutely excellent and it will make you care for these characters. The game is funny, but it's not a comedy. It's not Portal. The characters are real, with affecting back stories that feel real, and they find themselves in scary moments, but they joke and their conversations are filled with life.

I don't want to say a lot about the story. To me, the ending was satisfying. It might not be to someone else, and I think that will be dependent of what they go in expecting. But I will try to assure some of the fears people might have of the story disappointing them: The ending doesn't make everything you've done over the course of the story seem pointless (I'm not sure how much variation there is depending on your choices, but I doubt that this would become untrue even if someone went for very different options than me). The game doesn't pull a cheap twist out of it's butt or feel emotionally manipulative. The ending doesn't escalate in a way that feels unnatural to what has come before. It didn't wow me, or blow my mind, but it left me with emotions, and left me caring about it's characters.

If you're interested in the game because of how gorgeous it looks - well, you won't be disappointed. It truly is a joy to behold and explore, and you even get an option in the game to take photos via a throwaway camera. I missed a crouch option to help me get different angles on shots, but hey. Not enough games come with a camera, so that's already a big plus.

The music definitely is great too - and I'd recommend getting the soundtrack bundle if you've enjoyed what you've heard in the trailers.


As for the negative bits, that's just gonna be me nitpicking, but here we go:

There were very minor glitches here and there. My mouse would sometimes pick up an object I could comment on even though I couldn't actually see it (since it was covered behind a mountain or something). Also, in an option in the menu where you can type in something, that didn't seem to work for me (though it wasn't a big deal or an integral part of the game).

I also was disappointed there was no option to turn off your aiming reticule. I'll have to edit that out of all my screenshots! :(

Something that actually frustrated me? At one point in the story, it advanced before I explored everything I had wanted to in an area. And there wasn't any way for me to go back, because when I did go back, the things that were there before weren't there anymore. But it only happened that one time, and I doubt it will easily happen for other people.

And finally, something that's starting to become a pet peeve of mine in games such as these - indie story-focused exploration type affairs - is true here too, though talking about it might be a slight spoiler. It won't spoil the plot, but it might spoil your expectations of what can happen in the game. [spoiler]You're not going to see any of the characters as actual NPCs. I get that it's probably A) a matter of budget, and B) developers trying to avoid the uncanny valley, but I feel that it makes these realistic scenarios seem a little less immersive if I never actually see the people I spend the entire game talking to or reading about or hearing about. Now, Firewatch goes to great lengths to make Henry feel like a real person - you see your feet, your hands, he's animated incredibly well, and there are some moments in Firewatch where you see people (and not just on photographs you find!), but it's nothing like say, Elizabeth in Bioshock Infinite or Alyx in Half Life 2. And I'd really love to see something like that in a game like this.[/spoiler]


Anyway, to sum it up - Firewatch is a wonderful game. It sounds and looks gorgeous, moving around and exploring feels amazing. It's characters and method of interaction are very engaging and the story - at least for me - didn't disappoint, but instead dealt with unique situations not easily found in other games. If you think you might like it, pick it up. I think it's absolutely worth it at full price.

In my opinion this is one of the best looking games ever created. Similar to Life Is Strange, this game has a certain aesthetic to it that [i]almost[/i] made it a must buy for me from the graphics alone.

A game is ofcourse more than graphics alone. In my opinion, this game is a must buy if you enjoy story driven games that lean towards the 'walking simulator' catergory, because that's what it does, and it does so wonderfully. Sure, the game isn't the longest, it took me a little more 3 hours to complete, but I feel like that is the perfect amount of time to tell the story in and make the player experience what the gameworld has to offer. To explain this a little more, some games feel a little 'forced' in the sense that they make you do certain things that don't add anything to the game experience itself (see Fallout 4: "Another settlement needs our help!"). This game absolutely does not do that and that what makes it the perfect length for me. They also absolutely nailed the atmosphere in the game: it did make me feel certain things at certain times which made the game great for me. (I can't really elaborate without spoiling things)

However, there are 2 things I'd critisize the game for, and it seems like I'm not the only one in feeling that. 

First of, it doesn't really have any replayability, UNLESS you replay it for the visuals/dialogue alone, to try and see if you've missed something your first time around. Other than that the story is pretty much what the game is based around and I don't think it will have the same inpact the second time playing it. 

The second thing is the price point. I don't necessarily feel like the game is too expensive for what it delivered to me, but I can definitely see why you would feel otherwise. The ~€20 price point might be a little high for some people for the game it gives you and in that case I'd recommend you to wait for a sale.


Overall though, I loved this game and I would definitely recommend it simply for the game it is.
