You're going to hear me compare this game to two other games, Life is Strange E1-5 and Pony Island. Two other story-driven indie games that came out recently. If you want the TL:DR version, this is worth the asking price for me, and if you're a fan of story-driven indie games, it will be for you too. Now the 'did read' version. Spoiler free.

Campo Santo tells a compelling story, with a smattering of humor and witty dialog. The voice acting in this game is the centerpiece and it is fantastic. The game's leads pull off their roles with expert execution, pacing, and delivery. The game itself weaves the banter back and forth the entire length of the game, to make you feel like you're in the Wyoming forest. In this regard, it is as good as, or better than Life is Strange. Since Pony Island didn't have voice acting, there's no comparison.

As for the story itself, this could have been fleshed out a bit, and the Wyoming wilderness felt more like a game level than a place to get lost in. I wish Campo Santo had taken a page from Life is Strange here and given you more places to sit and reflect, as well as better platforming abilities. The game does give you the opportunity to take photos, but I felt like the landscape was in the way of Henry's wonky, sluggish controls most of the time, to make full use of the tool. And even slowing down to a crawl, I finished the game's story in 4 hours. In this regard, Firewatch is less value for money than Life is Strange. Both have the same asking price and you can spend three times as long working your way through the older story. Firewatch is roughly the same length as Pony Island, for four times the asking price. 

But is Firewatch four times the game of Pony Island? I would say it's twice the game of Pony Island. At 5 dollars, Pony Island is a steal though. Firewatch for twenty?--not so much. It's an excellent story, and I can't wait to look up the numerous real world book titles that have been dispersed through the game to read, but it wasn't as broad or as deep as I was hoping. Granted, the quality of the voices did make it FEEL longer than it was, but without spoiling anything, there wasn't really enough meat or potatoes to make the stew savory.

This is not to say you should stay away from Firewatch. Oh no. Definitely get this game. At 20 bucks, interested adventure gamers will enjoy the experience. At 10, casual gamers should give it a look. At 5, anyone can enjoy this creation at a great value. I sincerely look forward to what Campo Santo has to offer us in the future.

Firewatch does a pretty good job of setting you up for the experience the moment you launch the game. There's no flashy developer splash screens, no overly long unskippable intro videos - the game just opens to the main menu, featuring a sole fire watchtower and a blue sky, with relaxing ambient audio. And that's fitting, because for the large part that's what you can expect from Firewatch, which is more or less a walking game; if you're expecting puzzles, stealth, or some other form of gameplay, you may want to look elsewhere, because Firewatch is all about the story. The gameplay is primarily based around exploring the wilderness surrounding your tower, either doing whatever objective you have at the time or just exploring and searching for  supply boxes or interesting landmarks. The forest is pretty serene, and I'd recommend trying disabling the "Show player on map" and "Show new objectives" options in the menu because I found exploring based on using landmarks in the forest to be a lot more fun than just using the map as a GPS. The story is the driving force of the game, adding a mystery thriller storyline to what would otherwise be a relaxing nature hike. The dialogue between the two main characters is entertaining, and there are a lot of objects in the woods for you to ask your radio contact about. The only real issue is the length - it took me around 5 hours to finish despite taking my time and exploring around, but people on the forums have quoted 2 to 3 hours. I don't feel like I was cheated out of my $18, but if you're looking for a value you might want to wait for a sale.

The rest of the game is more or less a hiking simulator. That isn't a bad thing though. I found it to be deeply satisfying to wander through the beautifuly crafted world, accompanied by the many dialogue options you'll have when talking to Delilah on the radio. 

The story that ties everything together mostly kept me on the edge of my seat and therefore I found it very easy to finish the whole game in one sitting. Be warned though, even though the game's setting is certainly atmospheric and creepy, this is not a horror game. If walking through the woods alone, being paranoid about noises, is enough to grind your gears, then this will suffice to you.

Overall this is a very well crafted, albeit short, interactive experience with especially great voice acting. The price at about $20 is a bit steep but justifiable. If you're open to alternative storytelling and aren't appalled by the idea of hiking through the woods, this might be for you.

First and foremost: It's a very short game. Steam says I put in about 3 hours and I completed it. I didn't explore or anything since I was invested in the story but just beware that it is a short game. If you're interested but the price is too high then I suggest waiting for a sale before picking it up. If you're unsure then you should just wait for a sale to pick it up.

The game is fantastic though. I got really invested in the characters and story which is why I ran through it so quickly. The voice acting felt realistic to me and while the writing may have been a bit flat or subpar side characters, the relationship between Delilah and Henry (your character) feels realistic and fluid. There's banter and humor and emotion in every line and it feels like real people just having a conversation rather than some people in a studio reading off a script. It's what elevates this game from mediocre to fantastic for me.

The graphics are really stylized and pretty. It's got a cartoonish feel to it that looks great and keeps the forest you're wandering in feel colorful and alive. The lighting plays an important role because there are many moments right at sunset where the sun is shining through the trees and it just feels and looks majestic.

The audio is a good mix of ambience and music. When you're wandering through the forest you'll find that the only sounds you hear are the sounds of your footsteps and the wind. It's very quiet and lonely. When something dramatic is happening the music quietly comes in and becomes a part of the scene, creating emotion and driving you forward. I highly recommend buying the soundtrack because it's extremely good.

Without spoiling anything, the ending feels hollow. Not in that it's a poorly written ending or anything like that. Rather it makes you feel hollow, like this journey you've been on is coming to a close and it's not exactly the ending you wanted. It's not happy, it's not sad, it just is an ending. It's fitting and while it's not the most satisfying, it's the most fitting.

After all I've said praising this game there are some problems. Invisible walls and artificial barriers are prevalent throughout this game. Some of the barriers can only be cleared after you've progressed so far into the story, which is fine but still feels like the game is limiting your exploration abilities. By the time I could theoretically explore everywhere, I was far enough into the story that I didn't have the desire to explore anymore since I wanted to see how things ended. There were other small barriers that annoyed me. One example is a trail by the lake. I got lost and there's a literal wall of dirt and rocks that separates you from where you need to go. Instead of being able to climb over this mound (which was definitely possible mind you) I instead had to walk around it to end up on the other side. It's not major but it's annoying in a game that's about exploration.

There's also a lot of glitches and bugs in the game. Frequently I got caught on rocks and branches and things like that and had to back up and move around them like I was a car or something. I found a lot of seams in the world where they failed to properly connect them so I could see into the void below. I also saw a couple of rocks that had no bottoms. It's a lot of minor stuff like this.

Overall I enjoyed this game and plan to do another run through at some point to fully explore the environment. The presentation is spectacular and the main characters are realistic and engaging. The invisible walls and glitches take away from the overall experience but the glitches will be patched out.

This game is an interesting one to be sure.

I would have to classify this game as a exploration-themed walking simulator with dialogue options. Looking back on it I wonder how much of my choices really mattered, or if they changed anything. It would take another playthrough to find out. Of course minor things would have to change such as [spoiler] Ned's tapes and documentation of what you say, and what the image of you would be like, and what you name the Tortoise (Bucket Jr. for me!)[/spoiler]

Visually the game is simplistic but not to the point where it feels like laziness, though I did notice unusual clipping of moving things. Particularly of butterflies flying through rocks and a tortoise clipping into itself. [spoiler] Along with you not meeting a single person and the only people you see being entirely black. In fact the entire woods seems almost entirely void of fauna, not once do I remember seeing a bird fluttering by, or even the scampering of a squirrel. Only butterflies.[/spoiler] The park itself is lovely and well designed, I very much enjoy the variety of settings available from the lush patches to the rocky mountaneous regions to the cave to the open grassland. It makes it all the more exciting to explore and discover. 

Audio wise it's fantastic. The music does its job of inspiring awe and wonder when necessary, along with uneasiness and nervousness. Along with top notch voice acting. But, of course I can only speak for the dialogue I did hear, so there is the possibility they botched alternate dialogue I never heard. Also the sound of the environment and of animals (the few that you hear) work well.

Gameplay wise it feels reminiscent of a metroidvania in places, namely the "You found this, now all this is available". This would be more valuable if you could go back in time to before you have to "put your nose to the grindstone" and really start working with these tools that you find. Also the inspect, while cute, doesn't do anything. [spoiler]Along with that a great deal of the gameplay is dialogue options and I find myself wondering if any of it was worth the trouble. This is a make or break in this type of game, which can readily be seen in the recent Telltale lineup of games.[/spoiler]

The story is well written and well paced with a great deal of suspense. I enjoy how it turns out overall, though there are some gripes I have. [spoiler] There is an excessive use of red herrings and a great deal of things that are simply not explained. The fenced off area isn't explained explicitly, what happened to the girls isn't either (outside of them being attacked), along with the fact that Ned worked against himself by making himself known. Was this on purpose? Who knows? I certainly don't. And, again, I find myself wondering how much of it did I really impact? Did picking Bucket in comparison to Mayhem change that much? Did suggesting to have kids later rather than excitedly wanting kids change that much? Did anything you say to Delilah change anything at all (other than Ned's records)? Also, as a personal note, I didn't like the gap of days that were skipped. I would have preferred to complete day-to-day tasks with the option of skipping instead.[/spoiler]

All in all, it's a good game though not quite what I was expecting from the trailer and what was built in my head. I envisioned this as a game where you play as a park ranger, looking out for things, exploring, and having day-to-day activities. This is instead a rather linear experience, but with the opportunity to go and explore on one of the earlier days it does make it interesting.

Firwatch is a game where you play as a lonely guy named Henry who's trying to get away from it all by becoming a fire look-out for the summer. The story takes off sprinting with intrigue and, like a good book, leaves you wanting to know more and more about what's actually going on in this national park. 

The dynamic between "Hank" and "D" is phenomenal. The dialogue options and line delivery is absolutely perfect in every way. The characters are incredibly likable.

And that's about as good as the game gets.


As the story unfolds from it's sprinting begining, it begins to fizzle out and run out of fuel. There's no sign that they tried to fan the flame either. The story choices were deliberate and it makes you really question why the overall narrative takes a dive the way it did.

The whole story is the point of the game, there's nothing to do but walk around, climb up things, pick up objects, and talk to D. So when the story becomes we weakest part of the game, it's frustrating and disappointing.

I don't recommend this game. The pros just don't outweigh the cons.

Firewatch immediately begins with a seemingly benign choose-your-own adventure text game that evolves from touching to saddening within the first few minutes. It is this development that brings Henry to the Shonone to escape his problems and stew in his emotions alone in the Wyoming wilderness. However, that would make a boring game, and things quickly escalate after the first two days. Delilah on the radio serves as your only consistent human contact over the course of your adventure. She's witty and snappy, and you can choose how you'd like to interact with her. Snark back at her. Ignore her. The choice is yours. Shortly after their introduction, a mystery brews in the wilderness. As it turns out, Henry may not be as alone as it seems. All of this plays out in one of the most beautiful environments ever to appear in video games. Wyoming is vibrant and rich, dripping with an art style that is completely its own. 

The game is around 3 hours long, however. There is no combat to speak of, and most of the game is spent walking adn climbing.

If you can tolerate 3 hours and minimalist gameplay in exchange for rich character interaction and a beautiful world to explore, Firewatch is a must buy.

The game gives you the illusion of choices but ultimately they count for nothing in the outcome of the story. This is not really an issue, but it's worth pointing out, because this also means the game has little to no replay value. And despite what the developers claimed(6 hours long game), the game can be completed under 4 hours at normal pace. Of course, you could say, well, why not go explore? Why, of course, that sounds like a great idea! Except, there's not much to see, if anything at all. The game already shows off its best vistas and sights to you by just playing the story itself. And apart from that, there's nothing. No wildlife, no other people, no nothing. 

Overall, I expected more. I expected a more interesting story, and a more involved gameplay scenario. The game drops the whole idea of you being a park ranger way too quickly, and shoehorns a mystery arc in there that is about as interesting as a CSI episode. The presentation though, once again, beautiful. And great soundtrack, too.

A lot of games come out trying to do story, and end up being uninteractive walking simulators. Firewatch, on first glance, has all the signs of being the same. I have never been so happy to be proven wrong.

Don't get me wrong, this game is a short setpiece, at around 3 hours to finish it, it certainly isn't a timesink, but at no point does any of those 3 hours feel wasted.

You play Henry, who for reasons of his own, decides to become a volunteer firewatcher in Wyoming.  As part of the role, you talk to your supervisor: Delilah, on your radio. You never see her, only talk to her, and it's in her that the game shines through where other games like this fall down. Firewatch is not a game about hunting animals, or even fighting fires. Firewatch is about how you can become attached to someone without knowing what they look like. Firewatch is a game about atmosphere, and tension, and not being sure of your own senses.

I could explain more, but I don't want to spoil anything. Know that mechanically, Firewatch is a simple first person adventure game, driven by it's characters and a need to uncover more.

It's well worth the price of admission, and whereas people will have forgotten about games like Dear Esther within the decade, Firewatch is a game to rememver.

After the trailers, I was hyped for this game. I expected an open-world mystery / adventure game set in the middle of nowhere. What you get is essentially a linear walking simulator with nice art assets.

What looks like an open world is limited everywhere by obstacles that require a specific tool. Since you apparently did not think to bring literally anything with you, you have to collect ropes, an axe, and climbing gear when the story dictates it. This severly limits the places you can go / explore.
And even if you decide to go exploring, the only thing you can find are the supply-caches, which are marked on your map from the first minute; those usually contain a letter from someone you don't know, to someone you don't care about; writing about how they want to drink beer.

The radio is the only thing giving you a degree of choice, or the illusion of it. Often, you will be given a Telltale Games kind-of choice between 3 options of what to say, with a ~10 second timer counting down. Unlike Telltale however, these choices have 0 impact on the story and outcome of the game. You could remove the radio entirely from the game and end up with a genuine walking simulator, where you spend 10% of your time staring at the map, and the other 90% walking to the place, the map tells you to go.

This leaves the story as the only thing holding this game together, and while it starts out very intriguing, in my opinion it falls flat on its face near the end. I won't spoil anything, since this would ruin the game completely for you, but once you know the big twist at the end, the game has nothing more to offer you. This also leads to 0 replayability; I don't think anyone will ever play this game a second time.

To summarize: If you manage to stay unspoiled until the next sale, where the price drops below 50%, and if you enjoy the occasional walking simulator, then go for it. Otherwise, those 20€ could be invested alot better.

With Julia's descent into dementia, there is already an aspect of doubt regarding the sanity of the characters. The game even brings Henry's sanity into question in a conversation with Delilah. Then the game ends, no mention to Henry's sanity, just a sad man who lost his son running from the truth. I was personally hoping for a Bioshock Infinite type ending, but thats only my opinion. The game gives you the impression that the story is somewhat dynamic since you got so many different options talking to your colleague, but it has no influence on the story beyond the next five steps you take.

The scene where they first open the save and it's empty and the one guy just shouts out "DISAPPOINTED!"?

Firewatch: a short narrative driven video game that, in the 6 hours it takes to complete, engages the player in several scenarios that are up to you to discover what is happening.

In this 4 hour game, you wander around a forest cleaning up after unruly guests, taking in the attractive scenery, and stumbling upon a mystery that you can choose to solve (or completely ignore I guess.)

I can't really say much else without spoiling the story, but if realistic, humorous dialogue with very human reactions and interactions are your cup of tea, and a 2 hour completion time doesn't sully your view, then Firewatch is a nice little treat for you.

I, however, requested a refund as soon as the credits rolled. 2-3 hour completion time that left me with no interest in replaying does not to me a justified $17 price tag make.

EDIT: Firewatch has been successfully refunded.

First impressions:

Pros:
- conversations are always fun to listen to, and the voice acting fits perfectly.
- the visuals are beautiful
- navigating is quite easy with the map and compass
- music is great
- sound effects are great and can feel creepy at night
- if you're not sure if you can do something, try it out, chances are you can!

Cons:
- No FOV slider (only marking this because the devs said it would be in, and while it didn't make me nauseous, I did begin feeling a headache-like sensation, not very pleasant).
- sometimes I feel like you have way too little time to choose your conversation, but at least not short enough to where you don't have time to at least read the choices.
- will add more if I come across anything else.
EDITS:
- small visual bug where the screen jitters while zooming in on your map sometimes, not a big deal.
- small bug while looking at Delilah's tower, says there's more conversations with her by showing the mic icon after I've exhausted everything, but there were no options. (now I'm thinking the icon is just there permanently intentionally?)
- minor gripe: sometimes you have to really be precise where you're looking in order to get the mic prompt otherwise it won't show up.

Tips:
- make sure to keep an eye out on the queue to talk on the mic. There are many areas and objects that prompt it and I did miss a couple at the very beginning.
- Talking is timed and the timer can go quite fast, so decide fast.
- explore, there's enough detail around while you progress the story. (banging on the gate in the cave a bunch prompted the sign to fall off)

Overall:
The game is different from anything I've played, the story is intriguing and I want to see how it turns out. There are sad moments, beautiful moments, creepy moments, and tense moments. It's story-based, not much "action" but it's not to the point of being a "walking-simulator", it's much more involved than that. Will report back once I finish the game (see final thoughts).

If I could summarize the game, it would be a story-based mystery where choices matter and the atmosphere, setting, and conversations are the real meat of the experience.

FINAL THOUGHTS:
This was a great experience. I really wish it was longer, because the end does feel incomplete and anti-climactic, while other parts of the game were very tense. Because I let myself dive into the story with no distractions, the characters very quickly became likeable and was able to emotionally invest myself in them, whish is why I wish the last half-hour or so of the game was stretched out and fleshed out a bit. Parts of the game had me at the edge of my seat, literally, just wondering what is going on and feeling tense with every plot twist. The changes in pace are very well placed and I feel like the characters conversations grew based on the choices I made. I'll end up playing through it again, just because everything up until the end was an incredible experience. Don't get me wrong, some will enjoy the ending, but the characters were too likeable for me to have it end that way. There is more than enough to enjoy though, and would definitely recommend it to anyone who loves a good story and phenominal voice-acting, there really isn't anything quite like it out there now.

I pre-ordered this. Mostly because one of the writers was partly responsible for creating The Walking Dead back before it became totally boring. Season 1 of TWD was such a great practice in character creation. Im not sure if there is, or will ever be, an equal in TV in that specific area. The only thing I can compare it to comes from other genres; Kesey's "Sometimes a Great Notion" in Literature and in film the simple, more direct approach taken in the original Star Wars trilogy. I actually feel like Hank, excuse me, Henry, (we dont like being called Hank) from the first second. My new boss feels like my new boss. If the voice acting and writing wasnt top notch there would be no emotional attachment. Not the case here.

I dont want to spoil anything so I will leave details of the story out. But I will tell you this...Click on the first text and dont sit there like I did for 5 mins waiting for the scene to change. You will become Hanks conscious in perpetual limbo. My only gripe was that the intro was a little long. Not a problem for me but I know many people might get a little impatient. However, the story must be set. Think of it as the Prologue to a new adventure and possibly a new life, well, for Henry of course.
